column121: Shortly after takeoff from ZZZ-ZZZ1 both flight deck and cabin crew members detected a mild smell of burning oil or engine exhaust. Smell lasted for approximately 3-4 minutes during climb; with the strongest smell in the aft galley area. There was no fire; smoke or mist present; only a strange smell of what I would classify as oil burning. The fumes did not increase and began to stabilize and finally decrease after a few minutes. The crew began the Smoke; Fire or Fumes checklist but the fumes decreased before the checklist could be completed. The cabin crew investigated all lavs; galleys; and PEDs for any source of fumes. Dispatch and Technical Support Maintenance Control were contacted via Commercial Radio and an ELB write up was made. Since the fumes ended and did not appear to emanate from within the cabin or flight deck; I opted to continue the flight to ZZZ1. The flight concluded uneventfully and a written Smoke/Fume Report was filed with ZZZ1 Maintenance. Subsequently; the Chief Pilot was verbally debriefed. The aircraft was removed from service upon arrival at ZZZ1.

column121: We were on the ZZZZZ1 arrival into ZZZ and we had a clearance cross the ZZZ1 VOR at Flight Level 260 and then to descent via the ZZZZZ1. We were in a managed descent with 4000 feet set for the bottom of the ZZZZZ1 arrival. Nearing ZZZ1 I thought that we were high on the profile. I selected open descent intending to level off at FL260 and then continue on profile but I did not select FL260 in the FCU window. The airplane was very light at 113;000 pounds and descended very quickly right through the assigned FL260. I intervened by leveling off and we continued in a managed descent on profile for the remainder of the arrival.My estimation that we were high on the profile was inaccurate due to the fact that the airplane was light and capable of descending very quickly; I had not taken that into consideration. The pilot monitoring was heads down and I did not tell him I was changing the mode of descent from managed to open and explain why I was doing so. Had I done so; he would have caught it. This was my first day back to work after two months of leave. I had prepared to return by studying flows; call; procedures; etc. and had briefed the other pilot hoping to prevent errors from happening.Suggestions - Keep the other guy in the loop. Tell him when making a change especially if he is heads down. Always check the altitude selected when changing modes. Always focus on the next restriction.
column123: We were south of ZZZ1 arrival validation completed; arrival briefing completed clearance to cross ZZZ1 at FL260.  We were then cleared to descend via ZZZZZ1 Runway XXL.  The Captain set 4;000 feet in the FCU.  We both verified the altitude selected and the aircraft was in managed decent.  I verified the aircraft was on profile and would cross ZZZ1 at FL260.  I then updated the MCDU with the new ATIS; did an in range and verified arrival gate and set ramp frequency in the number 2 standby radio.  The Captain then said; 'I messed that up'; or something like that.  I didn't realize the Captain had changed modes to open descent and had descended through the FL260 restriction at ZZZ1.  He said he felt the aircraft was not descending quickly enough.  We crossed ZZZ1 approximately 1;000 feet low.  There was no call from ATC.  The Captain then went back to managed descent and we continued to ZZZ without and further incident.Cause - Lack of communication from the Captain letting me know he went to open descent.  Captain had been on extended time off the last 7 months.Suggestions - Communication of mode changes in decent to Pilot monitoring.  Resetting FCU to next altitude constraint when operating in open decent.

column121: After an unplanned diversion to ZZZ; we did not deplane since it was a short wait for our departure to ZZZ1. ZZZ Center closed from XA:00Z-XB:30Z for COVID cleaning. Because we did not deplane no passengers or bags left the aircraft. When completing the manifest we were unsure of how to get the clearance and passenger count without the station uploading via ACARS. I called Dispatch to help with some of the numbers like cargo weight and passenger zones. With Dispatch I could get weight for cargo but not zones; for passengers we were able to get the zones. I told the ground crew that if they could figure out the cargo bag count then we would be good. They tried to look into it but they were unable. So with Dispatch's help we got our manifest and had good numbers. After we left the station uploaded a new passenger count and later discovered the new passenger count from the station was about 300 pounds less than our original manifest.The main cause was the fact that the station couldn't upload an ACARS passenger count because they did not scan passenger tickets; everyone stayed on board. This caused an unusual hurdle where we had to figure out a way to get the numbers. But after we got it from Dispatch the station's last minute help with an ACARS upload caused a mix up with the passenger count and weight discrepancy.I should have printed the manifest before starting the new flight on the FMS. We need a way to maintain the passenger zones and cargo report since we don't have paper reports anymore. The close out report only has the total adults and children but not their zones; and the cargo only has total weight and not which bags go where.
column123: After an unplanned divert to ZZZ we did not offload because it was a short wait for our departure to ZZZ1. With Dispatch we were able to get the cargo weights and passenger zones. column121: Shortly after takeoff As the PF I experienced intermittent failure of both roll and pitch modes (with no flags; just the disappearance and reappearance in erratic random failures of pitch and roll indications separately) of my flight director during climb through approximately 6;000 ft. Obviously the auto pilot A disconnected and I was unable to reacquire it due to the erratic nature of the problem. Communicating to my FO (First Officer) of the issue; we recognized that his flight director appeared to be operating normally. This allowed us to use autopilot B to reassess our condition. With the auto throttle on with autopilot B the Number 2 throttle advanced rapidly approximately 5 knobs forward of the Number 1 throttle and I returned it to a symmetric condition (the auto throttle disengaged itself as well; Autopilot B still was working). While bringing the throttles to an asymmetric condition to stabilize the thrust setting the Stab Trim Light illuminated; the left fuel pump light of the center tank illuminated (approximately 22;000 lbs of gas in the center tank). We requested to level off at 16;000 ft. and 250 knots and indicated to ATC that we needed a few minutes to access a condition; that we would maintain our flight plan. We executed a transfer of controls to the FO making him the PF as he also communicated with ATC. After consulting the Quick Reference Checklist; it was clear the we had multiple failures not covered by the Quick Reference Checklist. In addition; the MA lights for both Flight Directors were alternating flashing in sequence. I Acquired the appropriate enroute Airinc VHF radio frequency from the chart and phone patched both dispatch and Maintenance Control. With no solution; both Maintenance Control and Dispatch agreed with my decision to divert back to ZZZ as opposed to continuing to ZZZ1 5 hours away in mountainous terrain with automation issues at night and a potential 12 hour+ duty day. FAs (Flight Attendants) were advised; ATC was advised (Requested priority handling and equipment requested to check brakes and tires); company was advised; and an announcement was made to the pax. We used the Landing Distance Normal Configuration chart for our aircraft to obtain landing distance as Saber wouldn't calculate for us the landing performance in our overweight condition at landing (approximately 161;000 lbs). It was my judgement to forego flying for however long it would take to burn 15;000 lbs of fuel to reach landing weight; so I opted to land overweight in light of the distance required from the chart. Once ATC cleared us on a vector heading for approach to land X in ZZZ; I assumed the PF role. Landing was inconsequential and smooth exiting X; X; holding short of X on X while ZZZ Fire assessed our brakes and tires. All normal; proceeded to Gate X.
column123: On departure out of ZZZ; the Captain experienced intermittent failure of his flight director. Both his roll and pitch command bars would randomly disappear and reappear without any warning annunciations. Autopilot A disconnected and was unable to reengage as we continued the climb. As the Captain and I began to analyze the situation; we recognized that my flight director appeared to be working normally and the Captain was able to engage Autopilot B. A short period after engaging the autopilot; the autothrottles disengaged as a result of the Number 2 throttle advancing several knob widths forward of the Number 1 throttle. The Captain returned the throttles to a symmetric condition and the autothrottles were reengaged. We had been given a climb to 16;000 ft. and decided to maintain that altitude and our current airspeed of 250 kts. as we continued our flight plan route. The Captain transferred the aircraft control to me; and I kept the radios while he further analyzed the situation and referenced the QRG. I told ATC we were working an issue but required no assistance at this time. The autothrottles once again disconnected as a result of asymmetry and we elected to keep them off for the remainder of the flight. During this time we also notice the MA light for the flight director switches was cycling back and forth from the Captain's side to the FO side. Additionally; the left center tank fuel pump LOW PRESSURE light illuminated with over 20;000 lbs. of fuel in the center tank. Lastly; the STAB OUT OF TRIM light flickered despite any changes in pitch or airspeed. It was clear that we had multiple issues not covered by the QRG; and the Captain quickly tuned the appropriate ARINC VHF radio frequency and established a phone patch with dispatch and Maintenance Control. Since there was no clear solution for our situation; dispatch and Maintenance Control agreed with the Captain's decision to divert to ZZZ as opposed to continuing. This decision was made after the Captain and I discussed the threats involved: automation issues; night landing in mountainous terrain; long duty day. The Captain advised the FAs (Flight Attendants) and made an announcement to the passengers. He then took the primary radio back from me and requested priority handling with ATC in addition to coordinating for aircraft rescue and firefighting to meet the aircraft to check our brakes and tires since we would be landing overweight. The Captain briefed the approach and calculated the landing distance using the Landing Distance Normal Configuration chart for our aircraft since Saber would not calculate at our current weight which was approximately 161;000 lbs. I agreed with the Captain's decision to land overweight; given we had the landing distance; as opposed to holding for almost 2.5 hours to burn fuel. The descent checklist was accomplished; and the Captain took over as the PF once ATC cleared us on a vector for the ILS X. A 30-flap landing was conducted and a normal landing was made. We exited on X; X; and while holding short of X; aircraft rescue and firefighting checked our brakes and tires. With an all normal; we proceeded to taxi to gate X.

column121: During passenger loading; ramp crew received a motorized wheelchair/scooter for an elderly passenger. The passenger declared that the scooter had a dry cell battery and the key was removed. Ramp agents filled out air carrier battery powered wheelchair form mobility device tag and gave the flight deck crew a copy.  Upon receiving this form and observing the type of chair through the cockpit window I became suspicious that this particular type of scooter probably contained a lithium ion battery and the tag was improperly labeled based on the passengers assumption.  The flight attendant also made a similar remark and I wanted to exercise caution before the scooter was loaded into the baggage compartment. We decided to have ramp personnel take the scooter out of the baggage compartment and with the assistance of the passenger open motorized mobility device to ascertain the actual type of battery. Upon opening the device we discovered it did have a lithium ion battery with 25.2 V and 11.5 a/h. Based on the formula the battery had less than 300 watts maximum for transport.  We elected to remove the battery and transport it in the passenger cabin to ensure we had access do it during flight. A new mobility form was signed indicating there was a lithium ion battery for the mobility device and I made a correction to the CLR [form] indicating the actual battery type.Members of the flight crew were able to spot a potential hidden dangerous good and miss labeled document based on passenger assumption. The flight crew worked with ground personnel to ensure the mobility device was not loaded onto the aircraft until we were able to ascertain the actual type of battery was confirmed and under the appropriate limits prescribed in our dangerous goods manual.

column121: On route to the airport the First Officer's Multi Function display failed. We decided to continue destination airport because it was not required equipment. Then we were informed the weather at the airport was deteriorating unexpectedly. We completed all the required tasks and checklist before the we were cleared for the approach. On approach we realized that we were too high and our descent profile was going to be unacceptable for a stable approach. Around 11;000 ft. the Captain called for the Missed Approach. We executed the Missed Approach with no issues and cleaned up the aircraft and started climbing to the missed approach altitude. We were at the missed approach altitude and Captain called for the auto pilot on. During this time there was a bit of confusion and the right turn and swapping the navigation displays and setting the new course for the back course was slow to be executed. We turned to the heading too slow and never intercepted the back course. Once we figured out that we didn't intercept the back course we had the Course Deviation Indicator full-scale deflection. ATC gave us a new altitude and a new heading to start the restart the approach. We got vectored around to the Initial Approach Fix to restart the approach and completed the second approach stabilized without any issues. Failure to comply with the approach profile and the missed approach profile.
column123: I neglected to call for the First Officer to start our descent. The First Officer noticed my mistake; but by this time we were very high. My initial reaction was to deploy the boards and steepen the descent in an attempt to get back on profile; however I quickly realized it wasn't going to work and we were unstabilized. I called for a missed approach when we were at roughly 11;000 ft.  Because we went missed early; I called for the autopilot on once we reached the published missed approach altitude of 14;200 ft. This caused confusion as to who should complete the tasks of spinning the heading knob to the 300 heading; swapping the RTU's; and setting the course to 303. I decided to have the First Officer complete these to stay as on-profile as possible. The first two tasks; the 300 heading and swapping the RTU's; were completed however the task of setting the 303 course was not. This led to ATC querying us about our progress on the missed approach and soon after issuing an altitude alert with an instruction to climb to 15;000 ft. By the time we figured out our mistake we were showing full-scale deflection on the Course Deviation Indicator. In addition to not setting the course; I made the mistake of accelerating to 200 kts. and calling climb sequence once level at 14;200 ft. instead of waiting until outbound per the profile. I should also add that the First Officer MFD failed enroute and this most likely caused a reduction in situational awareness throughout the rest of the flight. Failure to comply with the LOC/DME 15 approach profile; especially the missed approach segment.

column121: ZZZ1 went ATC zero due to a COVID cleaning around Xpm local for several hours. We had one non-radar route going north bound from my area to ZZZ2 Center. My area does not train or use non-radar procedures so we were very unprepared in terms of skill. We were told to get an estimate for the ZZZZZ Intersection from the aircraft and provide 10 minutes in trail between aircraft at similar altitudes. We were initially given 20 miles in trail from approach controls; but this quickly over loaded the sector and it was increased to 30 miles in trail which was insufficient.Things that went wrong:1) Printer at the XY position broke at the beginning; but was fixed by tech-ops in a somewhat timely manner.2) The automatic printing was not turned on for the XY position and no one knew how to turn it on.3) Manual printing the strips took up a lot of time for XY position.4) We did not have enough strip holders to post all of the strips for the aircraft in our airspace.5) The ZZZZZ Intersection sounds a lot like the ZZZZZ1 Intersection so we got a lot of incorrect time estimates as pilots got the confused.6) A lot of aircraft were still climbing before getting to the ZZZZZ Intersection to being the non-radar routing so they gave us incorrect time estimates for ZZZZZ1. Once some of these aircraft leveled off their estimates were changing drastically.7) Once we got the time estimate from the aircraft our Supervisor had to go and call on the area land-line. So we had no easy way to communicate with ZZZ2 Center.8) The XZ position was also open and 'merging' aircraft into the north bound rooting but did not have a d-side and given the strong westerly winds was getting odd ZZZZZ1 estimates.9) The combined amount of overflight traffic and departure traffic was greater than the number of available altitudes. Our area was not staffed properly; so I had been on position for about 2:40 when the event occurred; and was working my third different radar scope of the session.  I had been moved twice due to partially certified controllers kicking me out of my previous position.  I had also just returned from XX days off.The sector next to me (XY) was very busy; and part of my attention was diverted to that scope because there was inadequate staffing to provide them a tracker or D-side.  I know this is not something I should do; but the controller at XY seemed over loaded.I took hand offs on Aircraft X and Aircraft Y at about the same time.  I saw the traffic immediately; and turned Aircraft X to a 270 heading; and issued Aircraft Y 20 degrees left.  I've been certified at ZZZ1 radar for over X years; and have seen this same scenario thousands of times in my career.  I continued doing other things; then looked back on the situation and saw for some reason my 20 degree turn was not going to be enough.  I am not sure if Aircraft Y actually turned 20 degrees; or maybe wind was a factor.  I issued a 10 degree left turn to Aircraft X; confident that this would resolve the issue.  Upon checking back a minute or so later; I saw that this was not going to be the case.  I issued another 20 degree left turn to Aircraft Y and instructed them to expedite the climb.  I stopped Aircraft X at FL190; but did not issue further turn because it would have violated ZZZ2 RAPCON airspace.  About this time both aircraft responded to RA's.  I waited for both to complete the RA maneuvers and cleared them back on course and up to requested altitude.First; I feel that personally I should have used altitude separation instead of; or in addition to; lateral separation.  I should have ensured that the vector was enough before giving up vertical separation.  It is something I have told my trainees hundreds of times in my career; and something that I should have done.Also; I recommend that the area be staffed correctly.  We have been on COVID-19 schedules since March; and there seems to have been a shift in mentality regarding staffing.  As a facility we worked nearly X;X00 tracks yesterday; and my area's night shift only had X CPCs (Last year we would have had 5 or 6 on the shift.)  The result of this was that I was on position for nearly 3 hours without a break; during which my LoSS occurred.  I understand that we are trying to keep the crews isolated from one another; but we also need to staff appropriately for the traffic.  If we cannot staff enough people on a shift; then traffic needs to be slowed down.

In this scenario; ATC was juggling pushbacks; ground taxiing aircraft; and most crucially aircraft taking off while loaded with humans and fuel. Worse yet; aircraft on takeoff were hearing it. Pilots' ears are trained to be listening for certain things at certain stages of the flight. column121: Slow Pressure Leak at FLXXX.This trip started as a 3 day ZZZ1 airport.  Flight X was the second segment on day 1 from ZZZ2 to ZZZ3.  My First Officer; was the flying pilot for this leg.  Loading and boarding were normal; and the flight was full.  At push time a passenger stood up and ran to the lav; so we waited and pushed off gate X at XA:XXz.  We taxied to Runway XL for takeoff; the weather was beautiful.  With [FO] flying we departed XL on the ZZZZZ2 RNAV Departure to ZZZZZ.  Our route would take us from ZZZZZ to ZZZ4 ZZZ5 ZZZZZ1 into ZZZ3.  It was a beautiful day; we could see the front range clearly with [Mountain Peak] in the distance and nearly unlimited visibility.  The departure was uneventful; passing 10;000 feet I turned off the Sterile Cockpit light and gave a double ding; checked the pressure which was operating normally.  (A habit ever since my [X type aircraft] days; as they tended to be leaky airplanes; and because I read a story about an airliner that took off with the mode selector in the wrong position and all lives were lost). As such; I try to check it every so often in the climb.  Again passing 18;000 we did our flows; I checked the fuel which was feeding evenly and normally and again we were pressurizing normally.  I checked fuel and cabin pressure one more time and all was normal. We had a continuous climb to FLXXX without a single level off; which is unusual for ZZZ2.In level flight at FLXXX I checked the fuel passing ZZZZZ Intersection and all was normal 2 minutes ahead.  We were both still on headset with our speakers off at this point.  Shortly after ZZZZZ when we were just starting to settle in at cruise from ZZZZZ to ZZZ4 intersection; the Master Warning Illuminated with a Siren and a Cabin Altitude EICAS.  I glanced up and saw the Cabin Altitude light and the Cabin altitude between the 10 and 15 mark.  We immediately donned our masks.  Upon donning my mask the expansion strap knocked the ear piece out of my left ear; so it was dangling somewhere off the O2 mask.  With the Boom/Oxy switch in Oxy; I could not hear myself until I turned up my speaker.  Donning the mask was interesting; with earpieces; eye glasses; and not to mention the removal of a COVID mask that [FO] was wearing.  It took a few seconds to get the mask on and check in.  In any event with both our speakers up we checked in on O2 and I requested priority handling while accessing the QRC.  FO immediately started the descent.  We initially started down with 14;000 feet in the window which I knew would clear the terrain until I could check the Grid MORA's more thoroughly.  Running the QRC; we confirmed O2 on 100% with communications established; Engine Bleed Air switches were on and both Packs were on.  The next step; Step 5 says; Choose one:  Cabin Altitude is Controllable: or Cabin Altitude is uncontrollable:  When I looked up I saw the cabin steady between the 10;000 and 15;000 marks on the gauge and was not climbing; but was obviously higher than a normal cabin.  The Auto Inop lights were not illuminated and we were currently in Auto 2; so I decided to select Auto 1.  At this point nothing changed; but the outflow valve appeared closed and the cabin seemed to be steady.  I chose to continue the checklist with step 6 PASS OXY (If cabin Altitude 14;000 feet) ON.  I knew the masks had deployed because I could hear the flight attendants on the PA telling the passengers to put on their masks.Structural integrity was not in doubt; so I confirmed with FO that all the steps in step 8 were accomplished.  FO had done a great job and had accomplished all the steps; MCP was set at 14000; FLCH; Thrust was IDLE; Speed Brakes were extended; Speed was set at VMO; so I turned on the seat belt sign; ATC had been notified; so I did not set 7700 on the transponder.  I looked back up and at this point the cabin was slowly decreasing.  At no point did the cabin ever go out of the 10;000 to 15;000 marks on the cabin pressure.  At the most the cabinis estimated to have reached approximately 14;000 or a bit less (Maybe 13;000 or so).  Between the 3 of us in the cockpit; that is about the highest any of us saw.  You must interpolate because the gauge only has a marks for 10 and 15.  At some point during all this the flight attendants called the cockpit and I told the jump seater to take the call which he did.  I quickly checked the Grid MORA's and confirmed the 10;000 was safe; so FO requested 10;000 and I set it in the window.  At this point and altitude the cabin was stable.  We were well into the descent and the cabin had started descending.  I continued the checklist with the expanded items in the checklist; altimeters were set.  Initially we requested a divert to ZZZ6; as we were both familiar with the field and it was the nearest suitable airport.  I took the airplane from FO so he could set up which again he did very quickly.  I gave FO back the airplane and called the flight attendants.  They informed me that everything in the back was fine and I told them they no longer needed the masks.  Now we started a conversation about our divert options.With the passengers; all safe and no issues; we checked our fuel and determined that we had plenty of fuel to safely return to ZZZ2.  The cabin altitude was siting somewhere around 6 to 7 thousand feet.  I sent a quick note to dispatch to call me; so they sent me a frequency.  We were unable to reach them; so they sent me a second frequency which also did not work (Probably because we were at 10;000 feet).  I then established communication through the SAT Comm to the Dispatch; because there was no direct connection for sector X.  The dispatcher that answered handed me off to the sector X dispatcher; and he agreed that ZZZ2 was a good choice and said he would let everyone know.  After clearing with Dispatch; we discussed our plan and then informed ATC we no longer needed priority handling and that we were not an emergency and would like to proceed to ZZZ2.  They routed us direct ZZZZZ2...so I called the FAs and informed them of the new details and time.  They again informed me that everything was fine in the back and the cabin was secure.  I made a brief PA announcement to inform the passengers of our situation and our return to ZZZ2.  In the cockpit; we all started a discussion about the plan and confirmed that we had notified all the parties concerned and accomplished all the appropriate actions.  I asked Captain Y if there was anything else he could think of and he said; no you did everything you can do.  I requested landing data for [Runway] YL and FO briefed the Visual approach.  We accomplished the Descent Checklist and FO flew a beautiful uneventful visual approach to Runway YL.  Once on the ground we taxied back to gate X and handed the plane over to maintenance.Two things that are interesting about this situation:  First; when donning O2 masks and establishing communications.  Because we both turned our speakers all the way up; it made initial communication both inside and outside the aircraft difficult; due to feedback between the 2 speakers.  Also; I transmitted once outside the aircraft instead of inside with the rocker switch on the yoke.  The second and more interesting point is that whenever you practice a depressurization in the simulator; it is always an explosive rapid decompression.  This was not like that at all; this was an airplane that had a high cabin with a gauge reading between the 10;000 and 15;000 marks.   A higher than normal altitude but not climbing.  At the point on the checklist when it says 'Cabin altitude is controllable:'  It says 'Attempt to reduce cabin altitude by switching to the other auto controller (or manual mode if AUTO INOP is illuminated).'  I think it would be better worded to say Cabin altitude is controllable and can be returned to a normal cabin altitude.  In our case it was a high cabin; but not one that was continuing to climb. So is that controllable?  We decided to continue with the uncontrollable portion of the checklist and drop the masks etc.So; what went well?  Our planning and decision making; and workload management went well.  We constantly evaluated our situation and adjusted our plan as we gained more info and had the ability to discuss our options.  What could have gone better?  The communication while on O2 masks.  Next time I would make sure my ear piece stays in my ear and or I would turn down my cockpit speaker so that we do not get so much feedback over the speakers.  I feel that all in all; this was a well-executed event by all concerned ending with a safe return for passengers and crew.
column123: Aircraft X departed ZZZ2 for ZZZ3 on [Date] with Captain X (pilot monitoring); First Officer Y (pilot flying); and Captain Y (flight deck jumpseater). Takeoff from Runway XL and the ZZZZZ2 departure were uneventful; with no clouds; unlimited visibility; and light winds. Shortly after reaching FLXXX; with the autopilot and autothrottles on; the CABIN ALTITUDE EICAS message was displayed and its associated siren sounded.All flight crew members donned oxygen masks and crew communications were established. I noticed the cabin altitude indicator reading approximately 10;000 feet. Captain X ordered an immediate descent; and advised ZZZ Center that we were descending to 14;000 feet. ZZZ Center cleared us to descend; and advised that there was no conflicting traffic. I initiated the descent by putting 14;000 in the altitude window and pushing FLCH; followed by deploying the speed brakes and selecting a higher indicated airspeed. I continued increasing the airspeed as VMO increased.As I was flying the descent; Captain X ran the CABIN ALTITUDE checklist. Once the checklist was complete; Captain X brought up the Alternates page in the FMC and we discussed possible diversion airports. ZZZ6 was chosen as the nearest suitable airport and ZZZ Center cleared us direct to ZZZ6. Captain X focused on diversion planning and communication while I flew the airplane and talked to ATC; who cleared us to continue our descent to 10;000 feet.Once we were level at 10;000 feet; we reconsidered the decision to land at ZZZ6. Captain X confirmed that the situation in the passenger cabin was under control; the situation was stabilized; and our fuel state was sufficient to continue to ZZZ2. After coordinating with Dispatch; the decision was made to change diversion airports to ZZZ2.The flight to ZZZ2 at 10;000 feet was uneventful. ZZZ6 Approach provided a route to ZZZ2; which was then simplified to radar vectors by ZZZ Center and ZZZ2 Approach to a visual approach to Runway XL. A normal approach and landing were followed by a normal taxi to gate X.Other notes and observations:When the alarm sounded; I was wearing a surgical mask; glasses; and a headset; and holding my company iPad. I was startled by the warning; and before donning my oxygen mask; I reflexively checked the cabin altitude; and saw that it was approximately 10;000 feet. As I donned my oxygen mask; I knocked my glasses askew and my headset off; and left my surgical mask on. I had to release my oxygen mask to remove the surgical mask; and then get my glasses situated on my face. I abandoned the headset in favor of the speaker.Captain X had some difficulty with his earpiece; as well as with the comm panel (transmitting on the radio rather than the intercom at one point). Additionally; we both experienced feedback when attempting to communicate with each other. This resulted in poor crew communication during the initial stage of the descent; while Captain X was running the checklist. Once the checklist was complete; we were able to troubleshoot our communications and they improved. However; I was lacking situational awareness of the situation in the early stages due to the communication issues.During the descent; Captains X and Y reported a maximum cabin altitude between 14;000 and 15;000 feet. I did not observe the cabin pressurization system during the descent; as my focus was on flying the airplane.Captain X had difficulty coordinating with Dispatch. He sent a 'Call Me' request via ACARS and received several VHF frequencies; but all failed; possibly due to our low altitude (10;000 MSL; 5;000 AGL). He reverted to satellite communications; and was again hampered; this time because our dispatch sector did not appear in the SATCOM directory. He was eventually transferred to the correct sector and was able to coordinate our diversion.Captain X did an outstanding job of crew resource management; using me to fly the plane and coordinate with ATC; and using Captain Y as an additional resource for communication with the cabin. Additionally; he asked for and received input from both Captain Y and me; and used that input to guide his decisions about our diversion.All ATC agencies (ZZZ Center; ZZZ6 Approach; ZZZ2 Approach; and ZZZ2 Tower) were extremely helpful and professional; providing all requested assistance without delay.Captain X left the flight deck promptly once the parking checklist was complete to reassure the passengers and flight attendants. Several people commented that they were happy to see him in the cabin during the deplaning process.Debrief Items:What went well? Decision making. Looking back; the decision to divert to ZZZ6 initially was well considered and sound. We knew that Company had service to ZZZ6 and without knowing if there were any sick or injured passengers or flight attendants; a close airport was appropriate. Once the situation was stabilized; other factors could be considered (passenger accommodation; maintenance resources) and the decision to divert to ZZZ2 made the most sense.Workload and automation management also went well. By utilizing me to fly the plane and coordinate with ATC; and having Captain X assist with cabin coordination; Captain X was able to run the checklist; troubleshoot the problem; and stabilize the situation. And by keeping the autopilot and autothrottles engaged; I was able to initiate and manage the descent effectively.Finally; as I stated earlier; Captain X's leadership effectiveness was excellent. He remained calm when things got busy; and he actively sought out advice from all available resources; which led to a successful outcome.What could have gone better? My reaction to the alarm should have been to immediately put on my mask; rather than check the cabin pressure gauge. And I could have donned my oxygen mask more smoothly and quickly; rather than forgetting to remove my surgical mask and knocking my headset off. We could have done a better job establishing effective crew communications; which could have led to better situational awareness and crew coordination. Thankfully; all of these items were dealt with promptly; and none of them stood in the way of a successful outcome.

column121: We were on the ground at ZZZ for a prolonged time (Approx 1.5 hours) due to a previous flap issue on arrival. After contract Maintenance fixed the issue; we taxied to de/anti ice. That took about another 30 minutes before taking off. Prior to departure all takeoff protocol was followed with all checklists completed. The FMS was set up per the ZZZ2 Rwy XX Departure company page of TO-1/CMB-1 with flaps 2. We also used anti ice-all; with compact snow for the runway conditions. The terrain maps were configured to both our MFP's as well. ATIS was reporting light snow/ 1 to 5 miles visibility with about a 7 kt headwind for runway 19 at the departure time. Temp was around -4 C. It was also night. The First Officer (FO) was the Pilot Flying. I believe we had around 24 passengers with 9200 pounds of fuel at takeoff. Once cleared to takeoff; we taxied into position on the runway 19 threshold and the FO conducted a full static takeoff. We rotated towards the last one third of the runway and promptly retracted the gear. The FO pitched into the flight director with over a thousand foot climb rate. Everything appeared normal. At about approx 30 seconds to a minute into the climb; the terrain aural went off. We then conducted the CFIT profile and monitored our climb and speed. I paid particular attention to my RA which was showing -5 feet. I then looked at our course and we were perfectly centered on the course line and the terrain maps were showing nothing but green ahead. After the terrain warning seemed to be over; I pulled the thrust levers back to the TOGA detent. Once back in the TOGA detent; the terrain aural sounded again. Again; we conducted the CFIT profile. I scanned my RA a second time and it still bounced around -5 feet. The terrain overlays on both MFD's still showed only green ahead and around us. Once the terrain aural silenced the second time; the FO brought the thrust levers back into the TOGA detent. Tower then switched us over to Center. After contacting Center and with the terrain warning finally over; the FO called for and I completed the climb sequence and after t/o checklist. Once everything was stabilized; both the FO and I discussed at length what happened. We were both in agreement that we experienced an erroneous terrain warning. My RA continued to have the yellow bar and still showed -5 feet until about 10-15 minutes or 20;000 to 30;00 feet into the flight. The FO indicated he thought his RA was faulty as well. Once we landed and were at the gate in ZZZ; I wrote up the terrain warning and the faulty RA and I called Maintenance control. They had me run the RA test and returned the aircraft back into service. The controller told me that this can happen when the aircraft taxis on icy and snow covered runways/taxi-ways/ramps. After letting the controller know we had been on the ground in ZZZ for over two hours with those conditions; he was confident that's what caused our issues. He said when the ice and snow melts off the RA antennas; the RA returns back to normal. The subsequent flight to ZZZ2 was normal. I thought about this event and I'm not sure if I'm supposed to send in an ASAP; but I finally thought it might be a good idea. Please contact me if you have any questions or need more data. I believe the RA's functioned abnormally due to their antenna's prolonged exposure to snowy and icy conditions on the runway; taxiway; and ramp at ZZZ airport. I suggest an advisory could be sent out to keep the crews from being startled when this occurs in the conditions explained above. However; remind the aircrews to still comply with the terrain warning; whether it's an erroneous warning or not.

column121: On Date; I planned a flight to land at 23M Clarke County (a non towered field); then on to ZZZ. I obtained a full flight briefing through Foreflight prior to departure and confirmed that the only airport NOTAM for 23M was that the PAPI for runway 34 was unusable. I departed and had an uneventful flight en route to 23M. About 6 miles from 23M; I announced my position and intention to land on runway 16 on the CTAF. I made position reports again on turning left downwind; left base; and final. Abeam the numbers on downwind leg; I reduced throttle to normal MAP for landing. As I turned from base to final; I went to reduce throttle to idle; but the throttle stuck at about 12 inches MAP. As I approached the runway; I tried very diligently to get the throttle unstuck by turning the throttle tension knob and firmly pulling on the throttle. I was able to get the throttle to pull back to idle just before crossing the runway threshold and proceeded to land on runway 16 at 23M. Once on the ground; a voice came over the radio that said 'You can't land here; the airport is closed; didn't you see the yellow X on the runway?' I had not seen any X's on the runway on approach. At this point I reached the entry to the taxiway and saw that it was blocked off. I responded that I was having a semi-emergency and was troubleshooting a stuck throttle. They asked if there was anything they could do to help. I replied no and that I think I had the problem resolved and would immediately back taxi and take back off. I told them I checked NOTAMs before I departed and that I hadn't seen any NOTAMS about a closure; to which they replied 'Well I don't know how that happened.' He stated that they had no fuel and something about that being why the airport was closed; which did not completely make sense to me at the time. I cycled the throttle several times to ensure it was not sticking and the engine responded properly. There were no obstructions on the runway that would prevent takeoff and there were no workers visible around the runway. As I taxied back to the takeoff end of runway 16; I was thinking about how I did not see any X's on the runway and how there was no NOTAM for the airport being closed when I did my briefing just an hour or so prior. I felt like a real bonehead for missing this. When I got to the end of the runway; I saw that there was in fact NO X ON THE PAVED RUNWAY INDICATING IT WAS CLOSED. There was a yellow X laying on the grass leading up to the runway threshold; but there were no markings on the runway itself. I departed without issue and returned to my home airport. I checked the NOTAMs for the airport again and confirmed that there were no NOTAMs for 23M being closed on this date. Three issues stand out to me in this situation. First; if a runway is to be closed; the yellow X needs to be ON the runway; not in the grass leading up to the runway. All examples of runway closure markings I have ever seen have been ON the runway surface. Second; if an airport or runway is to be temporarily closed; there should be a NOTAM for that closure. Third; while there was an X on the grass leading up to the runway; I did not see it on final approach due to being preoccupied troubleshooting the stuck throttle. In the future; I will do a more thorough job of looking AROUND the runway for yellow X's while on downwind leg and on final approach. I am not sure if an unauthorized individual may have placed the X's in the grass and the airport wasn't really officially closed. The person on the CTAF did not identify themselves so I do not know if they were airport officials or someone else. The lack of a NOTAM and improper placement of the X's leads me to think this may not have been an official airport closure. Nevertheless; I will do a better job of scanning the area around the runway from now on for any indication of problems.

column121: The flight where this incident happened was a night VFR cross-country from ZZZ to ZZZ; as the final leg of a cross country flight along the route of ZZZ-ZZZ1-ZZZ2-ZZZ; which was being conducted for the purpose of instrument proficiency for me; using a view-limiting device while accompanied by a safety pilot.  Flight planning indicated that we had sufficient fuel for this mission; and indeed; I have flown this route several times with no issues in other similar aircraft.  I was using planned fuel burn of 10 gph; in accordance with performance charts for [this make/model]; such as the one we were flying.  We checked fuel state prior to the flight both on the gauges; as well as by visual verification on both tanks (both myself and my safety pilot) during the pre-flight inspection.  Both tanks were visually noted by both of us as being above the tabs.  The flight proceeded uneventfully until the final leg from ZZZ2 to ZZZ.  Approximately halfway between the two airports; at an altitude of 6;500 MSL (a little over 3 hours into the flight); the engine developed roughness; then sputtered and quit.  We had just changed tanks approximately 2 minutes prior; and I had adjusted the mixture slightly; so I immediately applied full rich mixture; turned the electric fuel pump on; and switched the tanks back.  The engine caught almost immediately; and I was able to initiate a full power climbing turn in order to remain near the town of ABC; which I knew had an airport; just in case the engine quit again; since we didn't know the reason for the engine stoppage.  After about 2 minutes or less; the engine quit again; and I pitched for best glide; and began searching for the airport; which we initially had difficulty doing; due to the obscuration of the airfield beacon by trees when approaching from the south.  We attempted to use the CTAF to turn the runway lights up; and eventually were able to do so; and spotted the runway.  Upon identifying my landing site; I then had my safety pilot read the emergency checklist for engine failure; while I performed the action items.  We were unable to affect a restart.  We then attempted to contact ZZZ Approach (just as this happened; ZZY Approach had handed us off to ZZZ; but before we could establish radio contact; the engine had quit the first time).  Unable to reach Approach on the radio; we squawked 7700 on the transponder; then prepared for an emergency landing.  We easily had the altitude to make the field; so I utilized S-turns and a forward slip to bleed off altitude for a straight-in approach to RWYXX.  We landed safely; (a textbook short field landing) and egressed the aircraft.  We could hear sirens as emergency responders from the city of ABC; both fire and police (having been notified by ATC) were en-route to our location.  I notified approach via cell phone that we were safe on deck (all personnel on board; as well as the aircraft); and the first responders assisted with towing the aircraft to a parking area.  Upon inspecting the aircraft afterwards; we discovered that both tanks were completely empty (both fuel tanks were still reading approximately 1/4 tank on the gauges when the engine first quit; and the left tank gauge continued to show this fuel state even after landing).  According to pre-flight planning; we should have had about 1.2 hours of fuel remaining at that point of the flight; which would have allowed us to make it back to ZZZ and have our legal VFR night fuel reserve plus some; so this gauge reading seemed reasonable at the time (although I have never entirely trusted fuel gauges in aircraft; and this incident has greatly deepened that distrust)!My understanding is that the owner will be doing an inspection in the next few days to confirm that there are no fuel leaks or other issues that might have contributed to running out of fuel early.  Assuming that no mechanical issues are found at that time; I believe that the following factors are involved:(1) For some reason I thought that fuel at the tabs on this plane was X gallons (Y per side); but I later found that in this aircraft it is Z gallons (A gallons per side out of a Y gallon tank).  A contributing factor for this may have been that most of my recent flight time has been in a [different model] for which tabs are indeed Y per side.  I may have confused this with the Y gallons per side TOTAL for this aircraft for full tanks; not tabs.  (2) It is possible that this aircraft was burning a lot more than 10 gph.  I was told afterwards that the aircraft burns more like 15 gph average if you are performing a lot of pattern work (and we had conducted 4 instrument approaches prior to heading home on the final leg).  None of the [aircraft] publications that I have substantiate this type of fuel burn for an IO360 engine; but if so; than that would partly explain why we ran out of fuel early.  I am not aware of whether this aircraft has any performance modifications that would increase fuel burn.  A 15 gph burn rate; even for a short time; would definitely run us out much sooner than expected.Thankfully we were able to safely land engine-out at this small rural airfield; especially given that this happened at night in an airplane that I was relatively unfamiliar with.  This incident reinforces the value of proper pre-flight planning and ensuring that accurate information is available in terms of fuel burn as well as fuel tank size; even when operating in the local area on a fairly short flight in terms of distance between points.  It also reinforces the value of cruising at higher altitudes when over rugged terrain; especially at night.  Lastly; it shows the importance of staying proficient at all aspects of an engine-out emergency.  My thanks to all that assisted; from the approach controllers; to the first responders; as well as my safety pilot.

column121: The following is a list of concerns and questions regarding ZZZ Center's decision to go ATC Zero in the middle of the day as well as the process by which it occurred. I'm going to divide the report into three major issues with details below. I'm not sure how many of my colleagues will file individual reports; but this is a combination of many of our concerns as discussed during and after the event. The three major places we believer safety was jeopardized were: 1) The decision to close in the middle of the day on short notice. 2) Confusion between the published contingency plan and the COVID contingency plan.  3) The decision to not transition into ATC Zero procedures until only 30 minutes prior to the event.1) Why close in the middle of the day?ZZZ Center has had multiple COVID positives since the beginning of the pandemic; and cleaning was always delayed until the mid-shift; when traffic is greatly reduced. In fact; in early Month 1; we had a Controller from the X Area report to work and leave in the middle of the shift because he was feeling sick. He took a test on his way home from work and reported back to the facility that he was indeed COVID positive. His crew finished their shift; the night crew worked their entire shift; and then cleaning occurred on the mid. This is after a confirmed COVID was in the building; working traffic that very day.Yesterday; management became aware of the COVID positive the day before and the person hadn't been in the building since Month 1. However; the decision was made that cleaning had to be done immediately. Why the urgency this time? Closing airspace on a very busy travel day on short notice introduced innumerable safety risks to the system; not to mention greatly impacted the efficiency of the NAS nationwide.2) Confusion regarding contingency plan.ZZZ Center has a published contingency plan; which we review at least annually. Procedures and routes have been developed to allow traffic to continue through the facility should it need to close unexpectedly. Apparently; a separate COVID contingency plan was developed outside of these procedures. There was quite a bit of confusion among the workforce regarding this discrepancy - including a NOTAM being published with the frequency from the existing contingency plan; which was actually not going to be used in this COVID plan.Additional issues from the Controller standpoint included a lack of understanding about what was actually happening to ZZZ Center airspace at XA:X0 local [time] when ATC Zero was declared. The contingency plan seems to indicate that ZZZ Center airspace is to be assumed by ZZZ1 Center and ZZZ2 Center; however ZZZ1 Center was under the assumption that ZZZ Center airspace was to be non-radar. To this end; approximately 25 minutes before ATC zero; an aircraft from ZZZ entered [Sector Y] airspace without a hand off. I called [Sector Z] to call radar on the aircraft; assuming that they were busy changing flight plans and forgot to initiate a hand off. The Controller told me on the line they had 'terminated' the aircraft and they were monitoring ZZZ2 frequency. ZZZ1 Center was in contact with ZZZ2 Center and passing ZZZZZ [Intersection] estimates to the controllers there. I told ZZZ1 we were still open until XA:X0 and Controller told me they were informed we were closed 30 minutes before XA:X0 local.Finally; the COVID route into ZZZ2 ended at ZZZZZ1 at which point we were supposed to issue 'rest of route unchanged.' First of all; most of these aircraft did not have ZZZZZ1 on their route; so rest of route clearance doesn't make sense. Second; any aircraft headed to a northeast airport that got tied back into their route with a direct after ZZZZZ1 went right back into ZZZ Center east area airspace. Once again; the question of who owns that airspace; is it radar on non-radar communications into play. We asked for clarification; which didn't come so we started to issue ZZZZZ1…ZZZ…next fix to go further north and around ZZZ Center.We were never adequately briefed on this new COVID contingency; neither when it was developed; nor on the day it was to be implemented. It seemed every time someone came down from TMU (Traffic Management Unit) or the watch desk; we were being told something different. There was a general feeling among the workforce that this was being made up on the fly.3) Too short of a time frame for implementing contingency plan.When airspace is blocked for special operations; routes are put out hours in advance. There are 'all aircraft must be out of the area by xxxxZ' notes sent to surrounding facilities and published in NOTAMs. These special operations have become fairly routine at ZZZ Center and we still get procedures started early.ATC Zero in the middle of the day is a much more complicated issue affecting a much larger piece of airspace and many more routes. Regardless; the decision was made to operate essentially as normal until the ATC limited at 30 minutes before XA:X0 local. Beginning with the fact that it takes significantly more than 30 minutes to traverse ZZZ airspace; this was not nearly enough time to sterilize the airspace and ensure all remaining aircraft were established on the only acceptable routes through ZZZ when ATC Zero (COVID procedure) has been declared. Below is a small list of the issues this created:- As late as 50 minutes prior to XA:X0; aircraft were still departing ZZZ3 and airborne from airports with 'bad routes.' This created increased workload for sectors ZZ and YY as they tried to get aircraft established on good routing prior to the XA:X0 local ATC Zero.- Sector YY needed a D-side and had (estimated) 15+ tracks as late as 35 minutes prior to XA:X0 local ATC Zero. At a time when we should be well into the transition into ATC Zero procedures; we were still working hard to separate aircraft and resolve conflicts.- Sector YX/ZX took hand offs on two slower moving aircraft near ZZZ4 at approximately 15 minutes prior to filed to ZZZ4 and ZZZ5. There was absolutely no way these aircraft could have been established on the legal contingency routes by XA:X0. We wound up negotiating with ZZZZ1 Center [named] sector to take radar on these aircraft after we issued routes southeast towards their airspace. When we were forced to leave by management at XA:X0 (due to 10 hour shift limitations); these aircraft were switched to ZZZ1 Center; but well into ZZZ Center airspace and not on the established COVID routes. While it is still unclear if ZZZ Center was officially non-radar airspace or not; these aircraft were not on legal non-radar routes. Several controllers were very uncomfortable leaving the airspace in the configuration it was at XA:X0 (myself included). We felt there was more to be done before each of the aircraft we were responsible for was in a safe and legal place.There was a feeling that getting us out before we hit 10 hours was more important than having the procedures fully running properly. Of course; both could have easily occurred if the transition to ATC Zero procedures started earlier.1) Closing in the middle of the day.In the future; short notice ATC Zero procedures should be reserved for immediate; dire emergencies and not be used for cleaning especially days after a positive person was in the building. The decision to go ATC Zero should not be taken lightly and the risks should be carefully measured before the decision is made.2) Confusion regarding contingency plan.A complete; thorough contingency plan needs to be developed and properly briefed to all involved - from OM down to controllers. There should be no confusion about what is going to happen and what each individual facility and sector's responsibilities are to be.3) Too short of a timeframe for ATC Zero implementation.When it is absolutely necessary to go to ATC Zero; the procedures must be implemented earlier. At a minimum; aircraft forecast to be in the affected airspace need to be given routing off of the ground.ATC Zero cannot be declared until each and every single aircraft in the affected airspace is accounted for and on an established contingency route.
column123: ZZZ Center went ATC Zero for a mid-day for COVID cleaning. This had not been conducted before during the day shift at ZZZ Center; only on the mid shift. The COVID cleaners were slightly delayed for their cleaning resulting in the airspace being closed longer than Command Center and Management had anticipated. The Operation Manager and all of the Front Line Managers were told that the cleaning was completed in the control room. They all came into the building to see and smell how the environment was inside the control room. Within minutes most of management came back outside dry heaving and coughing severely and said that the areas (Control Room) needed more time for the chemical to settle. After approximately 15 minutes; Management told us to come back into the building. We all initially thought the smell was bad. It was truly hard to breath. After a short amount of time; I was experiencing confusion; headache; sore throat; shortness of breath; nausea and could taste the chemical with my mask on. The taste of the chemical today has still not gone away. It smells and tastes like insecticide. My throat is still a bit sore. Several controllers went home on sick leave because they could not breathe and were coughing. The Operations Manager and all of the Front Line Managers left the control room multiple times because the fumes were so bad. They needed fresh air.There was not enough time between when the COVID cleaning taking place and when we were told to come back into the building. I want to know what chemical I was breathing in for over 5 hours. I believe this harmed me. Tech Operations stated that everything was saturated in the control room. What we were breathing in was not safe.

column121: Aircraft X departed JNU for ZZZ; but changed destination shortly after to return to JNU because the pilot reported that ZZZ winds would not allow for an approach. Aircraft X initially climbed to 090; but requested descent to 080 for moderate icing. I cleared Aircraft X back to the JNU airport via direct SSR direct; to expect the LDA Z 8 approach; as requested.I cleared Aircraft X for the LDA Z 8 approach; to cross SSR at or above 060. Shortly after progressing SSR; the aircraft transmitted that they were back in the icing and had 'quite a bit of ice on the wing' and said they were unsure if they would be able to maintain the transition altitude of 056 until LYNNS intersection. The aircraft then descended to 052; below the approach altitude. I issued a low altitude alert; and instructed Aircraft X to climb to meet the transition altitude. Aircraft X reported they would attempt to climb; but were unable and appeared to level off at 050 in a 060 MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude); and requested to transition over to the RNAV W 8 approach via JIGMI; as the approach had a lower transition altitude. Seeing as the aircraft had already progress JIGMI; I asked if they would be able to establish themselves on to a published portion of the approach if I provided a heading to join. the pilot said affirmative; so I issued a 10 degree turn to the right to join the RNAV W 8 approach; and to steer the aircraft away form higher terrain to the NW; as it was clear they would be unable to climb. I then informed the pilot that I was providing priority handling for them. Aircraft X was able to maintain 050 until joining the RNAV W 8 approach; at which time I issued the approach clearance and confirmed that the aircraft would be able to maintain the new transition altitudes of that approach. The pilot confirmed that they would; and was able to safely fly the approach to landing.

column121: During pushback; the tug driver did not use proper terminology. I understand that the contract ramp personnel work many different airlines; but they should have a working knowledge on the aircraft that they are pushing back; as well as some type of standard phraseology and verbiage.Upon completion of the pushback; the tug driver asked me to set the parking brake; which I did; and using proper terminology; I told him 'Brakes Set; Pressure Normal.' A few minutes later; he said to me; 'Have a good flight.' I asked him if the tow bar was disconnected and if the bypass pin had been removed; and he said 'Not yet; I'll tell you when they are.' A few minutes later; he said again; 'Have a good flight' and he disconnected the headset before I could ask him again if the tow bar had been disconnected and if the bypass pin had been removed. I rang the Ground Call button; and I was trying to use hand signals to have the wing walker inform the tug driver that I needed to talk to him on the headset. During this time; I did see the tug backing away from the aircraft; with the tow bar; and a ramp person walking away with the bypass pin in her hand. It appeared that the ramp personnel were finally starting to understand that I was trying to get someone back on the headset; when I gave them a thumbs up signal. The ramp person gave me the thumbs up signal; and they knew we were all set to go. I received the proper Salute; started engines and we taxied away.The tug driver never told me that the tow bar had been disconnected and that the bypass pin had been removed. The tug driver needs to have a working knowledge of the proper terminology to inform the Captain that the towbar has been disconnected and that the bypass pin has been removed; and to wait for the Captain to tell him that it is OK to disconnect the headset; not to just disconnect the headset on his own.Communication is paramount to prevent an accident; and in my opinion; this tug driver did not understand nor use proper verbiage/procedure during the pushback.

I also was having freezing issues with Jepp FD pro. After being handed to ATC; we had the approach and plan in place for the approach Runway XX. Inside the IAF I set the TDZE as normal and confirmed with crew; as we were cleared the approach. We had still been descending constantly from events before; we never really stopped descending since just after the divert was made. As we were in the arc; we were completely configured for landing and I noticed that we had descended below the published altitude on the ARC. I quickly realized we had been still in FLCH and immediately said to stop decent. We were approximately 400-500 ft. Low. And after arresting settled at about 600 below. The PF and crew were in VMC conditions. CAVOK. We were approximately 1/2 to 3/4 of the way through the arc once I noticed. We had the airport in sight and the PF elected to stay at the approximate pattern altitude as we were over water in VMC and had the airport in sight and about to turn final. The approach continued visually and the PF made a normal landing and taxi to hard stand.

Concerning the ZZZZ-ZZZZ1-ZZZZ legs; because of the 117 restrictions; depending how the Relief Pilot (RP)  and PM split the first leg or part of the 2nd; and the expected flight time of the ZZZZ-ZZZZ1 leg; no one gets decent rest. In our pairing; I as the RP slept first on the outbound leg for 2 hours; and the PM slept next for 3; and the PF slept the entire return leg (2.5 hrs). This was FAR117 compliant; but due to pairing construction is essentially too little; at the wrong time; and contributed to a degradation in safety. It is not helped by a 2-hour ground sit (during which it's impossible to rest because the countries authorities enter the airplane for a security sweep and postflight / preflight duties must be accomplished; and the constant loud noises and aircraft motion from cargo loading/unloading). So the RP and PM sleep a very small amount during the WOCL; and the PF doesn't get a rest opportunity until after the WOCL; when it may no longer be possible to sleep.This is bananas. ZZZZ1; and the country's airspace in general; is among our more challenging operations (language; altimetry; nonstandard ATC phraseology and procedures; night/weather; unfamiliarity with fix names; etc.). Setting up a minimum crew with back-to-back red eyes and little rest opportunity in that environment is dangerous. And the crew is then left to consider a fatigue call on the ground in ZZZZ1 - one of the worst places in the world to stop the operation for crew and airline alike.

I asked them to keep us informed if there were any changes of if anything escalated; they said they would.  At this point we had begun the descent on the arrival into ZZZ; the First Officer had been flying the whole leg.  He had been managing the radios as well while I was talking to the flight attendants.  I considered that while the situation currently was Level 1; I felt it was most prudent to get the aircraft on the ground to protect my crew and the other passengers.  Additionally; felt it would reduce my workload as well as my First Officer's if we requested priority handling.  I told the First Officer what I was considering and why; and asked if he had any considerations.  He agreed that was a good choice.  I then requested priority handling with ZZZ approach and informed them of SOB and fuel remaining.  I had sent an ACARS message to Dispatch informing them of our situation.  I called ZZZ ops and informed them of the same.  I then checked in with the flight attendants to ensure things were okay; which they were.  I informed them we were accepting priority handling and would be on the ground as soon as possible.  As we passed through 10;000 feet we kept the speed up around 315 knots to expedite our arrival.  We were given radar vectors to a visual Runway X and landed uneventfully.  We had to wait a few minutes for our gate as it was occupied.  We pulled into the gate.  The passenger disembarked and the situation was over.  There were no injuries.  After the plane was empty the crew got together in the front of the airplane for a debrief of the situation.  At the end of the debrief I asked the flight attendants if they were okay and would be comfortable with continuing.  They all felt that they were okay to continue.  When the First Officer and I debriefed; I asked him the same and he was good.  I took a moment to assess myself and determined I was good to continue as well.It is worth noting that the flight attendants did a very good job of keeping us informed as to the status of the situation.  This was helpful and good crew CRM.  They were clear in their communication; calm and professional.  My First Officer also was a model of CRM and performed exceptionally to include his aircraft handling to expedite our arrival.

column121: On approach to ZZZ; Initially the weather report was 3/4 SM visibility; so I informed the controller that I needed 1SM to shoot the approach due to my high minimums status. The Controller gave me direct ZZZ VOR and Hold northeast as published at 6;000 feet. I began heading direct to the VOR; when the controller came back and gave me the updated visibility at 1SM. So I accepted vectors to the approach. As I neared the FAF; I knew that I would need to be able to see the approach lights and runway in a low visibility situation; so I attempted to move the sun visor back to its stowed position. The visor became stuck; which is normal for these airplanes so I pushed harder. As I did that; the visor suddenly released itself and hit me in the face; causing a dull pain and immediate swelling. I touched the area and came back with a lot of blood on my hand; so I concentrated on flying the approach using standard procedures and call-outs and getting back on the ground. Unfortunately; I reached mins and did not see the runway environment; so I called out 'minimums; missed approach' and began the missed approach procedure according to standard procedures and call-outs. The controller attempted to give me a hold over the ZZZ VOR; but as I was bleeding and didn't know how long I would need to hold I chose to divert back to ZZZ1. I confirmed this decision after reaching cruise and having center call company Dispatch. Center informed me that I was a [priority] aircraft and would be treated as such as I had initially requested paramedics upon arrival. Upon reaching cruise however; I used my phone (which was off) as a mirror and concluded that I did not need medical assistance. So I informed Center of this change. I completed the flight back to ZZZ1 with no further issues. Paramedics met me at the ramp anyway; along with Airport OPS. They did not request my information and sent me on my way after cleaning the blood off of my face and neck. I then called dispatch and the Chief Pilots office to inform them of the situation.When the sun visor hit me in the face and I found blood on my hand. The sun visor in this airplane is in poor condition and gets stuck on the rail constantly. This in addition to the fact that I was very task saturated and didn't realize that the bleeding wasn't as bad as I had initially thought. I made the division to divert as I was performing a missed approach and wasn't aware of how severe the injury was. I knew the other airports in the vicinity were not suitable so I decided to go back to ZZZ1 as I knew it was 800-1000 foot OVC and I would have no issues. If I had moved the sun visor earlier that would have been beneficial; aside from that it could definitely use some TLC.

column121: I was the AFA (A Flight Attendant). Every part of the flight (boarding; climb; cruise; etc.) seemed to be going fine and seemed standard. When the pilots told us to prepare the cabin for arrival; I decided to look over the PAX (Passenger) manifest before tossing it. I had used it during the flight but only looked at part of it. To be honest; I didn't read over it before we departed. When I read over it toward the end of the flight; I noticed that one PAX was listed as a Special Assistance Passenger. This PAX was listed as needing a wheelchair and as blind. At no point was I aware that we had a PAX with a visual impairment. The PAX was boarded first and the person who pushed his wheelchair stowed the PAX's luggage. When interacting with the PAX on boarding; I handed him a sanitizing wipe and he seemed to have no trouble getting the wipe from me or getting to his seat; although I didn't really watch him go to his seat. At no point did the gate agent inform us that we had a PAX with a visual impairment nor did the person who pushed the wheelchair. When the B Flight Attendant asked the gate agent if we had any specials (for the PAX count form) the gate agent said we had one wheelchair. There was no mention of a PAX with a visual impairment.We did the standard briefings (announcements and safety demo); but neither of us provided a one-on-one briefing with the PAX. We were unaware of his visual impairment. After I realized our mistake on descent; I wasn't sure what to do. I had a brief conversation with the PAX; and he seemed to look me in the eye for the conversation. After I played the final descent announcement; I showed the B Flight Attendant the manifest and how it showed a PAX listed as blind. She was surprised to see it. We discussed our situation in regard to the PAX and the possibility of writing a  report.After we landed; the PAX gathered his belongings and deplaned without help. He also told the person waiting with the wheelchair that he didn't need it. He was traveling alone and without the assistance of a service animal. He only used a simple walking cane; not a red and white cane frequently used by people with visual impairments. He gave me no reason to think that he was visually impaired; but I understand that some disabilities are not apparent. When all the PAX had deplaned; I informed the Captain of what had happened and asked for advice. He said to fill out an report because we didn't do a required briefing. The B Flight Attendant and I knew that one-on-one briefings are required; we didn't know the PAX was visually impaired.I am concerned and upset that we potentially caused a safety incident with a PAX with a visual impairment. This is unacceptable. I hope to use this as a learning experience and pay closer attention to the PAX manifest before shutting the boarding door and proactively asking all gate agents about special assist PAX that we may have onboard. I say this with caution; though. We don't always receive the correct manifest; we sometimes receive incomplete manifests with no PAX information; and sometimes we don't even receive a manifest at all. While in the end; it was my responsibility to confirm with the gate agent about special assist PAX; I feel like there was a breakdown of communication between the gate agent and me. I wonder if the gate agent knew there was a visually impaired PAX on the flight. Perhaps there could be strengthened training for gate agents and flight attendants for recognizing special assist PAX. For flight attendants; also what to do if a special assist PAX is discovered during flight and certain briefings did not occur; as in our case. As stated before; I didn't know what to do in regard to the PAX.I understand the severe safety hazards not providing a one-on-one briefing could have caused if something went wrong during flight. I hope to use this as a lesson learned and not solely rely on being informed of all special assist PAX by a gate agent. In other words; I need to be more proactive; and I need to use my resources more wisely. My hope is that this can be used as a lesson for all flight attendants so that incidents like this don't happen again. We are first and foremost a safety industry; and we failed to keep to our safety standards.
