column121: While executing the ILS to [Runway] XXR at ZZZ; ATC informed us that we were following a heavy and instructed us to slow to 170kts. The Captain and I saw the other aircraft on TCAS and judged the distance to be six or seven miles. We discussed the possibility of wake turbulence but we didn't think the spacing was an issue. Then; after switching the tower; at around 3;000 feet; we were instructed to start slowing to our final approach speed. We then configured the aircraft for landing and started running the landing checklist. While listening and responding to the Captain's checklist callouts; I thought I heard someone say 'approach clearance canceled; maintain 3;000'; but I was unsure of the call sign. This was partly because the Captain and I were in the middle of running a checklist and partly because there was another aircraft on frequency that had a very similar call sign. We were Company X Callsign ABBC and the aircraft ahead of the heavy was Company X Callsign ADDC (there were at least three instances during the arrival where an instruction was given and we weren't 100% sure who it was for). I interrupted the Captain and told him that I thought tower had just canceled someone's approach clearance and asked him to query ATC to see if it was for us. The controller responded with a very urgent tone and said 'That is affirm; Callsign ABBC your approach clearance is canceled; maintain present heading and climb to 3;000. I'll have a turn for you in just a second.' As the captain was responding to ATC; I pressed the heading button to maintain our present heading as instructed; but I was confused as to what to do next. At this point we were around 2;400 feet (about 2;000 feet AFE); so a hard go-around using the TO/GA button was not required. I was not really mentally prepared for the go-around and was having trouble deciding what to do next; but ATC sounded like they wanted me to start climbing immediately to 3;000 feet; which was already set in the altitude window; so I reacted to his instruction by hitting FLCH. This caused the aircraft to apply full throttle and pitch up to maintain our current approach speed of about 145kts. We maintain this climb for several seconds until I was able to dial the speed up and get the aircraft accelerating. With everything happening so fast; and not really being mentally prepared for a go-around; I called gear up while the flaps were still at 5 which caused the landing gear warning to sound. It was a very sloppy go-around but I don't think the aircraft was ever in an unsafe state.This was my first go-around in the actual aircraft. However; I have mentally rehearsed and practiced enough hard go-arounds in sim training that the procedure is pretty much automatic and I can execute it without much thinking required. However; I can only recall doing a soft go-around once during FTD training and; as I recall; in that scenario we were not yet configured for landing and the altitude assigned was below us; so it was a simple matter of stopping the descent and flying the assigned heading. We also discussed soft go-arounds vs hard go-arounds in training and I had recalled that using TO/GA was optional but not really preferred during a soft-go around. I think there needs to be more training on soft go-arounds and the SOP should give more guidance as to preferred methods in various scenarios. Currently; the SOP does not give much guidance on the subject other than reminding the pilot to retract flaps at the F-bug or XX knots above green dot. After landing; the Captain and I discussed what I could have done better. He suggested; and I agreed; that the best course of action would have been to press ALT to stop the descent and then start accelerating before starting our climb. However; after replaying it in my head all night; I came to the conclusion that; given the fact that ATC wanted me to climb; it would have been perfectly acceptable to switch to heading mode and then press TO/GA and execute my normalgo-around actions and callouts; even though we were well above 1;000 feet AFE. This would ensure the aircraft was maintaining a safe speed while we began to reconfigure the aircraft and would have eliminated a lot of confusion that I created while I pondered what technique I should use to get us to 3;000 feet while also cleaning up the aircraft. Perhaps this should be the preferred method to execute a soft-go around when fully configured for landing and a climb is required. But perhaps there's another aspect of it that I'm not considering. The technique of pressing ALT and accelerating aircraft prior to starting the climb also seems like it would work in most situations. That's why I think the SOP should give more guidance on the subject. If there were a preferred method spelled out in the SOP; then it would eliminate a lot of the confusion and both pilots would be on the same page instead of debating on a technique for a procedure that is rarely used when there isn't really time to stop and think about it.This experience has also taught me to be prepared for a go-around at all times; not just when below 1;000 feet on an approach. Although; the spacing behind the heavy looked good to us; we should have been more prepared for the possibility that ATC would call for a go-around unexpectedly.

column121: The pre-departure checklists have the following added to the header of the checklist: 'NOTE: This check is to be done at the gate or hangar prior to taking the aircraft to the gate at the discretion of the Lead or Supervisor. column121: I was in contact with Chicago Center on our flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 on a direct flight plan at FL290. We were talking with Chicago Center when he transferred us to another Chicago Center frequency. I tried 3 times to contact the Controller as he was quite busy. The third time he said 'unless it is pertinent to the safety of flight; maintain radio silence.' I complied with his instructions. During this time I was working on other items pertaining to the flight. Some time had passed and I realized I have not talked to a controller in some time and the radio calls I was hearing were getting fainter. I called the Controller and asked if I needed to be transferred and was told that he did not have me on his list and was unsure of what frequency I needed to contact. I tried to go back to the previous frequency I was on but was not getting what I needed there. I then looked at my route and found that the closest larger airport was ZZZ2 and called their Controller asking for a correct frequency for Center and he asked for my position; squawk code; and tail number again. I gave him the information he requested and afterwards he recommended a new frequency to me. I contacted the Controller on the recommended frequency I was given and he was also unsure of who I was. He requested our altitude; tail number; and squawk code. I complied and he advised I contact the next control frequency he had. This next Controller was Cleveland Center. He seemed to have somewhat of a better idea of who we were but recommended the next Controller on Cleveland Center as well on a new frequency. As soon as I contacted this new Controller he knew who I was and kept me on the same altitude and course I had been on. Again; we were direct from ZZZ to ZZZ1 at FL290 and had not modified our course and ATC had not advised us of any course or altitude changes. Before we were switched to Potomac Center nearing our destination I was asked to take down a number and call it on the ground for a 'possible pilot deviation.' I complied and we were able to continue and land without any further incident. On the ground I called the number I was given and talked to ATC about the situation. They took my information and we talked about what happened. They advised me that in the future it is always a good idea to go back to your previous frequency if needed. I agreed with their advice and they said that I may be contacted in the near future about this incident. I said that is no problem and am more than willing to talk to whomever about it.To correct situations like this in the future I believe there are a couple things that can happen. For myself as a pilot that if I am ever unsure of who I need to be talking to that I can check in more often and make sure that we are all on the same page. The suggestion I would offer for the controller side would be that if anyone is in a NORDO aircraft situation that all the controllers in the area know of that tail number and are able to direct the aircraft to the correct frequency quickly rather than searching around.

column121: Aircraft X came to an abrupt stop on Runway XX at ZZZ due to snow on the runway. We were the only occupants of the craft. Neither of us were injured; nor was the plane damage. There was no damage to any other persons or property.A low approach was made to assess the condition of the runway before attempting a soft field approach and landing. We decided to make an approach to land after judging that the snow looked to be at or less than 2 inches. It looks like two layers of very thin snow. We could see tracks from another tricycle gear airplane. What we didn't realize was that that plane had landed in much shallower snow and that it had then snowed more on top. Being able to see grass protruding through the snow also gave the notion that the snow was not deep. I briefed my student on precautions to take with landing on snow before we made the approach.When we landed; the plane's mains and nose wheel sunk in causing us to come to an abrupt halt. We were able to taxi the aircraft most of the way up the runway. We agreed to attempt a soft field take off back down our tracks; which didn't get very far.Chief; Assistant Chief; Owner; and Lead Pilot were notified. We contacted the Airport Manager; who was able to come to our aid with a backhoe. We took off from the county road next to the runway as decided between myself; the Student and Chief Pilot; and as advised by the Airport Manager. A successful short field takeoff and climb out was performed by myself; the instructor and my student and I returned to ZZZ1.14 CFR 91.103; Pre-flight preparation; was not observed or fulfilled to its fullest. I will not get into the possible reasoning behind this; aside from that we decided to go to #X# during taxi.Lessons learned are abundant by our main takeaways that [we] I discussed were as follows:-New or unfamiliar airports need better preparation and scrutiny.-Snow depth should not be judged from the air. Until properly equipped and properly trained; no approach and landing should be made to a snowy runway that one is not sure they could take off from again.-I now have a new example of things not to do to use as a teaching tool with my students.We were extremely lucky pilots today. but we as pilots do not want to rely on luck. Lessons learned.

column121: Prior to the event; I came up from break and took a LC (Local Control) position that controls a satellite Class D airport with a gravel strip and water lanes. This position was combined with both CIC and Clearance Delivery/FD. This was never trained as a standard; but some work crews have made this a normal practice when staffing is short. Quickly after taking position; and before the event occurred; I did call up someone to split off the position but I should not have allowed it to remain de-combined in the interim. LC and GC (Ground Control) were de-combined; and while working I heard GC bring a potential conflict to LCs attention (good tower teamwork from GC). As I examined the situation I saw the same conflict- a heavy aircraft had taxied into departure position (Runway 33) with a large aircraft arriving behind on a non-intersecting runway (Runway 7L). With the spacing of the aircraft it did not appear that there was enough space to ensure compliance with our facility order. Our facility order details spacing required with aircraft arriving Runways 7R/L and departing Runway 33. I advised the LC that I did not believe adequate spacing would exist and suggested; but did not instruct; alternate courses of action to avoid a situation where the arriving aircraft might encounter jet blast. The LC insisted it would work and did not take any action. With the proximity of the aircraft; I don't believe a safety issue existed; however lack of compliance with facility guidelines with no standard for separation is an unacceptable risk to the users of the system.This event highlights many issues.As CIC during the event; I take responsibility for my own personal performance. I should not have taken CIC combined with an LC position. I should have had more engagement in the operation - if this situation had been detected earlier there may have been more time to correct it. I also should have given the LC instruction instead of suggestion when I saw action was not going to be taken.1. Lack of staffing. Perpetual lack of staffing leads this facility down the path of using what should be contingency practices into day to day practices. Positions are too often combined and because this has become the norm; controllers do not understand that they are providing a reduced level of service.2. Lack of safety culture. LC had two controllers address concern over this action and did not appear to consider an alternate course of action. This is not a behavior to this specific Controller but throughout this facility.3. Lack of training. The training culture and training at this facility has fallen short on ensuring that the staff of the facility have a thorough understanding of the rules we are expected to apply.4. Lack of supervision. Much like our Controller workforce; our supervisory staff is frequently understaffed and asked to do an excessive amount of duties that take them away from the operation. There was not a supervisor present at the time of the incident.5. Bad procedures. The facility; and region as a whole have done a poor job at creating procedures that are not easily followed by pilots or controllers. Many of these procedures don't have reasonable 'outs'; which put pilots and controllers in dangerous situations in a recovery situation.Consider revising ANC jet blast procedures.Provide clear expectations to CPCs on services we are expected to provide pilots.Provide adequate staffing to accomplish existing goals.

column121: I was notified about a report of a wrong surface landing. I was the Controller on the midnight shift.  I cleared Aircraft X for Runway XXC; but the Aircraft landed Runway XXR. Approach switched the aircraft on an extended base for the visual approach [to] Runway XXC. The pilot checked on the frequency for Runway XXC. I cleared the aircraft to land for Runway XXC. After I cleared the plane to land the janitorial guy comes to the Tower cab to vacuum the Tower and empty the trash. I usually go opposite of him so we can keep our space (we had our mask on) for social distancing. When he finished cleaning the Local 3 position I recognized the aircraft was short final to Runway XXR. I knew the runway had no vehicles on it because my strip bay showed no vehicle above Runway XXR bay header. I let the aircraft land Runway XXR due to the critical phase in flight. I taxied the aircraft to the ramp after the aircraft landed safely. In the past Approach would call me on the shout line to remind me that this aircraft is set up on the wrong approach. By me not being at the position walking around the Tower cab I did not recognize the aircraft on approach for the wrong runway.The recommendations I would use to prevent this wrong surface landing is to observe an aircraft turn onto the right approach for the right runway. If that pilot makes a mistake turning on to the wrong approach I can either send the aircraft around or correct the aircraft to land on the proper runway; or I can help the pilot get visual for the runway the pilot is lined up for and clear the plane to land for that runway. The key is catching the aircraft turning on the approach early enough so I can correct the pilot.

column121: I did not declare an emergency with ATC. We were already near Top of Descent with no traffic ahead. Getting medical attention was not time critical. The greatest risk was in the deplaning of our other passengers.While enroute to ZZZ; I was notified that 'A man in [seat] XX1 had declared that he had a high fever prior to boarding; and that he now felt very ill.' I queued an ACARS to Dispatch 'call me med' and waited for more information. Once I got this additional information and spelling of the man's name; I sent the message and spoke with Medical and Dispatch in attendance. In the meantime; I got another call indicating the man now said that he just had high blood pressure and would be okay. The load was light and we agreed to move the man to the back row and to move other passengers forward. The Flight Attendant's temperature strip was inconclusive. This information was passed to Medical. We issued the man an N-95 mask; and he wore it. The advice from Medical was to provide Tylenol and continue to ZZZ. Paramedics would meet us at the gate.IMPORTANT; it was then that FA called back to say there was an identity mistake. The actual seat assignment was XX6; not XX1. This meant that the passenger's name was incorrect during the Dispatch/Medical call. The incorrect passenger name is omitted to avoid confusion. I sent the correct name to Dispatch via ACARS.On approach to ZZZ; the man aspirated on the carpet and floor next to the last row and could not wear a mask. FA's notified me of this on taxi-in.Because of the concern for COVID-19; we made the decision that we would have passengers deplane quickly; then allow either the paramedics to the passenger; or allow the man to deplane. Inflight Supervisor and Customer Service Supervisor were at gate and aware of the de-boarding plan. The paramedic overruled the plan and rushed aboard. He proceeded to escort the man passed all the economy passengers and then blocked the jet-way several moments to get him into a wheelchair. I ordered the First Class cabin to deplane after the paramedic passed on his way to the back. I'm glad I did.The aircraft was towed away for disinfection. I checked in with Flight Ops enroute prior to landing and told a call would not be required. Checked in with Chief Pilot on the day after to determine COVID-19 result. There was no answer as of this writing.

column121: On a flight on a VMC day; all was going smoothly. After a beautiful landing; on roll out I took control of the aircraft; bellow 80 knots. I had no control of steering with the tiller. I used rudder and differential in-braking to exit the runway on the high speed exit and hold short Taxiway 1. Notified ATC that we could not taxi and were stopping on taxiway; clear of XXR and short of taxiway. Talked with ZZZ Maintenance and reset the A/SKID & N/W STRG; this cleared the ECAM. When I tried to taxi the plane the ECAM returned. Maintenance said they would send a tug to tow us to the gate. Sent a message for the fault. Notified Dispatch of our situation. After about 30 minutes; Maintenance arrived and talked with us. The mechanic said the nose wheel was canted. They asked us to try and reset a couple of circuit breakers. Discussed the situation With the FO and decided on no more trouble shooting and just be towed to the gate to get passengers off the plane. Maintenance agreed and we were towed uneventfully to the gate.

column121: We were assigned the RNAV Rwy 35; and given direct MEYRS.  We briefed the approach and confirmed altitudes in the FMS.  ATC gave us the clearance 'Cross MEYRS at or above 14;000 [feet]; cleared for the RNAV 35.'  I was the Pilot Monitoring; and I dialed 14;000 into to the autopilot pre-select.  The Pilot Flying entered 14000 in the FMS at MEYRS and executed a direct VNAV descent to MEYRS.  This caused the altitude to turn yellow in the FMS because the next altitude on the approach; at YARUB; was 14;800 [feet].  We discussed this for a moment and I deleted the 14;800 from the FMS.  The Pilot Flying then stated; and I agreed; that we should follow the charted altitudes and we entered 15;000 for MEYRS so that we would be above the published MEA of 14800 between MEYRS and YARUB.  With my intention being to put the YARUB altitude back into the FMS; I referenced the chart and then entered 12000 for YURUB (which was an error).  After crossing MEYRS at 15;000 [feet] we began a slow VNAV descent for 12;000 [feet]; but we should have been level at 14;800 [feet] all the way to YARUB.  While cross checking our position between the map display and the Jepp chart; I began to suspect that we had made an error.  Passing about 13;000 [feet]; I asked the Pilot Flying to level off; which he did; and then I stated that we were not at the correct altitude and that we should climb.  At that moment we received a GPWS caution that gave us a one time audible alert; and the Pilot Flying began a climb.  Shortly afterwards we passed the YARUB fix; and the MEA was now 12;000 so we continued the descent.While monitoring our progress on the approach; I noticed that our altitude was below the charted MEA.  I was confused for a minute while I tried to determine if we had made an error and then realized that I had deleted an altitude; and then re-enter it; but had in fact programmed the incorrect altitude.  Looking back I can't quite explain my thought process; and after the fact my mistake seems very obvious and amateur.  I did reference the chart for the YARUB altitude; and looking at it again '12;000' is written very close to YARUB; and that's my only explanation for how I matched that altitude to that fix; but of course 12;000 is the altitude after YARUB.  While I was monitoring our progress I remember thinking that something didn't seem quite right; and it took me a minute to piece together the ATC clearance; our ensuing actions; and to come to the conclusion that I had made a mistake.  The ATC clearance to an altitude that was already below a charted MEA caused a moment of confusion and second guessing.  I removed an altitude from the FMS that was auto loaded with the approach.  A few minutes later; when I realized I had made an error; I attempted to correct it but I put the wrong altitude back in the FMS after incorrectly reading the chart.  I asked the Pilot Flying to level off while I cross checked the chart and; FMS; and our position.  I then stated that we should climb; which we did.I should not have been so quick to delete an altitude from the FMS which was loaded by selecting the approach.  Also; when entering an altitude into the FMS I need to be more careful while referencing the chart and also confirm with the Pilot Flying that I am entering the correct altitude.
column123: While descending into MJT we were cleared by ATC to pass over MEYRS at or above 14;000 feet and cleared the RNAV 35 approach. We had already briefed the approach and checked the altitudes in the FMS. The first segment between MEYRS and the next point on the approach YARUB is 14;800 feet. Just before reaching MEYRS we decided to stop our descent to pass over MEYRS at 14;000 [feet]and hold at 15;000 [feet]. After YARUB the next step down is 12;000 feet. We had been descending in VNAV to make the cross at Myers. My First Officer put 12;000 feet at YARUB and I confirmed it. In VNAV we then started a slow descent to pass over YARUB at 12;000 feet. This was a mistake on my part. We realized at about 12;700 we where wrong and below a published minimum. I stopped the descent and started a climb. We did get a momentary GPWS terrain and responded according. We climbed about 20 feet and it was gone. We had already stopped descending when we got the GPWS. Realizing we where doing the wrong thing by descending in VNAV to cross YARUB at 12;000 [feet].Allowing the Pilot Monitoring to put 12000 feet n the FMS at YARUB. Immediate once we realized our mistake.. Autopilot off. Start a climb. We never did get to 14;800 [feet] because of how we where close to YARUB. I realized that we where low but also safe and never in any danger. I feel like I should have queried ATC about the descent clearance. I should have been more vigilant with the cross at YARUB.

column121: ZZZ to ZZZ1; visual approach into Runway XX; VMC weather conditions. At approximately 300 feet AGL two messages populated on the EICAS; PTRIM (Pitch Trim) MAIN INOP and PTRIM BACKUP INOP. Both crew members initially looked to see if half of the trim control on either side yolk had been accidentally held; which would cause the effected main control to become INOP; neither side was observed being pressed or stuck. The crew then quickly tested each main control and back up control; one at a time; each control switch failed to activate/ control the elevator trim. The airspeed was 145 KTS IAS. The crew briefed that the controls were trimmed for landing speed; 145 KTS; and due to the short final; now near 200 feet AGL; the landing would be continued. The crew also quickly briefed that in the event of a go-around special attention would need to be paid attention to airspeed due to the INOP trim and the traffic pattern and second landing would be flown at/near 145 KTS. The flight terminated safely and maintenance was called. Maintenance investigation found that when the autopilot disconnect button was pressed to disengage the autopilot it became stuck in the pressed position. This stuck position lead to the dual; main and backup; trim inoperative condition.I would very much like to know if this is a replicable condition with the AP disconnect button or if this failure was an anomaly. If this is a programming fail safe designed into the system; then awareness training might be beneficial to the rest of the group.

column121: I was soloing a new student pilot at ZZZ. After completing several warm-up laps in the pattern dual; I informed Tower that my student was about to solo and had my student drop me off in the non-movement area of the east ramp. On my student's first attempt at a landing; he flared high and initiated a go-around. On his second attempt he landed; stopped; and then initiated a takeoff roll. I realized that my student had mistaken the command 'Cleared to Land' for 'Cleared Stop-And-Go.' I used a handheld radio to call out my student by name and told him to discontinue the takeoff. He stopped on the runway; and he was switched to Ground for taxi instructions. I asked Ground to instruct my student to return to my location and discontinue the flight. While taxiing back to my location on south end of the east ramp; my student missed a left turn from A to F; stopped; and was directed by Ground to complete a 180 turn and return to his original taxi instructions. If had continued forward there was the possibility of crossing Runway XX-XY and committing a runway incursion.There were several contributing factors to both of these new runway incursions/violations.1) My student's confusion about ATC clearances. We had previously been issued 'stop-and-go' and 'cleared to land' clearances earlier that morning; but I did not confirm that my student understood the difference.2) Poor Aeronautical Decision-Making: My student informed me after the flight that he had only slept four hours the night before. I believe this contributed to both errors he made during his solo.3) Unfamiliarity/Lack of Training on Towered Airport Operations: We had one previous flight at ZZZ; but it did not involve extensive taxi instructions or various ATC clearances. Even that morning my student had the same repetitive taxi clearance after each of our landings completed together.Corrective Actions (To be completed with this student and future students).1) My student and I are going to have an extensive ground covering various ATC clearances; communication procedures; and possible taxi instructions at unfamiliar airports. I will require my student to complete a FAASafety.gov course on runway incursions.2) While I have my students use an ADM (Aeronautical Decision Making) checklist before each flight; I will audibly confirm the 'IMSAFE' checklist is complete before each flight.3) We will conduct another dual flight or two and ask for various different taxi instructions to diversify my student's experience.

At this point the Ground Controller told us we were supposed to stop 50 ft. further back. I looked behind us and noticed the left wing tip was over the east edge of Taxiway Mike. I could not see a hold line below the wing. We were switched to Tower. The Tower Controller gave us a number to call for a possible pilot deviation. Shortly after writing down the number we were cleared for takeoff. As we rolled down the runway I realized we failed to complete the final items.I spoke to the Tower supervisor later that day and explained the events as they occurred. He admitted that this hot spot is an ongoing issue; the hold area is not well marked and the Controller's intent was to have us pointed east to help move aircraft through the Runway 17R approach path faster. Unfortunately the Tower had to send around the landing traffic I was distracted with during the turn because they were not sure if we would stop. column121: First Officer and I flew our first leg of the day from ZZZ to Ashville Regional Airport. Most of the flight was normal and uneventful. About 15 minutes into the flight; we were cruising at FL190 and decided to prepare for the approach. We got the ATIS; landing performance information; set up the approach and First Officer briefed the approach. We noticed and briefed that AVL was on the FOQA list of top 10 airports for unstable approaches and briefed that they were for high speeds and descent rates. ATC then cleared us to descend with multiple step down altitude assignments (11;000; 7000; 6000; 5500; and 4700). We completed the descent and approach checklists when they were needed. Upon descending through 10;000 feet; ATC started vectoring us for the visual approach for runway 35. We continued the set up and called the runway in sight. We were vectored a bit high because of the surrounding terrain. While we were descending on our turn from base to final into Ashville Regional Airport; we got a GPWS warning (terrain; terrain; whoop; whoop; pull up). I decided to react first; since this was unexpected and immediate action may have been necessary with a GPWS warning. I started the recovery by leveling the wings; adding full power and starting a climb (simultaneously pulling back on the yoke and adding power). Then I called for a go-around. We notified ATC of the go-around and they asked for the reason. We told them it was due to the GPWS warning and they said okay and gave us an initial altitude and heading to rejoin the approach. After reconfiguring; calling for the autopilot; and After-Takeoff checklist; I transferred controls back to First Officer and we discussed what had happened and briefed how we would execute the next approach to avoid another GPWS warning. I made a P/A explaining the go-around to the passengers so that they would feel comfortable and safe. We then requested an ILS 35 approach and flew into to AVL without further incident.My First Officer and I concluded that the GPWS warning was likely due to the high closure rate in which we were descending to join final. We were joining final and descending right at the final approach fix (UMUXE); and the charts show multiple obstacles and rising terrain in the immediate area. Also; the FOQA alert page mentioned the obstacles/terrain in the report sent to us via ACARS.As a crew; it would help to always request an ILS approach when it is available. As the pilot flying; I would have slowed down earlier and planned a descent to be level while crossing the FAF. This would reduce the chance the that the aircraft EGPWS will calculate a high rate of closure between the aircraft and terrain that results in a GPWS warning.

column121: The flight crew received our flight release indicating the MEL for the RH EEC. When the crew arrived on the aircraft maintenance was already on and working numerous issues on the aircraft. The flight crew was informed that a bite test showed no errors with the EEC and and at the time it was operating normally. It was believed a ground air start error was what caused the EEC to trip off. The MEL was signed off and the release amended to show its removal. A ground air start was conducted at the gate with no issues; and the aircraft was pushed back. After a cross bleed start and concurrent with the tug disconnecting the RH EEC tripped offline. The crew ran the appropriate EEC QRH checklist directing both EECs to be selected off. Since we had previously reviewed the MEL we elected to continue. During the takeoff it was noted that the auto throttles were not responding and takeoff thrust was set manually. During climb and initial cruise it was noted by both crew members that the left engine EGT was fluctuating 30-50 degrees but stabilized with cruise power set. After approximately an hour of cruise at FL390 and 0.78 Mach the aircraft passed a front causing the airspeed to increase above the assigned speed. Power was gradually reduced to allow the speed to decrease to the assigned value. As the power was increased back to maintain Mach speed it was noted that the left engine was stuck at flight idle and was not responding to thrust lever movements. The thrust lever was positioned to the firewall with no response. As the airspeed was deteriorating rapidly the aircraft offset from the airway and began a descent while a revised clearance was received from New York via HF to return to JFK. ATC issued a revised clearance to JFK and approved the initial descent to FL360. At approximately FL370 the engine again began responding to thrust lever movement. Further descent was not considered necessary at this point and we continued to JFK since we couldn't guarantee that the engine would not stop responding again. After getting the aircraft stabilized; [we] notified via phone patch and the flight attendants and passengers were briefed on the situation and decision to return to JFK. No emergency was declared nor any emergency services requested. The flight continued normally to JFK and accomplished a normal approach and landing to runway 31R with no further incidents. Upon shutdown the crew briefed on site maintenance along with [Operations and Maintenance Control]. The issues were also written up in the log book.

My initial thought was that Aircraft X had misunderstood my assigned heading and had not switched to Departure Control and was still on my frequency. While the controller was speaking to me other aircraft were talking on the frequency. The cross-talk prevented me from clearly understanding the information that was being relayed in the coordination. In that instance I recognized what Departure Control was trying to coordinate and I sent Flight Number X around and vectored him away from Aircraft X and issued a traffic alert.Aircraft X checked onto my frequency on a mile final. I cleared him to land. Immediately after clearing him to land; the ASDE-X alerted with a taxiway proximity alert. It appeared to me that Aircraft X was correcting back toward Runway 1L. I asked the pilot if they requested priority handling. The pilot said no. The aircraft appeared aligned with the runway and the pilot confirmed they were; but because he was not a priority. I sent the plane around as required by the 7110.65. Coordination would have been easier and clearer had the radar data tag scratchpad entry for Aircraft X been changed to '01L' which would have indicated that he was inbound to land. The scratchpad showed the SID he filed; which contributed to my initial thinking that he was off course and not a priority. Additionally; had Departure Control requested priority handling in the coordination; I believe I would have immediately keyed onto the fact that Aircraft X was returning.The Airport Surface Detection Equipment (ASDE-X) ASDE Taxiway Arrival Prediction Software (ATAP) has had five alerts since its implementation on Date. In every case; the aircraft have been properly aligned with the runway and the alerts have been the result of poorly designed taxiway capture zones. The ATAP enhancement should be temporarily disabled and a full review of the ATAP system should occur.

column121: SNA Tower cleared us for takeoff on 20R but changed our clearance altitude from 5;000 feet to 3;000 feet for crossing traffic. We were very light and the max power setting gave us a very very high climb rate. We had a LEVEL OFF RA at 2;800 feet MSL which was the easy part. We complied and did not go above 3;000 feet as a light aircraft passed directly overhead. I believe the separation was 400 feet. Complicating this situation; and the real reason for this report; was the fact that we were given a 3;000 feet clearance and our performance was so high; we got ALT ACQ around 1;000 feet. Our automation did not provide proper guidance as the speed reverted to flaps up speed (15) and the autothrottles wanted to go to max power (takeoff power 100.6%). Also; the cutback N1 was 26% less than takeoff power! My FO had to disconnect the Autothrottles to prevent them from surging back to max power after he set them to cutback and flight directors were commanding a climb well above 10-15 degrees even though my speed was below the shark tooth. I had to fly out of the situation and my FO gave great communication as he kept our SA in focus. I am not 100% sure what happened with the automation but I believe the ALT ACQ at such a low altitude caused some serious issues. This would not have happened with a normal 5;000 feet clearance; or if we were heavy with less performance or we were doing a normal takeoff profile.However; I am concerned that with a few more variables or a crew that did not work as effectively as we did today this could have been a much worse outcome. I am wondering if we should be given 3;000 feet clearances with crossing traffic. With a normal takeoff profile it would have been fine but the max power setting and with the large power cutback for noise abatement this was a tricky situation. Compliments to my FO who took action on the autothrottles to prevent an automated max thrust climb after he pulled for cutback by disengaging them and clearly communicating that part of the problem.

column121: We arrived in ZZZ at XA:00 local time. The aircraft was to remain overnight and we were asked to leave the APU up and packs on due to cold overnight temperatures. This method was used by the ground personnel in lieu of a ground heat cart since one was not available. We left the APU running as requested and left the airport. Upon returning to the airplane the next day we found the left wing tank which the APU was being feed from only containing 200 pounds of fuel. This is a concern as there is no one on the aircraft overnight to monitor the fuel low pressure lights. If there was a delay or other situation this aircraft would have run the left tank dry causing the APU to shut down. Most importantly there would be an unmonitored low pressure fuel low pressure light. The other concern for this configuration was the outflow valve was closed manually with the APU and packs on. I understand this configuration with an external air cart on the aircraft; but not certain it is appropriate for the APU configuration. If the main cabin door were to be closed this would pressurize the aircraft completely making it impossible to access unless the fire handle is pulled in the wheel well to shut down the APU.

column121: On pushback the towbar broke. When I heard the noise I looked down and saw that the brakes were still set. I had failed to verify that they were released. Fortunately; maintenance found no damage on the inspection. The flight continued normally after we received a new release.There were numerous contributing factors that led to this place. This was my first international trip in quite some time. There were many issues related to COVID-19 and catering. Chief of which was no ice being available. I tried to coordinate with the station to get some even asking if the terminal restaurants had some they would spare. No luck. There was also a discussion between myself and the First Officer regarding the rarely used method to obtain the ATC clearance in ZZZZ.The First Officer said he wanted to get home early and I believe he initiated the call to ground for the push before I was ready. I hadn't yet removed my mask. I did not have my audio panel properly configured and my mask was blocking my view of those switches. Ground Control gave us a push clearance then added a last minute query as to which runway we wanted which the First Officer and I discussed and verified.I either missed the pushback crew saying they were ready or they did not initiate the standard sequence so I had to verify that they were ready. Ground then told us to hold our push and that stopped me from releasing the brakes at that point when I normally might have done so. There was also confusion with the pushback location. I could not locate it on the charts. We were also using a gate in a part of the terminal neither myself or the First Officer had been at before.As I was re-configuring my audio panel my watch flashed a [personal message.] Although I did not read it; I noticed it. That took my out of my routine and although I felt my legs relax after I thought I hit the pedals to release the brakes; they were still set.Although I have been with the company many years; I have also not been flying much lately; 4 legs in the last 90 days or so. I also don't know why my watch flashed a message when my phone was off.In the end it was a failure to verify the status of the parking brakes. I will redouble my efforts to ensure a verification that the brakes indicate they are released in the appropriate sequence going forward.

column121: The Captain briefed that he would fly the ZZZ ILS 27R. On the arrival abeam the FAF we called the airport in sight and were subsequently cleared #1 for the visual approach. In the turn towards the final approach I lost sight of the runway. I was expecting the Captain to maneuver the aircraft to align the airplane with the approach course prior to; or at; the FAF. He turned well inside the FAF to intercept a 3 mile final. I was not expecting this and felt behind the aircraft. While on the base leg we received a radio call from Tower 'low altitude alert; below minimum vectoring altitude.' This left me even more uneasy during the approach. I expressed my concern to the Captain. The Captain was able to re-cage my situational awareness and continued the visual approach. We rolled out on final; stabilized on glide path and made an uneventful landing. We thoroughly debriefed the flight; with much attention on the approach.
column123: The FO (First Officer) had never been into ZZZ; and I hadn't been there for years. Briefing the approach; I handled the terrain" item by saying something silly like "I don't know of any." In fact there was no high terrain; but there were close-in obstacles. I mentioned that we might well get a slam dunk visual but I did not communicate to the FO my idea of normally being comfortable joining the final on visual approaches inside the FAF; about 3 miles out at 1;000 feet AGL. If I had done that fuller briefing; he would not have been surprised when I later pointed the aircraft inside the FAF. Descending on the arrival; we noted that the procedure put us on a long final for the ILS to 27R; but we both got the impression that we would be #1 to the airport and slam dunked. On downwind abeam the airport we were descended to 3;000 feet and then cleared for the visual approach. I headed over toward the ILS FAF and descended toward its crossing altitude; 2;100 feet; while I evaluated the position and energy. I saw that we were in a position to join a 3-mile final in a stabilized condition. Focusing visually on the right base leg and the airport; we were at about 1;700 feet on about a three mile base. At this time ATC transmitted; "Low altitude alert; minimum vectoring altitude is 2;100 feet." Our path looked clear ahead and on final to the right; and I did not consider ATC's radar vectoring altitude to exactly apply to our operation. Still; they were trying to tell us something! I looked to the left and saw downtown; laterally closer than desired but certainly more than 2;000 feet horizontally. I shallowed the descent as much as I could without going too high to be stabilized on final. We joined the final and landed normally.By inadequately studying and briefing the airport's visual flying environment; I did a night visual approach that was safe but that (1) concerned ATC; (2) concerned my flying partner; and (3) worst of all; surprised me about our proximity to downtown because I had not identified the high buildings as a threat."

column121: The event occurred because ZZZ is working a busy airport with one Controller utilizing all three frequencies. This is a major safety of flight issue as multiple links in the safety chain were broken that day. If the sharpness of the crews from Aircraft Y and Aircraft Z had not utilized full four ear policy and patience it could have been an issue. The actions taken by the ATC operation in ZZZ are uncalled for and unsafe. If this is overlooked there could be fatal consequences in the future. There are a few local airports in the area of ZZZ that are non-towered. If the Tower Controller delayed any further for us to be handed over to Departure; we could have had a collision or RA with an unknown aircraft all due to the unsafe actions of one Controller handling a workload bound for a minimum of two personal.On the morning of date; I was in command of flight Aircraft X; ZZZ to ZZZ1. The ZZZ Tower had one Controller working all three frequencies: clearance; ground; and Tower. This day was a busy morning with Aircraft A bound for ZZZ1; Aircraft Y to ZZZ3; Aircraft Z to ZZZ4; and us to ZZZ1 all departing at roughly the same time.When we called for our clearance on the delivery frequency; we noticed there was some bleed over as the Controller was issuing takeoff clearances. We had to repeat our request for a clearance but were given it with no issues.I released the brakes and we called for push shortly after. Aircraft Y also called for push after us. In the middle of our push back the Controller called on the ground frequency to inform Aircraft A of a delay to ZZZ2 for them.  The two began to have a conversation on ground of a game plan to be made. As their conversation occurred our Ramp crew disconnected the tow bar and gave the wave off for an all clear to a taxi.I noticed Aircraft Y had pushed off gate X and we were pushed off of X+1 with our nose in the direction of travel to only exit at [intersection] with a head on collision. First Officer and I finished our 'After Start Checklist' and cleared the area to begin our taxi. I switched on our taxi and nose lights to noticed Aircraft Y did the same. With the Controller and Aircraft A conversation occurring to what was now a clearance being given with a read back to follow there was no way for me or Aircraft Y to have confirmation one was waiting for the other.There was dense fog and low visibility on the ramp that morning. Tower does not control the ramp and a courtesy call is requested. The weather was so bad we had a takeoff alternate of ZZZ5 that morning.It was a frustrating situation as Aircraft Y and I could barely make out the 2nd half of each other's aircraft; so it was a game of chicken. I tried to call over the radio and speak over the clearance being given but it did not work.Ultimately; I turned off my lights to give Aircraft Y the right of way. As we began our taxi to Runway X Aircraft Z called clearance to get their clearance to ZZZ4 and that now was being broadcast over the ground frequency adding to the safety issue that no one moving on the aircraft surface could talk to each other.The Tower issued Aircraft Y their takeoff clearance and told us we were next. After we got our takeoff clearance; we began the takeoff roll with no issues. As we continued our takeoff climb Aircraft Z called the Controller over the ground frequency. All we heard was the Controller responding over the Tower frequency meaning he was working all three frequencies still. This delayed our hand-off to departure and made us uneasy as the Tower radar could not see our path beyond a certain mileage. As we checked in with ZZZ Departure we were given an instruction to contact ZZZ3 Center as our time had been too long and radar services with ZZZ could not be utilized further.This told me the ZZZ airport Controller took too long to hand us off and impeded the Departure Controller from doing their job properly. We did not have sufficient air traffic control separation all due to the unsafe practices of the ZZZ airport and Air Traffic Control operation at the airport of ZZZ.ZZZ needs to hire another Controller! There must be at least one person working Ground and Delivery while another separate Controller works Tower. The operation in ZZZ has been compromised and it is scary to think that the unsafe actions are acceptable to those working in the ATC system.

column121: While in cruise flight (FL370) we were cleared to cross the ZZZZZ intersection at FL330.  The FO entered the new altitude and I confirmed it.  We agreed to start down at the TOD.  ATIS indicated that we could be landing either [Runway] XXC or XXR.  I noticed the runway condition was 555 and total runway distance for Runway XXR was 7500 feet; which required a non-standard landing assessment.  I started entering the numbers in the landing app; when I decided to look back at our progress.  I immediately noticed that we had overflown the TOD.  I alerted the FO and he selected 'OPEN DESCENT!  I knew this would be insufficient and called out 'My aircraft;' he acknowledged and I attempted to make the restriction.  I quickly realized there was no chance of making the restriction; so as I stabilized the descent; I instructed the FO to inform ATC would be unable to make the restriction (we would be high).  After that I called for 'autopilot 2 and we transferred control of the aircraft back to the FO.  ATC acknowledged the transmission and we proceeded to the destination airport without further incident.  I decided not to debrief until we were at the gate; so to avoid any further incidents.In an effort to stay ahead of the; all too often; last minute approach changes and subsequent rushed approach briefings at low altitude; I as the non-flying pilot; elected to proactively run the landing numbers and review the XXR approach plate.  The obvious problem with that is; that the check and balance system for aircraft control is compromised when both pilots are not concentrating on the more immediate task at hand. It should be noted that the FO had just come from a training event to restore currency after almost 3 months off.  My FO did list that as a threat on our very first flight of the day. As such; I had been trying to complete tasks earlier than usual; not only to avoid the problems associated with operations at ZZZ1 but also so I could more closely monitor him; but in this case it backfired.According to the report home page altitude deviations are the number one reported event; so I don't really know what could effectively prevent this type of event. Possibly; the best we could hope for is to reduce the frequency.  For my part in reducing the frequency of which this event occurs; I will not address any other actions until the descent is begun and the altitude clearance is assured.

column121: Inbound to ZZZZ on ZZZZZ Star.  Taken off STAR early and cleared direct to ZZZZ1 VOR.  We were instantly 1;800 feet above the path.  Proactively used speed brakes and planned to slow and extend flaps when below 20;000 feet; but were then told to keep speed at 250 KTS.  Lowered landing gear shortly after passing ZZZZ1 to get back on profile.  Was able to regain the VNAV path just prior to ZZZZZ1 and at Vref +10 per procedure.  Flaps were at 25. Frequency was very busy and sky hazy. Very late hand off to Tower.  Localizer did not correctly ID until just prior to FAF.  FO was very busy with frequency changes; configuration changes and checklist.  Tower did not clear us to land; but instructed us to continue as an aircraft was in position on our Runway; XXR. Another aircraft was holding short of XXR waiting to cross.  At 1;000 feet I was at approach speed and called 'stable;' but was distracted by no landing clearance and aircraft on runway.  Aircraft in position was cleared for immediate takeoff; we were cleared to land; and other aircraft was given clearance to cross XXR.  Departing aircraft was slow to accelerate.  Passing 500 feet FO made 'stable' call.  Shortly after we received an aural alert indicating we did not have landing flaps selected.  Flaps indicator showed flaps at 25 degrees verses the planned and briefed of 30 degrees.  I realized I had not asked for flaps 30 and was now below 400 feet. Elected not to make a configuration change to 30 degrees below 1;000 feet per procedure.  Hesitant to go-around per procedure because I wasn't sure if the crossing aircraft had not just departed the inboard parallel Runway XXL; and the late departing XXR aircraft had just rotated.  With the very hazy sky I was concerned about a conflict and /or overtaking the other aircraft during the go-around to increase speed to Vref+10 and land with flaps 25. Landing and rollout were normal.Despite adequate and recent experience into ZZZZ; these particular controllers were hard to understand.  FO had to ask for clarification a few times in the last 1;500 feet FAF. FO had just returned from 7 months of leave; was called out on reserve; and had only flown once earlier; and 4 times in the last 7 months.  I briefed the arrival and approach thoroughly and early; but it was a Max effort with the direct clearance.  I believe he got distracted from completing the checklist when the localizer did not ID until just before the FAF.  I was distracted from not calling for final flaps with the aircraft on the runway and the hazy conditions; and the late localizer ID.Add to the note of being at Vref +10 by the ZZZZZ1 fix; to be at final landing flaps. This may have helped me if I had a goal to complete that by the fix.

column121: Prior to Final approach in ZZZ; approach vectored us very close to the final approach course with a 30 kt tailwind on base and at 4;000 ft just outside ZZZZZ for the ILS XXR; assigned 190 kts. As we intercepted the course the autopilot flew past the localizer at close to half scale deflection; as it would not correct course timely. We also had to descend and slow down to configure for final approach within 3 miles of final approach fix. As the autopilot was correcting for that we set 3;000 ft for the missed approach altitude. A CAS MISCOMP status message appeared and the altitude alerter came on would not stop ringing. When we changed navigation source to green needles; the localizer would not capture with the autopilot; therefore the glide slope would also not capture. During the navigation source change; my flight director on the first officer's side became erratic and I lost the localizer transmission. We decided to execute a missed approach due to being unstable along with the flight instrument errors. Tower assigned us a heading and altitude and we reconfigured the aircraft for the go around all while the altitude alerter was blaring. During straight and level flight; we decided to reassign the FCP to heading and altitude. Once established; we turned the autopilot on and all instruments worked correctly. The altitude alert ringer was still buzzing so we decided to silence using Data Control Unit (DCU) audio buttons to declutter the situation. After completing proper checklists; we decided to continue on with another ILS XXR and executed approach and landing normally. After shutdown the altitude alerter still continued to ring until AC power was switched from the APU GEN to EXT AC. We wrote up the problem and notified maintenance.ATC giving us tight vectors with a tailwind on base along with our equipment malfunctions. The altitude alerter sounding loudly along our flight directors being erratic caused task saturation to the captain who was PF. As PM I helped the captain de clutter the situation and to reminded him to just fly the airplane which he did well as we tracked the localizer and conducted the go around. Once we silenced the altitude alerter it became much easier to fly the aircraft and we were able to conduct the next approach successfully.Possibly asking for a slower intercept speed or lower from ATC. The equipment malfunctions lead to the approach to become unstable and that's why we conducted a go around. I could have possibly contacted tower a few seconds earlier to ask for a vector and altitude but it was quite difficult with the task saturation being as high as it was; especially with the altitude alerter loudly sounding. Overall it was a great lesson in always being able to maintain control and fly the aircraft regardless of the state of automation it is in which I thought we did a great job of despite the system malfunctions during a high work load environment.

column121: In preparation for our arrival into DEN we briefed for the CLASH 3 RNAV arrival and the ILS to 35R as this was the expected runway from our direction of arrival. We also included in our brief the threat in DEN of runway changes and how we'd handle that especially during the descent phase on the arrival. About 20 NM from the waypoint CLASH on the arrival ATC informed us to expect runway 35L. We then re-set up for that runway and re-briefed. There was still plenty of time for this and there was little time compression. One point of confusion; however; was that the CLASH 3 has a transition for RWY 35R; but doesn't for 35L; which only has a point at which to expect vectors. We spent some time studying the arrival and approach plates to ensure that was the case to make sure we weren't missing something. I asked my F/O to double check as he was the PM and I wanted to concentrate on the descent as the PF. This has always been confusing as some arrivals and approaches have transition points and some don't. There should be some consistency. This was the beginning of some of the time compression which would later result in some workload management issues.Some point after this ATC broke us off of the arrival and instructed us to descend to 9000 feet and gave us a heading. They then assigned us to RWY 35R. We related that we'd just been assigned 35L and they reiterated we were now reassigned to 35R. This resulted in a very rushed set up for 35R as we were now pretty close in to the approach environment. I asked the F/O to set it all up so that I could continue to fly. I quickly dialed in what I thought was the 35R LOC; but it turned out not to be. I could see that he was struggling and tried to help him out. In hindsight; this was a mistake in workload management because I should have let the F/O do all of the set up. I verbalized that we didn't need to re-brief for 35R as we'd already briefed it and so had a plan. Again; in hindsight; I'm not sure this was a correct call; but we literally did not have time to brief at that point.Shortly after this we were cleared the visual approach to 35R.  We were roughly 7 miles from FRONZ and discussed not descending too quickly so as not to bust the floor of the Class B airspace. At about the same time ATC asked us to slow to approach speed for traffic ahead of us for 35R. After slowing we ended up just about 2.5 miles in trail.  At this point we were apprised of traffic for 35L and received a TCAS TA because of the assigned heading we were given to intercept the LOC for 35R. We both saw the traffic and I decided to hand fly from this point on as we had an overshooting crosswind and given our heading there would have been a good chance of an overshoot of the LOC.At FRONZ I asked for gear down and flaps 15. At about this point I noticed that neither the LOC or GS were engaging but I had the runway and the PAPI and decided to continue as we had been cleared for the visual. The FO asked if I'd like him to try and dial in the correct LOC and I said yes if he had the bandwidth to do so. Soon after we passed through 1;000 feet and we both missed the call out as I think he was still trying to dial in the LOC frequency. Also we never accomplished the Landing Checklist as we never got to final flaps. We got to 500 feet and we made those call outs. At around 400 feet AFL we received a Too Low Flaps GPWS warning and my knee jerk reaction was to call for FLAP 30 once I realized we were still at FLAPS 15. I don't know if the FO ever selected them; however. I quickly realize this was the wrong call and called for us to go around and the FO called for it at about the same time. We executed the missed approach with no issues and were vectored expeditiously for a second approach and landing without further incident.The FO is not submitting a report as far as I'm aware as we had no ATC deviations or non-compliance with FARS.
column123: This is a report regarding Flight X ZZZ-DEN regarding the changes and ATC clearances we received during our descent and approach to land in DEN.When we reviewed the flight plan in ZZZ we loaded the CLASH3 STAR with runway 35R being our selected landing runway. The flight plan had 17R; but DEN was landing North so that was the only change made to the plan on our part versus what dispatch had planned.Prior to TOD the CA fully reviewed and briefed the STAR and approach that we were expecting. We were fully prepared to execute this plan. Upon checking in with a close in DEN center controller we were advised to expect runway 35L with the EBBLR transition. There was some discussion regarding the EBBLR transition by myself and the CA as we were attempting to figure out if the transition and how the transition linked up with the approach. However; we did this again prior to TOD and were able to be prepared for the new arrival transition and approach. As we descended into Denver; we were handed off to DEN APP. This controller changed our runway back to 35R. We were well into the descent at this point and fairly close to the airport. The CA instructed me to load up the new approach and as I was attempting to do so ATC took us off the arrival for vectors and speed changes. At this point we were South of DEN but still fairly close in. I was still working on getting the FMC setup when ATC vectored us due West and then turned us on to final for 35R. The vector was vey poorly planned by the controller and both the CA and I could see that we were going to blow through the localizer if we allowed the A/P to handle the intercept. The CA disengaged the A/P and made a manual turn to join the localizer. At this point we could both see that the vector had us close in behind another airplane in final. ATC requested that we slow to 160 knots. The CA asked for me to deploy the gear and the flaps to down and 15. Shortly after ATC then requested us to slow to the slowest possible speed. Both the CA and I were closely monitoring the separation between us and the preceding aircraft. At this point I noticed there was a message on the FMC scratchpad that I had not seen before and did not recognize. I don't remember exactly what the message was but it did indicate that there was a conflict between the FMC selected approach and what the VHF radios were tuned to. I was rapidly trying to get the correct frequency on the NAV radios but my JEPP app on the iPad was not responding quickly as I was attempting to zoom in to view the frequency box. At this point we were somewhere around 1;000 feet AGL. The CA announced that he had the runway and the PAPIs in sight and was going to land and just disregard the FMC He was busy attempting to slow and again we were both concerned about the separation between us the preceding aircraft. That was what are focus was on at this point. I cannot recall if either the 1;000 ft or the 500 ft call outs were made. We were both totally task saturated at this time. At some altitude below 500 ft we received a warning message 'too low-flaps'. We both looked at the flap position and realized we were still at flaps 15. The CA called for flaps 30 and I monetarily selected flaps 30 before advocating that we needed to go around. The CA also realized we had to go around at almost the same instant I was stating that we needed to go around. So we executed the go around. We did have the 10;000 ft foot missed approach altitude selected in the MCP so we were climbing to that altitude. However; while just climbing through 7;000 the tower told us to maintain 7;000. I advised tower that we were at 7;200. Tower instructed us to maintain 7;100. We descended back to 7;100 feet and flew runway heading and completed the rest of the go around profile. Tower asked us for the reason for the GA and I replied 'configuration'. They handed us off to approach and we were vectored back around for another ILS to runway 35R. We ensured everything was properly setup and landed without further incident.Some comments about this incident. Both the CA and I had discussed the threat of Denver and how they often make changes to arrivals and approaches during cruise. In fact the CA had been reading in the flight ops newsletter on his iPad about the problems we have been having with arrivals into Denver. We were both fully aware that Denver presented a threat and thought that we had planned and were prepared for our arrival. Had we been cleared as planned per our original plan we would have been fine. Even after the first change to runway 35L we had time to plan and brief. It was only after the final switch back to 35R that we both began to become task saturated with the speed changes; the off route vectors; the FMC programming; the NAV radios; the poor vector to join final; and finally the separation between us and the preceding aircraft and the speed changes made while on final in regards to that aircraft. The amount of items needed to be accomplished while this was occurring in the terminal area was long and complex. We both became so overcome that we must have failed to accomplish the landing checklist; which would have had both of us realizing that we were not in the landing configuration.We made errors along the way; failing to get some of the call outs accomplished; FMC programming; and NAV radio frequency selection among some of the errors. However; many of these errors were driven by the nature of the changes being made by ATC in regards to arrival vectors; speed changes; runway and approach changes among other demands being made by ATC in a very time compressed period while flying within (or near) the terminal area.One more note about the runway changes in Denver. I know Denver and am aware of its threat even on departure. So while we were getting ready to depart and head to ZZZ2 I asked the ramp controller which runway was in use for the ZZZZZ SID. He stated XXR. Yet; when we received our push clearance 15-20 minutes later he told us to expect runway XY. I don't know if he was given bad information by the ATC tower or what happened; but yet again here we are in a high workload situation having to make changes to the FMC and request new TO data.Because of our short turn time in Denver the CA decided to debrief the entire arrival event into Denver while in cruise flying back to ZZZ2. We spent a good 30-40 minutes discussing the flight. Threat and errors were discussed; we used the briefing cards and identified what had occurred on the flight. I am not going to make excuses for the errors that we made; even if they occurred during a task saturated situation. However; a couple of my observations from this event were that we had talked about Denver ATC being a threat. We thought that we had addressed this threat by a good solid brief for the originally planned arrival; even after the change to the 35L arrival; we had time to plan and brief. We were ready; but ATC in Denver threw us some many changes and curve balls that we both were task saturated to the point leading to an undesired aircraft state. Fortunately; both the CA and I followed our training and SOP. safely executed a missed approach; and subsequently landed safely and uneventfully on the next approach.

column121: Flight crew noted a slight rumbling vibration on climb out.  The vibration increased with airspeed and as we reach cruise at FL300 and increased speed we noted the increased vibration and that there was a control yoke displacement of approximately 2 units right in straight and level flight with all other trim neutral.  After discussing the situation as a crew; we decided to contact [Operations and Maintenance] for further discussion and possible solutions.  Due to a known history and MEL addition affecting spoilers; we selected the flight control schematic page and noted that the right flaperon indicated a near full upward deflection in level flight. Through our discussion with [a] tech pilot; it was suggested that we try utilizing rudder trim to determine how much was needed to neutralize the control yoke; and we determined that 4 units of rudder trim was required.  Without being able to fully determine what was causing the vibration we decided that a 13 1/2 hour flight and oceanic crossing would not be prudent; and most likely would not be possible due to fuel over burn.  We discussed possible alternate airports and [Operations] ultimately requested that we return to ZZZ.  We were North West of ZZZ1 when we coordinated with ZZZ2 Center for our return to ZZZ.  We coordinated with ZZZ1 Center to jettison fuel in order to be below max landing weight.  The fuel jettison of 78;400 lbs. was accomplished just south east of ZZZ3 VOR at FL200.  Arriving back into the ZZZ area; we coordinated for runway 36C.  As we configured the aircraft for landing; we noted a drastic increase in vibration as the flaps were extended from 20 to the planned setting of 30.  We adjusted to flap 25 for landing and flap 25 speed.  Although the vibrations and roll control were abnormal on final; the landing was uneventful.  After landing we elected to leave the flaps at 25 until mechanics at the gate could verify that retraction would not cause further damage.  After block in it was discovered that the number 6 spoiler was up.  We could not see indications for the number 6 spoiler on the flight control page due to the MEL deactivation.  Initial indications are that the number 6 spoiler which was deactivated under MEL was 'floating' or extended when it should have been down.

column121: While waiting for the airplane to be towed to the departure gate; I ate a heavy breakfast and did not consume any coffee as this was an Air Carrier X operation and I anticipated coffee being readily available on the plane. column121: While conducting an aerial survey; operating a Cessna 206; I noticed that the camera crew person; did not respond appropriately to my questioning and had what appeared to be a sense of confusion during the flight. After speaking with camera person; I performed my own self-assessment and decided to descend and land at ZZZ airport.  Below is my summation of the flight. After takeoff; I leveled the airplane at 16;100 feet to start the aerial survey. I checked to see how much oxygen was flowing through my supplemental oxygen cannula and confirmed it to be set at 17;000 feet. I noticed my camera crew person who was sitting in the right seat next to me increasing his oxygen level intake. I asked him if he was OK and he responded; 'I don't know.' I then asked him if we are doing Lidar work. He replied no; why would you ask me that. Shortly thereafter I started to feel uneasy; woozy; felt my heart rate increase; slow to talk and making decisions was a bit more difficult. I decided to increase my supplemental oxygen cannula to 22;500 feet (to increase the oxygen intake). I looked over at the camera person to see how he was doing and noticed what appeared to me a discoloration of his face. At this point I took the following actions; started a descent; turned off the cabin heat; opened the air vents; notified ATC and activated the autopilot for the descent (in the event I passed out). Upon reaching a lower altitude and knowing that I was not going to pass out; I disengaged the autopilot and accelerated the descent to 3;500 feet and continued directly to ZZZ and landed. After speaking with the mechanics; it was learned that the flange was bent causing the number 2-cylinder leaking exhaust gases into the cabin.

I looked on final and down the runway and determined that it was clear. Runway 36 has an up slope and was not able to see the end. As I approached my rotation speed I could see that it was a vehicle (truck) on the runway moving in the same direction as me. column121: Finishing up a training flight with a student in Class G Airspace my student advised he was starting to feel nauseous. I took control of the aircraft from my student using the 3 part positive exchange of flight controls. As I took control of the aircraft I noticed the flight controls were extremely stiff on the longitudinal axis (ailerons). When asking the student if he was blocking the yoke from moving he responded with no and I visually confirmed he was nowhere near any of the controls. After maintaining positive control of the aircraft I started looking around both yokes for a reason why there was such an issue with the roll function as well as looking out at both ailerons. I could not find any reason why I was having such an issue maintaining level flight. We had just completed turns around a point and I wondered if a bird or something collided with the underside of the right aileron at just the correct time that prevented me from turning the yoke right or if there was something that caught up the control cables inside the wing that was preventing this. I was about 15 miles and a 180 degree turn from ZZZ1 and about 20 miles straight to ZZZ. I decided that ZZZ was not only straight ahead but 95% could be over water and wetlands versus ZZZ1 which would put me over populations and wooded areas for a majority of the flight as well as the services available at ZZZ (ATC; ARFF; Line services; Maintenance and the aircraft's Home base). The decision was made and I continued straight towards ZZZ and listened to the ATIS while having the student look through the Emergency Checklist for anything that listed flight control issues. I also verified that the elevators and rudder were not experiencing any issues. I attempted to go further to the right but was met with more and more resistance and did not want to risk snapping anything or causing any further issues/damage. I contacted the tower and advised I was approximately 20 miles south of the airport with some sort of flight control issue and requested a straight in priority landing on Runway 1. Flying straight I would have intercepted the extended centerline on a very shallow 10-15 degrees. Tower advised me to continue and expect the request as well as asked if I needed anything. I advised I did not and was trying to work the issue while maintaining in control. About 10 miles out I realized that while I was maintaining control at 107 KIAS I had no idea what the aircraft would do as I slowed to approach speed of 66 KIAS. I also noticed that I was applying a considerable amount of right rudder to maintain straight flight. At point I made the decision with the unknowns there and having to be uncoordinated as I would be approaching the ground I would prefer Fire Services standing by as well as identify as an emergency to open up any further options that could be available as I may only have 1 shot at the approach once I get down towards that 66 KIAS. I advised my student to tighten his seat belt and that my arms were starting to get tired holding the airplane level that I would need him to use CRM with me and help with Power settings and flaps. At about 1;000MSL I told my student that at 800AGL I wanted him to release the top latch of my door and by 500AGL I wanted him to release the side latch so the door could be unlocked and we can focus on landing in the last 500ft. As I crossed the threshold at about 80KIAS with 2 notches (25 degree) of flaps and about 5 degrees of intercept of the centerline I had my student reduce the power to idle and maintained control through landing but did end up left of centerline.After the aircraft was fully on the ground rolling out I released the yoke which went full deflection to the left. I taxied the aircraft back to the FBO apron and shut down the aircraft. I had my Senior CFI meet us to have him look for a possible issue. After the aircraft was completely shut down I had him go and try to move the yoke which he did with no issues. Further investigation it was noticed that the autopilot (AP); Single Axis; roll knob was turned to the left. The autopilot was never a thought as upon hiring over a year ago I was advised by the then-Assistant Chief Flight Instructor that the Auto pilot did not work; was disconnected from power but not able to be removed from the bottom of the panel. I never thought anything of it because during night flights the AP never had any backlighting to show it had power.  My senior instructor and I started up the aircraft and initiated the Autopilot which produced the same effect that I experienced in flight. We conducted a full check of all systems and found nothing else that could have caused the issue. We determined that the location of the AP the student could have inadvertently brushed the switch activating it with no knowledge as there are no lights to indicate it is powered or active. We also came to the conclusion that this incident was not a flight control malfunction as much as an unintentional activation of the AP as the AP did what it was told. Speaking with my Senior CFI we decided that I would personally verify any statements of inoperability from another pilot even if they are a superior with Maintenance and make sure the correct items are done for such items. I am also working on a full lesson for all of my students on the AP; how it works; issues experienced and multiple ways on how to shut it off until a decision could be made to keep the AP with it known active or make the AP inoperative and remove it from the aircraft.
