column121: We were on a quick turned from a late inbound flight and it verified in ACARS that we were going to keep the aircraft for the final leg of the day. We had flown 3 legs in and out of ZZZ under winter conditions; active snow and de-icing every leg. My attention had been high on the aircraft MEL items; airport NOTAMs and the changing weather conditions. We pushed back for gate de-ice in ZZZ; we had received a SELCAL/ACARS message (MSG) regarding a change and we were still good to go. However; the ACARS remained on this page and prior to de-ice I noticed there was still a SELCAL message posted. My FO and I checked the MSGs and it came to our knowledge that our Flight Attendant (FA) was being removed from our trip due to COVID Exposure. This ACARS message was received after push-back as we were getting de-iced. We then double checked the release and we realized there were 2 amendments. One was for the TAIL SWAP which we were aware of. However; due to the immediate boarding at our gate and activation of ACARS and upon finding that we were keeping the current airplane we did not see AMD # 2 with the FA change. We completed de-icing and that is when I called my Dispatcher and acknowledged the change. I advised him that we would be returning back to the gate; however due to extenuating circumstances; this should have been a notification that should have been sent earlier in particular VIA phone call to myself; the PIC; regarding this change. Prior to push; I had no knowledge of the situation or the change; the change I knew of was of the plane swap because I noticed the tail number in ACARS. Due to the quick turn; the FA had her phone off as we were boarding and was not aware either of the change and of the COVID exposure. However; since there was no acknowledgement there should have been an attempt to notify the FA through my FO or myself.I believe that the quick turn and the focus on the inclement weather distracted me from the information being received. I also believe there was breakdown in CRM from the PIC/Dispatcher point of view. This was a last minute change to our paperwork; and this change should have required a phone call to me; the PIC or an ACARS MSG PRIOR to push to acknowledge the change. At times there is lack of support from the Flight Ops/ Dispatcher level in being proactive to provide the most up to date information forcing the PIC to take attention away from other tasks; potentially like in this scenario and missing information.There needs to be a way to notify the flight crews of amendments made on the release. There are multiple reasons a release can be amended ranging from; CREW SWAPS; TAIL SWAPS; Weather; Alternate; NOTAMs; MEL; TIMES; etc. These amendments; can be essential to flight and ensuring both PIC and Dispatch is aware of the change is key. On our ACARS we have the ability to respond for numerous items; acknowledge TARMAC delays; acknowledge 'UNSTABLE APP AIRPORTS' via ACARS but we do not have a way to acknowledge flight release amendments. I am suggesting that prior to push should an amendment be made; if not acknowledged; it will NOT ALLOW crews to send for T/O DATA until it is ACKNOWLEDGED via ACARS or via telephone. After push back; you would have T/O data; but an acknowledge would be required VIA ACARS or Telephone. I believe this would also help with our AIRWORTHINESS Management system in ensuring crews have the correct MEL Listed on the release prior to push or especially after pushback. I strongly believe this would add an additional layer of safety that ALL Pilots could benefit from.
column123: We had to return to the gate because we became aware that we had the wrong Fight Attendant (FA) on board after push-back. There was an amendment to the release that we didn't receive notification for the FA change.Quick; late; and focused on the weather. Lack of system to ensure receipt of amendments. Break down in CRM between Company; Dispatch; and Flight Crew.I suggest better CRM systems between Dispatch and Flight Crew by implementing some type of acknowledgement when there are amendments to the RLS. Flight crews should not have to dig for information when Flight Ops and Dispatchers can also have the ability to provide the information to flight crews. Therefore; reducing workload on flight crews and staying focused on the things that require our full attention.

ATC asked if we had the airport in sight; we responded in the affirmative; and ATC turned us to a heading of 325 degrees; and cleared us for the Visual Approach to 35L. That heading essentially aimed us directly at the FAF DYMON on the ILS for Runway 35L.The Pilot Flying (PF) selected 7;000 feet in the altitude window and continued his descent visually. Shortly after arriving at 7;000 feet; ATC advised us Altitude Alert and stated minimum altitude was 7;500 feet in our sector. The PF immediately corrected our altitude to 7;500 feet and we stayed at that altitude until glideslope intercept for the ILS to 35L. We landed uneventfully in DEN.When cleared for the visual; stay at your last safe altitude assigned until intercepting glideslope; or have better awareness of the minimum altitude in the sector you are flying. Another option would be for visual clearance to land including a minimum altitude if required.

column121: When preflight planning; there is no way to accurately know which runway to expect at MHT. There is no digital ATIS. Weather for preflight planning is by a METAR.  This does give us the weather but not a runway.  Sometimes it is easy to know which runway to expect; but when the winds are light or calm there is no way of knowing. This would not be too much of a problem for many airports; but MHT uses complex RNAV arrivals with a branch point. We brief ahead of time. VHF ATIS is not in radio range at the normal time of our briefing. En route when the VHF ATIS is obtained it is sometimes necessary to change the runway which changes the arrival from the branch point. This is usually done while on the arrival in a high workload environment. Without the digital ATIS coupled with complex RNAV arrivals; we have the possibility of errors due to debriefing and reprogramming the FMC.

column121: Enroute from ZZZ to ZZZ1 at approximately ZZZZZ; we encountered chop at FL350 and decided to request FL390; which was granted. During the climb at approximately FL370 we encountered moderate turbulence. The airspeed increased into overspeed and the vertical speed increased significantly due to an updraft. Though I did not note the actual VS; I estimate at least 5;000 FPM based on the rate that the altitude tape was moving; which was where my focus was. I disconnected the autopilot; and as we went through FL380 I knew leveling at FL390 was going to be difficult because I couldn't safely decrease thrust any further; and pitching over would have made the overspeed worse. Using a little of each method; I was able to achieve a normal thrust setting and speed below max at approximately FL395 and returned to FL390; where we reported the event to ATC. We sent an overspeed code to Maintenance via ACARS. The sky conditions at the time were [VFR].
column123: During climbout through FL370 we encountered an increase in both speed and climb while the B autopilot was engaged. After the PF (Pilot Flying) disengaged the autopilot the aircraft continued to increase in speed causing an over speed condition by approximately 10-15 kts. The aircraft continued to climb through our selected altitude; FL390; by approximately 400 ft. while the pilot flying was executing his recovery techniques to return the aircraft by to the correct altitude and speed. Approximately FL350 I had already asked the flight attendants to be seated because we had a small amount of turbulence. During the event; both the passengers and flight attendants were seated. I relayed the turbulence/updraft to air traffic control as severe in nature so that other aircraft wouldn't be routed through the area. After the event both the PF and myself felt that is was probably more of a moderate turbulence and more of a severe updraft. Shortly after; I checked on both the flight attendants and passengers to ensure no one was injured. The event was not jerky or real rough; it was more of a pretty smooth continual pitch up that was very difficult to stop without really over speeding the aircraft more than we did. I felt like the PF did as good of a good as possible in this strange situation.

column121: While operating our flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 I was the Pilot Monitoring. At the time of the event; I was eating my catering and the Pilot Flying and I both found it easier for the PF to respond to ATC and manipulate the FMS. At some point at cruise altitude; ATC cleared us to fly direct from present position to 'ZZZZZ.' The PF responded to ATC and erroneously typed 'ZZZZZ1' into the FMS scratchpad and entered the waypoint as the direct-to navigation fix after both pilots checked the resulting dashed 'proposed course line' on the PF's ND screen. After several minutes; ATC inquired if we were proceeding direct to 'ZZZZZ' as he showed us drifting right of the intended course. This alerted us to double-check our navigation and to discover that we were navigating to the wrong fix; the misspelled 'ZZZZZ1.' The PF corrected the spelling of the assigned waypoint in the FMS; proceeded direct to 'ZZZZZ' and explained our error to ATC.I can identify three things that might have prevented this event: 1) The normal procedure and best course of action would have been for the Pilot Monitoring to stop eating; respond to ATC and manipulate the FMS. I do not; however; think this was much of a contributing factor. The PF is a 'strong' and extremely competent pilot highly experienced on the aircraft. I don't think the PF's assumption of those duties was particularly taxing/burdensome to the PF as we were in cruise at a very quiet and low-threat portion of the flight. It is not unusual for a PF to respond to ATC and manipulate the radios and FMS while a PM is eating. I have always personally tried to not touch anything other than my food while eating in the aircraft and think this is an especially important practice during the current health pandemic. While I could have sanitized my hands once I completed the radio calls and navigation tasks; it was more convenient to allow the PF to perform those duties for me. 2) The best course of action would have been for the PF to scroll the flight plan and chosen the assigned Direct-To waypoint 'ZZZZZ' from the flight plan. However; the aircraft's FMS is slow to respond; making scrolling through a long flight plan somewhat laborious; tempting one to effect the change via the scratch pad method. The PF alternatively could have checked the paper copy of the flight plan for the correct spelling of the waypoint before typing it into the scratch pad. 3) I had the 'PROG' page selected on my FMC and did notice that the course to the incorrect 'ZZZZZ' was almost 25 degrees to the right of the bearing of ZZZ1 and thought it odd to be navigating that far off the bearing to destination. This matched my curiosity about the dashed 'proposed course line' displayed on the PF's ND when the erroneous fix was entered into the scratch pad. However; knowing that the destination was more than 1200 miles away at the time; I assumed there was a significant 'bend' in the original flight plan. Had I mentioned my observation to the PF; it might have cued the PF to check the spelling of the waypoint as the PF made the entry from an assumed spelling. When checking off frequency with the controller who made the direct-to assignment; the PF apologized for the error and asked if we should contact anyone for further discussion/explanation. The Controller indicated that he did not believe that would be necessary.My time-in-type; time-in-position and total-time are not readily available and I don't want to delay submission of this report in order to track down those numbers. I therefore entered a generic '1' in each of those blocks in the report.  Each of the numbers actually totals in the thousands. Fatigue was somewhat of a factor in the event. It was the last duty day of a pairing that had us flying a mix of long and short legs; including international legs to and from an international country; and crossing the country and multiple time zones. We shifted between flying and non-flying duty periods several times and scheduled rest varied from long to short periods. Obtaining 'quality' rest was a challenge and I most definitely accumulated a sleep deficit by the day/time of the event. I estimate that I slept a total of 5.5 hours during the rest period prior to the duty period of the event; one sleep period of 4 hours and another nap of 1.5 hours; waking approximately 3 hours prior to reporting for the event duty period.
column123: First; I can't confirm all the information requested above.  I don't remember exactly which Center we were talking to or pinpoint where we were relative to a fix.  I think we were with ZZZ but it might have been ZZZ1; and we were south of ZZZ1 and west of ZZZ2 at the time; going direct to ZZZ2. I was the FO and the Pilot Flying. We were cleared direct to ZZZZZ. The Captain/PM was eating his catering so I was also answering the radio. When we received the clearance to ZZZZZ it was easier for me to enter the fix in the FMC than it would have been for him; so I typed that in.  About 10-15 minutes later the Controller said that he showed us about 45 degrees off course and asked whether we were going direct to ZZZZZ as cleared. We double-checked for NAV selected to the fix; looked at the course deviation; and checked the FMC; and they all confirmed direct ZZZZZ. On closer examination; though; we realized that we were actually going to a fix called ZZZZZ1; and that I had misspelled the correct fix when I typed it in. I didn't select it from the fixes listed on the flight plan; and should have done that instead of typing it in. That would have obviated the error. The aircraft made a fairly significant turn to the right when I executed the direct-to command and I thought at the time that if I'd known it was such a big difference in the track I'd have requested direct sooner. The Captain later said that he'd thought it was strange that the bearing/distance on the FMC didn't match what the airplane had turned to when we made the turn; and wished that he had said something at the time so that we could resolve the discrepancy.  I should have caught the misspelling at the time; but I also should have selected the fix from the list instead of typing it in. I indicated that fatigue was a factor with this event because I think I would have caught the error or not made it in the first place. We overfly ZZZZZ often and I've noticed the variant spelling before. It was the last night of the trip; though; and I'd not had more than 4 consecutive hours of sleep (or more than 5.5 total) on any of the previous days.

column121: We were cruising at FL370 when we received the EICAS message 'BLEED APU LEAK' even though the APU was not running. We ran the QRH but the message did not go away so we descended to FL310 and shut off the cross bleed; and bleed 1 per the QRH. We were in cruise for nearly 20 minutes when I noticed white smoke coming from under the CA (Captain) display units. Just as I saw the smoke; I smelled it. The CA had also seen and smelled smoke and we both commented on it at the same time. The CA used the EMER call button to contact the FAs (Flight Attendants). Both FAs immediately commented on the smoke smell when they answered. We told them we were [advising ATC] and hung up. Both of us donned our O2 masks right away and I radioed Center. The CA was flying and started an [expedited] decent. I saw ZZZ was only about 20 miles south west of our position. We told ATC to show that as our destination. As I was ACARS'ing dispatch; we received a frequency change so I dropped the message in the free text box without sending it to put in the frequency and then input the destination to get pointed in the correct direction. By the time I got back to it; Dispatch had messaged us saying that company in ZZZ was expecting us and to not worry about replying. Coming through 10;000 ft.; I pulled the mask away from my face to see if the smoke smell was still strong. It was not; so we decided to take the masks off and continued in. In an attempt to slow up further and increase our rate of descent; we dropped the gear at 250 kts. and the warning tape came up. We over sped the gear by maybe 2 kts. for less than a couple seconds. Once on the ground; we asked the FA's if there was still smoke in the back. They said there was a faint smell and no visible smoke. We made the decision not to evacuate and parked at a gate. The entire event lasted 13 minutes from starting the descent to landing.
column123: While at in cruise at FL370; we received the ICAS message Bleed APU Leak.  We completed the QRH procedure all the way through.  We had descended to FL310 and remained there for just under 15 minutes when we noticed smoke in the cockpit.  The smoke was gray-ish/white-ish in color and was accompanied by a very pungent smell.  The FO (First Officer) and myself very quickly put on our oxygen masks and I pushed the cabin emergency call button.  The FA's (Flight Attendants) both confirmed the smell but did not see any smoke.  Later; the FA's told me they were looking for smoke moments before we called them and after we called them; and several passengers started to ask the FA about the smell.  With oxygen masks on; communication established; and smoke in the air; we notified ATC of our need to descend.  It was during us trying to coordinate a plan with the FA and the FO that I realized the microphone in the oxygen mask was working intermittently.  The created an addition challenge with communicating with the crew.  We communicated with ATC our intentions to divert.  Just a few short moments later we received an ACARS message from dispatch that they noticed we were diverting.  We did not respond as we still had a little smoke in the cockpit and where focused on getting down and on the ground.  After a fast descent; and around 10;000 ft. I lifted my mask off to see if I could still smell the smoke.  I could not and because my mask microphone was working intermittently; we opted to remove our masks to facilitate better communication during the landing phase of flight.  Passing through 10;000 ft. we lowered the gear so we could continue our rapid descent.  In our haste to keep the descent going it appeared that we went above 250 kts. with the gear extended by 1-2 kts. for 1-2 seconds.  We continue the rest of the flight without any more issues.  After landing I confirmed with the FA that they did not see any smoke or smell anything.  It was at this point that we decided to taxi to the gate.

column123: Everything was good to go on my flight out to ZZZ this am. Until the last passenger boarded and demanded I move to clear the way to his seat in X6. As I was the A (FA); I knew that he was blocked in at X3 and showed him his seat. He told me that he didn't want that seat; he wanted what was changed for him at the gate. The Gate Agent was at the boarding door within moments and I asked her why he was moved into a social distance block seat. She told me that he wanted the seat. That isn't enough of an argument for me. The X FA; upset and arguably so came up and asked why this passenger wasn't in his previously assigned seat and the agent got very cold and told us he is technically allowed and wanted this seat; so rather than argue she gave it to him. (He's a premium passenger; go figure.) We pushed back as crew and told her that that isn't protecting the crew and that we still have over 10 minutes to have his seat changed; but I was met with a cold agent who refused to back down and shrugged off our frustrations and concerns with a nonchalant; 'It was a problem yesterday too but it's a short flight.' I was asked if we could close and that was that.About half way through the flight; I was cornered in my galley by the passenger in X6 and asked why the X FA was so unfriendly. In an attempt to cover for the Company I engaged in damage control apologizing for any discomfort and explained that the reason he was originally in X3 was due to a social distance block on his seat due to the health and safety of our flight attendants. I explained that if any crew member made him feel anything less than welcome; we did not intend to and that it was operational confusion between the agents and the crew. He told me then again that that was the seat he wanted and attempted to tell me that he understood where we were coming from but he just preferred that seat which is why he didn't want to move to any of the open seats on the flight that weren't right next to the flight attendant's jumpseats. He told me he knows a lot of people that fly for our Company and that he was thrown off that the X FA wouldn't engage in conversation during taxi and takeoff. I told him at this point that we are here for safety first and comfort second and that as flight attendants; we are observe a sterile galley allowing minimal distractions as we silently review safety procedures in the unlikely event of an emergency. He seemed pacified enough and moved to a point I could get around him and recirculate myself back to the isle. I am appalled by this incident on so many levels:1. Blatant disregard for FA health and safety from an agent that didn't follow protocol around the social distance block.2. FA should not be expected to sit next to a passenger who may or may not follow mandated COVID protocols. 3. The market we were flying into requires an online form filled out acknowledging the high COVID rates and need to quarantine due to ICU capacities and here you have the FAs sitting among the noise?! Nah. 4. It put both the X FA and the A FA in a compromising spot with the passenger and their perception of our service and this made us both highly uncomfortable when it wasn't at all called for or necessary to do so.5. Having passengers trying to talk our ears off and be chatty is not only UNSAFE because it is encouraging the virus to spread; 6. It's also unsafe because it is causing distractions during the times we as FAs need to be focused the most.7. For the Gate Agent to tell me that this was a problem yesterday too; it means that they have no clear understanding of the social distance block and no regard for their team mates who have to endure the flight with a sniffling; sneezing passenger for 2+ hours.8. A passenger preference for a window is not reason enough to forgo social distance block procedure.   This put me in a compromising situation with a dissatisfied passenger. I was cornered in my galley without warning and it startled me. Also; to have toback pedal over a topic that I felt the X FA was in the right and had every reason to be upset about was unnecessary and upsettingBETTER CRM.More education around social distance block for agents who don't know what it's like to be on the front lines and trapped with a plane full of passengers and no place to go without being bombarded with passenger questions as we fight for space over an arm rest.

TSM stated both flap actuators were required to be changed in the event of a jam with no faults due to known icing problem. Concurred with Maintenance Control that this was desired and safest step to continue. Gave all information to my crew chief; and supervisor and that the plane needs to be taken out of service until the parts are removed and replaced. Supervisor outlined that his boss argued that it's not the problem and proceeded to find any way to keep aircraft green. Both myself and work partner were pressured for well over the night to not ground Aircraft X and call it good. We raised the fact the TSM explicitly states with no faults both actuators must be changed. Due to ongoing peer pressure I reluctantly agreed to sign Aircraft X airworthy on the technicality that although the aircraft is reporting a flap jam; the phase of flight it occurred was in cruise and probably an indication error. However; prior to Date on Date-1 the exact fault and exact write up was entered. Corrective action from ZZZ2 base was a reset of LH #1 torque limiter. The TSM for this faults states that when resetting a flap torque limiter; the TSM refers to lubricate drive system; do a detail inspection and replace rotary actuator which have a tripped torque limiter. This was not done in ZZZ2 when an indicator was tripped; reset; and signed off. See [Logbook Entry]. I advised Maintenance Control and supervision of this oversight and advocated for replacing flap actuators.Event occurred because management doesn't take un airworthy as acceptable.Keep management where it belongs. Managing their supervisors and leave the technical aspect to the mechanics with the proper steps and actions from the manuals.

Did go around and followed vectors to 3;000 ft.; advised ATC and followed QRH; We did all steps but were both misinterpreted the checklist. Should have put lever to flaps 3; instead of flaps full and calculated the wrong approach speed as we now believe we misinterpreted the max speed chart for approach speed. 190 kts. instead of 165 kts. Report said we were 185 kts. I believe. On the approach I knew something was not right; thought about going around but was worried about the fuel time. During approach we had full slats no flaps. We requested longer runway (12;000 ft.); Landing was normal I let plane slow to 100 kts. before applying breaks. Never heated up beyond 150 [degrees] more or less. After firefighters looked over the airplane we proceeded to gate. Should have referred to SOP in performance for added info but thought we were right and worried about fuel. I have done this procedure in training; I ran the checklist and made the mistake that I was warned about. I believe frustration with a reassignment; irritated with a broken airplane (multiple problems) that was delivered to us and worried about fuel during checklist all added to my distraction and lead me to misinterpreting the checklist.Slow down slow read checklist slower; have more fuel to run all the way through.

He never exited his aircraft so we did not speak.I believe the other pilot was trying to beat me to the fuel island with his 'short approach' which must not have been all that short; considering where we met up at. I think he should have used better judgement and extended his downwind. My airplane is equipped with Lo Presti Boom Beam landing and taxi lights; and a precise flight pulse light. The effect is that even during day these bright lights which are alternating on the wings makes my aircraft highly visible. I always fly with these lights on; and they were on.My mistake was trusting the other pilot's judgement; that his short approach would have gotten him to the airport much sooner than reality. I should be more proactive and suggested that he extend his downwind; or just abort my approach.The other factor is another airplane was in the pattern; and was turning crosswind to downwind around the time of the near miss.My aircraft was a bit faster than he may have anticipated; as I was still slowing down with speed brakes deployed; but at time of incident was around 80 knots indicated.

column121: The previous week of flying was the most demanding experienced in over XX years of flying. In hindsight; these challenging events diminished and taxed my mental and physical abilities on subsequent flights leading to inadvertent decisions possibly contributing to my rejected takeoff.  On 3 out of last 4 flights encountered nearly identical events with the Environmental System Controller (ESC) Level 1 Alerts of Pack Flo/ Pack Disagree/ Bleed Off anomalies on two different aircraft during Max Thrust Takeoff with Anti-ice On flights. In the first flight event the anomalies presented on upwind; climb-out were corrected automatically by the ESC and Auto Anti Ice mode. Bleed Air Off; Pack Disagree; Pack Off; Level alerts all extinguished automatically. There was no input from the crew and the Level 1+2 checklists were reviewed for reference by crew. In the second flight event; relying on system knowledge; the previous flight; and anticipating the ESC would respond accordingly in same fashion it was discussed with crew that the ESC in Auto Mode would automatically resolve a pack flow disagree issue level 1 alert noticed late in taxi with a higher demand airflow presented in the system; when we were to run-up the engines for deice concerns for :30 seconds; in position prior to takeoff. Numerous distractions such as short taxi; checklist completion; deice fluid on windscreens making taxi turns difficult due to limited visibility on side windows; and significant deice delays made our departure later than normal allowing more body and mental fatigue to set in. The air synoptic was illuminated due to manual selection of Anti Ice because this air frame did not have an auto anti feature on it. This is important to note because it was normal looking to see AIR for our takeoff setup conditions. After engine run-up and brake release received a level 2 alert Pack not off alert; Pack Flow Disagree resulting in a decision to abort takeoff with a low speed <50 knots reject. Contacted MX resulted in a Block turn back and MX deferral for a malfunctioning Pack.Third flight event; subsequently occurred two days later with Bleed Air off/ Pack Disagree/ Pack Off level 1 alerts occurring on climb out on same aircraft first instance happened on. Close observation revealed in fact the ESC in combo with the Auto Anti Ice again fully resolved any anomalies without any input from the crew. It became more obvious to me the Auto Anti Ice feature once detecting no need for Anti Ice usage is securing Anti Ice allowing the ESC to revert to normal ops eliminating any level 1 or 2 alerts. Thus the ESC must be prioritizing the airflow; protecting the system if a potential leak is detected; turning off packs and bleeds in its process when Anti Ice was ON. On the rejected Takeoff the Anti-Ice was Manually turned ON; the ESC attempted to secure the Pack Flow /Disagree but was unsuccessful in doing so. The decision to conduct a low speed reject was correct but may have possibly been avoided by first contacting MX before takeoff. Checklist were reviewed by the crew but it was fully anticipated the ESC to resolve the Pack issue on run-up before brake release. In the future; it will be my priority with any confusing level alerts to involve MX early to form the best team based consensus and strengthen decision making.
column123: After deicing and during taxi out we received a level 1 alert for 'Pack 3 FLOW DISAG'. Level 1 checklist references: 'Consequences NONE'. It was our understanding that this was a cycling pack flow issue that the system controller would resolve with higher demand flow on run up once takeoff power was applied. This was our second leg for the night and we were already dealing with a lengthy delay; de-icing; icing conditions; snow; wake turbulence avoidance of a departing heavy jet and having to do an engine run up while holding in position in order to clear the engines of icing before releasing the brakes for take off. At the point of brake release to initiate the takeoff roll; neither of us noticed if the level 1 alert was still displayed. Once takeoff power was applied and we reached approximately 40kts ground speed we received a level 2 PACK 3 NOT CLOSED alert. The captain elected to reject the takeoff as is in accordance with company SOP. We cleared the runway with no further indecent and returned to the blocks where maintenance deferred pack 3. We ultimately departed without further incident and completed the flight as originally planned.  In hind sight we should have delayed the take off and mitigated the level 1 PACK FLOW DISAG alert before taking the runway.

column121: Saw a lightsport looking plane out of periphery of my vision while punching in a button or two on GPS on my panel. Immediately pushed forward and rolled away in steep descending turn to the left; as I was already positioned level and about 100 feet left of a head-on alignment with the other aircraft. I was heads down for less than 6 seconds estimated by time of noticing other aircraft due to relative movement in my field of view that would not have been apparent further out in distance and time from the near-miss. Immediate recognition of need to deviate to left (rather than right) was made along with recognition that a collision would not result due to the immediate evasive action taken. The other aircraft did not take any evasive action and is therefore assumed to have been unaware of my presence. I looked towards aircraft as I rolled and kept eyes on aircraft as it passed by me towards my 5 o clock position while I was rolled in a 70 degree left bank. I then recovered to level flight and continued to climb to 6;300 pattern altitude at my destination airport. I had ADS-B out from a modern solid state transponder unit as well as ADS-B in capability; but I was not referencing ADS-B in on any device screen at the time of the near-miss. The situation may have been avoided in the difficult to see case of a head on convergence had I had my ipad or phone connected to my ADS-B over wifi and a method for monitoring the ADS-B situation with auditory alerts in my headset so that an alert of impending collision would have taken my attention away from a cockpit task and diverted my eyes outside to search for a collision waiting to happen. I was lucky that my field of vision included enough of the view in front of me in my periphery to permit my vision to inform me of the near-miss by the time the aircraft was less than 1;000 feet in front of me. Closure rate was estimated to be 170-190 knots taking both of our speeds into account; with 100 foot lateral separation and less than 30 feet vertical separation before evasive action was taken about 2 miles north of Boulder reservoir; coming southbound from Longmont; CO.

column121: It has been hard to fly during the pandemic; and the aircraft had been in for annual inspection; so I had not flown for two months. I went out for practice. I chose the back-course approach at ZZZ; as it can be challenging. Also; during recurrent training in Month; we had noticed some odd autopilot behavior when flying this approach. My aircraft has Garmin avionics but these are mated to an older analogue autopilot.By the time I was told to switch to ZZZ1 Approach; I was still at 12;000 feet and quite close to ZZZZZ intersection on the approach. When I gave my request for the approach; the controller gave me vectors to circle back to rejoin the course while descending to 4000 feet. She then cleared me for the approach. I believed she said 'Maintain 4000 until established...'; but in our later discussion she said her instruction was 'Maintain 4000 to ZZZZZ.' I believe I read back the former. In any case; when back on extended approach course; but a short distance before ZZZZZ; I began to descend further. The chart showed 3000 feet for the segment between ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1; which is the FAF and 5.8NM from ZZZZZ. My GPS displayed an altitude of 3100 at ZZZZZ; which I believe is its indication of a safe altitude. So; I had set altitude capture for 3100 feet and was descending. The controller alerted me that she had expected 4000 feet to ZZZZZ. While we were discussing this; the autopilot failed to capture and the descent continued to 2900 feet. The controller told me to switch to tower.On my first attempt to call tower at ZZZ; I had not hit the switch correctly and was still with ZZZ1 approach. At the same time; I noticed the autopilot taking me off course for the approach and interrupted it while calling the tower. We were in the descent within the FAF by this time. The tower controller told me I was low for the course and left of course; and he asked if I was flying the approach visually instead of using the Back Course. Due to the autopilot issue; I was by that time flying visually. It was a clear VFR day; and at no time was I in close proximity to terrain or other aircraft. The problem arose for several reasons. The pilot (me) was rusty and needed practice. It was a mistake to do the more challenging BC approach as the first one. (After this event; I did the missed approach as planned at ZZZ and did two fine approaches at ZZZ1 and ZZZ2.) Also; I believe there anomalies with my avionics set-up and back-course approaches; and I should not have been trying to troubleshoot that as a single pilot; especially being a bit out of practice. Another contributor was my misunderstanding of the controller's instruction; along with using the 3000 foot altitude indicated on the chart for that segment ZZZZZ to ZZZZZ1) and the 3100 foot altitude indicated as the target for ZZZZZ on my GPS for the altitude I was trying to attain. All of these issues increased workload; which is better handled by an in-practice pilot (which is why I had gone out to practice). A final recommendation from this experience is that I will avoid flying BC approaches with my autopilot until I can do a flight with a competent pilot and avionics technician aboard. The BC approaches are quite rare; and almost all have GPS overlays nowadays. So; they are not really a high priority; I actually chosen this one to be challenging and give me practice monitoring the autopilot and taking over if it acted strangely. But given the altitude misunderstanding; resulting discussion; and then the strange autopilot behavior; it was a bit choppy. I flew the airplane in a safe manner throughout (there was no terrain issue along my path); but my adherence to published instructed and published altitudes on the approach was poor.

column121: Normal takeoff roll. After gear up and 400ft. flaps up. I noticed the aircraft would not nose trim down as the flaps were going from 10 to 0 as I tried to maintain 10deg to 12deg climb angle. The aircraft was trying to pitch up and it took increasingly excessive force on the yolk pushing forward to try to keep the airplane under 15deg nose up pitch. The trim switch on the yoke was ineffective.I was not using the auto pilot but pressed the autopilot disconnect switch thinking I had an electrical jammed trim motor. I then went to turn off the main trim switch in order to use to manual trim wheel and the trim wheel seemed frozen. We could turn the wheel but it took a lot of effort to get minor movements. At the same time we were getting FGC 1 and FGC 2 CAS messages. I went back to two hands on the yoke and asked for assistance from the non flying pilot. We noticed that we had a flight guidance computer 1 and flight guidance computer2 failure. At the same time the flight guidance panel went blank and the flight director disappear from the PFD. We had no heading reference and no pitch reference. The auto throttles were also not controlling the speed and when selecting Auto throttles 'off' they still appeared engaged but only 'holding' not moving. We were just trying to hold a basic pitch angle and heading and trying to level off. We were now still climbing through 2;500 ft. and ATC. cleared us up to 4;000 ft. we had a hard time controlling the airplane in the pitch mode. It wanted to climb! All of this happened within a few short minutes of flight.I had two hands on the yolk when NAME asked me if he could take the yoke and once he felt the yoke he agreed there was something serious with the aircraft and we notified ATC that we had flight control issues. We were able to adjusted the throttles to maintain pitch and we figured it was best if NAME controlled the yoke and I controlled the throttles adjusting power and I tried to trim the trim wheel. By NAME flying the plane I was able to try to regain some flight director functions. I pulled FGC1 and FGC 2 circuit breakers let them stay unpowered for a few seconds and reengage them and attempt to determine what systems were working and which failure we actually had. Resetting the circuit breakers brought back the heading indicator and the flight director. We switched the FD command to the Right side. We advised ATC we did not want to climb into the clouds we needed to stay VFR. ATC assisted us with radar vectors to final to Runway XX atZZZ1My thoughts are the pitch motor servo or pitch windings failed or became frozen thus causing the flight guidance computer 1 to not be able to get a valid signal from the pitch feedback then it switched over to flight guidance 2 that also was not able to see a valid signal from the pitch and disengaged. When the flight guidance panel did not have a valid signal from either FGC it therefore lost heading; auto throttles; vertical and lateral modes. The primary flight controls all worked (elevator ailerons and rudder all seem to work properly and the flaps could go up and down normally. The landing gear function was also normal. I believe this was a pitch trim issue which triggered a flight guidance issue and made the aircraft extremely uncontrollable. By splitting the pilot duties and using crew coordination we were able to safely land the aircraft.

column121: There was a pair of arrivals staggered by about 0.5-0.75 miles; with the Runway 28 Right arrival preceding Runway 28 Left arrival.  There was a solid 16-32 knots crosswind from the north depending on what altitude they were at.  Runway 28 Left glide slope is 2.85 degrees while Runway 28 Right is 3.00 degrees.  In this very rare set of circumstances; the left arrival is getting a rough ride form the right arrival. Aircraft X  [the first E175] was cleared to land Runway 28 Right and Aircraft Y [the second E175] was cleared to land Runway 28 Left. Aircraft Y was about 2.3 mile final when they advised going around.  I gave them runway heading and 3;000.  I advised them of traffic that departed north and stopped climbing in their southbound turn; an A320; and got visual separation transferred to the pilot.  I then coordinated the go around and was asked the reason.  I said I assumed unstable approach but was not sure.  The aircraft was coming up on level flight and so I confirmed the reason.  The pilot said they were hit by wake turbulence.  I shipped them to Departure; then coordinated with their coordinator the reason.  We logged it in the Tower log; but did not write an MOR (mandatory occurrence report). When the airplane came back around and landed; I inquired about the event.  They said that the airplane yawed to the right and then began rolling to the left so they went around.  That sounds very unsettling to me; however they made it out to fly another approach. No recommendations; it sounds like the pilots did what they were trained to do to save the ship.

column121: I was the Captain on Aircraft X (ZZZ-ZZZZ) on date.  I just wanted to give some details regarding ZZZZ's refusal to allow us to enter the country without a negative COVID test; and to give a well-deserved kudos to those who helped us.Upon arrival in ZZZZ; we were walking towards the customs area when we were approached by a man from the 'health department.' He asked us for our COVID-19 test results; which (according to our information) were not required for crews in ZZZZ. When we told him that we didn't have a test result; he said we could not proceed further; as a negative COVID test was a requirement for entry into Country.Two airline employees arrived to assist us - the Station Manager X and another employee Person Y.  Both were outstanding and went above and beyond to try to help us.  They spent considerable time attempting to explain to the health department official that crews were exempt from the COVID requirement.  This did not matter to the official; who insisted that 'All passengers must have a negative COVID test prior to entry.'   Manager X explained that we were crew; not passengers; and therefore were subject to the crew exemption.  He stated that he understood that there was an exemption; but he refused to change his position and stated that we couldn't proceed.Several calls were made by Manager X; attempting to get someone to explain to the health department official that we were exempt.  Someone then called the official on his cell phone; resulting in a somewhat spirited conversation.  After the call; the official decided that if we'd had a COVID test in the last 14 days we would be allowed to enter.  When we said we hadn't; he said if we'd had the vaccine; he would let us in; but of course we hadn't had that either.  Manager X pulled us aside and said that this official was simply trying to make a name for himself; and she again apologized; even though it was clearly not her fault.  It occurred to us later that perhaps he was fishing for a bribe; but while that's very common in small GA airplanes; I've never had that happen as part of an airline crew. Unfortunately; I was not able to get the name of the health official.By this point; we had the Flight Operations Manager involved; and he was working on getting us seats on the plane back to ZZZ as it was clear we weren't going to be allowed into ZZZZ.  Manager X and Person Y were both doing an outstanding job of keeping us informed since neither the F/O nor I spoke [the foreign language].We proceeded back to the gate while Flight Operations Manager got our seats worked out and worked with dispatch to make sure the outbound crew didn't leave without us.  As we were leaving; the health department official made one last offer - we could proceed; but he would 'Send a doctor to your hotel room to give you a COVID 19 quick test.'  A quick discussion with my FO; confirmed my thoughts that this was a bad idea.  Needless to say; we declined his offer.  When we arrived at the airplane; FO was physically standing at the bottom of the stairs to make sure that they wouldn't close the door before we arrived.While it was a frustrating endeavor; we couldn't have navigated this successfully without Flight Operations Manager; Station Manager X; Person Y; Dispatch and the outbound crew of Aircraft Y.  The crew desk was on the ball as well as I received a couple of pairing change alerts as we walked to the gate.  My FO; did an outstanding job; especially considering it was his first trip after OE.

column121: Ops normal from pushback to takeoff roll.  I was flying pilot; [the] Captain non-flying pilot.   Power was set and autothrottles and FMAs all had normal indications. At approximately 60 knots there was a loud bang and the jet swerved to the right.   I steered the jet back to centerline with rudder and the Captain initiated the abort.  We stopped quickly on the runway and told ATC we'd aborted and instructed the passengers to remain seated.  After quickly assessing the risk; and talking with the Lead Flight Attendant; Captain determined it was safe to taxi clear of Runway XX and we stopped on the parallel taxiway. We requested assistance from [the] Fire Department to look at the landing gear to ensure we hadn't blown a tire or had smoke/fire coming off the brakes.   After getting the all-clear; we coordinated with Operations/Tech Ops to return to Gate X.  We closely monitored brake temp indications during the taxi back and saw that they were all decreasing in normal fashion as expected.  We were met by many company personnel at the gate and Maintenance was able to quickly determine we had an Engine Number 2 compressor stall during takeoff roll.  Passengers deplaned in normal fashion through Door 1L; and the flight crew was then escorted up to ZZZ Flight Ops to discuss our readiness and ability to continue flying the trip.  Captain and I then proceeded to fly as scheduled.

column121: Descent and approach were briefed with expectation of [Runway] XXL at ZZZ. ATC advised during descent to expect Runway XYR. ATC was advised that we were a 747-8 and a request for [Runway] XXL was made. ATC advised that Runway XXL was not available unless operationally required. Runway change checklist was performed and performance obtained for [Runway] XYR. Captain briefed that a right turn [off] [Runway] XYR was not allowed except for Taxiway E. However we did not expect to make this exit so he briefed a left turn at [Taxiway] K or roll to the end. Arrival and landing were normal; after slowing through 60 kts. we were past [Taxiway] E and the Captain stated that he would be exiting left on [Taxiway] K. As we began our left turn toward the high speed taxiway I noticed a line of lights on the ground marking the taxiway closed. These were very dim and low to the ground. Very hard to see. I said very affirmatively; STOP; STOP Barrier. The Captain [stopped] the aircraft and then corrected taxi course. The aircraft did encroach on the first few feet of Taxiway K but not far enough that he couldn't correct back onto the runway. On our rollout ATC did issue an invalid taxi clearance that was a distraction. The taxi clearance was corrected after our [query] and the remainder of the taxi was uneventful. Post flight review of NOTAMS (Notice to Airman) and ATIS (Automated Terminal Information Service) revealed that the taxiway was NOTAM closed and was missed on our part. The poor lighting of the taxiway closure barrier was a large factor in us not seeing it sooner.
column123: Prior to top of descent we briefed and prepared to fly the ILS (Instrument Landing System) approach to Runway XXL at ZZZ. Our airport briefing page does say that arrivals between XA:00 and XB:00 should expect Runway XYR for landing; but goes on to state that 747-8 aircraft should expect XXL. Upon check in with ZZZ Approach; we were told to expect [Runway] XYR. I reminded the controller of our aircraft type and queried whether [Runway] XXL was available. We were told that due to noise abatement procedures at that time of day that we could only use [Runway] XXL if it was due to operational necessity. After a quick discussion with the Captain; we decided that due to our light gross weight; we could accept [Runway] XYR. We quickly reprogrammed the FMS (Flight Management System) and briefed the new approach; to include the many 747-8 taxi restrictions and the fact that taxi to parking was likely to be somewhat complex. We decided that a left turn off the runway on Taxiway Kilo was the most likely scenario. While we did these things quickly; I felt that we had covered all of our bases and did not feel rushed or that the workload was too high. What both the Captain and I missed however; was the fact that [Taxiway] Kilo was closed. We had both reviewed the NOTAMs (Notice To Airmen) and ATIS (Automated Terminal Information Service); but since we were planning on landing on [Runway] 8L; I believe we both simply failed to register the Taxiway Kilo closure; as it did not apply to our original taxi plan. The approach and landing were uneventful and both the Captain and I were focused on identifying Taxiway Kilo in order to vacate the runway. At no point during our approach or rollout did Tower relay any instructions on how we could expect to vacate the runway. As we began to make the turn for [Runway] Kilo; the IRO (International Relief Officer) forcefully stated 'Stop! Stop'. He had managed to pick up the extremely dimly lit barricades that marked the closure. The Captain managed to get the airplane stopped before we were committed to Taxiway Kilo. Around the time we stopped; Tower transmitted that [Taxiway] Kilo was; in fact closed; and that we could expect to make a right turn off the runway at Taxiway Charlie. This was an invalid clearance; as the -8 is restricted from using that portion of [Taxiway] Charlie. As we were about to query Tower; I believe he realized our aircraft type and issued a clearance to taxi clear of the runway at the end. The rest of the taxi was uneventful. I think there are several take-aways from this incident. First; the IRO was worth his weight in gold this morning. Had he not spoken out in a timely and forceful manner; I think there was a very good chance we would have impacted the barriers or at the very least been unable to continue our taxi. The IRO was the last link in the error chain and that link held strong. Second; I think both ZZZ Approach and the Tower Controller were both unaccustomed to a 747-8 arriving at that time of morning. Landing on [Runway] 4R presents a number of taxi challenges to a -8; and perhaps the best practice may be for -8 crews to declare 'operational necessity' and request [Runways] 8L or 8R unless there are other extenuating circumstances. In the event we must land on [Runway] 4R; a simple 'plan to vacate the runway at X' from Tower would be extremely helpful. Finally; while I do believe the way our situation evolved created somewhat of a setup regarding the closure of Taxiway Kilo; the information was in fact available in the NOTAMs and via ATIS. I overlooked that information largely due to an incorrect expectation bias. I am aware of my ultimate responsibility to digest that information and will make an effort in the future to pay more attention to the 'Plan B' options in addition to the expected one.

column121: Landing [Runway] XXL on final; aircraft in front of us reported a 10 knot loss. The FO was pilot flying at the time and over corrected for the wind; causing us to descend below glideslope very quickly on short final.  As soon as I was calling go-around the GS aural warning came on.  The FO executed a go-around. Because of the difficult wind conditions and seeing we were already at 2;100-2;200 LBS; I decided that I would land the second attempt as I did not want to get into a fuel situation. We were in agreement with this.  On short final for the second attempt; with me as pilot flying; at about 150 feet; we had the wind-shear caution alert and proceeded to execute our second go-around. ATC gave us instructions to set up for [Runway] XXR but due to fuel concerns I said 'Unable' and declared min fuel. Also; I added that if we did have to take any delays we would be declaring emergency fuel. ATC set us up immediately for a close pattern for [Runway] XXL. On this attempt; I stayed slightly high as the wind shear seem to be the worse right at the tree line at about 150 feet.  On this third attempt; we landed successfully and taxied back to the gate.Unstable approach recognized by me and a wind shear caution message for the second attempt.Inexperienced FO who had only flown once since May 2020 and challenging weather conditions with wind shear.Two go-arounds and declared min-fuel.Have pilots who have been out a while receive more recurrent training.  It was evident due to lack of recency the FO was struggling with the conditions that day.  Also; be vigilant on [Runway] XXL as I have had issues on windy days before where the tree line ends and the field begins. With the second attempt we had a 15 knot increase with the wind shear caution message.
column123: I was the Pilot Flying. The Wind shear changes in combination with the amount of time since I've been flying in the airplane were contributing factors. There were changes of +/- 15kts and on short approach I went slightly below glide slope and then the Wind shear happened which caused the Glideslope aural warning to sound. The Captain called for a Go-Around which we executed. Once we were at a safe altitude and being vectored back for another approach the we exchanged controls and the Captain became the Pilot Flying. As we were coming in on short approach the Wind shear Aural Caution message sounded so we executed a second go-around. ATC told us that they were going to vector us around for Runway XXR; but were now low on fuel and declared min fuel. They instead kept us close pattern for Runway XXL and we landed safely. Upon landing we had 1;450 LBS of fuel. We taxied to the gate with no issues.Glideslope Aural Warning System on first attempt and Wind shear warning system on second attempt.Wind shear affecting experience level.Go-Around executed twice.Keep crews more recent on flying or more time in simulator if it's been a while.

column121: We departed ZZZ en route to ZZZ1. Captain and myself; First Officer; noticed a light harmonic droning noise during climb out but no vibration. About 30 minutes after takeoff while in cruise at FL370 the LH Gen Master Caution illuminated. We ran the QRH and reset the LH generator. At this time the generator did not come back online. We then decided to reduce the electrical load on the remaining generator. The QRH indicated to land as soon as practical. With one hour and 20 minutes left in flight we elected to continue to our destination with the remaining generator.At this time we informed Dispatch. Along our route of flight we determined which airports were suitable for landing in the event we lost our right generator. This proved to be beneficial due to the events that happened down the road. About 40 minutes after the LH generator failed the LH engine rolled back. N1 fell back to almost idle and the ITT dropped immediately as well as fuel flow. We then advised ATC of our engine problem and determined ZZZ2 was suitable and asked ATC for radar vectors direct to ZZZ2.Captain pulled back the power lever on the LH engine at which time we noticed the engine spooled back up but was fluctuating erratically. We started our descent since we were only about 65 nm from the airport. During the descent the engine seemed to stabilize. The droning noise became louder and strangely seemed to come from the front of the aircraft. No noticeable vibration though. Descending into the pattern at ZZZ2 the droning noise become pretty loud and we felt a thump in the fuselage. The thump we latter determined to be a bird strike on the RH wing. (No damage to wing). Conditions on the field were night VFR and the runway was dry. With the loud noise that appeared to come from the front of the aircraft Captain decided during landing to hold the nose off as long as possible. We landed with no issues and no structural damage. We then taxied off the runway and were met with the Airport Fire Department. Priority handling was not requested; but fire was staged as a precautionary measure. As we were taxiing to Company; a repair station on the field; Captain gently pushed up the LH throttle at which time we both noticed it had spooled down by itself. He then went to idle cut-off. Being that Fire was following behind the aircraft a firefighter advised us that he saw a very large puff of smoke from the back of the LH engine when it died. Employees from Company were waiting on the ramp also saw the same plume of smoke. Upon the walk around inspection we found no evidence of structural damage to the engine or any damage where the bird struck had occurred on the right hand wing. The fan blades turned easily. We did observe underneath the LH engine cowl large black streaks from the starter generator cooling exit.

column121: I departed ZZZ at ZA:10 local on an IFR flight plan to ZZZ1 in [a rented aircraft]. A preflight inspection at ZZZ revealed no items of concern; and the brakes responded as expected when I tested them upon first movement from the tie down spot and throughout my taxi. The weather was VMC for the duration of the flight; and the weather I picked up on the ZZZ1 ATIS 15 minutes prior to arrival was winds 320@7kts; 9SM visibility; sky clear. I informed ZZZ Approach I would take the visual approach to Runway XX; at which point they cleared me for the visual approach and handed me off to ZZZ1 Tower. Tower requested me to continue on course to fly a left base for Runway XX and report three miles west of the field. Upon my reporting three miles west of the field; they cleared me to land runway XX. Upon nearing the extended centerline; I turned 90 degrees left and aligned myself on an approximately three mile final for Runway XX while at approximately 1;200 feet MSL and 90 KIAS. I completed my final approach and before-landing checks; including pumping the brakes to check for pressure; and crossed the runway threshold at approximately 65 KIAS with 30 degrees of flaps. Immediately upon touching down; the aircraft yawed violently to the left. I applied full right rudder deflection; which somewhat arrested the left yawing and increased the radius of the turn. However; the left main wheel by that time had entered the grass adjoining the runway; further aggravating left yaw. The aircraft continued to rotate about the left wheel until it came to a stop facing approximately due east approximately 75 feet from the west edge of the runway. After ensuring there was no immediate danger of fire or structural damage; I checked the main gear tires out the windows to see if one had blown; but they appeared to be OK. I advised Tower I would try to taxi back to the runway and proceed to the ramp. Upon applying throttle; the aircraft pivoted about its pitch axis into a slight nose-down attitude; which ceased upon decreasing throttle. I tried twice more to increase throttle to induce forward movement; but the aircraft continued to pitch forward when throttle was increased and pitch backward when throttle was decreased. At that point; I informed Tower I would need a tug. An airport crew came with a tug and attached a towbar to the aircraft. Upon attempting to pull the aircraft forward; the tug was not able to move it and subsequently became stuck in the ground. The airport crew then tried using a pickup truck to pull the tug while the tug pulled the aircraft; but the pickup truck became stuck. A 4wd pickup truck came and was able to remove the tug and the first pickup truck back to the runway. The airport crew used a shovel to dig the front wheel of the aircraft out of the ground; as it had become stuck during the previous attempts to taxi back onto the runway. They then attached the towbar to the 4wd pickup truck and were able to get the aircraft moving and onto the runway. I was then able to taxi the aircraft to the ramp under its own power; but noticed it had difficulty tracking in a straight line without additional brake inputs. Upon reaching the ramp; I did a quick inspection of the brake assemblies and discovered a metal-on-metal scraping noise when moving the aircraft back and forth by hand and no movement of the calipers when the toe brakes were actuated. At this point; I felt it was unsafe to continue operating the aircraft and arranged for a mechanic to inspect it the following morning. I called the owner; and he told me; 'that is why you shouldn't take that airplane places on a [weekend] afternoon - no one is around to fix it.' The mechanic inspected the brakes and found that the caliper slider pins were void of lubricant and rusted frozen; one brake lining was missing its rivets due to them rusting away; and several fasteners were loose. He replaced the linings on both slides; lubricated the assemblies; and torqued all the fasteners. I visually inspected the brakes; tested them on the ramp and during runup; and was satisfied that the aircraft was safe to operate. I departed ZZZ1 and had an uneventful IFR flight and landing back at ZZZ.In the future; I will add more thorough visual inspection of the brake assemblies to my preflight inspections; along with checking to make sure the calipers move when the brakes are actuated. I will also land prepared for a problem such as stuck brake; blown tire; or FOD and be more ready to immediately lift back off if safe to do so.

I assigned that to them; notified my Controller in Charge; and began to collect the information. I asked for the nature of their situation; which they told me there was high vibration in their left engine.I also gathered that they wanted to return. I then called Departure to forward the information and ask them for a heading and altitude I could turn the aircraft to. They gave me a 160 heading and 12;000 feet; as well as a frequency. After going back to the pilot; I called Departure back to ensure he was radar contact with them. Departure said yes; and asked if he needed to hold. I told them I had not asked. I then shipped the aircraft to TRACON. By the time the aircraft had turned back and I had shipped the aircraft; the aircraft did fly through and leave the southern tip of an adjacent Approach's airspace. However; I did not have a chance to call them as I was busy coordinating with the other TRACON and trying to get information from the pilot. I also never cleared the aircraft back to its departure airport. I simply turned the aircraft to a 160 heading and shipped the aircraft to Departure.I don't believe there was much I could do to prevent this situation. If I had the chance; I could have called TRACON; but in this scenario I didn't have any time to call due to the high workload.

column123: Upon returning to the flight deck from break; I was briefed on the ZZZZZ XA arrival and ILS XXL approach. ZZZZ ATIS broadcast that both XXL and XXR were in use. Runway data for both XXL and XXR were had been obtained earlier. Prior to descent we completed the descent checklist. At the FMC's; radios; item on the descent checklist; I intended to check the FMC to verify the approach and checked the item complete; but was interrupted by a radio call and never completed it. I did not catch the error that the FMC had ILS XXR programmed instead of ILS XXL; which had been briefed and anticipated. On the descent we were cleared the ZZZZZ XA Arrival to ILS XXL. Having briefed the ILS XXL; and believing we had ILS XXL programmed; no changes were made to the FMC. We did not catch the error until receiving radar vectors to the final approach. We were given a base leg and shortly after a vector to intercept. The turn to final seemed late and the aircraft but captured and lined up on the centerline. At that point; ATC gave us a 'right turn to 160' and then stated we were lined up for XXR and that we had been cleared for ILS XXL. He said there was no traffic for XXR and asked if we wanted to continue. We were at least 4 miles from the FAF so we accepted the approach clearance. We were able to review the approach noting the LOC identifier; changing the minimums and reviewed the Missed Approach procedure prior to descent on the GS. A stable approach was flown from the FAF to the runway for landing and was uneventful; as was the rollout and taxi-in.On the ATIS; gusty winds were noted and moderate; possibly greater; turbulence mentioned. This was a topic of discussion during the briefing and after. We briefed the cabin crew to have the cabin secured early and to take their seats as soon as possible after the chimes for the sterile cockpit notification. The aircraft was slowed early and we had begun configuring early as well so as to be stable early. The discussion was possibly an additional distraction during the briefing and Descent checklist.While we were able to comfortably get set up for the approach that was incorrectly loaded in and able to fly a stable approach; we should have asked for vectors to a new approach in order to properly brief prior to the initiation of the approach phase. We were lucky there was no traffic conflicts as there was little if any traffic due to time of day and the current state of airline traffic due to COVID.

column121: Fumes on flight ZZZ-ZZZ1.  This report is to highlight the procedures used to resolve fume events. It isn't to report the fume event. In summary; after the flight and cabin crew smelled fumes during flight and after landing; Maintenance worked to resolve the problem. After performing various procedures; Maintenance said the problem was fixed three separate times. Each time; the flight and cabin crew pointed out that the fumes were still present. Even so; a manager from another department was brought in to see if she smelled any fumes-she did not. So; as the maintenance policy allows; the aircraft was returned to service; overruling six professional and very experienced flight and cabin crewmembers' specific and detailed descriptions of the characteristics of the still present fumes' smell; the locations in the flight deck and cabin where the fumes were detected and the air supply vent locations from which the fumes were emanating. Approximately an hour later; a flight crew reassigned to ferry the aircraft to ZZZ2 started the #1 Engine; smelled the fumes and refused the aircraft. The fume event began during descent below at 5;000 ft.; at 15 miles from ZZZ1 airport when I noticed musty smelling fumes on the flight deck coming from the eyeball vents on both the overhead and instrument panels. I recognized the smell from previous experience (along with information supplied by both Air Carrier and the Pilots Association); as being from petroleum based fluid being heated and entering the air conditioning system. Being close to the ground and landing; I wanted to find a solution quickly so I closed the flight deck vents to see if there was any change. There was not; so I reopened them thinking that if the fumes were transient that air flow might move the fumes through and off of the flight deck. I also started to feel slightly nauseated so I donned my O2 mask. After donning my O2 mask the nauseated feeling subsided somewhat. Landing was made without incident. At taxi speed I opened my window; turned off the air conditioning packs and taxied to the gate. I then spoke with the flight attendants to see if any of them had smelled the fumes. The flight attendant at Door 3L said that shortly before landing some passengers asked him about a smell in the area. Once they had pointed it out; he said he had then smelled the fumes. No other flight attendants reported smelling the fumes at their jumpseat locations during flight. I wrote up the fumes in the AML (Aircraft Maintenance Logs); then completed and submitted a smoke; odor; fume form. When Maintenance arrived I described the smell of the fumes to them. None of the mechanics with whom I spoke (four I believe); smelled the fumes. From then until when the flight was cancelled at XA:00; one mechanic (of the four); acknowledged that he smelled the fumes 'slightly' and only one time. During this time; Maintenance completed procedure(s) three separate times and after each time said that they didn't smell the fumes and wanted to sign off the AML. Each time; my flight and cabin crew pointed out the smell of the fumes in the cabin and flight deck; so Maintenance continued their procedures. At some point after those three attempts to resolve the problem; one mechanic told me that the aircraft was going to be there until at least XB:00 that day. Soon after that; a manager from another department was asked to walk through the cabin and see if she smelled the fumes.  After a bit I checked my schedule and saw that we were reassigned to take that same aircraft back to ZZZ at XC:00 on [Date]. That was consistent with the last I heard from the mechanic who said the aircraft was going to be there until at least XB:00 that night. Around XD:00; I saw that another crew had been reassigned to fly our aircraft to ZZZ2 at XE:00. I texted the Captain on that flight to be sure he was aware of the seriousness of the problem. He replied; stating that after they had started the #1 Engine; the fumes returned. He did not accept the aircraft. I then called [Pilots Association] Safety for some guidance. I am concerned because; despite all the procedures in place to determine whether the source of the fumes is eliminated; the methods to determine whether the fumes are present or remain:1. Expose maintenance personnel and possibly other people to the fumes and their potential harmful effects (isn't that what we're trying to avoid?).2. Allow using the olfactory senses of random individuals that; (a) may not be able to detect the smell of the fumes; (b) have never smelled the fumes and/or; (c) have no knowledge of the seriousness of the smoke; odor and fume events and their potential and documented health threats.3. Allow the complaints and input of those that do smell the fumes to be ignored or overruled by any randomly chosen person that does not smell them. It seems that the goal should be that if just one person still smells the fumes; the problem isn't solved and the aircraft won't be released to flight status.

column121: I took the plane out to practice maneuvers etc. and was out for about an hour and a half.  There were a lot of planes in the area when I returned from the north and was asked to fly down the east side of the valley to enter a right downwind for Runway XX and to report midfield.  I repeated the instruction and entered the right downwind for Runway XX.  As I was about to report at mid-field; the controller stated that he saw me and cleared me to land on Runway XX.  A couple of minutes later; I believe he also stated that a plane was holding short for takeoff until I landed.I passed around the back of the landmark; made the right turn to the runway heading and saw the runway.  I then finished my landing checklist and proceeded to land on what I thought was Runway XX. Just as I was about two feet off the runway a second or so before the wheels touched; I heard the tower say to 'go-around' just as my wheels touched the ground. This was immediately followed by the tower stating-- [aircraft call sign] cleared to land Runway XX.I have no one to blame; nor any condition to blame for my mistake--I was shocked beyond belief that I had landed on the wrong runway and as many times as I've heard other pilots talk about it happening to them; I honestly thought it would never happen to me; as I have not had a single incident in 10 years of flying.  I have only one possible answer for my error and that is the 'confirmation bias' I've read about and heard discussed in the FAA courses and webinars I've taken.I take full responsibility for my error.  To say I'm embarrassed is an understatement; but one good thing has come of this:  I'm now acutely aware of the reality of confirmation bias from this first-hand experience and will definitely be intensely focused on confirming and reconfirming my runway prior to landing forever more.

column121: Corporate flight to ZZZ [Airport]. Approximately one hour from arrival airport we had multiple route changes. Final route change was ZZZ [VOR] VXXX ZZZ1 [VOR] ZZZ [Airport]. Had difficulty programing Proline Fusion with new route so I built each intersection on VXXX and reconfirmed route.Given a descent to 7;000 ft. by TRACON arrival. We had discussed and programed RNAV (GPS) Y Runway XX. We didn't ask TRACON for the approach we planned. TRACON cleared us direct to ZZZZZ [Intersection] for the ILS Runway XX. I had reviewed the ILS and knew ZZZZZ Intersection wan on the approach. I had the ILS programed in the number two Navigation unit under the number two FMS RNAV.I gave Captain a heading left to intercept the ILS as I had raw data up. Captain was not set up for the ILS and tried to load frequency and inbound course. Now we are high. I pointed the airport our to Captain. Captain had set up on his ILS navigation display 065 inbound.Speed was 250 kts. I told Captain to slow down. ATC asked if we were too high on approach. Captain advised we could make the field. Switched to Tower. I saw we were too high in altitude and speed to make a stable approach. I advised the Tower that we would like a visual approach with a right down wind for Runway XX. Captain was in agreement. Twice more I advised Captain to slow down. I put my hand over his hand and pulled throttles to idle. Captain brought throttle back up. I believe we were at 3;000 to 4;000 feet descending. Tower instructed us to make a right down wind to Runway XX. Again; I advised we are way too fast. Captain started his right turn. Tower advised us about an aircraft ahead of us. I am not positive; but I thought Tower said to climb to 4;000 feet. I did hear tower state pattern altitude was 2;000 feet. We picked up aircraft visually coming right to left as we were making the right turn to downwind. We received a RA but had visual sighting. I think the aircraft was about 1;000 feet horizontal and about 200 vertical feet above us. I advised Captain twice I had the aircraft. He handed me the aircraft and I slowed the aircraft and started to configure the plane for landing. Once configured for landing I gave aircraft back to Captain. I took aircraft back a second time when I did not think he was quite aware of where we were in relation to Runway XX. We were advised of VFR aircraft and cleared to land. Captain was preoccupied looking for VFR traffic. I brought aircraft around to final on the PAPI. Gave the aircraft back to Captain and asked if he was OK to land aircraft. Normal landing.I have been a Captain for a Major airline and told pilot and mechanic I wished to have debrief to address the errors we made with loss of situational awareness and getting behind on the aircraft.The proline fusion avionics system I believe has bugs to be worked out. Almost all numerical fonts are the same size. with all the color enhanced background if you do not know specifically where to look nothing stands out. None of the National flight training facilities have a simulator that has the Fusion avionics system. Flight Safety ZZZ2 has a stand-alone practice system that has no real time capability. We are pretty much self-taught to use the Fusion Proline Avionics system. To change an approach with the Fusion system also take time to set up an instrument approach means if you are in Navigation FMS mode you need to go to heading select. go to the VOR/ILS. set up the frequency and inbound course. then go back to FMS/NAV mode. I believe Captain made his error in the heat of the moment by putting the reverse course inbound with the tail of the VOR/ILS needle.My errors where I knew we were getting behind the aircraft and thought I could talk the Captain through what we needed to do verses taking the aircraft sooner.I have learned in Corporate flying that standardization in aircraft management means there is no standardization if you work for a small fight department. Especially as a contract pilot. This was without a doubt the most difficult flight I have had in many years. Pilots have great attitudes and always seek to learn and improve. I certainly learned but wish to not learn by making and compounding errors.
