column121: Please reference ZZZ [airport]; ZZZZZ 4 RNAV SID.  We were assigned the ZZZZZ 4 RNAV SID and departed Runway XXR at ZZZ.  After checking in with Departure Control the FO (pilot flying) called for the After TO Checklist.  This is when several things happened at once.   Before finishing the checklist the Departure Controller told us to climb to 10;000 feet and said we were clear ZZZZZ1 [Intersection] then ZZZZZ2 [Intersection].  At the same time we received an ECAM alert for a #1 Pressure Regulator Fault.  By the time I set the altitude in the FCP; read back the clearance; re-visited and completed the after TO checklist and trying to diagnose what the ECAM was telling me we were over ZZZZZ1 [Intersection] and the aircraft was starting to turn to the next point on the SID which was ZZZZZ3 [Intersection].  The FO put turned the auto pilot on and placed the aircraft in heading mode and started a turn to ZZZZZ2 [Intersection].  We got the aircraft navigating to ZZZZZ2 [Intersection] but apparently it was not quick enough for the controller.  He chimed in and gave us a heading for ZZZZZ2 [Intersection].  We told him we were in the turn and navigating to ZZZZZ2 [Intersection] at that time.  Probably not a big deal.  No conflict with other aircraft or terrain.  No airspeed or altitude violations.  Just a lot of things happening at once during a busy phase of flight.  The result was we were a few seconds late to make our turn when our departure instructions were changed from what was given to us on the PDC.We complied with the ATC instructions as soon as we could.  It was a busy phase of flight and we were task saturated at the time. Getting an ECAM message for a pressurization fault was an added distraction.   I have been off work for almost a month due to COVID leave and this was my second trip since returning.   I was a little slow to respond but I've been off work almost X weeks and I'm still shaking off the cobwebs.Not pointing fingers; but a change to our SID would have been nice to know BEFORE we took off so we could expect; brief; and build the change into the FMS.  When taking off on [Runway] XXR via the ZZZZZ 4 RNAV SID you are over the first point; ZZZZZ1 [Intersection]; seconds after TO.   Having a change to the SID when approaching ZZZZZ1 [Intersection] only gave us a few seconds to react. column121: Coming to ZZZ on the ILS [Runway] XXR; we were continually slowed by ATC for spacing of traffic ahead and behind.  At about 1;200 MSL on glide path still IMC Tower told us to go-around.  I was PF and hit GA button and advanced power levers.  We went through missed approach procedure; but as flight guidance was attempting to be set the aircraft was also capturing the level off of 2;000 MSL so took a little longer to complete.  Meanwhile we were a little late on turning to 195 heading.  ATC queried us as we were in the turn.  We had also climbed to 2;180 feet before stopping and returning back to 2;000 immediately.  After we got settled ATC vectored us back to ILS with no further issues.  ATC told us they had to send us around because aircraft on final for parallel Runway XXL behind us had gotten .99 miles from us.  Spacing needed to stay a min of 1 mile.I should have paid more attention to altitude and started turn to 195 even if flight guidance wasn't quite set yet.  Also pulled back power sooner or not add as much to avoid going through altitude.
column123: During our arrival into ZZZ; when told to run base (heading approximately toward ZZZZZ [Intersection]); we were slowed to 170 KIAS.  We were maintaining 4;000 feet throughout base turn and intercept turn onto final.  Once established on final (approximately 20 NM from ZZZZZ1 [Intersection]) we were slowed further to 160 KIAS; with traffic approximately 4 NM in front of us.  Once we intercepted the glideslope; we maintained approximately 1;000 feet above the preceding traffic; but gained to within 3 NM distance.  Meanwhile; ATC vectored a airline flight onto final for [Runway] XXL close behind us.I told the First Officer (PF) to potentially fly a half-dot high on the glide slope to avoid any potential wake from the preceding aircraft.  Once we reached approximately 10 NM from ZZZZZ1 [Intersection] we were slowed further to 150 KIAS.As we continued down the approach; the TCAS showed us to be approximately 2.5 NM from the preceding traffic; with the traffic behind us close in trail (unable to tell the specific distance).  At approximately 600 AGL; ZZZ Tower issued a Go-Around; with nonstandard missed approach instructions (Right turn heading 195; climb and maintain 2;000).  The First Officer initiated the Go-Around and the Captain (PM) proceeded to re-program the Flight Guidance.Due to the light passenger load; the subsequent climb rate caused the Flight Guidance to immediately switch from a Climb indication to an Altitude Capturing indication; which caught the Captain off-guard; and he tried to re-configure the Flight Guidance back to a Climb indication.  The Flight Guidance again sequenced to an Altitude Capture indication.  At this point; the Captain (PM) noticed the aircraft was off course to the left approximately 35 degrees and was rapidly approaching 2;000 feet.  The Captain brought this to the attention of the First Officer while also simultaneously acknowledging ATC stating 'Turn right heading 195.'  The Captain also prompted the First Officer to reduce the power setting; as the airspeed was approaching maximum flap speeds.  The missed approach up to leveling off at 2;000 feet was all hand-flown (i.e. not with the autopilot).Once the aircraft was established on the appropriate heading; altitude; and configuration; ZZZ Approach vectored the flight around for a second attempt at the ILS 16R; which occurred without further incident.  In researching the First Officer's seniority; he has been here less than X years (Date).  After debriefing the flight; he stated that that was his first Missed Approach / Go-Around in the actual aircraft EVER.Since we had been slowed down significantly early during the approach; we knew we could expect to be sandwiched in between other aircraft.  However; we did not know that ATC needed only 1 mile separation between aircraft on parallel ILS approaches (told to us by ATC during our second attempt).  There was no mention of spacing requirements on our first approach.Due to 'COVID loads;' the aircraft type climb rates are very good; requiring steeper than normal attitudes so as to not exceed flap speeds.  This factor; combined with the First Officer's relative inexperience with missed approaches; caused a momentary loss of situational awareness by the First Officer.This required the CA to not only re-configure the flight guidance for a missed approach; but also ensure the First Officer did not over speed the flaps; communicate with ATC; and ensure the aircraft was following appropriate flight guidance (which was a non-standard missed approach).Also contributing to the loss in situational awareness was the altitude at which ATC issued the Go-Around:  600 AGL.  This caused a significant startle factor in both the Captain and First Officer.  Had ATC mentioned anything about a potential missed approach; we would have been much more prepared.Last-minute ATC-issued Go Around instructions (below 1;000 AFE); caused by inadequate spacing with simultaneous parallel approach aircraft.RECOMMENDATIONS:1.  ATC NEEDS to let crews know 'be ready for a missed approach' if there is potential for a spacing issue.  We were given our Go-Around instructions at 600 AGL.  This is a very high-risk area to issue a Go-Around; when spacing throughout the entire approach was tight.  Some sort of notification to us would have primed for a potential Missed Approach and therefore could have avoided any loss of situational awareness and subsequent heading / altitude deviation.2.  STOP ISSUING NON-STANDARD MISSED APPROACH INSTRUCTIONS.  The ILS [Runway] XXR's Standard Missed Approach instructions are to fly runway heading to 900 feet; then climb on heading 195 to intercept the ZZZ 210 degree radial; maintain 2;000 feet.  This is VERY similar to what we were assigned (heading 195; climb to 2;000 feet).  However; when we're given nonstandard missed approach instructions; not only do we have to interpret what it is ATC actually told us; but also program that into the Flight Guidance.  This programming is CONTRADICTORY to what our normal Flight Guidance programming procedures are.  Had ATC simply said 'fly the published missed approach;' that could've aided in our appropriate handling of the aircraft.LESSONS LEARNED:Don't trust ZZZ ATC to not screw up.  If spacing looks tight; brief a missed approach; even if it's done on the Final Approach Course.  Also; do not trust your fellow crew member to fly a perfect Missed Approach.  Watch them like a hawk for course; airspeed; and altitude management; and IMMEDIATELY speak up if there is even a minor deviation.

They responded that she was having issues and they were correcting her. The weather was broken at 3;300 ft. with few clouds at 2;400ft. The tower called me back asking if we could take the aircraft back. I asked if the aircraft was VFR or IFR. They stated IFR and I had them issue her a 270 heading and a climb to 6;000 ft. By the time the tower switched her back to us; the aircraft was westbound safely above the MVA.Since she needed special handling; I asked SDMR (Miramar) radar to work the aircraft back in and she landed safely. I truthfully never considered this to be a pilot deviation. And since the tower was talking to her at the low altitude; I knew they were handling the low altitude alert; getting her back on course and trying to see if she could cancel IFR. Only when the tower advised me she was IFR and needed to come back to us; did I consider her a special priority case. But also with my years of experience; I assumed she was a low hour IFR pilot that needed special handling.I didn't tell the OM immediately about the event because she was with the tower when she was at a low altitude and I knew they were handling the situation and would be filling out the appropriate paperwork on their end. Only a little bit later did I think; I should probably have the OM watch the replay and if anything; it may be declared an priority handling. The OM advised me it should have been a pilot deviation; but I still don't understand why a disoriented pilot would get a brasher. In the future; I won't assume the classification of an event; I'll ask the OM for their guidance.

column121: [Aircraft X] was being vectored for an ILS approach into BFI RWY (Runway) 14R by the Arrival West (1W); Arrival East (1E); Boeing Arrival (1D); and Paine (1P) sectors combined. As [Aircraft X] was being vectored traffic was issued for two VFR aircraft on 1200 codes transitioning both north and south through the localizer for Runway 14R. Due to this traffic I left [Aircraft X] at 3;000 ft. and obtained a point-out with SEA Final (1F). Despite this altitude; [Aircraft X] responded to a TCAS RA and; in an effort to protect the sea final approach course; I turned [Aircraft X] right to a heading 220. As [Aircraft X] turned southbound I observed a C172; [Aircraft Y]; being vectored for the ILS Runway 20 approach into PWT. I turned [Aircraft X] further right to a northwest heading; and measured the distance between [Aircraft X] and [Aircraft Y]. I observed approximately 3.3 miles between the two and since I had already issued the turn; I judged that sufficient separation and attempted to continue working to not fall further behind. [Aircraft X] turned slower than anticipated and caused a separation error between themselves and [Aircraft Y]. The root of this issue is the continual constant conflict between IFR jets into BFI and VFR aircraft transitioning through the localizer in both north and south flow. It is a well-known; persistent issue that has been thoroughly reported for several years. Several solutions have been proposed; but none have been adapted.The only fix for this issue is a restructuring of the Seattle Class B airspace to protect the finals in both directions at BFI. I have personally submitted redesigns for this issue that both protect BFI; and in doing so protect SEA; and allow VFR operations in and out of BFI; and are not unduly hindering to the general aviation community. If safety is truly the priority of the FAA and the Seattle region; changes will be initiated immediately. I understand the process for airspace changes take time; however; the changes will never take place if the process is not started. When the inevitable aircraft incident finally occurs; I hope that no one dies and I am not on position.
column123: [Aircraft Y] was on vector; at 2;500 ft.; to ILS Runway 20 approach at PWT. [Aircraft X]; controlled by W Sector; was on final to Runway 14R at BFI and experienced a TCAS RA with an uncontrolled VFR aircraft. The W Controller was already at a high level of complexity and volume as sectors were combined. The BFI Runway 14R final is in close proximity to PWT 20 mile final and is also underneath the Runway 16 finals at SEA. With limited options [Aircraft X] was turned to the southwest towards [Aircraft Y] with only 500 ft. between them. There are many factors that lead to this situation. These include airport proximities; sector overload; traffic complexity. There is also the issue of lack of controlled and protected airspace in and out of BFI. This is an issue controllers have been bringing to local management for years. The workforce is metaphorically beating our heads against a wall as we are asking for help and are given zero assistance in return. The final to BFI is underneath the SEA finals so we are forced to descend large; fast turbojet aircraft out of Class Bravo airspace into a very high VFR traffic area. This leads numerous TCAS situations. Many suggestions have been brought up through established reporting procedures so I will not waste my time typing them out again. The feeling of a lack of support for change is disheartening. There needs to be change made into airspace and procedures for aircraft landing at BFI; and this should be done for both arrival directions at BFI.

It also said if we couldn't return to ZZZ. We were still climbing on the SID out of ZZZ and I was still running the after Takeoff checklist. I finished the checklist up and consulted the FO. We were both confused by this message. I went ahead and asked ZZZ Departure if they knew anything about it. They did not know anything then handed us off to ZZZ Center. I checked in with ZZZ [Center]. I responded to Dispatch asking which facility it was that was closing. They replied with ZZZ1 TRACON and that it was to be closed from XA:30 to XB:30z. After getting this response. I asked ZZZ Center if they had any information on it. They checked with their managers and didn't know anything about TRACON in ZZZ1 shutting down. I messaged Dispatch saying that we wanted to continue and see how things progress since ZZZ [Center] said they didn't know anything. The reply we received was a strong negative. Dispatch wanted us to turn back to ZZZ [airport] right away. At this point in the flight; we were half way to ZZZ1 [airport]. We were estimated to arrive in the ZZZ1 [airport] area around XB:00z and had enough fuel onboard the aircraft to hold for a while before having to go to an alternate that we would have added. ZZZ2 [airport] was close and had good weather. Dispatch didn't give us any time to explore other alternatives; so we complied with their demand to return to ZZZ [airport]. The entire time; my FO and I were trying to figure out why we were returning to the airport. The workload was high on the return. The risk for making mistakes was pretty high on both our parts. Thankfully; ZZZ [airport] wasn't busy and was able to cut down a lot of our workload by giving us a descent and direct a fix on the approach. Once on the ground I was able to call Dispatch and talk. They closed the TRACON for COVID cleaning and only gave about 20 minute notice. It sounded like the dispatcher knee jerk reacted to it and wanted us on the ground as soon as possible. That's why she didn't want us to continue. I complied because it was a safe course of action to return and because I couldn't get Dispatch to agree to continue. So this was the safest course of action that was mutually agreeable.Suggest going over delay options inflight with dispatch and to not make the decisions for the flight crew. Dispatch should seek the advice of other dispatchers and most importantly of the crew to come up with many options and narrow it down the best one in a non-time critical situation as this. Freaking out and demanding an air return is not a normal way to run an operation. Dispatch should be made aware that there are many options available to crews to stay in the air longer while saving fuel. We could have easily slowed down and held until TRACON opened again or we could have diverted to ZZZ2 [airport] and picked up some more fuel if we needed to. Both would have been faster options of keeping the operations going while being safe.

column121: After making the turn at ZZZZZ intersection at FL300; we had a bleed 1 leak caution message. We ran the QRH and isolated system 1 and after a few minutes the message returned forcing us to continue the checklist through the descent portion. As we were waiting the three minutes before the descent; I initiated contact with AIRINC to reach dispatch as our ACARS had just lost coms most likely to it transitioning from one frequency to another. However with the need for a descent arising we lost communication with AIRINC before establishing any plan with dispatch. We requested priority handling with ZZZ Center and initiated a turn towards ZZZ as the thought of continuing towards ZZZZ or ZZZZ1 was the longest stretch of open water on the route and worst case scenario we were 60-80 miles north of the coast and ZZZZ2 was the closest [authorized] airport around if we had to continue the checklist and shut down the engine. As we got closer to ZZZZ2 while still 130 miles from ZZZ we were able to get an ACARS connection and get dispatch caught up on the situation. They did not realize how bad the situation was and thought we were closer to ZZZZ and ZZZZ1 than we actually were. As the aircraft was stable and the bleed temp of system 1 was around 50C; the system still held almost 70psi throughout the flight indicating one of the valves was still open and not properly closed; we confirmed with dispatch that it was safe to continue beyond ZZZ to ZZZ1 for an uneventful landing. Throughout the communication black out center was very professional and extremely helpful. I hope our thanks and appreciation for their work can be passed on to the controllers working with us.
column123: Prior to ZZZZZ1 [fix]; flight sent an ACARS message stating a Bleed Leak. Flight followed the QRH and three minutes later the message returned requiring a diversion to nearest suitable. There was quite a bit confusion going on because the flight also attempted to contact us via ARINC. The ARINC call failed; and the flight seemed to be in an ACARS dead spot as well. A few minutes later; I received multiple ACARS messages stating the flight was diverting to ZZZ. Per the flight's location; ZZZZ1 seemed like the closer; more suitable option and would've had the flight avoid going EOW (Extended Over Water) at 10;000 [with priority handling]. After running numbers for ZZZZ1; flight informed me over ACARS that ZZZ or ZZZ1 was closer. Although [our equipment] showed the flight over ZZZZ1; in reality the flight was 250 nm to the east; indeed much closer to ZZZ or ZZZ1. With that information; we decided ZZZ1 was a more suitable airport. In addition to runway length; ZZZ ops informed us that pax would not be allowed off the aircraft due to customs issues. Flight landed and blocked in.While I was certainly caught off guard and should've opened the QRH a few minutes faster; I was seriously hampered by our lack of equipment accuracy; ACARS dead spots; and ARINC being unable to raise the flight. It's hard to have an accurate; timely discussion over ACARS when both sides of the situation are working quickly on fixing the problems. If this were being done via remote dispatching; I do not wish to imagine the consequences. In the future; I will remind myself to remain calm and follow step-by-step actions to reach a quicker; less confusing end.

column123: Upon arrival a ZZZ; we received a new cabin crew for the flight to ZZZ1. ZZZ to ZZZ1 was to be the flight deck crew's second flight using the same aircraft. TO fully understand; I also went aft to see for myself.  The FA showed me in her manual; the proper location and orientation of the equipment.  I went back to the flight deck; verified the same information in the aircraft operating handbook.  I advised the Captain of the discrepancy.  Maintenance was called.   This discrepancy was found on the second leg of the day; while utilizing the same aircraft.  The location of the equipment was inverted in its actual location vs. the location as stated in the manuals.Cabin crew may have not been facing forward in the cabin when pre-flighting the emergency equipment.  While the equipment was stowed in an overhead bin correctly; with the proper associated placards; the actual location of the equipment did not match the location stated in the manual.  As an example Oxygen is to be in the port side overhead.  Its actual location was starboard.  It is possible that during a pre-flight that a crew member facing aft will simply associate that the oxygen is 'on my left side'   This aircraft also had new overheads and added capacity within the last year. During that change; the equipment may have been installed incorrectly. Cabin crew may need to have greater situational awareness as to the actual right and left side of the aircraft; regardless of their orientation within the cabin.

column121: Prior to initiating descent to ZZZZ1; the flight crew contacted ZZZZ Center and advised that we were unable to accept RNP-1 (Required Navigation Performance) arrival procedures. At this point; Center instructed the flight crew to fly an RNP-1 arrival despite having been informed of the incapability and the flight crew reiterated the fact they were unable to accept the arrival. Instead; the flight crew requested to fly direct to ZZZZZ waypoint for the start of the RNP RWY (Runway) XX approach. However; Center ignored this request and instructed the flight crew to fly direct to ZZZZ1 VOR and expect the VOR-A approach (Jeppesen Plate [Page]). When the crew once again requested to fly direct to ZZZZZ for the RNP RWY XX; Center repeated the instruction to fly direct to ZZZZ1 and expect the VOR-A approach without further acknowledgement or explanation of denial. The flight crew speculated that Center's refusal to assign the RNP approach was due to misinterpretation of the flight crew's inability to accept the RNP arrival; and efforts to clarify this case were also ignored by Center. The Captain (Pilot Monitoring) selected the VOR-A approach in the MCDU (Multi-Purpose Control Display Unit) and verified the route information while the First Officer (Pilot Flying) briefed the approach plate. At this time; both crew members observed what appeared to be inconsistencies between the MCDU approach database and the Jeppesen approach chart; specifically that the waypoint on Chart X did not match the waypoint shown in the MCDU routing; nor did the MCDU approach procedure indicate the required procedure turn under routing [FLP page] or Procedure Turn Info page [NAV - Page 2 - Patterns - Procedure Turn]. As the workload for the flight crew increased due to the inconsistency between chart and MCDU database; Center's refusal to assign a more effective approach; continuing descent towards mountainous terrain; and multiple segmented and non-standard clearances from Center that threatened to interrupt critical flight deck operations (notably the approach briefing); the flight crew elected to fly the VOR-A approach under raw data (green needles). All elements of the planned approach thus far mentioned became void after the flight crew received the hand-off to Approach Control who instructed them to fly direct to the airfield and complete a visual left-hand traffic pattern from overhead the runway.This flight crew highly recommends that an investigation be conducted into inconsistencies observed between the Jeppesen approach plate for the ZZZZ1 VOR-A Approach [Chart] and the MCDU database for the EJET fleet; namely the incorrectly labeled waypoint identified as ZZZZZ1 on the chart. This flight crew also highly recommends that effective communications be made between [Company] Flight Operations and the [Country] Air Traffic Control agency to ensure better understanding of which procedures [Company] flights are able to conduct and which procedures they are not; specifically the differences between RNP-1 'Arrivals' and RNP Approaches.

column121: After I briefed the A Flight Attendant; she asked if I would be wearing a mask whenever they came in the cockpit for a lavatory break. She then informed me that they would not enter to give us a break unless I wore a mask.  I then initiated calls to Dispatch and Operations to inform them of this problem. I regret the inconvenience this brought to passengers and company alike but this difference in protocol needs to be resolved without imposing non safety operational constraints on the cockpit.   I realize this is a novel disease and the information from the CDC and NIH [National Institutes of Health] is at times confusing and conflicting but believe that we should not take information to extremes and compromise operational safety.Lack of cohesive policy between Cockpit and Flight Attendant protocols that plays between personal concerns over operational safety.  I also feel misinformation or agenda also play a role on differences regarding relative issues.Keep the current Pilot protocol which works well and imposes minimal restrictions regarding operational safety.  Clarify Flight Attendant protocols so they do not conflict with the cockpit.   To each individual this pandemic is relative and emotional.  Any preconceived or personal perception cannot be satisfied by one fits all protocols; so I believe individuals overly concerned should be required to get the vaccine.  I will at the earliest opportunity get vaccinated for myself; family and coworkers.

column121: I departed ZZZ East ramp in [a] R22 with a private pilot student for pre-solo training at ZZZ1. We practiced emergency procedures en-route. After listening to ZZZ1 ASOS we determined to set up to enter the traffic pattern for Runway XX. 8 miles west from ZZZ1 we announced our location on CTAF and identified there were two airplanes in the pattern. We entered a 45 degree left downwind for Runway XX at ZZZ1 at 1;100 ft. and 75 kts. We announced and turned left base for Runway XX at 900 ft. and 60 kts. during which I could see Aircraft Y in a close left downwind. We announced turning final and turned final on Runway XX rolling out at 300 ft. AGL (900 ft. MSL) and 60 kts. I instructed the student to perform a normal approach to the approach end of Runway XX and terminate to a 3 ft. hover directly over the numbers (just as would be required during solo or a check ride). The student initiated his normal approach at the normal 10 degree angle required. I then heard Aircraft Y announce he was on final for Runway XX and had the helicopter in sight. I assumed the airplane had misjudged his spacing in the traffic pattern would either adjust his airspeed; perform turns for spacing; or go around. This is not uncommon and simple courtesy to the lower aircraft. On short final for Runway XX I looked out the left rear of the helicopter and could see Aircraft Y on short final right behind us. Aircraft Y asked me my intentions on CTAF. I replied that I intended to complete a landing to a hover at the approach end of Runway XX and then conduct a normal takeoff. Three things were on my mind. First; an aircraft on final and at a lower altitude always has the right of way. Second; I wanted the student to have the opportunity to conduct a normal approach to a hover just as he will be required to do during upcoming solo flight and his PPL checkride. Third; I need to access the student's ability to terminate the landing to a stationary hover. I asked Aircraft Y if he intended to 'go around' as it was clear either we would have to rush off the runaway; before completing the landing; or Aircraft Y could go-around. Aircraft X immediately replied with a complaint over CTAF stating that 'you little black helicopters are hogging the runways here and as a local pilot I can tell you that we are sick of you'. Just as I decelerated to a 3 ft. hover over the numbers for Runway XX I heard the sound of an airplane at high rpm overhead. I looked up to see Aircraft X directly over my helicopter about 20-30 ft. As he overflew me; he stated; 'he intended to report me to the FAA' and requested my name. I provided my tail number for his use as I did not want to provide my name over CTAF. I then contacted Aircraft Y over CTAF and requested that he not over fly my aircraft (for fear of collision) and that I will work with him to gain proper spacing in the pattern. Aircraft Y insulted me over CTAF and challenged me to a physical altercation. I instructed the student hover taxi to the parallel taxiway for Runway XX. I then noticed a pickup truck [surveying] our helicopter. I instructed the student to land on a nearby taxiway intersection near parking and go to idle. I exited the helicopter and approach the truck. I greeted the driver of the white truck with a handshake; introduced myself; and asked if there was an issue. I was told by the driver that they are reporting me to the FAA and they are just 'sick of our little helicopters that are difficult to see and tie up the runways for airplanes.' I sympathized with the driver but told him this is a public airport and that we have a right to conduct flight training here just as much as anyone; provided we all adhere to the rules. Furthermore; I told him that the airplane made an error in spacing by turning downwind; base; and final too quickly and essentially attempted to push me off the runway while conducting a landing. I told the driver that I am sorry this happened; but I feel the airplane did not adhere to Part 91 Right of Way rules to a lower aircraft on final. I gave the driver my number and told him I'd be more than happy to work with him on any future issues. We shook hands and went separate ways. I returned to the helicopter and returned directly to ZZZ. My chief concern with this incident is that the airplane should not have rushed or crowded another aircraft on final approach. A change in speed; turns for spacing; or a go-around were all options for the airplane pilot. Furthermore; executed a go around directly over and in close proximity to another aircraft is dangerous. What if I had directed the student to execute a go around or immediate takeoff (because we were being rushed on final and had climbed up into the airplane. As a military aviator and civilian helicopter and airplane pilot of over XX years I had always striven to fly with the utmost safety and friendliness. I preach this to my students; and I hope that all Aviators practice this as well. My goal is simply to encourage friendly; smart; and safe flying by all pilots at both ZZZ and ZZZ1.

The engine was immediately shutdown and we exited the plane. All electrical (master/alternator/ignition) was shut off.Co-pilot grabbed the fire extinguisher as we exited. After exiting the Tower was called. The Tower called the on-field fire company. Response time was about <5 min as the on-field company was sent to the wrong side of the field.We opened the engine cowling to see if we could identify a source and possible extinguish. No fire was evident in the engine compartment. The fire departments had not yet arrived.The prop began a very slow rotation as if the engine was trying to crank.We went to check to verify that the Master Switch was off. It was.Smoke from the panel was much heavier. Appeared to mostly originate from the pilot side.Close evaluation showed flames from top of the left side-wall upholstery.We used the fire extinguisher to extinguish the flames along the sidewall. The amount of extinguishing agent or time for a full discharge seemed less than expected (perhaps 30 seconds).Fuel valve was moved to Off.A person called indicating that the Emergency Locator Transmitter had activated. We began a search for the beacon to deactivate. Determined that it is behind the panel in the back of the passenger area behind the stretcher. Requires panel removal.Fire department from ZZZ arrives.They verify that there is no excess heat in area where the flames were extinguished or other locations.The mechanic we used at [Company] arrived and began assisting with assessment and possible causes and removal of the ELT.Fire departments determined that no action on their part was needed and departed. On the scene perhaps 30 minutes.No immediate cause was noted the A&P from [Company].We returned the plane to the hangar. We called [Company1] to see if they could determine any immediate cause. We were trying to decide if we needed to use [Company1] vs [Company2].The technician from [Company1] saw no immediate issues.We disconnected the ground side of the battery; wrapped and secured to make certain no contact could occur that might provide a power source.We left the airplane doors open or ajar to allow for ventilation and secured the hangar.The plan at this point was to have the aircraft moved to [Company2].
column123: We pulled the aircraft out of the hangar; shut the hangar doors and climbed into the cockpit for the start. We completed the normal procedures checklist setting the parking brake; received our SFRA (Special Flight Rules Area) clearance and shut down the avionics for start and noted the time as XA:X0 pm. The engine was primed with the auxiliary fuel pump; mixture was set to full rich and throttle to full open. The ignition was turned to start and as the engine began to turn over it ignited; and the throttle was retarded to slow the RPM to approximately 1000 RPM. As the RPM was beginning to stabilize; there was a backfire explosion and almost simultaneously smoke began pouring out from the defroster duct? at the left side of the wind screen and from underneath the dash panel by the PIC (Pilot-in-Command)'s rudder pedals. The smoke intensified filling the cockpit and the door was opened to relieve the smoke. Since the smoke was continuing; the mixture was pulled; the ignition was turned off removing the key and the battery and alternator switches turned off. Co-pilot exited the aircraft to determine a cause of the smoke and as he was investigating; I pulled the fire extinguisher from behind the co-pilots seat. I then exited the aircraft while he continued to walk around the nose of the aircraft looking for any source of fire. None was noted and the smoke was ventilating and dissipating. I called the tower on my cell phone to notify them of our situation and asked for fire assistance. I told Tower we were [at] the hangars on the east side just south of the terminal building at hangar. Tower took immediate action to alert the airport firetruck and ZZZ City Fire Dept. We did not see any evidence of a fuel fire or flames exiting the engine compartment although we did notice that the propeller began to rotate slowly for a few terms before stopping completely. The engine compartment was opened and there was no evidence of any fuel or oil leaks or any fire or smoke damage to the engine compartment. We went back behind the right wing and looking through the cockpit door; co-pilot noticed flames between the sidewall and left rudder pedal. He activated the fire extinguisher and sprayed the area of the flame; extinguishing it.While waiting for the fire equipment to arrive; I called Maintenance to ask them to have a mechanic come over and evaluate the situation. Fortunately; their lead was on the way to the east side and he arrived to look at the aircraft. Shortly thereafter the Airport Operations Director was first to arrive on scene and supervised the arrival of the fire equipment. The airport team was first ARFF (Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting) unit on the scene and were very professional in evaluating the situation so that no unnecessary action was taken. The smoke gradually dissipated and the aircraft was checked for residual hot spots; none of which were found. The fire equipment returned to their stations and the aircraft was hangared until it could be moved to the local maintenance facility.

column121: During this incident I was on a checkride and we ran a partial panel VOR Runway X approach with a circle to Runway XY. This is normally a Class D airspace but the Tower at ZZZ is currently closed due to COVID and this has presented some challenges to the arriving and departing process given we share the airport with airline operations. We made it to the left downwind for XY and there was a carrier aircraft holding short of XY getting ready to take the runway and they requested over CTAF for us to extend our downwind so they could takeoff. We extended our downwind about a mile or so and decided to turn base. About the time we were turning base there was another carrier that called a 10 mile final for XY. With the position report given; we were under the impression we had the appropriate spacing for us to get on the ground and off the runway before they reached the field. We continued and turned in for final and the carrier taking off was on the roll. I made position reports and heard nothing back that would indicate an issue. When we were on short final carrier made a 6 mile final call. I then made a position call for short final and we were within a half mile of landing. About the time I was roughly 100 feet over the runway threshold; the carrier aircraft called and stated; 'Aircraft on short final; we are going around and will be flying above you.' We landed safely and had to extend our ground roll down the runway to exit because another carrier aircraft was taxiing to Runway XY via Taxiway A and we had to taxi beyond where they were. That concludes the incident. I do not know how accurate the position reports were from carrier or their speed but there didn't appear to be an issue on spacing and if they knew they were catching us that fast they could have let us know and I would have executed a go-around. This was not a near-miss event and we never saw the aircraft near us on ADS-B radar or receive any traffic notification. It seems to be more lack of communication in a non-towered environment with busy airspace as a root cause. I think they were well aware of our location in front of them and didn't speak up to let us know how quick they were catching us. I feel like there should be some additional measures in place when a tower is closed at an airport like this with heavier volume and many different types and sizes of aircraft operating. Sharing an airport between GA and airline ops in a non-towered environment is setting the stage for incidents like this to happen and truly presents some added challenges and hazards.

Looking at my PFD information I noticed I was 15 NM from ZZZ at this time. Suddenly I heard a 'thump' noise coming out of the engine; immediately followed by a loss of power of about 25%-30%.  I immediately initiated a 180 degree turn towards ZZZ. After the turn; I confirmed oil indications were in the green; I switched fuel tank; I engage [the] high boost fuel pump; but nothing changed as far as engine power; RPM kept dropping slowing.  I contacted ZZZ and informed the controller that I was experiencing engine troubles and returning to ZZZ. Control clear me for VFR decent and handed me over to ZZZ Tower. I could maintain altitude but I had a constant low rate of decent of 300 feet-400 feet. I decided to stay as high as I could until short final into ZZZ. Because I was coming directly from the north I planned on a short approach. I tried to move the throttle to full power but wasn't getting any change in rpm. At that time I decided that if I wasn't going to be able to maintain altitude to make it to the runway; as I reach the shoreline; I would activate the BRS/CAPS (Cirrus Airframe Parachute System) of the Cirrus. I had enough altitude though and made it to base; heard another thumping noise from the engine; landed safely.  Tower told me while taxiing that there was a lot of smoke coming out of the bottom of the pane; the Fire Department Captain of the CFR (crash fire rescue) crew who was following me during taxi came up on the radio and told me smoke was increasing and advised to stop the engine immediately. I had reached the FBO ramp at that point. There was lots of oil dripping from all the front of the aircraft and after first quick observation with the manager of the maintenance facility in ZZZ we noticed pieces of the turbo lodged at the top of the right exhaust pipe. At this point; Cirrus Aircraft has taken over the process to find out what happened with this Continental TSIO-550K. They have informed us that the right side turbo shaft sheared off and pieces went through the engine and oil system. The engine is supposed to be sent to Continental for further analysis.

column121: I released Aircraft X for departure from BFI in a south flow. Aircraft X reported climbing to 2;000 ft. on the NIRVANA1 SID. I radar identified Aircraft X and climbed them to 6;000 ft.. As Aircraft X was climbing through 1;800 ft. I noticed that Aircraft X appeared to be making a right turn towards the SEA VOR and not following the NIRVANA SID. I instructed Aircraft X to 'turn left immediately; left turn heading 130.' At this point; Aircraft X was starting to converge with Aircraft Y who was on final approach into SEA descending through 1;100 ft. on the ILS Approach to Runway 16R. Aircraft X was about 1.5 miles laterally separated and 700 ft. vertically separated from Aircraft Y and converging. I observed Aircraft X achieve vertical separation from Aircraft Y; then saw the turn to heading 130 start occurring. I gave Aircraft X the Brasher statement. The pilot of Aircraft X stated that it 'looks like the activation for the autopilot for the NIRVANA1 did not take place.'I honestly don't know how to fix this problem; but it is a recurring; systemic issue. This is not my first event with almost identical circumstances; and many of my co-workers have had very similar events. Attempts have already been made to alter the SID; or issue an initial heading for aircraft departing BFI; but these events still occur. The typical issue is that pilots are filing SEA.J5 and though BFI is issuing the NIRVANA1 SID and a Preferred Departure Route that would join J5 from TAOMA or SUMMA; pilot error including unchecked autopilot actions that result in a turn to SEA VOR will immediately cause convergence at the same altitude as aircraft inbound to SEA within the final approach fix; as well as any aircraft departing SEA during that time. There is very little and very subtle warning; and immediate action is necessary to recover separation and end the rapidly worsening danger of the situation. I believe in most cases it is a result of an individualized pilot deviation; and I don't know how to end those completely. The only other solution I can think of would be to completely remove/decommission the SEA VOR.

I made a quick and unexpected stop which occurred during the flight attendant demo. (No one was injured but it did get the attention of the flight attendants). I realized that the Ground Crew probably failed to ensure the towing lever was in in the normal position after removing the bypass pin which would have enabled the hydraulic nose wheel steering. I called OPS and they sent a ramp person out to lower the lever. The nose wheel steering then worked normally. I suggest the following: ensure the Ground Crew at all stations verify the towing lever is in the normal position after removing the bypass pin and that a warning is added in section X.2 of the AOM that proper nose wheel steering operation should be verified as the aircraft taxis forward. I recommend that the AOM is revised in section Y-1 to read: 'fuel verified; final is clear'. This ensures that the proper fuel on board is verified at the last possible moment before taxiing onto the runway instead of at the beginning of the Before Takeoff Checklist so unexpected delays would not cause a takeoff below the min fuel requirement.

column121: In ZZZ we attempted to start number two engine using APU air and it spooled up abnormally slowly; and I noticed that the EGT seemed to lag. At 45% N2 the start stagnated and decayed until a 2.5% N2 decrease and Engine Fail indication on the ECAM. We stopped the start; then following guidance in our paperwork; we started number one (which also stagnated a little bit but then started normally) and then attempted a second start on number two using cross-bleed from the number one engine. We allowed the engine to spool up to 25.7% N2; then added fuel. At starter cutout; the engine hung again; dropping to about 43.2% N2 and hanging there before slowly spooling up to about 43.8% N2 when it timed out for the start and Engine Fail was indicated on ECAM again. Our Quick Reference Handbook said we could attempt a second start after the first hung start; but that maintenance action was required if the second start failed. At that point we requested a tug and BTB to our parking space. This is where Maintenance Control got involved. At first they suggested that we defer the APU bleed; however it was obvious to me that the air was not the problem (we used a separate source for each start); so I told him the APU bleed deferral was not sufficient. Then he suggested that a problem with the Integrated Drive Generator might be causing the hung start and suggested we defer that; and I agreed it could be tried. As part of the maintenance action during start the Inetgrated Drive Generator was disconnected and deferred; and the Airworthiness Release in the log book was signed off; then we continued getting the jet started and were on our way. During the flight the APU was running as required by the deferral; and at 36;000 ft. it automatically shut down. I attempted to start the APU; and on the second try; it started. I requested and descended to a lower altitude of 30;000 ft. and the APU operated normally for the rest of the flight. If I had not been able to start it; I would have had to advise ATC and divert. I wrote up the APU under a P code for momentary or transitory malfunction. In ZZZ1; maintenance checked the APU for any failure codes; did the repetitive inspection for oil quantity for the Integrated Drive Generator deferral; and signed off the APU. The FO (First Officer) and I discussed the situation and agreed that the APU was not malfunctioning and may have had a momentary problem with operating at high altitude. We accepted the jet for the leg to ZZZ2. With a fresh Airworthiness Release in the log book; we started the number one engine first; then started number two using cross-bleed at the request of maintenance. The number two engine came close to exceeding time limits; but did eventually spool up. We were filed for 33;000 ft.; and at that altitude the APU did the same thing--it shut down--and we were able to get it started again on the second try. We requested and descended to 29;000 ft. for the remainder of the flight. Again; the APU operated normally from there on; and again; I wrote it up with a P code for the shut down. I also made a comment in the logbook about the number two engine start; even though our flight paperwork said that comments for a successful start were not needed. There I made a note that the EGT from fuel introduction to the point where the start stagnated; then started to spool up; seemed abnormally low and was at least 50 degrees cooler at 45% N2 than the other engine. The stagnated start was evident from fuel introduction until after started cutout when it became apparent that the engine was not ready to continue the start on its own. The Integrated Drive Generator has nothing to do with the EGT during start. I suspect something else is going on here; perhaps a Electronic Engine Control problem with the fuel mixture at high altitude; or a sensor malfunction. On further reflection; I feel that the deferral of the Integrated Drive Generator was inappropriate for the problem we had; and I should not have accepted it. It created a problem where we could have been forced to request priority handling and divert. It is likely that whatever is wrong with our engine starts does not pose a safety of flight risk once we get the engine going; so it makes no sense to do a deferral that could compromise safety. Until this is figured out; the guidance needs to be specific and it needs to go out to everyone in the maintenance and crew pipelines and it should be operations friendly. My recommendation is that everything in the fuel system be checked in case it is causing the starting problem for cold engines at high altitude. I think that the bleed system is less likely to be the issue because of the low EGT I saw during all four start attempts on that engine. I also recommend that maintenance be able to attempt at least one more start before the aircraft is taken out of service; and that crew get more guidance concerning the problem. 'Maintenance action' is not enough to let a Captain know what to expect or what to accept. I also have felt for a long time that our systems manual has been scrubbed of a lot of detail about systems with which we do not directly interact; so we are less able to make informed decisions and instead have to rely on experience. That will not always save us from making the wrong call. Everyone in this situation acted in good faith; and I am not writing this report to cast any doubt on anyone. I only want to point out a safety issue that we can avoid in the future.

column121: I believe complacency played a role in this error. I am always checking and double checking my work but unfortunately I missed an important piece of information on the Center of Gravity (CG) and Passenger Count (PC) data. Next time I will slow down and thoroughly check my work without rushing and recognize my complacency.We arrived to our aircraft in the morning to perform our duties for the first leg out of two for the day. Boarding was complete and I received the cargo sheet and CG/PC Data from the gate agent. As I plugged the numbers in for departure I noticed the passenger count seemed low.  Thinking that it was due to the slow season and COVID I continued to run the numbers for our takeoff data. With the low passenger count I figured we were going to also need a ZFW reset from the dispatcher. I confirmed with the Captain and went ahead and contacted Dispatch with our new ZFW and confirmation of our CG. New numbers were sent back and we took off uneventfully.While in cruise the Captain requested a lavatory break. Upon his returned; he voiced his concern with the passenger count from what he saw in the cabin while checking our CG/PC. That is when we realized that the incorrect CG/PC was given to us. As we were starting our decent; the Captain transferred the controls to me while he referenced the COM and tables to calculate our correct weight along with the landing data and Vapp. As a precaution we also added few knots to the Vapp. The Captain completed the tasks and I confirmed that all the information was correct and within safe parameters for a safe landing.  We had sufficient runway and the field was VMC at the time of landing. The landing was uneventfully and we continued to the gate.

column121: I was notified of my reserve assignment at XA:00 by Crew Scheduling. They stated when they called me to pack a bag because I might not be home as the airplane we were to repo back to ZZZ was still broken. They assigned me a XB:00 showtime on the phone. I however noticed later my show time was modified to XC:00. Either way I arrived at the airport and sat down at the gate that was on my schedule. The First Officer texted me and stated the hotel van was just pulling up. At XC:00 when no gate agent was around the gate area at [Gate] I called my Dispatcher at [the] desk. I asked if he could get someone to let us down to the plane. After placing me on hold he stated we would be originating from the maintenance hangar. He asked the maintenance department where we needed to go to be picked up. They stated [Gate1]. He then started to fill me in that we would be hauling two mechanics; their tools and few other miscellaneous items. We met the maintenance personnel at [Gate1] and was transported to the airplane near the maintenance hangar. Upon arriving we noticed a 5 gallon bucket of Skydrol hydraulic fluid in front of the airplane along with what appeared to be a hydraulic pump and some hoses that were located in an open top box. The maintenance personnel stated that Maintenance Control okayed this being transported onboard the airplane. The FO (First Officer) went up to the flight deck and stowed her bags. I called the pilot on duty to get some direction on this 5 gallon container and was also hoping he could put me in touch with the hazardous materials specialist. The pilot on duty tracked him down and he okayed it based on being less than 5 gallons and it was in a sealed container. The box with the pump; hoses and other miscellaneous items was also OK. I question that now based on the [Operations Manual]. The last bullet point is my question. While I was inspecting the cabin's emergency equipment the FO notified me that the maintenance personnel stated that there was a substantial amount of items loaded in the forward cargo bay accumulating to about 300 lbs. I asked if the items happened to get weighed as they went on. The answer was they did not and someone was going to come out with a scale to unload and weigh the items. I called the pilot on duty to confirm needing this information. The maintenance personnel did provide the information after unloading and reloading the cargo bay. During this time the 5 gallons of Skydrol was brought into the cabin and placed between two first class seats. The box with the pump also was. I called the scheduling and asked to speak to the manager on duty. I was connected. After explaining the situation to him he stated he would call me back. The maintenance personnel placed the Skydrol in a first class seat and placed a seatbelt around the container. Sometime after this they place an orange ratchet strap around this bucket also. After some time Duty Officer called me back. At this time Maintenance removed the Skydrol and the pump from the aircraft and stated we would be going without it. He stated they would remove it and place it below and secure it. He instructed us not to leave if it was placed below and not secured. At some point after this call with Duty Office crew scheduling called me questioning where I was at and why we have not departed yet. I explained to them we were on the airplane and attempting to safely depart after everything was in order. I called the Dispatcher and inquired about a new release because our release was timing out. We decided to add fuel to the airplane at that time because the APU has been running for along time now. While waiting for the fuel truck to arrive the maintenance personnel drove back up to the plane and loaded the Skydrol and the pump into the forward cargo bay. I went to look at how these items were secured. They were just sitting in boxes and not secured. I took a few pictures to send to Duty Office and the maintenance personnel asked me if this was OK. I stated I was told it had to be secured and that I was send this pictures to my manager. The maintenance personnel stated they would remove it from the plane and we could depart. The items were removed. While waiting for the fuel truck we also inquired with scheduling on what hotel we would be staying at in ZZZ1. They stated that we would be flying back because the 14 hours from our reserve availability period only was restricted to passenger flying and since this was Part 91 flying we were good for 16 hours. We were told we would have to call off if we didn't want to work the flight back. The fuel truck arrived and we departed soon after. The remainder of the flight was uneventful. We concluded the flight in ZZZ1 at XD:00.We were sent to the hotel and was scheduled for a min rest overnight. We called when we reached the hotel and had the show time adjusted to allow us 10 hours.

column121: For the ILS Runway 04R at ZZZ; performance numbers were run for a Flaps 30 landing with a good stopping margin at Autobrakes 3. ATIS winds were calling approximately 070/13 - no gusts. Upon switching to Tower at ZZZZZ on the localizer course and tracking the glideslope; Tower cleared us to land with winds now gusting to 20. As PF (Pilot Flying); I elected to add 4 knots to the Vtarget and as an added Safety measure at ZZZ; I selected Autobrakes MAX to compensate for a slightly increased approach speed. The PM (Pilot Monitoring) attempted to quickly re-run the performance data; but the gusts were not yet accounted for in the METAR. Rather than going heads down any longer inside 1;000 feet AGL; we agreed a 4-5 knot addition to VTarget and using Autobrakes MAX would be more than sufficient to account for the gust factor.At approximately 500 feet AGL; we received a GPWS Too Low Flaps Alert. The PM immediately called for the go-around and it was initiated. A quick scan of the flap handle and I realized that I had neglected to call for Flaps 30 from a Flaps 15 setting; and the Before Landing Checklist was not run. We were quickly vectored around for another uneventful ILS. The minor distraction of adding a gust factor and changing the Autobrakes setting sent me out of a normal approach configuration sequence and we ended up both missing the final flap setting and subsequent checklist.With the normal ZZZ procedure of not contacting (and often not switching to) Tower until reaching the fix at about a 5-mile final; it's possible for us to miss out on cues to changing weather on the ground. We were number 3 or 4 in a sequence of landings on 04R. Had we switched to Tower five or more miles sooner; we may have caught the gusting winds earlier and had more time to type in the adjusted winds and send away for the performance numbers prior to 1;000 feet AGL. This was another series of events combined with mild fatigue that led to poor task prioritization on our parts.
column123: The short version is that we got 'Too Low; Flaps' at 500 feet because we were at Flaps 15. We went around. Planned winds were 070/7. Tower winds were 070/12G20. I re-ran the performance landing numbers at 1;500 feet; but did not override the METAR and got back the numbers for 070/7. The PF (Pilot Flying) chose to add 5 knots to VTarget and we agreed to go from Medium to Max braking and continue.There is no guidance I am aware of as to when we would be required to re-run our landing numbers. I should not have tried to re-run the landing numbers at that point. That would have eliminated the distraction that led to not selecting our planned final flaps or running the Before Landing Checklist.

column121: With about 4 hours to go before landing; I had just emerged from the crew rest bunk when Lead Flight Attendant asked me if I could have the flight deck crew wear a face mask when a Flight Attendant was in the cockpit in flight. I told her no for the safety of flight reasons. I did not add anything further.I personally was not going to wear a face mask in the cockpit since I would be in the cockpit for the rest of the flight. I am required by the FAA on my medical 'Must wear corrective lenses; possess glasses for near/intermediate vision.' Since my glasses fog up every time I wear any type of face mask I know that wearing a mask at my flight deck seat is a safety of flight issue. About two hours later when the Lead came to in to give us a restroom break we; First Officer and I; offered her an N95 mask to wear for her safety and set it on the pedestal for her. She did not put it on and chose to wear what appeared to be a non-N95 certified black cloth mask.

column121: While in line for takeoff on Taxiway for XXR; we received a notification from the flight attendants that the cabin was filling up with smoke which was coupled with a foul odor akin to burning rubber. We smelled the odor at the same time the flight attendants notified us of the smoke. I asked them if it was thick enough to block view of the back of the aircraft and if they thought we needed to evacuate right away. They answered no to both questions. I then told them that we would be moving to a cargo ramp to run a QRH and if they thought at any point we would need to evacuate while moving to call me back and we would stop immediately. I also informed them that the next time we stopped would be the last time we would move without calling them and that once stopped; if they felt the need to evacuate; they were to do it. We taxied to the cargo ramp just south of taxiway after alerting ATC that we were [requesting priority handling] and would be pulling off to the side to run a QRH and to have the fire trucks standby. We ran the entirety of the smoke fire fumes QRH; which had us deactivate the PACs (Air Conditioning Packs) and close the bleed valves. We elected to not drop pass O2 or go on O2 ourselves as we were not having any adverse reactions; but just dealing with an unpleasant smell in the flight deck. We called the flight attendants at this time and asked about the passengers' condition and they stated that everyone was fine. The smoke slowly dissipated throughout the rest of the event. At this point; we decided to go back to the gate as the smoke was no longer producing from the vents and the passengers were not complaining about any issues when asked. We cancelled [priority handling] but requested that crash rescue follow us to the gate. Once arriving at the gate with the aircraft shut down and the flight deck door open and main cabin door; we had one woman reportedly having bronchitis coughing to a large extent. She was the first off. I was not aware she had an adverse reaction until pulling into the gate. We deplaned everyone as quickly as possible and had Maintenance confirm that PAC 2 was the culprit. To my knowledge; all passengers refused medical attention. We later got another aircraft and had all passengers board.The probable cause was something happened with the Right PAC as we were single engine no APU taxiing to XXR with Engine 2 running.

column121: TCAS RA on arrival into ZZZ [airport]. Assigned descent to 7;000 feet and vectors to final by ZZZ Approach. We reached 7;000 feet and noted approach was extremely busy where the Controller was being stepped on seemingly more than half of her transmissions. While level at 7;000 feet the TCAS noted a proximate target converging from 1 o'clock; 400 feet below. We attempted to contact Approach but there was zero opportunity to get a word in due to the sheer amount of communication on frequency. I advised the Captain PF to 'get ready' while we attempted to locate the aircraft visually. A few seconds later the TCAS noted traffic and ordered a very shallow climb. I announced to ZZZ Approach that we were responding to an RA; but I believe I was blocked; the frequency still jammed with constant communication. A very short time later the controller issued traffic to us and I again advised 'Climbing on RA.' Controller replied 'Roger' I believe and the event was over shortly after. We returned to 7;000 feet and were vectored for the visual; but the controller still had to vector us around multiple VFR targets on our way to the runway. Most significantly we were cleared for the visual approach; but were restricted to flying and intercepting between 5 and 7 NM from the airport due to area traffic. This caused a perceived limitation that pilots are not used to. The CA/PF then overflew the Localizer slightly attempting to maintain these limitations. The aircraft was clearly stable by 1000 feet and we continued in to land; but this was following an incident due to the same cause.Cause was due to the intense level of traffic in ZZZ Approach's airspace. I spoke with a contact at ZZZ [Approach] later who noted the Controller had 15 active aircraft not including the VFR targets attempting to get clearance from the closed airspace; Practice IFR traffic; and VFR flight following requests. The Controller was doing an excellent job and maintained a very professional demeanor throughout. There was just no reasonable way for Controller to maintain communications with the volume of aircraft. I am not sure; but this could have been a result of reduced staffing due to COVID. Maybe there was an East and West ZZZ [Approach] sector available; but no staffing to accommodate. My suggestions would be to either split ZZZ Approach or to draw a new arrival for ZZZ airport to reduce the amount of communications and possible routes needed for the controllers.

column121: Flew ZONNA1 arrival to TUS. I was PF (Pilot Flying) and did the arrival briefing prior to descent which included terrain hazards and the MSA. Both pilots had terrain selected. Approach control gave us a clearance to turn right to 270 and descend to 10;000' for sequencing. Soon after this clearance we entered IMC. Passing north and abeam Mt Lemmon at about 10;300'; we got an EGPWS TERRAIN PULL UP warning. I executed the EGPWS Recovery Action. Almost immediately we went VMC. After passing the MSA of 10;700 and visually verifying terrain clearance; I resumed normal flight; leveled at 11;000' and informed ATC that we had responded to a GPWS terrain warning. They acknowledged and gave us a descent to 9000'. Remainder of flight was uneventful.Either the Terrain system gave us a false alert or we were given a clearance to descend below the radar minimum altitude. We never got any indication on the Terrain display. STAR page showed us north of Mt Lemmon and the terrain depicted around it. While we had good terrain awareness; I should have queried Approach about an IMC descent below the Sector MSA.I recommend a Radar Minimum Altitudes chart be included in the Jeppesen pages for TUS.

column121: ATC turned us onto the approach while still at 4;000. Told us to 'maintain 3;000 till established cleared ILS [Runway] XXL. FO (First Officer) put in 3;000 in the altitude selector and I acknowledged it. Once established; instead of selecting 2;700 feet for the FAF altitude he rolled the altitude selector to 3;300 and started a slow descent. Stated he was going to just control the altitude himself. I thought that was strange; but let him do it figuring it was just a technique he liked to do.As we approached 2;700 feet; he was still descending at ~700 FPM; so I realized he was going to blow through the altitude. I told him he needed to stop descending and return to the FAF altitude until we intercepted the GS. The first time I said this he seemed confused and didn't really do much. I said more sternly that we needed to climb back to the proper altitude. This time he initiated a climb back to the proper altitude and we were still stabilized and fully configured by 1;000 feet AGL. ATC did issue us a low altitude alert as we were climbing back to the proper altitude and we got a single 'Glideslope' callout from the aircraft.The cause was the FO's improper use of the altitude selector and VS (Vertical Speed) mode. Contributing was me allowing him to do the method he did instead of asking him to just put the FAF altitude in the altitude selector till GS intercept.I should have insisted that the FO put the FAF altitude in the altitude selector; especially in IMC. I also told him afterword's that he could have just stayed at 3;000 once established and intercepted the GS from there since at that point we were already close to GS intercept.
column123: Cleared ILS [Runway] XXL; we were given an intercept heading and told to maintain 3;000 feet. The Controller kept us close and fairly high before clearing us for the approach. We were at 4;000 feet when cleared. Captain was PM (Pilot Monitoring); First Officer was PF (Pilot Flying). Once established; PF started down with vertical speed to capture glide slope by 2;700 feet at ZZZZZ. PF moved altitude knob up to 3;300 feet from 3;000 feet instead of to 2;700 feet causing us to go below published altitude by almost 500 feet. Was immediately corrected and aircraft was stabilized. Given a close proximity intercept; task saturation was high with intercepting; radio communications; and configuring aircraft. Should have cross checked better and stated intentions more clearly (PF to PM).If crew starts to feel rushed or task saturation is high; ask for longer final or a more stable intercept from ATC. Never let cross checking suffer due to task saturation; should always come first. PM should state approach intention more clearly while getting established. Don't have tunnel vision (Example Focusing on getting configured and not having correct altitude set).

column121: Operating flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. After landing on Runway XX; exited on Taxiway A and turned left on Taxiway C; and believing that Tower had actually cleared us to taxi to the gate; we started to slowly taxi; when Tower called us and asked that we call Ground. We called Ground and he stated 'You started to taxi without calling us; and crossed Runway XX; which is an active runway'. We had barely started to taxi on C. We had read the NOTAMs; and in fact; Runway XX was 'NOTAMed CLOSED'; so it could not be an 'Active' at all. Regardless; we asked Ground for taxi clearance to the gate; and received clearance to the gate via 'C.' We did not want to argue with the Ground Controller; but we do know that Runway XX is Closed at ZZZ1; so it's not Active in any way. We asked the Ground Controller if we should 'expect any paperwork'; and he said 'no'. I do not believe we did anything wrong; but it's better to be safe and proactive; and learn from our possible mistakes.We had flown into ZZZ1 previously (a few days before) and due to controller shortages or consolidation of ATC positions (During COVID-19 times); the Tower normally gives us the taxi instruction after we cleared the landing runway. This time; we cleared the runway and thought we had heard the Tower tell us to 'taxi to the gate' (as they have been doing recently). We started to slowly taxi on Taxiway C and that's when Tower asked us to 'call ground for taxi;' something they had not done in the past 3-6 times we had landed there recently. So; probably I was expecting the same ATC procedures to happen; but regardless; in the future; will come to a stop on the taxiway and not move until further taxi clearance is received.I would suggest to avoid being complacent; and instead of expecting the same type of ATC handling from small airports as we may be getting every day during COVID-19 (combined controller positions; where there is perhaps combined Tower and Ground; or even Approach/Tower/Ground Controller); and instead treat it just like a busy airport.

column121: I returned to work after a 3 month absence. I am still qualified on the module. I was assigned as the trainer to Mechanic Y. I was training him on the stator case assembly. I demonstrated how to tighten each vane segment foot bolts. The procedure that I was taught; and which had been in use as long as I can remember; was to slide the case and vane assembly; so that approximately one third of it overhung the table surface. Then the bolts were tightened from below with a ratchet with a socket and long extension; repositioning the case and vane assembly as necessary until all bolts were tightened. At the time of the incident; I was not in the work area; having gone to the restroom.Support the case with a hoist and sling before tightening the bolts. This should be added to the job card.
column123: One week after return from 3 months off and being the first time working on this unit as a trainee.On Graveyard shift I was working on the module and order # XXXX. I was tightening the bolts of the vanes. The bolts are tighten from the bottom while the case sits on the table. To access the bolts part of the case is moved slightly beyond the edge of the table. I was sitting in a chair with rollers while I was tightening the bolts. The chair moved; the wrench and its extension did come off the bolt head causing the case to slide off the table and fall to the floor approximately 30 inches.There was no visible damage to the case because it fell directly on my arm and that cushioned the fall. Inspection will be called to inspect the unit.I would add to the job card to support the case with a hoist before tightening the bolts. Or developing a fixture that would allow to reach the bolts from the bottom without having to move part of the case off the edge of the table.

column121: I was performing a functional test of the stall protection computer. On step XX; the task tells you to put the aircraft in the weight off wheels configuration. On the first page of the task for putting the aircraft in the weight off wheel configuration you are told to pull and tag Circuit Breakers (CB): CB P-1; A12; A13; A14; G14; & CB P-1 lower U7. On the second page to pull and tag CB P-1 lower T7; T8; T9; CB P2; N6; H8; CB P2 lower S1; V5 and CB P-5; B10.I pulled the circuit breaker on the first page but failed to pull the circuit breakers on the second page of the task. On the next step on the functional test of the stall protection computer you are told to set the air data test set to 90 kts and the altitude to 18;000 feet. During this step is when we noticed smoke coming from the left pitot probe. I ran out to check the pitot probe and saw that I melted the pitot probe test head to the pitot probe. I quickly removed heat from the pitot probe.To pay more attention to the Aircraft Maintenance Manual and to double check all the correct circuit breakers are pulled.
column123: While performing a functional check of stall protection system we were required to put aircraft in weight off wheels and put aircraft at 18;000 feet and 90 kts using pitot static test set. During the test; the test head on the LH (Left Hand) pitot static probe was melted to the probe.While performing the test I looked up and saw smoke coming from LH side of nose.My partner found the task in the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) and pulled breakers but failed to read far enough down and only pulled the breakers for the RH pitot static probe. Causing the heat to still be on to the LH probe.We quickly removed heat from probe.Pay more attention to AMM task and I should have double checked the CBs my partner pulled.

column121: While descending into LRU airport; I heard ATC call to another aircraft (Aircraft Y) that was also inbound. I was arriving from the west; and Aircraft Y from the north; North West area. I could see him on ADS-B. While Aircraft Y was behind me; he was much faster; however ABQ (Albuquerque) center had him climb and then hold as I continued my descent. Leveling off at my assigned altitude; I was still unable to see the airfield; despite the field reports of better weather. I was; however; still several miles away. At about the same time; Aircraft Y called in; cancelling his IFR stating that he had the airport in sight. ATC cancelled his IFR as he stated he was now in VMC. I then asked ATC for a report from the Aircraft Y; as he was able to see the field and I was not; despite me being at a lower altitude. (I asked hoping I would break out of the clouds soon; or find an area where I could; such as where Aircraft Y came from). Quickly after; I did get the airport insight below me and was able to descend VFR. I also cancelled my IFR at that time.Being almost over the airport; I extended away from it and then I called entering the Left downwind for runway 26. (The winds at the time were reported as being 240 at 22 - 27; making runway 22 or 26 the best options.) I then called a base turn; and then final. At that time I also heard Aircraft Y call in for the RNAV for runway 12. Being as he cancelled IFR with no mention of practicing approaches; I anticipated his landing before me; with no conflict. As I came on short final for runway 26; I heard Aircraft Y call out that he was going missed from 12; which would then be intersecting my landing path. At that moment I looked up and saw Aircraft Y just ahead and to my right; above me; but very close. I would estimate within 200-300 feet. Already being close to the ground; no evasion action could have been taken. I landed and taxied into the ramp. Shortly after; Aircraft Y landed on a different runway and parked as well. I called the center to report the incident and express my concern and safety issue that had occurred.
