column121: With a pre-checkride PPL (Private Pilot License) student; we were discussing pre-takeoff briefings and engine out after takeoff procedures. For our flight that day; I decided it would be good practical experience to get the student thinking about emergency landing options after an engine failure on takeoff. I believed it would be beneficial to see in reality what the landing options would look like with engine loss shortly after takeoff.The student performed a normal takeoff. Shortly after handoff from Tower Controller to Departure Controller (estimated 550 [feet.] AGL); I reduced the throttle to idle and instructed the student to pitch for best glide. I asked the student where an attempted landing might be possible based on our altitude and glide. I then asked if a 180 degree turn back to the departure runway seemed possible. After asking these two questions; I pushed the throttle back to full power and resumed normal climb. We continued to discuss procedures for engine failure on takeoff.Shortly after this; I noticed that our heading had deviated from the assigned runway heading by about 40 degrees to the south. Before I was able to correct; the Departure Controller assigned us an on-course heading. A few minutes later; Departure Controller asked if we had experienced an issue or needed assistance. I did not think much of it at the time and responded that we didn't need assistance.I later learned (from a phone call from Tower Controller to the flight school) that the Tower Controller had heard the engine power reduction and had seen the turn; and assumed an engine failure. I am not fully aware of what was experienced on the Tower Controller's end; but it is clear that my decision to practice an engine out procedure on takeoff caused a distraction to the Tower Controller that may have ended up impacting safety.Additionally; the fact that I did not notice the aircraft had turned 40 degrees to the south indicates that practicing that maneuver caused me to become more distracted that I had realized; or expected to be.Remedy:-Notify or request to Tower/ATC of my intention to practice any sort of maneuvers/procedures that are out of the ordinary from what is expected.-Be more aware of the probability of distraction while practicing any sort of maneuver during a high workload phase of flight.-Consider making engine out on takeoff procedures a ground instruction maneuver rather than in-flight.Human performance/Judgement:Ultimately; I made a bad judgement call by practicing an unusual/unexpected maneuver in controlled airspace. I did not expect or anticipate any disruption to the tower procedures; but I should have been more aware and given more thought to how my maneuvers would affect ATC.

column121: I was deadheading on Aircraft X. I identified myself to the A Flight Attendant (FA) (as I always do) as a safety and security asset.The flight was nearly full.  During boarding a man who I later learned was Mr. X approached my seat.  He was wearing a camo gaiter around his neck which was partially covering his mouth but was not covering his nose. As he approached; I identified myself as a crew member and politely asked him to pull his mask up over his nose.  He complied but said that I should pinch my mask tight over my nose.  I didn't quite hear what he said so I queried him.  He said; 'You should pinch down on your nose to close the gap at the top of your mask.'   My mask was an NP95 which had no gaps anywhere around my face.  It was my sense that the man was being sarcastic and antagonistic.  I said nothing further to him.I advised the FA A what happened before we pushed back.  She told me that the man had boarded without his face covered and was told to cover his face.  Thus he had pulled his face covering off his face between the time he boarded (when he was told to put it on) and the time he approached me; which was no more than thirty seconds. He clearly had no intention of complying with the mask policy.  FA A asked me to brief the Captain about the incident and asked if I would talk to the CSR agent whom she wanted to speak with Mr. X. I agreed.  Before departure I walked into the jet bridge and spoke with FA A and the CSR.  I briefly explained what I observed and what he said to me then I went back onto the airplane and took my seat.  A short time later I observed Mr. X walk back down the aisle past me.Sometime during the flight FA A advised me that Mr. X had been [violating other regulations].  She advised me that Mr. X demanded to know the crews names (including mine) but that she did not give him any names. She was clearly concerned about this and I could see how his actions were distracting to the flight crew and were thus interfering with their duties.  She told me that she was going to have CS meet the aircraft and asked me to stay as a witness.  FA A as well as the rest of the inflight crew were nothing but polite and professional the entire flight; when I observed her dealing with Mr. X or otherwise.After leaving the aircraft I was standing in the jet bridge and spoke with a CS Supervisor.  Mr. X walked by me and said in an aggressive and hostile tone; 'I want your name.'  I told him that I could not give it to him and that I could not speak with him about this matter.  He again demanded my name and moved closer to me.  I backed up.  He then raised his camera and said; 'I'm taking your picture.'  I stated; 'Do not take my picture.'  He said; I'm taking your picture.'  I quickly turned around and walked around the jet bridge corner toward the aircraft door.   I do not know if he took my photograph or not but felt that his forcing his camera in my face was one of belligerence; hostility; and aggression.  I felt threatened.  All of this simply because he was asked to properly wear his mask.  After the CSR Supervisor and Mr. X walked into the terminal; I remained in the jet bridge as I did not want to encounter Mr. X again.When the CSR Supervisor walked back onto the jet bridge; I explained to her that I could not have my photograph taken and suggested that if he loitered around the terminal waiting for me that she please call law enforcement.  I asked her if she felt he was being hostile and or belligerent.  She agreed that he was.  After some time; Mr. X left the area; and I departed the terminal.Based on his behavior and actions I would strongly urge that Mr. X is not allowed to fly on our airline in the future.

column121: It wasn't supposed to be a very long leg or a long day. The plan was to fly from ZZZ to ZZZ1; grab a quick snack and go to ZZZ2 for the overnight and good food. But; that wasn't what happened.  Snow flurries forced us into unplanned deicing. Bad alternates required reworking and refueling. In the middle of deicing; a sudden snow squall sent visibility plummeting and negating any holdover times. New takeoff alternates then had to be amended onto the paperwork; and re-validating required new paperwork. To describe our departure out of ZZZ as a struggle would be an understatement. But; ever so slowly and methodically; we did eventually depart to ZZZ1. It was on arrival that we were notified that our overnight had changed and to contact scheduling on the ground. So; you can imagine that when we landed in ZZZ1; we were mentally bruised; hungry; tired; and on edge. The landing was normal; as was the taxi to our planned gate. What confused us is what we saw upon turning to face south; looking at [Gate X]. There was nothing. No rampers; or wands or even lights. It was a completely empty and dark. I set the parking brake and asked my FO (First Officer) to send another in range report and commented that we should probably call ZZZ1 OPS and see if they had changed our gate. FO dutifully called OPS on the number two radio so I dialed the north ramp frequency into radio one to monitor. At that exact moment the ACARS message returned as my FO was repeating what OPS had just said; gate change to [Gate Y]! I released the parking brake and began a slow turn to the right when I realized I wasn't at an outstation in the middle of nowhere or on an uncontrolled ramp. I had lost all situational awareness and was in the middle of ZZZ1 moving without permission! I immediately stopped the aircraft and called North Ramp with the gate change. He replied yea there was a gate change and 'did i just do a 180?' I don't recall saying much before he asked 'and are you still moving???' I immediately replied we were not moving. At that point I was told I should never; ever do that and that he had numerous aircraft with beacons on trying to push. I should have apologized right then but instead fumbled though the gate change and having the pushing aircraft in sight. I still can't believe I would make such stupid mistake. I can't believe I didn't apologize. I was just beat up and wanting desperately to just take a five minute brake. Instead I let my guard and awareness down which led me to make a very stupid move.

column121: I was cleared on the RNAV departure to maintain 3;000 feet. When loading the departure an additional fix not noted on the chart was loaded in. I reloaded the departure to ensure I had the proper transition and the fix appeared again. This fix is not on the RNAV departure. I later realized that this is how the G1000 creates additional heading legs; but at the time I did not realize this and so I deleted the extraneous fix to have the flight plan reflect the proper departure.  After reaching 1;000 feet the departure states to turn left heading 295; which I had briefed. I began turning right and was adjusting the heading bug and noted it was taking a long time to reach 295 before I realized that I was turning the wrong direction. I corrected and initiated the turn back to the left heading 295. I was about 20 to 30 degrees off from the heading when ATC called and asked if I was VFR or IFR. I responded with that I was IFR and turning left to 295.There are a few contributing factors that lead to my error. First was my general lack of recency with the G1000. In the last 120 days I had amassed a total of only 6.7 hours in the aircraft. Additionally I only have a total of 24 hours in the aircraft since my check-ride last summer. This lack of familiarity; currency and comfort in the aircraft contributed to the error.  After passing 1;000 feet the G1000 was showing a magenta line to the right which is probably partially why I turned the wrong direction. An additional contributing factor was that I was operating single pilot IFR in icing conditions with little experience in the aircraft. This was a Part 91 flight and the 100 hour rule for commuter passenger operations did not apply.   While the General Operations Manual has a dual qualification policy it does not adequately address low time pilots. When a pilot is only qualified in one aircraft type they are afforded an opportunity immediately after completing their check-ride and Operational Experience to gain significant flight time and consolidate their knowledge and skills in the aircraft over the course of a few months.  In my scenario I have accumulated only 9 hours since the completion of Operational Experience. I am in full compliance with the policy and have been active in ensuring I fly the aircraft within the 90 days and make an effort to coordinate a flight when I haven't flown in over 30 days. As is evidenced by my low hours recently this does not afford a pilot new in the aircraft any significant flight time; nor the ability to consolidate their knowledge. While all aircraft are of the general purpose multi-engine variety this aircraft is the only Technically Advanced Aircraft (TAA) in the fleet. This adds a significant amount of complexity to it's operation.I would suggest that when a pilot is qualified on any aircraft we afford them the necessary time and hours to consolidate their knowledge and skills. Part 121 recognizes this issue and has the requirement for consolidation of knowledge and skills in new type aircraft. While again our aircraft are of the same type I feel with dramatic difference in this aircraft particularly; being a TAA; there should be a similar effort. Under Part 121 a pilot would be required to obtain 100 hours within 120 days of becoming qualified in the aircraft. I think we should model a policy to have similar protections. Consolidation was identified in a joint government/industry task force in 1993 to be of concern. One primary reason was 'in recent years manufacturers have introduced a greater number of new aircraft containing more equipment and systems variations within type. Pilots must not only learn different aircraft handling characteristics but they must also be able to work with a variety of aircraft equipment such as automated flight control and flight management systems.' (Federal Register Vol 60 No 81). As this aircraft aligns closely with the concerns listed here that resulted in the regulatory change (advanced aircraft systems)I think a policy to ensure a similar amount of experience is obtained in each aircraft a pilot is qualified in. This would not be to change the dual qualification policy; however; it would most often be triggered and impact pilots who are dual qualified. If a pilot were unable to accomplish the consolidation of knowledge and skills then I think it would be best to enter them into a recurrent training program. As a direct result of this deviation and review of my recent experience I have requested a training event from the flight training department to ensure that I have the requisite proficiency and after that I will make a concerted effort to add shifts to ensure I can achieve my consolidation of knowledge and skills.

column121: We departed on time for a XX minute flight. Climbing through 10;000 feet I chimed the flight attendants and we continued our climb to 21;000 feet. Center was telling me to expect bad rides all the way to our destination. So when we leveled off at 21;000 feet. I made an announcement stating that the ride was going to be rough and that I would keep the seat belt sign of the entire flight. I also asked the flight attendants to remain seated for the duration of the flight as well or so I thought. The ride was not good. Continuous light occasionally moderate turbulence. The arrival is challenging on a good day and today was no exception. We were dealing with a complex arrival; turbulence; icing and multiple changes to speed and altitude. We were cleared to descend via the arrival with no speed restrictions with about a 90 knot tailwind.We would be early. Around the time that we started our descent I noticed that someone was trying to use the door code to gain access to the cockpit. I immediately declined it and made sure door was locked. The Pilot Flying and I both thought that was strange so I tried calling back to a Flight Attendant to see what was going on. That was the first indication something was wrong. When I turned on the speaker for the cabin I could hear an audible cycling noise. When I tried to chime the flight attendants I couldn't hear the chime and I could not hear any voices on the interphone. I tried to make a quick announcement but nothing was coming out back in the cabin. As the Pilot Flying and I were extremely busy managing the descent and approach we heard a knock at the door and could faintly hear a voice. Pilot Flying turned around and saw a note on the ground that said INTERPHONE INOP.I wanted to get up and grab the note to try and write something back but we were too busy. A few minutes passed. The cockpit door lock code was entered again and I denied it a second time. I tried to yell as loud as I could that we got the message. I think they must have heard that time because they stopped knocking on the door. We landed and began our taxi to the gate. After clearing the active runways I had Pilot Flying call maintenance and inform them that our Cabin Interphone and Public Address system was inoperative. We taxied to the gate and shutdown. After the shutdown checklist was complete and before the forward door was opened I got up to check on the A Flight Attendant and see if everything was OK. He was visibly upset. After the passengers got off the other two Flight Attendant's joined us up in first class to discuss what had happened. A Flight Attendant said that it was the scariest flight of his life. He said that after we had hit a rough patch of turbulence the cabin lights in the plane started to cycle on and off. They were still doing it after I went back to talk to them. He then had tried to call me to see if everything was OK but couldn't reach me. He thought that maybe we had lost pressurization and that we might have been incapacitated. He tried the door code to maybe get a peek inside to see if we were OK. He left a note under the door in hopes that we would grab it and write back. Only after the last time that he tried the door lock and I denied it did he hear me yell through the door. The other two flight attendants were also upset that they couldn't communicate with me. I spent at least 15 minutes with them trying to explain why I couldn't respond to them even though I wanted to.Trying to unlock the cockpit door without my authorization put me on high alert. This is not something I expected. If this had been a different flight with more time I would have taken their note and responded to it and sent it back. That would have been the best way. I tried yelling through the door; but it is loud in the cockpit and only on the second time did they hear me. If we had lost pressurization the masks in the back would have dropped and they would have felt it in their ears. The first time I denied his access to the cockpit door he should have known we were OK. I cannot just open the cockpit door without knowing who is behind it. My first priority is to fly the aircraft. I just didn't have enough time to respond to them the way they wanted me to.I tried to address all of their concerns and I did understand that they were upset. I wrote up the Public Address system as well as the Interphone system with their input to give the mechanics all they needed to fix the system. Maintenance came on board and reset the system. I tested the PA and both forward and aft intercoms with the Flight Attendants and in front of maintenance to make sure everything worked. Maintenance signed off the system and we than headed back. After our initial conversation about what had transpired I thought all Flight Attendants were OK just a little rattled but good enough to continue. If I had known they still had reservations about what had happened I would have immediately responded to them. My crew always comes first.
column123: During our descent on the arrival we heard a knock on the cockpit door. column121: My first attempt at writing this portion did not save so I will attempt it again. We had an A321 sharklet. Every portion of the beginning of the flight leg from gate departure; takeoff and climb up to the fume event was normal and routine. At sometime above 10;000 ft. we got a call from our #1 FA (Flight Attendant) telling us that the FAs in Economy Class more towards the rear of the aircraft were smelling a sweat odor and a more robust glue type odor. I believe from my prospective that the odor came from the back from the wings black wards because we did not smell anything in the flight deck and no one smelled anything in first class; #1 FA or forward section of the cabin behind 1st class section. Captain began trouble shooting the problem with the QRH guidelines and the FAs that was smelling the odors. One of the FAs was feeling ill from the fume which was strong in the area they were working. Passenger in that area smelled the odors as well. Captain asked if she can continue or do we need to get back to the gate in ZZZ so she can seek medical attention. She was not sure if she wanted to continue on toward ZZZZ1 or return. Captain asked the #1 FA to monitor the FA's condition and if she worsened we will return to ZZZ. While we were discussing the QRH fume trouble shooting pages and making plans to return to ZZZ or another airport that may be closer to our position if we continued to fly farther away from ZZZ; the #1 FA called and told us the FA that was feeling ill was on O2 and was not getting better. So we notified ATC that we will be returning to ZZZ which was the best option to land. We [were given priority handling] to expedite our return to ZZZ and so the FA can get the medical attention she needed. As we began to descend into ZZZ I remember it was below FL180 and through landing that the odors began to infiltrate the flight deck and the #1 FA and passengers began smelling it too. We donned our O2 masks. It was a sweaty smell and it also had an Elmer's glue order to us. The odors continued until we arrived to the gate. The FA that was really ill went to the hospital and the remaining flight crew continued with us to ZZZZ1 with a replacement FA.I don't know of any causal factors that would cause a fume event other than fixing the problem of the source that caused the fumes from escaping and preventing and future leaks from going into the cabin.The only thing that would prevent this from happening would be a complete redesign of the airplane systems that keeps the cabin ventilation isolated from any possible fume leaking into the cabin.

column121: During climbout from ZZZ; above approximately 2;000 feet AFL; an amber GPS-L enunciated. I continued to hand fly the jet as we climbed into IMC conditions in the pre-dawn darkness. The GPS-L caution distracted me from calling 'flaps-up' at the appropriate speed. The Captain called my attention to this as we approached 240 knots IAS. I called for flaps up and the captain retracted them normally. I engaged the autopilot after flap retraction. At no time did we exceed the 250 knot flap placard limit. Maximum speed I remember seeing was 244 knots IAS with flaps not up. The rest of the flight to ZZZ1 was uneventful. I believe my recency of experience was a factor; this being my first unsupervised flight since re-qualification. Also; night; IMC in low marine layer clouds while hand flying the initial portion of the RNAV departure. The GPS-L caution was a nuisance warning that served as the distraction. I was focused on hand flying smoothly and lost situational awareness of aircraft configuration.Earlier use of automation may have helped with my situational awareness during the nuisance GPS distraction. My habit is to hand fly the aircraft until clean.

column121: Taxing from the device pad for departure we came very close to coming in contact with Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y had been given clearance to taxi to the runway while we were still finishing up de-ice and neither the Captain or myself as First Officer gave it much thought. When we finished the de-ice process I called for taxi and we were given clearance to taxi. The Runway Visual Range was being reported at the time of 1;000 ft. so the visibility was obviously a contributing factor in the described events. As we were on Taxiway A approaching an intersection; I began to notice some lights on the right hand side of the airplane. I assumed that I was seeing hangar lights as they did not appear to be moving. Looking back this was due to the fact that ourselves and Aircraft Y had roughly the same ground speed and therefore the lights were staying in the same position on my window.As we got closer the Captain and I both realized at about the same time that what we were seeing was Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y must have seen us about the same time because we both came to a stop. When we stopped on the slick taxiway we were probably no more then 20 or 30 ft. away from Aircraft Y. We began to taxi away and as we did I asked ground to verify that we were in fact cleared to taxi to the runway. They stated that we were. Aircraft Y then asked the same thing and ground replied that they as well were cleared to taxi to the same runway. Due to the 1;000 ft. Runway Visual Range I know that Tower could not see where either of us were. I think that the normal low visual procedures of reporting when passing certain points would have saved this from happening. I think that Ground thought that Aircraft Y was already at the end of the runway when we were cleared for taxi and for some reason Aircraft Y was delayed.
column123: We were departing. ATIS prevailing visibility was 1/4 mile in freezing fog. After start we went to device pad 1 and completed Type I and Type IV deicing. Ground gave us taxi instructions and to hold short the ILS critical area. Taxi was uneventful until reaching an intersection. Aircraft Y had been cleared to taxi to the same runway and we nearly met at the intersection. We both applied brakes. Aircraft Y told Ground they would 'give way to...' us. After starting to taxi we called Ground to confirm our taxi instructions. Aircraft Y did the same. We were both cleared all the way to Runway 12. Aircraft Y was cleared to taxi before us and either taxied slow or delayed their start. Ground could have confirmed their position before clearing us to taxi.

column121: While enroute at FL280; I noticed the radio frequency was very quiet. Since COVID has impacted US aviation; frequency congestion has decreased significantly; which makes longer periods of radio silence a new sense of normalcy.  My last handoff to ZZZ Center was eight minutes prior at which I made positive radio contact on frequency XYZ.AB. I was using COM 1 as primary radio and monitoring XYX.B on COM 2 with the proper audio panel selections to hear both radios simultaneously. After time passed by and I realized I was not hearing anyone; I transmitted my N number on COM 1 to ZZZ Center and did not receive a response. I selected microphone to COM 2 and reached out to ZZZ Center on XYX.B; no response. I switched the microphone back to COM 1 and tried XYZ.AB again; no response. I switched the microphone back to COM 2 and announced; 'All stations on guard; radio check.' After the second attempt; ZZZ1 Center answered and gave me a new frequency; XXC.DY. A Controller replied 'Aircraft X; possible pilot deviation; I have a number for you; advise when ready to copy.' I was extremely shocked at the situation as I was unaware the radio issue had escalated to that extent. I continued my flight to ZZZZ and called as soon as practical after landing. I spoke with a Controller. Controller said NORDO is a common issue but mine was excessive. I have no deviations on my record and strive to maintain a clean record. Going forward; I will be more diligent in recognizing radio silence and will reach out more frequently if I assume the silent period is excessive.

column121: On [Date]; an in-flight [problem] occurred regarding a Gulfstream GIV-SP. The details are as follows:On [Date]; [Aircraft X] was on a FAA Part 135 flight from ZZZZ to ZZZ1. There were a total of XX occupants on board of which included 3 crew members. The Pilot Flying (PF) was [Name]; the Pilot Monitoring (PM) was [Name]; and the third crew member; [Name]; was the Cabin Server (CS).The aircraft departed ZZZZ at approximately XA:00 on an IFR flight plan. The aircraft climbed uneventfully to an initial altitude of FL430. After about 20 minutes at altitude; a passenger came to the flight deck and asked if we could cool down the cabin. The PM set the cabin temperature controller to a cooler temperature. After about 5 minutes; the R COOL TURBINE HOT CAS message displayed. The crew performed the appropriate checklist and after a minute the message went out.At this point; the cabin was at a higher temperature than before and the passengers complained again. The PF decided to go back into the cabin to verify that all the gasper vents were open and to check if there were any other indications of potential issues. It was apparent that there was a significant temperature difference from the forward portion of the cabin compared to the aft. The forward cabin was at least 10 degrees warmer than the aft. Additionally; the PF noticed some warm air coming out of the vents. After checking the upper cabin gasper vents; the PF returned to his seat. After a short discussion on possible issues; the crew elected to descend to FL390.When the aircraft leveled at FL390; the CS came up to the flight deck and asked the PF if he noticed any haze in the cabin. The PF looked back and saw no smoke or haze. The CS went about her duties.After a few more minutes; the PF noticed smoke coming from the PM's vent and the crew received another R COOL TURBINE HOT CAS message. The PF immediately donned his O2 mask and requested to the PM that we ask for an immediate descent and to pull out the checklist. At this time; the cabin started to fill up with visible smoke and the Cabin Server came up to the flight deck to respond. The Cabin Server donned her O2 mask. After O2 masks were on; the appropriate checklists were performed. The cabin started to depressurize immediately after the right pack was turned off (as required by the R COOL TURBINE HOT checklist). At this point; a rapid descent was performed and [ATC was advised]. During the descent; smoke remained in the cabin. Due to the smoke in the cabin and loss of pressurization; the crew elected for vectors to the nearest suitable airport ZZZ2. While the aircraft was descending; the passenger O2 masks deployed and the CS instructed the passenger to put their O2 masks on. At about 15;000 ft.; the smoke started to dissipate. The crew continued their descent to 6;000 ft. and accepted vectors to the ILS XXR at ZZZ2. At this time; the cabin was completely free from smoke. The crew took off their O2 masks and completed all remainder checklists for landing. At XB:00 the aircraft landed uneventfully.On the landing roll out Fire and Rescue was approved on the runway to follow the aircraft to its parking spot. After shutting down the engines; the crew assessed the situation and verified that all passengers were OK and that no one was injured. At this point; the PM notified the airport that the crew and passengers will need to clear customs. After the crew and passengers were cleared from customs; the airplane was written up for multiple system failures including an abnormal cabin depressurization; the left pack unable to provide appropriate cabin pressurization under the above conditions; a malfunction within the right air cycle machine; and the aft [lavatory] O2 mask failing to deploy.

By the time we were clear we were through 10;000 feet and due to the distractions we forgot to complete the climb check. I initially began accelerating and reached about 265 knots before I decided to slow to complete the second part of the ice test. Once the test was complete (at around 18;000 feet) I began accelerating and again reached about 265 knots before we realized the flaps were still set to 9. We slowed; retracted the flaps; contacted Maintenance and continued the flight without further incident.No real suggestions. It was human error on my part. I should have been more vigilant and will be in the future.

column121: In our initial climb to 6;000 feet we were instructed by Departure to turn off course and given a fix to fly to. I confirmed the fix with the CA (Captain) and pressed Nav Mode on the FMS. I looked over to my PFD to set the new altitude assigned by Departure and the CA looked away at the same time. Shortly thereafter; Departure called and asked us if we were turning on course. We both looked up and realized that the Nav mode had not captured the course. I immediately turned the heading bug towards the course line on the display; while the CA notified the Controller that we were correcting and turning on course.While compensating for winds and flying via the heading bug; we started to analyze the problem. Shortly after changing the AP to the CA's side; we were able to correct the Nav issue; as the AP was functioning properly on the CA's side; I continued as the pilot flying. About 45 minutes out; the CA left the flight deck to use the LAV. As he returned; he noticed that we had about 8 status messages that popped up sometime after he had left the flight deck. I was engaged with a short conversation with the FA (Flight Attendant) and did not notice the display of messages until he returned. The status messages were flight control related; noting flight spoilers; rudder; etc. The CA referred to the QRH for landing data as a precautionary measure; in the event of a total system failure to those systems. The CA Then notified ATC of our potential systems status and requested deleting the LAHSO restrictions. ATC was unable to comply.Later; as we were given an intercept angle to intercept the final approach course; I selected the NAV button and was waiting for the intercept. We had a [heavy aircraft] on our left and we were paying close attention to that traffic; when we noticed that the aircraft had blown through the center line and was deviating right. The CA then asked me what was going on and while trying to process the information; I replied; 'I have no idea.' At that time Tower called to query our actions; It was as if the aircraft had a mind of its own and before I was able to kick off the autopilot; the CA then asked for the flight controls. We landed without incident and all flight control systems were operational throughout the landing phase; as all the spoilers had deployed. The AP had remained on the CA's side throughout the entire approach.Hindsight; I told the CA; that the one course of action we could have taken at the onset of discovering that the AP/Nav was not recognizing my side; we should have changed roles and allowed him to be the Pilot Flying. With the unexpected behavior of the FMS during the critical phase of flight; I was in total agreement with the CA's actions and decisions; I believe his actions were appropriate and timely while operating in the essence of safety for the passengers and crew.

column121: I checked in with the gate agent prior to my flight to ZZZZ.  I don't recall if any passengers were boarded but there were no passengers that I remember waiting to check in because it was still pretty early.  As I walked down the jet bridge I noticed a Flight Attendant walking the opposite direction.  I had not met her prior as I had not been to the aircraft yet. At no time did I notice any passengers boarding or on our aircraft.  After checking the aircraft maintenance log; flight documents; etc. I briefed the A FA.  I only briefed the A FA as passengers were now being boarded.  I assumed the other two flight attendants were on board.  I was completely unaware that we didn't have minimum crew while boarding.  Approximately 10-15 minutes prior to departure; the A1 FA informed me that she was informed that we had boarded without minimum crew.  I think the COVID-19 online form (for ZZZZ) was the reason that caused this problem.  I fly this trip nearly every week and it's generally always a bit of a scramble at the last minute to get the form completed by all crew members prior to departure.  In addition it is a very difficult form to electronically fill out for the first time.  I believe the FA was only trying her best to complete the form prior to boarding. Perhaps a reminder to both cockpit and cabin crew that a COVID-19 declaration form is required for entry into ZZZZ.  And that the form takes a while to complete as it NOT intuitive and can take a few attempts to complete it and requires sufficient WiFi or cellular signal.

column121: On DATE; Aircraft X was scheduled to depart on a two leg cross county trip from ZZZ to ZZZ1.  The trip was slated to depart at XA:30 but was delayed approximately 50 minutes due to unforeseen complications dealing with one of the aircraft preflight checklist items.  While checking the tire pressure of the landing gear tires; it was discovered that the left main landing gear tire valve stem was inaccessible due to the hub cap being installed incorrectly.  There is a small access door that allows access to the valve stem through the hub cap and the hub cap was clocked in the wrong position rendering the valve stem inaccessible.  A local A&P Service Center was contacted and on-site service was requested to remove the hubcap and re-clock.  An A&P responded to the location and removed the hub cap.  He asked to confirm the POH air pressure requirements; and continued to top off the air pressure per the POH.  The hub cap was replaced in the correct position.  All tire air pressures were serviced per the POH.  This was the last remaining check list item to be completed; and Aircraft X departed ZZZ2 at XB:20 en route to ZZZ3 for the first leg of the trip.  The taxi; take off; landing; and post landing taxi phases were normal.  On DATE; Aircraft X departed ZZZ2 on the second leg of this cross country trip to ZZZ1.  Taxi and takeoff were normal.  The trip was uneventful.  IMC conditions existed over ZZZ1 during our arrival time; with unknown tops and 4;400 ft. ceilings.  VMC conditions existed below the ceiling with winds reported variable at 3 kts.  The RNAV GPS approach was requested and granted into ZZZ1.  Following the approach; the main landing gear touched down with the aircraft near center line just beyond the extended threshold. The aircraft responded as expected upon main gear touchdown.  When the nose landing gear touched down the plane veered hard to the right.  Left rudder pedal was used to counter the uncommanded right turn and the plane veered left and immediately began skidding to the left.  The plane did not respond to input and skidded off the runway just short of taxiway F; into the landscaped area immediately adjacent to the runway.  The nose wheel collapsed while the engine was still running and dropped the spinning prop to the ground.  It was immediately obliterated.  The turbine engine abruptly quit running.  When the plane swerved to the right following the nose wheel touch down; the plane immediately felt unstable.  It felt as if the runway was icy and without good traction.  However; it was later determined there was no ice on the runway.  I advised the tower when the plane came to a complete stop that I had just hit ice.  This event duration happened extremely quick.  There were no injuries.  There was no known airport property damage observed.  There is no other property damage.  Emergency crews showed up quickly.  The aircraft did not catch on fire.  Emergency crews did not deploy any foam.  The ELT activated.  The airbag seat belts did not deploy.  Environmental observation:  Prior to decent; and while in cruise at FL270; I had been observing the OAT slowly creep down from around -45c to a max low of -51c.  The minimum in-flight temperature limitation of this aircraft is -54c.  When the temperature dropped to around -49c; I became acutely aware and concerned of the temperature as I knew I was approaching the maximum lower limit.  I advised ATC I needed lower due to temperature limitations and they advised expect lower in three minutes.  I was then instructed to descend to FL250.  The temperature increased to above -49c.  Shortly thereafter; the decent into the terminal area required a rapid descent of roughly 2;000 FPM.

I was definitely mentally fatigued at this time.  Aircraft Y was a departure from ZZZ flying west bound direct to ZZZZZ slow climbing from FL260 to FL340. Aircraft X was a southbound ZZZ1 arrival initially on a heading to avoid other traffic and descending from FL350 to FL270. I had turned the Aircraft X back on course to ZZZZZ1 thinking they were clear of all other potential traffic. When Aircraft X established to ZZZZZ1 they 'flashed' with the Aircraft Y aircraft heading west bound near ZZZZZ1. I had already switched the Aircraft Y to [the adjacent ARTCC]. So I turned Aircraft X and called traffic. The turn helped but still didn't fix the situation. Ended with 4.5 miles and 300 feet. We need to have the support from not only our local management but also national level management. Volume needed to be slowed due to staffing. column121: During the DINGO 5 arrival into TUS; after waypoint MAVVA; I continued on the charted 075 degree heading passing through the Runway 11L localizer course; not complying with the textual instruction to intercept the I-TUS localizer course. ATC gave me vectors back around to re-intercept the localizer course; and a normal landing was made.The cause of the event was a failure to cross-check the textual instructions with what is displayed on the chart. Contributing factors were as follows: 1) A 'Descend Via' clearance was not issued. ATC instructed to 'Descend and maintain 8;000 feet; and EXPECT a visual approach.' I misinterpreted that to mean he would provide vectors to the final approach course; or clear me for a visual approach passing MAVVA.  2) I found the verbiage on the chart confusing where it states 'Runway 11L EXPECT approach clearance'. I interpreted that to mean once established on the 075 heading from MAVVA; not upon intercepting the localizer; as normally you would not intercept a localizer without ATC clearance or prior to accepting a visual approach.To avoid a recurrence of this event; a thorough briefing covering all noted and textual information should be conducted and cross checked prior to every landing. While my briefing did cover all of the information on the plan-view of the arrival; I missed a crucial piece of information solely located in the textual description that was not well depicted nor defined on the plan-view. It would have been helpful if ATC had offered us a visual approach earlier; directed us to intercept the localized after MAVVA and THEN expect approach clearance; or have the instruction to Intercept I-TUS localizer clearly printed on the plan view. It is worthy to note; the ATC controller stated 'Yeah; you're not the first airliner to do this' both over the frequency and on the telephone while speaking with him after landing. This leads me to believe that this could be a common mistake that could be corrected easily with a revised; emphasized; note on the arrival chart.

column121: I was First Officer and pilot monitoring for a reposition flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. When I arrived to the airplane; the Captain was already there with multiple maintenance technicians working through a dual inoperative GPS situation. The consensus was to defer both GPS units; along with the associated MEL items. After processing our 9 MELs during our pre-flight discussion we waited approximately two hours for a flight plan to be filed due to the issue with ADS-B being inoperative.During the after-start checklist; the CONT CAB ZONE TEMP fault appeared on Master Caution recall. We complied with the QRH and MEL and contacted Maintenance Control for deferral under the 'flight crew placard' option. The Captain and I discussed the phrase in the QRH; 'if the light extinguishes when Master Caution System is reset; no further action is required' - and he noted that this does not alleviate us from the need to defer the item per the MEL XX-XXY. Along the same time; the Captain noted that the 'dispatch alert' box was unchecked; so after the deferral was complete we resumed normal operations.After takeoff we experienced two additional master recall lights - 'Anti-Skid Inop' and the 'Reverser' on the overhead panel.Shortly after we leveled off at cruise altitude the dispatcher asked if we had added a new deferred item after pushback. We responded that we had; that it was XX-XXY. He advised us to fill out a report; despite the 'dispatch alert' box not being checked.The reposition flights after long-term storage lend themselves to multiple maintenance related issues and could be planned ahead to be operated by Functional Check Flight pilots.The filing of our flight plan took nearly two hours. Not knowing the exact cause of the issue; it would be helpful for future flights to review the process for filing flights with inoperative GPS and ADS-B to minimize future delays.

column123: Airspeed unreliable event. Possible altitude deviation. I was deadheading on flight sitting in the observer seat. There were thunderstorms in vicinity and we were experiencing light to moderate rain and turbulence. CA (Captain) was PF (Pilot Flying) with autopilot engaged in climb to 14;000 MSL and also communicating to ATC on Com 1. FO (First Officer) was speaking to Operations on Com 2. I'm not sure exactly what altitude event occurred but happened around 14;000 MSL. There was a high speed warning and I noticed a large difference in airspeed between the CA and FO side. The CA-side airspeed was declining rapidly while FO-side was overspeeding slightly. The Captain recognized the issue and performed the memory items correctly and stabilized the aircraft. It was determined the FO-side was correct and the aircraft control was transferred to FO. The QRH was performed and CADC 2 was selected. There was no further incident. After the event we discussed the possibility of an altitude deviation during the recovery. There was a level off and delayed climb. I did not have a headset on and could not hear any altitude clearances or ATC communication. ATC did not inform the crew of any deviation. The crew handled the emergency well.[Responded by having an] in-depth discussion among the crew about the event and how to handle it better. Reports. Captain discussed event with Maintenance and entered it into logbook. In our event debrief it was discovered that this event has happened multiple times in this aircraft. The FO and another Deadheader both had separate airspeed unreliable events in the same aircraft in similar meteorological conditions. We read through the logbook to discover that this has happened multiple times recently and the aircraft has continued to be put back into service with no permanent resolution. The principle recommendation would be to correctly resolve the issue that is causing this. As for my part in this event; I realized I could have been more active in listening if I were using a headset. I could have verified the ATC clearance and assisted in communication.

column121: Outlet circuit breakers tripped overnight so the planes battery and engine was cold. I placed the heater duct under the RH cowling of the aircraft into the engine compartment to warm it up and left the engine cover over it to keep the heat in. Prior to departure; I decided that I was going to need an assisted start regardless so I moved the heater from the engine to the copilot door to heat the cabin (this is where I believe the latches were initially left unlatched). I left the engine cover on not noticing the latches and walked away. Prior to departure; I removed the engine cover from the pilot side and removed the tail stand and chocks and started up. There was no sign of anything wrong until I was on takeoff roll and the cowling caught wind and came up into my view. I immediately aborted the takeoff roll and taxi back to parking. I normally check the cowling during my preflight and ensure it is latched; but the heater event happened after I completed my preflight inspection. I think that many factors contributed; but the main reason for me was that I had never done what I did with the heater like that before so my preflight routine was off. I also failed to notice the latches on my walk around because the engine cover was on while I was on that side of the plane; which I normally take it off before I even go inside to get my final manifest. I will make sure that I stick to my routine when it comes to the pre-startup walk around and be very vigilant and aware when something non-routine happens. Having this event permanently in my brain will also help me never do this again.

After takeoff; during the climb; I was 'heads down' as I was PNF and was just assigned a frequency change from the Tower to Departure Control while at the same time we encountered a TCAS for VFR traffic off the parallel runway (NOT DUE TO ANY NAVIGATIONAL ERROR IDENTIFIED IN THIS REPORT). During the scan for traffic and putting in the new frequency into the FMS; I noticed we were making a longer left turn than I anticipated. I said to the SIC (in left seat flying the aircraft) why is it turning so far and where are we going? We both looked at the SID displayed as well as the FMS and it was evident the FMS decided to sequence us to our next fix - SAC VOR and in doing so commenced a 'smart turn' in that direction.Upon contacting OAK departure; they verified our position/altitude and shortly thereafter contacted us and said 'Just so we are on the same page; you made a left turn after departing APC towards SAC and did not complete the SID.' I responded that yes; we were looking into the FMS turn as we had verified that the SID was loaded correctly in the FMS.Upon completing our day; we decided it was best to get both OAK and APC Tower on the phone to discuss. Both controllers appreciated us contacting them and mentioned that this was not the first time they have seen this happen with the NAPAA4 departure and they were going to look into it. Both controllers indicated since safety was not an issue; they were not interested in any action on us. In addition to the above discussion with ATC; I am also going to contact Collins and/or Jeppesen in regards to a possible issue with the database and/or SID for the NAPAA4 departure.

column121: In the traffic pattern at ZZZ; my CFI and I were on the right downwind for Runway XXR when we were told to Continue for Runway XXR. We then continued and a few moments later was told to turn right base for XXR. When turning right base we noted traffic; but I didn't think it was a factor at first because we assumed it was for the parallel because we still were told to turn right base.  As we got established on base we saw the traffic was close and my CFI took controls to avoid a mid-air collison. We got no warning from the Tower and later found out that the tower told the other aircraft to continue for Runway XXR. Shortly after the Tower told them to continue for XXR that's when the tower said to turn base. I didn't think that traffic that was on final would be a factor for us and thought it was for Runway XXL. In the future; I think the Tower should be more clear and understand the traffic spacing better because if he did then he could've told us to extend a couple of miles so we could've passed behind the traffic instead of passing in front and coming within 1;000 feet horizontally of each other. I believe the talking between me and my CFI also contributed because maybe we would've heard the call for the other aircraft to continue and could've challenged that with the Tower but even then we still were told to turn base. I believe the tower should've noted the other aircraft and looked at the spacing; and told us this isn't going to work and this near-miss could've been avoided altogether instead we got turned directly into the path of another aircraft.
column123: I was flying with my student in the pattern at ZZZ. When we were downwind; Tower didn't clear us for a touch and go; but told us to continue. We continued downwind and waited for further instructions when Tower then told us to turn base.We turned base. There was some hesitation but then the Controller instructed us to turn directly towards the numbers. At this point; we were on right base unaware we were being turned onto an aircraft that was on final.   Before my students turn for final; I always have them look on final to make sure it is clear of traffic. At this point; I noticed the traffic on the left hand side and saw it on my iPad. I took the controls from my student and climbed to offset to the right where we avoided a near miss collision of about 1;000 feet horizontal distance and 300 feet vertical distance over a densely packed neighborhood of City. We never were told to extend or follow this aircraft.Prior to the Controller telling us to turn base; he had spoken to the aircraft on the straight in final and told them to continue. He realized the aircraft was there; but did not communicate the location and told us to turn base onto him. This situation demonstrates that pilots must exercise extreme vigilance at airports where ATC is so busy to provide clear instructions.The term 'continue' can be vague in that…does it mean we're supposed to fly the pattern as regularly; or are we supposed to continue downwind? In that case; the term 'extend' would make more sense.When I talked to the Controller on the phone later; I was told that this situation occurred due to a late runway switch by the other aircraft. However; in examination of the track log; the aircraft was on a straight in approach. The pilot also called up that they were approaching a point on the approach for XXR.  The Controller didn't acknowledge the mistake that had been made and the possible deadly consequences that could have occurred from this near miss.This is a serious near miss.

column121: Aircraft X; was a training flight with a student performing a practice ILS Approach to FDK Runway 23; authorized and approved by FDK Tower.  Aircraft X was 10 miles from Runway 23; approaching the NUMBE intersection on the 295-degree radial from the EMI VORTAC; the authorized feeder-route to the FDK ILS Runway 23 Approach.After receiving such approval; Aircraft Y; requested the same practice ILS Approach and self-announced they were 2 miles from NUMBE; but based on the ADS-B display in Aircraft X; Aircraft Y was approaching the inbound localizer course from the northwest; from which there is no authorized transition or feeder route.Aircraft Y told FDK Tower they would follow behind Aircraft X and slow down but at various points and times between NUMBE; the IAF (10 nm from Runway 23); and Runway 23; Aircraft Y was as close as 500 horizontal feet behind Aircraft X and was proceeding at a higher rate of speed than Aircraft X.Twice during the practice ILS Approach; the ADS-B-based Traffic Alerting System in Aircraft X (the leading aircraft) sounded an aural and visual caution (yellow); meaning Aircraft Y was closing in on the tail of Aircraft X.The flight student in Aircraft X was spooked by these warnings; as well as the radio calls from Aircraft Y saying they were 'too close'; and had difficulty controlling the aircraft and/or experiencing productive learning.Because of this high risk; and the student's unease with the entire situation; Aircraft X aborted the practice ILS 23 Approach and took evasive action (executing the missed approach 1.5-miles from Runway 23 and side-stepping to the left); to get out of the way of the closing aircraft; Aircraft Y.Subsequently; while on the ground; Aircraft Y's Certificated Flight Instructor and co-pilot approached the crew of Aircraft X and laughed at Aircraft X for 'flying too slow.'The crew of Aircraft X felt this was an inappropriate and unsafe display of arrogance; especially in light of Aircraft Y's violation of FAR Section 91.113 (f).

column121: Training flight on IFR Tower enroute clearance from TOA to ZZZ. Clearance was fly runway heading to intercept LAX 170 radial to LIMBO; V64; SLI; Direct. On departure from TOA my student was flying under the view-limiting device and I was pilot monitoring and looking outside for traffic. We departed Runway 29R; shortly after there was a departure from a parallel 29L of a light aircraft that was faster than our aircraft. While switching to Departure Control frequency we were advised of proximity of the overtaking aircraft and its altitude being same as ours. I was looking outside and was able to spot the aircraft in about 20 seconds and student flying advised ATC of us having visual contact. Another 20 seconds later I lost visual contact and took over controls momentarily using 3 step process to raise the left wing to check on the overtaking aircraft that was turning south at that time. I gave the controls back to my student using 3 step process. When my student was saying 'my controls' he blocked end of Controller's transmission for me. The part that I heard was only 'turn left 150.' Then; student read back 'Turn left 150 Aircraft X' and initiated a left turn to 150. At that time I started to question myself if this instruction could really be intended to us since it would probably put us below the MVA in the area. I clearly heard my student's readback to ATC about left turn to 150 and since Controller didn't say anything about his read back being wrong; I thought I shouldn't probably even worry. Just a moment later; because of the oddness of the situation I decided to clarify the instruction with the ATC; but by the time I was able to key the mic; Controller already was getting back to us questioning our actions. Only then I realized that my student responded to a call intended to another aircraft and Controller didn't even hear his readback because the transmission was blocked by the radio call of the aircraft that really received that instruction.I think contributing factors to this little misunderstanding was our scratchy radio. Because of it the student misheard the call sign and I couldn't even hear it; due to intercom on that particular plane being clearer than the radio and student was talking at the same time.Good thing there was no conflicting traffic and VMC conditions let me see the terrain.

column121: Taking off in ZZZ an incident occurred where we blew through altitude and we [were] slow to follow our heading assignment.I was PM on this flight; and it was the second flight of the day on this trip.Pre-flight was normal and we loaded up our passengers ahead of schedule with no pressure to rush.Upon receiving our takeoff clearance for Runway XX in ZZZ we were assigned a heading of 230 and an altitude of 2;000 feet. I performed the before takeoff checks and the PF armed the AT and the lateral mode (roll mode.) (SOP from manufacturer for takeoff with a heading assignment is either to activate heading mode and then spin the heading to the assigned heading at 400 feet; alternatively you can input the heading but leave it in roll mode until 400 feet upon which you can activate heading mode. Neither of which is particularly helpful during a high workload environment).Takeoff procedure was initially normal; we lined up on the runway and proceeded with a rolling start. The PF set takeoff thrust; and I made my first call at 40 kts. Sometime between 40 kts and 80 kts the AT Disconnect sounded. PF elected to continue. We rotated normally and after the call for 'Gear Up' and the '400 feet' call the pilot asked for me to engage the AT again. I hit the AT button; and continued with my climb sequence checklist. (Speed 180; FLC; Flaps to 0 and After Takeoff Checklist.)Around the time I hit FLC Tower called us to switch to departure. At approximately the same time the AT again disconnected (without an aural alert). I called AT disconnect and reminded the PF that he had to manually control the throttles for speed. As I swapped frequencies the PF attempted to rearm the AT's and blew through our initial altitude. The AT's again disconnected immediately after hitting the button and I called ATC informing them that we had blown through our ALT by 200 feet and were descending back to intercept as well and the late initial turn to a heading of 230.ATC acknowledged and asked us to IDENT and to turn to a heading of 260.At this point the PF had manual speed control; I finally armed the correct lateral mode. (Heading set to 230) PF and I had a quick discussion and decided now that the workload was lower we could troubleshoot. We armed the AT one last time however this time it did not disconnect; and we proceeded with the flight normally.There were a few contributing factors that caused this error.Firstly; we are both new on this equipment and are still learning the correct procedures and cadence of the flight.Secondly; due to COVID we have not been flying as much as we normally do further extend the period of settling into the new aircraft.Third; we believe manufacturer's procedure for setting the lateral mode during a very high workload stage of flight 400 feet during the climb sequence further exasperated the situation. The AP/FD should be programmed so that when you are in T/O mode that it will hold roll to 400 feet then will initiate the turn to a heading and revert to LNAV to HDG mode.Finally; the most critical error I believe was the PF's throttle technique. He would arm the AT and then bring the throttled straight to the stops whereas manufacturer procedure is to bring the throttle levers to around 40% TLA and then let the AT's set takeoff thrust. I hadn't noticed it in previous flight; but I noticed it on this takeoff because the throttle levers moved much to quickly to takeoff power. I believe that this movement overrode the AT logic and if he accidentally moved the throttles past the detent even momentarily it may have caused the AT's to disconnect. Then for the rest of the T/O roll the throttles were possibly still slightly past the detent not allowing engagement until they were finally moved to a lower power setting whereupon we could finally engage the AT's. We discussed this discrepancy during the cruise portion of the flight and the PF will use the correct throttle technique going forward.

column121: Our aircraft departed ZZZ at approximately XA:40Z on an IFR flight plan headed to ZZZ airport. Name was the pilot flying and I was the pilot monitoring. We climbed and cruised uneventfully at an initial altitude of FL430. After about 20 minutes at altitude; a passenger came to the flight deck and asked if we could cool down the cabin. As I set the cabin temperature controller to a cooler temperature. After about 5 minutes; the 'R COOL TURBINE HOT' CAS message came on. We performed the appropriate checklist and after a minute the CAS message went out.At this point; the cabin was at a hotter temperature than before and the passengers complained again. The PF decided to go back into the cabin to verify that all the gasper vents were open and to check if there were any other indications of potential issues. It was apparent that there was a significant temperature difference from the forward portion of the cabin compared to the aft. The forward cabin was at least 10 degrees warmer than the aft. Additionally; the PF noticed some warm air coming out of the vents. After checking the upper cabin gasper vents; the PF returned to his seat. After a short discussion on possible issues; we elected to descend to FL390.When the aircraft leveled at FL390; the Cabin Attendant came up to the flight deck and asked the PF if he noticed any haze in the cabin. The PF looked back and saw no smoke or haze. The Cabin Attendant went about her duties.After a few more minutes; the PF noticed smoke coming from my right-side vent and we received another 'R COOL TURBINE HOT' CAS message. The PF immediately donned his O2 mask and asked me to request an immediate descent and to pull out the checklist. At this time; the cabin started to fill up with visible smoke and the cabin attendant came up to the flight deck to respond. Now it has become our priority to get this airplane on the ground as soon and safely as possible. The cabin attendant donned her O2 mask. After O2 masks were on; the appropriate checklists were performed. The cabin started to depressurize immediately after the Right Pack was turned off (as required by the 'R COOL TURBINE HOT' checklist). I had to also switch the pressurization to manual and that increased my workload; as I had to control and visually monitor the opening of the safety valve. At this point; a rapid descent was performed. During the descent; smoke remained in the cabin. Due to the smoke in the cabin; a loss of pressurization; we requested for vectors to the nearest suitable airport which was ZZZ1. During the descent; the passenger O2 masks deployed; and the Cabin attendant instructed the passengers to put their O2 masks on. At about 15;000ft; the smoke started to dissipate. We continued our descent per ATC to 6;000 feet and continued with vectors for an ILS XX approach at ZZZ1. Now the cabin was completely clear of smoke. The crew took off their O2 masks and completed all remainder checklists for landing. The aircraft landed uneventfully on [Runway] XX.Upon the landing roll out; Fire and Rescue was approved on the runway to follow us to our parking spot on ramp. After shutting down engines and securing the aircraft; we assessed the situation and verified that all passengers were OK and there were no injuries.

column121: Flying the NAPAA4.NAPAA departure out of APC airport we loaded the departure into the FMS and verified the routing was correct.As we departed the airport on Runway 19R with a clearance to climb to 3;000 feet we had the autopilot engaged in LNAV and vertical speed. Autothrottles where set at 200 kts.As we started our climb there was a piston single that had departed Runway 19L ahead of us. As we climbed out I had the other aircraft in sight but did get a traffic alert on the TCAS. I think at the time we received the TCAS alert he was already passing off our left wing and 400 feet below us. The autopilot made an initial slight right turn towards the VOR and then sequenced the next leg of our flight plan from the SGD VOR to SAC as was filed on our flight plan.Due to the tight turn that would be required to fly the leg from SGD to SAC I thought it had initiated the turn early in anticipation of our proximity to the VOR and that we were approaching our assigned altitude of 3;000 feet.Between the TCAS alert and seeing that the FMS was sequenced now to fly to the next fix on our flight plan I was focused on ensuring we maintained our separation from the other aircraft and after verifying that the FMS was sequenced to our cleared route I continued in the left turn and established the aircraft on the leg from SGD to SAC.Tower handed us off to Oakland [Center] and it was then that they inquired as to why we had made a left turn after takeoff rather than flying the departure as published. We had a brief exchange with the Controller about how the FMS had sequenced us on the next leg of the flight plan prior to reaching the VOR.Upon landing at our final destination later in the day I placed a call to Oakland Center as well as the Tower at APC. The Oakland Controller that I spoke with did not think there had been any issue with what happened since we had not been given a phone number to call from our Controller. When I called the Tower at APC; I was able to speak with the controller that cleared us for takeoff and handed us off to Oakland when we departed. He stated that they have had a few aircraft making the same left turn after takeoff while flying that same departure. He indicated that they needed to look into it and said that there had not been any conflict with other traffic. He thanked me for getting back to him and talking to him about it and that he would be following up the next day with his colleagues regarding this departure.Our filed and cleared route was APC NAPAA4 SGD SAC ZZZ ZZZ1.

column121: During a practice RNAV (GPS) [Runway] 35 approach to Colorado Air and Space Port (CFO); we had just crossed the Final Approach Fix (FAF) at ARRES at the charted altitude of 7;500 feet MSL. The student at the controls was 2-3 seconds late in beginning the glideslope intercept; and our glideslope indicated slightly high. Knowing that we had to descend 500 feet in order to be below the upcoming 7;000 feet MSL Class B shelf; I reduced power to increase our rate of descent. There was also an air carrier [Aircraft Y] at our 1 o'clock; approximately 1;000 feet above our altitude according to ADS-B; which was making a right turn from a southerly heading to a northwesterly as it make its approach to DEN. Denver Approach contacted us saying; 'I need you below the Bravo shelf at 7;000 feet.' I replied 'roger; we are increasing our rate of descent; currently indicating 6;800 feet.' The Aircraft Y crossed above and ahead of us; right to left; approximately 1;000 feet above and 200 feet ahead. I did not hear any of the communications between the Aircraft Y and Denver Approach; nor did I notice any maneuvering by the Aircraft Y indicating it was reacting to our presence. The complex airspace around DEN is extremely challenging; and this approach's FAF is approximately 1.4 NM from the 7;000 feet MSL Class B shelf. Descending 500 feet in less than 1.4 NM at small aircraft approach speeds does not require excessive rates of descent; but it does require a timely descent. Any delay; or crossing the FAF above the 7;500 feet MSL altitude; quickly makes it likely that an airplane may violate Class B airspace during the Final Approach Segment. In our case; the timing of the arriving Aircraft Y was coincidentally exactly the same time we were at this critical place. As a CFI-I; I am reluctant to use this approach for training ever again. One suggestion may be to cross ARRES at an altitude lower than the charted minimum of 7;500 feet MSL - if; and only if; it's a practice approach under VFR. The potential negative training this would cause would have to be weighed against the extra margin of separation from the Class B shelf. Additionally; in the future; if I use this approach for practice again; I will have the student execute a missed approach and turn away from the 7;000 feet MSL Class B shelf if the aircraft is high at ARRES; does not initiate a timely descent; or if I notice DEN traffic that could cross above us as happened on this flight.

column121: We were doing approaches on an IFR flight plan because ATC currently won't allow practice approaches due to; we were told; coronavirus staffing levels.  Being on an actual IFR flight plan increased the complexity of what should have been simple currency training in visual conditions to get instrument currency.The aircraft; an Aircraft X type; was newly purchased and had been flown VFR by my student (I trained him and signed him off for an instrument rating; he passed on the first attempt almost a year ago); but he had yet to take it IFR.  It is nicely equipped with two Dynon combination PFD/MFD's and a Garmin GPS NAV/COM.  I have 1000-2000 hours on Garmin products; both GPS and G1000 systems; but only about a dozen hours on an Aircraft Y type with similar Dynon systems and no prior hours on an Aircraft X type.We took off from ZZZ1 and shot two approaches into ZZZ2 (about 15 NM away) and were being vectored for a last approach into ZZZ1 to a full stop.  I was simultaneously looking for traffic; explaining a point about GPS approach procedure; listening to another pilot on the radio report his position; and looking out for a scattered layer that was getting lower as the flight progressed and that we were just about to go into.  The autopilot was on and I noticed the aircraft climbing through 2;800 feet.  I thought I remembered that ZZZ approach had given us an altitude of 2;000 but I wasn't quite sure (my student was handling the radios); so I jumped on the radio and made an inquiry.  Approach confirmed we had been given an altitude of 2;000.  I immediately had my student hold the altitude we were at while I waited to jump in on the frequency as it was congested.  I reported that we were inadvertently at 2;800 and asked what altitude they wanted us at.  They replied 2;000.  I said we would descend to 2;000 which we did immediately.  ATC did not ask us to call a number when we got on the ground or make any other mention of it.The autopilot should have stopped the plane climbing at 2000.  Neither of us could determine why it didn't as it worked fine leveling off at altitudes both before and after.  I can only guess it was user input error on the part of my student.  When he changed it to descend to 2;000 and hold that altitude it worked just fine.I believe the reason why I didn't notice the altitude deviation sooner than reaching 800 feet over our assigned altitude was a combination of sensory overload of having to teach; look for traffic; listen to radio chatter; look out for entering clouds (which should have been less of a consideration since we were on an actual IFR plan); combined with a lack of experience on the Dynon systems which limited my rapid acquisition of altitude information.I shall endeavor in the future to practice with the Dynon systems more in VFR conditions before venturing into IFR.

column121: At approximately XA:45; I realized it seemed to have been sometime since I had heard from the Controller. This is not entirely unusual. Due to the pandemic; there are times of much less radio chatter. In fact; several times a week; there are periods where nothing is said by anyone on frequency for lengths of time as long as 20-40 minutes save the occasional 'You still there?' It seemed to have been a bit longer than normal; so we called on our last assigned frequency. We heard nothing so I tried Guard and heard nothing. Unbeknownst to me the volume of the radio receiving Guard was accidentally turned down. As I was trying Guard my copilot found a frequency on the chart; made radio contact and was given the proper frequency we should be on. We re-established communication with ZZZ Center. All seemed fine; until the hand-off came with a phone number for possible pilot deviation.Upon arrival at our destination I called the number I had been given. The Controller I spoke with asked if I knew why I was given the number to call. I told him I believed it was due to lost radio contact. He said it was. We then discussed how this might have happened and things to do to re-establish radio contact. He then said it seemed to him we had never been given a hand-off. He also said that sector was very busy at the time the incident occurred. I have no doubt they were. I suspect they were even a bit understaffed due to the pandemic.  we concluded our conversation and thanked each other.My copilot and I spent considerable time discussing how this might have happened and how to prevent it in the future. But it must be noted there is no recourse for pilots that find themselves in this situation. There is also no sure way of completely preventing this type of situation. Pilots have no way of knowing when a hand-off should occur or when they have reached a specific time limit. Sometimes we check on; only to be immediately handed off with 'short stay; contact center on XYX.AB'. Other times we listen for long periods time listening to a completely silent radio. Those long periods of silence do not help at all. They only make the silence seem normal. Maybe controllers should be required to inform us; at check-on; how long or how many miles we can expect to be with them. They always seem to have an idea how long we will be in contact with them.
column123: At approximately XA:45 local; at FL360; in cruise; we noticed that we hadn't heard from Center in quite some time.  During these times of COVID; it has become commonplace to go for long periods of time without hearing anything from Center or other traffic; especially in remote portions of the US. With the frequent occurrence that the only radio traffic heard is a pilot asking 'Still on?' just to make sure someone is still out there; it is impossible for a pilot to determine at what time/distance interval; he should be expecting contact; a hand-off; or any other instruction from ATC.This was the case on date.  During a long cross-country flight; we went for what seemed a long time without hearing anything from Center.  We acknowledged the fact and I keyed the mic to interrogate Center.  There was no response.  I tried again and even switched to the previous frequency; just in case.  Still no joy.  Pulled up the sectional to find the nearest Center and discovered ZZZ Center; Area X on frequency.  Called out to this Controller who brusquely inquired who we were; where we were; and informed us that we were on the wrong frequency; providing us with the correct one.  We immediately switched to the appropriate frequency; received a response and continued on our way.  Shortly thereafter; we received a call from Center that we had a possible pilot deviation and they had a number for us.  Number was copied; remainder of the flight continued without incident.Upon landing; we reached out to the Center phone number; who informed us that; after reviewing the recordings; we had not been handed off to the next sector; and it was no fault of ours.  Easy enough.  Controller called back a few minutes later; stating that the previous sector had filed a report on the incident; and needed pilot license number; etc.; for the reports.This brings me to the point where I ask; what can be done in this situation?  There is clearly no exact location where an aircraft is handed off to another sector/center/controller.  There is no exact amount of time flying through a sector before a switch is made.  What can we; as pilots; do to help with this situation?  Obviously; I cannot do my job as a pilot AND do the job of the controllers on the ground; so where is the happy medium?  Is there a guideline of the appropriate amount of time to go without hearing from ATC before inquiring?  Should we set a timer after each hand-off; or create a GPS way-point a certain distance down the line?It can be argued that 'I have a number for you to call; advise when ready to copy' are the most stressful 13 words heard in a pilot's day.  It generates fear; concern; trepidation and second guessing of the skills and abilities that we spend years honing and decades perfecting.  When we make mistakes; that is a definite way to bring attention to the problems and help find a solution.  What recourse do we have when a controller makes the mistake?  We spent the remainder of the flight and; arguably; the next 24 plus hours; stressing over what we should have done; when we should have checked in; how were we supposed to know; etc.

When I looked at my ground track after the flight; I did drift slightly right when I was on the extended downwind; but I never intercepted the final approach course. I did not receive notice from the Tower about the King Air on final before being switched to Approach and it wasn't until after I checked in with Approach that they gave me the advisory. The King Air's TCAS system showed that we reached within 100 feet of each other but myself and the pilots in the King Air agreed that it was much more that 100 feet. I overall feel like there was a lack of communication from all parts that could have possibly prevented this occurrence. I personally could have been more specific with tower on where I was going. I could have been more watchful of my track to stay clear of final. The winds were from the northwest so that could have been a factor in why I was slightly drifting. That is why it is important to know where your winds are coming from to maintain a constant ground track along the ground and prevent drifting.

I advised Aircraft X the minimum IFR altitude is 160 and to report reaching. I should have issued a heading south as soon as he advised me he was already turning to PUB. I know the highest mountains in that area are not above 140; but the terrain climbs so rapidly in that area I should have known he would not have topped the 160 MIA even though he did climb above the 130 MIA. He also reported turbulence and icing at this time.The pilot should not have exited the published holding without a clearance to do so. I should have issued a south heading as soon as he told me he was turning out of hold. It was poor service on my end.
