column121: While turning into Spot XXX on the cargo apron in ZZZZ; the plane was unable to stop in a timely manner due to what I believe was contamination on the apron. Due to the lack of braking ability the CA (Captain) briefly deployed the thrust reversers and the plane was then able to slow and we regained braking ability. I was not aware that there was difficulty braking until the CA deployed the reversers. We then proceeded to finish the turn into [spot] without issue. The entrance to the ramp was well cleaned and mostly free of contaminants; and according to the Captain; the braking condition was very good. However; further into the ramp; the contamination became present; although it was not very visible; almost like it was black ice on top of the pavement. When we exited the plane after shutting down and securing; the ramp and parking area was covered in a transparent; very slippery layer of ice with slush scattered sporadically throughout. I believe that this ice existed on the apron just outside of the parking spot as well. There was no active precipitation and all of the airport surfaces we had been on up until that point had had good breaking conditions. Thankfully the CA was able to control the aircraft without causing damage to the plane or surroundings. I do not have an exact recollection of the ground speed when we had the difficulty breaking; but I would estimate it to be in the range of roughly 5-7 knots. We notified the ground crew of the difficulty braking and hopefully they took actions to decontaminate that area of the ramp for the next aircraft.I believe the transition from well-cleared; contaminant free areas; to the contaminated area caused the braking issue. It was also night and the light did not reflect off of the ice on the contaminated areas of the ramp; making it difficult to see the contamination. I thought the Captain was maintaining a safe speed for the conditions and was surprised when the reversers were deployed.I would suggest that the entirety of the ramp is cleared to the same standard in the future if able. Crews should also be extra vigilant of contamination that is not easily visible in low light; or poorly lit conditions.
column123: Normal arrival. While taxiing to Stand XXX we were following a company aircraft. Due to the light weight of our aircraft it kept accelerating while at idle thrust. When entering the cargo ramp; the pavement was bare and wet. The last 500 feet of taxi had thin frozen slush. The aircraft ahead slowed; and we were slowing to turn into our stand; when the Captain noted the aircraft was sliding. He applied full brakes to no effect; then deployed reverse thrust on both engines; slightly above idle. The aircraft slowed and stopped after sliding about 50 feet. The reversers were stowed and the aircraft turned into the stand and parked. As it approached the stop point it again slid about 5 feet in the attempt to stop. Reverse thrust was not used a second time. Less than 30% n1 in reverse.[The cause was] thin ice on the ramp. Taxi speed about 8-10 knots. Unnoticed change in braking effectiveness. Fatigue from a 15+ hour day.Reverse thrust was a last ditch effort to not scrape paint. Parking brake might have worked also. Even creeping to the stop point; the aircraft still slid about 2 feet past the stop point.

column121: Towards the end of the climb segment; I glanced down at the ACARS screen and noticed we had a message. The chime did not go off since we were still in the climb. When I checked the message; it said something to the effect of; 'There was an error in the loading of DG (Dangerous Goods) on the aircraft. I'm working to get the details. Standby by for further details.' Several minutes later; a message came in stating that a can had been loaded in Position 1L in error. It was slightly lighter than noted on out weight and balance (about 70 pounds; if I recall correctly); not a concern. Of note; it had some DG; and the concern was that it included some radioactive DG (0.8 TI). The Dispatcher stated that it was up to all of us to decide if we would continue or not. The Captain and I discussed our options and referenced the FOM. We noted that up to 50 TI (Transport Index) could be loaded in Position 3 without a waiver and that it seemed that would probably be a higher exposure than the 0.8 TI loaded in [Position] 1L; but that we did not have the expertise or information to determine that for sure. As we were getting ready to forward some of our questions to the [Dispatcher]; he sent us a message stating that he was contacting the experts. After consultation with the Duty Officer; Safety representative; and DG experts; they determined that the exposure should be well within limits. This agreed with our hunch; and calmed any fears we had about continuing. We were also notified that the destination ramp would have a DG specialist meet us and take reading on the jet when we arrived; so we continued uneventfully to the destination. As promised; the DG specialist met us and took readings from both the supernumerary area and the cockpit. All were well below limits.The cause was either or combination of human error; inadequacy of training; or process breakdown. I can't say for sure as I'm not sure exactly how the error was made. During loading; I know the crew had problems loading a can. I believe they ended up off-loading the can and transferring the cargo to a new can. We were then delayed while the ramp agent and a manager had to confirm the loading of the can in order to get a final weight and balance. I'm not sure if this was the can in question; if that distraction led to the improper loading of this can; or if the two events were unrelated. Fortunately once someone realized the error; they brought it to attention even though we had already departed.

The flight returned to gate and was delayed several hours in order to allow for arrival to ZZZ [Center] after it opened at XF:30Z.I missed the original emails stating the closure which would have given myself; the crew; and the coordinator a heads up to be careful of our times deicing. column121: In preparing for the flight; I could not determine the engine-out minimum cleanup altitude departing Runway 16R for an engine failure that occurs after D3.0 IRNO. The complex special EFP reads 'EO - Established on H325 and above 5;500 feet MSL' - a condition that will not be reached if climbing via IRNO LOC SOUTH COURSE per the EFP. After talking to the Chief Pilot on Call; who then made inquiries to other internal resources; it was determined that 5;500 feet MSL is the minimum cleanup altitude. In fact; at the minimum all-engine climb gradient of 440 ft./NM any departing aircraft will be above 5;500 feet MSL (1;085 ft. AAE) before D3.0 IRNO. However; with an all-engine minimum cleanup altitude of 7;400 feet MSL an engine failure can occur with the flaps extended. The EFP does not provide a minimum cleanup altitude for that case.Our departure was uneventful; and our light-weight [aircraft] reached 7;400 ft. MSL as we crossed D3.0 IRNO. Winds were out of the south at 45 kts. On a side note; the [Runway] 16L/R EFP for IRNO OTS (Out of Service) appears flawed. If IRNO and IAGY are both OTS the procedure specifies runway heading to 8;500 feet MSL. At max crosswind for a V2 of 131 KIAS of 70 kts.; drift angle will be 32 degrees. With a ground track of 196 (degrees); the terrain at 7;862 feet is almost precisely on course from the FMG R-205 decision point. The crosswind limits appear to be for the early turn to H325; but may need to be more restrictive for a 164 heading climb to 8;500 feet MSL.

column121: Departing RJAA. I was PF (Pilot Flying). Captain was PM (Pilot Monitoring). Relief FO (First Officer) was sitting in observer seat. We were within a close margin of max structural weight but within all limits. It was briefed that the best angle speed (258 kts.) and flaps up maneuver speed (254 kts.) would exceed the 250 [kts.] below 10;000 ft. restriction so we opted to keep Flaps 1 until passing 10;000 [ft.] so that we could maintain maneuverability. Once we cleaned up to Flaps 1; I opened the speed window and manually set speed to 240 kts. The overspeed margin was currently 250 kts. The underspeed margin was around 225 kts. Flaps 1 maneuver speed was about 235 kts. Upon reaching 10;000 ft.; I put 245 kts. in the speed window to initiate an acceleration that would then continue past 254 kts. for the Flaps Up speed as the flaps transitioned. The transition was going as planned until we hit some moderate wake turbulence from crossing traffic. The speed started to shoot up dramatically towards the upper limit. I applied some back pressure while keeping the AP engaged to get the nose up and arrest the speed increase. I was able to arrest most of the speed increase but it still resulted in a 1 or 2 kt. overspeed. At this time; the turbulence became more intense and both the low and high speed regimes converged. I disengaged the AP/AT (Autopilot/Autothrottle) and hand flew to best maintain airspeed as I anticipated a drop in airspeed on the other side of the wake turbulence. The airspeed started to drop but was arrested with manual input. Once the high and low speed margins stabilized and the turbulence subsided; we re-automated the aircraft and continued our departure without incident.I did not anticipate the wake of crossing traffic to be such a factor in our tight tolerances. When so close to max structural weight on TO (takeoff); the transition from Flaps 1 to Flaps Up is always on a razor thin margin. Any significant wake; turbulence or even wind shift will put you into and undesired airspeed regime. I would suggest not loading the aircraft right up to max weights and this has always been an issue for flap transition on the 767.

column121: Due to the nature of wearing a mask due to COVID-19; it contributes to a couple safety concerns.  It is a matter of time before there is a serious injury or damage due to the policy of wearing a mask the entire time while on airport property.  I have been involved in a couple of close calls and have seen issues with my coworkers as well.First off; the communication issues.  We already have issues with radio communication and I know there have been reports filed in the past for this.  However; now there is another issue involving the wearing of masks and trying to understand what the person is trying to say.  The voice is usually muffled or broken up and hard to understand.  Most of the time requiring the person receiving the transmission to ask the other person to either repeat or in some cases just misunderstands the call.  Throw in the inherent environmental noises from jet engines or air conditioning packs and other loud noise; communication becomes very difficult at times.  As you can imagine; this can easily become a safety issue especially in times of urgency or clearing of flight control movement or other tests and engine runs. Second; visual impairment.  The wearing of masks impairs your line of sight looking down.  In order to actually see the ground in front of your feet; you need to actually bend your neck down to move your head to see and while you are looking down with your head down; then that is when you end up walking into something.  You are unable to just look down.  The obstruction has caused many trips due to the obstacles of power cords; tow bars; tools; steps on ladders; walking in cargo pits; and weather related issues; such as ice and snow.  These are just a few of the most common items; but the list is endless.Also; when wearing safety glasses or prescription glasses or sunglasses; there is the issue of them constantly fogging up.  Especially in colder weather.  This just compounds the issue with not being able to see what is in front of your feet.The easiest and fastest way to fix this is to not require the wearing of masks.   Maybe only wear a mask while stationary and unable to social distance as long as it doesn't affect your job.  TSA does give an option to not have to wear a mask if it is a safety concern as stated in the TSA website for the Executive Order. So my suggestion is to make the determination that due to a safety risk; the safety guidelines need [to] be changed to make masks optional on the individuals choice; depending on the job he or she is involved in due to the reasons stated above.

column121: While on an OE Refresher flight; I was the PM and my FO student was on his first PF leg in about 9 months due to being non-qualified during the COVID crisis.We were on a right down wind with a clearance to descend 2;000 feet. We were told to stop our descent and we leveled off at 2;600 feet. ATC alerted us to a helicopter crossing our path at 2;000 feet. We reported him in sight and ATC turned us for a right base. When we were clear of the traffic we were cleared to 2;000 feet and then for a visual approach with the airport in sight.  The FO called for gear down just outside the marker and managed the speed at the marker. We were at 170 knots at the time.  We had planned for a flaps 3 landing. With our encounter/interruption with the close traffic we didn't take into account that the marker was 3.4 miles from the runway and at 1;200 AGL. With the glide slope captured and a planned flaps 3 landing the airplane was having a hard time slowing down. I pulled the speed brakes to assist the aircraft and the FO was slowing the airplane down.  I pulled them just inside the marker and stowed them a few seconds later when the airspeed was near Vref. What I didn't realize was I had left them extended below 1;000 feet.  I think part of the issue is the approach seems a little nonstandard (standard: 5 NM; 1;500 feet AGL) and sneaks up on you with the marker at 3.4 NM from the runway at 1;200 feet.

column121: At approximately 100 kts; I noticed and called out a IAS Disagree warning indication on my PFD. I immediately looked at the First Officer and the STBY Airspeed indicators to compare speeds and saw the same warning on his. The difference in speed between both was about 5-7 knots (see FM; Airspeed Disagree Alert (amber) Indicates the Captain's and First Officer's airspeed indications disagree by more than 5 knots for 5 continuous seconds); and took about 5 to 10 seconds before the warning went away. My decision was to continue the takeoff since the IAS discrepancy was small and we were in the High-Speed regime. Following the disappearance of the warning indication; I closely monitored the speed differences which was reduced to 1-1.5 knots. Throughout the rest of the flight. An ELB write-up was made and local maintenance contacted to give a full description of the event after landing.Once we were at a safe climbing altitude; we discussed the situation further. I mentioned that if the difference in IAS had been larger I would have opted to reject. Interestingly; the First Officer expressed relief that we did not reject; and that we could have taken off even with the stick shaker going off; similarly as we experienced in a recent MAX training session (during climb); and that the company does not want us to reject other than for the exceptions stated in the FM. His honest answer left me to ponder and wonder if I made the right decision; and to take a closer look at our Normal and Non-Normal procedures; guidance; and its implications; and if any further clarification is needed or due. With that said; I would like to review on how would they apply in the following scenarios. For ease of page reference; I utilized FM dated XX-XX-XXX; however the manual date at the time of the event was [on] YY-YYY-YYYY. The information appears to be identical with the exception of a slight page numbering difference.  As a point of reference to determine a reliable airspeed indicator; the checklist states 'An airspeed indication that differs by more than 20 kts or 0.03 Mach from the airspeed shown in the table should be considered unreliable.' Also; there is NO guidance for pitch attitude on takeoff for this situation other than an initial pitch to 15 degrees followed by the immediate actions; which would call for a pitch and thrust reduction just off the ground following gear retraction. The immediate above action items seems contradictory to safe and sound practice of flying away from the ground and executing an emergency procedure at a safe altitude. Should safer guidance be included?It seems very clear; as always; that excellent flying skills and judicious Captain's Emergency Authority will be needed.

column121: We operated Aircraft X from ZZZ to MDW; and the majority of the flight was uneventful. Mr. Y was my Captain and PF; and we had setup well in advance for the RNAV RNP Y approach for Runway 22L at MDW according to their latest ATIS. Later we received an ATIS update showing that the ILS for Runway 31C was active; so we re-configured and briefed that; still with plenty of time. We had discussed the possible need of diverting to ZZZ1 rather than our filed ALT1 of ZZZ2 and ALT2 of ZZZ3; but the visibility at MDW stayed above the minimums we needed for either the RNAV or ILS approaches to 22L/31C respectively.Fast forward to our first approach attempt: we're established on the ILS to 31C; fully configured well before the FAF and I was thinking we've got it made. We broke out at around 1;700 MSL and inflight visibility was not an issue and better than reported. From around 2;000 feet and down we experienced constant light and moderate turbulence; but no icing or precipitation. Captain had turned the autopilot and autothrottles off to help deal with the winds that were gusting from 260 degrees at 21 to 39 knots. We were also landing with stall protection ice speeds; adding 10 knots to our Vref and Vapp speeds.Everything was going great until somewhere between 1/2 to 1 mile from the approach end of 31C we got multiple 'WINDSHEAR' automated call outs from the airplane. Captain elected to go-around which we did; re-configuring as needed and I let MDW Tower know at around 400 feet AGL per the SOP. They gave us a heading and altitude to fly; asked us the reason for the go-around and handed us back off to Chicago Approach. We cleaned up the airplane and got vectored in for another ILS approach to 31C behind an Air Carrier Y.The second ILS approach was almost identical to the first; albeit with slightly less wind and turbulence. This time; even though we were ready for the conditions and knew more of what to expect; we managed to catch a gust of wind right in the flare and didn't touch down on Runway 31C until between the first third and the midpoint of the runway. Captain did a great job of thinking quick and performed a rejected landing; setting and calling 'TOGA' almost immediately after touchdown and off we went. We reconfigured again; got vectored around and handed off to Chicago Approach again and came around for a third attempt at Runway 31C.The third time Captain was able to land normally and well within the touchdown zone; but when he applied the brakes we found out that the '5/5/5' runway condition codes advertised for 31C were optimistic at best with the airplane noticeably sliding and skidding as we rolled out. We also noticed that there was blowing snow obscuring at least 50 percent of the runway surface. Captain advised MDW Tower of the braking action we experienced; calling it 'poor' and; to their credit; they immediately directed the broom and plow teams out to clear Runway 31C again. The rest of the flight was normal as we taxied into our gate.If there's anything I learned tonight; it's that just because you're on short final that doesn't mean you're going to land. Also: just because the Air Carrier Y flight that landed ahead of you reported 'braking action good' doesn't mean you will. I remember being on short final during our first ILS approach to 31C feeling complacent that we 'had it made' being on the ILS rather than RNAV RNP approach with its higher minimums and having broken out early at 1;700 feet. My go-around call outs also could have been crisper and more prompt; but that was mostly due to the 'startle' factor which was my own fault.My one suggestion would be for the airport operations crews at MDW to conduct their own braking action tests more often and with a more pessimistic eye. When the ATIS states RCCs are '5/5/5' the Air Carrier Y flight that landed ahead of you reports 'braking action good' and yet you experience significant wheel slip/skid due to icy runway surface conditions upon landing; thatindicates someone is being either dishonest or overly optimistic on their own braking action reports. If we or our Dispatch had known that the 'real' RCCs for 31C at MDW were actually 3/3/3 or even 2/2/2; we most likely would not have had the required landing performance numbers that we needed to land at MDW's shorter runways and would've gone to ZZZ1.

column121: Descending via the NIIXX 2 arrival for the ILS Runway 35R in CAVOK conditions. Around the BSTON Intersection we were given a westerly to northwesterly radar vector and cleared to descend and maintain 10;000. As we got closer to the final approach course (somewhere between DEANE and DRUMM) we were cleared to descend and maintain 8;000 and cleared direct to the FRONZ Intersection (FAF for the ILS). The Controller asked if we had 35R in sight; after a pause; we had the runway in sight and advised ATC. We were then cleared for the visual approach to 35R. The FAF altitude at FRONZ is 7;000 so that is what we set in the MCP while descending through approximately 8;800 in FLCH. We had just gotten the '2;500' call from the Radio Altimeter and made our call outs. As we descended through 8;000 I noticed the Radio Altitude around 1;800 and descending. A quick look at JeppFD PRO showed our aircraft position just south and east of the DRUMM Intersection. I called out the altitude and the fact that we need to go back up to 8;000 (our last cleared altitude prior to the approach clearance) until we are north of DRUMM. I reset the MCP to 8;000 and verbalized that we need to climb back up. The Captain selected a V/S climb back to 8;000. We joined the approach course and followed the G/S and landed without incident.ATC never mentioned anything to us about violating airspace or going below the DEN Class B. Though it is nice to get directs; etc. However; I believe the direct to FRONZ clearance; if not really familiar with the DEN Class B; can set crews up to possibly violate airspace and even lead to an unstable approach.Once parked at the gate with all checklists complete; we debriefed and there certainly was some confusion as to exactly where we were when we descended below 8;000. We had a jump seat observer who thought we might have been a little low as he has a lot of General Aviation experience in the DEN area.

column121: As an LCA I was in the right seat and training a new B787 type aircraft Captain in the left seat. We had landed from on Runway  XXR in ZZZ and taxied to gate. Upon approaching the gate there was a marshaller and a wing walker on both sides. They were all giving us the all clear signal and marshalling us in to the gate. Gate X is a challenging gate because close proximity to other aircraft. We noticed tractors; baggage carts; containers; and container trailers all parked in the transgression zone on both sides of the entry path. We stopped the aircraft and attempted to contact Operations. As we waited the wing walker; especially on aircraft right; seemed to be frustrated and continued to try to get us to move forward. I witnessed a baggage tractor drive up and just push some of the baggage carts; not even taking time to hook up and pull them. Operations radioed back and told us they would call the ramp. A pickup truck showed up; presumably with a ramp supervisor. The person got out and started directing the removal of the equipment from the path of the aircraft. It was extremely hard for us to see the lines marking the transgression zone and we wanted to be able to rely on the ramp team; but it was more than obvious due to our experience with our aircraft; taxi training; and taxi experience; that we weren't safe to proceed. Finally they cleared all of the obstructions except for one container cart. Once that was cleared and could confirm that the transgression area was clear; we taxied in. What was most disturbing about this whole situation was the continued all clear signal from the wing walkers and the signal to continue the taxi from the marshaller.

column121: Coming in to ROA we were cleared for the visual approach for Runway 34; I was PM and Captain was PF. We were set up for a left base and kept our descent coming down to 4;000 feet. On the descent down we received a GPWS warning for terrain and Captain took immediate action and we climbed out of the terrain we were near. Captain and I both had our terrain mode on; but it was not showing up on the MFD for both sides. ATC also reported to us if we saw the terrain ahead before we received the GPWS.I believe this started from the beginning of our trip both Captain and I were deadheading from ZZZ to ZZZ1 and the aircraft had a hydraulic issue which made our flight delayed. Which got rid of 2 of our 3 flights that we were supposed to operate and made this flight our first flight of the day together. This was also my first time at ROA and Captain told me that he has been there a couple times before so I was unfamiliar with the airport and the surrounding terrain. With it also being a moonless night it was very hard to see the terrain in front of us and with terrain mode on but it wasn't showing us anything made it very difficult to determine exactly where we were at on the ILS approach plate when we were in VFR conditions. I also should have spoken up when I was looking on the approach plate that the highest terrain was 3;508 and Captain was setting the altitude bug to 4;000 feet. I believe our vertical speed was also a factor but I don't remember exactly what Captain had it set to. Captain and I also debriefed together to figure out what we did wrong and what we did right and learn from our mistakes.Add terrain photos or jepp plates on the 10-7 pages to help with situational awareness.
column123: Cleared for ILS 34 on an extended left base and received the ground proximity warning for terrain on decent to the final approach fix altitude. Initially cleared to altitude on our route to 9;000 feet crossing Pulaski (PSK) [VOR]. After PSK on rout to ROA we were then given a decent down to 6;000 feet. Clear night we called airport in sight for the sight of the rotating beacon we set up for ILS 34. On an extended left base approach control gave us heading 090 and we were cleared for the visual to 34. After our clearance I gave a further turn to heading 100 and tried to widen out the base for Runway 34. With our clearance I descended down to 4;000 initially keeping in mind we had a tailwind until turning on final for Runway 34. On our descent to 4;000 we both switched to terrain mode on the PFD and saw nothing. Initially I was still on my legs page on my IPAD and my First Officer on the approach plate. We got a call from Approach asking us if we know the terrain around us and while he asked leveling at 4;000 we got a a TERRAIN TERRAIN PULL UP WARNING. We exercised the escape maneuver and leveled at 6;000. We replied to the approach that we exercised the escape maneuver and discussed that we thought we were south of the terrain further back. At night it is hard to distinguish that but exercised extreme caution until back on final.Cause - No initial knowledge of the area of terrain at night even in terrain mode on PFD. Cross reference with iPad to select altitude until final. Suggestion - I will hold the last cleared altitude at 6;000 feet and go further out towards the IAF before turning for final and descending to final altitude before glide slope capture.

column121: The FO was on the very first leg of OE. The flight proceeded perfectly until arriving in the ZZZ1 [airport] terminal area. ZZZ Center descended us and never handed us over to the local [ZZZ] TRACON. Instead; we were told to expect holding instructions. It was clear the Center Controller was very busy (he was doing an exceptionally good job). Instead of issuing holding instructions we were asked where we wanted to hold. We told him we wanted to hold at ZZZZZ [Intersection]; the initial approach fix for the ILS Runway XX to ZZZ [airport]. He issued instructions to hold south. We asked if we could hold north inbound; right hand turns. He issued instructions 'cleared as requested' with no EFC. He asked how much fuel we had onboard and we replied 2 hours. I didn't push the EFC because it was clear he was saturated and we were holding at 11;000 feet above a lower layer in VFR conditions. ATC explained to other aircraft that ZZZ [TRACON] was ATC Zero and he was the only Controller handling all aircraft going into and out of 4 controlled fields. It was difficult to simply get a break on the frequency so I decided to just be patient.We had been sending ACARS messages to the company enroute and didn't get any responses; this is not that unusual; usually Dispatch will reply with 'OK' but not always. When we were issued holding instructions we sent Dispatch an ACARS message 'Holding at OM for Runway YY ZZZ; no reason given' and once again; we did not receive a reply. Incidentally; I instruct all my OE pilots; as I did in this instance; to look for the 'VHF IN PROGRESS' display after selecting SEND on an ACARS message to be certain the unit actually sent the message. In all cases it did.The airport pages indicated that ZZZ2 [airport] was just XX miles away and we knew they were not affected by this situation. The weather at ZZZ2 was also good. Our FMC fuel reserve was 4.0 since we had no alternate. At first I wanted to use 7.0 as a decision point on fuel. My thought it would probably take 20 minutes to get to ZZZ2 if needed and I wanted a cushion so I added 3.0 to the FMC fuel reserve to make my decision. If we hit 7.0 on the fuel it would be time to contact Dispatch and go to ZZZ2. While we were doing all this ATC was relying on us to contact aircraft going into and out of the airports below to issue instructions. Needless to say we were a bit busy. We were told to descend first to 8;000 feet in the hold; then to 6;000 feet. On several occasions VFR aircraft popped up on our TCAS (no alerts were issued) as we were holding in Class E airspace above the ZZZ Class D and the ZZZ1 Class C. We were keeping a keen eye outside. At one point ATC issued instructions to climb to 8;000 feet in the hold for traffic. Again; the Center Controller was doing an exceptionally good job. We were told on several occasions what our sequence was going into ZZZ; third; then second; then next.  Our intent; of course; was to get into ZZZ safely.ATC was issuing phone numbers for aircraft to call when on the ground. I was a bit confused as to why; I thought the towers were open; but paid it no mind. We heard the Controller mention COVID as the reason to another aircraft. Unfortunately; the aircraft landing ZZZ in front of us; Aircraft Y failed to call the phone number. This haunted ALL landings into all 4 airports. The Controller explained to another aircraft that his procedures precluded him from clearing any other aircraft for approaches into any of the four fields until had had a cancellation from the Aircraft Y. In fact; ATC had us attempt to call him on the frequency.I considered whether we could get in VFR but we could not get down into the class D with ZZZ Center and there was a layer between us and the field (I've forgotten where it was but probably about 3;000 feet). I then considered our fuel considerations; rather than using the 4.0 FMC fuel reserve I decided to use the actual FAR fuel reserve of roughly 3.6. The FO stayed on top of duties not only contacting other aircraft but complying with my requests as the flying pilot very well. Finally; when we reached 6;600 pounds of fuel remaining I asked the FO to contact Dispatch via ARINC phone patch. We had already looked at the ARINC Services page in the Jepps early on and determined that ARINC had a surface on ground frequency of XYX.XZ at ZZZ1; and we would be able to get a hold of them down low. I asked FO to come up with a diversion plan. FO worked with Dispatch who recommended ZZZ2 (of course) and said the fuel required would be 1;100 pounds at 10;000 feet. This seemed too low; I didn't see how we could climb to 10;000 feet; fly XY miles; and shoot an approach and landing on 1;100 pounds (and change) of fuel; so we declared minimum fuel and requested an immediate direct vector to ZZZ2. At no point did we use the words 'Mayday' or 'Emergency'. We were instructed to fly a heading (I believe it was 045 degrees) and issued climb instructions to 10;000 feet. We immediately complied and began to set up for an approach into ZZZ2.The FO did a great job juggling responsibilities; getting ATIS and setting up for the approach; contacting ZZZ1 local; etc. At one point ATC queried our fuel status and the FO initially used the word Emergency but then quickly corrected and said we had declared Minimum Fuel. We landed on ZZZ2 Runway XXL with 3.7 on the fuel. We pulled off the runway and asked ATC for a position where we could sit and call the company.We called Dispatch on the cell phone and were instructed to go to the 'Maintenance Ramp.' We complied and were met with a follow me car where we parked; right next to an aircraft with a full load of passengers (obviously there for the same reason; we were later joined by another aircraft). We were immediately met with a set of stairs and a representative who asked what we needed. Dispatch immediately gave us a field load and we ordered thirteen thousand pounds of fuel. We arranged for the proper fuel load. It took some time for the fuel truck to arrive.We then had to coordinate getting paperwork to the aircraft. While Dispatch and the team did a great job of getting that all set up; the young lady driving back and forth had to go quite a ways to get our paperwork which took a great deal of time.Once we had our paperwork we were able to depart for the short flight to ZZZ. We completed the legs without further incident.I am uncertain what drove ZZZ TRACON to close; whether it was a scheduled cleaning due to COVID or some type of emergency. We reviewed the ATC and FIR NOTAMs and did not have anything mentioning the closure. Clearly this was the beginning of the delay. Then; it was further exacerbated by the crew of Aircraft Y jet failing to call the phone number after landing. Had they called we were next to be cleared to land and we would not have diverted.Several suggestions: We need clear and concise ACARs policies in the FOM. Each and every time Dispatch receives a message from a crew inflight they should ALWAYS reply. Perhaps this is a policy with Dispatch; but since it is not in the FOM and once in a while we do not hear from them we have no idea and I was not concerned about not getting replies; until we mentioned holding to them and I got no reply. That's when we hopped on the ACARS Services chart and noted that ZZZ1 had a ground based frequency and we could reach them from our holding position (incidentally; many of our pilots don't even know that table exists). Second; It is not unusual for ACARs not to work. This needs to be cleaned up. We are constantly writing up aircraft for 'NO COMM' and ACARs failures and they don't work. Honestly; I'd say ACARS works correctly about 2/3 of the time; certainly not the spirit of FAR 121.99. Granted we have ARINC; but crews will rely on ACARS just to find out after the fact that dispatch never got anything from us. Next; if this was a scheduled COVID cleaning we should have known they were going ATC Zero before we arrived in the terminal area. Dispatch was even caught off guard about it. ATC must develop a means of communicating this so we don't find out so late in the game. They should also consider issuing a TFR. Perhaps the FAA should consider a new type of TFR for COVID. Frankly; I am a small aircraft owner and use it frequently. I don't want to be told I can't fly over class D airspace while in Class E airspace simply because they are cleaning TRACON. On a beautiful sunny day there are going to be aircraft all over. If I were flying GA in the area and knew the TRACON was down I'd probably stay away just because I don't want to get run over by a transport. Finally; the company should consider what paperwork we REALLY need at the aircraft. For instance; we can already get performance via ACARS. We can pull up our NOTAMS on our tablet. That would leave signing fit for duty and the release. Perhaps we could give Dispatch all the pertinent info (they already had the ZFW weight and balance) so all they needed was fuel onboard and they could simply give us the necessary numbers for departure. Next; send us an ACARS message for signatures - we could print 2 of them and leave one with the rep on the ramp. Had we been able to do that we would have been out about an hour earlier and would NOT have taken another delay. Incidentally; we obtained our PDC via ACARS in ZZZ2 correctly and it worked properly all the way back; including the summary page.

column121: I am submitting this copy of a fumes report submitted following a SOF event that occurred following deicing at the gate at ZZZ as a report. The only thing I might add pertaining to legalities is that after the event when we elected to attempt to fly the leg a second time before Maintenance took the plane out of service; that decision was made after conferring with the Duty Chief at Maintenance Control who had consulted with Maintenance following the SOF event. We had been running the packs with the APU for a long period of time after the passengers deplaned; and then did an engine run on top of that to blow out the entire air conditioning system and had no further issue with deicing fumes. The plane was only subsequently removed from service because it came to light that there might be an IOD claim from one or more of the flight attendants (3 of whom elected to deadhead home on the very same airplane they'd been working on when we had the fumes event) 'This is a report of a fume event that occurred post-deicing at the gate at ZZZ. A separate Fume Event form was also submitted. This is the third such occurrence I have encountered following ZZZ deicing in the past 2 years. In the previous 2 occurrences the effects were much less pronounced and not deemed a hazard because their duration was brief and the cause obvious. In those two cases when the aircraft was reconfigured post-deicing; when the packs were reinstated there was an immediate introduction of visible deicing fluid fumes entering the flight deck; with a much less pronounced but slightly noticeable effect in the cabin that did not warrant any action or alarm. In both cases the packs were turned off and cockpit windows opened followed by an eventual attempt to turn the packs back in one at a time with no further issues. In this case the same thing happened only to a much greater and somewhat alarming degree. When we ran the reconfiguration checklist using the HOT app in this event; turning the APU bleed on reinstated the packs which caused an immediate introduction of thick deicing fluid smoke into the flight deck. My memory of the next couple minutes is a blur because it felt like there were several things demanding my attention and not a lot of information to triage their importance and make a proper best decision given all the variables present. The cockpit smoke was so thick that I could barely see the First Officer and had to feel for my oxygen mask to find it. At some point the packs were turned off; oxygen masks used and the cockpit windows opened. At that point my primary concern was how bad did it get in the cabin? Based on past experience and the current magnitude of the problem; I suspected not nearly as bad as the flight deck but probably getting everyone concerned. Almost immediately the flight attendants called and said the cabin was hazy and what was going on? I said it was deicing fluid and tried to ascertain their assessment which while alarmed didn't suggest it was dire. (The QRH was never considered as the smoke/removal procedures are inflight procedures and rely on using the packs). At this point I was weighing the possibility of evacuating into frigid; arctic conditions with high winds onto a glycol-covered ramp (including 2 wheelchair passengers) vs getting the jetbridge up to the aircraft ASAP (as soon as possible) in case an [immediate] deplaning was deemed advisable. I asked the First Officer to contact ramp control to get the jetbridge attached immediately and tried to think of a way to provide some relief to the cabin air situation. I called the flight attendants back and instructed them to disarm all their doors and to the extent possible crack them open a couple inches to get fresh air into the cabin. That turned out to be unsuccessful because a tailwind was blowing the APU fumes from back to front so that idea was abandoned pretty quickly. Based on my previous two experiences I began wondering if enough time had gone by and perhaps turning the packs on might actually help to bring fresh air into the cabin so I experimentally flipped on the left pack only; but the smoke returned and I immediately turned it off again. It felt like a Catch-22 situation. I knew the only way we could clean out the air was to run the packs but I didn't dare turn on the packs again with the passengers on board. The jetbridge was eventually attached during which time I had assessed the cabin personally and there was a faint lingering odor but nothing I considered alarming. After the passengers were off I asked the flight attendants to self-assess whether they were okay to continue or did they want some medical evaluation and they all said yes they could continue. At some point I contacted the Duty Chief Pilot and after he consulted with Maintenance they suggested doing an engine run. It was at this point that the gate agent informed me that the flight attendants; who had also deplaned; that the flight attendants 'did not want to take this airplane'. We eventually did run both engines at the gate; using both APU and engine bleeds to blow out the pack air until we were satisfied that there were no further issues with fumes. At some point 4 standby flight attendants were assigned and we reboarded the aircraft and departed. My strategy this time was to take the APU completely out of the equation and we requested and received permission to deice at the CDF instead. Halfway into this deicing I was notified something to the effect that the previous flight attendant crew was claiming an injury on duty and because of that Maintenance was therefore taking that plane out of service. We eventually returned to the gate and deplaned to a different aircraft. As I reached the new gate boarding area I saw an off duty [Company] pilot [Name] waiting to board and I asked him for a candid assessment of his impression of what the cabin situation seemed like; and he confirmed my initial suppositions; namely that it was noticeable but not alarming. He likened it to the kind of haze that might be initially experienced when turning on the packs in very humid conditions; but nothing like the thick smoke we encountered in the cockpit. Once again we had to deice but the CDF was closed by then; so I modified our post-deicing procedure to turning the pack switches off prior to reinstating the APU bleed; and leaving them off through both engine starts and then turning them on after the APU bleed was off at the conclusion of starting the engines. We finally departed uneventfully.' I believe the cause of the fume event was 'inadvertent introduction of Type 1 deicing fluid into the APU intake'. I have one recommendation that I will personally use from now on; namely what I mentioned earlier which is not running the packs until they are set for engine bleed as the air source following deicing. I also have to wonder why this has happened 3 times now (all at ZZZ). Clearly there needs to be more emphasis on protecting the APU inlet door when spraying Type 1 fluid. I don't know their procedures; but maybe spraying in brief spurts above the inlet door from back-to-front might help; or just avoiding the area altogether and clearing it by hand in the worst case scenario; but I'm picturing the usual visual of Type 1 fluid cascading down the cockpit windows like a car wash; and if that is going on in the back of the fuselage that can't be a good thing.

column121: Captain was pilot monitoring. FO (First Officer) was pilot flying. Passing through 4;000 feet MSL on climbout from ZZZ we noticed a fuel imbalance developing - right wing main tank fuel indication already 400 pounds lower than left wing. Right wing main tank fuel appeared to be feeding at approximately twice the rate of the left and it appeared that the center tank fuel was not feeding at all. Engine fuel flow readings appeared normal and equal. By 10;000 feet MSL the imbalance had increased to the point that the IMBAL alert was activated. We coordinated with ATC to level off at 12;000 feet MSL in order to reduce fuel flow and begin taking appropriate action. Upon leveling at 12;000 feet MSL we observed the right fuel tank quantity feed rate appear to normalize and then observed a 50 pound increase in right main tank fuel quantity. Fuel imbalance at that point was 1;100 pounds. We initiated the IMBAL checklist in the QRH. Observing what then appeared to be normal tank quantity indications for a crossfeed operation; we coordinated with ATC to continue our climb and proceed on course to the destination knowing we would also coordinate with Dispatch and maintenance promptly to determine if proceeding to ZZZ1 was advisable. As soon as we established climb fuel flow settings and pitch attitude; the right main tank quantity began to decrease again at what appeared to be the same abnormal rate observed during the initial climb. We then requested priority handling initiated the return to ZZZ (nearest airport) and started the APU as a precaution. I advised Dispatch; the cabin crew; and the passengers of the situation using SOP. As soon as we stopped the climb to initiate the return to ZZZ the right main fuel tank indication again stopped decreasing at an abnormal rate. We concluded the IMBAL checklist and for the remainder of the flight we observed no further indications of abnormal rate of decrease in right main wing tank fuel. During the descent; I spoke with the flight attendants and they confirmed that there were no visible indications of fuel leaks on either wing or engine. We landed uneventfully at ZZZ with a total imbalance of 1;220 pounds with 8;370 pounds in the left wing; 7;150 pounds in the right wing and 13;470 pounds in the center tank - 29;000 points total. The aircraft was below max landing weight at touchdown. ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) personnel were standing by as requested. After landing and before further taxi; ARFF personnel inspected the aircraft closely and reported no leaks; no visible damage; and no abnormalities. We shut down the number 2 engine as an additional precaution and requested that the ARFF vehicles follow us to our gate. Maintenance personnel were debriefed in person at the gate upon arrival.Captain suspects suspect faulty fuel crossfeed valve.Reporter recommends company consider revisiting the IMBAL checklist in light of this particular malfunction.

column121: After pushing off gate and starting 1 engine; we received an Elevator Servo Fault ECAM message. We went through all QRH procedures to resolve the problem to no avail. After calling ZZZ Operations to coordinate a return to the gate; we were informed that we were not allowed to return to the gate for a maintenance problem without Maintenance Control authorization. This seems to be in conflict with 14 CFR 121.533; 14 CFR 121.535 regarding Captain's Pilot in Command authority; as well as the MEL preamble which states that Maintenance Control's role is that of technical consultation (Not Command and Control). In any event; we eventually reached Maintenance Control via personal cellphone; and; eventually; Maintenance Control concurred that we should return to the gate. We returned to the gate; maintenance personnel troubleshot the problem to no avail; and the aircraft was taken out of service. My concern is that; in this scenario; the flight crew was forced to go through a Maintenance Control process that has 3 possible outcomes. First; Maintenance Control directs some off book procedure over the phone that 'fixes' the problem. Second; Maintenance Control directs us to flight crew placard the malfunction (which is not allowed by the MEL in any event). Neither one of those outcomes are acceptable with a primary flight control malfunction. The last possible outcome; and the only realistic outcome; is to return the aircraft to the gate; which we were frustrated from doing by this Maintenance Control permission regimen. I am concerned we are being pushed into possibly unsafe operation as our judgment is automatically questioned by a corporate policy that directly conflicts with Federal law.[Reporter stated the need for a revision of] company policy regarding maintenance troubleshooting.We [flight crews] need clearer understanding of the roles and responsibilities of Maintenance Control versus the PIC.

column121: Description of Event: The aircraft with PIC as above and one passenger was returning to ZZZ from a 1-hour cross-country flight that originated at ZZZ1. The flight was uneventful in VFR weather; with altitude from 2;000 feet to 1;600 feet after takeoff and climbout until approach. Flight path was as depicted in the charted course; following VFR altitude restrictions as required within ZZZ2 Mode C airspace; and with ADS-B Out active on 1200 a required. Visibility was observed to be 10+ miles with a solid cloud cover (overcast) at 9;000-12;000 feet. Winds were variable 6-9 knots at approximately 230-260 degrees from surface to flight altitude. Within 10 nm on the approach to ZZZ on a vector of 220; while monitoring ZZZ voice radio on 123.00; little traffic within the airport operations area was observed or noted on the radio. At approximately 8 nm from ZZZ; an inbound aircraft was announced on my ForeFlight display through the ADS-B In signal at my 7 o'clock; 400 feet below and overtaking. That Cessna 152 pilot announced his intention for a straight-in approach to ZZZ runway XX. Communicated directly with that PIC and told him that we would slow down to distance behind him on my own straight-in approach to ZZZ runway XX; since he already had a 25+ mph speed advantage. Within 2 minutes; the Cessna 152 had passed us by on our left side and descended ahead of us to line up for Runway XX. In the process; I lost visual contact with that aircraft; and since there was no other traffic in the area; and ForeFlight did not show a blip for its position; I decided to perform a slight S-turn to the left to further delay our landing until the 152 announced he was clear of Runway XX. At approximately 4 nm from the threshold; with our speed down to 62 mph (58 mph Ground Speed); the Cessna 152 PIC announced 'clear of Runway  XX ZZZ'; after which I immediately announced a straight-in approach for Runway XX ZZZ and began to adjust our speed and trim to line up with the two VASI lights on the glide path. At approximately 2 nm; we were high (two white lights) but gradually settled to a nominal (white/red) glide slope on the final approach. We completed visual and verbal cockpit checks and I glanced outboard at the right Flaperon position (there being no flap setting indicator in this CH750 STOL; and no stall warning annunciation); but did not notice anything incorrect; even though I had earlier made a mental note that we would be making a flaps-up; standard landing instead of the full-flaps; STOL landings I usually make. We settled slightly low of nominal (two red lights) as we approached the threshold and at that moment; I made a mental 'flip' or attitude adjustment that we were about to land STOL; and I decreased power for a short-field landing. Our sink rate increased; but mentally; I still had confidence that the STOL nose-up attitude was safe; and did not add power but instead retarded it to idle as we crossed the threshold of Runway XX. Without flaps; our stall speed was 48 mph instead of 42 mph; and we stalled out at approximately 12' above the numbers and fell in a slightly nose-high attitude until impacting on the main and then nose gear. The aircraft bounced up and then impacted slightly nose-down; collapsing the nose strut; blowing out the nose tire; and stopping the engine as the fiberglass prop blades impacted and flexibly shattered.We immediately checked for fuel leaks even though the aircraft came to rest tail-high. I switched off the ignition and removed the key; exited the cockpit; checked again for fuel leaks (none); then shut down the avionics manually with the master switch; and turned the Fuel Selector valve to OFF. After ascertaining that the aircraft was not an immediate hazard and that both Pilot and Passenger were able to move about without difficulty; we called other airport residents; and cleared the CH750 from Runway XX.Conclusion: In summation; distracted flying due to traffic avoidance caused energy mismanagement resulting in a stall upon landing flare with flaps retracted and subsequent nose gear collapse without injuries.

column121: I was providing instruction on new avionics for a client in Aircraft X. An IFR flight plan was filed by my client on his certificate. I briefed prior to engine start that he was PIC and that I was there to provide insight on the use of his new GTN 750. He had flown previously with this equipment; based on what he had told me. This was our first flight together in his aircraft.Prior to taxi; I reviewed with him how to load and activate approaches in his new GTN 750. He seemed familiar with its use and only asked a couple questions prior to departure. His knowledge of the features was adequate when I queried him on the unit.After takeoff from ZZZ Runway XXR; we were given a left turn to a heading of 070 and a climb to 3;000 feet. He engaged the autopilot at about 1;000 feet AGL. My client requested from ZZZ Approach the RNAV Y XXR but asked for a non-standard transition. He stated that he wanted the RNAV Y XXR to ZZZ 'via the ZZZZZ transition.' This is not a published transition and not what we briefed prior to departure. We had briefed previously that he would ask for vectors for the approach and he would repeat that same approach three times to increase familiarity with the equipment and its use in the approach environment. A short time later; we were given the instruction to climb to 3;000 feet and after that; to 'turn left direct ZZZZZ.' The autopilot began turning the aircraft to the right; presumably because he had switched from HDG mode to NAV mode without my knowledge. ATC queried and he once again read back the left turn. By the time I caught the erroneous turn direction and autopilot setting; the aircraft was well into the right turn. ATC then requested that we continue the right turn 'since we were already turning right and I have to keep you away from other traffic.'My client did as instructed and I queried ATC to confirm that we would overfly the ZZZZZ waypoint; then proceed outbound for the full approach. I apologized for the error on that same radio call. ATC responded in the affirmative; then cleared us for the approach. No further communication about the incorrect turn direction was made and the rest of the flight proceeded without incident.My client and I debriefed this issue and shared the lessons we learned. We both looked at this with an eye toward learning and future improvement.First; I reminded him of the importance of flying what we brief and that we will commit to always do so in the future. Second; as his flight instructor; it was my responsibility to catch the turn error and take control -- an effort I began but could not finish before ATC requested that he continue the right turn. Third; reliance on the autopilot worked against us and I suspect he switched from HDG to NAV mode without my noticing; initiating the right turn direct to ZZZZZ. Finally; business has been slow due to COVID and I have not been instructing as much as I normally would. I feel this last point is perhaps the most important one. As the pandemic has continued for nearly a year now; its effect on skills as pilots and flight instructors is being felt industry-wide.

column121: On the downwind landing at ZZZ; I was #2 in the pattern when abeam the touchdown point. The plane that was #1 had just touched down; and around the same time my engine began stuttering and soon after failed. At that point; I had begun my descent and was at [approximately] 800 ft. AGL. I began to attempt to restart the engine and was unable to do so. I then decided to execute a power off 180 degree turn and land on the runway. Perhaps as a result of attempting to restart my engine and triggering the master on/off; I lost communication with ZZZ Tower (I had been previously communicating with them). The plane that was previously #1 was already quite far down the runway and not a factor. I ultimately ended up landing safely; although never received clear to land instructions from Tower due to communications failure. I attempted to advise ATC when the engine failed; however I don't believe this was communicated.Upon landing; I noticed that both of the fuel selector valves were turned off. I am not sure if these were inadvertently disabled when I was attempting to restart the engine; or perhaps I had accidentally turned both of them off before engine failure. I am skeptical that this would be the case; as I remember ensuring that they were both enabled as part of my descent checklist ~15 minutes before the engine failed. It is indeed possible that I may have turned both to the 'off' position accidentally during the descent checklist; but I do not believe the engine would have continued to operate for this long were they to be off.I do not have a clear recollection of what actions I took to restart the engine in the air as it is frankly quite a blur. After being on the ground; I enabled both fuel selector valves and attempted to restart my engine without success. I tried a second time; and it started and I taxied off the runway (at that point 2 fire trucks and a police car had arrived; and I taxied off in convoy with them).A takeaway for me is that; regardless of the cause of the engine failure; my previous flights had been in another model of airplane; and while I was very familiar with Aircraft X; I would say that I should have spent more time familiarizing myself with the emergency procedures checklist. Also; earlier in the day while pre-flighting; there were some irregularities with the communications systems in the plane; and also it was very difficult to start the engine. I did not feel that these issues were enough to warrant aborting the flight; but in hindsight perhaps I should not have flown that plane that day and had it serviced instead.

column121: This was my first time flying from PAO in this particular aircraft; and I had only been there twice before; in more modern aircraft.  Aircraft Y got clearance for a 'Right Dumbarton' departure; just ahead of me. The Controller explained the 'Dumbarton' departure to me and subsequently gave me clearance for a 'Left Dumbarton' departure; right behind Aircraft Y. Just after takeoff; as I was climbing out on runway heading; I noticed I was gaining quickly on the Aircraft Y; but I wasn't worried because I knew he would be turning right at the bridge.  Instead; he (or she) turned left instead of right.  I also turned left; and the Controller asked me if I had the traffic. I informed him that I did.  I was getting close to him but figured I would out-climb him and go above. My focus was on keeping Aircraft Y in my sight and avoiding the traffic.  I continued to climb.At the point we felt he was no longer a factor; I looked at my iPad screen and realized that something was wrong; and I could not figure out where I was. I spent several seconds trying to assess the problem; all the while still climbing.  I had full control of the aircraft; and I knew where I was visually; but I could not figure out where I was on the moving chart display; so that I could avoid airspace I shouldn't be in.Pretty quickly I figured out how to adjust my screen so that I knew my position; and at that point realized I had climbed into Class B airspace; or at least I think I did.  I had received no hand-off from PAO Tower and was so overwhelmed by that time; along with being very concerned about climbing into Bravo; I simply immediately put the nose down and descended below Bravo airspace.Here are the factors that precipitated this event: 1. I was flying an older aircraft with only one radio and an iPad with EFB for navigation. I was not as familiar with it as I am with the other aircraft I fly; which has a modern EFIS. I had not studied the airspace in my departure path from PAO; I thought I could rely on the iPad.  This was a mistake I'll not make again!  2. I've never flown in or out of an airport as busy as PAO.  I was very anxious about doing everything right; I wanted to be safe and not cause any issues or problems with the flow of traffic and the controllers.  The Aircraft Y's unexpected left turn and my focus on avoiding it became distracting factor that took me 'off my game'.In the future; I'm committed to more fully plan my flights; especially in congested airspace; and I will become more proficient in the use of my electronic flight aids.

We copied down the TRACON phone number to reach them on the ground. The engine then maintained full power all the way down to the runway and to the fuel farm. As it is a Tailwheel; the tanks tip back when on the ground and both tanks read empty; while in the air during our power issues they read just under 1/4 on each side; which should have been just under an hour of fuel to go for the remaining 10 mins ETA to ZZZ1. Once clear of the runway; I tried TRACON again; and [another] airplane relayed our safe message to TRACON as we were too low to reach them.Once parked and shut down; I called TRACON and confirmed we were safe on the ground. We elected to divert to the uncontrolled; closed airport out of an abundance of caution to avoid flying over populated areas with a questionable engine. Once on the ground; we decided to drain the rest of the tanks' contents fully and have a mechanic inspect the aircraft before we attempted to fly again. We are on the ground waiting for the mechanic as I write this report.

column121: Initially; cruised at 7;000 ft.  From ZZZ to about the ZZZZZ intersection on V185; I was between layers.  ATC requested that I change altitude to an even thousand because I was now westward bound and gave me a choice of up or down.  Up would have put me in the clouds. Just prior to a red X appearing over the G5's airspeed partition; the G5's airspeed tape quickly unwound and a stall indication began flashing.  Also; the GFC 500 autopilot had disengaged.  I told ATC I was in icing and received clearance to descend.The stall indication did not make sense.  But; I was confused by what was happening and pushed forward on the yoke so as to not take any chances. A recovery from a rapid descent and 180 degree turn was executed as I realized a stall was not happening and the auto pilot had disengaged.  ATC offered a 2;000 ft. altitude to get out of the clouds and in warmer temperatures.  I had turned on the pitot heat and the airspeed was functioning on both the airspeed steam gauge and the G5.  The plane was iced but flying without difficulty and the ice was melting rapidly. I turned back on course and continued without further incident below the clouds.  In retrospect; I should have descended to 4;000 ft. instead of stopping at 6;000 ft.  This would have put me in the clouds for awhile; but beneath the freezing level.

column121: This narrative highlights two incorrect published crossing altitudes on two different arrivals that can lead to altitude deviations and aircraft overspeeds. The first is the PASLY 4 (10-2C) arrival to BNA at GROAT intersection. The crossing is depicted to cross GROAT at or below FL 230. It is always 1000 out of 1000 times given to cross GROAT at FL 220 usually by Memphis Center and has been for at least five years. Sometimes this occurs very late. This can lead to a situation where the aircraft was on the path; is now high; and the aircraft then pitches down at the last minute to meet the unpublished altitude of 22;000 ft. This pitchdown can lead to an overspeed and a situation that still does not meet the crossing. The second instance is on the ENDEE 6 Arrival into MDW (10-2). The fix in particular is KAMBL and the published crossing is between FL 270-FL 240. The unpublished crossing that is given; very late; is to cross KAMBL at 24;000 ft. Now the aircraft is in the same situation as the PASLY 4 Arrival; only you may have a 100 plus kt. tailwind to deal with as well. Both these situations persist but are preventable by simply changing the published altitude. Finally; there are several Pilots who are rusty from not flying; due to low utilization; whose situational awareness and lack of currency make this situation even more grave. Please fix these easy to remedy issues and trap the known errors. Thank you. We did not have a deviation. I am only reporting to highlight these issues.

The deviation appeared to subside as we got closer to the field and we were within stable approach parameters from the Final Approach Fix until touchdown. Also; the NAVAID had been positively tuned/identified per company SOP prior to commencing the approach. Course deviation on the HSI followed by ATC advising us that we were right of course. Unreliable Localizer signal at PHL which is apparently a known issue.The First Officer disconnected the autopilot and hand flew. I notified maintenance and was told by multiple maintenance personnel both on the phone and in person at the aircraft that this was a known issue with runway 09R; it happens all the time; and that there's a NOTAM in effect regarding the issue. I searched all of the NOTAMs  and could not find anything remotely related to unreliable LOC/ILS on 09R. I do not believe that the FAA would allow a malfunctioning NAVAID to remain in service and do not think there is any merit in the maintenance department's claim that this is a known problem that we should just accept and learn to deal with. However; if there is a known problem with this or any other NAVAID that necessitates a procedure change; then the company should disseminate that information to the pilot group with an FIL; etc.

column121: While on approach to ZZZ in day VMC conditions; crew was instructed to fly direct 'ZZZZZ' - the FAF for ILS XX - for a visual approach to [Runway] XX. The crew had been left high by both Center and Approach; but was able to reach the 5;000 ft. and slow prior to intercept. The PIC/PF (Pilot Flying) briefed the SIC/PM (Pilot Monitoring) on speed/energy management and airspeed 'windows' prior to the approach. After reporting runway in sight and receiving the approach clearance; the PF initiated descent to 4;500 ft. (the FAF altitude) and began to lessen the intercept angle; and PM prompted gear down and flaps 22. Aircraft still slightly overshot the localizer but was able to capture both LOC and GS which happened simultaneously. 4;500 ft. is within 1;300 ft. AGL of field elevation; and due to the short distance both vertically to the runway and laterally (just outside 4 miles); the PM/PIC anticipated an unstable approach and called a go around. The PF pressed the TOGA (Takeoff Go-Around); disconnected the autopilot; and called 'check thrust flaps nine' and the PM set flaps 9 and checked the thrust to discover the PF had not yet increased thrust to detents. Concurrently with the 'check thrust flaps 9 actions'; and 'Sink Rate' EGPWS warning occurred; and momentary hesitation by PF prompted PM/PIC to take control and initiate the immediate action in response to the 'sink rate' AURAL as required for the EGPWS escape; with a 'Pull Up' Aural warning occurring concurrently with the initiation of the EGPWS escape procedure. (At the time of initiation the EGPWS escape; PIC noted an 1;800 fpm descent rate). Upon reaching a safe altitude; the aircraft configuration was cleaned up in line as normal; and flight continued back for ILS without further incident. One error was made during EGPWS escape; which was PIC only increasing thrust to detents and not to max. Upon completion of the flight; crew debriefed on a number of key items. These included energy management and the approach profile in the AOM; go around procedure and ensuring power is set concurrently with pitch and callout when conducting a missed; and the EGPWS escape maneuver.Crews should act very early to mitigate unstable approach situations; including in a situation like this requesting a lower altitude earlier and a vector out to the IAF in lieu of the FAF; this can alleviate the chances of an unstable approach long before the issue manifests. Missed approaches should be initiated immediately upon identification of an unstable approach. In the event of a missed approach; crews should ensure the action is taken decisively including the increase of power; and both pilots should remain involved in the process. Should a GPWS warning be received; decisive; immediate action should be taken - as per the AOM - superseding normal missed approach actions due to the time critical nature of high vertical speed close to the ground. Captains especially should keep a close eye on FOs conducting operations at outstations - in this situation; having approach offer a better vector to join or taking an actual ILS clearance may have prevented the situation from manifesting at all.

column121: During preflight; the crew noticed the Hazmat paperwork showed 15300 pounds of Lithium in position 15L.  This Lithium was in an AAD can.  This can only weighted 2800 pounds.  As the Captain; I asked for the Dangerous Goods [DG] specialist to explain what we were seeing.  I asked the ramp agent what the weight of the can was and that is when I found out it was around 2800 pound.  Clearly there was a problem.  First problem is that the two systems do not talk and crosscheck the weights.  Secondly; the DG system does not know the max weight of a can and therefore can't check to see that the maximum can weight is not violated. Third; did I have a CG issue? Fourth; how does the system generate paperwork that has such gross errors?I believe the cause is the systems for DG and W&B do not talk and the DG system Allows Lithium to be declared way above the maximum AAD can weight.  Also; the W&B system does not catch such gross errors.My suggestion is to ensure the DG paperwork system and Weight and Balance system learn how to crosstalk.  There should be no way for the system to produce paperwork that has gross errors.  The DG paperwork system must know and be able to verify the max can weight is not violated.  Further; the actual can weight must be known by the DG paperwork system as another crosscheck.  It should never be able to have more Lithium declared in the can than the can weights.

column121: Upon departing ZZZ early in the morning; both the PF and PNF flight directors failed shortly after takeoff; prompting the PNF to quickly reference the QRH after several attempts to rectify the situation. After the completion of checklists; during the climb out and initial cruise; it was discovered that the FMC had also frozen up; not allowing any keypad inputs for route modifications. Shortly after leveling off at our cruise altitude; the PNF continued to troubleshoot the problem and was eventually successful at restoring both flight directors and FMC's back to normal. Meanwhile; during descent into ZZZ1; ARTCC advised us of a crossing restriction that was not complied with. We immediately stopped our descent and apologized. ARTCC then handed us off to ZZZ1 approach; after which; the flight continued on without further incident. It is suspected that the electronic malfunction of both the flight directors and FMC's; may have deleted or affected the altitude crossing restrictions; or; ARTCC may have linguistically confused the pronunciation of ZZZZZ with the ZZZZZ1 arrival into ZZZ1; as our flight plan indicated. Per SOP (Standard Operating Procedure); maintenance was notified of the situation but unable to determine cause or reproduce the fault.As for the electronic equipment malfunction; both the PF and the PNF became aware of the flight director failures shortly after takeoff when trying to engage VNAV. The FMC was determined to have failed during climb out. As for the altitude deviation; this issue was brought to our attention by ARTCC after crossing the fix below the published crossing altitude.The cause of the electrical/ electronic failure involving the flight directors and FMC's was undetermined by maintenance and could not be reproduced. The failure to comply with altitude crossing restrictions at a fix; may have been due to ARTCC assuming we were given the ZZZZZ1 arrival instead of the ZZZZZ arrival; which was listed on our flight release and selected in our FMC. My reaction was calm but assertive in continuing to fly the aircraft as the PNF; troubleshot the problem.As for the electronic equipment malfunctions; these failures are unpredictable. As for the crossing restriction compliance; our flight planning documents indicate that the correct arrival procedure was selected in the FMC but ARTCC thought different. In the future; I will be a little bit more willing to question; and/ or; verify an ATC challenge rather than assume their always right!

column121: Arriving into ZZZ the altimeter setting was showing 0996 mb; so during our arrival brief we covered the VNAV limitation for altimeters lower than 29.70/1006 and put special emphasis on using FLCH (Flight Level Change) when transitioning. Transition level was FL070. ATC began descending us in small steps; they gave us a descend to FL070 but when we were passing FL080 they gave us a descend to 6;000 ft. then further lower to 5;000 ft.; during those step downs I missed switching the altimeter setting to the local 0996mb. Then when we leveled at 5;000 ft. ATC verified the altimeter setting stating that we were 400 ft. lower than we should have. I immediately realized my mistake; set the correct altimeter setting; took corrective action and called for the approach checklist. Since the airplane wasn't reacting as fast as I wanted; I disconnected the auto pilot; corrected the altitude and continued manual flying all the way until we landed. There is no excuse for missing an altimeter setting during transition. There were many factors/distractions that took place for this to happen and they all came pretty close together: long duty day; our bells to the flight attendants; re-route to a point not in our route; use of wing and Engine anti-ice; heavy rain during descent so continuous ignition was set; multiple small step downs from ATC; VNAV limitation; all of them occurring often simultaneously. We; as crew; came together and managed all threats that were thrown at us as best we could to bring the airplane safely to the ground.I will; from now on; better prioritize on the stuff that I delegate and ask my crew to keep an eye on me and remind me of things that could make us incur a deviation like this one. Even though we all had our hands full; I should have asked someone for some sort of reminder about the transition level.
column123: At the conclusion of a long duty day and the second flight leg of the day; I was PM (Pilot Monitoring) en-route. This was my second leg as PM (6th leg as flight crew) in an international theater in nearly 3 years. Prior to descent and during the approach briefing as well as once the relief pilots entered the cockpit; we discussed the lower altimeter setting of 0996mb and the associated procedure per Company limitations from not using VNAV when transitioning from QNH (Height Above Sea Level) to QNE or QNE to QNH when below 1006mb. We felt very prepared for the arrival and descent into ZZZ. The transition altitude of 7;000 ft. was also briefed however as we proceeded; we encountered winter weather requiring extra vigilance (icing conditions and heavy precipitation). ATC descended us in multiple small increments below 10;000 ft. but the last prior to this event was a descent to 5;000 ft. With the added attention to the weather and ensuring proper use of FLCH instead of VNAV during what should have been the transition; both the pilot flying; and the pilot monitoring did not switch the altimeters at the proper time to the local setting of 0996mb. Upon level-off at 5;000 ft.; ATC came over the radio to verify local altimeter of 996mb and stating the observation of being 400 ft. low. I quickly realized my altimeter was incorrect and took corrective action and confirmed the pilot flying did so as well both with the altimeter and the flight path. One of the observer pilots also confirmed and stated the MSA for situational awareness. The pilot flying disconnected the auto pilot and continued to intercept the localizer path while returning to the cleared altitude. The aircraft was hand flown to landing with no further incident.Multiple links in the chain led up to this event and while we thought we had sufficiently briefed the several unique environments (low altimeter/Company limitation; winter weather) we also were distracted by being vectored to a point not on an arrival or the approach expected. It only goes to show that even with the best preparation and briefing that events can change and compound quickly and while attention to detail is most crucial during all phases of flight; extra vigilance is needed for approach and arrival; especially in areas that have not been flown to in recent months or years. Ultimately; the crew worked together to safely return the aircraft to the desired state and ensured a lesson learned for the future when operating in areas with differing transition altitudes.
