Established on the approach between the IAF and FAF; I keyed the mic to establish contact with Tower inbound. The entire avionics turned off completely; losing intercom; transponder; GPS/Nav/Comm 1; and Nav/Comm 2. ZZZ was currently under IFR due to 2SM visibility; but we were in visual conditions on the approach course. I broke off from the approach and turned to the south; since we were no longer receiving navigational guidance along the approach; and I had no communications to contact Tower or Approach. I knew the weather towards the south was looking clearer so the plan was to continue south towards ZZZ1 or ZZZ2. We troubleshot the avionics; checking circuit breakers and cycling the avionics switch to no avail. No indications of ammeter discharge or low voltage illuminated; and the turn coordinator was still operable as well as engine instruments; so I presumed that the failure was based solely on avionics and not complete electrical failure. We descended lower; maintaining VFR so that we could receive cell signal; and I contacted ZZZ Tower via cellphone; since they gave us instructors their phone number another time when they had an ATC/instructor meeting. I told them we were okay; and had complete avionics failure. I asked for the phone number for ZZZ1 Tower so I could communicate with them if I decided to continue south to ZZZ1. At that time; the visibility and clouds around ZZZ began to clear up and we could start to see towards ZZZ. I asked ZZZ Tower if the field was still IFR; and they replied that it just went VFR. We proceeded inbound toward ZZZ; maintaining VFR; and were able to receive landing and taxi clearances for our aircraft through the cell phone. The aircraft was repaired; with the problem being a short-circuited avionics switch.

column121: This was my third solo XC (Cross Country). Flight planning was approved by the instructor. Weather and NOTAMs were reviewed by both myself and instructor and flight was deemed safe to proceed. There were no NOTAMs or field condition reports for the destination airport. One pattern was flown at departure airport with an instructor to update currency prior to departure of solo flight. Takeoff; climb; en route; and descent were uneventful. During a visual approach to Runway 02 at the uncontrolled airport; I noticed patchy snow on the runway. I noticed other aircraft had landed recently. I was expecting a normal landing to a touch and go. ASOS indicated the winds were from the northwest at 8 kts. I touched down on centerline at 67 kts. Before I set the nose down; the aircraft started veering to the left. I made the attempt to correct and the airplane continued to slide to the left. I believe due to the unresponsiveness of my control inputs; I was on ice. I made the decision to full stop and applied brakes. The aircraft continued to slide on the icy portion of the runway with no response to my braking or control inputs. The aircraft struck a snow bank on the left side of the runway. The aircraft tipped forward and to the right; resulting in damage to the propeller and the right wingtip. I'm not sure if this is a reportable incident/accident at this time. The following day; a NOTAM was issued for 30 PCT patchy snow and ice.	I believe I landed on a patch of ice. There were no NOTAMs published at the time of my departure. Had a NOTAM been published for wintery conditions; I would not have attempted a solo XC to this airport. I have not yet been trained to land in wintery conditions. Based on previous landing markings on the snow in the runway; I assumed it was safe to land. My relative inexperience resulted in not recognizing the ice under the snow. I should've gone around. In the future; I will take a harder look at my experience level and the conditions present in order to make a better decision. I have learned a valuable lesson to always err on the side of caution.

column121: Enroute ZZZ-San Salvador at FL390 we were able to ascertain through ATC Control that Runway 25 was in use and that we could expect to proceed via CAT VOR and execute the ILS Y 25. The FO (First Officer) was the Pilot Flying and thoroughly briefed the approach and his expectations for altitudes; automation modes and aircraft configuration throughout the approach. We were turned over to San Salvador Approach approximately 70 miles from the airport descending to FL200. San Salvador Approach cleared us direct CAT VOR; cross VOR above 5;000 [ft.] cleared ILS Y Runway 25. Both pilots confirmed clearance; altitudes and automation as we proceeded. As we neared CAT we were around 8;000 [ft.] at 240 kts.; still on the VNAV path. Although the FMC appeared to like the profile we both agreed it was time to slow down to meet the briefed approach profile. The FO selected vertical speed and dialed the speed back in the MCP window. With the selected vertical speed we weren't slowing down so I recommended Level Change. We slowed; configured and continued the approach passing CAT VOR. I set 2;500 [ft.] in the altitude window to fly outbound from the VOR as we completed the landing checklist. Once crossing the fix at [8.0 nm] we turned inbound via LNAV and set the FAF crossing altitude of 1;600 [ft.]; approach mode selected. We were in VFR conditions with the airport in sight on my side of the aircraft. As we turned towards the airport and descended I noticed we seemed low since we were more than 8 miles away and below the glide path. I looked back at the FMC and noticed fix [7.8 nm] with a crossing altitude of 2;500 [ft]. Shortly afterwards ATC asked what our altitude was and I replied 1;600 [ft.]. At that point both the FO and I realized we had missed [7.8 nm] on the procedure and should have crossed it at 2;500 [ft.]. [7.8 nm] is not clearly depicted on the approach plate with a crossing altitude nor is there an altitude depicted for the turn inbound. Also; we flew the procedure properly if the automation was in VNAV; but it wasn't. Although it was nighttime we were in VFR conditions with the airport in sight throughout the procedure. No GPWS cautions. At no time did I feel the procedure unsafe.
column123: I was the PF.  CENAMER approach cleared us to descend out of FL390 to FL 200.  We were expecting the ILSY Rwy 25.  We briefed the approach thoroughly and I explained I would stay in VNAV until lined up on final approach where I would select APP for the ILS.   Well above FL200; we were handed off to ElSal approach.  They told us to proceed to CAT VOR and cleared us for a full approach ILS Y Rwy 25 approach with procedure turn.  HOWEVER; we were high before arriving at CAT so I selected to use vertical speed and open the speed window to control speed.  The CAPT suggested I use LVL CHG instead since it would do a better job getting down and controlling speed.  I did so; while  flaps and gear helped slow us.  I was still well above 3500'; over the VOR beginning the procedure turn outbound to D8.0.  Still in LVL CHG; We were able to fully configure and be on the VNAV PATH at 2500' at D8.0.  We completed the LANDING CHECKLIST.  At this point we had the airport in sight and never lost contact the whole time.  We were both using TERR MODE for obstacle clearance.  After passing D8.0 I asked the CAPT to select the next lower altitude of 1600' as depicted on the approach chart; and he did so.  In my haste to get at the correct altitude; slow down and  configure for landing; I did not  realize I had not reselected VNAV.  The autopilot descended us to 1600' as we turned toward final.  We crossed D7.8 at 1600' vice 2500'..  There was no GPWS warning and we had the airport in sight the whole time.  On final approach I selected APP and we noticed we looked low and at the same time; the control tower queried us about our altitude.  That was when we noticed our error but were already capturing the glideslope at that time.  We continued the approach; landed safely and taxied to our gate without further incident.

column121: During the boarding of [Aircraft X] ZZZ - ZZZ1; I noticed a message on [Software] from the gate agent to station operations to inform the ramp personnel that there was a 'motorized wheelchair' on the jet bridge to be loaded onto the aircraft. I made a note to make sure we were provided notification of the wheel chair and when it did not come through the automated weight and balance data I asked the ramp lead. He just told me that it was 'very light' so he scanned it as a normal bag. I asked him if it was electric and if it had a battery and he said he did not know. He did not understand why I needed to know so after explaining that it was Dangerous Goods and required notification; he went to check it. I decided to go down with him to the cargo bin to make sure he knew what we needed. When he went in the cargo bin there was not a belt loader available so I was not able to also get in; and it was surrounded by bags so I was not able to see the base of it myself. He looked for several minutes; then informed me that it was 'not electric' and had 'no battery or electric parts' at all. I clarified this with him multiple times; both while standing at the cargo bin and also over the headset in the cockpit. After the flight was complete; we saw the agents in ZZZ1 unload it and the passenger get on it. I asked her if it was motorized and she said that it was. I asked her what type of battery it had and she said it was lithium ion and it was removable. She also showed me exactly where the battery was and how it could be removed. She also said that someone; it was unclear who and whether or not it was a [Company] employee; told her not to 'give too much information' during her check in process or she might have trouble flying with it. She couldn't remember if she had told the agent if it was a lithium ion battery. Regardless; multiple employees should have been able to figure out along the chain that it was motorized somehow; which meant it had to be electric.The cause was the ramp's misunderstanding of our DG (Dangerous Goods) policies and not being able to identify DG loaded on the aircraft; as well as possibly the passenger not reporting it as DG during check in.This is now the second time I have had an undeclared lithium ion wheelchair carried in the cargo bin in the past year and a half; which is indicative that this may be a larger issue than just one single missed item. Also; given that the ramp lead had no idea that electric wheelchair batteries had to be declared; it is impossible to know how many other events have happened where we simply didn't see the passenger after the flight.

I asked the other pilot to give it nose-up trim as he had done several times before. (The aircraft only has manual trim.) Suddenly; the aircraft nosed over. We have communicated the problems about the safety equipment not operating properly many times to our managers; and nothing ever happens to fix the problem.5. Other pilots have mentioned the same concern about lack of operating safety equipment to MCO Leadership and still nothing improves.6. One Ramp Supervisor explained that he has worked at four different (Company) Stations. column121: I departed ZZZ after topping off my aircraft fuel tanks. I flew VFR in VMC conditions to PDK. The traffic pattern very congested so much so that several aircraft had difficulty obtaining clearance to enter the controlled airspace at PDK. After monitoring the tower frequency; I elected to call ATL Approach to request a VFR ILS to PDK for a full stop landing. This would help me to practice a VFR approach; setting up the approach; capturing the localizer and glide-slope; Because I was solo I remained alert to visually remain clear of all aircraft nearby.I contacted ATL Approach and received a discreet transponder code as well as VFR vectors for the approach; I was vectored through the ILS localizer for sequencing and then cleared for the approach just outside of the FAF CHAMB and was transferred to the PDK tower frequency.The radio traffic was so heavy that I was not able to transmit before the tower called my call sign and cleared me for landing number 2 behind jet traffic. Because I was cleared to land #2 behind the jet; this contributed to my understanding I would land on Runway 21L; the longer runway used by Jets. The parallel Runway 21R is shorter and primarily used by piston and training aircraft.I continued on approach on the Localizer and Glide slope until short final. When I was approximately over the Runway 21 L approach end I observed Aircraft Y fly over head at approximately 75 ft. at a faster speed. I immediately called the tower and reported the aircraft overhead while side stepping to the right to go around. The tower sequenced me to land on the parallel Runway 21R and I continue to a safe landingThe issue was I was cleared for the ILS by ATL approach and expected to land on Runway 21L. Also I was cleared initially by the tower to land #2 behind Jet traffic However; the tower said that they cleared me to land on [Runway] 21R.I have been flying from this airport for over XX years and I as well as many other pilots regularly receive runway landing changes often on short final. In this case I may have misunderstood or did not hear correctly the landing clearance and as a result had a near miss with another aircraft.Contributing factors was the radio frequency congestion as well as the high volume of aircraft in the airspace; and my expectation to land on the longer runway behind jet traffic. Also the Aircraft Y pilot did not see me as he approached from above and behind my aircraft; which also contributed to the near miss. I have on board Aircraft X an L3 active TCAS as well as ADSB traffic advisory. I do not believe I heard or saw a traffic alert on my avionics.

column121: We departed ZZZ on a part 91 day VFR local pleasure flight with one adult passenger in this 1979 Cessna 172N aircraft flying approximately east south east. The weather appeared to be six plus miles visibility with some cirrus clouds; winds under 10 kts. with what seemed to be an occasional thermal. Approximately ten to fifteen minutes into the flight; was at about 1;800 ft. and began a gradual turn to the right.As the yoke was first being moved clockwise; or perhaps shortly thereafter; a pop was felt; the yoke then had no resistance whatsoever with the control yoke ending up being all but fully deflected to the right where it remained at that moment. A vibration in the airframe began. It was a light though consistent somewhat disconcerting vibration. Even with the yoke as it was (all but fully clockwise at that time; in other words; the yoke was about 90 degrees clockwise from level) the aircraft was not banking right. The left rudder pedal may have been instinctively depressed to pick up the right wing after the snap occurred; but uncertain. The aircraft now appeared to not be entirely controllable as the yoke and inputs to it did not seem to be having the effect which they should have.Thereafter; if the yoke was moved counterclockwise; especially if moved past neutral to the left; a distinct buffet of unknown nature was felt; and the yoke was immediately returned to the position which resulted in the least vibration; about ninety degrees clockwise. Not being a mechanic there was significant uncertainty as to what actually was broken and what effect it could have on the flight characteristics of the aircraft. When a shallow climb was introduced or the pitch was increased; a distinct buffet of unknown nature was felt and the climb with the associated pitch and power increase was immediately discontinued and not attempted again. When a very shallow descent was introduced the ongoing vibration seemed to decrease or cease. When the engine rpm was decreased slightly the ongoing vibration also seemed to decrease. That said; no further attempts were made to bank or turn left or climb or increase the pitch or power. All turns thereafter; which were slight with little bank; to the right; were accomplished with slight rudder pressure.7700 was squawked and ATC was advised on guard. Center responded promptly to the call. Due to the limited and questionable control problem; along with the ongoing vibration and buffeting issues; the best course of action at the time appeared to be not to continue the flight back to the closest and seemingly most prudent airport as it would have required a flight directly over a densely populated area. The next closest airport considered potentially usable in the situation appeared to be ZZZ1. However; ZZZ1 was much further than ZZZ (about 18 NM vs. about 10 NM); although few homes along the route it required a flight over water which would have necessitated a climb and a left turn. Due to the buffet experienced during the prior attempted climb; local knowledge of many times there being turbulence where the water meets the land; the distance (would something else happen during that longer travel time?) and the buffet experienced when a left turn was attempted previously; ZZZ1 did not seem to be a good choice at that time.There was an acceptable looking farmer's field which required a slight turn to the right and was just prior to the populated area of ZZZ2 and ZZZ2; it seemed to be the best choice. The aircraft was maneuvered slightly right using slight rudder pressure. After the turn was completed a gradual descent at reduced power was begun. Communication with Center was lost due to the descent although an airliner relayed our communications with Center.During the descent at reduced airspeed a very minimal amount of flaps were introduced to see if any negative effect was experienced. No negative effect was experienced. The descent continued; doors were propped opened; fuel was turned off;mixture to idle cutoff; mags and master switch off which all then culminated in an uneventful though spirited landing on a farmer's field. The airplane came to rest seemingly undamaged. Aircraft was exited normally and moments later Center called to my cell phone in order to check status and get information. FSDO's and local law enforcement were notified and responded accordingly.

column121: While on approach into CHO we were being vectored by Potomac Approach on frequency 126.4. We were on a right downwind being vectored for the ILS Runway 03. It was IMC conditions with light to moderate rime ice accumulating on the aircraft. At 3;000 ft. MSL we were given a right turn; a base turn; toward the final for Runway 03. We were just outside; south of the fix WULDU. I noticed were getting close to the localizer course for the final approach; and Potomac had not issued a turn for us to intercept the approach. I prompted Potomac approach and tried to establish communication. There was no answer on 126.4. I prompted again; and still there was no answer from Potomac. At this time we crossed over the localizer course without a turn to intercept given from Potomac. I had guard (121.5) already tuned in on comm 2. I heard Potomac approach trying to hail us on 121.5 on guard and advised us to switch to frequency 132.85. I switched to 132.85 and they gave us an immediate turn to the right to reestablish us on the localizer course. The coverage on 126.4 for the area was lost and I confirmed that with Potomac that we were trying to contact them. Apparently a Learjet overheard us trying to transmit on 126.4 and relayed it to Potomac. Once we re-established communication; Potomac gave us that right turn to intercept but it was 'too late'; The aircraft GPWS detected terrain and gave us a 'Terrain; Terrain' 'PULL UP' audio warning. I directed the First Officer to Climb the aircraft and disregard the instruction from Potomac Approach. We climbed up to 3;500 ft. MSL and got the aircraft clear of the terrain. I advise Potomac what had happened and that we were unable to intercept the approach from the vector that they gave us. Potomac than gave us more vectors to get re-established on the approach. From there we landed with no further issues. I conversed with Potomac about the drop in radio coverage on frequency 126.4. They agreed and confirmed that they could not hear us and we could not hear them on 126.4.[Problem was identified by] flight crew scan. No communication from ATC have prompting them several times. Having Guard (121.5) on comm 2 and have our audio on to re-establish communication. Being aware of the terrain in the area and seeing the aircraft GPS position on The Jepp charts. [Cause was] loss of two-way communication on 126.4 between our aircraft and Potomac approach lead us to not receiving an instruction to intercept the localizer course. Without that instruction we continued on our heading and had to re-establish communication via guard and switch to a different frequency that has radio coverage in the area. All of this lead to vectors in an area with terrain and caused us to be in a position where the aircraft GPWS was activated. [We] contacted ATC. Followed the aircraft GWPS system and climbed to avoid terrain. Advised ATC that we were responding to a GWPS annunciation. [Suggest] better radio coverage equipment is needed for the area around CHO. Suggest the importance of ALWAYS monitoring 121.5 on Comm 2 for flight crews.

column121: During the preflight brief by the Captain; specially as he completed the 'T' Brief; I observed the CYAN WX-A on his nav display; indicating that his radar was on.  I quickly looked to see if my radar was on also; it was not.  I know for certain his radar was not on prior to this as I cross checked altimeters and field elevation during my cockpit preflight and glanced at his Nav Display.  I am constantly looking to assure that the CYN WX-A is not displayed on the NDs this issue a big pet peeve of mine.  I believe this event occurred during the power transfer from GPU to APU as it occurred shortly prior to push and shortly after starting the APU and is a well known anomaly on the LDS (large display system) 767.  Further; on this day; the airplane had a bird strike on the nose cone which I noticed on the preflight.  The mechanic was working directly in front of the nose cone.  I'm glad that the radar didn't power on while he was inspecting the nose cone.  I have no reasonable assurance that a scenario like that can't happen as the radar powers on at various times when there is a power transfer.  As a matter of fact and ironically; I had that exact thought earlier as I completed my preflight and saw the mechanic on a ladder in front of the nose cone. I can't tell you how relieved I am to know that the radar didn't power on with the mechanic in front of it.  A known anomaly on the LDS Boeing 767 [is] the radar powers on at various times; which the technician believes is predominately tied to power transfers.  Further; the issue appears to be tied to whether or not the parking brake is set or not.  The design assumption of the radar assumes the parking brake is going to be set at the gate.  If the brake is set; supposedly the radar will not power on.   However; at my company; that is not the case as we release the parking brake once the airplane chocks are in place.  There is a belief by those in Flight Management that the Flight Manual has addressed this issue with a change to the Interior Safety Check and Power Application.  The change in the flight manual was a note stating that this power on anomaly can occur and the Captains should be looking for it.   However; the problem with that is that the radar powers on at various times.  I have seen it occur with a simple power transfer from GPU to APU; when the IRS selectors are moved from Off to Align with the APU already running and no power transfer occurring by the flight crew and I've seen the issue occur during a pushback following a pneumatic ground start as the generators come online.  I've also seen the Cyan WX-A displayed on one ND and not the other; and sometimes it is displayed on both NDs.  Further and a separate issue entirely; I'm not entirely certain the WXR button location isn't an issue itself.  It is a very easy button to toggle on/off.  The location is also very poor and is in a position that could be accidentally bumped by those installing the sun shades in the summer; those cleaning the windshields and by someone getting into or out of the seat.This anomaly needs to be corrected as soon as possible.  I've been on the 767 for nearly X years and this issue has been on going.  I have had discussions regarding this issue with many people over the course of several years; Standards; LCAs and most recently Fleet Captains.  There is a fix; LDS Software Update; which will correct the issue.  However; unfortunately; they are looking at a need to do a wiring change and at present time it appears that that will take 2 years to complete.  To make matters worse however; I have noticed this phenomenon is occurring on brand new 767s that we have just taken from the factory; like [another] aircraft which is a very new airplane.  It is unacceptable that we are taking new airplanes from the factory with this issue; knowing that the fix will not take place until Heavy Checks.  I feel this is irresponsible to all people on the ramp who are exposed to a radar in operation while parked at a gate.  We have pilots; crew bus drivers; ramp load teams; mechanics; fuelers; caters; lavatory service techs all being exposed to an operating radar when this event occurs.  I can't tell you how frustrating it is to complete the walk around; sit down in my seat and see the radar has been on because the Captain missed it or it occurred at sometime that he wasn't aware of.  This needs to be fixed quicker than a few years and some sort of procedure needs to be established soon to provide a safe/healthy work environment to all those I previously listed.  This really is not OK.

column121: On the ZZZZZ6 we were told to level at 7;000 feet for traffic. This was my 3rd trip on IOE and was practicing hand flying the departure. It was turbulent and we were in and out of IMC. Since we were extremely light due to light loads we were climbing at an extremely fast vertical speed. Passing through 6;000 I announced that I was going to use TCS to reduce the rate of climb to about 1;000 since there was traffic above and I wanted to avoid a RA. I corrected the VS to about 1;000 ft/min. I was not quick enough to override and reduce the autothrottles to avoid increasing airspeed. The airspeed quickly and momentarily increased to 270 knots as we were leveling at 7;000 feet. I reduced the autothrottles too late and while reducing them altitude deviated by 140 feet high. Both deviations were short and immediately corrected. Nothing was mentioned by ATC. We were later given higher once the traffic passed. The combination of hand flying in turbulent conditions in IMC and leveling at a low altitude with light loads was a recipe for distraction and error to occur. I could have eliminated some of these variables by engaging autopilot earlier or reducing autothrottles quicker. The CA and I debriefed and talked through what led to the event and how to prevent it in the future.I learned that when possible reduce extra variables that could lead to an error. I am new to flying with the company and new procedures; was hand flying in turbulent conditions and IMC; light loads with good performance; and was given a low level off. That is a lot of variables at once and the ones that I could control are the earlier use of automation to help alleviation some of the task saturation. Hand flying in turbulent conditions and maintaining altitude can be difficult and the autopilot can alleviate and sometimes do a better job to avoid deviations. Additionally I learned not to lag on overriding the autothrottles when using in FLCH mode. From this experience I feel that I can better identify and evaluate a handful of risks in a certain situation and will take prompt action to reduce these risks in a timely manner. The CA and I had a productive debrief and agreed on what variables led to the deviation and how to prevent in the future.

column121: During taxi to Runway 31L; ground control told us to hold short of the approach end of Runway 22 at Taxiway Z. As another aircraft was landing; ground told us to cross Runway 22 In front of the aircraft on landing roll and told that aircraft to give way to us. As we began to cross in front of the aircraft on landing roll; there was no indication that the aircraft was slowing down to give way to us. So I stopped our aircraft and the aircraft on landing roll passed in front of us. Ground said that we shouldn't have stopped.This event was caused by ground control setting up a disaster scenario by wanting us to cross in front of the aircraft on landing roll. If anything went wrong; like brake failure of the landing aircraft; then there would have been a potentially catastrophic aircraft accident.In the future; ground shouldn't cross aircraft in front of other aircraft on landing roll unless they are positive that the aircraft on landing roll has slowed down sufficiently to be safe.
column123: We were instructed to taxi from FBO to '[Runway] 31L via Zulu; hold short approach end [Runway] 22 at Zulu'. We exited the FBO ramp onto Zulu; turned left towards [Runway] 22 and noticed that [Taxiway] Zulu terminates before the approach end of [Runway] 22; and it becomes [Taxiway] Yankee. We discussed this on the flight deck that the taxi instructions should have been clearer because you can't really hold short of [Runway] 22 on Zulu; you would actually either hold short of [Runway] 22 approach on Yankee; or hold short of Yankee on Zulu. In any case; the Captain as PF (Pilot Flying) exercised some good judgement and decided to stop a bit back from Yankee; at least from the sign anyways. It's hard to figure where Zulu actually ended. That way we could respond to Ground if they modified their instructions to hold back further. Whatever is the case with Zulu or Yankee; we stopped and awaited further instructions. We noticed a bizjet (Aircraft Y) landing on [Runway] 4 so we suspected we were being held from crossing the approach end of [Runway] 22 (same as rollout end of [Runway] 4) due to the landing traffic. After a short wait; we heard ground instruct Aircraft Y which was now rolling out to 'give way to Aircraft X; he will be crossing at the end of the runway in front of you'. I cannot recall if the other aircraft acknowledged. The next thing we both heard was 'Aircraft X; cross Runway 22 and continue via Kilo'. I turned all the lights on and the Captain started to move forward. I looked right to clear and noticed the landing Aircraft Y was very close; it seemed to me he was past Bravo and Kilo 2 where I presumed he would have turned off; that his reversers were still deployed; and he was rolling very fast for so close to the end of the runway. I said 'STOP; we're not clear' or words to that effect and the Captain immediately stopped as he was now seeing Aircraft Y appear large in my windshield. It may have been hidden beside my windshield side pillar previously. We both agreed it would not have been pretty had we gone across the runway as it clearly appeared Aircraft Y was landing fast and rolling out long; and more importantly; evidently not giving way to us. After just a few seconds; Ground said 'Aircraft X; you're not moving' and we responded that it was not safe to do so. Ground replied; 'Aircraft Y is giving way to you' or words to that effect; and we replied that wasn't the case. After a few more seconds Aircraft Y exited onto Kilo in front of us; and Ground then instructed us to cross the runway and continue onto Kilo on our taxi to [Runway] 31L. Ground and Tower frequencies were combined per ATIS onto tower frequency 118.7; we were always using it; but when Aircraft Y cleared in front of us and we followed him until we turned left onto Charlie; we never heard him. Our subsequent taxi and departure was uneventful.The confusing or incorrect taxi instructions provided (i.e.; is it Zulu or Yankee to hold short) started us off with noticing ATC peculiarities as we spoke to Ground. The other aircraft not giving way to us; or appearing to do so; was the major cause of this averted conflict. Combining Tower and Ground on one frequency may also have caused some confusion; because the tower cab can hear everything but in the aircraft we can only actively hear the frequency we're currently using.First off; I think our alertness was the link in the chain that prevented an incident (or worse). I think that ATC made a procedural error in directing us to cross in front of the landing traffic without adequate time/distance to do so. I recommend [Company] request an official copy of the tape from the FAA if possible for review and development of lessons learned.

column121: Our flight departed from ZZZ enroute to EWY. Clearance was issued as follows: 'CLEARED TO EYW AIRPORT [via SID] FLY TOWER ASSIGNED HEADING THEN AS FILED MAINT 3000FT (ZZZ..ZZZZZ..MTH..EYW..KEYW)'. Established level at our cruise altitude of 14;000 ft. and on our cleared route we were handed off to MIA Center (ZMA). ZMA cleared us Direct to EYW and we proceeded on the new route. During our descent ZMA issued the cross a fix not on our route at 10;000 ft. We believed we heard GINGA as the controller pronunciation had the hard G sound. Looking at the chart the closest intersection with this sound was GIGIH. However; as we now know the fix was JANKA to the South. We requested clarification of the intersection 4 times from ZMA and received no response. Believing the clearance was to a GIGIH we started out turn to the West and continued our decent to meet the restriction. ZMA asked if we wanted to arrive from the North to EYW and we responded we had no preference. ZMA then issued at turn to heading 180 and we continued our descent to 10;000 ft. ZMA handed us off to Navy Key West Approach and the flight continued without incident. Upon landing and researching the charts in more detail we discovered the similar sounding intersections of GIGIH and JANKA in the EYW area; neither of which were on our flight plan. It is my opinion no violations occurred; and all altitude restriction were accomplished as published; however; the Safety of Flight is highest priority at our company and the crew felt this issue should be submitted as an ASAP report to further pilot education and professionalism. Similar sounding intersection names not on our flight plan. Controller pronunciation and being unable to confirm the waypoint.The ability to confirm the proper waypoint spelling with ATC.

column121: After departing [Runway] XXR from ZZZ [airport] on the ZZZZZX SID; began to accelerate through 9;000 feet MSL using speed mode. This caused the aircraft to level off around 9;300 feet MSL as it was speeding up from 250 KIAS. Captain was talking with ATC regarding our climb clearance when the acceleration began. ATC did not acknowledge the increased speed. After finishing the clearance readback the Captain noticed the increasing speed and changed to vertical speed mode to reduce airspeed. As pilot flying I reduced the thrust as well. Upon reaching 10;000 MSL we resumed normal profile climb.Limited experience taking off with wing and cowl anti-ice on. Normally upon reaching ZZZZZ1 intersection we have reached 10;000 MSL and can begin to accelerate. Because of the reduction in climb performance using the anti-ice system we were 1;000 feet lower than normal.  The use of cowl and wing and anti-ice also caused the aircraft to use a lower angle of attack to reach entered airspeed resulting in a reduced climb performance. Because of reduced loads from COVID-19 we have normally not encountered a problem reaching 10;000 MSL before the west bound turn resulting in a habit of increasing speed at ZZZZZ1 or west/east bound turn.

column121: Descending into ZZZ my First Officer (FO) and I noticed there was an unusual sound but we couldn't tell where it was coming from; I called the flight attendant and asked her if she could hear anything and she said no everything sounded normal to her in the back. We then pulled up the engine page and looked at the engine system followed by checking the electrical page but we couldn't see anything abnormal. We continued our descent and started our approach; it was visual conditions so we were on a visual approach to Runway XX; we had already canceled IFR. I called for flaps 12 and the FO put flaps 12 in; we noticed that the sound had changed a little so we again went through the engine instruments and everything still seemed normal. As we continued to add flaps we noticed the sound would get a little louder each time and when we went flaps 32 we could feel a small vibration coming through our feet. We checked the hydraulic page and everything looked fine; we then checked the flight control page and everything still looked normal. I was hand flying and did not notice any change to the handling of the aircraft; the only thing we noticed was the sound and then the small vibration. We continued to land with no issues; just a normal landing. After parking the aircraft and deplaning; I asked my First Officer to take a little extra time with his post flight to see if he could see anything that would have made the noise and vibration on the approach. After his postflight he came in and said he couldn't see anything unusual outside. I finished up my tasks and then decided to walk around the aircraft myself. When I got to the left side I noticed something sticking up on top of the wing maybe a foot or two from the fuselage. I grabbed a ladder and climbed up to look at it; I found that the trailing edge of the flap was cracked right next to the fuselage and then again about a foot or two away there was another crack. The top trailing edge of the flap had a piece that had come off and was sticking up. I took pictures and called the mechanic on call. I sent him the pictures and he called me back with a plan to send a mechanic down on a different aircraft that night. I went off duty at that point and when I got back to the airport the next morning my aircraft had been swapped out with a different aircraft for us to continue our day.

column121: On a descent into DEN; we were cleared to descend via the CLASH 3 Arrival. I confirmed that the final altitude was 9;000 ft. and selected it in the altitude window. About 10 miles from EVRLY; we experienced wake turbulence for about five seconds; and then experienced it again. I selected Vertical Speed and leveled off the descent to get above the wake turbulence. After we were clear of the wake turbulence; I selected a 2;000 FPM descent to get back on my vertical path. At that time; we were told to switch to Denver Approach. Upon checking in with Denver Approach they changed our runway to 35L. At this point I was concerned about changing the approach in the FMC. I forgot to re-engage the VNAV. Because I forgot to re-engage the VNAV; the aircraft did not slow down to 250 kts for EVRLY. The aircraft also continued a descent below 12;000 feet.; which was the lowest altitude at TWNSN. The aircraft continue to descend until I notice the deviation. By this time I was leveling at 10;000 feet. and was below the 11;000 feet. altitude required for PNBAL. ATC advised me to slow the 210 knots; and gave me a vector for the final approach to Runway 35L. They also gave me a descent to 9;000 feet. The rest of the arrival went as planned.

column121: The deicing crew at ZZZ briefed myself and the First Officer (F/O) where the deicing was going to take place and we requested FULL AIRCRAFT DEICE with Type 1 and WINGS AND TAIL ANTI ICE with Type 4. After we pushed back and parking brake was set; the QRH was complied with for configuring the airplane for deicing as instructed by the deicing crew. The ice-truck drove past the nose to the left side and disappeared. Approximately; 15 minutes later; the truck rolled up from the right side and told us over the radio that the deicing was completed without giving us the pertinent data that we need like the type of fluid used for the deice and anti-ice. Moreover; we were not given the start time for the anti-icing. The first officer had to ask them for the information even to the point of getting clarification for the type 4 used in the anti-icing. This baffled us! As we tried to figure out what was going on; I asked my F/O if he had heard the sound of the spraying on the fuselage. He said no he really didn't hear it and I didn't hear it. So just to make sure; I asked the F/O to verbally ask if Type 1 was WHOLE FUSELAGE and TYPE 4 FOR WINGS AND TAIL; iceman said YES!  So we got the holdover time; and stated to taxi out but I had my doubt on what was done. As I was telling the F/O that we will need to pullover and do a pre-takeoff check by going in to the cabin to inspect at least the wings; we got a call from the flight attendants telling us that the windows were still glazed over with ice.I decided to return to the gate to do another walk around inspection. When we arrived at the gate at my F/O did the second walk around inspection; he came back angry and furious; and rightly so because the airplane was still ENCASED IN ICE! I too was very angry with the UNSAFE Job the iceman did for us and LIED about it. And please note that there was NO precipitation since we arrived at the airport.
column123: During the night in ZZZ they had gotten freezing rain; so when we got to the airplane (10 minutes before departure due to the road conditions) we already knew that we had to deice; which my walk around affirmed that. At this point everything was pretty normal except for the fact we were late; (we did not rush nor did I feel rushed) and we had to deice. We ran all checklists and pushed back; we ran the QRH for de-icing and called OPS for deicing/ anti icing; and my exact verbiage was 'parking brake set aircraft configured for de-icing full body wings and tail Type I and wings and tail Type IV' when they were done which looking back; it didn't seem to have taken the usual amount of time; it was way shorter! We finished up with the QRH; started the engines; ran the checklists and started to taxi; to which we may have taxied 100 yards when the FAs (Flight Attendants) called and said that the windows in the back were covered in ice; the CA (Captain) was also listening to this; I than told ground that we needed to stop and work a problem; he stopped the airplane and we discussed the issue and both determined we CANNOT takeoff with ice on the airplane; we both made the decision to gate return and inspect the airplane; we got to the gate ran the parking checklist and they brought up the Jetway; I exited the airplane to do another walk around and discovered the airplane still covered in ice! When I returned to the Jetway the CA was talking to the station manager; I shared what I had seen on the walk around and returned to the flight deck and re-repaired the aircraft for departure; I was not part of the discussion with the station manager or the Chief Pilot; I was briefed by the CA as to what each had said; and the thing that gets me the most is that the Chief Pilot was making excuses for ZZZ Operations; as they 'don't do it very often'! Come to find out the person spraying our aircraft was the stations de-icing trainer!! After all the decisions and a call to dispatch for a new flight plan we pushed back again ran checklists; got property de-iced ( we think and hope) and departed about two and a half hours late for a uneventful rest of the flight.

column121: We were being vectored from the northwest to the ILS approach and descending to 2;000 ft. when Tower asked if we had the airport in sight. This was my first time in ZZZ and although I thought I saw the airport I was not in a hurry to call it in sight; just to be sure. I verbalized that with the First Officer but he had been there before and was comfortable calling the airport in sight; so I did. Our initial vector would have taken us just outside the Final Approach Fix. However; when Tower issued clearance for the Visual Approach; the First Officer turned to a heading that would take us inside the Final Approach Fix. At the same time; he continued to descend while configuring with flaps (I think at either 10 or 15) and landing gear; and the speed brake extended. As the descent continued; Tower issued an 'Altitude Alert' and instructed us to adjust immediately. I cannot remember the exact verbiage; but there was a mention of our altitude being 1;200 ft. and perhaps something about 'minimum vectoring altitude.' The First Officer immediately adjusted his attitude to level off at around 1;200 ft. and continued to fly towards the runway center line. We were approximately abeam the Final Approach Fix at this point. He then asked for more flaps; ultimately Flaps 30; for the landing. I realized at about that point that he still had the speed brake extended and told him. He immediately stowed the speed brake and intercepted the visual glide path to the runway. I think he asked me at about that point if I was okay to continue. He was on the glide path and stabilized; so I said 'yes.'On landing rollout I noticed what sounded like an open microphone on the Tower frequency. Since there didn't seem to be any other aircraft on the frequency; I suspected it was coming from our aircraft. The Tower made a broadcast to all stations on the frequency that they were broadcasting on an active ATC radio frequency; and that they should cease immediately. When I made the '80 kts.' call out on landing roll; I heard myself over the radio. That confirmed that the First Officer was holding down the microphone button in his grip on the yoke. As soon as he loosened his grip; the transmission stopped.
column123: I was the pilot flying. Based on the weather reported we briefed the RNAV Arrival to be followed by the ILS Approach. We made special note that we were not to utilize the Autothrottle for the approach due to MEL(Minimum Equipment List) restriction. The arrival went as planned until we were given a vector off the arrival and then direct to the Final Approach Fix and a descent to 2;000 ft. As we were a bit high and fast; the speed brake was being utilized to expedite descent. While proceeding to the Final Approach Fix; the weather was acceptable to proceed visually so we reported field in sight and were cleared for the Visual Approach. Due to the high intercept angle to the Final Approach Fix I turned to establish a more acceptable intercept angle to capture the localizer. My perception looking outside was that we were quite high so asked the Pilot Monitoring to set Touchdown Zone Elevation. I failed to engage Vertical Nav for better situational awareness in relation to my vertical path and relied solely on the visual sight picture until on final. While on a dogleg to final we received an ATC Altitude warning alert telling us that we were below the sector altitude. We were approximately 1;100 ft. just abeam of the Final Approach Fix on a dogleg to final. I then stopped the descent until approaching final approach course and engaging Approach mode for glideslope capture. Continued the Visual Approach to a landing.

column121: We had been vectored off of the WAZKO1 RNAV Arrival toward the final approach course for the RNAV Runway 4 at ELP. We broke out of the overcast around 9;000 ft. and were approaching KANTR at 7;500 feet. There was a lot of ambient light from the city below and the reflection of that light from the overcast above as well as the fresh layer of snow on the surface. Approach cleared us for the approach and gave us 'Direct KANTR; Maintain 7;200 ft. until KANTR;' which I read back; with an emphasis on the '200'. The FO (PF) selected vertical speed mode after I set 7;200 ft. in the altitude preselector and called '7;200 ft. set!'. The published altitude at KANTR is 7;500 feet; which is located above terrain at 5;851 ft. We leveled at 7;200 ft. and she called for Flaps 18; and we joined the final approach course with the runway; and the terrain below in sight since descending out of 9;000 ft. Just then the GPWS System chimed in with 'Terrain! Pull Up!'. The FO dutifully disconnected the autopilot and I told her NOT to go around; as we were on a published segment of the final approach in good VMC (ELP was reporting 10 SM Vis) and I had the terrain in sight the whole time. We were not descending; and we had been level for some time. We landed without incident and taxied to our gate. Upon docking; I asked Ground for the phone number to the folks at approach control. The fellow who answered offered that he was indeed the Controller. I told him what had happened and he said that it was not at all uncommon; and that 7;200 ft. was their Minimum Vectoring Altitude in that sector. I told him that I would be filing a report with respect to the incident; for his own information.If there are other similar incidents here a communique should be distributed to the pilot group.

column121: After deicing the aircraft we taxied to [Runway] 35L. Upon completion of all of our checklists we requested time on the runway to do a 30 second engine run-up for the A319. [Runway] 35L had just been plowed of snow before our taxi onto the runway. The Captain was the Pilot Flying and began to increase the thrust. At about 55% N1 the airplane began to slide and point away from centerline. The Captain tried to steer the airplane using the tiller with great difficulty. The aircraft rolled forward about 1;000-1;500 ft. I called Tower and notified them that we had a steering problem and requested to exit the runway. We decided to return to the gate to have the aircraft nose wheel inspected. The runway; although recently plowed; played a significant factor in our situation. Also; the recommended 70% N1 engine run-up per our [Operating Manual] is a lot of power to control in icing conditions on the ground. I think that the engine run-up procedure approved by Airbus can lead to very problem when operating on surfaces during icing conditions.
column123: After deicing we were cleared to lineup and wait on 35L and to conduct our engine run up. I ran up both engines symmetrically to 70% N1 [following the SOP]. It was then that the right main gear lost traction and the aircraft turned aggressively to the left. I immediately retarded both throttles to idle and used nose wheel steering to regain the centerline. There was nose wheel scrubbing felt. I then cleared the runway and returned to the gate for a maintenance inspection of the nose wheel. The factors were the unprecedented DFW weather. Although the runway was freshly cleaned and we were the first aircraft to use it. There was obviously ice in spots that were hard to see at night. The light takeoff weight of 116;000 lbs coupled with the high power setting for the run up played roles in the incident. Although I had operated two previous flight in and out of DFW that day the runway conditions changed rapidly. I felt that the runway had been freshly cleaned moments before I took to the runway and that it would be suitable for the run up. I will continue to be vigilant in inclement weather conditions. I have gained a newer understanding for the power of the engine on an A319.

column121: Significant freezing rain event the day of this flight led to 1/4 to 1/2 inch clear ice covering the entire aircraft. There was no attempt to de-ice the aircraft prior to the crew arriving for preflight. The engine inlets needed to be de-iced prior to block out so that we could start the engines after block out. This de-icing of the inlets took a considerable amount of time due to the significant accumulation of ice in the bottom of the fan section of both engines. By the time we were able to block out (2h 39min late) and taxi to the remote de-ice pad A; a short distance from our ramp; the de-ice trucks had run out of fluid and trucks needed to also be refueled. Another significant delay ensued. Almost an hour after block out; de-icing began. The entire airplane was de-iced with Type I fluid since there was no precipitation falling. Aircraft was fully de-iced and inspected by the de-ice team. We then proceeded to our departure runway and prepared for takeoff. The reason for this safety report became clear as soon as we began the initial climb segment immediately after takeoff. We began shedding ice from the entire fuselage and this shedding continued through 12;000 ft.; approximately 7-10 minutes after takeoff. All four crew members could hear the ice departing the aircraft and felt the airframe vibrations as large chunks of ice tumbled down the length of the fuselage. All four crew members each have 20-30 years of aviation experience; and no one had ever experienced anything like it. In my 30 plus years of heavy transport category aircraft operation I have never experienced this kind of ice shedding event. I believe that the de-ice procedure was completely ineffective for this amount of clear ice that covered the entire aircraft. With that amount ice being shed from the aircraft for that long; we had a significant amount of Ice still adhering to the airframe when we took off. The engine vibration was well within limits even during the climb out and so the crew chose to continue the flight. I was concerned about airframe damage from that amount of ice departing the aircraft; and because of that concern; I recorded an AML entry asking that the aircraft be inspected for damage after arrival in ZZZZ. [Cause was] inadequate de-icing for the amount of clear ice that was adhering to the airframe. Also the de-ice crew was possibly unable to see the ice after de-icing; since it was clear ice and fully covering the aircraft; and the airplane was still wet from the de-icing fluid used. [Suggest] re-evaluate the process of de-icing when so much clear ice is adhering to the airframe.

column121: We took off from ZZZ in normal conditions. At approximately 1;600 ft.; the pilot flying had problems with the controllability of the aircraft. The PIC took control of the aircraft and confirmed the actual problem - the aircraft was turning left by itself; without any reason. To maintain heading it was necessary to use abnormal force to the right with the aileron controls. The rudder pedals apparently were stuck. To maintain 2;000 ft. that was required; we asked for radar vectors to returned to ZZZ. ATC gave us vectors to downwind for Runway XX and cleared us for visual approach. Speed was 170 kts. column121: As I was setting up cruise at 11;500 ft. I noticed my speed was not what it should be with a bit of a tailwind and the plane was yawing severely to the right. I used a fair amount of left rudder to keep the ball centered for the whole flight. I tried to figure out what could be wrong with the plane to cause this; but could not come up with a plausible explanation. Checked the trim; looked at the flaps; ailerons; elevator where visible and could see nothing. [On a previous flight] there was pretty substantial turbulence and I thought maybe something happened to the rudder that I missed on the preflight. Other than being slow and requiring the constant pressure on the left rudder pedal; the flight was uneventful. Approach cleared me through the Bravo airspace utilizing the west transition to get to the south side of the Bravo airspace. Once clear of Bravo; they terminated VFR Flight Following and I contacted Tower about 10 miles west and indicated inbound for landing with ATIS. I believe Tower had me #2 with a 2 mile final. I had nice stable approach utilizing a fair amount of left rudder to align with the center line at a 90 kt. approach. I crossed the numbers at about 84 kts. and mains touched down at about 76 kts. When the nose gear settled; the aircraft immediately shot straight right off the side of the runway. I worked the left rudder pedal and brake to try and regain control and got the plane back on the runway fairly quickly. Tower asked if I needed assistance and I told them no. I tried to explain what happened but really did not know. Tower said to contact ground. I did so and they said the pilot waiting to depart said my nose wheel was canted 45 degrees to the right as I came by them. That would explain the yaw and the plane shooting off to the right on landing. I contacted a mechanic and he will be looking at the plane to [determine] what the issue is and what it will take to repair that issue. The mechanic said there is a pin on the strut that can break and cause this issue. He said I was very fortunate to have regained control and the nose gear released and was able to track again. He said when that pin breaks; very often the nose gear will not release and allow straight forward movement. I had no idea that this is a not uncommon occurrence with these aircraft. I had googled a description of what happened and got nothing coming up that would explain what the mechanic told me.
column122: Reporter stated that the mechanic said strut pin failure is not uncommon. Reporter added that the pin slides into a V groove to center the nose gear upon retraction. column121: There were snow drifts on the taxiway and runway.  Due to the snow; upon climb out; pilots side landing gear door would not close completely.  I cycled the gear several times to try and clear the snow to allow the gear to close fully.  We were unsuccessful getting the gear to close; so I decided to land and see if we could resolve the issue.  Feeling the departure airport was unsafe due to the runway conditions; I decided to divert to ZZZ1 to assess the situation.  I am familiar with the airport and they have a Tower and other facilities.  Roughly 20-30 minutes after ATC gave us our clearance to ZZZ1 (while we were at FL270); there was an explosion like sound and all cabin pressure immediately departed.  This blow out knocked off all of our headsets.  Understanding that we had a cabin de-presserization; I immediately pulled the power back to idle; dropped the landing gear and nosed the plane over for rapid descent.  Once we were going down; I changed our squawk to 7700 (knowing that this was our only form of communication with the outside world); set the autopilot to level off at 12;500 feet and re-engaged the autopilot in case I were to black out.  I didn't grab for my oxygen mask because at the time we were already coming down at a rate of over 8;000 ft/min and the wind/cold and just chaotic nature of the cabin; I didn't feel comfortable taking my hands off of the controls.  I also didn't go for my headset for similar reasons; as well as there being so much noise; I knew there would be no way for me to hear ATC let alone they be able to hear me. After we were able to level off at 12;500 feet; I looked for the closest airport (ZZZ2); brought up their weather and loaded the approach we wanted and turned to the appropriate heading.  I opened the inertial separator; turned on our landing and wigwag lights and decided to leave the gear down for the remainder of the flight.  I didn't want to accidentally add any other complications to our situation.  After what seemed like the longest approach in history; we finally touched down safely at ZZZ2; where I taxied the plane to the already waiting emergency vehicles.

column121: Aircraft is non-electrical with no starter; and based at a private airpark home.  Aircraft was tied down at tail and triple chocked. Preflighted and prepared for a normal start and flight. Aircraft traveled unoccupied down sloping yard and hit a ditch coming to rest on the taxiway; resulting in landing gear damage and propeller striking ground and pavement and engine shutdown. No injuries or property damage occurred. In retrospect I have always been careful to secure the aircraft for start correctly with triple chocks and tie down. It's possible; on this start; I may not have tightened the throttle friction lock fully which may have allowed the throttle position to travel partially forward after start. The chocks in front of all three tires started to strain; then failed and the aircraft rolled forward as I was moving around the wing. The last available restraint was a tiedown at the tailwheel position. Momentum and some slack in the tie down rope caused the tiedown stake to pull loose from the ground as the slack was taken up. The downhill slope of the yard added to the acceleration before impact with the ditch. I should have double checked the throttle setting and friction lock to make sure that throttle position would not change. The increase in power would not have happened.

column121: I am a CFI and I was flying a training mission with my client who is a licensed private pilot working on transition training to a new model aircraft (Aircraft X). This was my client's first flight in a Aircraft X. The lesson started with a detailed preflight; followed by a similarly detailed run-up. Once ready; we departed Palo Alto Airport for a familiarization flight in a practice area south and west of the airport. During our time in the practice area we maintained visual separation from another aircraft in the training area (each trying to stay in our own section of the training area; while we also maintained appropriate distances from scattered clouds in the area; and staying below the Bravo which starts at 4;000 in that area. During this time; we stayed in contact with the Tower having asked them for advisories during our training mission.After approximately 1 hour of Hobbs time (including the taxi and detailed run-up); we copied ATIS Quebec and informed the Tower that we would like to return to the field for the option; and closed traffic. We were instructed to fly over Stanford and enter the pattern for left traffic for Runway 31. We made our way as instructed and entered the left downwind for Runway 31. The Tower then told us that we were number 4 cleared to land; and that the traffic that we were following was roughly abeam us in the opposite downwind. We acknowledged the instruction and reported negative contact with the traffic to follow. Meanwhile; the Tower was very busy with numerous other traffic entering; leaving; and in the pattern. We were then told to extend our downwind; that we had extensive extensions into Moffett Field's airspace (it is very common for Palo Alto to have and use extensions into Moffett's airspace - this extension was even further than usual) and that the Tower would call our base. While extending; we saw our traffic to follow turn base and then final. But we continued downwind since the Tower said that they would call our base.Moments later; the Tower instructed us to fly 'straight towards the 31 numbers' which was a bit strange since we were so far from the runway (probably at least 3 miles at this point). But the frequency was very busy and it didn't seem to make sense (or even possible) to ask to verify the instruction. We turned left onto a long final and proceeded towards the runway. We were holding approximately 1;000 feet (+/- since my student was flying and this was their first time in the aircraft) this entire time on downwind; base and long final.Not too long after we turned long final; the Tower told us to climb 500 feet immediately for traffic. I immediately took the controls of the plane; quickly (re)checked nearby traffic on the G1000 MFD (with ADS-B traffic) and did a visual scan for traffic as I went full forward on the throttle; prop; and mixture and pitched the nose back for the climb. The quick scan of traffic (visual and ADS-B) did not indicate any traffic below or next to us; but it did indicate one aircraft above our altitude but not in the immediate vicinity. None-the-less; we tried to visually acquire the above traffic as we climbed.Moments later; the tower told us to stop our climb immediately and to turn right and fly directly towards Leslie Salt. Again; we immediately complied with the Tower's instructions as we continued to try to acquire and track any immediate threats visually. Just then; we saw another aircraft pass directly above us; slightly off to our left side; in very close proximity to our aircraft. The Tower then instructed us to make a right turn back to final for landing.I've been flying at PAO for nearly XX years; so I am familiar with how busy it can get. But even with that experience; it was particularly busy at this time. One of the things that I think was a factor in this situation was a partial callsign conflict. Our aircraft callsign ended in [--] while the callsign of another aircraft on frequency at the time ended in [--]. In fact; it is possible that the aircraft above us when we were instructed to climb; and the one that nearly collided with moments later; was the aircraft ending in [--]. My theory is that the instruction to climb was actually intended for Aircraft Y and not Aircraft X; and that the controller tried to stop our climb as soon as he noticed the error. Unfortunately; these problems were all compounded by the heavy radio traffic making it virtually impossible to verify instructions; especially in a timely fashion.My client and I replayed this whole incident both while still in the air; and during debrief on the ground; and we are both quite certain that we responded to our correct callsign and that this wasn't a case of us improperly (and unintentionally) responding to someone else's callsign. I wanted to use the G1000 PLAYback feature to check/verify the radio call; but; unfortunately; the radio traffic was so heavy that there was no way to use the replay feature successfully. I have replayed this entire situation a number of times trying to analyze what I could have / should have done differently to avoid getting this close to another aircraft. Unfortunately; I haven't really come up with a good answer given the details of the situation.Given that the only nearby traffic that I could observe at the time was the one above us; I could have held my attitude of 1;000 feet; in defiance of the Tower Controller's instruction; until I could verify that the climb instruction was for us; or until I could verify another nearby traffic threat. But this seems like a very bad idea. I have always operated that when ATC gives you an immediate traffic avoidance instruction that you follow that instruction immediately. There could have very well been another nearby aircraft that I was unaware of that was an even more of a threat that I was currently unaware of. Hence my immediate response as instructed.I believe that the similar sounding callsigns; heavy radio traffic; and large number of aircraft operating in the class Delta; all contributed to the confusion for all parties. I know that it made our task (mine and my client) much more difficult; and I believe that you could hear that in the voice and instructions of the Tower Controller and the other pilots. After landing; we opted to terminate rather than continue pattern operations. Once back in the flying club; we talked with another CFI and student who was flying (and returning to the airport) at the same time. I asked them if they heard the Tower 'trying kill us' and the CFIs response was 'yeah; the Tower Controller was clearly overwhelmed!' We asked him if he heard any indications that we responded to the wrong callsign. His response was 'no' and that; again; he thought that whole problem was that the Tower Controller was simply overwhelmed by the overall situation.I know that Palo Alto is an FAA Training Tower; and I'm fully understanding and supportive of that. But perhaps in this case maybe there should have been additional oversight of Tower operations; or at least a senior controller stepping in before the controller got too overwhelmed.

column121: Following a flight from ZZZZ to ZZZZ1 arrival at XA:50 local; I parked the aircraft on the north apron and installed all covers for protection.At approximately XF:00 local time; it started snowing lightly around the airport.Upon receiving a message from the passengers to inform me that they would be at the airport at XG:30 local; I went directly to the aircraft to prepare for departure. This involves taking the protection covers away from engines; pitot tubes and static wick dischargers also preforming a check on electrical heated pitot tubes; static sensors and various other checks and tests (pre-flight).The passengers arrived at the aircraft XG:55 local (approx.) and boarded. At this time; it had started snowing more heavily and I instructed [the] FBO to contact company for a Type I de-ice and Type IV anti-ice for the aircraft. The de-icing vehicle arrived shortly after XH:00 (approx.) and I spoke with the de-icing operator and FBO representative for the co-ordination of the de-icing and anti-icing of the aircraft. This involved me explaining exactly which surfaces I wanted to be treated and I showed the de-icing operator a diagram from the aircraft AFM to provide visual explanation.I was informed by the FBO that ZZZZ1 were to close the runway for snow removal from XH:00 - XH:25 local; I therefore requested the de-icing and anti-icing to begin at XH:20 to be finished within a 15-20 mins timescale and to be ready for start and taxi with taking into consideration the 'holdover time' tolerance.I was present on the apron ramp the whole time that the de-icing operator preformed the de-ice and anti-ice procedure and confirm that this was preformed correctly.Once the vehicles and personal had moved away and following a final external visual check of the aircraft; I secured the door from the inside and informed the passengers that we would be on our way shortly.Following a request for start; taxi and departure clearance and after performing all checks and aircraft test required; I started the taxi from the spot on the north apron. This was without event. ATC requested that the aircraft stop and hold short at holding point north apron 1 due to arriving and departing traffic. After a wait at 1 of maybe two minutes; ATC announced that we would not be able to depart; as they were to close the runway for a second snow removal. I informed ATC that we had de-iced and anti-iced; had start; taxi and departure clearance and was able to depart from intersection 1 with 2750 meters available. Cessna performance calculations based upon meteorological conditions at the time of aircraft start showed that 1027 meters was needed to perform and safe departure.After lining up on runway XX and upon receiving ATC clearance for departure; I applied approximately 75% power whilst holding the toe brakes to confirm that the engines were performing correctly following the de-icing and anti-icing. With engine parameters correct; I released the toe brakes; increased power on the engines to take off power (FADEC) and the aircraft started its ground roll. A cross check between the two airspeed indicators (PFD's 1 & 2) at 70 knots confirmed that I could continue the take-off roll. Upon reaching the calculated V1 (91 knots) and VR speed (98 knots); I applied a normal force to the aircraft yoke which moved in the normal manner; but the aircraft did not rotate. A little more the normal force was then used and still the aircraft would not rotate. The aircraft seemed to be 'stuck' to the snow on the runway. A rejected take-off (RTO) was performed without event.A considerable distance was required to stop the aircraft. Once controlled I taxied and exited the aircraft onto taxiway at 2 holding point on the south side. Conversation with ATC informed me that I was to stop and await the fire services who were on their way. Fire services gave the all clear and ATC requested that I was to follow the 'follow me' vehicle to the parking ramp. Once at parking position south side and after all required checks; I shut down the engines and spoke with the fire services about the RTO.Runway XX was now closed as scheduled for a second snow runway removal.I disembarked the passengers and after a visual check of the aircraft to establish if there was any evidence of why the aircraft would not rotate; I re-installed all protection covers and left the aircraft on parking ramp as it was now dark.Upon arrival at the aircraft [the next morning]; I completed a thorough visual inspection to establish a possible cause to the rejected take off but could not find anything for explanation.As the anti-icing fluid was covering the aircraft; the aircraft was clean of ice and snow. Following all ground checks and system checks; a normal departure was performed without event.

column121: I reviewed the weather at approximately XA00 hours; including visibility; winds; and turbulence.  When I reviewed this weather; the winds forecast for the ZZZ airport was indicated to be 18-25 knots; and mild turbulence was indicated through both visual and graphical reviews using the ForeFlight products.  At 1 1/2 hours later; two passengers and I boarded our SF50 Vision Jet and rechecked the winds at the ZZZ airport.  The winds had held steady at the previous levels.  We decided that we continue with our planned trip; understanding that the winds were mainly straight down the direction of the runway.  We filed for an altitude en-route at 11;000 feet; believing that it would be high enough to prevent any issues that we've encountered on the numerous trips we've flown to ZZZ with respect to turbulence.  We've flown over 100 missions into the ZZZ area over the past six months.  The takeoff from ZZZ1 was routine and without incident.  We climbed up to 11;000 feet without incident and no issues with turbulence.  Our issues began when we transferred to the TRACON frequency. Twice during the turbulence; we attempted to review the weather using the GTC 2 system within the aircraft and were having a difficult time stabilizing our inputs with our fingers; even using the bezel to support our hands and use our thumbs to do so was challenging.  During one of the larger turbulent events; the autopilot disconnect was engaged by the second pilot in the right seat; which we were immediately able to re-engage as the buttons on the aircraft's autopilot is not electronic but tactile.  Once we had the autopilot back engaged; we referred back to the GTC 2 to re-engage the flight plan and selected the approach that was already listed on the display; which was the visual approach to Runway XXL; using the VOR as a descend and entrance point.  We had not noticed that the VNAV aspect of the approach had been selected when we re-engaged the auto-pilot; at which point we were now consistently in moderate to severe turbulence.  During this period; the TRACON controller called us and simply said 'Why are you descending.'   We told them about the visual approach being loaded in and began to describe what our corrective action would be -- however; in that split second; we hit the single most severe turbulence I've ever felt in an aircraft.  The turbulence threw the aircraft up; then aggressively left; which then dropped aggressively; throwing everybody to the header of the cabin.  My headset  (a Bose A20) was broken on the upper hinge; which struck the upper panel and broke loose my supplemental oxygen mask; breaking the clamp.   Objects in the cabin flew forward and up.  At this point; I immediately placed the aircraft in recovery mode; with full power; level wings and attempted to contact ATC to advise that I needed an emergency descent.  In VFR conditions; I noticed that I was over the mountain and switched to [next] frequency; and immediately advised the same and was given the approval to descend to 6;000 feet with a distinct heading.   I was then advised other aircraft were experiencing similar issues with turbulence and had gone missed into ZZZ. On the new heading and altitude; I began a full systems check of the aircraft; landing gear cycle; ailerons; flaps and review the fuel system.   I advised the TRACON controller that we were fine and that the oxygen masks had been deployed.   The controller provided be vectors; then cleared us for the VOR approach into ZZZ.  We flew the approach; we decided about three miles from the airport to abandon our approach and return to ZZZ1; in which we were given vectors and an approach back into the ZZZ1 airport without incident. Many things happened on this trip; almost in serial.  Without a doubt; the level of forecasted and reported turbulence was well above what we had seen using ForeFlight; or based on our prior experience.  When recovering from the several avionics disruptions (auto-pilot switch shut-offs; etc.); we had maintained a fairly vigilant response to restoring our programmed flight activity - until the turbulence began to get violent.   In a similar environment; I would ask for a 180-degree turn to remove myself and the aircraft from the events that led to deteriorating events with even lesser conditions.  Our corrective action after getting clearance for the emergency descent was sound; but it should have never been necessary if we had more carefully judged the degree of the turbulence; which had caused us not immediately to identify the VNAV programming into the GTC 2.  The three of us debriefed the flight in detail; including a review of the ForeFlight products to identify in greater clarity about Airmets (Tango) and how we could set up levels of automation that we could defer in order to maintain more positive control of the aircraft.   In reviewing our training materials; we reviewed the SF50 process on how to accept lower levels of automation during events that require higher pilot concentration and how this aids in the better situational awareness in events that we experienced on this date.
