column121: A VFR flight was to be flown from BFL to ZZZ for the purpose of repositioning an aircraft for company business the following day. This flight was operated under Part 91 pursuant to all applicable FAR's and company SOP's. The intended route took the pilot from BFL to ZZZ2 to ZZZZZ to ZZZZZ1 then direct ZZZ at an altitude of 9;500. The pilot obtained a briefing via Foreflight at XA:21 local time for an intended departure time of XA:45. Upon reviewing the briefing; it was decided current conditions would allow for the safe operation of the flight. The pilot departed BFL at XA:45 local time and climbed straight out in VMC conditions to an altitude of 095. Cloud conditions in the valley were broken at various altitudes below 8;000 feet. As the flight progressed towards ZZZ2; the pilot then proceeded direct to ZZZ3. As the pilot approached the ZZZZZ2 intersection; traffic could be viewed on ADSB traveling opposite direction on the V197 (Northwest) at 10;500. This traffic was indicating a ground speed ranging from 50-70 knots confirming the PIC's suspicion of stronger than forecasted winds aloft. As the pilot continued southeast bound; it was apparent that the cloud conditions below and ahead were worsening and the PIC initiated a climb to 11;500 MSL. upon reaching 10;300 MSL just south of ZZZZZ3 intersection; the pilot turned east to avoid building clouds. During this moment; the pilot encountered a 2;000 FPM downdraft which they countered with a pitch up attitude to achieve Vy. Once established at Vy; the rate of descant had slowed to 700 FPM. Knowing conditions improved to the west; the PIC initiated a turn back to BFL and informed ATC of the intentions as well as the conditions. Upon receiving a handoff to BFL Approach; the pilot informed them of their intentions and that it may be necessary to notify ATC. As the ground speed began to drop below 45 knots still in a descent at Vy; the PIC saw a situation where the aircraft would not be able to stay above the cloud layer and safely away from rising terrain to the west. The PIC then informed ATC that they were turning southbound; notified ATC due to weather and squawked 7700. As this decision was made; the PIC was experiencing a severe downdraft where positive control of the aircraft's altitude was difficult to maintain. Upon descending to an altitude of 6;500' MSL; the pilot encountered a large updraft and used this to climb to an altitude of 12;00 MSL which allowed exceptional terrain separation. The pilot flew southbound; where it was visibly better weather and began to request PIREP's from ATC for a VFR field east of the terrain knowing that the area east offered high ceilings and lower terrain. ATC informed the pilot of a large hole in the cloud layer on a 090 heading and suggested the pilot land WJF. ATC then asked the pilot if they were able to accept a 090 heading and it was accepted. The pilot then sighted the large opening; measuring roughly 25-30 nm x. 5 nm and began a decent in VMC conditions. As the pilot descended below the surrounding cloud layer's bases (5;700 feet MSL); they verified ZZZ4 in sight and were given a handoff. Upon assessing the situation; the PIC decided against landing at ZZZ4 and determined an emergency declaration was no longer needed; relayed intentions to ATCT at ZZZ4 and were handed back to Joshua Approach. The declaration was canceled with them and the flight continued to ZZZ1 for a safe landing. Upon landing; the PIC contacted the Director of Safety for the company and informed them of the events that occurred. It was decided that the pilot made appropriate inflight decisions to ensure the maximum safety of flight. Further reviewing the events that took place; the pilot decided to reread the briefing to determine if any significant signs of these conditions were missed. No information was found to be omitted during the PIC's decision to conduct the flight. Numerous other aircraft had flown the same area throughout the day and encountered conditions well within the PIC's comfort; conditions were not reported outside of VFR regulations at departure; or at arrival. The only adverse weather reported was IFR at TSP to the north east of the intended route and winds aloft in that area in excess of 45 Knots. Going forward; the PIC will study material specific to the safe operation of a single engine aircraft over mountainous terrain to better be able to determine when such adverse conditions may be found and what to do differently when they are encountered. An action that could have been utilized by the PIC that was not was to request an IFR clearance east of the position where it encountered the first sign of severe downdrafts and flown via radar vectors to an area that was VMC away from rising terrain.

column121: Upon pushback from ZZZ Gate 1; it was soon apparent the Pushback Crew was experiencing a problem. They said nothing but it was increasingly clear the Tug was sliding as well as the aircraft not proceeding in a direction I would expect. I tried asking the Driver if there was a problem but did not receive an answer via wireless headset. When his Tug was starting to jackknife; I decided to use my brakes to stop the aircraft. By this time; the Tug came very close to impacting the aircraft on my side. I later learned that his headset was working; but he was trying to talk to the other Ramp Agents instead and not me. I also believe he was cognitively overwhelmed with the unexpected situation as that same phenomena (not responding to me) continued later when we attempted to another push after re-attaching the tow bar/Tug. The First Officer was also adding his input; which was not helping the situation with communication. It was a communications mess. We called the station to inform them of the situation and eventually a Ramp Supervisor came out and took over. We then discussed the option of attempting to move the aircraft to another part of the ramp where it was known to be less than nil braking. Going back to the same gate would only have been to an area of known poor/nil control. We eventually got to an area where the Ramp Agents could safely walk and feel that the ramp was in better condition and where other aircraft were not experiencing any problems.When I landed approximately an hour prior in a different aircraft; my taxi to Gate 2 took me to an area where I lost all steering and braking control for about five seconds. We immediately notified this on Ops frequency; and at least one other Crew stated they experienced the same. Luckily; we slid to an area where I regained control and then carefully proceeded to the gate when the aircraft performed adequately. I then called Dispatch via my cell phone immediately after block in. He said he would pass it on to the supervisor; but I did not hear any apparent immediate concern. Instead; he said I needed to alert the Station; as it is their job to manage that info (I was really puzzled that our Dispatch gave me that answer). I eventually found the Ops Agent and wanted to make sure the Station had this information; as I was very concerned that others could experience worse.Q1: What does it take for a Pilot to state before any real concern is expressed by those managing our operation? Was poor or nil braking not a big enough concern?Q2: Why had nothing been done to correct the situation or at least alert other Crews that some areas were okay but others were NIL? Or stop the operation?Q3: Why would a Push Crew try to fix this problem without getting any other assistance or guidance? I could see they were guessing and even willing to just leave us there as they told us to try to taxi out of it. They even tried to tow us forward on the re-attempt with our engines running. They were completely overwhelmed; which gave me even greater concern.Q4: As Crews; we have no accurate resources (ZZZ is a joke as it is often old and/or inaccurate) to tell us real time conditions on other parts of the airport other than asking Ground Control (which I did). I was concerned that everything was starting to freeze over; and I did not want to the PIREP stating I was in NIL or off the taxiway later on. Without having routine freezing rain experience; how can I know how quickly conditions can go from good to bad?Q5: What does it take for a pause or stop in our operation? Damage? Injury? Taxiway departure? It seems like we just continue pushing with no apparent oversight. That is not a comforting feeling nor does it give me much confidence our system has mechanisms to protect me before getting in a terrible spot.I would appreciate answers to these questions and would like to know if anyone in Headquarters feels this situation was acceptable or not?

column121: Pushed away from gate. Started taxing in ZZZ alley when I got a call from #1 Flight Attendant; (FA); that there were First Class; FC; passengers that were not wearing face coverings after being told to wear them by the FAs. Stopped the aircraft and made a very 'To the point' PA that any non-compliance with Flight Attendant instructions; particularly pertaining to facial coverings; would have 'un-favorable' consequences. I had already made it clear that facial coverings were required while on-board during my 'welcome aboard' PA. Conferred with FAs that my second PA was successful; and we continued taxi and takeoff. Once established in cruise; the FAs informed me that they were having problems with FC passengers willfully being non-compliant regarding wearing a facial covering after being advised as such multiple times by at least 2 different FAs. My FAs had even switched working positions in order to try to de-escalate the situation and convince the passengers to comply. I commenced communication with Dispatch and relayed the situation with advisement to contact customer representatives. Shortly thereafter; due not only to non-mask wearing; but also; disruptive behavior by passengers requested to be re-seated in Main Cabin. I further relayed this information to Dispatch. It was at this point the FAs gave the notification of passenger misconduct warning. Shortly thereafter passenger started harassing my FAs with constant cornering them in the FC galley and demanding trivial items. At this point; even after a tremendous amount of patience; de-escalation attempts and warnings by the FAs; and with building harassment and aggressiveness being demonstrated by passengers; I notified Dispatch that we would be diverting to ZZZ1. We landed at ZZZ1 non-eventfully; without being overweight and without declaring an emergency. Passengers were removed from the aircraft. We departed ZZZ1 and arrived in ZZZZ uneventfully. Please allow me to acknowledge my FAs for their display of 'Consummate Professionalism' during this flight. They were tireless in their attempts to de-escalate the situation in hopes of precluding a diversion. I would also like to acknowledge the support of Dispatch and company as reflective of the number of communications that were made prior to our diversion. And last; but certainly not least; I would like to acknowledge the expert airmanship demonstrated by my First Officer during our extremely busy diversion as well as throughout the rest of a very long day. Should you need additional information from me regarding this diversion; please don't hesitate to contact me.

While climbing through approx 18;000 ft; first one; then other flight attendants called to say they smelled a burning rubber smell in cabin but could not see smoke. Passengers were also complaining. The cause was unknown; but aircraft did have an MEL for avionics cooling extract fan that required it to remain in override. column123: The Captain (CA) and I noticed a smell in the flight deck while in the climb; roughly around 10;000 feet.  The FAs (flight attendants) called climbing through flight level 180 stating they smell an odor in the cabin.  The FAs also stated some passengers were complaining about the odor.   The Captain requested the flight attendants to call back in 10 minutes and state if the smell is dissipating.  The FAs call back shortly stating several passengers are having difficulty breathing.  At that time the Captain made the decision to return to the ZZZ.  I took over as Pilot Flying and ATC communications. I requested to return to the ZZZ and notified ATC for an overweight landing.  At that time the aircraft weighed roughly 180;000 lbs.  The CA took over Pilot Flying on the arrival shortly before joining the approach to runway.  The aircraft weighed approximately 177;000 lbs on landing.  When we arrived at the gate paramedics attended to several passengers who were having difficulties breathing. [Possible cause or related issue]; we were relatively heavy; had a slight tailwind and the runway was wet.  The TPS (takeoff performance system) called for config 2; TOGO; APU OFF.  As a measure of safety the CA decided to leave the APU and APU bleeds on.  I concurred.  The aircraft's extract fan was also MEL'd (MEL 21-05a).  The CA and I both felt the odor mostly resembled anti-icing fluid.  Though we also discussed the possibly the inoperative extract fan or the APU usage on takeoff was the cause of the odor.  But mostly we thought it was anti-icing fluid.  Once we realized passengers and the cabin crew were being affected the decision was made to return to ZZZ which resulted in an overweight landing.

column121: At 800 feet AGL; clicked autopilot off for a visual landing. At 500 ft.; FO called 'Stable; cleared to land Runway XX Center.' I replied 'Landing.' Clicked autopilot button again and crossed checked then confirmed that 'Flight Director' was displayed in PFD. Landed uneventfully but elevator movement was very heavy in flare. After landing at taxi speed; I tried to move the yoke left and right and there was very limited movement. The First Officer tried as well with the same result. We checked the Flight Control and Hydraulic Displays and both were normal.I considered a go-around but quickly [determined] a go around would be extremely difficult with big power changes and limited flight control capability. column121: On initial climbout of ZZZ off Runway XXC we experienced loss of power shortly after passing 400 feet and received the 'Landing gear' aural warning. I double checked the gear handle and verified gear position; then verified N1 rollback; momentarily thinking we had dual engine failure. FO exclaimed startle; I replied 'fly the plane'. FO disconnected auto throttle; brought the thrust back up to takeoff position. We momentarily lost altitude and airspeed as Startle and surprise delayed our recognition slightly. Timing of the event was before flap retraction so we were near flap over speed during recognition and recovery; I said 'watch the speed pitch up pitch up' until flaps were retracted. FO later indicated his flight director was not giving correct indications for phase of flight. FO was able to recognize and manually control the aircraft; resuming normal climb out. Once the aircraft was under control; auto pilot and auto throttle engaged normally and no further anomalies were experienced.Unknown; weather was stormy; with moderate turbulence and lightning flashes in vicinity; in full IMC.We teach hand on thrust levers at all times during arrival and landing phase; but not during takeoff...had the FO had physical contact with the thrust levers during the climb; the AT retarding would have been instantly detected. I recommend the same procedure is taught for takeoff as is for landing...one hand on the thrust levers.
column123: After checking everything was normal we lined up on runway XXC in ZZZ. We verified our automation was in the correct mode including TO; ROLL; and FLCH were verified on our FMA as well as the crosshair flight director was up. As I advanced thrust the auto throttles took and the captain confirmed that ATTCS armed and we had normal TO thrust. at 80 knots while verifying the speed I saw the AT were in their normal HOLD mode. At this point everything was completely normal. When I went to rotate and was transitioning in the instruments I noticed that the FD had switched during the roll to the diamond mode which is supposed to happen at 1000'AGL. (Latter the captain confirmed that there's was normal). I had a normal rotation and pitched towards a normal takeoff attitude disregarding the flight director. At approximately 400 AGL the auto throttles commanded idle thrust suddenly. The startle and surprise nature of this took a second to process where we lost approximately 50 feet. At this point I disconnected the auto throttles and set climb power. The automation was still not working correctly including the flight director. Once we climbed through sterile we turned on the auto-throttles and they worked throughout the flight but we watched them very carefully and called Maintenance writing up the experience on the ground. The cause is unknown. before Takeoff we both verified we were in the correct automation modes. Once in cruise flight we verified all out take-off date and departure limits were set correctly and they were. Contributing factors to the loss of altitude was the thunderstorms in the vicinity; night; and moderate turbulence. More effective startle and surprise training in the sims. We are taught to keep both hands on the yoke throughout departure I think at 400 feet though 10;000 we should be guarding the thrust levers like we do on approach to landing.

column121: After detailed pre-flight inspection according to manufacturer checklist; we noticed that both fuel tanks are full; samples from each fuel sump and sump under the engine are clear; we checked the color - blue color for 100LL; there was no water or other contaminants; oil level was in the operational limits for our airplane; and we decided that airplane is in the condition to make a safe flight. After listening the ATIS and getting all necessary information about the airport; we contacted Clearance Delivery requesting VFR Flight to NW (northwest) to our practice area; and after that Ground Control for taxi instruction.We completed the runup at the runup area next to Runway XX; as instructed by Ground Control; following every step on the checklist. During the runup we didn't find any issues with the airplane; magneto check was within the manufacturer limits; oil pressure and temperature were ''in green'; engine was working and responding normally like any other day. After completing runup; and agreeing that there is nothing wrong with the airplane; we decided to proceed with our flight. After contacting Tower; we departed NW to practice area. Student was flying the airplane and I was monitoring his and the airplane's performance. During takeoff roll we checked engine instruments; everything was normal; and we continued with liftoff and climb. When we arrived at [the] practice area we practiced Steep turns; S-Turns over the road; and turns around the point. During the time from takeoff; climb and during maneuvers; the engine was performing normally as well; without any issues. Once we completed the maneuvers we decided to go back to our airport. After gettingATIS information; [student] contacted the Tower and requested a full stop landing on Runway XY. We were told to proceed directly to the Airport.At that moment we were at around 1;700-1;800 feet and decided to slowly start our descent. Around 20-30 seconds after that we experienced engine roughness; loss of power and the airplane started shaking; and we started losing altitude. I took over the controls from [student] to try to troubleshoot and to find out what exactly could cause the airplane to behave like that. After checking the fuel selector (BOTH); mixture position (FULL RICH); carburetor heat (ON); primer (IN AND LOCKED) and ignition (BOTH); and noticing that everything is in position for normal operation; I started reducing the power to see how airplane will behave. With less power; shaking was reduced; but still present; and altitude losing was increased. After that I advanced power to maximum to see how the airplane will respond; but rough running increased again; shaking increased; and altitude loss was reduced but still present.At that moment we were at around 1;300-1;400 feet and descending; and I decided to contact the Tower again and to try to explain our situation. Tower asked me if we can come back; and after finding out that we are constantly descending regardless of our power setting; I acknowledge them that we are unable to do so. I decided to [follow] the [the] Expressway; to stay away from busy streets and populated areas; and to try to at least maintain the present altitude which was at that moment around 900 feet. They cleared us to land at any runway at any airport around; but not being able to maintain altitude using different power settings; I knew that we were not going to make a safe landing at any airport around; because we were getting too low; and airports were 8-10 NM far from us. At that moment we were at around 700 feet and descending; when I told the Tower that we will probably land somewhere around the Expressway. Having the populated area and narrow streets on our left side; [marsh] on our right side; and low altitude; I decided the best option will be to land on Highway; which; we were lucky; was not too busy. Having the wind from [the south] and traffic flow towards it; landing in the southbound lane was the best choice I could make at that moment. We touched down in the middle lane; and immediately started moving the airplane to the right side so traffic can keep moving. After noticing that we landed safely; without any injuries and damage to other persons and property; we secured and exited the airplane.

column121: I was enroute to ILM. As I began my descent into the Wilmington terminal area the ATIS and Approach Controller indicated ILS Runway 06Z was the approach in use. Weather was reported as 400 overcast and one mile visibility. Winds 030 degrees at 4 knots. A cold front and convective activity was approaching the airport and I requested a short vector to final. I was cleared for the approach and began my descent. I ended up too high on the approach and executed a missed approach at minimums. As I was being vectored back for another approach I was advised that the aircraft following me also executed a missed approach due to being too high. I looked at the wind vector on my PFD and realized that I had a 50 knot tailwind at 1;500 feet on my last approach. I advised the Controller about the strong winds at altitude and asked if Runway 6 was still the best runway.I also asked the Controller if he had any real time winds on the ground and was reminded that the Tower was closed; he would try to get me an update from the automatic reporting system. I was told that the automatic reporting system still indicated winds out of the NE (northeast) at 11 knots. I continued for a second approach but at 700 feet AGL my wind vector was showing a 50 knot tailwind and my groundspeed confirmed that. I deemed it unsafe to land and executed another missed approach.The Controller suggested ZZZ as an alternate. I began vectors to an approach to RNAV GPS Runway XX. I quickly realized that I would have the same 50 knot tailwind situation at ZZZ and began questioning the Controller about any real time wind information on the ground. He said the only info he had still indicated winds on the ground were out of the NE about 7 knot. He said the convective activity situation at Wilmington was improving and asked if I would like to go back for another approach. I was beginning vectors to another ILS Approach 06Z. I was still seeing the same 50 knot winds at altitude and began doubting the wind reports on the ground. I asked for an approach to Runway 24. I was cleared for the RNAV approach 24. As I was descending on final approach; I had a 50 knot head wind at 1;000 feet.When I reached minimums and began to go visual; I encountered a windshear. I increased power to MCT (Max Continuous Thrust) trying to climb out; but to no avail. As I was continuing to recover from the windshear; my landing gear contacted a treetop about 1/4 mile from the runway. At this point I deemed the safest course of action was to continue to land. I made a normal landing to a full stop; turned off the runway and taxied to the FBO. After exiting the airplane minor damage was noted. At this point the winds on the ground had shifted to the SW (southwest)) and were gusting to 35 kts indicating to me that I had landed during frontal passage.The biggest contributing factor to safety I noted; was the lack of any real time winds on the ground. If I had real time wind data from the Controller as I was conducting my approach; I would have been advised of the wind shift occurring; and might have been able to take preventive action before I encountered the windshear. My recommendation is to not have a system that solely relies on the automatic reporting system which is not real time. I would have each Approach Control have the ability to see and give real time winds just as an operating Tower would have.

column121: Upon arrival at ZZZ Maintenance notified us that there were multiple damaged fan blades in the number 1 engine. While we do not know when or how this occurred; we can only guess that it was due to snow/ice ingestion on takeoff roll; improper de-icing and inspection of engine inlets prior to engine start; or de-icing prior to takeoff. While there was no active precipitation; upon arrival at the aircraft; the crew noted snow and ice on the aircraft to include in the engine inlets. Per [company] procedures; after the doors were closed; before blockout; the crew call Ramp to have engines cleared. The clearing crew showed up. The Tug Driver noted them moving around the aircraft and appeared to be clearing engines. They left shortly thereafter; and we confirmed with Ramp Tower that the clearing and inspection had been logged complete. After push back onto taxi; we noted that the taxi lane had not been completely plowed. There was a large snow berm; approximately 2 ft. high about 10 ft. left of centerline; which converged toward centerline all the way until Taxiway XX. After some discussion with Tower and the Pushback Crew; we opted to have plows come and clear an area in front of us; that they could pull us to clear of the berm before engine start to avoid ingestion. Engine start was slow; even for Pratt & Whitney; but no starter or engine limitations were exceeded. N1 started around 20-25%; well below the 40% limit. After engine start anti-ice was turned on due to temp/dew point spread. We taxied on cleared pavement to the de-ice area. The taxi took less than 15 minutes so no engine clearing was used. During de-ice we noticed B777 push back out of a gate on [taxiway XX]. It was pushed back through a berm of snow and ice. After de-ice we taxied and took off after this B777. It is possible that the B777 had some snow/ice on its trucks that was deposited on the runway on takeoff. From de-ice; we taxied to Runway XX. The turn from Taxiway XY onto Taxiway XZ could have been cleared of snow better; but the turn was made using minimal thrust. It is possible that some compact snow or ice was ingested here; however; once cleared for takeoff; we did a 30 second engine clearing procedure and all engine instruments appeared normal. After takeoff; the Captain mentioned a rumble; which sounded like it was coming from a pack. It was faint enough; that we didn't feel it was an issue; as all packs checked out normal. Later on climb out the number 3 engine EVM fluctuated up to 5.0; then back down to normal ranges only slightly above the other two engines. The captain sent a message to [Operations} asking about engine telemetry; and we were advised it was good; so we decided to press on.

During the final approach; the aircraft was within standards: the airspeed and glide path were stable; and the aircraft was aligned with the runway's extended centerline. As the airspeed decreased and the nose contacted the runway; I immediately felt a strong vibration from the nose followed by the nose continuing to fall to an abnormally nose-low attitude where I could see the runway directly. Seeing this happen; I immediately shut down the engine. Once the aircraft came to rest; I secured the rest of the cockpit. After exiting the plane; I was informed by the airport operations staff that they had retrieved the nose gear from somewhere on the runway (they did not specify where they found it). ZZZ Tower then closed the runway and airport for operations until both the runway and aircraft were secured. I do not believe any human performance considerations negatively affected this incident. As the events unfolded; I performed to the best of my ability to ensure that I was safe while also ensuring that the aircraft was not damaged further. while this incident ended safely; it has definitely inspired me to further my proficiency. I will focus on modules that will improve my knowledge on maintaining stabilized approaches; ADM; and preventing and recovering from bounced landings. As a flight instructor; I hope to use this experience as a lesson to any future students.

column121: We were on a Part 91 ferry flight. On climb out we noticed the ground idle annunciation light was illuminated which we concluded was not normal as the ground idle is on a squat switch and shouldn't be on in flight. We further discussed other system items which would possibly cause the issue. In addition we noticed that the takeoff V speeds were still showing on the airspeed indicator which should have been cleared out after takeoff. ATC cleared us up to FL390 and we were crossing our first fix. We tried cycling the ground idle switch during this time and were in the mid teens. The ground idle annunciation remained illuminated. Shortly after this the Captain noticed that our cabin was not pressurizing; as the cabin altitude was not increasing nor was the cabin rate increasing. He selected the cabin rate knob to high to try and get the cabin to pressurize. Shortly after; the cabin rate immediately went to approximately 6;000 fpm. He said lets get our oxygen masks on. We put them on and at this time we were at approximately FL220. Suddenly the master warning illuminated along with a cabin decompression annunciation. He disconnected the autopilot and leveled off and said lets advise ATC. I advised ATC and requested a return to our origin. ATC gave us a descent to 10;000 ft. with direct to the airport. Once we accomplished memory items for cabin decompression and emergency descent we ran the emergency checklist and returned with no further issues. I believe we handled the situation appropriately by advising ATC and going to a lower altitude and returning to our origin airport. Once we reached 10;000 ft. the cabin decompression annunciation extinguished and we landed with no further issues.

Eventually they removed the 1.4S cargo from the fwd cargo leaving the lithium ion battery on the fwd cargo and one package of the 1.4S on the aft.   We departed and operated safely to ZZZ1. [Caused by] rushing to comply with departure times and not listening to what our priority is: Safety. I suggest training for our colleagues so their main focus is open communications for a safe environment so we can have a safer operation.

column121: While on final approach the PF was having difficulty slowing the aircraft and continuing the descent. The headwind we had been fighting quickly turned to a crosswind. The PF elected to re-bug and use flaps 40 well above 1;000 feet. As the PF I selected the new flap setting in the FMC and verbally called out the Vref and target speeds. As we were slowing past our previous target speed the PF called for flaps 40. We had no amber band visible for flaps 40 placard speed; so I verified the placard; 162 knots; and selected the flaps seeing 158 knots and slowing on my tape. As I verified the speed brake was armed he again called for 40. The flaps were still at 30. At this point we were now below 1;000 feet but above 500 feet. We discussed the non-movement and load alleviation. As the PM; I suggested; pitch up and slow; the flaps moved to 40 as we suspected they would. The checklist was completed and we were able to be stable by 500 feet AGL; so we continued the landing. We did not observe any limitations being exceeded on the flaps or in procedure as the PM was able to manage the approach prior to the 500 foot gate.In discussing this event during our debrief we believe that we did meet our approach gate criteria. We were in our first 'heavy' approach in many months as the flight was full. The weight may have contributed. The wind was also a contributing factor as it shifted down the final enough that by the time we departed the traffic flow had reversed.Neither of us were averse to going around but it did not seem necessary in the moment as it seemed we met our criteria to continue. Having said that I'm certain eyes further from the instrument panel may have captured data we missed but I believe we trapped and corrected the situation.
column123: While on final approach I; PF; called for final landing flap (flaps 40) and flaps did not move to commanded position (they were at 30); despite being slower than max speed for flaps 40. Since we were within a few knots of max flaps 40 speed; I slowed further and flaps extended to commanded position. I believe the flap extension occurred right around 500 feet.  The final approach speed was within stabilized approach criteria and the outcome of the approach and landing were not in doubt. Landing was uneventful.We have been flying mostly empty airplanes for almost a year and this flight was almost completely full. I believe the higher landing weight coupled with a significant loss of headwind on final contributed to the airplane taking a while to slow down to an acceptable speed for final flaps. When I called for final flaps; we were 3-4 knots below the max flaps speed and I believe the aircraft's safety system was restricting flap movement until I was a little slower. As we return to Pre-COVID passenger loads; I will have to adjust lead time for decelerating the jet. Today was a good reminder.

column121: The Number 2 and 4 Flight Attendants (FA) called to report strong odor in aft galley. I continued boarding while the Number 1 FA went in to speak with the Captain. She returned and said we were to continue boarding. I could hear the aft FAs calling Captain while we stood in entry area. The Number 1 would go in to cockpit to get updates from the calls. A deadheading pilot then came from the back of plane and went to the cockpit to speak with the Captain. There was some question about it being a urine smell and perhaps the cleaning of the lavs. We had neared the end and I walked through closing bins; etc. As I got to row 25 I smelled a very strong and pungent dirty sock smell. I went to aft galley and told them it was a dirty sock smell and where I began smelling it. I asked them to relay that info up front. The Number 2 and 4 wanted the Captain to come and smell because they disagreed with that assertion. I had returned to the front of aircraft and the Number 1 and Captain went to the back. When he returned he seemed perturbed that the Number 1 was not immediately behind him and wanted to close up. I said I would close the remaining overhead bins. The Number 1 returned and we departed. First; I believe we should have stopped boarding and deplaned the passengers and crew until the cause/type/potency of odor could be established. Following the operating procedures for deplaning at the gate would have allowed a quicker review of the situation and the concerns for safety until a definitive answer could be established while removing passengers and crew from a potentially harmful exposure.
column123: We commenced the boarding and Flight Attendant #2 and I walked to aft galley and both smelled a noxious odor. I called the Flight Attendant 1; three times and she in turn told the Captain. He said 'it is probably a leaky trash bag or rotten food.' Flight Attendant 2 called the Captain directly and he again blew us off. We had a deadheading pilot also go to cockpit to relay information and when he got back; he said the 'theory is that it is a leaky trash bag'. We had been on the aircraft for 4 hours prior to this event as we brought the aircraft in from ZZZ. The fumes were coming out of air vents in galley and aft lavs and was going into c zone. 33 minutes after we first notified Captain; at the end of boarding; he came to the back and said 'I don't smell anything; we are going to ZZZ1'. With that; he turned and walked back to the front. Yes; the fumes had just dissipated by that point; 33 minutes later. There was no interaction; NONE. He obviously did not care about the noxious fumes in the aft section of aircraft. For 33 minutes; he continued to disregard every attempt to tell him what was happening in the back. He's a Check Airman; really? He's supposed to be the best of the best. I felt like my safety was jeopardized and I would never feel safe flying with him again. What if I reported smoke; would he say it is stale cigarette smell on someone's shirt? The one important bit of information he might need might come from the most junior Flight Attendant or even a new hire. In this case he had 4 very senior Flight Attendants and disregarded all of us when we made 5 attempts to get his help in telling him about the noxious odors. Captain obviously needs some intense CRM training. Maybe giving a check ride to another pilot and trying to manage fume events are just too much for him. It obviously was.

column121: Aircraft X was an air return back into ZZZ; for the standby display cool fan malfunction causing the display screens to overheat. This aircraft was ferrying to ZZZ1 for a repair. During troubleshooting it was decided that the problem could be relays K7HK and K11HK in JB2. The relays were replaced per the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) CH24/ESPM (Electrical Standard Practices Manual) and did not fix the problem. The next likely part was the avionics cooling control panel; it was replaced per AMM CH21 and did fix the problem. Because I had removed JB2; a retest had to be performed per the AMM CH24. The first half of this complex task was done in the hangar. The second half requires the engines to be ran. Everything was checking out good per the AMM; until the final engine start. During the start sequence on the LH (Left Hand) engine everything seemed to be normal; then I received an APU Overtemp red warning message which distracted me from watching the LH engine parameters. After the APU Overtemp message cleared I noticed the LH engine ITT (Interstage Turbine Temperature) at 998 degrees. I immediately put the LH thrust lever to fuel cutoff and motored the engine until the ITT was below 120 degrees. The MDC (Maintenance Diagnostic Computer) engine exceedance history showed the LH engine to be at 1110 degrees for 10.6 seconds. This is the first time I have ever encountered 2 overtemp events or 2 red warning indications at the same time while working one of our aircraft. I was working hard to get this task done so the crew could move the aircraft yet that day; as they were standing by in the hangar to depart after repairs were completed. I must admit I did feel pressured and hurried; however I did complete the retest task per the AMM; with everything checking satisfactory. As for the engine hot start event; I really regret it happening. It seems like it was one of those situations that does not occur together all that often. I felt I was distracted and was task overloaded for maybe a second or two which played a factor in this unfortunate event.

column121: We departed ZZZ on DATE at approximately Time LCL with two charter pax. All preflight checks were normal. We were fully topped off with fuel. As we were climbing through 26;000 ft I noticed that the number 2 oil temperature gauge was rising. I alerted the first officer (NAME) to consult the checklist and prepare for a possible engine fire or failure. There is no guidance in the checklist so we were left to use other resources such as each other; prior experience and MX techs in ZZZ1 through conversation via flight phone. We brought the number 2 engine back to idle power and noticed a brief reduction in oil temp. Within a minute or two the oil temperature gauge was at red line where it remained for the rest of the flight. We leveled off early at 33;000 ft. and made contact with Maintenance in ZZZ2. With the number 2 engine at idle we were able to maintain altitude at a speed of .68 Mach which was sufficient to troubleshoot the issue. I transferred control of the aircraft to the first officer and spoke with NAME1 (Maintenance tech). During the phone call we tried to find other indications that would lead us to confirm that the indication is accurate or erroneous. We did notice that the oil pressure did start to rise into the yellow arc when we advanced the power lever. However this could have been normal or unrelated. We took an SPR (snapshot) of the engine settings. We also reset the Oil 2 circuit breaker which isolates the oil 2 gauge for temp and pressure. The indication was as before... a red line temperature situation. We decided the best course of action was to shutdown the engine and divert to ZZZ3 as a landing could be made safely. Our Maintenance tech agreed. Given that a more serious condition could occur; such as an engine fire; failure or an engine damage/separation event we the crew elected to shutdown the number two engine and divert to ZZZ3. We performed the engine shutdown procedure then; due to the fact we were over Max landing gross weight and would require priority handling and would be landing at a high elevation airport without one of our three engines... I elected to declare an emergency. I declared with ZZZ center at 33;000 ft. and they gave us direct ZZZ3 and began our descent. We advised approach that we would require extended vectors to run through the applicable checklists and burn fuel for a safe approach climb in the event of a two engine go around. And to land below Max landing weight. The appropriate checklists were performed as a crew and the a visual approach and landing was executed uneventfully.We taxied to flight support where we shut down and began our company reporting process.

Pilot Flying became distracted with updating the speeds on the arrival and did not see the aircraft was still descending in Vertical Speed mode. Upon passing 14;000 feet; the Pilot Flying realized the aircraft was below the arrival descent profile and began reversing the descent. About the same time ATC called to query our altitude as we had descended below their Minimum Vectoring Altitude. We were issued a climb back to 14;000 feet which we complied with and then a vector off the arrival to final and further descent. The rest of the arrival was without incident.

column121: On the morning of an international departure that was scheduled to depart later that evening; the Captain emailed and informed both FOs of how the flight would be conducted in regard to face masks.  During the pre-flight phase; the #2 FO challenged the decision and said he was walking off the trip unless the Captain agreed to wear a mask whenever he was on the Flight Deck.  In an effort to maximize safety and also to address the #2 FO's concerns; the Captain offered the solution that he would wear a mask during cruise; whenever the #2 was performing his relief duties; but; with safety concerns about glasses fogging and hindered communications during critical phases of flight; said that #2 could sit in the cabin rest seat during those phases if it would make him more comfortable (since masks would not be worn).  The Captain believed this was 'legal;' since an #2 actually wasn't required by the FARs on the planned 6 hour and XX minutes flight and was also the safest option since; if the #2 dropped the trip; the flight would likely be sent un-augmented with zero inflight rest periods then available to the 'flying' pilots. The #2 agreed with this solution and the flight departed.Prior to the later descent; the #2 stated that he believed that an FAR's had been violated by him not being in the cockpit for takeoff.  He said that he would be in the cockpit for descent and Captain said he was welcome to be there but reiterated that masks would not be worn during critical phases of flight.  The #2 did then come up for the descent and landing.After the aircraft was parked and debrief conducted; #2 said he would be submitting a report over his belief that an FAR was violated by him not being in the cockpit for takeoff and departure.The Captain and #1 FO are not aware of any 'violations' of FAR's in this instance but decided to report the incident in case there's something they are not aware of.
column123: During takeoff; the #2 FO stayed in overhead flight crew rest area instead of on the Flight Deck.  Erroneously thinking his presence was not required on Flight Deck on takeoff. Captain and #2 chose that course of action; as #2 wasn't comfortable with staying on Flight Deck with the Captain who had a cough. Captain was unable to wear a mask due to fogging of glasses.

column121: Dispatch notified us that the release was not signed at cruise.   I immediately realized he was correct.  I added 2000 pounds operational fuel on the way to the airport and discussed this with the crew.  I planned on signing the release and talking with the Dispatch in Operations (Ops); because this is one of the last places internationally that we still go to Ops.  The van takes us through security then to Ops then to the bottom of the jetbridge.  All 3 of us had done this recently and knew of no change and in fact the 10-7 page states that we are not allowed to go through the terminal.  However; upon reaching the airport the driver brings us to the terminal; stating that this is the new procedure.  We verified on our iPads and even called Ops to verify this change.  Indeed; due to COVID; we go through the terminal.  The security was extensive; overly extensive and time consuming.  The walk to the gate is long and although we hustled; we still arrived at the jet later than desired.  I called Dispatch for the brief once arriving to the cockpit and received a standard brief which included a new release; release 2 due to ZFW increase.  I agree that was okay; but after the call; we realized the 2000 pounds I had added via app was not added; so I called the Dispatch back.  The Fueler arrived during this call and he agreed to add the extra 2000 pounds for us and I told Dispatch it was done so no new paperwork was needed.   I wondered why the Dispatcher had not included the 2000 pounds. In retrospect I should have realized something was amiss; for example; the release not being signed.  We then had discussions with Ops regarding the extra 2000 pounds; but it was all resolved.  During this time; the FO saw the dispatch release; stated it was #2; but neither of us noticed it said 'not signed' at the top; only noted that it was release 2 and that we were all fit for duty.  We had the Oceanic checklist out and looked through it; but missed the dispatch release on it.  I have been signing the release lately enroute from the hotel to the airport since we never go to Ops anymore due to COVID; except today; since this is one of the few places that we do go to Ops.  However; apparently; we don't.  A note in the 10-7; an Ops alert; or something stating this would have been helpful.

column121: Aircraft X departing from ZZZ bound for ZZZ1 scheduled to depart at XA:45. My FO (First Officer) and I both discussed the hydraulic maintenance write ups from the previous day and saw no obvious irregularities. All ground activities were normal; I.e. engine start and taxi. FO was the pilot flying; I was the pilot monitoring. Climb to our cruise altitude of FL380 was uneventful. Approximately 40 minutes into flight we got the B system engine low pressure light; we used the QRH procedures for this malfunction which resulted in the switch being turned off. We checked the system page and saw that our fluid quantity was rising and stabilized at 106% and pressure was at approximately 2700 psi. The #2 oil filter bypass light came on; we again used the QRH which had us reduce thrust on the #2 engine to see if the light would extinguish. After moving the throttle to idle the light was still illuminated which; as per the checklist; required us to shut down the engine. Immediately prior to shutting down the engine I contacted Purser with our plan to secure the engine; our ETA to ZZZ1; and state that no cabin prep would be necessary. He told us that a deadheading pilot was onboard so we asked that he send him forward to the cockpit. Upon completion of the Engine Failure or Shutdown Checklist we advised ATC; got a more direct turn to ZZZ1; and descended to FL240. Once established at FL240 we saw that our closest divert airport was ZZZ2; we requested and received ATC clearance direct to the field. Our decision to proceed to ZZZ2 vs. ZZZ1 was passed on to Purser. We tried initially to contact Dispatch by sending a 'Call me' message from the ACARS. It took quite a while to get a response containing a frequency and I think the actual first response we got from Dispatch was that they had noticed that we had descended and wondered if we were having an issue. We did confirm that we had shut down an engine and once a decision had been made to go to ZZZ2 we confirmed that with Dispatch through ACARS messaging. We had good communication with Center but were never able to speak to Dispatch; though as we got close to ZZZ2 we did hear ZZZ3 ARINC; though they could never hear us. At about the same time Center notified us that our company was trying to contact us on the frequency that we had previously been given; we told them that they could not hear us so they relayed our final intentions to the company. I can only assume that our altitude might have played a role in this poor communication with Dispatch; though we had no issues with ATC. In the approximately 45 minutes of cruise prior to descent into ZZZ2; we discussed steps taken; checklist to be completed (One Engine Inoperative Landing Checklist) and other considerations. As a result; I switched pilot flying and pilot monitoring duties. At approximately 60 miles from ZZZ2 we commenced our descent. With all checklists complete and planning for a flaps 15 approach to the ILS at ZZZ2; we were given an intercept heading and selected flaps 15 for landing. The flaps did not move; so we requested vectors across final while we troubleshot the flaps. At this time I assumed the duties of flying the aircraft and talking to ATC. [The other two pilots] took on the task of determining why the flaps did not extend. Shortly after; we checked our system page and discovered that we had zero B System hydraulic quantity; I do not recall the B system pressure. We decided to run the Loss of System B checklist which led us to electrically extend the flaps. After one more series of turns to intercept final; we fully configured and executed an uneventful approach and landing at ZZZ2. After being inspected by Fire and Rescue Crews we taxied to our gate.

column121: Normal takeoff and climb out. We went to FL400 for cruise altitude. We got to cruise; made our PA turned off the seatbelt sign. I was Pilot Monitoring. FO (First Officer) said;'uh oh we have a light on the HYD overhead.' I looked up and ENG2 engine driven pump said low pressure. I canceled the master caution and got out the QRH. Simple checklist; select the HYD pump switch to off. End of checklist. We pulled up the hydraulic display on the center screen. B system 106%; normal pressure. We started a what if dialogue. We agreed it was OK to continue with present condition. We looked up Loss of System B in QRH; and discussed it. We looked at flight plan divert circles and discussed scenarios. After 5-10 min the system B quantity started to decrease; slowly at first. I asked ATC for a descent to FL 320. Now the System B started to decrease rapidly. We knew we were about to loose Hyd Sys B. We selected Autopilot A to fly the aircraft; still descending; we were now over Location X but before ZZZZZ fix. We texted Dispatch we were going to lose System B and wanted to confer if we should divert or continue; Note-Loss of SYS B checklist did not say land at nearest suitable airport. We were almost to FL 320 and the ELEC 1 low pressure light illuminated; as the system quantity reached 0 and system pressure was 0;pump switch off per checklist. We got a few more lights and confirmed we had a complete loss of system B. Unbelievably we now got an ENG 1 hyd low pressure light illuminate; pump switch off per checklist. ELEC 2 HYD pump only hydraulic pump now functioning. It held autopilot A. We looked at each other and said lets head to ZZZ1; we had previously talked about divert points and where to go if the situation had gotten worse which it did. During this time we noticed A HYD quantity decreasing from 90+% to low 80's(we thought we might loose A too)I requested a descent and a turn direct to ZZZ1 from Center for a hydraulic loss. He gave us a different heading and said to expect to hold for sequence. We were now clearer to the controller and requested priority handling. The lead FA dinged us and asked if everything was OK; I told her no; type of situation; and to prepare the cabin for a divert to ZZZ1; I asked her to have the cabin ready in 10 minutes; no evac prep necessary. We got direct from ZZZZ Center; reprogramed the FMC and let dispatch know we were diverting. We started in on the loss of System B checklist as we were making a dive for ZZZ1. We ended up taking a vector to lose altitude. We completed the loss of system B to the ALT Flap extension. I then called back to the FA confirmed TEST; no evac; trucks would be standing by; we might seem like we were landing faster. I made a PA to the passengers. The FO did an excellent job of flying the airplane first; great CRM working with me on the checklists; with ATC ; keeping me in the loop where we were when we were being pulled from so many directions (We were getting pulled from ATC; Dispatch; FA; PAX; checklists...). We completed the ALT Flap extension and then landing checklist. The landing was normal for a flaps 15 landing.After the parking checklist; we debriefed. ZZZ1 station manager entered the aircraft and said they might have an aircraft swap if we could fly to ZZZ2. Sent Maintenance report. I talked to the FO and cabin crew and they all wanted to continue and fly to ZZZ2. We called dispatch and he elaborated on the possibility of us flying to ZZZ2. All the crew members wanted to finish the flight to ZZZ2; so we started in on this plan. I spoke with the Operations Manager and the ZZZ2 Chief Pilot for clearance for all of us to continue to ZZZ2. We did have to also fill out a simple report and give copies of our licensed to the [local] authorities. We informed the passengers. The plan did come together and we did an aircraft swap and an uneventful continuation to ZZZ2.
column123: In cruise; the System B Engine Pump 'Low Pressure' light illuminated. The Captain (non-flying pilot) accomplished the QRH checklist and the pump switch was deselected. Hydraulic quantity in the 'B' system was over 100%. Approximately 5 minutes later the 'B' system quantity starts to rapidly drop to zero. After reaching zero; the 'B' system Electric Hydraulic Pump unexpectedly illuminates 'Low Pressure.' We also receive the associated caution light for the flight control system. While the Captain was completing 'Loss of System B' checklist and we were discussing our options (ZZZ1 vs ZZZ2); we received another caution light for System 'A' Engine Pump 'Low Pressure.'We immediately decide to divert to ZZZ1. The Captain advised ATC; and notified the Dispatcher over ACARS. We completed the checklists; notified the Flight Attendants; and informed the passengers. There was a very clear division in the flight deck workload. The Captain worked the problems; communications with the company; and in cabin communications. I flew the aircraft and communicated with ATC. This workload division not only works well in the simulator but also in real life.We completed the 'Loss of System B' deferred items and Alternate Flap Extension procedure. We shot the ILS in ZZZ1 and landed without incident. Clearing the runway we taxied to the gate. The System 'A' Electric Pump continued to function and we fortunately had no other problems.This whole situation was extremely similar a recurrent training scenario that we had not that long ago. Having 'seen it before' was strangely reassuring.

column121: TCAS RA on flight route from ZZZZ AFB to ZZZ. We were on Y52. We noticed two aircraft on TCAS and with audio in contact with Fukuoka ATC Control radio in front of us heading directly in front; 12 o'clock towards us head on. Altitude of two aircraft varied from below 1000 and to our altitude of 26000 ft. TCAS alerts were activated. One of the involved aircraft's call sign was Aircraft Y. Opposing aircraft now at our same altitude; 26000 ft.; closing fast.TCAS warning; 'Traffic-Traffic;' aural followed by TCAS RA and; 'Descend;' aural warning followed. Initiated evasive maneuver. I; the Captain; with minimum map scale on display could see opposing aircraft also now descending into our flight path. Initiated flight control input with verbal command that co-pilot continue to fly while I also inputted left lateral evasive maneuver to avoid collision. I noted our separation on TCAS was less than 100 ft. in red color. Increased separation was noted and aircraft flight was stabilized back to 26000 ft. No visual contact. Possible loss of 300 to 1000 ft. of altitude of our aircraft due to evasive maneuver. Cabin crew felt evasive maneuver with no injuries reported of passengers or crew.

column121: At cruise altitude FL380 approximately 40 minutes into the flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 the Engine 2 HYDRAULIC PUMP LOW PRESSURE light illuminated. The Captain (Pilot Monitoring) performed QRH Non-Normal procedure and selected the associated HYD PUMP switch OFF. No further action was required at that time. I don not remember exactly what Hydraulic Qty and Pressure values were at this time but I recall that they were relatively normal as the Electric Hydraulic Pump remained functional.Approximately 15-20 minutes later; the Engine 2 OIL FILTER BYPASS indication illuminated on the Upper Display Unit Primary Engine Indications page. The Captain performed the ENGINE OIL FILTER BYPASS QRH procedures. The OIL FILTER BYPASS light remained illuminated after closing the Engine 2 thrust lever which directed us to the ENGINE FAILURE OR SHUTDOWN QRH checklist and the required shutdown of Engine 2. We elected not to attempt a restart of the engine. As PF (Pilot Flying); I continued to fly the airplane. I disconnected the autopilot and auto throttles and hand flew the airplane; adjusting rudder trim to approximately 13 units of left trim in order to maintain wings level; yoke level.We advised ATC and requested a descent to FL240 due to Engine Out Altitude indication of FL245; and slowed to 233 kts. per the Engine Out speed indication. Center cleared us to descend; as requested. I descended in LVL CHG to FL240. Shortly thereafter were handed off to [adjacent] Center. Initially we elected to continue toward ZZZ1 and were cleared direct to ZZZ1 by enter. After approximately 10-15 minutes of hand flying and after reaching FL240 I engaged Autopilot A (Autopilot B was unavailable due to the non-normal events).The Captain communicated with the flight attendants; made a PA to the passengers; and coordinated with flight attendants to have a deadheading Captain join us on the flight deck as an additional resource/additional crew member (ACM). This was the Captain I had flown with from ZZZ4-ZZZ the previous day and we therefore had the added familiarity and comfort of having just flown together. The Captain attempted to contact Dispatch via both ACARS and on Comm 2 via a frequency that was received in an ACARS message. We could hear Dispatch calling us but they could not hear us talking to them (possibly due to our low altitude?). ACARS availability was intermittent in our location. At some point later on; Center informed us of the frequency that Dispatch was trying to communicate on. We told Center that we had been trying to contact Dispatch on that frequency to no avail; and asked them to relay to Dispatch that we probably had little additional information to share with them beyond what had already been successfully exchanged when ACARS was available and beyond what Center already knew about our situation. During this period of time; the Captain and I periodically exchanged communication roles as necessitated by the multiple overlapping tasks required to be completed; while the deadheading Captain also assisted with some communications to passengers; to Dispatch; and reviewed and confirmed the QRH procedures we had followed; as delegated by the Captain (PM).Approximately 10-15 minutes after shutting down Engine 2; performing associated QRH procedures; and dealing with intermittent communication issues with Dispatch; we discussed and confirmed the fact that ZZZ3 was actually the closest suitable airport and asked Center for direct to ZZZ3. Prior to that decision; given our location over the Gulf; our direct route to ZZZ1 had been taking us relatively close to what would have also been a direct route to ZZZ3. Therefore; there had been no significant delay in getting us on a course to our nearest suitable airport ZZZ3. Weather at ZZZ3 was procured; Dispatch was successfully notified of and supported the decision to divert to ZZZ3; Flight Attendants and passengers were notified; and ACARS divert communications were completed. Initially we had elected not to balance fuel but after the center fuel tanks were empty; we elected to balance fuel; opening the crossfeed valve and turning off Engine number 1 fuel pumps.The Captain discussed with me and the ACM Captain whether or not we would elect to exchange controls at some point and it was agreed upon that the Captain would fly the approach and landing. I recall that transfer of controls occurred while at FL240; approximately 10 minutes prior to descent to lower altitude. Non-Normal landing distance was calculated by me (and backed up by the ACM) and other One Engine Inoperative Landing checklists were reviewed. I made a PA to the passengers explaining that they could expect a relatively normal landing at ZZZ3 with the exception of possibly seeing fire trucks there as a precaution. Below 10;000ft. I completed the portion of the One Engine Inoperative Landing Checklist for configuring for a Bleeds Off landing. Despite having calculated non-normal landing distance; normal landing data was also procured (as suggested by the ACM Captain) in order to determine whether or not any special engine out missed approach procedures existed; which did reveal a missed approach procedure of flying runway heading to ZZZ VOR.While on a final base leg vector to final approach for the ZZZ3 ILS at 2;000 ft.; the Captain called for Flaps 1. However; the flaps did not extend when selected. We discussed why that might be occurring; trying to determine whether or not it might be associated with our original HYD LOW PRESSURE situation which had initially been resolved by turning of the engine drive pump and utilizing the remaining electric pump. We informed Approach that we had a flap issue and requested vectors away from the approach. I selected the SYS page on the Upper Display Unit to observe Hydraulic indications and saw that System B Hydraulic Qty was 0 or close to 0 and Pressure was low; if not also 0 (I do not recall the exact value). In post flight discussion with the Captain we discussed that there may have been a time (when flaps 1 was selected?) that a Master Caution light illuminated; we both looked up at the overhead but did not notice any new lights illuminated that were not already part of our previous non-normals. The Captain also recalled that when I had performed the Master Caution Recall as part of the After Start Checklist; the annunciator panel lights had not necessarily all illuminated without one or both of us having to push on the panel; as is often the case; and therefore it is possible that when/if the Master Caution light illuminated during the high workload single engine approach phase of flight; we may have failed to see a HYD indication on the annunciator panel or if it did illuminate; we might have considered it to be associated with the original HYD LOW PRESS non normal. Postflight; we discussed the possibility that it was the demand placed on the hydraulic system by the selection of flaps in conjunction with some other cause of a leak that caused the hydraulic quantity and pressure to go to zero at that time. In any case; given confirmation of 0 HYD QTY on the SYS page; we now performed the LOSS OF SYSTEM B QRH checklist and procedures which eventually directed us to the Alternate Flap Extension procedure.Once we had completed and reviewed the LOSS OF SYSTEM B QRH checklist and procedures; and the Captain discussed his plan for configuring flaps (taking into account the additional time required for alternate flap extension); I asked the ACM to reference the deferred items (e.g. landing checklist) for ONE ENGINE INOPERATIVE APPROACH AND LANDING while I referenced the deferred items (e.g. landing checklist) for LOSS OF SYSTEM B; to make sure they were the same or comparable and that we did not miss anything; given that I could only run one landing checklist and we simultaneously had two separate non-normals with deferred items. When ready; we were cleared for the approach. We successfully extended the flaps to 15 usingthe alternate flap extension procedure. Upon contact with ZZZ3 Tower I informed them of our special request in the event of a single engine missed approach per the landing data information.The approach and landing by the Captain were excellent. He stopped the aircraft on the runway with manual brakes per the QRH procedure. ARFF equipment came to the runway and personnel examined the aircraft prior to our taxiing to the gate. We left the flaps extended in case Maintenance wanted them in that position and informed ops and station maintenance of their position. We discussed with a mechanic some of the details of the non-normal events. We had to wait for customs to get ready for us; which caused a delay in deplaning. I took advantage of that time to go to the cabin to talk to the flight attendants and First Class passengers to see how they were doing and talk a little about our situation and answer questions while the Captain continued discussion with mechanics and Chief Pilot; etc.One final note I would like to add is that we received outstanding; professional support from all ATC facilities during the flight and from Flight Operations (Chief Pilots; Safety Committee; etc.) postflight; and our flight attendants were totally professional and did an outstanding job. Utilization of the deadheading Captain's input and support was extremely helpful; too. Thanks to everyone who supported us.

column121: During our approach briefing we planned to exit the runway at Taxiway V near the far end of the runway to facilitate our taxi to parking. After landing on Runway 31R I followed the green leadoff lights to exit the runway at what I thought was Taxiway V and was already committed to continue onto the taxiway when Tower told us to exit at Taxiway V join [Taxiways] B and S to the ramp. The First Officer noticed that we had exited at Taxiway WW and asked the Tower if okay to exit there. The Tower then advised us that [Taxiway] WW was closed but no problem. We noticed that a couple of low and narrow snow berms across the taxiway that were left over from snowplows and we continued forward without any problem. I also noticed at the time that there were other aircraft tire tracks through the snow and did not appear to affect our progress. The taxi to parking was uneventful. During the landing rollout I tried to locate our position on the moving map airport diagram which I pre-positioned as much as possible at Taxiway V area; but could not ascertain exactly our current position. I saw the green leadoff lights; and thinking that we were at [Taxiway] V continued to follow them onto the taxiway. There was also another aircraft on short final behind us and it was my intention to exit the runway expeditiously so as not to complicate its arrival. I did not see a taxiway sign prior to the taxiway and determined that we must be exiting at [Taxiway] V. The Tower Controller did not seem to be phased by our encroachment onto a closed taxiway. We were already committed to Taxiway WW and there was no way to stop the aircraft and safely make a 180-degree turn to get back on the runway to exit at Taxiway V. There were not any cones or barricades with caution lights across Taxiway WW; and as it was not a construction area I felt that we could safely exit on [Taxiway] WW. To complicate matters; taxiway signage in that area is not sufficient as I did not see a WW sign prior to the taxiway - only the sign on the right side of the taxiway after entering [Taxiway] WW. Also of concern is that the green leadoff lights were illuminated allowing aircraft to taxi off the runway onto a closed taxiway. The lights should have been extinguished. I did not see any green leadoff lights at Taxiway V.

column121: We were flying; from ZZZ to QRO (Queretaro; MX). During preflight inspection; the FMC database was current as well as both pilots' Electronic Flight Kits. While in-flight; the weather was reporting clouds at 1;200 feet 5 mile visibility and light winds. The runway in use was [Runway] 09. While in cruise flight; Mexico Center informed us to expect VOR DME 2 for RWY (Runway) 09 approach in QRO. The aircraft was set up; and the Pilot Flying (Captain) completed all briefings. While in cruise flight; Mexico Center gave us a late descent clearance which is very common on this flight that required LVL/CHG mode and speedbrakes to get back on path. While we were descending to our first cleared altitude (around 14;000 feet MSL); Mexico switched us to QRO Approach. Upon contact with QRO Approach about 15-20 miles out; they advised of a traffic on a ten mile final; and informed us to now expect the VOR DME 1 RWY 09 Approach. We were recleared direct to QRO VOR; provided another descent; and then shortly thereafter; Approach cleared us for the approach. The First Officer went into the FMC and configured it to fly direct to QRO VOR. After the aircraft was established on course to the VOR; the First Officer selected the QRO VOR fix in the FMC and inserted the VOR DME 1 RWY 09 approach after verification with the Captain. Because of the angle the aircraft was approaching the VOR (straight in Runway 09); and relative to the approach procedure (an outbound heading 292 followed by a left procedure turn inbound); an additional procedure turn was required just to begin the approach. The procedure turn would normally be done at the VOR. Due to the FMC not having a procedure turn at the VOR to begin the approach for arrivals from the west; it immediately started auto-sequencing fixes to fly the aircraft directly to the outbound procedure turn DME 10 from the QRO VOR. The First Officer had to re-enter the VOR into Direct To and build a holding pattern into the FMC. There was a missed approach holding pattern depicted on the approach chart; therefore; the First Officer built a hold based on the holding pattern published. The First Officer informed ATC that a procedure turn was required at the VOR and also notified approach that the aircraft would enter holding as published to begin the approach. ATC advised us to descend to 11;000 feet and cleared for the approach. ATC seemed confused as to what we were doing. It appears that they were expecting the aircraft to make a hard left after crossing the VOR (almost a 180 degree turn) into unprotected airspace that contained mountainous terrain. The minimum safe altitude for that sector is 12;800 feet and if the aircraft would have flown that; there could have been a CFIT event. Once the aircraft entered the holding pattern; making a procedure turn to enter the crew selected IMM EXIT and the aircraft completed the current holding pattern; just a procedure turn; and exited the hold to fly the entire approach as planned and expected. There seems to be an issue regarding the Jeppesen Charts; and FMC database for this specific approach. The FMC did not contain any proper procedure to join the approach legally. Also the FMC sequencing the approach could have presented multiple issues including CFIT; TCAS; or lost of Situational Awareness.
column123: We were heading to MMQT to shoot the VOR 1 approach from the west. We were headed direct to the VOR with the approach loaded after that. Approximately 9 miles prior to the VOR the airplane started a left turn to join the outbound portion of the approach. This was not appropriate or legal. We turned the airplane back towards the VOR and realized there was nothing loaded to turn the airplane around to join the approach legally. There is also no procedure turn depicted on the chart. There was a holding pattern at the VOR and a missed approach procedure associated with the approach. We decided to enter the holding pattern at the proper altitude and told the controller we were doing that. That allowed the airplane to turn around and we were able to join and commence the approach that way. The rest of the approach was uneventful

column121: We were left base descending at 1;800 feet turning final for a visual landing 15 into MOB. As it all happens so fast there was no time to react in the moment; but as we turned to what looked like a single lone bird turned out to be a drone quadcopter zipped by me on my left at eye level and went directly over our left wing within 15 feet. I immediately reported this to MOB Tower described it as quadcopter at our altitude and within 15 feet of the aircraft and that If it had been any closer it would've struck us or potentially went into our left engine possibly causing failure. This drone was in the critical approach corridor in our path on final to land. Luckily after we landed we did a thorough pre-flight and  there was no damage nor evidence of a collision. I saw the drone as we quickly passed it in a split second.Cause - Careless drone operator operating a drone illegally in vicinity of airport.Always be vigilant of the airspace and treat them as if they were birds even if not always avoidable. Report any such activity to hopefully avoid an emergency in the future.
column123: While being vector for final approach to runway 15 in MOB we experienced a near miss was a drone at approximately 1;800 feet. column121: After an uneventful approach and touchdown with Captain as Pilot Flying; the aircraft was decelerating normally with speed brakes and reversers deployed. The crew accomplished a normal exit of the runway when smoke could be seen in the flight deck and sirens sounded in the cabin. Purser was immediately contacted and told flight crew that there was smoke in the cabin and detectors going off. The Purser was asked to assess the situation in the cabin as simultaneous contact was made with the Tower. Cabin was asked for any signs of a fire or source of smoke and none were present. The Tower advised crew that a runway treatment had been used two days prior and that upon crew request no signs of smoke or fire were visible coming from aircraft. Crew determined it was safe to exit the runway taxiway due to smoke being from possible ingestion into the packs or reversers from chemicals in the runway area and proceed to the ramp with constant contact with the cabin to ensure no escalation or fire warnings.A short time later an evacuation message and siren was triggered in the flight deck. Once again we verified with cabin crew that no fire or source of smoke could be assessed. We requested that the emergency equipment be available and accompany the aircraft to the gate out of an abundance of caution and increasing warnings in the flight deck. A normal shut down was accomplished and the flight mechanic entered the flight deck and informed crew that he had inadvertently set off the evacuate warning while trying to cancel the smoke detectors in the cabin.Crew was met by local airport authorities and emergency personnel. During the interaction with crew we were informed that two compounds 'Sodium Formate' a liquid treatment and 'Potassium Acetate' mixed in with 'aviation grade sand' had been used two days prior and could possibly have been ingested by reverser system and packs leading to smoke. A giant smoke cloud could also be seen at the midpoint of the runway at least 200 feet tall but centered in one location; the possible site where chemicals interacted with the aircraft. Crew taking over the flight was briefed on the situation and Maintenance was in the process of examining the aircraft. By all logic with no indications of a fire and smoke being generated inside the aircraft an external source was deemed the most likely cause. The pebble sized compound that may have been present along runway edge and some portions of runway; even though runway appeared perfectly clean and clear were brought by airports OPS Crew after an inspection of touchdown and mid runway areas.With the compounds mentioned not being familiar to crews not much comment can be given; I would suggest familiarizing crews with this event to help discern an actual fire with a foreign contaminant causing indications of smoke and fire. I would also point out that procedures need to be followed in regards to on board mechanics response to dealing with abnormalities; rather than helping in trying to cancel an alarm after it was deemed non-threatening the issue was compounded which could have forced an evacuation had flight deck and cabin crew had poorer communication.

The plane ahead of me cleared the runway.  On short final; I saw a headlight at the far end of runway rapidly approaching. I announced that I was going around for plane on opposite side of runway. I climbed and turned slightly right.  The plane from the other direction was rolling on the ground and about midfield took off and turned slightly right. I then announced that I would be staying in the pattern.  I then landed uneventfully.  He came and found me to apologize. He said that he had keyed in the wrong frequency and had been announcing his intentions to land on the opposite direction runway.
