column121: We landed in BTR. We were instructed to roll out to the end of the runway and exit left onto Taxiway Foxtrot. I remember seeing a NOTAM that B between Alpha and 4R was closed. Foxtrot was on the opposite side so we confirmed that Tower wanted us to exit left onto Foxtrot. They said affirmative left on Foxtrot and we complied. The CA (Captain) slowly steered us off Runway 13 and onto Taxiway Foxtrot. He was on centerline the entire time. At this point; I was getting the flaps up; clock started; APU started; and the rest of the after landing flow. Immediately after this; I called up ground for further taxi instructions. I felt a slight dip in the left side and we were unsure of the cause. The Captain said he added some power and the airplane continued to roll forward taxiing. I was focused on getting some complex taxi instructions from ground that were abnormal and a bit confusing. It took several calls for me to clarify the taxi instructions. When we parked at the gate; I went out to do my post flight walk around. The ground crew was already taking pictures and I could see dirt on the left side wheels. That's when it clicked that the left wheel had gone into the grass. I informed the Captain of the left wheel; and he called maintenance as well as informed Dispatch.Tower advised us to 'exit left at the end on taxiway Foxtrot' and to contact ground when off. We complied with their instructions. There is no mention of wingspan restrictions or weight limits for Taxiway Foxtrot. The company documentation does not make mention of any restrictions to Taxiway Foxtrot either. While the CA was on centerline; oversteering is needed for this taxiway - there is no mention of this on the 10-09.A note should be added prohibiting air carriers on Taxiway Foxtrot. At the very least; there should be wingspan restriction or weight restrictions. Additionally; tower should have instructed us to back taxi on the runway rather than tell us to exit on Taxiway Foxtrot.A note should be added prohibiting air carriers on Taxiway Foxtrot. column121: While receiving an application of Type 1 De-Ice fluid to Aircraft X; EMB-145 aircraft prior to a scheduled revenue departure in ZZZ airport; FO (First Officer) was indirectly sprayed in the right eye with the Type 1 De-Ice fluid by the ground crew due to a concentrated high pressure stream of De-Ice fluid being applied directly to the seal of the Right side DV window of the aircraft for ~2 seconds. Since the aircraft was not pressurized at the time due to Standard aircraft De-Icing configuration; the seals of the cockpit windows were not air-tight; allowing for fluid passage into the cockpit. The FO was not just sprayed in the eye; Type 1 fluid also covered his forehead; right cheek; right jawline; headset; shoulder; pants; iPad resting on the window; and shelf. Type 1 fluid was seen to enter the front left and top DV window seals. CA (Captain) and FO made a crew decision to return to the gate to seek medical attention for FO for verification of the potential harm Type 1 Fluid could cause. FO got the Safety Data Sheet from a ramp manager on the fluid being applied to the aircraft. The fluid was Clariant Safewing MP 1 LFD 88 Type 1 De-Ice fluid; Substance Key 000000702835. Per instructions on the Safety Data Sheet; FO and the Emergency Response Paramedics flushed FO's right eye with Honeywell eyesaline sterile isotonic eyewash until burning sensation in FO's right eye went away. After application of the eyewash; paramedics recommended to FO to seek a follow up medical exam with an optometrist to determine if there was any further damage to the right eye or not before returning to work.[Suggest] Re-training of basic de-icing procedures required on behalf of the ZZZ de-ice crew.
column123: Due to the snow and rain showers in ZZZ the aircraft had to be de-iced/anti-iced with type I and IV fluid. While in spot XX in hold bay XX in ZZZ; towards the beginning of the type I application; the de-ice crew sprayed high-pressure type I fluid directly on and around the FO's (First Officer) DV window. The high pressure fluid entered through the seal of the DV window spraying fluid around a section of the DV window on the inside of the flight deck. The FO was also sprayed on his headset; shirt; pants; his right arm; and small amount of fluid entered his right eye. I then informed the de-ice crew that they sprayed in the inside of the flight deck via the DV window. Dispatch; the Flight Attendant; and the passengers were informed we would be returning to the gate. Once back at the gate the FO's eye was assessed and treated by EMS in accordance with the safety data sheet on the type I fluid that was provided by station personnel. It was also recommended by EMS that the FO follow up with an optometrist for further evaluation. The FO was removed from flying status. I then contacted Maintenance Control and entered a discrepancy in the aircraft's maintenance log book in regards to the DV window. De-ice fluid was observed spraying into the flight deck through the First Officer's DV window during the de-ice application. AOM Volume I section 3.2.2 defines 'sensitive areas' as 'Areas where direct high pressure fluid application should be avoided during the deice/anti-ice process'. 'Windshields' is listed as one of these sensitive areas. During the deice process; the individual applying the type I high pressure fluid directly sprayed the FO DV window causing fluid to enter the flight deck around the seal at a high rate of speed.We returned to gate; the FO received medical attention for his eye; and a discrepancy was entered into the aircraft's maintenance log book for fluid entering the flight deck via the FO DV window. I suggest that the individuals applying de-ice fluids to the aircraft are properly trained on the 'sensitive areas' of the E145 and that direct high pressure fluid application is avoided in these areas.

column121: Flight was all normal until we were cleared for a visual approach. Approach vectored us about 2 miles outside of the Final Approach Fix. When cleared for the a visual approach the First Officer turned inside of the Final Approach Fix. We had briefed the towers and their height and had them visually. The First Officer turned off the flight directors and turned directly towards the runway; about 20 degrees angle.  At 1;000 feet Tower called and asked if we had the towers in sight and said he had gotten an altitude alert.  At that point we were still visual with the towers and a half dot low on the glide slope. I directed the First Officer to come left and get on final. We continued the approach and landed. Found out afterwards this was the First Officer's first time to this airport and that he really didn't have a good visual on the runway. I felt his turning off the flight directors added to his lack of situational awareness. We discussed this approach afterwards and he felt I should have directed a go around. I believe he was waiting for me but I was in the green.  I didn't know he was lost. I explained to the First Officer that there is a reason we brief instrument approaches at night; to use them.  I shouldn't have allowed him to make the turn directly towards the runway but told him to intercept closer to the Final Approach Fix. The First Officer needed to communicate he wasn't in the green and execute a go around if he felt it was needed.
column123: Cleared visual approach after I stated to the Captain that I had the beacon in sight. I turned toward the airfield and began my descent referencing the glideslope. I only saw the beacon; not the runway. Tower issued a low altitude alert as I flew too close to the towers west of the field. I had the towers in sight and the Captain gave me verbal commands to help me orient the runway. The landing and rollout were uneventful. I accepted a visual approach based on the beacon alone. I was also distracted by the airspeed going below the hook for reasons I didn't understand. After landing; the Captain and I thoroughly debriefed the approach and landing.

column121: After a 2 hour delay for other related maintenance issue we took off from ZZZ on our way to ZZZ1. Right after take off as we were climbing an AMBER CAS message showed indicating IRS 1-2 COOL FAIL we were climbing to 2;000 ft. then we were cleared to 10;000 ft. we kept on climbing with CAS message still showing AMBER at around 8;000 ft. I instructed SIC to get the QRH as we were still climbing; we reached 10;000 ft. then we were cleared to FL230 as we passed 10;000 ft. we started working on the problem QRH indicated to SHUT DOWN IRSs as we kept on climbing to FL230 I was hoping perhaps the cool air would cool IRS and I wouldn't have to shut them off because if I did I will lose automatization and navegation as we were going thru the QRH the IRS 1 and 2 shut themselves OFF at that point I lost all automatization; AP AT; Yaw Damper; Navigation and DUs 1 and 6 showed a RED ATT (no attitude indicators). At that point We manually shut off the IRS and I went to the display controller and selected IRS3 the RED ATT indicator went away I had my attitude indicator back but not any automatization still no AP AT Yaw damper and Navigation then we were cleared to climb to FL320 at that point I made my mind of not more climbing did not want to get to RVSM space without automatization and I instructed my SIC to call ATC and request return ASAP and PRIORITY; ZZZ2 ATC was very busy it took some time for my SIC to get the request in so I stayed at FL230. After communicating with ATC they asked for our intentions I instructed my SIC return to airport but DIVERT to ZZZ4 (ZZZ4 has a longer runway than ZZZ they are closed to one each other and the winds when we took off were very strong) ATC acknowledged the request and were giving some turns and step descents I don't really remember what headings or what altitudes however I was trying no hand fly the airplane and land safely. It was very bumpy we had severe to moderate turbulence I instructed the Captain to go the cabin and tell passengers we are returning to airport fasten their seat belts she went back there and instructed passengers to do that then she came up front and asked if bracing position was necessary I said no but I want you seat in the back with them and make them feel comfortable she said two little girls were crying but they were OK we also had 2 Dogs on board. We started our descent and turns as per ATC instructions preparing for the visual approach latest winds were 08018G23 during the descent at some level off altitudes it was hard to keep the airplane stable or on assign altitude as it was very bumpy it fell like like the trim was working at half rate and without yaw damper I had to use rudder input also. During all the flight from the take off on I couldn't hear my SIC when she was transmitting to ATC when pushing the push to talk button on the yoke; I could hear ATC but not my SIC... I also instructed Captain to call Operations on SAT PHONE but was not working either. I hand flew that airplane for about 40 minutes almost from takeoff to landing we landed safely and exited the runway on our own; Fire trucks were waiting and asked if we needed assistance we said no; then on the ground ATC gave my SIC a phone number for me to call. I also spoke to NAME County fire and rescue they wanted a statement from me as well as my name; I called ZZZ3 ATC on NUMBER they also wanted a statement of the failure and I said we had the NAV computers overheat and the shut off we lost all automatization but I was able to control the airplane however it was very bumpy at some times....they asked for my name; my pilot certificate number; address phone number and said they will write an incident report and I should do the same. After landing I spoke to passengers I explained to them in a way that they could understand why we came back and why we choose ZZZ4 they were fine with it and just wanted a recovery flight. Captain fed them on the plane while I went to FBO I talked to chief pilot I spoke to Operations and Maintenance and I called Center as requested. I came back to plane and right at that time a recovery GV landed we helped the passengers to transfer to other plane and transfer their luggage. After they left SIC and I did a radio check on the ground checked all the buttons in the right position and they were still could not hear her were she pushed the push to talk button not in VHF1 or VHF2. We secured the airplane added some oil helped the Captain with the cleaning and got to our hotel almost 3 hours after we landed.

column121: I was holding short of Runway 29R on Taxiway B2 at Stockton (SCK) in preparation for a VFR departure en route to ZZZ; waiting for a [Company] heavy aircraft to land and clear the runway. The prevailing conditions were night VFR; with unlimited visibility; clear skies; and minimal wind. Stockton Tower was closed; and traffic was coordinating via CTAF. After the heavy aircraft landed and cleared; I made my CTAF call indicating that I was taking Runway 29R for departure. The heavy aircraft crew acknowledged my transmission and noted that they were clear of all runways. While beginning my takeoff roll; a ground vehicle; self-identified as a tug; made a radio call on CTAF that they were crossing Runways 29L/29R en route to the cargo ramp. This was the first call the tug made on CTAF. I made another radio call noting that I was in my takeoff roll; and began visually searching for the tug. I reduced engine power to idle; and applied heavy braking. At that time I saw the tug's anti-collision lights cross in front of my aircraft. I stopped on the runway and made an additional radio call noting that I was aborting takeoff and returning to RWY (Runway) 29R. At no point did the tug acknowledge any of these radio calls or change behavior. I returned to RWY 29R and made an otherwise uneventful departure.Primary cause of the problem: runway incursion by airport tug vehicle that was broadcasting on; but possibly not monitoring; the CTAF frequency.Proximate causes of the problem: airport ops vehicles likely unused to operating on CTAF after-hours at normally tower-controlled airport. Night conditions may have made it difficult for the ops vehicle to see my aircraft on the runway; and made it more difficult for me to see the ops vehicle. Complacency: SCK is a cargo airport; and extremely quiet at night. It's possible that the ops vehicle crew was accustomed to only seeing large cargo aircraft operating at SCK at night; and so my comparatively smaller (and unscheduled) aircraft may have not been noticed/ignored. Finally; the airport operations staff may not have been aware that entering a runway - even several thousand feet down the runway from a takeoff aircraft - is still prohibited.Preventative measures: training for airport ops crews on proper radio use; importance of clearing runways prior to crossing; and runway incursion avoidance best-practices.

column121: Arriving at the aircraft and checking the logbook; I noticed that the last crew had written that the Takeoff Configuration light and horn activated on takeoff (speed of activation was not noted). I surmised that the crew rejected the takeoff and subsequently swapped out of the aircraft after returning to the gate and the aircraft was not flown afterwards. The corrective action was a check of the Takeoff Configuration Warning System with no faults noted. Since nothing was actually corrected; the Captain and I discussed the possibility of it activating again on our takeoff. We pushed late due to an unrelated finding of damage in the floor of the Forward Cargo Bin C. The bin was deferred and bags transferred to the aft bin. We were relatively full on this flight and our V1/VR speeds for Flaps 1 on Runway XXR were 125/135. The engine start and taxi out were uneventful with the throttle burst yielding no takeoff warning. On the takeoff roll at approximately 130 knot (5 knot after V1) the takeoff warning horn and light activated. We elected to continue the takeoff. The initial climb was normal and we discussed that we would be writing this up in ZZZ1. The Captain called for 'flaps up' at the appropriate speed and I moved the flap lever to UP. We had a few distractions from ATC due to hold-down altitude that was cancelled. Before I moved the landing gear handle to OFF; I checked the flap indicator and noticed that the flaps were still at 1 with the LE FLAP EXT green light illuminated. After confirming that the flap handle was up; I told the Captain the issue and that we need to keep our airspeed below 250 kts. and level off to handle the problem.After notifying ATC that we would need to level off; they gave us vectors for terrain while we ran the QRH for Trailing Edge Flap Disagree. Since the QRH doesn't really address the disagreement when attempting to RETRACT the flaps and only deals with setting the flaps for landing; we turned our attention to coordinating the air return. Dispatch was advised of the return as well as Station Ops in ZZZ. Our current gross weight was a little over 130;000 pounds so we extended the gear to add drag and burn off excess fuel for landing. The F/As (Flight Attendants) and passengers were notified of the return. Since this was a flight control issue; we [received priority handling] and notified ATC that we were requesting [Runway] XYL but would need time to reduce our landing weight to 128;000 pounds. We felt this was the safe option as time was not an issue. We then ran the QRH; ran the performance calculation for the Trailing Edge Flap Disagree QRH; and then the brake cooling module. The flaps extended normally with the Alternate Flap system to 15 degrees. The only slight issue was although I read the section directing the flap lever to be moved to the final flap position (15); we were sidetracked by discussing slowing during the extension and this was not done until after the QRH was completed. This allowed us to see our Flaps 15 maneuvering speed. After the delay vectors were complete and we were below the maximum landing weight; we made an uneventful landing on [Runway] XYL. Brake cooling allowed us to take right to the gate and the ARFF (Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting) trucks followed. No other issues occurred. We swapped into another aircraft and continued the pairing.
column123: The aircraft was an originator. The previous day a takeoff had been rejected because of a spurious Takeoff Config Warning and the maintenance resolution was no faults noted. The F/O (First Officer) and I discussed possible reasons for a false warning lasting a few seconds; which refreshed our memories of the warning system and thankfully prepared us for a repeat occurrence. We pushed late due to an unrelated finding of damage in the floor of the forward cargo bin. The bin was deferred and bags transferred to the aft bin. On takeoff; approximately two seconds after the F/O's V1 call; the configuration light illuminated and the warning horn sounded. The F/O called VR; and we lifted off. The light went out and the horn stopped about the time the wheels left the ground. The F/O's performance and adhering to procedure during this event was flawless; which combined with our earlier discussion allowed the situation to be handled easily. We briefly mentioned writing the issue up again in ZZZ1. I called for Flaps Up; from their takeoff '1' setting. F/O moved the flap lever to Up; and then moments later told me the flaps didn't go up; and instructed me not to go over 250 [kts.]. We were still at about 200 knots; so no airspeed issues. I told F/O to tell ATC we needed to level off and maintain low airspeed. Initially we told ATC we would follow the SID and get back to them. ATC gave us a terrain clearance altitude. We confirmed the flaps were not up. I called for the QRH and we agreed that 'Flap Disagree' was the appropriate checklist. The checklist starts off by saying 'to prepare for landing' so we paused the checklist; agreed we were not going to ZZZ1 with flaps out; and I messaged Dispatch we were returning to ZZZ; told ATC; and received clearance to return to ZZZ. I notified the F/A (Flight Attendants) and told the passengers we were returning to ZZZ. We ran the QRH for Flaps Disagree; the procedure went mostly uneventfully. We were at 130;000 pounds; so we took delaying vectors to burn fuel to 128;000 [lbs.]. We checked the brake cooling for Autobrake 3; no issues. We did [receive priority handling]. We landed Flaps 15 and taxied to the gate. Positive takeaways. The CQT training from (year)?; (year)? that emphasized flap malfunctions prepared us well to handle the stuck flaps. Negative takeaways. The QRH for Flap Disagree was obviously written with a failure occurring during approach in mind. For our situation of failure on takeoff; the procedure kept us with the flap handle up until we had returned to ZZZ and were preparing to land; which meant we had flaps out; but no maneuvering speed. We know that Flaps 1 speed is 180 knots approximately; but it would have been one more item in our favor if we had moved the flap handle to match the flaps to give us the normal sight picture on the displays. While we were extending the flaps with the alternate switch; between watching the flap gauge and calls from ATC; we momentarily missed the instruction in the QRH to move the flap handle with the flap movement. We followed proper flap speeds as flaps were extending; but that that was because of our experience; not the display. The QRH should have the instruction to move flap handle with flaps before the actual instruction to move the flaps so that crews can discuss the handle in advance. We ran the brake cooling for Autobrake 3; and then tried to run again for Autobrake 2. The brake cooling module did not work the second time. We recalled a recent (Company communication piece) about Dispatch doing something to mess up performance calculation results; which could be rectified by requesting landing data again; but that did not work. Something in the performance calculations needs to be corrected so that brake cooling can be run more than once. Brake cooling was not an issue; even with Autobrake 3; so this was a small nuisance. Based on passenger comments; F/As did a great job. F/O's performance was excellent; our teamwork together allowed the situation to be handled easily.

column121: While taxing to the gate and on the terminal ramp the 4th Flight Attendant called up and stated there was smoke in the cabin. She stated 'could be electrical'. I stopped the aircraft; I got a minor whiff of something but it dissipated immediately. FO (First Officer) smelled nothing. We reported smoke in the cabin to ground and requested Airport rescue and Fire Fighting. We considered running the Smoke/AVIONICS SMOKE/Fumes but needed more information; (global assessment). I called up the 1st and she stated she was unaware of what was going on. I called back to the rear of the aircraft and 2nd stated it had begun to dissipate. After a brief discussion with FO; I elected to taxi to the gate and have Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting follow us and access the situation. Aircraft deplaned normally. 1st was unaware there was an issue 4th thought it was an electrical odor 2nd stated there was an odor but not a burning odor. He noticed a lite haze in the reading lights. [The possible cause] was primarily due to the dark cabin; communications among cabin crew. In a perfect world; there would have been better communication between all of the flight attendants; prior to calling up the flight deck. A more concrete assessment could have made with all eyes on the situation. Then the degree of urgency; and solid information can be transmitted more efficiently to the Captain.
column123: Taxiing to the gate on the terminal ramp we received a cabin call from the #4 FA (Flight Attendant) reporting smoke in the cabin. column121: Upon arriving at aircraft; noticed the crew O2 supply read zero. I reviewed the AML (Aircraft Maintenance Logbook) and found the aircraft had been on the ground for approximately 5 days. I also noticed the last MX (Maintenance) action taken was to change the crew bottle due to low crew O2. That got my attention. The bottle had been changed 5 days ago and the bottle had emptied while the aircraft sat on the ramp. So; I went further back into the AML pages and found the crew O2 bottle required changing 4 other times in 30 days (meaning this was the 5th time it required changing in a month). This led me to believe there was a deeper problem with the crew O2 system. Therefore; I refused the aircraft. Lack of meaningful automated historical oversight of AML discrepancy/corrective actionAs AMLs are being moved to more remote electronic system with less transparency to the flight crews; a system that compares discrepancy code numbers so that when one is able to detect a system failure that is repeated often. As this aircraft has been imported to the new AML storage system (which is MUCH less accessible to flight crews than the old [software] system); the only reason I was able to see the problem was because the old AML discrepancy book hadn't been removed from the book yet.

column121: While cruising at 0.82 Mach at FL350 with an FMC calculated optimum altitude of FL370; aircraft experienced unforecasted severe turbulence with the autothrottles immediately becoming disconnected and the airspeed immediately accelerated to approximately 320 kts. 0.85 Mach (5 kts. over VMO Max speed). As Pilot Flying; I manually managed the throttles to avoid any further overspeeds and requested that Pilot Monitoring coordinate for a descent to FL330. This request was made and we received a 'Standby' message. [Two minutes later]; the airspeed fluctuations became more severe and the autopilot had trouble maintaining altitude. I then advised the Pilot Monitoring that I was initiating a descent to FL330 and to advise Gander that were doing so prior to receiving ATC clearance. The PM sent this message to Gander that were descending due to severe turbulence and as we were descending through FL33.5; Gander approved our previous request for descent to FL330.
column123: The plane was in cruise at FL350; the aircraft entered abruptly into severe turbulence without warning. The auto-throttles disconnected and the airspeed accelerated into the barber pole (approximately 3-5 kts. overspeed) for approximately 2-3 seconds. Followed by an abrupt deceleration and continuous vibrations of the aircraft. Previous cruising airspeed was .82M. The PF (Pilot Flying) was manually controlling the throttles to the best of his abilities. We then asked for FL330 via CPDLC. The aircraft was becoming extremely hard to control at an appropriate airspeed and altitude. We received a Standby message. [Two minutes later]; the aircraft began to enter constant severe turbulence and the decision was made to descend immediately to FL330 for the safety of flight. I advised Gander Radio that the decent to FL330 had been initiated due to the severe turbulence. We received an approval to descend to FL300 at approximately FL350. No other deviations were noted. We called Gander Radio to issue a Pirep and contacted the Dispatcher or subsequent Pireps and reports.

column121: We were at FL320 on the HLYWD arrival into LAX; and we had been given a vector off course for spacing. Upon rejoining the arrival we were given slower speeds until we actually saw an aircraft 5 nm in front of us. We were then assigned a speed of 250 kts indicated; then descend to FL240; followed by a clearance to descend via the arrival. I was concerned as we started our descent as we were clearly descending at a higher rate than the aircraft ahead of us and would be flying through their flight path at a close proximity plus winds at altitude were approximately 110kts. Suddenly our airplane began a roll to the right; I would estimate 20-25 degrees of bank; then it began rolling to the left at least 30 degrees of bank if not more and the autopilot disconnected itself. We were having an upset due to wake from the aircraft ahead of us so the Captain quickly recovered and I advised ATC what was happening and that we needed something different. They approved an offset to our course; and then advised the aircraft ahead was a B777. 5nm is inadequate spacing between a heavy aircraft and others. Fortunately we recovered well and landed safely. 99 percent of the time our folks in ATC do an absolutely outstanding job; and we couldn't do this without them! This event is unusual; but highlights an opportunity we can improve.I would also like to see better communication from ATC and a better understanding of the safety ramifications of wake turbulence - I frequently get the impression that they don't understand this risk adequately. I want to know if I'm in trail of a heavy aircraft! Sooner than later! It matters; it changes my expectations and I'm not consistently getting this information. I recommend more spacing; more and consistent communication about heavy aircraft ahead; and if I need to be vectored for spacing then let's address speed at the same time so I'm not constantly changing my configuration when I need to focus on flying.

column121: I departed from an airport which lies in a cutout from the adjacent airport Class C airspace. My desired on-course heading was 021. I knew that the adjacent airport Tower handled the nearby airspace; and I was comfortable contacting them and requesting clearance through Class C toward my destination.Immediately after lifting I established contact with Tower. Tower responded; and I requested clearance through Class C climbing to 3;500 feet. The Tower controller responded with the phraseology 'Cleared to operate in Class Charlie;' approved my course heading and told me that he only controlled to 2;500 feet. I took that as an altitude limitation; and continued north north eastward. About the time I was getting ready to level off at 2;500 feet; the Tower Controller cleared me to 3;500 feet; and handed me off to Approach.Upon establishing contact with Approach; that controller asked me if I was familiar with Class Charlie airspace and scolded me; telling me words to the effect of 'You can't just fly around here not talking to anyone.' I informed her that I had been in contact with Tower and he had handed me off to her however; I sensed that explanation didn't satisfy her. She then gave me a phone number that I could call later if I needed to talk with someone about it.At my next fuel stop; I contacted TRACON at the phone number that was given to me; and I was told that I had violated Class Charlie airspace. I explained to the gentleman on the phone that Tower had cleared me using the proper phraseology; 'Cleared to operate in Class Charlie.' The gentleman from TRACON went on to say that the Tower Controller shouldn't have done that. At this point; I didn't know what to do; and I certainly couldn't undo what I had done; so I thanked him for his time and told him I'd be filing a Report when I reached my destination.This airspace is remarkably busy with training aircraft. That is why I contacted Tower immediately with my request. If the Tower Controller didn't have the authority to grant me clearance then it's my opinion that he should have told me to remain clear of Class Charlie airspace; but he didn't do that. Instead; he specifically used the clearance phraseology that is taught in flight school and my company's recurrent training. Given those circumstances I proceeded in good faith with the clearance given to me by the tower controller. I believe that air traffic controller communications are recorded and stored. If so; I believe someone with the proper authority can verify this narrative and correct whatever caused this potentially dangerous situation.

Upon changeover to Oakland Center; we advised the Controller that GPS jamming had been in progress; and that we still had a navigation flag. He then issued a clearance to follow the fixes listed above; and we then asked how much longer the GPS jamming would continue. He said a few more miles. we advised him we still had a navigation flag on our GNSS; but apparently he was distracted; and told us to continue without issuing a heading. We were then turned over to another controller who apparently had not been informed of the ongoing issue. Hence once over SFO VOR; was when the issue listed above was encountered. We were not told if there was a near miss; he just gave us a heading to 180 and vectored us to the airport after that. Once on the ground; we were advised to call approach control for a possible deviation. We attempted to call but could not get through to anyone. We advised the Tower we were not able to reach anyone; so he tried to call and failed; but then he got through with another number. They said to disregard; and we then proceeded to ZZZ1 where the flight terminated.

column121: Was cleared visual approach [Runway] 23 / asked to turn short final inside of GS Intercept Altitude for traffic. Changed Alt Select from 2;300 feet to 1;500 feet and selected VS (Vertical Speed) descent of 700 rpm to get below GS. Descending below 1;800 feet or so; received Low Altitude Alert from ATC / Tower. Second causal item was over aggressive selection of Altitude Select to 1;500 feet . . . In retrospect should have selected something like 1;900-2;000 MSL given field elevation of 700 feet.De-selected AP and climbed to 2;000-2;100 feetWe actually discussed not accepting a short turn to final as part of approach briefing . . . When cleared for the visual; initially turned right to extend final leg; but then was asked by ATC to turn to a left heading given other arriving traffic behind us. In retrospect; could have indicate unable; but that seemed unnecessary given overall regime; weather; etc. Second suggestion would be to double-think / exercise caution in selecting an altitude above the DH but below the FAF / GS Intercept Altitude.

column121: Prior to departure Maintenance was called due to FOs (First Officer's) MAP failure on navigation display. Maintenance did a reset and signed off logbook as reset ok for service. FOs MAP was restored. Approximately 2 hours into flight and approximately 30 mins from ZZZZ1 enroute to ZZZZ; FOs MAP failed; followed by Captain's CWS (control wheel steering) fail; autothrottle failure; and SINGLE FMC operation message. Very shortly later; approximately 10 seconds; LNAV/ VNAV failed; both FMCs failed. Opposite autopilot selected; autopilot B. Captain's CWS was restored and one FMC was restored allowing for the engagement of LNAV/VNAV; and autothrottle was restored. FOs MAP still indicated a failure. Within approximately 60 seconds we had another dual FMC failure; followed by another LNAV/ VNAV failure; autothrottle failure; Captain's CWS failure. At this time with over two hours left to ZZZZ and navigating by raw data we decided it was the best course of action to divert to ZZZZ1 where the weather was favorable for landing with these navigational failures. We notified ZZZZ1 Center of our issues and intent to land in ZZZZ1. Around this time the Captain's FMC was restored automatically and we were once again able to navigate with LNAV/VNAV and the autothrottle and Captain's CWS was restored and autopilot was operational. As we neared ZZZZ1 we informed ATC of the need to hold to burn off fuel due to being overweight for landing which took approximately 10 minutes. The remainder of the flight was uneventful; we landed on Runway X and commenced the ILS approach in VFR conditions. The FOs MAP warning flag remained in view for the rest of the flight. My FO; Fas (Flight Attendants) did outstanding jobs. Great communication. ZZZZ1 ATC also very professional and helpful. In the 21 years I've been on the 737 both as an CA (Captain) and FO I've never experienced a dual FMC failure. I've experienced several single FMC failures; but not dual failures leading to several other navigation failures.

column121: The aircraft had several maintenance scheduled items that needed to be addressed before we could fly the aircraft. It was supposed to be the first revenue flight after long term storage. There was one maintenance schedule item X which needed to be accomplished before the aircraft can be used for revenue flight with passengers. The item was signed off on the completed items sheet and the aircraft was released for flight. When we were taxing; Dispatch notified us to hold. We called them and they said there was a maintenance schedule write off not signed off properly. So; we returned to the gate to have to addressed. The reason for this report is that you cannot leave the gate with passengers unless maintenance schedule item X had been signed off. Our paperwork showed it was signed of yet the electronic AML [Aircraft Maintenance Logbook] said it was not.  We returned to gate. We found out later that it was a clerical data entry error made by someone in maintenance and the maintenance schedule item sign off was entered incorrectly.The cause is easy to figure out. The only way to fix it is to have a computerized completed items sheet that only shows items cleared and then the computer copy and paper completed items sheet would always match!After items are cleared in computer; print out new completed items sheet for AML so paper and computer always match.

column121: Upon arrival the inbound crew advised us that the nose strut might possibly be low. I advised them that we would look at it on the walk around and that we would write it up if necessary after doing the walk around. Prior to boarding with the only occupants on board being the two flight attendants and myself;  my FO (First Officer) went out and did the walk around; he motioned for me to come down and look at the strut which was nearly fully collapsed and not showing any chrome. Not having a ruler or protractor available we took an informal measurement. The distance between the top and bottom was two fingers or less; which was certainly less than two inches.  At this point; I contacted Dispatch and Maintenance Control to advised them of the situation; at which point Contract Maintenance was dispatched. I made an entry into the logbook stating that the nose strut was nearly compressed and needed to be serviced.   Once Contract Maintenance arrived; he originally rolled out the tanks; as if he were going to inflate the cylinders; he attempted to open a valve in the nose wheel strut area and then after some difficulty stopped. He then made a phone call to Maintenance Control. After this phone call; he said that per the AMM (aircraft maintenance manual) the measurements that he took indicated that the strut was showing 2 inches and was legal for dispatch as outlined in the AMM as is and that he was to sign it off as instructed by Maintenance Control. At this point we boarded; and just prior to closing the door; under all prudence and caution; I decided to do another inspection of the nose wheel strut to find it fully collapsed and actively leaking foamy fluid. I contacted Maintenance Control and advised them that the strut was compressed and leaking foamy fluid; which I then entered into the logbook. We deplaned and Contract Maintenance then added nitrogen to the strut and signed it off again. At this point; the on duty pilot; Name 1 called me to gather more information on the situation. I informed him of all the events that had occurred up to this point. He then asked me why I would do a preflight walk around with passengers onboard and he stated because we aren't really sure of what the strut compression should look like after passengers had boarded and additionally why would I need to do that after I had a legal sign off. I informed him that in the interest of safety that I felt it was OK to do a walk around after a maintenance procedure and; as well as to comply with the CFM (company flight manual) guidance for exterior inspection; which is to ensure that gear struts aren't fully compressed and that there are no fluid leaks. I also added that we should still be able to see some chrome on the strut and that there shouldn't be any leaking fluid. After the Contract Maintenance inflated the strut we then began to board again as we waited for the book to be signed off. As the FO and I were briefing; the Contract Maintenance asked me to step outside. After stepping outside; the Contract Maintenance guy pointed out the strut which may have been inflated to the legally required two inches and but was leaking a solid stream of foamy liquid and not just a couple bubbles as Maintenance Control contends. I then contacted my Dispatcher Name 2 and Maintenance Control. They then advised me that they would remove the aircraft from service and schedule us to take the RON aircraft that was coming around XA:15pm.   I also sent pictures of the compressed strut and leak to Maintenance Control. I attempted to send the video too but was unable to do so because of the file size. The following morning; I was contacted by Chief Pilot Name 3; who asked if I was OK with how everything turned out and to get my side of the issue. He also said that I was scheduled to fly the airplane several more times the following day and would I be OK with taking the aircraft. I told Name 3; that I'm perfectly fine flying the aircraft as long as it's legal and safe; which in this case would mean the strut would be showing a normal amount of chrome and not streaming foamy liquid from the cylinder.  He also shared an email outlining the events from Name 2 which directly contradict several key facts from the evening. 1. The inbound crew didn't write up the aircraft. I wrote up the aircraft three times. 2. When Maintenance came back there was foaming bubbling liquid coming from the strut which can be be seen in the pictures and videos that I took or are visible on the ground which appears wet from the leaking fluid. Name 2's email incorrectly characterized this leak as a couple small bubbles. The cause narrative for this series of events is pretty straight forward. I feel like my Dispatcher was very accommodating and I feel that the real issue here lays with how Contract Maintenance; Maintenance Control; On Duty Pilot and indirectly Name 2; Maintenance Control; Maintenance Director interact with the pilots after the fact. Contract Maintenance from the very beginning expressed his hesitation with the situation once he saw the foamy liquid coming from the cylinder. Finally; his insistence that I look at the leaking cylinder after we boarded and he once again expressed his hesitation and ultimate concern about the issue thus giving me a moment of pause. I had the opportunity to speak to Maintenance Control several times and they didn't really seem to understand why we wouldn't go because in their opinion; because they signed off on it that it was good to go; even though it was leaking. The On Duty Pilot questioned why I would do a walk around after Maintenance was performed; expressing that we didn't know what the nose strut would look like after boarding and why would I do that even though I had a legal sign off; as if I was supposed to accept the sign-off carte blanche. I expressed to him that I needed to be not only legal but safe and that I could do a walk around whenever I felt it was needed on confirm to expectations set forth in the manuals. I didn't see that email from Name 1; until Chief Pilot contacted me to inquire if I was OK with flying the aircraft on my next trip. I told him that I was was fine with flying the aircraft in the future; as long as it was in serviceable condition; which would mean showing a normal amount of chrome on the strut and not leaking fluid. The concerning part of Name 2's email is where he ends with 'This is bad when Maintenance is using appropriate AMM references for the checking of proper servicing being refused with a legal sign off; but we are taking the delays for no reason at this point.' This sentence is challenging because it assumes that I'm making a refusal for no good reason and that the sign off were legal to begin with. If it had only a couple bubbles as his email suggests then I would have certainly taken the sign off but upon receiving the sign off and seeing the stream of foamy fluid still coming from the cylinder; along with input from the Contract Maintenance and my First Officer we needed to again assert our concern with the aircraft.  Fortunately Name 2 wasn't there; he doesn't know the extent of the issue and his comments are a direct challenge to the safety reporting culture that the Company has developed.

column121: Captain (CA)=Pilot Monitoring (PM); First Officer (FO)=Pilot Flying (PF). Discovered pressurization outflow valve in the full open position during the after takeoff checklist (no Auto Fail lights; both Packs; ISO valve and bleeds all in proper position). Discussed with the FO and advised ATC we needed to level off at 10;000 ft to investigate an issue and asked for straight ahead to avoid terrain (initially assigned 15;000 ft on the SID). FO was PF and had them take the radio. Pulled the QRH and referenced AUTO Fail or Unscheduled Pressurization Change 2.2. At this point we discussed and surmised we did NOT have an AUTO Fail issue nor and unscheduled pressurization change as the Cabin appeared to be modestly; although suspiciously pressurizing; as we were building some differential and the cabin altitude was relatively low.  Troubleshooting forbids switch manipulation unless inclusive of a QRH or other written procedure hence we chose not to manipulate cabin pressurization controller from AUTO to ATLN. Additionally; we recalled a bulletin from Standards Department dated 7/xx/2020 titled 'Cabin Pressure Controller Blinking/Blanking issue'. This bulletin states that on our 900ER fleet from (tails)(we were in tail) the digital controller can blank and or blink or become so dim its unreadable. Additionally; the bulletin states the controller should right itself shortly...We did not have any blinking/blanking or dimness. Our outflow indicator was bright and solid indicating full open and remained so for the duration of our flight. In an attempt to determine if the cabin would hold we elected to continue our climb to 12;000 ft at which point we got a significant bump felt by the entire crew.... At this point I attempted to contact Dispatch via ACARS to establish two way radio communications. We had plodded along south at a low altitude for a good duration in an attempt to solve the issue. I became concerned with our flight plan fuel. We were dispatched with no reserve for ZZZ1 (weather severe clear at arrival time). Was there enough to complete the mission or might we find ourselves having to divert for fuel 'if' we felt the cabin psi was solid enabling us to continue? We we're now down near (mountain) at 12;000 ft IMC picking up a fair amount of ice as weather was now an issue. After multiple attempts to get a hold of Dispatch to no avail; Flight Attendants complaining about ears; a QRH procedure that didn't quite fit; no ability to troubleshoot; a bulletin that didn't match enough to convince me and a possible fuel stop with an open maintenance issue stranding passengers....in consultation w/ my FO I made the command decision to return to ZZZ. In my mind; this was the safest option and provided our passengers an opportunity to reset. Additionally; it brought the aircraft back to a maintenance base for investigation and repair. We informed Dispatch via ACARS and setup to return and received an amended release via ACARS. We did not declare an emergency as it did not appear warranted/necessary. We ran performance including our LTP (landing threshold point); discussed our TPC and landed significantly under max landing weight as we had a light load. During block in as L1 was opened we felt another pressure bump despite the outflow valve remaining in the full open position. I greeted all deplaning passengers and answered questions; debriefed full crew and discussed scenario and concerns. Flight Attendants met with supervisor and were replaced. No crew members/ nor passengers asked for medical attention. Swapped aircraft; checked duty time and pressed on.Lesson learned:I should have used SATCOM to raise Dispatch in lieu of ACARS. We traveled a fair ways south and company frequency became weak. We switched to XXX.X and sent a message but never could get radio contact. We became distracted by the accumulation of ice buildup at that point in the journey. Bulletin concern: If it is related to the digital controller bulletin why would the company continue to allow problematic controllers be installed? NOTE: The original design Pressurization Control Panel may be installed in any 9ER aircraft from (tail) and subsequent as a repair for a Pressurization Control Panel issue. Therefore; even though (tail) and subs were delivered with the upgraded panel; this issue may occur on these aircraft if the upgraded panel has been replaced with an original panel.

column121: During the approach we were cleared direct down to 8000 feet from 12000 feet. During the descent Autopilot was engaged and following LNAV and VS we were encountering continuous light to moderate turbulence throughout the descent. As we passed through approximately 12000 feet and beginning to slow; we experienced severe turbulence mixed with continuous moderate [turbulence]. When we initially encountered the severe turbulence; the Autopilot disengaged; the aircraft was changing altitude and air speeds abruptly with several hundred feet of altitude change and at least plus or minus 20 to 30 knots airspeed changes. The Captain was thrown hard enough to hit the overhead panel with his head and we received a report one of our Flight Attendants had been hurt and several passengers had hit their heads. I as the Pilot Flying took manual control of the aircraft and flew the remainder of the descent and approach. The aircraft was extremely hard to control throughout most of the descent and approach as we continued to encounter continuous turbulence; strong crosswinds and wind shear. During the ensuing descent and approach the aircraft was extremely hard to control as we continued to experience moderate to severe turbulence; strong crosswind and wind shear throughout the approach. Once established inbound and cleared for the approach we were pushed several degrees off course and had some airspeed fluctuations of plus or minus 20 knots. We quickly discussed missed approach but prior to reaching 1000 feet we had regained the course; were on glide path and stabilized (properly configured) to continue the approach. We continued the approach while receiving some lower wind shear of plus or minus 10 knots down to approximately the 500 foot call. At 500 feet we were still stabilized and continued the approach to landing without further issue. Throughout the approach and landing; we had airspeed; altitude variations and heading deviations that were extremely hard to control due to the turbulence and wind shear events we were experiencing. I do not believe at any point we had any exceedances or violations; however; it was a very task saturated environment. There were no reports of the severity of the turbulence ahead of us and it was a very unexpected event.This was an example of good Crew Resource Management as the Captain and I maintained good communication throughout the event and helped to cross monitor the aircraft systems and instruments. As the pilot flying; I was entirely focused with aircraft control and the Captain doing the pilot monitoring was ensuring all the descent and approach tasks were completed. We kept good crew communication with what was happening with aircraft control and situational awareness. A recommendation is for pilots to ensure they continue to practice hand flying skills for situations like this. The autopilot was unusable; and I was thankful I constantly practice hand flying the airplane. It helped me with confidence to control the airplane to the best of my ability in a situation where the aircraft is being tossed around by turbulence.

column121: As [aircraft] was being loaded; a cart was brought to my airplane that contained a bunch of dry ice boxes. 16 boxes in total; each containing a reported 18kg of dry ice. I multiplied 18 by 16 and got 288kg. I remembered that there had been an alert bulletin released recently that limited the  Aircraft X to what I thought I remembered was 320kg of dry ice; and I confirmed this number with a pilot standing near me. However I didn't recall that the limit was in pounds; not kilograms. So I completed the PNF; submitted it to Dispatch via email and completed the flight as scheduled. I then received an email several days later from the director of safety asking to confirm the weight of the dry ice; we spoke on the phone and he informed me that the limit was in fact 320lbs and not 320kg. We discussed the issue and I now have this number etched in my brain.[Weight limit issue clarified] when the director of safety spoke with me on the phone about the discrepancy.[Captain further stated the following statements]. Instead of breaking out my GOM or confirming in the hazmat binder; I verbally discussed the weight with another pilot and thought that 320kg was the correct limit for the  Aircraft X. This was compounded by the fact that the jet was several hours late and thus everyone was in an enormous rush to get the cargo loaded and sent on its way.I felt rather crestfallen; as I pride myself on doing everything in exactly the same way and by the regs/procedures to the letter. When in doubt I will always refer to documentation in the future instead of verbally discussing it with someone or relying solely on my memory.Confirming with actual paperwork instead of verbally with another pilot. As I am the PIC the responsibility falls directly on my shoulders to ensure each flight is flown in compliance with company policy/procedure and the FARs and I shouldn't rely on my own memory and word of mouth information when I have questions with regard to important matters such as this.

column121: During our initial climb-out we noticed the rate of climb on the pressurization gauge was acting erratic with various climb and descent rates. As ATC continued to assign higher altitudes we both noticed that the cabin altitude was climbing but the differential rate needle was not increasing like normal. As we climbed through 10;000 feet the cabin altitude needle started to decrease and the differential rate needle started to increase. After leveling off at 23;000 feet everything appeared to be stable. The cabin altitude was decreasing below 9;000 feet after nearly getting up to 10;000 feet and the differential rate needle started to increase between 5 and 6 psi showing that cabin was pressuring like normal. After ATC clear us to 25;000 feet I then requested climb to 27;000 feet because of the moderate chop/turbulence at 25;000 feet. Once we reached 27;000 feet we proceeded with running the cruise checklist. Moments after completing the checklist our pressurization rate of needle showed a descent of 6;000 feet depressurizing the cabin; triggering the cabin high altitude annunciater and the master warning lights. At that time we both donned our oxygen mask; performed abnormal checklist and asked ATC for a lower altitude because of our depressurization issue. Once we reached a safe altitude we removed our oxygen masks and decided to return back to our departure airport.Although I believed this incident was handled safely; declaring an emergency would have been the right thing to do. Anytime an emergency checklist is used or a return to field situation arise should trigger one to declare an emergency regardless of the severity. By doing so helps the pilot in handling the emergency more effectively.
column123: Upon initial climb out we felt our ears straining and popping so I as Pilot Monitoring looked at the pressurization gauge; and it was fluctuating between climbs and descents. We continued to monitor it and it stabilized acted as normal as we climbed through about 10;000 to 11;000 feet. The cabin needle stabilized just below 10;000 (cabin altitude) feet and started a slow descent down to 9;000 (cabin altitude) feet. As we climbed into the Flight levels up to our cleared altitude of 23;000 feet; it appeared stable at 9;000 feet; and the differential needle pushed to a higher differential as its design to do.ATC then cleared us to our filed altitude of 29;000 feet. As we continued the climb; the pressurization continued to operate normally; with the differential increasing and the cabin altitude slowly descending just below 9;000 feet. The Pilot in Command asked me to asked ATC for 25;000 feet as a level off altitude. We leveled there and were getting continuous moderate turbulence at 25;000 feet so we requested 27;000 feet as our final. We climbed up to 27;000 feet. We leveled off; and shortly after running the cruise checklist; we both felt high pressure in our ears; and I instantly saw the cabin needle jump up too a 6;000 foot a minute climb and then the Red Cabin above 10;000 foot annunciator illuminated and as well the master warning. We then both put on our mask and made sure oxygen was 100% and notified ATC that we were having an issue and needed to descend. The decision was made to return to our point of departure. ATC cleared us direct to the field and we descended down to 6;000 feet. We ran through the abnormal checklist for the cabin above 10;000 foot annunciator. Once were low enough to safely remove the oxygen masks we did. We did not declare an emergency. We continued without any further incident and landed safely.

column121: In flying return flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 at 3;000 feet; we were anticipating B clearance into the ZZZ 1;500 feet shelf northeast of ZZZ VOR. This expectation was due to the fact that clearance was received shortly before going the same route but opposite direction; and that ZZZ was landing Runway XX; so arrivals would not be a factor in receiving clearance.  We were receiving VFR flight following from ZZZ1 followed by ZZZ1 [TRACON]. Upon hand off to ZZZ Approach frequency from ZZZ1 [TRACON]; the frequency was extremely congested. We established two-way communication and made initial Bravo request with ZZZ around ZZZ [VOR]; but only received 'radar contact' in return with no further clearance. I queried the Controller at least two more times for clarification; but communication was blocked and the frequency was extremely congested. We initiated descent near ZZZZZ [Intersection] to avoid the 1;500 feet class B shelf; but may have penetrated the B airspace in the descent down to 1;400 feet MSL.  We remained below the floor of the Bravo and received no further communication from ZZZ until handoff to ZZZ2 Approach near ZZZZZ1 [Intersection].Contributing factors leading to this possible deviation are that the PF was the senior pilot on the flight and is very experienced in the area but may have been somewhat out of practice as COVID has significantly decreased flying. Also; the Controller seemed to be slightly overwhelmed; possibly working multiple frequencies; we weren't anticipating the business of the frequency although we should have known better. Additionally; the strong tailwind increased ground speed; although the descent was rapid; the ground covered during descent was greater than normal. Finally; as we just flew the same route the opposite direction; we were (falsely) anticipating the B clearance.While these factors are no excuse for possibly entering the airspace without clearance; the notion that business is picking up again means we all need to be more diligent in our planning and flight execution. As Captain; I should have anticipated not receiving the B clearance; and planned descent accordingly.

column121: Entering the traffic pattern for the airport I turned to enter final which positioned my aircraft directly into an extremely bright setting sun.  The sun then blinded me at that point and I lost visual contact with the airport and runway and altitude information.  After regaining sight from the sun and while establishing my position along with altitude in relation to the airport and runway I observed another aircraft that appeared to be flying in the opposite direction about 200 feet away.  I then took an evasive maneuver and cleared the traffic.  At that point I was no longer in position to continue the landing and I executed a VFR go around and re entered the traffic pattern and landed without further incident.  What caused this incident was turning on final directly into the extremely bright setting sun which blinded me. To prevent this from happening again I will use a runway if available that is not in line of sight with the sun or fly to an alternative airport without conflict with the setting sun or wait until sunset.

column121: While approaching Mt Jefferson area on course direct ELKES at 14;000 aircraft encountered a mountain wave. First indications were not unusual; a loss of altitude followed by the autopilot pitch correction to maintain and resulting indicated airspeed loss. It is not uncommon for a momentary loss of a couple hundred feet and airspeed to drop to 90 KIAS; however; at the point where it would 'normal' the situation quickly escalated into an uncontrolled altitude loss as the autopilot rapidly pitched above 15* and I noted a 90+ headwind on the G600 wind vector indicator. I immediately contacted ATC that I was unable to maintain altitude; which they issued a lower clearance (13;000) and vector away from terrain. With the autopilot turned off; I maintained about 10* nose up at 75 KIAS; flaps 10; full throttle and noted a 1200FPM altitude loss. As I approached 13;000 I informed ATC I was unable and inquired about the MVA. I was fully prepared to activate emergency power; declare; and turn back; however ATC stated that the heading I was on gave me about 9000 for an MVA. I elected to ride the wave as the uncontrolled altitude loss was trending up and was able to stabilize as I approached 12;000. While altitude was stable; I remained below the MEA and published minimum off route altitude unable to climb or increase indicated airspeed above 80KIAS for several minutes. As the aircraft exited the mountain wave to the south; I was able to recover the airspeed slowly back to normal cruise as the aircraft moved over the ridge lines.This is the second time a mountain wave event has resulted in altitude loss of more than a few hundred feet. During the 'normal' events I have always notified ATC that I was encountering a wave and only one time previous did the incident result in the necessity for a lower clearance at 13;000'. However; in this event; I would characterize the resulting altitude loss as uncontrolled at minimum control airspeed and max continuous power for the altitude. I would consider this to be an escalation of what might be a normal inconvenience; and causes me to inquire about alternate routing. In all cases of my experience; these waves seem to be encountered over the Mt Jefferson area and a southerly re-routing of to the south is the normal avoidance procedure when the waves are encountered. But why wait until one is encountered? Might it be more prudent to take a different airway further south to begin with? Might be worth exploring.

We contacted company via ACARS and Aircraft X replied at Time that Dry Ice of less than 5lbs will not show on close out and that our close out was good. Then; multiple company messages that followed updating the load closeout and that it was determined to be 8 lbs of Dry Ice. The corrected load closeout was received at Time. The flight was operated to ZZZ1 uneventfully.[Situation was caused by] I believe that the casual factors are a communication disconnect between the ZZZ base and loaders to loads and planning in ZZZ2. Captain [recommends] a fix [to correct] the way we automate the communication of Hazardous Goods to Load Control & Dispatch.

column121: When accepting the flight the Wx (Weather) report at base/sending hospital was 10 sm and clear. Wx at receiving hospital was 6 sm and clear. Although cameras showed haze down the mountain I was confident with the visibility reported and knew that the sun set made it look worse. Descending down the mountain the layer of haze did look more dense than forecasted and arrived at receiving hospital without issues. I checked all weather before return back to base and all were still reported the same. Now it was fully dark and cameras gave a clear view of the basin. I chose the return leg through ZZZ as this gives a good indication of visibility due to the lights up the mountain and all the way. Due to 0% moon there was no reference than the lights on the ground. I climbed to 8;000 ft. which provided proper clearance along that flight path. From ZZZ I could see the lights at the airport from about 10 sm. When I got to ZZZ1 valley the visibility rapidly decreased and within seconds we were IMC. I started my climb to about 9;000 ft. and because my crew did a fantastic job immediately giving me report on visibility left and right; I made a left turn which got us out of the clouds fairly quickly. My crew kept on briefing me their view/visibility on both sides which got us back on track on the north side of the lake. Here we could see the haze/fog/clouds spilling through and over the south mountain range. From that position we had a clear path to the airport and landed without further incident. Weather reporting in our area is spotty. We have wx reporting up in the mountain at the airport and down the mountain at two other locations. The weather 'out of control' factor here is the mountain ranges. There are several tools like cameras that supply information and you make your best judgment; but if the weather is very dynamic you can be caught by surprise like we did on this incident. The additional factor of 'no-moon illumination' added to the fact that we did not see the forecasted clouds rolling in. The 'in-control' weather factor here was that I could have been severely cautious and decline the flight on the haze shown on the cameras. Although I kept positive control over the aircraft when initiating IIMC [Inadvertent IMC] protocol I do want to mention that an autopilot would be a great tool in circumstances like this. When practicing the IIMC procedures in the SIM I am spoiled with the situational awareness and added 'second pilot' of the autopilot. Due to the fact that we are dealing with mountain obscuration and often weather that is not reported and can only be identified with visual cues; we should be first in line for a helicopter with these kind of capabilities.

column121: Earlier in the day I wrote up the airplane for a pack 2 overheat. We were flying an airplane with an MEL on pack 2. We were cruising at FL250 about 90 miles north of our destination when we got a red 'bleed 1 leak' warning message on EICAS. I notified ATC that I wanted an immediate descent to 10;000 ft. for a bleed leak. The FO (First Officer) handed me the QRH and we began the descent and notified the FA (Flight Attendant) to take her seat because hot air was going somewhere it shouldn't and that we would call her back. I began to run the QRH. ATC gave us FL200 as the initial descent. He asked if I was requesting priority handling; I said YES. He asked for clarification on what a bleed leak meant for us and gave us 10;000 ft. subsequently. Our initial descent rate was about ~3500 fpm; faster than normal; to get out of the icing conditions and closer to a safer pressure altitude. I ran the QRH as written until I reached END. Once I finished running the QRH and put it back in the storage cubby; we began to breathe a sigh of relief that things are probably going to be okay. I directed the FO to slow the descent rate to ~1000 fpm. We were at about 16;000 ft. by this point. The FO then pointed out to me that cabin pressure dropping as indicated by the amber boxed Cabin Alt reading on the EICAS. Cabin altitude was at roughly 9;800 ft. and climbing. We elected to keep pace down to 10;000 ft. in order to get in front of the reducing cabin pressurization. The checklist list was not written with a pack 2 MEL in mind. I began to realize the ramifications of what I had just done by turning off Bleed 1; Pack 1; and closing the cross-bleed switch.The priority handling request with ATC and the events we had just gone through had my mind racing from adrenaline. I decided that 'worrying' about the pressurization system wasn't necessary. We were at 12;000 ft. and descending and if I recall correctly cabin pressure differential was about 2.2 psid. I decided to press dump on the cabin pressurization controller after looking over at the FO and mentioning that pressing the dump button wouldn't harm anything and that we weren't in dangerous territory as far as what happens if I press it. We felt a minor pressurization change as the airplane equalized. In hindsight; this was entirely unnecessary. I should have simply let the airplane depressurize on its own.I then began to evaluate how much fuel our descent to 10;000 ft. would burn instead of being at FL250. It took a minute for the FMS to catch up to the descent we had done. The initial fuel numbers it gave us led me to believe we would be very close to divert. I gave it some time and the numbers got more accurate for fuel calculations. I determined we had no need to divert on account of fuel. I notified dispatch; ATC; and the FA that the urgency was over and we would continue to our destination.Next; the airplane began to get hot and stuffy. One consideration was diverting to the nearest airfield. I didn't want to have a heat casualty in the back. The other was to get air into pack 1 so that it was useful in cooling the cabin. I looked at the overhead panel and discussed with my FO the notion of starting the APU to feed pack 1. This was a risky decision because if the leak was closer to pack 1 then feeding APU bleed air into the system would induce basically the same situation. I figured that I could simply turn the APU back off if that turned out to be the case. I figured the air and pressure coming from the number 2 bleed was hotter and higher pressure than the APU. The checklist had given me the steps to solve the problem perfectly if only my number 2 pack weren't MEL'd. I had a short mental struggle with my decision to do something that contradicted what the checklist had just made me do a few minutes earlier and really felt strange using Captain's authority to bypass it. I pride myself on checklist discipline and following the books as best I possibly can. In hindsight; I think alittle thermal discomfort and more rigidity with regards to the checklist would have been wise.I selected auto on the cross-bleed switch and turned on the APU and fed the number 1 pack. The airplane cooled down inside. I spoke with the flight attendant once more to ask about the faces of the passengers and if anyone knew about what just happened. She said they didn't have any idea and that we would keep it that way. We shot an ILS approach and landed normally.This situation was a learning experience of the highest caliber for me. I have since re-learned how the cross-bleed switch logic works. I have studied the layout and function of the bleed and pneumatic systems and learned much more about airplane pressurization. Pressing dump was not the right decision and I wouldn't do it that way again. Selecting the recirc fan off to bring in fresher air would have been a better choice than turning on the APU.

column121: On departure from SEA; ATC warned us that a drone had been sighted at approximately 6;000 feet at the cloud tops in the vicinity of our flight path. Both my First Officer and I maintained a lookout. Climbing through 6;100 feet; I spotted the drone about 200 feet off my right side; about 100 feet below our altitude. Due to the clouds and small size of the drone; I spotted it less than one second before we crossed its position. Had there been a conflict; I would not have had enough space to execute an avoidance maneuver. The drone near miss was promptly reported to ATC with the recommendation to not send any aircraft through this airspace. There were no TCAS indications of the drone. A timely report from ATC alerted us to that hazard; but ATC did not provide any specific instructions to avoid the traffic.ATC knew a drone was operating in the vicinity of NEVJO; but continued to send aircraft on the SUMMA 2 departure. A simple vector on departure would have eliminated this potential threat to our aircraft. The drone was large enough and our rate of closure was great enough; that if could have caused significant damage to our aircraft had there been a midair collision.

column121: I was in command of Aircraft X schedule service from ZZZ to ZZZ1. We departed normally and were climbing to our assigned altitude of 32;000 ft. when just prior to level off our Flight Attendant called us in the cockpit to report that she had a smell of smoke in the cabin. We maintained communication with her as she said it seemed to be coming from Row 4 emanating from the lighting valance on the aircraft left side. We told her to monitor the situation and let us know if there was any sparking visible. She told us that she physically checked the valance and PSU's and they were very hot to the touch and that the smoke and heat was migrating rearward now from Rows 4 thru 10. I told the FA to get the PBE [Protective Breathing Equipment] out along with the fire extinguisher and prepare to fight a fire if one erupted. I then told the FO (First Officer) to notify ATC of our situation and that we needed to return to ZZZ. We were then cleared to return and given a decent clearance to 24;000 ft. Still not sure what type of smoke we had in the cabin I asked the FA to come forward so we could have the FO check the smoke for type of odor (electrical or engine based). FO advised me that the smoke odor seemed to have been not electrical. I then had him get the QRH out and run the procedure for SMOKE IN THE CABIN procedure. We accomplished the memory items and in coordination with ATC requested priority handling and were given an unrestricted decent to 8;000 ft. and vectors to a visual approach to Runway XX at ZZZ. The ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) trucks were standing by for our arrival. The QRH procedure was completed and the smoke seemed to dissipate a little according to the FA. We landed without incident and upon initiation of communication with the ARFF commander we were told there was no smoke evidence on the exterior of the aircraft. Since it appeared the internal situation was under control we decided to taxi to the gate for normal deplaning. Fire Dept. followed us to the gate and upon arrival ; they boarded the aircraft and I advised the commander of what had happened and where it had been located. The ARFF members then checked the aircraft over with their thermal heat locater and found no heat source in the Valance or PSU. They then left the aircraft. Dispatch and MX were notified of the situation. Aircraft passengers were deplaned without incident.

column121: Boarding a nearly full flight began at XA:30 AM. We had power (i.e. lights) but; we did not have any airflow (air conditioning). We were beginning to sweat profusely. I (FA) contacted the terminal Supervisor who patched me through to Agent; in the tower. I told him of our plight and passenger complaints and concerns. He said he would send someone immediately to turn on the air. This was approximately 20 minutes later. About 15-20 minutes later we still had no air. Passengers were getting very upset and many took their masks off. We made announcements stating that without airflow; it was even more important to keep their mask on since they could not social distance. I contacted the Supervisor again and insisted the passengers be let off the aircraft if we were not going to get airflow and we still didn't know anything about when the pilots would arrive. Approximately 10 minutes later the pilots boarded and stated we should never have begun boarding under those conditions. They got air up and we departed 15 minutes later. 1 hour and 10 minutes after boarding. I felt very; very unsafe in those conditions as did many passengers.We should never board without air conditioning during COVID. If the pilots are running late; a mechanic should be brought down to turn on the air. A few minutes would be acceptable but when the tower is contacted; something should be done in a timely manner. Flight attendants should be allowed to let passengers deplane under such extreme conditions where everyone's safety and health are put at risk.

column121: I had just departed Manassas (HEF) Runway 34R. Tower had me maintain runway heading; then turned me on course to the west (out to the SFRA FLUKY gate); and switched me to Potomac Departure.  On my ADS-B in; I noted a target 100 feet below me; and simultaneously Potomac Departure called out that traffic and asked if I had it in sight.  I replied; 'No because it is directly under me.'  The low-wing light sport aircraft passes the wing directly under the pilot; so nothing directly under me can be seen.  I started to climb but Departure warned me there was also traffic above me.  It was then that I noticed that I had climbed into the bottom of the 2;500 foot ring of the Class Bravo.  Then Departure informed that traffic was no longer a factor; and I descended back below 2;500 [feet]. I believe Manassas Tower had me continue on runway heading to clear traffic that had just departed Runway 34L.  Perhaps Tower was not aware of the traffic which eventually found itself under me. HEF traffic is very constrained by Class Bravo to the North; the East and directly above; and R6608 directly south; leaving only two narrow paths for arrival and departure--to the west toward the FLUKY gate; or narrowly to the SSE between the Class Bravo and FRZ to the East and R6608 to the West.

column121: We were flying from ZZZ to ASE and I was the pilot flying. As we approached Aspen; which at that time was reporting VFR; we were given vectors to intercept LOC DME E into ASE. I looked over and noticed the LOC approach was not properly set up. I warned the monitoring pilot of this but at that point we made visual contact with the airport. We accepted clearance to maintain 13;000 ft until established and clearance to execute LOC DME E approach. Having visual contact with the airport we started our descent. A layer of clouds moved in below us as we made the final turn inbound. At the entire time we had full visual contact with all the terrain around. We lost sight of the airport due to the cloud layer; at the same time ATC issued an altitude alert. I emphasize that we were in full visual contact with all the terrain and that visibility at our flight level was unrestricted. The pilot monitoring advised that we had terrain but lost a visual with the airport and said that we would be going missed and starting a climb. We got another altitude alert from ATC. We advised we are in a climb and asked for vectors to give time to decide what to do. We proceeded to ZZZ1 airport afterwards. We were NOT in IMC conditions at any phase of the flight and we maintained visual clearance from all the terrain. The mistake was communication breakdown with ATC and in part CRM in regards to the intentions to execute a visual approach. At no time aircraft was in IMC conditions and we were maintaining clearance with terrain at all times. The aircraft was never put in any unsafe condition. I learned from this how CRM and communication has to be mastered the entire time.
