column121: I was PF in the left seat and we were cleared for take off on Rwy XL.  As we were lining up on the runway; I heard the Tower clear a helicopter for an eastbound departure from the ramp; but I did not visually see the helicopter yet.  Once we were on the takeoff roll; I saw the helicopter lifting off from the ramp (ahead and to our left); but it appeared to be turning parallel to our runway to I diverted my attention back to the runway.  Right after initiating rotation; I saw the helicopter begin to cross over our runway; left to right; at approximately 200 feet AGL.  Because we were past V1 and already rotating on a short runway; I quickly determined an aborted takeoff was not an option so I continued our rotation.  During these few seconds; there were some communications between the Tower and the helicopter; but I did not comprehend them due to my focus on avoiding hitting the helicopter.  Shortly after liftoff (~100 feet AGL); I had to make an evasive maneuver to our left and reduce our climb rate for a few seconds to avoid hitting the helicopter.  Luckily; there was no terrain or obstacles to the left of our runway heading.  Once the helicopter passed off our right at what I estimate was 200-300 feet; I resumed a normal climb rate and a right turn back to our departure heading.  The Tower controller apologized and then handed us off to Departure.  Looking back on the scenario; I believe continuing the takeoff roll as we did was the right call; as we certainly would have had a runway excursion if we had attempted an abort at that point in the roll - passed V1 and already rotating.  Additionally; I am not sure how I could have anticipated the impending conflict earlier because helicopters maneuver on a dime and it was hard to tell its intending heading after liftoff.  After the event; I listened to the ATC recording on a publicly available website and it seems the controller tried to tell the helicopter pilot to remain north of the runway at all times; but that transmission was not acknowledged.

column121: I was 10 miles north of ZZZ and flying heading 220 at 1;500 ft. MSL and 105 knots in a Mooney inbound for a VFR traffic pattern entry on a right downwind to Runway XX. Three airplanes had just landed and I was maneuvering for the 45 degree entry to Runway XX. I heard the Cessna announce it was 4 miles ahead and also maneuvering for the same entry to Runway XX. The sun was setting to the west which made it difficult to spot aircraft to the southwest and west of my flight path. I announced on CTAF that I was 10 miles north and maneuvering for the 45 degree entry right downwind Runway XX. At 5 miles northwest of ZZZ; I announced that I was 5 miles northwest maneuvering for the 45 degree entry; right downwind; for Runway XX.At that point; I heard the Cessna was on the 45 entry to right downwind Runway XX. I turned to a heading of 180 at 1;300 ft. MSL; 113 knots; and remained 5 miles west of ZZZ; while visually scanning ahead; left and right; for the Cessna. It was very difficult to see southwest and west due to the sun setting. At 5 miles west of ZZZ; I announced Mooney is 5 miles west of ZZZ maneuvering for the 45 entry; right downwind; Runway XX".Within a minute; I spotted the Cessna approximately 100 ft. below and 400 ft. to the right. The CFI onboard called on the radio; and said "did you see us?" I responded; "Yes I just did. Would you like to go ahead of me or do you want me to proceed on the 45 entry?" He responded that they would continue the entry and go ahead of me. I continued to fly a heading of 180 and then executed a turn to the west followed by a 360 degree turn to the east to enter the pattern after the Cessna. I landed and did not see the Cessna on the ramp.Afterwards; I called the CFI in the Cessna; whom I've known for years. I listened to his remarks and explained that I had no intention of overtaking him in The Cessna. This is not something I would ever attempt nor have I ever done in 18 years of flying. He mentioned they had requested my position in the air (around 5 miles out) and I said that I never heard that request nor that they were in the Cessna. I was only monitoring CTAF and visually scanning for traffic. I heard they were already on the 45 degree entry to Runway XX. I believe that 1 or 2 of their position reports or requests for my position were not transmitted or heard because we may have both pressed the mic button at the same time to give or request position reports. One of the Cessna's communications may have been incomplete which could explain why I heard that the Cessna was on the 45 degree entry to Runway XX; as I was 5 miles west northwest of ZZZ."

column121: A flight of 2 helicopters called Ground Control on for VFR flight following. They were on a non controlled ramp. Ground Control issued departure frequency and squawk. No readback was heard. Generally; this is an issue with military helicopters; and they usually call up local shortly after; when ready to depart. I reached out several times on Ground Control; inquiring if they had the ATIS information; and if they wanted to taxi to a runway or a present position departure. They were non responsive.I passed the strip to Local Control; thinking they would call him. Moments later a Aircraft Y who had been in the pattern was departing and I saw the 2 helicopters departing the ramp; right in the path of Aircraft Y. I alerted Local Control and he had the Aircraft Y make an evasive left turn to avoid the traffic. Both Local Control and myself on Ground Control made multiple attempts on all frequencies to reach the Aircraft X flight. They both almost had a NMAC with the Aircraft Y. TRACON was calling on the shout line and I answered on Ground Control as Local Control was trying to move the Cessna to a safe position. The TRACON controller alerted me Aircraft X had called them and they mistakenly thought they were calling from a different airport so the TRACON controller gave them a departure clearance which resulted in the unauthorized departure from ZZZ and the NMAC. Once Aircraft Y was safe Local Control and Ground Control both advised TRACON to issue a brasher.Military helicopter pilots need better training on how to depart here and learn to give appropriate readbacks. TRACON should have verified where the helicopters were. Assuming they were at ZZZ1 created a dangerous situation. The VFR flight plan was in the system. TRACON Flight Data should have seen it originating from ZZZ.
column123: Aircraft Y departed climbing to remain in closed traffic for stop and goes.  Aircraft X helicopters on a ramp near the departing Aircraft Y began to lift climbing in front of the Aircraft Y who did not have them in sight. Local Control issues immediate traffic for the Aircraft Y and told to turn left immediately. Local Control called out to Aircraft X on Local Control frequency several times and on guard frequency.  Aircraft X did not answer and continued to fly toward Aircraft Y which was maneuvering to avoid the helicopters. Aircraft Y made an inadvertent low altitude turn to avoid colliding with the helicopters. Coming out of the turn the Aircraft Y reported them in sight.Approach Control called Local Control in a panic about Aircraft X saying she gave permission for departure to the helicopters saying she thought they were at another airport nearby. She did not know they were actually located at this airport. Aircraft X continued toward the Aircraft Y and eventually called local control once they departed the airport.  Local Control told Aircraft X that they were not cleared by Local Control for departure and advised that they almost hit Aircraft Y that was climbing directly toward the helicopters.Aircraft X replied that Ground Control gave them the departure frequency.  In error Aircraft X thought that they needed to contact Approach for takeoff from the airport.  When Aircraft X called for VFR departure; Ground Control issued Aircraft X a squawk code and told them the departure procedure which is normal handling for VFR aircraft.  The next expected sequence of events is that the VFR aircraft then contacts Local Control for takeoff clearance. Aircraft X bypassed Local Control and went directly to Departure Control thinking that is who they needed for departure.My recommendation is that there is clarity made to pilots that their receipt of the departure frequency is not a directive to contact them to depart while the Tower is actively controlled by a Local Controller who is issuing control instructions and safety alerts.

column121: My second report regarding aircraft from the Palm Springs area performing erratic maneuvers in the face of IFR arrivals.  Aircraft Y departed Palm Springs and terminated services outside of the PSP Delta. They proceeded to fly just north of UDD and start performing aerobatic maneuvers between 050 and 060. This aircraft climbed right in front of Aircraft X; who was cleared for the RNAV visual 31L approach.  Traffic alert was issued to Aircraft X and while the pilot did not say 'near midair'; they did say 'he's right in front of us!' and the altitudes were the same.The pilot for Aircraft X said they had to respond to two RAs for that one aircraft.The pilot of Aircraft Y may have also been in violation of FAR Sec. 91.303 which prohibits aerobatic flight within 4 miles of a federal airway (V137) and over an area of congested population.I am requesting; again; for the PSP airspace to have a Charlie or Bravo airspace.  My colleagues and I deal with dangerous situations every day that could easily be avoided by having non-voluntary protected airspace.  This is the second event in one day where PSP Tower has terminated a VFR aircraft who ultimately got much too close to an IFR arrival. A Class C/B airspace and a requirement for Tower to hand off departures to approach; would allow the radar Controller to determine if a dangerous situation is imminent.As of now; the only controlled airspace in the Palm Springs valley is the Tower's Class D. Class E airspace exists around TRM; but only prohibits flight for poor weather. This airspace is a free-for-all with half of the aircraft talking to ATC and the other half are not; and just blasting through everyone else. This needs to change.Also; the local pilots should know better than to be flying in these congested areas doing aerobatics.  The safety culture of these pilots is questionable and should be discussed.

column121: I was working the Springs sector and noticed a high performance aircraft depart PSP and then the tower dropped them and they went to a 1200 code.  I kept my eye on them because we have had high performance aircraft interfere with arrivals/departures before. Over the next 30 minutes; the aircraft flew around the airspace; but it wasn't until around XA:45z that they started doing maneuvers around UDD.  I believe it was Aircraft X that was doing aerobatic maneuvers just east of the UDD airport.  The aircraft rapidly change altitude; turn very quickly; and all of this at a high rate of speed.  It's next to impossible to anticipate what their intentions are and makes it very difficult to keep other aircraft out of their way. These aircraft fly through the airspace; creating havoc; and then just call the tower for pattern entry; instead of calling approach for sequencing.  One of the aircraft was right next to a regional jet; but below; and keeping up with them; while they were trying to descend on a visual approach in to PSP.  This aircraft called the tower; instead of approach; and was sequenced by them.  I; however; was left focused on the situation; unsure what this aircraft was doing; and if they even saw [the regional jet].The lack of a mandatory controlled airspace in the PSP area makes it very difficult to make any sort of plan; since anyone who wants to can fly right down the final legally.  PSP tower is also terminating these high performance aircraft; right as they leave their Delta airspace; where they go on to get in the way of arrivals coming in PSP or other nearby airports.  These high performance aircraft are out every weekend; constantly getting in the way; and making the approach controllers bend to their will.  The workload on the Springs sector is already very high; but add in the lack of guaranteed controlled airspace makes everything much more difficult.  We are approach; departure and clearance delivery; all in one sector.  It is incredibly frustrating to make sense of all the aircraft criss crossing; formulate a plan; and then have someone who deems it not important to participate in the TRSA; blow up your entire plan; making you change everything.  While that did not happen exactly in this instance; it has happened many times before; and is what has brought me to file this report in hopes to prevent it from happening more.I recommend that we change the airspace around PSP to something that is mandatory controlled airspace.  The voluntary participation makes sequencing and separation difficult; and in the cases of these high performance aircraft; they are creating an unsafe situation; but still 'following the rules'.  Some sort of protection needs to be added to the area to help us ensure our separation and allow controllers to have a safe space to sequence.I would also request that someone look in to the legality of the aerobatic activities that these aircraft are doing in the Palm Springs valley.  Are they aware what they are doing is unsafe and potentially illegal?

I began to depart the other aircraft of the crossing runway with turns and to also have them stop at 2000 feet for the picture takers. When Aircraft Y checked on; I cleared him for the option. My biggest mistake was putting expeditiousness over safety. I overlooked Aircraft X in two important ways.  I had an expectation bias that he would exit the runway before the intersection and  even the I scanned the runway; I missed him sitting at the intersection. The color of the plane and the concrete made it difficult to notice him. Not until Aircraft X keyed up to talk did I remember he was there but by then Aircraft Y had touched down; saw the aircraft and was stopping to avoid.This situation very poignantly reminded me (because it was a very close call and so thankful it was not more serious) that safety is our number one priority. As a facility we need to have a clear reminder that a runway is occupied as opposed to one single light that carries multiple meanings.  We should clearly define a procedure for LAHSO as well.

column121: Aircraft X on an IFR flight plan was being vectored for an ILS approach. The weather was marginal but apparently had some very strong winds aloft as the aircraft kept flying off course when given any heading. The initial heading of 115 looked like a 125 heading. I gave him a 115 heading down to 1800 ft. for the ILS approach but when I saw that he was heading toward the higher MVAs; I asked him to turn 10 degrees left. The pilot asked if I was painting any weather but I didn't see anything and I told him that. I also told him to advise if he wanted to deviate for weather. It looked like the weather was clearing up and the winds were calm enough for an approach. Since he kept getting blown off course toward the shoreline and away from the water; I asked him if he'd like an instrument or visual approach instead. He said that he had the shoreline in sight so the visual approach might work.As he got closer to the field; I noticed that he looked like he was heading 145; even closer to the MVA. And so I told him to turn left heading 090 but he delayed his response; much like he'd been doing the whole time. He flew out of the 1500 ft. MVA and into the 2100 ft. MVA and I issued a safety alert and again told him to turn left heading 090 and to climb to 2100 ft. After what felt like forever; he finally turned left heading 090 and climbed to 2100 ft. I then safely vectored him for an ILS approach and he landed without incident. Throughout the conversation there was a major delay in the pilot's responses and I believe that that made a big difference. I could have sharply turned him much earlier though and had I done that I believe that this would not have happened. Given that he was such a small aircraft and was being so greatly affected by the winds; I've learned my lesson. When the pilot departed ITO after landing; he was very thankful; and quite honestly I am too. It was a good learning experience. I know that pilots are quite busy and he was probably fighting the winds more than he knew. I discussed the matter with my Air Traffic Manager who was Controller in Charge at the time and we went over safety alerts. Weather can make a big difference and here in Hilo it is very unpredictable.

column121: Aircraft X departed CGI airport pop up wanting an IFR clearance to ZZZ at 030. I cleared him and climbed him to his requested altitude; not thinking about the MIA northeast of CGI being 035 because of the towers. I was concerned more about his speed and losing 5 miles separation with an arrival to CGI from the northwest and getting him to report the field in sight and then he did and cancelled IFR. I was busy tending to other traffic and the MSAW alert never went off. The MSAW normally would go off instantly when the aircraft departed northeast bound because it's a large area that has to be missed. The tower had gone home almost an hour before. They would have asked about it also. When he was roughly 1 or 2 miles east of the tallest tower; a controller at ZKC called me and asked if the aircraft was really at 030. I realized immediately what had happened and I said yes. It was too late to to anything different with the aircraft at that point. He was missing the towers. But after I hung up the landline I realized the MSAW never was flashing telling me he was at an unsafe altitude. I called the other controller back and asked him if his MSAW was going off. He said right after he had called me it started to go off. I fully accept responsibility for making the mistake of not realizing 030 was an unsafe altitude on his route. However; the MSAW should have been going off for several minutes and this is a safety issue. I have been working at this facility for almost 30 years and have never even known it would be possible for me to disable the MSAW and I would never try to do such. The first thing the tech ops guy asked my supervisor was if it was turned on. Like I said; I didn't know it could be turned off on an individual sector any more than you could disable Conflict alert. You can suppress it individually for and aircraft but it is always on as far as I know.

column121: ZZZ ATIS advertising ILS Runway XY; winds 24008 favoring [Runway] ZA but it is normal for ZZZ to use 12 until winds are 10 KTS or greater due to terrain and approach undesirability of Runway ZA.Aircraft checked on with correct ATIS descending from Center and asked for RNAV ZA. I only heard RNAV.  The common request from airline is for the RNAV Z Runway XY when we are advertising ILS's because it saves flying miles/time.I should mention that the cleaning/disinfecting person was starting my station so I had to move out of the way and move items away for her cleaning process. This is a nightly routine and is highly distracting.I cleared Aircraft X for the RNAV Z Runway XY approach. To which they read back 'Cleared RNAV' (pause) 'Zulu; Runway XY' (the XY was dropped and due to the cleaning I only heard Y which I assumed was part of X-Y) [Note: there is NO Runway YA at ZZZ].I observed the aircraft making a right turn at ZZZZZ intersection instead of the left turn for Runway XY this alerted me the aircraft was following the Runway ZA approach path. I immediately canceled the approach clearance; assigned an appropriate altitude and heading and informed the pilot it appeared he was on the wrong approach and I was now vectoring for the correct approach. The pilot was still above all MVA's so there was no immediate danger. There was a short discussion with the pilot and he set up for the correct approach which was completed with no issue.1st; Cleaning/Disinfection of control position and its immediate vicinity by contract staff should be done only when the position is not being worked at that station. Our facility closes the TRACON at XA:00 and has a 5hr XX min window this could be done in with no distractions and eliminate the danger to the NAS is currently poses.2nd; this was a clear hearback/readback issue with expectation bias on both the controllers and pilots part.A- Because of distraction; I failed to hear the initial request for Runway ZA and followed up by issuing a standard clearance for the RNAV Z Runway XY with no other warning to the pilot such as 'Unable Runway ZA' as I would normally do with an opposite direction request I was unable to approve.B- The pilot readback a completely wrong clearance in many ways; The RNP approach he wanted to Runway ZA is called 'RNAV Runway ZA'. It does not have a Z and is to ZA not YA. By reading back 'Cleared Rnav Z Runway YA' it greatly increased the chances of my hearing it as I expected.C- In listening to the recording the pilot obviously was unsure of the clearance he got as there was a long pause between RNAV and Zulu; which leads me to believe the pilot had a flag going off in his head that he neglected to properly follow up on.  Had I not been involved with dancing around the cleaning person to be able to see my scope I probably would have picked up on this better. As it was I must have had a flag of some kind in my own mind because I did give extra vigilance to ensure the correct turn at ZZZZZ so there must have been something warning the back of my mind as well.In the end the system did work as it ultimately should and the error was caught and corrected with no risk. I know a last minute correction like this can cause stress on a flight crew and this crew handled it with high professionalism and safety was insured by both them and myself.

column121: Aircraft X; was on the CORRL STAR landing SFB.   Aircraft X checks in level at 5;000.  There is an un-tagged target Aircraft Y in their proximity at 5;900.  At that time; they are not in conflict; and the targets do not appear to be on a course to merge.This area is Class E airspace; there is no requirement to be in contact with ATC; and it is a practice area for flight schools.  Yes; this seems extremely unsafe; and it is!  We have numerous commercial aircraft; loaded with potentially over 100 human lives; going through a VFR practice area all day; every day and nothing is done to stop it.In this practice area; you can expect to see aircraft doing such things as stalls; steep turns; rapid altitude changes; just to name a few.After assigning Aircraft X a runway assignment and seeing no traffic that they are in immediate conflict with I move onto another task.  Aircraft Z; cold calls me requesting VFR practice approaches.  I get them a code and assign them the code of XXXX.  I wait a few seconds; and they aren't tagging up.   So now; I ask the call sign of the Aircraft Z requesting approaches; the aircraft tells me and that's when I see the primary target change to a code of XXXX.  I identify the aircraft; however; it won't tag up. I'm diagnosing why the target won't tag up and discover it's because they filed an IFR flight plan to be picked up in the air.  So now there are 2 codes for this aircraft in my tab list.  While I'm trying to delete the IFR code; Aircraft X keeps up and states they are responding to a TCAS/RA.  I immediately did issue a traffic alert; but it was too late.After looking at the replay; I watched the targets merge; and what the playback showed was the in-tagged target made a hard-left hand turn; and descended rapidly causing the TCAS/RA. It appears the the target was almost diving at the aircraft and 'buzzing' it.The Aircraft X company itself; has identified the area between OMN and SFB as the area they receive the most TCAS/RA's in.  But yet; we still fly them through there knowing this!  Why?  We issue multiple traffic advisories and traffic alerts in the area throughout the day.  It isn't a secret this is a dangerous area.  What would you expect; a major VFR practice area placed right in the middle of a published STAR; and at the published STARs altitude.  With no airspace (Class C; Class B) protecting the aircraft.This isn't the first time this has happened; and if nothing is done it won't be the last time.  The risk for a mid-air catastrophe in the area is extremely high.  Something needs to be done. My recommendation is either move the practice area or change the STAR.  We have 2 STARs into SFB; one over OMN and one over OCF.  This event happen on the OMN STAR.  The other STAR (OCF); is much safer; but yet we continue to receive multiple Aircraft X aircraft over the OMN STAR.  In fact; the majority of the Aircraft X [company aircraft] are assigned the OMN STAR!  I know; it doesn't make sense; but this is done all day every day.Now the provider (F11); the user Aircraft X [Company] has identified a significant safety risk to the FAA; and yet we are still in this predicament.Stop using the OMN STAR; that is my recommendation!  Unless weather or other safety factors are more dangerous than this. I would be hard pressed to find a more dangerous spot than this.Also; flight schools should be picking up their airborne IFR with us and telling us on initial contact they have one on file.  This will prevent 2 codes being generated for the same aircraft and aircraft automatically tagging up when assigned a code.  We are going to work with them locally to see if they will start doing this.

column121: Aircraft X called Local Control for departure IFR. The aircraft was cleared via the SID and this was reiterated at Local Control when they were released. With their release; Local Control also advised them to remain north of the runway for an aircraft rolling out as well as the next arrival. The aircraft departed and was transferred to TRACON. I observed an unsafe proximity to terrain as this aircraft was climbing form 800 ft. to 900 ft. on the update when it grabbed my attention. The aircraft was approximately 3 miles northwest of the airport and approaching the hillside. I called over to the coordinator fir the two departure sectors and brought their attention to the aircraft and asked if they check on them. This seemed to startle the coordinator who said they would check. About twenty seconds later the Low Altitude Alert went off showing 1;100 ft. and I can only assume Aircraft X was IMC as I could not see them out of the window. Still progressing towards the hillside. The aircraft then began to turn to the west and away from the hillside. The coordinator called back; which goes directly to Local Control; and said the pilot understood they were to remain north of the course. Local Control explained what they had told the aircraft and all was back to normal. With the wind we were having they would have drifted north a little anyway; but this was a lot of drifting; so this statement made sense. Around this time; the Supervisor came back; as I was starting an incident report. I called TRACON Supervisor and asked if they were filing anything on this event. They said no because there is no climb gradient on the SID. But there is and I do not believe this aircraft was meeting it. I left it at that and said I was filing a report. When I filled out the report I entered 800 ft. for the required and observed altitudes because that was the first altitude I saw. The pilot should have understood what was issued and to not over fly the runway. I do not know if this would be considered a Pilot Deviation; but I have a hunch it was: The vector SID has a required climb gradient. They were near that; but I do not believe they were legally meeting it and off course.

column121: This was at the very end of the swing shift; where I sent down the other two controllers for COVID clean-up protocol.  There were four arrivals - 2 pairs - so I paused on cleaning to work them down and to their ramps.   Aircraft X landed Runway XY Right; with an aircraft rolling out on Runway XY Left; with another aircraft on Taxiway T.  It looked like Aircraft X would exit T as well.  I gave the Runway XY Left arrival turn left on D join A to the ramp this frequency.  I then gave the first aircraft at Taxiway T cross Runway XY Left; turn left to D while crossing and join A to the Ramp this frequency.  I gave them both A because they were parking at the D Ramp.  Then I gave Aircraft X cross Runway 28 Left; turn left on D; then left on B; taxi to the Ramp via B; H; A; this frequency until switching over to Ramp Control.  I gave Aircraft X; B due to parking at the B Ramp; and to not get stuck behind the other aircraft should they not have marshallers to enter the ramp.  Once this was all communicated; I resumed cleaning and the first mid shifter came upstairs.  I noticed at this time that Aircraft X had joined Taxiway A behind the other aircraft and watched to make sure the other aircraft were able to get into their ramp space.  They were and I was satisfied to file a report.  The mid-shifter plugged in and I began the briefing with mid shift closures; and then followed the check lists to cover CIC; Local; Ground; and Clearance Delivery.  As I was covering the Ground traffic; I noticed Aircraft X was now on B between G and H as they should have been originally.  I am not sure why they corrected when the other two aircraft were out of their way.  I completed the briefing and left.  I have no recommendations for this event.  I would however; like to hypothesize why I believe this occurred.  I think that the preceding 2 aircraft crossing T to D to A; created an expectation bias with Aircraft X to follow them without having been told to.  I believe they were finishing up their after landing checklist and confirmed between them that they were to have been on B; and joined B at F1 hoping that the diagonal versus 90 degree turns would be subtle enough that ATC would not notice.  I further believe that we are all running around 10% acuity with the pandemic and all of the circus atmosphere of the recent political debacles.  This would explain the simple mistake and due to the reduced traffic there was no harm to the operation.  Finally; there is a chance that with nighttime and possible lack of familiarity; the crew was confused by the taxiway lights at the junction of Taxiway's A/B/D.

column121: I was working Aircraft X as a visual approach to PSP. They were cleared about 15-20 miles NE of the airport. I noticed a 'Z' tag (PSP Tower) on a downwind departure that was moving quickly; so it caught my attention. I clicked on it to see that it was the local [aircraft type]; Aircraft Y.  This aircraft is notorious in our area for getting in the way of IFR arrivals to PSP; so I kept my eye on the data tag.Aircraft Y dropped off the Z tag and turned southbound after passing an arrival to 31L. This put them on a converging course with Aircraft X. I still had some altitude separation to work with; so I called traffic to Aircraft X and told them to stop at 045 since Aircraft Y appeared to be momentarily level at 040. I thought maybe Aircraft Y saw the arrival. After I stopped Aircraft X; tower called and said Aircraft Y had Aircraft X in sight. I then saw Aircraft Y start climbing; and issued a traffic alert to Aircraft X. At the same time Aircraft X started descending.Aircraft Y was never pointed out to me; and no coordination was performed by the tower. Aircraft Y pilot is notorious in our area because they fly around at high speed; in highly congested areas; doing aerobatic maneuvers without talking to anyone. Then they fly back in the PSP; skipping approach every time; avoiding any sequencing from us. They force us to move around them; since we don't know what their intentions are; and then call the tower right before the Delta to get pattern entry instructions. This is all legal; but unsafe. The plane is from a local area; and they are very aware of the procedures and traffic in the area. However; they continue to avoid talking to approach control because it is not required in a TRSA.The few times the pilot has been on approach frequency; they are argumentative and obviously frustrated with our instructions.  The safety culture has obviously left this pilot and they feel they are above the rest of us and our mission of safe and efficient flow.The issue in this event is the conflict happened right outside the delta; with no coordination; and probably some pressure from the pilot to get on course and on their way. The Tower probably felt pressure to terminate the aircraft; as they were already outside of their delta airspace; and the TRSA has no requirements for participation.PSP airspace needs a Class Charlie or Bravo airspace around it. We provide no protection to a steady stream of arrivals by having a voluntary participation airspace surrounding it. The airspace is BUSY. The controllers have no safe airspace to assume separation. Aircraft fly through our arrival and departure corridors at leisure; stopping departures; corrupting sequences and causing unstable or aborted approaches.UDD is located about 10 miles east of PSP and has VFR jet departures launching all day long; right at aircraft in the downwind for PSP. What major airport allows for aircraft to fly into the radar downwind?  This creates an incredibly confusing situation for the controller; as we have no idea what the intentions are of any of the aircraft. When you look at the amount of traffic; the speed; and the lack of maneuvering room; the Springs/Desert sector is a time bomb waiting to explode. We as controllers do the best we can to alleviate these situations; but with mountains surrounding almost all quadrants of the valley; there are few routes to take in and out; which results in many head-on situations.I have a similar report that I filed a few years ago where a YAK converged with an arrival for PSP 13R and the pilot reported a NMAC with the aircraft.  Protected Class Charlie or Bravo airspace would have avoided both of these situations. The controllers and pilots deserve to be afforded some level of protection when close into the airport. RA's and and NMAC's 5-10 miles away from a major airport are unacceptable.

column121: Aircraft X entered the airspace for 4 miles south of HIO at 020 heading eastbound. I used the ADS-B function on the radar display to determine the call sign. Aircraft X turned north and re-entered the airspace at 2100 ft.; 4 miles southeast of HIO. Aircraft X then made a right turn and joined a 5 mile final at 1800 ft. Aircraft X overflew the right runway and began circling in the north portion of the airspace. Aircraft X was given the green light gun signal multiple times but never landed. In total; 6 different aircraft had their flight paths adjusted to avoid Aircraft X. Aircraft Y called ready for departure; IFR on a SID. I called Approach and requested a 5 minute release to attempt to avoid Aircraft X's erratic flight paths. Aircraft X was on a left downwind heading for the opposite direction runway and had been circling for approximately 15 minutes. I cleared Aircraft Y for takeoff assuming that Aircraft X would continue their right turns and not be a factor for Aircraft Y. Ground Control advised that Aircraft X is cleared to land on any runway. Aircraft X intercepted a left base for an intersecting runway but flew through final. column123: As the pilot in command; I departed in my airplane on a VFR cross country flight to ZZZ1. The aircraft has an installed GNS 430W GPS and GTX-330ES transponder providing ADSB capability. The route of flight followed a basically southerly course direction; with route guidance provided by the G430W direct to my destination. Approximately 15 to 20 miles from my destination; I announced my intention to land. The GPS map course indicated that I was closing in on what was indicated to be my destination; and I made preparations to land; with a call to Tower; indicating my intentions. Having received no response; I maneuvered the aircraft west of the airport in an attempt to gain some time for working out the communication problem. Eventually; I received a broken communication that provided clearance to land. I set up my approach and noticed that the runway markings did not match up to what I expected and did not land. I found out later that I was at a nearby airport however; and this did not correspond to my Garmin 430W readout. Given the communications issues I was having; I contacted my son with my cell phone; who was on the ground having traveled there independently. He contacted the Tower; indicating there was a problem with my flight. The Air Traffic Controller on duty; at that time; was able to locate my aircraft almost immediately and provided vectors. Communications between my aircraft [and ATC] improved as I flew closer to the airport. I made a safe; uneventful landing.To summarize; it is apparent that there were significant issues with medium to long range communications and erroneous GPS information that directly caused concerns with this flight. There was nothing obvious indicating that there was equipment failure on board my aircraft; at that time or subsequently. The return trip was perfectly normal; with support from ATC flight following the entire way; later that evening.The real concern comes down to bad GPS tracking data; which placed me in the wrong airport airspace unintentionally; whereas; I had reason to believe; based on erroneous information; that I was receiving correct information pursuant to an airport arrival at my intended destination There have been published reports of military GPS interruptions for testing and training purposes in the area that are known to have impacted civilian aircraft. Perhaps such jamming activities disrupted my GPS on board; thus would have provided inaccurate location guidance to my Garmin 430W.

Professionals should; regardless of the root cause; be able to recognize his or her own deficiencies; and continue to put effort into doing a better job every time.

column121: Upon reaching rotation speed; PM called for rotate. At rotate; the flight control (elevator) felt unresponsive. Both pilots noted the unresponsiveness. The aircraft felt unsafe and unable to fly; and the decision was made to land the airplane back on the runway. Max breaking action was not needed to stop the aircraft with a safe margin of runway still ahead. Upon stopping; communication with the passengers and cabin crew was established; as well as with the Tower. All passengers and crew members were safe; and no one panicked. Tower needed an explanation/reason for the rejected takeoff. Later we called tower and everything was fine. They were concerned about injuries; which did not happen. We returned to the gate; and upon deplaning the passengers; they seemed calm and praised the crew reaction to the situation. Dispatch was notified and Maintenance was called in to inspect the aircraft.Good Crew Resource Management (CRM) is paramount for the safe operation of an aircraft on all phases of flight. Training; focus; attention to detail; and quick reaction are all fundamental during times of abnormal circumstances. Pilots should not become complacent; since most flights are non-eventful. Though not a procedure that is trained/performed/demonstrated during simulator training; it could be suggested to be implemented for situations like this. Overall; good aeronautical decision making; experience; and a safety mindset is crucial to the safety of passengers; crew; and aircraft.

I walked to the front of aircraft to get some air; but also to get water for the poor passengers. Thankfully; the plane did cool off in the air; but it was still extremely uncomfortable.Extreme heat conditions on the airplane combined with mandatory mask compliance for passengers and crew caused this event.  Crews can be terminated/lose benefits if removing masks on board the aircraft in front of passengers. Until recently; FA's were not required to wear masks while making announcements. Passengers can be fined/lose flight privileges for removing masks. The threat of the FAA fines and penalties under the new federal mask mandate appears to supersede common sense safety practices and concern and care for crews and passengers.Masks; may help prevent viral spread (there is much data to refute those claims); but prevents the passengers and crew to breathe much needed fresh oxygen. The effects of not getting enough oxygen and the potential for hypoxia were ingrained into me during FA training. I am greatly concerned that airlines and the FAA are continuing to put the safety of passengers and crew at risk with mandatory mandates that restrict fresh oxygen; which can cloud judgement and critical thinking abilities. Heat exhaustion and the need for fresh oxygen when wearing masks was acknowledged by the CDC. Of course; the CDC recommended spacing of self 6 feet away; but plane passengers and crew do not have the luxury of a 6 foot distance. Mandatory mask mandates on planes should also come with the ability to tell passengers and crew to remove masks when feeling anxious or stressed or when breathing is compromised. If one feels sick or faint because of heat and a mask; the ability to lower a mask on a plane should be allowed. FAs should be empowered to use their common sense when enforcing masks in extreme heat conditions. The 'appearance of safety' seems to be aviation's new standard of practice rather than 'actual safety' of anyone on board an aircraft. This is a very serious shift in thought for the FAA and airlines.  The unintended consequences of these 'appearance of safety' standards are frightening.

column121: Upon doing the cabin sweep; I notice [Passenger in] X1 talking on the phone and asked her to turn it off. I can't identify a bad actor hiding in a mask from an innocent one in a mask. I can't smell alcohol; smoke; or even jet fuel when wearing a mask; which is required of me at all times - especially in my jump seat.The ability to do my job as a safety professional on an aircraft is greatly reduced thanks to these mask mandates. I am really surprised that the FAA and airlines care more about the optics of safety than the actual safety on board a plane these days.

column121: After doing a prolonged run up [in] the PA-28 on Runway XX (after having massive avionics upgrades at a shop on the field) we noticed slight elevations in CO (Carbon Monoxide) in the cockpit. 25-40 ppm. My student and I were aware and I said to keep the window open and keep the heat and vents closed (which resolved the issues) and the levels went back down to an acceptable range. After being cleared to depart with a right turn out to the east of the airport the student and I briefed our takeoff and emergency action that would be taken in case of an emergency. A few seconds after rotating I stated feeling symptoms of what I believed to be from the CO. I was going to give the plane to my student so I could open the door for air as he warned me of the sensor reading close to 250 ppm of CO. I got tunnel vision as well and extreme dizziness and headache and told him to open the window; which is in the left side. Fearing we only had seconds before I lost consciousness and that he would be not far behind me I entered into a steep right bank nose lose attitude [received priority] and tried to make it to the intersecting Runway (XX) I was unable to make it to the runway and was able to land on the taxiway. As soon as we stopped I opened the door and then responded to the tower and waited for emergency personnel. A mechanic on the field informed us the next day there was a crack in the exhaust (unsure of the size) in a place I would not have been able to see. I believe my actions were correct both in timing and place of landing.

column121: I listened to the ATIS and prepared to taxi out for the short flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 in the new to me aircraft. We had come in a few hours earlier and had no adverse radio issues at all. Reviewing the NOTAMs earlier I had filed away that the Tower was on part time status; most likely due to COVID; and would be closing in the afternoon.After startup we called Ground and did not hear a reply. On our arrival they had told us to stay on the Tower frequency; so we tried that one. Still no response and we tried each a few more times.We listened to the ATIS again and noted that it talked about the Tower closing and that it was many hours old. The passenger in the right seat was also a very experienced ATP rated pilot and CFI and he told me 'The Tower is closed'. I remembered that possibility from my NOTAM search earlier in the day and asked him how he knew. He said it was on our Foreflight app and he heard XA30 on the ATIS.That seemed plausible to me; so we reverted to CTAF procedures; announced our taxi on the Tower frequency; and proceeded to Runway XX. I did glance up at the Tower; just in case; and saw no light gun signals but the Tower was soon out of view. Part way to the runway we were intercepted by an airport vehicle and the driver pointed to his radio. I switched our radio to the second nav/com and was able to establish communications with the ATC facility.In retrospect; this was a good example of a display of expectation bias. We fit the facts we were experiencing into the theory we had developed for what was going on and we were mistaken. I knew that when a Tower closes they say so on the ATIS broadcast; but being so old I thought maybe they had just forgotten to do so. We both had XA30 in our minds as the closing time and discussed that it was now XB30; but we missed the fact that on the ATIS and the NOTAM XA30 was the opening time and it was UTC; not local time. The radios worked fine on the way in; they must be working fine now; etc.In reality we were wrong on all accounts and it is a good thing that we were able to establish ATC contact before taking off which would have only complicated things for all.

column121: I; the First Officer; executed the charted Visual Approach. Landing was uneventful and rolled to taxiway Tango before passing controls to the Captain to taxi to gate. As we exited the runway Tower gave taxi instructions to the gate. and to '... stay with me'. I read back the taxi instructions and the Captain repeated them as he commenced taxi from the runway and stated 'flaps up'. I then commenced my after landing flow; raised the flaps; checked speed brakes stowed; autobrakes off; flight directors off; wing lights off; steady and strobe to steady; trimmed to 5 units; check weather radar off; cycled ramp (though not needed) to active in VHF2; and started removing flight pertinent printer strips. By this time we were somewhere near the Bravo; Golf; Sierra taxiway junction. I briefly looked up as Captain stated; 'There's Golf'. I don't remember what I heard exactly that caused me to look up again; some reference to Golf taxiway perhaps. But when I looked up I did not recognize where we were. I saw lighted taxi signs for Sierra; Golf; and Bravo in the distance to the left. I could see blue taxiway edge lights all around but nothing in front of us. The blue taxi edge lights were very disorienting especially without a lit taxi center line. Our taxi and turnoff lights were so dim that they were essentially useless. The moon was providing more light than they were. On my IPAD I could see our own ship; we were on Golf but heading the wrong way. The Captain had turned right instead of left. At that point he turned left in an attempt to get back to Alpha taxiway; I assume. He did make me aware that he was concerned about accidentally crossing on to the runway. Due to the very poor lighting and the sea of blue taxi edge lights; taxiway was difficult to discern from anything else. All you could see was directional taxi signs in the darkness and blue taxi lights scattered about. The Captain turned left until there was a break in the blue lights with the Bravo sign visible just a little further away so it did appear as though we were turning on taxiway Bravo though I could see no yellow line. I told him I didn't see the taxiway; I think we're going in to no man's land; and Captain said; no; we're on Golf; there's the sign for Bravo. I was confused about the blue lights; they didn't seem to be oriented right and the our ship was sort of on Golf but pivoting so I allowed the events to progress thinking maybe I was just disoriented. When we proceeded ahead the ground before us was just dark. Really no discernible features except for blue taxi lights up ahead that seemed to mark the edge of Bravo. I said I think we're off the taxiway. Captain stopped. We exchanged thoughts on the best way to proceed from that point. We called tower to confess. Tower took a look; said we were just near Bravo; or Golf; I can't remember exactly but he was not concerned which taxiway we ended up needing to get to the gate. I thought we might not be on prepared surface but the Captain was sure we were still on the taxiway just facing the wrong direction. So I told him clear to the right; let's turn all the way back around and take Bravo. The Captain turned tight right and proceeded back the way we came. The jet stopped and thinking it was an incline the Captain added power and we rolled back on taxiway center; turned left on Bravo; took Foxtrot then Alpha to the gate; tower then stated; 'Not a problem guys; the snow plows do more damage than you'. No other occurrences from then on. We did discuss the possibility that we may have left the taxiway. The Captain was confident we had not and I was inclined to believe him since I could not see the ground beneath us; we were just avoiding taxi edge lights. I told him I would check and do an external walk around once we shut down. During deplaning maintenance met me before walking out. She asked me if the landing was rough and I said; actually; no; the landing was great... WHY? She showed me a shot on her cell phone of our nose strut and this is your nose gear. It was covered with dirt. I went down to look at it and it was dirty but both tires were still intact at that point and I saw no evidence of anything else on the mains or the engines. The mains were spotless; engines were clean. I came back up; told the Captain the mains were covered in dirt on the tires and on the lowermost part of the strut. I then stepped out of the cockpit while he talked to maintenance. We turned the plane over to maintenance; they said they would check out the gear and clean it off and we left; still not sure we actually left the taxiway. The wind was blowing in excess of 30 knots and dirt was blowing all over. We chalked it up to that.It was dark; really dark on that end of the airport. The taxiways are a conglomeration that looks more like spaghetti. The whole area is labeled HS1; for good reason. They are difficult enough to navigate in daylight; much less at night with no centerline lighting; a plethora of edge lights all outlining various 'islands' on the field; taxiway ID and directional signs for every taxiway that intersects in HS1 and a useless taxi light. That is a lot of scattered lights with no reliable taxi light to help gauge distance. The Captain was disoriented. Golf taxiway is constructed right on the curve at a 45 degree angle. The directional sign at night can make the left turn on Golf easy to miss especially with the opposite direction of Golf being directly in front of you. I; the First Officer was task distracted. I was performing after landing flow and cockpit cleanup. The Captain had told me during this trip that he was once based in [the area] and was very familiar with this airport; not to mention he was a check airman. My guard was down and I was not as diligent as I normally am during the taxi operation. Being tired and expectation bias. It was night; the end of the day in serious winds. The Captain and I were exhausted most of our mental energy on planning the approach and landing given the conditions that night. The approach was not exactly a standard one we do all the time; and we were not landing on the usual runway you get at this airport. A better taxi light would have alleviated much of the confusion. The lights are not adequate. Neither of us was really sure that we ever left the taxiway. Taxiway centerline lights. There are many islands outlined in blue and no green center lights to actually show the trail through the maze of them. Distance judging is difficult in the dark and it was dark for us. Those lights would have helped. I should have stayed more engaged in the taxi phase to back up my Captain. Getting lost is going to happen and there are two of us for a reason. I allowed myself to get disoriented as well.
column123: Landed Runway 31 LGA. Cleared at taxiway T. ATC gave us T;B;G;A to gate. Turned right on Taxiway G instead of left. column121: ATIS reported active Runway 28 with winds 300 at 23 kts gusting to 37 kts and potential for low level windshear and light snow. Prior to push; the First Officer briefed performance data departure brief for windshear with engine anti-ice on; Runway 28 with less than 1/8 in. wet snow. Captain directed deice type 1 given a break in the light snow and increased visibility while awaiting push. Aircraft pushed back onto deice pad; type 1 was applied; ground crews confirmed clean aircraft surfaces; and engine starts were completed. Ground Control provided initial taxi instructions 'Taxi Runway 28 via Alpha; cleared cross Runway 33'. After making the left hand turn from Quebec to Alpha taxiway; Ground Control informed us of a wind shift from 300 to 320 degrees; a 27 kts. crosswind for planned Runway 28 departure; and offered Runway 33 instead. We accepted the Runway change given the nearly 40 kts. gust aligned with Runway 33.Captain elected to continue taxiing on Alpha given the concern of additional snow; while the First Officer completed the Runway change in the FMS and briefed the updated departure heading of 330. Approaching the intersection of Alpha and Mike taxiways Ground Control directed 'Taxi M; cross Runway 28'. Remembering the initial taxi instruction of Alpha cross Runway 33; the Captain mistakenly continued straight instead of turning right on M; leading to a Runway incursion on Runway 33. The First Officer was distracted in verifying all Runway change steps had been completed and did not recognize the error until holding short of Runway 28 on Alpha. The First Officer called tower and reported position; at which point crew reoriented; finished the Runway change discussion; and departed Runway 33 without issue. The root cause was misapplication of previous taxi clearance by the Captain; combined with insufficient First Officer backup due to the Runway change tasks. I would suggest adding the intersection of Mike and Alpha taxiways as a potential hot spot worth pre briefing prior to push back. Stopping the aircraft on Alpha to complete all necessary Runway change steps and briefings would have allowed the First Officer to be more proactive with taxi instructions.
column123: After receiving Type I deicing  we called ground for taxi. Winds were very strong and ATIS advised ILS in use to Runway 28 and Runway 28 for departure. This was briefed and expected. Ground Control cleared us to taxi from the  ramp to Runway 28 via Alpha; cleared to cross Runway 33. Halfway down taxiway Alpha; ground gave new winds and offered Rwy 33 for departure. It was a 27 knots crosswind for Runway 28 so we accepted. New taxi instructions were taxi to Runway 33 via M; cleared to cross Runway 28.There was no SID to change or rebrief so I slowed the jet while the First Officer ran the numbers; changed the runway in the FMS and greened up the speeds which were the same. This all occurred before the missed right turn on taxiway Mike. I turned on the turnoff lights and said; clear left; clear to cross; lights are on and rolled across Runway 33. Approaching the end of Alpha; we switched to tower frequency and was asked our position. We said we were about to make the turn onto Lima; short of Runway 33. The error was brought to our attention. We advised we were holding short of Runway 33 at Lima and we were ready for departure. We were cleared for Take-off; with no further dialog regarding the error. Runway 33 was not closed but it was not the active runway and we followed our original taxi instructions.There were several things going on that contributed to the error. De-icing and holdover considerations; wind shear advisories in effect forcing non-standard takeoff procedures and a late runway change with taxi instructions similar to the original. Failure of both pilots following along the 10-9 chart at night with blowing snow.We reviewed the expected taxi route from the ramp to the expected departure Runway (28). There were no Hot Spots to brief and getting there via Alpha is very simple. I think we could benefit from a Hot Spots circle and reference on the 10-9 chart here in SYR. We may have felt a little rushed as we blocked out late and were trying to get airborne before the snow started again.

column121: The flight was cruising at 35;000 ft. (FL350) in Instrument Meteorological Conditions (IMC). The flight attendants had been briefed earlier about turbulence along the route of flight. When the turbulence became constant moderate; the flight attendants were informed via the public address (PA) system to 'take their seats.' The flight was deviating around weather and needed a left deviation and attempted request a deviation from ATC; however; due to frequency congestion this was causing a delay in deviation. The Captain executed the deviation out of safety (emergency authority) and had the First Officer announce the deviation to ATC; not long after the deviation severe turbulence was encountered lasting approximately one minute. The aircraft was out of control with large airspeed; attitude; and altitude deviations. The severe turbulence caused a 500 foot altitude deviation (35;500 ft.) which triggered a TCAS alert. All automation disconnected in the turbulence and the Captain assumed manual flight control. The second aircraft was acquired visually; and the Captain manually maneuvered to regain control; avoid the aircraft; and return to 35;000 ft. Once clear of the turbulence; the auto-throttles and autopilot were re-engaged; and ATC informed about the location and magnitude of the severe turbulence. The First Officer was tasked to check on the status of the flight attendants and passengers. There were no flight attendant or passenger injuries. Both during flight and upon landing; Maintenance Control; Dispatch; and Operations was kept informed of the severe turbulence encounter along with crew and passenger status. column121: My student and I were returning to the home airport from the local practice area after a training flight. Since this was the student's 2nd training flight; I was explaining the correct traffic pattern entry and radio calls to him. I made the initial radio call 10 miles away from the airport and stated location; altitude and intentions. A short time later; a Mooney checked on to the CTAF and announced his location and intentions. I noted to myself that the Mooney was near us; but behind and decided to be vigilant. The wind favored landings on Runway XX that day; which meant that we would have to fly from the practice area to the northwest of the airport to an area southwest of the airport in order to make the 45 degree entry to the right traffic. I was a bit concerned as the student and I were flying in a Cessna 150 which is very slow and was worried about being overtaken by the faster Mooney as we both set up for the traffic pattern entry. I made my next radio call at a location approximately 4-5 miles northwest of the airport and stated that we intended to maneuver for the 45 degree entry to the traffic pattern. I also directed the student to descend to traffic pattern altitude. I continued to visually scan for the Mooney. Since I expected the Mooney to overtake us and since the right of way rules state that overtaking aircraft should pass on the right; I spent most of my time searching on our right. The pilot of the Mooney made a radio call and stated a position and distance from the airport that was very similar to ours. I became even more concerned about the possibility for a collision and made an additional radio call with our revised position and stated that we were in a Cessna 150; in an attempt to inform the Mooney pilot of our speed and the possibility for collision. The pilot of the Mooney made another radio call and stated his position; which was very similar to ours; 5 miles west of the airport. I became very concerned about the situation and began to aggressively scan for them. I didn't feel that it would be appropriate to divert towards the airport; as it would cause me to conflict with the traffic pattern. I also didn't feel that it would be appropriate to divert away from the airport; as I expected the Mooney to pass on the right. A very short time later; the Mooney passed by us on our left and slightly above us. It appeared to me that we were vertically separated by less than 200 feet and laterally separated by less than 200 feet.I realized after the fact; that I had allowed myself to continue into the possibility of a collision because I felt I had the right of way as the slower aircraft and because I did not want to cause my student an undue expense of maneuvering away from the airport. I noted that the other pilot made three radio calls that expressed essentially the same position and distance from the airport; yet I made no attempt to escape the situation. In the future; I will be more aggressive about maneuvering out of or away from potential traffic pattern conflicts.

column121: I am a private pilot; multi-engine student. I was working with my instructor on a variety of things that morning in the practice area. We came back to the airport and proceeded to perform some touch and go landings on Runway XX; left traffic. We performed two touch and go landings; then a full stop landing. We taxied back and performed two more touch and go landings before the tower asked us to switch to right traffic (five landings in total). On downwind; the nose gear light didn't come on immediately. The hydraulic lever would kick back telling us it was pressurized and I had visual confirmation that the front gear was down.We performed three more touch and go landings to do our best to confirm that the gear was down and locked. I recall the nose gear light would flicker from time to time. We performed the checklist items accordingly but could not get the nose light to stay on when extending the gear. Every time the hydraulic gear lever would return to neutral and the gear was visible in the mirror.  My instructor requested to the tower that we switch to the non active Runway (XY) so that he could land and get out to see what was going on with the gear. With the instructor flying; he chose to feather the left engine after the gear was lowered. No flaps were used. Upon landing; he shutdown the right engine. The plane initially acted normal but started to veer to the right as we continued down the runway. I could feel that he had very little directional control. He also has no brakes on the right seat position so he yelled 'left brake!; left brake!' I pushed the left brake as hard as I could and the plane turned left enough to stay on the runway; however shortly thereafter the nose gear collapsed. We skidded to a stop; shut everything down and exited the plane. The right engine hadn't stopped in time so the prop was damaged from contacting the runway. The left engine was feathered so there didn't appear to be any damage to it. The plane was removed from the non active runway and brought back to the hangar. I have no idea what we could have done differently as we had hydraulic pressure and visual confirmation that the gear was down (bad switch?). The previous touch and go landings were fine with no adverse steering issues. Perhaps the nose gear wasn't getting a lot of contact during the touch and goes but I still had directional control prior to him landing. Feathering the left engine obviously saved that from damage. The intent was to only gently land and inspect prior to taxing back to the hangar; but due to other circumstances the plane veered right; was corrected with left brake and the nose gear still ended up collapsing.

Several touch and go landings(3) were performed during which we attempted to lightly touch nose wheel to move into locked position and get the safe indication. Some of those attempts were firm enough to confirm gear was actually down and locked. Landing gear hydraulic lever had returned to center and gear was visible in mirror every time. Checklist items for a single light out; handle returning to neutral; gear warning horn active was followed and in addition three touchdown taps indicated to me gear was extended. Discussed with student all actions and elected to land on Runway XY instead of active [Runway] XX so we could land; roll out gently; stop; and shut down so I could visually inspect the gear. After we were cleared to land on Runway XY I feathered left engine on base; continued approach; conducted gump's and final checks. As main gear contacted runaway I pulled mixture on number two engine and although initial touchdown was normal; aircraft began a slight yaw to the right along with some unusual noise like rubbing or scuffing. Felt similar to right main tire going flat quickly followed by greatly increasing yaw; much worse than a flat tire. We applied left full rudder pedal but yaw was increasing dramatically aircraft was nearly 30 degrees to centerline and about to leave runway. As there are no wheel brakes on my side of aircraft so I loudly instructed student 'left break; left break; left brake; left brake 'which he did; straightening out aircraft parallel to centerline approximately 6 ft. from edge of runway. Shortly after this nose gear collapsed and remaining 1 to 200 ft. of runway was done on the nose of the aircraft and the main gear. Once stopped; we shut off master; generators; avionics; fuel and vacated aircraft. Myers aviation removed airplane and put in our hanger. Upon inspection and disassembly it was discovered that nose wheel was turned past the stops to the right; tire scuff marks; and hydraulic actuator bent 90deg in fully extended position most likely due to excessive side load. Upper drag link assembly tubing cracked; separated; other parts bent or damaged and all located except one turn limit stop pin.

column121: While training a student pilot in ground reference maneuvers and lazy eights; we suffered a complete loss of power. engine restart procedures were executed and were unsuccessful. Our area of operation is in a humid coastal area. We are well versed in the use of carb heat and many times it is on for most of the flight. It was on continually this day. The area that we use for this training has many good hay meadows and pastures to complete a forced landing. Our landing was very good and we were able to land our Piper j3 with no damage or injuries whatsoever. We used less than 1/2 of the field to execute the forced landing.After the landing and securing the aircraft it was noticed that we had several areas below the carburetor where fuel was continually dripping out of the airbox in substantial amounts. We assumed the carb float was stuck and flooded the engine out.After disassembly of the Stromberg carburetor in the shop we found a good amount of small gray beads and flakes in the float bowl that could be easily crushed into a powder. one of these beads was lodged in the carburetor main fuel jet cutting off the fuel flow to the carburetor venturi. In maintenance during the [previous] annual the carburetor fuel bowl plug was removed and the fuel that was captured was visually inspected for contaminates. There were none. during an inspection of the disassembled carburetor after the forced landing it was found that this drain is not the lowest point in the fuel bowl and the only way to really be sure that all of these contaminates are out is to disassemble the carburetor. We also checked the carb fuel screen and it was clean. The gascolator had a small amount of what appeared to be rust and aluminum flakes in it but not enough to cause any issue. We purchased a lead test kit and tested the gray particles from the float bowl. They were found to be lead. We have been running nothing but locally sourced 100LL fuel for the past year. This event seemed to be a big enough deal that it was worth sharing to possibly prevent others from suffering a forced landing due to a similar issue.

He did not reply this time either. This is when I first became aware of this aircraft being NORDO (No Radio). I began to reach out multiple times to the aircraft and after a little time I heard him reply that he went back to the tower. I then questioned him as to why would he return to the tower frequency and gave him another instruction.The aircraft again did not respond. I also asked him to ident if he could hear me transmitting and that failed. Now I was becoming worried as I was aware this aircraft was level at 2;000 ft. and there is a Minimum Vectoring Altitude (MVA) south of him 5 to 6 miles that is 3;000 ft. I reached out to Tower to ask them if they could try to reach out to the aircraft. I also had another aircraft in the vicinity that I inquired if he could hear me and if that aircraft could transmit for me and try to contact the aircraft. Both of those attempts failed as well. I was now getting nervous as he was headed towards the two antennas with the MVA's at 3;000 ft. I then reached out to him on guard frequency and stated that if he heard me to climb immediately to 3;000 ft. I also alerted the Supervisor what was going on. Now I was seeing the aircraft entering the MVA area of 3;000 ft. and I transmitted in the blind a MVA alert and for them to climb immediately. There was still no contact with this aircraft. Now another aircraft was also trying to reach the NORDO aircraft as they heard the concern in my voice. After some time the pilot called me and said he was ready for the vector onto the ILS. Thats when the other aircraft transmitted the climb information and they began to climb. The aircraft then called me and stated he is having a serious problem with his radios and wanted to return to their departure airport. I then gave him vectors to return where the aircraft landed safely.I have no recommendations. This was an event that as a controller I did everything I could think of to get in contact with the aircraft but he was truly NORDO. In conclusion it was a equipment issue that caused the incident.

column121: During climb out from ZZZ; passing FL330 we noticed the Master Caution light flickering. We discovered it was the Low Pressure light for Hydraulic System A Engine Driven (ENG 1) pump. After leveling at FL370 the ENG 1 low pressure light then came on steady. We executed the checklist and turned the pump off. We then referenced the Hydraulic quantity and noticed the A system quantity was at 20% and B system was at about 88%. The quantity in system A then continued to decrease; reaching 0% within a few minutes. The System A ELEC 2 low pressure light was not illuminated at this point. We decided to divert to ZZZ1 and advised ATC. We reviewed the Loss of System A checklist and planned our diversion to ZZZ1. On downwind for Runway XX in ZZZ1 we lowered the gear early as planned. After the gear came down we got the low pressure light for the System A ELEC 2 pump. We completed the checklist for Loss of System A and continued our approach. After landing we discovered the Alternate Nosewheel steering was not working. We stopped the aircraft on the runway. We checked the hydraulic quantities and noticed the system B quantity was now at 47%. We were subsequently towed to the gate.

column121: First leg was a block turn back in ZZZ. Fluid leaking under right main gear. Maintenance performed the following corrective action: REMOVED AND REPLACED RH GEAR TRIM CYLINDER RELIEF VALVE. I asked the maintainer whether he needed to bleed the brakes since he cracked the closed system. He told me to cycle the brakes and if they felt good we were good to go. Legs 2 was the subsequent takeoff. After takeoff; gear handle would not move. QRH procedure offered no resolution. Declared priority handling. Conferenced maintenance and Operations Control in the air. Uneventful landing ZZZ Runway XX. The following was the maintenance corrective action: CONFIRMED FAULT; GEAR HANDLE WILL NOT RETRACT IN ANY CONFIG. T/S SYSTEM AND FOUND MLG HYDRAULIC INTERLOCK CYLINDER NOT EXTENDING WITH SYSTEM 3 PRESSURE; WHICH MECHANICALLY INHIBITED TRAVEL OF GEAR HANDLE. DUE TO TRIM CYLINDER RELIEF VALVE RECENT CHANGE; SUSPECT RESIDUAL AIR IN SYSTEM. BLED TRIM CYL RELIEF VALVE; NO AIR. BLED HYD FUSE; FOUND A SIGNIFICANT AMOUNT OF AIR-ENTRAINED FLUID. BLED INTERLOCK CYLINDER. NO FLUID CAME OUT AT FIRST; FOLLOWED BY A SIGNIFICANT AMOUNT OF AIR ENTRAINED FLUID. AFTER BLEEDING; SYSTEM WORKS NORMALLY; INTERLOCK EXTENDS AND RETRACTS AS NORMAL; REF [type aircraft] AMM 32-31-05-2 AND AMM 32-37-03-2. JACKED ACFT AND SWUNG GEAR TO VERIFY A POSITIVE FIX. GEAR SWINGS NORMALLY WITH CORRECT INDICATION MULTIPLE CYCLES. ACFT OK FOR SERVICE. Is it reasonable to draw a connection between leg 1 and leg 2 as to cause and effect for the gear handle stuck in the down position? After extensive research; I wasn't able to find a definitive answer as to a correlation. However; during my research; I discovered that it is maintenance procedure to bleed the hydraulic system after relief valve replacement. Interestingly enough; I even asked the mechanic about this. He response was to me was to set and release the brakes a few times; and then he asked me if they 'felt okay'. When I replied that 'They seemed normal' he said 'You're good to go'. Obviously; I wasn't good to go. I should also mention that after the job was declared complete; I went down to observe the new valve. There was hydraulic fluid everywhere including a 3 foot diameter puddle under the valve. As the Captain; when I ask specific questions about a maintenance procedure; it is unacceptable to be given incorrect information by maintenance or be lied to by maintenance. Why wasn't the procedure completed correctly? Why isn't there a check and balance system in place to verify mechanics are completing maintenance actions? I demand an answer to these questions as well as why there was so much air in the hydraulic system which inhibited gear handle movement.

column121: Descending on the STAR arrival around 11;000 ft. the FO (First Officer) deployed spoilers to slow and as the handle was moved we received a EICAS message for Hyd system pressure 'L'; hyd quantity; spoilers; rudder ratio etc. We selected hydraulic synopsis and noted left quantity '0' and pressure was low. As the fluid depleted the PTU engaged and L hyd pressure came up to 2800-3000 psi. We asked for an extended downwind for Runway XX and referenced the QRH HYD SYSTEM PRESSURE (L ONLY). We leveled at 6;000 ft. heading southwest. Slowed to 210 kts. and the FO continued flying as I accomplished the required items. After checking landing distance we decided to request Runway XY in case of steering issues or fluid leakage to not shut down Runway XX. We [advised ATC] asking for men and equipment standing by even though pressure was adequate. In the event any other systems were compromised. We configured to Flaps 1 normal. Continued to configure and slow and lowered the landing gear on an extended 15 mile final so we would have time to deal with any other issues that may arise. I took the controls as pilot flying and briefed the FO on various options we had in case of missed approach or control issues on the ground. FO did a tremendous job monitoring and capturing errors as they arose like finalizing checklists and call outs. We landed normal and stopped on Runway XY; cleared the runway at XX and stopped for crash rescue inspection of left wing area. We were informed fluid was leaking aft of number 1 L engine and shut down the L engine. We started the APU and shutdown R engine. We were informed brake temps were less than 150 and no smoke or fumes present. I referenced the various checklists regarding fluid loss and was told the leak had slowed. We coordinated with ZZZ operations; maintenance and ground control when fire rescue requested a clean up for hydraulic fluid on taxiway. Then maintenance tugged us back to the ramp at Gate XX. Failure of hydraulic component during descent while deploying speed brakes/flight spoilers. But I missed the fact at first that the loss of pressure on checklist has various systems and at first I referenced the pressure loss of L and C and then realized it was just the L quantity and pressure we were dealing with.
column123: I was the Pilot Flying; on descent through 11;000 ft. I deployed the flight spoilers. Shortly after; we had a master caution 'L HYD SYS PRESS' along with associated messages and lights on the hyd system panel on the overhead panel. The CA (Captain) checked the status page; when I looked at the status page L hyd quantity was at or near 0; and the pressure was normal (near 3000). There appeared to be a hydraulic leak with the PTU operable. I continued flying; we asked for vectors for an extended approach. The CA ran the checklist and [advised ATC]. We ran the HYD SYSTEM PRESSURE left only found on QRH 13.1.5. The checklist refers to a situation where the PTU is inoperable or complete loss of hydraulic fluid. We considered either one of these situations conceivable; so we opted for extended vectors and early configuration in case we needed alternate extension on either the flaps or the landing gear. We also elected to land on Runway XY so we wouldn't shut down Runway XX in case nose wheel steering was unavailable. The CA took the aircraft for the approach and landing. We configured and landed using flaps 20 per the checklist and cleared the runway uneventfully. Upon clearing; the fire trucks met us and informed us that we were leaking hydraulic fluid out of our left side. We turned on the APU and shut down both engines and the leak stopped. Maintenance towed us to our gate uneventfully.[Cause was a] Failed O Ring on left hydraulic system equipment.
