column121: This was the first leg of a 3-day trip and my 2nd trip in several months. I had not flown in several months due to COVID scheduling (but I have remained current with a PC simulator).  I was having difficulty in clearly hearing ATC and through the interphone in flight.  I was the pilot flying at the time of the event.  My First Officer has been enduring a highly antagonistic situation in the home life; which may have found its way to the flight deck; creating an unanticipated stressor.  My First Officer was distressed over these interactions; resulting in a secondary distraction.On approach; my First Officer (the pilot not flying) believed we were issued a clearance down to 2;400 feet and read back the misunderstood altitude of 2;400 feet.  I did not catch the altitude clearance.  Descending below 3;400 feet; ATC advised us of a low Altitude Alert and informed us that we were meant to be at 3;400 feet.  We apologized and explained it was a misheard clearance.  ATC asked us to climb back up to 3;400 feet and advised us we were still cleared for the approach.  We complied and continued without incident.We discussed as a crew the intention to submit a report that evening.  Being a bit rusty on operating in the physical environment and with the remainder of a 3-day to focus on (including a line check); I inadvertently forgot to write the report.  After our first 2 legs; I was scheduled to split from my First Officer to fly with a line check pilot (per my request prior to the trip) out of an abundance of caution; due to being out of the physical environment for so long.  It may be because we were no longer operating together that my First Officer and I forgot to submit our reports in a timely fashion (without having each other as a reminder).My job as a Captain is to ensure the aircraft is flown in a safe manner and that we comply with ATC instructions. The responsibility comes down to me to maintain total situational awareness in all phases of flight.  I became inadvertently disconnected from the communications loop as pilot flying.  This resulted in a breakdown of a good multi-crew concept; as well as an unsafe situation and unintentional deviation from ATC instruction.  I must remain more diligent and vigilant as a crew member in all aspects of flight; regardless of assigned duty in order to maintain safe and compliant operation.It is also imperative that I participate in SMS in a timely manner; consistent with company standards.  To be an effective team leader; it is also my duty to ensure my crew members take part in SMS.  This can only enhance safety for our colleagues and industry as a whole.  It was never my intention to neglect to submit a report; but unfortunately it was mistakenly forgotten.  I should make reminders for myself to stay on task with necessary reports.  In the future I may find it helpful to set reminders in my phone whenever issues like this arise.
column123: On approach to land; as the First Officer and PM for the leg; I responded to ATC's instruction to descend to 2;400 feet.  My Captain did verify with me the altitude to descend too; since Captain had not heard it clearly.  I advised that the assigned altitude was 2;400 feet.  It wasn't until we were descending below 3;400 feet that ATC checked in and advised that we were to level off at 3;400 feet.  We did proceed to climb back to 3;400 feet and continued the approach to land.The altitude of 2;400 feet was above the FAF altitude and ATC did not correct me when I replied to ATC with the confirmation to descend to 2;400 feet. It was then that; with the 2;400 foot altitude assignment being a bit lower than expected; even though ATC had not corrected me when I responded with a 2;400 foot altitude assignment; I should have verified the altitude assignment.In the future; as a First Officer and soon to be Captain; I will be more vigilant with all procedures and in the interest of safety and full compliance; verify that all direction and communications are clear; concise and without question.  If this is ever in doubt; I will take full responsibility and take all steps necessary to ensure a safe and compliant flight.

column121: Shortly after takeoff we received a bird strike in our Number 1 Engine that caused considerable damage. Based on the engine vibration as well as the unusual noises coming from the aircraft; we determined it was necessary to immediately return for landing at ZZZ. I received priority with air traffic control and the First Officer continued flying the aircraft. There were no ECAM actions or QRH follow ups. Although there were high vibration indications as well as some initial fluctuations with N1; N2 and EGT (Exhaust Gas Temperature); the engine parameters remained in the realm of normal. Therefore; the First Officer and myself did not see any reason for shutting the engine down in flight. We landed safely; let the airport personnel do a quick inspection of the aircraft on the taxiway and then returned to the gate.It all went fairly well. There was a startle factor with this event. But; in general we followed everything we learned in training. However; I may have delegated the re-configuring of the aircraft to the First Officer a bit too soon. He did that on his own. It was all done correctly. But; I don't remember doing the normal acceleration altitude call outs. I did all the standard communication procedures to ATC; cabin crew; passengers and Dispatch. Then; rejoined the First Officer for the approach preparation. The First Officer handled flying the aircraft as well as his communication with ATC perfectly.There is nothing that I can suggest that would prevent this from happening again. We always have to contend with the hazards associated with migratory waterfowl. Always consider that as a threat during that time of the year as well as keep a vigilant lookout.

column123: Transferring from Approach to Tower and upon passing Lexington VOR (HYK) we were asked to descend to 3;000 [feet]. Flying towards the departure end of [Runway] 22 we were asked if we had a visual of the airport. The Captain was non flying and answered yes. Then the Tower said that we were cleared for visual [Runway] 22 and a helicopter on the north end of the field was operating. That put us on a 45 downwind and once on the downwind; I then put 2;000 [feet] on the altitude selector. As per procedure 1;000 [feet] AGL is the lowest we can put in the selector. I then gradually decreased my descent from 3;000 and called for flaps setting three at speed 160 [knots] then gear down to be configured by the Runway 22 touchdown zone point. My descent was shallow and we did have the ILS 22 in the MCDU as reference. Turning within the outer-marker BRIDL we got an obstacle call. I was referencing an obstacle as referenced on the approach plate at 1;997 [feet] marked with an arrow at 1;997 [feet]. We were at 2;500 feet still descending as I looked to the right. I was about to call obstacle and perform the go-around procedure as per SOP but the call quickly ended. The call as per SOP is the trigger call 'Obstacle; Pull Up.' The call ended and we continued the standard turn. We were configured flaps five on the base leg and the continued on final. We descended once we captured the glide slope. We put 3;100 [feet] which was the missed approach procedure. The startling part of the flight was the obstacle call which we then started to look for something else; since we already had the tower obstacle in sight and we both confirmed the sighting.I think that in the future it's best to enter the traffic pattern and just follow the approach itself.

column121: We had a charter flight to ASE. The passengers wanted to go to Aspen but the weather and winds prohibited us from going there. We filed a flight plan to RIL and proceeded. I was the flying pilot. About 30 minutes away we saw the weather in ASE had improved so that we could get in and out. We called ATC and let them know we wanted to make the change. We changed the destination in the FMS and started the new routing to ASE. At one point we had trouble loading the approach into the FMS and I allowed myself to get involved in fixing the FMS. We were given a descent to 13;000; but 12;000 got set in the altitude selector. We were in visual conditions and were looking for the field. passing 12;600 we were told by ATC that we needed to climb to 13;000 as the MSA in our area was 13;000. I began a climb back up When ATC call back and said climb now low altitude alert. While climbing We immediately called the field in sight and were given a clearance for a visual approach. The approach was stable and we landed without incident. As we were taxing in we were given a phone number to contact for a possible deviation. I called the Tower and gave them my name certificate number and contact phone number for their paperwork. I believe that being the flying pilot and allowing myself to get involved in an FMS issue distracted me from catching the wrong altitude being set in the altitude selector. Following company procedures of flying the aircraft while letting the non-flying pilot program the FMS would have allowed me to recognize the altitude error and correct it.
column123: We were filled into RIL airport but passengers wanted to get into ASE. The weather cleared out of Aspen so we changed flight plan to arrive into ASE. We were cleared to ASE airport and getting set up for the LOC DME E. While being vectored for the visual approach and watching the weather in the area; we descended below MSA close to JARGU by 300 feet. ATC informed us. We were in VMC conditions and saw airport but descended before calling airport in sight and before being cleared for the visual approach. We should have followed altitudes on the LOC DME E. We rushed ourselves because it was getting late and we wanted to get in and back out of Aspen before sunset. Resolved by getting back to altitude and calling airport in sight and cleared for the visual.

column121: After completing maneuvers in the practice area; we went to shoot the RNAV Runway XX into ZZZ. This approach was done under the hood with the left engine throttle closed for a simulated engine out approach. This approach was done successfully with a few touch and goes done afterwards. After completing the touch and goes we contacted approach; and went back to the Practice Area. After the engines warmed up to ideal operating temperature; due to the warmer weather we decided we were going to shut down the right engine entirely and feather the engine. Pulling the mixture to idle cutoff; and prop lever to feather; we did just that. After 1-2 minutes we tried to restart the engine. After running the checklist the engine prop turned over a few times but did nothing more. As the prop was turning over the electrical system stopped working and we had no avionics; nor could my instructor and I hear each other in our headsets. We tried to start the engine several more times; but the prop wouldn't turn over; as the battery wasn't charging and what we assumed at the time; the electrical system had failed. We then squawked 7600; ran the engine failure checklist; and my instructor contacted Tower over his phone; for clearance back into the airport; and from there we squawked 7700. On the final approach my instructor and I could talk to each other once again; but after running the descent before landing checklist and turning on the left fuel pump; my instructor and I no longer could hear each other as the electrical system seemed to be overloaded. After landing; around 5-7 minutes our avionics came back on; and we could then talk to the controllers and was able to taxi back to the parking area of the flight school. During the incident the weather was clear; winds were calm; and pressure was roughly 30.35 inches.

column121: The Deviation event occurred over or around the HLMET intersection on the LDA Runway 35 approach into Salt Lake City International. ATC instructions were to proceed direct to HLMET; Cross HLMET at 11;000; cleared for the approach. Somewhere just seconds before or after crossing HLMET I descended to an altitude of approximately 9;600 MSL. The altitude on approach after crossing HLMET is 10;000 MSL until crossing the nest fix PEDLE. However after becoming distracted (which I will explain later); I noticed my altitude got down to that approximately 9;600 MSL for which I knew was not right; and immediately began corrective action while simultaneously ATC queried my altitude and I made mention of correcting. I saw I was just passed HLMET and quickly climbed back up to the crossing altitude of 10;000 MSL. Shortly later the controller mentioned the possible pilot deviation may have led to a loss of separation; although no TA/RA's were issued by either aircraft. Here is where I want to bring to attention the possible safety issue as related to the situation and what resulted in me becoming distracted and task saturated. Starting at an ATC controller back before TRACON; which was Salt Lake Center and while on the QWENN 5 RNAV Arrival off the MLF VORTAC transition; I was left extremely high by the center controller; for which I was expecting to receive the 'Expect' crossing restriction at FRNZY intersection at 15;000 MSL on the chart. I could hear multiple aircraft in front of me getting the FRNZY at 15;000 MSL restriction; but also complaining of being left very high and possibly not being able to make it. As I started to see the FMS computer show a required 3;500 FPM decent to make that restriction; I thought I better ask the controller for a descent; however the frequency was congested and it took many more minutes until finally the controller just issued me to now cross FRNZY at 16;000 MSL and 250 KTS. I replied that I would do by best; but it would be tight to make. Mind you that this new altitude required my attention to reprogram the altitude into the FMS as I anticipated and setup for 15;000; and still it showed a required 3;800+FPM decent to make it. I immediately initiated the decent for which I used the VNAV mode in the FMS/autopilot to make the crossing; which also required idle power and the activation of the aircraft's speed brake system to induce drag to not over-speed in the decent. During the decent on the arrival there was also light to bordering on moderate rime icing in IMC and snow showers. When the engines are at idle power they do not produce enough bleed air to keep the Anti-Ice/De-Ice systems operating; for which I got warning that they were not being kept hot enough; so I was trying to introduce small amounts of power to try and get more bleed air flowing to those systems; all the while trying not to over-speed and setup for the instrument approach. Being single-pilot this induced a very high work load; which caused me to become task saturated and behind on preparing for the approach. After finally passing FRNZY at the 16;000 MSL altitude and still in icing conditions and IMC I was simultaneously passed to TRACON approach control which issued me the direct HLMET; cross at 11;000 MSL; cleared approach restriction. I continued the decent down out of 16;000 MSL to 11;000 MSL still using VNAV on the autopilot (more on that later). I noticed I was still nearing around idle power and adding what I could but was still having trouble keeping the speed under control and still behind on setting up the approach. Somewhere around 12;000 MSL I got an indication that the speed brake panels went down; even though I didn't select it. Wondering what happened I looked out the pilot side window at the wing and noticed they were in fact still up; just no longer indicating it in the cockpit. This distracted me; as I knew I needed them extended to maintain my speed and help to try and keep power up and bleed air flowing. It took mybrain a few moments to try and figure out what was going on as there is no abnormal procedure for that in the checklist. I decided to recycle the speed brake switch; for which they then operated normally (retracted and extended); and then gave all normal indications. Throughout that situation is when the altitude deviation occurred; as after I was confident there was not a problem with the speed brakes and they just needed a reset; I accidentally went through the 11;000 MSL attitude down to the approximately 9;600 MSL altitude. Upon speaking with Maintenance later on the ground they feel that the system was activated for so long throughout the decent continuously; they work trapping hydraulic pressure to hold it up; that logically that pressure must have bleed down some; causing them to blow in-trial/down just enough to give an indication in the cockpit that they were sent fully down; and that this was not a malfunction or cause for investigation for repair; especially since they functioned normally after the reset. The indication only looks for full up or full down deflection; so if they blew down a little due to reduction in trapped pressure; it made sense to them. Again they continued to function and indicated correctly the rest of the flight. Back to the VNAV function I used on the autopilot to meet the crossing restriction; as that is the recommended function to meet crossing restrictions; and the function I always use to reduce pilot workload. Somewhere during the sequence of the approximate 3;800-4;000FPM required descent the VNAV system apparently kicked off and defaulted back to just a raw pitch autopilot decent; in which with everything else going on I failed to notice. I can only attribute this to it not liking or taking issue with that rapid of a required decent; and thus defaulted out of it. With 1500+ hours in type; I cannot recall ever descending so rapidly; to were I would have seen or noticed its inability to function through that rapid of a decent. Had VNAV stayed activated; it would have saved the deviation from happening as the approach was loaded with all crossing restriction altitudes and it would have followed them; for which I was also expecting it to do. Although this 'event' happened in Tracon airspace; I feel the safety issue started back in Salt Lake Centers airspace by being left very high on the arrival. ATC needs to be cognizant especially when icing conditions are possible/present some or most aircraft cannot descend that rapidly and keep critical anti-ice/de-ice systems operating properly with idle power descent. Additionally; giving instruction to meet a crossing restriction that requires 3;500+FPM descents is unsafe and not conducive to being able to setup and properly execute a stabilized approach; and leads pilots to get behind. After giving this event thought I am recommending to our flight department to not use the VNAV function of the FMS/autopilot for required descents over 3;000 FPM; but rather use vertical speed mode and monitor carefully. In addition; we will no longer accept any crossing restrictions from ATC that would require over 3;000 FPM; and rather state unable and require a re-sequence back on the arrival via a course reversal to help lose altitude and keep from the pilot getting behind the aircraft and task saturated. Us pilot use the term 'slam dunk' when ATC tries to do this; where they keep you very high and then plop you right on the arrival/approach. This condition does present safety issues due to the above mentioned items.

column121: The sector had been very busy. I had earlier dealt with the breakup of an ALTRAV (Altitude Reservation Flight Plan) where almost all of the original information was incorrect and the breakup required coordination with multiple sectors. I had a Radar Assist trainee training on position next to me with approximately 15 hours of training time on that position in the last two months during the flight breakup; and he had left to go assist another sector with the same flight breakup. While the training team was gone; I took the handoff from the adjacent Center sector on Aircraft X. He was level at 6;000 feet and needed a beacon code change.I lost radar contact with him around the boundary; which is not uncommon in that area. He did not check on; but radio coverage is not normally an issue in that area. I don't remember what I was doing; but I was talking to aircraft and looking at the south area of my scope for a while. When I realized Aircraft X had not checked on I tried him on multiple transmitter sites. I then dealt with some other aircraft requests before returning to Aircraft X. At this point; Aircraft X position was identified by ADS-B. The data block was still in coast track because he had never gotten the beacon code change. I had another aircraft near him at 12;000 feet and asked him to relay. I was off line coordinating during the relay. When I returned to the frequency; I dealt with aircraft checking on and their requests before asking the 2nd aircraft if he had gotten a response on the relay. He did not. I called the adjacent sector and asked them if Aircraft X had returned to them or if they had issued any lost communication procedures. The sector said they would reattempt the aircraft and call back. They called and said they were able to get Aircraft X via relay and that he would be coming to me. Aircraft X checked on; and I issued the new beacon code. The data block paired and I radar identified the aircraft and issued an altimeter. As this was happening; the Assist training team returned to my sector.I had an IR (instrument training route) for Aircraft Y that I was blocking for with an exit time of XA44Z; but I had not written down that the aircraft would be exiting at a point which is is my airspace. There is currently a radar outage at one of the radar sites and we are unable to see aircraft southeast of Approach's airspace below 7;500 feet. For the past week; when I have had aircraft come out of an IR route; I instruct them to maintain a VFR climb to 9;000 feet and issue their clearance once I can radar identify the aircraft. When I did that procedure with Aircraft Y; the pilot stated she was in IFR conditions and could not maintain a VFR climb. I was trying to get my Assist to coordinate a block altitude with another sector so I could issue a non-radar clearance; but I was also asking the Assist side trainer if there was a correct way to do this. I had no idea what the correct procedure was.The trainer was not paying attention to the scope and thought it was a hypothetical question; while the trainee had no idea who or what I was talking about. I was very focused on getting Aircraft Y her clearance because she was non radar in IFR conditions with icing in the area. At some point I noticed that Aircraft X was flashing an MSAW (Minimum Safe Altitude Warning) alert. I pulled up the IFR altitude chart; saw that Aircraft X was still at 6;000 feet and entering a block of 6400 feet and issued a climb. I issued 'Aircraft X climb and maintain 7;000 for a low altitude alert' but did not actually issue the low altitude alert. Aircraft X climbed quickly; but I believe they did violate the 6;400 foot block.We should have written procedures for non-radar IR exits. If there is one; I am unaware of it and should receive more training in that area. Since the radar site outage is a daily occurrence right now; and the IR routes are very frequent in this sector I feel like I should know exactly what to do instead of coming up with something that could be completely incorrect and continuing that procedure until it didn't work. I believe my focus on that event is what led me to miss the altitude until the MSAW alert went off. I have had specialized training in MSAW alerts and the issuance of a low altitude alert; but this is my first time ever actually seeing it and I failed to issue it.

column121: I was training a Controller on the sector. He gave a descent to an aircraft from 4;000 feet down to 3;000 feet. When the pilot read it back multiple aircraft keyed up at the same time. One of them was the correct pilot; another was another aircraft checking in; and the third was a C17 that thought the transmission was for him to descend to 2;000 feet. The Controller gave the instruction very clearly; and the descent was to a different aircraft to a different altitude. When the pilot called later he said that he always gets a decent to 2;000 feet there so he thought that's what the call was. When [the C17] descended to 2;000 feet that dropped him into a 2;000 foot (Minimum Vectoring Altitude). The altitude was recognized but not before penetrating a 2;500 foot MVA. A climb was issued and the pilot said he could maintain his own terrain and obstruction clearance. But that was after the MVA was already violated. It was obvious when the altitude read back was happening that more than one aircraft were keying up; it wasn't obvious that 3 were. Let alone an aircraft with a very different call sign descending to a very different altitude. This was a pretty clear case of expectation bias. The pilot was made aware of the situation. He said it was a very clear VFR day so he saw all the terrain just fine; and he just thought that is where aircraft got their descent to 2;000 feet.

column121: Aircraft X was holding at 4;000 feet at the missed approach fix (and also initial approach fix) for several instrument approaches at. They had already executed the Missed Approach Procedure once because of weather below minimums. The pilot advised me that they wanted to try again. Since they were already established in a holding pattern published for the ILS approach; I cleared them for the ILS approach and issued the altimeter.The procedure is clear that the only route of flight allowable from holding is via the 10 DME arc to a straight-in course on the localizer. That is what I expected them to fly. I quickly redirected my attention to a sequence of three other aircraft I was trying to shoot a gap with; through a band of weather. At the same time; I had another arrival that was opposite direction; outbound from the same gap. When I was able to finally scan back to Aircraft X I noticed that they were not on the 10 DME arc; and had strayed into a 4;000 foot Minimum IFR Altitude at 3;000 feet. My first thought was that they decided to shoot a different approach; but when queried; the pilot responded that they still planned the ILS. However; their current position did not correlate to any possible point on the Approach.When questioned further; the pilot said that they were direct to a fix to intercept the localizer. They had received neither a direct clearance nor a descent clearance. Without any more questioning; I informed them that the Minimum Vectoring Altitude (technically minimum IFR altitude) in that area is 4;000 feet; and issued a 'cancel approach clearance' and 'climb immediately; maintain 4;000 feet.' The MSAW (Minimum Safe Altitude Warning) did not activate. Because there was no audible alarm; and the fact that I knew 3.000 feet was still a safe altitude; I chose to not use the 'low altitude alert' portion of the phraseology. Later; after discussion with; and as recommended by the Operations Manager; I issued a warning to the pilot.Because this occurrence was a pilot deviation; there is not much from the ATC perspective that would have changed the outcome. Undoubtedly; the pilots' workload was high; due to the missed approach and bad weather. The design of the approach is also somewhat complicated because there are variations including the arc; published holding; and an outbound course on the localizer (which they apparently wanted to fly); but they don't all connect logically. However; the pilots should've queried if unsure.

column121: ASE Approach has a very bad habit of violating Sector 06's airspace; especially on busy days. Today was a very heavy traffic day; there were continuous EGE departures and arrivals every 5 miles. ASE approach busted our airspace with Aircraft X at 140; called me the D side up for a too late point out. When I wouldn't immediately say point out approved (they only gave a call sign; no CID; and there were data blocks everywhere making it impossible to see) they became belligerent saying he was already in my airspace I needed to approve their point out now! column121: Fuel leak discovered prior to pushback. Maintenance says 'no big deal happens all the time.' So we ran an engine to see if the leak would seal and shut down and ran 70.20 QRH. Maintenance tells me leak is gone no drips. I opened my window and visually checked the engine and saw fuel leaking at an alarming rate from the bottom of the number one engine. FO (First Officer) and I went outside and measured the rate of drips and we recorded 175 drips per minute. Asked Maintenance why they told us the engine was not leaking; and they denied seeing any leak. We would have taken off with a major fuel leak had we not checked ourselves. Maintenance in ZZZ was pushing us to depart because they needed the gate. ZZZ Maintenance's overriding concern was obviously not for the safety of the passengers and crew. 8 fire crew surrounded the aircraft after the leak was discovered and they said they would not authorize another engine start yet Maintenance asked us to try again to start even though fuel was pouring out of the engine.
column123: Just prior to engine start ground crew reported fuel leaking from Number 1 Engine. We performed QRC Fuel Leak. It failed. Logbook entry accomplished. Asked to do engine run. Got permission; coordinated with all; did 5 minute engine run. Shut down engine. Ground personnel said there were no leaks. Captain looked outside window and steady stream of fuel was leaking from engine.Captain and I went down to look at leak and count drops per minute. 175 drops per minute at that point which progressed later to a steady stream of fuel coming out. Fire Department responded with 2 engines. During the ensuing hours; MX (Maintenance) kept trying to get us to do another engine run. Fire Department said due to the amount of fuel leaking they would not allow it at the gate. We absolutely agreed. MX kept coming up to us with documents telling us this was OK; and if we would just do this engine run; all would be well.In spite of this; MX wanted to run a procedure for a 60 or 100 drops per minute engine leak. We were originally at 175 drops per minute and progressed to a steady stream. Clearly this procedure did not apply. Both Captain and I were very uncomfortable with all of this. Jumping back to the leak first being discovered and the need to do an engine run; MX attempted to get us to hurry up with the engine run because a 777 needed the gate. This was mentioned several times; to the point where the Captain became so uncomfortable he had to tell them to slow down; follow procedure; and focus on what we were doing. As the engine run resulted in an even worse problem; Captain refused the aircraft and we left the scene. Operations refused to cancel the flight for a considerable period of time. This delay was so bad; the Captain and I eventually left the airport for a hotel. Scheduling talked to the Captain and informed him we would be flying into our day off; a new part would be flown in; jet fixed; and we were scheduled for an MX ferry flight on the [Date1]. We got to aircraft only to discover no part had been flown in. Nothing had been fixed. MX had done several engine runs and said there was no leak. This was; in my career of flying jets for Company since [Year]; and having done many thousands of walkarounds; by far the worst leak I have ever seen. Something in the jet broke. We were told it would be fixed. Nothing was fixed. At this point; we had lost confidence in anything local maintenance was telling us because they were still trying to use a checklist; which they showed us; with very minor 60-100 drops per minute leaks. The part you see in the attached photo was not replaced. Nothing was replaced. We refused the jet again. Numerous attempts were made to get us to do a high powered engine run; which we are 1) not trained 2) there was heavy rain and standing water; making for slick surfaces; so we would not have done it under those conditions anyway. Captain refused jet; and due to the pressure put on us from local maintenance; we left airfield. Scheduling put us on a deadhead flight home the following day. Scheduling sent crew out on [Date2]; DH to ZZZ & MX ferry jet Aircraft X back to ZZZ1; even after no repair was made to this part.

column121: As pilot monitoring; I was handling the radios. Center cleared us for the 'RNDRZ 1 arrival Runway 26L' which I read back. We had set up for that arrival and runway; validated it; and briefed it thoroughly to include the issues with turning early if cleared for the visual which presented a terrain problem. Upon selection of the Runway 26L runway and the RNDRZ 1 arrival in the box; the aircraft automatically selected the Runway 26L transition which we understood we were cleared for. The Captain and I both verified with the other that we were cleared for the transition and we agreed that what the box presented to us was what we were cleared for. At the waypoint BERBN the jet turned onto the Runway 26L transition as planned. We received a radio call to turn back to a 130 heading and then given subsequent vectors to final and landed without incident. We were told by ATC that we should not have turned onto the transition. Looking back over the arrival and approach plates again and again; I still think we did what we were cleared for. If receiving the clearance for the 'RNDRZ 1 Runway 26L' doesn't mean clearance for the Runway 26L transition I'm not sure what does. Such verbiage at other airports indicates clearance onto the transition. The arrival plate is confusing however because at BERBN it directs the reader to 2 different things at once. It directs the reader to the Runway 26L transition found on the approach plate and also the possibility of continuing on the present heading to expect vectors to final. Even with that; to be cleared for the arrival and runway has always meant cleared for that runway's transition. Furthermore; the transition does not connect with the approach to Runway 26L giving greater weight to the fact that one need not be cleared for an approach to be cleared for the transition. I believe the Captain and I did exactly what we were cleared to do and that our understanding of that clearance corresponds to our experience and training.Causal factors were incorrect chart depiction and the aircraft navigational system automatically linking the Runway 26L transition when that arrival and runway are selected.Chart needs to be revised to make clear when the transition is to be used and when not. The aircraft navigation system needs to be updated to reflect how ATC wants the approach flown.

column121: FO (First Officer) and I both believed with confidence that ATC had instructed us to turn right to a heading upon reaching CLUSO. Neither of us had any doubt about the matter. That was the first instance we had any doubt about what our clearance had been. At that point; second-guessing ourselves; the FO and I began to wonder whether we had read back 'KAYTO' or 'CLUSO' when first given the heading clearance. Both waypoints sound similar when pronounced; and this similarity may have contributed to this new doubt. So; we were not sure if the error was ours or ATC's. In any case; ATC informed us that there was 'no problem' with the turn and then gave us further vectors. There was no traffic conflict.In retrospect; the only thing that may have played a role in any confusion that may have occurred with either ATC or with us is that 'KAYTO' and 'CLUSO' can sound similar; causing the wrong term to be ensconced in memory.Consider not having waypoints in close proximity to each other that may sound similar when pronounced.

column121: We pushed off the gate and taxied out to spot XX to switch to ground. Upon reaching the spot; we contacted ground a minimum of 6 times and sat for more than 5 minutes before finally getting a response. We had planned for runway XXL but were given XY which was unusual for a northbound departure out of ZZZ. We were told to taxi 1; 2 and to give way to company traffic which was passing right to left on [Taxiway] 1. Once the traffic had passed; we made the left turn onto 1 and I announced to the Captain that I was going heads down to change the runways. I changed the runway on the route page and it did not uplink so I glanced at the iPad for a quick check of the numbers. During that quick look; movement caught my eye out of the rear right window and I turned to see another aircraft quickly approaching the Captain's blind spot on either [Taxiway] 3 or 4. I alerted the Captain of the traffic and he aggressively applied the brakes and stopped the aircraft prior to the intersection. The other aircraft taxied past without noticeably altering its speed and we continued taxing once clear. I am confident that both aircraft would have experienced a fuselage to fuselage collision had we not noticed the traffic at the precise moment that we did.  Ground controllers were busy and weather was in the area. I don't know where the other aircraft came from but we were never given any reference to the traffic or hold short instructions. Additional staff working the ground frequency for that particularly busy bank in ZZZ. Also; make crews aware that when two taxiways intersect at less than a 90 degree angle on the right side; there is a significant blind spot for the captain which makes checking for traffic very difficult.
column123: We were cleared to taxi to runway XX from spot XX via [Taxiways] 1 and 2.  The airport had just reopened after being closed for weather.  Controllers were swamped trying to give clearances and deal with multiple aircraft.  We were not advised of approaching aircraft nor were we issued hold short instructions.  Another aircraft was approaching the [taxiways] 1 and 2 intersection on [Taxiway] 2 while we were approaching on [Taxiway] 1.  They were coming from our right rear at a 45 very fast.  My FO (First Officer) saw him first as he broke into his field of vision he alerted me.  I applied mildly aggressive braking to stop while the other aircraft showed no signs of slowing down.  If I had not been alerted or even alerted 2 seconds later there would have been a collision in the intersection.  It was a dangerous near miss that even after the fact neither ground nor the other aircraft seemed aware of.  I contacted ground and told them it was near miss.Airports are starting to get busy again but I feel controllers and pilots are not as current as we were.  Someone should have caught this before it happened.Ground is going to have to step up their game if airlines are adding flights to ZZZ.  You can't be giving clearances on ground frequency when you are already overloaded.  That's crazy.

column121: Departed ZZZ after an unexpected runway change from Runway X to Runway YL due to high winds. After takeoff I was the PM and the FO was the PF. We were assigned Runway YL ZZZZZ. ZZZZZ1 departure. There was a fair amount of turbulence due to the strong westerly winds flowing over the mountains. On the departure you are supposed to cross the fix ZZZZZ2 below 10;000 feet MSL. We were climbing in VNAV Path and the FO was hand flying. We ended up going thru 10;000 to approximately 10;400 feet MSL due to VNAV not commanding the FD to level off. As the FO who was the PF was returning to 10;000 feet MSL the Controller told us to level off at 10;000 feet MSL; which we were already doing. It was clear and VMC at this time. There were no targets on TCAS and nothing was said about any loss of separation. I immediately rechecked the box to ensure the departure was there and the rest of the altitude constraints were correct; which they were. The flight continued to ZZZ2 uneventful and nothing else was said by the Controller.Last minute runway change was a contributing factor as we more thoroughly briefed the Runway X departure at the gate. The moderate turbulence on departure affected aircraft controllability and instrument scan. The fact that we departed from a field elevation of XXXX feet MSL and 10;000 feet MSL came a lot quicker than normal (flying from home base). The fact had I recently transitioned to the aircraft and have only flown less than 50 hrs since October 2020 and often go 2-4 weeks without flying.   Another contributing factor is my lack of HUD experience and the division of duties when looking thru the HUD but not having any navigational information presented on the HUD. Long sit time in ZZZ Departure airport.Take more time to rebrief a departure after runway change. Emphasize the high field elevation and how much quicker we will be at 10;000 feet MSL than what we are typically used to flying out of ZZZ1. Use the HUD for the takeoff but develop a better scan with the navigational display to enhance situational awareness on a departure procedure. Consider the use of a higher level of automation to reduce workload in turbulent conditions.

Flight crew then requested an additional low approach and ZZZ Tower indicated that the nose gear still appeared to be retracted; but that the nose gear doors were open. PIC executed missed approach and departed traffic pattern to complete speed turns in attempt to lower the nose gear. Procedure proved to be unsuccessful. Another low approach was conducted and ZZZ Tower said the nose gear still appeared to be up; with the gear doors open. PIC requested priority handling; then gave passengers onboard an additional briefing. Flight crew briefed the landing procedure multiple times and then entered an approximately 15 mile final for Runway XXL at ZZZ. Flight crew fully configured aircraft for landing (with the exception of three gear indicators in down and locked state) at 10 mile final and briefed landing procedure again. PIC landed disabled aircraft on Runway XXL at ZZZ in accordance with procedure for nose-gear unsafe state. Flight crew and passengers evacuated aircraft after it came to a stop on Runway XXL ZZZ. While ground personnel and local responders worked to remove the aircraft from the runway; a police officer came into the FBO with an (estimated 9-10' long) chrome socket/ratchet extender in his hand; and informed the flight crew that he had removed that item from the retracted nose gear. Police officer stated he removed the tool from the location where the aircraft tow pin/head is supposed to be installed for towing and that it was almost as wide as the nose gear door opening on the aircraft.I suggest an additional line item be added to the aircraft's certified Pre-Flight Inspection Checklist and Before Start Checklist that includes wording/verbiage to identify and confirm that a certified tow head; tow pin; or otherwise foreign or unapproved object is not in the nose strut of the aircraft. I also suggest the identification of a clear nose strut tow-pin location be added to the PIC's final before flight walk-around. I suggest additional training and oversight of FBO line personnel that includes a mandate of using certified; tagged and visually identifiable; approved tow pins for the aircraft they are moving and the importance of removing them immediately after ground movement/towing is completed.

column121: I operated Aircraft X from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. The weather was low; approximately 600 OVC at ZZZ and rain. I believe we had an alternate of ZZZ2. We planned to shoot the ILS to Runway 7 at ZZZ. I was the pilot flying. We operated the flight to ZZZ normally and got set up for the ILS to Runway 7. I was established on the approach and fully configured at approximately 1;000 feet when I noticed that both the localizer and glide slope were flagged. I was looking at the PFD (Primary Flight Display) and slightly startled by the lack of information. I then glanced to the First Officer's side and noticed his PFD looked normal. I never felt any erratic pitch attitudes but according to FOQA (Flight Operations Quality Assurance); we reached 12 degrees pitch down and up to 2700 FPM descent below 1;000 feet. I remember hearing the aural 'glide slope glide slope' The FO (First Officer) then questioned; 'should we go-around?' I responded yes and initiated a go around. We climbed up to 3;000 feet and requested radar vectors back around for the same approach. I then transferred the controls to the First Officer because his navigation equipment was operating normally. We continued on the approach. At approximately 600 feet I called runway in sight; and he responded landing. We drifted to the right of the approach course; due to the First Officer not reacting to the left crosswind. We were also a bit high on the glide slope. I told him to correct; and asked him if he was able to correct the flight path; he responded correcting. We ended up landing hard and fast. I taxied off normally. I forgot to write up the discrepancy that the airplane lost localizer and glide slope. I believe the cause of this event was due to the gradual failure of the glide slope and my reaction to that. It took us approximately 38 seconds from when the failure occurred until the missed approach was executed.  I don't think it would hurt to see this event repeated in a simulator so that I can see it again and understand how I could have reacted better.
column123: I was Pilot Monitoring for an approach into ZZZ1. We were conducting the ILS to runway 7 at ZZZ1; and had just passed the final approach fix when the Captain's glideslope malfunctioned and presented a red 'GS' flag. My instruments appeared to continue to provide accurate glideslope indications; and the autopilot remained engaged; coupled to the Captain's side; and continued to fly the aircraft. I don't recall noticing which vertical mode took over in the absence of the GS. I suggested to the Captain that a go-around be made; she waited several seconds to see if the glideslope indications would return; then disconnected the autopilot to execute the go-around. The Captain applied TOGA (Takeoff/Go-around) power. Upon applying go-around power; the pitch attitude further decreased; and the vertical rate of descent correspondingly increased; causing a GPWS sink-rate warning. Visual ground contact was made briefly before the descent was arrested. We continued the climb straight out and contacted Approach for missed approach instructions. This event began with the malfunction of the Captain's side glideslope. This led to a breakdown in situational awareness and crew communication as the aircraft continued to descend in the absence of the glideslope until a go-around maneuver was executed. I believe additional training may be required; both on go-around procedures as well as on equipment malfunctions during approach.

column121: We were cruising at FL390 and we called the back for a break. I was the second pilot to exit the flight deck and while in the main cabin I noticed the pitch of the aircraft.  I then made a brief break and called to return to the flight deck.  Once the flight deck door opened and the A came out I noticed the thrust levers advancing to max power and the airspeed indicator slowly approaching the amber band.  I then immediately called for a lower altitude as I took my seat and once I was in my seat I looked at my First Officer and said we need lower now.  My First Officer then dialed a lower altitude on the FMC and selected descent via V/S (Vertical Speed). I then gathered all info on what we were experiencing and thought either we had an unreliable airspeed or runaway stabilizer.  As I looked back at our altitude; I realized we weren't descending and our airspeed was slowly approaching amber pole.  At that time I disconnected A/T (Autothrottle); A/P (Autopilot) and started a slow descent and requested my First Officer to call in our descent to ATC.  ATC then notified us that we needed to stop descent at FL370 due to lower aircraft.  My training kicked in and I figured if this went back we would need around 10;000 feet to recover so I then requested a vector off course.  We then were given 10 degrees left and I leveled off at FL370 continued to hand fly and one by one acquired A/P; HDG; VNAV.  Our Airspeed gained approximately 30kts and we were stable at FL370 on a heading.  ATC asked why the need to descend and I replied we encountered mountain wave and could not hold altitude. ATC then replied that we were the first to complain of mountain wave. Seconds later an aircraft at FL470 notified of +/- 1000 gain/loss and another airliner requesting lower due to mountain wave. We were then given direct to a waypoint on our flight plan and landed at destination without further incident. Be more vigilant while single pilot operations.

column121: While boarding the ramp manager arrived to the flight deck with a NOTOC regarding 20 KG of dry ice being loaded onto the aircraft. The Ramp Manager informed the Captain that it was freight containing pharmaceuticals; not a UN3373. She also told the Captain that [this] was not an expedite item. Moments later the Dispatcher sent an ACARS to tell the Captain to verify that the package was an expedite item. The Ramp Manager again confirmed that it was NOT an expedite item. The Captain called the Dispatcher and they discussed that the package was not a expedite medical supply item or an expedite UN3373 and was therefore limited to 2.5KG per package. Because the package was 20 KG the Captain asked that it not be loaded. After swapping aircraft due to an unrelated Maintenance issue; the Captain went to look at the package and noted that it had a handwritten label saying it was the X Company Vaccine. The Captain noted that because it was not an expedite item it was not labeled normally; i.e.; it did not state 'Contains dangerous goods...' and did not have the dry ice placard. It also had a marking indicating that it contained no dangerous goods. When speaking with the Dispatcher again the Dispatcher told the Captain that we were indeed authorized to carry it citing the national state of emergency due to the pandemic. Captain read the FOM chapter pointing out that it was not an expedite medical supply item and not an expedite UN3373 and should therefore be limited to 2.5 kg of dry ice; but the Dispatcher assured the Captain that we could take it. The Captain confirmed that the package would not be able to fly on any other flight that day. After conferring with Dispatch; and the manager who brought up the NOTOC who confirmed the contents the package was loaded on to the aircraft. There were no further issues.Flight crew and Dispatch worked together to determine if the item was safe for transport.Speaking with Dispatch and the Ramp Manager; it became clear that each party agreed that the 20 kg of dry ice would normally exceed the limit for an individual package that is not an expedite medical supply item or expedite UN3373; it was; however; also agreed that this vaccine shipment was somehow excepted from that normal requirement. The cause would seem to be some confusion as to whether or not freight which is not an expedite item that contained medical supplies; specifically the Vaccine; were allowed. Perhaps a lack of guidelines specific to the transport of the vaccine was a possible cause (if such an exemption from policy exists). The Captain determined after speaking with the individual parties that it would be safe to transport.Better guidance; including up to date flow charts; to help navigate this issue. It is not entirely clear whether a medical supply needs to be an expedite item in order to be exempt from the individual limitations of 2.5 kg. Although both the Captain and the Dispatcher initially thought that it does need to be an expedite item to contain more than 2.5 KG; the chapter in the FOM does not expressly say either way. The exception to the limit of 2.5KG appears to be listed under the expedite item section on the maximum limits page of the FOM; but it then states; 'Dry Ice weight may exceed the 2.5 kg (5.5 lbs) limitation; if contained within the UN3373 expedite item or medical shipment.' The use of the word 'or' may indicate that a medical supply need not be an expedite item even though it is located under the expedite item section. This could use clarification. If a medical shipment can exceed 2.5 KG without being an expedite item; then it should be listed as a separate exception. Similarly; if the medical shipment MUST be an expedite item that should also be clearly stated. If there is some exception due to the pandemic for the COVID vaccine that should be conveyed. The current flow chart contained on our system could stand to be updated. Specially; it lists all limits in pounds; but the NOTOC is in KG; which in itself renders the tool useless. Also; the flow chart ask the question 'is dry ice in an expedite item?' This is a yes or no question; but the flow chart only has an option for 'YES.'

column121: On climb out at SFO; on initial contact with departure control ATC advised us that the preceding aircraft reported a drone near OAK at approximately 4;000 ft. After flap retraction I deemed it prudent to maintain a best rate of climb till out of 4;000 ft. At around 3;600 ft. the FO (First Officer) verbalized he had visual contact with the drone pointing to the 11 o'clock position. Shortly after; I then established visual contact. The drone passed just to our left and under us. I would estimate we came to approximately 500 ft. of it. ATC was notified and flight proceeded to destination without further incident.I'm assuming the drone was not being operated under any legal clearance. Furthermore the drone had no transponder making our TCAS useless in this case. I am pleased with my decision to maintain a good rate of climb until clear of drone.Unfortunately drone sightings around busy airports are becoming more rampant. And like bird strikes; very little is known exactly what type of damage can occur to a jet airliner if a collision occurs. It is my hope that the FAA and law enforcement will do whatever is necessary to protect the airspace that is crucial for safety of flight.

column121: Somewhere after Burns Flat (BFV) at 38;000 ft. and until ZUN VOR; we had encountered first an ATC Fault EICAS message. Oddly then on both transponders. First Officer was the Pilot Flying. So; we discussed and went into the QRH and complied. I had then though to ask ABQ ARTCC if they were able to see us on their radar scope. The controller had replied yes. So when I remarked of our issue; he knew right away that jamming was taking place. Now I didn't clarify if this was any kind of military exercise and if this was normal. He acted as though it was. Shortly after this; we started slowly seeing other EICAS messages. I can't remember the exact order though. I believe the next was EGPWS TERR or so. Then L GPS appeared not too far after this. Maybe R GPS as well; maybe. Eventually we saw UNABLE RNP. So we definitely knew GPS jamming was making sense. The RNP ANP scales on the Pilot Flying Display bottom was like RNP 2.00 ANP 2.93 in amber color. It was clear our GPS was in an inertial mode. I did select radio updating eventually per the QRH's procedural instructions. Center never seem too concerned as nothing else was said. The weather was quite good and while concerned; I had a good idea as we made our way towards ZZZ1; the start of the RNAV star; the GPS navigation would probably return to a normal state and it did. There wasn't any flight safety breaches or traffics conflicts as this event happened entered at cruise. Although; I did forget to make a maintenance log entry required by mandatory reports. I may have been more fatigued than I was aware. Sleep was fragmented in chunks of multiple 2 to 3 or so hrs. on this day. Intentional GPS jamming I suppose. I've never encountered this in my entire career here. Wondering if the military does these exercises; but I would expect we'd be notified via a NOTAM and on our [flight plan] if it was known. I suppose if we knew we could of had a different routing? I don't believe compromised safety as in this case was an issue. It never degraded to a more severe off course deviation and didn't cause traffic conflicts. Don't get me wrong we were concerned and a bit miffed. I will file a security report and read more on the subject of GPS jamming interference's.

column121: We were taking off behind an EMB-170 on 26L. ATL will routinely clear you for takeoff before the aircraft in front of you has rotated and that was the case for this takeoff as well. After we rotated and selected the landing gear to the up position; I noticed some left and right wing rocking which usually indicates wake turbulence. We were climbing out at V2+10 and suddenly we had airspeed fluctuations and received a WINDSHEAR Warning message. Following the windshear escape procedure; I followed the command bars and selected full thrust due to the low airspeed and close proximity to the ground. I believe we received the warning below 600 ft AGL. As I was following the command bars; I noticed the right engine Aircraft X was flashing red. Shortly thereafter; the warning ceased and I pulled the engines back to the flex carats and requested the autopilot be activated to alleviate workload. I monitored the engine for the rest of the flight and it all seemed normal. Once out of sterile; I informed the Dispatcher and Maintenance Control via ACARS of the event and called them arriving at the destination. While on the phone with Maintenance Control after the flight; I checked the engine exceedance log in the maintenance computer menu and it showed that the engine encountered a level 3 event for 6.9 seconds and that the peak temperature was 927degC. The Maintenance Control technician checked the GE engine manual and informed me that while it wasn't outside of limitations; to write it up and they would have local maintenance come and sign it off. The weather in ATL was not gusty and no wind shear was reported in the area.I believe ATL is clearing aircraft too close to other aircraft. Wake turbulence encounters are a threat. Despite being of a similar size; the Aircraft in front of us put off enough wake to rock the aircraft and cause airspeed deviations strong enough to activate the windshear warning system. Encountering wake turbulence in ATL is a common occurrence though it doesn't typically cause windshear warnings to go off.I think there should be either more separation or perhaps a study into whether ATL Tower is following proper spacing procedure. I feel that if we encountered the wake of a larger aircraft; the airspeed deviations could have been more severe and there is not much margin for error when you're climbing at V2+10.

Just prior to engine start; ground crew said fuel was leaking from Number 1 engine. Followed QRC; ended up doing engine run. Ground crew stated no leaks after engine run. Captain looked out window to see fuel streaming from number one engine. This was never resolved. We refused to fly aircraft. Were told by scheduling a new part was being flown in and we would Maintenance ferry jet home on the XXth [Date]; our scheduled day off.On XXth [Date]; discovered; at jet; no part had arrived but we were told to ferry jet to ZZZ1 and it would be fixed. After consultation with numerous agencies and several hours; we again refused jet. Nothing had been fixed. Worst engine leak I've ever seen. The directives Maintenance was following were for leaks in the range of 60 to 100 drops per minute of fuel. This became a steady stream the day prior. We refused to fly jet as nothing had been done.Took some time to get hotel; had to self-help. Arrived to hotel. Scheduled to deadhead home on XYth [Date]. Due to mix-up; transportation went to wrong hotel. We missed XA00 flight home. Rescheduled for XD:50 pm flight home. I had a ZZZ turn today; XZth [Date]; with a XA50 report. This was illegal crew rest so the crew desk did a mini-pack of my schedule; combined the now 4-day trip with 4 duty periods into a 5 day trip and 5 duty periods with near absolute minimum rest.I spent some time checking on the legality of what was done; with company. It turns out; this extremely onerous now 5 day pairing with very limited rest opportunity was legal. Legal doesn't mean smart or does it mean a pilot really has adequate rest.I gave every effort in an attempt to get adequate rest; but the pressure; once finally in bed; and reflection on the maintenance issues; the mental fatigue caused by the ever-changing schedule; flying into now two days off; and then paired with a trip packing with minimal rest caused sleep to be very difficult. Two-hour time difference; though seemingly minor; comes into play as I'd become acclimatized.I finally realized; as I was about to go to parking lot; I was not safe to fly nor could I certify FFD. I called fatigued.

column121: Descending into ZZZ; we received an RA from a VFR traffic crossing our path below us at approximately 5;500 ft. MSL. We were descending to initially 3;000 ft. MSL to setup for landing on Runway XX (VMC conditions prevailed and the ATIS advertised a visual to Runway XX); but then were told to maintain 6;000 ft. MSL by Center for VFR traffic she was not talking to in our path. Hearing and seeing this scenario develop we shallowed our descent rate to level at 6;000 ft. MSL in an attempt to mitigate a predictive RA scenario. Once level and seeing the traffic was continuing in our direction; we also attempted a turn to avoid the traffic prior to the RA; however the frequency was congested and the turn was too late. Once we received permission to turn and initiated it; we ended up receiving the RA. We complied with the RA; disengaged the autopilot; and also climbed to approximately 6;500 ft. MSL to avoid the traffic showing at one point 400 ft. below us and advised Center of the RA. We were given permission to climb and; once clear of the conflict; to proceed to ZZZ without further issue.The event occurred due to a few factors coming together. The main issue is that the VFR aircraft was maneuvering without talking to ATC so as to avoid traffic. It was also a beautiful day; so there was a lot of GA aircraft the Controller was working with causing the frequency to become very congested. Secondly; the Controller should have issued us a vector or higher altitude to maintain to avoid the traffic as we never had or called aircraft in sight. We could have tried to turn earlier; but the congestion on the frequency prevented this from happening as well.I feel that this issue could have been prevented had the Controller issued us a higher level off altitude; or given us a vector once it was determined that the VFR target could become an issue. I feel that we tried our best to avoid this scenario by shallowing our descent and even requesting a turn. It just came down to the VFR traffic had an unpredictable flight path; the frequency was very congested; and once we received our clearance to turn it was too late.

column121: We departed ZZZ on a Part 91 leg to ZZZ1. Reaching our initial assigned altitude from approach we were given a climb to 17;000 and that's when we lost EDC2 without making any changes to anything. We were caught totally by surprise. As a result there were several alarms and aural warnings sounding that could not be silenced. That's also when we realized that we could no longer communicate through the intercom and the First Officer had zero radio communication. We communicated through hand signals and loud talking. I was the Pilot Monitoring on this leg but I took controls at this point since I was the only one with radio communication. I pressed the autopilot disconnect button to ensure everything was disengaged and never made an attempt to reactivate it. I leveled at 14;000 and asked for a heading to troubleshoot and run the appropriate checklist. I announced that we had a failure of EDC2 and asked my First Officer to run the checklist. I couldn't hear any part of the checklist but he announced that the last step was to land as soon as practical.  I [requested priority handling] and asked for vectors back to ZZZ. I received a heading and a descent and [the] First Officer competed the appropriate checklists for descent and approach. On final approach during our before landing checklist we realized the gear did not indicate down. We aborted the landing and tried to see if the Tower controller could confirm if the gear was down or not. We made the first pass and he thought it was down but asked us to make one more pass with all the lights off in the Tower so they could try to get a better look. Again he said it looked like they were down. I considered calling for the emergency gear extension procedures but I felt a sense of urgency to get on the ground. There were several alarms sounding and we were still struggling to communicate. I was attempting to troubleshoot mentally but hand flying the airplane was my priority. At this point I realized I was getting overloaded and we still had no idea what had caused the failure in the first place. I was worried things could continue to get worse at any moment and I decided to land because so believed it was the safest thing to do. Just before touch down I recognized the gear was not down and I gently applied pressure on the power levers backwards against the flight idle stops to fully committed to the landing. At this point I knew a go around was dangerous. We touched down smoothly on centerline skidded down the runway. We finally came to a gentle halt just slightly off the runway in the grass. We ran the shutdown procedures and evacuated through the door where we were greeted by fire rescue. After walking away without even a scratch I discovered things were starting to come back to me that I couldn't seem to remember during flight. Details about the systems that I've learned in training that I could not dig out of my head while we were in flight. I've learned a lot about myself and how I react when the workload gets high and I know I can handle any future emergency better than this one. That being said; my First Officer and I were the only ones involved and we walked away completely unscathed.

column121: After landing at MLB I turned off of Runway 9L at Taxiway Mike and was instructed to taxi Mike to the ramp. Due to it being dark and taxiway markings in poor condition. I got confused and accidentally taxied onto Taxiway Kilo. This was despite using a taxiway diagram and being very familiar with the airfield. I realized my mistake when I realized that Mike shouldn't have taxiway lights and turned off of Kilo as soon as possible. Luckily; due to the airport being empty at night; there were no aircraft on the taxiway at that point and I believe this reduced any immediate risk from the mistake; which I attempted to correct as soon as it was safe to do so. ATC did not mention my error to me. This means that either ATC did not notice my mistake or they did not think it was significant enough to mention. I was lucky that there wasn't an aircraft on the taxiway which could have resulted in a major situation. I believe it was a combination of fatigue (hour long night flight at the end of a day) and the dark conditions made it difficult to notice the proper taxiway markings. I believe having aircraft taxi on an unlit taxiway at night is risky as it could be easy to miss on a dark night especially next to a lit taxiway which would draw a pilot's visual attention. Additionally; due to it being my home airport I may have subconsciously paid less attention to the airport diagram than I would have at another airport. Going forward I will pay extra close attention to the airport diagram especially at night when I may have to taxi to an unlit portion of the airfield. This combined with verbally briefing the taxi route out loud could prevent an incident like this from happening again. It is easy to get distracted at night; especially if tired at the end of a flight; and make mistakes like this. So definitely; always use a diagram; double check the route and signs; airports should make sure markings are in good condition. More importantly than just using a diagram is actively reading it and understanding it no matter how familiar with the airport you are.

I had a big headwind so my internal timer felt right to be descending but the reduced ground speed I was still outside of the FAF.My reaction to realizing the issue was fast. column121: While enroute (cruise); an aircraft (C182 tail dragger) suddenly passed over and overtook us in our Piper Warrior at a distance that was close enough to almost cover the wind screen.  The student and I were discussing where we would land in the case of an emergency at the time of the incident. My fault in the incident was that I should have been monitoring and announcing on 122.8 instead of 122.9.  I do not believe that the Cessna saw us or even realized that we were sharing the same real estate.  In the future; I will be more attentive to local frequencies and stay at a higher altitude in that area.

column121: Aircraft X; cleared Visual Approach  off a downwind turn behind a Heavy. Aircraft X was pointed away and behind Heavy when cleared to follow the traffic and issued caution wake turbulence. The pilot turned to follow the Heavy at his discretion towards the traffic and the field to a dog leg at about 5.5 miles in trail of the Heavy. Aircraft X joined final approach behind the traffic and I; the Final Radar Controller; observed what looked like a quick radar track anomaly. Quickly followed was an observed turn and quick descent and climb by Aircraft X back towards the field. The pilot promptly advised of a 'complete upset' and that he was back on the turn towards the traffic and on the Visual Approach with out a chance for me to issue any instructions.Later to find out this verbiage meant the aircraft had been sent into a complete roll to the right in which the pilot continued to recover the aircraft. No official cause but I can only guess wake turbulence from the Heavy traffic sent him into an uncontrolled roll. I acknowledged; inquired if any assistance was required to which the pilot responded in the negative; and I continued to work the traffic to include breaking out a Heavy behind him to allow him to continue the Visual Approach. The aircraft continued on the approach and double confirmed that everything was okay and no assistance was required before sending him to the Tower for landing.No recommendation; but awareness for all pilots of potential wake turbulence induced events. I personally could have ensured the aircraft was at a higher altitude to possibly prevent the wake trajectory; but I was originally setting up Aircraft X for an ILS Approach to follow at the appropriate  wake turbulence minimums. Only after the pilot called traffic and field in sight was he given the Visual Approach clearance to follow. If the pilot did not feel comfortable with this; I did not know or could have recommended a different method of approach.

column121: Briefed low level level off at gate.  On taxi out; ship phone rang in cubby hole and I couldn't reach it.  Dispatch informed us that we needed to hold on the ground for a maintenance carry over item that would expire before the completion of the mission.  We waited ready for takeoff for almost an hour with several updates from Dispatch that sounded like we were going back to the gate.  Then suddenly told to go.  Briefed again the low level level off while waiting.  Took off and did not execute the maneuver as we briefed.  Got ATC call to switch to departure control right before ALT CAP.  Noticed the FMA was not matching the calls.  I switched my eyesight to the FO's hand on MCP.  Once correct; I returned to ADI and discovered altitude was approaching 2;500 feet.  Corrected pitch to return to 2;000 feet.   ATC then assigned us 5;000 feet.  No comment was made about the altitude deviation.  Cleaned up aircraft; engaged autopilot; no further incidents.Cause - Pilot flying distracted to monitoring.  Pilot monitor error in MCP.  Pilot proficiency played a role.  This was my first flight in 2 months and second in 5 months as pilot flying.Pitched down to correct altitude.  FO contacted departure and we got an immediate climb to 5;000 feet.The main thing that sticks out is pilot proficiency.
column123: Briefed low altitude level off thoroughly. While taxiing; received phone call to hold for Maintenance waiver issue that affected later flights. Held for nearly 45 minutes at end of runway. After MCP operation; noticed altitude deviation. Made deviation call out and pilot flying corrected immediately. Pilot flying became distracted with MCP operation. Pilot monitoring procedural error in MCP operation. Pilot proficiency. Time compression. Aggressively corrected and contacted departure. No comment from them and received immediate climb to 5;000 feet.Pilot proficiency should be maintained/bettered through flight/simulator scheduling efficiency.

column121: Approximately 20 minutes after departure I received a call from the Flight Attendant that we had a couple passengers that weren't complying with the mask mandate and asked me to make our announcement reminding passengers of the Federal mask mandate. I made our announcement. Just prior to going through sterile flight deck period the Flight Attendant called again with passenger seat numbers X3 and YX4 and asked me to relay non mask compliance to the station. We made several attempts to contact Operations. After being unable to do so I sent an ACARS to Dispatch notifying them of mask non-compliance and asked them to have a CSR meet the aircraft. Being so close to the destination we elected to continue to the destination. After landing we tried several more times to contact Operations on taxi in and were unable to do so. Upon arriving at the gate the CSR came on board and informed me they had LEOs waiting at the counter and the TSA had been notified but she wasn't sure if they were sending a representative to speak with the passengers. She requested keeping the passengers on board for several minutes; so they could make sure everyone was prepared to receive the passengers. Given the all clear; the passengers disembarked without incident.The Flight Attendant mentioned she made multiple announcements and handed the passengers the information describing the penalties for non-compliance that are included in the packs of masks/alcohol wipes. It sounds like she made every available effort per SOP to have the passengers comply with the mask mandate. As states continue to withdraw mask mandates I foresee this becoming an increasingly widespread issue. I thought the idea of handing the passengers the information card was a very smart idea as seeing this in writing may carry more weight. Perhaps aircraft can be stocked with additional copies of these cards to hand out. Also our current guidance on the mask mandates in the flight crew memo make this policy sound like it is just per company policy. Updated guidance stating that this is a Federal mandate may make it more clear to the passengers that this is a serious federal violation. Every day we see passengers wearing masks that are not allowed on our flights and have to be given masks the meet standards; gate agents policing masks that required standard would also be helpful.

column121: While descending through approximately 20;000 feet on the arrival we encountered a compressor stall with self recovery on engine number 1 (heard loud popping; aircraft experienced slight yaw moment).  All engine parameters indicated normal. PM (Pilot Monitoring) briefed the Flight Attendants and made a PA to the passengers explaining what happened.  Approximately 3 minutes later we had an indication of N2 overspeed (~103%). PF (Pilot Flying) reduced thrust on the engine to bring it within normal limits which was immediately followed by a ENG 1 FUEL CNTRL FAULT. FO (First Officer) continued to fly the airplane while CA (Captain) was completing the ECAM procedure. The ECAM procedure directed the ENG 1 to be shut down. PF notified ATC and requested vectors to final approach for Runway XXL. PM completed the ECAM procedure and the QRH follow up for the ENG FAIL. PM briefed the Flight Attendants on a Precautionary Landing according to the Non Routine Landing Considerations. PM conducted a PA to the passengers to explain the situation and to expect ARFF (Aircraft Rescue & Fire Fighting) to check the airplane on the outside. We were cleared for a visual approach to Runway XXL which we backed up with the ILS. PF conducted a normal approach and landing and stopped the aircraft on the runway short of Taxiway D.  PM requested that the Fire Commander check the outside of the aircraft for any damage or leaks. After ARFF inspected the aircraft and reported no signs of damage or leaks we taxied to the gate.  After arriving at the gate; we called Dispatch to notify them of the precautionary landing.  Dispatch patched us through to Maintenance Control.  We discussed the ECAM / engine indications with Maintenance to aid in the log discrepancy write up.

column121: Turning for a 7 to 8 NM final from left base to Runway XX with aircraft configured flaps 20; PF established aircraft on ILS Runway XX GS and LOC for visual approach. PM made a VFR traffic call for an 8 NM final landing Runway XX. Another jet on the ground at ZZZ made multiple calls for a radio check and the PM responded he could hear the jet loud and clear. PF called autopilot off; and request the visual approach for Runway XX in the FMS. The PM entered the Runway XX visual approach into the FMS.  PM made a 5 NM final call on CTAF. The jet on the ground informed the PM they were taxiing on Runway XX and would clear the runway prior to aircraft landing and then engaged the PM in a conversation about their inability to contact ATC Clearance. PF called flaps 30 and flaps 45 and slowed the aircraft on speed and Glide Slope. PM read the before landing check and at the LANDING GEAR DOWN call both the PF and PM noted the lack of DOWN 3 GREEN on the display panel and then visually checked the gear handle and noted it was in the up position. This occurred at about 1;100 feet HAT and was follow by the gear horn going off. PF immediately began a go-around and made call outs PM preformed G/A TO actions and traffic calls. The aircraft descended to 900 to 1000 HAT before entering the upwind for Runway XX and performed an uneventful left traffic pattern landing on Runway XX.This was my first day back from a month of leave and my Captain had also recently returned from leave. Rust may have been a factor. Additionally; we were flying at a high altitude airport with terrain at night with no Tower. There was definitely a communication break down and I was tasked saturated and should have let the Captain know I was in the red; and I could have missed the gear call. The final distraction was the jet on the ground taxiing on Runway XX where they should not have been; and fixation on them clearing the runway and engaging in a conversation about contacting ATC to get their IFR clearance was also a factor taking my awareness outside the aircraft.In the future I need to be more aware of my saturation level and communicate this correctly to my captains and avoid engaging in extraneous ground communications with other aircraft. Also; I need to visually and verbally verify my actions and confirm call outs by myself and other pilots regardless if I am PM or PF and verbally verify ambiguous calls or situations.
