column121: I was told by my Captain we are to expect two FAMs (Federal Air Marshalls) and one LEO on our flight. When boarding commenced; one of them showed his ID and asked me if he could check in with the Captain. After doing so; I asked him if he was aware of 'the other two.' He seemed confused. I told him we were supposed to have 'two FAMs and a LEO. Are you the LEO?' He said yes. I told him we have two FAMs too; but I'm not sure yet what seats they're in. He said OK and sat in seat. As he walked away; my Captain called me into the flight deck and said LEOs aren't supposed to know about the FAMs; but the FAMs are supposed to know about the LEOs. I was dumbfounded and anxious because I thought all armed persons are supposed to know about each other; with the exception of FBI agents; which is not in our manual anywhere; but was told to me when I inquired years ago at recurrent. I asked if ever someone can be armed on our plane and not have to tell us. The trainer answered FBI only. In flight; I looked it up in my manual because I hate not being sure of a rule; and I needed to read it to verify. I found two spots referencing FAM discretion; and to me; it says LEOS ARE supposed to be informed about the FAMs. All armed persons are informed about each other. Is our manual wrong? Am I interpreting it wrong? I informed my Captain what I had found. He said the Company gate agent was the one who told him LEOs aren't supposed to know about FAMs.My thought is; what if the FAM steps in to help us and pulls his gun out and the LEO shoots him. It could totally happen; because there would obviously be a commotion; the LEO thinks he's the only one on board with a gun; it's his job to help.Later that day; I asked a different company gate agent what their policy was. I wanted to verify. She said if the LEO asks if there is anyone else armed; she will answer 'yes; but they are not in your category;' but she will not disclose the seat number(s). If he or she (LEO) does not ask; she (gate agent) does not tell.Unless I'm reading my manual wrong; I think we have a policy discrepancy. Please let me know what's correct so I may comply in the future.

column121: We were cleared approach RNAV Z XXR.  I looked at the navigation display and saw a solid unbroken magenta line from our position to the runway.  LNAV and VNAV displayed in FMA's.  Prior to this we were given delete speeds and at some point; I think we were assigned 210 knots.  Weather was clear VMC.  We were looking for traffic.  At some point traffic was called to us.  I did not see the discontinuity at ZZZZZ in the MCDU.  Approaching ZZZZZ I felt the plane was not turning to follow the path as it should.  I disengaged the autopilot and hand flew the rest of the procedure.  ATC asked us if we were turning and then asked if we could land.In the 10 months preceding this incident; I have 18 hours of block time.  I have 2 hours of block time in the last 90 days.  I was an X type aircraft Captain but was retrained as a First Officer (FO).  I have 0 hours as an FO in this aircraft prior to training.  My training consisted of one 4-hour sim period and two OE legs.  I believe the Captain was just back from a medical issue; had done a short training course and this was his second trip on the line.
column123: Arrival into ZZZ during daytime VFR conditions with excellent visibility. Our FMC was programmed for the arrival as well as the RNAV RNP Z to XXR with the transition at ZZZZZ intersection. Our primary error was that we did not close the FMC discontinuity between the arrival and the approach. The result was that we overflew ZZZZZ1 intersection and corrected immediately after recognizing that we were not turning at the appropriate time. In hindsight it appears that multiple distractions contributed to our failure to remove the discontinuity. The change in speed assignments as well as a request by the Controller to watch for Aircraft Y traffic on a parallel runway and the timing associated with the issuance of our approach clearance.We were able to visually identify the Aircraft Y parallel traffic and kept visual separation. Once established on the extended runway centerline we received TA/RA warnings associated with the proximity of the Aircraft Y on XXL.  Also; there was never any indication that our aircraft deviated laterally of the extended runway centerline that would have compromised separation.Immediately after arrival at the gate I called approach control to discuss the late turn on the approach. (I was not asked to call.) I requested to speak with a Supervisor and we had a 5-10 minute discussion. I was told there was 'nothing on their end' in the way of a complaint. We also had an additional discussion about the traffic advisories associated with our approach given the close proximity of parallel traffic.One of the challenges of flying into ZZZ is that we typically are issued our runway assignment; approach; and transition in the latter stage of our arrival. Also; once issued; it seems to be relatively common to be reassigned to yet another runway; approach and transition. It is also common to receive speed modifications on the arrival.We were prepared for the RNAV Z to XXR and per company procedure we had the default arrival transition programmed. In hindsight I believe that if our clearance to fly the approach had come earlier in the arrival phase (when we had less distractions) that we would have been more likely to close the link between the arrival and approach and avoid our error.

I believe there was a count error that was missed by us or the cabin crew.Although every effort was made to ensure we had accurate zones for departure; we ended up with three extra passengers than what the final location/count included. We were doing our best to ensure we had accurate numbers before block-out and perhaps the final count was overlooked as we were pressured for time. I am often notified of these changes with only minutes to spare before departure; so I feel that letting the passengers move rushes us and exposes errors like this one.While I understand some peoples need to distance on an airplane; I think there should be a cutoff in time before departure for this to be allowed. This creates an unnecessary distraction for the crew; and could create potential discrepancies like this one for the location/count. I think it could easily be explained to a passenger that they are free to move at some point after departure.

Almost everyone touched my hands when I served the drinks. And immediate contacts with them handing over the drinks; it makes some passengers quite uncomfortable and distracted events for the crews.The fourth problem is that WiFi is inadequate and lots of people ask how or where to find the menu; it may sound simple to do it but it's not something that generally people are familiar with our website and not many frequent fly members on board. It takes lots of crew time and distraction in fact.Lots of crew members are still not having the access of the vaccine yet. I feel that our company put our crews in great danger in our work environment. If we follow the federal guideline; I strongly believe that we are not ready for this; yet.Thank you for your consideration and help in advance.We must vaccinate the crews 100%. column121: While at 3;000 feet about 21 miles southwest of Deland (OMN) (and flying southwest enroute to LAL); I saw on my EFB a possible convergence between myself and two other aircraft. The first aircraft; a twin-engine; was at my five o'clock; slightly higher than me; flying southeast. The second aircraft; a single-engine high wing was at my ten o'clock; slightly below me; and flying southwest. I found myself in the middle of this impending convergence; so I turned right and behind the twin; knowing that the aircraft would safely pass me. In this position; I could observe the other two aircraft quickly converge. I could see they still had vertical separation during the convergence until I saw the high-wing perform a climbing left turn towards the twin's path. There was no collision; but I genuinely think neither aircraft saw each other considering the higher aircraft was a twin-engine low-wing and the lower aircraft was a high-wing. I estimate the aircraft were within 500 feet of each other.

column121: I departed Wings field while a TFR was active. Wings field has a cut-out for the TFR but I still got a discrete code and frequency from Philly ATC before departing. When I departed; there was one plane that had just done a go-around and another coming from the north to cross the field and enter the pattern. Rather than do a left turn out and add congestion to the left downwind; I decided to do a right turnout to stay away from the traffic in the downwind and provide room for the incoming traffic to enter the pattern. I announced my intentions on CTAF and the inbound plane acknowledged my intent. The runway I departed (24) headed directly at the TFR. My plan was to call Philly; turn into the TFR and get clearance through the Bravo airspace. As I climbed; the TFR was coming up very quickly. I was not at TPA (Traffic Pattern Altitude) but I was also not talking to Philly yet. I was concerned about entering the TFR without talking even though I was transmitting a discrete code. So; I made a hard turn to the right to stay out of the TFR but was anxious about calling Philly. I changed off CTAF and called Philly (but was still climbing to TPA). Just as I did; my traffic alert system started sounding an alarm. I could not hear what Philly was saying because the traffic alert system was extremely loud. I assumed it was alerting me to the traffic in the left downwind and I tried to silence it. As a result of trying to talk to Philly and trying to silence the traffic alert system; I got distracted and failed to keep my head outside the aircraft (failed to aviate above everything else). When I finally looked outside there was another plane crossing about fifty feet from me. I have asked several people; but it is still not clear to me whether I can enter the TFR while transmitting a discrete code but not talk to ATC until I reach a safe altitude clear from the traffic pattern at the airport. I would think that is the case; but I don't want to assume that. I also think more room should be given for airport cut-outs for TFRs. The TFR starts about .9 miles from the end of the runway which should be enough to get to TPA; but it still requires a pretty sharp U-turn to avoid the TFR.

column121: We were held down at 5;000 feet for traffic while essentially on a left downwind departure. After flying level at 5;000 feet for a couple of minutes we were cleared to climb to 16;000 feet. Once established in the climb and climbing out of 6;000 feet; we were climbing at a rather high rate. As we were established in climb; we received a TCAS TA on traffic at 1 o'clock; which appeared to be converging on us. No sooner than we noticed; we received a 'DESCEND; DESCEND' TCAS RA. I disconnected the autopilot and autothrottles while simultaneously idling the thrust levers and pitching down to comply with the RA. Essentially; we went from full climb thrust in a climb at 250 knots below 10;000 feet to needing to descend promptly. That's a pretty dramatic change of aircraft energy state. I saw from the corner of my eye that it appeared to be a twin turboprop. The conflict aircraft passed right over us; most certainly less than 500 feet.  As we were descending in our RA maneuver; ATC warned us to stop climb immediately. We informed him we were responding to TCAS RA already. After the threat aircraft was behind us; we resumed our climb and queried ATC as to why they didn't point out the traffic to us. The Controller said he 'didn't see him and wasn't talking to him.' I found that answer to be strange; but as it turned out; the top of the Class B airspace was below us. We reported the event to Dispatch and the Captain filed an incident report as per the policy. The question I have is whether the ATC can somehow remove VFR targets outside of their airspace band that are squawking VFR and wonder if that's what happened here. The threat aircraft was well within his rights to fly VFR above Class B airspace without talking to ATC; but without TCAS and without Controller pointing out traffic; because they may be 'squelching' VFR traffic outside of Class B; this could have ended really badly especially considering several cloud layers that we encountered. I recently flew an aircraft with TCAS MELed and I'm sure glad this happened when we actually had a functioning TCAS.

column121: This flight was a planned departure from ZZZ to ZZZ1.  Weather was overcast; rainy with relatively calm winds and temperatures decreased during preflight from around 10C to 4C prior to departure. Pushback was delayed due to ramp congestion but only delayed takeoff slightly.  The Captain was operating as Pilot Flying (PF) for this flight.  The First Officer was Pilot Monitoring (PM).  Takeoff was uneventful. The departure was flown autopilot off.  While heading toward ZZZZZ and climbing at 280 KIAS; sometime after passing FL180 and climbing to FL230 in Instrument Meteorological Conditions (IMC); Boeing 737-800 aircraft experienced extreme airspeed indicator swings on both sides of the cockpit.  Indications wildly fluctuated between 300 KIAS down to 180 KIAS.  The PF asked the PM if his indications were normal and the PM responded that his indications appeared erroneous as well and he had an airspeed disagree indication. The pitot heat was verified ON. The autothrottles started to chase the airspeed fluctuations and were subsequently turned off.  PF maintained the climb power and pitch angle and asked the PM to get a higher altitude from ATC.  ATC responded with a 'standby for higher' response.  The PM attempted to select Vertical Speed and it would not engage.  All vertical guidance was unavailable.  The PF asked the PM for a groundspeed and the PM responded that he did not see one.  There was no groundspeed on the Captain's (PF) side as well.  The Standby Flight Instruments were difficult to read as they had been dimmed for the takeoff and now the sun was coming up. Simultaneously; we were approaching a turn from ZZZZZ to ZZZZZ1.  PF elected to maintain wings level and continued straight ahead as to not compound the problem by turning in IMC conditions with obvious airspeed errors.  Since the sun was just rising we could see the top of the weather was very close. As we approached FL230 we continued to climb and notified ATC.  ATC cleared us to FL380.  After reaching an altitude; probably FL240/FL250 in Visual Meteorological Conditions (VMC) the aircraft returned to nominal limits.  The flight continued under VMC to ZZZ1.  The aircraft flew normally after the event and landed safely.  Discrepancies were noted in the Aircraft Maintenance Logbook (AML) and maintenance personnel were debriefed by the Captain. Recommend a third air data inertial reference unit (ADIRU) on the B-737 so the bad ADIRU can be removed from the equation during a failure and still have a comparator feature.
column123: Early morning departure out of ZZZ to ZZZ1. During climbout on the SID just after passing through the transition through FL180 I noticed we had lost the flight director and a yellow 'speed disagree' flag on the PFD (Primary Flight Display). I then looked at the MCP and VNAV/LNAV was off. Tried to re-engage and it wouldn't due to the PFD flag. About that time I noticed the speed had dropped from 280 KIAS to about 260 KIAS and we were off course having missed a slight turn on the SID. The Captain then said his was not right and asked me what mine said. I had said mine didn't seem correct either. Then he asked me what our ground speed was and I looked and mine was blank; not showing and wind/GS/TAS. At that time I told Center that we were having a problem with our instruments since we were off course and altitude. He came back and gave us present heading and FL230. The Captain then asked me to see if we could continue our climb since we weren't far from being on top of the weather; I asked and was told to stand by. A few seconds later Center gave us FL380. At this time I notified ATC having noticed we were getting further off our heading and the situation was getting worse. As we started to climb everything came back; air speeds matched; flag went away; was able to re engage LNAV/VNAV and flight directors. Few seconds after that we were on top in VMC. Everything came back just as quickly as we lost it. We were cleared to our next fix and resumed normal operations. We discussed our options and mutually decided that since there was clear weather for the rest of the way to ZZZ1 and everything was working that it was best to continue rather than turn back into the weather and return to ZZZ. The rest of the flight was uneventful and sent an ACARS message to let Maintenance know we would be writing the aircraft up when we landed. We landed in ZZZ1 and the Captain made the entry in the logbook when we got to the gate.

column121: On the arrival in MGGT; winds were reported out of the south at 10 kts; so MGGT was landing Runway 20. Referencing WSI (Weather Services International); there were two active areas for volcanic ash; one for Pacaya and one for Agua. Both had plumes and ash clouds from the surface to 14;000 ft; and both were moving west. While selecting what approach we were planning; we looked at the different missed approaches and decided the VOR Z Runway 20 would be best in the event of a missed approach and avoid any ash cloud. The Missed Approach procedure for the VOR Z Runway 20 is AUR; 1 DME past the VOR; a slight left turn via the 169 radial to 17 DME and then hold at 11;000 ft with no special climb rates associated with it. Then our briefing turned to the Engine-Out (EO) Procedure. We immediately noticed the EO procedure splits the gap of the volcanos Pacaya and Agua; and right through the SIGMET area.We thought about what to do in the event of an engine-out missed approach. I decided; in this situation; the EO procedure would not be appropriate due to the active SIGMETs for volcanic ash; and I decided the missed approach for the VOR Z Runway 20 would be more appropriate and safer than the EO as published. We reviewed the terrain that shows on the EO procedure; terrain charts; and considered our landing weight. Landing was normal and no missed approach was accomplished. But planning for worse case revealed challenges to our procedures of following company EO procedures as published.Our training has us brief and setup EO procedures for missed approaches as well as takeoff; and fly them as published in the event of an engine-out event. This particular procedure; on this night; sets a crew up for a terrible scenario of going missed approach or takeoff; losing an engine; and flying directly into a volcanic ash cloud with one engine while these volcanoes are active.My suggestion would be to give the aircrews more options; have the EO procedure ready but review all the missed approaches as published and note whether we can fly them as a published engine-out. In this case; I believe we could have safely executed the missed approach for the VOR Z Runway 20; and possibly an engine-out scenario on initial takeoff; but I just don't have access to the information to confirm this. Blindly following EO procedures when other factors encroach on the procedures could result in a worse outcome.

column121: Winds were moderate; variable; and gusty; but within limits for the aircraft. In accordance with accepted technique; half the gust factor; approximately 6 knots; was added to the final approach and landing speeds. Just after touchdown on the centerline; with all three gears established on the runway; a gust was felt and corrected for. As the correction was made with what was perceived as moderate aileron and rudder input; the airplane veered sharply to the left. With the thought that over-controlling back to the right could lead to the left wingtip dipping and then digging into the runway resulting in the aircraft tumbling (worst case) or a ground loop at high energy (best case); I elected to input enough control to keep the aircraft tracking as straight ahead as possible. This resulted in departing the runway surface to the left of the runway. Once in the gravel that was lining the left side of the runway; my entire focus was on maintaining enough control not to hit obstacles or dig in gear or wingtips so as to cause tumbling. In the process of dissipating energy; I crossed two high-speed taxiways at almost a perpendicular angle and at a still relatively high-speed resulting in the aircraft becoming lighter on the struts. The struts compressed again on the other side of the taxiways resulting in enough energy depletion to safely steer back to the runway surface.Upon re-establishing safe contact with asphalt; the aircraft was taxied a short distance to parking. Upon the post-flight walk-around inspection; there was visible damage to two of three propeller blade tips (of composite material made by Hartzell) from contact with gravel likely occurring when the struts compressed after crossing the taxiways. No other visible damage to the aircraft was observed nor were fluids observed to be leaking. It is very likely the root cause of this event was the application of too much rudder for the capabilities of the aircraft in countering the cross-wind gust after landing.The PA-46 line of aircraft is known to have very sensitive nose wheel steering; especially at higher speeds; and while being aware of it and managing it were trained to extensively; it's entirely possible that too much rudder was applied as was appropriate for this aircraft type. Habit pattern transference is a likely contributing factor in that I have several thousand hours in other type aircraft; to include very recent and continued professional flying experience in the Pilatus PC-12; and all of which do not exhibit the level of sensitivity in nose wheel steering that the PA-46 does. In instinctively applying the crosswind gust correction I'm used to; it is very possible that I applied an amount that was too much for safe control of the PA-46 at the time of occurrence.I do not feel training was a contributing factor as I received very thorough Piper-authorized training and initial conditioning in the aircraft with a Piper-authorized instructor. However; overall low time in type is definitely a contributing factor. Up to the time of this event; I had logged 20 landings in the PA-46 and several of which were in gusty conditions and or crosswinds similar to what was experienced during this event. In the future; the biggest take away from the event for me for flying the PA-46 is to concentrate on keeping the nose wheel off the runway as long as possible as energy depletes so that when the nose wheel does contact the runway; it's at the lowest speed practical. During this event the nose wheel was centered upon initial contact with the runway; as was emphasized in training. Any application of nose wheel steering at higher speeds should always be done very lightly at first to ensure the aircraft remains under control.

column121: While working [sector] X there were significant areas of weather that were impeding aircraft transitioning the sector.  One area in particular was south of ZZZ and it was causing large deviations for aircraft inbound to ZZZ.  Due to a recent Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) that drastically alters Controller's working conditions on sector; which mandates the wear of facial coverings due to COVID-19 communication began to break down with aircraft on frequency.  While trying to describe the precipitation to pilots the mask created interference and the pilots could not decipher what I was trying to relay; which was weather that would affect their route.  This was especially the case with a handful of aircraft inbound to ZZZ that needed information on the weather and on the other aircraft they would have to follow into their destination airport.  My only option was to remove the face covering so that I could communicate directly and effectively to the aircrews trying to navigate these storms.  I am simply trying to comply with the duty priority.  Management at this Center is more concerned with complying with the MOU regarding face coverings than they are about safely moving aircraft about the National Aerospace System. If I were to be seen without my face covering on sector I would undoubtedly be reprimanded for the 'face mask violation.'  Ironically enough; if I were to not be able to communicate with the aircrews effectively and they enter an area of severe turbulence associated with thunderstorms I would also be reprimanded by management.  We have now entered a situation where controllers are going to be forced to decide what is more important; the aircraft on frequency or the arbitrary rules being enforced by management due to a 'pandemic' that is now over a year old that has proven to represent little-to-no risk to the controlling workforce. By the end of the session I had several instances where separation errors almost occurred because of deviating aircraft and having to repeat transmissions to climbing/descending aircraft...this was even after I removed the face covering.I would recommend that someone in the Air Traffic Organization stand up for the safety of the system and issue some direction for controllers that need to communicate with aircrews.  It is unreasonable to expect controllers to day after day wear a face mask while on position that causes distractions and limits the ability to safely conduct air traffic control procedures.  There is currently no direction as to when a Controller can remove a face mask in order to promote safety.

column121: This is a very large sector that when worked on its own has 6 different VHF frequencies spread apart for coverage. In between these frequencies is a fairly large gap where aircraft below about 7;000 feet may have a brief period of no communication with ATC depending on how the Controller handles the frequency change. I received a handoff from Approach Control on Aircraft X which was level at 4;000 feet. An experienced Controller's first thoughts would be that this aircraft could not only go NORDO (No Radio) but also that the Minimum IFR Altitude (MIA) gradually increases to 5;100 feet to the western part of this sector. These thoughts came to my mind; and to be proactive; I issued a climb to 5;000 or 6;000 feet (don't recall which). Immediately after checking in; I realized this aircraft wouldn't need to be at 6;000 feet for a while and by then I'd be in communication with this aircraft on another frequency.Aircraft X requested to remain at 4;000 feet for better winds and flight conditions. I saw where the aircraft was landing; which was a few miles west of my sector; and measured from there to where I'd need the aircraft to be level at 5;000 feet. I instructed the aircraft to cross 120 miles east of the destination airport level at 5;000 feet and also to eventually check in on a different frequency when I was no longer coming in on the current frequency. Approximately 10 to 15 minutes later; MSAW (Minimum Safe Altitude Warning) was going off on this flight and flashing 4200 feet. It took a second for me to realize I made a mistake and overlooked a section of the MIA chart that was 4;200 feet. When MSAW flashed; the aircraft was beyond my frequency reach and we were unable to communicate.The aircraft was also just barely clipping the corner of this particular MIA section and then it was back to at or below 4;000 feet. Instead of trying to relay through an aircraft; I allowed the aircraft to fly through this corner since it was a 200 feet. difference we were talking about and it was such a brief time period. I was confident with my knowledge that although not ideal; this aircraft wasn't in danger. The Aircraft went on to meet my previous requirements of crossing at 5;000 feet at 120 miles from destination and checked in the next frequency and no further issues arose.I frequently skip a frequency that would likely work in between the check in frequency and the frequency at the western part of the sector. It's never been an issue because we very seldom allow an aircraft to make it that far west at 4;000 feet to begin with. I was confident I had been proactive and covered my bases when indeed I had not. I used a type of crossing restriction; at least for this purpose; that I never use and one that I had never used prior and I overlooked an important section of the MIA. I need to start using this intermediate frequency even if for a short time period. Pay more attention to detail when issuing a restriction of this kind. This was completely my fault.

column121: There were storms in the area; and we were given a reroute by ATC; to go south to the coast; and then follow the coast west to IAH. The FO (First Officer; Pilot Monitoring) had made a passenger announcement telling them that we were expecting storms along the route of flight; and that we were anticipating a bumpy ride. I; the CP (Captain; Pilot Flying); had advised the FA that it was going to be bumpy. In the climb out; we encountered light turbulence. Upon reaching cruising altitude of FL280; it was smooth; so we briefly let the passengers up. Upon reaching the coast; ATC advised us of multiple storms and cells along our route of flight; and had mentioned that several aircraft ahead of us had gone south of these storms; had stayed within 50 NM of the coast; and had reported nothing worse than light turbulence; and advised we do the same. After discussing with the FO; we agreed that flying south of our route; and staying within 50 NM of the coast; was our best option. At this time; I had my radar up; and the FO had his terrain map up. We advised the passengers and the FA to expect a few bumps; turned the seat belt sign back on; and to remain seated. We also decided to slow to turbulence penetration speed. We were painting multiple red and magenta cells which we were staying south of; and had a lot of green all over the radar. We were dodging and avoiding the cells to the north; while staying within the 50 NM range of the coast. We then must have hit an embedded cell that the radar did not pick up; as it was only reading green. Almost instantly; we went into severe turbulence; and lost approximately 400 feet. The aircraft did not go into any unusual or upset attitudes; and the Auto-Pilot remained on. During this turbulence; we also had a suspected lightning strike - we saw a flash of light all around us; heard a bang; and smelt the 'fireworks' smell that you usually smell associated with lightning. After being struck; we got a Stall Protection System advanced master caution message appear. It disappeared within 5 seconds of it showing. As quick as the severe turbulence hit us; it disappeared. ATC queried us regarding our loss of altitude; at which point the FO reported the severe turbulence and suspected lightning strike. ATC asked if we needed further assistance; to which we replied no. As previously mentioned; this happened very quickly. All in all; I would say it lasted no longer than 30 seconds; and closer to 20 seconds. Once we were back at FL280; we had completely exited all weather (which we had been in for a majority of the time upon reaching the coast); and were in clear blue skies. I spoke to the FA; and asked if she was OK; to which she replied she was. She then asked if it was OK for her to check on the passengers; which she did. There were no injuries; and the only thing she mentioned is that the passengers were staring at her wide eyed. ATC asked if there were any injuries onboard; we replied with none. The flight continued with no further incidents. Upon landing; both pilots thoroughly inspected the outside of the plane on the walk around; noting a black mark on the right side of the nose which may be the entry point to the suspected lightning strike; but with no damage seen. I wrote up the plane with 3 write ups - Severe turbulence; Lightning strike; and Lock out/Tag out installed.CRM was effectively utilized during this event; with the PF using the radar; and the PM using the terrain. With the information available to us at the time; with ATC advising us of going south of the cells; as opposed to north; the decision; at the time; to go south was the correct one. That being said; I think it would have been smarter to go north of the cells; but we did not have that information. Utilizing the radar was key during this event; by staying out of the red and magenta cells. However; the radar has its limitation; especially considering they are older pieces of equipment; and can not 100% accurately paint embedded cells; of which we hit. After the event; ATC began recommending to other aircraft to go north of the cells. Ultimately; I would say the crew were stuck between a rock and a hard place - staying within the 50 NM boundary of the coast; but staying as far south as possible of the mega cells to the north. Additionally; I would like to mention the extraordinary job that the company did after the incident. Upon reaching the gate; multiple members of both [safety teams] reached out to me and the crew; checking that we were OK; and that the passengers were OK. I feel our company truly encompassed themselves with the company values; of which we stand for; and has made me thoroughly proud and joyful to be a part of.

column121: While in cruise at 35;000 feet and in excess of 90 knots of wind from the tail; the flight had been in constant light and occasionally moderate chop. I requested 37;000 feet after confirming performance capability; and hearing ATC advice that higher altitudes were better than lower and the closer we got to 40;000 feet the better the ride. We were told 'Aircraft X; I have your request' and we were handed off to three subsequent controllers each assuring us that the next would assign our climb. Both PM (Pilot Monitoring) and PF (Pilot Flying) recognized the flight path was taking us directly into a cloud bank; and the turbulence levels were becoming more of a solid moderate chop. As a result; PM (the Captain) advised the Cabin Crew to secure themselves and instructed the passengers to take their seats and securely fasten their seat belts. This event took place less than 10 minutes from entry into extreme turbulence.On the last handover; we had a converging aircraft 1;000 feet above us and traveling in the opposite direction. When ATC called the traffic for each of us; we were just entering the cloud bank into IMC conditions. Almost immediately; we encountered an increase in turbulence to solid moderate (changes in aircraft attitude and altitude occurred; but the aircraft remained in positive control). However; within seconds; we encountered severe turbulence including large abrupt changes in altitude; attitude; airspeed; as well as wind shear and updrafts. The result was initially a traffic alert. Within a few more seconds; we were in extreme turbulence and the aircraft was being tossed about violently; control was practically impossible; and the aircraft was being pushed upwards.The PM called the increase in speed and retarded the thrust levers as the aircraft was being shaken so violently that it took both hands of the PF to maintain positive control. Then a TCAS RA alerted us with a 'LEVEL OFF' command with the converging traffic icon in the PFD illuminated yellow. Almost immediately after; the icon turned red and PF pressed the FORCE TRIM INTERRUPT" button and shoved the yoke forward into the RA box to comply with the given guidance. The turbulence continued so violently that the autopilot was fully kicked offline; and the aircraft remained in a diving attitude per the TCAS guidance.During this period; and as a result of the wind shear and turbulence; the aircraft's speed fluctuated between a momentary illumination of the green PLI (Pitch Limit Indicator) and the triggering speed for a stick shaker activation. PM continued to apply speed brake and retard thrust levers to maintain the aircraft speed within limit (at no time did we encounter either a yellow or red PLI; or the stick shaker). At 30;500 feet we came out of the most violent turbulence and were able to reestablish a climb back to assigned altitude. Immediately after; the Captain contacted the cabin crew for an evaluation on any injuries or known damage. Beyond all the drinks and unsecured items being thrown around; none were reported; so we continued to the assigned destination. After landing; the post flight walk around revealed what appeared to be abnormal alignment or misalignment on the right outboard aileron."

column121: I was sitting in the left jump seat. Less than an hour into the flight from ZZZZ to ZZZZ1; a status message alerted the CA (Captain) and FO (First Officer) to an Oil quantity of '4' on the number four engine. Another CA; sitting center seat; was direct by the PIC CA to call dispatch and begin discussing options. During this conversation with Dispatch and Maintenance the oil quantity continued to fall. By the end of the conversation the oil quantity was '2.' As there were no secondary indications; and the procedures call for continued operation of the engine; the crew; Dispatch; and Maintenance concurred that continuing to ZZZ1 was best. Shortly thereafter; the oil quantity indication read '0' but oil pressure and oil temps remained normal. At approximately XA:50; oil pressure began to fall on the number 4 engine. Dispatch and Maintenance were again consulted. As an engine shutdown was imminent; it was agreed by all that returning to ZZZZ was the best course of action. ATC was contacted and provided return routing. The crew reviewed all checklists and reviewed the emergency section of FOM. When oil pressure dropped into the 'red' at '10' the engine was shutdown IAW the QRH. ATC was notified; and the PIC landed uneventfully at ZZZZ. Overall; I believe the aircrew effectively utilized all resources and employed effective CRM during this inflight shutdown.
column123: Takeoff and climbout were uneventful. Shortly after top of climb the secondary engine indications appeared on the lower EICAS. The #4 Engine Oil Quantity indicated around 5 quarts. I called the second Captain back to the flight deck. I had him Satcom Dispatch and Maintenance Control. I checked engine out performance and noted that an altitude change was not necessary. We discussed the issue and had Dispatch calculate 3 engine cruise to ZZZZ1. Several minutes later the Oil Pressure began to slowly drop. We updated Dispatch with the deteriorating indications. We contacted Dispatch and Maintenance control to update them as to this not being an indication error. We discussed proactively returning to ZZZZ verses waiting for an engine shutdown to steer our decisions. This time a Duty Pilot was brought into the conversation and it was agreed by all that returning to ZZZZ would be the best course of action. We asked Maintenance Control if we should consider shutting down the engine to avoid damage. Maintenance Control wanted us to wait until the QRH called for the shutdown. We turned back to ZZZZ at XA:50. At XB:24 we shut down the engine as required by the QRH due to Oil Pressure. We followed all guidance in the FCOM and FOM and notified ATC of the engine shutdown. The arrival; approach; and landing were uneventful. Ground Maintenance later told me that the O-ring was not installed when the starter was replaced causing the oil leak.I would suggest that Duty Pilots are included in all calls to Maintenance Control. They could easily be subject experts on simple MEL applications in line operations as well as help steer events such as Diversions. I feel as they are the liaison between flight operations; Dispatch; and Maintenance departments and they bind the working groups together. Without the Duty Pilots input; it feels like an uphill battle between departments where no department wants to be responsible for a decision. There is a lot of resistance from the mentioned departments until the Duty Pilot enters the conversation at which time everyone seems to concur when the Duty Pilot agrees with the crew.

column121: Turning final ZZZZ fully configured at 150 knots I armed the Localizer first than the Approach mode. First Officer inquired and received the landing clearance. I noticed that the glide slope didn't capture and that we were going above the path. I tried to descend in Vertical Speed; but it didn't come active; so it wouldn't work. Approach mode light still on. I disconnected the Autopilot; lowered the nose and started a descend using the VGSI (Visual Glideslope) path indicator and the outside PAPI (Precision Approach Path Indicator). During the descent we tried to reset the Approach/Glideslope unsuccessfully. The approach was pretty bumpy with some good downdrafts. The aircraft went below the glide slope and I started to correct back when the pull up warning came on then stopped right away. Then the glide slope warning followed. I was just under the path recovering and had 3 red lights and 1 white on the PAPI. Speed around 10 knots above Vref and decreasing toward Vref. I was very focused on the approach and continued to an uneventful normal landing.We were configured early; ready for approach; but the Glideslope not capturing and the uncertainty concerning the landing clearance created a distraction that put me behind the aircraft and I developed some tunnel vision trying to remedy the approach. I became fixated and continued when I should have discontinued the approach and gone around. After landing the First Officer said to me that she had mentioned going around; but it hadn't registered with me during the approach. I tell First Officers that there is no mission; but today I didn't follow my own advice. It's easy to become over focused without realizing it. When in doubt; go-around.
column123: The event began while beginning the ILS Approach. The company notes on the approach dictate not to arm the ILS until reaching a certain position because of the possibility of false localizer signals. The Captain was the Pilot Flying and I was the Pilot Monitoring.  I remember thinking that the Pilot Flying armed the approach later than I would have since we were well beyond the designated point. My best guess on what happened is that because of the delay the localizer armed but the glideslope never captured because we were already too high. Whatever the reason for the automation not doing what we had expected; the result was that we realized that the Glideslope never captured and were trying to get the aircraft to come down.Not only were we distracted with being above the intended glide path; but we were handed over to tower late and I was busy with getting clearance to land while the Pilot Flying was flying the plane trying to get back to a stabilized approach. As the aircraft was getting back to a normal glide path (3 red; 1 white on PAPI) around the 500 foot mark I gave my stabilized approach callout and realizing we were slightly above speed and correcting; but the vertical speed exceeded what is acceptable. At this point I said 'I think we should go around'. I can't remember if it was just before or after I said this that we got a 'PULL UP' alert. The Captain elected to continue the landing. Later after discussion; I learned he may have had tunnel vision to the point where my go around call didn't register with him.My unfamiliarity with ZZZZ did not help our situational awareness as well as being distracted with getting switched over to tower (late) and attempting to get landing clearance around the same time we realized the automation did not perform as expected. As a FO/PM not being assertive enough when a go-around was needed.Abiding by company SOP to the letter. No matter what; at 500 feet if stabilized approach criteria aren't met; it's an automatic and firm 'GO AROUND'.

column121: Once established in descent just below FL180; we received a call from the Flight Attendants that there was an odor in the vicinity of row X. This odor was described by FA 'A' as something similar to fuel and/or oil; but not a burning or acrid smell. The odor was not detectable to any other passengers or crew on the aircraft except the passengers in row X; to whom it was very noticeable; which was also confirmed by FA 'B'; but only when they walked up to row X. There was no visible plume anywhere in the airplane. The pilots did not detect any irregular odor in flight.The FO was flying the airplane (PF) so they took the radios as the CA (PM) looked in the QRH checklist. The comment about a fuel smell drove the pilots to suspect a fuel leak; but after running through the fuel leak checklist; no fuel leak indications (per checklist) were confirmed (fuel imbalance normal/not increasing; both engine fuel flow rates equivalent; quantity as expected for phase of flight plan). CA then confirmed with FA 'A' that the smell was indeed still noticeable; but there was still no plume and the odor was still confined to row X.We continued descent into ZZZ1 on what looked to be a fairly expedited vector; while we requested ARFF to be on standby at time of arrival. However; after we received another vector away from an expedited intercept course; we quickly [advised ATC] to gain traffic priority; which ATC quickly accommodated; clearing other aircraft from our path. We were cleared to land and we confirmed with Tower that ARFF would be standing by. Tower indicated we would exit [Runway] XXR at Taxiway 1 for ARFF coordination.Upon exit at Taxiway 1; we were cleared to cross runway XXL; and brought the aircraft to a stop on Taxiway 1 clear of runway. We requested ARFF check/scan the exterior of the aircraft for leaks/heat/fire/abnormalities. CA made a PA to pax noting that ARFF would be approaching the aircraft as a precaution. After ARFF indicated no abnormalities; we taxied to the gate; making clear to Ops that as an extra precaution; we would not start the APU. After we had taxied into the gate and set the parking brake; we immediately shut down (left-hand-side) engine #1; confirmed good/stable AC external power connection; then shut down (right-hand-side) engine #2. Prior to departure from ZZZ; we were sprayed with both Type I 'Deice' and Type IV 'Anti-Ice' fluid; with engines running; at the X Pad.After landing; FA 'B' said passengers had complained that the odor became more noticeable after landing gear was extended on final approach. FO also said that after landing they briefly noticed an odor.We could have [advised ATC] earlier on in the event. This would have allowed us traffic priority earlier in the descent (and speeds above 250 KIAS once below 10;000); getting us on the ground sooner and reducing the overall time of pax/FA exposure to fumes.We flew the same airplane the following day; and the airplane was cleared by Maintenance with no defects found. Nothing was wrong with the airplane itself. Fumes remaining localized in a certain area of the cabin suggests internal point source emission rather than external ingestion or airplane system malfunction. However; at time of writing; we still do not know; definitively; what caused the fumes.The FAs are commended for their prompt notification and accurate description of the nature and extent of the fumes. FO is commended for flying the aircraft while coordinating with ATC and requesting ARFF; while the CA ran checklists and coordinated with the FAs; then flying the approach almost to minimums. Working together seamlessly is key in these situations; and the CA commends the crew for a job well done.
column123: Prior to departure from ZZZ; we were sprayed with both Type I and Type IV fluid; with engines running; at the South De-Ice Pad.Once established in descent just below FL180; we received a call from the FA's. I (the FO) assumed it was the FA's notification that they were seated. Instead; they communicated to the CA that there was an odor in the vicinity of row x. This odor was described by FA 'A' as something similar to fuel and/or oil; but not a burning smell. The odor was not detectable to any other passengers or crew on the aircraft except the passengers in row x; to whom it was very noticeable. The pilots did not detect any irregular odor in flight.I (the FO) was flying the airplane (PF) so I took the radios as the CA (PM) looked in the QRH checklist. Since the CA was communicating with the FA's; I trusted his lead on necessary checklists to run; as he had the first hand information on the situation in the cabin. During this time; we had entered IMC conditions; and I was flying the airplane and working the radios; receiving several heading; altitude and speed changes during this time.The comment about a fuel smell drove us to suspect a fuel leak; but after running through the fuel leak checklist; no fuel leak indications (per checklist) were confirmed (fuel imbalance normal/not increasing; both engine fuel flow rates equivalent; quantity as expected for phase of flight plan). CA then confirmed with FA 'A' that the smell was indeed still noticeable; but there was still no plume and the odor was still confined to row X.We continued descent into ZZZ1 on what looked to be a fairly expedited vector; during which I requested ARFF to be on standby at time of arrival. However; after we received another vector away from an expedited intercept course; we quickly [advised ATC] to gain traffic priority; which ATC quickly accommodated. We were cleared to land and we confirmed with Tower that ARFF would be standing by. Tower indicated we would exit XXR at Taxiway 1 for ARFF coordination.Upon landing; I cracked the Thrust Reversers (TRs); and briefly noticed a smell in the flight deck. I then decided that the use of TRs may not be the safest procedure; as it was still unclear what was causing this smell. Thus; I immediately stowed the TRs and decelerated using only the brakes (long runway; good braking action).Upon exit at Taxiway 1; we were cleared to cross runway XXL; and brought the aircraft to a stop on Taxiway 1 clear of XXL. We requested ARFF check/scan the exterior of the aircraft for leaks/heat/fire/abnormalities. CA made a PA to pax noting that ARFF would be approaching the aircraft as a precaution. After ARFF indicated no abnormalities; we taxied to the gate; making clear to Ops that as an extra precaution; we would not start the APU. After we had taxied into the gate and set the parking brake; we immediately shut down engine #1; confirmed good/stable AC external power connection; then shut down engine #2.After landing; FA 'B' said passengers had complained that the odor became more noticeable after landing gear was extended on final approach. This was my 2nd precautionary ARFF event on 2 consecutive workdays (though separated by a period of leave). Having had the time to reflect upon the first event; I felt calmer and more prepared this time. I focused on making a successful approach (almost down to minimums).One error I made was to start configuring and thus slowing down too early. Due to several heading changes and an ATC request for us to slow down while the aircraft in front of us on the approach sped up to best forward speed; I had felt momentarily disoriented regarding our distance to the ZZZ1. Luckily; my brain was about 5 miles ahead of the airplane. Once I realized my error; I paused further configuration (which was gear down flaps 3 at that time) until closer to the ZZZ1.Considerations that were made were items for fire and emergency evacuation; should a fire develop after landing. Luckily; this was not the case.To my knowledge; it is still unclear what caused the smell. If it would have been more severe (filling the entire cabin and flight deck); then the checklist for smoke/fumes would have been appropriate.Overall; I feel that this event was handled well by everyone involved.

column121: I had just assumed responsibility of the position about a minute prior when the pilot of Aircraft X informed me that they were 'Over HOMAI; what do you want?' The previous controller; still observing the 2-minute overlap; confirmed what she stated in the relief briefing; that Aircraft X had been assigned direct HOMAI; which ties into their flight plan routing of the LNDHY1 STAR into OGG. I responded to the pilot that he should track outbound of HOMAI on the LNDHY1 arrival; which publishes a 204 degree track. The pilots were obviously confused; but began to correct. In the process of doing so; the aircraft may have clipped the boundary of a higher 6;300 ft. MVA. Aircraft X was level at 4;000 ft. in a 3;500 ft. MVA; and would have had no problems remaining so if they were established on the STAR. In an effort to salvage the situation; I asked the pilots if they had the airport in sight for a visual approach. They replied in the affirmative. Then I asked if they had traffic to follow in sight. They replied in the affirmative and I issued the visual approach clearance. The MSAW (Minimum Safe Altitude Warning) did not activate and I did not issue a low altitude alert. The pilots did not question the 'direct HOMAI' clearance they received from the previous controller until they were about a half mile past the fix. If there was any question about their routing; they should've clarified much earlier. But the confusion is not infrequent; and I have had pilots question the routing before. The published STAR clearly shows a 204 degree track after HOMAI on both the visual layout and written description. When I state this fact to querying pilots; the confusion is resolved. But the lack of a fix after HOMAI may cause pilots to ignore the track; or (as some controllers suspect) cause the track to drop out of the FMS when an approach is pre-loaded. My recommendation is for another fix to be added on the 204 degree track after HOMAI; to resolve the confusion; and to help ensure that aircraft don't fly on a free heading toward a higher MVA.My other recommendation is to look into how the LNDHY1 STAR is being programmed into FMS displays; and whether the addition of a (yet to be assigned) approach (e.g. RNAV Z RWY 2 from HOMAI) erases or otherwise obfuscates the 204 degree track outbound of HOMAI.

column121: Aircraft X was released IFR off UDD; which off of RWY (Runway) 28 would be an immediate left turn (Southeast) to TRM; climbing to 4;000 feet. I issued a traffic alert; and Aircraft X eventually said they had to turn to avoid the traffic.I am recommending that there be some sort of real controlled airspace in the Palm Springs valley. The TRSA is not mandatory; and there are frequently aircraft (many high performance) that choose not to call the approach controllers and just go straight to the tower. The airspace in the months between September and May is extremely busy at times; and the controllers/pilots have no safe space in which to operate. It is called 'The Wild West' over there for a reason. Everything is shoot from the hip; because you have no idea what is about to happen next. We can not plan on anything; we can never assume anything. The most controlled airspace in the valley is the PSP Delta; which requires participation; while the approach controllers work 20x the traffic and have no 'safe space'.I ask that the airspace be reviewed and considered for a Class Bravo/Charlie airspace to avoid future NMACs or worse.

column121: Aircraft X was southbound at 030 for a visual approach to Runway XX at ZZZ. I accepted a VFR point out from ZZZ1 facility on a XXXX code just a few miles east of ZZZZZ intersection going a few miles west of ZZZZZ to turn back to ZZZ1 airspace along the coastline at 015.  I did not tag up the point out because there was no traffic in that vicinity; and I was busy messing with my COVID mask. I was trying to put my mask on which I had in my pocket.  I cleared Aircraft X into Runway XX for the visual approach. I switched Aircraft X to the Tower when the point out aircraft was 7NM East of Aircraft X at 015. The tower controller issued traffic to Aircraft X three times. The first traffic call Aircraft X reported seeing the aircraft on TCAS. The third traffic call Aircraft X reported the traffic insight. No traffic alert was given to Aircraft X and no TCAS RA was performed. Aircraft X continued inbound and landed without further incident.  I lost track of the point out because when I took it I was working planes while trying to fix my COVID-19 mask.  When I decided to just work without one; I had moved on to other traffic and forgot to tag up the point out.The fact that I was more concerned with getting in trouble for not having my mask on rather than doing a completely efficient job is the FAA's fault.  The FAA is making us fear the repercussions of the mask mandate; so much its eroding the safety of the NAS...DO NOT REQUIRE MASK TO BE WORN ON POSITION IF WE ARE ALREADY SIX FEET APART; which we are based on the distance of scope to scope. Whether its distracting; [probably] muffles transmissions; the mask mandate on position is depleting the safety of the NAS.
column123: I was working LC. Runway XX was the active Runway; advertising RNAVs.Aircraft X; checked on Tower frequency on an 11 mile final at an altitude of 1;700 feet.  I noticed a target moving east to west at a high rate of speed (240 knots) and was not tagged up.  I called traffic to Aircraft X at his 2 o'clock 3 to 4 miles moving westbound at 1;500 feet.  Aircraft X said he had it on his TCAS and he was looking for traffic.  I continued to watch the westbound traffic realizing it was going to potentially become a conflict for Aircraft X and continued to call traffic to them.  I advised Aircraft X to try and maintain 1;700 feet based on the fact the westbound traffic appeared to be holding 1;500 and Aircraft X was on an instrument approach.  I also told Aircraft X it appeared the traffic was going to pass underneath. Aircraft X reported the traffic in sight right as my Ground Control and I realized the target was making a hard 180 degree turn back to the east while climbing up into Aircraft X's flight path and altitude. I responded back to Aircraft X to maneuver at his discretion to avoid the aircraft. The target continued eastbound.  Aircraft X landed without incident.  I asked Aircraft X if he would give me a call so that I may ask questions.  I told him he was not in trouble; he obliged and I gave him the tower number.  I then attempted to call the Supervisor from our communications counsel to ask what was going on with the target to no avail; the Supervisor did not pick up. Once on break I was able to speak with the pilot: The Pilot said it was a [description].  He caught a glimpse of it while it passed underneath then Aircraft Y did the 180 degree turn back east and passed right off the nose of his aircraft at his altitude.  The pilot also mentioned that his passengers had asked about the aircraft; leading me to believe in fact Aircraft Y was extremely close and causing this to be a significant event.  The pilot said he was also going to file a report.I took the information down to my Supervisor.  My Supervisor called the ZZZ [TRACON] Supervisor who said he didn't know anything of the event and that he was too busy to look into at the moment.  Seeing as how Aircraft Y came from ZZZ's TRACON airspace; my Supervisor gave them a call to see if they knew anything about Aircraft Y and what it was doing.  ZZZ4 said they were talking to Aircraft Y and had coordinated with ZZZ with a point out; ZZZ accepted the point out on Aircraft Y.  There was never any coordination from ZZZ to myself on LC in reference to Aircraft Y.Note: I did not issue a Traffic Alert because I had no clue what Aircraft Y was doing; I was focused on calling the traffic from the beginning;  and with the 180 degree high speed turn I felt like giving the pilot discretion to maneuver as needed (since he had him in sight then) was the best course of action for the pilot to be able to keep his passengers alive.Note:  Aircraft Y was never tagged up on the scope.  They appeared to be VFR but I'm really unsure if they were.Events like this in the ZZZ [TRACON] airspace and ZZZ [Tower] environment in my opinion are a consistent problem.1.  ATC 101: coordination and positive control. ZZZ1 [TRACON] coordinated with ZZZ [TRACON] as a point out.  ZZZ [TRACON] accepting the point out.  In all reality both facilities should be monitoring what Aircraft Y was doing.  The original point out coordination was that Aircraft Y was going 6 miles west of the fix ZZZZZ.  Once Aircraft Y passed 6 miles there were 2 possible controllers to notice and do something about it.  ZZZ [TRACON] should have questioned ZZZ1 [TRACON] and myself reference Aircraft X; ZZZ1 [TRACON] should have reached out to Aircraft Y and ZZZ [TRACON].  Because no one did Aircraft Y was 15 miles west of ZZZZZ and crossing through the final of Runway XX at ZZZ.2. Take responsibility when you have accepted a point out by keeping an eye on the target as well as looking at your current traffic and what may be aconflict between the point out and current traffic. Do NOT lose track of your traffic and or point outs (which was the excuse of the ZZZ [TRACON] Controller). If you're busy do not accept the point out potentially causing yourself to 'lose track' of traffic.3.  CARE! This job is not a game.  There is not time to not care when human lives are at stake.For my side:1.  I have re-played this 1000 times over in my head.  I think maybe I could have called a traffic alert but what I can't see is what I would have suggested to Aircraft X.  I called the traffic early and continued too; once he got it I felt like the pilot knew how to fly that plane better than me; and could see what Aircraft Y was doing better than me as well.  If I had given him a suggestion based on how erratic Aircraft Y was I truly think it would have ended badly.   The pilot's RA never went off; and speaking to the pilot he wasn't sure why but he said it probably had no idea what to do based on what that Aircraft Y was doing.2.  Suggestion; call the pilot if able or the airport and question said pilot.  Potentially file a deviation or ask what was going on.3.Stop the 'holes in the swiss cheese'.  This was always my favorite CBI [Computer Based Instruction].  In order to not have the holes line up you have to be vigilant always.  I try and will continue to try. Maybe I could have even been more vigilant today?  Saw it coming earlier?4.  Encourage pilots to file reports so this information can be turned into learning experiences.Thank you for reading some recommendations; and there are probably 100 more things that could be done.  This event took a toll on myself the rest of my shift.  Some things you just can't un-see; but for myself it makes me better and care even more for our pilots in the sky and their passengers.

column121: We were cleared to FL 230. Passing through 17;500 feet; #1 engine rolled back to approximately 30%N1.  The N1 and EGT had flashing red and yellow arcs and the lower section had a red flashing box around both engine indications. Our initial analysis was engine failure.  We requested to level at FL 180; communicated to ATC our situation and requested vectors to return to ZZZ.  Upon further analysis of the engine condition; the Captain (Pilot Flying) stated the engine was still running but noted the indications were not normal. We also saw the EEC in ALTN mode.  Captain continued to fly and directed me into the QRH for the EEC ALT MODE checklist since the engine was running and not surging; stalling; or any indications dictating complete failure or the need to shutdown.  We completed the QRH for the EEC ALT MODE according to our situation and indications.  We discussed and agreed to also reference and ran the QRH [for] One Engine Inoperative Landing.  I continued communications with ATC; while the Captain communicated with F/A's and made a PA to passengers. I computed [landing] data and set up the FMC. Captain flew the approach and landing; taxiing clear of the runway to a safe location.  Autobrakes were used and no manual braking activated until slowed (approximately 50 knots) and prior to the exit of the runway.  Based on our weight and configuration [calculations] prior to landing required the use of autobrakes and brake cooling calculations.  I calculated the [landing data] for Non-Normal One engine Inop with 15 Flaps landing.   Brake Cooling calculations returned a 58 minute cooling period; which we accomplished at the turnout abeam runway.  Emergency Rescue Crews communicated to us no visible smoke from brakes and heat signature negative. After the 58 minute cool down; we were given clearance to taxi and proceeded to our gate.
column123: When we arrived at the gate; Maintenance was working on the #1 engine. The previous crew that had the aircraft had returned to the gate. When they started the number one engine they got the Engine Control light. Maintenance cleaned the cannon plugs did an engine run and returned the aircraft to service. Our engine start and initial climb were all normal. We were on radar vectors for our route and climbing through 17;500 feet or so when the #1 N1 Gauge flashed yellow twice. We both saw it; then the #1 engine rolled back to 31% on the N1 but the engine didn't quit. We leveled at FL 180 and requested vectors back to ZZZ. We ran the EEC ALT Mode Checklist and the Engine Failure or Shutdown Checklist from the QRH. Landed Flaps 15; autobrakes 3. We ran the brake cooling calculation prior to landing. We had a 58 minutes of break cooling.

column121: I was PF from ZZZ-ZZZ1; during the climbout at 17;000 feet with the autopilot engaged we had just started to get some trace ice on the windshield wipers (probe heat and engine anti-ice on) when we got 'IAS DISAGREE' caution lights on both CA (Captain) and FO (First Officer) PFDs. No other alerts. We requested priority handling with ATC. We looked at the IAS disagree checklist in the Quick Reference Handbook which then told us to go to the 'AIRSPEED UNRELIABLE' checklist. I performed the initial Quick Reference Checklist procedures and then the CA read through the rest of the Quick Reference Handbook as I followed procedures and continued hand flying up to cruise altitude of 34;000 feet. We determined that the problem was on the FO side so once the checklists were complete and we were leveled off at cruise altitude; we swapped controls and the CA became PF since he had the accurate airspeed indication. 'IAS DISAGREE' flashed on and off frequently as the spread between CA and FO IAS +/- 10-15 kts and then it stayed on consistently for ~30 minutes during climb. Once we were at cruise and clear of icing and clouds then the 'IAS DISAGREE' indication went away and the FO IAS indicator appeared to work normally. We discussed with dispatch our possible diversion choices but all of them either involved going through a line of weather or re-encountering icing; we decided that the safest course of action was to continue on to ZZZ1 where the weather was VFR. Then as we started our VFR descent into ZZZ1; we got the 'IAS DISAGREE' indication flashing on and off again sporadically several times with no further issues associated and landed uneventfully.The logbook had showed that an inspection had been performed on pitot static system overnight in ZZZ. Icing conditions present during taxi and climb. ATC gave us everything we asked for. Captain said that crew phone to contact Dispatch was valuable. Recent MAX training definitely made our response simple and effective. We found out from the mechanics that met us at our gate that this aircraft had had multiple pitot/airspeed problems in the past. Aircraft was a MAX.I've heard now that we are the 2nd 737 (ours being a MAX; other being an NG) that has had 'Unreliable Airspeed' in the last week! Need to ground these aircraft until the source(s) of the problems are resolved.

column121: We were level 5;000 feet 250 knots approaching ZZZ VOR on the ZZZZZ2 Star. Approach gave a heading 280 and slow to 180 and asked if we had the field in sight. The sun was just above the horizon as I looked west and across the cockpit for the field.  Simultaneously I was looking cross-cockpit and programing the speed and heading change into the FMC. I could make out the field so I said to the Captain (PM); 'I can see the field; you can call it in sight.'  I noticed another aircraft on TCAS at our altitude on TCAS and then saw them visually less than ten miles away; also headed west toward ZZZ [Airport]; I noted the  paint scheme and relayed to the PM all that information and that they were probably headed to the north side of the airport.  In my head I was thinking that our airplane was not slowing down as fast as I would like when the PM said 'where is that airplane; I think we need to turn.' I pushed the localizer button on the FMC but the airplane did not turn so I turned the autopilot off and manually turned to intercept final for [Runway] XXR. As I did; we received at TCAS TA then a few seconds later a TCAS RA to climb.  The ADI showed a red boxed area from level flight down (I was descending) so I just leveled off until we heard 'clear of conflict.'   Then Approach gave us a 180 heading; paused; and then said 'you guys can't do that;' and switched us to Tower.  I was able to correct the high energy level of the airplane using gear; flaps; and speed brakes and continued the approach and landed uneventfully.Fast close to the airfield; sun in eyes; failure on my part to use automation.Something from ATC that I was going to turn towards the runway instead of downwind in the [Runway] XXR pattern or an advisory where we were in the sequence.  My recency of experience led to not arming the localizer; while I did brief that at the start of the first leg I could have reemphasized it during the approach brief.

When the PF re-cruised he inadvertently typed in '320' instead of '230'.  There was not an immediate erroneous depiction on the ND.  Everything looked normal; however we continued past the descent point.  Just as we realized there was something wrong; the ND descent point disappeared.  The PF has been on reserve and has flown very little in the last two months.  The next two flights went well with no problems.The two pilots were on the first leg of the trip.  It was the first time they'd flow together.  They were working well together and both were attempting to follow policies/procedures.  This was a dumb mistake by one pilot that was not caught by the other.  By re-cruising; the goal was to have the ND provide usable descent point information.  I listed this as a 'Moderate' risk rating because we easily received relief from ATC.  If they had not assisted us; the risk would have been higher.

column121: On date; our aircraft took necessary evasive action to avoid a Near midair collision while on an IFR Flight Plan in Night-time Visual Meteorological Conditions. Our aircraft was descending to an assigned altitude 7;000 feet while established on an assigned heading of 220 degrees. While descending through approximately 7;700 feet; at approximately 17.5 DME from BAPPA Intersection (Initial Fix for RNAV approach Runway 19 at GEU) approximately 229 degrees bearing to the fix; the onboard TCAS System issued a 'Traffic-Traffic Advisory'. About one second later the approach Controller issued a 'traffic alert' in conjunction with an 'immediate left turn' heading assignment of 170 degrees. After hearing the tone in the Controller's voice; I immediately complied with the Controller's (initial) request. As I glanced over to the TCAS portion of the screen; the conflicting traffic and our aircraft appeared to be converging; almost touching our aircraft's position on the screen. Scaled down to lowest distance ring/range; I estimate the distance between aircraft was less than a mile and the traffic was at about our twelve to one o'clock position. The traffic's altitude indicated 700 feet below our current altitude while we were descending before I looked away from the screen. I believe the traffic continued on a converging trajectory relative to our position prompting the Controller to re-issue the traffic alert combined with the immediate left turn heading assignment. I am not sure if the Controller did not receive our first acknowledgement of their Traffic Alert or if it was the fact the Controller saw our targets practically merge on their scope; but the tone in the Controller's re-issuance of the clearance convinced me the conflicting traffic had closed the distance between our aircraft and I was more focused on flying away from the traffic than verifying our distance by staring at the screen. My copilot confirmed the altitude separation was as little as 400 feet on screen and the traffic's position along with our position had merged on screen. At first glance; our distance to the conflicting aircraft appeared so close; I didn't have enough time to try to gauge the aircraft's performance or our convergence trajectory on screen. At that moment I felt there was not enough distance between us to wait for a Resolution Advisory from our TCAS System either. I discontinued the descent and level-off assignment of 7;000 and initiated an immediate power and pitch up maneuver. As a result; I climbed about 1;000 feet about our then current altitude of approximately 7;700 to an altitude of approximated 8;700 and the speed of our aircraft increased by about 30 knots from approximately 250 knots to approximately 280 knots indicated airspeed. When I was clear of conflict; I resumed the descent to 7;000 feet; resumed normal speed and complied with the Controller's new clearance. I am convinced the Controller's immediate left turn heading assignment alone was not sufficient to avoid the conflict. While performing the evasive maneuver; I heard the Controller correcting another aircraft on frequency advising them of a possible pilot deviation by that aircraft; however I don't recall if the term 'Pilot Deviation' was actually used and am not sure if that aircraft the Controller corrected was the same aircraft that caused our Traffic Alert/ Traffic Advisory. The Controller seemed extremely busy at this time; so we opted not to query the Controller on frequency regarding our near-miss. The area in which this occurred lies just north of DVT airport near a practice area; an area notorious for intensive pilot training. The brightly lit city lights on a clear night sky while descending may have masked the exterior lights of the conflicting aircraft just ahead and below us; as we never caught a visual of the aircraft.

column121: Sat in ZZZ for hours for a delayed flight coming from ZZZ1. During the swap; the outgoing Captain informed me that the Crew that brought the aircraft into ZZZ1 said that upon landing the right thrust reverser malfunctioned. The delay was due to Contract Maintenance MEL'ing the right thrust reverser. During pre-flight I checked the logbook; Release; and stickers as well as looked up the MEL on my EFB. During this time the 'A' Flight Attendant informed me that a passenger was refusing to wear their mask and creating a scene and that the CSR had been called. Eventually the passenger was removed and an updated report was sent to the aircraft. During the distraction I neglected to click on the hyperlink in the MEL in the Maintenance portion labeled MEL SP#XX Thrust Reverser System. If I had I would have noticed on that a Circuit Breaker for the #2 Engine should have been pulled and collared. Upon landing in ZZZ2 I informed the outgoing Captain of the MEL. During my commute home I received a text from said Captain that he found the wrong CB had been collared and that he had written it up and ZZZ2 Maintenance was fixing the issue. Upon reviewing the SP#XX I can only assume that the CB for the #1 Engine had been pulled instead.
column123: Inbound Captain advised that they had received the aircraft late in ZZZ due to Thrust Reverser MEL applied in ZZZ1 on previous flight and then further delayed on their flight due to a Passenger refusing to comply with mask requirements.In reviewing the logbook I found that the MEL sticker in the front of the logbook was not completed. The MEL number was not entered; the Special procedures performed were not entered and the circuit breakers pulled and collared were not entered.   When I reviewed the logbook entry; the special procedures were references SP-XX.  I also observed C/B's  #2 Engine TR Sync Lock and #2 Engine TR INTLK pulled and collared.I then reviewed the MEL and SP-XX and discovered the following errors.1. SP XX calls for the #2 Engine TR Sync Lock c/b and the #2 Engine TR Control c/b to be pulled and collared.  the Control C/B was NOT collared as prescribed in SP XXnd the INTLK c/b WAS collared contrary to SP XX2. There was no MEL sticker placed on the Inoperative TR lever.3. There was no MEL sticker placed above the respected N1 gauge.I contacted Maintenance Control to confirm my understanding of the MEL regarding the incorrect Circuit Breakers and they confirmed the wrong circuit breaker had been pulled.  Notified ZZZ2 Maintenance and entered the discrepancy in the logbook. ZZZ2 Maintenance arrived and corrected the circuit breaker configuration and signed off the discrepancy I had entered. Missing information on the logbook sticker was also corrected.I have long felt that our MEL is VERY inadequate when it comes to circuit breaker identification.  In this particular instance the nomenclature is correct and was just applied incorrectly by the Mechanic; but if the C/B locations were included  it would have been much more apparent to the Mechanic as well as flight crew that the two C/B would not be immediately adjacent to each other.  I have brought this to the attention of Flight Ops previously with regards to other MEL's and have been advised that changes are slated for a future revision that has been delayed due to aircraft out of service returns; COVID and other issues. I also feel it should be reinforced to flight crews that MEL compliance is not solely the responsibility of the Maintenance department and that we should always verify (to the limits of our abilities) those aspects of MEL compliance which we have ready access to on each airplane we accept regardless of previous crews acceptance of the aircraft.
