column121: About XX minutes after we reached our cruise altitude; my FO (First Officer) and I observed the level on our #2 Oil Qty gauge go from 11 to Y then Z; then blank rather quickly.  It had been normal up until then; we just caught the decrease at 11. After checking the QRC and QRH for Low Oil Qty to no avail; we noticed our #2 Oil Pressure dropping. It stabilized at 29 psi but fluctuated from XX to XY with 29 being the median amber band.  This continued for the remainder of the flight until TOD (Top of Descent).  I referenced the Engine Low Oil Pressure Checklist in the QRH on Page X.XX.  It states that if the oil pressure is at or below the redline: Go to the Engine Failure or Shutdown checklist on Page X.XY. The oil pressure never reached the redline; so the checklist stops there.  All other engine parameters were normal with no vibration.  My FO (First Officer) continued to fly and talk with ATC while I set up a phone patch with our Dispatcher as I decided that there was too much information to use ACARS.  I told them what was going on and that we were continuing on to ZZZ but we were also prepared to divert if need be later on.  They were in agreement as there was no need or requirement at this time to shut the engine down or divert.  I talked with the Flight Attendants and we had a good discussion about the situation.  I told them that our aircraft was operating just fine and that it seems that we have an indication issue and that I was not going to make a PA.  I also asked them if they could discretely look at the aft portion of the right hand engine to see if they saw any oil.  My FO (First Officer) and Flight Attendants did a great job along with our Dispatcher and Maintenance Control.  Later in the flight; our Dispatcher gave us single engine landing data for ZZZ.  Descending into ZZZ when the thrust levers were slowly retarded to idle; the oil pressure and qty actually increased.  By the time we were on final approach; the said indications were normal.

column121: I was the First Officer and the pilot monitoring. We were cleared to descend via the ZZZZZX. Approaching FL200 on the descent; I noticed my airspeed start to decrease rapidly without any change in airplane thrust or pitch. I called out 'airspeed' while inspecting the standby and Captain's airspeed indicator. We called unreliable airspeed and started the QRC (Quick Reference Checklist). We followed the QRC followed by the QRH (Quick Reference Handbook). We were able to confirm that the Captain's airspeed indicator was accurate based on the pitch and power settings and correlating with the standby airspeed indicator. The QRH instructed us to reengage the autopilot and change the ALT SOURCE selector to the Captain's side. This allowed my airspeed indicator to correspond with the Captain's and standby airspeed indicator. After we dictated which airspeed was accurate; ATC had given a heading and altitude to continue into ZZZ. I completed the QRH checklist for Unreliable Airspeed but kept the unreliable airspeed tables open to make sure the pitch and power settings correlated with our speed. We continued to fly the ILS approach into ZZZ without any further incident. The Captain notified Maintenance and Dispatch once we were blocked in and the door open. We were unable to conclude the cause that created the unreliable airspeed situation. But; I will become more familiar with the airspeed unreliable checklist and table so that I may refer to it and utilize it more efficiently in the event of another similar occurrence.

column121: I was the First Officer and pilot monitoring on this ZZZ to ZZZ1 flight; XXX on [aircraft]; arriving into ZZZ1 from the south east; at night; in VFR conditions. Due to the winds out of the north at ZZZ1 (310 at 12 gusting 21); RWY XX was the only landing runway on the ATIS.   Upon loading RWY XX; the ZZZZZ [arrival] would not show as an available arrival in the FMC.  ATC did not assign the ZZZZZ arrival but instead gave us direct ZZZZZ1 (a waypoint on the ZZZZZ); and then direct to the airport. These ATC instructions were given near ZZZZZ2 [fix] on our flight plan. With the Captains concurrence I executed direct ZZZZZ3. Additionally; the Captain had me select ZZZZZ3/12;000 as a hard altitude in the FMC to help with descent planning (12;000 was a crossing altitude restriction on the ZZZZZ1). I then placed ZZZZZ5 as the waypoint that would follow.   As we got closer to ZZZZZ3; Approach directed us to maintain present heading with a further descent to 10;000. This heading did not keep us in a direction tracking the ZZZZZ arrival over the water along [geographic fix 1] ; but instead brought us on a more westerly heading over terrain on the southwest side of [geographic fix 1].Approach then directed a descent to 8;000. Then directed a right turn to 250. Then directed a further right turn to 260. And finally; a descent to 7;000.   Approach then asked: 'Do you have the field in sight? 2oclock 21 miles'   The Captain and the Observer both spoke up to speaking that they could see the airport. I as well saw the lights of the airport and felt comfortable concurring.   The Captain said he could accept the visual and so I then relayed this to  Approach. Approach than cleared us the visual approach RWY XX.   At this point the Captain looking at his descent planning showed us slightly high on the VNAV descent path and started a descent below 7;000.   Shortly after this and around 6;200 ft; a GPWS alert 'CAUTION TERRAIN' enunciated. Looking at my Terrain display; the AMBER terrain mapping showed terrain off to our right. The Captain immediately arrested his descent and the Observer and the Captain and I visually confirmed the terrain off to the right of our flight path.   Shortly after this ATC further directed us to begin our right turn towards the field.   The Captain and I continued to maintain visual separation with the terrain and delayed further descent until comfortable the terrain clearance was no longer a concern. We then conducted an LVSA on the MCP and an uneventful landing in ZZZ1. [Reporter added concerns] accepting a visual approach at night. Although we could see the lighted airport environment ahead; what was not so apparent was the dark terrain just below the city lights that was still ahead and to the right of our flight path. At night; the city lights in the distance can cause night vision to be affected and spotting unlit terrain between your flight path can be potentially more difficult to see. Accepting a visual approach is not something that should be done lightly. The better course of action was to recommend to the Captain we delay accepting a visual until we were closer to the field and the terrain well behind us.  ATC did not help matters by asking us to an accept a visual approach as early as they did. A mistaken assumption could be made that the terrain protections of 7;000 was past us and a descent to establish an already slightly high VNAV path to RWY XX could be initiated. Clearly the terrain ahead was much closer to our altitude; we had several miles to go before a descent below 7000 should have been initiated. The GPWS 'CAUTION TERRAIN' was a very clear on this point.   The importance of GPWS Terrain monitoring [is that] GPWS is an essential situational awareness tool and one the pilot monitoring only had displayed initially. Had the Captain also had TERR selected this may have mitigated the early descent; but as pilot monitoring I should have done a better job monitoring the TerrainMapping display. Clearly after the 'CAUTION TERRAIN' annunciation appeared; the Yellow Terrain mapping became very clear on both our displays.   Additionally; when descending in mountainous terrain it's also important to remember that the GPWS system will only display terrain data that is 2;000 feet below or closer to the aircraft. Depending on your range ring and your location and rate of descent; you can quickly go from no terrain colors to quite colorful ones in short order. Vigilance in monitoring Terrain Mapping along your flight path is key.   Lastly; had this situation happened in [different type aircraft]; the terrain profile view function would have provided significant situational awareness to the crew on the terrain that was still ahead.   [Regarding] RNAV approach to XX; the [company] aircraft behind us had received approval to fly to a point on an RNAV approach to XX; an approach that is currently not available on our aircraft. Had this been available; this would have been a valuable tool providing altitude protections and a significant aid to situational awareness.   Even if not an RNAV approach; a visual approach page like the ZZZZZ3 VISUAL Rwy XY that is available in JEPPS would have also aided in better descent planning for the RWY XX visual approach.

column121: We conducted the ZZZZZ4 arrival and joined the ILS XX approach from ZZZZZ [Intersection] as briefed. When the Captain contacted the Tower; the Controller cleared us to land XX Right. The Captain read back the clearance. I said; 'Can you confirm Controller wants us to land on the right? We're on the ILS XX Left.' The Captain confirmed with the Controller cleared to land on the right. The Controller responded 'Affirmative. XX Right; Cleared to land.' At the time; we were well above 1;000 feet in visual conditions with the runway in sight and; so I had no objection. I clicked off the autopilot and side-stepped to XX Right and we landed. No issues arose with ATC or any other traffic. The next day; the Captain reached out to me and we spoke over the phone. Captain learned that we had actually been cleared for the ILS XX Right approach and Captain intended to file a report. A couple of days later I was finally able to confirm that this was correct. We aren't able to determine if it was being read back correctly or incorrectly; but there was never a clarification type of response from ZZZ Approach. It's also important to bring up that the Captain was wearing a face mask throughout the flight operations which did contribute to difficulties in communication with myself and with ATC at various times during the trip. This likely was a contributing factor to our deviation. Another contributing factor was the violation of sterile cockpit below 18;000 feet by the Captain and myself. Personally; I was distracted by our conversation as well as the fact that Captain was wearing a mask during the flight.Complacency is also a factor as the ZZZZZ4 Arrival usually results in the ILS or visual to XX Left.I think our company needs to take a harder stance on mask-wearing during flight operations in the flight deck.  I recommend that the company forbids the use of masks by pilots during flight operations to ensure that communications are clear and effective. In this case; it can be assumed that the Captain was repeating the clearance saying 'XX Left' but the Controller did not hear it clearly and assumed Captain was saying XX Right. Therefore; Captain was never corrected and we continued with what we had expected in our heads. There were multiple points throughout our trip that ATC did not understand the Captain and asked who was calling or needed clarification on what Captain was saying because it was difficult to understand with the mask. I thought on several occasions throughout our trip that it was the Captain's choice to wear it but if we have an emergency situation that I really hope Captain would take it off so that effective communication could be established and maintained. An emergency situation did not occur; but clearly an issue did arise with our approach to our destination.
column123: ZZZ had a broken layer at 1;700 feet and we were expecting to do an approach. Descending into ZZZ on the ZZZZZ4 arrival we had set up for the ILS [Runway] XXL. We were assigned to join the ILS [Runway] XXR at ZZZZZ [Intersection] and then later cleared for the ILS XXR approach. We did not fly the ILS XXR. We flew the XXL approach and when we were on with Tower; we told them we were inbound on the ILS XXL. Tower cleared us to land XXR. By the time we contacted Tower we were out of the clouds and could see the runway. We verified two times that we were cleared to land XXR and not XXL. And Tower confirmed that we were to land XXR. Since we had visual on the runway; we side stepped and landed on XXR. We were probably at 1;500-1;600 feet AFE when we side stepped. We were confused as to why they had changed runways on us; but we knew that XXR was longer than XXL and that the landing speeds were the same and we were familiar with the airport. As we side stepped; I programmed in the ILS XXR so that we had a backup source even though we visually had the airport in sight. Later in the evening it still didn't sit right with me that we had a runway change that late; especially since we had been on an IFR approach. I realized we had in fact been assigned ILS XXR all the way back on with Approach. They never corrected me. So; I either read it back correctly but we were really hearing what we wanted to hear (ILS XXL) or they never corrected me and we all missed it. The approach was stable all the way through for XXL and the sidestep was done in a safe manner.I attribute not being sterile in the descent as a factor even though we were assigned to join ILS XXR at ZZZZZ prior to FL180. I would say complacency and expectancy were the primary factors. XXL wasn't closed and we were set that we would be doing the ILS XXL. It was also the last leg on the last day of our trip and we had had a long day. I had been up since 8 or 9am and we had flown 4 legs. This flight landed around XApm.I can say that I once again am reminded how serious our jobs are and that miss hearing a simple 'L' vs 'R' can be life changing. I can only say that I am thankful that this took place during a low traffic period and that we were able to maintain a safe condition. I'm honestly not too sure how to avoid this situation. I believe that writing down my clearances would assist in allowing me to verify and that maybe I need to make sure to turn my headset up so that I won't miss ATC.

column121: After completing a fuel stop at PEO; I taxied from the fuel pump near the FBO to Runway 28 for departure. Prior to taxiing I completed my pre-taxi checks and self announced my taxi on CTAF. The wind was 220@17G23 and I wanted to complete my run up into the wind. Runway 28/10 doesn't have a parallel taxiway to the East requiring a back taxi for approximately the half the runway length. The runway; departure and arrival corridor appeared clear and I announced taking the runway for back taxi with no other traffic heard. I completed a short run up; scanned the runway and announced on CTAF I was taking off Runway 28. I applied power; checked instruments and accelerated down the runway. Shortly I noted something in the distance down the runway; a second later noticed engines rise above the crest of the the runway and I immediately aborted takeoff. I was close to rotation speed; pulled power back and aggressively braked. Once at a safe speed I announced I was aborting and vacating the runway. I was close the the north/south taxi and uneventfully exited the runway at that point. At that time I saw a Falcon jet exit runway 10/28 via the next taxiway about 800 feet down the runway heading to the fuel pumps. I turned my aircraft around announced my back taxi and departure. Concerned that I had an equipment issue or was on the wrong frequency I asked for a radio check while I was departing downwind and received a good check. Due to a significant crown/slope in the runway it is not possible to see the opposite ends of the Runway 28/10. The other aircraft operator should follow the best practices identified in AC 90-66b par 10.1 self-announce their intentions and monitor the frequency for other traffic as well. Additionally; the aircraft was taxiing from the west hangars to the fuel pumps and if there's sufficient wingtip clearance they should use the parallel taxiway instead of the runway as an increased measure of safety.

column121: I was wrapping up a long training flight with my instructor and we were practicing approaches and landings before wraping up for the day. On the third landing approach there was a Cessna 150 ahead of us in the pattern.  I extended the downwind to make room and turned base and final much further out than typical. One of the things we had been practicing is making sure to be low enough on the approach to not overshoot since it is such a short runway.  On this approach I was quite low and setup a little low on final when I realized that while I had seen the C150 land I wasn't certain it had cleared the runway. I thought it might still be on there and asked my instructor if we should go around. He said no and to go ahead and land since we didn't see the other aircraft on the runway anymore and we would be landing very short. The previous loop around the pattern I initiated a go around because it didn't feel right but was assured that we were setup just right for landing and should've landed.  I think that I was reluctant to do another go around 'for no reason' if I didn't need to according to the instructor.Shortly after landing and rolling out several feet and up the incline in the runway we saw the other airplane at the far end. At just about the same time we heard frantic calls for the other airplane to get off the runway as soon as possible.  I was setup for a short field landing and exited the runway after a very short landing roll about 1;700 feet from where the other aircraft had exited the runway.  We were shaken from the realization that we had shared the runway and scared the other training aircraft.Contributing factors:1. Fatigue- This was one of the first training sessions after a 4 month break and my instructor and I were exhausted.2. Human Factors - I deferred to my instructors experience and decided against the go around.  We have since discussed this issue and agreed that if either of us feel a go around is a good idea we will go around.3. Airport -  The runway X landing zone is at a significantly lower elevation than the XX end of the runway. because of the geography is difficult to see aircraft at the other end.

column121: Aircraft X was IFR inbound to ZZZ requesting the LOC RWY XX; however; the tower still on their COVID hours closes early. When the tower closed they put the localizer on RWY YY so the LOC RWY XX was unavailable. Due to winds Aircraft X was unable RWY YY. They requested the RNAV Y RWY XX. I had traffic for Aircraft X as they were approaching ZZZZZ with the crossing altitude of 051 and the traffic at 047 I gave a restriction for traffic. This confused the pilot so I went back and cancelled the approach clearance and told the pilot to expect clearance at ZZZZZ1; but this was a mistake; what I meant to say was ZZZZZ. The pilot did not question me but did seem confused. Rightfully so. When Aircraft X was clear of the traffic they reported that they were direct ZZZZZ. I then cleared Aircraft X to cross ZZZZZ at 5;100 cleared straight in RNAV Y Rwy XX approach. Aircraft X appeared to over shoot ZZZZZ before turning to ZZZZZ2. I questioned the pilot that the next fix past ZZZZZ was ZZZZZ2; is that where they show their self going. The pilot stated they just passed ZZZZZ2 and I can't quite understand what they said after that. But at the time I thought they said going to ZZZZZ3 the next fix on the approach. While this was going on I had a couple other aircraft waiting and another facility call me for point outs. When my attention took me back to Aircraft X their path appeared off and had began a go around and the moment they called me I issued the low altitude alert and an immediate climb. They attempted the approach and landed safely on the second attempt. My initial reaction to this approach was that something was off; which is when I questioned the pilot. I gave them the benefit of the doubt and hoped that they had corrected the overshoot at ZZZZZ and was properly on the RNAV Y RWY XX at ZZZ. However; I should have just gone with my gut and broke the aircraft off the approach when I noticed the error and vectored back around for a second attempt. Hindsight when you look back is always better. We try to not delay aircraft and hope that they are truthful when we question them about approaches. However; safety is our number one priority and concern and I did feel like there was something not right and looking back I wish I would have just broken the aircraft off the approach and re-sequenced. It is always easier to watch a replay to see how we can improve; but that is important so we do not repeat our mistakes.

column121: Uneventful flight to ZZZ. On final ILS XXR at ZZZ; below 2;500 feet; inside ZZZZZ but prior to ZZZZZ1; LOC and GS Captainured; flaps 20 set; Captain called for leg gear down and disconnected AP and A/T. At this moment; the L HYD SYS PRESS Master Caution Lt illuminated. At first I thought the light was associated with the AP and A/T being disconnected. It took a couple seconds to recognize that it was the HYD pressure light. At this time also we were checking in with  XX_1 r outside ZZZZZ1 and were cleared to land. Very shortly after I accepted the leg clearance; the Captain alerted to Go Around and made the Go Around call to Tower. We accomplished the normal go around procedure and shortly received a LDG GEAR DISAGREE caution as the gear did not retract due to the initial emergency. We repositioned the gear handle to the down position and that caution extinguished. After reaching 3;000 feet and completing the GA procedures; the Captain continued to fly the AC and I accessed the Non Normal procedure through the FM on my EFB. The HYD section has a large index and initially I inadvertently selected the HYD SYS PRESS L and C non-normal and after the first two steps realized we were in the wrong checklist and switched to the HYD SYS PRESS L (only) Checklist. I ran the checklist aloud as the Captain continued to fly. Step 7 instructed not to use auto brakes. When completing the deferred items; the flaps and gear were already in the proper configuration and due to the post Go Around altitude and box pattern vectors; though not unduly rushed; I inadvertently failed to re-run the descent checklist as part of the deferred items; missing the last reminder to not use autobrakes. We did run the deferred landing checklist; and the Captain flew the approach to landing. After touchdown the auto brakes engaged firmly and the Captain immediately moved the speed brake lever slightly fwd to disengage the autobrakes and proceeded to manually brake the AC along with use of the RT engine reverser. We slowed to a gentle stop with approximately 1;500 feet remaining on Runway XXR. Due to the lack of runway steering we remained on the runway; coordinating with ground personnel; and monitored brake temps. After an initial external check by ground personnel; we secured the engines; remaining on APU power for the remainder of the ground ops evolution and tug to our gate.
column123: Communicating with ZZZ approach on the ILS XXR to ZZZ between ZZZZZ and ZZZZ1; with the flaps at 20 and after lowering the landing gear; we received an EICAS message L HYD SYS PRESS. I was Pilot Flying; hand flying with the A/P and A/T off. The First Officer was Pilot Monitoring. At ZZZZZ1 we switched to ZZZ Tower and informed them we would abandon the approach. We were given a northerly heading and a climb to 3;000 [feet]. I decided to abandon the approach using V/S mode as we were at approximately 1;600 feet; and to reduce my workload; engaged the right autopilot. I inadvertently called for 'Gear Up' which did not occur due to the loss of the left system. We realized this error when a 'GEAR DISAGREE' EICAS message appeared and returned the gear handle to the down position. The gear remained down from the prior approach through the eventual landing.I stated the I had the airplane and the radios and directed the First Officer to run the L HYD SYS PRESS non-normal checklist.We also pulled up the status page and noted the loss of quantity from the left system; less than .2 with RF showing.We initially started the L and C HYD SYS PRESS checklist but caught the error when the checklist called for an action regarding the center system.We then proceeded to run the L HYD SYS PRESS checklist; but made an error; missing the 'do not use autobrakes' step. I would eventually select Autobrakes 4 for landing.ATC asked me at this point if I needed the equipment standing by and I declined.Upon completion of the checklist up to deferred items; I [advised] with ATC.ATC asked us which runway we would like; and I inquired about [Runway] XYL. ATC said it would be available as a visual approach. I decided to re-use the ILS to XXR as we were set up for it already; would benefit from the precision guidance at night; and it had an approach light system that [Runway] XYL did not. The length of [Runway] XXR provided our required landing distance; with margin; plus around another 4;000 feet.I sent a brief ACARS message to Dispatch stating I had [advised with ATC] and would be landing in ZZZ. I should have included the nature of the [event] and our need of a tow in the body of the message. Despite being somewhat concerned about the time available as I was stuck in a high drag configuration; I still had enough time to send a more complete message and should have done so- it would have been a few more keystrokes. I also had enough time to re-run the non-normal checklist. Doing so would have caught the autobrake restriction. The First Officer and I discussed this in our debrief.I then briefed the purser using the TEST acronym; advising that we would NOT need to prep the cabin for evac.I do not recall asking for the equipment to be standing by; other than stating we would need to be towed off the runway. The equipment was in fact standing by for us at landing and detected hydraulic fluid that contaminated the runway.ATC had provided a modified box vector for us; and as we were approaching base I exchanged roles with the First Officer and assumed aircraft control as Pilot Flying. I called for the deferred items. Another opportunity exists in the deferred items with a descent checklist step stating the autobrakes should be off. In our debrief; we discussed that the were a number of items in the deferred items checklist that were not applicable to our situation such as alternate gear and flap extension. This may have led to the error and missing the descent checklist step. We committed to running future checklists step-by-step.The flaps 20 approach was uneventful; and I used the autopilot and autothrottle until short final. Approach had given us a discrete frequency for ZZZ Tower and the rescue equipment. At landing; I felt a sensation similar to anti-skid activation and immediately disengaged the autobrakes by slightly advancing the speed brake lever; and came to a stop using the operable reverser and manual braking.ZZZ Fire and Rescue assessed our aircraft and we set up for a tow-in. ZZZ Fire and Rescue noted hydraulic fluid contaminated the runway.We proceeded under tow to gate. At the gate; I discussed the event with Dispatch and the [Chief Pilot].In my debrief with the First Officer; we went through the debrief card. The items that seemed to go well included workload management; automation management; and our planning and decision making. The humbling items that could have gone better would include my monitoring and cross check of the items on the non-normal checklist. In a future event; with time available; one of us will independently re-run the non-normal checklist before committing to the approach. Calling for the gear up as we abandoned the approach was a rote response. With a hydraulic issue on arrival in the terminal area; next time we will maintain the existing configuration unless performance reasons dictate otherwise.Communication with Dispatch should have been more thorough; next time I will spend an extra two minutes to send a more informative message to Dispatch.

column121: Prior to performing the engine start checklist; we noticed the main cabin door was not indicating closed. We asked the Flight Attendant to try to reopen and close the door and after multiple attempts it would not show closed so we called Maintenance. To my surprise; they offered to defer it under MEL52-3-1 without sending Maintenance to the aircraft. In my experience; mechanics have always gone over to the aircraft whenever there are issues relating to the main cabin door so I found this a little odd. We reviewed the MEL and Maintenance Control asked about nuisance messages which did not exist at the time; so we put the MEL in the logbook but shortly after I realized that we did not have any nuisance messages because we did not have engine 1 running which would prompt a Master Warning MAIN DOOR OPEN. We went back to Maintenance Control and discussed how the maintenance action required to remove the micro switches was required because once we start engine 1 the system logic will generate a MAIN CABIN DOOR EICAS warning. They argued that was not a 'nuisance' because it was only going to triple chime once and not continuously and I had to reiterate multiple times that a Master Warning EICAS being displayed is inappropriate and a distraction/nuisance. I was passed over to the Maintenance Supervisor; and another Maintenance Control person who all seemed generally confused with what I was talking about. I suspect they misunderstood the system logic or which door we were deferring because they said they issue this MEL '2-3 times a week' which I highly doubt. Eventually; we told them they need to send a mechanic out because we had already made a PA that the aircraft would need to be inspected by Maintenance. A mechanic came out and removed the micro switches faster than it took to stay on that circular conversation with Maintenance Control. Shortly after applying the MEL and pushing back; we started engine 1 and MAIN DOOR OPEN EICAS warning presented. This was extremely confusing because that message should not appear when the micro switches are removed; similar to when they perform that same procedure on the bag door micro switches. Additionally; when a message is going to be displayed after an MEL is applied it usually includes that information as a note on the MEL; like with MEL 21-13. I called a friend in Flight Technical for some clarification on why that message appeared and he agreed it should not be present and it was possible the maintenance action was not done appropriately because an Embraer manual shows the need to remove 4 micro switches but the AMM Task only has the Mechanic remove 2. I called Maintenance Control again and explained the situation; and the supervisor was adamant the AMM Task was completed correctly and only required the removal of 2 micro switches and reiterated multiple times that the message should be displayed because the micro switches were removed. At this point; we had been racing against a DOT 3 hour limit clock and an FAR 117 max duty time limit; so we elected to take the aircraft because the supervisor confirmed all maintenance actions required of this MEL had been completed; we verified compliance with the MEL; and we knew why that message was presented.Either there is a discrepancy with the AMM that doesn't tell them to remove all of the required micro switches or the MEL should include a note that says the Master Warning displayed. Accepted aircraft after confirmation from Maintenance Control Supervisor that there was no other option to make the EICAS Master Warning extinguish. First of all; is this an MEL we really want our planes flying multiple days with? The aircraft flew an entire day the following day; so this MEL was not applied to get the aircraft to a maintenance hub. If we had an RTO (rejected takeoff); how would I know which door is really opened and closed? That's literally why we have the door pages up during takeoff. Next; the company needs to investigate the inconsistency withthis MEL not saying the EICAS warning should be present or the improper maintenance action that caused it to appear.

column121: Captain advised we had a maintenance issue to have checked out before boarding our return flight to ZZZ. I believe pilots saw something had leaked under the engine; observed by FO walk around. Mechanic looked for AC left engine fuel leak suspected by pilots; after a period of time (I do not recall) mechanic could not find leak; he signed off on logbook. Pax began boarding; entry door was closed; on push back; FA's were doing safety demo when FA 4 was called over by passenger sitting in right window seat a few rows aft of the wing. Passenger stated something was dripping from wing. Demo was almost complete; FA 4 continued with demo then looked out to see pax concern. Upon seeing fluid dripping from several places along the underside of the wing; she went to get another FA to see the issue. FA 4 took FA 3 to see the dripping. FA 4 and 3 went to the forward entry area to inform FA 1; I was working FA 4 and standing next to FA 1 so I was also informed at this time. FA 1 called Captain (CA) to advise. Several minutes later we were notified by CA that we were going back to gate and need to disarm doors. Same mechanic (only one I saw) returned. Passengers remained onboard while he checked the issue further. It is my understanding he reported he still found no leak. Sometime later CA advised crew and passengers via PA that we would be starting engines at the gate to further troubleshoot the problem; he advised passengers to remain seated. I was told this test was done at the Captain's request; not the instruction of this mechanic. Engine test was completed; seat belt sign turned off; more time passed and it was decided to deplane passengers. While crew waited on the AC for info from the company as to our schedule and whether this plane was going to be able to be repaired; our FO showed CA a video of the fuel leak while the engine test was running. I saw this video; fuel was pouring from the engine like a running garden hose. CA stated he had no confidence in this mechanics ability to perform his job as he appeared that he had no idea how to handle it. While I was discussing this with CA he told me he asked the mechanic earlier to call Company Maintenance base for instruction. The mechanic told CA yes he did call Company. CA told me he was angry with this mechanic because he himself called Company and was told mechanic did not contact them.  Aircraft was taken out of service hours later.
column123: Upon arrival at Gate 1 in ZZZ; ground personnel connected to headset after engine shutdown to report a fluid leaking from number 1 (left) engine. He smelled his fingers; reported that it smelled like fuel; and asked me to investigate the fluid. The First Officer and I both investigated; and felt; to the best of our knowledge; that the fluid smelled like fuel. At that point; there was a puddle under the #1 engine; 3 feet in diameter; and fuel was dripping at a rate of 2-3 drips per second. As we stood there discussing; the dripping reduced to 1 drip every 4-5 seconds. The FO and I agreed that we were unfamiliar with any allowable drips on the 737 MAX LEAP engines; and I proceeded to the cockpit to make an entry in the aircraft logbook; dispatch a code in ACARS; and call the Maintenance Control to coordinate for a maintenance technician. The technician arrived and we conferred on the above information; and he proceeded to investigate and coordinate with the maintenance team in Company (my assumptions; although I did hear his telephone conversation at one point). After his investigation; he returned to the cockpit to inform me that he had opened the engine cowl; performed his checks; and found all valves ready for service. He signed off the write up and dispatched the aircraft for service. We boarded the passengers and pushed from the gate at XA:40. Push back was normal; engine start on engine #2 was normal. After push back was complete; we started engine #1. After engine start; and after the push crew had disconnected and given me a salute; ground personnel came back; pointing to the #1 engine. At the same time; the Cabin Crew called to alert me to a passenger that was reporting fluid leaking from the RIGHT side of the aircraft; and a Flight Attendant confirmed that we were leaking fluid. The report that fluid was leaking from the right was incongruous; and caused the FO and I a couple minutes to confer and investigate what that could be. We later found out the leak was in fact from the LEFT side; and was from the #1 engine. I did note in my investigation; that the #1 main tank fuel quantity differed from the #2 main tank fuel quantity by nearly 400 lbs; a discrepancy that didn't exist before pushback as I had noted the fuel during the Before Start checklist. By this time; the same ground coordinator who had reported the previous leak connected to headset and reported that we were again leaking fuel from the #1 engine. His report was that fuel was gushing out from under the engine cowl. The FO and I coordinated and elected to taxi back to the gate to expedite arrival and engine shutdown. The ground crew quickly assembled and we returned to the gate at approximately XA:48; and shut down both engines. I made another logbook entry and called Maintenance Control to inform them that we had returned to the gate and required the maintenance technician to perform more checks before we could depart. The maintenance technician returned; and we performed an engine run at the gate on the #1 engine; which resulted in identifying a large fuel leak; with the technician recording video. At this point the aircraft was taken out of service; and I began coordinating with station personnel and Crew Scheduling for subsequent actions.

column121: My Captain and I were in the descent phase of our flight initially level at 4;000 feet MSL while on frequency with DFW TRACON.My Captain and I both heard the Controller give us a descent clearance to 2;400 feet MSL; we both accepted the clearance and my Captain read back/acknowledged the clearance to ATC.The clearance to descend to 2;400 feet did not seem unusual or out of place as we were approximately 20 NM from the RBD airport; upon leveling our aircraft at 2;400 feet my Captain and I were discussing visually seeing radio towers at our 11o'clock and approximately 10 SM in ahead and to the left of our flight path and we were expecting to be vectored around the obstacles.A few seconds after we had discussed the mentioned radio towers DFW TRACON challenged our altitude of 2;400 feet insisting we were supposed to be at 4;000 feet MSL upon hearing that radio call; and confirming with ATC we expeditiously initiated a climb back to 4;000 feet.At no point in the flight did I feel like we were in danger or in an un-safe proximity to the obstacle radio towers or in the vicinity any other aircraft as we were in VMC conditions; with good visibility.In my perspective; the Controller seemed to be over worked at the time of the occurrence and did not verify with my Captain after his read back to descend to 2;400 feet; indicating we had read back a correct clearance.After completing our flight; getting ready to taxi into parking on the ground at RBD; we were informed there was a similar sounding aircraft call sign on frequency and that the descent clearance to 2;400 feet was for the similar sounding call sign and not for us.We were also informed that we were 'stepped on' during our radio transmission; unknown to us during our read back to DFW TRACON to descend to 2;400 feet. It seems to me DFW TRACON should have confirmed who was supposed to descend to 2;400 feet when they did not receive a clear read back.
column123: While descending for landing at the Dallas executive airport; we were given a delayed descent with a crossing restriction which required an expedited descent. We hustled down and made the assigned crossing altitude restriction.  Shortly following that; we were assigned a new frequency and cleared to descend to 4;000 feet.  We initiated a normal descent and almost at the same time we were leveling; we were cleared to descend to 2;400.I acknowledged the clearance to descend on the radio and we initiated a normal descent to 2;400 feet.  As we were descending; I pointed out the radio towers at our 11 O'clock position to my co-pilot.  My thoughts were that the controller would give us a slight vector to the right; otherwise I would request a turn.Very shortly after that; the Controller challenged our altitude.  I replied that we were cleared to descent and that I had acknowledged the descent. The Controller stated that they needed us back at 4;000.  We immediately complied.The Controller appeared to be very busy.  I tried to keep all communication correct and prompt.  In speaking with the ATC person he stated that there was another aircraft with the same registration ending - same letter and that the Controller referred to that aircraft with an abbreviated call sign.In my opinion; if the Controller does not get a clear read back from an aircraft; especially if there are similar call signs on frequency -- then the Controller should state 'That clearance was for N--- only' I have heard that many times.'Contributing to this was the fact that there were several aircraft that the Controller was working and may have been challenged doing so.I never felt in danger at any time as we saw the radio towers and am not aware of any conflict with any other aircraft in our proximity.

We made a comment that perhaps rotary traffic was using the right pattern for separation. We got called by Tower and the Controller thanked us for our patience and said Runway XX clear for takeoff. We proceeded to takeoff and climbed in the upwind to around 650 feet before making a turn to the left. Whilst we were in the crosswind segment; still climbing we noticed a plane that appeared to be 200-300 feet below us in right downwind for Runway XY off to our left; on its way to pass underneath us. It was probably 600 feet away when we first noticed it and it passed underneath our nose. We were both puzzled as to what they were doing. Once we were clear of them; we made another left turn into left downwind for XX the Controller came on the radio and said to us that we had come very close to 'my' ILS traffic for ZZZ1 and that they had it written down that we had requested right traffic; which was incorrect. Our inactions were verifying left or right traffic; assuming left traffic was standard especially due to all the rotary traffic using the right downwind for XX. The Controller was particularly busy and perhaps as we were heading to ZZZ1 they figured it was more direct to make right traffic. We climbed to 200 feet of TPA [Traffic Pattern Altitude] on the upwind so to make sure we were as close to TPA before being in Downwind at the wrong altitude.
column123: We were cleared for takeoff for Runway XX.  Prior to takeoff; I was monitoring entry of all aircraft entering the traffic pattern. I never communicated which way I was going to turn crosswind since I was following the other aircraft that have been in the pattern throughout the morning.  After departure; I climbed to about 700 feet and started to monitor other traffic in the area prior to making my crosswind turn.  I saw a small aircraft to the left of me that was descending about 200-300 feet below.  I then started to make a left crosswind turn from XX0 degrees to approximately YY0 degrees.  I flew over the traffic and continued heading south for ZZZ2.  ZZZ Tower Controller then addressed me on the radio that they had me down for a right downwind turn.  I never once communicated I was making a right downwind turn nor heard the Controller mention; 'make right crosswind upon departure'. column121: After takeoff; during climb phase; clearance was given from ZZZ Approach [Control] to climb restrict to 12.000 feet direct ZZZZZ intersection. No answer from ZZZ [Center] also. I tried to contact back ZZZ Approach and ask for a different frequency; but had no answer from ZZZ Approach also. I started looking on my charts and started calling ZZZ Center on other frequencies; but no answer again. I tried to contact XYX.ZB; but no answer also. This was when I realized that I was facing a communication fail. At this moment; I selected 7600 (communication fail code) on my transponder (squawk). Decided to continue the flight following my flight plan clearance received; towards my destination. Over ZZZ1 tried to call ZZZ [Approach] but no answer. During all time I tried to use different radio equipment on board and also keep trying contact with ZZZ Center; ZZZ1 Approach; ZZZ Tower; another aircraft that sometimes I could listen very weak; but no answer.When approaching ZZZZZ1 intersection; on XYX.ZB I started listening ZZZ Center transmitting blind for me a telephone number for me to call. I also could listen if I received the message to press ident; I did. After that; ZZZ transmitted to me; blind again; to turn left heading 270 and descend to 6;000 feet; and asking me to press ident if I received. I pressed ident; and followed the instruction given. ZZZ [Controller] replied that they see my ident; and weather information for ZZZ [Airport] was given to me; together with a VFR approach and landing clearance on ZZZ3 Runway XX; and ident was requested again. I understood and pressed ident again. ZZZ Center said to me to try contact with ZZZ1 Approach on XCY.DZ I tried; but no answer was received again; and I kept monitoring both frequencies; the reception was very weak and noisy. After few moments I could listen a last transmission saying me the weather and clear to land on Runway XX; after landing try to call ground.I did land on Runway XX; and after landing; vacated the Runway via Taxiway 1; stopped and tried to call Ground. Again; no contact. Decided to turn left on Taxiway 2 and look for a place to park. I couldn't see any signal from Tower or follow me car at that time. When I was closer to the Tower; I could listen to Ground calling me; and I replied back. He said he was receiving me too weak. Instruction was given to continue Taxiway 2; hold short Runway XY. Next instruction; cross Runway XY turn left on [Taxiway] 3 and hold short Runway XX. At the holding; communication was lost again. Parking brakes applied. I took my phone; called ZZZ [Center] and asked ZZZ1 Tower telephone number. I tried to call Tower but phone didn't complete the call. After few minutes; I decided to make a 180 turning back; to not cross the runway. I did it and followed Taxiway 2 back; when I received a transmission on the ground frequency saying to turn left on Taxiway 4 and park. This was what I did. After stopping the aircraft; I didn't move from inside until police and the airport ground personnel came to me and said me that I can leave the aircraft. Before leaving the flight deck; I took my phone and called the ZZZ Tower again and after speaking with [the Controller]; situation explained; he asked me to call ZZZ center on phone number given. I did call ZZZ; asked to call with the supervisor. I explained all the situation and the same I am writing here on this report.After all done; I was asked to taxi the aircraft to another apron. I asked to park the aircraft at the hangar; closer to the FBO; where an aircraft technician could help me to troubleshoot and fix the airplane. A follow me car was provided to me and the taxi was done following the follow me car; and aircraft parked in front of the hangar.

column121: After pushback; while centered on Taxiway D8 in the alley between terminals [1 and 2]; I noticed multitudes of vehicle traffic (Passenger buses; tugs; fuel trucks; etc.) moving along the edge of the alley. Unfortunately; those Ground vehicles have no defined lane to stay within that guarantees wingtip clearance from taxiing aircraft. As a result; the Ground traffic did not move in a standardized flow/distance from our aircraft in the alley. In fact; depending on size/type of aircraft parked at their gates; the ground traffic was not able to move in a straight line and would move out toward the center of the alley. In my assessment; the risk for misjudging vehicle/aircraft wing tip clearance; by either Aircrew or Ground Personnel; will increase during low ambient light and/or low visibility conditions.Airport Operations should paint a Ground vehicle taxi lane that guarantees clearance from aircraft pushing and entering/exiting the length of the alley between Terminal 1 and 2. Operations should emphasize the higher risk/potential for collision in this area during annual Ground Operator refresher training and initial qualification. At a minimum; update Company bulletin to warn Crews about uncontrolled vehicle movement in close proximity to taxiing/pushing aircraft and the need for increased vigilance.

column121: During single-engine taxi out; the A FA called the cockpit; informing us of passengers' non-compliance with the facemask policy.  The decision was made to return to the gate. As we taxied back toward the Ramp; I coordinated with the Captain; advising that I felt it was appropriate to perform an After Landing flow prior to returning to the gate. Captain agreed; and I accomplished the flow.  While holding for a gate; and on the apron with the parking brake set; the A FA called back to the cockpit; advising that the passengers were now willing to comply and that the three FAs were comfortable with continuing the flight.At this point we re-accomplished a Before Taxi flow (as appropriate for our single engine taxi configuration); then ran a Before Taxi Checklist.  We then coordinated with ATC to proceed with a taxi clearance for departure. The Number 1 engine was started and the rest of the taxi and takeoff proceeded uneventfully.  Once airborne; I noticed that we had departed with the autobrake selector in the OFF position. As I thought about the sequence of events leading to that I thought of two things:  placing that switch to RTO takes place in the Captain's Before Start flow.  I also recalled that when I performed the After Start flow (following the Passenger incident); I placed the Window Heat switches to ON; another item that is normally accomplished in the Captain's Before Start flow.Clearly; in our unique situation; a Before Taxi flow; followed by a Before Taxi Checklist was insufficient to reposition all switches to their appropriate positions prior to taxi and takeoff. Of note; neither of us felt rushed; and we both felt that we used good CRM to methodically think through our situation before continuing; yet in the end; something was missing. I've referenced the manuals; looking for a procedure that would have trapped our errors; but am still left wondering.  Since we started the original taxi single engine and never shutdown that engine; the procedure in Flight Ops Manual never entered our minds; yet that guidance probably would've caught the error.Non-standard Ops lead to inadvertent takeoff with auto brakes selected off.
column123: On taxi out; the A FA called to tell me that there was a family being non-compliant regarding the face mask policy. I made the decision to taxi back to the gate. At that point; we completed the Before Taxi Checklist and taxied to the runway. After takeoff; the FO pointed out that RTO switch was not re-selected to 'armed.' Our unique situation made it impossible for autobrake re-selection to occur.In this situation; our normal checklist does not catch the error. I should have triple checked everything because our routine taxi out was interrupted.RTO reengage missed during a taxi back to the gate and subsequent cancellation of that.

column121: DFW has an odd system of ground-frequency assignment for the east side of the airport; that has long concerned pilots for the very reason this incident highlighted. Outbounds from the remote; E Terminal spots of XX to YY are often assigned the discrete Ground frequency of 121.80; even though all other east-side operations for the apt are issued 121.65. However; those of us assigned 121.80 are never switched to the 'main' frequency of .65 that everyone else is operating on.On this day; as we taxied out we were assigned 121.80; but the First Officer; to his credit; decided to take the initiative to also pull up 121.65 on the other radio; so we could hear what was being said to and by the other aircraft operating in the same area and taxiways and the same controller. Northbound on Taxiway K approaching Taxiway Z there was a B737 waiting to pull out. Ground issued instructions to them over 121.65 to pull out ahead of us; and then transmitted to us on the same frequency to give way. The only reason we were aware of these transmissions was because we were monitoring both frequencies. We gave way to the B737 without incident and everyone went on their way none the wiser; except us. Had we not been monitoring 121.65 but just on our assigned frequency of 121.80; there's every reason to believe both aircraft would have gotten much closer together before the ground controller might have discovered his error; and ultimately; it was not his error but the assignment of two; discrete frequencies to different aircraft taxiing on the same taxiway.

column121: Pushback was delayed due to catering (and vehicles impeding the catering truck from approaching the aircraft).  Following push clearance; the tug began the push but we came to a stop after approx. 15 sec. I thought perhaps something crossed behind us and we would resume the push.  But; after a few more seconds; the tug driver said that a catering truck wasn't moving.  That seemed odd; and the Captain and I wondered why a catering truck wouldn't clear a moving aircraft.  That's when the Captain looked through his side window; over his shoulder and told me; 'THAT'S why the truck isn't moving - it's sitting under our wingtip!' We hadn't felt anything and the tug driver was asked if we were touching.  He said that he couldn't tell.  A crowd gathered.  I informed ramp of our situation and our intent to remain in position to investigate. A maintenance rep came on interphone and let us know it was difficult to determine how close the wingtip was to the roof of the truck.  It was judged safe to set brakes. After some time; it was decided to let air out of the truck's tires.  Personnel climbed atop the truck and after getting a closer look; the truck was moved.  No visible contact/damage was noted but the possibility was mentioned that the winds were moving the aircraft slightly and the wingtip may have bounced off the roof and that may have not been enough to show damage but that an inspection would be the best course of action.  We were cleared to be pulled forward to the gate and the aircraft was taken out of service and the crew and passengers deplaned to the aircraft at the adjoining gate.  The remainder of the flight was uneventful.Since we were being pushed straight back; we did not see the events leading up to the potential contact.  It would seem that a combination of catering truck driver and wing walker inattention may have contributed.[Suggest] Company communications to [the catering company] and maintenance re-iterating the need to be vigilant.
column123: About 60 feet into a routine pushback; the aircraft stopped.  The Tow Driver told us a 'catering truck driver is refusing to move.'  I asked if I should set the Parking Brake.  The Tow Driver said 'No.'  I looked out the left window and saw a catering truck with no driver in the cab.  I called Ramp Control on the radio to report the situation.     I looked out the window again to see a Maintenance Technician on the catering truck's over-the-cab loading platform.  He was leaning on the railing to look toward the aft-right side of the truck.  I opened the aircraft L2 Window to get a better view.  I saw the Left Wing apparently resting on the middle; top-right of the back portion of the catering truck.  I saw numerous Ground Crew and Maintenance personnel walking around the catering truck gesturing at the apparent contact point.     A Maintenance Supervisor saw me looking out the window and got on the Ground Interphone to tell me what was going on.  She said they thought there was actually no contact with the catering truck but couldn't be sure until they employed an operable hydraulic work lift - the first one they tried was inoperative.  I asked how big/small the gap was.  She thought the wing was about an inch from touching the truck; but the wind was causing the aircraft to gently rock; possibly bouncing the wing off the top of the truck.     After many minutes; a plan emerged to deflate the tires of the catering truck and tow it out of the way; preventing any possible further contact with the wing as the wind blew.  After the catering truck was clear; the Maintenance Supervisor got back on the Ground Interphone to tell us the aircraft was being taken out of service as a precaution and a replacement Ground Crew would tow us back to the gate for deplaning.  We were not to set the parking brake until safely at the gate.  Company Operations and Maintenance coordinated a different aircraft for us to continue the flight.     The tow was uneventful.  Once parked; we ran the Shutdown Checklist.  Maintenance Technicians boarded and asked us to not shut down the aircraft.  They also invited the First Officer and me to go outside and get on the work lift to inspect the wing.  To my eye; there was absolutely no indication of any kind that the wing had contacted the catering truck; however; I know that painted panels of modern materials can deform; return to shape; and not show outward signs of damage.  Not that it was my decision; but I concurred with Maintenance in taking the aircraft out of service.     Passengers and crew boarded the new aircraft and departed uneventfully.Cause Unknown.  I would only be speculating on events that occurred out of my view.I can only speculate how this event occurred; so I cannot provide prevention suggestions.

column121: We were on the TIPTOE Visual Runway 28L. We were paired up with a heavy that was on [Runway] 28R. column123: On final approach in SFO we were paired up with a heavy jet on the right side with very gusty cross winds from the north.  On 5 mile final we encountered wake from the heavy and it induced a roll upset. The recovery procedure was utilized and aircraft control was regained at which point we encountered the wake again and it induced a second roll upset. Proper upset recovery techniques were utilized and we went around without issue. The cause of this event was due to high gusty winds out of the north and being paired too closely with a heavy jet upwind. The resulting wake was blown directly into our flight path. Having known about the winds and the pairing of the heavy jet closely spaced upwind; I would suggest staying a minimum of 1 dot high on the glide slope and requesting a long landing so as to avoid potential wake in the future.

column121: We were returning to ZZZ from ZZZ1 late on the afternoon. The enroute environment was apparently busier than the recent 'new normal' for that time of year as we had been limited in our climb clearances to between one- and three-thousand feet per climb clearance since our departure 25 minutes earlier.  Our most recent climb clearance was to FL400 (on our way to our filed FL410). Subsequently; ATC called traffic (I don't recall the model or the horizontal distance away) at '1;000 feet ABOVE YOUR ASSIGNED ALTITUDE' (emphasis mine). I would have replied 'Looking' or some similar acknowledgment. I did look and then subsequently noticed my FO (who was PF and in the left seat) had shallowed our climb to 100 FPM or so out of FL390 -- significantly less than the 5 or 600 FPM I would have expected. We were also very light; so a climb rate that shallow would have soon required a power reduction. At about the same time we got a TA and the Controller asked us to confirm we were level (or leveling?) at FL390.  I don't recall the exact exchange; but I would have replied something to the effect that we were climbing to FL400; he would have said something to the effect of maintain FL390.  At that point I fully processed what was happening; gave silent kudos to my FO for correctly interpreting the bad direction this was going; and directed him to 'push.'  As what we had was a TA; not an RA; the autopilot was left engaged; but he did direct the nose down and I dialed 390 into the ASEL.  The Controller asked us to confirm we were at FL390. I interpreted that as him wanting that confirmation on tape and I gave it to him; although we were; in fact; changing our vertical direction from up to down at FL393 at that point.We are a very structured flight department. In order for an airplane to be directed to an altitude during enroute climb or descent; the Controller has to assign that altitude; the PNF has to read it back and dial it into the ASEL; the PF has to verbally and independently repeat that altitude for both of us to hear; and has to acknowledge that he sees that same altitude displayed in front of him. Owing to that routine sequence and cadence of events; we are both 100% certain that we were assigned FL400.That said; I can allow as how I have possibly been wrong at least once in my flying career. My FO was hired on just as COVID came on the scene last year.  With the reduced amount of flying we've been doing since; he is still considered 'new' to the operation and as such not fully comfortable with our procedures. By that; I mean that I sometimes sense a hesitation for him to be as assertive as he should be and as assertive as he would be by now had this been a normal year. That notwithstanding; I would expect any pilot in our organization to question; in no uncertain terms; anything they were uncertain about; especially an ATC clearance. Likewise; no one in our organization; from Director of Flight Ops down; would hesitate to ascertain verification of any such uncertainty; no matter who questioned it. That's the way we move airplanes without bending them. I'm still 100% certain we were cleared to FL400.In retrospect; and we observed this at the time; the primary thing that would have alerted us to this unfolding conflict would have been for the Controller to have called the traffic as '...opposite direction at FL400.' That would have raised the hackles on the back of my neck and elicited from me a request to confirm our assigned altitude. There is no error-trapping possible when traffic is called as '1;000 feet above your assigned altitude.'Additionally; and this is not a negative; just observation and fact: we're flying the oldest; and by far the most reliable; airplane in our fleet of four; however; owing to her age; we're looking at a pair of >XX-year-old TCAS displays on dedicated three-inch round screens. There are no course overlays; no distance rings and; especially on the longer ranges (20 and 40 mile); no way to preciselyassess the relative position; direction or closure rate of traffic approaching; especially when doing so nearly head on. Technology is good. Newer technology can sometimes be better.On a positive note; we did visually acquire the traffic while far enough apart that had evasive action been necessary (it wasn't); we would have had plenty of time to take it. We did debrief this incident immediately after its occurrence; replayed the events out loud and decided the error was ultimately ATC's; that we had done everything we could to mitigate the repercussions to the controller and that we were not at fault.

column121: I was working Sector X (AOA [At Or Above] FL360) and another sector was being saturated (Y/Z/A combined. Training was being done at this sector); so they split off A to me. There was a lot of traffic and weather in the area. Apparently; restrictions were put in place that aircraft entering ZZZ1 [Center] from us and landing at ZZZ [Airport] needed to be AOB FL260. I was working an Ultra High Sector. When I was given the briefing by the trainee; the trainer ran over to my scope and said that Aircraft X needed to be AOB [At Or Below] FL260. The aircraft was at FL430 and maybe 40 miles from the boundary; on top of same direction and opposite direction traffic. Aside from that there were numerous conflicting aircraft issues already fixing to happen. My EDST [En-route Decision Support Tool] had a bunch of red alerts of which should have been fixed prior to the aircraft entering our area. Again; this was on the sector I was gaining; NOT the one I was already working. I was bit overwhelmed taking the sector just due to the amount of work that needed to be corrected due to the neglect of the training team.I descended Aircraft X to FL390; knowing I would have to move or quickly descend the aircraft through two others converging at FL390 and another directly below at FL380.I assigned the altitude and realized the speed gain was great enough that I could get Aircraft X down to FL360 (base of my stratum) and miss Aircraft Y; heading the same direction at FL380. To ensure I had room and miss opposite direction traffic at FL390; I turned Aircraft X. My turn was a bit too aggressive and in doing so; the wind caused the aircraft to lose a bunch of speed; resulting in the CA going off. I turned Aircraft Y to the left to keep separation; but it was already lost. From my observation; I showed a loss of separation to where they were separated by 4.9 miles and 900 feet vs the 1000/5 I need. I didn't stare too long as I had to go on to other separation tasks that were not completed prior to receiving the additional airspace/traffic.First; splitting sectors at the last minute has become all too common an occurrence with this COVID schedule and working 'more with less.' The whole environment is unsafe and the things we do are dangerous; resulting in issues like the one I had.Secondly; I won't be taking sectors from a person who doesn't have it all figured out; no matter what the Supervisor says.I take pride in what I do and having separation errors is unacceptable. I had the pilot helping me out the best he could and I second guessed myself that the aircraft would descend through the altitudes fast enough in a straight line Aircraft X started to outrun Aircraft Y as he descended. My turn was too aggressive; and I never played it into my head how much the wind would impact the turn. I think just trying to take action to descend the aircraft to meet a restriction overruled my common sense to think how my actions would play out. Solely my fault; but it could have and should have been avoided had other things been done in a timely manner prior to my taking the airspace. It seems to be a trend to do everything last minute; which is what creates such mistakes. Had I worked that aircraft and known of the restriction; Aircraft X would have descended below all my traffic 100 miles prior. Maybe not to FL260 so as to penalize the aircraft; but at least below those who were deviating and being rerouted around the weather.

column121: Aircraft X checked on approximately a 6 mile final on the Visual Approach and I cleared him to land.  At approximately a 4-mile final Aircraft Y asks for an 'S turn to the North' to which I state 'Approved'.  About 30 seconds later; Aircraft X asks for another s-turn to the south to which I also state 'approved as requested' and inform him that there is no traffic in his vicinity and also issued the wind. Aircraft X is now on a 1.5 mile final and well east of the airport and asks 'Tower; Aircraft X we are still plenty high; can we do a left tun and a left 360 around?' I state 'Unable' due to traffic in trail and ask Aircraft X if he needs to go around. Aircraft X replies 'affirmative'.At this point Aircraft Y is approximately 2 miles well east of the airport and it appeared that they were turning toward the airport. Not wanting Aircraft Y to overshoot finals; I issue 'Aircraft Y; fly heading 195; climb and maintain 2;000'.  When Aircraft Y becomes established on the heading; I issue 'fly heading 210 and maintain 3;000'. I did this without coordinating with Approach first because things were rapidly developing as Aircraft Y was indicating 190 knots and they appeared to be headed toward terrain east of the airport.  I realize that this was a vector below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude (MVA). The MVA east of the airport is 2;400 feet but at this point; I wanted to get Aircraft Y away from terrain as quickly as possible without issuing any vague or confusing instructions to the pilot. I did coordinate with Approach with the 210 heading when I got the chance and it was approved.As I stated in my above narrative; I realize that the vector that I issued was below the MVA but from my perspective from the Tower; I needed to get Aircraft Y away from terrain as quickly as possible. This was a unique situation where I had to utilize my best judgment with the circumstances that were presented. I realize that I was breaking the rule of vectoring an aircraft below the MVA but what was the alternative at this point? Let Aircraft Y head toward terrain and possible result in a catastrophe? It was the best of the two bad choices that were presented to me at that point and I had to quickly make a judgment call.

As Aircraft X was right over ZZZZZ; I noticed moderate precipitation was beginning to appear; but I did not have time to issue the weather before the pilot reported turbulence. The pilot stated they were in moderate and basically severe turbulence and asked for a vector or different altitude. I immediately descended the aircraft to 13;000 and coordinated with the next sector; since they had track control. I again asked the pilot if they need anything and they asked for a lower altitude. I coordinated with ZZZ Approach; to point out the aircraft descending to 10;000 due to the turbulence. I then descended the aircraft and asked the pilots if there was any damage or injuries. The pilot stated that he and the other pilot were the only ones onboard and they were not injured and did not suspect any damage to the aircraft. When the aircraft was level any 10;000 and clear of the now depicted weather; I asked the pilot again how they were doing. They said that the ride had improved. A short time later; the weather in that area grew rapidly to moderate and heavy precipitation.  I transferred communications of Aircraft X to the next sector. After the incident; I needed to vector numerous other aircraft away from that hazardous weather.COVID schedules; low staffing and long time on position were all contributing factors. My area has been extremely short staffed during our COVID schedule and tonight was no exception. We only had 5 CPCs scheduled for the shift; and also needed to staff the CIC position all night. There were numerous instances when all 5 controllers were working over 2 hours on position and we had 4 sectors open; plus the CIC and no controllers on break.The fact that I was working a non-typical configuration (outside of COVID) was also a contributing factor. column121: Very light 757; 16.7 on the fuel; almost empty payload; operating from ZZZ to ZZZ1; daytime VMC. High winds in effect. Vref was 111; Vapp is 126. I was PF (Pilot Flying); and decided to fly faster on final since we were in a light 757; and my limited experience with this situation led to this. Missed approach procedures were reviewed multiple times as other jets had to go around several times. Runway was dry; over XX;000 feet long; plenty of distance. I decided to fly a new Vapp of 135; as the jet was having problems controlling the airspeed since the winds were about 060/22G30. Our divert was ZZZ1; and we knew that several aircraft attempting to land had to execute missed approaches. All this into account; I decided to fly around 135 KIAS; as this felt like a more stable approach. The airspeed wouldn't stabilize safely below this number; as it was all over the place and I had to fight with the autothrottles to maintain within 15 kts of the initial Vapp of 126--it just wouldn't stabilize at a speed below 135. My reasoning is that since I was light; in a 757; long runway; daytime VMC; and super gusty winds; I had plenty of room to stop safely without encountering hot brakes or running out of concrete. We landed uneventfully; although long; as I touched down past the touchdown zone--this was the only cost of flying faster; and I felt it was worth it; all things considered. We landed and were able to taxi clear on taxiway; no problem.  If I was in a 767 or a heavier 757; I wouldn't have even thought of this; and we would have flown the Vapp given; for better or worse.  Were we technically unstable? Yes; I believe we were. Were we safer; in my eyes; flying a more stable approach with the winds we had? Yes; I also believe this to be the case. We never had a windshear warning; and we never felt unsafe; but looking back; I was in the wrong; even though I felt more stable; which led to a safer approach. However; the AOM procedures don't allow for this; so I was technically in the wrong; even though the airplane flew better and safer; in my opinion. Next time; I will fly the Vapp given; and if we have to divert; then so be it.

column121: Since COVID; these particular international schedules have been in a lot of flux. Most sequences; up until now; have been 'rockets' where we only get to rest a relatively short amount of time during the day after an all-night flight; and then fly back all night. I have written about this before; and this is to reiterate: these sequences are sub-optimal in terms of safety due to the limited rest. The threat on these sequences is NOT a virus; it's the cumulative fatigue after being up for two straight nights. There is no reason not to make ALL these flights have a longer sleep opportunity with a 30 plus hour layover.  Three times in the last 2 months we lined up for the wrong runway in ZZZ after the double all-nighter. Fortunately; someone caught the error before it was critical; but it is reflective of the fact that the three of us are sleep-deprived. In this aircraft category; you have an older pilot group to begin with. Give us the opportunity to get enough rest.Upon arrival in ZZZ; I was extremely tired; and felt my ability to monitor was degraded.Schedule all these international trips as longer layovers. It's a safety issue; pure and simple.

Just before passing FL200; Captain queried ATC to confirm FL230; but received a response approaching FL220. A clearance was given to descend FL200; and we complied. It was then that we reviewed the textual part of the chart and noticed our error. The expectation that other SID's do not include this exception is biggest cause. Also; not detailed re-reading lengthy textual descriptions on SID's every single use; contributes. ATC clearances can include 'climb via; except maintain...'. This clearance would easily eliminate this oversight and airports like DEN; should have knowledge of the departures to aid in this. Also; Jeppesen charts should include these little nuances in the top altitude box on the SID; since this isn't true of all SID's.

We had a semi-hard landing and bounced and go-around selected all simultaneously. We were slow to put the speed brake back in after touching down but did eventually secure it and maintained attitude as we executed go around. Go-around procedures were completed airborne. Vectored back around by ATC for uneventful approach; landing and taxi in. The Captain and I both did a walk around of the aircraft post flight to ensure integrity of aircraft and check tail skid as a precaution but didn't notice the skid was ground down as we later were informed from the Director of Operations and Maintenance. We debriefed the event. Windshear/airspeed loss at low altitude while simultaneously executing go-around and didn't maintain proper go-around pitch once touching down as indicated from tail skid damage. Quicker reaction from crew with go-around with instantaneous airspeed loss and loss of lift and maintain proper attitude of aircraft on touchdown when executing go-around. Follow rules to live by; do not make large control inputs when in flare/go-around close to ground.

column121: Climbing through 16;000 feet to FL 200 we experienced a high whistle sound from the front of the airplane. I felt pressure on my ears; nose; and head and had the air pushed out of my lungs. We identified a cabin depressurization and I reached for my O2 mask. I took a long inhale from the oxygen and then proceeded with additional memory items. The Captain began an priority descent. I reached for the Pax oxygen switch with my right hand and the PA button with my left hand. I communicated with the Captain that I was going off comms to tell Pax to put on oxygen masks. The Captain stated 'Wait. They are going to be fine here in 2-3 seconds and I don't want to replace the masks.' This occurred around 13;500 feet. So I did not complete memory items per the Captain's instruction. I contacted ATC and advised we were on an priority descent because of depressurization. We received a new assigned altitude of 10;000 feet. The Cabin started to repressurize around 11;000. ATC asked if we wished to declare priority handling and the Captain declined. We were able to continue to ZZZ without incident.There were several deviations from our normal operating procedures that concern me. First the disregard from memory items on the checklist. Second; the captain did not have his O2 mask plugged in. He believed he could plug it in fast enough if needed and that he doesn't plug it in because he forgets to unplug it after a flight. This caused a delay in performing a memory item. The Captain was able to plug his oxygen mask in but never donned it during controlled handling decent. Also; we did not formally ask for priority handling with ATC. We could not diagnose the problem for the rapid depressurization so we were unaware of what triggered it. I suggested declaring priority handling to cover our bases if anything else occurred. This flight had already been abnormal with the priority descent. The Captain disagreed saying the problem is over. Lastly; I do not believe the cockpit acceptance was completed for this flight. It is typical that the FO (First Officer) does the walk around and security check while the Captain is completing the acceptance. While doing the walk around it is very apparent that the shaker pusher test is being tested from outside the airplane. You can hear the shaking on the horizontal stabilizer. I did not hear it that morning. Also upon startup; the Captain found a popped circuit breaker on his side for De-Ice. I'm not sure when the circuit breaker popped but no de-icing equipment was on so I assume it was before startup. This is another missed item on the acceptance checklist. Now; these deviations did not cause the priority handling to occur but they could have added on to make the event worse.

I took control of the aircraft and told him to tell ATC we were descending because we were unable to maintain altitude at the time. Once we were clear ATC cleared us down to FL330 and we continued on to ZZZ2. At the time of the initial shear we were talking and did not detect the variations in airspeed that were the telling signs of the shear coming. At the time I did not declare an emergency but looking back at it I would now because we were unable to maintain altitude at the time.
