column121: We had returned to the gate 2 times for passenger related issues. We then taxied out to the hold short line. We sat there awaiting the final closeout for ten minutes or so. When the close out came; there was no performance uplink; so I went to change ZFW and CG to match the latest closeout. I then verified that the V-speeds matched the takeoff performance page and we departed. The flight plan had us filed for FL380; but the VNAV page capped us at FL370.  We then leveled off at FL360.  After some discussion given our light weight and nearly standard day temperatures; we began looking for the reason for the low Maximum Altitude. We found that I had entered the ZFW incorrectly from the final closeout.Causal factors could include feeling a little rushed to get going after the half hour delay. Another factor could have been the lack of an uplink that led me to manually enter data.  Additionally; while I have been to training recently and am fully current; there is no smoothness or rhythm to my flying due to a lack of consistent time in the aircraft.  Hopefully having a regular line in Month will improve my proficiency.
column123: After returning to the gate for a passenger issue; we were running slightly behind schedule.  Original closeout deleted and after starting the second pushback; we had a new closeout (Rev 01) with good numbers which were accepted by the FMS.  During the second pushback; we were directed to tow back to the gate for a baggage issue.  Finally pushed back a third time and during taxi for departure; we received an ACARS message that closeout had been deleted and to wait for new numbers.  Received revision 02 (one pax less) of the closeout.  Did not get the prompt to accept new numbers.  Got another message of a deleted closeout and to wait for new numbers.  As we were getting more behind schedule; we ran through the numbers with the latest closeout (Rev 02) and confirmed the numbers as OK for a Flaps 10 degree; 10 knot tailwind TPS; with a plan to then cover the changes (if any) in the next closeout revision.  Waited approximately 20 more minutes at the end of the runway; number one for departure and finally got Revision 03 of the closeout; which was unchanged from Revision 02.  No prompt to accept the new numbers; so we manually updated them.  After I had checked the PERF page TOW numbers with the latest closeout numbers; the First Officer noticed that the ZFW was slightly off and updated it; but entered XYZ.X instead of correct number XAZ.X.  (Unnoticed at the time) Original number had been XAB.C.   V-speeds did not delete from the FMS; and with a slightly lighter TOW than the plan; I figured we were good to go.  V-speeds did not need to be changed; so we didn't.  We then completed all items of the Before Takeoff checklist and took off normally.  During the climbout; VNAV showed a max altitude of only FL360 instead of the planned FL380.  I found this odd; as we were lighter than the original planned weight and the temp at altitude was normal.  When we leveled off at FL360; I looked again at the closeout and compared it to the FMS perf page and then discovered the ZFW entry error.  Corrected it then and the VNAV max altitude fixed itself.  Remainder of flight uneventful.Because we were late and at the end of the runway; I may have rushed the FO to enter the ZFW data too quickly; which resulted in wrong data in the FMS.  I did not specifically verify the entered ZFW number because I had previously seen that the revised TOW was below the planned TOW and we didn't need to calculate new TPS numbers.  Even though the entered ZFW was incorrect; it was not used in calculating new QRH V-speeds; so the error went undetected as we went with the planned TPS.In the future; if a closeout does not uplink; I will call up the perf page on my FMS (as opposed to looking at the FO's perf page) and confirm each entry with the closeout.

For experience in the hours to clarify I went to flight school and earned a PPL (Private Pilot License) and have roughly X00 hours flight in helicopters combined with instrument and commercial type training; along with XX hours of fixed wing flight experience. 10 hours in drones however that is measured in flight logs stored within the aircraft flight logs and is subject to some error like all things are. The issue with drone operations vs. commercial manned aircraft operations is that the infrastructure is built around manned flight and to precisely pinpoint a physical address on a sectional is quite cumbersome. For the most part a sectional is helpful for areas in general but you could literally find yourself operating inside a hole within several boundaries. This is where applications such as Airmap; B4uFly; and UASidekick can be a huge help in checking and re-checking an area. I do understand the responsibility falls onto the PIC in this case and that I should have been more diligent and this is a lesson learned. But I cannot imagine that professional operators would be pulling out plotters for every address they fly at to pinpoint the coordinates. My concern lies with the applications accuracy not that the developers do not try but 4 of the top applications did not alert me to an airspace issue; this along with my presumed thought that the restriction was much farther north let me to believe I had the all clear. As drone operators the only official source we have is one that is geared towards manned flight and as usage continues to grow my fear is that a more serious incursion is inevitable. Helicopters operators have a chart that is most helpful to them when operating at low level; and this is very helpful as I have used these to navigate Los Angeles and San Francisco class B. Drones are an emerging business and as a responsible operator I am always concerned about flight safety. But usage is only increasing; something as simple as doing a roof inspection of a residential home reduces risk increases productivity and improves the accuracy and level of service. column121: On VMC descent on the PIGLT6 Arrival just past JAFAR intersection at 12;000 feet; aircraft on autopilot started to bank left up to 20 degrees with associated turbulence. Shortly after aircraft stabilized level; aircraft rolled to the left again and started to go past 30 degrees in the roll without any corrective action by the autopilot. The downside to all of these satellite based RNAV arrivals is that it puts everybody on the exact same spot in the sky over a path and makes the trailing aircraft susceptible to upsets. The controller could have slowed us or spaced us out but it wasn't his fault that we are all tracking in line. This effort to get more aircraft throughput by ATC will end up in more of these incidents and could hurt somebody. We need to space out more on the arrivals and only ATC can make that happen. This isn't all their fault. It is the very design of these procedures by non-pilots that put pressure on our controllers.

column121: I was a CFI giving instruction to a first-time tailwheel student in a Aircraft X. The Aircraft X [vintage aircraft] primary trainer that lacks an electrical system and therefore has no radios with which to communicate with other aircraft. The only electronic equipment onboard is a 406 ELT and a battery powered intercom to allow communication between instructor and student. We had finished the airwork/aircraft familiarization portion of our flight and had returned to the traffic pattern for takeoff and landing practice. We operate out of ZZZ; [local city]; just north of downtown. ZZZ is a busy GA airport with heavy flight school traffic; helicopter traffic; and [vintage aircraft] traffic in the form of [vintage military]; aerobatic; and vintage aircraft. The local flight school is well aware of our [aircraft type] operation and it always extra vigilant of possible NORDO traffic because we operate regularly. Worth noting is that Runway XX [north] utilizes a left-traffic pattern while Runway XX [south] uses right-traffic. This is due to obstacles east of the airport and to keep all traffic over the river rather than over the city. The weather at the time of the incident was good VFR; nearly unlimited visibility with northeast wind of 5-10 kts. The windsock unmistakably favored Runway XX [north] all day and was consistent. I had been at the airport since late morning and everyone had been using Runway XX [north] all day. When in the pattern and scanning for traffic; I noted that we were the only aircraft in the area; but a flight school aircraft was taxiing out for departure on Runway XX [north]. On approach to our first landing; I noticed the Aircraft Y holding short and appeared to be waiting for us to land. After we crossed the threshold; the Cessna taxied into position to depart. After our touch and go and on the upwind leg; my student exclaimed 'dude what's that?' I leaned around him (I was in the rear seat) to see an airplane filling our windshield. I quickly took control and aggressively turned into the downwind. While in the turn; I observed an Aircraft Z pass behind us on final to Runway XX [south]. I estimate the horizontal separation to be 1000 feet or less and vertical separation to be less than 50 feet. Once in the downwind; I observed the Aircraft Z that had taxied into position behind us execute an emergency turn off the Runway; presumably as surprised as I was to see an airplane landing on the opposing Runway with a very obvious tailwind.From the downwind; I witnessed Aircraft Z land and clear the Runway. The Cessna was still holding short; so I executed a short approach and put the Aircraft X on the ground as quickly as possible; student and self very shaken. I taxied to parking in front of the hangar and shut down. I noticed the Aircraft Z pilot was walking toward us; presumably to apologize. Instead; he verbally accused my student and me of causing a dangerous situation by not having a radio. I reminded him of the windsock and weather conditions which clearly favor Runway XX [north] to which he replied that he got his weather report from 'Center' and they told him winds were calm. He then informed me that he made several radio calls; including 'left downwind; left base; and final for XX [south]'. I reminded him that Runway XX [south] utilizes a right traffic pattern; so nobody would be looking for him on the east side of the airport. After a short discussion with the instructor in the aircraft involved; he never heard any radio calls from the offending Aircraft Z other than his last call that he was clearing Runway XX [south]. His account of the entire incident was identical to mine; as we discussed it with the event still very fresh in our minds. He has offered to provide a written statement as well.I am 100% confident that we did nothing wrong nor did we violate any FAR's. I am submitting this report purely for the need for such a close call to be documented and hopefully learned from in the future. The negligence of an irresponsible pilot nearly caused a mid-air collision; and did cause a Runway incursion. If it were up to me; some serious remedial training would be required for the offending pilot to continue to use his privileges as a pilot. Everyone makes mistakes or misses a 'RP' [right-hand pattern] note on a sectional chart from time to time; but when that minor error almost gets people killed; something should be done. His defensive and rude 'I didn't do anything wrong; its your fault for not hearing me' attitude certainly didn't indicate to me that he realized the seriousness of his actions. I sincerely hope this report can be of use to others in the future and a harsh reminder to us all of the unforgiving nature of flying at an uncontrolled field.

column121: I was flying from ZZZ to ZZZ1 via [airway] at [altitude].  I had just leveled out at cruise altitude when the engine began to run rough. This part of the route was most treacherous in terms of landing options being in the mountains. I chose to turn from my position direct back to the ZZZ2 airport and towards [land mark] which I thought would be a better landing spot to put it down if the engine did decide to quit. I maintained altitude to stay high while enroute back to ZZZ2 to keep our options open. The power did not fluctuate it was just running rough. I did go through the checklist to which nothing seemed to change the roughness. I held off on the magneto check because I wanted to get to a spot; I was comfortable with losing power to do the mag check (over ZZZ2) I listened to the ATIS and was going to begin my call up to the Tower from 15 miles to the north.  At this point before I made the call the engine began running extremely rough. This prompted me to request priority handling with Tower.  Tower gave me the landing clearance then and there for Runway XX.  We communicated and I decided to stay high until over the top of the field then spiral down for the airport to stay within gliding distance. I did this because I know that historically most engine problems just seem to get worse when you make changes to the throttle and since I had to reduce power at some point to land the plane; I decided I was going to stay in a position to land safely with no power if it did happen. I spiraled down to join a left downwind for Runway XX and landed and taxied in. On the ground shortly after we performed a magneto check in which the L magneto dropped approximately 800 RPM and the engine began running extremely rough. The pre-takeoff magneto check was performed prior to the flight with no issues and magneto drops within tolerances.  The airplane is in maintenance right now and I have just heard today that there was apparently a plastic piece on the magneto that should've been removed when they were installed that came loose and somehow affected the timing of the left magneto. In terms of the human factor; I had my girlfriend who is an instrument rated private pilot in the left seat; and her mother in the back. Geographically I didn't want to take any chances so we turned back towards the [landmark]; airport with a long runway; and flatter terrain because I have never dealt with an engine running that rough and couldn't figure out why and expected the engine to fail. I believe my only inaction was checking the magnetos which I purposefully refrained from until we were over the airport. By the time we were over the airport and had the field made; I just decided we would focus on landing and deal with it on the ground.

column121: I was cleared to land on 10R and planned to exit at the first available taxiway (H) which was within the landing performance data but required accurate; prompt control to do so. I successfully landed and slowed to normal exit speed; acquired what I thought was the lead-off line for H; and the taxiway edge lights on the far side of the lead-off line. What I didn't perceive was that the lead-off line had been blacked out recently as H had been moved during construction. Given the poor ambient lighting (even accounting for the excellent forward lighting from the landing lights); there was no immediate visual difference between the runway surface and the transition to the gravel surface and as the airplane departed the runway; the extra drag of the gravel and ~4' of underlying mud brought the airplane to a stop. After realizing what had happened and that I wasn't going to be able to taxi further; I coordinated with Tower; was instructed to switch to Ground and asked for a tow and passenger transport; then shut down the engine.Everything but the runway exit went as planned. I followed aircraft procedures; but departed from my usual night time post-landing technique of acquiring the lead-off line; then verifying the taxiway signage and seeing the lead-off goes between the edge lights. The erroneous lead-off line combined with the adjacent line of taxiway edge lights and the still-night-but-approaching-daylight contributed to my disregard of my usual next exit criterion that the lead-off lights guide between the taxiway lights; resulting in exiting the runway surface next to the intended taxiway exactly on the blacked out lead-off line that led to the previous location of Taxiway H.The bottom line contributors were fatigue after an earlier transport; planning an aggressive landing while fatigued; and visual cues that combined with my disregard of solid techniques in the process of achieving the required performance to meet the plan. In the future I will accept and use the available runway rather than plan for an expedited profile that approaches the limits of my current capabilities.

column121: Cleared to line up and wait Runway XX. When cleared for takeoff; pushed power to approximate 40% then selected TO/GA. We ran the Engine Failure Checklist; and discussed running the Rejected Takeoff Checklist. Since the event happened as the aircraft had just started to roll (probably less than 10 knots) we didn't run the Rejected Takeoff Checklist; knowing that brake energy and cooling wouldn't be an issue. After we taxied to the gate; I made calls to Dispatch; Maintenance; and the Chief Pilot on call; while the First Officer went to the ramp to inspect the aircraft. He discovered bent and broken turbine blades with metal pieces loose in the engine. He came back upstairs and called ZZZ Ground to do a runway check for engine debris. I made a PA to the passengers explaining that we had an engine failure at power up; and the aircraft would be taken out of service. They would receive more flight information in the terminal. After the passengers had deplaned; the crew got together and debriefed the event. I informed the F/As of what had happened and let them ask questions.

column121: The NIITZ 1 RNAV Departure from Runway 8L depicts FLAAR as prior to the lake.  The E/O (Engine Out) Page for 8L shows it as past the lake. I realize that DP1 is an altitude (3;500 feet - 6;000 feet) but the diagram does not match up. I expressed my concerns to a Check Airman friend and he did a better job of analyzing the problem. He noted the brown arc on the E/O (MSA circle we assume) shows FLAAR to be at 25 NM. I used the FIX Page of the FMC and put the LAS/12.7 arc and it lands on top of FLAAR. So; I see two problems. The 'terrain' and the omission of 'Not to Scale' could create confusion when you are trying to build a visual model of the E/O. Also; I'm not sure we recognize the hold at FLAAR is really only 12.7 NM from LAS; not 25 where it may seem less threatening to following traffic.My friends words: I agree that if you were trying to create a mental image of what you were doing in case you lost an engine; then the engine out diagram (picture) would lead you astray. The dilemma arises from the 12.7 ring and FLAAR being almost coincident. It gets worse; because 12.7 and FLAAR have nothing to do with one another. 12.7 only matters if you are below 3;500 feet. And FLAAR only matters if you are above 3;500 feet. So we are mixing altitudes with rings with fixes with terrain features with no warning that the drawing is not to scale! The disturbing part to me is that the E/O has the standard 25 NM MSA ring (at least that's what I think it is; and it is at 25 NM); which lends credence to FLAAR being 25 NM out (not about 13). So you are totally right! The written text is fine; but the diagram is very misleading.  I think we need to put 'NOT TO SCALE'. Or get rid of the terrain features. But the mixing and matching just leads to confusion (at the worst time).

Ground Control advised them to hold position and issued us no further instructions so we were continuing with our previously assigned clearance to taxi via H; G to XXL. Approaching the taxiway the Captain cleared left and noted that Company aircraft was waiting; while I cleared Right. While making the turn onto the taxiway; the Captain did one more glance to the left and brought the aircraft to an abrupt stop. Just then I noticed a (other carrier) 757 taxiing down G that we had had no prior information on. The Captain was able to stop the aircraft and maintain separation. We held there for (other carrier) aircraft to pass by on G and then re-cleared both left and right and proceeded onto G as previously instructed. We confirmed our clearance with Ground Control to which they again verified we were to taxi XXL via H; G. No hold shorts or information concerning other aircraft were given other than the inbound Company aircraft being told to hold his position when he made the inquiry about entering the ramp in reference to us taxiing out. The PF (Pilot Flying) immediately retarded the throttles to idle; and applied smooth breaking; which brought us to a complete stop.  We were angled left by about 30-40 degrees in relation to the center line of Runway 4; just prior to taxiway. I immediately informed ATC that we had stopped on the runway; the PF informed the PAX (passengers) to stay seated.  At that point we began to assess the situation. Initially we thought it was a blown tire or nose wheel steering issue. In that moment of assessing I noticed the #1 Engine Fail Caution illuminate in the #1 EGT Gauge. I informed the PF of the indication. It was the only indication we saw. No fire; no red lines only the engine failure alert caution. We reviewed the Rejected Takeoff Procedure; completed the QRH for Engine Failure. We then assessed the rolling and breaking capability of the aircraft and we found it to be normal.  We got clearance to exit the runway and return to the gate. As we pulled in to the gate; we remembered that we had not run an After Landing Checklist and quickly completed that; followed by the Parking Checklist. Then; the jetbridge malfunctioned and we had to wait until Airport Ops came to fix it. Once the jetbridge was attached I exited the aircraft to inspect Engine #1. I found the N1 fan blades and the stators directly behind them to be in a normal appearance. When I looked into the tailpipe of the turbine section; I found metal debris from the engine and both the aft fan blades and stators in front of them to be damaged and missing pieces. I hustled back to the Flight Deck to inform Ground Control that they needed to do a FOD check of the runway as we had; had and engine failure and that they needed to check for small engine parts.

If I remember correctly we stopped the descent at approximately 5;300 feet. We then flew over the towers and after clearing them we continued our descent to 3;900 ft and commenced the visual approach to a successful and safe landing. We were never given any warning about the towers and did not notice the towers on the approach plate until after landing and getting to the hotel. column121: Knowing that Runway XX would put us on a straight visual; while we were still in cruise; we thoroughly briefed the landing. There is rising terrain NE of ZZZ1 at the approach end of [Runway] XX necessitating close in maneuvering. Airport elevation is at XXXX so we decided to be fully configured with gear down and final flap selection at 7;500 feet 5NM from the Runway XX threshold to approximate a glide path. This would give us X;XXX feet buffer to get down. (Much more was briefed; this is just a highlight.) After we were switched from Center to ZZZ Approach we were told to expect vectors to Runway YY ILS. This was preferable because that would give us an instrument approach without terrain for visual backup; and it's within the 10 kt tailwind limit. However when we got switched to ZZZ Tower we were told they were not using YY and to expect vectors for a visual XX. We requested [Runway] YY again but this was refused by Tower; so we elected to get delayed vectors to allow time to set up XX again (we already had landing numbers and we had briefed it so it didn't take long). As had been briefed; we were fully configured 2;100 feet above field elevation at least 5 NM out and the FMS was used to draw an extended line from the Runway XX threshold to give better situational awareness of runway positioning during maneuvering. Green needles were used with the ILS frequency for Runway YY to give a visual indication of when we were approaching the runway centerline knowing that this would also give us reverse sensing and a false glide slope--this was briefed as well. My First Officer was flying but if it had been my leg I would've transferred controls to him anyway. I had flown with him for three days and seen him perform hand flown approaches and was supremely confident of his skills. And since we were being vectored in the NW sector for a right base to final to XX he would have the best view to make the turn to final. On final we got a visual GROUND PROX caution box on the PFD as well as aural 'glideslope' messages with an associated flashing caution some 3-6 times. Each time I canceled it and said disregard it's a false glideslope which was acknowledged by First Officer. First Officer had me cancel his flight director and he flew the visual raw data with me backing him up on descent rate; speed; and how it looked. He did a nice job and set it down without incident. [Unrelated] runways were NOTAMed closed. Runway XX PAPI was NOTAMed OTS. The reason to bring this attention is so that other crews will have notification that they may be required to land with minimal instrumentation backing them up on a visual. Other flight crews may not have the experience nor may benefit from mild weather condition. Please notify other crews that while [other] runways are closed they may be required to shoot a straight visual to XX near rising terrain; so that awareness may be raised and overall risk mitigated.

We had a tailwind which made it exceptionally difficult to get configured. The Captain continued to descend and try to reduce speed. He called for gear; however; I was unable to extend the gear because we were not at the appropriate speed. We were switched to Tower. The Captain continued the descent all the while attempting to reduce speed. Best guess we were at approximately a 7 mile final. We received an EGPWS 'TERRAIN TERRAIN'. The Captain shallowed the descent. It was then followed by a 'TERRAIN TERRAIN PULL UP' and I called for the go-around. We followed the escape procedures; were vectored around the pattern; and landed without incident. Neither pilot had been into the airport. We had reviewed documents; however once cleared for the visual we did not comply with the prescribed speeds on the arrival. In retrospect; we should have continued on the RNAV arrival since we were unfamiliar with the airport. Additionally; better awareness of wind may have assisted in getting configured.

column121: During a tour in ZZZ; at straight and level flight on my way to the landing zone; the helicopter seemed to be operating with reduced power when at max continuous power (MCP). Please keep in mind that during my preflight inspection of the helicopter in the morning; before conducting tours; I noticed no visible abnormalities. There was no low rotor RPM condition and no visible change in RPM throughout the tour. I noticed that with 2 passenger flights; earlier in the day; I was able to maintain MCP and 100 KIAS. Then; at the time of the occurrence; I noticed that with relatively the same weight in another 2 passenger flight that I was only able to maintain MCP and fly at 80 KIAS without decreasing in altitude. Given the 20 knot loss; I felt I should shut down prior to taking any more flights and just give the engine a once-over. Upon my inspection; I noticed oil spray over the engine on the helicopter's right side and some on the firewall. As a pilot; I felt at that point I needed to call our maintenance guy to give me his opinion on the situation. Our maintenance guy is also the Chief Pilot and Primary Manager of the company. He instructed me not to sell or take up any other flights with passengers. He then proceeded to tell me to fly the helicopter to ZZZ for him to come inspect it and make necessary repairs. Given the amount of oil I started with during pre-flight and the amount of oil in the engine after 2 hours of run time (the difference was 1.5 quarts burned; 8 quarts in the morning and 6.5 in the engine at the time of shutdown and pilot inspection) I felt I was within limits to fly the helicopter not even 5 minutes from the landing zone to Company at ZZZ. There was no oil light illumination in flight during that time or any time during tours. Both the oil temperature and oil pressure gauges were in the green. There has been a cracked cylinder on this helicopter before which resulted in reduced power as well. Given that; in my experience as a pilot; I believed this to be another cracked cylinder or maybe even a bad valve. I felt that my flight back to the airport was within limits. I topped off the oil; performed a power check and a magneto check prior to takeoff from the landing zone. I made my call to Tower; lifted off from the landing zone; flew my .03 flight over to Company; shutdown; and left back to ZZZ1 for Maintenance to handle it. This is the facts from my perspective; from what I was experiencing; to what I was told from Maintenance/Management; and how it was handled.

column121: On the evening of March XXth I was piloting a Bonanza VFR from ZZZ  to ZZZ1. In order to stay below the shelf of the class bravo airspace I would have to fly the x-c below 2;000 feet which I didn't want to do; both for safety and for efficiency. While on the ground at ZZZ  I requested flight following at 3;000 feet; with the intent of transiting the bravo airspace enroute to ZZZ1; and was assigned a departure frequency and squawk code. The takeoff and initial climb was uneventful. We checked in with Approach; and were informed that in order to fly to my destination at 3;000 feet we would initially have to take up a westerly heading before turning south. After flying west of ZZZ2; the main cabin door opened in flight; severely inhibiting communication with ATC due to the loud wind noise captured on the front seat passenger's headset microphone. In addition to the sudden distraction; the loud wind noise picked up by the front passenger's microphone inhibited communication with ATC; requiring me to ask approach to repeat a few transmissions. I tried talking the front seat passenger through closing the door; which was unsuccessful; then I unsuccessfully attempted to close the door. Finally; I had the passenger unplug their microphone so that I could establish good communication with ATC. While still dealing with the open door and noise I heard ATC tell me to fly a heading direct to my destination of ZZZ1 and cleared into the Bravo; which I read back; and then I turned direct to ZZZ1 at 3;000 feet. After unplugging the front passenger's microphone; and reorienting myself to the aircraft's position the passenger/pilot riding in the back commented that I was inside the Class Bravo at 3;000 feet; when the floor of the Bravo was 2;000 feet at our current location. I replied that while we were attempting to close the door we were vectored on current heading of 145 and cleared into the Bravo. The pilot/passenger replied that he heard the assigned heading from ATC; but did not hear us cleared into the Bravo. Contributing factors: 1) Distraction from cabin door popping open in flight.2) Distraction/impaired communication related to wind noise.3) Distraction related to trying to close the door in order to quiet the wind noise.4) Distraction related to trying to instruct the front seat passenger on how to close the door.5) Distraction from trying to close the door myself when the front passenger was unable to do so after two attempts.Corrective Actions:1) Unplugging the passenger's microphone2) I told ATC that I wished to descend to 1;500 feet; which would keep us below the floor of the Bravo; and began my descent.My perception was that as PIC I had to 'fix' the problem myself; either through instructing a passenger; or by physically manipulating the door; when in reality; the only action that needed to be taken was simply having the passenger unplug his microphone.  I exhibited poor judgment in struggling to close the door. I did so in order to reestablish good communications; but I allowed the process to distract me. The simplest; and quicker solution would have been to immodestly tell the front seat passenger to unplug his microphone. This would have saved time; confusion; and extra radio calls; as well as prevented a distraction in the cockpit. Factors affecting the quality of human performance:1) Being startled by the open door and noise.2) Failing to seek out the simplest solution.3) Possible affects of mild fatigue affecting the ability to problem solve quickly (it was the end of a long day).

I noticed that a departure Aircraft X was taxiing to XC; so I decided to give the next aircraft (Aircraft Y) a hold short at the taxiway (north) parallel taxiway prior to the runway (Taxiway 4); just as an extra precaution. However; I inadvertently said the taxiway name that was the south parallel to XC (Taxiway 5); and did not catch my error. I switched the aircraft to the XC Local Controller's frequency. They had rolled their departure (Aircraft X); and Aircraft Y continued to taxi past the hold bars of XC before they stopped. I did not clear the aircraft to cross Runway XC; nor did the other Controller. Despite my mistake in issuing the incorrect taxiway name; I do not believe anything but the phrase 'Cross Runway ##' gives them the clearance to cross a runway. I; and most other controllers are questioned frequently about runway crossings or unclear taxi instructions. The taxi instruction I gave this aircraft made no sense; because to execute it; they would have needed clearance to cross Runway XC. I made an error by using the wrong taxiway name; but there was no accompanying runway crossing given.I don't know; as I was trying to be extra safe by holding an aircraft at a point further from the runway since there was a departure; as opposed to at the runway. I suppose next time I will just have them hold short of the runway; instead of a taxiway; just so there is no confusion or possibility of mis-stating a taxiway name whatsoever. Additionally; I think that the drop in traffic due to COVID may have played a role. Pilots may have not been to ZZZ since Runway XC was under construction; and they were able to cross it at will before there were proper pavement markings. There are proper markings now; but possibly expectation bias that they were previously able to taxi in this manner played a part.

column121: All preflight items complete INCLUDING Main Electric STAB TRIM CUTOUT switch with normal results. Student Captain was Pilot flying for this leg. Shortly after Takeoff the PF commented that his electric trim switch was not working and asked me to try mine; which also did not work. I asked him if the elevator was working and he replied that it was and felt normal. We asked ATC to level off at 12;000 ft to work on a flight control issue and was approved. We did not ask for priority handling at this time...we engaged the A Autopilot successfully but shortly after the 'STAB OUT OF TRIM' light came on. As we began to look up the appropriate Non-normal; the PF disengaged the autopilot and tried to manually trim the stabilizer. Although he was successful it looked like it was difficult to rotate so I asked to give it a shot to feel the force required to rotate. The force required to rotate was abnormally high but did provide results and we were flying a trimmed aircraft at 240 knots. By now I was considering that a Jammed Flight Control (the stabilizer in this case) was the source of our STAB OUT OF TRIM  problem. So the first checklist we addressed was the Jammed or Restricted Flight Controls Non-normal and also the Jammed or Restricted Flight Controls procedure (the script/expanded explanation). Around this time we requested priority handling with ATC because checklist called for landing at nearest suitable airport. We were hoping that we might get electric trim back when moving STAB TRIM switch on pedestal to OVERRIDE. Did not happen. Called Dispatch with Maintenance Control on the line hoping for some systems expertise. Ended call with where we started. We began to discuss possible value of running STAB OUT OF TRIM checklist. We did. But before doing so we noted the hazard of running multiple checklists and capped our STAB TRIM OVERRIDE switch to normal. The Jammed Flight Control non normal resulted in moving both STAB  TRIM switches to CUTOUT but also called for landing at nearest suitable with Flaps 15. About this time we got on radio again with Maintenance Control; Dispatch and also the Flight Operations. Our hope was that Flight Operations might be able to get a Hydraulics of Flight Controls Maintenance expert on with us. We discussed both checklists and Flight Operations talked about the potential effect of slower speeds. This call ended with general consensus we were on the best track and we discussed whether to land sooner or burn down to below Max landing weight. Because we felt the aircraft was stable and our condition was not likely to get worse we chose to burn fuel. I talked to PF and told him it would be prudent for me to do landing since that would be his first one from left seat in aircraft. We briefed our arrival plan which included our trim plan as we reduced airspeed and extended gear and flaps. As we descended and slowed we reminded ATC of need for priority handling equipment. Only significant thing to report was that by the time we had fully configured and slowed to final approach speed it was extremely difficult to trim manually. In fact; with one pilot exerting maximum effort; you could maybe get the manual strection about a quarter turn. All of this led us to believe that the Stabilizer was DEFINITELY jammed. Landed uneventfully; had equipment check us out then taxied to gate. Flight Attendants were given TEST brief and told there was no need to prepare for evacuation.

column121: I was a passenger on a flight to Spokane. I was sitting in seat X. I was traveling with my spouse who was seated on the opposite side of the aircraft in seat Y. The flight enroute was uneventful. On descent; we were again in VMC conditions. A visual approach would be likely as there were no clouds between our position and the airport. The active runway was 21. As an airline pilot I have done the visual arrival into GEG Runway 21 many times from the south and am aware of the several high towers that are southeast of the airport and directly in line with the arrival into Spokane. Two of the towers are nearly 950 high; so this is a significant threat to arrival aircraft; especially if pilots are heads down and not noticing the towers. If pilots are only focused on clearing the terrain by 1;000 ft. that will clearly put the aircraft in near contact with one of these two towers since the towers themselves are nearly 1;000 ft. above ground. Having been a commuter for much of my career; I have flown over these towers as a passenger no less than 100 times. I know what the normal proximity is to those towers should be and look like from both within the cabin and flight deck on this visual approach. From my vantage point in seat 2A; our vertical proximity to the towers southeast of GEG was not normal and appeared to be dangerously close. We appeared to be much lower over the towers than I had ever seen before in nearly two decades of flying into the airport. I was definitely uncomfortable with what I was seeing and even a bit shaken by what appeared to be a 'close call'. Our arrival into Spokane was mostly normal after that event. The landing appeared to be a bit long; perhaps even out of the touchdown; but nothing of great significance. Upon arrival at the gate; my spouse and I deplaned. Once inside the terminal; my spouse asked me 'Did you see that arrival?' I said 'You mean; how close we were to those towers?' My spouse said;'YES! My God I have never seen those towers so close in my life- that wasn't right.' My spouse is also an airline pilot and commutes so he too is a valid witness to what occurred on that flight. We discussed whether or not to say something as we understand that events can happen from time to time. Because of the seriousness of what we saw; we felt it was appropriate to contact ALPA in an effort to highlight this real threat to all airlines and general aviation regarding the visual arrival into GEG. Over the years I have seen certain deviations from standard that were noteworthy but nothing that alarmed me the way this did. My hope is that additional training can be provided to all airline pilots regarding the towers in proximity to GEG. Perhaps a greater emphasis on arrival procedures. Maybe even a bigger emphasis on the Jeppesen chart itself. I also think the arrival gate coming into GEG from the south should not be allowed over the towers; either VMC or IMC. They are a threat in either scenario. Lastly; a possible change to ATC protocol would be for Approach to require visual confirmation of the towers to arriving aircraft when a visual approach is expected.

column121: On final approach into ZZZ I was Pilot Flying. After calling for gear down we received a BRK RH FAULT advisory message. We finished configuring for landing and I called for the Quick Reference Handbook(QRH). The QRH procedure had us run the 'Landing Gear/Brake malfunction landing checklist'. At this point I called for a go around so we may accomplish the necessary items and let ATC know. After the go around I made a PA advising the passengers we had a faulty brake indication and had to go-around to run the checklist. I spoke to the Flight Attendants and told them I would update them; shortly but we should be landing in the next 5 to 10 minutes. Immediately after; I sent a free text to Dispatch advising them we had a brake fault and were executing a go around and running the procedure. I do not recall receiving a response from Dispatch.The First Officer completed the procedure as I prepared the aircraft for landing. The procedure called for a flaps full landing and longer roll out. At this point I decided it would be best to [receive priority from ATC] and have the fire equipment standing by as this was a brake issue which would cause asymmetric braking. I also requested ATC to switch our landing runway to a runway that was longer than our planned runway. After the procedure was complete I called the Flight Attendants and told them we had [an urgent situation]; we will be landing in 5 minutes; expect emergency equipment and we will not be bracing. I then made another PA to let our passengers now we had an issue with one of our brakes and out of an abundance of caution I have requested the airport to deploy its safety equipment but I did expect the landing to be normal with an extended roll out. My voice remained calm and I made no mention of an emergency during the PA. At this point ATC vectored us to final and we configured and ran the appropriate landing checklist. We touched down and I used reverse thrust and very gently applied brakes.I immediately felt the right hand brake was not biting. I had to mainly use the left brake with right rudder to maintain centerline. Once the plane slowed below 60 knots I was able to slow with both brakes and used the tiller for directional control. The right brake was working but did not feel as effective. We exited the runway and were able to taxi normal; albeit at a slow speed. At this point I noticed on the STATUS page the right outboard brake temperature did not rise leading to the conclusion that it was indeed that brake which had failed. I elected to taxi with both engines to reduce asymmetric thrust. Parking at the gate was normal. I entered the discrepancy in the logbook; called Maintenance and headed to our overnight.In hindsight I do believe [advising ATC] was the right call even if the issue did not end up being serious. I was worried about asymmetric braking and was also not sure if the brake had failed released or with full pressure. I felt it was best to declare and have the trucks standing by and not need them. The only thing I would have done differently would have been to call Dispatch before talking to Maintenance. After discussing the event with the company it seems Dispatch was not aware of the issue until after the plane arrived at the gate. I usually call them first when we have maintenance issues but In this case since the flight was terminating I figured it would be best to go directly to Maintenance but I can see how the lack of communication can cause confusion with Dispatch.

column121: Aircraft requested an RNAV Approach. The Radar Controller cleared the aircraft direct to the Initial Approach Fix. The route was updated in the computer to reflect. Aircraft was level at 13;000 feet and told to cross the Initial Approach Fix at 13;000 [ft.]; cleared RNAV Approach. I was talking with the Radar Controller immediately before saying this was a common error point where aircraft descend below the 12;100 [ft.] MEA (Minimum Enroute Altitude) to the intermediate fix. We observed the aircraft cross the Initial Approach Fix and begin descending. The Radar Controller drew a circle around the next fix for reference. When I came back around on my scan I observed the aircraft already below the MEA of 12;100 feet. I do not recall the exact altitude but it was below 12;000 feet. I brought this to the attention of the Radar Controller. Immediately they transmitted 'Aircraft X WHAT ARE YOU DOING?...' The Radar Controller told the airplane they were below the 12;100 [ft.] MEA. The pilot immediately asked for a visual approach and the Radar Controller asked if they had the field in sight. Upon the affirmative response; the visual approach clearance was issued. I inbounded the aircraft to the Tower and a brasher statement was issued. A low altitude safety alert was never issued.First action should have been to issue a low altitude alert and verify they have surrounding terrain in sight. This approach has had multiple MEA violations and we have been briefed that issuing safety alerts is utmost priority. I should have told the Radar Controller to issue the alert but they responded quickly to the aircraft asking 'what are you doing?' and got them cleared for a visual approach. Perhaps the placement of the MEA step downs is not as apparent as required on the approach plate. The other transitions have both caused issues before on this approach.

column121: I was working a fairly busy session at the beginning of my mid shift. Aircraft X checked on to the NE of ZZZ and was given a heading of 280 and descended to 80; which they read back correctly. Aircraft Y was being vectored from the SW of ZZZ and was descended to 60; which they read back correctly. A little while after descending Aircraft Y I noticed that Aircraft X was at 60 just about to exit the NW corner of the 65 MVA entering the 60 MVA. When I realized that Aircraft X was at the unexpected altitude; there was not enough time to issue a safety alert before they entered the 60 MVA (which was fine for their current altitude).I talked to the pilot of Aircraft X and they indicated that they were sure that they had read back to descend to 60. I reviewed the incident multiple times and only heard Aircraft Y confirm that they were descending to 60. However; both aircraft were on separate frequencies and there could have been a 'stepped on issue' that caused Aircraft X's incorrect read back to not get through to me.There are a couple of things I will work on in the future:- The call signs of Aircraft X and Aircraft Y were similar enough that I should have informed them; that they were both on separate frequencies. I will work on making that a priority in the future.- Aircraft X descended 2;000 feet before I realized the deviation. I was fairly tired after a long work week and think under normal circumstances my scan would have caught the deviation. I should have recognized I was not operating at 100% and asked for an extra set of eyes from the ZZZ [TRACON] Controller. In the future I will work on recognizing this and ask for help.- I don't normally put in assigned altitudes on IFR aircraft data blocks but after this incident I will probably start. Keeping up with strip marking can be difficult when busy and take your eyes away from the scope. Maybe having the altitude in the data block may have helped me recognize Aircraft X was descending past their assigned altitude.- I don't normally come in for XA:15 mid shifts (Usually start at XC:15 or XB:15) and should have asked to work a slower position knowing I was fatigued and on my 6th day.From a technology standpoint there are a couple of issues:- I didn't ever see the Low Altitude (LA) alert go off when I reviewed the falcon replay. The LA indication would have definitely got my attention to issue a safety alert. In my experience working and training it seems like it rarely goes off when it is actually needed. That alert system needs to be revamped; it could be a very useful and a life saving tool!- I wish we could somehow keep everyone on one frequency when we are combined. I think there may have been some kind of 'stepped on' issue with this situation; that one frequency may have helped with.Our staffing has been really bad lately and controllers including myself have been working lots of overtime since last fall. I know management doesn't have many options to alleviate the problem and I don't mind helping out with working overtime. However; here are some recommendations that might help:- We have X supervisors that are certified and can work positions. With COVID vaccines going on they should absolutely be used as staffing until we get people through vaccines and some stability in our staffing. I feel like having well rested controllers that are working less overtime is way more beneficial to safety; then having a stand-alone supervisor in the operation as often possible. Once we get out of our current staffing slump; having stand-alone supervision is a great idea! However; it is currently NOT A GOOD use of our resources.- Plan ahead and be proactive. The entire facility was aware over a month ago that controllers were going to be eligible for COVID vaccines in March. However; there was nothing done to try and stay ahead of all the sick hits that we're going to be happening. There could have been COVID vaccine signup sheets back in January or February to find out who wanted it right away; who would wait; and who didn't want it at all; then plan the schedule based off of that. In addition; the union put a schedule together well ahead of the vaccine eligibility to help mitigate the problem; but it was not implemented for some reason. As a result of no planning or forward thinking; for the past few weeks staffing has been very unstable. There have been many last minute changes to controllers schedules with extra OT to make things work. This is not a safe way to run things and could have been avoided.

column121: I was conducting training. Aircraft X was level at 12;000 feet. The trainee noticed Aircraft X was about to enter into a higher Minimum IFR Altitude (MIA) due to Minimum Safe Altitude Warning (MSAW) alert. Unfortunately a minute passed before he noticed due to handling a new VFR flight following on the other side of the scope. At the time I was on the information display looking up an approach plate. The nearest display was not configured for use so I was with my back to the scope on an adjacent sector. My trainee issued a 15 degree turn and climb to 13;000 feet and then issued a low altitude alert. The pilot unfortunately did not appear to begin his turn or climb for approximately 40 seconds. The turn is first seen on the radar right before the aircraft enters the 12;700 foot MIA at 12;100 feet and the trainee turned the aircraft an additional 30 degrees (45 total degrees) and the pilot complied immediately. Separation from the MIA was reestablished.With the help of the radar replay we identified that when the training team had pulled up the route to check the MIAs; the route line obscured the '27' of 127 and unfortunately we didn't notice and we both individually believed the route and altitude were safe. If either one of us had immediately observed the MSAW or if the pilot turned and climbed in a timely manner instead of delaying; I believe the aircraft wouldn't have entered the higher terrain box. As an aside; the event occurred before a position relief briefing had begun; but the relieving Controller was plugged into the position. I will use this as a reminder to carefully check routes for minimum safe altitudes and keep in mind that the route line can cover the text. I will and remind my CPCIT to use the phraseology 'immediately' for pressing clearances. I will remain vigilant; especially during times when I am training.

column121: On Date; ZZZ [TRACON] experienced a positive COVID-19 test that required facility cleaning.  This cleaning required the facility to shut down radar operations; known as an ATC Zero event.  ZZZ ARTCC contingency plan would then be put into place.  Earlier discussions before I arrived at work discussed the options of how to work the ZZZ [TRACON] airspace.  ZZZ [ARTCC] was advised that ZZZ [TRACON] would be working radar in the Tower; and the option of ZZZ [ARTCC] assuming the airspace did not become an option.  The contingency plan states that ZZZ [ARTCC] clear the airspace and hold aircraft; not assume the airspace.  [A telecom was] convened to discuss the plans for the closing and cleaning of ZZZ [TRACON].  It was clear to me and those listening at ZZZ [ARTCC] that the decision had been made for ZZZ [ARTCC] to take control of the airspace and continue operations at ZZZ [TRACON].  After the call; ZZZ [ARTCC] was given an hour to work through any issues and develop a plan to accomplish the mission.  In conversations with the ATM; I advised him of what the Contingency plan stated; and even had a copy of the plan [sent] to him so he could read it.  I also advised him we were creating a plan to work the airspace and we would be ready to go for the XC:00 deadline.  I immediately brought together TMU; Tech OPs; FDCS; ZZZ [TRACON] ATM and area X staff to put a plan together to carry out the continuation of ATC services into and out of ZZZ [TRACON].  NOTAM was published closing the ZZZ [TRACON] airspace; TMU had instituted an X hour ground stop to slow the initial volume; I conferred the command center the request and they agreed and put in the ground stop.  The plan was delayed for about XX minutes due to traffic volume at ZZZ [TRACON]; and we assumed the airspace about XC:XX pm.  I sat in the area during the entire event; just to ensure what procedures we had developed were followed.  I also ensured correct phraseology was used concerning arrival traffic being cleared on the ILS [Runway] XXR.  Overall; the professionalism of all involved provided for an orderly outcome of the event.  We controlled the airspace for a little over an hour until the cleaning was complete.  My only concern was that we did not follow published procedures during an ATC Zero event.  I am filling this out today because I just received a call from another person at ZZZ [Center] concerned that I did not follow proper procedures concerning the ATC Zero event. I did not fill one out that night because I believed I was acting with approval from my ATM and District to assume the airspace and continue operations at ZZZ [TRACON].We proved that we could operate the airspace in a controlled manner for short periods.  ZZZ [ARTCC] needs to develop basic procedures for all of our underlying 24 hour facilities in the case of an ATC Zero event.   The controllers on the floor working the airspace need to have the basic information in front of them as they work through the basic issues during such events.  While I know that all contingencies can't be covered; that list would be exhaustive; we could have a strong baseline to follow during a similar events in the future.

column121: While being radar vectored to the visual final for Runway XX at ZZZ; Approach Control issued a descent to 6;000 feet MSL. We read back the clearance and proceeded to descend to 6;000 feet MSL. The Captain did observe that we seemed closer to some radio Towers on a hill than what would appear normal; but we received no GPWS Alerts. We continued on vectors and flew an uneventful approach and landing. After a call from Tower a few hours later; it was explained that the descent clearance to 6;000 feet was issued to a (other carrier X) whose readback was on a different Approach Control frequency. Our readback to that clearance as Company A (very similar sounding call sign) must have occurred at the same moment as (other carrier's) reply. Since the (other carrier X) aircraft had been on a different approach frequency; we had yet to hear any other communications to or from that aircraft; and ATC had not issued a caution for the similar sounding call signs. Additionally; ATC did not issue a low altitude warning if we had gone below the Minimum Vector Altitude in the sector we were within.When managing multiple frequencies; ATC should ensure that aircraft with similar call signs are alerted to possible miss interpretations. Furthermore; ATC should minimize the use of simulcasting on multiple Approach frequencies and consolidate traffic to one radio frequency.
column123: We were being vectored for the visual approach to Runway XX at ZZZ from the east. ZZZ Approach Control issued a clearance to 6;000 feet MSL. We were later contacted that the clearance was for (other carrier) X; on another frequency and not for Company A. The clearance apparently took us below the MVA for that sector. The Controller was controlling multiple frequencies (he was busy) and never advised us of similar sounding call signs. We did not receive any terrain cautions from the aircraft or Controller.  The subsequent approach and landing were uneventful.Listening during communications is always the most important.  Being advised of similar sounding call signs is an important step to help alleviate threats and for Crews to be more vigilant.

column121: After being cleared for a visual approach to Runway XXL in ZZZ we received an EICAS 'E2 OIL LOW PRESS' red master warning message on the EICAS display. I cancelled the red warning and advised my First Officer (FO) to reduce the thrust lever to idle on engine number two. I observed the oil pressure for engine two indicating in the red at about 34 PSI; but fluctuating around the top of the red level; and with occasional fluctuations into the bottom on the green range; and which caused the EICAS warning to extinguish; but then reappear once again triggering another master warning for the same condition about 30 seconds to a minute later. Engine number one was still operating within normal engine parameters (green indications); however. The FO was the pilot flying the aircraft; with the autopilot coupled to the [Runway] XXL ILS. As engine number two was still operating at idle thrust; and as I deemed that there was insufficient time to safely compete the required QRH checklist items during the approach prior to landing; I advised the FO to continue the approach. Therefore; rather than perform a go around so as to provide an adequate amount of time to complete the QRH inflight engine shutdown checklist; I made a call to ZZZ Approach and advised the Controller of the situation - that the aircraft had low oil pressure on engine two and that engine failure was imminent. The Controller queried me if I [needed priority handling]? I replied in the affirmative; and subsequently advised the Controller that the we did not require immediate assistance [for the time being]. The ZZZ Approach controller requested the number of souls on board and approximate fuel. I advised the controller that we had XX passengers and X crew for a total of XX souls on board and that we had XXXX lbs of fuel; and approximately 2 hours fuel (endurance - at single engine burn). ZZZ Approach gave instructions to contact ZZZ Tower; who issued a landing clearance for Runway XXL. I advised the FO to disconnect the autopilot and continue to hand fly the approach to landing with the engine number two at idle thrust. The low oil pressure master warning occurred shortly after the glideslope intercept and normal thrust reduction at an altitude of approximately 10;000 MSL; at around the ZZZZZ fix; on approach to runway XXL. The aircraft configuration at the time of the first EICAS warning was flaps 9; gear up; with a speed of 200 KIAS.  As we had already planned to make a normal flaps 22 approach and landing; I elected to continue the approach configure the aircraft for a flaps 22 landing as originally intended. I advised for the aircraft to be slowed to 190 KIAS and the approach to be continued. Landing gear down and flaps 22 was selected at ZZZZZ1 FAP and at which time the before landing items were completed. I then communicated with the flight attendant an abbreviated brief on the CABIN EMER intercom - that we had a low oil pressure indication on engine two; and that we had about 1 minute to go before landing; and to make sure to be seated. A normal landing was successfully carried out; and upon rollout I advised the FO to activate just the engine number one thrust reverser to aid slowing of the aircraft. I took control of the aircraft at the 80 knots and continued to slow the aircraft using moderate braking to a safe exit speed off the runway at the high speed taxiway exit 1. I taxied to a stop just after turning onto Taxiway M. I instructed the FO to advise the tower the we momentarily stopping on Taxiway M to perform checklist items. The tower advised us to contact ZZZ Ground. I then instructed the FO to shutdown engine two and back this up with the QRH and to then perform the after-landing checklist.  A number of ZZZ rescue fire service trucks were approaching the aircraft. Cognizant that the close proximity of emergency service vehicles would cause some concern for the passengers; I made a PA announcement to the explaining the situation and that once the personnel hadperformed a visual check for any smoke emanating from the rear of aircraft fuselage; we would continue the taxi to the gate as normal. Once personnel confirmed that there was no visible fire or smoke present we requested to continue the taxi to the gate as normal. We then taxied to the gate as normal with the exception that I elected to not set the parking braking - due to a possible risk of smoke or fire developing; as the brake temperature on the left inboard brake was indicating in the amber caution range - but requested for the ground personnel to chock the wheels instead to give time for the brake temps to cool down.  A normal shutdown check was performed and with normal passenger disembarkation. I immediately wrote up the discrepancy in the aircraft logbook and contacted the company dispatch to explain what had occurred and requested to speak with maintenance to discuss the write and the event. I advised Maintenance Control of the discrepancy details and what occurred. Maintenance Control then advised that they would need to place the call on hold while they checked if I needed to be transferred to the Maintenance Duty Manager or to receive a callback from a Maintenance Supervisor. I then performed the aircraft terminating checklist and went outside to inspect the aircraft exterior. I then received a call from a company Maintenance Supervisor to needed some additional information about the event. While on the phone call with maintenance I received a call from someone else in Maintenance (possibly the Duty Manager). As no voicemail or text was left by on my phone; I expected another callback from Maintenance Control; but which did not occur; however.In my view; appropriate decisions and actions were made by all crew members. And given the dynamics of the situation; that these decisions and actions were necessary to mitigate the safety risks; to the passengers; to the aircraft; and in the interests of other relevant aviation stakeholders; and which contributed to a safe resolution and satisfactory outcome.
column123: We were cleared for the visual approach to [Runway] XXL; when we received a master warning and EICAS message E2 OIL LOW PRESS. The Captain identified and cancelled the warning and we verified the oil pressure in the red on EICAS as well as checking the oil quantity on the to data page; where we saw only 4 quarts in the number two engine. I was instructed to bring the number two thrust lever to idle to prevent further damage. At this point we were between the IAF and FAF on the XXL around 190 knots with flaps 9. The Captain and I agreed due to the time available before touchdown and severity of the situation to leave the number two engine at idle thrust. The Captain called ATC and advised ATC of our situation; ultimately [requesting priority handling]. The Captain advised ATC of souls on board and remaining fuel onboard; stating we did not need immediate assistance. ATC handed us off to Tower where we got our landing clearance for XXL. The Captain then called the Flight Attendant and gave her a report to prepare for normal landing; advised the situation; gave her time till touchdown; the flight attendant stated cabin was secured. As we neared the FAF I called for gear down and flaps 22 for the final configuration with a landing checklist. We had already briefed to do a flaps 22 landing due to forecasted wind. The Captain had me disconnect the autopilot and hand fly the approach to maintain best control of the aircraft. We performed a normal landing with number two engine at idle thrust; which was successful. At 80 knots; we transferred controls and captain advised me to tell Tower we would need to stop once clear of the taxiway; which I promptly did. ZZZ Tower instructed us to contact Ground and cleared us to stop on the taxiway. The Captain instructed me to shutdown the number two engine; and promptly back it up with the QRH to verify all necessary steps were taken for the E2 OIL LOW PRESS master warning. We completed the QRH items and after landing checklist at this time. Operations vehicles contacted us and the Captain asked them to verify no smoke; fumes; flames etc.; coming from the number two engine; which happened to have no indications. We then contacted ground control to taxi into the ramp area. Prior to movement we noticed the left hand inboard brake was in the yellow arc; in which the Captain elected to leave the parking brake released and have the wheels chocked at the gate. After parking; we accomplished the shutdown checklist; deplaned all passengers and cargo. I stepped outside to do the post flight walk around and found the bottom navel covered in oil; therefore verifying the oil leak. After returning to flight deck the captain was on the phone with Maintenance control; writing up the discrepancy; the Maintenance Duty Manager explaining the situation. We completed the terminating checklists to finish. I believe the decisions by the crew and actions performed; were the best course of action for the dynamics of the situation and time frame we worked with.

column121: Only upon my meeting with the chief pilot was I aware that I had a close range encounter with terrain.  We never received any type of warning.  The Ground Proximity Warning System (GPWS) did not notify us nor did we get a terrain alert from ATC.  A previous report was submitted regarding this flight due to other reasons.  I viewed the flight path in question as a go around (not anything to hide).  The following is what I recall.  We planned and briefed a Localizer Approach.  When transferred to Approach we were informed the Localizer Approach was not available.  We were left with the RNAV Approach. I requested the First Officer to brief the approach.The RNAV Approach was showing in the FMS. Approach gave us a clearance to a fix; the First Officer responded; but I did not understand the fix.  A fix I was expecting to hear was not what I heard.  I asked the First Officer to request the fix again.  Approach replied and again I could not understand what was said.  I am not seeing anything on the approach plate nor FMS what I am hearing.  Approach mentioned that the fix is on the approach plate then spells it out. Now I understood and knew where to go.  We are heading to ZZZZZ and at ZZZZZ I notice the aircraft is not turning.  The FMS had a discontinuity then direct to ZZZZZ.  I turned off the auto pilot and hand fly to get back on track.From ZZZZZ to ZZZZZ1 the course was centering. Inside ZZZZZ1 was going IMC I wanted to go missed [approach].  Somewhere during this time; the flight in which I was following shifted.  The First Officer tried twice to call Approach for a heading and altitude. No answer.  I transferred the controls and called Approach.  Approach responded.  Approach said something about not to continue the descent and gave an altitude and heading.  The second time around we landed. In reviewing the flight; I can see many errors.  I allowed to many little errors become a larger error.  With the little errors I allowed myself to become distracted.

column121: Approximately midway through the pushback; the ground crew indicated that the tow bar had broken and requested that I set the brakes. It caught me off guard as I hadn't felt anything unusual; so I asked them to clarify that they indeed wanted me to set the brakes. They confirmed that they wanted [me to] set the brakes; so I complied. The push crew lead left the radio to retrieve an aircraft mechanic before I was able to obtain more information. The FO and I had a brief discussion as I had a vague recollection that broken tow bars might require a logbook entry; but the only reference we found was that it required a safety report. When the lead returned to the frequency; he indicated that the aircraft mechanic had inspected the nose gear and there was no damage (I witnessed a gentleman with an aircraft maintenance safety vest walk out from under the nose; but I did not speak to him). I asked him to please clarify the nature of the issue; and he indicated something to the effect that the bar had 'cracked where it hooked to the tug; not the airplane.'  I asked the FO if he was satisfied with the response; which he indicated he was. They swapped the bar and we continued without further incident. I filed a report after the trip; and was contacted today by my union advising me that I failed to recognize that this event required a maintenance write-up and sign off.The biggest causal factor is my limited time in the seat; exacerbated by little flying during the pandemic. I had logged only XX hours since completing my upgrade in Month X of 2020; and that trip was the first live leg I'd flown in over five weeks. I remembered that a broken tow bar required additional acknowledgment; but I let myself be satisfied that I was compliant when we found the safety report reference. I think I also reasoned that since a mechanic knew what happened; he would have advised me if further action was required; and I see now that's not dependable logic. I will be spending more time reviewing my manuals in hopes of eliminating future oversights.The best suggestion in this case is the one I must make to myself- to know my company policies/procedures better; as well as striving to clearly understand how to access required information when I need it. I did search the FOM while we were stopped; but now know the reference I needed was actually in the OM. In the future; I will call the maintenance center as well; but this only provides another layer; not absolute protection; as they may not be certain of the policy either. Bottom line is that it's my job to know my manuals. I believe that the return of regular flying that looks to be unfolding over the coming months will help tremendously as we all get reacquainted to the tools of our profession.
column123: During push back the ground crew advised the Captain to set the parking brake. After setting the brake he was advised that the tow bar had malfunctioned. They then decided to get a new tow bar and push us out the remainder of the way. I told my Captain that I think we have to do something for a malfunction of the tow bar so I looked in the FOM and told him he needed to file a safety report. It was later brought to my attention by a union safety representative that we should have returned to the gate and made an AML entry and had a maintenance inspection.I did a search in the FOM for tow bar and didn't see anything that would have led me to believe we needed a AML entry for our situation.Better training on this type of event.

column121: SGU is notorious for near mid-air collisions and RA events.  I was monitoring the CTAF while we were between ETIYR and PIETZ prior to being cleared for the GPS (Runway) 19.  While monitoring I heard an aircraft state that they were having difficulty getting the runway lights to turn on via the CTAF.  I heard multiple series of clicks on the frequency.  After a minute the other plane said he saw the lights and all was normal.  That plane made position reports and was doing a circle to land to a MAP (Missed Approach) for the HIVKA SID.  Everything was uneventful until an aircraft at Mesquite Municipal began trying to cycle the lights at Mesquite.  Hey; what do you know SGU and Mesquite share the same frequency along with Kanab or maybe 2 more fields.  So; inside the FAF our Runway 19 lights cycle through all 3 settings of low; medium; high and turn off 3 times before we land.  We landed with the lights on low with no incident. Too many airports on the same CTAF.  Get a new CTAF for SGU that is it's own

column121: We were assigned an aircraft to take from ZZZ to ZZZ1 that had the BLEED 1 system on MEL. The FO and I discussed before departure in our threat based briefing about how the BLEED 2 system would have a hard time pressurizing the entire aircraft all the way up to our cruise altitude of FL XX0 and how we should make the climb as shallow as we could without exceeding VMO or any airspeed restrictions in order to help the BLEED 2 system pressurize the aircraft.After takeoff the aircraft was pressurizing normally but then somewhere around approximately 7;000 feet on the climb we noticed that the cabin altitude was increasing at about the same rate as our actual altitude and there was only about a 2;500 foot difference between the two. Knowing that only one bleed system was trying to pressurize the aircraft we continued with the hopes that it would catch up and pressurize normally.At 12;500 we got the Cabin Press warning so we leveled off and asked ATC for the lowest altitude they could give us; we were over the [name] Mountains at this time so the lowest altitude they could give us was 12;000 feet. At 12;000 feet the cabin pressure was holding steady at about 9;500 feet but wasn't increasing or decreasing any further.The FO and I discussed running and looked at the pressurization fail checklist but both agreed that the checklist was designed for a 2 bleed operating system and that this was a unique situation.At this point I called Dispatch and Maintenance to discuss the best plan of action; after some discussion Dispatch told us that we needed to return to ZZZ because we didn't have drift down performance for our route of flight at 12;000 feet. By the time this was decided we were almost on the other side of the mountains and I could see the town of [name] about 30 miles to the southeast of our position. My decision was to not turn around and cross the mountain range again at 12;000 feet without drift down performance. When Dispatch became aware of our position we both decided that the best plan of action was to continue to ZZZ1.We landed in ZZZ1 without any further incidents.In hindsight there are two things I wish I would have done differently. The first thing I should have done was to not continue over the [name] mountains with the pressurization not adequately pressurizing the aircraft. I think my continuation was due to the fact that I was unfamiliar with how the pressurization of the aircraft performed with only one bleed system operative and it was my first time operating the aircraft with that particular MEL. If I had it to do over again I would have asked for delay vectors while we waited to see if the pressurization would catch up with our altitude and that way I could have avoided crossing the mountains at an altitude without drift down performance and just returned to ZZZ.The second thing I would have done was to at least run the unpressurized flight checklist; it was a short flight with a very high workload and even though we were still partially pressurized it would have been a good checklist to run just to see if there was anything else we were missing.
column123: Bleed 1 was consistently giving a #1 bleed hot caution on previous flights. Therefore; the bleed 1 source was placed on MEL. The only guidance from the MEL was that we shall not turn on the affected bleed valve. Climbing out of ZZZ; we were filed too FLXX0. Bleed 2 was on bleed 1 was off. Upon reaching 12;000 feet the cabin press master warning light appeared. We leveled off and descended to 10;000 feet. We contacted Maintenance Control and Dispatch. I took the radios and was already PF. Due to not having drift down performance and already being pass the mountains Dispatch and the pilots agreed that it was best to continue to ZZZ1 as we had a lot of fuel.   We noticed the aircraft was very slow at pressurizing during the climb we attempted to help the system by reducing the rate of climb. This seemed to have little affect. It was almost expected by us that the master warning would go off. Once it went off we noticed the aircraft was at 12;000 feet. But the cabin pressure was at 10;000 feet. So there was a small pressure differential. We therefore decided that we would not put the masks on as this would make commutation more difficult with each other and there was no need for an emergency descent. We descend to 10;000 feet as soon as possible this allowed the cabin to descent to 8;000 feet which was much more normal. We contacted Maintenance Control first as we knew what caused the problem. They advised us to call Dispatch. Drift down performance was not available for our altitude so by the time we contacted Dispatch we had passed the mountains and we agreed with Dispatch that it was safest to continue to ZZZ1. Due to the aircraft not pressuring and knowing the issue causing the problem we did not run the cabin press checklist as this would have advised us to turn on bleed 1 which is specifically what we were told not to do in the MEL. By descending down to 10;000 the master warning went away. We continued to ZZZ1 with no further issues.1) It's important to continually monitor the pressurization panel. 2) Maybe contact [Dispatch during preflight for other options]. 3) Knowing that if the bleed source is on MEL; we should expect the aircraft to not pressurize.4) I would not feel comfortable flying an aircraft with this MEL again unless we were filed below 10;000 feet know the system would not pressurize.5) The MEL was not clear on what to expect with this system inop.
