column121: On the LIBER 3 arrival; ATC instructed 'after GLOWS fly heading 020 descend 4200 ft. for traffic; vectors for the approach.' Approximately 15 miles from the runway; ATC instructed '5 miles from CIGNI left turn to intercept the inbound course; maintain 4200 until established; cleared approach.' PF (Pilot Flying) tuned heading; drew a line out from WUNDU; set 1700 in the altitude alert and armed the approach.As course came alive and captured we noticed path continuing to drop below us on the vertical guide. As course came alive; PF pushed VS then VNAV. ALT turned to FLCH and the aircraft began to descend. Rather than capture; it descended through the path. PF pushed VS in attempt to regain the path. We heard 'Terrain warning.' PF turned off AP; began a climb and asked PM (Pilot Monitoring) to rest 4;200. ATC questioned the low altitude alert and asked us to confirm we were established on the approach due to the MSA of 4;200. We confirmed due to laterally established and visual contact with terrain. PF leveled at 4;200; engaged AP and we worked to re-engage the APP while continuing; landed and debriefed.After being vectored off the arrival; it may have been a better course of action to load the RNAV Y for 20R due to better altitude protections. Also need to wait for LNAV to be in magenta.
column123: Due to traffic we were on a heading and descended to 4;200. 5 miles from CIGNI turn left maintain 4;200 until established; cleared approach. I turned to the heading; pressed approach and spun the AA down to 1;700 and lined out from WUNDU; entered in the inbound course and activated.Waiting to intercept I noticed VNAV path was dropping below us. I as saw the course come alive I pressed VS and VNAV; ALT turned to FLCH. Aircraft began a descent to capture PATH but we went through it. My first reaction was to press VS and climb back to path. We heard a terrain warning; I clicked AP off and began a climb asked PM (Pilot Monitoring) to spin AA to 4;200. ATC notified us of a Low Altitude alert; he said if we were established we were okay; We were laterally established and had visual contact with all terrain. I leveled at 4;200 and engaged autopilot. column121: I am a flight instructor at a 141 school. I am currently one of the instructors teaching the Private Pilot curriculum. The error I committed was sending one of my students on a solo flight without a current solo endorsement. Normally in our curriculum; a student pilot solo endorsement would not expire before the student earns their PPL. Due to COVID; our curriculum got pushed back and winter break put a pause on the private curriculum just a few flights before the check ride. The time added was enough for all student solo endorsements to expire. Knowing this; we added a reminder in our CFI guide that follows along with our Private Pilot Training Syllabus. The reminder was placed on the flight just before the solo flight. Due to the lost proficiency over winter break; I was not ready to give this student a new solo endorsement at the beginning of this spring semester.The issue began on the flight before the solo flight. This particular flight was the fourth time I had instructed this curricular period in the last 30 days so; I felt confident on the expectations of the flight. Because of this; I did not review the CFI guide before or after the flight and therefore missed the solo endorsement reminder. With my full permission; my student then flew solo the next day.I discovered the issue when I went to send that student on their next solo flight and I asked them to prove to me they had their required documents and endorsements. I then quickly gave a new solo endorsement.

column121: Approximately 30 nm north on the 340 radial from ZZZ at 3;000 feet MSL engine failure was experienced.  Approximately 3 minutes prior to engine failure fuel tank selector was moved from both to left tank to compensate for uneven fuel burn.  Before and at the time of engine failure aircraft was on flight following with ZZZ approach.  Immediately upon experiencing engine failure ZZZ Approach was contacted and requested priority handling.  At this time; aircraft pitched for best glide speed and made 180 degree turn to ZZZZ.  Emergency procedures were followed; aircraft descended to 2;300 at 65 kts at which time fuel selector was placed back to both and engine power restored.  ZZZ Approach was contacted and made aware of restored engine power.  Aircraft climbed to 4;500 enroute to ZZZ to check and monitor systems circling over ZZZ.  Once definitive evidence showed that engine failure was related to fuel tank selector in left position and that all other systems were functioning normally ZZZ Approach was contacted and aircraft resumed heading from ZZZ to ZZZ1 at 4;500 with no further system failures.

column121: I was the second in command on a charter into Bermuda Dunes airport in California. We landed on Runway 28; the aircraft was being flown by the PIC. After landing we exited the runway on a taxiway prior to the end of the runway. Once clear; I began to run the after landing checklist and was activating controls and switches as the pilot in command taxied the aircraft. As the PIC turned onto the parallel taxiway to proceed to the FBO; PIC started the turn slightly early and the left main landing gear departed the prepared surface into soft sand. We stopped the aircraft and evaluated the situation. It was determined that we needed assistance from airport personnel. Experts on the field in conjunction with our company determined the best plan of attack was to pull the aircraft back onto the prepared surface and tow it to the FBO. A plan was made with our Operations department; Maintenance; and the airport personnel who had experience pulling aircraft from the same location previously. The aircraft was safely returned to the asphalt and towed to the FBO where a qualified Maintenance Technician who was hired by our Maintenance department; inspected the aircraft and returned it to airworthiness status. Bermuda Dunes has a history of aircraft getting stuck turning onto the parallel taxiway and I was told that two other airplanes had already met the same fate in the sand this year that we were faced with. An evaluation should be made of the Bermuda Dunes airfield and notes placed in the Jeppesen plates; to alert aircrews of the hazardous situation that exists with narrow taxiways and a lack of turning fillet areas to prevent departing the prepared surface at Bermuda Dunes.

column121: During arrival into HPN; I noticed the PAPI seemed different. After a few moments I realized that the light indications were backwards. The PAPI for 16 is on the left hand side of the runway but the red lights began on the left (farthest two lights from the runway were red).  The FAA requirements per FAA AC150/5340-30G Chapter 7.4 (d) are that the 'light housing assemblies nearest the runway (inboard) must be seen as red and the two farthest from runway (outboard) must be seen as white.' The VGSI (visual glideslope indicator) was at a corresponding angle to the ILS glideslope which we were using as a backup; despite the red and white being 'flipped'.  I wasn't sure the reference and didn't want to address my concern without being certain and without a reference so I did not immediately notify operations. In addition to my hesitation that evening; the Tower closed just a few minutes after we parked at the gate. The next morning when I arrived to the aircraft; I asked for a contact number for the Tower and gave them a call. The Controller who answered seemed helpful and keen on ensuring that the issue would be resolved. Controller said they would send OPS out to check on the system. Address with HPN operations to resolve the PAPI indications.

column121: There are two waypoints near Truckee; CA; with identical identifiers: VERDI.  One is a useful visual reporting point for aircraft approaching Reno.  It is shown on the San Francisco Sectional over the town of Verdi on Interstate 80.  The other is an airway intersection on V200 and V392; 12 miles out on the 241 radial of the Mustang (FMG) VOR.  This location is about four miles southeast of the town of Verdi.  It is in the northern portion of the Mount Rose Wilderness Area; on a ridge at a much higher elevation than the town.  This is very mountainous territory.  The aforementioned ridge rises to the south of I-80; reaching 10;785 feet due east of Donner Pass and Truckee.  Minimum IFR enroute altitude is 11;500 feet on V200 and V392; and 13;000 feet on nearby V6.  Even in VFR conditions; the mountain tops are frequently obscured by clouds.  Many pilots plan their route over Interstate 80 and utilize the VERDI reporting point as part of that route.  The town is strategically located at a 90 degree bend in the Truckee River canyon and I-80. VERDI the airway waypoint appears on IFR enroute chart L09; but it does not appear on the sectional chart. A pilot relying upon the sectional chart when programming a route into his or her GPS navigator will reasonably enter VERDI as a waypoint.  It will be happily accepted by the instrument; since there is such a waypoint in its database.  The problem of course is that the location is not over the intended route; but instead is over a mountain ridge in a designated wilderness area almost four miles to the southeast. This is an unnecessary hazard to navigation.  One solution would be for FAA to rename the VERDI visual reporting point as part of its series of five-character VPxxx waypoints which are in the navigation databases.

At this moment ATC gave us a clearance up to our cruising altitude of FL410. The crew declined the request and relayed the need for a lower altitude (initially FL310). The appropriate memory items where accomplished; requested priority handling and descent to 10;000 was initiated. During the descent; the high cabin altitude and decent QRH procedure were accomplished by the First Officer while the Captain negotiated the descent. Passing through 27;000 feet the cabin altitude reached a level which activated the automatic deployment of the oxygen masks. Reaching 10;000 feet; the Captain verified aircraft was stabilized; crew was checked for any injuries; and the FO attempted to reach company via AIRINC. With the low altitude prohibiting any contact with ARINC and the aircraft was not equipped with datalink; the discussion began on where to go next. Departure airport ZZZ was approximately 200 NM behind us. ZZZ2 was 190 NM in front of us. And the Destination of ZZZ1 was an additional 300 NM past ZZZ3. The crew discussed the options and in an abundance of safety elected to divert to ZZZ3. The crew notified ATC of the decision to change destination and asked the ATC facility to notify our company of the situation and destination change. The flight continued to ZZZ3 and landed without further incident. After being cleared for the approach; The FO intercepted the inbound course on GPS guidance. The Captain's localizer guidance initially appeared stable. The FO disengaged the autopilot and we immediately descended below the cloud ceiling; which was approximately 1;100 feet MSL or 1;200 feet MSL. The Captain and FO both sighted the runway at 1;100 feet MSL. At some point below 1;000 feet MSL; the localizer appeared to be stable. The remainder of the approach was uneventful. During the approach; the winds were 40 knots from approximately 200 degrees; prior to the FAF. After clearing the runway; we reported the problem to the Control Tower. The FO informed the Tower Controller he had problems with the Runway 15 localizer on two previous occasions. The Tower Controller said he had not received any other notifications about problems with the localizer from any other aircrews. At no point was the approach unstable. [Request] inspection of the localizer antenna. A query to the LCH Control Tower to determine if other aircrews have experienced the same problem. Passing approximately 11;000 [ft.; high elevation airport]. Cabin Alt Red warning light illuminated and horn sounded. Horn silenced - pressurization panel checked - and confirmed correct positioning of switches as terrain noted and communication coordinated with ATC for 'safe' altitude and significant weather avoidance required. Aircraft climbing at normal rate and leveling at 11;000 [ft.] was not an option. O2 masks donned and immediate action items of QRC executed. Remainder of checklist executed as Flying Pilot coordinated deviation with ATC and Captain with regard to safe altitude and course for primarily terrain avoidance and significant weather avoidance as a secondary threat. 17;000 ft. deemed to be safest altitude based on position of aircraft. Requested and set. Executed checklist items concurrently with NO resolution to regaining aircraft pressurization. All indications were normal; but obvious that aircraft was not pressuring at all. Plan determined by flight crew to coordinate safe corridor passage through the 'valley' - again based on terrain primary and weather secondary. Coordination with FAs indicated that passenger O2 had deployed automatically (and of note was deployed manually too during procedure); and that crew and passengers were 'safe'. ACARS NO COMM was illuminated likely due to A/C altitude and mountains blocking signals. Crew coordinated for lower altitudes as safe MORA (Minimum Off-Route Altitude) conditions permitted to account for passenger O2 eventually being depleted. Initially 15;000 [ft.]; then 12;000 [ft.] coordinated to attempt to get cabin altitude below 10;000 [ft.]. At 12;000 ft. with the pack switches selected to high - crew was able to get the cabin altitude to below 10;000 ft. On initial communication with the cabin crew - communication with the forward cabin was nearly impossible due to loud noise by door 1L (our apparent source of no pressurization). Crew communication conducted via aft galley inter phone to determine crew and passenger status. ZZZZ2 considered and subsequently determined (in coordination with Dispatch) due to familiarity; the fact that we have been routinely using it as an alternate for ZZZZ flights; safe passage from our current location to airport at 12;000 ft. and relatively easy weather avoidance to get to airport. Aircraft integrity was addressed and deemed not to be an issue to choose the more distant diversionary airport. As we continued to slow down; he contemplated a need for flaps 30. Due to it being almost XA PM; the flight deck was dark; so I grabbed the speed cards and turned on my chart holder light to verify if we needed flaps 30 to stay above maneuvering speed. I noted flaps 20 provided a 4 knot buffer above slowest maneuvering speed; however; the flight conditions caused some light turbulence stemming from gusty wind conditions. The PF called for flaps 30 to provide a bigger margin of safety above Va. Unfortunately; as I got distracted with our Va and speed cards previously mentioned; I failed to notice that the APPR mode was not armed. As result; staying in HDG mode and distracted we flew through the Localizer. Approach called and queried us on our flight path. The PF disengaged the autopilot and corrected back without delay while I responded to ATC that we're correcting. The PF landed the aircraft shortly after without any further irregularities. Despite a warranted concern to make sure we're at a safe speed for the given aircraft configuration; I let myself become distracted with said task and should have done better dividing my attention. As soon as the words 'cleared for the approach' are broadcasted; focus should shift to the FMA by both pilots for confirmation that APPR Mode is armed.

The Company must be able to immediately communicate with the aircraft at all times.We both failed to do this on both legs of the day.Although I finished training on Date; my first OE trip started approximately 3 weeks later. This was my second OE trip. There have been huge time gaps in my training and I was still feeling very much in the yellow on this airplane. My inexperience with the airplane and domestic flying kept me very firmly in the yellow while flying those legs. It wasn't until I was able to decompress from those flights the next morning that it occurred to me that we didn't adhere to the above referenced FOM.Even though I am flying with a Check Airman and said Check Airman has signed for the airplane; I still need to be in command and take my time to check all of my available references. column121: Climbing through 34;000 feet we encountered a noise and grinding sound with a significant vibration through the plane. I noticed an odor and told the Captain and at that exact time the flight attendants called up saying that there was smoke in the cabin. We looked at the instruments and noticed both engines were erratic in their readings and a high vibration occurring on the number 2 engine. All of these events were happened at the same time.  I flew the aircraft the Captain worked the checklist and requested priority handling.  We shutdown the number 2 engine. An airport was right in front of us and we decided to divert there. Captain took care of the passenger PAs and flight attendants while I controlled the aircraft and flew.  After completing all the checklists and on downwind Captain took the aircraft and landed the plane. Fire Department was on scene and looked over the plane after we landed. They didn't noticed any leaks or fires so we taxied to the gate with them following us.  We had paramedics meet us at the gate to treat any passengers or crew members in case they needed assistance.After we made it to the gate and the passengers deplaned we inspected the number 2 engine.  There was damage to the nose cone and fan blades and inner engine cowling.  Something happened in flight for the parts to become damaged.  We were at FL340 so I doubt there were any birds or anything we hit; not sure why this happened.
column123: Climbing through 34;000 feet at climb power we encountered a cyclic; significant vibration through the airframe. The First Officer then noticed a toxic odor which I then noticed. This was immediately followed by a call from the flight attendants advising that the cabin was filling with smoke accompanied by a toxic odor.  This all happened over a period of about 15 seconds. We then looked at the engine instruments and noticed erratic engine indications along with reduced thrust and high engine vibration on the number 2 engine. The First Officer continued flying the aircraft and I communicated the situation to ATC with a call and a request for lower altitude. I completed the engine severe damage/separation checklist resulting in a precautionary shutdown of the number 2 engine. I then advised ATC we would be diverting for landing.After that I called the flight attendants to check on the status of the cabin. They told me the smoke and smell were dissipating rapidly. I advised them of the situation and that we would be making a precautionary landing  and would be landing in about 25 minutes. I then advised Dispatch through the ACARS message of our situation. After checking in with the First Officer on the status of the diversion I made a PA to the passengers advising them that we were having problems with one of our engines and that we were going to make a precautionary landing.  I also told them that in an abundance of caution they may see some safety equipment inspecting us after landing. Through the descent I made several more calls to the cabin to check on the status and made another PA to reassure the passengers. I also completed the one engine inoperative checklist along with the non routine landing checklist. I elected to assume control of the aircraft for landing and took the controls after we briefed the approach and after landing considerations. After landing without incident; we cleared the runway on a high speed taxi way and stopped so that the Fire Department could make an inspection of our aircraft. After Fire Department told us they saw no abnormalities I elected to taxi to the gate.The FO and I made a visual inspection of the number 2 engine and saw damage to two compressor blades along with damage to the spinner and the inner engine cowling. I was surprised at the small amount of damage considering the effects to engine performance and the smoke and fumes in the cabin.  I'd like to add that the First Officer did a great job in his duties which allowed me to focus on my duties. His calmness; superior airmanship and advice were instrumental in the smooth handling of our situation. I'd also like to commend the flight attendants especially the number 1; on their calmness; communication and professionalism in a very stressful situation.

At this point; we got clearance to level off at 4;000 feet while we ran the compressor stall QRH and decided to return to ZZZ shortly thereafter. We dumped approximately XX;000 lbs of fuel in about 15 minutes.  Once our dump was complete and we landed uneventfully and taxied back to the ramp. column123: Passing approximately 1;000 feet MSL on departure from Runway XX and ZZZ we heard several (4-5) loud bangs and felt aircraft vibration. We experienced no further abnormal engine indications for the remainder of the flight. We coordinated with ATC to return and made a quick call to Operations to appraise them of our situation and ask them to relay that information to maintenance. We ran the ENGINE COMPRESSOR STALL checklist in the QRH. Although the engine operation appeared normal; we opted to increase bleed air demand on all engines as a precaution. Furthermore; even though the engine operation appeared normal; we decided that it would not be prudent to remain airborne for 3 to 4 hours burning fuel.  We therefore asked ATC for fuel dump instructions. The controller instructed us to climb to 12;000 feet and to prepare to hold.During a slow climb to altitude; being careful not to approach the thrust level that existed at the time of the compressor stall; we [advised ATC]; reviewed the FUEL DUMP checklist and sent a diversion ACARS message to Dispatch. Shortly after level off ATC cleared us to commence dumping fuel while proceeding to the holding pattern. We dumped roughly XX;000 lbs over the next 15 minutes during which time we thoroughly discussed our situation; reviewed contingencies; and built and briefed an ILS approach to Runway XY. The Captain flew an uneventful approach and landing with Autocontrols off inside 1;000 feet. We exited the runway; waved off the responding emergency vehicles and taxied to our ramp. Due to lack of parking; we blocked in on the ramp main taxi line; checked in with Maintenance on the intercom; shut down the engines; made Maintenance Log entries; contacted the Duty Officer then scurried to the recovery bird.

column121: I was conducting a flight in the pattern following some avionics upgrades. After being cleared for Runway XX; I unintentionally demonstrated a (scary) non-violent; flat ground loop upon landing. No damage to the airplane or the airport environment. The only damage was to my pride! I was fortunate that the grass was as wide as it was adjacent to the runway and that the transition from the runway edge to the grass and the grass itself was as smooth as it was. I am quite glad to have had a passenger (another pilot) in the right seat as we were able to debrief and I was able to assess the errors that created this event.1) I was carrying too much power (throttle) into the approach and upon landing. While my approach speed was correct; I failed to reduce the power to idle over the threshold. My examination of 'why I would do this' is attributed to my very recent multi-day return to flight training in a Turbo Cessna 182 which is very nose heavy and requires a bit of power to avoid sinking on final. This isn't an excuse! It is a reminder to me specifically that different aircraft require different techniques.2) I bounced. Albeit small; I bounced - caused by #1 and the fact that I landed too flat with too much momentum. I should have immediately gone.3) I didn't hold it off and I didn't have the yoke as far back as needed. I was trained to verbally say to myself 'hold it off; hold it off; hold it off' - I have gotten out of the habit and have re-instituted it.4) I wasn't lined up and there was a small crosswind. Crosswind landings are an area for me to work on. My passenger noticed a difference between the windsock at the approach end of the runway which was straight down the runway (my observation) with a calm to slight wind and the mid field sock indicating a 45 degree crosswind at about 7 to 8 knots. I didn't observe this as it was on the right side of the aircraft my view was obscured by the round out and flare (albeit flatter than required)Those are the ingredients in the recipe for inducing a ground loop - plain and simple.As I was able to taxi back following this incident with no physical damage to anyone or anything; there were a few things I did right...1) I did not panic - panicking never makes things better - that is not to say it wasn't serious - one of the scariest moments in my flying career for sure!2) I kept my heels firmly planted on the floor and did not apply the brakes. 3) Once it was clear that the rudder walk was not going to correct this situation; I put my full concentration into managing the energy and keeping the wings level so we could ride it out - the aircraft did end up rotating about 180 degrees in a decent sized arc - thank goodness for ample room and smooth terrain.I am a big believer of getting back on the horse when you fall off (doesn't mean I wasn't nervous or finding it hard not to think about it too much and psych myself out). I took some time to review some videos I have for Tailwheel Essentials. After all; I was bringing the aircraft back the following day and would need to land safely at home.I am glad to report that it was a good landing as I was lined up; on glide slope; with the correct approach speed; idle at the threshold and I held it off and pinned the tail to the runway with full back pressure - a nice three point landing. So I proved to myself once again that I can do it; and can do it safely. I have arranged some additional remedial training with a Tailwheel CFI to reorient my brain and strengthen my muscle memory.I consider myself extremely fortunate to have learned a VERY valuable lesson that I WILL NOT forget; with only a small loss of pride and a degree of embarrassment!

column121: I was coming from the North and was entering the right downwind.  I was given an extended downwind by the Tower Controller and a 'number 3 clear to land'. I had switched to my ADS-B traffic page on my GTN 750 navigator; which I always do to improve traffic identification in the traffic pattern.  Tower Controller mentioned that number 2 is over a VFR reporting point.  I saw the traffic over that point at my 1 o'clock position.  In hindsight; I am not so sure anymore whether this was actually number 2.  The 1 o'clock angle looked right to me and I saw the traffic; a high wing; and pointed it out to my copilot. It was about where the reporting point is located (at least that's what I thought).  I did not verify with my ADS-B traffic page; which would have clearly shown the number 1 and number 2 traffic.I was focused to look outside for the traffic.  I let the traffic pass on my right and continued a little bit further downwind; since my plane tends to be faster; so to give it more separation. Then I turned base; then final.  I was slightly high so extended full flaps. The gear was already down.  All of a sudden on short final; I saw 50 feet left; 200 feet ahead and 100 feet below of me at about 11:30 o'clock position a high wing plane. I immediately turned right and did a 360; and let the Tower Controller know.  Rest of [flight was] uneventful. I am still a little bit unclear about the exact positions of number 1 and number 2 traffic. I was number 3. The most likely case was that I mistook number 1 as number 2; and thought number 1 was on short final. So I did not pay attention to number 1 but only looked for number 2. If I would have paid attention to number 1; I would have recognized that there is no number 1 on short final; and that the plane that I thought is number 2 is actually number 1.Further; I did not cross check with my ADS-B display. This is exactly the kind of situation; where ADS-B helps greatly and in the most important moment I did not cross check; a clear mistake. In summary: When number 3 or number 4 and cleared to land; make sure all ahead are accounted for. Identify number 1; 2; and 3; so to not mistake number 2 for number 1; or number 2 for number 3.  Usually; I do that; but in this case; I was sure; I had identified the position of number 2 correctly. Cross-check with ADS-B traffic page. Contributing factor was that the audio traffic alert from the GTX-345 transponder to my headset does not appear to work. This may have been due to a recent avionics upgrade and I have to fix.

column121: During a VFR flight; I noticed a slight aircraft vibration that concerned me and I made the decision to land and investigate the issue on the ground. While entering a 45 degree entry to left downwind for Runway XX at ZZZ; I became aware that my radio had become inoperative. I visually cleared for traffic and completed a standard traffic pattern and approach to land. I landed slightly long and slightly fast and made the decision to go-around for a second landing attempt. On the crosswind to downwind turn; while visually clearing for traffic; I saw Aircraft Y on climbout in the pattern behind me. I assessed that either the aircraft had taken off immediately after my first landing; or the aircraft had entered the pattern behind me on a straight in approach. While completing a second pattern; Aircraft Y maintained a relatively close spacing to my aircraft. While on the initial phase of my landing roll; Aircraft Y passed me airborne at approximately 100 feet AGL; and offset to the right on either a go-around or low approach; indicating that he had not maintained sufficient spacing in the pattern behind me to conduct his landing option before I had exited the runway. I exited the runway at the departure end taxiway and positioned at a stop in the south ramp area to do a ground run-up and mag check. While I was performing this action; Aircraft Y completed a pattern to a full stop. Aircraft Y was clearing the runway as I was taxiing north to park. I noticed Aircraft Y come to a hold short of the parallel taxiway while I was still approximately 500 hundred feet from the intersection. As I approached his position; I slowed to give way to Aircraft Y to enter the taxiway ahead of me; but I assessed that the aircraft had remained stopped in the same position and the pilot was holding his cell phone up in the windscreen with both hands; as if waiting for me to pass and take a picture of my aircraft. I did not come to a complete stop. While taxiing past; I noticed the pilot; the single occupant of the aircraft; appeared to be taking pictures of my aircraft. Aircraft Y then entered the taxiway and maintained an uncomfortable distance behind me; so much so that I pulled over on the ramp to let the aircraft pass me. While Aircraft Y taxied past me; with his aircraft still in motion; the pilot had both hands holding his cell phone and appeared to be taking more pictures of my aircraft. He continued to do so even as he was past me; leaning over his left shoulder and looking backwards with his cellphone in both hands while his aircraft continued to move forward. I assessed that I had made the correct decision to allow the aircraft to pass me as he was clearly distracted from operating his aircraft. We both taxied to park in the north ramp. Minutes later; the pilot approach me and identified himself. We spoke about the occurrences. I explained my lack of radio calls due to the inoperative radio. I explained that I did not visually see him on his straight in possibly due to distraction from the engine issue; but that I will continue to enforce my own vigilance and VFR lookout. I expressed my concern for the uncomfortable pattern and taxi spacing and he seemed unreceptive. He also expressed significant concern for the fact that I did not allow him to enter the taxiway ahead of me as the aircraft exiting the runway; which I have addressed in this report.

In fact; the situation was incredibly dangerous. The aircraft probably were only separated by maybe 200 to 300 feet laterally and 0 feet in altitude. column121: Aircraft X checked on from the East and requested the RNAV Approach. I cleared them for the approach over HILIE at 8;000 feet and they read the instructions back correctly. I had the approach plate pulled up initially on the Information Display System (IDS) to verify that 8;000 feet was an appropriate crossing altitude but then toggled back to the normal IDS screen; to keep an eye on the weather. As they got further along on the approach; I noticed the aircraft was at 6;400 feet inside of the 6;500 foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude (MVA).  Unfortunately; I didn't review that section of the approach during their check on and it didn't set an alarm bell off in my head because we do have approaches in our airspace that have published altitudes below our MVAs. I quickly pulled up the approach plate on the IDS to double check.When I started comparing the approach plate and the radar overlay of the approach; I initially thought they were between NAXAF and CUGEV; not outside of CUGEV.  If you look at the approach plate on the IDS; going from the runway out the fixes are: WIVUP; NAXAF; CUGEV; and OZOLA. However; the RNAV Y 26 approach that is available on the radar display is missing the fix 'WIVUP;' so going from the runway out on the radar displayed map you have: NAXAF; CUGEV; and OZOLA).  I then asked the pilot if they were outside of CUGEV and they responded 'Yes'.  I realized they were descending way too early and I issued a safety alert to climb to 6;700 feet. After they climbed; I asked what their intentions were and they wanted the Visual Approach. I cleared them for the Visual Approach.I was not pleased with my recovery time and felt like I should have reacted quicker. We are very rarely on a Runway XX flow and I should have reviewed the radar display map; approach plates; and appropriate altitudes in more detail before and while on position.  I should have just gone with my gut feeling and immediately issued the Low Altitude Alert and asked questions afterwards.  The Low Altitude Alert never triggered which seems like a common theme in these situations. It would be really nice if we could somehow make that thing more accurate.  I think that the fix 'WIVUP' should be added to the radar displayed map so that is correlates exactly with the approach plate. I think it would have helped me recognize more quickly where the aircraft was on the approach and that they were low.My phraseology was not perfect with the low altitude alert but I really think the phraseology needs to rewritten. By the time I got to the 'advise you climb and maintain part' it seemed like they had descended almost another 200.' That small amount of time could be the difference between impacting terrain and not. column121: Initial CPDLC clearance was SID La Guardia 7 Runway 13 Whitestone.  During taxi out Ground changed SID to the GLDMN 7. When you select GLDMN 7 as the SID; numerous complex special engine out procedures are available.  The first; and only engine out procedure; with GLDMN in it for 13 says 'GLDMN NTHNS.'  My FO (First Officer) asked Ground if we were cleared the GLDMN7 NTHNS Departure because of that title listed in the engine out procedure list.  Ground responded with 'It's just the GLDMN 7 RNAV Departure.'  Our confusion was we were originally cleared La Guardia 7 Runway 13 WHITESTONE; so with the change to the GLDMN 7 we were expecting WHITESTONE; and if not; then another transition such as NTHNS. We set the parking brake and informed Ground we'd need a few minutes to brief the new departure. As we further investigated the GLDMN 7; if you select the 'COMPLEX Special EFP Runway 13 GLDMN NTHNS' engine out procedure; it shows the title as 'Runway 13: GLDMN Departure; NTHNS Departure.'  This clearly shows GLDMN and NTHNS and separate departures; not GLDMN Departure with a NTHNS transition.  There absolutely needs to be a Jeppesen title change there either adding a separating comma between GLDMN and NTHNS; or just list them in two separate lines.  For such a simple punctuation mark missing; it took a radio call (which didn't clear up our confusion; and further investigating to clear things up for us).  Either way; we set the brake to brief the change and accomplish the Departure Plan Checklist.  We departed with no issues after that chart confusion.  This report is to support that title change.
column123: During taxi out for departure from LGA; ATC assigned us a new departure from our original clearance of LA GUARDIA 7 WHITESTONE for Runway 13. The new clearance was to depart on the GLDMN 7 for Runway 13. Pulling up the procedure was easy to do; along with programming the FMC. But; the safety concern was that the emergency departure labeling in the Jeppesen Charts was confusing. We requested; for some time; for Ground Control to brief the procedure and to get clarification about the assigned departure.  In the Jeppesen charts; it looks like the emergency procedure is with a NTHAN transition; which we were not assigned; because such a departure doesn't exist. We quickly realized that the NTHAN is a separate departure entirely. We noticed the confusion was because the separate departures were not differentiated with the usual ';' (comma); like at other airports. We then made sure we were on the same mental model and briefed the departure with the appropriate emergency procedure; ran the Departure Plan Checklist and continued on without incident.

column121: Upon arrival in ZZZZ; we were instructed to taxi on Taxiway E and hold short of the ramp since our gate was occupied. I was watching the activity on the ramp that was indicating a possible gate change to hard stand X. During that time with the parking brake set and while I was looking at the airport diagram the First Officer informed me that we had reached the 3-minute required cool down of the engines. I asked him to shut down engine 2. I instinctively followed his movements and noticed that he was holding eng1. Without thinking I said 'no no no' and as a result he moved the engine master from off back to on and the EGT momentarily entered the red zone. All other indications were normal and no ECAM or STATUS messages were displayed. I then asked the First Officer to shutdown engine 2 which he did. We taxied to hardstand X with no incident; shut down engine 1; and performed the parking and terminating checklists. We debriefed the incident and it was obvious that the First Officer was really affected by the mistake. After the last passengers deplaned; I called Maintenance Control to discuss the incident. Local Contract Maintenance also arrived because they were going to move the aircraft. I asked the crew to head to the hotel and I stayed with the airplane to make sure everything was taken care of. The EGT exceedance was considered transient and the required inspection was minimal so the airplane was available to return to service quickly and caused no delays. Later I met with the First Officer and we had a long conversation regarding what went on; the threats this pandemic had brought to us as a pilot group especially the fact that we don't fly much; what we both learned from the incident and what we could have done better next time.
column123: Taxing to the gate; ramp told us to hold short of the ramp on [Taxiway] E.  While holding short of the ramp on E; I told the Captain that we had our 3 minutes for engine cool down.  The Captain told me to go ahead and shut down engine 2.  I ran my flow and instead of selecting engine master 2 I select engine master one.  The Captain saw that I had select the wrong one; and said; ' no no no'.  With the Captain saying that; I took that as put engine select one back to on.  I put the selector back to on and the engine stayed running but the EGT came up and momentarily touched the red arc.  Once we got to the gate; and accomplished all of the checklist and got the passengers off the plane the Captain called Maintenance and was talking with the local Maintenance guys on the situation.  He stayed behind to make sure everything was being taken care of properly and making sure Company Maintenance and local understood what had happened instead of just writing it up and walking away.  Kudos to the Captain!  I was disappointed in myself for making the mistake and during the debrief the Captain could see that.  I apologized to him for making the error that I did. We talked about it and he mentored me through it. I believe not flying that much in the past year do the pandemic played a factor into my error.  I am not blaming the pandemic; but do to not flying as much it's a link to the error.  Another link to the error; is I reverted to the last plane I flew.  We would shut down engine one while taxing in.  What I learned from this situation is that when you are not flying as much as you normally do; you really need to slow down and be more deliberate in your flying and flows.  Think what you are doing and what you will be doing next. Do more chair flying to help close the gap from not flying as much. Do to flying not as much before each trip I will review flows; procedures; and do more chair flying to keep this from happening again.

Ground personnel are also throwing heavy bags constantly; in all weather. The WHO does not recommend wearing masks during heavy exertion; and a wet mask is a worthless mask.The front-line workers of the airlines were forced to wear a mask based on the potential that the mask would prevent transmission of a virus. I argue that not enough research and consideration was made into the potential harms of wearing masks in and around aircraft. OSHA recommends mask fit tests; education; breaks from masking; and studies into the effects of mask wearing in workplaces. I do not believe cost benefit analysis were conducted.We should not be masking children younger than 5 years old. This is a recommendation by the World Health Organization.I would like to see a survey or study done on the effects of mask wearing on employees in the aviation industry. I understand a study was conducted on mannequins in regards to viral transmission on aircraft; but this is inadequate.

We safely accomplished all checklists and briefings and managed to make it down and 'ready for takeoff' at approximately XX:00 z. The whole time from pre gate to this point we had been 'reminded' multiple times by everyone including dispatch (who did a fine job) of the impending 'return' to the gate if we didn't get airborne on the hour. Upon check in with tower we were told to stand by. I was fully expecting them to tell us that we were unable to depart and to return to the gate. We waited and were ultimately cleared for takeoff. Our off time is XX:03 z. It is my belief that; despite the accounting of this event; the entire crew did an outstanding job and I believe we did not compromise safety despite multiple opportunities to do so. I am filing this report the unsafe nature of this 'setup' and also to account for a 'late' departure from ZZZZ at XX:03 z (XA:03 L). The rest of the flight was; thankfully; uneventful.I believe my previous description outlines the factors. How anyone can plan for a 10-minute window on a full international flight; departing at XA:00 am body clock time in a foreign location is beyond me. This is an accident or a incident waiting to happen that is totally unnecessary. This is a peacetime operation; not wartime.Change the schedule. Put some realistic thought into how pilots can be pushed into rushing to comply. As the Captain I had to balance the needs of our passengers; the demands of the local airport personnel; the well-being of the crew and the safety of entire operation leading into a stressful 10 minutes of 'getting it done'. column121: Sequence XXXX is paper legal but challenges common sense.  Bottom line up front; the overall experience level and proficiency of the [aircraft type] pilot group; the training for ZZZZ; ZZZZ itself and the lack of an opportunity to get real rest while flying creates the perfect storm of factors with the potential to cause a true safety event.   We had no safety issues on training flight X into ZZZZ and on training flight Y out of ZZZZ. However; this trip inherently causes the whole crew to be 'in the red' at the gate day one.The [aircraft type] Pilot Group in normal times run on the low end of the proficiency spectrum with 4 takeoffs and landings a month being a good month as compared to a narrow body pilot who will get close to that in one trip alone.  With COVID; the reduced flying schedule; and pilots taking leave of absences this proficiency has diminished even further.  There is also a steady stream of new [aircraft type] pilots entering the fleet despite the flying downturn as retiring pilots are often [aircraft type] Captains.  For example; on this crew; the Captain had XXXX hours; the Check Airman and myself had in the XXX-hour range; and the experienced pilot was the Relief Pilot with around YXXX hours. I would say this is typical with two of us have less than a XXXX in the equipment and one pilot being experienced.  Point being the [aircraft type] pilot group in a COVID world with diminished proficiency is not at their peak performance capability.  Now we add in ZZZZ and the training into ZZZZ.  My training into ZZZZ took place at night on the jump seat.  Again; this may be paper legal but to me negates the intent of in person training.  After this trip my spouse asked me how did the mountains look.  My reply;' What mountains?'  On our VFR night; I could see none other than the EGPWS red and yellow dots.  Luckily; I have a strong memory of going into ZZZZ in a [type aircraft] model and my flight engineer sweating as he ran spaghetti charts trying to figure if we could climbout.  With training at night into ZZZZ; it is like someone asking you to find the bathroom in a dark hotel room never seeing the room in the day.  You know there are some walls and furniture for obstacles but until you turn on the lights you don't get a sense of how close you are to smacking into something.  Also; the elevation and ground speed while sensed was reduced due to being night. We as a [aircraft type] group fly through mountainous terrain to mountain airports that are not high altitude.  Thus; we are 'new' as a group on this equipment despite previous experience on other equipment.  Finally; we have the problematic rest issue which is paper legal and perplexing of how it meets the intent of rest.  Typically; the Relief Pilot gets the first break.  On our Continent Y flights that depart at similar times; most don't sleep but the key difference they land 1-3 am body clock time.  So; staying awake the whole flight and not being fatigued is more attainable.  This sequence; however; lands at XA am body clock time and flies through the whole WOCL.  If a flight is going to this location area; they also land close to XA am body clock time but most Relief Pilots will sleep as the flights takeoff closer to a normal bedtime hour. On this sequence; I would suspect most Relief Pilots will not sleep as they are past the normal circadian dip in the afternoon but not ready for nighttime sleep.  End result landing in ZZZ or ZZZ1 with a fatigued third pilot. Now for the PF/PM.  Usually; the PF takes the second break.  But this is inherently problematic on this trip.  If you alternate legs; the PM from the first leg now will be the PF on the second leg.  The concern is that typically on a long-haul flight requiring three pilots the workload at this point has decreased and that pilot is winding down for their break.  This sequence is the exact opposite.  Everyone after sitting on the ground for an hour plus is at a heightened awareness due to the ever-present terrain and typical weather. So; the usual 15 minutes after takeoff to start a break might not work in that it may be less than ideal while still climbing out navigating storms to swap seats.  Since we had four pilots this played out differently.  Once the PF is able to commence a break that heightened awareness may work negatively against sleep.  Also; on long haul flights this is the quietest break as the first service is done and the second hasn't started.  Not the case with this sequence as their will be a service because it is a new flight. There is a strong potential that none of the pilots get sleep. All this will be repeated the second day with the added potential for hotel sleep issues etc.; and maybe not being able to get the restorative sleep needed to make up for the first night deficit. The second night the takeoff out of ZZZZ will be the most critical in my opinion especially if there is strong weather and or any maintenance issues.  But will a pilot really call-in fatigue on the go home leg to attempt rest at 8;000 feet? Finally; there is the human element that no one wants to talk about.  What are the options for a crew who knows their limitations when it comes to this trip such as proficiency; experience; fatigue; age etc.  All four of us didn't think this sequence was smart and were cautious about being there.  Most [aircraft type] sequences are 1 leg and 1 leg or it is a day turn.  COVID has changed this but not the expectation level of the [aircraft type] pilot group for this type of flying.  When I was junior in the company on reserve; I flew a lot of ZZZ2; ZZZ3 and ZZZ4.  Why because the senior pilots could avoid these high workload cities.  Now we are on a senior fleet that by definition is older. There is no true junior pilot on the fleet.   Pilots are doing their best to see and avoid this sequence understanding their limitations.  I think this adage sums up the situation there are bold pilots and there are old pilots but there are no old; bold pilots. The sequence is ripe with pitfalls and I think the group would rather be old than bold.Somethings we can't overcome no matter how good or professional we are as pilots.  One is fatigue.  Two is experience and proficiency.  This sequence challenges both of these.  [Airline] pilots will fly to ZZZZ. This is not in question. How we do this and how smart we are about this is the reason for this report.  First examine if the loads and cargo warrant the use of the [aircraft type].  If yes; can it be flown into daylight hours letting the pilots be at their peak waking performance? This would allow two of the challenging factors of this trip to be negated which are night operations into ZZZZ and rest issues.  If no; can the trip be divided into a ZZZ1 turn and a ZZZ turn at night that leaves earlier?  Still not ideal but better.   Finally; can training be accomplished in daylight hours.  We can't change the challenging nature of ZZZZ's terrain and weather; but we can change how we operate in and out of the airport to recognize rest concerns; crew limitations and thus optimizing safety every flight.

column121: I had just arrived for my shift for the day. It was mostly slow to start with; however bad weather had already moved through the airspace and another; much larger weather system was moving into the sector below me. I was told the ZZZ [Airport] and ZZZ1 [Airport] arrivals were shut down over ZZZ2 [Airport] and would be coming my way. Next thing I know; I have about 20 planes flashing at me from sector X West of me and every airplane was routed ZZZZZ [Intersection]; ZZZ [VOR] next fix. A lot of those next fixes were bad routes and would have not been per the letter with how we would give planes to ZZZ Approach or ZZZ1 [Approach]. Besides that; though; a lot of those airplanes were not properly separated and would have been in conflict shortly after entering my airspace with not only the airplanes they were handing me but with the airplanes I already had. They needed ZZZ1 [Airport] arrivals down to at least FL280 or lower at Sector Y (the sector I was feeding) and we were receiving them. Stacked from [Sector] A and [Sector] X some as high as FL400. That gave us approximately 20 miles to get them down all the while receiving north bound traffic over the same 10 miles stretch that we were putting south bound planes through because ZZZ1 [Airport] departures and overflights from ZZZ3 [Airport] had not been shut off. After it become so congested at the south end of my sector that I could no longer separate planes or data blocks; I requested a D Side. One was not available because the only staffing we had was currently plugged-in working. I then told informed my Supervisor that I could no longer accept hand offs from Sector X. He said he would tell them. Sector X; however; continues to drive airplanes into my sector without a handoff or point out. I had to take evasive action on one airplane and turn one of mine 35 degrees to avoid hitting an airplane that was 10 miles in my sector with no hand off or point out. Once we finally got that sorted out; those airplanes continued south to [Sector] Y who became so saturated that he could no longer take handoffs from me so I had to put airplanes into holding with nowhere to hold them because military airspace was active and I was still very congested. I may have violated military airspace because of trying to descend airplanes to avoid another aircraft at the same altitude. I also had to pull my mask off at one point when I started to get bad read backs because I didn't have time for bad read backs. Every second counted when you are solid red with no D side. I did eventually receive a D side sometime later.There NEEDS to be better pre-planning. Especially from TMU. Also; when it is requested that TMU shuts down departures from ZZZ1 [Airport] they need to do it! Telling ZZZ1 [Airport departures] we can still take them but 15 in trail doesn't work. Also; the masks are a safety hazard when we are busy!  Pilots cannot hear us properly and if we are having to repeat ourselves; wait for another read back it is taking away precious seconds we could be giving the next plane a control instruction and breaking our thought process to the next airplane. Also having only enough staffing for one D side in the entire area is ridiculous!  Every sector needed a S side and there was only one available. We are back to normal schedules and working 6-day work weeks with overtime and the staffing is still not enough for safety! Not to mention we are tired working 6-day weeks. It doesn't allow us to properly recoup after long days working. There also needs to be more organization when something is shut down. Planes should come to us sequenced so we can then Sequence with the airplanes we already have and not aimed at the same fix.

column121: I was the Captain and Pilot Flying for Aircraft X. Prior to departure from ZZZ; the FO (First Officer) and I discussed the weather and turbulence we were going to encounter along our route through Central Florida. We had also spoken with Dispatch about possible routes due to being a non-EOW (equipped over-water) aircraft for this leg. Dispatch informed us that most aircraft were staying on the east coast to get around the weather. Just south of Orlando; we started approaching the line of thunderstorms and began deviating to the east. Dispatch has us request MLB-COMET-JAWSS-VIYAP to avoid the weather and keep us within the 50 mile limitation of a non-EOW aircraft. We passed the request to ATC and was told the route wouldn't be possible; however; he did say that most aircraft were on NE deviations and staying around 30 miles off shore. We passed this info along to Dispatch. As we continued with our deviations; the FO was keeping vigilance on our route with the terrain display on his MFD and the Jepp app. As we approached the 50 mile boundary; we advised ATC that we had to stay closer to the coast as we were not capable of extended overwater operations. We began a more N-NW heading around the weather. We once again requested JAWSS to maintain the 50 mile boundary. ATC told us to plan on headings around the weather. As the flight progressed; the frequency became congested with traffic requesting vectors as well. Dispatch advised us we were approaching the boundary and to turn back. We tried to get a word in to ATC but unsuccessfully. I advised Dispatch it was busy and we would turn back when we could. Dispatch advised us we had gone past the 50 mile boundary. FO confirmed we were around 60 miles offshore. When we finally got a word in to ATC; we were rerouted on a route that took us further away from the coast and declined it; advised them we could only go 50 miles off the coast. We were told to continue on the heading and they would try to get us closer to the coast. We were then assigned HATMA-CRVET.[STAR]. We verified that HATMA would be within the 50 mile limitation (which it was) and proceeded towards HATMA. We told Dispatch of the route and it being within 50 miles. He informed us he had spoken with the company; who told him exceeding the boundary was OK; for weather deviations. Dispatch said he would be filing a report and we should as well. I informed him that while we were aware of the limitation; we were not going to jeopardize the safety of the flight and did our best to stay within the 50 miles. He agreed safety first and to file the report when we had a chance. Once over HATMA; we were within the boundary again. The rest of the flight was within the boundary.  While it was helpful to have communication with Dispatch for weather deviations; it became an unnecessary distraction to respond to multiple notifications of approaching the 50 mile boundary and exceedance of the boundary. It's my opinion that dispatch should be more aware of our possible task saturation of flying the aircraft and dealing with ATC; traffic; weather. I believe informing us of a possible deviation could have been relayed to us after we were past the weather.

column121: During preflight; discovered both O2 walk around bottles mounted in the aft section of aircraft with masks attached to the incorrect port.  Masks found attached to the (Lo) setting when they should have instead been connected to the (Hi) setting.  I corrected both bottles by attaching each hose adapter to the Hi setting.  This issue brings forward two significant risks. While flight attendants are responsible for ensuring masks are corrected to the appropriate setting; it is highly unlikely that a flight attendant switched or incorrectly connected these masks.  More likely; both bottles were provisioned to the aircraft incorrectly by Line Maintenance.  Since these types of bottles came to Company X during the merger with Company Y; it is suspected that Legacy Company Line Maintenance Techs are unfamiliar with the correct setting of the mask.  The hazard is that a passenger in medical distress; or flight attendant during a decompression will not receive an adequate flow of O2 -- placing both at increased risk for injury and/or death.This event also further underscores the substandard (or lack of thorough) pre-flight checks accomplished by flight attendants. It is also highly likely the majority of Legacy Company flight attendants are still unfamiliar with these types of bottles due to inferior training; thus increasing the risk for error during pre-flight.

column121: We experienced a weather radar power on anomaly; which is noted by an Amber WXR FAIL or CYAN WX-A on one or both NAV Displays. This issue is a long known issue on our B767 fleet. The weather radar anomaly is tied to a known issue involving the parking brake; IRS Selectors and electrical power transfers. There is a note in our flight manual to look for this anomaly after the IRS selectors are moved to the align mode. That is typically handled by the Captain early on during the preflight; however; the anomaly seems to be occurring at various other times as well. This morning we experienced the anomaly after arriving at the gate while preforming post flight duties. The Captain had completed the Shutdown Checklist and was waiting for me to complete the ACARS Post Flight Summary. After receiving the message the Captain complied with Company Bulletin. This bulletin came out [recently] and per the bulletin; we have to comply with this procedure to assure there are no [duplicate] messages tied to our CPDLC. We had used CPDLC on this flight. The Captain complied with the procedure; which is simply put; cycling the BUS TIES from closed to open to closed with a 15 second wait in between cycles. This was the first time we had done the procedure. When completed there was a SIGNIFICANT electrical power shift. The noise for the relays was amazing. It was significant! With the BUS TIE switch back in AUTO; I noticed on both NAV Displays the previously mentioned radar power on anomaly. The message was displayed on both NAV Displays; however it stayed on for just a few seconds on both NAV Displays; then switched to other message on both NAV Displays. I told the Captain what had occurred and once he saw the message I de-powered the Radar. Both messages on both NAV Displays cleared as expected. Cycling the BUS TIE switches in compliance with the directed procedure per Company Bulletin [causes this]. Further there is a known Radar Power On Anomaly which is not being corrected in a timely manner. The new message procedure seems to be causing a known and dangerous Radar Power On Anomaly. It is NOT OK that we have had a radar power while at the gate issue for over X years NOT get fixed in timely manner. This Radar Power on anomaly is a risk to anyone working around the airplane. Further; adding a procedure that appears to be causing this radar anomaly is very; very troubling. I would have thought this procedure would have be verified for not causing any other issues. Really is unacceptable and disturbing that it doesn't appear to be properly researched. It also leads me to believe that the company does not understand the causes of the radar power on anomaly to begin with. column121: I was taking off on my 3rd and final takeoff and landing for my first solo. I had 3 great landings with my instructor and had landed twice solo and was going in for my final takeoff and landing. I was climbing in the pattern and was at 800 feet when I turned right over [road] then leveled the wings. Waited 3 seconds and turned parallel to the runway at 1;100 feet. Powered to 4500 RPM got the clearance to land from Tower and radioed back for clear to land. I pulled the carb heat and when I got to ¾ of the runway I powered to 3000 RPM which is normal for a descent. I put in 2 seconds of flaps and took out the trim. I noticed I was a bit high at 900 feet when I turned over the shopping center so 100 feet above where I normally am. Put in some more flaps to about 20 degrees and turned in to final. I saw 3 whites and 1 red light; so I knew I was a bit high; I reduced power to get the plane to slow and reduce elevation. This gets me to the railroad tracks and descending in normally. Power is reduced to idle over the railroad tracks near Runway XX airplane starts to decent quicker than the last 2 times that I landed solo. As a result; I pitched up to get the glare shield on the horizon as that happened; I touched down and bounced on the runway. As the aircraft rose; I pitched for a decent angle thinking I was high above the runway; as the nose came over; I was surprised how close to the runway I was. Then I pitched for level flight; as I did this the aircraft touched down for a second; I thought It touched flat. But the nose dropped even more; this is when I heard the prop strike the runway. The aircraft went out of control veering to the left; as it departed the runway the nose gear collapses and digs into the dirt. The forward momentum of the airplane has the tail lifted off the ground before aggressively landing on the mains. the aircraft has come to a full stop; after stopping I paused for 3 seconds and then I contacted Tower and let them know what happened. After contacting Tower; I Opened my door and took off the seat belt; took the headset off and stepped out of the plan. I went out of the aircraft for 30 seconds before going back and turning the ignition off and turning off the master switch. After that I was met by airport ops.  After the initial shock and recuperating my thoughts I have found what mistakes I made on this solo and how this should have been avoided. Firstly; there is the initial bounce and when I caught air; I should have pushed into full power and pitched up to have the glare shield on the horizon which allows me to climb and then radio into Tower for a go-around. Definitely do not pitch down like I did and try to save the landing but rather go full power and pitch up for a climb. I was very appreciative of the airport ops and their quick action to make sure that I was safe and getting all the information to see how I didn't land correctly.

on the descent I noticed the Cessna coming towards my position.  he was calling downwind for XX; he was level and I didn't think he could see me due to our closing angle so I descended to remain clear of his path; calling traffic in sight and called final XX continued to the landing...I had inadvertently aligned for XY and was not in the position I announced; I was free from traffic and made a routine otherwise uneventful landing.During my after landing self-critique I realized / reviewed my errors:1)FPL mode on G1000 PFD and MFD displays were not showing real time position due to the cursor mode and Runway XX GPS approach data being left on screen.2) Navigation around some lower clouds and traffic had me looking around and distracted me from dialing in the new runway alignment which is typical practice for our operations.3) Looking for traffic and distractions led to the disconnect between my perceived and actual position.Corrective actions:  will be to enter traffic patterns from more typical locations instead of shorter direct to downwind entry; We have seen this at the facility over the last few days. The aircraft are being handed off relatively late and very high. The weather was not very good and the winds aloft were making the aircraft faster than normal; so the descents have been difficult. column121: When checking in with SEA Tower; Tower told us 'Cleared to land on [Runway] 34L'; and he then asked us which gate we were parking at. We then heard him ask every other aircraft the same thing. Somebody said that's not important right now (which I wholeheartedly agree with); but Tower insisted that it was. I know they want to make their runway exit and taxi plan but asking us which gate we're going to is not necessary; and it's a huge distraction at a critical part of the flight. We're trying to complete our landing check; make sure we're landing on the correct runway; and flying the jet. I don't want my First Officer looking up a gate; or being distracted away from his monitoring duties; and I don't want that for myself when I'm the monitoring pilot. Another thing that SEA Tower is famous for is giving taxi and/or runway hold short instructions while we're slowing through 100 kts. after landing. That also is a critical time; and we're often transferring controls right about then. Tower needs to WAIT until the aircraft is clear or almost clear of the runway and SLOWED down before they start issuing instructions. Nothing further. Educate the tower controllers on critical phases of flight and the their taxi plan is NOT critical. They need to understand that they are there to help the pilots; but instead they're a huge distraction.

column121: After opening my IFR flight plan the Controller cleared me [with] radar vectors climb 2;000 ft. heading 130 expect 3000 ft. [in] 10 minutes and contact Departure. I departed IFR and turned on course while climbing to 2;000 ft. At 1;000 ft.; I attempted to contact Departure but didn't get a reply. I thought maybe I wasn't high enough so I continued my climb. At 1;300 ft.; I heard the Controller talking with another aircraft so I waited until he was done and tried to make contact again. There was no reply. I confirmed I had the correct frequency and channel selected and tried again with no reply. The Controller then asked if I 'was up' and I immediately replied thinking he heard me. He didn't reply back; so I tried again to contact him. Again; no reply. He again asked if I 'was up' and I replied again with no response. At this point; I was level 2;000 ft. so I decided to contact Tower to let them know I couldn't contact Departure. The Tower Controller gave me another frequency and I contacted Departure with no issue. I was asked to climb to 3;000 ft. and was cleared to my destinationEnroute; the Controller asked me to contact him when I landed. After landing; I called him and he asked why I didn't contact him after Departure. I explained that I tried several times and that I could hear him but he clearly couldn't hear me. He then informed me that I was 400 ft. below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude shortly before I finally contacted Departure through the different frequency. I honestly don't know what I did wrong. I know for a fact I had the right frequency in because I verified it several times and asked my medic to confirm. I also checked all other switch positions and even made sure my helmet was plugged into the correct jack. Everything was correct. In addition; I could hear the departure controller so I had to be on the right frequency. From the point I was switched from one frequency to the other; there were no communication problems. I can't explain how it happened.

column121: Approximately 30 minutes after reaching cruising altitude; the lower display illuminated indicating low oil quantity in #2 engine. It indicated 3. Oil pressure and oil temp matched #1 engine. We opened QRH and learned there is no NNC (Non-Normal Checklist)  that covers low oil quantity. Upon a deeper review of our manuals we learned via the 737 FCTM (Flight Crew Training Manual) that the controlling engine indications that could lead to an inflight engine shutdown in regards to engine oil are only pressure and temp. We decided that as long as pressure and temp were good we would continue normal operations. Also based on aircraft logbook and Local Maintenance briefing regarding an earlier flight with a low oil quantity indication we felt it was an indication issue.We monitored pressure and temp and also made contingency plans for an engine shut down just in case. Within 15 minutes the quantity indication dropped to zero; but temp and pressure still matched the #1 engine.  After another 15 to 20 minutes we noticed oil pressure was slowly declining with  temp still good. Oil pressure continued to decrease until illuminated red. Ran QRH LOW Pressure NNC; which directed us to the inflight engine shutdown NNC.We informed ATC that we were performing a precautionary engine shutdown and will need to divert to ZZZ. ZZZ was chosen based on our cruise altitude and distance at providing the best drift down and descent airport. We completed the inflight engine shutdown NNCWe then completed engine out landing NNC and proceeded to ZZZ and landed without further incident. Upon landing we stopped on runway and were towed to ramp.Low oil quantity.

column121: Just below 1;000 feet AGL; ATC directed us to go-around; due to previous aircraft still on the runway. I performed the soft go-around procedure. I called for go-around flaps and the FO selected flaps 2; but the correct flap setting for go-around was flaps 3; as this was a flaps Full approach. I noticed the incorrect flap setting when I saw the airspeed was down in the aircraft's amber 'hook' indication. Normally we would be five knots above the top of this hook; the top of which is Vref. I manually selected a higher airspeed and accelerated before commencing the turn away from the runway. The rest of the go-around and subsequent approach and landing were normal.Lack of recency of experience due to short term leaves of absence may play a role. My FO hadn't flown a lot since returning from a six month hiatus. I also had close to a month off; due to COVID. I feel that I could have reduced my approach speed earlier and thereby increased our spacing. However; we had been assigned 160 knots to a 5 mile final. We complied with that ATC instruction.When I am pilot flying; I brief that a go-around is a successful outcome and encourage my FO to call it out if I don't meet stable approach criteria. I think in the future I will include in my approach briefs which flap setting corresponds to the 'go around flaps' call. This aircraft family uses flaps 3 and flaps full for landing; but 'go-around flaps' is a command to go either from flaps full to flaps three or from flaps three to flaps two.  We don't do that many go-arounds; so a quick review might help. Additionally; watching the preceding traffic more closely on TCAS could have prompted an earlier speed reduction and notice to ATC that we were unable to comply with the previous speed assignment.
column123: During go-around I inadvertently selected flaps 2 instead of flaps 3 during the flap retraction sequence. The PF noticed and compensated; and we continued with the cleanup and subsequent climb and re-vector back runway for a landing with no other issues.I inadvertently selected single engine go-around flap setting of flaps 2 instead of full flaps to flaps 3 go-around.Continue training go-around procedures in training and being more mentally prepared for a potential go-arounds in the landing phase.

column121: The APU went out on this plane before landing initially in ZZZ.  Of course; it was deferred and we were cleared to return to ZZZ1.It was a warm day - not exceptionally so; but hot. These airplanes retain heat all the time; but with a broken APU; the plane becomes a miserably hot metal tube.I had a plane at maximum capacity with a lot of large; hot passengers.  I also had a plane with elderly passengers; small; crying children; and people who did not understand English. All were compliant with the masks; but I also know those masks are dangerous in heat.  The CDC has listed these warnings on their website and in their tweets.  I was very concerned about their health and the heat inside the cabin.While returning the cart to the galley after service; I began to get light headed.  I stood behind the bulkhead (away from passenger view) and removed my mask to breathe oxygen.  I also had to fill a glove with ice to put on the back of my neck to cool myself.  I was very concerned; if I felt that way on a spring day what are the rest of my plane of passengers experiencing?Masks are a very serious and concerning safety issue on hot planes - especially this type and especially when temperatures are climbing.  The summer is going to be a hazard to everyone's masked health - including customers and crew.The mask policy on airplanes needs to be reviewed by the FAA - especially on this make and model.  There are serious safety issues caused by the mask mandates.  Anyone with asthma; heart conditions; lung issues and those who are extremely obese are already at risk when their bodies are exposed to heat.  Constricting their ability to breathe oxygen and fresh air is a danger in HOT spring and summer conditions.  I was taught in training that crew members are more susceptible to hypoxia in the air; but now that threat is greater with FAs flying in masks in hot metal tubes at high altitudes.

column121: I departed around XA:30 and was set to arrive at ZZZ1 at XC:35. Upon my descent into ZZZ1 I began experiencing loss in power and noticed my low voltage light turned on. I tried turning the pilot-controlled lighting at ZZZ1 on; but my radio was not transmitting a signal. To make sure it was not just a problem with the lights at ZZZ1; I flew over to ZZZ2 and also could not get the lights to turn on there. With my landing light being inoperable because of power loss; landing at a dark airport was not a safe option. At this point a tried making a call but had no luck transmitting and [advise] by squawking 7600. I started flying to ZZZ3 to see if the airport was illuminated but when I arrived it was dark.At this point I only had 30 minutes of fuel remaining and concluded I needed to start flying towards ZZZ immediately to ensure the safety of myself and my passenger. I flew towards ZZZ at 2;000 feet; stayed clear of Class B airspace for as long as possible; and was closely watching for traffic visually and on my iPad with the ADS-B in device I had connected. After flying above ZZZ4 and seeing the airport was dark I continued flying to ZZZ and concluded that it was my only option to land safely. Since I was low on fuel; when the airport was in sight; I began my descent into Runway XXR. During my approach I saw another aircraft taking off Runway XYL; I immediately turned left and landed on the parallel Runway XXL to stay clear of departing traffic. I taxied off the runway as fast as possible and worked with airport operations to safely secure my Cessna.This experience has taught me a lot of things to prevent [a situation] like this from happening in the future. I have purchased a handheld radio to have as a backup at all times when flying in the future and am actively talking and learning with my mechanic to better understand the electrical systems in my aircraft. I will always fly with a backup radio in the future especially at night to have the ability to turn on lights at uncontrolled fields and have an extra line of communication if necessary.

column121: I was Flight Attendant 1 on Aircraft X; ZZZ-ZZZ1 on [date].  Upon descent we; the inflight crew; experienced a fume event or 'stinky sock smell'.  The other flight attendants and I experienced severe eye irritation and I also had a headache.  There was no smoke or fire.  After landing I notified the flight deck of the non normal odor event.
