column121: During walk-around; [the] FO (First Officer) found a dent in [the] aircraft; aft left side; near lavatory service. [The case was] entered into [the] AML and [we] informed Maintenance. Contract Maintenance took pictures; detailed measurements; and notes for submittal to ZZZ2 Maintenance Control. After approximately an hour; it was determined that [the] aircraft was good to go; item was deferred; and the paperwork was completed. Flight was uneventful to ZZZ1. At the gate in ZZZ1; a Mechanic came out to the aircraft with some ACARS paper that was requested inbound. We mentioned the dent; so he said he would go take a look. During this time; [the] aircraft was serviced; passengers were boarded; and the flight was 'ready' for departure. The door was actually closed when the Crew Chief informed us that we were on a maintenance hold. The same Mechanic returned and told us that the dent was very significant and the aircraft should be taken out of service for repairs. He mentioned that the aircraft shouldn't have flown and was a 'blowout' waiting to happen. A Maintenance Supervisor came out; evaluated the situation; and the aircraft was subsequently taken out of service. Why and how was it determined that the aircraft was 'good to go' at an outstation; but when the plane gets to a hub it's taken out of service? I understand a forward-leaning mentality when it comes to serving our passengers but this should never be at the expense of safety. We were informed by the Maintenance Supervisor that the discrepancy was deferred in ZZZ but the aircraft was to undergo further evaluation when it arrived in ZZZ1. This sounds plausible; except; the only reason the discrepancy was 'further evaluated' was because we needed ACARS paper and happened to mention the dent to an experienced and highly trained Mechanic; who applied the brakes to this situation. Mistakes can happen; but in situations where there is doubt regarding airworthiness; it is better to err on the side of caution.

column121: We were flying in IMC and received an IAS comparator on both the Captain and F/O (First Officer) PFD (Primary Flight Display). About 30 seconds later the autopilot disconnected. We knew that we had an Unreliable Airspeed. The F/O continued to fly the plane and we went through [the] unreliable airspeed checklist.  We then spoke with ATC and received a block altitude. We then went through the QRH procedure for unreliable airspeed. We determined that the Captain's airspeed was inoperative. We completed the checklist pulling from the F/O CADC (Central Air Data Computer). We got #2 Autopilot and NAV working. The Captain landed the airplane without any issues.Cause: We believe the Captain's pitot tube could have been frozen when we were flying in IMC.

column121: At initial entry into the flight deck; a large amount of coffee was spilled on the aft; center; pedestal of our Airbus A319. Despite an immediate clean up with a large number of paper towels; the first noted impact may have been the failure of the ACARS printer; as indicated by an MCDU message; and the failure of the 'Slew' button to advance any paper. We then began a long series of phone calls with our dispatcher and Maintenance Control (conferenced in) to both attempt a reset of the printer or secure an MEL entry. The total time on the phone was likely over 30 minutes; after which we had an ACARS printer MEL. During our extensive time on hold; I began to suspect that some of the coffee may have also entered other components; such as the Flap/Slat and Spoiler control modules; all near the ACARS printer. After advising Maintenance Control of this; their guidance was to cycle the various components at the gate to see if they worked; we did so; but that generated a FLT/C ECAM Slat Sys error message. Maintenance Control suggested that we try the tests again; once both engines were running; which we did. Both systems appeared to operate nominally so we dismissed our push crew for taxi out. Within 2 to 4 minutes of commencing taxi; I noted an electrical odor; followed soon thereafter by visible whiffs of electrical smoke coming from the ACARS printer area. I directed the First Officer to immediately pulled the ACARS printer Circuit Breaker (as we knew from our earlier Maintenance Control-directed troubleshooting); but found it had already popped. We returned to the gate after consulting with Maintenance Control and local operations; whereupon our aircraft was eventually removed from service.This was arguably the greatest failure of my entire aviation career; I am aghast that we allowed this situation to progress as far is it did; particularly in light of the 'What If's?' We almost took off in an aircraft with grossly uncertain airworthiness. An after-the-fact Google search reveals a long history of potentially catastrophic aviation emergencies and incidents from cockpit fluid spills; we would have added to this list if the ACARS printer had happened to begin smoking a few minutes later; or if the spoilers or flaps/slats had had an uncommanded movement; or if the Engine Master Control(s) had detected a false 'Off' signal...all from a stray drop of coffee migrating to the wrong place at the worst time.While there are many parties to this series of mistakes; I feel that Maintenance Control guidance in this matter was woefully incorrect and caused a serious; negative; impact on our flight's safety. Furthermore; our own flight training has been deficient; we should have known to ground the aircraft. Had we been correctly trained on this threat; we would have never left the gate. Prior to this event; I had little understanding of the potential damage from fluid spills; now I know better; particularly after seeing the coffee stains near the cannon plugs and wiring of essential items inside the center pedestal. Lastly; we were not the first; nor will we be the last; to spill something on the flight deck: the FAA and other aviation authorities should quickly establish Technical Standard Orders for all equipment in 'spill zones' so as to prevent potentially catastrophic outcomes going forward.

column121: The mission was to reposition Aircraft X; a Cherokee 6; from ZZZZ to ZZZ1 where the owner would meet me. I had previously flown this aircraft a few years prior; and it was one of the nicer planes in ZZZZ. During pre-flight in ZZZZ; I noticed that there was a lot of dirt in the fuel. We spent a good amount of time draining the tanks both with the fuel drains on the tanks and out of the gascolator to remove any debris. After that; I had an uneventful flight across the Gulf of Mexico; stopping in ZZZZ1 and eventually ZZZ3. After clearing customs in ZZZ3; I taxied out for departure. After getting clearance for takeoff; I applied power to taxi onto the runway and the engine suddenly stopped. I restarted the engine and taxied to the ramp; thinking that I had put the fuel selector accidentally out of its detent and that caused it to quit. However; upon taxiing to the ramp; the engine quit again. I saw the fuel pressure was quite low; and decided to spend the night in ZZZ3 and have the mechanic look at it the next morning.I met with the mechanic at XA:00 and we worked on the plane until XC:30. He removed the gascolator and cleaned it; finding that it had water and other contaminants. We did the same with the wings and ensured there were no contaminants in the fuel. After discussion with the mechanic; he thought cleaning the gascolator should fix the problem but that at the higher temperatures the plane could be experiencing vapor lock at lower RPM settings and that I should run the boost pump at low power settings and idle. He put a logbook entry in the airplane's logbook for the work performed. Upon taxi out and run up all engine indications (fuel pressure; etc) were within limits. I took off from ZZZ3 and stayed within gliding distance of land. After about an hour in flight and when I was about 30 miles east of ZZZ4; I noticed the fuel pressure gauge was showing fluctuations and it moved from 30 to 25 and continued down. I knew at this point the engine driven fuel pump was failing and decided to divert. Suddenly; the engine quit and I completed a restart using the electric backup pump. I [received priority] and headed to ZZZ5; near ZZZ4. At first the electric pump couldn't keep up with the fuel demand and was causing engine power surges (extremely lean mixture) and it was fluctuating. I reduced power significantly to maintain a lower speed and altitude but the electric pump continued to fluctuate. After the power reduction I had good fuel pressure and decided to divert to the nearest suitable airport that had maintenance available - ZZZ5. I didn't believe this was a land immediately [situation] due to the fact that the backup fuel pump was operating and engine indications were normal and I had no reason to believe that would deteriorate. I landed uneventfully in ZZZ5 and taxied to parking; with the engine barely running.In hindsight I shouldn't have let the plane owner and mechanic pressure me into going when we suspected that the engine driven pump was 'weak.' Ironically; the owner has the fuel pump sitting in his house so he knew it was having problems and failed to tell me before I flew 5 hours over water outside of gliding distance of land. I should never take failing to perform to minimum mechanical or operating standard as an 'airplane nuisance' as the mechanic and owner stated. If the POH doesn't call for running the boost pump on the ground and it requires running the boost pump to run; that is an airworthiness issue and should be addressed prior to flight. Overall everything went well and the backup performed it's purpose.

column121: After an Instrument Proficiency Check and Biennial Flight Review with the aircraft owner the last landing of the day was proceeding normally with the owner/operator pilot-flying. There was a crosswind on final approach but nothing abnormal. As the aircraft was entering the flare and about 5 feet above the runway (with power at idle; on centerline; at 75 knots) the aircraft nose suddenly slewed about 45 degrees left immediately taking the aircraft off the runway and over the grass. The pilot initiated a go-around with full power. The aircraft touched down on the grass and rolled straight for several hundred feet before the right wing settled to the ground and the aircraft rotated 90 degrees right and stopped.As instructor I did call for a go-around as directional control seemed lost; but that call was simultaneous with the pilot initiating a go-around. I cannot explain the initial sudden yawing moment. I speculate that the plane was hit with a gust during the flare and there was inadequate energy; even with full power; to keep the plane from contacting the grass. The attempt to prevent the plane from settling onto the grass caused a nose high attitude; along with full flaps; probably created excessive drag preventing acceleration.The METAR at the time showed wind 30009KT The 3 METARS before the incident showed wind 24011G17KT to 28009G14KT. The landing METAR was well within the Demonstrated Cross Wind for a Cirrus SR-22; but perhaps unexpected gusts were starting as we landed.There were no injuries but the airport was closed for several hours.
column123: Just prior to touch down on Runway 20 a wind gust pushed the airplane extremely hard to the left; I initiated a go around but was unable to climb and regain control. There were no injuries. I was flying with a CFI at the time and had just completed a Biennial Flight Review and an Instrument Proficiency Check and everything had gone fine; the day was done and were landing at my home airport. I feel the cause was a combination of a strong wind gust and wind shear.

column121: I was parked on the gravel bar with the tail of the plane oriented significantly downhill. I had the parking brake set but also used a good size piece of driftwood to chock the left main tire. When it was time to leave; I released the parking brake while still outside the aircraft; which is the only practical way to release it since the lever is situated deep within the footwell. However; when I removed the log (so as not to hit it with my tailwheel when taxiing) the plane started to roll. Therefore I reset the parking brake; deciding to release it from inside the cockpit after starting the engine to provide enough thrust from rolling backward while I reached within the footwell to release the parking brake lever. I struggled slightly but was able to reach the parking brake lever and satisfied it was released I increased power and the plane began to move forward. Taxiing was sluggish but this was expected due to the low-inflation bush tires combined with two other factors: the 'digging' or plowing of the tailwheel and the soft gravel/sand. The tail wheels of all aircraft were digging that day; causing extra power to be needed for ground operations. We deal with this situation every time we land and takeoff from gravel bars and had dealt with it the previous 10 takeoffs and landings earlier this day. So at the time I didn't notice or feel anything unexpected during taxi.As I lined up for takeoff; I took notice of the same small bush I always use on this gravel bar as an abort point if my tail isn't up and flying as well as a familiar tree I use as my abort point if I am not airborne by the time I reach it. I applied full power and well before the small bush abort-point; my tail was already up and flying. This was unusual as it normally takes much longer for the tail to come up but I mistakenly saw this as a good thing so I continued the takeoff roll. A second or two later; I was suspicious that I wasn't accelerating normally so began preparing to abort if not airborne by my second abort point. I momentarily diverted my eyes from outside the cockpit to check my airspeed and this check confirmed my suspicions - I was not accelerating normally. As I began to pull the throttle off; I hit a small rut and momentarily became airborne a few inches so I hesitated a fraction of a second to abort the takeoff. However; I settled back to the surface and instantly; before I had a chance to pull the throttle to idle; it felt as if the tires 'grabbed' and the resulting inertia put the plane on its nose and the remaining momentum caused it to flip over onto its back. I was able to exit the aircraft quickly and within seconds; several people were there to assist me. Multiple people then assisted me with carefully turning the plan back over and we were all very surprised at the lack of damage. Other than the propeller; some scrapes and scratches to the paint and a crack in the top of the [type] windscreen; there were no other obvious signs of damage. We pushed the plane out of the way and secured it and I was given a ride with one of my friends to ZZZ1 where we spent the night as planned.Unable to figure out what happened I began recreating the events that led up to the incident and became suspicious that even though I was able to taxi; maybe I had not fully released the parking brake. Returning to the plane the next day; I opened the door and several of us looked inside and saw the position of the parking brake lever. It was barely to the halfway position. I'm not familiar enough with the internal valving to know for sure; but the halfway-released parking brake lever seemed to confirm my theory. The chain of events leading up to this incident were extremely interesting and like any error chain; there were numerous opportunities to break it; beginning from the moment I landed on the gravel bar and picked my parking spot.  I only parked my plane in the same manner because everyone else was parked that way. However; I could have simply chosen to park farther away from the bank on more level ground; thus avoiding the need to use the parking brake to begin with. The next opportunity came when I first removed the log and the plane began rolling backwards. I could have simply asked any one of 10 people to help me keep the plane from rolling while I released the parking brake (from outside the cockpit as I always have in the past) thus enabling me to get in and start the engine. The next opportunity to break the error chain came when I accepted the sluggish taxi as 'normal' thus exhibiting confirmation bias. Rather than being more suspicious I was actually being complacent. Yet another chance to break the error chain was when my tailwheel came up unusually quickly. Had I recognized this situation as abnormal (rather than welcoming the unusual 'bonus' of the tail coming up so quickly) I could've accomplished an easy; low speed abort and checked everything to see what was amiss. Finally; the last chance I had to avoid this outcome was to abort as soon as I became suspicious of my lack of acceleration rather than focusing on my predetermined abort point. Once I went beyond that last opportunity to abort; I believe my fate was pretty much sealed. Contributing factors (in my opinion) were an unusually large 'audience' of fellow pilots watching our group of planes takeoff. This probably reveals the biggest failing on my part that day. Ego. Not wanting to screw up in front of a bunch of fellow pilots. Looking back; a simple aborted takeoff would never have been seen as a screw up but the exact opposite. Everyone on that gravel bar would've been extremely supportive of the prudent decision to abort. For ANY reason whatsoever. Maybe another contributing factor could be the design/location of the parking brake lever of the [Homebuilt type]. Though I hesitate to include this as a factor as the location of the parking brake lever had never been an issue in the past. But this unusual scenario may have shined some light on a potentially troubling aspect of the location of the parking brake lever deep within the footwell as opposed to someplace in plain sight and easy to manipulate and confirm whether it is set or released. All in all; this was a scenario fraught with poor aeronautical decision making and will inform my attitude towards flying for the rest of my time spent piloting aircraft; regardless of which type of aircraft I am flying. Lessons learned.

column121: During single runway operations immediately after a runway change from 31R to 13L due to winds; all Admin; Ground Operations; and checklists through taxi out were uneventful until Taxiway B; holding short of Taxiway M5. We estimated being #10 for takeoff. The Ground Controller gave us a slot time of (time) Zulu time; cleared us to cross 13L at M5 and told us to continue taxiing A5 then Alpha to Runway 13L. On the same radio the Ground Controller advised us the RJ (Regional Jet) ahead was cleared for takeoff and another aircraft was on three-mile final. That left one RJ on Alpha at the end of runway to taxi past while contacting Tower and running the Before Takeoff Checklist. With Lots of urgency in voice with words and tone from both Ground and Tower Controllers to all aircraft; the Tower Controller cleared us to line up and wait. We completed the Before Takeoff checklist and noticed an aircraft begin to taxi expeditiously; on taxiway Bravo on the other side of the runway. The Captain noticed the aircraft taxi and landing lights; stated his observation and asked F/O (First Officer); 'Why are his lights on?' F/O noticed the rate of Taxi Speed and lights then queried Tower Controller; 'Tower Confirm Aircraft X is cleared to line up and wait?' Tower responded but the radio call was quick and interrupted by another person transmitting. Captain and F/O were 100% confident Aircraft X was originally cleared to line up and wait. Due to a visual conflict with the other aircraft possibly receiving the same clearance; our Captain stopped our aircraft during the query and response. The other aircraft appeared to slow down on the other side of the runway. The next radio call was; 'Aircraft X; CLEARED FOR TAKEOFF 13L (text represents a QUICK radio call strung together). This was followed by 'Aircraft X you are past the hold short line 13L; continue to cross without delay join Bravo and Contact Ground. F/O repeated the call including 'Sorry for the mixup'. The rest of taxi; ground operations; and return to 13L for takeoff were uneventful with the following exception: all communications from Tower; although a different voice assumed to be a supervisor; continued to contain LOTS of urgency in voice; words; and tone from both Ground and Tower Controllers to all aircraft. When conducting single runway operations; especially during deteriorating weather conditions; Ground and Tower Controllers should make a conscious effort to avoid speaking too fast and share information when similar sounding flight numbers are on frequency. When recognized Controller saturation and urgency; we can increase our guard and awareness against expectation bias. Additionally; we could possibly slow the cadence when appropriate while reading back clearances.
column123: Scenario in DAL wasn't optimum. Runway change had just occurred due to winds out of limits. 13R closed. Winds shifting and Rain/low visibility to the south of field. During taxi; four to five Aircraft are shutdown on Taxiway B due to weather at east gates. Six Aircraft shutdown on M for the same reason. Taxi instructions for Aircraft X; 'Taxi to 13L via B hold short of M5;' given initially. EDCT (Estimated Departure Clearance Time) time now given (not known prior to this) by Ground of (time) void by (time). Ground then gave us hold short 13L at M5. Cross 13L; A5; A; 13L; contact Tower. Corporate jet in hold area just north of Taxiway A; approaching 13L holding short. Ground Controller and Tower Controller sounded rushed / voice inflection during transmissions from taxi out to this point with all aircraft. Tower Controller stated; 'Aircraft X; lineup and wait Runway 13L.' F/O read back instructions to Controller verbatim; to lineup and wait 13L; with no response from ATC which seemed normal. 'Before Takeoff Checklists complete; final clear; 13L verified;' and I looked right; to double check final clear; rounding corner on A I looked left and saw a Company aircraft rounding corner on M6 toward 13L with LUAW (Lineup and Wait) Lights configured. I stated this to F/O; while simultaneously stopping aircraft at 45 degrees facing 290 degree estimate; just past the hold short line. Tower Controller then cleared other Company aircraft for takeoff 13L. He then stated to us 'Aircraft X; it appears you're past hold short line; taxi without delay across 13L to B; contact Ground and we will get you right back out. Never heard COMM jam or readback from other Aircraft X. When we were cleared LUAW and we read it back (all sounded normal in headset and transmission) and therefore I don't know how I could have prevented mistake. First time we knew of other Company aircraft call sign was when Tower cleared the aircraft for takeoff. The rest of DAL Ground Ops through departure phase was uneventful. Runway change / single runway operations / weather changing / departure gate closed; definitely played into non-standard operations both for ATC and Aircrew. Similar call signs should have been noted or announced by ATC to help prevent any confusion on ATC to aircraft instructions. Cadence and voice inflection are critical components in managing risk during less than optimal conditions for ATC. Although the task loading and pace for our phase of flight and internal communications did not feel rushed; the additive conditions; especially late notice EDCT could have contributed.  When I recognized Controller saturation potential and their urgency; we could have slowed down our transmissions and pace or have been more directive to them to slow down. Not only our craft; but all the aircraft that were on the taxi; could have helped slow things a bit.

column121: Flight was scheduled to depart ZZZ. We arrived in the flight deck and performed all the normal procedures we have for a normal push back. Captain did the preflight walk around and I loaded the FMC. We agreed the OFP (Operational Flight Plan) looked good and the rest of the flight plan looked sufficient for a potentially bumpy ride to ZZZ1. Captain advised to Flight Attendants to stay seated out of ZZZ until we knew the ride would allow for their safe duties. I was the flying pilot and after Captain did his first flight of the day and PM (Pilot Monitoring) duty brief; I briefed the SID. We planned for a normal pushback with 2 engine start for a quick taxi for departure. We performed the BEFORE TAKEOFF CHECKLIST on taxi out down the ramp for takeoff on runway XX.While we were taxiing down to runway XX; I noticed there was a split between the L and R duct pressure. I made note of it to Captain and we briefly discussed these splits we have seen before in this aircraft and recall it being a known normal occurrence. I cycled the L PACK (Left) switch to OFF and back to AUTO as well as the ISOLATION VALVE switch to OPEN and AUTO and saw the duct pressure needles sync together. We decided it would be a safe action to depart and noted we would keep an eye on the duct pressure and pressurization.We departed runway XX and CLIMBED VIA THE SID. I hand flew the departure to the mid 20s and then turned the autopilot on. I noted Captain mentioned 2 different times that the aircraft was pressurizing normally though the duct pressure still was split. The ride was mostly good and the flight attendants were up but the seat belt was still on. As we approached our level off altitude of FL340 the CABIN ALTITUDE horn and the MASTER WARNING lights illuminated. We verified the CABIN ALTITUDE was high on the pressurization panel and performed the Immediate Action items for CABIN ALTITUDE WARNING OR RAPID DEPRESSURIZATION/EMERGENCY DESCENT. The CABIN ALTITUDE was not controllable; and we continued with the descent. There was a definite issue with immediate communication over the inter-phone with the masks on and all the noise. Getting the mask on and the audio panel correct to be able to speak and hear over the speaker poses a threat in this airplane if not practiced. We were able to communicate with each other and ATC but it was challenging with all the noise and distractions.Captain identified as a priority flight with ZZZ Center and we began the initial descent over the mountains. I initially turned off the AUTOPILOT to pitch over and begin the procedure. Once we were established in a descent; I turned the AUTOPILOT back on and descended to FL190 with the high terrain in mind. We saw an aircraft below us on the TCAS and had to shallow the descent initially before we were cleared lower. Captain proceeded with completing the checklist and communicating with the Flight attendants; passengers; and dispatch. Descending through approximately 16;000 feet I noticed the CABIN ALTITUDE was in a normal range of around 7;000 feet and we took off the oxygen masks. We leveled off at 11000 in the vicinity of ZZZ2. Initially we were planning on diverting to ZZZ2 because we were so close; but Captain's experience and familiarity with ZZZ3. This led to the decision to divert and there was difficulty communicating with dispatch possibly due to our low altitude so we opted to landing in ZZZ3. The flight attendants and passengers were all briefed for the diversion to ZZZ3. I left the AUTOPILOT on and we flew the RNAV (GPS) Runway XY 29 approach and landing. All checklists were completed before ZZZZZ intersection and the landing was normal. CFR ( Aircraft Rescue & Firefighting) was there upon arrival.We were parked at the hard stand in ZZZ3 and the ramp personnel brought over the ramp to allow the passengers to vacate the aircraft. Operations were there to help while we figured out the plan of action for the passengers. Captain discussed the situation with the ChiefPilot; Dispatch; and Maintenance and I aided the flight attendants with passengers. I walked to the OUTFLOW VALVE and noted a mesh substance blocking the OUTFLOW VALVE from fully closing. Captain manually opened and closed the valve and I videoed the movement.

column121: On Departure out of ZZZ the crew experienced significant audio distortions on COMM 1. Switched to COMM 2. In the vicinity of ZZZ1 contact was lost with ATC for a period of approximately 10 minutes. ACARS was also lost at this time. Upon reestablishing contact ATC was able to hear the crew loud and clear but on board the ability to receive ATC transmissions was significantly degraded and there was significant static and noise on both frequencies. As the flight progressed the quality of the reception continued to degrade and COMM 1 became completely unusable. The QRH was run and the MEL; FOM and AOM (Aircraft Operation Manual) were utilized. The decision was made to Identify as an emergency and continue to the planned destination. Due to the inability to contact the company; ATC was requested to tell the company of the communication issue. As the flight progressed the quality of the reception continued to degrade on COMM 2 until it was barely usable. Upon entering the approach segment of the flight NAV 1 and 2 provided unreliable lateral and vertical information. The flight concluded safely at the destination. Flight crew that handed off the aircraft noted issues with the ACARS no other pertinent information was provided by the crew as they departed. ACARS was usable for the preflight and initial departure portion of the flight.The cause of the radio communications failure is not known by this crew member at this point in time.Air traffic control was very professional and they were immensely helpful and indispensable throughout the event.
column123: While departing ZZZ; on climb out and then more noticeable as we neared ZZZ1; static / screeching distortions were noted on COMM 1. At least three times; we asked ATC how they heard us; and the reply was 5x5. We could hear ATC at a 2 or 3. We advised ATC of this. Conditions deteriorated throughout the flight; causing us to utilize COMM 2 as primary.After a short period; COMM 2 began a degradation similar to COMM 1. All flight instrumentation; engine gauges; etc. showed normal parameters. QRH / FOM checked; Captain and I monitored and with COMM 2 not improving; and notification updated information to ATC; Identified as an emergency. Plan and back up plans were made by crew; flight attendants briefed; company notified. Flight continued with no further issues. It should be noted that during a period of time; no COMMS were heard; and we queried ATC to make sure we had not lost all communication. Additionally on approach (visual conditions) both lateral and vertical guidance was observed unreliable. Furthermore upon accepting the aircraft from the previous crew; the Captain noted issues with the 'ACARS' noting we may have to reset the ACARS.The cause of the action is outside of the scope of this crew member. ATC was outstanding. Helpful professional and went above and beyond.

column121: Pushed back from the ZZZ gate X; during push back; we received the okay from ground crew personnel that we can start engine 1. During engine start of the number one engine; it was noted that we had a hung start as the N2 gauge only got up to about 31 percent. Once the Captain and I noticed the indications; we went into shutdown procedures of the number 1 engine. We did note the engine 1 ITT temperature rapidly increase; before it decreased. After shutting down the engine to prepare to restart; ground crew personnel attempted to notify us that there was a fire. However; due to faulty headsets of ground personnel; this information was hard to make sense of. At this point to confirm a potential fire; we contacted the flight attendants to check the rear of the aircraft and look out the windows to confirm the fire potential. The flight attendants did not see any flames or smoke. The decision was made to open the main cabin door; to allow the pilot in command to visually verify there was a fire threat. After the pilot in command visually inspected the area; he was able to confirm that there was a fire and we promptly called for an aircraft evacuation of the passengers and crew. Fire units were notified promptly by ground crew and notification to ZZZ Ground Control of evacuation of passengers on the ramp. The Captain and myself (First Officer) continued to do the Engine Fire (on the ground) Emergency Procedure Checklist and the Passenger Evacuation Procedure Checklist.
column123: Pushing back we were cleared to start the number one engine. While starting the engine we noticed the engine went to 30 percent N2 and N1 was hanging at 6 to 7 percent. When we were doing the shutdown procedure we noticed the ITT gauge started going up rapidly then went down to zero after we shut down the engine and had no other messages appear on the aircraft. After we shut down the engine the rampers were trying to tell us something; but their radio had a lot of static and I could not understand them. I thought they said fire; but I was not sure because of all the static on the radio. We had no indication on the EICAS of an engine fire. I had my First Officer call the Flight Attendant and check to see if there was a fire. They called back and said they could not see anything. Still unable to understand what ramp was saying; I decided to open the cabin door to visually check; and there was a fire on the number 1 engine. I ran back inside and told the Flight Attendants to evacuate the aircraft. The First Officer and I ran the Engine Fire (on the ground) Emergency Procedure Checklist. After we finished the checklist I shut off the aircraft and made sure everyone was off the aircraft.

column121: We were flying back to ZZZ on a clear dark night; arriving on day four. It was my leg (Captain); PF (Pilot Flying). About 20 miles out we were given a vector to ZZZZZ which is about 6 miles south of ZZZZZ1; the final approach fix for runway XXL. The controller asked us to keep our speed up to 210 or better until final as she had other inbound aircraft that she was sequencing in. We switched to green needles and sequenced the approach according to our normal procedures. When we were about 10 miles from ZZZZZ; approximately abeam ZZZZZ1; we called the field in sight. The controller gave us a heading of 080; cleared us for the approach and switched us to tower. She noted that the other aircraft would be following us and to keep 170 or better to final. At this point we were about 5 miles from ZZZZZ1 at about 90 degrees intercept. The heading the controller gave us would take us inside the final approach fix before we intercepted the final bearing. Seeing this; the FO (First Officer) noted that we had not begun our decent to final approach fix altitude yet. I called for the descent; flaps 20 as we slowed to final approach speed. As PF; I noted that the flight guidance would not give us a good intercept because the intercept was too great. At this moment; the autopilot began the turn to final too soon. I turned off the auto pilot and began hand flying. As we began the turn to final I called for flaps 30; and then flaps 45 as we neared the final bearing. As we were completing the turn; the FO (Pilot Monitoring) noted that we were still high and that we should increase our rate of decent; we were about 2000 MSL; I steepened our decent and he selected 1000 fpm as we rolled out. I called for and we completed the landing checklist. Tower came up and checked us in. We had not called at the FAP (Final Approach Path) as we were busy flying. At this point; we were about 4 miles from the end of the runway at about 1800 MSL. The tower gave us landing clearance and noted that we were low as the PF I called for us to stop our decent; and I leveled the aircraft at about 1500 MSL. I noted that I had not completed the turn correctly and we were not quite on final bearing. I corrected and called for zero VSI (Vertical Speed Indicator) and adjusted to get on final. The FO complied and we continued inbound. At about 3 miles from the runway on final bearing our GPWS alarm went off; PULL UP. As PF; I called for a climb and began a climb at about 5 degrees nose up. As we began our climb; the GPWS alarm went off again; saying PULL UP; I increased the climb; and we climbed about 200ft; as we were very close to glideslope. I was about to call for a missed approach; when I noted that the climb had put us on glideslope; and the PAPI's confirmed us on glideslope. Seeing this; I reestablished our decent and the FO called stabilized at about 3 miles. We landed normally; completed our checklists and shut down the aircraft in accordance with our normal procedures. We have procedures and training guidance that should have prevented this. In this case; there were several errors I made on this approach. As PF; I should not have accepted the vector inside the final approach fix with such a large intercept heading. As Captain; I knew that the flight guidance would be unable to make the turn correctly and we would need more room to make the turn to final. I should have asked to continue our course and give the controller other options. This likely would have prevented the whole series of errors. I should have started my decent to FAF altitude sooner. We were at 3;000 feet; 5 miles from ZZZZZ1 as we turned; and I delayed our decent to 2;400 ft. for several seconds as I turned off the flight guidance and began the turn. If we had been at 2;400 MSL we would not have required a large decent in the turn to final. When the tower checked us in at 4 miles and noted that we were low; I should have called for and established a climb back to glideslope instead of just leveling out. We were very close to glideslope and we should have re-intercepted it first. When the GPWS alarm went off; I should have immediately called for a Missed Approach. We were low (hence the alarm) and there is no space or time for altitude errors on final. Any delay calling for a Missed Approach puts safety at risk. Finally; there was probably some 'get-home-itis' in our minds as we were flying. Arriving late at night; at home field on day four; we were tired and wanted the trip to be over. Going missed would have delayed our landing. Also; we were also trying to satisfy the controller who was sequencing us in front of another aircraft. We needed to focus on our flight; not her decisions or problems.

column123: We were positioned at ZZZ ramp spot XX. An aircraft at spot XX1 was cleared to taxi to [runway] XXR; but I wasn't paying attention to his routing. I thought I heard via 'Kilo.' Immediately after that; we were cleared to [runway] XXR via Kilo; and told an airplane on Kilo to our right waits on us. The airplane at spot XX1 began taxiing and I began my taxi so as to be in front of the airplane on our right that was taxiing; but waiting on us. I can't be positive; and it may have been just my expectation; but I thought I saw the airplane from spot XX1 (on our left now) start a left turn on Kilo. With him safely in front of us (I thought); I briefly looked down at the FMC then to my right to make sure we were clear of the airplane on Kilo. The First Officer then said; stop; stop; stop." The aircraft from spot XX1 had turned to the right not left; and was now right in front of us. He had been cleared to the runway via Kilo; K5; Lima. We had not been moving very fast since we had just left spot XX; but I applied the brakes quickly to ensure safe separation. This; I learned later; had caused our number one Flight Attendant; who I did not know was standing; to lose her balance and fall against the galley area. Ground Control then apologized for not letting us know; or to give way. We continued to the runway and I spoke with the crew to make sure they were okay; our number one especially. They all said they were okay and that they were good to continue to ZZZ1. In flight; the number one Flight Attendant told me she wanted to file an injury on duty report. I was very concerned for her at that point; but she said she was just a little sore; she could perform all her duties; and we would be okay to continue. I concurred with her that it would be safe to continue to ZZZ1. We were scheduled to turn around and fly back to ZZZ.I was still very concerned; so I asked the number one to coordinate with her supervisor and get guidance since she wanted to also fly back to ZZZ. I called safety to get guidance as well. Our Flight Attendant stated she was fine to fly back and could perform any and all her duties. After observing; and speaking with her; the First Officer and I both concurred with her assessment that it was safe and reasonable to continue. We landed uneventfully in ZZZ and a team member met the airplane for our number one."

column121: Upon arriving at ZZZ; I asked the local FBO to fuel my aircraft. At their request; I allowed them to fuel the aircraft without me after hours. During my preflight inspection two days later; I noted the fuel quantity indicators in the wings indicated full fuel in the inner tanks. I noted that no water was present via a fuel sample despite heavy rain the day before; and that the gas caps were present on both wings. I was then distracted during my preflight inspection and did not remove the pilot side gas cap to visually inspect fuel level. The co-pilot side gas cap had previously been removed to observe fuel level in the tank. Engine start; taxi; and run up were unremarkable. Shortly after takeoff on runway XX; I noticed that the pilot side fuel cap had departed from the airplane and fuel was coming out of the wing at a tremendous rate. Fearing a severe weight imbalance; I Identified as an emergency and returned to land on runway 18 without further incident or damage. Extensive search of the airport grounds failed to locate the missing gas cap. No damage was noted in the gas cap receiver. I suspect that the gas cap was either damaged or installed incorrectly and the preflight inspection failed to uncover the fault.Chain of events:- Local airport staff removed both gas caps and fueled the plane unobserved.- Pilot side gas cap was either damaged or incorrectly reinstalled after fueling- Preflight inspection was not specifically performed on the pilot side gas cap- During takeoff; the gas cap came loose and departed from the aircraft- In-flight emergency was declared- Landing was successful without further incident or damageHuman Performance Considerations:- Other factors; such as lack of water in the fuel and fuel quantity indicators; gave the impression of properly installed fuel caps- Other activities occurring around the aircraft during the preflight inspection provided distractions that prevented a full inspection of the aircraft- Failure to remove and inspect the gas cap resulted with in-flight failure

column121: Immediately after takeoff the #1 inverter failed. I inadvertently switched off the avionics master instead of the inverter switch I was intending to bring the backup inverter online. As we were in a turn to assigned heading and just starting to enter the clouds; I reduced power to stop the climb and stay below the clouds and continue back towards airport while I sorted things out. I saw the airport and by that time had my avionics back and had switched to the other inverter. I contacted the Tower and informed them I had an electrical problem and was requesting to return for landing. I was in a little too tight to land on runway XX which was the runway I had just taken off from so I requested to enter a left downwind for runway XY as there was basically no winds. The ceiling I believe was probably ragged between 500-700 feet above the ground...approximately 1100-1300 MSL. column121: First Officer; Pilot Monitoring. Captain; Pilot Flying. 3;000 feet MSL inbound to AWLEE 210 KIAS or greater assigned. Cleared for a visual approach approximately 5 miles from AWLEE 170 or greater to 5 mile final assigned. Continue on heading; allow spacing for visual approach at 210 KIAS. Abeam CRDNL given 080 heading and still cleared for visual and switched to Tower. 080 heading gave a perpendicular intercept course for final. Captain armed approach mode. Aircraft began an early turn to final simultaneously the Captain input a command that caused the plane to enter into pitch mode. I called out pitch mode and he turned autopilot off. I advised the Captain that he needed to begin a descent since we were inside the final approach fix and were 600 feet high. I entered vertical speed mode and put in a thousand ft per min rate of descent and dialed in a 45 degree intercept into the heading. Captain began slowing down and called for gear down; flaps 30; and flaps 45 at appropriate speeds I called for level off when I realized we were at 1;500 feet MSL (acceleration altitude). Simultaneously we received a call from Tower advising us that we were low for our area. I informed Tower that we were leveling and continuing our visual approach. At this point I went outside the cockpit and became focused on looking for towers that would pose a danger to our flight. I didn't recognize any threats. I thought that we could maintain this altitude and intercept the glideslope without issue. We then received a call of terrain. I said we needed to climb. No climb was initiated. We then received the audio alert of woop woop terrain. Pull up. At this point I stated we needed to climb. I began pulling back pressure and a climb was initiated. The audible signals ceased and we continued to intercept the glide slope. Once established on glide slope and on course I called out 1;000 feet stabilized and we completed the approach to a landing.  As soon as we were at 1;500 MSL I should have called for a go around. I knew the Captain was disoriented and was confident that I could act as a back stop to get him onto final. I didn't call for a go around after we stopped getting the audible warnings because we were at that point established within the safe and standard parameters of the approach. However; a go-around may have been the pertinent thing to do to increase everyone's situational awareness.

column121: Event took place right after takeoff. I was PF and had manually leveled off at 3;000 MSL using the 'Low Alt Cap' procedure which went as briefed. At this time the PM had called Departure Control and we were issued a climb to 4;000. The PM set 4;000; I confirmed verbally and then commanded VNAV. I continued to manually fly since we were assigned a heading. I had briefed a speed of 200 knots due to being below Class B Airspace and now came to the realization that I had just commanded the aircraft to speed up while we probably weren't high enough yet to legally accelerate. As I held the pitch to hold the airspeed; the altitude alert went off at 4;300 feet. I then clicked off the autothrottle; pulled the thrust to idle and pitched to return to 4;000 feet as the Controller called to remind us to maintain 4;000 feet. We reached 4;500 feet before descending. Flight proceeded without further incident.I had not flown much recently. Reserve lines in my home town had recently materialized and I was enjoying the absence of commuting. I hadn't flown since February with the exception of a PT and upset training in March. I felt that hand flying would be good to help regain proficiency. Our clearance was to fly runway heading for vectors; so I thought this would be a great opportunity. In hindsight I should have waited for a little less busy environment to ease back into it. The FO had flown out of ZZZ1 before and was aware that things could get busy. I should have taken this as a bit of a warning. I could have also thought about how to handle this departure a little more thoroughly. FLCH would have been the better choice in this situation. It would have held 200 knots and commanded a 500 FPM climb. Far more manageable.
column123: I was PM. The Captain was PF. Our initial clearance was 3;000 feet and runway heading. The Captain briefed a low altitude capture using 200 knots as we were under the Class B shelf and relatively light. He briefed the intention to hand fly until we were given the intercept to the initial fix on the departure. The initial level off went well and according to the brief with the Captain hand flying. Were quickly given a new heading and a climb to 4;000; which I read back to ATC and set. The Captain confirmed the altitude and called for VNAV. I watched to confirm the start of the climb; then turned to switch my iPad view to the chart page. I heard the altitude alert; looked back to see the airplane pitched higher than the flight director and realized we were climbing past 4;000. At the same time the Captain disengaged the autothrottles; reduced thrust and pitched to return to 4;000 feet. At this time the Controller called us to tell us she needed us back at 4;000 feet. The altitude was about 4;500 feet. The PF corrected back to 4;000; then were soon given another climb.  Upon debrief we both realized that FLC would have been the better mode to engage as the VNAV reverted to the programmed speed that was too fast for what we were trying to do. The Captain mentioned he increased the pitch to control the speed and that caused us to climb thru the assigned altitude.As we were still in a critical phase of flight; I should have been more vigilant in monitoring the rate of climb; the speed and the vertical mode. If I had; I could of called it out to help the Captain arrest the acceleration and rate of climb in time to avoid the overshoot. I suggest that more emphasis be placed on the use of FLC and also VS mode. We seem to minimize their use as we rely on VNAV so heavily. The call to engage VNAV becomes a reflex. In this scenario; FLC or VS would of been a better mode that would of prevented the increase of speed that in turn contributed to the overshoot.

About 50 miles north of ZZZ1; we were cruising at 280 kts in IMC conditions at +2 degrees TAT with engine anti-ice on. The Captain was flying. We then noticed the airspeed start to go way down then go way back up. It indicated maybe 40 kts to 300 kts (unsure exactly). 'Airspeed low' kept announcing as well. The Captain turned off the autopilot and autothrottle and set 4 degrees nose high and told me to set power. I pulled the power to 70% N1 and we compared PFDs. My airspeed indications would indicate properly for a few seconds then jump up or down. The Captain's was constantly moving up and down so we transferred control to the First Officer. I called for the QRC and the Captain read and accomplished the steps (we had missed flight directors off). We had climbed a couple hundred feet during this and I asked the Captain to notify ATC and I turned the airplane eastbound in an attempt to exit IMC. It worked and a couple minutes later we exited IMC and started a descent to warmer air. While the Captain ran the QRH for unreliable airspeed and informed ATC/dispatch; I continued to fly. As the air warmed and as we exited IMC; airspeed indications returned to normal. We reviewed pitch and power setting in the QRH to make sure the airspeeds were accurate. The rest of the descent and arrival to ZZZ was uneventful. My guess is we accumulated ice on the probes enough to make the airspeed indications go unreliable. I didn't see abnormal icing on the windshield wipers nor was icing reported. Being in IMC at +2 degrees was about perfect conditions for it. After landing; the Captain and I talked about how we were thankful for 737 MAX simulator training we had both recently completed. The training prepared us so well for this and I am thankful to our check airmen in the sims. I felt well prepared for this as described above thanks to 737 MAX training.

column121: On Date there was an unfortunate damage to the Right Horizontal Stabilizer of Aircraft X. This damage drove Safety Bulletin on Date 1; which suggested a breakdown in communication as the root cause of the damage. However; most technicians (and supervisors) believe the real root cause of this damage was caused by the inability to use the correct equipment to accomplish the task at hand due to [the] Stores Department using both sides of this bay as staging and storage for their various equipment and items (tires; crates of all types and sizes; stacked at heights of over 10 feet in some instances). The work to be accomplished was on the right hand wing tip but because of all the equipment on the ground a small 35 feet JLG or widebody lift could not be used; instead a much larger JLG was necessary; positioned much further away; resulting in contact/damage to the right horizontal stabilizer. If this was a one off; the technicians probably would not have as much heartburn but this issue of stores using Bay 3; one of our prime widebody aircraft bays; as a storage has been going on for years and has resulted in other aircraft damages in the past.  This has been a well-documented and hot topic of discussion in ZZZ meetings; crew briefings; safety team raising it with messages; every level of management has been made aware of this over the years.  Sadly; the situation is getting worse instead of better.At our latest ZZZ meeting Date 1; a supervisor questioned the findings of the investigation stating that in his experience working the service center; he felt the stores equipment was more of a causation factor than the loss of communication. The reply from another member of management 'I am not aware of this being an issue'. Another participant suggested there was a lot of documentation but was told 'we can look into it and maybe build a case to get the stores equipment moved'. Since the damage; this stores equipment problem has been highlighted at the daily crew briefings and what is glaring to most techs since this damage is the fact that not only has nothing been done to mitigate the issue; it has actually gotten worse since the latest damage. This aircraft has been out of service now for almost 3 weeks; (if we are to believe the finance people when they tell us that a wide body generates X money on average a day); that's a costly stores area; just looking at it from that perspective!The unfortunate reality is in the event of a damage the technician is grilled in the investigation; sent for drug and alcohol testing; always made to feel at fault; always told it was self-induced pressure; and of course have their records pulled showing they signed off a specific training course; maintenance & engineering bulletin; awareness class etc. I have examples of this from many investigation reports.  I'm filing this report because the front-line mechanics don't want to for fear of repercussions if they did.  Sure; there are many human factors that come into play when incidents like this happen but when you look at it; this is not complacency on the part of the mechanics. There are real pressures to get these aircraft in and worked in BAY 3 and we crutch the system on a daily basis because of these pressures.  My question; how is Company living up to their values of safety always being #1 when this issue has been ignored for years despite the attention and spotlight?What is staggering to most; weeks after the latest very costly damage the situation is actually worse. The only answer could be; if you investigate and find the root cause that suits; then of course it will be impossible to mitigate and address the real root cause! I won't gain any friends for pointing this out but this issue needs to be addressed. It is our responsibility; from safety; to Management; coworkers etc.; to do the right thing; provide a safe work environment; which helps keep us all safe from injury and our assets from being damaged. We owe it to each other and ourcustomers. At this juncture this needs to be a priority from senior leadership because constant suggestions and concern from the floor have hit a brick wall and frankly we on the front line don't have the authority to fix the problem.

column121: On flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2; which was at the limit of our aircraft range unless there are decent tailwinds; had a hard time getting a climb; barely any tailwinds and was expecting a cumbersome arrival.  So; when we were over West [State] and assigned the ZZZZZ arrival I was wondering if we would land with minimum IFR reserves.  Asked Center to keep us high as long as possible and they did a pretty good job except this involved lots of vectors and altitudes when getting closer to ZZZ.  So; during descent I was delaying a steep descent until closer and lower to save fuel.  All of this ended up working and we landed with more than minimum reserves but it caused me to be really busy in IFR conditions.While direct to ZZZZZ1 to cross at 9;000; I was given an eastbound vector through the arrival track between ZZZZZ2 and ZZZZZ1 while descending at close to 3;000 FPM.  Then told to head direct to ZZZZZ1and cross it at or below 9;000.  This involved a 135 degree right turn within 10 miles of ZZZZZ1 but all was good on making the crossing altitude.  Then was given 5;000 at ZZZZZ and told to cross ZZZZZ1 at or below 9;000.  I entered the 5;000 in for ZZZZZ but made the error of entering a vertical 'Direct to' for ZZZZZ and engaging VNAV.  Looked up and the descent rate had switched from almost 3;000 FPM to just above 1;000 FPM.  Very quickly disengaged VNAV and dialed in the 3;000 FPM on the VS mode.Finally figured out there was no way I was going to make the crossing at ZZZZZ1.  Told the Controller I wasn't going to make the crossing altitude at ZZZZZ when within 2 miles of ZZZZZ1 - a little late.  We ended up crossing ZZZZZ at a little below 10;000 and the rest of flight went very well.Causes:  1st would be doing that VNAV to ZZZZZ - if I left everything alone; we would have been fine.2nd was coming in high and having to do a steep descent while being vectored around and given the direct-to really close to the ZZZZZ1 fix which involved lots of turning.3rd was flying a little slow and descending a little slow to save fuel which caused problems for ZZZ Approach.4th was getting barely any sleep the night before - had taken a natural energy booster later in the day and it didn't wear off until XAam or so then had to get up early.5th was keeping the flight smooth for the passenger despite the steep descent and all the turns - without a passenger I would have been more positive about getting down.6th was the low fuel situation I was concerned about - during COVID with lower air traffic I became used to getting unobstructed clearances but it is busy again - really busy this day and I didn't figure that I would have any problem getting a climb to 450; but I did and that burned more fuel than I had planned.How to avoid in the future:  1) Plan fuel for busier air traffic.  2) Don't do a VTO to the last of 2 fixes when given crossing restrictions for 2 fixes.  Either VS it or if using VNAV just do the VTO to the first fix and let the VNAV figure out how to get down to the second fix.  3) Don't take that energy booster after lunch time!  4)  I forgot that during descent the fuel gauges read a little low - just remember this next time.

column121: Conducted a part 91 flight ZZZ1 to ZZZ2.I initiated a crew brief of the SID while still on the ramp...I had the chart display mainly zoomed in on the text description box to make the text bigger.   I focused on the final altitude of 17;000 to the right of the text box that pertained to all runways. I had showed the PF the altitude and said 'I will set 17;000 in the altitude select if you agree'.   He responded 'affirm'.   I began to read the text version of the SID to myself and it read 'Climb on a heading of 216 to intercept course 185 to ZZZZZ; then on track 108 to cross ZZZZZ1...'  I announced we will arm LNAV for departure as the FMS matched this.At that point I did not finish reading and zoomed in and looked at the SID graphically but focused on the runway departure and how it fed into the initial FIX ZZZZZ.  I noticed all runways fed into ZZZZZ.  I knew that fix would be important on readback; (as it is at ZZZ3 for example); to ensure safety on parallel runway operations.Very short taxi out from FBO.  Took off runway XXR; normal operations.  Positive rate; gear up; '400 feet; flaps up select VS.'  Thus; we were in VS speed as is often the case for climbout.Tower sends us to departure.  I call twice; no joy.  Switch back to Tower and ask to confirm frequency.  Call back through 6;000 and departure responds climb and maintain 7;000.  We received this clearance at approximately 6;800 feet.  We executed this clearance immediately however given out pitch attitude and climb rate we overshot 7;000 feet and reached an altitude of 7;400-7;500 based on my best recollection.No TCAS alerts were issued.  We maintained 7;000; were given another climb clearance and then before the ATC Controller switched us over; we were told of the possible deviation.What I have learned from this incident is to read the entire textual description in the SID and to take in the whole SID graphically as opposed to taking into account just the post departure/runway routing.I also learned poor habits can be formed from other airports; particularly our home base airport.  We receive a SID on our clearance every time.   We then get a heading on takeoff clearance from home base ZZZ2 ATC voiding the initial part of the clearance 99 percent of the time.Another factor is the scarcity of climb via SIDs that do not mainly incorporate 'at or above.'  This incident taught me not to assume or have a bias to SID instructions.Another factor in this error was rust due to the COVID shutdown.  Our awareness and CRM need improvement which will come with more recent operations I believe.

ATC advised us of the weather and gave us a reroute to the ZZZ2 VOR which was significantly off route from our original flight plan. Unfortunately; after re-calulating our new flight plan and fuel; we noticed that due to our reroute we would be landing at ZZZ1 with minimum fuel. Letting them know that if we continued to fly to the ZZZ2 VOR that we would be landing with min fuel. We were given 'deviations as necessary direct ZZZ1 when able'. Our radar showed two storm cells about 3-5 miles in diameter. We decided to deviate around these cells and proceed direct ZZZ1 once clear of the storm. While navigating around these storms we began to experience updrafts and downdrafts. During our course of route the autopilot was engaged and suddenly began to deviate from FL290 by +800/-300 ft. The VSI (Vertical Speed Indicator) showed a climb and descent of +/-4;000 feet per min and the cockpit windows became fogged. During this time the airplane did not feel like it was pitching this extreme and did not exceed +5/-2 degrees. Altitude miscompare flags appeared on our PFD'S (Primary Flight Display) and the VSI had a RED X for less than 5 seconds. I began to run the QRH. ATC contacted us about our altitude and asked if we were having a rough ride. We responded and advised of the situation and were cleared to descend to FL240 at pilot's discretion. After the airplane was stable at FL290 we descended to FL240 and landed at ZZZ1 with 2;400 pounds of fuel and no further incidents.

column123: We were at FL410.  We knew about the weather before we left.  There were some high top reports but not many.  We got closer to the line and asked for FL430.  We started on top but then went into IMC conditions.  We had our radar on the 100 mile range and pointed down so that the 50 mile line was painting the ground and any storms that were between 50 nm and 100 nm.  If there is a storm between the 50 nm and 100 nm and it is severe the ground behind it will not paint.  It will be black.  Also; if the storm crosses the 50 nm line and starts to disappear then you will top that storm.  We deviated to the left of course to an area that looked clear and was disappearing as we got closer.  So we should have topped it.  We got into the top of a buildup.  First Officer turned off the auto pilot and hand flew.  We got some rain and an updraft followed by a down draft and then numerous up and down drafts. we went up to 43;300 and I saw 41;800 on the down side. column121: While on initial descent into SFO; I obtained a METAR and D-ATIS for the airport prior to my briefing. On this particular day; the wind was from the west and quite gusty between 35 to 40 knots. I wanted to ensure the crosswind component was within my limitations as a First Officer. At the time; I noticed a discrepancy between the METAR wind direction and that of the ATIS. METARs provide wind direction in reference to true north whereas ATIS and D-ATIS provide in reference to magnetic north. At SFO; the magnetic variation is 14E; meaning we would subject that amount the direction in reference to true north to get the wind direction in magnetic north. For simplicity; I will round to 20 degrees. At the time; the wind on the METAR was 280 degrees but that on the ATIS was 300 degrees. Both reports had the same reported time and date and the rest of the information including peak wind was exactly the same on both reports. There seems to be a large discrepancy between the two since if the METAR says the wind is 280; then in magnetic that is 260 and not the 300 that was advertised by the ATIS. This 40 degree difference is quite large. I was curious and began to observe the ATIS and METARs over the next couple days and found that SFO is consistently reporting; on the ATIS; a value that is 20 degrees greater than the METAR. Possibly explanations for this could be that the wind information is coming from different sources; but it seems quite peculiar that the wind direction on the ATIS is consistently 20 degrees greater than the METAR.  Any pilot would use the METAR; subtract 10 or 20 degrees; and get a wind direction of 270 or 280 degrees magnetic. The ATIS is reporting it as 310 degrees. This discrepancy can be large enough to cause confusion with crosswind landing limitations for the aircraft and pilot. I have noticed this issue prior to this flight; but did not think much of it until I noticed it consistently wrong over the past few days. If you view the METAR and ATIS for OAK and SJC; the ATIS for both reports a wind direction that is 10 degrees less than that of the METAR. This is as expected. SFO; however; reports 20 degrees greater. I addressed SFO Tower about this directly; to which they responded that they do not control this data as it comes from the 'weather people downstairs.' I am just curious if this is intentional or if this is; in fact; an error. Perhaps SFO Tower quality assurance can take a look?

column121: I was providing instruction to my instrument student.  He was in the left seat; flying the plane on autopilot; having been cleared by me (simulating ATC) to proceed via direct to the ZZZ VORTAC at 9;500 MSL; there to commence the RNAV XX approach; expecting a circle-to-land.  I obtained approval from the ZZZ tower for this practice approach; with the usual caveats about maintaining VFR; no traffic separation provided; etc.  That approval was granted while we were still about 10 miles west of the VORTAC; inbound to it at 9;500 MSL and perhaps 130 mph indicated. The top of ZZZ Class D is XX00 MSL; and we had no need to enter the Class D until we were final approach fix inbound.Soon after getting approval from the tower for the practice approach; the tower informed us that there was traffic at about our 10 o'clock; southeast bound.  I saw it immediately both visually and on our GPS nav screen.  It appeared to be a white high-wing LSA (Light Sport Aircraft); either a Remos or a Flight Design.  I can't recall if the tower was talking to that plane; but I'd guess not; as the traffic advisory was issued only to our own tail number; as I recall.I watched the LSA carefully as my student (via our A/P (Autopilot); in NAV mode) took us towards the VORTAC.  We seemed to be converging slowly; with only a 20 or 30 degree difference in our headings; and exactly the same altitude.  The LSA was rock-steady in maintaining its heading and altitude; and seemed to be on A/P; also heading for the local VORTAC.We were slowly closing on the LSA; holding a constant bearing about 30 or 40 degrees behind its right wing.  As the distance between us decreased to about a mile; I instructed my student to make a serious power reduction; which he would have done anyway over the VORTAC.  I thought that this would change the equation enough that we would fall behind the LSA.  After half a minute (or less); I realized that we were not slowing enough to make an appreciable difference in our closure; so I told my student to put his heading bug about 45 degrees off to the left of our heading; and punch the HEADING button on the A/P; which he did.  Our 185 then made a nice standard-rate turn to the left; and we passed directly behind the LSA; exactly at its altitude and about 500 feet away.  The LSA never wavered - as if he never saw us.After about a minute on our new heading; I 'cleared' my student from present position direct to the VORTAC to commence the approach.  We heard nothing from the LSA; nor did we see it again.  The practice approach and landing were without incident.As I recall; we were always behind the wing of the LSA; so we were the overtaking aircraft.  I fault myself for waiting too long before starting the turn to break the slow-motion convergence with the other airplane.  There was no chance that we were going to collide with it - I never stopped watching it; and I am an experienced formation pilot; good at judging closure rates and angles; etc. But I did not allow for the possibility that the LSA might make a sudden sharp turn towards us; or that its pilot might look out to his right rear and be unpleasantly surprised to see us there. If such a situation were to arise again; I would make an earlier turn or altitude change to get a good resolution; and try to keep a mile away from the converging traffic.  It makes more sense; doesn't cost any more; and sets a better example for my student pilot.

column121: On a day; VFR approach to RNO just to the north of waypoint URATE as depicted on the RNAV (RNP) Y to 16L; EGPWS alerted 'Caution; obstacle.'  The FO as pilot flying altered his flight path; yet we then received 'Obstacle; pull-up!' which the FO did.  Both the hill and obstacle at 5;101 feet MSL were in sight the entire time.  We then continued for a normal uneventful landing.  Enroute; we had discussed extensively the challenges of RNO; including terrain; single runway; engine failure considerations; and higher than typical descent rates and true airspeeds; and were comfortable with our position and closure rate with the hill and tower.Cause - EGWPS will alert for terrain or obstacles for either proximity or closure rate sooner than I expected.  By being carefully studied on the terrain and obstacles in the vicinity of RNO prior to arrival; we were well aware of the tower and hill located at the location of the EGPWS alert.Suggestions - Give a wider avoidance to high terrain or obstacles both horizontally; vertically; and with respect to closure rate.
column123: Cleared visual approach 16L RNO. Turned to intercept extended final near FAP WORTH. Had briefed and set up for RNAV (RNP) Y 16L and using it as backup to visual. Dialed in 6;400 and began descent to FAP altitude turning base to final. EGPWS alerted 'Caution; Obstacle'. As PF I verified obstacle in site and continued turn to final away from it. Soon after alert 'Obstacle; Pull up' occurred. I disconnected the AP and initiated a climbing turn away from obstacle that we had kept in site the entire time. Alert ceased very quickly and we continued an uneventful and stable approach and landing. Approach briefing had included a good discussion on RNO hazards including single runway operations; EO considerations; mountainous terrain; high descent rates and TAS. We knew where the obstacle/ hill was on the approach and felt comfortable with our position relative to it on the visual approach.Cause - The preceding aircraft was denied the instrument approach. Visuals in mountainous terrain create unique challenges. Being cleared to follow proceeding aircraft and maintain spacing may have also caused a more square pattern than desired which brought us closer to the obstacle.Suggestions - Maintain the practice of following IAP ground track even on a visual approach if not intimately familiar with the terrain. Also; be cognizant of how EGPWS tracks descent and closure rate. The warnings certainly came quicker than we expected. I would give high terrain an even wider berth.

Immediately after reporting this transition; and well prior to entering the Delta Airspace of ZZZ1; I switched my COM2 radio to ZZZ1 and got the latest automated weather report. I do not recall what the letter designation for the report was at the time; but the weather was clear with good visibility of 10+ miles; winds relatively calm; and a clear sky. I then radioed the tower at ZZZ1 on their frequency and identified myself as a student pilot solo flight along with my relative position west of the airport and requested a full-stop landing while approximately 15nm away.The Tower answered saying they were having difficulty hearing my transmission and to restate my position. I spoke more loudly and clearly; identifying my position as west at about 14.6 miles. They advised me to re-contact them when less than a mile from the runway.  I began a descent appropriate to arrive at pattern altitude prior to radio contact. When I got within a mile I radioed the tower and the tower advised me to turn for my base and that I was cleared to land. I executed turns to base and final without issue and extended full flaps incrementally. Upon entering final approach with full-flaps I was just high of the glideslope as indicated by the PAPI system. I entered my flair and 'ballooned' slightly. When I came back down from ballooning; I came down hard and in the process; experienced prop strike; front gear collapse; and damage to my right wing before coming to a stop on the grass to the left of the runway with the help of the grass to arrest my momentum. The plane came to rest in a nose-down fashion at an approximate 45 degree angle to the edge of the runway and in the direction of the landing. After announcing over the radio that they have a crash on the runway; the tower radioed me to ask my condition and I replied that I was fine. I then noticed fuel leaking from my right wing and elected to shut down electrical items as a precaution. When the airport firetruck arrived; the operator sprayed foam on the area leaking as a precaution for the fuel leak. After several minutes; the responding airport staff strapped the nose wheel to the fuselage and were able to pull the plane to a storage hangar with a tractor by keeping the plane on the main landing gear and tugging the plane via the tail tie-down.

column121: I completed a run-up at departure end penalty box and observed an airport vehicle depart the same place. As I was preparing to taxi; a jet called my aircraft identifying by location to request my intentions. I stated 'run up complete but he can start a back taxi.'  I started the taxi to the active runway. He declined in favor of my departure. I called 'taxi and departure Runway X; VFR to the east.' I rolled on to the runway displaced threshold while checking for traffic on final. I observed the jet had not moved but he called and requested if anyone else was inbound to land; to no response. I checked the plane was secured; and after rolling some of the displaced threshold; checked instruments and passengers; and applied full power. After reaching rotation speed; I observed the airport vehicle cross the runway in front of me. It appeared he was playing chicken. I considered rejecting the takeoff but could not be certain the power changes and braking would help avoid the collision. Thankfully the vehicle cleared the runway and I was off the ground moments later.  I think safety can be improved by having ground vehicles at uncontrolled airports stating their intentions. A simple call of 'crossing the active runway' would have improved safety as I could check and delay my takeoff. I called on CTAF during departure that the ground vehicles crossing was 'not good' and another voice agreed. I met the driver later and he was the voice that replied. As pilot in command; I will improve by maintaining situational awareness of aircraft and NORDO ground vehicles. It was a busy time with other traffic and that is a good reminder to double check your aircraft and intended path.

This high and tight turn is very hard to capture a stabilized approach. I would recommend that SoCal gives additional downwind distance prior to turning base leg if the requirement is to stay above 2;500 feet MSL when turning near LEMON or HUKEM."
