column121: Once on final for [Runway] XXR; we got a TCAS RA event from what appeared to me an (other carrier) aircraft that overshot the final for XXL. We did not have the transponder in TA mode because we were never given a Traffic Advisory from ATC; and did not have the aircraft in sight as instructed by our guidance. The RA instructed us to Adjust Vertical Speed. It commanded approximately 1500 FPM descent. We were at flaps 10 and 1;500 feet AGL. As we descended per the RA we continued to configure the aircraft. We were below 1;000 feet by the time we got to flaps 30. The aural glideslope warning sounded. We knew we needed to go-around but couldn't because of the aircraft above us. When I looked at the ND (Navigation Display); I saw the red square showing the intruding aircraft right above us at +5. It was at 800 feet when we got the clear of conflict aural message and elected to go around.The (other carrier) aircraft; in my opinion; went through their intended final for XXL. A contributing factor was the lack of notification by ATC.
column123: While descending through approximately 2;000 feet AGL on the visual approach and on the ILS glideslope to Runway XXR in ZZZ; we received a TCAS RA Descend. The conflicting traffic was slightly above and behind us on Runway XXL. We believe the Descend RA extinguished at approximately 800 feet AGL (although a review of the FRM (Fault Reporting Manual) afterwards says it should be inhibited 'below approximately 1;100 feet radio altitude'). After following the Descend command and by the time the command extinguished; we were not in a stabilized position to land. We executed a go-around. We were not informed about the traffic by Approach and therefore did not meet the requirements to switch to TA Only for Runways XXL and XXR in ZZZ. We were vectored around for a normal landing on XXR. As we switched to ZZZ Tower; another aircraft in front of us also experienced a go-around for the same situation.Presumably the conflicting traffic met the requirements to switch to TA Only because they keyed up on the MIC and said they didn't overshoot and we should/can switch to TA Only. However; we didn't meet the requirements to switch to TA Only.  ATC never asked us to report them in sight; presumably because they were behind us! So; what happens to our RA resolution when the conflicting traffic is in TA Only and transgressing on us? Presumably they can't be offered an RA resolution (which would likely have been for them to climb). If they had climbed the Descend RA 'pressure' on us could have been alleviated sooner. Instead we were forced lower and lower. And all of this was close to the ground. Even though the RA inhibits reaching 'approximately 1;100 feet radio altitude' the conflict with the other aircraft still exists; and we were pretty sure we were below 1;000 feet before the RA extinguished (as evidence by being already slightly into the 1;000 feet white tape). When the RA finally went away we executed a go-around from about 600-800 feet; but the traffic conflict doesn't magically go away.This event occurred right as we were configuring to land; so we never had a chance to fully configure prior to 1;000 feet AGL; as maneuvering for the RA was taking up our attention. The time in the RA resolution mode was more than momentary. It seemed long and sustained enough that it felt like it would just RA us into the ground. As I now knew a go-around was imminent there was a slight moment in my mind I thought about going around right then and there; but the RA continued. I can see where a Crew may be spring loaded to go-around even though the Descend RA is still present.The FO recognized that the traffic showed '+500' on the MFD display. The FAA defines a Near Midair as 'an incident associated with the operation of an aircraft in which a possibility of collision occurs as a result of proximity of less than 500 feet to another aircraft...' We were likely very close to meeting that definition.There was a slight tail wind at altitude for aircraft joining final from left base to runway XXL allowing for increased potential for overshoot. Maybe a very slight overshoot by the other aircraft and the tight sequencing by ATC created this incident; but we can't be sure. It's possible ATC was sequencing aircraft too tight.

column121: Climbing out of ZZZ in moderate rain and passing through about 18;000 feet; with the FO flying; we got an airspeed disagree and altitude disagree on our displays; a Master Caution for Engine; autopilot (B) kicked off; and VNAV disappeared all within a few seconds. We compared instruments and determined that the Standby and Captain's displays matched with airspeed at 280 and close to the same altitude still climbing. We transferred aircraft control and ran the airspeed unreliable checklist/altitude unreliable checklist. After reporting our difficulties with ATC; we leveled at FL250; to finish checklist and run checklist for EEC alternate mode. At that time the FO instruments showed an airspeed of 130 KIAS and 25;500 feet. It took a while to get through checklist; but we were able to get autopilot-A back.  We talked about the bad weather at ZZZ and decided to continue to ZZZ1 due to VMC conditions there. On descent passing through 15;500 feet; FO instrumentation appeared to recover. Approach and landing were uneventful.  Priority handling was requested to ensure ATC was aware of our indication problems.

column121: The hydraulic reservoirs have a big red caution label. It reads; 'CAUTION DO NOT OVERFILL HYDRAULIC RESERVOIR. FILL TO APPROX. 2/3 BETWEEN REFILL(RFL) AND FULL (COCKPIT PANEL SHOULD READ 92% FULL) REFER AMM 12-12-00.'Below the caution label there is an ATTENTION label. It reads; 'ATTENTION Do Not Overfill the RESERVOIR. Overfill can Cause Hydraulic Fumes To Enter the Flight Deck and Passenger Cabin'Some years ago I had an air return when the cabin filled with acrid mist causing eyes to sting and some to choke. The flight attendants thought we were on fire! The Captain and I used goggles and oxygen to safely return. This event was caused by both hydraulic reservoirs being filled to capacity. I believe the cockpit panel read 107%. If I'm recall correctly this is the most that will register.Although I have not since had visible or detectable odor; I believe crew and passengers are breathing atomized hydraulic fluid whenever the reservoirs are over serviced. The leg noted in this report from ZZZ-ZZZ1; started with both reservoirs reading 100%. At shutdown they were at 92%. Where did the difference go in a three hour operation? The day before; my aircraft had 107% in system A and 92% in system B. I alerted Maintenance of the over service. The Technician proceeded to move System A to B. The result was both reservoirs at 100%.I have dealt with this issue individually before. I find a small portion of our technicians understand the significance. Sometimes I meet with great resistance.[Recommend] a notice for Aircrew to remind them of the placards and similar or more specific training for all our Maintenance Technicians and Maintenance Control.
column125: B737-800 Captain reported loss of Hydraulic Reservoir quantity when reservoir is overfilled. Reporter theorized that hydraulic fluid is being atomized resulting in harmful cabin fumes and physiological symptoms.

column121: When cruising at 8;000 feet direct to ZZZ1.The flight attendants called us stating they smelled a burning smell coming from somewhere in the cabin. The Captain also stated he smelled something and we immediately ran the immediate action items and the QRC for smoke/fire/fumes. Donning our oxygen masks; the Captain delegated the flight controls and radios to me and told me to notify ATC and he would run the checklists and talk to the flight attendants. I notified Approach giving them souls and fuel on board. We were so close to the airport they gave us a vector for the approach into Runway XX. At that time the flight attendants told the Captain that the smell had gone away but for per cautionary reasons we elected to keep the masks on and the fire trucks on standby as we continued the approach. After landing we taxied to the ramp and stopped short of the gate for the emergency vehicles to inspect the exterior of the aircraft. After confirmation that nothing was smoking outside we canceled the emergency and taxied to the gate. Emergency personal came on board inspecting the inside of the aircraft deeming it safe we deplaned. The flight attendants did an excellent job in paying attention to everything going on in the aircraft. They informed us in the flight deck immediately allowing us to take action and get on the ground quickly and safely. Maintenance found that an electrical outlet had short circuited and started to smoke in row XX. The aircraft's systems worked and the circuit breaker tripped and the fire was never fully ignited. As soon as the flight attendants notified us in the cockpit the Captain called for the immediate action items for smoke fire flames. This reaction was precautionary but notifying ATC and donning oxygen masks was the safest solution when we did not know if something was on fire or even where it was. Great communication is key in emergency situation. Our crew worked together perfectly and shows how our training has paid off. The only suggestion I have through this experience is to regularly clean the oxygen masks because you never know when you will need them.

column121: I was the PF (Pilot Flying) when we initiated takeoff from Runway XXR at ZZZ.  Flex power was set and prior to the 80 knot call; we had an ECAM Caution for #1 Engine Bleed Vane Failure - or words to that effect.  CA (Captain) and I recognized the ECAM and CA called 'Reject; my aircraft;' I responded 'Your aircraft'; a positive transfer of control was made; the auto brakes engaged; and the aircraft was promptly stopped per SOP.  Of note is the fact that this ECAM Caution was not inhibited; but the auto brakes did activate; so our speed must have been below 80 knots at the time of the ECAM caution; but greater than 72 knots given auto brake activation.  During the stop; CA had difficulty advancing the thrust levers out of the reverse range and briefly pushed them significantly into the forward thrust range of travel.  As the engines accelerated in forward thrust; I advised CA of the position of the thrust levers and he promptly retarded them to the forward idle position.  We made a quick assessment of the situation and CA proceeded to exit the runway at the first available forward high-speed taxiway; with me advising ATC of the situation.  While doing this; CA advised the FAs to remain seated via the PA.  As we exited the runway; CA noticed the ECAM Caution directed us to place the #1 Engine Master in the 'Off' position.  CA instructed me to do this and I promptly complied.  CA then brought the aircraft to a complete stop and assessed brake temperatures and other factors.  Correctly judging that we were in a stable and safe situation; CA checked with the FAs to ensure they and the passengers were safe and to advise them that we had experienced a low speed rejected takeoff and he would contact them to advise of the next steps.  CA and I then consulted the QRH to see if there was an ECAM Exception or Follow-Up to our ECAM Caution.  There was no further guidance in the QRH; so CA advised me to inform ATC we would be contacting Maintenance and then getting back with ATC to advise them of our intentions.  CA contacted Maintenance; who said they definitely wanted us to return to the gate; I advised Operations and Ramp Tower of our need to return to the gate and they assigned us gate X.  I subsequently coordinated with Ground our return to the gate while CA advised the FA's and passengers of the situation.  We returned to the gate without mishap; deplaned; and continued the flight on a different airplane.I have no idea why the ECAM Caution appeared.  Other than a brief excursion into forward thrust due to the mechanical difficulty of moving the thrust levers out of the reverse thrust range; this rejected takeoff followed SOP and was unremarkable.Increased training and guidance for low speed rejected takeoffs would be helpful.  Perhaps a section in the QRH with emphasis that it is the sole source for immediate guidance following a low-speed reject.

column121: We checked in at ZZZ for flight to ZZZ1.  Walking onto aircraft to preflight and get ready the FA's (flight attendants) commented that they smelled a strong fume odor in the rear of the cabin.  The prior crew had left the APU running and that was providing the air to the cabin.  We were not immediately sure what it was but the longer we were inside the aircraft the more it seemed to smell all over the aircraft.  One flight attendant soon commented that she had been in a fume smell diversion and that she felt it now smelled exactly like what she had experienced before. As I was contacting Dispatch and Maintenance Control; the ZZZ station without our knowledge or consent had sprayed the entire aft cabin with some kind of disinfectant spray to cover up the smell and had begun to board passengers.  When I was made aware of this I radioed them to stop spraying the aircraft; halt the boarding; and remove the passengers that were onboard.  Maintenance Control had called a contract Maintenance Tech to investigate the odor.  Meanwhile; we had shutdown the APU and connected the ground air. When the Maintenance Tech arrived; he had a bunch of paperwork for items to check; and mentioned that he was going to inspect the APU.  He did not seem to know what to check or how to check it.  Ultimately he handed me the pile of papers and ask us to run the engines.  In an effort to help we did so.  We could not specifically determine the source of the smell; but it seemed stronger with the APU providing air.  We were unable to isolate the source and could not fly the aircraft or do a maintenance ferry flight. Afterward; Maintenance Control then informed us that the residual contamination in the air ducts would have to be cleaned and tested with special equipment; and that they would have to send a road crew down from ZZZ to perform those functions.  So Maintenance Control knew from the start that this type of contamination issue required special procedures and equipment to deal with and withheld that critical information unnecessarily exposing us to who knows what kind of long term health hazards instead of just informing of this up front. After we officially could not use the airplane; it was around XA:30pm.  We were assigned to fly another aircraft for the flight now departing at XG:15pm.  We then spent the next few hours trying to get a day room so we could get a meal and away from the airport before the later flight.  Each time were verbally told we had a room from Crew Tracking; Hotel Desk; etc.; we called the hotel and were told there were no such rooms available for us.  After wasting a considerable amount of time on this effort we were finally given rooms and arrived at the hotel just after XF:00pm. I walked down the highway from the hotel to find something to eat after having nothing for several hours.  Finally sitting down to eat a sandwich; I realized that I had a dull headache from trying to determine if the fumes were no longer present in the aircraft when isolating certain ducts for Maintenance Control.  It dawned on me that I was fatigued and I reported this to Crew Tracking. The cause was Maintenance; fume smells; lack of timely day room. [Captain suggested] better communications with Maintenance and Dispatch.

column121: We departed the gate and were instructed to taxi to Runway 28 via 'D; A; A1 to the Runway 28 holding point.'  Upon glancing at the taxi diagram; referencing the our Airway Manual (AM); to verify our taxi route; I quickly realized a discrepancy between the instructions we were given and the chart -- there was no A1 taxiway that reached the runway.  Before we could inquire about these instructions; the controller gave us a 'follow the aircraft ahead' instruction.  Digging a little farther; I began to notice that this discrepancy was worth a report submittal because the 10-9 Chart for MMGL differs from the AM; and neither the 10-9 Chart nor the AM agrees with the airport in reality.  Upon your own review; you will discover that there is a difference in taxiway names between the 10-9 chart; and the AM; specifically as it relates to the A taxiway.  Additionally; in reality there is an A1 taxiway; properly signed; that parallels the A taxiway toward the approach end of Runway 28.  There is also an additional taxiway; A2; that connects the A taxiway to the runway; prior to the approach end of Runway 28 which is not charted on either chart. The airport NOTAMS reference a change in taxiway naming convention; however; the NOTAMS do not make sense with either the current charts; or with reality; and in fact lead to more confusion.  I believe that by paying attention to aircraft position with reference to the published chart; I was able to help the Captain remain in the green; and hopefully trap this threat from snaring other crews.  In deliberating whether to submit this report; I concluded that since this threat affects the broader aviation community; the report would be more appropriate for resolving this discrepancy to the benefit of everyone.

column121: Some really troubling events unfolded on our flight; ZZZ-ZZZ1. After ground power failed and the high pressure air carts were removed to be repositioned for a gate start (APU is on MEL) the cabin environment was no longer safe or acceptable to have nearly XXX passengers onboard. I had the FO call ZZZ Operations on the radio to have them send an agent to open the cabin door and deplane the passengers. The jetway was still attached to the aircraft but nothing was being done to get the passengers safely off the jet.  I turned on my cell phone and called the ZZZ ramp manager's phone number and requested immediate assistance. After further needless delays several flight attendants came to the flight deck to tell me they could see the agents standing in the jetway but there were doing nothing; my request to begin the deplaning was being ignored. I next called the flight office and requested a Chief Pilot and a manager to come ASAP to gate XX to assist. I have attached several photos to include the air synoptic of the excessively hot cabin temperatures after the air start units were removed and the jetway power failed! It gets much worse; and I will provide the whole narrative as it unfolded.When I arrived at the gate 50 minutes or so before departure I was informed that only the first officer had arrived and was onboard. The gate agent had just received a call that the cabin was very warm and ZZZ Operations wanted us to start the APU (why did Operations not know the APU was placarded). I assured them that the FO was most likely already addressing the matter. When I arrived at the flight deck I saw the FO had the air synoptic pulled up and I noted the aft cabin temp showed 102F. The FO pointed out that the APU was placarded inoperative. Air start units were being connected at this time to power the air conditioning pacs. During the FO's walk around he had taken a picture of the way the ground crew had connected the PCA hoses. How long had the PCA even been hooked up is unknown; the jet arrived at this gate at XA:00 in the morning; but regardless; it was all to evident the PCA air was not making it into the cabin do to the improper connection. The FO joined me and we returned to the terminal; I spoke with the gate agents and told them it would be a fairly long delay waiting for the cabin to cool.  I asked them to keep the flight attendants from boarding the hot jet when they began arriving at the gate area.  After the ground crew had finished hooking up the air start carts; the FO and I went to the flight deck to check that the air conditioning was functioning. Nearing the schedule departure time we were finally getting the cabin temp to where boarding could begin. After boarding was complete and the cabin door closed the ground crew checked in and cleared us to start the right engine. I informed them that on this aircraft; per the manual; the left engine is started first with ground air start. The ground crew had positioned the air start units incorrectly to start the left engine. I told them to let me know when the left engine was clear for starting. The crew then shutdown the air start; even though they did not have a tug hooked up to reposition the equipment!  We no longer had ANY cooling airflow into the cabin. A couple of minutes later the electrical power from the jetway fails. The ground crew begins fiddling around but can't get the power restored and there are no portable power units near this gate. I later learned; after speaking with a facilities manager; that this jetway power supply had a service tag hanging from the power panel and should not have been used do to erratic 400HZ service. So with only battery power on the airplane; recirculating fans have shutdown; there is no cool air being provided; you can see [on] our air synoptic the cabin temps quickly were above 95-98 F.  In the interest of safety for the passengers it should be obvious why I requested an immediate de-planning of the passengers.  Unsatisfactory that ZZZ station was delaying opening the cabin door and safely removing the passengers.  I even resorted to threatening a ground evacuation after a repeated request for help to draw their attention to the seriousness of the issue at hand.  Passengers are wearing face coverings in a cabin approaching 100 F with all the cabin and cargo doors closed.  Still the gate agents would not open up the cabin to begin deplaning the passengers until some passenger service manager gave the go ahead; why?After the passengers had begun deplaning the ground crew finally located a portable electric unit and began reconnecting the air start carts so we could operate the air conditioning. The ramp supervisor was now on the flight deck with us with along with some other manager in tow. They were questioning why I had their ground crew shutoff the air start units and have them moved. I said that is not what I told them to do. I only stated that per this aircraft manual the left engine is to be started and to let me know when the area was clear to start the left engine. While discussing the horrible failings and going over the situation I looked up and noticed the ground power had only been restored to the PRIMARY GRD source. This aircraft requires two ground power feeds or one from the ground and the APU; our APU was still placarded INOP! There is a risk of overheating the eclectic connection the way they had provide power (see PIC). I pointed this out to the manager. I also asked him that when they provide the correct ground power and air conditioning and we can get around to re-boarding the passengers are we going to have a ground crew available so we can start and pushback as quickly as possible. The manager assured me they would have a crew there for us. He lied!  After we had closed the cabin door with our original passengers minus 20 or so that chose to not fly with us; I called the ground crew to get the go ahead to start. No ground crew at our gate!  The FO called ramp to ask where our ground crew had gone? Twenty seven minutes later a crew arrives at the nose but does not check in on the headset. I have the nose camera on so I can see them as they fiddle around with connecting a tow bar and what not. I had flashed the nose taxi light to get their attention and made many interphone GND crew alert chimes; all of these signals were ignored. When they did finally get on the headset I expressed some frustration that we could have been starting the engine while they prepared for the pushback. They were quick with the excuse that they had just arrived and were unaware of the situation. When we were cleared to start the left engine the air start units were not running in the high flow position and the duct pressure has only 16 PSI; 25 PSI is minimum to start. I asked them to check the start units were set correctly. This ground crew had no idea how to operate their equipment. The AutoStart of the left engine failed on the first start attempt. The second start attempt reached idle and stable barely.Almost three hours late and somewhere about half way to ZZZ1 from ZZZ I noticed that ZZZ1 had us arriving to gate XX; even though the APU was on placard. ZZZ1 gate XX is a tow in only gate with engines shutdown per the ZZZ1 airport pages. FO wants to send a message to dispatch right away. I say lets just give them a little more time to do the right thing and see if they get it sorted out. Sure enough about an hour from arrival we send for the changeover info for ZZZ1 and they still have us arriving gate XX! I sent dispatch a message to ask if ZZZ1 is really planning for us to use gate XX with an INOP APU? Dispatch calls ZZZ1 Operations and they finally get around to changing our arrival gate.Ground crew not following procedures and failing to correct errors.  Station management not supporting a safety culture to support flight operations in the interest of passenger safety.Attention to details in preparation for supporting an operation with a aircraft that has an MEL placard affecting normal ops; in this case the APU inoperative.  When the PIC Captain of the flight; after all the doors closed and ready for flight; calls and radios the station that the passengers need to be immediately de-planned due to safety concerns; then this decision needs to be supported and executed without delay!

column121: On STAR into ZZZ I was high and was not going to make a mandatory crossing altitude. Prior to it I asked the controller if I could be relieved of that restriction and he said yes.I had not been into ZZZ since COVID and as such didn't realize that ZZZ; being a large International hub; was still operating way under capacity compared to domestic airports; meaning vectors to final were fast. column121: After intercepting the glideslope it was noted by both pilots the aircraft was not slowing down normally.  Despite lowering the gear and deploying speedbrakes we were having a difficult time getting 10 knots below the next flap speed to continue to configure a variable tailwind was noted between 5 & 10 knots which helped explain what we were seeing.  Continuing to investigate however both pilots thereafter realized we were abnormally low and the PF disconnected the AP and leveled off.  Tower called with a low altitude alert shortly after that and we acknowledged it; configured normally and were stable by 500 feet AGL.  Landing and roll out was normal.  There were multiple approach NOTAMs that day and we miscalculated the effective times on the one stating the ILS XXL was unusable.  We were an hour off and were arriving inside the last 30 minutes of the effective time.  It turns out NAVAIDs maintenance was manipulating the glide slope signal at the time; causing the glide slope to appear lower.The ILS to XXL was OTS and NAVAIDs maintenance was transmitting a lower than normal glidepath. It would have been helpful if ILS status had been repeated on the ATIS; as it normally is; but it was not.  During the low altitude call from tower they were even quick to add to the call that it 'was in the NOTAMs'.  Further investigating with my prior position with FAA Flight Inspection it is still in their guidance that NAVAIDs maintenance is not supposed to transmit a localizer signal if they are going to manipulate the glide slope signal to avoid this hazardous; misleading; information.  The localizer and glide slope both were transmitting; with a proper ID; at the time of the incident; we even crossed ZZZZZ at the appropriate altitude of 3;000 and showed on path.  It was after that when the aircraft would no longer slow; as it was chasing a depressed glide path.  In the end we missed the NOTAM but then multiple holes of the swiss cheese lined up; thankfully it was day VFR and we saw the solution with our own eyes in time.  The other layers of protection normally there (ATIS; maintenance procedures) would have helped overcome our oversight.

The flight and landing went without incident; until ZZZ1 reported the damage to the flight crew after arriving at the gate.It is impractical for the flight crew to perform an external inspection after all external service equipment is removed and the cabin door is closed.  The last opportunity to look over the aircraft is the push back crew.  Perhaps wing walkers could walk all the way back to the tail on their respective sides and examine the airplane for anything unusual.  This information could then be forwarded to the tug driver; who would in turn forward to the flight crew.  Something like 'external equipment clear; inspection complete; no damage noted.'

During the final of the first touch and go of his session of 3L heard the Aircraft Y on the frequency asking landing information. I gave him 3L in use with right hand circuit and 2 aircraft doing touch and go training. When coming in right downwind again Runway 3L we got a traffic warning on the GPS screen. PIC didn't see it but I spotted the traffic head on almost same altitude and called the conflicting traffic to warn him being opposite in the downwind head on. He replied to join right downwind 3L. As PIC still couldn't see the traffic and a collision was going to happen I took the yoke and turned the aircraft to the right with a slight down input. Conflicting aircraft never saw us neither did any avoidance maneuver.PIC had back the controls and we did a second touch and go. Meanwhile the Aircraft Y joined the right downwind 3L and landed when we where again end of downwind. Turning on final for full stop ( final call was done) the Aircraft Y reported entering back track 3L. Being surprised as we where already on final I saw he could however vacate heaving 3 taxiways ahead. Nevertheless the pilot of the Aircraft Y called us that we better did a go-around as they would not be able to vacate in time. I replied that his behavior was very unprofessional; first positioning his aircraft opposite ours in a downwind leg and then entering and blocking the active runway with an aircraft on final. After we landed and shut down the aircraft I expected at least that the PIC of the Aircraft Y would come to apologize; but no one came to us. When checking the airport register I also noticed he never registered his inbound nor outbound flight.  When checking FlightRadar24 you can clearly see that the Aircraft Y flew opposite the downwind descending through 1;700 feet of the 03L to do a 180 turn to join his opposite track. The Aircraft X is at the same moment at 1;500 feet flying correct downwind position for the 3L. Closing speed was around 250 kts.

column121: While on the ENDEE 6 Arrival to MDW we encountered a near midair collision and the following is a narrative of that event. Time stamps are from 'Flightaware' app and may not be 100% accurate. I added these to recreate the event to the best of my knowledge.I was the Pilot Flying on this leg. At about XX:26Z ATC began to vector us off the arrival for spacing. During these vectors we were cleared to descend to lower altitudes. I had even made the comment jokingly that we were being 'over-controlled' by ATC after several heading; altitude and speed changes. At approximately XX:45Z we were cleared to descend to 5000 feet. Our flight path at the time was approximately over top of Morris Muni airport (C09) about 6.6 miles southwest of STKNY on the arrival. Crossing altitude at STKNY is published is 6000 feet. We were then cleared direct to ALQUE for the ILS 4R at MDW. While still level at 5000 feet at approximately XX:47Z we had a TCAS TA (solid amber) showing an aircraft in front of us and +100 feet above our altitude. I do not remember the scale set at the time on my navigation display but it was very 'close'. This was this first time we had seen a Traffic Advisory of any kind on the display (no open white diamond) and had not been advised of traffic from ATC. One second later ATC told us we had 'glider traffic' ahead and to 'deviate as necessary' to avoid the traffic. I immediately began a right hand descending turn. About two seconds later we received a Resolution Advisory RA to descend and the First Officer told ATC we were responding to an RA. At about 4500 feet; I saw the glider slightly higher and to our left. Once clear of the conflict; ATC cleared us to descend to 4000 feet and stated he was not in contact with the glider and asked if it was clear of clouds. ATC warned aircraft behind us on the arrival about the glider and it's altitude. We estimated the distance from the glider was 150-200 feet as it passed to our left. The event happened in the proximity of Channahon; IL Glider Club (IL59) south of STKNY on the arrival.The takeaway from this event:The TCAS did not operate as we would expect in time regarding a TA caution providing 40 seconds warning and an RA providing 25 seconds warning. It's hard to tell if the glider had just turned on its transponder or if the slow speed of the glider had an impact on our TCAS. The glider was in Class E airspace and outside the 30 mile equipment requirement (transponder) from the ORD Class B. What rules apply to gliders here; to me; is unknown to be honest.ATC had vectored us off the arrival and was assigning altitudes lower than published crossing restrictions by 1000 feet (5000 feet abeam STKNY).Vectors took us almost directly over a glider airpark with no warning about that on any chart we would ever use readily available. Some warning symbology or quick access information would assist considering the low altitudes we fly over these areas.In hindsight; I would have made clear to ATC we experienced a near mid air collision in that language as described in our FOM.

column121: Climbing through FL180 I engaged CMD (Command) A autopilot. When I pressed the button the airplane instantly had a loud banging noise; jolted very aggressively; nosed down; and started oscillating.  It was almost to the point I thought I was going to accomplish upset recovery procedures.  I was quickly able to level the airplane off and safely hand fly.  We contacted Maintenance and unanimously agreed that the airplane was safe enough to continue to hand fly the plane for the duration of the flight. Maintenance asked if we tried autopilot B. The jolt and aircraft response was significant enough that we did not want to try arming the autopilot again.  We safely hand flew the aircraft back to ZZZ1. In our debrief we discussed that for a split second we initially thought it was so severe that we were losing aircraft control. We were greatly startled and hands were shaking for a good 5-10 minutes after the event happened. We were scheduled to fly to ZZZ2 after the flight; arriving the next morning. We hit an emotional lull after the flight and we both determined we were not emotionally; nor physically; fit to continue our pairing.  We called in fatigued and were given hotel rooms immediately.
column123: We were climbing through 180 out of ZZZZ.  The CA (Captain) went to engage CMD (Command) A and the aircraft made a loud bang and had a violent nose down control input. It was so severe that we thought the flight attendant could have been injured.  It was so bad for a moment I thought that we might have hit something mid-air.  I was completely shaken up and so was the Captain. We refused to attempt to re-engage any autopilot. We were just about to divert but we had Dispatch run the numbers for us at non-RVSM altitude. We calculated 6.0 remf on this 700 so we opted to hand fly it. We worked in 30 minute shifts. The arrival was busy with many changes enroute. We were both shaking at the initial event and were completely calmed down enroute but we both started to feel drained after the adrenaline started to wear off. We were both obviously not fit for our next leg which was scheduled to arrive after midnight into ZZZ1. We both got a hotel at ZZZ even though I could have commuted home that evening; I was toast at that point and just went to bed.

column121: There is a group of towers on right downwind/base to 14R and 14L that are a potential hazard when visual approaches are in use. As shown on the approach plates; at least one of these towers is 148 feet higher than the glide slope intercept altitude for these runways. Although the VFR traffic pattern for both runways is left; the PAWNEE CITY 1 and HOWRY 2 arrivals set IFR traffic up for a righthand pattern with the towers situated between them and final. Unlike the approaches; these towers are not charted on either arrival.When flying a righthand traffic pattern; such as from PAWNEE CITY 1; HOWRY 2; or on a visual missed approach; pilots are susceptible to colliding with the 2;548 feet towers while attaining the glide slope intercept altitude of 2;400 feet.1) Add a page in Jeppesen for OMA which calls attention to the towers. 2) Provide easier access to traffic pattern altitudes and directions in Jepp in the event of a visual missed approach. As of right now; this information is buried in a 4;000 plus page document. 3) Obstacles and terrain that are considered significant to approaches should also be charted on arrivals. 4) Pilots should thoroughly review significant obstacles and terrain depicted on procedures and enable ownship on Approach in Jeppesen for increased situational awareness. 5) ATC should ensure pilots see these particular towers; not just the airport; when clearing pilots for the visual from the west. Alternatively; pilots should be vectored well clear of the towers before being issued a visual.

column121: During walk around; a ground crew man informed the Captain of need to push prior to darkness as ground crews have difficulty seeing. Pushback happened after dark due to weather delays. Initially; the tug driver wanted to drop the airplane with a minimal push which would have resulted in a max pivot turn. We felt we were unable to have wingtip to wingtip and/or tail to tail clearance so we asked the tug driver to pull us out further telling him it was too tight. He complied. The right wing walker seemed confused as he walked in front of the engine and not at the right wing-tip; the closest point of potential impact. Walking in front on an engine had no value to us as an aircrew. Once we were released from the tug; taxiing was extremely difficult due to several factors. These were narrow alleyway; very poorly unlit alleyway; at least 1 heavy jet parked on low D gates; construction on the south side of the alley way; no hazard O4 lighting for the construction fence; ramp and construction vehicles parked outside the fence on the ramp; and poor surface markings. Taxiing out was extremely slow and challenging and we notified an inbound aircraft to be careful. Poor visibility due to rain and the glare from wet added or exacerbated the taxi out difficulty. Poorly lit area; poorly marked area; new operational area; construction. Our first warning came from the ground crew when they express difficulty with completing the pushback after dark. If not for the interior lights of the terminal; I feel we would have struck the aircraft parked at gate. Our second clue was the attempted drop spot which showed us the degree of difficulty these crews were operating in. Better training for wing walkers. Better lighting in this area. Better surface markings to assure wingtip clearance in this area. Hazard lights on construction fence. Removal of all equipment and vehicles on ramp parked up against the fence. Reevaluation reflective paint stripe/J line coming from this alley. Until at least some items are addressed; all night operations should be towed to the top of the alley with lighted vehicles to protect rampers and cover far distance as wing walkers. I feel this is an aircraft damage event waiting to happen; even without the low light low visibility conditions.

We attained VNAV PATH and 150 KIAS approximately 3 miles after STEFN. We verified both our altimeter settings and altitude.  We advised Tower that we could see both terrain and the airfield. Otherwise; the approach and landing were normal.  Of note there was no GPWS alert with flaps 20 and gear up. He indicated they sometimes get an altitude alert activation; but usually on vectors to visual Runway 24. He also indicated he was not as familiar with the Tower sector.   I asked him to look into it a bit more given that the only difference between what I flew and what I would have flown in IMC is I would have been 25 KIAS slower which would have resulted in a descent rate difference of just 133 FPM given a constant wind.  The wind in this case was a light headwind during the approach.Had I been in IMC and/or could not immediately determine by visual reference terrain clearance; the approach would have terminated with an immediate climb and terrain escape maneuver.Recommend the altitude alert system be de-conflicted to ensure aircraft on FMS glide path for the RNAV Z RWY 24 do not get erroneous alerts and/or note on company chart outlining requirements for speed on the approach or other requirements to successfully complete the approach in IMC.No deviations noted by Tower or aircrew. column121: Two flights ago in flight training my instructor had taught to keep fuel in mind and to switch tanks periodically during flight as well as when following the checklist. The next flight an engine failure was simulated and upon switching fuel tanks my instructor restored power to the aircraft. Both lessons were among the flight training lessons I had learned were in mind during this flight. I had rested well the night before; had eaten a good breakfast; was not on any medication; and all my paperwork was current. After taking off with full fuel tanks; the plane flew normally during VOR practice and soft field landings at ZZZ1 airport and the fuel tanks were switched about every 15 minutes. Upon returning to ZZZ; I followed the checklist and in doing so switched fuel tanks again. I then completed two landings and take offs. On the third my instructor initiated another simulated engine failure abeam the numbers on downwind. I thought of the previous lessons and decided to switch fuel tanks again after establishing the glide speed and planned to land on runway X. Once I was set up to land and on final for runway X my instructor allowed me to add power as I deemed necessary. The landing was successful and since we were doing touch and go's I set up the aircraft and added power for takeoff. After successful rotation I established the initial climb. About 50ft above the runway surface the engine lost power. My instructor took the flight controls then and landed back on runway X. We rolled off the runway threshold into the grass along the center line. The plane stopped before hitting the fence. The engine was still running at idle at that point; so my instructor radioed ZZZ Tower and they gave us clearance to taxi off the grass and onto the ramp but no further. After looking at the fuel selector switch my instructor and I determined that it was past the left fuel tank mark between it and the shutoff position. The stop that prevents pilots from going past the left fuel tank was not there.
column123: I was the instructor giving instruction on a training flight to a student in an airplane owned by a flying club.  The student is a member in good standing with the club; and is nearing completion of his Private Pilot training.  We were in the process of prepping for his Practical Test by practicing VOR navigation; short field takeoffs and landings; and soft field takeoffs and landings.  We were returning from ZZZ1 to ZZZ after practicing on a sod runway.  We had entered left traffic on runway X per ZZZ tower instructions; and were remaining in the pattern for the option.  Tower had switched us to right traffic on runway X; which is normal procedure at ZZZ.  After several touch and goes; the student applied power; initiated rotation; started the climb and the engine lost power.  I took the controls and successfully landed on the remaining runway; but was unable to stop prior to running off the end of the runway and rolling out into the grass.  Fortunately; the aircraft was able to come to a complete stop prior to the boundary fence.In the past week leading up to this flight; I had to keep reminding the student to switch fuel tanks; stressing that it is most likely going to be the cause of an engine failure if he doesn't.  I had the opportunity to reinforce that during another subsequent flight prior to this one.  He was in the habit of not utilizing the checklist - not sure why; as it is something I mention on every flight.  Today's flight; I again had to remind him when to use the descent and before landing checklists.  Both of which call to verify that fuel is on the fullest tank.  We have previously discussed having a designated time to switch tanks on numerous occasions.  For some reason; he has never accepted any of the instruction I have been giving him.  Perhaps now he will.I noticed he was very busy on final this last trip around; and it appeared at this time he was switching tanks.  I have never instructed him to switch tanks on final before.  For some reason; he continues to do things in the airplane that were not taught; or are in direct opposition to what was being taught.  Most of them are minor; but fuel is something I'm very passionate about having on board.After the landing was completed; I looked over at the fuel selector valve which is hidden from my view in the right seat.  'Right' is at the 3 o'clock position with the plastic frame to guard it from going further.  'Left' is at the 12 o'clock position with the spring loaded stopper at the 6 o'clock position so you feel a 'click' when it is in the detent.  Off is at the 9 o'clock position; requiring the stop button to be depressed before it can be selected.  It was evident the stop button had broken off at some point.  When I examined the physical position of the selector switch; it was at the 10-11 o'clock position.  Not fully 'Off'; not fully 'Left.'  An engine run performed by us after being towed back to the FBO ramp verified the engine ran fine.  That's when we discussed the broken fuel selector valve.As the instructor; I monitor my student's preflight actions; but never really perform the preflight myself to verify the students actions unless I notice they miss something.  I have no reason to doubt my student did anything wrong during the preflight.  During the debrief; we reviewed the importance of a thorough preflight and proper maintenance.  We also performed an engine run per Maintenance's request.  There was nothing noted on engine performance; but while switching the fuel tanks; it was discovered that there was no 'click' when the Left tank was selected.My student may have felt a need to hurry things along with his training since he is leaving the area at the end of this semester.  Perhaps some basic knowledge was missed; he may have been stressed with school coming to a close; or any number of things that distracted him from truly paying attention to flying.I believe with the debrief we had; my student will now pay attention to appropriate times to switch fuel tanks rather than being so focused on one thing at a time.

The controlled airspace advisory button was dimmed; but I clicked it anyway to be sure and it said 'No Airspaces found here'. I took that to mean no controlled airspace was where I was; at my AGL (0 ft). I should have checked against the LAANC system. I am sorry about that. The iFly GPS sectional also referenced service (svc) times for the surface extension; which was confusing to me; since the popup window said no controlled airspaces were found.  I should have spent more time pouring over the sectional and have recognized the meaning of the magenta dashed lines. Although I also found out today they are on reduced service hours; so not sure if this applies. But I should have been aware. It was not until today; that I happened upon the LAANC for the area. Recommendation: To avoid this; remote pilots should always check against the LAANC system for controlled air space; especially if relatively unfamiliar with an area; as I was. Remote pilots should not rely on general aviation EFBs that may or may not call out things that are significant to remote pilots. I have taken some manned pilot flying lessons. Again; I am sorry. I am definitely going to be more diligent; and take extra precautions in unfamiliar situations to watch for controlled air space. I will pore over the sectional closer; and check the LAANC system. column121: The Autopilot A was engaged. The RNAV ZZZZZ3 Arrival and the RNPZ XXL were programmed in the FMC. The  approach was not connected at ZZZZZ; as we were not cleared for the approach.  Approximately five miles prior to ZZZZZ1 [fix] we were told to expect vectors for the ILS. We selected the ILS XXL in the FMC; and upon executing the selection; we received an Autopilot Disconnect message; and an A/P Disconnect Caution light. The aircraft went into Control Wheel Pitch. I; the Pilot Flying; immediately selected Vertical Speed to keep the aircraft in a state towards the impending crossing restriction. I also reset the Altitude Alerter for X;000 feet; as we now were in Vertical Speed and needed altitude protection at ZZZZZ2 [fix].A few seconds later we passed over ZZZZZ2. The Autopilot Disconnect Caution light illuminated; and the Autopilot Lateral Mode switched to Control Wheel Steering; and the aircraft didn't turn and follow the still illuminated and displayed LNAV PATH. I immediately engaged heading mode; and turned to rejoin our intended course. Approach gave us a heading; as the minor deviation from our path was most likely noticeable.  The rest of the flight proceeded uneventfully.  We assumed we programmed the FMC incorrectly; in some way; and we needed to be more vigilant.  ZZZ to ZZZ1 [airport]; we were on the ZZZZZ2 RNAV; Autopilot B engaged; on PATH. We were given an intercept heading to join final for [Runway] XX. Heading mode was selected. The aircraft flew heading and was in VNAV. The final approach course was entered into the FMC; and upon executing; the Autopilot B Vertical mode disengaged; with the A/P Caution light and the aircraft descended in Control Wheel Pitch.  We selected a pitch mode and proceeded without further incident.My concern:  I don't know why these disconnects happened. If they are normal for the -800 MAX; I am unaware of this. I thought all of our fleet types were programmed and responded to Pilot programming the same; in this scenario.  I've never experienced [other model] aircraft revert to CWS Pitch or roll; even with faulty Pilot programming.  We both assumed that perhaps; since neither of us had flown a MAX in a few years that we missed some training; or company notice.  We assumed that the error was a Pilot programming error.   I called the Chief Pilot on Call and told him of the occurrence the first time; and he was unaware of such a thing happening normally. We confessed that we actually had more experience than him in the MAX. He indicated I should call later and talk to the MAX programming expert and he perhaps could explain why the MAX behaves in this way. That is why we flew the aircraft a second leg with the anomaly; I assumed it was Pilot programming error.  A few days later; I was contacted by a Chief Pilot; who informed me that our experience was a malfunction; and that a logbook entry and maintenance resolution should have taken place.  I assumed it was a MAX anomaly; but it was a malfunction.

During that briefing we identified a threat of possible turbulence around 20;000 feet based on a PIREP. Upon arriving at the plane; I briefed the lead Flight Attendant. That briefing included a discussion on turbulence. I directed that the Flight Attendants stay seated for the departure until I call. Ground operations through takeoff and climbout were normal and uneventful. Departure cleared us to 17;000 feet. We leveled there awaiting hand off to Center and were in light turbulence. After a short delay we were cleared to climb to approximately 25;000 feet and to contact Center. I initiated the climb via VNAV. Almost immediately we encountered severe turbulence. The airspeed was fluctuating and the plane banked +-25 AOB (Angle of Bank). The autopilot remained engaged and made appropriate corrections. However; I put my hands on the controls in anticipation of needing to take control. The ride was so violent that my First Officer could not get his hands on the radio knob to change frequencies. By 18;000 feet the ride eased to moderate turbulence. When I deemed it safe; I then picked up the PA and asked 'Flight Attendants check in.' They checked the cabin and reported all passenger; crew and plane were safe. The First Officer made the check in with Center; reported the severe turbulence.At an appropriate time; I notified dispatch of the event. He published our PIREP. Later we submitted the log entry for maintenance. Further down line ZZZ1 Station was notified and I discussed with them an appropriate response upon landing. The remainder of the flight was uneventful; not even a ripple of turbulence. Once blocked in and checklists completed; I greeted passengers in case any were still concerned. They all seemed very appreciative; and thankful. Many even commented on the smooth landing and offered thanks for a safe trip. Customer Service; Maintenance and Flight Operations and met us at the gate. I provided full debriefs to each. The flight operations manager said we did a great job but also advised we submit a safety report. I want to offer that I believe the system; Standard Operating Procedures; and tools made available work. While I could not foresee the severity of the turbulence that awaited us; we knew a rough ride would be encountered in that area and took precaution. The result was no injuries to crew or passengers or damage to the plane. I offer this report mostly to help improve the system. And I am happy to answer any questions if necessary.
column123: WSI (Weather Service International) indicated a narrow band of turbulence on our route from roughly 17;000 to 20;000 feet due to shear below a jet stream.  Larger jets reported moderate (PIREP symbols) turbulence on WSI so the Captain had the flight attendants remain seated after takeoff until we called them.  At the time of the event the seat belt sign was ON and everyone on the plane was seated.  As we climbed through 17;000 feet the turbulence worsened from moderate to severe.  Large and rapid airspeed deviations of +/- 25 knots and sharp rolling moments of roughly 25 to 30 degrees occurred for roughly 2 minutes; all estimates.  As Pilot Monitoring it took me awhile to tune the ATC radios for a frequency change as I couldn't grab the tuning knobs in the turbulence.  I believe ATC instructed us to climb from 17;000 to 19;000 feet and that put us into the worst of the turbulence.  Once we were cleared to climb higher (above 19;000 feet) the ride improved quickly.  I believe a hand off from TRACON to Center caused much of the delay but I am not certain.Again; the seat belt sign was on and all flight attendants were seated per the briefing.  No injuries and no damage.  We did not make the 'be seated immediately' announcements as everyone was still seated since takeoff.  We were focused on getting a higher altitude and a better ride. Once we were clear of the turbulence we asked the flight attendants to 'check in' per our turbulence training.  We filed a PIREP with ATC and notified Dispatch.

column121: Upon departure from Runway XXR; just as we reached acceleration altitude I received an emergency PA from the flight attendant informing me there was smoke in the cabin. I immediately shut off the gasper fan; the recirc fan; the packs; and the APU bleed. I inquired as to the severity and was told 'it's bad.' My First Officer and myself did not see or smell anything resembling smoke. I immediately informed ATC we would like priority handling and requested vectors for an approach back into ZZZ. I asked the flight attendant if the passengers were in danger and if I needed to drop the oxygen masks. I was told at this point 'no' and was informed that the smoke had stopped. I asked the flight attendant to remain on the PA and to inform me the instant any more signs of smoke appeared.We were given vectors around to shoot the ILS to Runway XXR. I told the flight attendant we would be landing soon and to plan for a normal landing and taxi back assuming the smoke remained stopped. After a successful overweight landing; we exited the runway and taxied into the ramp. We had fire trucks follow us into our gate. They informed us they saw no heat signatures on our aircraft. The aircraft was successfully deplaned without injury or incident. Contract maintenance arrived a short while later and found a panel light in above seat X had shorted out and burned through the contact casing.Hindsight 20/20 I wouldn't have requested priority handling. In the moment; given the information I had to work with; I made a decision based on the fact that I thought there was a fire in the cabin and wanted to get the aircraft on the ground as quickly and as safely as possible. Crew Resource Management was almost nonexistent during this event. There was a very big language barrier between myself and my First Officer. During normal operations I often struggled to understand what he was saying. I took the lead on the radios; navigating; the communication with the flight attendant; and piloting the aircraft.

column121: While descending into ZZZ; my student elected to make a midfield entry into the downwind. We briefed the approach and announced our position on CTAF at about 4 miles outside of the airport. Following our call; another aircraft asked our location in relation to the airport. We attempted to reply; but severe radio congestion prevented a response. The student and I began scanning for traffic; but it appeared that no other aircraft were in our area. Just after crossing midfield; we began our turn to downwind when the previous aircraft announced a midfield downwind. We spotted the traffic 100 to 150 feet below us and passing underneath us to our left. We took evasive action and initiated a climb; then rejoined a normal downwind behind the aircraft. No evasive action was taken by the other aircraft and it seemed he was not aware of the near miss. The rest of the flight occurred without incident.I believe the cause of the near miss was a result of extreme frequency congestion in the area. Communication in the area was encumbered by heavy usage and several radio calls we made were blocked due to other transmissions; leading to confusion over aircraft positions at the airport we were using. A review of the chart showed a large number of airports with 50NM operating on XYY.Z and several of those airports were surrounding the busy nearby metro areas. My recommendation would be to evaluate the airport usage of that area and assign unique frequencies several busier airports in the area.

This error was not made on any recent instructional flights. Following the procedures taught to him by his instructors (keeping the stick full aft; minimizing brake usage; and taking the next exit) would have prevented the event from occurring.

Seeing as that we had flown an aircraft that had the potential to be unairworthy; I will be much more careful next time I take a maintenance flight and see if I can get a double check on aircraft that need to flown; with other mechanics. column121: I was working Sector 18 Woodstown; but not actually Woodstown (sitting at Sector 17). I was to be only working the Compton and Reading military airspace; which had Aircraft Y's and a Aircraft Z in it at the time. I witnessed the Aircraft Y refueling with the tanker at FL256 with out communicating that to me. Shortly there after; Aircraft Y separated from the tanker without communicating to me; and what I assume was descending back to the fighter cap altitudes of FL230-FL240 of which he was initially cleared to be at. Aircraft Y turned at the southern portion and descended; and then I saw him at FL227 below his assigned altitude. Aircraft X; was at FL220 right underneath him. I immediately asked the pilot if he was FL230-FL240; he responded that he was. At the same time the altitudes on the data block went back to FL230-FL240. The Sector 19 Controller; who was working Sector 18's airspace (even thought Sector 18's airspace was assigned to me sitting physically at Sector 17); said that Aircraft X was responding to an RA and descended. I immediately called the traffic to the fighter jet at that time. Filed previous reports regarding the Presidential airspace over Delaware. Procedures are not defined; there is no LOA or SOP; and the workforce was not properly briefed. There are many sited violations FAA Orders associated with this unsafe operation in addition to automation issues that can cause unsafe situations with Sector 18 not being utilized correctly. Request an LOA for the procedures; and for the boundaries; altitudes; refueling operations; and reroutes to all be negotiated with affected parties and implemented correctly in an LOA. A fighter jet got too close to an airliner jet in this situation; and the pilot did not even seem to understand the issue or care. They need to at the very least stay at their assigned altitudes; and they should be communicating with us on refueling operations to avoid situations like this.

column121: I was providing training on Ground 1 when Aircraft X exited Runway 25R and the trainee instructed them to taxi via C; N; north route. The Aircraft X pilot read back the instruction correctly. A minute later; I heard the OS (Operational Supervisor) advise us that Aircraft X taxied up L and not N which we; the training team; had not noticed. (Background: Taxiway K & L used to be the north route; but those are now a ramp area controlled by the City of LA for pushback from the international terminal. Taxiway N is now the north route.) This situation began to present itself several months ago when the taxiway routes first changed from L & K to N & P. It does not seem to happen as often; but I've now noticed four different scenarios in the last week (two last weekday; and two this same weekday.) It still seems to be a possibly systemic problem. In addition to Aircraft X; while the OS was telling me and the trainee that our 'scan needs to be better' to prevent this situation; Aircraft Y was under tow to Gate X and began to turn on K instead of L. (Per the LOA with the city; all arrivals to the ramp must enter via L & hold short of K1.) I immediately instructed Aircraft Y to stop; called the Ramp Tower to coordinate any potential traffic conflicts; then allowed the Aircraft Y reposition to continue. I'd recommend additional signage; a change to the charts; or added emphasis in the text of the 'north route' that emboldens how N is now the north route; not K or L. Or all of the above. The above recommendations would help alleviate the issue from the IFR/pilot side. Regarding the repositions/tows: the City of LA should disseminate refresher training to every airline that repositions aircraft on the LAX airfield. This training should be mandatory for any reposition operator and clearly explain the new procedures for the ramp. The response from Aircraft Y for why they turned on K instead of L was that they 'temporarily lost communication with their tow driver.' This response is unacceptable. Unless specifically instructed; no revenue flight or reposition is ever to enter the ramp via K.

column121: Coming into IAD the errors started when we were intercepting the localizer for Runway 1R. I was the pilot monitoring and the FO (First Officer) was the pilot flying. Approach cleared us to intercept when we were basically already crossing the final approach course so we had to navigate back to the localizer on our own. At the same time we had been getting hit with some minor wake turbulence from the airplane ahead of us which Approach informed us was a Boeing 777. We were then cleared for the visual approach and advised of the caution for wake turbulence and to maintain 170 kts. until 5 miles out. At this time we configured gear down flaps 20. I had just recently had training in the sim for wake turbulence and remembered how dangerous it could be so I advised my FO to use caution and I believe I recommended maybe staying above their path since we had already hit a small portion of their wake prior when we were on downwind. He elected to turn the autopilot off and hand fly slightly above their glide path. We then continued down and around 100 ft. got a terrain warning. Our first reaction was this was because we weren't on glide path and the FO called out; 'visual; landing.' around 50 ft. we got another aural message stating 'too low terrain'; at this point I realized something was wrong and quickly scanned and noticed we were still at flaps 20. At this point I immediately called for a balked landing. The FO restated in a question; balked landing? I said yes and he immediately executed the maneuver. We advised ATC of the go around and they asked for the reasoning and I stated we were unstable. We continued the go around and came back to land on [Runway] 1R after some vectoring without further incident. To add to this and to summarize; we did not complete a landing checklist; we were not fully configured and were at gear down flaps 20 degrees; and our speed bug was still at 170 kts. We received a terrain aural warning that we misinterpreted followed by a second aural warning and executed a balked landing at a medium energy state with lower power setting but high airspeed. Our attention started deviating from standard starting with the poor intercept angle of the localizer. I further complicated the situation by over concentrating on the wake turbulence from the 777 and focusing too much on the FO's glide path and what I would call tunnel focusing on his flying. I believe my statements to him about the wake turbulence also led to distracting him from normal flight operations as well. He was talking through his thought process on staying a half dot high on the glide path and I was responding with statements like I agree; not necessarily breaking sterile cockpit but also causing more distraction on both of our parts. This was the first time that I had not completed a landing checklist. It has made me realize that while being aware of threats like wake turbulence is important; it's even more important to maintain a greater situational awareness and take a step back and not tunnel focus on one threat while other threats could arise. While I am glad we did not try to force a landing. This is a mistake I never thought would be possible or would happen to me. I have definitely learned a lot from this experience.

column121: The situation happened on leg 1 on the second day of a 4 day sequence.  We departed ZZZ for ZZZ1. As the First Officer I completed both the interior checklists and performed the exterior inspection.  I noticed during the walk around that one of the red navigation lights was inoperative.  When I got back to the flight deck I confirmed that it was previously written up and had been deferred in the AML.  No other issues were noted during the preflight. The Captain was the Pilot Flying and I was the Pilot Monitoring. We departed ZZZ on Runway XXL. The takeoff and departure were uneventful.  Weather was clear with unrestricted visibility. The climb was continued until we leveled off at FL340. At approximately XA:13Z; I started to smell something.  It smelled like burning plastic. At the same time I noticed the smell the Captain asked 'Do you smell that?' Before replying we both saw smoke coming from the 'FL' button on the transponder located on the center console.  At this time we both we executed the items for 'Smoke; Fire; or Fumes'; donned our oxygen masks and established crew communication.  At that point the Captain gave me both aircraft control and the radios so he could focus on the abnormal. While I monitored the autopilot the Captain continued with the 'Smoke; Fire; or Fumes' checklist.  I confirmed with him that the proper switches were being turned off in accordance with the checklist. We noticed that the smoke and fumes were decreasing and did not need to run the 'Smoke or Fumes Removal' checklist.  While the Captain attempted to locate the transponder circuit breaker to isolate the problem he noticed that the 'ELEC PANEL LIGHTS AFT/CENTER' circuit breaker located at the base of the front of the center pedestal was popped. We were confident the problem had been isolated and the Captain informed me that he was about 90% sure we were going to divert but he wanted to check with company to see if we were missing anything.  We quickly realized that a step in the checklist had us turn off the internet and he would be unable to use the crew phone app to communicate with the Dispatcher. The Captain then took the radios back and attempted to get phone patch with the Center Controller.  The controller was unable to give us the phone patch but was able to relay information.  After communicating through the controller and using ACARS; it was decided that we would divert to ZZZ2.  The Captain notified ATC and informed Center we wanted to divert to ZZZ2. The controller asked if we want ARFF (aircraft rescue firefighting) and the Captain said yes. The Captain then gave me back the radios so that he could run more checklists.                                                                                                                                                                             The Captain continued with the checklists the controller asked what runway we wanted to land on. The Captain and I agreed that we wanted the longest runway due to the fact we would be landing overweight. I then requested Runway XXR. I got the airplane set up for an ILS approach to XXR. I started the descent into ZZZ2 while the Captain finished checklists and briefed the passengers and Flight Attendants. Then the Captain told me that he ran the 'Non Routine Landing Considerations' checklist and that the passengers and flight attendants had been briefed. He talked about the heavy weight landing and did a landing assessment. He asked if I had anything to add or could think of anything else we might need to do before landing. I told him that I think we had covered everything and I had nothing else to add. He then briefed the approach and took aircraft control.  We completed both the descent and before landing checklists. After landing we cleared the runway at taxiway. I relayed to ARFF that unless they see anything abnormal from the outside our plan was to continue taxing to gate. They informed us that they did not see any unusual readings on thethermal scan.  ARFF followed us to the gate.  The Captain had me make a PA to the passengers that we would be taxing to gate and they would be accommodated after deplaning. The taxi and engine shutdown at the gate was uneventful. At the gate we were met by a member of the company Flight Office and he asked if we needed to be checked out at the hospital. We both said we did not require medical attention and that no more than a few seconds went by that we breathed in fumes before getting on oxygen. He then told us that he was pulling us off the remainder of the trip and could positive space home.  The Captain completed writing up items in the AML. We then debriefed when it was just the two of us left on the airplane. I told him I thought maybe I could have done more to help.  He said I did what he needed by flying the airplane and communicating with ATC while he ran the appropriate checklists and backed him up in his decision making process. We both agreed that we handled the situation in the way we are trained to handle abnormal at the school house. The cause was smoke coming from the 'FL' button on the transponder located on the center console.

column121: I was cleared to land. As I came over the end of the runway; I was getting some weird wind shear that was pushing me around; but my approach felt controlled and so I went through with it. Right before I touched down; I got a strong crosswind gust of wind (from the left) that pushed my super cub sideways (nose pointing to the left) as I touched down. Being a tail dragger; the plane responded accordingly; and I began to skid sideways down the runway. I was already down and too sideways for a go-around; so I pulled the throttle all the way back; stick back and left; and rudder full right. The plane continued to skid to a stop sideways on the runway; but all three wheels remained on the runway at all times; and no damage to the runway or aircraft occurred. After coming to a complete stop; I proceeded to turn the plane around to the left; leaving the asphalt for a brief time on the left side of the runway and taxing to the exit ramp on the other side where the Tower then informed me to stop; and I was later met by a foam truck and a service vehicle. I believe that the main factors in this were the wind gusts from the side; which in turn caused me to land sideways. I could have performed a go-around; though in the moment my approach felt controlled up until the last minute. column121: My student and I departed on a training flight to the southeast practice area where we were going to run through Private Pilot maneuvers (stalls; steep turns; engine out; ground maneuvers and landings). After climbing to 035 and completing steep turns; we set up to do power on stalls and climbed to 050. We then set up to do power off stalls. After completing 4 power off stalls; we still had significant altitude and I decided to give student an engine out by pulling the mixture. The student set up the aircraft for best glide and selected an airfield that was about three miles away and ran through the restart checklist. Every 1500 feet I would advance the mixture and push forward on the yoke to make sure the engine was staying primed. We then simulated part of the forced landing checklist (ELT; squawk codes; emergency calls) and performed the landing brief.The student chose to try to get to the airfield by going down the downwind then realized that student was too low and close to the runway to safely make it to the field. I asked student what the backup plan was and student selected a field to right of the aircraft that student could easily turn into. Student turned the aircraft to the field and I estimated that student could easily make the landing and that student had the engine back and to do a go-around. I advanced the mixture and the engine sputtered and died and the prop stopped. The student announced that I had the controls and I pointed the airplane to the field that student had selected. I checked the mixture in; shut off valve on; then attempted to restart the engine with the key. After two attempts; I determined that we were too low and shut off the fuel valve and pulled the mixture and landed the plane in the field.There was no damage to the plane; no injuries to myself or my student; and no property damage. Fuel levels were still visible and greater than half way from the top of the tanks (well over 1/2 full; I didn't have a fuel stick to check total actual levels); oil level was still at 5 qts. We were able to later restart the airplane and taxi it closer to the property owner's barn with permission.The biggest thing that I learned was that I will not pull the mixture to simulate an engine out any more. That was the mistake that I feel caused this. In the future; all engine outs will be initiated by pulling the throttle. Though this has been common in my training from private to commercial; it put us in a dangerous situation that I could have avoided.
column123: At the altitude of 4;000 feet my Instructor pulled the mixture in the aircraft to simulate an emergency landing. At that moment I trimmed the plane all the way; pulled the carb heat and pitched the airplane for 60 kts. Next I looked for a place we could simulate the landing and we were just 2-4 miles from [an] airport. We were descending approximately 500 feet per minute. The closer we got I realized that I was too low to make the obstacles. I made the error of not looking at the altitude of the field. Therefore; I looked to my right and there was a large field and I pointed to my instructor that at that moment the safest decision was to do the field on the right. My instructor said that was a good decision and I started my turn to the field.My airspeed was 60; my right hand was on the throttle; which at the time it was all in. My left hand on the controls and my feet on the rudder. A few seconds later my Instructor looked at me and said 'you would have made it' and he decided to end the simulation by putting the mixture all in. However; the engine would not work and my instructor said 'my controls' I restated 'your controls' and he took charge of the plane. He tried turning the engine on a couple times and the propeller would just not move at all. It happened in a matter of seconds. Since I had already lined up the airplane to the field; my Instructor worked hard to fly the airplane until it touched the ground where he applied the brakes after he had landed it safely. We turned all the systems off and removed the key from the starter. We opened the doors and got out of the aircraft. We called the flight school and they came to get us and to see the airplane.

Aircraft was returning from ZZZ1 with X passengers aboard. It was thought that a fuel pump had failed; but further investigation revealed that I as the PIC had misread my fuel gauge.
