column121: Very poorly written NOTAM creating a dilemma in operations. After landing on Runway 6; Napa Tower cleared us to back taxi on Runway 6 and exit on Taxiway C. We stated that we were unable Taxiway C due to our aircraft weighing more than 30;000 lbs. There was a NOTAM 04/006 in effect stating 'Taxiway C closed to aircraft more than 30;000 lb'. Tower then stated that it was OK and reissued the clearance for us to exit Taxiway C. I was hesitant; but we complied with the clearance and exited Taxiway C so as not to create a potentially bigger problem with other traffic. But I also stated on the frequency for the tapes that we are exiting on Taxiway C in compliance with our clearance despite weighing more than 30;000 lbs per the NOTAM. I think we made the wise decision to comply with ATC under the circumstances; but the pilot should not be put into that situation of either violating a clearance or violating a known published NOTAM. Per many NOTAMs at APC; Runway 1L/19R was closed with many other taxiways closed also. We were very aware of the NOTAMs and pre-briefed our certain back taxi on Runway 6 during our approach briefing before top of descent. We were very situationally aware and not surprised except for the clearance to exit on Taxiway C (it was supposedly closed to us). I politely had a short discussion with Ground Control during taxi in to the ramp and expressed my concern about being issued a clearance that made us technically in violation of the NOTAM. He said it was OK; but he would discuss it with the supervisor. I did not mention this to Ground Control; but the NOTAM should have stated more clearly and accurately that Taxiway C is closed north of Taxiway H to aircraft over 30;000 lbs. The NOTAM for Taxiway C has been in place for a long time-- certainly before the NOTAMs for Runway 1L/19R and other taxiways were more recent. Somebody didn't review the consequences of the older Taxiway C NOTAM when they published the more recent ones. It created an operational problem needlessly. Napa Tower did not appear concerned; but I hope they and Airport Ops fix this situation.

column121: During the final minutes of a long training lesson of emergency procedures my student and I were hovering at the departure end of Runway XX. We had just finished our last emergency procedure training pattern and were ready to head back to the ramp to stop our lesson. Where we were located; we needed to cross Runway XY/XZ to get to the ramp on the east side of the airport. Since my student is getting ready for a check ride and I am very comfortable with both her flying and communication skills with ATC I left it up to her how we would reposition. Due to the light wind an air taxi crossing the field and Runway XY/XZ was both appropriate and her final decision. She keyed up the mic on tower frequency and requested the air taxi back to our ramp as she; and others at the school; normally do many times a day. Unfortunately; the first transmission was blocked by additional traffic on frequency and her request did not go through. She knew this occurred since she heard the end of the other traffics transmission; and ATC was advising that traffic that we were still on the runway. Once there was silence on the tower frequency; she made her request again. The next thing I heard was a traffic report from ATC advising her of an additional helicopter about two miles to the west and inbound to the same location we were going. My student acknowledge the advisory and advised we would be looking for that traffic as she started to proceed to air taxi to the ramp crossing Runway XY/XZ. Just as we were about to cross XY/XZ we heard an advisory from ATC that an airplane was cleared for takeoff and as the pilot was acknowledging his clearance; he inquired what the little helicopter was doing (us). I thought it was weird of the clearance for takeoff since we were in the process of air taxing and about to cross the runway. Once past the runway and starting to land; ATC inquired with my student if she requested to cross Runway XY/XZ and she replied yes (thinking her transmission was received and by ATC giving her the traffic advisory he was aware of our movement). Unbeknownst to her or I; her second transmission was also walked on and not received by ATC. My student took the coincidental advisory of traffic as ATC's acknowledgment that we were intending to air taxi and cross Runway XY/XZ. It was confirmed upon landing by someone listening to ATC that neither of our requests had gone through. ATC had not heard her first or second transmission for the request and the traffic advisory was merely coincidental looking back on it. Luckily the traffic that was advised they were clear for takeoff on Runway XY had not even started rolling at the opposite end of the runway for their takeoff and they had also seen us and not started rolling until we past the runway.Looking back on the incident I know as an instructor I CANNOT let comfort and confidence with a student lead to complacency. I need to be on top of my game 100% of the time and make sure both myself and my student is both listening to and understanding radio traffic; and if we do not; we need to make sure we completely understand and get clearances before moving. This had the potential for a worse outcome and I most definitely have learned from it. I need to keep my eyes and ears 100% concentrated on the task at hand; and looking back on it I know my mind was still partially concentrated on our last emergency procedure training and how to debrief my student about it; and not on the 'simple' task of taking the helicopter back to park it. Complacency has no place in the cockpit and this event has taught both my student and I a valuable lesson.

We continued climbing and turned further right (net 180 by then); while it appeared target was still at their previous altitude (now -700 thanks to our climb) and maintaining a roughly easterly heading but still in a right turn. After we continued our right turn (now heading west); I for the first time caught a visual on the other aircraft at roughly our 4:00 position and 700 feet below (where ADS-B said they were at that moment). They appeared to be still turning right; perhaps practicing 360s -- I don't know. In any case; we were continuing to put distance and altitude between us such that we resumed our northerly heading back to home airport without further incident other than perhaps a minute during which our altitude was 3;800 MSL -- not a legal VFR cruising altitude -- while we made sure the other aircraft was not trying to chase us. column121: I was conducting a training flight on Airman Certification Standards (ACS) maneuvers to prepare a student for the practical test to be taken within 4 days.  Initially; we conducted normal; short field; and soft field takeoffs and landings without incident.  Then; we departed to the practice area and practiced unusual attitude recoveries; steep turns; slow flight; approach stalls; and departure stalls from 3;000 feet MSL.  That complete; I directed the student to return to the home airport.  On downwind entry; we were 500 feet above pattern altitude.  I considered this a good opportunity to give my student a simulated engine failure and have him continue to the runway.  On downwind; we were at an altitude lower than the student felt comfortable.  He stated that he didn't feel we could make it.  However; to demonstrate that the landing could still be made if the conditions (engine out) were real; I took the controls made a short approach (a banked continuous base to final turn) and lined the aircraft up with the runway in a landing attitude. Unfortunately; during the maneuver I became obsessed with monitoring our airspeed for proper glide speed and maneuvering during the turn at the neglect of ensuring the landing gear was extended.  We landed with the gear retracted. The flare (round out) was at normal altitude and attitude. Overall; it was not a bad landing.  The student caught the error prior to me when we heard scraping.  The aircraft slid and eventually slid off the runway to a point between the runway and taxiway.One human performance consideration may have been a factor.  I have been conducting training in both straight gear and retractable gear C-172s switching between the two on the same day.  That was the case on this day.  I had flown 0.7 [hours] practicing landings with one student in a fixed gear 172 in the morning; driven to a different airport; and flew in this student's retractable 172 in the afternoon. My mindset was fixated on making the landing and not on the differences between the two aircraft.

column121: We had been cleared the ILS 25L Approach while on the ANJLL Arrival and assigned 250 knots. At about 12;000 feet; we got a call from the cabin that the passenger we had called STAT-MD for earlier in the flight; was feeling worse. I asked the First Officer to call OPS for medical assistance to meet us at the gate. When he returned back to the ATC frequency; we were approaching 10;000 feet and hit wake turbulence sufficiently strong to cause the airplane to go into control wheel pitch and roll. I redirected the aircraft to KRAIN; re-engaged LNAV and VNAV; and asked ATC what we were following.  I was told we were following nothing. This didn't make sense since we had just hit very strong wake turbulence. While established on final; ATC told us to slow to 170 knots. This surprised both of us; because the last speed assignment we recalled being given was 250 knots. 170 knots would be a huge speed reduction and we were still about 25 miles out. ATC then asked us if we were at 210 knots. We told the Controller no; and that we had been assigned 250 knots. He told us we had been instructed to slow to 210 knots back when we complained about the wake turbulence (approaching 10;000 feet). We were now overtaking a B777 ahead; so our approach clearance was canceled. We were given vectors for spacing and vectored back onto the localizer and then re-cleared the ILS 25L. column123: Climbing through FL240 on our way to our final FL280 we receive a call from the (FAs) flight attendants. The Captain took the call because I was responding to a frequency change to ATC. The Captain returns from the call and informed me of what was taking place and that he was trying to receive more information from the FA's. column121: I am a Private Oilot who currently lives in ZZZ; and I was in ZZZ1 for the weekend. I am currently working on my instrument rating; and I do not have a complex endorsement. I was looking to book a plane for that day; and I decided that it would be best to look at renting a complex aircraft and hiring a CFI as PIC so I could get my first lesson in flying complex. This way; the time would count towards my 10 hour requirement for complex or TAA aircraft for my commercial license; which I plan on getting after my instrument rating. I knew that I would be required to hire a CFI as PIC since I do not yet have my complex endorsement. We arrived on the morning of Date and took off from ZZZ2 at roughly XA:00am after a preflight with the CFI; who is employed by Company. The lesson took place in the school's 172RG. Our flight consisted of an intro complex lesson where we flew down to ZZZ3 for a touch and go. Following this; we flew back to ZZZ2 and prepared for landing. We were cleared for Runway XR by Tower and made a straight in approach. The before landing checklist was completed; and we extended the landing gear as required. We noted that the light on the landing gear instrument had turned green as we were on approach; indicating that the landing gear had been deployed. There was a crosswind out of 070 with winds at 17kts; gust 22kts as reported by Tower. We performed a side slip to correct for the crosswind; and approached the runway at normal speed. The side slip was performed well and the airplane touched down straight and in the middle of the runway at appropriate touchdown speed. Once the main wheels touched down; the plane started to wobble on the left side; and it became clear that the left main landing gear had not locked in place. The left landing gear then folded back into the plane during the rollout. By this time our ground speed had slowed considerably; but the plane was supported partially by the left fuselage. While the main right gear and front gear had deployed; the main left gear was now back inside the plane; and the aircraft veered off to the left and into the grass. Informed Tower; and the airport closed the runway and deployed emergency services to come meet us.Nobody was hurt during the event; and we safely exited the aircraft where we waited for the airport personnel. I did not notice any damage to the airport; and no runway lights were hit. The only damage to the plane was minor; and from what I could see it was limited to the landing gear and possibly the left wingtip; which was touching the ground when the plane came to a stop to the left of the runway. The engine; prop; and the rest of the plane seemed undamaged.The airport informed the FAA of the event; and eventually I was dismissed after giving the airport workers my pilot certificate. I made a quick call to inspector. We briefly spoke; and I gave a brief oral statement. In my opinion this was a clear mechanical failure and was not due to pilot error. Also; this event does not fit the definition of an accident or reportable incident to the NTSB; per NTSB part 830.
column123: Take off at ZZZ2 at XA:40 AM local time Eastbound after clear ZZZ2 Delta airspace; right turn southbound direct to ZZZ3 at 1;500 feet MSL. column121: I was cleared for takeoff from Runway 23 (gravel runway) in Merrill Field Anchorage Alaska by the Tower of the airport. The Tower had given me the so called 'Chester Creek Departure' with the Altitude deviation across the Knik Arm of the Cook inlet; after I had talked to the Tower on the Ground frequency 121.70 about my intentions and asked for the deviation across the cold water. All normal procedures here in town! After getting cleared to takeoff I responded with repeating my clearance and that I am taking the runway for departure (on 126.00). After liftoff I climbed; as there are obstacles to clear etc. As I clear the obstacles I am still on runway heading and after clearing them I turn right about 20 degrees or so to go onto my 'Chester Creek departure' route: as cleared and as advertised by Tower and me. In this moment I notice a Cessna C172 coming at me head on; right down 'My' 'Chester Creek departure' at low altitude!!! I take evasive action by stopping the climb and banking right; bringing my flight path parallel and below to the head-on coming-at-me Cessna C172. - As I saw the Cessna C172 in time and evaded it there was no big danger but If I had not seen him it would have been head on for sure or an extremely close near miss. Had I flown a C185 it would have been head on for sure; had I been by myself or less fuel on board it would have 'fit' too!This should not have happened and it happens often in Merrill Field. There is nothing wrong with any of the airspace of the Airport or the procedures; its just that there are certain individuals on that tower that fail to warn of traffic conflicts in their airspace or they fail to warn certain flight instructors about their deviations!!! This C172 was LOW and should have been at full pattern altitude as it was on a downwind for Runway 25 !!! This is not the first close call I have had with this Tower. I am flying in Alaska and Anchorage for XX years. Depending on who is on this Tower I am either relaxed as I can trust the person I hear (and Know as known good) or I am nervous as I hear who it is ( and I know who I am talking about ) and I worry 'what will be messed up today?' again. As I am leery whenever I hear this person on the tower I do all I can to make it easy; and clear and precise and yet again this happened. How often will this continue to happen? I am pretty disgusted with the services of some (very FEW) of the controllers of Merrill Field Tower...

column121: Operating flight ZZZ-ZZZ1. Myself and other Flight Attendant during taxi noticed a musty like fume smell moments after pilots turned on the engines. Followed by extremely hot temperatures in the cabin which overtook the cabin. Immediately we noticed the majority of the customers reaching for their air vents and received multiple comments about the aircraft blowing 'hot air'. We walked through the cabin and were able to identify the fumes were coming from the Air supply vents towards the FWD of the Cabin. The intensity was Level 2 Moderate. Flight Deck was notified immediately. The moment the engines turned on I immediately felt a sudden rush of heat and immediate chest pain/tightness; nausea; and the air felt very thick making it slightly harder to breath. Ones the Flight Deck was notified they immediately responded and shut off the engines. I gradually began to feel better and my symptoms eventually went away. We returned to gate and deplaned the aircraft. Maintenance requested details of the Fume Event which we provided. Maintenance deferred the P.A.C.K. located in the FWD of the aircraft which stopped the Fumes. We re-boarded and departed from ZZZ -ZZZ1.These fume events are happening more than it is being reported. The company procedure for these events are misleading crew members into reporting to the company as an ODOR (Smell) event vs Fumes event so that they don't have to report it properly. Out of fear of retaliation crew member choose to not report and ignore symptoms. These too common mechanical issues are exposing us to harmful chemical exposures and causing us to get sick at the moment and then experience more severe symptoms later. Myself and many crew members. If we can enforce and install Carbon Monoxide sensors on the aircraft which is something we have in our own homes and is not costly; we can prevent and attend to these fume events in a timely manner and prevent Crews/Customers from getting sick or worse situations that can cause a more severe safety incident.

Simultaneously; Aircraft Y was observed over the approach end threshold; but we could not VISIBLY VERIFY if the pilot in Aircraft X still had forward progress when he went passed the runway edge lines at the end of Runway 24.  Being unable to see the aircraft moving (or not moving) passed the hold short on taxiway Alpha off of Runway 24; limits ATC ability to make informed decisions on having to send following aircraft around or safely land.  The new hanger blind spot has been creating unnecessary problems in the way ATC is conducted on BOTH Runway 6 and Runway 24.Recommendation - Build a new taller tower; add height to the existing tower; lower the hanger to eliminate the blind spot.

column121: I was the First Officer and Pilot Monitoring for our flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. After an uneventful departure and climb we established our cruise at FL360. Approximately 15 minutes into our cruise the Captain noticed a bright light near the top of his side view window. He brought my attention to the window heat unit which was glowing. From my vantage point I initially thought the unit itself was aflame but after several seconds it became apparent that a short existed which was contained within the window panes. A glowing line similar to a light bulb's filament began snaking downwards from the heat unit between the window panes. The Captain tapped the window several times which managed to briefly extinguish the light. We both acknowledged the need to descend as soon as possible and I requested a lower altitude with ATC. ATC mentioned traffic directly in front of us and stated he would try to give us a descent after the traffic passed. During this time; around 10 seconds after the Captain tapped the glass; the short reignited and continued to grow. The Captain noted an acrid smell; unusually high heat emanating from his window; and again expressed the need to descend. I pointed out the traffic; now visible to us; at our 12 o'clock and stated that we can descend shorty after they passed underneath us. For a third time I requested a lower altitude with ATC. The window failed shortly thereafter. The Captain's side view window let out a loud bang and fractures spider-webbed its entirety. For the first time since this incident began we received a L WSHIELD HEAT EICAS message followed by another L WINDOW HEAT EICAS message.Considering the potential for smoke/fumes and loss of cabin pressure we both immediately donned our oxygen masks; ensured they were at 100%; and established communications between ourselves and ATC. As I was donning the mask I saw the previously mentioned traffic pass safely below us. I relayed this to the Captain who began an emergency descent and told me to notify ATC. I [advised ATC] and let the controller know we were beginning a descent. As the Captain was flying our descent I sent an ACARS to Dispatch notifying them of the L WINDOW failure and that we would need a diversion. The Captain noted that we were close to ZZZ2. I plugged ZZZ2 into the fixes page; identifying that we were 55 miles away and subsequently plugged ZZZ3 into the fixes page; identifying us to be 90 miles away. Our first thought was to proceed to ZZZ2 as it was so close. I requested a heading from ATC as the airplane was about to turn north towards ZZZ1 along our original route and that we would likely be diverting to ZZZ2 but were still weighing our options. ATC gave us a heading which we accepted. As we were established in our descent I told the Captain I'd notify the flight attendants. He continued to fly the airplane as I called the FAs. I provided them a brief note of what had happened; that we were diverting; and that we would make an announcement to the passengers when we knew where we were going. They were professional and calm throughout the notification. The Captain handed control of the airplane to me so he could run the QRC and QRH. I accepted the aircraft and he quickly and effectively ran both checklists to their completion. By the end of his checklists we received a message from dispatch identifying ZZZ2 and ZZZ3 as good diversions. We were closer to ZZZ2 but still in the flight levels. We discussed our options. Considering ZZZ3 was a crew base; maintenance base; and nearly perfect to descend to from our present position we elected to proceed to ZZZ3. After establishing ourselves at 10;000 feet we removed the oxygen masks and donned our normal headsets for easier communication. The Captain gave the flight attendants a full briefing and updated the passengers on what had happened and why we were going to ZZZ3. I flew the airplane with autopilot engaged; managed ATC communications; notified dispatch that we were an [priority] aircraft and going to ZZZ3; and proceeded to obtain ZZZ3 weather; performance numbers; and set up the approach in the FMS. By the time the Captain completed his duties we were at 5;000 feet and on delaying vectors for Runway XXL into ZZZ3. We discussed what both of us had done ensuring we had not missed any items seeking immediate attention. Satisfied; he briefed the approach; we ran the descent checklist; I transferred the aircraft controls back to him; and I notified ATC that we were ready to proceed to the airport. The rest of the flight continued uneventfully. I called Ops to ensure we had a gate; we shot the approach; several emergency vehicles followed us after landing; and we canceled [with ATC] while taxiing in.The Captain detected a light in his peripheral vision. He discovered a short working its way through the window pane.Repeated cycling of the windshield heat in a prior checklist revision likely led to the unit's failure and short. We knew it was likely a matter of time until the window failed. We immediately began planning our descent and diversion choices.I was surprised at how challenging it was to hear ATC and/or the FAs with the oxygen masks on. Our breathing was very loud over the intercom/speaker which made it very hard to hear other voices. It might be worth noting in sim sessions.

column121: As Pilot Flying; at approximately 1;050 feet AGL on the ZZZZZ3 departure; we experienced a rapid succession of three bursts. At the same time; I was reducing the thrust levers to CLB mode. The gear was already up and the Captain; Pilot Monitoring; was just checking in with departure. Both of us weren't sure if we had hit a bird or something else. We had another rapid succession of three bursts with associated ECAM that almost instantaneously cleared the screen. The Captain quickly recognized the right engine (#2) indications were 'rolling back' and stated so clearly. He then ensure positive aircraft control by verbally stating; 'Your aircraft'. I responded with 'My aircraft'. The right engine ECAM message went away just as quickly as it displayed. The right engine then showed normal parameters and 'parallel' with the left engine. The Captain reviewed the Quick Reference Card and determined no action from the QRC required. He [advised] ATC while I simultaneously flew the aircraft on crosswind and turned downwind. The thrust levelers remained at CLB setting and flaps 1 on downwind with no other associated engine indications at approximately 2;500 feet MSL. We both agreed the best resolution was to land the aircraft ASAP. Our current weight was below max landing weight. I very quickly briefed a visual approach to Rwy XXR while the Captain loaded an approach in the FMGC. With gear down; I made the right turn on a base leg. I pushed the SPD button for managed speed as I thought we were in APPR Mode however; I quickly pulled the SPD button for selected speed once I noticed the engines were increase thrust for a higher speed. At this point we experienced one more rapid succession from the right engine which quickly resided again with speed now selected and winding back to approach speed. We configured final flap setting to 3 and briefed our potential go-around if required. The Captain successfully ensured our Descent and Before Landing checklist were completed with clearance to land. Upon a successful landing; the Captain ensured the passengers and crew were informed to remain seated while we taxied to the gate. ARFF did a complete review and temperature check of the engines with nothing significant to report. Noteworthy items...the aircraft was hand flown until downwind. Auto pilot was engaged briefly once at 2;500 feet MSL. The autopilot was disengaged when turning base leg and hand flown for the visual approach.Definitely a startle factor; particularly since it happened just above 1;000 feet AGL while thrust levels are normally set to CLB mode. Additionally; the initial confusion as to whether we had hit something (bird?) since the ECAM did not display an action. Furthermore; once the ECAM action did display it was nearly instantaneously gone as the engine continued to attempt to resolve the problem.Since ENG Stall isn't on the Checklist; this scenario could be used in future training events to increase awareness and action based on a low altitude scenario during take-off phase.

column121: The Captain and I were scheduled to depart ZZZZ in a 737 MAX. The flight was full and we knew we had max takeoff weight issues for runway limit. The outside temperature was 16 degrees C and winds were variable for Runway XXR. On our first pushback; we did not have our load closeout and we pushed from gate and began to taxi; even while seeing potential overweight issues. After calling ZZZZ Operations; we received our load closeout and ran the numbers. The temperature increased to 18 degrees C and that significantly degraded engine performance at our weight and required configuration. We noticed that we would be overweight by about 1;100 pounds. We discontinued taxi; messaged Dispatch via ACARS and coordinated a return to gate for overall reevaluation. Dispatch and the flight planning team determined we needed to offload passengers and associated bags and that would fix the problem.Now; enough time elapsed that we needed more fuel and needed a new ATC flight plan clearance. ZZZZ Clearance informed us that we had no clearance in the system and we needed to contact Dispatch. We did that via ACARS as well as through ZZZZ Operations. This disconnect with the clearance occurred more than 10 times over a 4 hour period before they finally got a clearance through ZZZZ ATC. We were told that the issue was that ZZZZ ATC did not like something in the clearance request that ZZZ1 Dispatch submitted. However; ZZZZ ATC would not talk to ZZZ1 Dispatch; nor tell them what was wrong with their submission. ZZZZ ATC would only work through ZZZZ Operations; who does not submit flight plan clearance requests and had no idea what is required. We; the aircrew; decided to not push back until we had our clearance and a valid load closeout. It began to rain during our delay and I requested approximately XX different updates based on new weights; temperatures and runway conditions. Also during this 4 hour delay; Dispatch and the flight planning team repeatedly pulled off many passengers and bags. This required continuous updates for accuracy. The passengers were told to deplane after X hours and were given a time to be back at the gate for departure. We got everyone back on board; received our flight plan clearance; a valid load closeout and departed via ZZZZ Runway XXR. The flight was uneventful and we landed safely in ZZZ2.The main issue on this flight was planning and execution by the company. The company tried to leverage the 737 MAX in an environment where it does not need to be flying with full loads and the flight planning team tried to execute an inherently flawed plan. In ZZZZ; rain is constant; but the temperatures and winds that day were very moderate compared to what routinely occurs in the summer months. Even at 18 degrees C; the 737 MAX is extremely weight limited at this airport's altitude. The 737 MAX should not be flying in ZZZZ during even moderate temperature months with full passenger and cargo loads. The ATC flight plan clearance issue is a procedural or communication issue between the company and ZZZZ ATC. ZZZZ Operations should be able to intercede in these situations and fix any issues that come up; but training and awareness is required. Ultimately; this was a non-issue due to the more time-consuming weight issues associated with this flight. Our flight planning departments must continue to gather data related to the 737 MAX during normal operations at all airports throughout the year. This data will lead to an executable annual route schedule for the 737 MAX and ensure smooth operational tempo while maintaining appropriate safety margins.

column121: During TO out of ZZZ thrust levers anomaly- TO thrust setting as I remember was 84.6; however; when First Officer selected TOGA the thrust increased to over 90% N1 before reducing. column123: On the take off from ZZZ when I pressed the TOGA button; the throttles rapidly advanced to near full forward; and then slowly retarded to the selected takeoff thrust as we were rolling down the runway.  The throttles came forward very rapidly and went further forward then I would expect.  We were set for a 22K takeoff with an assumed temperature reduction. After takeoff the Captain and I discussed the anomaly.  It was very unusual. The rest of the flight; up to the landing flare; was normal.  I was flying the new visual approach. The approach was loaded into the FMS. The autopilot was engaged. I think I remember disengaging the autopilot if the final turn to final.  In the flare; below 50 feet the throttles began to advance by themselves. I remember being right on speed prior to this. I felt the throttles move forward; and I remember trying to hold them back.  I think the autothrottles were attempting to go around.  I felt the aircraft 'ballooning' and I saw that I was now going to fast (I remember seeing 155 knots). At this point I said go around and pressed the go around button. We climbed out and tower gave us a visual downwind to return. The go around was a normal go around. After cleaning up; I went right back to flaps 1 for the downwind. I was trying to process what just happened and the Captain and I discussed it. We were both surprised by the auto throttle. While turning base; the auto throttles were doing a poor job of holding command bug. They were very slow to respond. I turned off my flight director and visually flew a visual pattern (I had no lateral guidance from the FMS; the approach had not been resequenced. I know the airport very well could see where I needed to go.  I left the auto throttles engaged but I had a firm hand on the throttles. While on base; the air speed got 5 knots slow and I manually pushed the throttles up to speed up. I completed a visual approach and normal flaps 40 landing with flight director off and auto throttles engaged. The auto throttles functioned normal after I had manually pushed them up; but in retrospect I should have disconnected them and flown manually. They were definitely suspect at this point. The flaps 40 approach and landing was normal and smooth. The auto throttles worked as they should.  We had a mechanic at ZZZ1 meet us and we wrote up what had happened. The next morning while eating breakfast; I was 'bothered' by what had happened and I called Name to discuss the anomaly.  We discussed the anomaly in detail. He didn't have any answers either; but said he would keep an eye on the aircraft; X. Additional note; the approach was stable prior to the auto throttle anomaly. We were following an [aircraft] that was going very slow. We were minimal space behind them so we were right on speed throughout the approach to flare. I believe the autopilot was engaged until the turn to final.I am not sure if this was a fault with the airplane auto throttle; a 737 Max anomaly or a coding issue with the new visual approach? Thinking about what had happened on the takeoff; I suspect something was wrong with the auto throttles. I am fairly new to the Max. [No suggestions]; however in retrospect I should have turned off the auto throttles when it became clear they were not working correctly after the go around.

column121: I departed with one passenger to ZZZ on an IFR flight plan. The flight was uneventful until on a 5-mile final when I heard the Tower clear a 'Heavy' cargo plane to take the runway for departure. As we got closer to the runway; we noticed that the heavy cargo plane was just getting off the runway as we were on short final. With traffic behind us in the pattern; I continued the approach opting to land slightly below the glideslope on the first third of the runway so as to avoid any potential wake turbulence put off by the departing aircraft beyond its rotation point. While in the landing phase of flight; approximately 1' off the ground and near stall speed for a normal landing; we encountered sudden turbulence that caused the plane to destabilize resulting in a brief touchdown followed by a balloon and a subsequent stall that caused the aircraft to bounce on the runway. As I saw we were losing directional control; I added full power to initiate the go-around maneuver; regained stability; and completed a left traffic pattern. We came in shortly after another Cirrus on short final and had a normal smooth landing. It was not until after taxiing to [FBO] and performing engine shutdown that I noticed the tips of the props were frayed as the obvious result of a prop strike on our initial attempt.It is my opinion that the cause of the turbulence encountered on the runway was the jet blast from the departing heavy jet rather than wake turbulence as we landed well before its point of rotation. While I do not have a copy of the Tower's audio; I do not recall any warnings from the Tower. Apparently; the 'heavy' jet took an extended amount of time to take the runway after being cleared and departed less than a minute before our touchdown. Since we could not see the plane delay taking the runway from a distance due to haze; the Tower should have warned us to avoid wake turbulence and jet blast during our approach. This would likely have prompted a decision to break off our approach at a safe altitude to allow the jet blast to dissipate; and follow trailing traffic to an uneventful landing.At 120 kts. approach speed; our ETA to land on a 5-mile final was approximately 2.5 minutes. Had the Tower held the 'heavy' cargo jet for the additional few minutes; substantial loss of property and the potential for loss of life could have been avoided. In hindsight; as PIC I could have made the decision to break off on short-final and abort the landing when I noticed the heavy cargo plane had departed so shortly before we were to land. I trusted the Tower to provide safe and adequate separation for our arrival and it could have cost us a lot more than a prop strike. I will not make that mistake again.

column121: I was working the Eagle Lake sector. Our area was getting all of the west arrivals as well as our normal arrivals due to weather. I had been coordinating with Houston Approach as to what was working best for them in terms of arrivals and how they wanted them situated since we could not get in on a normal flow. We had worked out BELLR intersection for both IAH arrivals and HOU arrivals. We were crossing HOU arrivals at 11;000 feet and IAH arrivals at 12;000 feet. After a few had made it in Houston Approach called and indicated that they did not want the aircraft stacked and wanted everyone in trail. He had also indicated that all of the aircraft were deviating upon check in with him. At this point I told him I would take care of it.Because of the weather building and starting to slowly close in I shut our corner post off. We had about 15 inbound and in terms of safety and using my best judgment I thought it would be smoother and safer if we took everyone to the southeast corner post. After I had made the decision and told the supervisor this is when the issue really began. The Supervisor; along with TMU (Traffic Management Unit) did not like this plan. They specifically told us to continue pushing these aircraft through the weather because it 'Wasn't bad enough yet'. That is a complete and utter lack of regard for safety. The mentality at Houston Center is to push aircraft through as much weather as humanly possible until a pilot decides they physically cannot make it happen. This has been the mentality for years and needs to be corrected immediately. I cannot in good conscious work airplanes through an unsafe situation just because someone with a higher position than me thinks it's OK.Ultimately when I am on position the decision should be mine on what is safe and what isn't. I am the Controller talking to the pilots; getting PIREPs and watching the weather develop real time. No one in TMU is talking to airplanes real time. They do not know the flow of the sectors real time. Houston Center's TMU is ungodly bad. They have been for years. There is never a plan and the Controllers are the ones who suffer for it. This needs rectification immediately and needs to be taken to the top of the food chain. Its not a matter of if; but when something happens because of poor judgment on managements part. This needs to be taken very seriously. It has gone on this way for far too long.Management needs to listen to Controllers when they are being told something isn't working or something isn't safe. Yes; any Controller can make a bad plan work. That doesn't mean we necessarily should.This unsafe mentality of pushing aircraft to the limit through weather will result in a safety event and it needs to get fixed before that happens.

column121: This was the second leg of an OE for the First Officer who was returning to the line after more than one year on leave. We had planned and briefed a Single Engine Taxi (SET). I asked the Pushback Crew to push the aircraft 'towards ZZZ' to better align us for SET Ops. As we were pushing; I noticed a Company aircraft on the adjacent gate was also getting ready to push and commented to the First Officer that we might have to start both engines to safely taxi away. I then realized we could make a left 270 to make our turn towards the east; to taxi to the planned runway. The Pushback Crew asked for me to set the brakes and I complied; then asked me to set the brakes as they were pulling away. This caused a chuckle from both he and I as he got jumbled with his scripted words. The First Officer had completed the #2 engine start and started his flow. He got to the Air Conditioning panel and asked if it was set correctly.I reached up and turned the #2 engine bleed on and commented that the pack was now being powered. Between the chuckle with the Pushback Crew and the First Officer query; I lost my focus and didn't notice the FO did not complete his flow and callout. I was also concerned with getting the aircraft moving in the left 270 before Company pushed. The FO called for taxi and we proceeded down CS and Mike. After being cleared onto Mike and seeing there was no line for Runway XX; I called for #1 engine to be started. The FO started it and did his After Start Flow; noticing and announcing that we hadn't set the flaps. I verified this; stopped the aircraft and commanded flaps 1; Before Taxi Checklist. These items were accomplished; we continued with normal operations and took off and flew to ZZZ1 without further incident.Don't get distracted during critical phases of flight; specifically when very specific cues are used to command flaps and run checklists.
column123: During the Crew brief; and prior to pushing back in ZZZ; the Captain briefed a single-engine taxi (SET). The Captain requested from the Tug Operator that the pushback be angled toward the turnout direction; to facilitate an easier SET break away to begin taxi.  When the pushback was complete; we discussed whether or not to start the remaining #1 engine; and abandon the SET plan; because the Pushback Crew had not pushed the aircraft in the position instructed. Ultimately; we decided to request; from the Ramp Controller; a turn in the opposite direction and continue with the SET plan.  Being on the second leg of OE; and getting familiar with the switch positions of the pressurization panel; I had stopped my after start flow at that panel; to ask the Captain a question. Inadvertently and after that interruption; I neglected to continue the flow to its completion.  Subsequently; we began our taxi without setting the flaps; which helps to trigger the Before Taxi Checklist.  When we eventually started the #1 engine during taxi out; I noticed that the flaps had not been set; as I usually re-check the items on an after start flow.  We stopped the aircraft; set the flaps; and completed the Before Taxi Checklist.  The flight continued as normal.I think that getting further comfortable with the pressurization panel; and that particular flow; will increase situational awareness and become less of a distraction.

column121: Proceeding directly to ZZZZZ intersection on the ZZZZZ 2 RNAV arrival. Was cleared to descend via ZZZZZ 2 RNAV arrival on [Runway] XXR. Prior to ZZZZZ; at approximately FL220 during descent; noticed that the cabin altitude was at 8;300 feet and increasing. I called attention to the First Officer that we might be losing cabin pressurization. The Pressurization screen on ECAM was displayed and noticed that both the inlet and extract valve were fully closed but the safety valve had opened.Since we had already been cleared to descend via ZZZZZ arrival and had an altitude of 12;000 set in the MCP I decided to expedite the descent to see if I could control the rate of ascent in the cabin. At approximately FL180 it appeared that we could not control the rate of ascent in the cabin and that at its present rate the cabin would exceed 10;000 feet shortly. I then [advised] with ATC and requested 10;000 feet which was granted. I advised the Lead Flight Attendant that we were experiencing cabin pressurization problems but to expect a normal landing. As we leveled at 10;000 feet I monitored the cabin and noticed that it had climbed to 12;000 feet but stabilized. It took several minutes before the cabin normalized at our cruise altitude of 10;000 feet. I asked the First Officer  to see if he could find an applicable checklist to run. During this time I maintained control of the aircraft and communicated with ATC. The First Officer advised that he was able to manually control the outflow valve and that the checklist recommended shallow descents thereafter. I continued to ask for delayed vectors from ATC just north of ZZZ as the First Officer and I reviewed the state of the aircraft and decided it was safe to proceed with the landing. I asked ATC for shallow descents on the arrival to [Runway] XXR into ZZZ. The landing and taxi in were uneventful.

column121: I was Pilot Flying.  The right thrust reverser was inoperative and disabled by maintenance; the left thrust reverser was available for use.  After touching down and derotating; I deployed the left thrust reverser.  When I attempted to move the thrust lever backward from idle reverse to increase reverse thrust I found that the thrust lever would not move and my hand position somehow felt different from usual.  In that same moment I realized that instead of lifting the thrust reverser unlock lever I had lifted the shutoff lock and moved the thrust lever into shutoff; shutting down the left engine.  I called out the problem to the Captain and told him I would be using only brakes to stop the aircraft.  There was plenty of runway remaining and heavy braking was not required.  We taxied to the gate using normal single engine taxi procedures.After performing several thousand landings in this aircraft I have a well developed muscle memory for engaging reverse thrust.  I also have a well developed muscle memory for shutting down the left engine during taxi.  With the right thrust reverser disabled; thrust reverser use required touching and moving only the left thrust lever instead of both thrust levers.  I am fairly certain that this interaction with only the left thrust lever subconsciously triggered the muscle memory motions for a left engine shutdown instead of those for activating the thrust reverser(s) which usually involves moving both thrust levers.  I had landed the same aircraft the day before with the same inoperative right thrust reverser and properly deployed only the left thrust reverser.  I have no other explanation for how I managed to perform the motions for an engine shutdown instead.I will be much more aware of this possibility for inadvertent incorrect hand motions possibly caused by muscle memory triggers when operating an aircraft with a deferred thrust reverser.

column121: Arriving in San Diego; we had been cleared for the RNAV Z Runway 27 approach. We checked in with the Tower and were cleared to land. I heard Tower instruct a [heavy jet] to; 'Line up and wait; traffic on an 8 mile final'. Checklists and callouts may have masked additional communications on the frequency because I can't recall whether the [heavy jet] flight was cleared for takeoff; or not. We broke out of IMC at approximately 1400 feet. The Pilot Monitoring called 'Runway in Sight - Landing'. Shortly thereafter; the First Officer said; 'Is that an airplane on the runway? I looked closer and honestly could not tell. The navigation and beacon lights were blending into the approach lights and it was difficult to distinguish the aircraft. We had to get closer before the actual structure of the airplane was apparent. We had already determined that a go-around/missed approach was necessary; but before we could communicate that to the Tower Controller; she issued the go-around instruction; 'Fly the published Missed Approach; and contact Departure'. I had observed that the offending aircraft was stationary on the runway; and not in the midst of a takeoff roll; so I knew that the published missed approach or runway heading was appropriate; and that a sidestep departure for spacing was not necessary. So we complied as instructed. We had already determined our BINGO fuel enroute and knew that we could accept one more approach before diverting to our alternate; so we accepted vectors back for another approach. The subsequent approach and landing was uneventful. The [heavy jet] had been removed from the runway and was still holding short when we landed. No mention of the reason for the go-around was given by the Tower; nor did we ask. Because we knew. There was an airplane on the runway.     Cause: [The] decision to work a Maintenance Irregularity while on an active runway. The Tower's decision to put the [heavy jet] on the runway when they were not ready to depart; and then forgetting about them. And our loss of situational awareness based on the radio communications that were; or were not; taking place on the Tower Frequency.In the future; if the First Officer questions the security of the runway; or the landing clearance; I will instruct them to simply; and without delay; to ask the Tower. This would NOT have prevented the necessity to go-around; but perhaps would have initiated the maneuver a little sooner."
column123: While on the RNAV Z 27; we were handed off to Tower and were cleared to land. This occurred at approximately SAYAE intersection. The approach continued normally and we broke out about 1;400 feet and then called 'runway in sight'; 'runway in sight landing'. Sometime after the 1;000 feet stabilized cleared to land call; I noticed what appeared to be an airplane on the displaced threshold of Runway 27 and said; 'Is that an airplane on the runway? The darkness of the displaced threshold area against the runway lights and the fact that the aircraft was in position pointed away from us made it difficult to tell. However; by the times the words were spoken; we were close enough to see. At the very same moment we began our go-around; the Tower issued instructions to go around and fly the published missed approach; which we did since the aircraft on the runway did not appear to be moving. We proceeded with a normal go-around and returned for a normal landing since we had sufficient fuel. In the simplest terms; we executed a normal go around due to an aircraft on the runway. Why was there an aircraft on the runway? I am not sure. Shortly after we were cleared to land; we heard the tower instruct [another aircraft] to line up and wait; traffic 8 mile final. I honestly don't recall hearing a take-off clearance; perhaps due our being engaged with our tasks and callouts during the approach. We did see the aircraft short of the runway when we returned. It wasn't until later that we read that they had a mechanical issue.Maintaining better awareness of traffic utilizing the runway particularly when we can't see it yet. Better awareness would have allowed us to question if the runway was indeed clear. That may not have prevented the go around this time; it would've depended on how soon we became aware."

column121: Immediately after lift off; we experienced a continuous light shudder. Gear and flaps were retracted on scheduled. The unidentifiable shudder continued to increase as airspeed increased. No shudder was felt at the control column. We requested an immediate  return to ZZZ. Following an uneventful return to land; taxi in; and shutdown at the designated parking position; it was discovered that the aircraft had a detached elevator balance tab. During the previous flight; when flaps were partially extended; a similar shudder was felt. The shudder ceased when landing gear was extended; and flaps were extended to the 30 position. During a detailed post flight inspection of flaps and gear doors; nothing was detected. The shudder was first felt in the previous approach; when flaps where partially extended. It then disappeared when landing gear was extended; and final flaps were selected. As a result; the post flight inspection was heavily focused on those two main components; flaps and landing gear doors. The balance tab; although included in the post flight inspection; did not appear to be completely loose. A more detailed inspection of all secondary flight control surfaces may have exposed the potentially damaged balance tab.

column121: I arrived to the airport of departure (ZZZ) with the owner for a reposition flight. I was referred to this owner within the Bellanca Crusiair community since I had recent time in make and model; and I am an active tailwheel CFI. The day prior to this flight I met with a very competent and experienced Cruisair owner/pilot; who has 600 hours in make and model to refresh me on systems and flying characteristics of the aircraft. 	The new owner and I had briefed the route of flight and pertinent details over the phone the days before; as well as in person prior to pushing the aircraft out of the hangar that morning. I conducted a thorough preflight in accordance with the 'Bellanca Crusiair Senior 13-14 Handbook of Instructions.' I also discussed recent maintenance that was conducted on the aircraft with the local mechanic and owner. I found no discrepancies with Aircraft X and proceeded to enter the aircraft along with the owner for our flight. Engine start was normal; as I saw a prompt rise in oil and fuel pressure. Oil temperature closely followed. Soon after I proceeded to taxi to the run up area for the active runway at ZZZ. A run up showed instruments; flight controls; and the engine to be performing as expected and normally. The aircraft was properly configured for takeoff and I made a radio call on CTAF to indicate we would be departing Runway XX straight out. The take off and climb were normal given the high altitude and density altitude conditions that existed. Upon climb out; and at a safe height; I performed the procedure to switch tanks. Switching the tanks resulted in no issues and fuel pressure and engine power was maintained. Shortly after this time I had leaned the mixture to provide adequate power as we ascended in our climb.	After 5-8 minutes in a cruise climb configuration and on the left tank we experienced an unprovoked gradual reduction in power. This was indicated by a loss of RPM; thrust; and fuel pressure. I quickly enriched mixture; suspecting that the mixture may have creeped out and the engine was running too lean. This did not completely restore the loss of power; but it did not make the situation worse. I lowered the nose and promptly swapped to the right hand tank; which completely fixed the issue. I turned back towards ZZZ so that I would be closer to an adequate landing area and to decide on the continuation of our flight. Another power loss event occurred; this time with the right tank selected; with a slightly more profound loss in power once I was enroute to the airport. After running the engine in this configuration at a safe altitude and within ample gliding distance of the airport I swapped back to the left tank. I was unable to replicate the issue over time and deemed that it could have been a random anomaly; perhaps air in the fuel lines; and proceeded on course. It was also at this time when I received flight following to ZZZ1; from Center. 	After 5-8 minutes in a cruise configuration we experienced the issue again; except this reduction in power was longer and more severe. From this point forward several things happened consecutively in order to keep the engine running. I was swapping tanks to hopefully remedy the issue; excising the wobble pump whenever power loss or fuel pressure was nonexistent; and exercised the mixture and throttle controls. We experienced the power loss events regardless of which fuel tank was selected. I was operating each of these systems independently and deliberately; actively attempting to keep the engine running and hopefully avoiding a possible prolonged power failure. Over time the loss of power was random and increasing in severity. It was also during these actions I informed Center of our situation; but not [requesting priority] at that time. After repeated engine failures that seemed to be gradually increasing in frequency and intensity; where at least two of which caused complete power loss for at least 1-2 seconds; I decided to notify ATC in fear of landing in the barren terrain between us and ZZZ. ZZZ3 Approach provided an accurate heading back ZZZ and timely ASOS information; all of which contributed to the safe outcome of this event. Upon reaching the airport; and after deeming a safe altitude; I performed a deliberate power to idle approach since I could not rely on on-demand power. I performed a tight pattern and landed smoothly on the runway. We taxied off the runway under our own power. I contacted ZZZ3 Approach via the local clearance delivery phone number and by radio to inform that we safely landed. We then proceeded to taxi to the hangar of origination and informed the mechanic of what we just experienced.

column121: I called the [Radar Controller] for a briefing. During the briefing Aircraft X was given an approach clearance for the ILS XX [at] ZZZ. The [Radar Controller] indicated it would be a missed approach by point at a flight plan on file departing ZZZ. When he asked if I had questions at the end of the briefing; I inquired about the ZZZ1 radar outage and made a comment about its implications. We were now on the same page. The missed approach on the ILS goes to 4000 ft. We had traffic at 5000 ft. looking for a visual approach to ZZZ2. The [Radar Controller] said they would vector the ILS traffic on the missed approach. VFR conditions prevailed at ZZZ. Aircraft X checked in on the missed approach and mode C indicated 1000 ft. Radar was not lost during the approach. The [Radar Controller] immediately vectored the aircraft to a 040 heading. We commonly utilize vectors below the MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) at ZZZ; but this is not available when the ZZZ1 radar is out of service. In this case; both the [Radar Controller] and [Radar Assist] didn't catch the error in a timely manner. I noticed the error occurred when I called ZZZ3 Approach to [request] the aircraft direct ZZZZZ and climbing to 4000 ft. I immediately told the [Radar Controller] after. We commonly use vectors below the MIA and know the implications of ZZZ1 radar outage. Many use a visual memory aid by marking a cross over the radar station when its inoperative. The outage window on the EDST (Enroute Decision Support Tool) and radar screen are suppressed during normal operations. Outages like VORs and RADAR are easily missed or disregarded. Perhaps better memory aids could be used.

column121: Yesterday we were flying ZZZ1-ZZZ. I was Pilot Flying. The flight was smooth and VFR going into ZZZ. ZZZ was landing Runway XX. The aircraft was downwind and I was at speed 230 and asked for flaps 1; speed 190. Once the flaps started coming out we noticed a light vibration which was consistent. Like driving down a bumpy road. The vibration continued until the gear came out and we slowed to 150. The rest of the landing I did not notice the vibration continue on landing. We landed; exited the runway and parked. Our Maintenance person went outside to do an inspection of the airplane and see if he could find the cause of vibration. The pilot monitoring and me also went out to see if we noticed anything unusual. Extended the flaps and the spoilers checking everything. Maintenance did not see an issue. The second flight going from ZZZ-ZZZ2 I was pilot monitoring. After lift off we noticed the same vibration very quickly. We retracted the gear and flaps on schedule. Then the PF (Pilot Flying) leveled off at 3;000 feet. We still had the same vibration and decided to return to ZZZ. Not exceeding 210 knots. The weather was still VFR and we landed Runway XX. We did not [request priority with ATC]. Once parked; our Maintenance person started a full inspection of the airplane. Into the inspection the elevator trim on the left of the tail was different than on the right. The Captain went into the cockpit and moved the flight controls up and down and the left trim tab was not moving the same as the right side. Maintenance personnel went up and inspected the trim tab on the left and found the control rod was not connected and it moved freely. Making a strange sound. Shortly after this we were told to head to the hotel so Maintenance could work on the issue. The aircraft recently sustained substantial damage in ZZZ3. The aircraft tail was damaged. I believe the two are connected. We came back and landed in ZZZ; very quick flight.

column121: I reviewed the maintenance log when I arrived at the aircraft for the first flight of the day. It had just been released from maintenance. It had previously been written up for a strong smell coming from the lavatory. The corrective action stated that the lavatory had been leaking into the cargo bay. It had been repaired the same day and I was the first to fly the aircraft. I included this information with my crew brief.During the descent to ZZZ1; sometime prior to FL180 because the descent checklist had yet to be completed; the FO (First Officer) and I heard what sounded like an extra loud flushing noise from the FWD LAV (Forward Lavatory); but then developed into a loud sound similar to an engine spooling down; immediately followed by a strange; slightly chemical odor. We both looked at each other and confirmed what we heard and smelled. I called the A F/A (Flight Attendant) to verify if anyone had just flushed the toilet. She said someone was in the lavatory; had just flushed; and it smelled strongly like excrement.The odor quickly subsided. We discussed the possible sources. The LAV was a different style from most of our aircraft so it could have just been a sound [different] than what we were used to. The LAV had just been repaired so the odor could have been related. Since there odor was gone and there were no other indications of abnormality we continued to ZZZ1 but I had the FO start reviewing synoptic pages for any clues and I started reviewing possible diversion airports. We made a list of airports closest to our position as we got closer to ZZZ1; ZZZ2; then ZZZ3; then ZZZ4.During descent after passing through FL180; I started to hear and feel the aircraft surging. It sounded like it was coming from the engines. I de-cluttered the EICAS to check for vibration. There was a notable difference in engine vibration; but they were still in the green and there were no other indications on the EICAS.At approximately 13;000 ft. the FO and I both noticed a strong acrid odor. I called the A F/A who confirmed the LAV was not in use. I then called for the Smoke; Fire; Fumes QRC (Quick Reference Checklist). We donned our oxygen masks and the FO started through the QRC. We were almost exactly on top of ZZZ3; which we had already decided as a suitable airport; so when the FO [read the steps related to ATC] of the QRH (Quick Reference Handbook) I told him to [request priority handling] and ask to land at ZZZ3 immediately.ATC assigned an ALT of 9;000 ft. As I started to descend; the aircraft began shaking violently. ATC continued to vector and assign lower altitudes. When the FO turned off the RECIRC fans per the QRH; I asked him to put the checklist down and set up the aircraft for landing. We were very close to the airport and descending quickly. I decided the priority was for the FO to get our landing numbers and set up the approach while coordinating with ATC and the FA's. I could not help because I suspected external damage to the control surfaces so I did not want to take my attention away from maintaining positive control of the aircraft.Somewhere around the 9;000 ft. mark or lower we received an EICAS PACK 1 FAIL. This was the first time the EICAS provided any kind of indication of an abnormality. We had experienced a loud noise; strong odors; violent shaking; and now a PACK 1 FAIL. It felt as if the aircraft had suffered major damage and safe completion of the flight was at serious risk. ATC had placed us on a downwind for the ILS but; fearing we may be losing more systems and controllability; I told the FO we were turning immediately to final. As we slowed to approach speeds the shaking reduced. The FO contacted the FA's to go over [procedures]. I did not order a brace and I did not intend to evacuate. The aircraft was stabilizing and there weren't any smoke or fire indications in the cabin or flight deck. I landed and stopped on the runway. I requested an inspection by the fire trucks to make sure the aircraft wasn't on fire and we were safe to taxi. I made an announcement for everyone to remain seated and that we had landed due to a maintenance issue; but that the aircraft was safe and we were taxiing to a gate.In our judgement; due to the order and severity of events; we thought the aircraft may be in serious jeopardy. An immediate landing was the safest option available. I have often conducted a very similar scenario with FO's on long flights out of the area and near ZZZ3; during cruise. The scenario is a fume event. The reason this is important is because the QRH for fumes is very long and involves a lot of system isolation for troubleshooting. It would take 20-30 minutes for us to review the QRH in a relaxed; stable environment. Only at the end of the QRH do you see just how much runway would be required if you're heavy and have taken a lot of performance penalties due to the QRH troubleshooting process. Because we were so close to the airport and descending quickly; I prioritized performance and navigation over completing the QRH. There simply was not enough time for the full checklist.Parked at the gate; I called Dispatch and explained what was going on. They weren't aware of the diversion. The FO had asked ATC to notify our company during descent. I was getting bounced around a lot between Dispatch and [Administration] with Maintenance talking to them in the background; but Maintenance immediately insisted that it was a simple air system failure and that the aircraft was safe. Both the FO and I conducted a walk-around. I said the aircraft was not safe to fly. I wouldn't have landed in ZZZ3 if I thought the aircraft was safe. This aircraft needs a full maintenance inspection based on the severity of conditions we had just experienced. [In the past] I've had a hydraulic line rupture at FL200; I've had a brake failure on landing; I've had a full system failure. This was like nothing I had experienced and felt far more severe at the time than just a simple air system failure. It was serious enough that I didn't know if we would make the runway. This aircraft had a recent history of fluids leaking into the cargo bay. How much unseen damage was caused by these fluids? Why wouldn't an inspection be required if the maintenance department is saying 'oh yeah the smell and shaking is from the system blowing out'? As I'm trying to convince Dispatch and Maintenance that an inspection needs to be conducted; this is already approaching about 2 hours after landing; the adrenaline started to fade and the fatigue settled in. The entire crew was exhausted to the point that even the FA's were fatigued. Having drilled this scenario; I believe I acted appropriately given the circumstances. QRH calls for system isolation to identify the source but with odor being cause of the [diversion] and no EICAS indications there is no way to verify the source without taking the O2 mask off; which is extremely dangerous. We were so close and working with so little time that getting on the ground immediately became the top priority.

column121: This was not a good flight because of compounding errors that happened and the negative effect that they had.  The good part is that the flight remained safe; but here below are several things that I learned.  The events started when on decent into ZZZ when the lights on the autopilot mode selector began to flicker erratically; however the autopilot appeared to perform normally.  This was in IMC descent thru layers with occasional moderate turbulence.  (The was second flight after the power supply to the EFIS system failed resulting in loss of the primary attitude indicator and HSI which was repaired and return to service.  I mention this only because it attributed to my increase lack of trust in the flight instruments.) The autopilot was on altitude preselect with a vertical speed selected.  During the decent I was evaluating the autopilot issue and I think; after the fact; I pushed the altitude capture twice; resulting in me disengaging the capture and descending below the desired altitude.  At the time I attributed this to a malfunction autopilot and I decided to disconnect the autopilot and manually flew the plane.  This increased the workload.  Weather was also a significant factor.  There was a line of thunderstorms that were moving over ZZZ (destination) and I was watching the satellite radar utilizing a portable GDL52 communicating to Garmin pilot on my I pad. For this flight I was using ForeFlight for navigation/charts and Garmin Pilot for weather; because the GDL would not communicate satellite radar information to ForeFlight.  I have been using ForeFlight for charts and weather in previous aircraft for many years; but this aircraft has only ADSB-out and is scheduled to have an avionics upgrade to a GDL69a (sat WX) and Garmin 345 (ADSB IN/Out) installation in Month.  I was also utilizing the onboard radar; but am learning to use this system.  Bottom line was too many nav / weather systems in use that resulted in unnecessary and additional workload. Another factor was that I had transitioned from a piston to a turboprop and had about 80 hours in the TBM time at the time of this flight. So I was still low on the TBM experience curve.   Based on the weather I requested GPS XX and activated the approach on the 530s. However; as I proceeded to ZZZ GPS XX; the weather changed and the IAF for GPS XX was near the line of thunderstorms and center offered ILS XY and left turn to heading for the IAF - I made a right turn to that heading.  I should have recognized that I was starting to make small mistakes. During this time I also was varying from assigned altitude due to increase workload.   I entered ILS XX in to the 530S and activated and Center vectored me to the approach.   I began the approach and was able to see the ground occasionally.  I was handed off the Tower and I waited to capture the glideslope. I continued the approach; my position and altitude were not cross checking; and I began try to determine why.  I was high when I was on a 2-3 mile final.  While making this evaluation; I was able to see the runway lights and able to make a visual decent and landing.  I was not confident after this flight; there were too many mistakes in this flight.  When I was on the ground I contacted my flight instructor and went over flight and discussed the avionics and my reaction/ decision I made.  We made a plan of how to determine the effect of the flickering light on the mode selector and insure that it was safe for flight.  I altered my plans so that weather would have a minimal impact and returned back to ZZZ1.  To learn and avoid these errors in the future; I did a full debrief with my instructor when I return home.  This focused on both the avionics and cross reference that he recommended to determine status of the navigation system.  We also spent a considerable time on how I responded to the apparent situation and decision making.  It was at this time; I realized how much some minor errors in my part had a large impact onthe flight.  The avionics have also been evaluated by Company in ZZZ2 and determine that the malfunction was limited to the mode selector display and that the autopilot is functioning normally. It is schedule to be repaired.   Further I have also flow approaches in VFR conditions to verify operations of the navigation and autopilot systems and apply some of the procedures that my instructor and I discussed.

column121: While doing pattern work on Runway 30L; we requested a full-stop on Runway 3. Tower instructed us to 'make left downwind.' My student and I turned left to enter the left downwind Runway 3; at this time; Aircraft Y traffic was mid-field downwind Runway 30L. Traffic was cleared touch-and-go Runway 30L. Without further instruction; my student and I proceeded with a standard left pattern Runway 3. On 0.25 nm final; I see the traffic landing the parallel is still rolling on the runway; and I did not anticipate them being clear of my runway by the time my student and I crossed the threshold Runway 3; so I instructed my student to execute a go-around. This resulted in our Aircraft X directly overflying the Aircraft Y right as they rolled across Runway 3 on Runway 30L. They were not yet airborne.In hindsight; I believe Tower's instruction to make left downwind may have been intended as extend downwind; or they would call my base. Since this instruction was not given; we made a normal pattern and did not anticipate a conflict until short final.Earlier on the same flight; we had been doing full-stop-taxi-backs; and we landed Runway 30L; and exited left onto Taxiway B. The same controller gave us taxi instructions 'Runway 30L taxi via Delta' and I asked if I needed 'cross Runway 3.' During this same flight; I had prompted the previous controller a couple of times; and gotten the instruction to cross each time; but only after prompting for it. The next controller volunteered; 'we don't normally do that.' She did give me the crossing; but I am wondering why we do not volunteer that crossing since it is necessary to cross the full-hold bar for Runway 3 in order to turn left onto Taxiway D from Taxiway B; or the other way to turn right onto Taxiway B from Taxiway D.

column121: I was flying with a family member to go sight seeing around downtown Pittsburgh when we encountered a hazardous situation with another aircraft. In this report I want to describe exactly what happened; how I think this situation could have been avoided; and what could be done in the future to prevent this from happening again.At about XA:30 local time; I was approaching Pittsburgh from the east in Aircraft X. cruising at about 80mph at 2;100 ft. MSL. My intended course of flight was to fly west over the Monongahela river; make a shallow turn over the north side; then proceed outbound over the Allegheny river. When I was approaching downtown; I saw Aircraft Y about 1.5 miles ahead of me flying on a head on course at my altitude. I rocked my wings a few times and turned to the right. When the Aircraft Y pilot saw me; he turned to the right and proceeded behind me.I then continued along my intended route along the Monongahela river and flew at 2;000 ft.. After passing point park; I turned northbound to continue with my plan. I saw off my 2 o'clock position about 1.5 miles out the same Aircraft Y flying westbound towards my intended route. At this point in time; I could not turn to the right due to the skyscrapers downtown and if I continued going straight or to the left we would be converging. I decided to take evasive action and turn around back over the Monongahela river by performing a steep turn to the left. While I was performing the turn to the left; Aircraft Y changed course and was flying over point park at this time doing another lap around the city. At this time; Aircraft Y was converging on my location by flying a southeast heading while I was flying an easterly heading. To give way; I flew as far south as I could with out causing any obstacle hazards; but Aircraft Y continued towards my location. Due to Mt. Washington (a large hill with more skyscrapers on top) was to the south; I could not turn to the right. I also could not turn to the left due to the traffic. I decided to add full power and pitch for Vy to slow down; as well as regain the altitude I loss during my steep turn. Aircraft Y; traveling at a faster speed; turned right directly in front of me and proceeded to AGC to the south.For this flight; I calculated ground elevation to be at 765 ft. using the Pittsburgh TAC (1613-848=765). I decided 2;000 ft. would be a good buffer for obstacle clearance and Class B Airspace clearance. During the steep turn I descended to 1;800 ft. due to lack of concentration caused by the traffic I was avoiding. During this flight; I was flying an aircraft that was not originally manufactured with an electrical system and was complying with Part 91.225(e) and 91.215(b)(3).Reflecting on this incident; I believe this could have been easily avoided if the Aircraft Y pilot would have been scanning for traffic and noticed me. In both encounters; I began making evasive maneuvers over a mile in advance while the other pilot continued turning towards me. If an emphasis on see-and-avoid would have been done in this busy airspace; this problem would have been mitigated.Going forward; I believe that there could be some regulatory measures to improve safety in this particular environment. From my experience flying sightseeing flights over Niagara Falls and the Hudson River; I believe that providing a CTAF frequency for VFR aircraft to communicate with makes flying in dense traffic much safer and organized. My suggestion in the future would be to add a note on the Pittsburgh TAC chart with a CTAF frequency; insert a note requiring pilots to contact AGC Tower or PIT Approach; or add a Part 93 regulation standardizing the direction of traffic flow around the golden triangle area. With Class B boundaries above and to the west of the city; large buildings in the city itself; a mountain with large towers to the south; large radio towers to the north; as well as multiple hospital helicopter pads in the city; I believe this is a very complex airspace that could afford to have special procedures to be complied with in this airspace. In conclusion; this occurrence was a result of lack of visual scanning procedures. With this airspace being particularly complex as well as congested due to medical flights and sightseeing flights; I believe all pilots should exercise extremes caution in this area.

column121: I was flying a helicopter near the south end of the ZZZ Class C airspace. I was flying over the ridgeline at about 1;700 feet when the Tower advised of Aircraft Y east abound approaching my location. At that point Aircraft Y was about 500 feet above us and a mile west of our location. ATC tower also told the other aircraft of our location and he informed the tower that he had visual contact with us. I immediately descended near the ridgeline (to about 1;500 feet MSL) and turned south east away from the approaching aircraft. I saw him pass behind me. column121: Runways 8/15 in use. Arriving Runway 8 and departing Runway 15.I was on CIC at the time of this event. After I finished talking with GC; I sat back down at the CIC position. Aircraft Y was on about a 1.5 mile final to Runway 8 as I saw Aircraft X taxiing onto Runway 15.
