I asked LC; 'Is Aircraft X rolling? Did you LUAW him or clear him for takeoff?' LC said he didn't think he had cleared him for takeoff. I told him to cancel Aircraft X's takeoff clearance immediately; which he did. The aircraft had rolled about 1;000 to 1;500 feet by the time they aborted.After this incident; a supervisor listened to the tapes and confirmed that LC had indeed cleared Aircraft X for takeoff. I'm not sure whether it was inadvertent and he meant to give him a LUAW clearance or whether he just forgot about Aircraft Y on final.Don't fall into a sense of complacency.Don't allow distractions to take your focus away from your primary duties. I am often teased about it; but when we are busy with many critical situations happening at once; and especially when we have CIC combined with GC; I will not answer the outside phone line until our traffic isn't as busy. I don't want to take my eyes off the busy operation in order to get a phone call from the airport authority about a NOTAM for a taxiway light bulb that's going to be OTS (Out of Service) during the mid-two weeks from now. (CIC was not combined in this situation)LC's scan should have been focused more heavily on making sure that Runway 15 traffic was not moving when Runway 8 traffic was on short final. column121: IFR flight to ZZZ. Weather was not a factor. Departed PHX from Runway 7R; runway heading assigned. After approaching 1;000 feet AGL; assigned heading 050. Switched to Phoenix Departure on 119.2; then 120.7 within a minute or two. Controller gave me instructions to 'turn left heading 360; vectors to intercept the PXR 350 radial.' Knowing I was on a diverging path away from my flight-planned route; I was waiting for at least one more turn that would take me toward the radial. This turn occurred within the next few minutes with the controller saying 'turn left heading 270'. Now on an intercept heading with the radial; I made a right turn to join the PXR 350. The Departure Controller quickly gave me instructions to fly heading 260 (which I immediately complied with) asking why I had made the turn north. The remainder of the flight occurred without incident.In hindsight; here's what I learned during this exchange. Despite the numerous flight hours operating in the PHX ATC system; I somehow mistakenly interpreted 'intercept' with 'join'. I knew a 360 heading would not intercept the planned radial. So; I was expecting that next turn to put me on course to do so. What I wasn't told; was the 270 heading was for spacing from other traffic; not necessarily to intercept or join the PXR 350 radial. Had I known why (traffic) I was being turned to a 270 heading; then my thought process would've completely changed and I would've known; without question; to continue on the assigned heading. Instead; I was thinking this was simply the heading that would allow me to intercept the 350 radial. Despite my error; I should have questioned the heading as the intercept angle was 80 degrees; not the standard 30 degrees one would expect. In doing so; the Controller would have simply advised me to remain on the 270 heading and expect another turn to intercept and join the airway. As pilots; we must deal with many human factors on a daily basis. Some of those factors thwart our efforts to fly safe and reasonably. I feel this was a situation where 'if it doesn't look right or feels oddly different' then say something. Questions are always free. Accidents are costly. Routinely flying the same routes and hearing the same instructions from ATC can also create a unique set of issues. We don't always hear what was said; we hear what we expect. And this human factor is one that all pilots must concentrate on avoiding.

column121: There was a momentary unreliable airspeed followed by a brief failure of the PF's (Pilot Flying) PFD. Once the PFD was restored; airspeed was still momentarily unreliable.While operating the flight from ZZZ to ZZZZ; I was the pilot flying. After deviating for weather; we were proceeding directly to ZZZZZ to perform the VOR DME 2 [approach to] Runway XX at ZZZZ. Approximately 20nm from ZZZZZ and descending; we encountered IMC and light precipitation and light turbulence which gradually increased to moderate turbulence. We were partially configured at flaps 1 and gear was down at 200 kts and beginning our turn for the arc when my airspeed began having deviations of +/- 15 kts; I attributed this to the increasing turbulence and precipitation we had encountered. While banked and descending; the PLIs (Pitch Limit Indicator) presented and I had a loss of airspeed below the green dot and a gain of airspeed that presented amber digits. At this point my airspeed completely went away; as if I was on the ground; a grey box was present where the digits would be but there was no V-Speed information. Shortly after this occurred; my PFD went black for a moment; but never reverted to a different display. Once this happened; I transitioned to the IESS (Integrated Electronic Standby System); rolled the wings level; advanced the thrust levers; climbed to ensure terrain clearance; and we returned to VMC.Nearly immediately after establishing the climb; the PFD and all information on it returned; although there were errors with the airspeed. Initially; the airspeed showed faster than we were; as if we had been repositioned in the simulator; and we received one aural 'High-speed' until the airspeed settled back to what the IESS was showing. Our altitude at this point was approximately between 17;000 ft. and 16;000 ft. with a high peak around 9827 ft. in our vicinity. From our descent; I knew I could find VMC around 19;000 ft. so I directed the pilot not flying to tell ATC we would be present heading and climbing to 20;000 ft.I did not direct the PNF (Pilot Not Flying) to declare an emergency as we were busy figuring out what just happened and coordinating a plan between each other. In the climb; we cleaned the aircraft up and ran an after takeoff checklist. Once we were in VMC; we worked with each other to determine that all of our instruments matched and were reliable. We also determined that we could remain mostly VMC by performing the approach from ZZZZZ1 and asked to proceed directly to ZZZZZ1. We successfully performed the approach and landing at ZZZZ. Upon exiting the runway; we received both AFCS (Automated Flight Control System) Fault; and ADS Probe 1 Fail messages. We felt that we could have been struck by lightning; but we could not find any strike points on the aircraft; and all static wicks that were visible to us were found intact. We entered both messages above in the AML as well as an AML entry for a possible lightning strike.I feel my actions were appropriate given that we were not in radar contact any longer. I was unsure if I could trust any pitot or static instruments and I knew where I could find visual conditions away from terrain. I should have declared an emergency but at the time I felt that doing so with the language barrier would have broken down my communication with my First Officer when we needed to focus on flying the aircraft. Additionally; he was able to secure a clearance for the same heading up to 20;000 ft. as soon as I asked him to do so.

column121: After a normal flight from ZZZ we descended for the visual approach to ZZZZ; due to no response from anybody on the ground at ZZZZ; I elected to do an over flight of the airport at pattern altitude of 1;500 ft. with the autopilot disconnected; crossing over midfield from north to south on the east west runway to enter a left hand crosswind for the left pattern landing east; we started configuring the aircraft for landing by selecting flaps to the #2 position; on the left downwind leg we selected the gear handle down; at that point we received an amber CAS message of GEAR MISCOMPARE R The nose gear and left main indicated down(GREEN) the right main gear was an AMBER X. While the First Officer (FO) looked for the message in the Emergency Procedures checklist I engaged the Auto Pilot and Auto throttles and climbed to 2;000 and stayed in an extended racetrack pattern around ZZZZ. At this point we informed the passenger of the situation and was thinking that the procedure should work and we would land at ZZZZ. We followed gear will not extend checklist; pulling the blow down handle; no change; the pulling the main gear uplock handle; no change the last procedure in the checklist was to try and yaw the airplane. We informed the passengers what to expect; and tried the yaw left then right twice; no change. At this point I made the decision to divert to ZZZ1 again informing the passengers what the plan was; they were fine with that because they had used a local company at ZZZ1 to take them to ZZZZ before. We pickup a clearance to ZZZ1 with ZZZ2 Center; and informed them of our situation. After that hand off to ZZZ2 Approach Control; the controller asked us if we would like a fly by for visual verification of the gear status. We chose to do this option; and he coordinated with the tower. I felt very confident that the gear was down because when the FO pulled the uplock handle he felt very little resistance; from my past experience that is a good indication the gear was not in the uplock. With blow down in the system the gear only has one place to go; so I felt with a very high degree of certainty that the right main was down and locked. The weather at ZZZ1 was VMC 10 miles 5;000 ft. Scattered wind was 110/18 gusting 24. After being vectored for the visual low pass over Runway XXR at ZZZ1 Tower informed us that Airfield Operations was in a position to observe our low pass; we had the aircraft fully configured for landing and made the low pass at 300 AGL and 140kts. Airfield Ops confirmed that he saw three gear. We executed the climb out instructions cleaned up the aircraft except for the gear remaining down; then we were vectored for another visual approach to land Runway XXR at ZZZ1. During our patterned we went ahead and [received priority]; to have the trucks just in case. Also the FO radioed Company ZZZ1 if they could have a van meet us to take our passengers to their requested destination on the field; and if they would call the Company1 maintenance facility and let them know we were inbound. We reconfigured the aircraft for landing while on a 3mile final we slowed to final approach speed and with Airfield Ops and the fire trucks standing by we made a normal landing with an extended rollout; confirming the gear was indeed down. We cleared the runway and taxied to the Company1 maintenance facility. We deplaned the passengers and got them on their way immediately. I informed the maintenance staff of the issue and they pulled the aircraft in the hanger and did a visual inspection of the gear. They found that the uplock switch; which is a plunger type; was stuck in the gear up position making the computer think the gear was still in the well.

My intention was to run a new before Takeoff checklist to clean it up and be ready to go. At this time; a FA called to ask if someone could use the restroom to which I said no. Then ATC called 2 or 3 different time to inquire about a desired heading on departure. The stop was then lifted and we departed. Upon reaching acceleration altitude the FO realized we were still at flaps 1 when he was looking to clean up. At that point I realized I had failed in following up on the before Takeoff checklist.The takeoff itself was uneventful with no more than light chop and moderate rain during initial climb. We debriefed our error for the next hour and a half on our way to ZZZ1. I clearly had failed in letting the distractions take my focus off of the checklist. The weather itself was just a rain shower with no gusts; no wind shear; no lightning and our fancy MAX radar didn't show any of the severe weather cues that it is capable of showing. My FO had told me he had flown very little during the pandemic so my flaps 1 vs 5 concern was more related to his recent experience that to the weather.Another threat was the MAX. We don't get to fly them that often (yet) and I find my eyes are 'lost' when trying to scan the gauges that have always been in the same place for the last XX+ years. Now; many of them have moved. The flap indicator was not where it normally is. That may have caught my attention before accepting a takeoff clearance in an NG.Fortunately for us we were utilizing VR max procedures as this gave us additional speed over and above the flap 1 speeds. Our flaps 5 VR max was 167 which was 8 knots higher than our flaps 1 VR of 159. The tail strike potential of utilizing the published flaps 5 speed on a reduced takeoff with flaps 1 selected is very clear to me. I will no longer be doing flaps 1 takeoffs in [other make/model] airplanes.  Most FOs ask me about my flap preferences for takeoff. I gather many captains don't do flaps 1 in the bigger airplanes.

column121: ZZZ is [near] the BDL 5 nm Class C surface area. During a training flight while returning to ZZZ from BAF; we were using flight following from Y90 TRACON and squawking a discrete code. We were in the Class E airspace beneath the 2;100 MSL shelf of the Class C. As we approached our destination; ATC told us 'Radar services terminated; squawk 1200; frequency change approved.' At this time; we were approximately 1 mile from the Class C surface area. Given our trajectory; it was obvious to the Controller that we were headed direct to our destination and would enter the Class C airspace. Since we were in communication with Y90 and had not been advised to change course or remain clear of the Class C airspace; we assumed that we were cleared into the Class C surface area. We continued into Class C surface area and landed. TRACON usually either advises us to remain clear of the Class C surface area or switches us to the tower frequency.We did not conflict with other traffic in the area as traffic departing BDL was turning away from us and climbing well above our altitude. We were later advised that there could have been an incursion into the Class C airspace.This could have been avoided if we had questioned the Controller to confirm that [we] were cleared into the Class C surface area. We also could have not assumed that we were cleared into the Class C Surface area and altered course to remain clear. The Controller could have told us to remain clear of the Class C airspace or switched us to tower frequency rather than terminating radar services.
column123: During a training flight to ZZZ from BAF we were using flight following from BDL TRACON and squawking a discrete code. We were in the Class E airspace beneath the 2100 MSL shelf of the Class C.As we approached our destination; which is located [near] the BDL Class C surface area; ATC told us 'Radar services terminated; squawk VFR; frequency change approved.' At this time; we were just outside the Class C surface area. Given our direct trajectory to ZZZ; and the fact that we had communicated this was our intention to both BDL TRACON (and prior to that; the BAF Tower); we thought it was obvious to the Controller that we were headed directly to our destination and would imminently enter the Class C surface area airspace.This was because we were in communication with BDL TRACON and had not been advised to change course or remain clear of the Class C airspace. This was (in hindsight) a possibly incorrect assumption on our behalf that we were cleared into the Class C surface area.As such; we continued into the Class C surface area and landed. In the past; TRACON BDL has usually either advised us to remain clear of the Class C surface area or has switched us to the BDL tower frequency if they did not want us to pursue a direct route from BAF to ZZZ. We were later advised by BDL Tower (not BDL TRACON) that there could have been an incursion into the Class C airspace.My learning: this could have been avoided if we had questioned the BDL TRACON Controller to confirm that we were indeed cleared into the Class C surface area. We should also have not assumed that we were cleared into the Class C Surface area and we should have altered our direct course to remain clear. I do realize that the BDL TRACON Controller could have told us to remain clear of the Class C airspace or switched us to BDL Tower frequency rather than terminating radar services; but I have to focus on what I can directly control in the future in order to remain a safe pilot.

Prior to reaching ILC ATC initiated change in my routing to keep me clear of 'military airspace '. Revised routing was direct KITTN direct KATTS direct OAL then flight planned route. I entered above fixes in FMS and selected direct KITTN. At this point I pulled up every Jeppesen and government chart available to me and tried to understand this revised routing. ATC said it was to keep me clear of military airspace but there is no charted airspace on J58 above 17;999 ft.Was ATC lying? Was ATC mistaken? What is my elevated level of risk from deviating from flight planned route due to ATC ERROR . Should I query ATC? Is ATC error of immediate danger to me? As I was pouring over charts trying to determine if there was some charted military air space at my altitude that I was simply missing ATC advises turn right 30 degrees . I turn right 30 degrees. ATC advises that I was off course and had appeared to proceed from KITTN direct to OAL rather than KITTN KATTS OAL. I reviewed FMS and ATC was correct. Although I had entered the revised routing in the FMS ; the FMS glitched and sequenced in error from KITTN Direct to OAL .I explained what appeared to have happened to ATC . Controller said I had come within 1 mile if penetrating this military airspace which I still could not find on any government or Jeppesen chart at my altitude. I took down the Controller's telephone number and agreed to call him after I landed to discuss this and the reason for me being issued a revised clearance. When I called the Controller he explained that the government has lots of military airspace that represent a hazard to normal flights which they purposely do NOT publish on government Enroute charts. He explained ATC was aware of these uncharted portions of military airspace and it was their job to keep the public away from this hazard. I was somewhat shocked by this admission that the government is publishing knowingly false Enroute charts that do not show military airspace hazards which the controller said in fact do exist and around which they had given me a revised routing. My FMS glitch resulted in a deviation from revised routing. But what I am concerned about is that the Enroute charts we rely on are being willfully and purposely falsified and do not reflect what controller described as many military airspace hazards that do in fact affect the flying public.

column121: Aircraft was directed to taxi from gate 1 to Runway XXL via Taxiways 1; 2; 3; 4. While on Taxiway 3; turning right to join Taxiway 4; both crew members noted an aircraft that appeared to have just been pushed back from gate 2. It was also agreed by both crew members that the tail of the aircraft appeared to be just inside the ramp boundary line. Approaching the aircraft at gate 2; the FO noted that the right wingtip was on the boundary line. The Captain then stated that he was going to deviate left of the taxiway centerline for additional clearance and the FO acknowledged. Approaching the aircraft; the FO was monitoring the right wingtip. From the cockpit angle the wingtip appeared to have approximately five feet of clearance and this was communicated to the Captain. The FO continued to monitor the wingtip until it appeared to initially pass the tail of the other aircraft outside of gate 2 and then announced it was clear to the Captain. It was at this time the right winglet struck the horizontal stabilizer. (Aircraft  speed was approximately 5 knots.)  The FO then called out to stop multiple times. The Captain stopped the aircraft and made an announcement for the Flight Attendants and Passengers to remain in their seats. The Captain verified with the Flight Attendants that everyone was OK. The crew then coordinated with Ground Control and Operations to return to gate 3. An ACARS message was also sent to Dispatch while waiting for a gate assignment. It is the FO's initial assessment that the wingtip must have started to pass on the opposite side of the horizontal stabilizer of the aircraft outside of gate 2; but incorrectly determined that it was on the near side based off the cockpit angle and understanding that the Captain had deviated left of the taxiway for more clearance. There were no distractions and the crew communicated clearly.  Actions that could have prevented this incident would have been if the crew had stopped on Taxiway 4 and waited for the aircraft at gate 2 to move and provide more clearance. Additionally; the FO could have better assessed the wingtip spacing.
column123: We were cleared to taxi from [gate] 1 to [Runway] XXL via [taxiways] 2; 3 and 4. As we were joining 4; I noticed an aircraft facing terminal at [gate] 2; which appeared to be just inside of the movement area line. I mistakenly assumed it was an aircraft that had just pushed and that he was waiting to taxi. My expectation bias was that he would not have been pushed deep enough to interfere with Taxiway 4. As we were NE bound on [Taxiway] 4; I steered aircraft left of taxi; centerline to give more clearance around other aircraft. I asked FO how we looked on wingtip clearance. The FO stated; 'We are clear by 5 to 10 feet.' As we were passing behind the aircraft I felt that a main tire hit a pothole. As I asked what that was; I felt another 'bump'. The FO stated 'Stop. Stop.' I brought the aircraft to a stop and the FO told me we struck the other aircraft. I would estimate we were at a speed of 7 to 8 knots when the contact occurred. We began our taxi on #2 engine. I believe the second engine start was complete prior to contact. There was a typical level of chatter on ZZZ Ground frequency; which was busy. After the contact; I stopped the aircraft on Taxiway 4 and set the parking brake. We reported the incident to Ground Control. While I made a PA to the cabin to remain seated; the FO notified operations to coordinate a gate return and contact Maintenance. We returned to Gate 3 without further incident.Task Loading - I did a poor job of managing task loading. ZZZ is very busy and congested on the ground. With multiple aircraft moving in a densely packed area; I should not have opted for Single Engine Taxi (SET).  This would have reduced the workload on both crew members and perhaps allowed for better situational awareness as we were moving towards the departure runway. Risk Management- I did not properly balance the risk of aircraft contact with continuing on the taxiway. Had I stopped and waited on the other aircraft to move well clear of taxiway; I would not have assumed that unnecessary risk. This also relates to rushing and trying not to clog up a taxiway. I should have set the brakes and not moved forward until aircraft in question was well clear.

column121: Upon finishing my three-day paring in ZZZ1 at (time/date) I received a phone call from Scheduling; as I was leaving the aircraft. They told me they had added on to my schedule; they needed me to deadhead to ZZZ; then ferry an aircraft back to ZZZ1. I was concerned because I had already flown quite a bit that day and was afraid that I would not be legal for it. The Scheduler assured me that I was legal and that it was all okay. I asked them to look into it again because I had my doubts. I then asked if they could provide a hotel for rest at the end of the turn as I would be extremely tired. She claimed she would pass it on to the hotel desk. Upon contacting the hotel desk they said they could only provide a room if there was an unused ZZZ1 overnight room; which there was not.I proceeded onto the gate for the first leg of the ZZZ turn. Inside 30 minutes to departure there was no crew or other deadheading crewmember present at the aircraft. The flight to ZZZ was scheduled completely empty except for the Operating Crew; myself and one other deadheader. Again; I was concerned that I would time out before we could complete the turn so took it upon myself to prepare the aircraft for departure and set up the cockpit for the Operating Crew; in order to expedite our departure. We eventually departed 18 minutes later than planned. Upon reaching ZZZ; the operating First Officer left to recover a diverted aircraft back to ZZZ1 and I quickly prepared our aircraft for our return to ZZZ1. Unfortunately; once again; our aircraft experienced multiple delays due to random unexplainable maintenance locks; issues with load and balance calculation and performance. As we sat on the ramp at ZZZ I could tell that I would soon be in danger of timing out and verified my legalities. It showed a Table B Limit of XX42C without extension. At roughly XXX25CI called Crew Scheduling and notified them I was within 20 minutes of reaching the latest takeoff limit; and asked them what their plan was. The Scheduler on the line said that there was someone looking into my legalities and that they would call me back. That call never came. Shortly thereafter the aircraft issues were resolved and we were able to depart at XX37CF; just five minutes before the XX42C takeoff limit. With the aid of computer program and the printed crew legalities sheet; it appeared we had taken off within limits and were completely legal to fly the flight.Upon landing at ZZZ1 at XX04C; we were told that there were no gates available we would have to hold on the pad until one became available. Shortly after parking in the pad; we received an ACARS message referencing my employee number and requesting a flight delay extension. It showed several times; but those times did not match any times on the calculator on computer program. It was confusing and seemed to be in error. Since we were parked in the pad with the parking brake set; the Captain took the radios and I called Crew Scheduling. I explained we were on the ground waiting for a gate; I told them I had received the ACARS message and that it did not make sense - I asked for clarification and the implications of accepting or rejecting. They placed me on a brief hold but when they came back they were not able to answer any of my questions and essentially didn't seem too concerned since we were on the ground in ZZZ1. Since Crew Scheduling was not able to explain the ACARS message I neither accepted nor rejected the extension. Once again I asked for a hotel room; and they said they were not able to accommodate.A gate finally opened; we terminated the aircraft and I left the gate. As I was walking away I got a call from Crew Scheduling; a different Scheduler was on the line telling me that I had violated the limits. I explained to him that I had taken off five minutes before the limit time and that I should have been legal to fly the flight. The Scheduler explained that even though that was true I had violated the 'Last Block In' time of XX15C. I told him that I was not aware of any Last Block In Time; it is not a number that is published or provided to us in the cockpit; either by the Crew legalities sheet or the computer calculator. I also explained that I had called Crew Scheduling multiple times this evening to voice my concern over my proximity to the limits and not once during any of those calls did any member of Crew Scheduling even bother to mention a 'Last Block In' time limitation. The Scheduler tried to explain that it was all okay as long I say I was aware of it and that I was in acceptance. I countered that no; I was not aware of the limit despite my multiple requests to Crew Scheduling to evaluate my limits; and no; I was not aware I had exceeded any limit; yet when I called for an explanation of the ACARS message; it would have been the perfect time to tell me; and finally no; I did not accept the extension; nor did I reject it because nobody at Crew Scheduling could explain it to me. However; by default; a lack of acceptance should be considered a rejection. This was obviously not what the Scheduler wanted to hear; so he told me that he would forward it to a Supervisor; who would subsequently call my Chief Pilot. I said that was fine; asked that he have the Supervisor call me as well and we ended the call.This experience has taught me that Company does not have either the capability or the desire to adequately protect its pilots from exceeding FAR Part 117 Flight Duty Limitations and Rest Requirement restrictions. I understand that FAR 117 responsibilities are shared between the certificate holder (Company) and the pilot (myself). In this case; however; the pilot had expressed concern about the limits three times; asked for clarification from the certificate holder; yet was repeatedly stonewalled with evasive or non-existent guidance in order to complete the operation. Finally; after successfully and safely completing that operation the pilot was criticized for exceeding a limit the he was never provided; warned of; or explained ahead of time. Then finally the certificate holder attempted to coerce the pilot into accepting the extension after the fact.Resolution of this issue and prevention in the future should include: 1. Provide pilots with the latest block-in time on the crew legalities sheet and computer in additions to latest takeoff times for every flight. This allows pilots to clearly understand all limits of the flight. 2. Better and/or more extensive training of Crew Schedulers on FAR Part 117 duty restrictions. 3. Clearer and more proactive communication from Crew Scheduling to pilots about approaching limits. 4. Make available crew rest accommodations; on request; to a pilot that has been flown to the extent of or over the flight limits on the last day of a paring. Accident prevention should extend beyond the confines of the cockpit. After working 13 hours and 48 minutes on duty operating aircraft; nobody should be behind the wheel of a motor vehicle late at night.
column123: This event involves a potential exceedance of the Part 117 Maximum Block In (MBI) time for the First Officer at the end of a long duty day that included a re-route (involuntary assignment). It has already been reported by the First Officer; and I agree with and support his report. Rather than repeat his whole narrative; I will highlight important points and add one or two additional observations.In ZZZ; we experienced multiple unexplained maintenance locks which prevented us from receiving takeoff data. (Unknown if this malfunction was due to the new maintenance software; or ZZZ Ops not entering our actual fuel on board - which was tankered in and approximately 3;000 pounds more than expected on the release.) After about 30 minutes; we were able to resolve the situation by correcting fuel on board on a new release (and new takeoff reference number.) Feeling pressure to simultaneously deal with First Officer's legality issue while resolving the maintenance lock issue was a distraction and threat that (unlike weather; passenger issues; or aircraft malfunctions) is created by the system. In other words; although Part 117 is intended to help improve safety; the way it's applied ends up being an unhelpful distraction and a threat to safety.The First Officer tried to raise legality questions on the original call. Later; during the re-assignment; the First Officer called Scheduling at least three times to try to discuss the situation. Although I could not hear the other end of the conversations; it sounded like each time he was told they were aware of it and 'working on it.'The First Officer had accepted an extension the previous night. This caused him / us to wonder whether he was even legal for an extension on a 2nd consecutive night? He attempted to bring this up to Scheduling but never got a good answer from them. (Like everything else in Part 117; it's not as easy to answer as it should be. It certainly isn't a yes/no answer.)Once on the ground in ZZZ1 and holding in the pad for a gate to become available; we received an automated ACARS message asking to accept or reject an extension. This was done at the very last minute; when the only realistic options were: accept the extension; or violate Part 117. That doesn't really give the pilot any option to reject the extension. As previously stated; he had already been trying to work with Scheduling prior to this. And; he also (unsuccessfully) attempted to clarify his block in time and options with Scheduling after the ACARS message. When there was still time to address the issue; Scheduling would only give him a 'we're working on it.' It seems like the only option Scheduling would consider was strong-arming him into accepting the extension 'or else.' As we approach what looks to be a very busy summer flying schedule; with the strong possibility that the pilots being brought back in July from extended time off will arrive on the line too late to fill the gaps; Scheduling and Dispatch might consider being more proactive looking for other solutions (offering more premium open time trips; not diverting aircraft into airports where we only have one scheduled flight per day; etc.) versus pushing so hard and flirting with legality issues. In the interest of fatigue management and safety; I don't think it's reasonable to assume that a pilot who has been involuntarily reassigned more flying at the end of a long trip will automatically desire to voluntarily accept an extension to his flight duty limits. The discussion needs to happen much earlier; and not through an automated message giving the false appearance the pilot has an actual choice in the matter.

column121: Denver airport is becoming hazardous to fly into due to non-specific ATIS; poor communication between DEN Center and DEN Approach; and the normalization of multiple arrivals and approaches being programmed during a normal arrival into Denver. This has increased substantially in the last few months and is resulting in aircrews being nearly continuously heads down reprogramming and briefing arrivals/transitions; approaches; taxi plan; getting appropriate landing data; briefing such changes; reviewing NOTAMs associated with these changes...etc. This is usually done while dodging weather; and mitigating turbulence; while descending into high terrain and congested traffic into an airport with multiple; parallel; similarly named runways. I feel there are three root causes. 1) ATIS is not very useful. Basically; a direction of traffic flow and a listing of all available approaches DEN has. 2) There seems to be a system now where approach tells Center what runway transition to assign aircraft. This transition frequently doesn't make sense and was not anticipated; programmed and briefed. Then; upon handoff to approach; the transition to another runway is often assigned. Then when the actual runway and approach is assigned; it frequently results in another reprogramming. This is acceptable during rapidly changing weather...it is commonplace all the time; however. On Aircraft X we programmed and briefed the FLATI 2 RNAV; RWY26 transition; RNAV Z Runway 26 approach. (Winds were 25024G34.) After starting the descent; we were given direct BYYKE; for the LONGS RNAV arrival. We programmed the LONGS arrival; Runway 26 transition; Runway 26 RNAV Z approach. We told Center that we were requesting Runway 26. Center directed us to fly the Runway 16R transition. (even though we were planning not to accept this approach). They said they are directed by DEN approach what transition to assign). We reprogrammed the ILS R16 transition and approach (we are now well along in the descent...moderate turbulence; and a VNAV discontinuity resulting from the reprogramming not being executable because of an approach transition altitude in-congruence) This was resolved quickly and safely and flown uneventfully with a 25 knot crosswind landing. The forecast approach winds were spot on; the ATIS hadn't changed substantially in an hour (Though there were about 5 or 6 of them). The point is; there was no significant change in weather driving this. I could have written the same report the last time I arrived to DEN on my last [arrival] from the east. On the flight today; we planned and briefed two different arrivals; one of the arrivals changing the transitions twice; two different RNAV Z approaches; an ILS approach and two different runways/performance numbers; NOTAMs; engine failure procedures taxi plans etc. I wouldn't spend time filing this report if it was a 'one off' It is becoming the norm and accepted scenario into Denver. It is also a contributing factor with DEN historically having issues with RNAVs. Each of these arrivals is complicated with at least 5-10 different altitude or speed constraints associated with them.

column121: Approach control cleared us direct to WESEN for ILS [Runway] 08 [approach] at SJU. Captain was Pilot Flying; First Officer was Pilot Monitoring. This was the second leg of the night for this three day pairing of a long duty day. Level at 3;000 ft. (pilot selected) then cleared descent to 2;500 ft. (pilot selected) accomplished in vertical speed. Aircraft pilot selected speed was 180 kts. Controller assigned heading 110 to intercept and then cleared us for ILS [Runway] 08 approach. Approach/Land was armed and 'Land Armed' was displayed on PFD. The localizer remained identified and aircraft turned to intercept inbound course. Glide slope was above. Halfway through the intercept; the aircraft made an abrupt pitch-up followed by a thrust increase. This was very unusual as I have never experienced or seen an aircraft climb to capture a glide slope. While this was happening the aircraft exited approach/land mode and reverted to heading mode and solid bow tie altitude (2;500 ft.) All FMAs were 'white'. During the automation the aircraft pitched up and altitude was approximately 3;000 ft. in an attempt to capture the glide slope. The FO made a quick analysis and quick calls to the pilot flying while I was simultaneously disconnecting the autopilot and manually retarding the throttles to correct this anomaly. The aircraft was stabilized and a hand flown ILS was accomplished without autopilot assistance. This aircraft was scheduled for an 'auto land' for currency requirements and subsequently not accomplished. The First Officer monitoring that was accomplished and the verbal inputs from the FO were timely and appropriate; solid CRM. A note in our company aircrew briefing guide notes: Safety Alert Runway 08 Intermittent Glideslope Weak or intermittent glideslope signals have been reported when using ILS Runway 08. Exercise caution and intercept glideslope at the altitude depicted on the approach chart to guard against following a false glide slope signal. If the crew experiences any anomalies while conducting the approach; report the incident to tower and file an event report.

column121: After being cleared for takeoff on Runway 1 in DCA; the Captain transferred the controls to me. Shortly after the '80' knot callout and my response; I noticed Aircraft Y approaching an intersection ahead and it appeared they were moving faster than if they planned to hold short of the runway we were departing. We continued the takeoff uneventfully and Tower gave us their phone number to call upon landing in ZZZ; assuring us we were not in trouble or at fault but wanted to hear our side of the situation. The Captain asked me if I saw the aircraft and after a brief discussion it was obvious we both saw the same situation unfold.I am unaware of Aircraft Y's communication with ATC. With that said; I'm assuming it was either a lack of situational awareness on their part or ATC giving incorrect instructions.I do believe the system in place will normally prevent these occurrences. Maintaining situational awareness. Verifying clearance prior to crossing an active runway. Both pilots being heads-up. Physically checking the runway for aircraft should be the last barrier.
column123: We were cleared for takeoff on Runway 01. I turned control of the aircraft over to the First Officer (FO); and after he applied takeoff power I took control of the throttles. Several seconds later I made the '80' call; which the FO acknowledged. About this time I noticed an aircraft (Aircraft Y; I think) up ahead approaching Runway 01 perpendicularly on a taxiway (probably Taxiway G; but maybe M) at a fairly rapid taxi speed. I focused on the aircraft and began to wonder if it was going to stop as it got closer to the runway environment with no sign of slowing. At this point I mentally prepared for performing a rejected takeoff. Just as the aircraft reached the point where I was thinking I would reject the takeoff I noticed the aircraft stop with a pronounced 'dipping of the nose' from hard braking. At this point I knew the aircraft had stopped and takeoff could continue. I estimate our speed to be about 120-130 knots at this point. A second or two later the Tower Controller made a somewhat excited call; 'Aircraft X!...no further transmission'. As we passed the other aircraft I looked over and couldn't determine if it was over the hold short lines; but could tell it was very close. We continued the takeoff and shortly after getting airborne; the Tower Controller asked us if we had the number to call the tower when reaching destination. After retracting gear and flaps I asked the FO 'Did you see that other aircraft?' He replied he did and after further discussion I determined he saw basically the same things I did (aircraft approaching the runway; considering a rejected takeoff; 'dipping of the nose' with hard braking; knowing the aircraft had indeed stopped and comfortable continuing the takeoff). I called the tower when reaching ZZZ. The Controller taking my call informed me the other aircraft had entered the runway environment and asked if we noticed anything. I replied we did; but continued the takeoff because we knew the aircraft had completely stopped and we couldn't determine if it was over line or just very close. The person taking the call also mentioned the Tower Controller started to issue a rejected takeoff command to us but didn't finish because the Ground Controller confirmed the encroaching aircraft had stopped; hence the 'Aircraft X...'SMGCS lighting installed at DCA and used in all weather conditions; not just low visibility. Red lights are very effective in reminding pilots they are not cleared to cross/enter a runway.

I continued to read the remainder of my announcement and also stated once we are in the air we will demonstrate the life vests once again.  We did so at level off...Now after level off the passenger at XXF returned to her seat and I knew that I could not send the military service dog (over 80 pounds according to the handler; 2 tours in Country X and 1 in Country Y) and the handler to XXF...so I had the active military officer and his special forces dog sit at the 1L door for the remainder of the flight (he strapped in as needed) and he returned to XC for landing and the passenger once again went back to XXF for landing. I sat down on the D-side and attempted to get a briefing but the controller was too busy.During the stint; the controllers work was sloppy; he did not seem to have any idea what was happening in the sector at any given time. Several times throughout the stint he did not use positive separation between IFR aircraft and had what I would describe as 'separation by luck.'The reason I decided to report this stint is because the controller nearly caused a midair collision between Aircraft Y that had departed ZZZ1 and Aircraft X that was descending for ZZZ1.When Aircraft X called for a clearance airborne off of ZZZ; the controller did not issue him and IFR clearance but instead instructed the pilot to remain VFR and take up a westerly heading for active military airspace. The only problem with this plan is that the airspace didn't start until 17;000 [ft.]. The aircraft should have been given the clearance to 170 and a heading to get out from under the airspace.Aircraft X was on a heading (for the military airspace) and was descending quickly because he had been left high.I made the following suggestion to the controller. Clear Aircraft Y on a 190 heading and leave Aircraft X on his present heading until they pass.The controller instead cleared Aircraft X direct ZZZ; putting him in conflict with the climbing Aircraft Y that had not yet received a clearance. I just don't understand why he would do this. Direct the airport wasn't even a good way to set the airplane up to land had there not been traffic.When he finally saw the conflict (did not respond when I pointed it out to him). He froze. The control instruction he gave was 'UHHH Aircraft Y maintain VFR' He then called the traffic to Aircraft Y which was at 12'oclock and 10 miles (estimated) opposite direction. Descending.He then followed up the instruction to Aircraft Y to maintain VFR at 8;500. At the time he issued the instruction; Aircraft Y's indicated altitude was 082 and he had been climbing in excess of 3000 ft. per min. The pilot said he could not stop at 085 but could go back down. The next radar hit was at 094. The controller then said 'UHH just maintain VFR.' He should have left Aircraft Y climbing and turned him. It would have cleared the conflict quicker.He then turned Aircraft X 15degrees right for traffic. But when he issued the instruction; he didn't say it with any urgency at all.I don't remember if he eventually issued Aircraft Y a turn or not; but I do remember thinking I was about to witness a midair collision because a bad controller was sitting on the sector.The traffic was not busy; it had some complexity due to the military airspace; but it wasn't bad. It could easily be worked by a competent controller without a D-side.In summary: Bad control judgement; Bad control technique; lack of control instructions; inadequate control instructions; failure to scan the radar environment; and a controller being completely overwhelmed by traffic nearly lead to a collision at near 10;000 ft.

As the discussion with Dispatch/Maintenance Control/ Chief Pilot continued; the hydraulic quantity continued to drop and then stabilized around .17 (where the standpipe sits in the reservoir?). At that moment; the status message POWER TRANSFER UNIT popped up. The captain relayed to Company this information and with the concurrence of all; the election to divert back to ZZZ1 was made based off of all the available information of system degradation; weather conditions in ZZZ and time to complete the extensive HYDRAULIC SYSESTEM  PRESSURE - Left (Only) checklist. column121: I was called to assist in an aircraft spill situation on an A300 aircraft. I arrived as the First Responder was finishing up. I initiated the spill form and another AMT (Aircraft Maintenance Technician) documented the spill in the aircraft logbook. The aircraft had been in ZZZ since about midday and the spill was reported by the unload crew. The aircraft arrived with no containers in the aft lower compartment where the spill was located so a determination as to the source of origin for the spill would not be possible. The aircraft had operated [two] previous flight legs. The spill affected all areas of both the LH side and RH side outboard positions 5 through position 6. The responder said the spill was a 'mild' alkali and that he had used gray spill pads to try to absorb and clean up the unknown material. He said that a sample should be sent out to positively identify the substance. I documented this on the spill form which I completed down to the corrective action field. I inquired as to obtaining an [reference number] but there seemed to be a hesitancy to issue one and the spill form seemed to be met with the same response. The responder showed me the reference material that he used and stated that sodium bicarbonate could be used to clean up the unidentified spill. I informed both him and several on site Supervisors that since it had been identified as an alkali; the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) Chapter 5 procedures (as per the GMM) would take precedence for any cleanup actions. It appeared that they wanted to load the aircraft but sometime later; the aircraft was ultimately removed from service. I later spoke briefly to the incoming supervisor prior to my leaving my shift for the day and mentioned the spill form which needed the [reference number] and remaining entries after corrective actions were completed. The following day I pulled the history and saw that the log item had been cleared and noted that there was no deferral for a spill on the aircraft. Since I had initiated the spill form; I was concerned and called Company and asked if they had a copy of the completed form. They controller looked but could not find one. I reached out to the [records department] who had the applicable log page but no attached spill form. I inquired as to whether the form had possibly already been scanned and the log page was there but the spill form was not to be found. I informed my Supervisor of my concerns. I understand the GMM (General Maintenance Manual) procedure directs that once the area has been cleaned and a visual inspection accomplished by the AMT; no further action is required but there is more to that procedure. GMM spill response procedures cover roughly two pages and are fairly specific regarding spills determined to be an alkali; a spill that does not have a known source and the requirement for a deferral for a reinspect of the spill area at a later date. The GMM also provides guidance for the disposition of the aircraft spill form. I went upstairs to my manager's office and asked the questions regarding this procedure with the GMM in hand. The response that I got was that the spill was cleaned up by a [company name] vendor that we pay good money for (cleanup service) and at that point; the aircraft spill form is no longer necessary and that is the end of it as far as I was to be concerned. I mentioned that his answer is not in line with what the GMM says. My ultimate concern is for the aircraft and for the AMT's who signed the logbook if any part of this process was misrepresented to them in the name of getting the aircraft back into service. Hopefully this is not the case. The ZZZ Aircraft Hazardous Material Spill Flow Chart; the GMM and the Aircraft Substance Spill Form are very specific with the responsibilities for spill events such as this. It seems like every spill event in ZZZ is like the first time with decisions being made on the fly.

column121: Last night I flew the airplane across the border from ZZZZ to ZZZ to clear Customs on my way to ZZZ1. Customs held me for about 30 minutes. I was quite tired and stressed because this flight was scheduled very suddenly and I had to drive to ZZZZ to make the flight. By the time I was released from Customs; jumped in the airplane; started the engines; and tried to get my clearance to ZZZ1; ZZZ Tower was long closed. So I tried a phone call to TRACON first; but since ZZZ is so close to the border; my cell phone could not get the proper signal; between Mexico and U.S.; so the call did not go through. At that moment; I switched the ZZZ Tower frequency to see if I could get my clearance from TRACON with no success. So; I decided to taxi to the head of Runway XXR; and try it again there. No joy. I began to feel desperate. I tried again calling by phone and this time I made contact; but the call dropped in a second. I kept trying for about four times; until I finally could get my clearance.My 'void if not off by' time was about 8 minutes; so I rushed the flight plan into the FMS; and put Tower frequency again in Comm 1. I then made the call that I was taking off from ZZZ for a straight out departure. Nobody answered; so I began my take off run. I saw some lights down the runway but; from my perspective; looked beyond the runway. Only when I was about to rotate realized and almost froze to see what I think was a helicopter on the runway! I pulled hard on the yoke; since I could not stop the airplane on the ground without hitting the other aircraft. I tried to calm myself down as I was scared to death. I was surprised that I did not hear the helicopter on the Tower frequency. That is when I realized I had not put in the correct Tower frequency! My blood went to my feet and my heart was racing and I felt so bad and miserable to think I could have killed some innocent people along with myself just for that 'little' error. I still feel awful.From now on; I will double and triple check my frequencies; altitudes; headings and runway holding instructions. I assure you that I learned my lesson on how external factors as stress and fatigue can and will affect your judgment. I will do my best to prevent this from happening to me again. Just the thought of the terrible disaster I might have caused; makes me realize the importance of proper focus; concentration and compliance with SOP's; no matter how tired you are. Besides; I will try to fly with a copilot from now on. Another set of eyes and mind are better than one.

column121: On a training flight with a commercial single engine student around ZZZ. After performing some airwork north of the airport we came back in for a full stop landing. Instead the Pipeline finished his work inspecting the line and requested to exit the airspace to the southwest. This took him right through the final approach course of our runway.At that moment we saw him turn on a collision course with us. ATC would ask the Pipeline twice if he had us in sight to which he responded yes; but made no course correction. He did not hit us because my student and I made the prudent move to forget our approach profile and level off to avoid descending into this aircraft. He went under out aircraft at maybe 75 feet. After the aircraft passed we had to use a large amount of forward slip to get down to our proper glide path because of that incident and the fact that we had to level off to avoid collision. ATC allowed this aircraft to fly through the final approach course with an aircraft on approach and as a result this aircraft was too close to us. The Pipeline aircraft that called us in sight did not show up on my ADS-B; either due to altitude or other reasons; but if he saw us he intentionally passed very close to us.

column121: On takeoff from ZZZ we felt a rough bumping at 100 knots. I was distracted by the cause of the roughness and didn't notice the exact speed we initiated the rejected takeoff at but felt it was at least 100 knots; but not above 120 knots. I determined the aircraft was unsafe to fly; called for the aircraft and rejected the takeoff. The First Officer (FO) alerted Tower as we were slowing to a stop. Once we were stopped; I made a Public Address telling the Passengers to remain seated. I was surprised to find that I didn't have a non-normal checklist for the situation and it felt odd as we had so much time to wait for the Fire Trucks to arrive. During that time I communicated with the Flight Attendants FAs to check on them and asked them to look for fire or smoke. They verified no indication of either and also confirmed that there were no injuries. Crew Fire Rescue pulled up and reported the two left main tires were blown and no fire; though they did hose them down briefly. The FO suggested starting the APU; which we did; and I was able to shut down the engine as the Fire Department was tending to the aircraft. We coordinated with Operations by radio and Dispatch by ACARS; and made Public Addresses to keep the Passengers informed and calm. The Passengers were then deplaned by air stairs and bused to the terminal.
column123: I had done the walk around and hadn't noticed anything unusual about the tires. The brake-wear pins looked fine. Taxi out was normal and even the initial takeoff roll was normal and didn't notice anything. After I heard the Pilot Monitoring call 80 knots; we felt a jolt and then the aircraft started shaking and getting progressively worse. We rejected the takeoff at about 100 knots with the appropriate flows and callouts. As we were slowing (I believe I saw 43 knots); I called Tower to let them know we were rejecting the takeoff. We got the plane stopped. The Captain called the Flight Attendants. The Tower let us know they actually heard the tires blow and that they were sending out the Fire Department and the Airport Operations. They then switched us over to another frequency to coordinate. We started the APU and shutdown the engines and then the Fire Department sprayed something on the aircraft left side. They used the word hot-spot. The people were then deplaned via air stairs and bused to the terminal; and we again confirmed that no one needed medical attention and were uninjured. After thinking about it; I know in training we had been told to wait until below 60 knots to call the Tower; but I'm not sure if that had changed to being at a complete stop or not before calling and could not find guidance in our manuals.

column121: On Aircraft X we received an ENOTOC (Electronic NOTOC) from Load Control. While we reviewed the ENOTOC   I noticed that there was no UN HAZMAT number and pointed it out to Captain as something I believed was supposed to be on the ENOTOC. Having flown cargo at multiple previous jobs I am very familiar with the HAZMAT paperwork requirements. However; as the ENOTOC is fairly new and the printout is overly confusing to read and decipher Captain contacted Load Control to get further clarification on the matter and to insure that we were in compliance with the procedure and regulations. Load Control assured us that everything was in order and correct for the flight. I do not recall whether we sent to NOTOC acknowledgment before or after we contacted Load Control for clarification. Apparently my initial intuition that something wasn't right with the paperwork was correct and we should have requested new paperwork be sent. Even today I have no idea what HAZMAT was actually on our aircraft. I believe the primary cause of this error is the cumbersome layout of the ENOTOC format to begin with. Every time we receive an ENOTOC it's like trying to decipher a sudoku puzzle. The columns (location; weight; UN number) don't seem to align with what is being listed for the HAZMAT. Even figuring out the location of the HAZMAT requires finding a number on the form and then referring to the bottom of the form for the actual position (at least I think that's what we do because it's a form that is in such disorder that I'm not even sure if I'm looking at a position number or a weight). To compound this ENOTOC issue was the fact that when we inquired with Load Control they assured us that the paperwork was correct and everything was in compliance with procedure. Where the error occurred is unknown; but more awareness from everybody involved could have easily prevented this error.  I [suggest] a reevaluation of the ENOTOC procedure and paperwork is in order. The ACARS printout needs to be simpler and easier to read. If it can't; then we should return to the previous procedure with a hard copy of the NOTOC paperwork.

column121: At ZZZ we were notified by the maintenance technician as part of the maintenance briefing that the autoland system was 'still' deferred and that a part was to be installed when the airplane returned in a few days. We noted that the previous crew had performed an autoland to Cat II standards; and had not written up the airplane with an items. An inspection of the logbook showed multiple issues with the First Officer (FO) raw data glideslope (G/S) indication and other failures over the last few landing cycles. During the flight we received messages from dispatch asking us to perform an autoland in ZZZZ1 to recertify the autoland system as that is how the airplane was deferred; i.e. the aircraft could be recertified by a satisfactory autoland being performed. We thought this strange as the previous crew performed an autoland to cat II standards and did not write anything up. The captain needed a landing for currency anyway; so a few messages were exchanged to that effect with dispatch; which led us to be directed to do an autoland in ZZZZ because the weather at the destination that the airplane would be flying were cat III. We said we would and performed the autoland. On approach we had a no land 3 message on the EICAS and a status message cue. The airplane then indicated the CAT II only on the PFD. We also saw that; as per multiple write ups; the FO's side G/S indication for the raw data portion was not in view. At about 1500 feet above the ground; the FO side glideslope came into view; but the aircraft showed slightly high on glide slope according to the raw data indication (note very slightly high; not out of any parameters; but still a bit unusual for the indication while on autopilot). Atmospheric conditions were VFR and the runway was in sight during the whole approach sequence. At about the time that the FO's raw data for the G/S reappeared; the Captain's side G/S raw data indication disappeared from view; though there was no indication of fault noted on EICAS with either of these issues. We continued the approach and the captain let the airplane land and it landed normally and tracked the centerline normally. The autoland was written up as unsatisfactory due to the loss of both raw data indications during the approach; the FO side data came back; the Captain side never did once it was gone. It appears to me that the autoland system deferral perhaps was not deferred properly as multiple failures over weeks of time suggested a problem with the system; and in the case of our monitoring of the autoland during our flight resulted in the same G/S issues on the FO side as well as a new failure on the Captain side of the raw data indications.

column121: After diverting to ZZZ we arrived at ZZZ1 a few hours late. Upon arriving at the departure gate for our next leg we discovered the flight had already been boarded an hour or so early. The ground service bus was connected and the battery switch and emergency exit lights were off. We discovered there were two open write ups in the book which were a LAV water heater issue and a pack issue. We called maintenance to let them know about the write ups. A little bit later we were told the aircraft was being taken out of service. A replacement aircraft was eventually found. During preflight I called Dispatch to discuss ZZZ2 operations during late night tower closure procedures. About ten minutes later I received a call from Dispatch that the runway lights were NOTAM'ed out that night and we were not going to be able to go. He was; however; going to call ZZZ2 and ask if they could keep the lights on. The  Concourse Manager and the tower came up with a 'plan' to depart and if I couldn't get into ZZZ2; due to no runway lights; to divert to ZZZ3 and they would bus the pax to ZZZ2. This was not a plan I was in favor of to say the least. ZZZ2 equipment maintenance agreed to delay the runway light not/closure till after our arrival; which was approximately XA:30PST. About an hour from arrival we received a GPS 1 and 2 message with an accompanying TERR POS message which was the result of a [name] NOTAM regarding jamming. We discussed the situation of a late night RNAV arrival into mountainous terrain with a tower closure and no GPS and terrain warning. Just prior to descent the GPS returned. Reporter stated the cause of the late departure was maintenance deciding to take the aircraft out of service after it had been on the ground for three hours. Boarding a flight an hour before aircrew showing up and the ground service bus as the only power source. The emergency exit lights were not on as well as the battery. The decision by non pilots to fly to a 'special airport due to terrain' not knowing if the runway lights would be working only to divert to another airport. [name of area] jamming and the loss of GPS and terrain warnings.Operations management needs to change from reactive to proactive.

column121: Aircraft was dispatched with the RT INNER fuel quantity indicating system inop. Per the MEL; the RT INNER fuel tank quantity would have to be verified by an alternate means. Arrived at the aircraft; fueling was complete and the fuel service form had been signed but the alternate verification had not been recorded in the system. Called Maintenance and they said it was in progress and would be signed off shortly. First Officer (FO) confirmed that they were dripping the tank while he was on his pre-flight walk around.Received an ACARS alert that the system had changed; verified the MEL signoff and it confirmed 6;600 pounds in the right inner verified by Magnetic Level Indicator 2.Fuel Service form showed block in fuel of 19.2 lbs. and that 11.0 lbs. of fuel had been added to bring us up to a total 30.2 lbs.Climbing out of ZZZ got RT INNER FUEL tank pump fault. As Pilot Monitoring (PM) complied with ECAM and turned the pump off and consulted the QRH. When I brought the FUEL page back onto the ECAM I noticed the RT OUTER tank was burning and we had a fuel split of 1000 lbs between the RT and LT outer tanks. The working pump in the right inner tank showed a green line which I took to mean fuel pressure from the RT inner tank but the RT outer was burning down.I put the crossfeed valve in line so that LT inner tank was feeding the #2 Engine. Fuel stopped burning from the RT outer tank at that time. After a minute or two closed the crossfeed valve to see if the RT inner tank would now burn. Fuel started burning out of the RT outer again. Put crossfeed back in line to manually manage the fuel burn and to minimize the imbalance between outer tanks.FO and I discussed what we thought was going on. At this point I believed there was no fuel in the RT inner tank. We both agreed that we could not continue on to ZZZ1 and talked of possible diverts. We discussed returning to ZZZ but I believed there was no fuel in the RT outer tank and if that was the case; we already had an almost 7000 lb split between left and right sides.At this point we were about 50 miles to the west ZZZ2 and decided that was our best divert option. FO continued flying and worked with ATC to change destination and begin descending. I tried to contact ZZZ2 Ramp on VHF 2 but got no response. Informed operations via ACARS of a fuel discrepancy and that we were diverting to ZZZ2. He acknowledged and sent us routing and new numbers. Coordinated arrival with ZZZ Center and ZZZ2 Approach and shot a visual approach and landing to RWY XXR ZZZ2. Left inner tank was empty by the time we started the approach and were burning tank to engine on both engines.Once in the chocks we discussed what had happened and ran numbers on how much fuel we should have and how much we actually had. We blocked out with 29.2 and as per the fuel burn indicators had burned just a little over 10;000 lbs. We should have had 19;200 lbs. RT inner tank; inop FQIS; showed 5;900 lbs; but was empty. LT outer showed 7.4 and RT outer showed 6.0 for a total for a total of 13.4.ZZZ2 Maintenance verified fuel on board with MIL sticks. LT outer 7.7; LT inner 0.0; RT inner 0.0; RT outer 6.0 for a total of 13.7.A failure in the system ensuring required fuel is on board when dealing with a Fuel System MEL.
column123: Aircraft assigned had MEL for RT Inner fuel tank quantity indicator inoperative. When we got to aircraft and I began my walk around; I noticed maintenance moving a ladder over to the right wing inboard of the engine. As I got around to pre-flight the right main gear I asked the maintainer if they were checking the fuel quantity and he confirmed they were. This struck me as a bit odd since the system indicated Flight Ready when we were in ops. I finished my pre-flight and when I got to the cockpit I mentioned to the Captain they were checking the tank on pre-flight; but we both agreed there was no record of the check in the maintenance history. He called Maintenance and they said it was in work. We received an ACARS informing us the aircraft status changed to not flight ready. Shortly after we then received a Flight Ready ACARS notification. I then confirmed the fuel added from the previous flight block in and the fuel slip using the APS. The APS; fuel slip and fuel page all were within +/- 200-300 lbs of total quantity. We blocked out and departed on Runway XXR. After getting a turn east and a climb; ECAM indicated a RT Inner tank pump fault. The Captain began handling ECAM and QRH as Pilot Monitoring (PM). As Pilot Flying (PF); I was not head's down much but I did notice we had approximately a thousand pound split between the LT and RT outer tanks. The fuel page also showed the left pump in the RT inner tank still operational with a green line leading to the right engine. The RT inner showed approximately 5.7. The Captain informed me he was going to place the cross feed valve in-line to feed the right engine from left inner tank. When he did that the RT outer tank burn stopped. After a few minutes he closed the cross feed and again the RT outer tank quantity began decreasing after monitoring it for a minute or two. We then paced the valve back inline to manage imbalance. At this point we were leveling off and we began discussing what was taking place in the fuel system. Despite what the fuel system was indicating; we both came to the conclusion that there was no fuel remaining in RT Inner tank. Based on where we were; and the headwind we would have turning around to ZZZ; we elected to inform Center that we needed to land at ZZZ2. As PF; I took over ATC comms and FMS management to get a descent and set up for approach to ZZZ2 while the Captain attempted contacting operations via ACARS to tell them our situation and plan as well as call ZZZ2 Ramp. We descended and landed at ZZZ2 uneventfully. Once we were blocked in we discussed what we blocked out with-29.2 and had burned-10.0 per the fuel consumption gauges for each engine. The aircraft showed we had 19.2 onboard. We discussed this with Maintenance and they did the manual verification of the tanks confirming that the left and right inner tanks were empty and the actual fuel onboard was 13.7.Unsure other than a discrepancy between what amount of fuel was added and what reading was taken to manually verify RT inner tank quantity.I do not know what took place during the fueling / manual verification timeline to offer feedback on how to prevent future occurrences

Also; we never had been to this airport before. Everything was normal as far as boarding; we started both engines at the gate because the end of the runway was very close to the ramp. I called them when we landed in ZZZ1 and he said it was common (it happens about once a week) and they will soon be posting that area as a hotspot. The rest of the flight was normal ops.Causal factors: It was the first flight of the morning and it always seems rushed; combined with the new weight and balance and a new crew; it felt like I was trying to catch up. Also; it was a new unfamiliar airport with the runway about 100 yards away; combined with a somewhat vague restricted area on the other side of the field. I believe this was the subtle chain of events along with a brief disruption in my situational awareness that was the direct cause.I believe I should have looked a lot closer (zoomed in) at the airport diagram; and should have briefed the FO exactly where the runway entrance was at [Taxiway] A5 and where the restricted area boundaries were. Also; as I mentioned before; and ATC also told me; they need to revise this chart and put that area as a hotspot because it's so easy to pass if you're not completely focused. Also; I should have waited to ask the FO about the hydraulic procedure till later. Also; as far as the chart goes; not only should this area be a hotspot but it should be magnified in the corner of the chart as well as having a description on the 10-7 pages that covers both sides of the airport where the boundary is.
