All of us did not feel right; and felt ill. I called the Captain with our concerns and told him I would call him with an update. I called him again and he said to for each of us to fill out a report which we did; and he collected all of them. I eventually called him back and told him we needed to have the paramedics meet the plane upon landing at ZZZZ1 and that all the Flight Attendants #1;#2;#3;#4 need to go to the hospital. Once on the ground the paramedics met the plane but stated that all four of us could not be transported in the only ambulance that showed up to take us to the hospital after telling us all to get into the ambulance. we had to get out and go back up the stairs from the ramp and back into the terminal and wait on the logistics to be figured out on how they were going to transport us to the hospital.  I had reported that 'All' four Flight Attendants need to go to the hospital. That lack of preparation on the ground to transport us to the hospital became quiet the debacle; and took a long while.  Once back inside the terminal we contacted medical company to report our illnesses. The paramedics left then had to be called back to come get us; I was told that they were on another call and that they would come back. Eventually they did; they took some basic vital signs; were missing some medical equipment (CO2 monitor)and worked with the ground personnel to figure out how to get us to the hospital. after at least of over 2 hours after landing In ZZZZ1 they finally took us to Hospital X in City which is 45 minutes from the airport to be seen in and Emergency Department. We were  never given oxygen as a basic  medical resource after complaining of possibly being in a 'Fume  Event' by the paramedics. At the Hospital X we were given  [medical treatment]. No blood work was ever done; again; oxygen was never administered to any of the Flight Attendants. I had an X-ray done because I was complaining about my lungs hurting. The x-ray report came back normal; after being read by a regular doctor; but a specialist said after he reviewed it that I  had fluid in my right lung. We finally were released from the emergency room after they secured payment by Air Carrier name ; as they told us we could not leave until the bill was paid. I had to use my own credit card to pay for  all the Flight Attendant prescriptions; as the pharmacy  was off site. We were transported back to the hotel and checked in for our overnight. We were grounded by medical. We were given  instructions to go to another hospital the next day which was in their network Hospital Y. We complied with this request and we received IV therapy; were given prescriptions; and blood work was done which showed a lot of our levels out of normal range. We remained at the hotel for 5 days under the care of Medical until we were released to fly to our home base of ZZZ2. Once back in the United States we were contacted by Company; [Air Carrier] employee medical provider and were told to go to a US hospital to get checked out and have test done.  I was seen at Trauma Center in City where I reside with the approval of Company.  My final diagnosis was- lung injury. I am still taking prescriptions; and I am still on my inhaler. I continue to experience pain in my lungs and I am still under the care of Company. I want to be contacted by the FAA about this report. - [F/A Name; Employee No.]
column123: Please accept this report; as this is the first opportunity I've had  to file this report.  As soon as I stepped onto the aircraft; I noticed a dirty sock smell- an oil smell. It was strong to me. I mentioned this to the #1 and #3. I then stepped into the cockpit to introduce myself. After a few cordial words; I asked 'Do you guys smell that?' The Captain said 'What?'- I said 'it's like an oil; fume or dirty sock smell'. The Captain said 'no; we just brought this aircraft in from ZZZ and had no problems; and the other crew (other flight attendants); never mentioned anything'. I went back to the back galley where I was working. We started boarding; and then departed. I did walk back up to the front during boarding and the smell CLEARLY a dirty sock smell; which we all know only comes from oil; was still lingering.  Approximately an hour and twenty minutes into the flight; (maybe and hour and thirty) the number 1 came back to the back galley where the rest of us flight attendants were sitting. I said to all of them 'Hey; I just want you all to know I have a mad headache and I don't feel right and I know it's from that smell I smelled before boarding'. Each flight attendant then shared that they too had headaches; and the number #3 said his fingers were tingling; the #4 said she felt dizzy and had vertigo; and the #1 said he felt like he was going to pass out; was nauseous; and had a bad stomach ache. The #1 called the Captain; and he went through the cabin fume event checklist. He asked each of us several questions. We had a few different conversations with the Captain and the #1 had called the Captain several times. At one point in my conversation with the Captain he said something about why we didn't say anything; and I said 'wait a minute- I did say something and you told me you brought this aircraft in from ZZZ and there was no problems and the other flight attendants never mentioned anything'. The Captain replied; 'Yes; you did; I dropped the ball'. As the flight progressed to ZZZZ1; the cabin crew felt worse. The Captain was informed that we wanted the paramedics to meet the flight AND that we ALL needed to go to the hospital. We landed in ZZZZ1; deplaned the passengers and walked up the jetway; we had to wait about 5 minutes for the paramedics. We immediately called Medical to inform them of our situation and our symptoms. Medical wanted to go into grave detail about our information and the crew was getting more and more anxious and feeling worse. One of us finally said 'Please; can you just get us on the way to the hospital and we can call you on the ride to give this information?'  We all sat in wheelchairs. The medics took our blood pressures; however; were lacking in any other medical equipment. They used my SPO2 monitor to complete our initial vitals. Never were we placed on O2.  The lack of ground logistics for the transportation to take us all to the hospital was a huge fiasco. We sat for over two hours before getting transportation that took ONE HOUR to get to the hospital. We had repeatedly stated we wanted to go to the hospital and the delay of care was unacceptable. At one point we were all brought down the stairs to the bottom of the aircraft where an ambulance was waiting. We all got in the ambulance; and then about 20 minutes later were told to get out as the paramedics would not take all 4 of us. Back up into the airport we went. Not to mention that it was about 90 degrees outside and we were in full uniform. I then began to feel like I was going to pass out. We were placed back in the wheelchairs. Finally a van was procured for our transportation to The Hospital X. This took over an hour. Name was an agent for Air Carrier in ZZZZ1 and went with us to the hospital. She was extremely helpful. We arrived at the hospital and eventually were all placed in separate rooms; examined; were given IV medication and then prescriptions to go back to the hotel with. NO X-RAYS; EKG's or other tests were taken at this hospital. Not one of us were given oxygen therapy. No blood work was taken. We were cleared to leave after about 4 hours HOWEVER we were not allowed to leave because the hospital had not received any payment! It took several phone calls with Medical; and the company to get the bill paid. This part is unclear as most was spoken in  [local language]; but from what I gathered; Name (our liaison) was given a credit card to pay the bill. Furthermore our #1 took ALL of our prescriptions across the street and paid for them out of his pocket!!! After another hour long drive back to the hotel; the crew checked in; changed clothes and barely made it down to the restaurant to eat before it closed for the night. The next morning Medical called to check in on us and determined we all needed to be checked out again. This was after Medical questioned WHY we went to THAT hospital last night. I've never been to this Destination before and it's not like any of us picked a hospital. Medical set it up for us. Well Friday morning; Medical said that wasn't the hospital they are affiliated with and we need to go to Hospital Y. This was about XA:00 am local time. It was XD:00 local when we got into a van to take us to the hospital. This was another huge fiasco; there should be measures in place to easily get medical attention when needed! The company (daily Ops) had told the #1 to take an ride hailing service!!!! He informed the person on the phone of the dangers of ZZZZ1; and that you do not take a ride hailing service as kidnapping is a serious threat. But I digress. We finally arrived at the second hospital an hour later and there we proceeded to get another IV placement with medication for our individual symptoms; X-rays; blood work; & EKG's. We were also given different prescriptions to take with us. This time it was all covered and the scripts were filled right then and there. We were not medically cleared to fly out of ZZZZ1 until Date. We landed in ZZZ2 and were met by each of our supervisors. We talked with them for awhile. We each eventually went on our way home. I then called Company because I wanted to get checked out in [domicile]. Finally on [following day] I was contacted and was given instructions to go to the hospital as now my symptoms included a chest tightness; a continued head ache and just a feeling of being 'off'. I went to General Hospital Z on Date & Time I gave the doctor there my union provided card that explains aircraft fume event procedures and what I was exposed to. My doctor at the ED decided he wanted to contact his colleague who was an infectious disease specialist.  I was given IV medication; a 12 lead EKG; chest X-rays; oxygen therapy for 1 hour; and several vials of blood work; some of which were repeated after an hour. The doctor determined that the symptoms I was having were in line with inhaling a toxin. He advised me to follow up with my primary care doctor; to get plenty of rest and to take it easy. As I am writing this report; my head aches are managed by Motrin; I still have a chest heaviness and feel my heart racing at times and have had two episodes of feeling like I am going to pass out. I have finished the prescription medication I was prescribed. I am worried about the long term repercussions of this fume event. I am also worried about losing time and pay away from work. I want to be contacted by the FAA about this incident.

column121: This was a flight [to] ZZZ for pickup of an item. I monitored the AWOS and listened to UNICOM for traffic. I announced my intention to enter the traffic pattern for Runway XX and land at ZZZ with a FULL STOP. It was observing that several aircraft were in the pattern in close spacing on the downwind with an estimated speed of approximately 70 Knots. My pattern entry speed was reduced to 130 KIAS for landing gear deployment and spaced about a 1;000 feet to right; outside of these aircraft. Again; I announced my intention to make a Full Stop landing without interfering with the numerous aircraft doing Touch & Go landings. I reduced the speed 110 Knots on base and 100 Knots on Final Approach. Expecting these aircraft to extend downwind about 30 seconds to give me room; I was surprised when one of them continued on a tight base and turn to final directly in front my plane. At 100 Knots approach speed; I easily overtook the 70-knot aircraft and passed successfully at about 500 feet right of ZZZ Runway XX centerline. I accelerated my plane while retracting the gear and flaps and maintained 180 knots for the climb and turn to crosswind. Again; I observed several aircraft on close spacing downwind and I entered a downwind slightly outside the pattern. For the fourth time; I announced my intention to make a Full Stop landing and turned the normal base for my plane's speed. For a second time; an aircraft made a turn to base and turned to final directly in front of me instead of extending their downwind about 30 second to allow much-faster airplanes to make a Full Stop. On this pattern; I was grateful the other aircraft decided to go-around when the pilot observed the rapid CLOSURE from behind. I said 'Thanks' on the radio and completed a safe Full Stop Landing.After my safe landing; I proceeded to the FBO to pick up the item. Upon reaching the FBO desk; I heard on the FBO radio that Runway XX is now CLOSED for an airplane stopped on the runway. From the FBO windows; it appeared to be an aircraft was sitting on Runway XX without its Landing Gear. The poor soul and retractable aircraft were still out there when I departed. If these aircraft belong to a Flight school; perhaps the instructors should talk to their students about allowing faster; dissimilar airplanes into the traffic pattern for a single full stop landing. There are MANY corporate airplanes that land at ZZZ Airport with approach speed in the 100 - 120 knots range. This would be appreciated by many and certainly may save unwanted distraction during landing. Perhaps the instructor input may save some distracted soul from making a gear-up landing.

column121: Flight for Part 141 Multi-Engine Instructor (MEI) applicant. Preflight was claimed complete; both instructor and student walked out to [the] airplane; started engines; and taxied out. Run-up was normal; as was taxi. On takeoff; engine checks were complete and in the green. Upon rotation and climbout; both oil temperatures and cylinder head temperatures were rising rapidly. At 500 feet; instructor told MEI student to return to airport; [the] temperatures were rising too fast. Lowered power output and maintained 700 feet AGL. By the end of the downwind; both temperatures were in the red; oil pressure still in the green. Base to final had normal airspeeds. Landed safely with engines operating.Upon landing and rollout to taxi; engines began to stutter. Mixtures were pulled as we exited the runway and airplane was shut down. Post-shutdown examination showed engine plugs were not taken out. Thus; pre-flight had not been completed. Engine malfunction was due to student not completing pre-flight and instructor placing too much responsibility and trust upon [the] student to complete such actions. It is the student's responsibility to complete the pre-flight; but the instructor's responsibility to ensure pre-flight is completed. Corrective action would be for instructor to check the MEI student's pre-flight responsibilities and checklist items.

column121: This was the first time flying into RIC for both crew members. Captain was PF and FO was PM. Crew planned to fly the SPIDR 4 RNAV Arrival and to connect to the RNAV (RNP) Y Runway 16 (RIC was landing Runways 16 and 20). Crew requested and was approved by Potomac Approach to fly the RNAV (RNP) Y to Runway 16 from DEEER (Potomac directed crossing DEEER at 4;000 feet MSL). We received the approach clearance around REDNG. FMC had given ALERT MESSAGES all flight long there was a steep descent after HEMME waypoint (280 KIAS/11;000 feet - 12;000 feet crossing restriction). FMC was correctly programmed. After passing HEMME; the aircraft began to deviate from the RNAV path by getting high. It became very clear; pilots had to intervene substantially in order to correct the aircraft back onto the VNAV PATH to successfully fly the RNAV (RNP) Y Runway 16 Approach. PF used maximum inflight speedbrake; elected not to use extending flaps. Aircraft airspeed was restricted to 250 KIAS or less as aircraft was transitioning to below 10;000 feet MSL. The only technique to slow the aircraft and attempt to re-establish the RNAV vertical path was to extend the landing gear about 30 miles from the field. Crew was able to correct aircraft back to RNAV path and complete the approach + landing. If this was another crew with little or no experience flying this RNAV Arrival to RNAV (RNP) Approach into RIC with actual weather; there is a high probability they would not successfully complete the approach and landing (would have to go missed approach; other altitude/speed deviations and/or compromise safety).

column121: While serving as PF (Pilot Flying) into ZZZ on the ZZZZZ arrival; I was flying the aircraft with autopilot; autothrottle; and VNAV. We had programmed the STAR along with a transition to the ILS XXR into ZZZ and reviewed all the fixes and block altitudes on the Pro Line Fusion MFD screen. The aircraft flew the STAR without incident from FL280 all the way down to about 13000. The VNAV and autothrottle were working. I became distracted when the autothrottle failed to reduce 'FMS speed' for ZZZZZ1 to 250. I manually selected 250 and slowed. I reactivated the FMS speed function and verbally announced that we would monitor the speed and to make sure it made the next speed slowdown proactively at ZZZZZ2. What I failed to properly notice is the VNAV set a floor altitude of 13000 and leveled off. I did not think much of it since the next fix was an 'at or above' 9000 so I thought it was a level-off in lieu of an overly shallow descent.While being distracted in over-monitoring the FMS speed reduction; we got caught in an undesirable aircraft state. To make the alt window at ZZZZZ3; 9000-8000; I manually selected VS and adjusted the descent rate and flight spoilers in order to make that fix's alt window. I believe it was too close to notice if we made it or not and we did not seek relief with ATC since the Captain seemed unsure how to query ATC since he too was interested in watching the VNAV and FMS speed since he had little time on this Pro Line Fusion avionic suite. I flew the remaining alt windows in VS mode since that higher level of automation was not trustworthy or compatible with my state at that time. Later in the arrival; before ZZZZZ4; ATC gave us relief off the arrival and gave a descent to 3000. I dialed 3000 into the FGCP and the Captain confirmed the ALT. Continued down in VS. Since the previous UAS - Undesired Aircraft State - was around 10000; it impeded on the 'in-range check' being completed. We were at about 6500 when the in-range check was started and it distracted us from noticing the aircraft was still in VNAV and had captured the floor of the arrival; 6000; and did not continue [the] descent to 3000. ATC would query us shortly and again I would notice that the aircraft in a UAS. I noticed VNAV still active and disabled it; and continued down. We intercepted the approach and landed without further incident.In hindsight and a word of caution; this is the first avionics suite I have seen where altitudes on a STAR can be superseded by altitudes on an approach. In this example; the ZZZZZ STAR with the ILS XXR ZZZZZ5 transition. There was a discontinuity between ZZZZZ6 and ZZZZZ5. I want to know why in what world should VNAV look ahead of a discontinuity and block the VNAV windows on the STAR. All the stepdowns on the ILS XXR were there for reference as there no way knowing how far in the downwind ATC would take you before a base turn. I don't have a lot of VNAV-capable aircraft experience and I see tremendous issues with not being properly trained in how the aircraft will respond based on what is programmed into the FMS. In general; the avionics differentiation training was lacking and laughable and the differences from the standard avionics in the CL604. It seems half-finished and very retrofit. Having to train on-the-line with the suite to new crew members is frustrating at best and dangerous at worst. I will continue to step up and down levels of automation as my comfort and knowledge adjusts and will try to look for any potential red flags in FMS programming beyond the basic comparing to the approach plate.

column121: According to my student: While he was doing solo touch/goes at ZZZ; on his second landing; he touched down left of centerline. While rolling with the throttle in the idle position; he turned off the carb heat and began to retract the flaps. The nose of the plane began to veer right. When he applied left rudder he said the plane felt as if it would skid; spin or drop the nose onto the ground. Therefore; he applied just enough left rudder to straighten the nose wheel and rolled onto the grass adjacent to the runway. No contact was made with any runway signage or lights. There was no damage to plane; runway; or grass area; and there were no injuries. Tower cleared for continued movement to the Alpha taxiway. He continued to the transient parking area and called ZZZ Tower per their instructions.As the instructor; my student called me to inform me he had run off the runway; no damage had occurred; and he had spoken with the tower and FAA. I did not know he was flying by himself that day and had received no notification from him. I asked him to recount what happened to me several times trying to understand what happened. I called the Tower and confirmed that the winds were variable at 3 knots and visibility was very good. Based on his recount; I do not fully understand how he thought going off the runway was his safest option. I have not offered him any training or instruction that would indicate that was good judgment. He has never landed far off centerline with me in the plane and has never demonstrated that he would ever act in such a way. He and I have logged extensive dual hours at ZZZ doing pattern work; and he has never flown in a way that indicated he would act or make a decision in this manner. He had demonstrated consistently with me that he was able to maintain directional control of the airplane both in the air and on the ground. I have informed him that all of his solo endorsements are no longer valid. I was planning to spend an extensive amount of time with him on the ground and in the air addressing what happened yesterday through re-training; but he has decided to discontinue his flight training at this time. As a result of this incident; I have re-clarified to all students that they must inform me of any time they plan to solo and must receive my permission before doing so. I have also implemented a strict rule of no solo touch and goes. Solo pattern work will from now on only be full stop landings.

column121: Approximately 80 miles before top of descent MIA Center descended us to FL360 behind a widebody which was left at FL380. There was a quartering left tailwind of approximately 30-35 knots. We were given 280 knots assigned for spacing. The widebody entered the STAR from our left or the east. Our separation grew from less than 10 miles to just at or slightly over 10 miles with our descent and speed. At approximately 60-55 miles from the new top of descent from FL360 we experienced a rapid roll to the left of approximately 30 degrees. I turned off the autopilot and the plane then rolled right rapidly; about 20 seconds later. We [asked] for a speed of 250 [kts]. ATC gave the speed when we reported the wake turbulence. I continued to hand fly for a while until we could assure ourselves the wind dropped a bit and our separation had increased. I had the FO (First Officer) call the FAs (Flight Attendants) everything was secure and everyone was okay. We had them take their seats [and] the seatbelt sign was on at the time of the event. Upon leveling at 8;000 [feet] and turning westbound we had a second event even though the 777 was turning base ahead and we were just entering the downwind and crossing the bay. Approach had kept the 777 high and gave them relief on the restrictions as they descended. The next day; MIA Approach cleared us to 8;000 [feet] behind an aircraft ahead with tight spacing. We did get a slight roll left then right but I immediately slowed to 230 and had the FO tell MIA we were slowing. This time the aircraft ahead was not kept high and so I hand flew slightly above VNAV path to assure at FL230 we would not have wake turbulence. Later [that day] Tower cleared us to takeoff before [another air carrier aircraft] had rotated. After I lined the jet up on the centerline and after takeoff clearance; we waited 8-10 seconds for [the other air carrier aircraft] to rotate. We then took off. We were given heading 105 [on departure; and the other air carrier was given heading 120]. The aircraft behind us was given 090. We encountered wake turbulence behind [the other air carrier aircraft] due to crosswinds. MIA has minimized separation and rushed operations such that it is my experience safety is impacted.First; the next time MIA says keep it rolling and cleared to takeoff; I will ask to exit when an aircraft is still not near rotating. Second; MIA needs to review the operating practices in play. Lack of separation at FL380; being placed below and behind a heavy with a quartering tailwind; 10+ miles separation was not enough with 30+ knot tailwind. Change the practice of [descending] a non-heavy behind and below a heavy to descending the heavy below the following aircraft.

column121: At start of shift; we were informed that NOTAMs had not been available since approximately XA:00z due to damage to the FAA servers.  Several messages sent by [the] domestic manager to get NOTAMs by calling Airport Operations at our airports to obtain NOTAM information.  However; this wouldn't work with many international airports due to language barrier (later resolved when international NOTAM access was restored;) and even with domestic airports; the information is only good until the phone call would be terminated because without new NOTAMs coming in; we would have no way of knowing if a new NOTAM was added later.  Additionally; Center; FIR and FDC NOTAMs were not being updated either; so that information also not available as required by FAR and FOM.Consequently; I elected not to release any of my flights until the NOTAM system came back up.  I attempted to have the flights all prepped so they could be sent immediately when the NOTAM system started coming back; but I fell behind even doing that; and all 13 flights on my desk released late and took the associated delays.  Contributing to the late releases were thunderstorms approaching ZZZ during the inbound and having to focus my attention on those rather than getting flight plans prepped.  My purpose with this report is to both self-disclose the fact that I sent releases later than specified by the manual but also to raise concerns about management's solution to 'mitigate' the NOTAM issue.  The manual is clear about our requirement to check ALL NOTAMs; and merely calling airport operations does not ensure that all NOTAMs are received.  Some NOTAMS; like runway closures; taxiway closures; approach light outages; etc; may come from Airport Operations; but others may be issued by the FAA NOTAM office (FDC NOTAMs;) others are issued by the ATC centers.  It's simply unrealistic and imposes too much of a workload on both international and domestic dispatchers to be expected to call dozens of airports (9 alone on one of my ETOPS flights;) along with multiple centers to try and get NOTAM information while also dealing with thunderstorms and all of our other flight following duties.It seemed very much that the overriding concern was getting releases out regardless of whether it was legal or prudent to do so. Apparently; the FAA puts the NOTAM servers on the top floor of one of their building.  When thunderstorms moved through; the roof leaked and allowed water to soak all of the servers. Better server placement by the FAA would be a good start along with a robust backup system in a completely different location along with the necessary programming and bandwidth so that failing over to the backup system is a near-instant process rather than requiring hours.

Then the call for gear down and flaps 30 at 180 knots. PF was approaching the localizer course; called flaps 45 at 160 knots. To reduce automation workload the autopilot was disconnected and was preparing to make a left turn to intercept the localizer and glide slope. The stick shaker activated at this time because the flight computer detected a pending stall with the flight spoilers deployed. Immediately after the flight spoilers were fully retracted; the stick shaker stopped and the aircraft was on speed with flaps at 45 degrees. A left turn was made intercepting the localizer and the aircraft was on a stable approach by 1;000 feet.ATC gave direct to the final approach fix for the visual to RWY XX while still descending out of 6;000 and needing to slow to configure for landing. PF could have anticipated needing more distance to reduce airspeed; possibly without flight spoilers; and fully configure the aircraft by 3 miles of the final approach fix by descending sooner and leveling off earlier. This would have reduced pilot workload and automation management allowing for a more thorough scan of the aircraft and its systems before deploying flaps and slowing to final approach speed.

column121: At 7;000 feet during climb the flight attendants called the flight deck and reported fumes and a smell in the cabin. Both flight attendants reported it and said multiple passengers were aware of it as well. I didn't smell anything in the flight deck. I might have gotten a slight acrid smell but now I'm not sure. I contacted ATC and requested to return to ZZZ and reported fumes in the cabin. They [gave us priority handling]. I sent an ACARS to Dispatch saying we were returning to ZZZ. I called the flight attendants and told them we were returning to ZZZ and would be on the ground in 15 minutes. First Officer was the pilot flying and setup for the approach. I briefed it for him. I pulled the QRH and looked at the fumes procedure. I turned off the recirculating fan and pushed in the dump button. I called the flight attendants again to confirm if they were still smelling the odor and they were. I asked if they saw anything. They started telling me about what they saw on the wings. I clarified my question. Did they see anything in the cabin? Smoke or other signs of heat / fire? They did not. On final to XXC we were number 2 to land when an aircraft reported a bird strike. Tower told the aircraft ahead of us to go around. I asked tower about the bird strike and they told me to expect a low approach. I made the decision to land despite the possibility of bird remains. I felt that was the safer course of action. First Officer agreed. We landed. I had instructed the flight attendants to inform me if the conditions worsened otherwise we would taxi to a gate. [Airport response] services followed us to the gate and inspected the interior with an infrared camera and didn't find any sources of heat. Due to no airflow onboard and the temperature rising in the cabin we deplaned. All passengers were grateful for a safe return.As a crew we worked together; kept each other calm and controlled. We communicated well and I'm grateful for the professionalism each member of the crew displayed to have a successful outcome to this event.

column121: We were given an ILS clearance into ZZZ in VMC conditions. A VFR airplane was at our altitude and seemed to be tracking to cross the final approach course. We both had the aircraft in sight and changed to a visual approach to maneuver behind the aircraft. At that point the airplane made a sharp right turn and we had to turn further right (away from the final approach course) to maintain separation. It seemed like the plane was on a long final for ZZZ1 and we were then at 90 degrees off of the final approach and unable to make a stable approach into ZZZ. We called the go-around with Tower and were given a heading and altitude toward the east before switching to Approach Control to come back and try it again.The main issue was the VFR traffic no one was communicating with. The crew did not fully brief the location and potential for conflicting traffic for ZZZ1 when approaching from the south. Had the crew not changed to a visual approach and been given ATC vectors; we may not have had the same issues. A go-around may not have been avoidable due to conflicting traffic but a more thorough brief of the airspace and threats may have increased situational awareness and avoided confusion. We should also have not changed the type of approach at the last minute.
column123: We were given a heading to intercept the localizer to Runway XXL and given a traffic call that was not on frequency. Controller then had us maintain heading and fly through the localizer to avoid traffic which was about 500 ft. above; crossing our path and that of the localizer track. We decided as a crew that if they gave us clearance for the visual; we could maintain separation from the aircraft into ZZZ. We were given just that and made the right turn back towards the runway and began to descend for landing. The general aviation aircraft ahead of us descended into our path and made an unexpected turn as we were continuing. I disconnected the autopilot and continued the turn towards the east to avoid ZZZ3 airspace and aircraft. Once clear of the aircraft; we elected to scrap the approach and were given vectors for another uneventful approach. We were originally on a 5 mile final to Runway XYR when ZZZ swapped runway configuration and we were then rerouted to the south to land north. We briefed the new approach and had the approach loaded and armed. With the change of runways; perhaps there was not enough time to fully brief the new approach and surroundings to point out a runway to the east that could cause some confusion. Some cumulative fatigue was present; as well as it being our third of four legs for the day added to the stress of the situation. I do think the spacing given into ZZZ was a partial factor with a GA aircraft that wasn't talking to anyone. There are steps to help mitigate issues like this; like ensuring complete situational awareness of self and the possibility of others; but ultimately there might always be general aviation aircraft out there operating around controlled airspace's not on frequency.

column121: Landed without a locked nose gear. Heading into ZZZ; I did the before landing flow and put the gear handle down. The gear lights only indicated 2 green mains and the red unlocked light with no nose gear indication. Seconds after the lights illuminated for both the Left and Right Hydraulic Flow. I informed Tower I needed to break off my approach for a gear indication issue and troubleshoot. They gave me a heading and altitude then sent me to approach. Approach gave me vectors while I troubleshot. I performed the landing gear will not extend hydraulically checklist. Part of the checklist is to pull the emergency gear extension handle; I did so briskly and without twisting the handle. The indications did not change and I did not hear or feel a thump. I then pulled even harder on the emergency gear handle and braced myself by putting my feet on the floor then tried again and still no response. I finished the checklist then read through the next checklist to land with defective gear. I called approach and said my checklist was unsuccessful. I asked to return to ZZZ and told them there was no indication for the nose gear; and [advised ATC]. They brought me around for [Runway] XX; I ran through the checklist multiple times to ensure I had the procedure down; then left the book open. I landed softly and held the nose off for as long as possible. Performed the ground evacuation checklist then shut everything off and got out.

column121: Arrived at aircraft. I reviewed the Aircraft Maintenance Logbook (AML) to verify what I had already reviewed on my IPAD. The aircraft had three MEL's: Auto-brakes inoperative; Auto speed brakes inoperative; and External power inoperative. I then found an open write up for the Anti-skid system; and called maintenance to address the issue. (This was the first flight of the day; aircraft was in ZZZ all the previous night).Maintenance arrived; and I showed them the open write-up and gave them the logbook. I then discovered that the B system hydraulic was at 69% with RF displayed. I again called maintenance to address this issue. The technician showed up and filled the system to 88%. I told the technician that I did not put the discrepancy in the AML; and if he wanted me to; I would get the AML from the other maintenance technicians and make an appropriate entry. He said; it's okay. We then pressed on with the other issues. I never made a HYD B low" entry into the AML. Upon landing ZZZ1 and accomplishing our post flight duties; I again noticed that hydraulic system B was at 69% with the RF displayed. I made an AML entry and called Maintenance Control regarding the issue. I then left the aircraft and debriefed the oncoming Captain on all of the above issues. I later called the oncoming Captain and was told that during trouble shooting in ZZZ1; a hydraulic leak was discovered in one of the wings.With the many MEL's and the newly discovered maintenance issues; I failed to make an AML entry regarding the low system B hydraulic quantity prior to having it serviced. I also allowed it to be serviced without an AML entry.Suggestions: Maintenance could clear MEL's on overnights and service low fluid quantities. They could also investigate low fluid quantities that are out of the ordinary."

column121: Upon landing; we were advised by Ramp control that our gate was occupied and to have Ground Control hold us off of the gate.  Ground Control cleared us to taxi north on [taxiway] 1 from 2; make a u-turn in the pad; and then hold short of 3 on 4.  We did so and were the third aircraft in line.  A B737 was first and an E-175 was second.  After a while; the E-175 was cleared to his gate and made a hard right to get out of line and proceeded to his gate.  Because the Captain was on the radio with Operations and I was on the radio with Ramp Control; we did not immediately move away to close the gap left by the departing E-175.  Upon completion of our radio calls; the Captain dropped the parking brake and began slowly moving forward to close the gap between us and the B737 that was now the first aircraft in line.  I noticed Aircraft Y coming from my right at a higher than normal rate of speed but was initially convinced that he was cutting through the pad and would be turning south on taxiway 5 to form a second line of aircraft holding short of 3.Both the Captain and I realized at the same time that the Captain of Aircraft Y was trying to squeeze between us and the B737 ahead. The Captain hit the brakes hard enough to make the aircraft stutter to a stop. Had we not noticed Aircraft Y and the Captain of my aircraft not hit the brakes; it is possible that the left wingtip of Aircraft Y that was rapidly cutting in line might have come across our flight deck window.  We were both stunned.  No clearance had been given for that aircraft to squeeze between us and the aircraft ahead of us.  No heads up had been given on either the Ground Control frequency or the ramp frequency to alert us that he was going to try and squeeze in ahead of us.  In my over 20 years of flying for an airline; I have never before seen such a reckless move and it is the closest I have ever come to an aircraft accident. I have thought about this for the past 22 hours and cannot for the life of me think of anything that would cause a pilot to think that taxiing in this manner was safe; a good idea; or in the best interest of anything I know about the safe operation of an aircraft and the protection of the passengers in one's care. I cannot speak for the mindset of the Captain in Aircraft Y.  I cannot think of anything that would cause me to operate an aircraft in this manner and therefore have no idea what to suggest.
column123: Our gate was occupied; so we were instructed to get in line on the taxiway behind a company aircraft. During this time; the line began to move and I taxied forward. Another company Aircraft Y approached at a fairly high taxi speed and cut in front of us. I was able to stop in time after realizing where they were planning to go. If I had not seen them; their wing would of hit the front of our aircraft. We had switched off ground frequency to get an update on our gate. I returned to the frequency and asked what that was. I believe Aircraft Y answered that there was no room at the end of the line (the reason for cutting in front of us). Later; I asked the Ground Controller  what their flight number was; and I was told 'Snitches get stitches'.  I asked the Controller if I heard them right and Controller responded that it was a joke. I responded that I didn't think it was funny; I took it as a threat; and asked for the Tower phone number. I believe Aircraft Y taxied in front of us not knowing with certainty that we would see them. They did something that could of potentially damaged aircraft or injured persons. I can't speak for the crew of flight Aircraft Y or why they thought that was good practice and safe to do.  As far as my crew; I don't believe there was anything we could of done to change the outcome.  As far as the Ground Controller; I believe by what Controller said; Controller saw what had happened and didn't intervene. This created the possibility of two aircraft colliding on the ground. Instead; I believe; Controller thought the best course of action was to make a joke out of the situation.

column121: First Officer's landing. After touchdown and roll out to the end; we were issued taxi instructions while still on the runway and during transfer of control from FO to Captain for taxi. I heard taxi Alpha to the gate which I read back. As we turned across the hard stand for gate X from Alpha the controller informed us we had been instructed to taxi Alpha Fox. Busy airports should have a standard and understood initial taxi route so that you have time to clear the runway and listen to further instructions. Maybe they could be depicted on the approach plate or in the airport diagram or the controller could issue with landing clearance.
column123: On the landing roll out while we were transferring controls we were issued a taxi clearance to gate X. The Captain still had the radios as we were decelerating through about 80 knots. He responded to the radio call and I can clearly remember him saying taxi to the gate via Alpha. There was no correction from ATC so we taxied to the gate. As we crossed the ramp area the Controller advised us the instructions were Alpha Echo Foxtrot. We apologize and proceeded to the gate with no further issues.The inability to hear the controllers instructions clearly at a busy time in the landing roll out combined with the lack of correction by ATC when our read back was incorrect. In the future I will restate the instructions from ATC once I have the radios on the ground after the roll out is complete. I will also plan not to respond the ATC during task saturation like this.

column121: On arrival at ZZZ; winds were variable and began to favor Runway XX for landing. We were set up for landing on Runway XY. I; acting as Pilot Monitoring for this leg due to special qualification airport; suggested to Captain that we swap our planned arrival runway due to winds and additional available landing distance (approximately 500 feet) for landing on Runway XX. The FMC was reprogrammed correctly; briefed; and we accepted a heading to intercept final Runway XX. With approximately a 30 degree intercept; approach control cleared us for the ILS XX. Captain selected approach mode early. This caused the aircraft to capture a false glideslope and the aircraft began a descent prior to capturing the localizer. I called this to the Captain's attention; of which he was also aware.Prior to localizer capture I recommended a discontinued approach. Altitude was well above Minimum Safe Altitude and the approach was salvageable but due to my experience level in the jet; I suggested a soft go-around. The Captain elected to continue; to which I agreed and remarked that our subsequent protected altitude would be 2;600 feet; which we were currently above; and that I would monitor. The Captain; slightly flustered about the false glideslope capture began to fiddle with Auto Pilot disconnect; Flight Director reset; and approach mode was re-armed. The new capture mode now is LOC but with a failed Glideslope. The aircraft has defaulted into the current vertical speed. I call slightly below glideslope; Captain again resets Auto pilot; Flight Director; and re-arms the approach mode. Localizer captures; Glideslope has been armed; and we are currently in a 700 to 800 FPM descent; very slightly low on Glideslope; at a safe speed; and safe altitude.I call attention to our protected Final Approach Fix altitude and glideslope intercept at ZZZZZ 2238 feet. If I remember correctly; we were approximately 3 miles from ZZZZZ when I remarked that at our current Flight Path Angle would have us slightly below our target altitude without any correction at ZZZZZ. Let me be clear; the aircraft was; based on our current descent rate; projected to be only slightly below 2;300 feet at the Final Approach Fix. A minor correction would have rectified the approach path angle and captured the glideslope. I called our altitude to the Captains attention once more approximately 1 to 2 miles prior to ZZZZZ; where we had now reached 2;300 feet; the charted approach value. Right as I was going to call for the Go Around at ZZZZZ; the tower controller issued a Low Altitude Alert; the Go Around was called and initiated; and the aircraft was at approximately 2;100 feet; a little less than 200 feet low at the charted glideslope intercept altitude; as well as above 1;000 feet above ground.The Go-Around was accomplished without error and a subsequent ILS was flown to Runway XX without any additional complications. Upon debrief; I became aware that the Captain was unaware that he had not captured the Glideslope. I re-framed the situation for us to consider alternate action and explained my reasoning for a requested discontinued approach prior to localizer capture. I am still low time and in consolidation. I had no reason to expect that we could not become stable with glideslope capture prior to Final Approach Fix. Hindsight is exactly that and this event began and ended all within 4 miles. The Go-round was completed to qual standards with safety and stable approach criteria in mind.False glideslopes capture prior to localizer capture due to not allowing the aircraft to capture in LOC or LNAV prior to arming the approach mode. Again; I believe I was very clear about our impending altitude deviation; however I don't believe I heard any response from the Captain from 3 miles(my initial call) and 1 to 2 miles(my second que). I could be wrong. The whole event spanned a time frame of less than 3 minutes from 'looks good' to 'doesn't look so good' so I could NOT have fit many more altitude callouts in that span. Due to my low experience in the jet; I incorrectly expected a correction that I did not receive. The go around was initiated at or just seconds after the Final Approach Fix. An assumption of understanding is not the greatest way to handle approaching a go around. I do not believe I was hinting and hoping but I will be more aggressive with my descent planning awareness callouts so as not to enter into a [undesirable situation] in the future. However; the correct decision was made concerning the safe operation of the aircraft and the proper response was executed.
column123: Trip was third leg of the day.  Landed from second leg at around XA:40 local and got to sleep room at XB:10L.  Awakened 30 early of show time at approximately XB:40L.  Weather was marginal regionally and at ZZZ. ZZZ1 was filed alternate but also monitored weather at ZZZ2 for second option.  First Officer has less than 75 hours and ZZZ is Special Qual field. Identified the CFIT (Controlled Flight into Terrain) hazard; short runway; marginal weather; etc.  Pre briefed the ILS XY enroute as winds were favoring that runway.  Also talked about EFVS (Enhanced Flight Vision Systems) and auto land contingencies.  Upon contacting ZZZ approach; they asked if we wanted ILS XX due to a wind shift.  Initially decided to stick with XY but reversed the decision seconds later due to shorter usable runway on XY due to displaced threshold and winds favoring XX slightly.I was flying the approach while the First Officer set up and briefed the ILS XX.  We re-accomplished the approach checklist and accepted a clearance direct to the Final Approach Fix to cross at 2;600 feet and maintain until established; cleared for the ILS.  We put the 2;600 foot hard restriction at the Final Approach Fix and were navigating LNAV/VNAV.  Just prior to Final Approach Fix I mistakenly selected the approach mode.  The aircraft immediately intercepted what I believe was a false glide slope and begun to descend before intended.  I turned off both flight directors and attempted to get the aircraft out of approach mode. The aircraft stayed in approach mode because I did not disengage the autopilot.  So; after re-engaging the aircraft tracked the localizer in LOC mode and Vertical Speed with Glideslope Flight Mode Annunciation struck through as a failed mode.  Realizing the error; I disconnected both flight directors and autopilot and immediately re-engaged and re-automated.  At this point I believe the aircraft momentarily intercepted a glide path; and almost immediately and simultaneously with the Tower Controller realized we were about 250 feet low of the glide slope intercept altitude.  We immediately performed a discontinued approach and climbed to 3;000 feet.  We received vectors for another ILS XX and auto landed uneventfully.Fatigue was undeniably a root cause although not the only issue here.  Flying two legs and then getting only 30 minutes opportunity to nap between legs was just a little too much for me despite 'feeling pretty good' ahead of the flight involved. In retrospect I should have used LNAV/VNAV to get solidly on the ILS final before selecting approach mode.  And; also; I should have and will in the future decide to discontinue an approach as soon as any serious mode switching starts happening on the final approach. In the light of day and after a nap I know this solidly; but it is much more difficult with a foggy brain at XF:00.  So; in the future; I'm going to use LNAV/VNAV more and not use APP until later in the approach. Revision of the flight pairing to allow for more rest time...even an hour nap; would help.  Also; making sure to use LNAV/VNAV and protect GSIA (Glide Slope Intercept Altitude) at 1 NM prior to the intermediate fix.

column121: After seeing my flight was delayed; I called Maintenance Control and they said they weren't able to service the hydraulic system I had written up the night before. The local maintenance didn't have the correct parts or fluid. The technician told me they were flying out the parts; fluid; and mechanics from ZZZ. I asked if hydraulic fluid was allowed to fly and they said it was fine. After the aircraft arrived and the mechanics finished servicing the aircraft; I arrived and began my preflight duties. The mechanics said they had one sealed can of hydraulic fluid and the pump tool they used to service the system. I called the on Duty Pilot and he told me it was fine as long as it was sealed and the partially used can was being left. This didn't sit right with me so I tried to find information about it in the manual. Hydraulic fluid wasn't listed but there also wasn't a phone number for the company HAZMAT specialist. I escalated the issue to the Union and they were able to find a reference in the Dangerous Goods Manual (DGM) appendix about hidden hazards. I also googled the hydraulic fluid (Mobile HyJet IV-Aplus) and found the safety data sheet listed the fluid as a Class 9 Dangerous Good. After leaving a voicemail with the Duty Pilot saying I was going to deny boarding to the fluid and equipment; the duty manager called me and asked why I was going to leave the items and that it was going to cost a lot of money to get it back to ZZZ. I referenced the DGM and they said I was good to depart.This [Hazmat violation] was either caused by ignorance of our DG policies or was negligent behavior on the part of operations. I've been told before from them that hydraulic fluid is Hazmat. They once drove 3-4 hours to another airport because of this same issue. Either way; this was a significant safety violation. A comprehensive review of DG policies and the quality of training need to happen. Either they actually didn't know or they disregarded safety policy for the sake of operational convenience. Either is scary in a 121 airline.

column121: The flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 was the third leg of our day. We had landed at XA00Z which was an hour advance of planned passenger's arrival. Our passengers soon notified us of late arrival upon which I checked to ensure we would not be affected by EDCT (Estimated Departure Time Clearance) and that weather wouldn't be a factor. I then obtained our flight clearance which included a full route meaning we weren't getting our shorter overwater route. That route would also avoid any of the approaching weather by a wide margin. I re-ran our flight plan to ensure we had adequate fuel as the new one was 110 NM longer and would slightly change winds. The original route required 3;570 lbs total including enroute burn; 45 min reserve; and alternate based on cruise altitude of FL400. No alternate was required though as destination weather was > 5000/5 for the entire day and projected to remain so. Still; we plan and carry alternate fuel anytime we have the ability to do so. I had rounded the final fuel load up to 4;000 lbs total as it's all too common flying in or out of ZZZ3 airspace and suddenly getting significantly different routing or held down below cruise altitude for a bit. That decision would prove critical in preventing a divert later in flight. We boarded passengers at XB30Z and were given taxi clearance to 30. Upon nearing the runway; we were told to taxi to the holding area and would start taxi again at XB50Z for a XB54Z release. Approaching XC00Z; we were cleared to taxi and then into position and hold where we sat for approximately 3 minutes before being cleared for takeoff. Shortly after checking in with departure; we were given a 250 kt speed restriction and then given multiple vectors 90 degrees off of route. During most of this we were held below 15;000 ft. After being cleared back onto our flight plan; we were step climbed 6 times until we reached FL 330 about 30 minutes into the flight. During this time we also had to request deviations for weather. A slight left deviation would've allowed us to safely clear all the weather even at the lower altitude; but all aircraft were being directed that right was the only choice. Based on what traffic we had directly in view and on TCAS; it didn't make sense as it looked clear with all possible conflicts being to the west. We attempted to work right but even with significant deviations directly westward we were going to be boxed in by cells. Both NEXRAD and our onboard radar indicated yellow to red echoes well above our current altitude. We and other aircraft at higher altitudes continued to request eastward deviations and were denied. We also repeatedly requested higher as that would've been a satisfactory way of being able to comply with what they needed; but again were denied. At this point; I told the ZZZ3 Center controller that we had no choice but to go left as there was no place we could safely penetrate the weather. They finally relented and after a short deviation that was within 2-3 NM east of the course line; we were around it and back on flight plan. I was prepared to declare pilot authority to deviate for safety of aircraft; passengers and crew had they not. Between the additional ground time; ATC vectors; deviations; and hold down; we had eaten significantly into the additional fuel and were showing below a 45 min reserve if we remained at the lower altitude. This was even after seeing the deteriorating fuel state early and slowing down significantly from cruise speed to M.65. After again requesting further climb and being denied; I declared minimum fuel. Instead of the controller acknowledging; we were shifted to the next controller. Upon checking in; we were still held down and told to expect some time before climb. I again interjected on the radio that we were minimum fuel which was acknowledged by the new controller by him stating; 'uh..ah...well; ok.' He then stated we wouldn't get any further climb until with ZZZ4 Center. By that time we would be over State andstill at FL330 just over an hour into flight. The PM and I evaluated the fuel state and knowing the potential ATC delays we could face in ZZZ1 area airspace despite the great weather that we may be facing a divert. I kept our home base of ZZZ5 and ZZZ6 in mind should that be required. We set 1;000 lbs as an acceptable; safe fuel state needed to both put us above minimum fuel and give us some additional in the event of further delays. After ensuring ZZZ4 Center knew of our fuel state; we were held down for nearly another 10 minutes and then stepped 4 times from FL330 to FL400. After reaching FL400; we pulled back to M.67 and finally saw 1;100 lbs overhead destination and decided to continue. I considered requesting FL430; but based on less tailwind and the increased burn to climb I decided it wouldn't be beneficial. Fuel state improved to 1;280 lbs as the winds shifted and thanks to a small shortcut by Center. During decent with ZZZ4 Center; we were turned roughly 120 degrees off the arrival and it wasn't until questioning the controller if he knew that we had declared that he stated no and turned us back towards ZZZ1. Even though I had never rescinded the previous declaration; it apparently had not been passed to some of the subsequent ATC sectors. I told the controller that we were currently above min fuel but would not continue to be with continued vectors away from destination. We were shortly passed off to the approach controller and landed uneventfully from the RNAV XX. Final fuel state at shutdown was 1;145 lbs.Our passengers being on time might have alleviated some of this as weather had not moved onto our route at that time. More fuel would've have also created more pad; but the additional alternate fuel that wasn't required by regulation or the situation plus additional contingency fuel should've been more than sufficient to prevent it. Getting held down well below planned cruise altitude until almost halfway through a 2.5hr flight is pretty uncommon but played the biggest role in this.

column121: After departing we were flying the ZZZZZ departure.  At around ZZZZZ1 intersection on the departure; at approximately 18;000 feet; the Captain (Pilot Flying) called the transition; followed by ATC giving us a frequency change. As I (Pilot Monitoring) looked down on the aisle stand to change the radio frequency; I heard the Captain say something while there was a sharp right rolling movement of the aircraft.  I looked up and saw a red AUTOPILOT disconnect EICAS message; and the Captain with his hands on the control wheel.  I had assumed that we had experienced wind shear; being in the terrain that we were located.  After the Captain appeared to have the situation under control; I asked the Captain if he wanted me to report the incident; to which he replied yes.  I reported to the controller that we had hit a strong gust on departure; which he acknowledged.  The Captain then said something along the lines of did you see that?  We almost hit a glider.  He had disconnected the autopilot and rolled the aircraft to avoid the glider.I believe I said; is that what happened; to which he said yes.  I can't remember my verbiage; but I believe I then reported to ATC that we had almost hit a glider. ATC acknowledged; and then passed along to the aircraft behind us the information.  At no point did we receive any type of TCAS alert; nor any warning from ATC about a target in the vicinity.  After that last transmission to ATC during which the incident happened; we switched frequencies and continued on with the flight uneventfully.  Later when we were over the ZZZ track; we spoke to the aircraft behind us but they said they had not seen the glider.  Looking back with hindsight; I should have reported the incident to the controller by saying; 'I wish to report a near-midair collision.'  I cannot say enough about Captain's quick thinking and airmanship to bank away from that glider and avoid what would have potentially been an air disaster.
column123: During climbout from ZZZ on the ZZZZZ departure at an altitude of about 17;500 feet we encountered a glider. The Pilot Flying turned off the autopilot and banked right to avoid a possible collision. This event occurred just as we were given a frequency change to Departure Control. At no time during this event was there any traffic depicted on the TCAS nor was there any traffic alerts given by ATC. The Pilot Monitoring passed this information to the controller before switching to our new frequency.

column121: Departing Munich; we were given a push clearance that said; after the crossing Medium Transport aircraft; cleared to push to face north. This was relayed to the push-crew and acknowledged. Push commenced shortly thereafter. We couldn't see; but assumed the Medium Transport passed. A brief time later; Apron control asked us to stop our push; which was relayed to me and the me to the push-crew (there was the lift tug driver and another person on the headphones). I allowed a reasonable amount of time to transfer the stop; but they kept on pushing. I asked them again to STOP the push. The person on the headset seemed confused. I again told them to stop the push; stop the push. The push slowed but never stopped and then began to pick up pace. I then with louder; more stern voice told them to STOP; HALT THE PUSH; figuring the German stop command might do the trick. Nope; the push just continued. After we came to a stop on the start spot; I asked him if he understood what STOP meant - he was flustered. I overheard the FO talking to apron trying to convince them that we had told the push crew to stop multiple times. They mentioned it was a reportable event; hence the filing. This is very rare for Munich or any German airport. I am convinced; this was purely a language issue and the gentleman on the headset did not understand the bigger picture. The tug driver was also dependent on what he told him and I don't think he was aware of what was going on either.
column123: Upon receiving our push clearance Ramp control instructed us to wait for an aircraft to taxi by; then push.  This was relayed to the push-crew; and they immediately began to push.  Ramp control instructed us to stop; as the aircraft we were supposed to wait for had not yet passed by.  The Captain instructed the push-crew to stop and had to tell them several times; before they would stop.  When they did stop; they just paused and began to push again.  This happened; I recall about 3 times; and ramp control kept instructing us to stop; but we could not get the push-crew to do so. The push-crew eventually just pushed us all the way back; contrary to our instructions to 'halt.'  No explanation was given; as to why they would not stop.  Ramp Control informed us of our deviation; and their intention to write a report regarding this. We gave them our apologies and explanation that the push crew was not following our directions to stop as they requested.
column125: Air carrier flight crew reported EDDM ground crew would not stop push back as instructed; possibly due to language barrier; resulting in a ramp excursion.

column121: Departed ZZZ 4L in windy gusty conditions with a normal takeoff. Passing approximately 500 feet; a Rudder Ratio EICAS caution message appeared. I followed the QRH procedure after doing the 'after takeoff' checklist. This procedure stated: Above 160 knots avoid large or abrupt rudder inputs; Crosswind limit is 15 knots; Do not autoland. I made a maintenance write up and we continued. Climb was in IMC with light chop since there was a weather system moving into the east coast.Approximately an hour and half into the flight at FL340 received a Cabin Alt EICAS warning along with Cabin Altitude light and aural warning. We performed the immediate actions: Donned the oxygen masks and established crew communication. I followed the Cabin Altitude checklist and when I came to the decision tree: Cabin altitude is controllable (I switched to the other alt controller without any change) or Cabin altitude is uncontrollable; I felt that I was in between the two since the cabin was slightly above 10;000 feet and HOLDING STEADY. I advised ATC and asked for a lower altitude to the mid 20;000 feet thinking the cabin would decrease below 10;000 feet. I was also reluctant to go any lower because there was weather and turbulence below us. I called the purser and asked if the cabin oxygen masks had dropped and she informed that they had not confirming that cabin altitude never got above 14;000 feet. The cabin altitude decreased below 10;000 but the EICAS message was still illuminated so I asked for lower again. Passing 20;000 feet the Cabin Alt warning went out and the cabin showed approximately 6;000 feet so I elected to stop at FL190. This kept us right above the weather with the FO deviating around the tops.I informed the purser of the situation and made a preliminary PA. Contact with Dispatch was next with Maintenance Control on the line. Maintenance Control was not able to rectify our situation so the Dispatcher and I started looking for a divert airport. Due to the weather and the cross-wind limit of 15 knots due to the Rudder Ratio issue I was very limited in airport selection since the cross winds were in excess of 15 knots in ZZZ1; ZZZ2; ZZZ3; ZZZ; ZZZ4. ZZZ5 was the only option with calm winds; 400 Feet broken; 3 MI visibility and rain.I made the decision to divert to ZZZ5 with dispatch concurrence. I informed the purser and made another PA.We began planning for landing into ZZZ5 and was told of moderate turbulence ahead. I seated the flight attendants. Approaching the IAF for [Runway] XXL ATC informed us of an aircraft ahead of us Going Around since they were unable to see the runway at mins. I inquired about XXR and was told there was another aircraft on approach for that runway. That aircraft landed and we proceeded to a normal landing. Fire and rescue greeted us and after getting the all OK we taxied uneventfully to the gate.

column121: Planned fuel was 6;040 and got fueled to 6;200. We took off with roughly 6;000 pounds of fuel and minimum fuel was 5;564. So we left with well above minimum required fuel according to release. We were enroute and about halfway to 2/3 of the way through as I monitored our fuel burn. I noticed based on current conditions at that time (winds aloft were greater than planned and ATC requested Mach .77 or greater while .76 is planned); that we would be about 700 pounds under planned landing fuel. So as a crew we quickly setup for long range cruise and contacted ATC that we needed to slowdown even though they insisted we maintain a high speed. So we slowed to Mach .63 for long range cruise and then ATC descended us to 27;000 feet from 31;000 feet starting down early because we were slower than surrounding traffic.Then we get instructions shortly after to change arrivals keeping us away from other traffic. Once we finally got situated with the changes; dispatch beat me to notifying them and sent us an ACARS asking about the route changes and fuel. So we told them current plan and situation and based on the information back from dispatch; we had sufficient fuel as long as we maintained LRC (Long Range Cruise speed) to ZZZ allowing us to land with just 100 pounds of fuel more than planned and dispatch had us landing at roughly 1;850 pounds. At some point ATC also queried us asking about why we would be taking off with less fuel than we need to do the flight; even though we didn't. We actually took off with more fuel than planned. ATC was actually being unprofessional about the whole thing and giving us a hard time; because we asked to slow down to conserve fuel as stated over the radios in order to avoid getting into a bad fuel situation later or having to declare minimum fuel; and then he put us on different arrival and etc. It just created more workload and pressure by his attitude and questions as if it was our fault than it needed to be and ATC did not help with that even though they're there to help us.He made us sound bad on the radio as if we didn't know what we were doing about our fuel. Then sometime later while setting up for new arrival; ZZZ does a runway change as well after we got our LDR (Landing Distance Required) and brief; so that added more workload trying to update everything and re-brief in addition to ACARS taking longer than usual to respond. During all of that; Center then instructs us to level at 19;000 feet after getting the first descend via due to VFR traffic at 17;500 feet!  After traffic passes Center then gives us descend via again with immediate handoff to Approach in the same transmission. So First Officer does the handoff while I'm assessing and starting down seeing how quick we need to descend.  I saw we needed to do 6;000 feet or more a minute in order to meet the crossing restriction. I knew that wasn't going to happen so right as I was going to tell First Officer to let ATC know we can't make the restriction because of the level off earlier due to traffic as he was checking on; Approach immediately on initial contact asked if we would make the crossing restriction and we said no.He immediately then got upset and asked if we told the previous controller who would be Center and we said no because we didn't have time as we literally just switched and got the clearance at the same time and literally a few seconds later discovered we couldn't make it work. So we explained that to Approach but he wasn't accepting that and blamed us for not making the restriction or notifying Center before talking with Approach. But we literally had no time between the clearance and handoff at the same time and during the frequency switch that's when we noticed the issue and first transmission with Approach we weren't given the time to tell him that before he asked and queried us. So Approach then gives us two small delay vectors and rejoin arrival. But Approach said we should've told them early on we couldn't make itbut again we explained the situation and that we were not given that chance to do so. So we then continued on after that with no further issues.Insufficient fuel planning on release as it never reflects the actual fuel burn since release doesn't account for delay vectors or vectors on approach. The issues with ATC and last second changes to arrival and runways were a result of not having enough fuel at normal cruise followed by slow ACARS affected our ability to fly the planned arrival causing a higher workload for us and ATC which then caused the hiccup with crossing restrictions and with crossing traffic as well.  For fuel; we slowed for LRC and got a couple shortcuts once on the banker arrival. We were able to gain most of our fuel back because of LRC and landed with 2;200 pounds. For the crossing restriction; we just explained the situation to ATC and along with Center; Approach gave us a hard time and we notified them we couldn't do it; then we carried on with no further issues after that.For fuel planning and fuel contingency; we should be doing a minimum of like 500 pounds and 750-1;000 pounds extra on IFR days. Also for holding fuel; that should be 600 pounds minimum as we realistically burn more than 400 pounds on a go-around on a VFR day. As far as ATC goes after discussing with my First Officer as the situation that unfolded after another as a result; we maybe should have declared Minimum fuel early on knowing we wouldn't have enough unless we slowed down. But because of LRC and little to no delay vectors we determined to have enough hence why we never declared. However; if we declared min fuel early on that would've maybe given ATC more understanding even as frustrating as it may be; and allow us priority to slow and not have to descend via and etc. And that maybe would've avoided the issue with crossing at ZZZZZ1 and etc. One thing led to another; so next time maybe declare min fuel and decline a descend via to stay up high longer and to reduce workload. It was a good learning experience except for lack of professionalism and help from ATC.

The Captain reported Center and Approach Controllers criticized and questioned them on the frequency over both issues.
