column121: We departed on a Class II international trip. The previous day (with a different Second in Command); we had tested the HF radios by receiving a time hack on the WWV atomic clock HF frequency. We had a good operations check and assumed the HF radios were working properly. The day of the trip; we again tested the HF by receiving a time hack on the ground; however; we could not transmit on the primary and secondary frequencies at the time due to our close proximity to the FBO hangars. After departing and prior to coast-out; the Second in Command (SIC) (also an experienced Captain who happens to have a lot of experience with HF in the military) attempted to test the HF radios using the Primary Frequency and a Secondary frequency while I flew the plane and managed the VHF radios. Prior to coast-out; the SIC determined that the HF radios were not transmitting. We reviewed the Operations Manual to make sure we were operating the HF radio properly and to make sure we weren't missing anything. We determined that we were operating it accordingly and that we had tried everything we could in order troubleshoot the problem. We briefly discussed our contingency options again prior to coast-out (including returning to our departure airport) and informed Center of the issue.  Center informed us that there was a flight right behind that we could relay our position with until we got back in radar contact. After that; there would be a southbound flight that was paralleling our course that would relay for us until we reached our destination.After discussing this with ZZZ Center; the controller also assured us that this was a legal option. We made radio contact with the relaying flight on the VHF air-to-air frequency. After we were confident we could continue to communicate and relay; the SIC and I again discussed our options and contingencies and we both elected to continue. We relayed our positions successfully until we reached ZZZ Center on VHF again. Our next contingency plan was that if we couldn't relay with another flight we would divert as ATC did not have any northbound traffic for us to relay with in order to return state-side. During this time; we briefed the passengers on the possibility of [diverting]. I transferred the controls to the SIC so that he could fly while I coordinated with ATC; relayed our position; plotted our course; and kept up with the NavLog in an effort to reduce each other's workload. He had worked hard attempting to troubleshoot the HF radios; meanwhile having me manage the radios and navigation allowed me to handle the lost HF event. Once talking to ZZZ Center; we made VHF contact with the southbound flight and we were confident that we could continue relaying position reports; we elected to continue to our destination via relay.We recorded each waypoint along the route on the NavLog and plotting chart; and successfully relayed each one. The other flight in turn would verify that each reporting point was received by ATC. Once we were within range of ATC; we contacted via VHF; they confirmed radar contact; we again exchanged the flight controls (I resumed pilot-flying duties and the SIC resumed pilot-monitoring duties) and we continued the rest of the way to our destination on VHF radios in the radar environment. The rest of the flight was uneventful. After deplaning our passengers at the destination; I called Maintenance Control to create a write-up and MEL the HF radios. The MEL restricted us to VHF communication. The log was completed and the MEL was complied with. My next call was to Operations to inform them of the issue and restrict the aircraft to 'Class 1 navigation only' until maintenance could fix the HF radios. The remainder of our scheduled trips were within radar service areas; so there were no additional operational issues concerning the HF radios and the MEL. As a side note; despite being a stressful situation; I believe the SIC (another Captain) and I handled the situation quite well all thingsconsidered. We communicated; risk assessed; and split duties effectively. If ATC hadn't assured us this was a legal option (it sounded like we weren't the first one to have this problem) or other flights had not been willing or able to help us relay our position; then we would have definitely had to have returned to our departure airport or diverted  after burning off a bunch of fuel to get the plane below landing weight.These HF radios probably have not been exercised in over a year due to COVID-19 international travel restrictions and lack of Class II flying. While we did test the HF the previous day by receiving a time hack; we did not check the transmit function of the HF radios. We checked the HF radios reception the previous day by receiving the time hack; however; we did not test the transmit function of the radio. Checking the transmitter the day before would have allowed us to MEL the HF earlier and prevent this trip from occurring on this tail number. Also I would recommend that as we continue to develop  training scenarios as part of our  recurrent training programs; that we include Class II navigation scenarios to supplement that training. In a normal year (without pandemic-level travel restrictions); we don't individually get to perform very many Class II trips. I believe including Class II training scenarios; including what to do during lost-comm events as well as other emergencies such as single-engine failure; depressurization; and medical emergencies); would be extremely beneficial in building decision-making processes in a Class II environment.
column123: During the departure; I told the PIC that I would conduct the FMS navigation check and the HF check. The FMS navigation check was conducted almost immediately using a VOR.  The HF check was another story. On deck at departure airport; I was having issues getting a radio check on the ground with ZZZ Radio; but after discussing with maintenance; we collectively thought it was interference from the hangars right at the ramp.  An air check was required.  We could hear the HF clock on 10000 MHz but just could not raise ZZZ Radio.As the departure airport is very close to the ocean; we coasted out as I was attempting to get the HF to work.  Both HF radios seemed to be having a common issue with transmitting; this despite being able to hear intermittently HF traffic.  I was able to tune the radios but continued to fail in any contact with ZZZ Radio.  (HF1 seemed to not electronically tune as I pressed to transmit; HF2 seemed to tune pressing transmit; but no one could receive).  While the PIC flew the plane (and spoke with ATC); I continued to trouble shoot the radios exhausting all system knowledge.  We even pulled the manual out to make sure I was not missing anything.During my troubleshooting of the radios; the PIC was provided an option from ATC of relay with other aircraft.  Specifically; there was another aircraft very close by our position.  The other aircraft pilots agreed to take our HF relay if we needed that option.  At this point; I reported to the PIC that our HF radios were failed.  We were pretty much at the final fix prior to HF operations (20 minutes after takeoff). We both discussed the options prior to committing to the HF relay.  We could turn around and head back.  We could relay with other aircraft.  We could also pick up another relay that could take us all the way down (or perhaps back to ZZZ if we wanted that option).  We decided to continue with company to keep the flight going safely.  The clients were kept informed.  ATC was kept completely in the loop.As we entered radar control; ATC called to tell us that there were no northern flights that could help us get back but there was an Air Carrier flight which was willing to relay HF the remaining way.  Since the remaining oceanic airspace had 3 more fixes; we decided that this was a safe option allowing us to keep the mission on track.  With ATC facilitation; we contacted the flight while in radar control and established the link for our HF relay.  The HF relay with the Air Carrier took us into ATC airspace.  The rest of the flight was uneventful. Primarily; we both felt comfortable that we could continue to our destination safely. Secondly. This HF teaming; thanks to ATC; [and other flights] allowed our passengers to get to their destination with all the COVID restrictions compliances intact for their entry (a significant travel issue). Cause; aging equipment. I am not sure that this HF failure can be avoided.  Perhaps we need to do more checks of our equipment and keep them at a higher standard of repair and readiness.

On reflection; I should have positioned the aircraft more aggressively to drop the left wing to see the other plane earlier. I also could have immediately asked for a vector from Approach to keep me clear; although this traffic appeared to be climbing out of Dan Jones (T51) or Dry Creek (TS07) and presented a late radar contact for the traffic call.

column121: On go-around Aircraft X had a gradual loss of power which resulted in having to land in a nearby field. The airplane had been sitting (pickled) for three years a week before but had recently been flown from and to maintenance for the annual inspection (at ZZZ) and back to ZZZ1. The same day the off-field landing occurred; I had performed several landings and had no problems at all with the aircraft until this last takeoff/climbout.The RPM seemed to drop and the aircraft was not producing thrust. The engine has a massive carb heat system. Carb heat was used and possibly left on in the climbout however nobody thinks that carb heat would cause enough power loss to cause a catastrophic thrust - lift scenario in low density altitude flight conditions (sea level 65 degrees).Other issues might have been debris in the recently fueled tank; carburetor float issue and then possibly a prop governor issue. We could not reproduce the problem on the ground. So far; the issue is unknown as to the continual loss of power.In looking back at this event; I think that it would have been prudent to take a newly run aircraft that has been sitting for a while and just out of annual to a large airport where there is more room for errors. Only after several hours or days of 'testing' should you exercise an aircraft to other shorter riskier areas. You just never know what can go wrong. They say hindsight is 20/20 but I will need to take a better look at risk management when it comes to flying an aircraft that has an unfamiliar history or has just come out of hibernation and or annual inspection.

column121: I was returning to my home base of ZZZ from ZZZ1. I am flying my newish Aircraft X; of which I have about 19 hours in. It should be noted that most of my flight hours are from 25 years ago. I knew ZZZ had some crosswinds but I thought they were manageable and I felt I needed to push myself a bit. If I remember; the winds were about 13 at 260 (260 at 13). Part of my challenge was that they were not reporting winds on METAR only ATIS. Upon approach the winds started gusting to 19. This would give an 8.4 kt. crosswind gusting to 12 knots; something I should be able to handle. So; on the first attempt; I think my approach was OK; but I flared high; bounced and quickly realized a go-around was the best option. Not perfect but decent decision making.The second attempt is where things went very wrong. This time I came in with 20 degrees of flaps. My approach was probably a bit fast; but seemed OK as I got closer to the airport. First of all; I flared too high again; bounced; but then made the mistake to try and salvage the landing. On the second bounce I recognized that the plane was proposing and I'd have a prop strike if I let it drop again. So; I started another go-around; but the plane would not climb; more importantly I wasn't facing down the runway but more towards the left side. At this point the helicopters parked left of the runway are getting bigger in my windshield but I know I've got to gain air speed. The one correct decision I made was to keep the nose down until I gained some airspeed. Eventually I got the speed and was able to climbout. At some point in this I realized why I couldn't climb; I had raised all of the flaps! I then came around and successfully landed the plane on the third attempt. It was bad enough that after I parked; the fire department came over to 'congratulate' me on my recovery; but I really think it was to make sure I was OK.I learned the following on this landing attempt. I need more time with my instructor with landings; especially crosswind landings. I need more practice on Go-Arounds focusing on flap management and right rudder.

column121: After flying a practice RNAV (GPS) approach into ZZZ; I was climbing through 2;000 feet on the missed approach when I checked in with Approach. Approach provided an altimeter setting (30.12; which had changed since my last check-in of 30.11) and a few seconds later provided a heading for vectors for the ILS at ZZZ1.  I leveled off at the assigned altitude of 3;000 feet and shortly after; ATC asked me to maintain 3;000 feet.  Considering my altimeter was reading 3;020 feet; I knew this call meant something was not right.  I scanned the instruments and saw the altimeter setting was now set to 29.92. I requested the altimeter setting again and when I entered the correct setting; I was approximately 300 feet above my assigned altitude.  After landing I was able to determine the sequence of events that caused this deviation.My airplane has an Aspen Avionics Evolution 1000 PFD.  I have had this for the last X years and feel I am proficient in operating it.  It has a feature that; in my piston powered general aviation airplane; is not used.  If you press the 'baro' button and then push the right knob; the altimeter setting will change to 29.92.  Since I never climb to FL180; I have never used this feature. In this situation; when I contacted ATC; they gave me the altimeter setting; and since it was different; I pushed the 'baro' button and turned the right knob to the correct setting. When ATC then provided me a vector; I needed to move the heading bug almost 180 degrees (it had been set during the southbound approach and now I was flying northbound).  Instead of spinning the heading knob (the same right knob) 180 degrees; I pushed the knob which automatically sets the heading bug to the current heading.  What I didn't realize was that when I pushed the right knob; the 'baro' function was still active and therefore set the altimeter to 29.92.  The heading bug also aligned to the current heading; however since I was in turbulence; I assume I bumped the knob twice instead of once.  I didn't notice the change in altitude because I was in a climb.  When I reached 3;000 feet; I leveled off like normal without being aware that I was higher than I should be.Moving forward I will need to be more careful and aware of what function is active in the PFD before making changes.  However; my fear is that it may be another X or more years before something like this happens again and as time moves forward; we tend to forget these events.  I do think this is an opportunity for Aspen to make a software revision.  If this baro reset feature is meant for aircraft passing through 18;000 feet; it would be nice if this feature could be disabled for installations in aircraft that cannot reach that altitude.  Alternatively; if this feature is meant for aircraft passing through 18;000 feet and it is utilized at an altitude well below that; a flashing yellow flag (similar to what happens when approaching the selected altitude) would help to visually annotate the change that was just made. I'm not trying to remove responsibility from the pilot; but the pilot has hundreds of things to remember when flying.  Modern avionics should not be adding to the list of quirks that need to be remembered.

column121: With one passenger; took off from ZZZ1; was circling the west side of [the island] intending to land back at ZZZ1. At 2;000 feet MSL; abeam ZZZ; lost 400 RPM engine power; engine got very rough; with bad vibration. Requested priority handling for Runway XX at ZZZ. Upon reaching threshold; aircraft was much too high and too fast for landing; was still at maneuvering speed from descending from cruise; made low pass and went around for another attempt at Runway XX; at about feet 200 AGL; with throttle at max power setting; and barely able to maintain altitude. Runway surface was shortened to about 2;600 feet by construction. There were two orange construction barriers; one at the end of the shortened runway length; and a second one about midway within the remaining 3;000 feet of runway closed for construction. Construction barriers were not apparent to me as such from the air. I was not able to touch down at the threshold; and touched down just beyond the first barrier; within construction area.At that point; I still did not see that the barriers were barriers (they looked like flat tarps or orange police tape on the ground). Still at high speed from rollout and heading towards the second barrier; my passenger called for me to go to the left. Steering to the left side of the runway; I passed beside the barrier; and avoided hitting it; and with full braking; came to a stop at the end of the paved surface; and shut down. Nothing was damaged; nobody was hurt; but I had barely avoided the construction barriers; made of concrete. But only on the ground and nearby are they visible as barriers. From the air they look like orange flat tarps or bags. The potential for catastrophe in the event of [a] landing is great. If construction barriers used on runways were made of soft rubber; like traffic cones; or constructed to be collapsible on impact; there would be no hazard; and they would still fulfill their purpose.On my part; my landing was poor. My speed and altitude were too high. Reducing power and using a large amount of flaps; or planning on making a downwind to Runway XY instead would have been necessary to avoid the overrun into the construction. My mindset at the time of the accident was one thing 'get on the ground in as few seconds as possible'; based on training for the total engine failure scenario; where there truly is no time. This scenario was not like that; and needed essentially a normal landing procedure. A partial power loss; like this; is a more common [event] than a total complete engine failure. But the general training syllabus based on the FARs emphasizes the total engine failure scenario; almost to the exclusion of other emergencies. I thus suggest that the training syllabus mandated by the FARs be changed to put more emphasis on a partial power loss; and assessing the difference between that and a more total power loss. I intend to take a flight review in the short term; with emphasis on practice for a partial power loss; like this scenario; and being on proper approach speed for short field landings at the threshold in such scenarios. Next day; mechanic found electrodes had been bent away from contacts in both spark plugs on one cylinder; causing that cylinder not to fire. He repaired those plugs; and we did a successful ground run; and per his determination that it was fixed; I took off again; from Runway XY; at the beginning of the usable runway surface before displaced threshold; to return to home base; ZZZ2. At 1;200 feet to 1;300 feet MSL (about 400 feet to 500 feet AGL) after takeoff; the problem recurred. I did a 180; reduced power; and with flaps extended; made safe landing touching down at threshold of Runway XX; and came to a stop within the usable runway.The following day; mechanic prepared to pull the affected cylinder; whose spark plugs had been affected the same way as before; to investigate the problem. He found a small black cylindrical object; 1/4' diameter and 3/8' long; out of hard plastic or scratched metal; in the cylinder; and concluded that it was knocking against spark plug electrodes and bending them. Neither he; myself; nor FAA could identify object or its origin. Mechanic is certain it did not originate from within the aircraft; and concluded that it had to have come in through the carburetor heat intake; which is unfiltered. This is unlikely to have happened during operation as carburetor heat inlet is far off the ground. I believe a careless operator did a run-up beside where my aircraft was parked at an outside tie-down; and that run-up kicked the FOD into the carburetor heat intake. On an earlier unrelated occasion; similar carelessness caused my entire windshield to get pitted by kicked up FOD (I had to replace the windshield); making the scenario plausible as my aircraft is always tied down outside. Pilots are taught to avoid doing runups near persons or other aircraft or vehicles due to this danger. But as I cannot control the carelessness of others while I am not present; and hangaring the aircraft is unfeasible; I intend to get cowl plugs for when the aircraft is parked; to avoid this. While I don't feel that they should be mandated; perhaps the FAA needs to officially recommend them for those who must park outside. The FOD removed; I departed from Runway XY again; and this time; there were no problems; landed safely at ZZZ2. Hence; the FOD had been the cause of the engine problem.

column121: I departed ZZZ; climbed normally; received vector for a right turn to a heading of 290 and a climb to 10;000. I complied with all of the uneventfully. West of the airport was cell of precipitation that I couldn't see through. It was depicted as yellow on my weather display. The precipitation was west of the airport and oriented along the axis of about 290 to 300 west of ZZZ.I was doing the ZZZ4 departure. The tower controller advised in the initial climb that in substance that I'd be boxed around on vectors for the climb before being going to the route.A previous departed reported the ceiling at about 6;500 which was basically true. I changed frequency to ZZZ TRACON and got a heading of 290. When I entered the IMC the rain was very intense and it was turbulent. I noticed changes on the vertical speed indicator up and then later down. The temperature was near freezing; but I did not see any actual ice. While climbing in IMC; the radio frequency began to screech such that I couldn't hear anything. That ultimately occurred on both radios and both frequencies. The marker beacon lights were flashing. I received a traffic alert for traffic on my left. It was very turbulent; but I stayed at 10;000 feet as assigned. With no communications (coms); I squawked 7600.I decided to turn 90 degrees right still in IMC because that resolved the traffic; would get me out of the precipitation; was a heading basically on course; was consistent with the expectations from the departure briefing and ZZZ4; and would restore coms. The precipitation was aligned with the vector so remaining on that heading was not viable. There was traffic there. I didn't change altitude (I was at 10;000 ft. the whole time).After the right turn; I exited the side of the precipitation; I was able to hear ground responding to one of my calls (on COM2 on the bottom antenna); so I went back to the departure frequency on COM1 (on the top); re-established communications and departed.The ATC TRACON controller was upset seemed to think that I was in VMC and just turned randomly or something. I've flown through 'yellow' precipitation many times uneventfully. The lost coms procedure when you're on a vector is to either stay on the vector or turn on course. I turned on course because it solved all of the problems; but seemed to surprise ATC. I think that the confusing thing for ATC was that it was fine weather straight over the airport; which is probably what he has on his computer. But west of the airport was unexpectedly intense rain.I'm not sure that this incident could have been avoided given what everyone knew at the time; although once I squawked 7600; the turn on course shouldn't have been a surprise.

My radio transmission was cut short mid-sentence. Immediately thereafter I noticed a burning electrical smell. I quickly shut off the master switch to reduce the risk of an electrical fire. At this point it was clear the flight could not continue and a landing at a nearby airfield would be necessary. My home base; ZZZ1; was only 20 NM north of my current position. I elected to execute a climbing 180 degree turn to reverse course within the SFRA; north-westbound at 4;500 feet MSL. Once north of the SFRA; I remained clear of Class B; C; and D airspace; staying well west of ZZZ2 and the ZZZ3 Class C shelf. As I approached ZZZ1 from the northwest; I contacted the Tower Controller from my cell phone; and he cleared me to land. The no-flap landing was uneventful.As for lessons learned and next steps; I have a handheld radio; but the battery was unfortunately dead. I need to check this more regularly so that it can be relied upon in the event of lost comms. I've also printed out a list of ATC phone numbers in case I need to reach other facilities using my cell phone (I luckily had ZZZ1 Tower saved as a contact on my phone). I also think I should have more seriously considered descending immediately and landing at a closer airport; such as ZZZ4. By climbing to join the reverse course of the SFRA; I put myself in a more dangerous position if an inflight fire had actually developed. Additionally; I have a fire extinguisher in my airplane; but it was secured under the back seat; and I never touched it. I should have removed it from its harness and had it ready to go in case it became needed.I think it's extremely important that pilots regularly think about what they would do in these types of abnormal situations. These situations don't happen often; but when they do quick action is sometimes required to avert a real emergency. I'm lucky this occurred during a daytime VFR flight. A couple weeks ago I was flying at night in IMC on an IFR flight plan. Had this occurred then the situation would have been far more serious.

column121: We began the day at XA:00; the plane had 13 gallons of fuel on the pilots side; and 11 on the other. Generally we plan for 5-6 gallons per load of jumpers. After releasing jumpers I descended down from 9;000 feet AGL a couple miles east of the airport. Under 3;000 feet AGL on a 2/3 mile straight in approach to Runway XX @ ZZZ; I continued losing altitude as plane with the throttle fully out to lose airspeed. (It was put in every couple thousand feet descending to 'clear' the engine.) When the desired speed and altitude was reached; I pushed the throttle in with no response. I enriched the mixture and pumped the throttle; and that also made no change. Checked fuel selectors; mags; etc; all with no luck. I realized the aircraft would not make the runway fairly shortly. Continuing straight in; I would have hit the side of an adobe hill.Right was rougher terrain; so left was the best option. I made an announcement on CTAF but may have been too low at that time. I navigated to the smoothest looking area i could find given the very short amount of time I had to deal with the situation. Dropped full flaps; and slowed down as best I could. The plane touched down; bounced over a few hills; and came to rest slightly upward on another hill. I exited the aircraft thru the pilots door; and looked over the plane; then called Person X to inform him of the situation and was able to text him GPS coordinates While waiting I checked the fuel level in the aircraft; and the passenger side was empty; while the pilots seemed to have about 7 gallons; however the plane was at a slight angle so could have been inaccurate.Burning 17 gallons of fuel for 3 flights is about normal. Especially considering the slightly lengthy times to climb today.

The cracking is right around the pilot point for the front motor supports.  I've done some research online and noticed that this apparently is a common problem among other DJI Mavic Air 2 operators. column121: When I got to Aircraft X; it had a writeup for (paraphrasing) '#4 tire worn'. We were scheduled to take aircraft from ZZZ to ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 to ZZZ to ZZZ3. On our second pass through ZZZ with about five minutes to push the Ops Agent informed us of a Maintenance lock on the Release. About that same time we got an ACARS message from Dispatch saying the same thing and that it was something about a tire change. I called Dispatch and the guy answering the phone said he had tried to call Maintenance and no one answered so he would try again and let me know. I called back seven minutes later and asked to be transferred to Maintenance Control to talk to them directly. Maintenance Control said the tire was allowed only three cycles and the aircraft was 'dead' until it was changed; that it was supposed to be done the first time we went through ZZZ but somehow it didn't happen. This is five minutes before push with no one in sight to change the tire. Five minutes or so after scheduled push; a crew came out to change the tire. The guy that changed the tire took the logbook and came back about 45 minutes later with it saying we were good to go.(As an aside; I informed Maintenance Control the aircraft was coming back to ZZZ for the night and could they change it then. Maintenance said it was only good for three (3) cycles. In 15 years I've never seen a tire written up that wasn't changed immediately and the first I've ever heard that a 'worn' tire is good for only three cycles. This information would have allowed us as a crew to be more proactive to get the tire changed the first time we went through ZZZ or at least set up for the next pass through. This could have prevented over an hour delay.I looked at the logbook and saw in the lower right corner 'MTO W/O Closed' with the 'YES' circled. I didn't look for any narrative in the pink Maintenance part. That is my bad but I took MTO W/O Closed to mean the work was done. We did the 'Before Start Originating' checklist and departed without incident. I noticed a missed call and a text from the succeeding Captain about the logbook having a problem. Being out of the aircraft and in the hotel room by then; I have no way of knowing what the problem was for the logbook but apparently the Captain had to call Contract Maintenance to verify the #4 tire was changed and enter it in the logbook. The long and short of it is I may have flown an aircraft with an open writeup because of improper documentation and my ignorance in seeing that.

column121: During our taxi-out and takeoff role; the Captain and I noted a Number 1 Fuel Filter Bypass Master Caution Light.  We both felt this was part of a MEL condition entered into the aircraft's ELB; but feel the MEL procedure to be both ambiguous and poorly written.  The condition should not be available for ER [Extended Range] operations.During our pre-flight planning activities; the Captain and I noted a defect of 'Repeat. LH Fuel Filter Bypass warning light was on for 5 minutes' written up on the Electronic Log Maintenance Logbook (ELB).  Maintenance indicated that 'Fuel Filter Signal Disagree' on EEC #1 was the actual issue causing this light to indicate. Maintenance deferred the fault by placing the #1 Fuel Filter Bypass Light on MEL 7304A.The ELB indicated that maintenance replaced the #1 engine fuel filter; did an engine idle run; and noted no gross contamination of the fuel in the filter.  No further CDU faults were noted by maintenance.  The number #1 engine 'Fuel Filter Bypass Light' was placarded.  Upon referencing the 737NG MEL; as far as we could tell; this is all the maintenance action items that need to be completed.As for the flight crew actions to be completed for MEL 7304A; we must only assure that the:1. 'Remaining fuel filter pressure warning system must operate normally.'2. 'Maintenance is required to verify malfunction is in fuel filter bypass warning system on initial deferral.'We noted that the flight crew actions for this MEL are rather sparse: Our normal pre-flight activities would ensure that the #2 Fuel Filter Bypass Light was extinguished and maintenance indicated they performed step 2.During our pre-flight briefing the Captain and I discussed this MEL; verified that the system was not needed for ER operations - as our flight to Destination would; of course; fall under this category.  Unfortunately; a complete discussion and briefing about this item may have fallen slightly short as we became mildly distracted with a separate and unrelated new maintenance fault in the parking brake accumulator system that was noted during our flight deck pre-flight activities.  In turn; our flight became delayed at the gate in ZZZ as the parking brake system needed to be deferred using another MEL.  Additionally; we waited for connecting passengers from an inbound ZZZ1 flight.We pushed back from the gate in ZZZ started to taxi out for a departure on Runway XXR.  During a turn on our taxi to the runway; we both noted that the Master Caution light illuminated for the Number 1 Fuel Filter Bypass Master Caution Light.  I canceled the light and the Captain decided he wanted to stop in a safe area to deal with the possible issue. I agreed and ground control in ZZZ allowed us to stop on Taxiway 1.As the Captain stopped and set the parking brake; we both stated how confused we were about the fuel filter bypass light illuminating.  I checked the 737QRH for this light and it only indicated that 'erratic engine operation' may occur 'in flight'.The Captain and I discussed how it was extinguished after engine start; and only illuminated momentarily on taxi out; during a turn; and it was now extinguished again.  We referenced MEL 7304A again from the 737NG MEL.  Nowhere could we find whether the 'inoperative/placarded' light should remain illuminated; extinguished; or momentarily indicate.  We discussed that most MELs similar to this deferral would explain to the flight crew that a caution light may illuminate.  (See example MEL 78030: 'NOTE: The 'Master Caution' and 'ENG' MAY illuminate when performing master caution recall.')The Captain decided to call Dispatch and conference in maintenance while stopped on the taxiway.  We told our Dispatcher about our issue and he brought in Maintenance on the phone line.  The initial maintenance personnel transferred us to the 'Specific area.'  The 'Specific area' advisor told us that this momentarily illumination was normal and part of the MEL; the write-up was already in the ELB; and that it is 'OK to continue.'During our conversation the Captain; Maintenance; Dispatch; and I came to the conclusion:1. There is no maintenance procedure to deactivate this light.2. The issue is already indicated in the ELB.3. Maintenance stated that was a normal and 'very common' occurrence on the 737 fleet and we are OK to continue.After finishing our conversation with maintenance and dispatch; the Captain and I amended our takeoff briefing to be prepared for this light to illuminate during the takeoff roll.  I; as the PNF; would indicate it was this light; cancel the alert; and the takeoff would continue in both the low speed and high-speed regimes.During the takeoff roll; at approximately 120 kts (at least 20 kts below V1); the Number 1 Fuel Filter Bypass Master Caution Light did illuminate.  I called out that the fault adding 'expected!'; canceled the Master Caution Light; and we continued the takeoff.  The light extinguished itself shortly thereafter.  The light never illuminated again throughout the rest of the flight.  The flight continued uneventfully to ZZZ2.
column123: The maintenance release had an open write up for the 'fuel filter differential pressure warning system'.  We read both the maintenance release and the MEL (7304A). Not much information other than the other system must be operative and if you do get the other filter bypass light; you should assume both engine filters have an impending bypass condition. Startup was normal. On taxi out; we got the left fuel filter bypass light; the side that was written up. It caught us off guard; because no where did it say that the light might come on. We pulled over and got a phone patch to Maintenance Control to discuss the light. Maintenance Control said it was normal with the problem and we were OK to continue. The light went and we taxied for takeoff. At approximately 120 knots; the light illuminated again. We continued the takeoff and the light went out shortly after we were airborne. The light did not illuminate again until taxi in.

column121: While flying flight ZZZ - ZZZ1 the gear did not come up on takeoff when the gear handle was raised. I was flying and immediately recognized that something was wrong. I kept the airspeed at 220 kts. while we climbed out to 4;000 ft. MSL. I put the auto pilot on and checked the Aux Gear Extension Door; it was down. I called for the QRH and the FO ran the checklist for Gear Disagree with the handle in the off position. It did not help. I gave the aircraft to the FO and directed him to inform ATC that we were going to return to ZZZ. I then contacted Dispatch. Maintenance Control and the [Chief Pilot] were brought on the line as well. While all the parties were assembling; I talked with the Flight Attendants and the passengers. Maintenance Control and I ran the Gear Disagree checklist with the gear handle in the up position. This checklist had me lift and reseat the Aux Gear Extension door. As the checklist was completed; the gear was able to be raised. In conference it was decided to land overweight versus burning down fuel to 157.3. Dispatch sent landing data for our weight on Runway XXR. I took the aircraft back from the FO and then flew an approach to Runway XXR in ZZZ. We configured early and got a normal gear extension. We landed normally with max auto brake set. Our landing weight was 168.0; 10.7 overweight. We taxied clear; the fire trucks checked our brakes and we then taxied back to gate.
column123: I was the pilot monitoring on the flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. The flight departed the gate and taxied to the runway for a normal takeoff from [Runway] XXL. The visibility was slightly reduced due to rain; and there were overcast clouds at 800 ft. After rotation; the Captain called for gear up and I retracted the gear. We started the right turn on the departure; and the flaps were brought up on schedule and the Captain called for the after takeoff checklist. I checked in with Departure and we were given a 270 heading and 6;000 ft. Departure then gave us Direct to XXXXX; which I programmed in the FMC and LNAV was selected. This was a relatively high workload time; in IMC. I completed the after takeoff checklist flow; electing to leave the engine anti-ice on; ensured the flaps/slats were retracted; and placed the gear handle in the off position. I completed the after takeoff checklist and noticed that there were lights illuminated at the gear panel. At this time; the Captain and I both noticed that the plane did not sound right; and we started trying to diagnose the issue. The Captain used speed intervene to set the speed to clean maneuvering speed of 225 kts. I mentioned that it sounded like a gear door was open; and we looked at the gear lights and that the landing gear lights indicated 3 green on the instrument panel as well as the overhead panel. There were also 3 red lights on the gear indication. The Captain called for the QRH; and I completed the QRH for landing gear disagree. The QRH was completed and we determined that the gear was in the down position. At this time; we both looked at the alternate gear door; which was closed. During my preflight; I had confirmed the alternate gear door was closed visually; and then by stepping on it. I had also confirmed the gear pins were present on the flight deck.At this time; we advised ATC that we would like to stop at 6;000 and get some delay vectors for a landing gear issue that we needed to work on. The Captain transferred controls and radios to me; while she contacted Maintenance Control via the radio. Maintenance Control instructed her to place the gear handle in the up position and then open and close the alternate gear door. Then the gear handle was placed in the down position; and back to the up position. At this time the gear retracted and all gear lights went out. From the time we took off; until this moment was approximately 15 minutes. We decided to [advise] ATC and requested that fire rescue meet us at the runway. We decided that a return to ZZZ was our best option. Due to the fact that we tankered an extra 16k [lbs.] of fuel we were overweight for landing. The Captain talked to Maintenance Control and Dispatch to see if they wanted us to burn off fuel or land overweight. Were sent overweight landing data and determined that a safe landing could be made back in ZZZ; and used auto brakes MAX. During this time; the Captain made several announcements to the Passengers explaining the situation and also briefing the FAs on our expected plan of action. We briefed the approach; and discussed our plan in case the gear failed to come down on the approach. A normal landing was made and we exited the runway and stopped to allow our brake temperatures to be read. Fire rescue said everything looked normal and followed us to the gate.

column121: Received a Level 1 'Emerg Power On' message while at cruise; FL380. We referenced the QRH; which states moving the Emergency Power Switch to OFF; and then to ARM; which we accomplished. The message remained. We monitored the Electrical System Synoptic for battery status; and created a plan in case the battery started depleting. Per the QRH; we had the option to deploy the ADG. During descent; the battery started losing charge; and we deployed the ADG. It came on-line without issues. Approx 2 minutes later; we received multiple messages on the EAD indicating an electrical system failure. The Capt lost his 3 MFDs; however I still had my 3 MFDs. I assumed PF duties; the Capt took over PM (Pilot Monitoring). We lost Radio #1; and maintained comm on Radio #2; where we notified ZZZ center of our electrical issue. No flight control issues were noted. No other system issues were noted. We [requested priority handling] passing through 10;000 ft. The ADG worked as advertised; and we were prepared for the loss of some systems if the ADG became the sole source of electrical power.
column123: During cruise at FL380 we received a level one alert 'EMERG PWR ON'. We went to the QRH which told us to cycle the Emergency power switch to see if [the] alert would go away; which it did not. It said to monitor battery power and if needed to deploy the ADG. Power stayed steady at 26 for the battery for 35-40 minutes. Then [the] battery started to deplete and the decision was made to deploy the ADG while we were descending on the arrival. When ADG was deployed Captain's instruments and radio went away and control was given to the F/O and radio 2 was used. We [advised ATC] and were descended to 2;000 ft. and became visual with the airfield. My HUD was working and I decided to take the aircraft on base leg in case any other unforeseen problems arose. Normal landing and [priority handling] was called off after landing rollout.Battery system and emergency power malfunction. column121: On the arrival into the ZZZ area; ATC kept us high due to departing IFR traffic. We heard the departing traffic calling ATC on the radio after departure; but got no response. Because we were getting very close to the airport; we elected to reduce speed in order to make the impending descent easier to manage. We were monitoring both the ATC Center frequency and the CTAF frequency at ZZZ. There was a significant amount of General Aviation traffic operating in the vicinity of the ZZZ airport. As the speed was reduced below 200 knots; the First Officer; who was the PF; asked for Flaps 8 and 20. I verified that the speed was below 200 knots and selected Flaps 8 and 20. As soon as I selected Flaps 20 I realized we were still at 16;000 ft.; and said; 'We can't do that yet;' and immediately retracted the Flaps back to 0.  At this point we were only six or seven miles from the airport; still at 16;000 ft. We had identified the traffic threats on TCAS. In order to initiate our descent to the airport; we canceled IFR. After descending through 15;000 feet the First Officer again asked for Flaps 8 and 20. Because we had extended the flaps earlier above 16;000 feet; I was focused on the altitude. Due to the fact that we had slowed to below 200 knots the first time we extended the flaps; I failed to look at the airspeed indicator; thinking we were still below 200 knots. We were discussing the maneuver we would need to make to circle around and descend to the airport at the time. ATC and CTAF radio traffic was also heavy at the time. As soon as the flaps were selected the overspeed clacker started up. I looked at the airspeed indicator; saw that we were above 200 knots; and reached for the flap lever with the intent of retracting the flaps. At this point I'm unclear what EXACTLY happened next.  There was some turbulence; we were beginning our turn; and there was a lot of radio traffic.  We were also focused on the traffic displayed on the TCAS. All of this created a great deal of distraction. My hand was on the flap lever at the time; with the intent of retracting the flaps. Whether it was because of turbulence causing me to inadvertently move the lever; or me simply moving it the wrong way because of the distractions; I did; in fact; move the flap lever to 45. The overspeed clacker; interestingly enough; added to the momentary confusion. In fact; at one point I believe the First Officer said; 'What the hell is going on?' I was mortified to see the indication that the flaps were at 45; because there was no intent; plan; or call for further flap extensions. It was simply a mistake. I immediately retracted the flaps to zero. We did not receive any message associated with a flap problem; i.e. 'Flaps Fail'; etc. After everything calmed down and things were back in order; we continued the approach; which ended up resulting in a go-around because a general aviation aircraft cut us off on short final. After landing and proceeding to the gate; I wrote up the flap limitation exceedance. Maintenance arrived later; inspected the flaps; performed functional checks; found no irregularities; and returned the aircraft to service.In my opinion there were several factors contributing to the event. Distraction was probably the primary cause. We were distracted by all the radio traffic on the CTAF frequency. Sometimes it was difficult to differentiate between the CTAF traffic and the Center traffic. Also; being left so high so late on the arrival created a self-imposed sense of immediacy...'We need to get down'. Interesting to note that this urgency was never 'real'; but rather something we imposed on ourselves. Assumption was another contributing factor. Because we had originally slowed to below 200 knots; I assumed we were still at that airspeed when flaps were requested the second time. This assumption caused me to neglect the airspeed indicator before selecting the flaps because I was more concerned about the altitude.This is primarily an exercise in self-discipline and patience. The training and procedures are all in place to help prevent these types of events from occurring. It simply becomes incumbent on each pilot to be disciplined enough to not allow external factors to get in the way of simple; straight-forward procedures that can and will keep the aircraft; passengers; and crew safe.

column121: I was [the] pilot flying; headed into ZZZ. It was VMC; severe clear; and in the afternoon. We were being vectored toward Runway XX in ZZZ. I was in green needles; with the [Runway] XX ILS frequency active. My FO made a comment [that] we weren't picking up the right identifier; but because it was visual; and we had just called the field in sight; I was not going to reference the glideslope anyway. I could clearly see the PAPIs and was going to reference that since I had a visual. We were then cleared for the visual for [the] runway; so I kicked off the autopilot; and began a stable descent. We had noticed the glideslope and the PAPIs were not lining up; so I made a comment I was just going to fly it visually and use the PAPIs as the guide; not the glideslope. After all; it was only being used as a back up. Well; as we proceeded along; even though I was 2 white/2 red on the PAPI; the glideslope annunciator started yelling at us (later; we found out the ILS was OTS; which explained why it was not working correctly). Instead of asking the FO to switch his and my frequencies back to standby; I elected to fly higher on the PAPIs to shut the annunciator up. I ended up being 4 white about at about 300 ft. Because the winds were calm; the runway was clear and dry; and I knew a safe landing could be accomplished; I elected to continue the approach. I still landed softly and safely in the touchdown area; and stopped in the usual amount of runway required. It was an uneventful landing.When we taxied clear of the runway; I asked Tower and asked about the frequency and asked the FO to pull up the current ATIS to see if there was a NOTAM about the ILS frequency; and sure enough; it was OTS. In hindsight; I'm not sure how I missed that on the ATIS; but I should have read it more carefully and I could have avoided this situation altogether.
column123: I was the First Officer and the Pilot Monitoring for this flight. Having received ATIS for ZZZ and setting up the approach the CA (Captain) briefed the Visual Approach Runway XX to be backed up by the ILS and I concurred and had no questions on the briefing. I mentioned to the CA that I did not have the proper identifier and I double checked the frequency to ensure that it was correct and it was. The CA acknowledged and [said] that we had been cleared for the visual approach. During the approach the CA noticed that the GS (Glideslope) and the PAPI were not matching and informed me he was strictly using the PAPI for the visual approach. While continuing on the approach the GS annunciator was sounding a notification and the CA ended up high on the PAPI at about 100-200 ft. The CA called he was high and correcting and continued the approach into ZZZ and landed in the landing zone with no issue and was able to slow the aircraft and exit on taxiway. Once on the ground the CA asked the Tower to confirm the frequency for the ILS and the Tower responded it was released to Maintenance. At that point the CA asked me to bring the ATIS back up and that is when we both noticed the ILS was NOTAMed OTS. We discussed the approach and landing and decided to both submit reports.

I notified ZZZ Tower that I would be exiting the runway at Taxiway XD.ZZZ Tower asked if I would like fire services and I replied in the affirmative. The flames had burned through a portion of the brake lines and there was a steady stream of hydraulic fluid issuing from the hosing. The brakes' temperature was continually monitored. I called [the] Ramp Supervisor to coordinate for a tug and was towed back to the Company A Ramp by a Mechanic and escorted by ZZZ response crew.

column121: We were flying the ZZZZZ RNAV arrival into ZZZ inside of the ZZZZZ1 waypoint when ATC instructed us to descend via except cross ZZZZZ2 at 10;000 ft.; 2000 ft. higher than published. We informed ATC that if we comply with the assigned crossing restriction that we will have trouble making ZZZZZ at 6;000; [which was] only 8.2 miles from ZZZZZ2. ATC then replied; 'If you will be high on the arrival let me know.' We then decided to slow down the aircraft to prepare for making the crossing restrictions and recalculate our descent inside of ZZZZZ2 to advise ATC if we will be high or if we can comply with the ZZZZZ restriction.Once the Honeywell FMS reached waypoint passage over ZZZZZ2 and cycled to the next fix; we started down to make the next crossing restriction. Within a few seconds of starting our descent; we received a TCAS 'TRAFFIC' alert followed by a TCAS RA. I immediately disconnected the autopilot to comply with the RA and resolve the conflict. After the resolution advisory was resolved; [the Pilot Monitoring] noticed that the FMS had cycled to the next waypoint early and found that we were still a few tenths of a mile from ZZZZZ2 during the event. The assigned altitude at ZZZZZ2 was 10;000 ft.; we leveled off during the RA around 9;750 - 9;800 ft. There was no communication from ATC to us regarding the event. The rest of the arrival and approach was flown successfully and we landed safely.The Honeywell FMS cycled waypoints early; leading us to believe that we had reached waypoint passage. [I suggest] finding a solution to prevent the Honeywell FMS from making premature smart turns/waypoint passage cycles.
column123: Operating [the] flight as SIC (Second in Command) and PM; we were assigned to descend via the ZZZZZ [arrival] but cross ZZZZZ2 at 10;000. We leveled off at 10;000 prior to the fix and set the next appropriate altitude. At about 2.5 miles prior to the fix; the Honeywell FMS prematurely sequenced to the next waypoint. We began an initial descent and quickly noticed the discrepancy in distance between current position and waypoint. [There was] an RA to 'monitor descent' annunciation. The Pilot Flying immediately climbed back to 10;000 and we waited until the correct DME was displayed. [The cause of the crossing altitude deviation was the] Honeywell FMS [working improperly]. I have noticed this problem in almost all company aircraft containing Honeywell FMS. The airplane will sequence to the next waypoint prior to the actual position. This can; and does lead to; altitude deviations and potential RAs and possibly worse. I would like to either see the problem itself fixed or the company to implement an SOP or training that covers this issue.

column121: After canceling IFR on a visual approach into ZZZ; we switched to CTAF and began making position reports. Center had advised us of 2-3 aircraft in our vicinity as we approached the airport. We had one aircraft in sight and were looking for the others. There were several aircraft on the CTAF and no immediate conflicts were noted until a departing aircraft was shown on the TCAS display at 12 o'clock and climbing towards our altitude followed by an automated 'traffic' callout. We could not see it immediately or infer its exact course so started a slight right turn away from the airport to avoid [it]. After several seconds I spotted the other aircraft on a converging course from the left and advised my copilot to increase descent to increase separation as he continued flying and searching out my window. It was difficult to spot due to very little relative movement and it was more difficult to spot from the copilot's seat. During the correction I saw that we were on a collision course and directed a climb/level off before taking [the] controls and beginning a more aggressive climb. My copilot spotted the aircraft immediately after the control transfer and we passed approximately 500 feet above the other plane. I had the opportunity to discuss with the crew of the other aircraft on the ground. After checking in with Center and receiving a traffic advisory; it seems they saw us before our initial ('blind') right turn and began a left turn to increase separation; then a level off to allow us to pass above. The mirrored lateral and vertical corrections contributed to the closure. Our 'blind' turn was initiated due to the TCAS return; which displayed their position and climb; but no lateral movement information. Lateral movement information may have provided better situational awareness in this case. Spotting the aircraft sooner would have also helped prevent the conflict.

column121: My wife and I were flying to IOW. The nearest airport to IOW with a TAF is CID; 16 NM to the northwest. The CID TAF at our estimated time of arrival was... 4SM -RA BR OVC015We planned on flying the flight VFR with only CID being a little marginal VFR. About 30 NM from IOW we encountered light rain and the OVC015 ceiling started to drop. We maneuvered right and left as we made our way toward IOW. The IOW ASOS at the time was reporting the ceiling 1100 scattered. At 15NM west of IOW at 500-600 feet AGL skimming the cloud bases; I turned around to get back to better weather; but found that the weather had closed in behind me; or my route in could not be duplicated out. I knew there were antenna towers in the area and got a visual on one of the towers which appeared to be near my altitude. The safety of the flight was now in question. I called CID Approach and requested an IFR clearance to IOW. The Controller cleared me to the IOW airport via radar vectors and gave me a heading and instructions to climb to 2;500 feet. I advised the Controller that I wanted to shoot the RNAV (GPS) 30 approach into IOW circle 7. We shot the approach; broke out around 1100 AGL; circled; and safely landed on Runway 7. I hold an ATP certificate; however my last instrument proficiency check I had was a 135 check [several years ago]. Therefore; I was not instrument current.Our airplane is equipped with a Garmin 400W and a Garmin 335 ADS-B out transponder. The 400W had a current procedures data base and the pitot static encoder check was completed [two years ago]; making [my aircraft] legal for IFR operations. Additionally; I had flightplan.com app loaded onto my phone; which allowed me to have current IFR low altitude charts and approach plates for IOW; as well as the surrounding area.My brief IFR flight and approach was performed to ATP standards and did not alarm ATC in anyway. I have reviewed my ADS-B track and found that the lowest I got on that flight was 422 feet AGL; which is lower than I recall. The antenna tower I saw is at 320 feet AGL. The low flight occurred in Class G airspace during the day. Complacency on my part was definitely a factor and I have taken steps so as to not repeat this occurrence. I have scheduled an Instrument Proficiency (IPC) check.

I looked over to the Captain and we both nodded; at which time I stated that we did indeed have the ILS 26L LAS loaded into the FMC (from the direction of PRINO intersection). The Approach Controller cleared us to fly the ILS 26L with a clearance to cross BERBN at or above 7;000 feet MSL. I then queried the Approach Controller about whether or not they would like me to call our base leg for Runway 26L.  The Controller replied that our base leg would be visible on their radar; and that a call was not necessary. Not realizing that there was INDEED a transition from the BERBN intersection to HUXAR on the ILS 26L; we proceeded turn north whilst descending to intercept the Runway 26L localizer just outside of RELIN intersection (D7.2 IRLE) Runway 26L.Shortly thereafter; we were told by the Approach Controller that we had initiated the turn too soon; and we were given a heading to the East in order to avoid traffic (other carrier) that was already established on final for Runway 26L.  We did receive a TCAS TA (no RA); and after completing the turn to the East; the TCAS TA was resolved. After the turn to the East; and with proper separation between our aircraft and Aircraft Y; Approach Control vectored us back to the north to join the localizer and clear us for the visual to LAS Runway 26L. We were then handed-off to LAS Tower. Landing was uneventful. After landing; we were provided a phone number to call LAS TRACON. The COKTL 1 Arrival and the latest ILS 26L charts for LAS are dated (date). I can tell you that I was certainly not familiar; nor had I ever been assigned the ILS 26L from the COKTL 1 Approach (I wasn't even aware that there was a transition from BERBN intersection; as that transition is located on the new ILS 26L Approach chart). My apologies to the LAS Approach Controller for our misunderstanding.As an added measure; I would prefer to see more information added to the COKTL 1 Arrival; like a ball note referring Pilots to the BERBN transition on the ILS 26L LAS. column121: Aircraft was dispatched with an inoperative Pack #2 due to a regulator fault and [the flight] was in full compliance with the MEL at departure. Flight was completely full in the cabin. Due to Pack #2 being inoperative it was difficult to cool the main cabin temp using only Pack #1. Using only Pack #1 at FL370 we were able to maintain 72 degrees in the cabin using max cold and high flow. Approximately 200 nm west of ZZZ at FL370 we received an ECAM AIR PACK 1+2 FAULT. ATC was notified and [priority handling was requested]. Upon checking the pressurization and bleed air page; it appeared that Pack #1 was overheating showing an output temperature in amber yet we never received a Pack 1 OVHT ECAM. The cabin altitude was still under control. A descent to 10;000 ft. was initiated without exceeding the cabin altitude before we complied with the ECAM to turn off Pack #1 leaving us unpressurized. Contact was made with Dispatch and Maintenance Control to discuss the situation resulting in a diversion to ZZZ.
column123: Approximately 240 nm from ZZZ; at a cruise altitude of FL350 and while in communication with Center; an ECAM aural and Master Caution sounded for AIR PACK 1+2 FAULT. The CA (Captain) said he noted a momentary amber overheat temp in Pack 1; but it did not trigger the PACK 1 OVHT caution. I (Pilot Monitoring) did not see this indication that had subsequently returned to a green inlet temperature. Pack 2 was previously secured and turned off per the MEL deferral on our 2nd release. Pack 1 showed a fault light. The AIR PACK 1+2 FAULT ECAM directed us to secure Pack 1; descend to 10;000 ft. MSL or MEA and then turn on the RAM Air when the pressure differential was less than 1.0. Even though Pack 1 had a fault light in the overhead panel; it appeared to be partially functioning; the cabin pressure holding and the cabin altimeter only increasing at a very slight rate. A flight crew decision was made to begin an immediate normal descent to 10;000 ft. without the use of oxygen while closely monitoring the pressurization page to ascertain the true nature of the Pack 1 malfunction. The CA directed me to assume pilot flying duties and ATC responsibilities while he coordinated with Operations; Dispatch; flight attendants and the passengers. We began a coordinated 1500-2000 fpm rate of descent via two ATC-assigned step down altitudes of FL300 and FL200 before ultimately reaching 10;000 ft. The aircraft was lowered in a steady continual descent with no pauses which I believe helped our situation. Cabin pressure held steady around 8;000 ft. during the normal descent. Upon reaching 10;000 ft.; Pack 1 was secured; differential pressure reached less than 1.0; RAM AIR was selected on and the cabin altimeter climbed from approximately 8;000 to 10;000 ft. as expected. We completed all remaining ECAM items until the screens were normal. The rate of fuel burn at 10;000 ft. MSL made reaching our initial destination of ZZZ1 impossible; and it was decided that ZZZ was a suitable diversion while 200nm away and with 11;600 pounds of fuel aboard along with the best Maintenance; aircraft and passenger accommodation options. We informed ATC; Dispatch; Operations; and proceeded accordingly. We switched to the next Center and the Captain [requested priority handling] and returned to the pilot flying role while we coordinated an uneventful arrival via the ZZZZZ to Visual XX approach at ZZZ and ultimately parking at gate XY. We were then met by the ZZZ Chief Pilot at the gate and proceeded to fill out a risk mitigation form following the event. We then accepted a new aircraft and release at gate XZ and ultimately brought the same passengers to ZZZ1 two hours later than originally planned.In totality; I felt the event was handled safely and professionally. The CRM skills taught and utilized allowed both the CA and First Officer to properly divide duties while ensuring sufficient cross checks and communication. At no time did I feel rushed or stressed. I believe the deliberate delay in securing the faulty Pack 1 that appeared to be functioning along with the continual scanning of the pressurization page allowed us to avoid an unnecessary priority descent; use of pilot oxygen; or the deployment of passenger oxygen that might have accompanied a rapid depressurization. All in all; I felt the CA was composed and handled the event in line with Company desires. While I regret the delay the passengers experienced; I believe we handled the event in a safe and caring manner.

column121: I was the PF (Pilot Flying) on this flight from ZZZZ1 to ZZZZ. On arrival into the ZZZZ terminal area; we were cleared direct to ZZZZZ and cleared for the ILS XXL approach. Weather at ZZZZ was reporting winds 280 at 12; few clouds at 3;000 ft.; altimeter 29.62; and no other significant weather. The initial approach was uneventful and we were fully configured and stable by about 1200 ft. AGL. At approximately 800 ft.; I turned off the autopilot and began hand flying. Then at approximately 700 ft. we received an audible wind shear warning that lasted for 3-4 seconds. This caught us both by surprise as there were no other conditions that would be associated with wind shear. There was no convective activity in the area; the weather was good; and the wind readout showed stable at 12 kts. The aircraft showed no airspeed fluctuation nor an increasing or decreasing trend vector; the thrust setting was normal; pitch attitude and vertical path were stable. During the alert; the weather radar showed a lot of red radar return that wasn't previously there; and did not correlate with what we were seeing visually out the windscreen. We both assessed the situation; and agreed that the alert was erroneous. At this point we were at about 300 ft. AGL; and the Captain told me to continue. I agreed with this assessment and decision; and continued to land normally. Not once did we receive any other indication that wind shear was present; it wasn't even 'choppy'. It was smooth all the way through landing. After reflecting on the event; I still believe that the alert we received was false. With that being said; as a crew; we probably should have discussed making a logbook entry and discussing the alert with the mechanic once we were parked at the gate in ZZZZ. Going forward if I encounter something like this again; I will handle it differently for a couple of reasons. First; the FOM does state that if a wind shear warning is received; to follow wind shear escape maneuver or to execute a normal go around. Secondly; I do not want to get into a habit of second guessing the warning systems on board the aircraft. Regardless of a suspected error; and as long as safety is not compromised; follow procedure then once at the gate; make a logbook entry for a suspected error.
column123: We were operating this flight from ZZZZ1 to ZZZZ arriving approximately XA:30 UTC. Captain was PM (Pilot Monitoring) and FO (First Officer) was PF (Pilot Flying). We were set up for the ZZZZZ1 RNAV arrival for the ILS XXL. The aircraft (a B767) was empty and our landing weight was 198;100 lbs. VApp was calculated at 122 and VRef at 117. The weather was VFR. There was no convective activity; a few clouds at 3000 ft.; winds 280 at 12 reported on the field; and altimeter at 29.62. We were cleared to the fix ZZZZZ to begin the ILSZ XXL at 4000 ft. We intercepted the localizer and armed the APPCH. We continued to configure the aircraft for landing maintaining VFR conditions. With the aircraft fully configured for landing (Stabilized Approach criteria met) at approximately 700 ft. AGL we received a wind shear alert. The weather was VFR; and the winds at our altitude were showing stable at 12 knots. There was no airspeed fluctuation (including the airspeed trend line); the throttle position did not change; the thrust setting did not change; and the aircraft pitch attitude did not change. As PM; I did not elect to call 'Go Around' as the aircraft was fully stabilized; fully configured for landing and we were passing through approximately 300 ft. AGL with the PF hand-flying the aircraft. Given the situation with all of the present conditions and the state of the aircraft; I believed the alert was erroneous. I should have made a logbook write up on the EPGWS (Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System) to check for errors. There were no reports of any wind shear activity in the area and the weather conditions were VFR. Also given the location and state the aircraft was in; I thought it would create an unnecessary 'non-normal' situation that could have potentially caused more problems than just continuing the approach and landing the aircraft. As I stated above; the aircraft exhibited no indications for us to believe that there were any type of wind shear occurrences at the present time or in the immediate time prior to landing.

column121: We were on a visual approach to Runway XX at ZZZ.  During the approach we received a GPWS Caution 'Terrain' or 'Too Low Terrain' just after the '500 ft stable' call. As the PM (Pilot Monitoring); I failed to call for a go-around.  The PF (Pilot Flying); Captain completed the approach and landing uneventfully. Everything about the approach was normal and I have seen it many times in my 3 years here. PF was stable at 100 ft above field elevation as well as at 500 ft above field elevation; the only exception was that the winds that had recently shifted and gusting were causing the airspeed to deviate by plus or minus 10 knots; but not dramatically.  The fact that we were visual with the runway; on path and speed and properly configured; made the GPWS caution surprise me. After hearing it; I reverified that we were within all our approach criteria and it appeared safe so I did not call for the go around. However; being that it was not day VMC; I should have called it. In the future I will be sure to comply with the GPWS alert immediately and call for the go-around.

column121: Original First Officer (FO) called out from the trip. I was assigned a new FO; he informed me that he was low time FO and hasn't flown much during the past few weeks. I took the first leg to ZZZ1; and I let him [have] the leg back from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. He flew really well during the entire flight. We were cleared for the visual approach Runway XXL with great weather. FO did a great job during the approach and he was properly configured and stable at all times. It looked like he was going to have a great landing because he was doing everything by the book. Unfortunately; when it came time to do the flare he barely flared and took the power out a bit too quickly and the main landing gears made contact with the runway firmer than normal. Everything happened too quick; I saw him initially starting to flare but then at the end he let the nose drop a bit and the mains contacted the runway. I didn't get a chance to note the VSI at the time. As soon as we arrived at the gate I called Maintenance and informed them of that I was writing the aircraft for a possible hard landing with minimal flare. We originally had a plane swap; while on the swap I grabbed some dinner. And eventually received a call from the Chief Pilot confirming that there was damage to main landing gear and he wanted to hear from me what had happened. I explained to the Chief Pilot what had happened; and Chief Pilot took notes and said to follow up with an Ops report.A firmer landing than normal due to minimal flare that caused the main landing gears to come into contact with the runway quicker than normal due to minimal flare. FO barely flared during a visual approach at Runway XXL in ZZZ that ended up causing a hard landing situation.[Reporter recommends] possibly rotate brand new FO's and make them fly more often. FO informed me he had not flown in a while and was still low time FO. He did a great job on our leg to ZZZ1 as Pilot Monitoring (PM); and then a great job on his leg from ZZZ1 to ZZZ until his landing flare where everything happened to quick and he ended up barely flaring and making contact with the main landing gear a bit firmer than usual; which prompted me to write up the landing.

column121: I loaded the route into the FMC. We received and acknowledged revision 1 sent from Dispatch asking if we had received the revised flight plan. It was the route I had loaded earlier. It started with the ZZZZZ departure. But the route assigned in FD Pro did not match the route from Dispatch; but it too started with the ZZZZZ. I assumed the FD Pro flight plan was the original flight plan. We received the PDC clearance which stated 'Cleared to the ZZZ airport ZZZZZ then as filed; climb via SID. Expect FL340....' After takeoff; prior to completing the ZZZZZ SID; BOS ATC requested we fly direct to ZZZZ intersection as a short cut. We searched our legs page in the FMC but could not find it. We advised ATC we had no such fix. They had us go to ZZZZ regardless.  They then asked to confirm the route we were flying. The route we had loaded from Dispatch was NOT the route ATC had on file. But it was the route that was originally in FD Pro for [us].  ATC then had us fly that earliest FD Pro flight plan to ZZZ. We were asked later during our flight to call BOS Center once on the ground. I did. They wanted to figure out what might have been the reason our flight plans did not match up. They said we had not deviated off course as we were on the filed ZZZZZ which was on both flight plans. I stated to him I had loaded the revised flight plan from our Dispatcher and that I accepted the PDC flight plan clearance message as it appeared to match our revised flight plan.  I called our assigned Dispatcher and informed him of the problem. He thinks PDC did not load the revision but he should have gotten some kind of rejection notification if it was kicked back. Which he did not. So we do not know why ATC did not get the revised route that we flew. I would suggest that if the ATC PDC message that acknowledges our clearance was a complete route; not 'as filed'; I would have caught the discrepancy in the flight plans. It was unique in that both flight plans began with the ZZZZZ. It worked out in our favor that ATC gave us a short cut before we left the ZZZZZ. If not; somewhere after the ZZZZZ we would have deviated off the ATC filed route. The route that Dispatch sent us matched the route in [our] flight plan. The PDC acceptance message was not enough to make us doubt we had a route difference. PDC clearance could read the full route instead of 'as filed'.

column121: Clean configuration. Airspeed 280 knots. Autopilot on. IMC conditions. Being radar vectored around significant squall line. Anti-ice on. Climbing to cruise altitude and passing altitude about 20;000 feet when my airspeed indicator suddenly went erratic with plus or minus several (at 30 knots greater and less than commanded) indications. Airspeed indicator never reached stick shaker or over-speed warnings limits. Immediately took control of aircraft from autopilot and crosschecked the primary flight display with the Captain and standby indicator. Recommended Captain become pilot flying as his indications were consistent with standby indicator and airspeed indicator was not as erratic as mine (more consistent with turbulent air flying in the 737). After transfer of aircraft control to Captain; I completed the Quick Reference checklist (QRC) and QRH for unreliable airspeed indicator. When double checking the pitot heat was on I notice both Engines Electronic Control (EEC) were in soft alternate mode. During the entire time the aircraft was in IMC the airspeed indicator was erratic and EEC remained in soft alternate. A few minutes later; at level off at cruising altitude (low 20;000s) and out of IMC the airspeed indicator returned to normal along with EEC. Remained clear of clouds and landed uneventfully at ZZZ1. We did not return to ZZZ after [Notifying ATC] because we were more than half way and the squall line was over ZZZ.Unknown as to why airspeed indicator was unreliable and erratic in IMC turbulent air and then returned to normal when clear of clouds. Also did not know why EEC went to soft alternate and then returned to normal.
