column121: The incident happened during our descent on the ZZZZZ arrival into ZZZ. As far as I remember; we had been cleared by the previous Controller and told to do the XXL transition. I had already programmed the FMS for that specific arrival and pre-loaded the ILS XXL. The weather was not an issue with a clear sky and great visibility. I briefed a visual approach for XXL; backed up with the routing of the ILS for that same runway; and made sure we had the discontinuity between the last point on the arrival - ZZZZZ1 and the first point on the approach - ZZZZZ1. We were then told to contact the next Controller and assigned different altitudes on the arrival while maintaining the routing. For some reason; at one point; I thought/assumed we were cleared for the visual and got rid of the discontinuity by linking the first point on the approach with the last point on the arrival - ZZZZZ1. I turned to the Captain to ask him to 'confirm' and proceeded by removing the discontinuity. Because we were not cleared for the approach yet; the aircraft proceeded past ZZZZZ1 on a XXX as expected; but because it was now programmed to fly the approach it started turning at ZZZZZ2. The Controller asked us if we were flying the RNAV; we responded that we were doing the XXL transition and as the Captain said these words we realized we had made a mistake by leaving the XXX. The Controller kindly reminded us what we were expected to do and gave us a heading to intercept the localizer for the visual XXL. What led to this mistake is mostly my fault. I was fixated on flying the visual; and I forgot to actually make sure we had been given the clearance before getting off the arrival. My mind was too focused on the preconceived idea of what was expected rather than what we had actually been cleared for that I failed to properly communicate with my Captain. I was complacent; and this led to confusion in the cockpit and with the Controller.
column123: During our descent on ZZZZZ arrival into ZZZ; we were cleared to descend via ZZZZZ ; XXL transition. We programmed the FMS for that particular arrival and transition and preloaded the ILS XXL. The weather was good with clear sky and great visibility. Pilot Flying; briefed the visual approach XXL back it up by ILS. We made sure the discontinuity between the last point on the arrival ZZZZZ1 and the first point on the approach ZZZZZ1. We were told to contact the next Controller and assigned us different altitude on the arrival while maintaining the routing. I contacted the next Controller and for some reason we thought; we were cleared for visual via ZZZZZ1 transition. As we past ZZZZZ1; we continue to fly heading XXX as we approached ZZZZZ2 the plane was about to transition to the new fix. At this point ATC assigned us a heading 350 and asked us if we are flying the RNV transition? Which responded yes and I realized the error. At this point he assigned us 310 heading to intercept the localizer and cleared us for visual to XXL.We were both fixated and our mind was set on the preconceived idea of what was expected rather than what we had actually been cleared for; especially when the proceeding traffic receives that clearance. I (we) failed to confirm and communicate with each other and ATC. I got complacent and side tracked; the combination of these two led to the confusion in the cockpit and with the Controller.As a (Captain/Pilot Monitoring) I should have communicated and confirmed that we are both on the same page and understood the clearance and when in doubt ask the ATC for clarification. I want to make sure and get the confirmation before removing the discontinuity and not to rush. Do not assume if previous aircraft receives particular clearance we will get the same and avoid complacency. I will emphasize this on my future arrival briefings to ensure this doesn't happen again; FOOLISH ASSUMPTION/MISTAKE.

column121: During the pre-start check; the crew confirmed that all three altimeters were set properly.  I have a clear memory of personally checking all 3 altimeters.  As Pilot Flying I was hand flying a vectored departure and given a clearance to climb and maintain 10;000 ft.  Approximately 200 ft prior; as I was leveling off; I was given a new clearance to climb and maintain 16;000 ft.  I continued to hand fly and completed a smooth level off at 16;000.  As I was doing so; ATC gave us a notification of opposite direction traffic 1;000 feet above us which we had on TCAS and immediately saw visually.  All appeared normal and I believed ATC was simply letting us know why we had not been cleared higher and was giving a normal notification of traffic.  The transmission was partially garbled; and the Pilot Monitoring (PM) requested that ATC repeat it.  ATC simply responded with 'maintain 16;000' which the PM acknowledged.  The PM then noticed that our altimeters did not agree and informed me that my altimeter was set at 29.92 instead of the local altimeter setting.  I reset the altimeter and discovered that I was actually at 16;180 ft; which likely had prompted the call from ATC.  We were just short of 200 ft high.  I descended and was at 16;000 before passing under the opposite direction traffic.  We did not receive a TCAS TA or RA.  I have no memory of resetting my altimeter to 29.92 but surmise that I must have done so as it would be very difficult to have hit the button accidentally.  While allowed to set 29.92 once assigned a climb above 18;000 ft; my normal practice is to wait until the altimeter setting flashes approaching 18;000 ft to reset it.  Normal practice meaning I don't recall ever doing it differently.  I cannot explain when I reset it to standard; except that it was after the pre-start check and prior to leveling at 16;000.  My best guess is that I did so at 10;000 for some reason; as that was the only altitude I passed that I would have considered significant; although I was on profile in a 250 knot climb both before and after 10;000 ft.  In this case; the local altimeter setting was close enough to standard that I did not exceed the 300 feet limit for a flight violation or cause a traffic conflict.  This was just luck however.  Had the altimeter been significantly different from standard; I don't believe I would have been more likely to notice the error and could have been responsible for a conflict.I'm not sure what the cause was except that I simply made an error.  Why; how; or when escapes me.  However; I did have to call in fatigued that morning as we were on a late in the day pairing but had been delayed overnight to a morning departure two time zones to the east.  When I called in fatigued unable to fall asleep early; I was given my 10 hours and a later show time; though to make the later show time I still needed to get out of bed two hours prior to when I was accustomed.  After I woke up to my alarm; I was notified that the aircraft was still in maintenance and was given an even later show time; and I took a short nap.  In the end; the error happened during a time I'd normally be awake; but I did not get my normal sleep routine.  I had legal rest and did not feel particularly fatigued; but I can't discount that fatigue very well could have contributed to such an unusual error.  I utilized the Fatigue Risk Management Plan (FRMP) to the extent I felt necessary and neither Crew Scheduling nor the company pressured me in any way to fly fatigued.  Perhaps I should have insisted on an even later show time.  My feeling of responsibility to our customers who had already been delayed over 12 hours was a factor in making a show time that was earlier than normal for me; considering time zones; but again; I didn't feel overly tired at the time. Obviously; having made this error for the first time; I'll be more cognizant of when I hit the button to bring the altimeter to standard going forward.  As far as the possible fatigueaspect; our promise to our customers to transport them to their destination at the time we say can sometimes conflicts with our promise to transport them as safely as possible.  I have availed myself of the risk management plan several times in the last year and have never received any negative feedback or pressure to fly fatigued.  There are times when I feel the probability of losing pay has pressured other pilots to fly with less rest than they needed; but in this case pay was not a factor as I was the only pilot available to fly this leg to an outstation serviced only once per day.  So; I was going to be paid for the leg no matter when I flew it.  Therefore; I can't recommend any changes to the risk management plan.  I simply need to do a better job of anticipating and assessing my own fatigue level.
column123: Climbing out we were assigned to maintain 16;000 ft. First Officer (FO) was pilot flying. Altitude was verified at '1;000 to go' call. As we went through 15;000 feet; I said 15;000 climbing 16;000. FO was hand flying; as we near 16;000 (about 100ft to go) I noticed he wasn't slowing down the climb rate. I looked over and his altimeter was set to 29.92 instead of the altimeter we've gotten when I checked in of 30.16. As I looked over ATC asked if we had the 16;000 ft altitude assigned which I replied affirmatively. As I was done talking to ATC I told the FO he had the wrong altimeter setting; and that our Altimeter was 30.16. FO did level off at 16;000 ft but he had a wrong altimeter setting. column121: This was a maintenance reposition flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I was flying as the PIC with a Captain in the right seat. Pushing back from the gate; we had a zero fuel weight (ZFW) of 52;000 lbs. The gross weight on the performance was off by over 4;000 lbs from the data received; and we were out of balance. The aircraft had no passengers; no flight attendants; no baggage; just 14;700 lbs of fuel and two pilots and all galley carts.  We called the Dispatcher to inform her that we were out of balance. She told me on the phone that she was [gone] the previous week when we were transitioning to 5 zone weight and balance and she didn't know what was going on; and literally just handed me off to the pilot on duty to figure out. This was totally unacceptable. She is the dispatcher of record; has equal legal responsibility for the planning of this flight and upon being informed that we're out of balance and had our ZFW change by thousands of pounds in a few minutes time; she just hands me off to an unrecorded phone line with the pilot on duty?! My head is still spinning.  At the gate; our ZFW was 52;000 lbs. Now we are being told to put numbers in the box for ballast but I have no idea what it means 1.0 2.0 3.0 etc; what does that correspond to? We are not actually moving any ballast anywhere etc. The pilot on duty and some other manager on with him; and myself went back and forth for a good amount of time trying to figure out what the accurate zero fuel weight was; what an accurate gross take off weight was; and my main concern; if our stab trim; and V speeds were accurate and safe. I want to reiterate; this was a total and complete debacle. There was so much confusion on the phone as to how we got these numbers from computer and what they meant; and if they were accurate. I had to ask the pilot on duty and manager point blank on the phone; are you telling me these numbers are accurate; and safe for us to depart; before I would continue this flight any further. This 5 zone weight and balance makes no sense how we could be out of balance with only fuel on board. It does not seem like this 5 zone system was well thought out; or that ferry / reposition flights were accounted for. How this got approved by the FAA is beyond me. Additionally; our FOM states that 'the amount to be considered unusable shall be noted on the dispatch release and be considered as unusable by the flight crew'; no such comment on this release is present. If were using fuel for ballast for CG limits which is totally news to me seeing as we never had a problem with CG on 3 zone weight and balance; then the PIC must be notified because if that fuel is used; an in flight emergency would have to be declared because the aircraft would no longer be within CG limits.

column121: I was working the arrival and final position with an arrival rate of 22 [aircraft] sent in the NTML [National Traffic Management Log].  However; at the time of the incident I had 19-20 aircraft in my sector landing MCO.  So; needless to say; the Center was not complying with the 22 rate.  Which for sure contributed to this because my supervisor called Miami Center to slow the COASTR [COSTR] arrivals down to 210 kts. Aircraft X was on the COASTR [COSTR] arrival.  I was fed Aircraft Y from TPA Approach at 11;000 [feet]; and normal speed.  I descended Aircraft X to 9;000 [feet]; not realizing that Aircraft Y wasn't given 210 kts by TPA.  When I descended Aircraft X there was probably at least 5-6 miles between the aircraft.  As Aircraft X was descending; the CA [Conflict Alert] went off.  I issued an immediate turn to Aircraft Y and called the traffic.  Aircraft Y read it back and said they were responding to an RA and then subsequently; Aircraft X keyed up saying they were responding to an RA.First of all; the rate is not a joke!!!  This is a normal occurrence; here at F11; we ask for one rate and get fed way over the rate.  It's been okay until now when something happens.  I would encourage you to look into this; and stop the games; because safety is being compromised.  The rate is there for a reason.  It wasn't being followed; no one will be held accountable for it.  When the rate is established; that is the rate.  The rate is there to ensure safety.  This is a shining example of why the rate is necessary. The advertised rate was 22; and I had 19 aircraft landing MCO in my sector at the time of the incident.  That's not a 22 rate.  I can assure you; that if the rate was being followed; that situation would have not occurred.  Because Aircraft X would have been normal speed over the COASTR [COSTR] arrival; and Aircraft Y and Aircraft X would have been compatible.  And the two airliners wouldn't have to respond to RAs; and make it uncomfortable for the people in the back; and safety wouldn't have been compromised.

column121: On arrival into EDF we were on ANC Approach. After initial contact; ANC asked what approach we wanted at EDF. The Pilot Monitoring replied the Visual 34. ANC instructed us to turn left heading 260 and descend and maintain 8;000 (we were at 13;000.) While rolling out on a 260 heading and still descending; ANC came back and said they were going to take us the other way and to turn back right heading 330. We rolled out on 330 still descending. At around 9;000 descending; ANC asked us if we wanted Runway 16 and that the winds were 330 at 5. Taking into account our position and high altitude relative to EDF Runway 34 and our weight; I decided that this would be acceptable; but wanted the IRO to double check the numbers before accepting this change. I said 'standby' and the Pilot Monitoring transmitted 'standby' to ANC. ANC immediately instructed us to descend and maintain 3;000. At the same time of ANC transmission; we were leveling at 8;000; and I was asking the IRO to run the numbers for 16. The Pilot Monitoring replied '3;000; Aircraft X'. I reset the altitude selector to 3;000; verified the altitude with the Pilot Monitoring; engaged FLC; set speed and we began to descend. This clearance seemed logical considering we were clearing terrain; there was no traffic on TCAS; no terrain indicating on the HSI (I was in terrain mode) and we needed to lose altitude to make the airport. There was no further contact with ANC ATC until they instructed us to maintain 8;000.Descending through approximately 6;700; ANC contacted us and instructed us to maintain 8;000; low alt alert and that the MVA in that area was 8;000. After landing and block in; I was notified by EDF Tower (via the military) that ANC TRACON wanted me to give them a call (which I did after speaking to the Chief Pilot.) They took my info and said he would be forwarding to quality control (assurance?) and they may contact me as they were looking into it. There was either an error by ANC Approach or we mistook instructions for another aircraft. After the flight while discussing with the crew; myself and the Pilot Monitoring thought we heard the same instructions. Considering we may have accepted a clearance for another aircraft on frequency; I later looked at the flights in and out of ANC at the same time. There was another flight that arrived in ANC shortly after we landed. It is possible that the instruction were meant for them. It is also possible instructions were meant for an entirely different aircraft and we mistook it for us. There was high workload at the time while considering a runway change; configuring the aircraft and checking landing data.The Pilot Monitoring immediately replied to maintain 8;000. I rolled the altitude selector back to 8;000; clicked off the autopilot; added power and hand flew the airplane back to 8;000 and then reengaged the autopilot. If in fact we did accept a clearance from a different aircraft; caution must be used when similar flight numbers are on the same transmitting frequency; especially during high work loads. Unfortunately; we were unaware of the other aircraft at the time of the event.

column121: Upon arrival to the aircraft; an ACARS message from our dispatcher was already on the printer asking if we had Revision X to our flight release.  I opened and downloaded the flight release to my iPad.  The release was indeed Revision X.  We replied to the Dispatcher telling him that we did have Rev X onboard.  I never saw the original Rev Y.  When uploading the flight plan to the FMC; the route that loaded was consistent with Rev X.  This route was: BLZZR4 BLZZR BAF Q480 CANDR RAV J64 [...].  I logged into the CPDLC and we received the clearance via CPDLC.  The CPDLC clearance was: 'CLEARED TO ZZZ ARPT BLZZR4 THEN AS FILED. [...]' We accepted the clearance.  From this point the flight progressed normally.  After departure while flying the BLZZR4 departure we were talking to Center; we had not yet reached the BAF waypoint.  The controller gave us a shortcut and cleared us directly to TRIBS intersection.  We couldn't find that fix on the legs page and replied that we were not showing TRIBS on our route.  The controller inquired as to what our route was and I replied with the route that was on our release (noted above).  Controller replied that they had a new route for us and cleared us from our present position direct to TRIBS Q406 BWZ J6 HVQ J78 FAM SGF [...] to ZZZ. We accepted the new clearance; entered it into the FMC; then notified Dispatch via ACARS of our new route.  Later in the flight; while talking to the next Center; the controller notified us of a possible pilot route deviation and gave us a phone number to call Center upon arrival in ZZZ.  The flight continued uneventfully to ZZZ.  Enroute to ZZZ; the Captain and I discussed what possible route deviation could have occurred.  We could only speculate that there was a difference between the flight plan on our Rev 01 Flight Release and the route that Center had cleared us via CPDLC and expected us to fly.  We were confident; however; that we were never off course since both the CPDLC clearance and Rev X flight plan had us flying the BLZZR4 departure; and the shortcut and subsequent reroute issued by Center occurred while we were still on the departure route.  At BAF (Barnes VOR) is where Q480 & Q406 diverge).After the Captain called Center from ZZZ; we suspected that the cause of the problem was that the Rev 01 route wasn't processed by BOS prior to issuing us our CPDLC clearance.  Since both the Rev X route; and the original route that BOS expected us to fly both began with the BLZZR4 departure; we had no idea from the CPDLC clearance of 'CLEARED TO ZZZ ARPT BLZZR4 THEN AS FILED.' that there was any discrepancy.  We are unsure why the updated route wasn't processed by BOS prior to issuing our CPDLC clearance.   Perhaps there is a cut-off time where changes are no longer accepted or processed. Even when being issued a 'Cleared As Filed' CPDLC; listing the entire filed route at the end of the message would be another way to confirm that the ATC facility has the same route as the crew does on their flight release.  In addition; being able to print the entire CPDLC message would also be helpful to not only have a hard copy of the clearance; but also to avoid having to step through multiple pages on the FMC and potentially miss something.  This would be especially helpful when there is an unexpected reroute as part of the CPDLC clearance.

column121: Due to construction in the southeast portion of the airport; I did not enter the ramp for [the] gate at the correct entry point.  Even though I thought I was intimately aware of the LGA environs; my expectation bias; compounded with non-standard taxi marking that made it appear that I was at the end of the taxiway; caused me to make a mistake.  The irony of this event is when we departed Runway 31 earlier; both of us noted the crazy construction and the potential for mistakes that could happen in the close quarters.  Prior to operating out of LGA for the first time in a long time; I reviewed the company notes/memos and our 10-7 pages.  Both of us had our taxi charts up.  When I noticed we were in the wrong position; I stopped the aircraft.  We coordinated with the Ramp Control and was safely marshaled out after we restarted our left engine.  Causes included expectation bias; poor taxiway markings; construction congestion. This was in daylight. Experienced crew.  While I take responsibility; better markings would have made the difference; especially since we are all not at the top of our game with the reduced flights.  Even though taxi configurations change during construction; this does not alleviate reasonable signage or markings.  It is the cost of doing the work.  I am sorry for the mistake.  However; if this is the worst thing I do----it has been a good career.  For me; it illustrated that I can always do better.

column121: Showed up to the gate at XA am from being assigned trips off reserve; met the Captain and the gate agent where we learned from the Gate Agent we had 2 non rev maintenance guys coming along with us. Went down to the aircraft where I started doing my checks and setting up my stuff; I came round from my walk around and started doing my 1st flight of the day checks. In the middle of while I was doing my 1st flight of the day flows the maintenance person asked me if he could bring his stuff up to the aircraft instead of the cargo bay I said sure (I heard him say tools and something else) as he walked out the jet bridge I paused for a minute and the Captain walked into the cockpit; he asked me where the maintenance guy was going. I told the Captain he went to get his tools and I think he said something about hydraulic fluid; I told the Captain I haven't read DG (Dangerous Goods) in a while but don't know if we can take it he agreed and went outside to tell the maintenance personnel to hold on for a second; he came back in sat in his seat pulled out the FOM and searched [but] could not find anything specific so decided to ring the duty pilot; at this point I carried on with my first flight of the day flows over hearing the conversation the Captain was having on the phone with the duty pilot; I heard something along of the line as it being explained as a hydraulic pump by hand in a little crate basically a little hand pump; and Captain was assured we are not taking any hydraulic fluid it's been emptied out might have a drop or two that was missed with a paper towel that's all... Captain looked at me and said don't know if you heard most of that which I replied I have he assured me we are not taking any hydraulic fluid and if I was comfortable going in which I told him in that case I have no issue going to fly. Well I believe we did everything that could have been done to ensure we were following SOP and company policy and procedure but there was a breakdown in communication between duty pilot / Maintenance Control and base Maintenance Manager where they forget to tell us we're taking canisters of hydraulic fluid.
column123: I was given Aircraft X on my first day of a four day reserve stretch. When I arrived at the gate I was informed that this was a maintenance (MX) reposition flight for an aircraft in ZZZ1. The two mechanics were sitting in the gate area and I went over to speak to them. I was informed the aircraft in ZZZ1 had issues with its hydraulic 2 quantity and that they had to head over and look at the system. I went back to the gate and got the paperwork; met my First Officer (FO); [Name]; and went down to the aircraft. As we began doing our first flight of day items and loading the flight plan; I told [name] that I would go upstairs and inform the gate agent he could let the mechanics board. Unfortunately the agent was having issues with scanning the mechanics on; so I called our Dispatcher so we could have them put on the release and they could come down. On the jet-bridge with the mechanics one of them told me he wanted to go check if they had got the tools out to the aircraft yet and that he wanted to also 'make sure the pump would not be leaking'. I immediately asked him if he was referring to a hydraulic pump and he confirmed he was. I told him I had to contact the Operations Controller because there should be no hydraulic fluid on the airplane; especially not any that could be leaking. at XA:01am I called the Operations phone tree and connected myself to the Chief Pilot; [Name 2]. I told [Name 2] that Maintenance told me they were worried about a hydraulic pump that could leak in the cargo compartment and needed to know exactly what was going on with this reposition and the equipment I was bringing. [Name 2] agreed with me that no hydraulic fluid was allowed to be transported and we went through the FOM looking for any guidance on hydraulic pumps and transporting that type of equipment. Our joint search of the FOM was in [the] chapter under the Hazardous Materials and Dangerous Goods section. This call lasted 13 minutes and 7 seconds and we agreed that there was no exceptions about equipment such as a hydraulic pump and [Name 2] told me he was going to talk to the Maintenance Head in the Operations. at XA:18 am I missed a call from [Name 2] and he left a message saying 'I just got a little more info on that hydraulic pump so to speak on your guys repo flight. Apparently it's a ground servicing pump; basically a tool we are bringing down there for maintenance.' I called back at XA:19am and he explained to me that we were bringing a pump that Maintenance would use on the ground to pump fluid into a hydraulic system on the other aircraft. He told me that Maintenance confirmed it was washed out and did not contain any hydraulic fluid.  I then went back and spoke to the mechanics to confirm this was the correct information. They said yes; the pump was indeed a servicing pump and it had been cleaned thoroughly prior to transport. With this information I and the conversation with Maintenance and the Operations Controller I decided that this was indeed a legal fight with cargo that was permitted in accordance with our FOM. On Date 2; I received a call from [Name 3] from the safety committee. He informed me that a Captain on the return flight for the broken aircraft was being asked to transport canisters of hydraulic fluid from ZZZ1 back to ZZZ and asked me if I knew anything about how they got there. I told [Name 3] that I had not transported any canisters from ZZZ to ZZZ1 and was under the impression that the pump and two tool kits were the only items aboard my aircraft. [Name 3] told me he would investigate further and call me back. [Name 3] called me back and informed me that we had unknowingly transported 2 canisters of Hy-Jet IV-A+ to ZZZ1 and informed me to fill out an ASAP with all pertinent details. Two Canisters of Hy-Jet IV-A+ were brought aboard Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZ1 without knowledge to the flight crew. There was clear confusion and either misinformation or lack of information between the flight crew; Operations; and Maintenance. In the future on maintenance reposition flights; or any flight requiring equipment to be flown for maintenance; an itemized list of equipment that is being transported should be signed my maintenance personnel; one copy should go into records and the other copy should go to the flight deck to be reviewed by the flight crew. This way there is a clear paper trail of evidence and accountability in the event that anything like this should ever happen again.

column121: Just prior to the EEP(ETOPS Entry Point) on a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 we received an ACARS message from Dispatch informing us that a possible 'hoverboard' might have been loaded in the cargo area. It should not have been and with the dual concurrence of us and Dispatch it was decided that the safest course of action was an air return back to ZZZ. We discussed with Dispatch if they wanted us to burn down to a normal landing weight or land overweight. It was decided to land overweight and that Maintenance would met us at the gate and conduct the overweight inspection. We requested and received Runway 8L for landing due to its length and to minimize brake heating. The landing was normal and the overweight inspection was successfully accomplished and the 'hoverboard' was removed. Clearly; there was a breakdown somewhere that allowed an item of non approved Hazmat to be placed onboard the aircraft. How and why this happened is beyond the limited facts that I have available but I think a in-depth review of our processes and procedures with regards to these items would be warranted.
column123: Prior to reaching the ETOPS Entry Point and Oceanic Airspace; we received a message from Dispatch informing us of a safety of flight issue regarding some luggage onboard. A Hoverboard (non-permitted item) had somehow passed through TSA screening and had potentially been loaded in a cargo compartment. In conjunction with Dispatch; we felt the safest decision was to return to our departure airport of ZZZ. This required an overweight landing and maintenance inspection. Not only was the item found on our aircraft; but apparently two Hoverboards were found. More extensive checks or passenger questioning during the check-in and security phase. Passengers need to also be made aware of the seriousness of having such Hazmat items onboard a plane.

Following that work; the aircraft and its logbooks were returned to me by the maintenance facility. Those logbooks had remained in the continuous custody of the maintenance facility from the time I delivered them to the maintenance facility; until they were returned to me on or about Date 3.A maintenance-related event occurred with respect to the aircraft on Date 3. It was the subject of a report submitted by me. I have discussed that event with the owner of the maintenance facility. I have also reviewed the confusing logbook entries for the inspection and maintenance work described above. In the course of those discussions and that review; I have become aware of what appear to be errors; inconsistencies; or alterations in those entries; and I have brought them to the attention of the owner of the maintenance facility; for such corrective action as may be necessary or appropriate. Yesterday the owner of the maintenance facility agreed that corrective action may be necessary with respect to those entries; and I am therefore submitting this report today.

column121: My Controller in Charge (CIC) issued a clearance to Aircraft X on the ground at HCR. The new procedure at HCR is that pilots are required to fly a Visual Climb Over Airport (VCOA) and remain within an arbitrary 5 mile radius of the airport and call us as soon as they're airborne.  Aircraft X was given all of this information and chose to fly directly south into the SLC arrival flow. He called me initially at 14;000 feet; 10 miles south of HCR airport; in another sectors airspace. Prior to this his transponder was not on. I gave the pilot radar contact; and asked him to confirm his position; to which he stated he was 'south of the airport'. This procedure is unsafe. Other airports have higher terrain than we do and they have SID's off both directions that actually work when it's IFR.There's no reason that we can't have a Runway 22 SID that goes over NONTY. The aircraft could climb to cross NONTY at 15;000 feet which would deconflict from Sector 32's traffic; and the arrival flows into SLC. Other airports have these procedures and their terrain is much more complicated than ours. This procedure was called completely illegal and unsafe a year ago and all that's changed is you deleted a footnote from the 7110.65. We can't keep pretending this is safe; until someone gets hurt. We have a responsibility to the flying public to do better.

column121: Training was in play at Local and Ground all day.  There was flow with delays to ZZZ.  Aircraft Y was taxied to Taxiway L short of M for eventual taxi via M to 1L for departure. Aircraft X was taxied to Runway 1R on the SSTIK4; which requires a red 'R' if requested/required by the pilot.  It is unknown at this point if that was the case.  My only assumption is that the Ground CPC-IT taxied the aircraft incorrectly to Runway 1R and the OJTI did not notice.  As their flow time came up; Local CPC-IT taxied Aircraft Y across Runway 1R at M and LUAW Runway 1L.  Aircraft X was given Runway 1R LUAW.  The CPC-it then; unbeknownst to the OJTI; launched Aircraft X on the SSTIK4; and shortly thereafter launched Aircraft Y also on the SSTIK4.  The only reason I became aware is when I heard the CPC-IT issuing visual separation and the Local Assist coordinating the same with NorCal.  When I looked up at the display; the aircraft were approximately 2 miles in trail with Aircraft Y lower and following to SSTIK.  Of note; with OJT occurring on both Local and Ground simultaneously; and Local Assist open; but apparently not engaged dynamically; the FLM could not possibly monitor both positions and all that the Local Assist was doing.  Subsequent discussion by the Local Control OJTI dictated that they were sorry; as they missed it and 'Use of RNAV To... will save you every time.'  This has been my complaint about people who refuse to use it and ignore that its use will in fact keep this exact scenario from occurring.  The numbers of neigh-sayers are reducing thankfully and we will eventually have the majority compliance.The traffic has picked up over 700 operations a day a few days of the week and is expected to get busier by the month this summer.  Use RNAV To... and; when working as OJTI; pay attention to what the CPC-IT is doing.

column121: The Captain was flying and after takeoff the white FMC message dealing with the autothrottle appeared and the Pilot Flying noticed an amber EGT exceedance.  The autothrottles and VNAV were inoperative at that point after takeoff.  The TAT probe was indicating a higher than normal temperature which we determined to be the root cause of all the problems.  We consulted with the QRH and Dispatch and all agreed to air return to ZZZ without any further issues.
column123: Just after takeoff the aircraft experienced a loss of data from the TAT probe (repeat gripe).  This initially manifested itself as an autothrottle limit error and a rapid increase in #1 EGT (yellow backfill on gage but no other indications) and loss of VNAV and related FMC functions.  We continued to climb to 16;000 feet MSL and informed ATC that we may need to return to ZZZ.  I passed aircraft control to the FO and initiated radio contact with Dispatch.  After initial contact; radio communications with Dispatch were lost; but Dispatch replied via ACARS that they agreed a return to ZZZ was prudent.  Release was amended.  ATC; cabin crew and passengers were informed; no emergency was declared.  The aircraft returned to ZZZ without incident.TAT failure is a high workload event similar to unreliable airspeed.  The number of items that rely on the TAT is huge; and once the event occurs there is (a) no real clue as to what the causal factor is; (b) no QRH guidance for the NN; and (c) a plethora of conflicting data and flight deck indications.  Thought should be given to educating our Pilot group to the risks and indications associated with TAT failure.

Altitude deviation was noted and a correction was made around 1;600 feet; shortly thereafter the tower issued a low altitude warning.  Altitude was corrected back to 2;000 feet; approach and landing was accomplished without further incident.  During debrief; crew agreed that expectation bias was a major contributing factor to the deviation.  The PF was still thinking about the altitudes for the Runway XX ILS.  It was the last leg of a three-day pairing so the PM did not properly back up the PF due to Pilot Flying's strong performance during the entire pairing.  PM should not allow previous performance or experience to impact critical backup role.
column123: Initially set up and briefed for the ILS XX. New ATIS was obtained with runway change to XYR just prior to runway transition point on the ZZZZZ Arrival.  Re briefed and set up for ILS XYR. I armed the localizer and set 2;000 feet; localizer captured and upon reaching 2;000 feet at ZZZZZ; I reverted to my previous briefing of the ILS XX and set 1;500 feet and proceeded to descend to 1;500 feet. Several hundred feet into the descent; Approach Control told us that we were low. Upon realizing what I had done I initiated a climb back to 2;000 feet from now 1;600 feet prior to ZZZZZ1. Reaching 2;000 feet prior to ZZZZZ1 and being stable again; we now continued to configure and resume the approach to land with no further incident.I should have verified my actions as I was accomplishing them and verified them with the PM. column121: Pushed off of gate X - ramp told us to taxi to spot X.  Taxing out of alley from [gate] X - there are ZERO taxi lines.  Paint has been removed.  I was going to taxi out to spot X then turn on taxi line there; but there was a plane stopped waiting to enter spot X.  I turned where the taxi lines used to be toward spot A.  Passing by spot Y; there was a plane coming in spot B blocking me from A.  There were ZERO taxi lines to be able to get around aircraft at spot B that started taxing. I told ramp that there were no taxi lines for me to get around other jet.  He asked me if I had my charts - which I did. He said it was construction.  Nothing in Jeppesen showed any 'alternate' taxi procedures.  There was a dashed yellow-black line to the North of standard taxi lines; but it went no where.  Later I could not find any mention of what a dashed yellow-black line meant in the AIM.  This was the first time I have taxied from X concourse to spot Z.CLT ramp just wants to move metal.  Having to switch to 3 different frequencies to get from one side of the ramp to the other is distracting.  Having ramp ask me if I have my charts or that due to construction I can taxi where I want is an accident waiting to happen.  There are ZERO lines to follow.  For us at night; unfamiliar - WITH our current charts out giving ZERO guidance and getting no help from ramp was was very uncomfortable. We stopped several times to make sure we had wing clearance with other aircraft taxiing.Publish and mark standard taxi lines during construction.

column121: During initial climbout; I was the pilot flying. We were flying runway heading off of [Runway] XX to 4;000 feet as assigned. We had not yet received our clearance to climb higher. I began to reduce power and pitch in order to level off at 4;000. At 3;500 feet; and speed 240 KIAS; we were instructed to climb and maintain 10;000 MSL. I then smoothly added thrust and adjusted pitch to continue climbing utilizing FLC. Once I increased thrust; there was a loud bang; followed by the engine indications and crew alerting system indicating engine # 1 was out. Additionally; a yawing tendency towards the INOP engine. Once identified by both pilots; controls were transferred to the Captain and I assumed PM duties. Normal checklists were complete; ATC and company was notified and the QRH procedure for engine out was accomplished. Engine fluid levels were normal; and the engine was shut down; which did not require the pulling of the #1 fire extinguishing handle. Once concluded a restart was not advised after discussion; due to the loud bang and sudden shutdown; we then were directed by the QRH to execute one engine inoperative approach and landing. The FA was notified and provided a [crew] brief; followed by the passenger announcement. We then coordinated with ATC for radar vectors for the visual; backed up by the  RNAV XX in ZZZ. Once landed; we stopped on the runway; had the engine inspected by the ZZZ fire department. Verification was made that there was no fire; fluid leakage and we then taxied off the runway and parked at [the] gate for deplaning.   Loud bang; aircraft yaw and EICAS indications by both pilots leading to the engine out procedure. Cause is still to be determined; from the initial inspection; the mechanical issue caused small metal fragments found in the compressor blades. After identifying the issue; we transferred flight controls; had a brief discussion and executed the pertinent QRH procedures for engine failure and a single engine approach and landing. No suggestions to report at this time.
column123: We were climbing out of ZZZ of Runway XX on runway heading and were just about to level off at 4;000 ft so the FO (PF) reduced thrust. Just before we leveled off we were given a continued climb up to 10;000 ft. While reintroducing thrust at 4;000 ft we heard a loud bang followed by aircraft yaw.  I immediately looked at the EICAS and saw an abrupt stop in the #1 engine. I called for my Aircraft.  The First Officer and I briefly discussed the situation then promptly ran the QRH for Engine OUT. The engine was shut down and our fluid levels (hydraulic/oil) looked normal so we decided against pulling the fire extinguishing handle. We discussed the possibility of restarting the engine but decided against it because of the loud bang we had heard followed by the abrupt shutdown of the engine. We were then led to [procedure] and proceeded to get set up for the Single engine approach.  After finishing talking to the passengers; flight attendant and sending a message to dispatch we completed all other  normal checklists. We then executed the visual approach backed up by RNAV RWY XX into ZZZ without any further event. We landed and had the fire department check out our engine for signs of smoke; fire; or fluid leak and then proceeded to the gate.The first indication of the Engine failure was a loud bang followed by aircraft yaw. We then looked at the EICAS and saw the indications of a #1 engine failure.  We were not given a definitive cause for the failure. It seems to have been a mechanical issue inside the Engine. Upon inspection after landing chunks of metal were found inside the compressor blades. After noticing the event. We transferred  flight controls then briefly discussed our situation and decided to run the checklist for Engine Failure in the QRH .

column121: On the departure; the First Officer (FO) had requested Heading Mode (HDG); Flight Level Change (FLCH) during the climb out as we were given a heading.  It was bumpy and he was trying to comply with the SID instructions to speed up to 250 KIAS while hand flying in bumpy air.  As we approached the 5;000 foot altitude restriction; he started to slow his climb for the level off; but didn't pull back on the thrust levers. The autothrottles were on; but we were not quite close enough to the altitude for the flight director to switch to 'ASEL' on the FMA and begin capturing. In a climb; the auto throttles remain at full thrust in green FLCH until ASEL is annunciated; and since the FO was hand flying and beginning the level off before the Altitude Select (ASEL) annunciation; the speed began to pick up.  As pilot monitoring; I noticed the airspeed at 255 KIAS with an increasing trend and I called out 'airspeed' to alert him to the airspeed.  He seemed confused and did not make any corrections. I then called for him to 'pitch up' which he did slightly; but he mentioned the level off altitude that was approaching.  I said to 'pull the thrust back' and he seemed confused again and replied that the auto throttles should do that.  I then pulled the thrust levers back myself to slow the aircraft down as the speed was starting to go past 260 KIAS.  ATC gave us a 'climb and maintain 7000' and a direct to one of the fixes.  The FO pitched up for the climb and I was able to let go of the thrust levers as the speed was again under control.  As we were climbing; ATC instructed us to climb to 16;000 and the FO called for 'Autopilot On' prior to the next level off so there were no further issues.  I reminded him that there is no speed protection in the level off for the FLCH mode if he is hand flying it and levels off early.   ATC didn't seem to notice the increased airspeed;  and the flight continued without further incident.The FO said that he finished IOE and for the next month was unable to get any flying from crew scheduling.  He had less than 30 hours on the aircraft.   The following month; he had to be in Country to check on family due to the COVID pandemic.  He said that he had flown earlier that day and seemed to be comfortable in the plane.  It became clear that he was rusty on the details concerning the FLCH mode.  After I spoke with him about what happened; he said he understood and he did not make the same mistake on his flight the following day. Any time a pilot has less than 100 hours (consolidation) on an aircraft; and doesn't fly for more than 30 days; they should be given a trip with an IOE instructor both to give them recency of experience and to refresh any forgotten material.
column123: During take off climbing to the assigned altitude of 5;000 in flight level change plane accelerated to 250K; during last 1;000 ft I shallowed the pitch as climb was getting a bit bumpy due to builds up around [the] area and I was trying to avoid flying through a cloud straight ahead. Captain advised me of speed increasing and passing 250 and I assumed the auto-throttle would have compensated for that as it was engaged. Leveling off to 5;000 speed past 260 and the Captain reached out the thrust lever decreasing power avoiding further deviation. Soon after cleared to 7;000 climb and flight continued with no further deviation. After IOE I was put on reserve and didn't fly for about a month; I then was able to pick up a line and fly just one sequence as a tragic event forced me to drop the rest of the month and travel overseas; as a result in 2 months I only flew 19 hours and that was my first day flying after a long stop. As newly typed on a new airplane I didn't immediately recalled the different ways the autothrottle responds; however soon after the event my Captain explained [to] me what happened and refreshed my memory on it. After IOE it would be good to assign some extra flight to help consolidate; maybe assigning more frequent flights and not letting more than 2 weeks without flying would avoid skills deterioration until the first 100 hours are reached.

column121: The following narrative is due to a complete lack of threat and error management and operation performance.   This was the first leg of a 4 day trip and I would be flying with a First Officer for the first time.   We were heavily delayed to start our day and weather was terrible.   High winds and windshear were reported throughout the whole Company system with several crews diverting.   Yet my release for this flight indicated nothing other than I should evaluate the use of Runway XX for ZZZ departure.   When the aircraft arrived I met the arriving Captain and he explained to me the auto pilot master warning EICAS message occurred at 1;000 feet on the coupled ILS approach into ZZZ.  The Captain stated maintenance refused to take the write ups as it was going to ZZZ1 and they would casually look at it there.   I immediately called maintenance and asked why they wouldn't take write ups and said from what it sounded like a write up was not warranted.   The maintenance controller asked if I wished to MEL the autopilot and I stated how can I?  At this point I should have immediately refused the plane; but at Company; refusing to fly gets us an immediate phone call from the Chief Pilot office.   We Were now operating in the red of the threat and error management philosophy.   On the way to ZZZ1 we experienced moderate turbulence as expected and when we turned base for Runway XY the field was surrounded by virga.  The FO and I briefed a go around and the windshear escape maneuver once more.   On final at about 1;200 feet the Autopilot Fail master warning EICAS  message appeared and the Autopilot disconnected.  I continued to hand fly the aircraft and remained stable to about 300 feet where I encountered increasing performance and the approach became unstable.   A normal go-around was executed and we called positive rate gear up; we received the windshear caution.   Immediately after we hit severe turbulence.  We diverted to ZZZ without further incident.  The remainder of the flight was performed without the autopilot.Company maintenance did not take a write up from a Captain. I wrote up the AP failure and the encounter with severe turbulence. All write-ups must be taken by maintenance.

column121: Shortly after reaching cruising altitude of 5000 ft. MSL I was just about to cancel my IFR clearance and proceed to ZZZ1 with VFR advisories with a decent to 3500 ft MSL. In that moment I was able to determine it was a white; 4 bladed drone; approximately the size of a microwave. The light I had seen appeared to be just that; or a possible camera that the sun was reflecting off of. There was not enough time to react; due to this; I continued on my IFR clearance for a few more miles; while I reported the incident to ATC. After the report to ATC; I notified [company] of the event and asked them to issue a PIREP for those heading into ZZZ. There was one passenger onboard; however; they were unaware of this incident. column121: After completion of pushback and after receiving salute I flashed the landing light.  The push lead and a wing walker were observed walking away as the tug backed away from the aircraft.  Approximately 10-15 meters off the nose a small bag which apparently contained the push headset fell out of the tug cab where the bag and the headset fell apart laying on the ramp.  The tug driver saw it fall out his side of the cab and stopped.  As the tug driver stepped out of tug it began to roll towards our aircraft with the tow bar still mounted on the front like a battering ram.  The tug driver immediately jumped back in the cab and stopped the tug and manipulated some controls.  The cab driver was the only one in tug and rest of pushback crew was oblivious as they walked back to gate area.  I don't know if the tug has a parking brake but the tug driver again stepped out of the tug while it idled away from the aircraft towards the terminal.  The unmanned tug continued towards the terminal at a walking pace while the tug driver scooped the headset into the bag and then he jogged back and jumped in the moving tug.  The tug now under manned control continued back to the gate are and we taxied out for departure.I don't know if it was complacency or rushing to get out of our way or both but I would like to think push tugs both have a park position as well as a park brake both if which should have been used in this case in my opinion. Emphasize safety to ramp members to protect persons and property.

column121: I acted as the pilot-in-command and sole occupant of a Cessna 402 aircraft on a flight in visual meteorological conditions. Prior to departure; I conducted a preflight inspection in accordance with the manufacturer's recommended procedures; and I followed the preflight checklist. All systems appeared to operate normally during takeoff; climb; and cruise flight.During the approach to landing; I monitored the UNICOM frequency when another pilot approximately 4-5 miles ahead of me; approaching the same runway; advised that there was turbulence on final approach. While on short final approach; I experienced turbulence and added power to maintain a proper glide path.  At that point; I noticed that the left (i.e.; critical) engine was no longer producing power. As a result; the aircraft nose yawed left (i.e.; toward the dead engine) and I applied full right rudder to maintain directional control.Since I was on a short final approach to the runway; I reduced power in order to land while maintaining my airspeed above Vmc (i.e.; minimum controllable airspeed with critical engine failure). However; the gusty wind drifted the airplane to the left of center line. Since I had applied full right rudder to maintain runway centerline while in flight; upon touchdown the airplane aggressively spun to the right and departed the runway; which caused the landing gear to collapse.When the aircraft came to a complete stop; I shut down the right engine; secured the aircraft; and exited through the cabin door without incident.

At that moment the student (who is also commercial multi rated but learning to be an multi engine instructor) rotated and began initial climb. column121: I was in the traffic pattern doing touch and go landings with a student at ZZZ (one of five aircraft in the pattern).  We were approaching mid-field right downwind for Runway XX; and tower advised that we were following another aircraft on base; which we advised we had in-sight (which was number two; making us number 3.) As we approached our base leg; tower told us the base turn was our discretion; and we began turning base.  As soon as we did so; the traffic we were following (Aircraft Y) called tower and advised that they needed to do a 360 for spacing (it appeared they had turned their base leg too soon; and were too close to the traffic they were following.  Tower approved and notified them that once they completed their 360 to watch out for us; and that they would be now following us (making us now #2 for the runway; and them #3).My student turned final and we were on an approximately 1.5 nm final; descending through 700-800 feet; when my student stated; 'I think they're turning right at us!'Simultaneously Aircraft Y had apparently just completed their 360 turn and Tower inquired if they had us in sight and were to follow us; they stated they were looking for traffic.I looked up to suddenly see the other aircraft heading directly across our final approach path; and almost on a head-on course; coming at us approximately from 45 degrees off of our left nose.  As I looked; I also simultaneously received an ADS-B traffic alert from Foreflight on my iPad; indicated the other traffic; heading directly at us and at the same altitude.I immediately stated 'my controls'; took over control of the aircraft; and quickly began a descending turn to the right to create distance from the other traffic; I looked up again and saw the other aircraft also start a sharp bank to their right; while simultaneously telling the tower that they now had us in-sight.  I remained in control of the aircraft and executed an (otherwise) uneventful landing.Tower did not acknowledge the event.  It seemed that the controller was very task saturated with the five aircraft in the pattern.  It seemed they were also distracted by a King Air 350 that was handed over to tower from ZZZ Approach and setup for a right downwind for Runway XX. Initially tower had told them to enter left downwind; but they were adamant that they wanted right downwind; which I believe both added to the confusion; as well as tied up the tower frequency unnecessarily with their continued back and forth communications. It did not help that the King Air had requested and was then doing a 360 turn for spacing of their own; right on the upwind leg of Runway XX when there were multiple other aircraft in the traffic pattern.It should be noted that while we were on short final; the Aircraft Y involved in this incident had once again turned base too soon; and I noticed that they were less than 0.5nm behind us.  They were so close that they in fact were ordered to go-around by the Tower because we had just touched down and were still rolling out when they crossed the runway threshold behind us.I believe contributing to the incident were: The pilot of Aircraft Y failing to maintain situational awareness resulting in inadequate spacing thus requesting multiple 360 turns; their failure to adequately scan for traffic and maintain a proper rectangular course in the traffic pattern causing them to cross our final approach course at a 45 degree angle; tower controller being task saturated with multiple aircraft in the traffic pattern; and the King Air traffic adding to the confusion by adamantly requesting to enter the right downwind (which conflicted with the other aircraft already in the traffic pattern for Runway XX; which is right traffic.)

column121: It was a busy day in the pattern at LMO and BJC was closed for pattern work. I had already done one lap in the pattern at LMO and was in the downwind for another lap. In the downwind; the skydiving operation announced a few times; 'Jumpers away'. I saw them and told my student to make a slightly wider pattern to accommodate them. Just as we made a slight deviation; an aircraft; Aircraft Y; entered the pattern mid field downwind and my ADS-B indicated they were the same altitude as us. Aircraft Y announced they had 'downwind traffic in sight' but it was likely another plane. They cut us off not only in the downwind; but also headed straight for the jump zone. The jump plane announced frantically 'parachutes have been deployed'. I was careful not to climb or descend while I did not have Aircraft Y in sight because ADS-B indicated they were same altitudes. We did not see them until they were passing just under us. Once I saw them; I asked their intentions with no response. I decided it was best to depart the airport back to BJC. Upon returning to BJC; I spoke with many instructors from different flight schools in the area and it seems like the traffic pattern at LMO has become increasingly dangerous. Many instructors have had near misses with other pilots not making calls or entering the pattern however they wish.

column121: All events through pushback were accomplished without note. During pushback; a puddle on the ramp aft of the normal oil spot was noticed behind the #2 engine. Puddle was not present on the walkaround. A stream of drops along the ramp was also noticed while the #2 engine was run. After five minutes the fuel leak had not stopped and we towed back to a gate. Maintenance was called; ran several tests; and two engine runs. The leak dissipated as the tests were completed. No fuel appeared to be leaking while engines were running; except for one within limits from the heat exchanger. Forms were completed to indicate it. Aircraft pushed and started again. No leaks were noted.Shortly after takeoff/cleanup; Captain announced a split in the thrust levers. Autothrottles were used for takeoff with VNAV (climb page 2L adjusted for 202 knots at 1;000 feet AGL). Looking at the engine instruments; I noticed the #2 thrust lever about three knob widths ahead of the #1. #1 N1 was at commanded power with the #2 N1 showing the white commanded power bar of about 95%; but the engine only producing about 88-89%. Further advancement of the throttle lever produced no increase in power. Vertical Speed was selected and we reduced our climb rate to bring the power back. As the power came back; the throttle synced and power matched. VNAV was reselected and as the power returned to full climb; the split reappeared with the #2 indicating a commanded increase without the engine delivering the power.As this was being discussed; the center tank fuel pumps were turned on (750 pounds in the center tank). Immediately after the pumps were turned on; the power matched and all indication were normal. As soon as the center tank fuel was exhausted; the split returned. Crew leveled at FL 270 and elected to return to ZZZ. As power was less than full climb at cruise/descent; and no abnormal indication were present during these flight conditions; no QRH Checklists were run. The rest of the return to ZZZ was completed without note. Engine performed as expected from level off to shutdown.Contract Maintenance expressed an increased level of calls from aircraft coming from the paint shop; fuel leaks were common with these aircraft.  Would recommend a Maintenance individual check and run engines prior to returning the aircraft to the line.
column123: Origination flight on an aircraft that had just come out of the paint shop. Preflight was uneventful with no fuel drips or puddles noted. We pushed five minutes early. On push back #2 was dripping fuel and did not stop after a short time and engine was shutdown. After consultation with Maintenance Control; we returned to the gate and called Contract Maintenance. Contract Maintenance did four motoring tests as directed by [company's] Maintenance. With each test; the dripping became improved. Then an engine run was completed with decreased dripping; but not to a small enough level to allow Dispatch. Contract Maintenance then opened the cowl and did an engine run to determine location of drip. After that run; the component dripping was identified and the dripping had decreased to an amount that allowed MEL. MEL was completed. This was about a 2.5 hour process. Ground Ops and Operations were very helpful with accommodating the Passengers as well as they could. I had given periodic in-person updates to the passengers. Finally; we pushed-back and the engine starts were uneventful without any drips. Uneventful taxi. We took off on Runway XX with a headwind 20G30. On push up of thrust; #2 lagged a bit and I pushed the thrust lever up to get closer to match and continued my crosscheck.  As we approached V1/VR I noticed #2 still lagging by a few percent and pushed up the throttle some more. Normal on centerline liftoff and climbout. After liftoff; I informed the F/O  (First Officer) that we had a split throttle situation. We cleaned up on schedule and began to evaluate the situation (again the aircraft had no adverse flight characteristics). With the aircraft cleaned up and climb power set; we observed that although the #2 demand pointer was correct; the #2 N1 lagged approximately 2-5% N1. Once our climb rate was reduced in Vertical Speed and at a slightly lower climb thrust setting; the engine was normal and tracked normally with the demand pointers and thrust lever position. To this point we had continued to follow ATC instructions to keep it simple. We found that the engine reacted the same with the autothrottle On or Off. Also we had 750 pounds of fuel in the center tank; so once established in the climb we turned the pumps on and immediately #2 N1 returned to normal operation at full climb power. When center tank was empty and pumps turned off; the malfunction returned. With this information we leveled off and informed ATC that we would probably need to return to the airport. While level we reconfirmed no other abnormal conditions or switches out of place. Also at level flight in this situation there were no conditions that warranted a QRH Checklist although it was discussed. F/O and I discussed the situation and decided that without the aircraft able to achieve full climb thrust on Main Fuel pumps only; the safest choice was to return to the airport. F/O flew and talked to ATC; while I informed flight attendants and passengers of need to return to the airport for safety reasons and gave them our ETA. I called Station Ops on VHF and informed them of our need to return; get a gate; and asked them to contact Dispatch. We also confirmed via ACARS with Dispatch the need to return due to engine unable to achieve full climb power (or something like that). The F/O did a very good job and stayed ahead of the aircraft preparing for the briefings; descent; and Approach Checklist. We referenced the Diversion Checklist to ensure we had covered the suggested items. We accomplished a normal descent and asked for a long visual approach to increase probability of a stable approach and landing without the need for a thrust needful go-around. F/O flew stable approach and landing with normal braking. No emergency was declared; no special handling requested; and a normal weight landing occurred. Uneventful taxi-in and shutdown. Flight was canceled and the passengers accommodated as best as Ops could. Debrief with the flight attendants yielded that although disappointed in their flight being cancelled; they were appreciative of the Safety of turning back. Immediate notification with XXXXXX was done after engine shutdown with Dispatch; Supervisor; Maintenance; and Chief Pilot.The Location X crews both above the wing and below the wing were very familiar with the Maintenance trouble shooting of engine drips on starts because they have seen it more the once from aircraft coming out of the paint shop.  An engine run after paint shop would have found this problem before a revenue flight was disrupted.  Maybe this may be a prudent practice--an ounce or prevention may have saved a pound of Customer frustration.  Perhaps a faster crosscheck by myself might have allowed a reject option in the 70-90 knot range; but even then there was no decrease in power and I perceived the N2 engine thrust close-enough to N1 engine thrust to ensure a safer option than a medium speed reject.

When we contacted Ramp Control they said we had entered the ramp without clearance; but we were still on a designated taxiway. There were some alternating double-dashed lines in FLL around what I would consider 'the ramp' that were about 100 yards off the various concourses; but we were nowhere near those when we taxied in. One factor in this whole thing is the FO contacted the Ramp control frequency on the 10-9 page for North Ramp but only South Ramp was open. But we still were not in or on the ramp when we got that mess sorted out.

column121: We finished the first leg of three on the last day of a three-day trip. We pulled into the gate at LAS with a scheduled plane swap. After completing the Parking Checklist and other post-flight duties; I cleared the FO to head out while I stayed with the aircraft while passengers deplaned. Ground power was connected initially but air was not. As deplaning commenced; I asked the agent to call for ground air. It was 106F OAT and I was concerned about cabin temp. I understood from the agent that the aircraft would be on the ground for some time. After all passengers were off; I went outside and asked Ramp to connect ground air. A few minutes later one of the guys came to the cockpit and informed me that ground air was inop. In the meantime; one of the new FAs (flight attendants) came onboard saying she came down early because the terminal was very crowded. As the situation progressed I decided to leave the APU on for cabin cooling; informed the FA and agent and went on to my new aircraft. At the time I didn't give it a second thought. It wasn't until I got to the new aircraft; finished preflight duties and had a few minutes to reflect that I realized my error. Sick feeling. I told the FO that I would be back and hustled back to the previous gate to remedy my mistake. Probably 30 minutes or so had elapsed since I had left it. By the time I got back to the gate The new crew was onboard and passengers were boarding.I must say that I didn't feel any type of particular time pressure or any major distraction. I'm not sure why my thought process went so awry. While this situation is not common; I'm sure it's not unheard of and I should know better than to leave the APU running and Terminating Checklist incomplete. I certainly could have stayed with the aircraft until the new Crew arrived.I am sure that I hadn't reviewed FOM in some time so unless I'm the only one who has messed up this way; adding that to our training profile may raise awareness to this issue and prevent someone else from making the same mistake.

column121: After starting the #1 engine during a single engine taxi out; I shut down the APU. This was done immediately after my workload increased significantly. Since we were on a MAX we chose to start the second engine early on the taxi out to [Runway] XXR; but engine motoring continued until we were crossing Runway XXL. My attention was split between monitoring the engine start and looking outside during the runway crossing. By the time we were clear I was concentrating on the remaining taxi distance for our three minute warmup. I went through the normal After Start Flow without thinking about leaving the APU running. My mistake was not caught by either of us on the Before Takeoff Checklist; only on the climb out through about 8;000 feet.We should have slowed down. There were many factors causing us to rush. The gate was unusual for (Company) operations; and we had to deal with broken jetway stairs and ground power that was disconnected during boarding. These were both stress inducers; and we should have recognized that we were being pushed into the Yellow before we even left the gate. The Captain was unfamiliar with the airport. I could have done a better job walking him through the taxi procedures. I should have realized this would cause a distraction while starting the second engine. We were on a MAX departing for an ETOPS flight; and fuel is almost always a consideration during taxi out. We chose to delay APU start at the gate and single engine taxi to conserve as much as possible. We even briefed the earlier start because of lengthy MAX engine motoring; but it still wasn't early enough to be complete before crossing [Runway] XXL. We should have started the engine earlier so I could concentrate on one thing at a time. Both the Captain and I were new to ETOPS flying. We were in and out of the Yellow during preflight as we worked through the extra preflight procedures. We should have given ourselves more time to complete these tasks.
column123: During taxi out; at an unfamiliar airport; a delayed engine start of engine #1 was performed by the F/O; due to a long taxi to the runway. During the After Start Flow performed by the F/O; he inadvertently shut the APU off; which was required for this ETOPS flight. I missed the fact that the APU was OFF during the 'Before Takeoff' checklist; and a normal takeoff was performed. During the climb; at approximately 7000 feet; it was discovered that the APU was off; so I started the APU prior to reaching 10;000 feet. The flight continued without incident. At no time did the aircraft fly in Class II operations with the APU off.

column121: The event happened at night on taxi out from gate to Runway XXL. There were significant amounts of thunderstorms surrounding ZZZ requiring the airport to only have Runway XXL for takeoff and XXR for landing. Upon leaving the ramp area; we were given clearance to taxi to XXL via Taxiways '1' then [Taxiway] '23.' We turned north on [Taxiway] '1' and followed a B737. The B737 aircraft stopped holding short of [Taxiway] '23.' After about 30 seconds it proceeded and turned onto [Taxiway] 23 and we followed. It was as we turned onto [Taxiway] 23 that both the Captain and I heard the ATC Ground Controller give excited directions to 'hurry up/go fast.' The key point here is that we never heard our call sign used for any of these calls and assumed he was talking to someone else. As we advanced to a position abeam Runway XXR on our right; the Ground Controller called our call sign and I responded. He then told us; using our call sign; to 'go fast; aircraft on short final to Runway XXR.' We saw the conflict and tried to move faster but it was too late and the aircraft was forced to execute a go-around. The Controller told us the aircraft had to go-around and chastised us for missing several calls. I responded that we 'never heard it.'Ultimately; I believe one of two things happened--either the Controller made several excited transmissions either omitting our call sign or used an incorrect call sign; or both the Captain and I missed several radio calls made to us until a conflict happened.
column123: We had been reassigned after a long weather delay and misconnect out of ZZZ.  We had to consult with dispatch to confirm our clearance and routing. ZZZ ATC had reconfigured airport and were landing and departing runways XXL/R. At spot X we were instructed to taxi to XXL; [Taxiway] 1; [Taxiway] 23. As we approached [Taxiway] 23 a B737 was stopped ahead of us. That aircraft then turned onto [Taxiway] 23. We followed; no instructions to hold short of the XXR approach was given. The Ground Controller then told the B737 to hurry; then told us to hurry and cross XXR approach; saying that we were expected to hold short of [Taxiway] 23.  We were not instructed to hold short of Taxiway 23.

column121: During climbout from CVG; we were given a climb to 13;000 feet and cleared to WADAL intersection. Passing out of 9;000 feet (climbing at 1500 feet/min) we were told to contact Indy Center on 135.57. We checked in with Indy Center (135.57) and stated we were climbing to 13;000 feet. Passing through about 10;000 feet; the TCAS gave an aural TA warning and the display popped up on the MFD.  It showed an aircraft 800 feet above us descending at our 12 O'clock position towards us (about 6 miles out). At the same time; Indy center issued a turn 15 degrees to the left. Simultaneously we got a descending RA (indicating 2;000 feet/min down). I commanded my OE student to immediately disconnected the A/P comply with the RA; which he did. As we were descending per the RA; we visually acquired the aircraft as it pop out of the clouds at about 200 feet above us. It passed off our right side and directly over us. This appeared to be low wing aircraft; single engine type. This aircraft was squawking 1200 and appeared to be VFR.  They nor Indy Center were not controlling this aircraft at the time. I did speak with the Indy Center manager afterwards; he was unaware at that point what had transpired.Cause - VFR aircraft not controlled by ATC and flying in the clouds without an IFR clearance.Suggestions - I learned the importance of always complying with TCAS instructions in an expeditious manner. Had we not done this and utilized our training; it may have ended poorly.

column121: At approximately 130 knots I saw a flock of seagulls coming from my peripheral right side and they started impacting the aircraft with multiple strikes. The Captain was diligent and assertive to abort the aircraft at this time and we came to a complete stop with auto-brakes; spoilers and reversers. I notified the Tower of the abort and requested the AARF and made all the appropriate call outs (spoilers; 80; 60) to back the Captain up on the abort. Once stopped the Captain made the PA 'remain seated x3' and I rolled the flaps to 40 once we verified no doors were open. We held position to run the brake cooling chart and determined we needed one hour. We then had the AARF follow us to the ramp as well to be sure no personnel approached the aircraft. Once parked at the gate; we requested chocks to be inserted on the nose wheel so that we may release the brake pedal pressure as setting the parking brake was not an option. When the AARF confirmed it was safe to have the jet-bridge brought to the aircraft we did so and AARF remained ever ready throughout the entire process. Once the brake cooling was confirmed complete; the Captain; the mechanic and I inspected the tires to find #2 tire flat with fuse plug melted and #3 tire scalloped badly. Both would need replacement. No other damage identified. Too many birds on the airport property that were not easily seen. Adding an air cannon to the airport property to scare off the birds for arriving and departing aircraft.

column121: We were operating our flight ZZZ to ZZZ1. This flight operates at close to if not at its max weight where maximum performance from the aircraft and crew are required due to the short runways. Headwind operations; or more importantly; absence of any tailwinds; should be the main concern of ATC and pilots when utilizing this airport when such performance is required.In the hours prior to this flight ZZZ was running a south operation; departing RWY XX; as one would expect with a reasonable headwind (180/7kts). Approximately 20 minutes before departure; they switched to a north operation; now departing RWY XY. This change seemed illogical as it now was using a runway that had a 7 knot tailwind for takeoff. With this change our flight was unable to depart as we were too heavy due to a tailwind weight penalty of 9;030 lbs from our runway limit.I asked ZZZ Ground/Tower Control why they had changed to a north operation. The answer we received was that arriving aircraft on the XXXXX Visual were encountering a tailwind at altitude and therefore the change. This puzzled me. Is this an official procedure that the FAA ATC has at ZZZ or shouldn't runway selection for takeoff and landing be based on surface winds?We had no choice but to wait for an opening for RWY XX; which caused a significant delay to our companies reliability operation; not to mention putting other aircraft in an awkward position of either compromising safety margins or accepting lengthy delays. Switching runways around based on winds at altitude rather than safety of landing and departing on short runways with tailwinds; puts the pilots in the position as the last line of defense for safety.  Just FYI; we also only had one reverser. Although RTO does not include the reversers in its stopping distance calculations; it was still a consideration to us.ATC changing runways from a headwind to a strong tailwind. Putting pilots in a less optimal position to operate their aircraft.The additional work load and max performance requirements when utilizing a short runway with a tailwind should be avoided as much as possible especially at ZZZ. Every foot of runway concrete is paramount to operating safely at this airport. Therefore every knot of tailwind compromises that safety margin.
