My original plan was to fly towards the FAF at 6;000 [feet] then turn base leg then final just inside of it to start my descent after being fully configured. I decided to turn earlier and mistakenly followed what I thought to be my glide slope; therefore; I believed myself to be too high and needing to descend for a stabilized approach. Turning base to final; we got an audible alert of 'obstacle' to which I was searching outside but did not see. Then at the Captain's prompt suggestion I tried to level off but was not aggressive enough. The slow descent resulted in a 'pull up' alert and I was able to maintain altitude but the Captain noted the RA of being around 650 AGL. I was able to continue my turn base to final stabilized and had no other incidents with the event. Lack of situational awareness on my part and last-minute decision to keep a tighter traffic pattern which would require compressed time to configure the aircraft. Mainly; my mistake in believing/following a false glide slope which lead to my confusion. Following the ILS profiles even in VMC conditions for terrain/obstacle clearance. Keeping my situational awareness outside of the cockpit more & remaining vigilant especially in VMC conditions.

column121: I was Pilot Flying. I triggered a stick shaker/pusher at the Final Approach Fix. I recovered per SOP.[There was] a northbound squall line west of the field. A last minute wind shift caused us to switch runways. Although it was fast; we were able to set up and brief before intercepting course. ATC forgot to turn [us] on the ILS; so we went through the localizer course. This led to reactionary vectors and the aircraft doing S turns until we passed the final approach fix. At this point we were flaps 30 with the power reduced. I called for the go-around; but when I pressed the autopilot disconnect button; I became fixated on the lack of a missed approach course. (I didn't press the TO-GA button.) While troubleshooting; the airspeed continued to decrease leading to a simultaneous stick shaker and pusher. I lowered the nose and recovered per the training; paying special attention to the radar altimeter. I briefly oversped flaps 8 on recovery.Stall recovery training works. I was able to accomplish the recovery quickly without having to think about it. However; it shouldn't have gotten that far. It was my first go-around since OE. I was task saturated and in the moment couldn't remember where the TO-GA button was. We were able to handle weather; ATC error; runway changes and an instrument approach at the same time. However; because our go around was triggered at a relatively untrained aircraft state/position; I missed a critical aspect of the maneuver. I don't believe this is a common problem; but incorporating go-arounds during recurrent in various positions may be beneficial.

column121: Climbing out at approximately 5000 ft; we received an R 14 DUCT warning message on the EICAS followed by a ANTI ICE DUCT warning. While running the QRH; we received a HI PACK Press caution message. I assume it was a left pack since we had to pull power back on the right engine; but honestly I don't remember which side the pack high pressure was. I knew from a previous 14th DUCT warning message that we could not continue and requested a return to ZZZ. I told the FO (First Officer) that I had the radios and the flight controls and asked him to read the QRH for R 14 DUCT. After we finished the QRH; I requested that the FO talk to the Flight Attendant and tell her that we had to return to ZZZ and that we are not evacuating and that she has 10 minutes. We completed the descent and approach checklist. I completed the flaps 20 landing and let the aircraft come to a stop after max reverse thrust use and only needed braking to the end of the runway to minimize brake temperatures. Left inboard brake temp did reach a white 8 and 6 while the right stayed green at 5. We taxied back to the gate keeping an eye on the brake temperatures. I asked the FO to run the pack high pressure QRH on the ground; the message cleared. Once we made it back to the gate; holding short waiting for the ramp to park us; we received a SMOKE TOILET caution message. I asked the FO to call the FA and ask her to check the lav for smoke. We could hear the smoke detector from the cockpit. The FA reported nothing unusual in the lav. The smoke detector stopped going off. In the meantime; requested the fire department inspect the outside of the aircraft. By the time the fire trucks came we had already hooked up the jet bridge and deplaned.
column123: On the initial climbout we received a R 14th DUCT warning message. The Captain directed me to inform ATC we needed to return to ZZZ. Shortly after the first warning message; we received an ANTI ICE DUCT warning message and an R PACK HI PRESS caution message. After we were established on a course back towards ZZZ; the Captain took the radios and called for the R 14th DUCT warning QRH. After completing the first half of the QRH procedure; the warning message persisted so I completed the rest of procedure; preparing for a landing at the nearest suitable airport.Shortly after completion of the full QRH procedure; the R 14th DUCT warning and ANTI ICE DUCT warning messages cleared while we were still in the air. Given the potential severity of a 14th stage bleed air leak; we agreed that an immediate return to ZZZ was warranted and prioritized our remaining tasks with that in mind. I called the flight attendant and informed her that we had a warning message and would be returning to the airport; and we had about 5-7 minutes until landing. She acknowledged and requested I make a PA. I made a brief PA informing the passengers that we had a maintenance issue that required us to return to ZZZ and that we would be landing in about 5 minutes.I resumed responsibility for the radios and proceeded to assist in getting set up for the approach; setting frequencies and getting the appropriate landing data requested. We completed all normal checklists and then had an uneventful approach and landing. After clearing the runway; and having no persisting warning messages; we stated that we did not require any assistance and taxied to the gate. After we were safely on the ground; the Captain asked me to complete the R PACK HI PRESS caution QRH procedure; which cleared the message. We also reviewed the QRH procedure for the ANTI ICE DUCT warning message.While holding short of the gate waiting for a parking crew; with no remaining warning or caution messages; we received a SMOKE TOILET caution message and I could hear the smoke alarm sounding. The Captain called the flight attendant; who went to check the lavatory; and asked me to run the associated QRH procedure. I contacted the Ramp Tower and advised that we were getting a smoke toilet caution indication and requested the fire department. The flight attendant called back and reported there was no smoke in the lavatory. The SMOKE TOILET caution message cleared shortly after this with no further crew action. Passengers deplaned via jet bridge. I sent an ACARS message to Dispatch and Maintenance at the gate advising of the situation. While in the air the Captain had mentioned (and I believe attempted) messaging Dispatch of the return; though given the time critical nature of this [event]; this message was not sent until we were on the ground.[The cause was] right 14th stage bleed air leak in flight.

column121: While taxiing into [spot]; it was raining with lowered visibility. The ramp agents were standing in position with the exception of the marshaller. The Safedock system was in operation; and I saw an agent by the controls. I followed the line clearly marked [spot]; which was between both wing walkers. Directly in front of this line; which was angled to the left; was the door marked [spot]. I had line of sight to Safedock. As a newer Captain; I did not have any reason to doubt that this was my 'J' line to follow. As I approached and passed the large [spot] painted on the ground; I realized that it was a dashed line; rather than a solid. Just as I noticed this; a marshaller appeared to my left. The marshaller then waved his flags at me and pointed to my left. I then realized that there was another [spot] line; and that I was in the wrong one.The marshaller emphatically waved his batons to my left; and I believed he was directing me left to exit the ramp. I had my FO [First Officer] call Ramp Control and got clearance to turn left and swing back around for the correct 'J' line. I received that approval. I conducted the turn after the marshaller again waved me to the left.I was able to gain clear sight of the vehicles on both sides and noticed no impediment to my progress. I turned around on the taxi lane and entered the straight in 'J' line using Safedock.My FO said that he then saw some markings for the slanted line that indicated it might be for an B737.I was approached by a Ramp Supervisor upon exiting the aircraft. He stated that I had 'jet blasted' his rampers during my exit turn. I explained my perspective; given that I believed I was following the ramper's direction. He told me that 'Next time; call for a tug.' I told him that I understood his concerns; expressly apologized for my confusion during the parking; and that I would heed his advice in the future.[Causes]1) My inexperience as a Captain2) The addition of 'J' lines for B737 aircraft that lined up with safe dock; were labeled exactly the same as the ones for Airline aircraft3) Rain and visibility issues4) Last leg of a day that began [early]5) Confusing and very late directions given by marshaller[Suggestions]1) Use this as a learning tool with respect to ground operations2) Given the human factors present in this event; I believe there needs to be changes to the paint for B737 'J' lines.3) More focus in inclement weather4) Recognize that fatigue can play a role at every stage of a flight; including taxiing to park5) Use my own judgment when given instructions that don't seem to be correct/ safe.

column121: While in cruise at FL400; I noticed cabin altitude display illuminate Amber on upper EICAS showing cabin altitude of 8300 feet and rising at 300-400 ft/min.  Aircraft was dispatched with one pack deferred; two operating. I brought up the ECS schematic to verify Packs 2 and 3 were both supplying pressure and in High Flow. They appeared to be operating normally; but I then noticed a Status message with a Pack 2 fault; cabin altitude was already 9;000 ft. and still climbing. At this point I requested a descent from ATC to FL 360.  They gave us a vector for descent.  A minute later; with Cabin altitude of 9300 ft.; I informed ATC we had a pressurization issue and needed to descend.  We were given FL390 and then a few minutes later; FL360.  Pressurization stabilized at 8;500 ft.; but began to climb again at 100-200 ft/min. We requested and were given FL 320.  I notified Operations Control via ACARS (SATCOM inop); that we had a Pack 2 issue and that we had descended as cabin altitude had been increasing. They were given our fuel and told I would keep them advised. We were at FL 280; where cabin altitude at stabilized; but showing slight increase. I recommended to divert to ZZZ along our route of flight; but they informed me they wanted the airplane in ZZZ1.  I informed ATC that we needed to change our destination for 'maintenance' from ZZZ2 to ZZZ1.  We were given proceed direct ZZZ1; about 350 miles away; where we landed uneventfully.Cruise flight when cabin altitude appeared amber on Upper EICAS.Strictly a maintenance issue with the aircraft. We had Pack 1 deferred and any issue with the remaining Packs was going to cause pressurization issues.To assess the situation; attempt to bring pressurization under control; and descend as necessary to reduce cabin altitude.  QRH was utilized to validate what pressurization reading we should have at the various altitudes.Aircraft was dispatched to pick up freight in ZZZ2; and then proceed with a Pack deferred.
column123: Pushback; taxi; takeoff and climb were completely normal. Weather on departure were calm winds and decent VFR in the terminal area. The weather became more marginal upon leveling at cruise. On this leg I myself was the First Officer and Flying Pilot. The Captain was the Pilot Not flying. We also had a Relief Pilot on board and loadmaster.  The event began somewhat early in cruise at FL400 when the Captain noticed a cabin altitude display Amber on the Upper EICAS display. He then immediately selected the ECS page and we both were made aware of a 8;300 foot cabin and rising at 300-400 fpm. The aircraft was dispatched with Pack #1 deferred; therefore packs 2 and 3 operating normally. After diagnosing the situation via the ECS page; both packs 2 and 3 appeared to be supplying pressure and in High Flow as designed when one pack is selected off.  However on the Lower EICAS we both noticed a Status message with a Pack 2 fault. Cabin altitude was still climbing and at this point showing 9;000 feet and still climbing. At this point we agreed to suggest a decent to FL360 and were given a vector for decent. About a minute later with Cabin Altitude of 9;300 feet the Captain informed ATC that we had a pressurization issue and needed to descend now; we first were given a decent to FL390 and shortly after to FL360. At FL360 we observed the cabin initially stabilizing at 8;500 feet; but shortly afterwards began again climbing at a lower rate than previously of 100-200 FPM.  We again agreed to request a lower altitude of FL320 and ATC cleared us to FL320. The Captain then notified Operations Control of the situation via ACARS (SATCOM Inop) that we had a PACK 2 issue and we were descending with a cabin altitude still slowly increasing. The Captain requested further decent to FL280 and ATC complied. At FL280 we experienced a cabin altitude almost stable at around 8;000 feet but still trying to climb at a slow interment 100 FPM. The Captain notified the rest of the crew including the Relief Pilot and load master. The Relief Pilot was taking his rest but immediately returned to the cockpit to help in CRM and dealing with the situation. I suggested the Relief Pilot pull up the cabin altitude chart showing what the cabin altitude should be for our current altitude so we would know how far off from normal we were.  All 3 crew members talked about possible diversion airports and relayed our ideas to Operations Control. After communication between Operations Control and us it was decided by Operations Control to divert to ZZZ2 to address and fix the situation. The Captain immediately requested to divert to ZZZ2 and informed ATC as to why; and I put us on a course to ZZZ2 via ATC instructions. At this point we were about 350 miles north of ZZZ2 with plenty of fuel and sufficient weather for landing. We landed at ZZZ2 uneventfully and maintenance was made aware of the present maintenance issues.While in cruise flight the cabin altitude appeared amber on the Upper EICAS.Pack 2 was failing for unknown reasons. Pack 1 was already deferred on departure so any remaining pack issues was going to cause a pressurization issue.Crew did their job in noticing the system fault and working the problem. We were dispatched with Pack 1 deferred so any further pack or pressurization faults would cause a pressurization issue.Dispatching an aircraft with a pack deferred which would and did cause a pressurization issue when any further pressurization problems would happen. In this case pack 2 also failing to perform up to specification; therefore; causing an increasing cabin altitude at a higher level cruising altitude.

column121: I am reporting an unsafe situation we as an aircrew encountered on the flight back from ZZZ to ZZZ1.We had an APU failure and lost at least one of our packs; so we had no air conditioning inflight and the temps in the cabin became dangerously high; I knew once we got off the ground and we were climbing out that the situation was going sideways; so I formulated a game plan and as soon as we reached altitude instead of using the cart I just pulled every tray of water I had on the plane; it was at that point Flight Attendant who was deadheading on the flight immediately came to the galley and introduced herself and asked what she could do to assist me and I just told her jump in and start handing out water and asked her to make ice packs for 2 moms that were on board.One was an expecting mom around and her husband were seated in X12 and an infant and mom in Y3 the expecting mom became pale and very hot and I was really concerned for her and her unborn child's safety and the infant and mom in 6 were red and very warm.What little bit of ice we had that hadn't melted we fashioned ice packs after emptying the Purell packets out of the zip lock bags they were in for both moms and we together pulled every bottle of water we had on board passed them throughout the cabin until we ran out; our flight crew were miserable as well as the flight became very unbearable.At one point I became so dehydrated NAME sat me in my jump seat and handed me one of the large bottles of water we had left onboard and made sure I was hydrated while she attended to pax needs and then I swapped out with her so she could hydrate as well. The teamwork was amazing and I am so grateful to have had her assistance.We kept everyone calm and hydrated as best we could until we got on the ground in ZZZ1; while I was tending to landing prep Flight Attendant deadheading went ahead and filed her report inflight for me so I could tend to the pax.Together we were able to keep both moms and their babies born and unborn safe the flight deck was very concerned and called me to ask if we needed medical personnel to meet us at the gate but I told them no that everything fine but if the situation changed I would advise as soon as possible.In closing the conditions onboard when we lost the pack was dangerously hot and it was definitely a test of my training but like I said as soon as so realized we had a problem I already had a plan in place to deal with it.

column121: On final approach to Runway 13 into MDT; we were cleared to intercept the visual final approach course. Due to the haze and unfamiliarity on the airports on separate sides of the river; we mistook CXY Runway 12 for MDT Runway 13. We had the GPS 13 approach loaded for reference due to the ILS 13 being out; but prior to turning inbound on the final we were given a vector for the intercept final approach course. I mistook the Capital City airport (CXY) Runway 12 for MDTs Runway 13. We were asked if we had MDT in sight; thinking we did; and cleared for a visual approach; I made a descent for CXY Runway 12; still not realizing it was not MDT Runway 13. MDT Tower asked then told us we were aligned with CXY and gave a low altitude warning. I immediately added power and climbed. I then aligned with Runway 13 at MDT and landed.
column123: We were approaching Harrisburg Int'l from the west when we were instructed to intercept the final course for a visual approach to RWY 13. It was hazy with visibility low enough that the only airport in sight was Capital City (CXY).  Its RWY 12 is oriented similarly to RW 13 at MDT; so when we were asked if we had the airport in sight; we said we did.  The airport was closer by a few miles than our FMS was indicating so we configured for landing and steepened the approach. MDT Tower then asked if we could be approaching Capital City as we were lower than we should've been. At that point; MDT was also visible. The pilot flying applied power and climbed enough to conduct a normal approach to RWY 13.The haze contributed; as did the vector for a visual.  Interestingly; the proximity of these two airports is compounded by the fact that the airport on the south side of the river (CXY) is actually north of MDT; which is on the north side of the river due to bends in the river.We could've avoided the error if we'd been more familiar with the area and/or declined the visual approach.

column121: I began instructing a student pilot for their private pilot certificate under Part 61. This student had been with 2 other instructors before coming to me. The first instructor he was with was from April to December 20XX and had flown 24 hours dual. The second instructor was from February 20XX to November 20XX and had dual of 50 hours and 3 solo flights; one in June; July and November of 20XX. As I began instructing this student; he had 74 hours total time and had soloed. I asked him if he had his student pilot certificate and medical; and his answer was yes. I did not do my due diligence and physically look at those 2 documents because I assumed with 2 previous instructors; 74 hours and solo flights; he had them. That was 100% my error. I paid more attention to verifying he was a US citizen and getting that endorsement in both our logbooks; then giving the proper consideration to the other documents. I realized this on May XX; 2021 as I was thinking it is time to start prepping for a potential check ride in the next couple months. I asked him to provide a copy of those documents to me; and that is when I realized he did not have the appropriate FAA issued student pilot certificate. He had his medical and he had another form; FAA Form 8500-8; Medical Certificate Third Class And Student Pilot Certificate. His medical examiner told him that Form 8500-8 was his student pilot certificate. Therefore; my student believed he had the proper student certificate; and that is why he told me he had both documents. As soon as I realized that this was not correct; I immediately called him to confirm it and advised him as to what must be done to get the correct FAA student pilot certificate. We met the next evening; June XX; 2021 and completed the application. I told him he could not solo until he received his temporary certificate. His temporary was issued on June XY; 2021. This student had 15.7 hours of solo time up to this point; which will not be counted as his solo requirements. He will complete all the solo time requirements after the issue date of June XY; 2021. As for myself; I learned a valuable lesson; never assume a student has the proper paperwork; regardless of the number of instructors or previous flight hours. I will always do my due diligence; and never assume anything moving forward. Moreover; I feel ashamed and embarrassed that as a professional CFI; this situation occurred.

column121: I have departed ZZZ airport to the south to practice landings in ZZZ1. On the way back to ZZZ I have contacted ZZZ Tower around 7NM to 8 NM south of the field; the Tower has replied standby so I have tuned to easterly heading so I will not enter the airspace; a few minutes after that the Tower has instructed me to join mid left downwind for Runway XX and to report when established on the downwind; after I have established on the downwind I have notified the Tower. To the best of my knowledge and memory the Tower has replied the following instruction: 'you are number 3 for Runway XX continue'; I have given the Tower read back and then I looked forward to visually scan for the traffic in front of me; I remember clearly that I saw 2 aircraft in the final for Runway XX; the first one was an airplane in the short final and the second one was a helicopter that was also in the final behind him. I remember that I have pointed the 2 aircraft to my students and explained to them that these are the aircraft that are in front of us and we will follow them as we are number 3 in the sequence. After the helicopter was abeam to my position; I continued to fly on the downwind for an extra 30 seconds to 1 minute so I will allow some extra spacing between myself and the helicopter as I'm flying with students on their first ever fly day. As I was told I'm number 3 in sequence and I visually saw the 2 aircraft that are in front of me I have continued the traffic pattern and turn left to the base leg; and then when I was in the appropriate position I have turned final. Between 30 seconds to 1 minute after I was established on the final for XX the Tower has instructed me to 'immediately turn heading 090 and break the approach'; I have immediately took controls from my student and turned to the heading 090 while giving a read back to the Tower. As I have established on the heading 090 I saw that there was a jet aircraft on the final approach behind me; approximately 1;200 feet horizontally and 300 feet vertically in my evaluation. after that I have continued to comply with the Tower instructions and followed a different traffic that was on the downwind to join the final for Runway XX again for a full stop. Before landing when I was on short final I have verified with the Tower that I had clearance to land.I have strong belief in self critic and self evaluation and after this event has occurred I have come up with the following safety measures that can help prevent this situation from reoccurring:1. When you have been instructed to follow traffic while on the downwind; you should always verify with Tower that you can start your turn towards the base leg.2. When you are told that you are number 3 in sequence and you see the 2 aircraft in front of you; that absolutely does not mean that you should stop looking for other traffic in the area; you still need scan for traffic very frequently.3. When flying on the base leg; even in a controlled airport; you should always try to look for more traffic coming on the final; both behind you and in front of you; and make sure that there is no traffic that can jeopardize the approach before actually making the turn to final.4. Do not think that just because you are flying in a controlled airspace under ATC supervision; you are protected. Always actively scan for traffic and verify ATC instructions.I believe that if I had used these safety measures that I have mentioned above this event could have been prevented. I am glad no damage has been done in this event; and I'm committed to learn from this experience and actively seek to improve myself as a pilot and as flight instructor.

column121: I was working a sector with weather building. The warning areas were hot with numerous aircraft deviating into active military airspace. I was unaware at the time that the only plan was to depend on the military to take point-outs to work aircraft through that area. With no notice the adjacent sector said I can't take anymore northbound aircraft because the controlling facility will not take point-outs. At the time I had several aircraft within minutes of their airspace that required 90 degree turns to miss the sectors airspace. I had to reroute almost every aircraft on my frequency. This reroute put aircraft into weather and overloaded the next receiving sector. This last-minute major increase in workload resulting in Aircraft X not being issued weather. The aircraft flew through moderate to heavy precipitation and encountered severe turbulence which resulted in two passenger injuries.I have NO recommendations this will absolutely happen again. For the years I have been at ZJX; aircraft deviating into active military airspace is normal operations. Look at my previous reports and my co-workers in other areas. Numerous conditions happen in ZJX south area to overload the sectors that cause weather not to be called. After this incident I returned to the south area to see this exact scenario unfolding again. An air carrier flight was in active military airspace [requesting priority]. The only reason this is even being discussed is because a passenger was injured on Aircraft X. If an injury would not have occurred nobody would have investigated what was going on in the ZJX south area. This has been going on for years in the south area with numerous reports. Nothing will change and this will happen again.

column121: Event occurred during descent phase. Captain was the pilot monitoring; First Officer (F/O) was the pilot flying. Aircraft had sat for several days down for maintenance. [The maintenance airport] experienced heavy rainfall for an extended period prior to flight. Flight was uneventful until the descent phase of flight. At approximately FL220; the radar showed 'Weather (WX) FAIL' accompanied by a grinding noise; as if the radar was stuck on one side of the sweep. Radar was secured. At approximately 15;000 MSL and 325 knots in the descent; an additional loud bang and excessive airflow noise occurred; accompanied by multiple EICAS messages; including 'IAS DISAGREE.' Captain's side display was showing approximately 250 knots. F/O's side display was showing approximately 330 knots; which agreed with standby instrumentation. F/O called for 'AIRSPEED UNRELIABLE' checklist. The autopilot and autothrottles (A/T) were disengaged; and the A/T ARM switch was turned off. F/O continued flying manually throughout the remainder of the flight. Captain elected to leave the Flight Directors on; as the lateral guidance was still valid; we were VMC; and at that range we already had the field in sight. It was agreed that the F/O would disregard the pitch guidance until the instrumentation issue could be corrected. Captain continued running through the checklist from the QRH; it was determined that the F/O's instrumentation was valid; and the Captain selected the right side Air Data Compute (ADC). From that point forward; as we slowed to 250 knots; the airplane essentially flew normally. F/O continued to manually hand fly the descent and approach to an uneventful landing. After inspection; the aircraft was taxied back normally. On post-flight inspection; the radome had a large structural failure; which likely caused an asymmetric airflow disruption which affected the Captain's instrumentation.

column121: Taxi clearance: taxi from ramp position XX;  right turn onto W3; left turn EW; right turn S7A; then S7; hold short S7C.    As a crew; we were a little bit tired from our 1st leg in the middle of the night; our scheduled ground stop time plus the delay as maintenance took care of a Pressure Regulating Valve issue.    In any case; if you take a look at the VVNB Airport Moving Map (AMM) taxi chart; it appears as though EW is a separate taxiway. The color differentiation of light gray versus the ramp coloration of dark gray gives the impression we would be taxiing from the ramp onto a separate; defined taxiway; not onto a yellow line that is at the outer edge of a parking ramp. In addition; S1 (the taxiway that is adjacent and parallel to EW) had green lights illuminated; again giving the impression S1 was the active taxiway EW. So as we taxied via W3; EW looks like it's part of the ramp. In other words it does not appear to be EW taxiway. S1 appears to be EW. The poor signage does not help as well. Clearly the main issue here is that we had never been to Hanoi and never experienced this. That said; as we taxied out and entered S6A; the intersection between EW and S1; my copilot notified me we had passed EW. We stopped there. We advise ground we missed EW and needed to take S1. Ground control gave us S1; routed us back onto EW; then S7A; S7 and then our takeoff. That said; no conflict with any traffic; only one maybe two other aircraft moving on the airport at that time. Ultimately it was a non critical event.    To help prevent this from happening in the future; a caution note regarding taxiing at any time (i.e. taxing in or taxing out) when given EW would be helpful.
column123: After setting up the cockpit for the ZZZZ1-ZZZZ leg; we sat in the back to rest while Maintenance was working with an MEL item.  The aircraft was one hour later than schedule to allow extra time for maintenance.  Fatigue was now starting to show after two 18-24hr overnights in lockdown.    After final setup and brief; we received our taxi clearance; from spot XX; E3.EW.S7A.S7.S7C hold short [Runway] 11L.  We discussed the route that appeared clearly marked on the Airport Moving Map (AMM) page and began taxiing.  We realized we had crossed beyond the centerline of EW and were unable to make the turn and stopped.  After calling the controller of our position; he gave us S1.S6A.EW....the rest was normal.    Looking back; the green taxi lights were lit on S1.S6A.EW and FD Pro AMM page in dark mode makes EW look very different from the ramp area.  Expectation bias may have played a role in how controllers have started using follow the greens (used in SIN but not in HAN) and what we interpret as a clearance.  I will personally pay closer attention to where we are in the future.

column121: The crew flew the RNAV X RWY to 34R at RNO in day clear weather with winds reported at 260/26G31. During the flare; the crew executed a go around due to a strong gust destabilizing the approach. During climb out; the Tower Controller called the winds stronger out of the West and suggested a visual approach to Runway 25. Although having reviewed the 10-7 Special Considerations page earlier in the flight; the crew did not recall the takeoff and landing restriction on Runway 25.The crew configured for a 5 mile visual approach to Runway 25; then briefed and commenced the approached. Descending on the approach with the terrain visible and safely below the aircraft; it became apparent that the terrain east of the airport would not allow a safe approach. At approximately the same time; our descent rate in combination with the terrain resulted in a brief 'Terrain' warning; the pilot flying adjusted the aircraft flight path and then executed a go-around. The crew then flew and landed from the RNAV X to RWY 34R. I believe rushing and a false sense of familiarity with the airport led to an incomplete recognition of all the information in the 10-7 pages. I have operated into RNO regularly but not often and always to light winds down the primary runway. Arrivals and approaches are briefed extensively and flown according to standards. The day of the event; we conducted a thorough briefing for the approach; to include reviewing the operating manual about the exact procedures for executing the EO (Engine out) SIDs at RNO and which RNAV approaches we were authorized to fly.Despite my review; to include Special Considerations/Restrictions; I did not refresh the [Runway] 7/25 restriction in my mind and in the moment I did not recall the critical restriction. Additionally at the time; I did not feel like we rushed the visual approach. However; I now realize that I was focused too much on flying a stable visual approach and landing into the wind and not taking the time to truly review the approach and missed approach. Take the time to thoroughly familiarize yourself with all the applicable notes during your airport review and briefings.
column123: RNAV X 34R to RNO in day VMC; reported winds were very close to limits (260/26 G31). Due to an extremely strong gust which destabilized our approach we executed a go around. After max effort go around and stabilized climbing clean; Tower suggested we use Runway 25. Even though we had both reviewed the 10-7 pages earlier in the flight; at that particular moment we did not recall the prohibition to landing on that Runway. After agreeing that we would look at it; I as Pilot Monitoring set up the box for a visual by extending a 3 degree GS to an extended 5 mile Center Line to give us VTI.The Pilot Flying double checked the 10-9A page and the landing app. While still considering this option; we maneuvered towards the extended Center Line and set and then descended to an altitude above the depicted altitude in that area. Our rate of descent combined with rising terrain triggered the EPGWS (Ground Proximity Warning System) to a 'TERRAIN' call. The Pilot Flying immediately altered his flight path and the terrain remained visible and well below us. It became abundantly clear that a stable approach would not be possible and we abandoned this option. We opted for another attempt at the RNAV 34R; and despite strong gusty crosswinds were able to maintain a stable condition to touchdown and landing.Things I have taken away from this event: The winds Tower reports may not be the winds you experience at the Runway. By sticking to a ridged stable approach and associated Standard Operating Procedure's mantra we kept from bending metal; violating a FAR; exceeding a limit or attempting something really stupid. And although RNO is a complex city and we review the notes every time we go there; the [Runway] 25 note was momentarily forgotten. We reviewed the 10-9a pages but somehow forgot to review the 10-7 pages in that situation. A mistake I (or my First Officer) will never make again.I firmly believe that this is a onetime incident. A few moments either way and we would have missed the gust and landed uneventfully. And I have a hard time imagining that another crew; or me again; would ever forget the 10-7 notes in a complex city. But again thanks to our training department's dogma regarding stable approaches; we are self-reporting not something far worse.

column121: I was the Relief First Officer sitting in the right aft seat with a very limited view of the PFD;s and MFD;s of the aircraft. Shanghai Approach Control issued us a different arrival than what the company had filed and what we already had planned. The communications were ambiguous at best and we all agreed to get a clarification on which arrival was being issued. There were four arrivals that had the suffix '81A'.  The pronunciation was tough to understand.  It took some clarification but we all confirmed the new arrival as the 'DUM 81A' arrival. At some point after DUMET there was a transmission from Shanghai Approach to 'comply with all restrictions' At the same time the PF was slowing down and trying to get down with deploying the speed brakes to meet the restrictions of PD230.  Shanghai approach made the same transmission again. I unbuckled my seat belt to stand up see what the displays were showing and wanted to confirm the altitude in the alt window was correct. It was set correctly to 6;980 feet which was equivalent to 2;100 meters issued to us. The aircraft showed a little high on the path but was correcting and it showed very close to the speed restriction of 230 kts.  I sat back down and verified the restrictions on my tablet. There was a lot of foreign language chatter on the radio. Upon crossing the fix; Shanghai issued a clearance direct to MPI which was the IAF for the approach to [Runway] 16L.  It wasn't until after we landed that the PF and PM were talking about being high over the PD230 fix however they agreed they were on speed.Understanding which arrival they were trying to issue took more time than necessary.  The pronunciation of the arrival was very hard to understand. This complicated things more than usual and it cost time. The frequency congestion in a foreign language complicated things when trying to get them to repeat the clearance.  On a side note this was the first time I've ever heard an approach clearance to a runway with a Left designator as 'Cleared for 16 Lima' ...the PM was corrected to say 16 Lima after she responded with 16 Left.  it didn't make sense.  When passed on to the Tower Controller; they correctly said 16 Left.My only suggestion is if you look high on a path; Flight Level Change works pretty good to hustle down to the altitude.  I can't say for sure if this descent was done in PATH or FLC.  The language barrier is what it is and probably won't change much.

During this time; we noticed the ammeter showing a very high charge.A pilot on the CTAF asked if we intended to stay in the pattern and I reported our problem. They offered assistance; so I turned back to the airport and asked if anyone could visually check our nose gear. A pilot on the ground at midfield confirmed our nose gear was down during a low approach. With this information; I decided to return to ZZZ; where the aircraft is based; about 30 miles away.I initially planned to [advise ATC] at ZZZ.I called ZZZ Tower 20 miles out and explained the situation; and my concern that the nose gear was not locked; even though it was down. The Tower asked if we would like to do a flyby of the Tower for them to check the gear; which I accepted. The Tower asked for fuel amount and time; and passengers; to which I replied we had 60 gallons and plenty of time; 2 souls.We did a low approach over [Runway] XXR; and the Tower confirmed that the gear was down and locked. They asked if we would prefer to land on the north runway; which was the active runway. I said yes and planned a soft field landing to [Runway] XXL. Since the gear was locked and I was being given priority and any resources I needed; I amended my decision to [advise ATC]; as I felt it would not get me anything else I might need to land safely that I wasn't already being provided.My passenger pointed out that the gear pump circuit breaker was popped. She tried pushing it in; which caused the ammeter to spike; so we pulled it out and left it out.The Tower asked if I wanted additional resources waiting on the ground. I decided no additional resources were needed; and proceeded to land using soft field technique; holding the nose gear off for most of the ground roll. Tower again confirmed nose gear was locked and I made a sharp turn to exit the runway once I confirmed steering was good.I was cleared to taxi to the plane's flight school where an airport ground personnel met me to get a report. He then asked us to call the Tower; which also asked for a report detailing my route of flight.After the plane was repaired; Maintenance reported that the gear switch actuator was replaced; but I never got an explanation for the gear pump electrical problem.

column121: We were climbing out on the SID when we realized that our onboard weather (WX) Radar might be inoperative (INOP).  Just then; ATC asked us if we would like to deviate left or right around WX.  We asked if we could stay on our present heading (HDG) 325; which was a left deviation; and that our radar might be INOP.  He cleared us to continue; and advise. Unbeknownst to us are present HDG would take us direct to ZZZ.  The importance of that will be apparent; shortly.I transferred control to the First Officer (FO) and began to troubleshoot the problem.  Finding no approved procedure I contacted Dispatch. They advised that if we cannot continue to ZZZ1; we should consider a divert to ZZZ.  I determined distance; checked WX; and did a non-standard landing assessment.  All were satisfactory; we would be under maximum landing weight (MAX LDG WGT) and outside visual reference showed no convective activity ahead; to the horizon.  I notified dispatch that we agreed. Dispatch amended our release for diversion to ZZZ and we informed ATC. At this point we were approximately 94 nautical miles from ZZZ. I asked the FO to handle the radio while I briefed the Flight attendants (FA's) and the passengers (PAX). I briefed the FA's that we were diverting for INOP WX radar and that it would be a 'Precautionary landing'. The FO was already given a routing to ZZZ so I had an accurate arrival time. Next; I briefed the PAX and I sent the diversion report to dispatch.After; completing my briefings I rejoined the FO and he briefed me; that we were cleared direct to STAR and descending to 24000. We were told to contact ZZZ approach.  I informed them of our situation and notified ATC.  We completed the arrival briefing and accomplished the Descent Checklist.  I called ZZZ operations to verify that they had been informed of our arrival and reconfirm our gate assignment.  I asked them to send a Customer Service Manager to help with the PAX.  We landed and taxied to the gate without further incident. Roughly two hours later we departed for ZZZ1 and landed there; also without further incident.The reasons for submitting this report are as follows.                                                 1.  To voluntarily share the details of our event so that the program can glean important data; and use it to remedy any deficiencies or discrepancies discovered.2.  To afford me the protections guaranteed by the program; should; during the course of it's review; company discover that any actions or omissions on my part; though inadvertent and unintentional be determined to be in violation of applicable FARs or company policies.

column121: At approximately XA:30 hours; just moments prior to boarding; I smelled a very strong; musty; wet dog like odor inside the cabin. As I walked back towards the AFT galley (at approximately mid-cabin); the odor became much stronger. I immediately called out to the lead F/A and asked her to come back to observe what I was smelling. [Lead F/A] stated she could also smell the odor. Accordingly; I immediately made my way to the cockpit. The odor became so strong that my throat started to burn; and I began coughing. I told the Captain that we were being fumed and that I was going to notify the boarding agent to immediately stop boarding in order to prevent further issues (i.e. passenger exposure.) The Captain stated that he was notifying maintenance and agreed to hold boarding. I left the aircraft (no passengers were onboard). While making my way up the jet bridge to notify the agent; customers were beginning to walk down the jet bridge since boarding had commenced. I was able to stop the passengers and advised them to stop; turn around and go back into the terminal since we were having maintenance come to the aircraft. I did not advise them why. I entered into the terminal and advised the agent in a discreet manner to stop boarding as we were experiencing an aircraft fume event. I then returned to the aircraft briefly to advise the Captain that the agent was notified. The crew exited the aircraft and we remained in the jet bridge area for a few moments until maintenance arrived. We collected our belongings and exited the jet bridge into the terminal to gain better air quality. I continued to experience a burning throat and my cough continued. At that time; it was prudent to seek medical attention; therefore; I contacted Medical to seek advisement. I was given a clinic appointment at [medical name] and was seen by a doctor accordingly.Improper aircraft maintenance was the cause.Recommendations  - Contacting numerous departments; is too much following an incident like this. One call should automatically provide the needed support; guidance and direction that we require during events like this. Because this is my 3rd fume event; I was able to more quickly identify the inherent risks; take appropriate action to limit passenger exposure; and limit extended exposure; however; it was still medically concerning and we should have less calls to make following these dangerous occurrences.
column123: During the preflight the ground air was not sufficient to cool the aircraft.  I had the ground crew turn off the ground air and the CA started the APU. No passengers were on board yet.  A FA came up to the flight deck saying he noticed a smell.  At the point I radioed maintenance about the problem and we all exited the aircraft.  A few minutes later the maintenance staff said they could smell the problem in the jetway.  The whole crew then started the Fume Event process.  We were all checked out at the on airport [company name] clinic.  Reporter stated the cause was Aircraft XXX [which] is a known Fume Event multiple offender.  I remember from my walk around that the belly of the aircraft had a high amount of oil streaks.  When was this last belly washed?   Airbus knows this is a problem and does not take it seriously.  Reporter suggested company take known Fume Event aircraft out of service.  Use them for parts; excluding the APU.  Put filters like [other air carriers] has to protect crews and passengers. I shut the display down to start the engines and forgot the flight plan would drop out and need to be reloaded. Mistake number four. So; no initial heading information was available. at that point I tried to retrieve my pen to get the clearance. while my head was down in the floor I climbed to around 1;500 feet. 300 feet inside class C airspace. Mistake number five. I called ZZZ for clearance and was instructed to remain clear of Class C. Due to the partial disorientation of not having a route; I wasn't sure whether I was in it or not. to be safe I descended to 1000 feet and reloaded the flight plan. The point here is after a series of mistakes I ended up with an airspace deviation. How could it have turned out differently? I could have used the autopilot. I could have used my spare pen. I still could have departed [Runway] XY after the jet departed [Runway] XX. I should have checked that my flight plan was still in the aircraft's computer.

column121: We were enroute back to home base in early evening on after dropping passengers.  Two Crew were onboard.  First indication of any concern was a 'Chip Detect' annunciation.  Following the checklist all oil temps and pressures were noted and observed normal.  While in cruise we began noting very small needle deflections in the oil pressure and the real likelihood that the left engine was in distress.  Following the checklist we began a decent to single engine altitude and prepared for an engine shut down.  Within short time of this action the engine began to loose power and fail. Engine securing procedures were followed using the checklist ATC was advised.  We were still at higher altitude over and passing ZZZ [Airport] so several options were available as far as final landing destination.  Given the current state of runways at home (Only +/-3900ft available per NOTAM) and lack of any onsite support service that might be needed we decided to reverse course and divert to ZZZ; without further incident we landed safely.

Approaching the five mile call; crew noticed Aircraft Y coming from the right to left directly in front of crewed aircraft. Crew was getting ready to call the five mile distance; but instead crew executed an immediate left turn to avoid a collision and notified the tower of the situation. Crew continued left turn per tower instructions and climbed to 2;000 feet. Crew was advised to fly back towards the runway at 2;000 feet and contact Departure Control. Departure Control gave crewed aircraft vectors for right downwind and crew conducted an uneventful landing at TME. Crew was advised by tower personnel on the ground that there is no radar at the field and they depend on position reports. Crew was approaching the five mile call when they noticed Aircraft Y cut in front of the crewed aircraft. Crew asked the tower personnel if the Tower knew the aircraft was inbound then why did they not inquire the position of our aircraft before they turned Aircraft Y.

column121: I; RPIC; was tasked with conducting cell tower inspections in the greater pacific northwest area for the drone company. I was using a drone that had known issues with camera gimbal yet with no other options or support from the company; I had to continue to fly with this drone. This drone was known for its gimbal locking and or becoming unresponsive to the drone's heading when flown. Problems with this drone were brought to my attention by my flight trainer prior to me taking over the drone; and I had also informed my mission coordinator of the problems with the gimbal after I had taken over the drone to continue the operation. Upon take off; I encountered the gimbal lock again. Before I could land and calibrate the gimbal; a substantial gust overcame my area of operation from the West/Southwest. As a reactionary response; I pushed the right stick forward (into the Southern Direction) to send the drone away from the traffic behind me; to the North. The gusts appeared to be above the operational limits of the drone and I adjusted the right and left stick to aim into the wind. I looked back up in the air to find the drone to evaluate if it was safe to do an emergency landing into the grand land; or to find a safe descend path. With the gimbal unresponsive to the drone's heading; I was unable to correctly judge the drone's flight path which was directly into an oncoming tree. This tree was outside my operational area; and therefore was above my MOCA (Minimum Obstacle Clearance Avoidance). It was not my intent to fly beyond my operational area; but as an inadvertent contingency for safety of those on the road; the safest area for an emergency landing was beyond the grounds of the tower. My thought was that the grass seed would have been a suitable/softer area to land; versus the hard gravel of the maintenance road; or induce the hazardous possibility of a highway incursion with highway traffic. The justification for my flight response is that by flying towards the grass seed land; I would have absolutely mitigated the risk of causing serious injury or death; and or substantial damage by causing an aviation accident with the highway or any case that could have been defined by the 49 CFR 830. By the time I reacted to the tree being in frame of my camera; my counter maneuvers did not prevent the drone from colliding with the tree. The anti-collision sensors of the drone also did not prevent the drone from colliding with the tree. The drone has and always was in Position Hold mode and was not deviated from. Even with the wind gusts pushing the drone to its limit; the anti-collision sensors should have detected the tree and stopped the aircraft from colliding with the tree or at least assisted my counter maneuvers in preventing the accident. In response to the weather; my anemometer was reading 2-9 mph on the ground. This wave of gusts was unexpected and arbitrary to the regular wind speeds I had been enduring for the entire site audit. To the Southwest; I did notice very dark cumulonimbus clouds which may have been a severe thunderstorm forming; which may have caused instability upwind. I was able to find the drone near the tree in the grass seed bush. The camera has completely broken off; the landing gear had sustained fractures; the main profile has been disconnected; and one propeller was broken. This drone is not safe to fly in its current state and will need repair from manufacturer. In this flyaway accident; there was no serious injury; death; or substantial damage that occurred beyond the aircraft and the surrounding environment. I wanted to bring this accident to light because of the post crash situation. The drone was lost in grass seed bushes that were at least 4-5ft tall. I had to walk through the bush with my best guesses to where the drone was actually at. Since the drone battery had disconnected with the drone; I was not able to use the GPS homing software on the tablet to find where the drone was. After some timesearching; I eventually found the drone and the camera. But I have yet to find the battery. From my understanding of the DJI drones; if the battery is disconnected while it is in the 'on' mode; the battery will continue to discharge. After some time; the LiPO battery will eventual become depleted and not pose as a threat to the grass seed bushes. However; in any case that the battery should still pose a threat to the grass seed bushes; I think a contingency should be put in place with modern commercial drones that would benefit and promote safety in post crash events. My thought is that audible micro speakers could be places with the intelligent flight batteries that will sound an alarm if the battery is armed and not in a fixed / connected position with the aircraft. It is the same principles as black boxes for manned aviation. In this scenario; this battery is lost in some field of very high and very dense bush that does not allow me to find the battery without extra aid from more people; metal detectors; or other mechanical means of detection. But; that some chime or sound be presented by an improperly disengaged 'on' battery; I would have been able to find and locate nearly all components of the air craft swiftly and with haste. The fact that even with me scanning a 50ft radius of the crash site and I could not find the most critical and unsafe component to the drone raises the question of 'how can we improve post commercial drone crashes.' I think by having some alarm attached to the battery would aid in the post crash finding time and recovery. Even with the battery discharged; it may still pose a threat to the field; making it unsafe for its presence to be there. In theory; by attaching a speaker to the battery; you would add a safety system as another line of defense in protecting the crash scene environment from future substantial damages.  Contributing factors are company's lack of critical response for repairs or replacements of a commercial aircraft; extreme weather phenomena changes; hardware failure in the anti collision sensors; and hardware failure in the main visual optical sensor.

column121: After arrival landing Runway 19L we were given instructions to proceed eventually Taxiway C enroute to Gate X. After switching to Ramp Control; we were given instructions to enter Spot X to Gate X. However; there was an aircraft outbound toward Spot Y. Taxi light on; still moving; and uncertain clearance in my opinion between two large transport category aircraft if I continued. Ramp came up again to state go to Spot X and enter and 'You can't stop there.' Before I could speak to ramp on be radio suggestion allowing the outbound aircraft to taxi out our outbound Company aircraft just went for it; scooted over to Spot X and went left on C toward [Runway] 26R and begged forgiveness with Ground Control. This never should have been an issue. In every other city we would have been held short of the alley a minute or two; wait for outbound aircraft to clear the alley; then taxi to the gate. And there is even a parallel Taxiway B available if jamming up C at that point is so critical. We try to embrace Ramp Resource Management (RRM) as Pilots. Maybe LAS Ramp Control needs a tutorial on this. And perhaps include LAS ATC if the Ramp Controller is not authorized to hold an inbound aircraft on Taxiway C to allow an outbound to clear. Looks like barrier to Safety for the back C alley in LAS needs some fixing. LAS Ground and Ramp Control should be advised that holding an inbound aircraft for the back alley to allow for outbound aircraft to clear is by far the safer and most stress-free option and will only delay their taxi plan less than a minute.

column121: As this report is not timely; it is to the best of my recollection. Approach phase of the flight to DEN. Briefed and installed the SSKII 2 RNAV/ILS 16R. On arrival we a received multiple speed and heading changes but we were back on course and LNAV/VNAV path were engaged. At some point prior to CLIFF; for whatever reason ATC changed clearance to RNAV 16R for us and the Aircraft (AC) behind us. I was Pilot Not Flying (PNF) so I installed the approach/transition. The AC ahead of us was in sight and was on the arrival but still assigned the ILS 16R. The approach was verified by both the First Officer (FO) and myself. LNAV/VNAV were still engaged and the speed window was open as ATC had already been assigning speed changes. The FO located the Approach briefing guide for the RNAV/RNP approach and RNP values for the approach were line selected and installed. All altitudes for the approach were verified.  I made the comment that 'Since ATC has been messing with our speed so much; the speed window is already open'. So far the approach was flawless and the aircraft (AC) was on the vertical and lateral profile.Upon reaching CLIFF the AC began a descent as it should have. TDZ had been set and VNAV Path was engaged. As we approached CEPEE the MCP/FMA's had not changed SPD/LNAV/VNAV path were engaged. The magenta track depicted CLIFF;CEPEE;AAGEE;JABRO;JETSN; RW 16R; as it should. It was upon arrival at CEPEE that the event occurred. The AC continued to descend and VNAV path remained engaged. But; the AC continued to track straight ahead. CEPEE had not become active and the vector leg out of CLIFF was still engaged. I had been so concerned with the vertical profile that I failed to notice CEPEE was not active. Realizing what had happened I went to the FMC to LS AAGEE; but ATC noticed at the same time and assigned us either a 080 or 090 heading. ATC also canceled the RNAV approach clearance for the AC behind us. We landed without further issue. Once inside the terminal; still pissed that I allowed this to happen; I located the Captain of the AC that landed behind us to apologize. He informed us that ATC had mistakenly given him the # to call. I took the number (#) and called immediately. After a conversation with the supervisor I was informed that there was no safety issue; no loss of separation; and no need to file a report.Looking back; how this could have been avoided... first of all; I could have just said 'unable' when ATC switched us to the RNAV RNP 16R. Although not a big deal at the time...after flying all night; briefing and installing one arrival and approach then; at the last minute being reassigned to a RNAV/ RNP approach which requires lots of briefing and changes; and programming; was probably not the thing to do. What else could I have done...I allowed myself to get distracted. I should have continually monitored the lateral path to insure the AC was doing what we thought it was going to do. It was very clear and it was easy to look outside to follow traffic. It was also the FO's first Pilot Flying leg so there was instruction taking place and attention was diverting to multiple places.The FO did a great job when we were reassigned to the RNAV RNP Z 16R. He did not miss a checklist; procedure; or setting.I'm disgusted that I allowed this to happen. I am unfortunately or fortunately very familiar with the airspace and lateral/ vertical deviation issues in the area. I'm not the first and sure won't be the last; but I know what I will and won't do next time.
column123: During the SSKII 2 RNAV Arrival phase; we were advised by ATC to expect the ILS 16R approach. A few minutes prior to CLFFF; the last point on the SSKII 2 arrival; we were assigned the RNAV (RNP) Z R16R approach. We were on a northerly heading in HDG mode at this time for vectors for the previously expected ILS. The Captain; as Pilot Monitoring (PM); selected the correct RNAV Z 16R approach as well as the correct transition (CLFFF transition) in the FMC. I verified the selected approach and transition after he did so. I then set up the approach per all steps of the Approach Briefing Guide and briefed the approach. We were then given direct CLFFF and selected LNAV. We were cleared for the RNAV RNP Z R16R approach shortly before arriving at CLFFF. Upon arriving at CLFFF; I verified that the CLFFF waypoint sequenced in the FMC to ensure we were now on a published segment of the approach. I selected LNAV; VNAV; opened the speed window for the appropriate speed; requested the PM set touchdown zone elevation (which he did); and verified that the ENGAGED FMA's were in green LNAV and VPATH. The aircraft began a descent per the VPATH glide slope. I ran through the items again to verify that the approach was proceeding correctly. I verified again that the FMA's showed an engaged green LNAV and engaged green VPATH. The approach was proceeding as expected. At the CEPEE waypoint; the aircraft should have begun a right turn towards the AAGEE as part of the track towards the final approach point and final approach course. The aircraft did not turn and continued in a straight course after passing CEPEE. I immediately checked the FMA's again to ensure it did not revert to HDG mode. The FMA's were still in green; engaged LNAV and VPATH. The aircraft was also still in an expected VPATH descent to the TDZE. Within a few seconds; and before we could figure out why the aircraft did not turn; ATC called to cancel the RNAV approach and gave us a right turn for a visual approach to runway 16R and gave clearance for the visual approach. We proceeded uneventfully for the visual approach and landing. After arriving at the gate and leaving the aircraft; a pilot from another aircraft that was behind us during the arrival and approach advised us that he was mistakenly given a phone number by ATC to call regarding the RNAV Z 16R turning issue that we actually experienced. We got the phone number from him and the Captain called. The ATC supervisor said that no report would be required; there was no loss of separation; there was no safety issue; and how just wanted to know what happened. The Captain and I reviewed everything we did in setting up; preparing; and executing that approach and could not figure any reason why the aircraft did not initiate a turn at CEPEE and continued straight while engaged in LNAV with the proper approach waypoints; altitudes; and sequencing verified in the FMC.

column121: Flight was cleared for approach into Runway XX at ZZZ. After noticing the approach was too high; the flight crew executed a go-around and missed approach. The flight crew then tried to re-establish contact with ATC but was not successful. After reaching missed approach altitude the flight crew decided to turn and make left hand traffic for Runway XX; where we made a visual approach and landing while making position reports on the local CTAF frequency. After landing; it was realized that the flight crew could have potentially violated the proper missed approach procedure or additional approach clearances into ZZZ after not being able to contact ATC. After parking at gate; Captain called ATC via phone to cancel IFR.One possible cause could be the relatively rare experience of flying into an uncontrolled field at night and the procedures that are associated with that. There was also some confusion about the type of approach the flight was cleared to execute; in this case; RNAV or visual approach into Runway XX. We believed we were cleared for the visual approach. However; being unable to contact ATC added confusion and doubt to the situation after landing. Flight delays most likely added stress as well.The first suggestion for future experiences would be to be more mindful and diligent about confirming the type of approach we are cleared to execute. This would have clarified the proper procedure when executing a go-around. A second potential solution would have been to gain altitude in order to try and contact ATC. As for the approach; the flight crew could have requested vectors to leave and then rejoin the approach when the aircraft was at a more appropriate altitude before needing to execute the go-around.
column123: After executing the go around; [we] climbed to pattern altitude to make a left traffic pattern instead of executing the published missed approach. [We were] unable to re establish contact with ATC after the go around. [We] did a visual approach to a landing. Crew believed ATC cleared for visual approach; therefore not requiring the published missed approach. [We should] clarify approach clearance with ATC [next time].

column121: Upon accepting Aircraft X; the inbound Captain; told me details about an MEL for Bulk Fuel Temp. He stated that there was an associated CAS MISCOMP" (Crew Alerting System Miscomparison) status message and that this was relayed to him by the previous Captain. They had no issues on their flight. We accept aircraft and depart ZZZ1. Not long after reaching cruise about 60 miles SE of ZZZ we lost our left fuel tank quantity indication along with our total fuel quantity indication. I had also recently updated the fuel in the FMS after reaching cruise altitude. Due to the MEL; we had been monitoring the fuel system for any possible errors and we had additional fuel after reaching altitude than planned. Right before we lost our left fuel indication both tanks were even. We did not receive any cautions; nor any indication on the fuel EICAS page of a "Fuel Channel Fail" status or caution like you are supposed to. After approximately 3 minutes of no left tank fuel quantity indication; we referred to the QRH for "Fuel CH 1/2 FAIL" for guidance and equalized our fuel flow between engines. In this circumstance; in addition to another aspect of already have a MEL on the "BULK FUEL TEMP"; along with not receiving EICAS indications like the system is designed to; we decided to divert to ZZZ. At some point during the beginning half of our descent to ZZZ; our left fuel quantity indication came back but my decision to divert was already made. We didn't have any fuel indication for approximately 8-12 minutes. We followed all procedures as far as alerting Dispatch; Flight Attendant; ATC; made a PA to passengers; In range to the line; followed by below the line and ensured we would not be overweight. We did not declare an emergency at that time. Upon getting vectors to final approach for runway; we intercepted the localizer below the glide slope. Approx 7-8 mile final when I called for 'Gear Down; Flaps 30;' but the gear did not move. Shortly after we received a "GEAR DISAGREE" master warning. We were at approx 3;400 ft flying the glide slope and not yet past [the] FAF so instead of calling for a go around; I disconnected the autopilot and asked for delay vectors to troubleshoot. We received an altitude assignment of 3;000 ft; heading 190; which required a descent.We then ran the QRH for "GEAR DISAGREE"; and after multiple attempts using the gear handle we used the alternate gear extension as called for in the QRH. All three gear came down and were indicating green. At this point I let ATC know we were ready to return for landing and we requested priority and to have trucks ready just in case. We also followed procedures to inform company of the [situation] and informed the flight attendants (FAs) of new situation. We also told the FAs to perform a "BRACE" command just in case due to the QRH stating directional control on the runway might be difficult. We ran through all the proper procedures except for the Go Around checklist. Looking back; we should have even though we did not miss any items. At the time; I did not consider the vectors as a go around due to being 6 miles out and having to descend to the assigned altitude. Upon touchdown; we received a "STEERING INOP" caution and I noticed directional control required more rudder than normal. Runway XXL does not have any high speed exits so we stopped on the runway; coordinated with airport command; and waited for buses to deplane the passengers.We did not use a tug to be pulled off the runway because I was unsure if the alternate gear extension was applying pressure to the nosewheel similar to nosewheel steering. I talked to Maintenance and they were also unsure. We did our best to keep the passengers up to date while waiting for the buses to deplane the passengers. We did not evacuate as there was no imminent danger after landing and the runway being closed. Unrelated to the gear; I should not have assumed and trusted another persons word that a CAS MISCOMP (Crew Alerting System Miscomparison) status message was in association to an MEL without verify the MEL procedure; and not just reviewing the MEL. We should have written that up at the gate in ZZZ1 although it may be completely unassociated to all our issues. I should have called for the go-around checklist to reconfirm we completed all the items even though we did not do a go-around maneuver."

column121: I was given clearance to depart RWY XXL in ZZZ. Up through that point everything went okay. I had no issues with Preflight; Engine start; Taxi etc. After taking off; rotating; and pulling the gear handle up with a positive rate of climb; I was awaiting all the proper lights to extinguish. All lights did extinguish; except the NOSE gear light. I do not recall hearing or feeling the normal audible 'thump'. Although these things happened while I was communicating with Tower on Frequency 1; I was transferred over to Departure on Frequency 2 and waited until I was with Departure to state that I had an issue with the landing gear. I recognized the issue almost simultaneously with the transfer and instinctively pressed the annunciator light check button to see if all the proper lights came on; and they did. The first Departure Controller sounded female. She asked what I wanted to do; what I recall saying is that I thought I might have to return to the airport and requested extended vectors so I could run my checklists. She leveled me off at 2;000 MSL. I believe once leveled off she asked me if it were an emergency; and I said not yet; but not completely sure. I grabbed the company QRH while climbing and started reading the Abnormal Landing Gear Will Not Retract Hydraulically checklist. After level at 2;000 [feet] and configured for cruise; I read the note and checklist; then fully cycled the gear once. When I put the gear handle in the down position; I watched all the proper lights illuminate; until everything indicated fully down and locked. When I retracted the gear; I watched all the proper lights illuminate; but continued to receive the initial result. The NOSE light remained illuminated; while all the other lights were extinguished. At this point; I knew I could not proceed over water to another destination. I let Departure know I would definitely need to return to the airport. She asked if I was [advising]; and initially I said no; because it was an abnormal checklist; but then said yes because it was the NOSE wheel and I was afraid of a possible tip over and prop strike. At this point I didn't know if I could trust the gear being up or down. Since the checklist flowchart answer was YES; I immediately moved to Abnormal Landing Gear Down and Locked Light Illuminated with the Gear Switch Up and HYD PRESS Light Out checklist as it instructed. I read the complete checklist and slowed down to 120 KIAS; to meet the 130 KIAS requirement; put the gear handle in the down position; and pulled the HYD circuit breaker. Departure checked on me to see how I was doing; and asked me to tell her when I wanted to turn back. I was still running checklist and said OK. Once I completed all steps; I read the Abnormal [checklist] Landing with Defective Nose Gear asked to return to the airport; as the checklist instructed. I let Departure know I was ready to return; she asked which way I wanted to turn. I requested turns to the right. She asked me which runway would I like to use and I said [Runway] XXR. She asked if I was sure; so I changed to [Runway] XXL since it was longer; but had already started vectoring right. She asked me what happened. I said the landing gear light remained illuminated after takeoff. I cycled the gear to see if it would go out and it didn't; I went through my checklists and now I was flying at 120 KIAS to keep from damaging the gear. She clarified by asking something like 'so one of the landing gears would not go up; right?' and I confirmed that and said I could no longer trust the lighted indication; so I pulled the emergency gear down. After a few moments of silence; a different Departure controller came on. This controller sounded male. The rest of them from now until I safely parked did. At this time; I was flying a downwind direction and I prepared for the approach to Runway XXL. Departure stated that he would have me turn base XX miles away. I set up the GPS and briefed the approach plate for RNAV XXL. Once done; I kept reading the checklist to ensure I was clear on what to do and when. All other aircraft landings and departures were continuing on XXR. I was vectored to final for XXL somewhere prior to the FAF approach; and asked to intercept the LOC for XXL; but since I'd selected the RNAV XXL and briefed that approach already; and it was VMC; I didn't change my configuration to the ILS to keep from becoming task saturated prior to an [urgent] landing. I was switched to Tower; who notified me of traffic landing on XXR and cleared me to land. I turned off all switches except mags; flared and landed with the nose wheel kept high; then turned off mixtures and mags. Everything seemed to be done safely with no issues. When the nose wheel came down; it was slowly; gently and the plane remained upright. On the rollout; at about taxi speed; I turned on the battery and avionics (only) to speak to ATC; and stated that I had left over momentum and was exiting left on Taxiway Q but the engines were off due to completion of the checklists.
