column121: We were taking off from ELP on Runway 22 and had an initial clearance for the TDOWN3 RNAV Departure.  Tower cleared us for takeoff with revised clearance to turn left to 200 and climb to 17;000 [feet].  I was the flying pilot manually flying.  As we were accelerating and getting the aircraft to a clean configuration we were issued a frequency change to Departure.  Upon checking in we were immediately given further instructions which included a right turn after reaching 6;200 feet to 060.  Both of us misunderstood the turn right part of the clearance.  The FO (First Officer) read back 'passing 6;200 heading 060' and had no response from the controller.  We climbed through 6;200 and turned left. We were about half way through the left turn when the controller saw the mistake and told us it was a right turn; but then told us to continue the left turn.  He later asked us to call them for possible pilot certificate action. There are several causal factors [due to direction of turn by flight crew].  First; having a clearance for an RNAV departure that has a left turn from Runway 22 sets you up to expect a left turn out for protected airspace even after receiving a last minute change to the departure plan using radar vectors.  Because the radar vectors are given last minute the old departure stays in the FMC showing the original route on our map displaying that left turn; so even though we were not following the route displayed it probably influenced our thought pattern.  There is no published departures turning out to the right from Runway 22 due to mountainous terrain if you are departing east.  Secondly; we also had prebriefed the engine failure procedures that have you turn out to the left for the same reason.  Third; from a 200 heading to turn right to 060 is counter intuitive because it is more than 180 degree turn. All of these factors I think caused expectation bias to turn left and not hear the right turn instruction.  Fourth; the controllers failure to emphasize the right turn part when it is more than 180 from current heading and his not ensuring the read back was correct. Controllers need to emphasize the direction of turn especially if it's more than 180 degrees and ensure they get a correct read back.  On the phone the controller said this was normal to avoid traffic from Mexico.  If this is a common procedure to use radar vectors to turn us out an opposite direction of our assigned clearance then there needs to be some notes somewhere in our charts so we can prepare for that ahead of time.  This non published procedure could cause conflicts with terrain in the event of an engine failure.
column123: The missed approach and takeoff engine failure profiles for Runway 22 tell you to turn left.  The TDOWN 3 SID; we were assigned; tells you to turn left off of Runway 22.  The reason all of the departures turn left on Runway 22 at El Paso is because there is high terrain if you turn right.  On takeoff; we were told to climb to 17;000 feet and turn left to heading 200.  When we contacted Departure; the controller quickly blurted out a long; involved clearance.  I responded; 'Passing 6.2; turn to 060.'  He did not respond back to my radio call.  On a heading of 200; the heading of 060 is to the left.  As we entered the left turn to 060; the controller informed us that he had told us to turn right to 060; he also told us to expedite our left turn and continue to a heading of 010.  When we rolled out on the heading; he told us to call a phone number because of a potential violation.  I read the phone number back to him and asked him to verify.  He did not respond because he was working two frequencies; and was talking to another aircraft on the other frequency. When we called the phone number for El Paso Departure Control; they told us that left turns off Runway 22 often conflict with traffic at a Mexican airport.  So; they often vector you to the right.  The Captain and I have both been in and out of El Paso numerous times; and have never gotten a right turn off Runway 22.  None of our guidance for El Paso says to expect a right hand turn.  Expectation bias caused us to hear 'turn to 060' instead of 'turn right to 060.'  Also; the Departure Controller was working two frequencies and did not catch that we said 'turn to 060.'  Here is what he blurted at us at 1;000 feet AGL while we were retracting the flaps; '[company name]; radar contact; turn right to 060 and climb to 17;000.'  He also had a thick; Hispanic accent.  If the keyword was 'right'; it didn't help that he placed it in the middle of a sentence with no emphasis or follow up. If left departures off Runway 22 conflict with Mexican air traffic; perhaps they need an updated departure procedure.  The ATKNN 5 Departure off Runway 22 turns right; but it continues west bound.  There are no departure procedures for Runway 22 that turn right initially; and then continue to the east.  Also; none of our guidance tells us to expect a right turn off of Runway 22.

column121: Approached Runway 28 into GMU and had the Pilot Monitoring turn the pilot controlled lighting up to max (7 clicks). The runway lights for Runway 28 did not appear to turn on. WHEN ATCT CLSD ACTVT MALSF RWY 01; REIL RWY 19; HIRL RWY 01/19; PERIMETER LGTS H1; H2 - CTAF. However; the FAA Chart Supplement contains this remark: ACTIVATE perimeter lights H1 and H2--CTAF. We recommend that the FAA Chart Supplement be updated with the correct information.  Also; consider adding the pilot controlled lighting limitations information to the Airfield Sketch and on the Runway 28 Approach Plate; as these products are much more likely to be referenced by a flight crew while in flight.

column121: This is a recurring issue. FNL and AIA both have weather-reporting equipment on the same frequency and are only 139 miles apart from each other. Our routing typically originates east of FNL and due to ATC preferential routing; our descent into FNL typically takes us over the GLL VOR/DME.  As a result of the interference between the AIA ASOS and FNL ATIS; neither station can be understood during the initial descent. When arriving into FNL; the ATIS is unreadable until we're approximately 30 miles from the airport; and by then we're already talking to Denver Approach and usually getting vectored for an approach. Likewise; descending into AIA; the ASOS is unreadable until we're about 50 miles out. I suppose it goes without saying that changing the frequency of one of these two stations seems like the best solution; but I know that reducing the power of either station could be an option as well. Personally; while I know the aviation frequency spectrum is crowded; I really hope that an effort is made to find an unused frequency for one of these two facilities.

column121: I was CIC (Controller in Charge) of the Approach control facility. The Radar Controller was working North South Sectors combined; which is standard for our facility due to traffic volume not being as high as it used to be. The Radar Controller Had an IFR aircraft (Aircraft X) off of one of our satellite airports; ZZZ; climbing high with the center level at 8;000 feet northbound. The Radar Controller also had an IFR aircraft (Aircraft Y) level at 8;000 feet southbound. Both aircraft on a collision course at 8;000 feet about 5 or so miles apart. Prior to this moment an adjacent facility sector called and the Radar Controller answered the shout line. The other line left unanswered. They called again and I answered working CIC and Data combined realizing the Controller needed assistance. They requested we climb Aircraft Z to 17;000 feet. I acknowledged with my initials. Immediately after I told the Controller to climb Aircraft Z to 17;000 feet pointing at the scope at the aircraft (now 4ish miles apart.) Controller told me to 'hold on' and went to Aircraft A a VFR aircraft in the northeast part of our airspace who was descending out of 6;500 feet southwest bound towards a Aircraft B (IFR) who was descending out of 9;000 for 5;000 feet who could of been a factor but currently were 10 ish miles apart and told Aircraft A to turn on a heading of 270 (I believe) reference traffic. The Conflict Alert alert is now going off; the Controller realizing her mistake asked me what to do; I told her to crank one to the right. At this point Aircraft A got back on frequency asking 'say again.' I told the Controller to now Climb Aircraft X to 17;000 feet ; she keyed up climbing him to 10;000 feet. He acknowledged the climb. I told her to give Traffic alert; to the other aircraft (Aircraft Y). She did not; and kind of froze. We did not have a hand mike plugged in to the adjacent scope so I was unable to get on the frequency myself to do anything. Aircraft X and Aircraft Y went right over one another by 100 feet. Neither knowing about each other. The Radar Controller just certified on radar and had her two RDO's (regular days off) right after. This may have played a factor on her not prioritizing the two IFR aircraft on a collision course before the VFR and IFR aircraft 10 miles apart. My recommendation would be to remind controllers working position that the CIC has say in the operation and should be listened to when they give an instruction. Because they may see something you have missed; and are trying to avoid a catastrophe. I should of been more adamant after I told the Controller to climb Aircraft Z instead of letting the Controller tell me to 'hold on.'
column123: Aircraft X was level at 8;000 feet. Aircraft Y was level at 8;000 feet. VFR Aircraft A landing ZZZ1 requesting RNAV Approach and IFR Aircraft B at 5;000 feet landing SWF were merging and I turned the VFR aircraft on a 270 heading. Due to this situation I was late to resolve the conflict between Aircraft X and Aircraft Y. Center approved higher for Aircraft X to 17;000 feet. I did not answer the line; CIC (Controller in Charge) did and advised me to climb Aircraft X. Other contributing factors were that the whole session I was working radar; the CIC was hovering over my shoulder making comments and telling me what to do. One instance was with a VFR aircraft over already radar with the adjacent TRACON sector and requested a IFR clearance to his destination. The CIC did not allow me to handle this situation how I wanted to and immediately made coordination with other sectors and was telling me what to tell the aircraft. I then went ahead and told him to take the position and for him to speak to the aircraft since he had made all the coordination. The whole session he pointed out minor things that when an actual important situation came up I could not tell he was urgent and I had not noticed the two aircraft at 8;000 feet. CIC was micromanaging me and was hindering my ability to work my traffic with his constant comments. Such as 'I didn't want to sit here and watch you'. Due to all these factors it was extremely difficult to work my traffic and focus. The one time I needed my CIC to advise me of an urgent situation; he did not until Center called to climb the aircraft. But when there were minor things in the way he wanted to work my traffic then he was yelling. This CIC took approximately over 600 hours to certify on radar and constantly had talks to during training. He also had his facility CIC waived a few months after he certified on radar. They should not have two recently checked out controllers working radar and data alone. CIC should not comment unless it is a safety issue. The CIC should allow the Controller to work traffic and only interfere when extremely necessary. I should have rerouted Aircraft Y through a less congested area.

column123: I was flying direct to ZZZ. I was IFR in clouds; rain; and turbulence at 7;000 feet approximately 35 miles from ZZZ. I noticed the artificial horizon had 'tumbled' and the 'vacuum' warning light came on. I turned off the auto-pilot and attempted to level the wings with multiple left and right corrections. Also noticed I was now in a dive. I saw the ground through an opening in the clouds and aimed for that. I broke out of the clouds at approximately 3;000-3;500 feet. Once I regained control below the clouds I tried contacting ZZZ Center. They were very difficult to hear/with broken reception. I notified them I had a vacuum pump failure; was below the clouds in VFR conditions and would call when I landed in ZZZ. Not sure if they heard me. I maneuvered the plane as necessary to stay out of the clouds and rain showers to ZZZ. Once on the ground I called Approach and Center to notify them of what had happened. I guess you can never know when a vacuum pump may fail; but it sure does affect many crucial navigation equipment. My assumption would be to have a secondary vacuum pump or artificial horizon as a safety back-up. I will be checking into that.

Captain ensured AC control; while the First Officer [advised with ATC] and asked for level off at 8;000 [feet]. Cleared as requested. The Engine Failure Checklist was completed. During this time we leveled off at 8;000 feet and received additional vectors from ZZZ departure. I sent an ACARS message to dispatch to inform them of the engine failure and subsequent return to ZZZ and requested a gate be assigned. We continued with the approach. column121: Upon taking the aircraft; the number 3 MFD was inoperative which; per the MEL; required the Captain to complete all flying duties. While at ZZZ the Captain noticed that the GPWS Inop; Windshear Inop; Terrain Inop; and Terrain fail message were indicated in the EICAS. The Captain called maintenance who immediately deferred the issue and the Captain completed the logbook entries. Prior to push I entered the appropriate information into ACARS which did not match the PERF INIT which the Captain entered. We verified the numbers multiple times and determined that the ACARS had to be inaccurate. We also verified our numbers with the updated AOM. After calling Dispatch it appeared that their was a fleet wide issue with ACARS. It appeared to me that some information that is generally manually input may have already been calculated in the zero fuel weight of ACARS (85lbs for crew bags). Prior to the ACARS issue we notified Ground Control to receive an off time into ZZZ1 which we were given a departure time. At that point the Captain decided to complete the paper form X. We notified the ground crew of the delay who informed us they had to leave for another aircraft and would not be back for about 30-40 minutes. The Captain decided to have them push us from the gate in the event our issue was solved prior to their return. We completed the appropriate checklists and pushed but did not start any engines. Then notified ATC of the delay to void Off Time. The Captain then called the company for approval to open the cabin window to hand the form paper copy to the ground crew. Once the form was completed we called ops; handed the W&B out the window; and re completed the before start checklist all the way through. We also discussed not utilizing ACARS W&B throughout the flight (added workload). We then notified Ground that we were ready to verify off time prior to starting engines (fuel management). They gave us an immediate wheels up time so we started the engines and taxied to [Runway] XX. I used my IPAD to verify weather at ZZZ1 prior to push which was reporting calm winds ; few 050 TCU and 10 miles vis and again I checked prior to taxi which they were reporting calm winds; 046 CB; 10 miles. On departure from [Runway] XX we were given a turn to the west and eventually a heading to the north with a climb to 8;000 [feet]. When given direct to ZZZZZ for the ZZZZZ4 Arrival we had to vector around a few storms. We also had to vector around storm clouds on the arrival and were given vectors off the arrival by approach due to flow into ZZZ1. Within this period we both discussed the weather; verified the TAF; and discussed needing an alternate and potential fuel issues. After updating the D-ATIS we verified that the field visibility had dropped below 3 miles so we messaged Dispatch asking for/if we needed an alternate due to visibility. Dispatch responded that the TAF was good and we didn't need an alternate. The Captain started to become concerned because he was showing extreme areas of precipitation along the arrival and approach. Other aircraft ahead reported heavy rain. There were multiple discussion with ATC about getting in to ZZZ1 but I don't remember if they advised aircraft were going missed. We received normal vectors into the approach to Runway XYL and my first awareness of wind shear is when the aircraft in front of us called wind shear and missed. With our Windshear capabilities inoperative we were both paying very close attention to the aircraft's instruments. After intercepting the localizer and passing the Runway XYL FAF the precipitation was worsening. Somewhere between 1;700 and 1;200 feet the aircraft instruments were showing increased gains and losses and began to vibrate significantly. The Captain called wind shear and we completed the wind shear procedure up to the missed approach altitude of 3;000ft. Tower gave us runway heading and eventually turned us to the west with a hand off to approach. Prior to the handoff we began discussing fuel and alternates. The Captain suggested ZZZ2 which we messaged to Dispatch. Dispatch recommended ZZZ3. I recommend that we not go to ZZZ3 because of all the weather that was building between ZZZ1 and ZZZ3 and it also appeared weather was building at ZZZ3 per my IPAD. We asked ATC about ZZZ3 and they indicated that ZZZ3 had similar weather to ZZZ1 so we determined based on fuel and ATCs information that ZZZ3 was not an option. It seemed to me that Dispatch was adamant about diverting to ZZZ3. We also discussed other airport near ZZZ1 (off field) that could be potential alternates. After the check in with Approach they asked us our intentions which we replied stand by and began rough fuel calculations to ZZZ2. The Captain quickly determined that fuel to ZZZ2 was inadequate due to a 15-20 minute flight and approximately 2200lbs of fuel on board. (Increased fuel burn at lower altitude; storms in the area; and potential unknown issues on arrival at ZZZ2). We then asked ATC about aircraft success in to ZZZ1 which they replied that some aircraft were making it in and some were not. We then requested Runway XYR because it was the closer runway and informed ATC of our minimum fuel situation. The Captain notified the Flight Attendant; we ran the appropriate checklist (ATIS; build it; bug; brief it) and continued vectors to Runway XYR. There were two aircraft in front of us which one was able to land and another missed (aircraft in front of us) due to wind shear. After recalculating fuel requirements the Captain determined that a missed would put us in an emergency fuel situation therefore we [advised ATC]. I believe that upon intercepting the localizer we were somewhere around 1700-1800lbs. During the approach the gains and losses of altitude did not seem significant but it appeared to be difficult to maintain the localizer although I did not see anything greater than one dot. There was also added pressure to continue the approach due to the fuel situation. During the approach tower asked the aircraft that made it in where they broke out and they replied 'right at mins'. At around 800 feet I called out that I could see the ground which was not visible as we got to 500 ft. At 300 feet I called approach lights in sight 12 o'clock and continued to call out the approach lights. The aircraft began to drift right and I called the runway environment insight at 11 o'clock. Throughout this period it was apparent that the Captain was having difficulty seeing the runway. When he finally looked up and determined that he did not have adequate references; and the aircraft was not in a safe position to land; he called the missed. Immediately on the missed it was apparent the at least 90 percent of the airfield was VFR. We could see all of Runway XZ/XA; including approach paths; so we made a decision request XZ and due a VFR pattern into XZ. Tower provided we could use whatever runway we needed so we continued with XZ; entered the left crosswind; base; and landed. During the miss we did not climb to the missed approach altitude; left the gear down; and kept the flaps at nine because of the immediate landing after the missed to Runway XYR. We updated the FMS with Runway XZ and extended a line for reference because there are no approaches in our pubs for XZ. We did not rerun the performance information again because the field length was 10;500 [feet] which was longer than Runway XYR and it was an immediate landing. We also received fuel EICAS alerts during the missed and a fuel critical prior to landing XZ. All approaches were conducted with flaps 22. Emergency vehicles were on scene which we did not require. Upon taxiing into the gate the field went in to a ground stop due to lightning. In all the entire flight segment from door closed to door open was 3.4 hours. I would say that this flight provided the crew with several threats. To name a few; my PFD was inop so only the CPT could fly; windshear; GPWS; and TCAS were inop; pop-up weather wasoccurring throughout the flight route; fuel considerations; ACARS not accurate due to new AOM changes; delays prior to departure; delays in route; other aircraft encountering wind shear; and potentially an inexperienced dispatcher. There was also a significant pressure to land the second approach. I felt that we handled the situation very well as a crew and discussed and analyzed any and all potential alternatives but were cornered due to the fuel situation. I do wish I had analyzed the winds better throughout the duration and been more aware of the weather at the field during the Runway XYL wind shear event. With most of the airfield being VFR it was absolutely possible to successfully complete approaches to the XB runways and XZ/XA [runways]. The only area impacted by the weather was the XY runways approach segments. Therefore; if winds were within landing limits we could have immediately requested an alternate runway from ATC.
column123: While conducting the setup check in ZZZ; the GPWS Inop; Windshear Inop; Terr Inop; and Terr Fail messages appeared on the EICAS. Maintenance was called and the affected system was deferred per MEL. The aircraft also had an MEL for the First Officer MFD; and an NEF item in the cockpit. ACARS would not produce accurate weight and performance numbers; and Dispatch informed us that this was a known issue. We elected to perform a manual weight and balance with the Form X. The TAF for ZZZ1 was forecasting VFR and radar looked fairly benign. The First Officer obtained the D-ATIS for ZZZ1 which showed Winds Calm; visibility 10SM; Few at 5000; Scattered at 8000; with no other weather (information M). Due to this; extra fuel for weather was not considered by us or Dispatch. While in our initial descent the First Officer and myself noticed the weather in ZZZ1 was deteriorating and sent an ACARS to Dispatch asking if we should get an alternate. Dispatch replied that no alternate was needed; and we assumed that they had more up to date information than available to us in the air. Our radar was depicting areas of extreme return (red and purple) blanketing the approach and airport with other aircraft saying it was a smooth ride; but heavy precipitation. While outside of the final approach fix on the ILS Runway XYL; other aircraft were heard going missed due to windshear. ATC informed us that some aircraft were landing and some were going around. We elected to continue the approach as we were not experiencing any abnormal flight conditions. Inside of the final approach fix; I was unable to maintain positive aircraft control on the approach path due to airspeed; altitude; and course fluctuations. I made the determination to execute a windshear escape/go around. The Flight Attendant was notified of our situation. We contacted Dispatch to request a diversion and suggested ZZZ2. Dispatch replied that ZZZ3 was a better option; but ATC informed us that ZZZ3 was having similar weather to ZZZ1. I used the FMS to determine a rough fuel burn to ZZZ2 as 1400 lbs not including any deviations or approaches. We were also low on fuel; approximately 2;200 lbs after the missed approach. We discussed and agreed that we did not want to end up in ZZZ3 with such low fuel and similar weather issues. We decided to attempt a second approach at ZZZ1 after ATC stated that some aircraft were landing successfully. It was apparent that we would be below divert and possibly final divert on the second approach so we declared Minimum Fuel. We requested ILS Runway XYR due to perceived improved conditions and the closer approach for that runway. During the approach; the Flight Attendant called and said that a passenger was in the bathroom and asked if we could delay the landing. I advised her that due to our fuel situation; it would not be possible. She was able to get the passenger back to his seat before final approach. While on the approach; we overheard the aircraft in front of us go around for windshear. Our fuel level was low and a go around would put us in a fuel critical situation. We [advised ATC] and continued the approach. We experienced difficulty in maintaining the approach course and I used my PIC authority to continue the approach since a missed approach would leave us with inadequate fuel for much option. The First Officer called approach lights in sight; and we continued to 100 feet above the field. The First Officer called Runway in sight; and when I looked up; I did not see a runway and was disoriented due to the extreme precipitation and reduced visibility and immediately executed a go around. We were now showing a very low fuel level; and it was unlikely we would have enough fuel to get to another airport or reattempt an approach. I used PIC emergency authority to request a circle to land Runway XZ. We were able to maintain visual contact with Runway XZ during the maneuver. We had no time to get any type of performance numbers; and reasoned that since itwas longer than Runway XYR we could land. The landing was conducted without incident. As we engaged E/TO Reserve on the windshear escape; I entered this in the logbook and contacted maintenance. See attachments for reference if needed.Many threats existed in this incident including: pop up weather; weight restrictions; the need for paper performance calculations; an inoperative MFD; an inoperative Windshear system; and lack of an alternate. The weather and TAF looked ok during the planning portion of the flight; it was not until enroute; that everything deteriorated. I believe we acted in the best manner possible given the stressful situation and lack of backup options (fuel and/or alternate). It was a unique scenario that required a unique response. I believe we made safe decisions based on the current parameters. In hindsight; I would have been more assertive about requesting an alternate enroute. I do not believe we could have forecasted such bad weather; which is why we did not ask to remove passengers to add fuel in ZZZ. As we could not find a suitable alternate; we had little choice once we were low on fuel than to attempt to land on any runway. A third go around would have likely had us considering an off field landing.

column121: I was Pilot Flying operating the ZZZ flight. On short final; we received a sink rate aural alert. My First Officer called continue; I agreed; and we continued. It happened around 100-200 feet. We never observed more than 1000 fpm on the VSI; and the PAPI indicated 2 white and 2 red and the landing was made safely in the touchdown zone. Once the runway was assured; I elected to nose down slightly coming over the threshold to give myself some more room to get the airplane safely to the ground with the given conditions. Gusty winds; and bumpy conditions made for a more difficult approach; but at no point did it seem unsafe to either one of us.After landing in ZZZ; left hand brake temperatures were relatively high upon exiting the runway and entering taxiway A. We landed Runway XXL. Visual approach; winds 250@18G30kts. Once on taxiway; left hand outboard brake temp indicated around 380C and the inboard was around 340C; temperatures still climbing. Quick decision making and thinking; I as the Captain decided to notify Ground Control that our brake temps were too high to park at the gate; and that we would like to continue taxiing around the airport to get them to cool off enough to allow us to park safely. A few moments later; temps were above 400C and climbing; and we got the BRK OVERHEAT amber EICAS message. Called for the checklist; and complied. Basically; do not set the parking brake. The highest temp seen was 495C where it stopped climbing and finally started trending back down. I elected to taxi single engine; and only use the right hand brakes (which were under 300C the entire time) in order to get the brakes to cool off and to prevent an unsafe condition at the gate with hot brakes and the possibility of having a brake fire. Once cooled off below 300C we parked at the gate; and the message had cleared prior from the EICAS.

column121: On station arrival at ZZZ our marshaller used incorrect/non standard marshaling signals to bring us into the ramp area. Rather than marshal us into what is probably the most congested ramp in our system he continued with the move forward signal and offered little or no guidance for a turn onto the J line. Once we were parked he appeared agitated at where the jet ended up being parked. I attempted to talk to the marshaller to see what the issue was and ask that he be directive with his marshaling signals. I was intercepted by the Ramp Lead who told me that he would relay any comments I had. When I told the lead what my intent was he responded with 'you guys don't pay attention to our signals anyhow.'On our departure; the same marshaller we had inbound was used for engine start and departure. When we were ready to taxi; I flashed the landing light and got a very soft/non standard signal that appeared to be 'move ahead.' It wasn't clear that was what he was signaling so I flashed the landing light again. The marshaling signal did not change. I came forward using the marshaller for guidance and realized that he wasn't going to offer effective guidance for our turn towards the taxiway and started my turn late. Because of the close proximity of the neighboring ramp and taxiway construction and the ineffective marshaling I didn't have the energy to make a departure towards taxiway delta at idle thrust. I chose to make a right turn back towards taxiway charlie which is contrary to our 10-7 procedures. I verified that the thrust levers were at idle and the N1 rpm were at idle before making the turn.Once clear of the ramp I asked the station if there were any problems caused by the non standard turn. Nothing was mentioned.Standard marshaling is a problem throughout our system. In a perfect world; I would be able to park the jet using nothing but guidance from the marshaller. In reality; it's rare to get a marshal-er that actually marshals the jet. This leads to a combination of using the marshal-er and pilot experience to park jets. This generally works OK in stations that don't have congested ramps. Not as well in stations like ZZZ.The company needs to provide more/better training for the people marshaling aircraft and they need to ensure the supervisors enforce standard marshaling practices. As a pilot; trying to overcome a systemic problem with marshaling by using the marshal-er as a secondary source of guidance rather than a primary source; I contribute to the problem.

column121: The following narrative describes an event that took place while operating a passenger flight  - the second segment of a two-segment day. For this particular flight; the Captain (CA) was the Pilot Monitoring (PM); the other First Officer (FO) was the Pilot Flying (PF); and I was positioned in the First Observer's seat as the additional crew member; aiding in pilot monitoring duties. The flight itself was uneventful and could be described as a straightforward intra-European flight. We continuously checked the weather on our way to ETAR in order to remain cognizant of the weather conditions expected for landing. Well before the top-of-descent; we pulled the final weather report; requested aero-data performance; loaded the expected ILS approach; and once all crewmembers were present on the flight deck and ready to discuss the descent/approach/landing; the PF conducted the approach briefing. All checklists were completed on schedule and as we approached ETAR; we confirmed with approach controllers that we would expect the ILS to Runway XX. As we came within approximately 20 or so miles from the field; we were given radar vectors to final. At the time; ETAR was experiencing a large number of air traffic; both inbound to the field; outbound from the field; as well as training aircraft in the traffic pattern. On the downwind leg; the PM programed the course fix intercept and executed the change with the PF's verbal concurrence. The winds at ETAR were light; visibility was great; skies had a higher scattered layer; and overall it was a nice VFR day. Due to the heat rising from the surface; we did have some convective and mechanical turbulence as we approached the runway; but nothing too far out of the ordinary for a summer afternoon. The aircraft was configured on schedule (if not slightly early to be conservative) and was stable (on speed; on path; configured for landing) well before 1;000 feet. After the 'Stable' calls were made and we continued the approach; the PF disconnected automation (as briefed earlier) and continued the approach. The approach itself never destabilized as we approached the runway; however once in the flare; I noticed we were floating quite a bit. I had preloaded in my mind that floating beyond the touchdown zone would be a 'go-around' call. As we began approaching the end of the touchdown zone (and below 10 feet RA); the PM made a comment that the end of the touchdown zone was approaching. As soon as the final touchdown zone marker disappeared under the nose and before I could make the call myself; the PM called 'Go-around!' Almost as soon as this statement was made; the main tires touched down; the PF stated 'too late' and the reversers were pulled. By the time the aircraft had touched down; the flight deck had just momentarily passed the end of the touchdown zone. The aircraft decelerated normally and we cleared Runway XX on taxiway Bravo. During taxi to the terminal building; the PF stated that we would discuss the landing at the gate; to which the crew agreed. Once we were safely at the gate with the engines secured; all checklists accomplished; and the deplaning process was well underway; we had an open discussion about what had happen and why a go around should have been conducted; especially since the call was made. The debriefing was well received by the PF; who expressed that he understood why his decision to continue the landing was not correct given the circumstances. The PF mentioned that from his perspective during the landing; he believed he had still been in the touchdown zone; whereas from my perspective; we were 100-200 feet beyond it. The PF also mentioned that he saw a low altitude balked landing as being more hazardous than continuing the landing; however we reminded him that this is why bounced and balked landing recovery are part of the Extended Envelope Training received on a bi-yearly basis. After a thorough discussion and debrief; the PF stated that he agreed that we should have conducted a go-around and remained open to any suggestions/recommendations/critiques as we conducted the debrief as a crew. We discussed the no-fault go-around policy that exists and I mentioned that the response to a go-around call made by any crew member should not; and can not be 'too late;' as this breaks down CRM; places the crew in an uncomfortable situation; and establishes a scenario similar to disregarding a statement of 'I'm not comfortable with this' where one crew member's decision to continue becomes dictating (even with deteriorating safety margins) when other crew members had already expressed concern. We discussed that; although ETAR's Runway XX was long and we had ample room to decelerate after touchdown; the decision to disregard a go-around call on a shorter runway could have drastically different results. With every critique or debriefing item mentioned; the PF was incredibly receptive; understood the points being made; and was internalizing the information being discussed. I also recommended that we as a crew file reports to take advantage of a program designed for reporting slips; lapses; and errors; as well as allow each crew-member to reflect on the event in order to further analyze what could have been done differently. This event outlines a deviation from stabilized approach criteria; simply due to the landing touchdown beyond the touchdown zone. Although the correct go-around call was made; the PF continued the landing due to the immediate touchdown occurring almost immediately after the go around call was made by the PM. Expectation bias and continuation biases are incredibly powerful by influencing decision making well into the landing maneuver. Experience of landing on runways and stopping with thousands of feet remaining can cause a false sense of security when procedural drift occurs. With this event; it was incredibly beneficial to not only take time to debrief as a crew; but to see the value in each crew-member submitting an ASAP report to simply share individual perspectives from the landing. Due to the debrief; we were able to discuss company policies; procedures; as well as determine what could have been the best course of action in order to mitigate similar threats in the future. The value of a debrief can allow for crew-members to internalize constructive criticism; rather than brush off an event as an outlier. During an event such as this; I believe a tremendous amount of learning was accomplished simply by following up and discussing the events as a crew. I recommend that the normalization of debriefings after a flight; especially after flights with an event; should be standardized among the pilots. Not only are debriefings a form of mentoring tools but setting aside ego and discussing areas of possible procedural non-compliance; performance deficits; CRM breakdowns; or unmitigated threats could reinforce learning among crew-members. This ties in directly with professionalism as aviators. Although I do not believe there was an intentional violation of regulations or disregard for safety; addressing this event as a crew served to promote learning; enhance safety; and build up colleagues rather than put them down. Emphasizing the normalization of go-arounds due to unstable approaches has also been viewed as a beneficial adaptation within the Atlas culture. However; although we are seeing a statistical decrease in unstable approaches resulting in a landing; I believe this is still a work in progress as we evidently have not reached the milestone of 100% go-arounds from unstable approaches. Emphasis can also be placed in recognizing that stable approaches can still destabilize in the last 10 feet during landing; whether drifting from center-line; landing beyond the touchdown zone; or excessive pitch during the flare. This is of course in addition to ability for any operating crew member to call for a go around at any point during the approach. The go around procedure should be accomplished assoon as the call is made; and the discussion of 'why' should be reserved for when the aircraft is in level flight with checklists completed or once the aircraft is safely on the ground; parked at the gate; and checklists completed.

column121: Glide slope alert flying into RST. During approach phase of landing into RST. I was the Pilot Monitoring. We were cleared for the visual to runway 13. I recall we were descending and the Pilot Flying had the FAF altitude of 2;600 set; and the banana bar was indicating that we should level off at that altitude at approximately 0.25-0.75 prior to Ellie (FAF). I believe the approach mode was also activated; and we were fully configured. At the same time we were setting up for the approach there was a GA aircraft taking off; and a [air carrier] taxiing and holding short of Runway 13. I was focused outside and listening to ATC. We were both surprised when we received a glide slope alert. I believe that we were approximately 200 feet below the FAF when we received the alert. Around about this time I believe the 757 was cleared for takeoff. When we received the alert the Pilot Flying kicked off the autopilot; increased power and worked to re-establish a stabilized approach. We were still operating in visual conditions and had the runway in sight. From my perspective it seemed he had re-established a stabilized approach. Around 200-300 feet; or so; we received another glide slope alert. I do not recall us being excessively low to have activated the glide slope aural alert. The aircraft landed normally and safely. The Pilot Flying was frustrated that we had by all indications an unstable approach. In rethinking the events I am confident that we had the aircraft correctly configured and ready to fly the ILS with the aid of the autopilot. While we could not confirm this; our best guess was that the taxiing air carrier had somehow interfered with the glide slope and we began descending prior to the FAF. I felt that he had established a stabilized approach prior to 1;000 AGL; so the second aural alert was also a surprise. I believe it was the PF's first time flying into RST. After the first aural glide slope alert we probably should have called for a go-around. The alert caused a couple moments of confusion. We probably should have just gone around and removed the distraction.

column121: The Captain and I were operating a flight to MDST from ZZZ. We thoroughly briefed and read the pertinent information for the arrival into MDST since we had never been to that airport. We briefed and expected to get the SEKAR 2P [Arrival] for Runway 11 at MDST; which we did. Upon descent; we received clearance to 6000 ft to SEKAR. Upon passing SEKAR; we were cleared direct to OMRUP and cleared approach to Runway 11. OMRUP is not on the arrival; but the approach portion going into MDST. In the FMC; we brought OMRUP up and inserted it into the line below SEKAR and verified the route. Aircraft was still in VNAV PATH and because the altitude along the route was a descent from 6000 to 4000; we selected 4000 and continued the descent in VNAV. This is where we realized something wasn't right. There is high terrain surrounding the airport and it is briefed on the briefing pages in the EFB (Electronic Flight Bag). We reached approximately 5000 and decided immediately to climb back to 6000 because the MSA along the arrival track is 5500 from RETAK to OMRUP. We climbed and maintained 6000 until we passed the high terrain. Once we cleared the high terrain; we proceeded to fly the approach without further incident. We never got a terrain alert as we didn't allow ourselves to descend further into high terrain. The Captain and I used excellent CRM to avert a potentially serious situation. The Captain's situational awareness and experience arriving at an unfamiliar airport were a tremendous asset to recognizing and correcting a potential hazard.

column121: Climbing on the SID the forward Flight Attendant called the flight deck about noise coming from the main cabin door. We verified that the doors indications were all closed. No pressurization abnormalities were noted with the CPAM system. The noise was not audible in the flight deck. Shortly after the Flight Attendant called again saying the noise was louder; at which time the CPAM and doors EICAS (Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System) page indications were checked again. Pilot Monitoring advised the Flight Attendant to verify all door securing pins were in the green position and to try and detect if air was passing through. During this time ATC amended our climb instructions from 37;000 feet to level at 32;000 feet for traffic. When the Flight Attendant called again she said she felt air coming from the right side of the door.At this point the noise was audible through the flight deck door and inter-phone rapidly increasing in volume. We then donned our oxygen masks and decided a descent was immediately required. Pilot Monitoring advised ATC that we were beginning a descent. Upon completion of the emergency descent and at a safe altitude; Pilot Flying gave aircraft control to Pilot Monitoring. At this time an announcement was given for a precautionary landing. The Pilot Flying began setting the aircraft up for a return to ZZZ; via straight in. The approach and landing phase was conducted in accordance with normal operations and checklist procedures resulting in a standard landing and taxi to the gate. Once at the gate; the Flight Attendant had difficulty opening the MCD (Main Cabin Door). This was in addition to difficulty experienced closing the MCD for departure. Both Flight Attendants reported hearing a loud pop prior to the sharp increase in sound from the MCD in flight.The risk was a complete and rapid; possibly explosive decompression of the aircraft. Suggest extra vigilance in verifying the airworthiness of MCD seals.
column123: As were climbing after departing ZZZ; our Forward Flight Attendant called the flight deck advising us that she was concerned about a loud noise coming from the main cabin door. We verified that the door was secured and all systems reported normal. We continued our climbout. She then called back and said it was getting progressively and rapidly louder and she can feel air coming from the right side. Systems were still normal. After being given an amended altitude of 32;000 [feet] from a previous altitude of 37;000 [feet]; we were cleared higher. It was at this time we heard the sound from the main cabin door through our flight deck. It was very rapidly getting worse. As a crew; concerned about pressurization issues; we immediately decided to initiate a descent. We donned our oxygen masks as a safety measure. During the descent; all systems still reported normal. However; the issue with the door was still evident. Once the descent was completed and we were at a safe altitude; as pilot flying; I handed controls to the pilot monitoring.I stated that this would be a precautionary landing and to prepare the cabin. I also made my passenger announcement. We then set the aircraft up for a return to ZZZ. The return and landing at ZZZ was completed under normal procedures and checklists. We returned to the gate as planned. After talking with the flights attendants upon landing; they reported that just prior to the sound becoming very loud they heard a 'pop' further exacerbating the issue. It should also be noted that there was trouble closing the main cabin door prior to departure. There was also trouble opening the door once we arrived at the gate. Cause MCD (Main Cabin Door) seal.

column121: During boarding Name in seat X came on board aircraft and told me the gate agent had told him to give me his battery for his wheelchair/scooter.  He asked his wife if she knew what type of battery it was and she said she did not know as she looked all over the battery for an indication of the type of battery it was.  She then handed me the battery and I tried to find any indication of what type of battery it was to no avail.  The battery did have a hazmat fire symbol sticker on it.  I let the Captain know about the battery and explained to him that the passenger didn't know what type of battery it was nor was there any indication on the battery to its type.  I called the agent on the Jetway phone that was in the Jumpseat; to let them know we had an issue with this battery.  The agent sent a manager down and I explained to the manager that we didn't know what type of battery it was.  She then called the Ramp Manager to come up.  I gave the Captain the battery to see if he could see something on the outside to indicate what type it was.  When the Ramp Manager came up she told us it was a lithium-ion battery.  I asked her how she knows that and she said that the passenger told her that.  I then explained to the Ramp Manager and the Captain that the passenger told me that they didn't know what type of battery it was.  The Captain then called someone to clarify what type of battery it was and if it was accepted on board in the cabin.  The agent then pulled up a photo on her phone showing a recycle symbol similar to the recycle symbol on the battery; except the symbol on the battery didn't have the words Li-ion in addition to the symbol as the picture that she displayed on her phone did.  All the symbols I have seen for lithium-ion have that addition Li-ion indicating it is a lithium-ion battery.  The Captain thought that she pulled the photo from a manual that they have access to and made the decision to now close the door.  It wasn't until later in the flight when I had explained to him that she just googled it and pulled it up on her phone so that she could shut the door.  I was then able to find in my manual that if the agent had been told by the passenger that indeed the battery was a lithium-ion battery she should have made a notation in the passenger record with a code and instead of the passenger handing me the battery; as per procedure in the manual the agent should have brought the battery on board the aircraft and stowed it either in the overhead bin or under the seat and informed the Lead Flight Attendant and the Captain of the location so that we could inform all other flight attendants on board to then monitor the battery throughout the flight for excessive heat; smoke or other potential fire indicators. [Reporter recommends] not allowing a lithium-ion battery of that [large] size to be boarded on an aircraft or coming up with a safe location to stow that type of battery knowing that there is a potential for a fire hazard.  25 grams of lithium-ion is the max [allowed] per our manual states that we can transport.  This size battery was the max.  On board we have a sleeve [containment bag] for a laptop or tablet or cell phone battery that may catch on fire; this battery would not fit in that sleeve!

column121: ZZZ MX (Maintenance) called and informed that the LH eng took 19 Quarts. MX inspected the inside and outside of the eng cowl and eng; tailpipe; inlet and behind fan blades with no evidence of a leak. The inbound crew did not write up a problem with the oil QTY. We reviewed AHM (Automated Health Monitoring) report with was posted inflight an hour prior to landing and showed good QTY and oil pressure and no high oil temp. We reviewed the oil service screen in work bench and no servicing has been done for a while which showed no oil consumption issues. We asked to MX service the oil tank and run the engine; no leaks found and a good oil gulp at start which tells us the tank is not over serviced. We put the engine oil qty on MEL for two reasons one that the oil qty transmitter was giving false readings and MX may have thought when they checked the gauge in the cockpit that the engine was full and that's why the oil screen also showed very little oil servicing of the engine. Second reason is that by putting the engine on MEL that forces the mechanic to check oil at the tank and document it. There for showing if we truly have an oil consumption problem. We monitored the take off and looked at the takeoff report and it showed good oil qty and pressure. About an hour later we got a report of the engine having high oil temp. We looked at AHM; it did show a high oil temp with oil Qty and pressure good. On post landing at ZZZ1 MX did a look at the engine and once again no leaks found. With the oil temp high that's when we asked them to pull the master oil chip detector and it had metal shavings on it. With the oil temp over limit that requires an engine change.I'm not sure we can prevent this kind of failure this was a really oddball problem we have not seen before. I think we were a victim of a failing lube and scavenge pump or gearbox the oil may have been hiding in the gearbox. If we were to do this again I may have asked MX to do a high power run instead of just an idle run; But it may not have shown the problem.

The student then turned to final and made his radio calls. Flaps were extended about 25 to 30 degrees and the student was coming in at about 70 to 75 MPH. At about 500 feet and 1/4 mile final; the Stearman came down in front of the students C172 about 400 feet away in a rapidly descending base to final and cut right in front of the student. The student had no choice but to abort the landing and go-around since they descended to a lower altitude in front of him. The made a CTAF call on 122.8; '<tail number> going around; aircraft on runway'. Adding full throttle and waiting for a positive rate of climb the student retracted the flaps. The student's initial thought was to just fly runway heading and perform a go around but because of the lack of communication his instincts told him they would perform a touch and go. He then made a 30 degree turn to the right of the runway then turned left to fly parallel to the runway and watched below for the Stearman as he gained altitude. To no surprise the Stearman was performing a touch and go.If my student had flown runway heading the Stearman more than likely would have ascended from under him. If he was any lower on my glide slope; and due to lack of communication from the high performance Stearman; his high wing aircraft would not have seen anyone above him; and the Stearman biplanes nature would not have seen him below them and they would have collided on the displaced threshold. The student had plenty of fuel and flew to the west of ZZZ and waited for them to land before returning. The way the pilots of the Stearman were flying a high performance aircraft with no radio; contrary to the flow of traffic; and without observing Part 91 right of way rules while conducting their operations poses a significant safety hazard.

Request approval with FAA if my location would be in any controlled airspace (my location was not in controlled airspace).3. Be sure all 4 propellers are secure and not damaged.4. Battery is fully charged.5. Check for any magnetic interference.6. Set my RTH.7. Make sure drone is connected to controller.8. Be sure my remote pilot license and current certificates are on or next to me before flying.9. Take off and hover drone to about 5 feet and check that all controls are functioning.10. Fly mission.I recalibrate the drone after about every 6 to 8 flights. As I was flying the drone to where I wanted to go; the property manager watched over my shoulder at my controller screen to see the view of the property. Once I flew over the playground; I yawed the drone 180 degrees to frame up the playground in my camera with the rest of the property. At this point; the drone was hovering at 357 feet (109 meters) above a wide open area of land with trees with the camera pointing North West. I took my photos; then I yawed to face the camera West and began flying to the next corner of the property to where I would yaw to point the camera North East for the photos. (The pool area would be the far North East corner where I was controlling the drone from this angle when I would take the photos.)About 5 seconds into this direction (West); my controller beeped; and I looked down. The property manager was still watching the controller.  We saw the camera on the drone flip up at the propellers and the app froze. The Kittyhawk app (now called Aloft) displayed 'Drone Disconnected' at the top of the screen. I quickly hit the RTH button on the controller; but the app was still displaying 'Drone Disconnected' and the RTH button would not activate. At this time; I looked up to find the drone; but I could not see it anymore. Since the controller disconnected from the drone; I presumed the drone fell to the ground; and the property manager and I (and two of her maintenance workers) performed a search where we thought the drone may have crash landed in the fields.We notified the owner of the land where we were searching as well as a restaurant closest to the fields and asked them to be aware of a possible drone on the ground or in the trees and to notify us if they find it. I also tried connecting the controller to the drone while we searched; but it would never reconnect.The weather was partly cloudy; 92 degrees; and Wind 7 mph during the flight. Further south where I took pictures from the playground area were two towers; but the drone was nowhere near them.The drone did not log the duration of flight; but it was about three or four minutes into the flight when the malfunction occurred.

column121: I was working the combined sectors as R-Side (Radar Controller). About the time Aircraft X called requesting flight following while he conducted a practice approach to ZZZ; ZZZ1 Tower called for a release on Aircraft Y. My D-Side (Handoff/Assist Controller) released Aircraft Y heading 270 climbing 4;000 feet while Aircraft X was still southbound approx 3;700 to 3;800 feet. I cannot get the replay to work properly so based on my fuzzy memory I remember multiple aircraft calling airborne for clearances and flight following as Aircraft Y called airborne off of ZZZ1. Two of the other aircraft were calling up. Aircraft Y checked on noting the transponder code he had selected. It was interesting because I did not see a transponder code; only a primary target where I expected Aircraft Y. I requested Aircraft Y ensure his transponder was on. While waiting for that I continued with other tasks including clearing the other aircraft calling. I noticed the continued primary only target and multiple times requested a recycle of the transponder on Aircraft Y. Looking back; I should have still climbed Aircraft Y to a higher altitude while we sorted the transponder issue. However; I allowed the other aircraft to distract me. Meanwhile; Aircraft X made a course reversal and was now northbound and had climbed to 4;000 [feet]. At one point I noticed the primary target headed towards Aircraft X. I believe I asked Aircraft Y's altitude. They reported 4;000 feet; the same altitude as Aircraft X right in front of them about 3ish miles. Looking back; I should have immediately climbed them but I only issued an immediate left turn to heading 210. Slowing down to the microseconds; my thought process had added complexity from an extreme precipitation cell just south of Aircraft Y; thus a few more microseconds of processing to come up with a heading far enough away from Aircraft X but not so far to have the possibility of it being too close to the precipitation and thus risking Aircraft Y refusing the heading and having back and forth transmissions to find a suitable heading. There wasn't ANY time for back and forth transmissions; I had to get it right the first time. So this caused me to pause what seemed like a long time but was probably an extra second to give the heading 210. I wish I would have climbed at the same time. I immediately went to Aircraft X and issued a left turn away to I think 320 or 330 along with an immediate descent to 3;000 feet. All I could think was I had to separate these two aircraft heading close to each other. The 3;000 foot clearance was below my MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude); But I knew I had to immediately get SOME vertical separation and I know; from being a pilot myself; a C182 can drop fast. It was the fastest way to create separation I had. Climbing Aircraft Y; while I should have done that; would have a delay in response. The headings would have a delay in response. Telling a C182 pilot to turn and descend immediately while simultaneously issuing traffic was the quickest way to pull these planes apart. It was below my MIA; however the aircraft was VFR in VMC. It was the safest option I had; with the note I wish I would have ALSO climbed Aircraft Y. To recap; I first issued an immediate left turn to 210 to Aircraft Y; then quickly issued and immediate left turn to the NW and an immediate descent to 3;000 feet while calling the traffic to Aircraft X. Then I went back and issued traffic to Aircraft Y who I believe said he had visual on the traffic. There was a combination of garbled radio and foreign accent from Aircraft Y. Looking back I technically should have used the term Traffic Alert to both aircraft; but I still got the traffic calls out as soon as possible after attempting to separate the traffic. I asked Aircraft Y if they passed the traffic; they said yes and at some point I climbed them. I told Aircraft X to resume own navigation and altitude their discretion. There wasn't time to dwell as I still had many other tasks to complete. In the middle of this all another aircraft; possibly Aircraft Z questioned why they were leveling off. I had to instruct my low time D-side to do several tasks including point outs and coordination on Aircraft Y and other aircraft. It was probably 10 minutes before I slowed and was able to report the event to my supervisor. Before the two aircraft came together I attempted at least once; unsuccessfully; to track the data block on to the primary target. I don't recall exactly why my attempts were unsuccessful and the data block stayed near ZZZ1 coast track. I may have typed the input out of order or didn't click directly on the target.I should have climbed Aircraft Y earlier and I wish I was more successful at tracking the data block on the primary target. Having the data block tracking with the primary target would have prompted me to respond quicker. Task saturation fought me on all of this. While not directly related to this event; the sector frequencies have been absolutely horrendous for weeks. Well; they've been very bad for years; but especially awful the past weeks. We have 2 transmitter sites with Mains; Standbys; and BUECs (Backup Emergency Communication System). I; and everyone else; have to CONSTANTLY switch between all 6 radios to communicate with aircraft in various portions of the sectors!! Even high altitude! My supervisor has begged us to report the frequency issues. It is a disaster waiting to happen; and I'm not exaggerating. I think even this session I had to switch multiple radios to talk to aircraft in the flight levels. Not helping the issue is bad feedback on that frequency. Its actually some other constant transmission like someone talking. You can usually hear it as soon as you unkey the microphone. Since the 2 radio sites are cross linked; the site that is receive only usually picks it up when you unkeyed. Its hard to explain but VERY frustrating. Please fix this. Someone needs to go out there and track down that rogue transmission station and either shut it down or fix it. Someone is either transmitting on the same frequency in FM or some other mode or some other harmonic frequency issue or something.

The Pilot Monitoring called out the PAPIs (Precision Approach Indicators); which showed all white; but the glideslope guidance was taking me higher.  I called for a go-around.  My go-around was sloppy; but the Pilot Monitoring brought his A game; so it was manageable. On the second approach; a visual approach backed up by the ILS 13L; both lateral and vertical guidance were erroneous.  I had to fight the tendency to cue on the vertical guidance; which again was taking me high. The Pilot Monitoring turned off both flight directors. On short final; we got an audio glideslope alert. The glideslope raw data showed me way low. The PAPIs were three white and one red.  We should have also turned away from the ILS on the NAV tuning panel. On both approaches; an Aircraft Y was parked right at the hold short line in front of the glideslope antenna.  I suspect we will see more aircraft stopped at the hold short line with the runway closure at DAL; and so we will see more ILS interference.  I have seen similar ILS behavior at other airports with an aircraft stopped at the hold short line.  We did not write up the aircraft.  An ILS test was completed and passed prior to the flight. NOTAM (or other reminder) that the 13L ILS may be unreliable with aircraft in the ILS critical area. More training on go-arounds.

column121: As our wind speed and direction reporting determines which type of approach should be flown (AOM 3.2.7); we used the advertised ATIS of LIMA (which indicated ILS XX was acceptable; if I recall correctly; landing data only showed a one (1) or two (2) knot tailwind when we used LIMA; wind 290/06). When we ran data for landing; the latest ATIS was (time); and we subsequently broke off of the RNAV5 Arrival approaching way point ZZZZZ for severe weather avoidance. We were set up for a left downwind for Runway XX (number five in the stack). We were approaching ZZZZZ1 on Runway XX shortly after the normal ATIS changeover. As we were cleared for the ILS XX; we heard preceding aircraft went around (I quickly downloaded the current ATIS to see if there was a SPECIAL).I discovered ATIS NOVEMBER was current (without being advised by the tower or approach control). I queried APP CTRL (before tower hand off) as to why Runway XX is the preferred runway; with an advertised tailwind being observed at the surface? Approach Control said 'We're keeping you on Runway XX for the sequence (or words to that effect); then he immediately handed us off to the Tower. I ran new landing data; then queried the Tower why they're landing Runway XX when ATIS NOVEMBER is advertising Runway XXR? He had no good reason. Landing data propagated around 800 feet AGL; and data showed Runway XX was all dashed lines; and we did not have the landing performance required; so I told the Tower we were going around. The Tower then asked if we were unstable on the approach as being the reason for the go-around. I said; 'No. The reason was you're landing aircraft on a runway not advertised as the landing runway; due to the wind being beyond our limits.' This wasn't a subtle wind change at the last minute; as we reported information LIMA (and we weren't corrected -- as LIMA was the current ATIS); but information MIKE had apparently occurred already; then information NOVEMBER was advertising runway XXR while on approach for Runway XX; and them knowing this; they continued to allow an unsafe operation to continue; to the extent; as we learned later; there wasn't just one go-around before ours; but three!

column121: On the ORCKA 5 Departure; after passing the 160 SMO radial and DOCKR below 3;000 feet. We were given heading of 030 and climb to 12;000 feet as prescribed by the SID (expect vectors). As we were climbing and turning he gave us direct 'KLIPR at or above 10;000; climb to 15;000.' I could not find KLIPR on the legs pages. I checked several downline pages; went back to page 1/9 and then checked the route page to verify the ORCKA 5. It was loaded but still no KLIPR. I told the controller it isn't apparently on our route. He spelled it out. I was moving too slow. He gave us 030 heading and told us to let us know when we are heading there. I though we were heading in the right direction but the intersection is now behind us. As I was jamming the box; perhaps KLIPR got eaten or dropped out as we passed it. It's location is right by DOCKR.  I can't figure out why it wasn't there initially as we turned. We were going through 10;000 feet easily so he then gave us direct KEGGS and to go to next frequency. The next controller gave us direct NNAVY.  Altitudes were no issue; if anything our climb rate was quicker than my cumbersome effort towards KLIPR. What could we have done better. I had expectation bias from the old Loop departure. If I remember after DOCKR you loop back to LAX at or above 10;000 feet. With this departure giving an initial vector and our climb rate much better than my 737 experience.  I was looking for KLIPR to be farther down the road than between LAX and DOCKR. I still don't know why I didn't see it because I was looking at the' top of the flight plan' legs page. I was just too slow for the expectation of the controller so he vectored us on down the line. Although I haven't been to LAX in two years I am comfortable there and fell behind unexpectedly during this event. Errors were automation Management; FMC / CDU and similarly spelled waypoints.
column123: The following narrative describes events that occurred over a very short period of time; perhaps only a few minutes in total. It is my sincere intention not to cast blame; but to offer an explanation for what happened from my biased point of view as the PF (Pilot Flying) on Aircraft X. Our flight began normally from LAX; with the exception that we were pushing back about 45 minutes late due our aircraft's late arrival into Gate 77. Preflight duties were performed fairly routine; but under some time pressure to complete everything thoroughly but as quickly as we could in an attempt to make up some of our delay. This time pressure was self-induced; as no other employee was pushing us for an on time arrival in ZZZ. Red flag #1. During the pre-departure cockpit preparations; we received notice that the passenger boarding was complete; followed shortly by ramp informing us that they were ready for the parking brake release and pushback. At this point I gave a cursory PF brief from the briefing card we all carry - too cursory. Red flag #2. Taxi and takeoff were normal from Runway 25R on the ORCKA5 Departure. I was manually flying; enjoying only my second flight as PF in over a month. We switched from Tower frequency over to SOCAL Departure; and shortly after checking in we received instructions to continue climb I believe to 5;000 feet and turn left to a heading of 030 degrees. Quickly after that we were given further climb to 12;000 and direct to KLIPR.  At this point things went wrong; rapidly. The Captain; as PM (Pilot Monitoring); couldn't find the KLIPR intersection on the legs page; and informed ATC that it did not appear to be on our departure. SOCAL spelled out the intersection phonetically; and then I think confirmed that we were on the ORCKA5. Things were happening fast. While hand-flying; in the turning climb; I tried to locate (unsuccessfully) KLIPR on the 10-3 page displayed on the iPad. Red flag #3.At this point; I should have turned on the autopilot to assist with the FMC and MCP inputs; as I could detect the stress and frustration in the Captain's voice in being unable to find KLIPR on the legs page; or on the departure plan view. Red flag #4. In my divided attention between flying the aircraft and searching for KLIPR on my iPad; I failed to find it as well. I was looking too far down the flight segment to see that the this waypoint is located right off the departure end of the 25s at LAX. This was the key moment; I think; and the last opportunity to correct the error. All I needed to do was put on the AP (autopilot); join the Captain and assist with the repair. But I did not; at least not immediately. The Captain inserted KLIPR on the legs page; got my confirmation; and executed the entry. When I had looked at the route modification; I thought it was correct. The waypoint showed in the correct direction (I thought) but much further down line than it should have; off the scale of my selected range on the navigation display. Red flag #5. Passing around 10;000 feet I engaged the autopilot at the Captain's urging to finally get back in the cockpit as a crew and together correct the problem. I engaged LNAV; but we were not turning fast enough for ATC and the controller gave us a new heading of 010.  I'd like to add at this point that our controller was patient; helpful and professional throughout our fiasco. The only way he could have helped us more is if he teleported into the cockpit and handed us our crew meals. Somewhere in the fray I had suggested that we reload the departure and that would bring KLIPR up; and now the legs page had a discontinuity and we had lost the LAS transition. Also we were given further climb; and now the KEGGS intersection to get us back on the departure. It was at this point I saw we had not been heading to KLIPR at all; but to 'CLIPR'! How did I miss that?! I had set up that problem by not giving proper confirmation of the legs page entry; having not used proper procedures (see Red flag #5). Further climb; and now direct to NNAVY were issued; but we first had to reload the lost LAS transition. After that was competently accomplished; our 'helmet fire' was apparently extinguished; and we were switched to the next Departure Controller. He gave us direct Las Vegas; and kindly spelled 'LAS' in the clearance for the lost crew.What followed was probably a good 2 hours of discussion and self-examination of what went wrong and why. I believe that two primary factors set us up for these errors. The first was my too-brief departure review. This was the first time the Captain had been on this departure; and only my second. Although we both verified the FMC route and legs page; and had confirmed the proper altitudes; we were not familiar with all the new (to us) waypoints; such as KLIPR. A more thorough review on the ground was paramount; and I failed to do it. The second was my desire to manually fly the aircraft during what rapidly became a complex departure. At the first sign of things getting too busy; it became mandatory for me to engage the autopilot; and thereby engage my brain in helping eliminate the threat. I failed in that regard. Adding mistakes such as 'CLIPR' vs. 'KLIPR'; was due to my attention being more in the HUD than on performing proper FMC verification procedures. That was entirely on me. I still have no explanation for why KLIPR was not on the legs page. I had displayed on my CDU the Takeoff Ref page; and did not give due diligence to the ND or the legs page on the Captain's side. What I saw was '_ _ IPR'; and a magenta line in the direction I wanted to go. Not good enough!  Additionally; in my attempt to find KLIPR on the Jepps I zoomed in and slid the page right-to-left; taking the desired waypoint right out of sight. Using the autopilot undoubtedly would have enabled me to do this search more thoroughly. We had only seconds; it seemed; to prevent this entire undesired event.

column121: This was in a B737-8 MAX which is not selectable on the menu.  Inbound to ZZZ; deviating west of the arrival due to a severe TS over ZZZZZ and also another TS touching ZZZZZ1 along with multiple significant CB radar returns just west of our direct line to ZZZZZ1.  We checked in with ZZZ Center and descended to or level at FL340. We were made aware that our deviation west of the arrival was causing the Controller difficulty in de-conflicting our descent due to departing traffic which was below us and to my understanding west of us.  Very busy controller with no time to discuss options.  I was approaching the west edge (absolutely as close as possible) of the last significant CB when the Controller told us in an excited tone to turn right 15 degrees and descent to FL280 (or maybe 240; I don't recall now).  The CB was about 4 mile ahead and 2 miles across in both directions and 15 degrees right would put us straight through the middle of it.  I started an immediate right and tried to ask my First Officer to tell the Controller we had to have farther right; but he saw me turning and read back the 15 degree instruction.  The Controller was immediately on to two or three other calls.  I asked my First Officer to tell the Controller the heading that we needed to fly and about then the Controller noticed that we had turned a bit extra and shouted at us because apparently another aircraft was departing in the corridor between the last CB and the big TS.  I immediately corrected back and flew through the middle of the CB I was trying to avoid which was where the Controller wanted us in the first place.  I also paused my descent very briefly to verify with the Controller that we were going to be safe still and we agreed on a heading of north as we passed directly through the cell.  Fortunately; despite passing though the small cell with a solid yellow return; there was no significant turbulence and no injuries.  I don't believe we caused loss of separation and my intention was to coordinate and return to the desired heading as soon as possible. The frequency was too busy; departures probably should have been pushed farther west; I was trying to comply with the Controller's guidance as best I could while not creating a dangerous turbulence situation for my flight attendants and passengers.  The B737-8 MAX radar might be overly sensitive.  Had the Controller asked 30 seconds sooner we would have had time to coordinate; or a minute later we could have taken any heading.  In retrospect; we should have said we were unable to turn for another 6 miles; but given the urgency in the Controller's voice; I thought I was doing the right thing.Whenever an airplane is cleared to deviate for weather and is operating around thunderstorms and significant CBs; it seems like the Controller should always ask if you can accept a turn; not just assign a heading into the direction of the things we are avoiding.  Also; if there is any way to make these frequencies less congested; that would help also.  And finally; the other company's aircraft was apparently flying outbound and closer to our assigned arrival than we were comfortable with flying inbound.  Maybe ZZZ Center should develop and publish alternate Departure and Arrivals that could be assigned for weather avoidance as widespread thunderstorms are so common in this area.
