column121: We were cleared for takeoff on Runway XX in XXX and completed the before takeoff checklist. We lined up on the runway and I gave flight controls to the First Officer as it was his takeoff. He initiated the takeoff roll and all was normal. I called 80 knots and a few seconds later we noticed a large bird flying in front of the aircraft; flying at engine height from left to right in front of the aircraft. We presume that we were around 90-100 knots of airspeed. Upon the bird flying past the right side of the aircraft we heard a loud bang with a simultaneous shake/vibration. (Between seeing the bird and the noise/vibration was about 1-2 seconds) As this happened I called for the reject and applied braking and reverse thrust. We came to a stop on the runway and I advised the passengers to remain seated and the First Officer advised ATC. The engines were idling normally; (although the vibrations on the #2 engine were briefly amber) and our brake temperatures were below then amber range. We exited the runway at exit and stopped as CFR (requested by us) evaluated the exterior of the aircraft; we had shut down engine #2 prior to them approaching the engine. They reported some damage to the engine but no other visible damage to elsewhere on the aircraft. I elected to taxi to the gate and we parked at Gate XX without issue. I had briefed the passengers and FAs about the situation and everyone was kept informed. While parked; I was advised by the B-FA that in addition to a loud bang and vibration (presumably when we hit the bird); there was a bright orange/yellow flash on the right side of the aircraft at the same time as these noises/vibrations. Upon inspection of the aircraft at the gate it was obvious that a bird was ingested into the #2 engine as there was debris inside of and damage to the engine.

column121: Aircraft X [requested priority handling] while enroute to KTN from an airport in the lower-48. The pilot reported a loss of navigational avionics including the heading indicator; and could navigate solely by compass heading. Using a series of no-gyro vectors; I attempted to guide the aircraft over the airport in order to establish visual contact with the ground to allow for a visual approach or cancellation of IFR. Without the use of navigational equipment; I assumed that all instrument approach procedures would be impossible.During the initial vectoring; the pilot reported a momentary loss of engine power. He was able to restart the engine; which remained functional for the duration of the flight. When the pilot was over the airport at the minimum IFR altitude but could not make visual contact; I guided him to an area with a lower MIA in the hope that he would find visual conditions. After a descent in the lower MIA area; he indicated he was beneath the cloud layer and I gave him further instructions based on the aircraft being in VMC even though he had not cancelled IFR. This included allowing the pilot to continue a descent below the MIA while I continued a series of no-gyro vectors utilizing the terrain map on my display. I attempted to keep the aircraft over the water while maneuvering to enter the Tongass Narrows from the north. This stretch of water leads directly to the airport and is regularly used by VFR traffic operating locally. While maneuvering; the pilot lost visual contact with land. I issued a climb instruction to regain the MIA altitude; 060; over the airport in order to recover adequate separation from the terrain. Shortly thereafter; with the pilot level at 060 and flying over the airport; a Company A pilot [in] Aircraft Y called on frequency with weather information and indicated he could see the aircraft as it passed overhead. Additionally; a local frequent flyer; Aircraft Z; was instructed possibly by KTN FSS to abandon its VFR approach to Runway 11 and continue southeast toward the aircraft [with priority handling] and [to] join my frequency. I utilized that aircraft as an airborne spotter to aid in guiding Aircraft X into the airport from the south below the MIA.At this time; the pilot of Aircraft X advised he had approximately 13 gallons of fuel remaining and was exhausting it at a rate of 18 gallons per hour. Given the limited fuel quantity; lack of navigational options; and uncertain weather; I determined I would have to take the aircraft on the most expedient path to the airport. The pilot of Aircraft Z was VMC in the same area; having climbed from less than 1;000 ft. north of Runway 11 to nearly 4;000 ft. all while over terrain. Depictions on the Company A RNAV M 29 approach plate indicated that the terrain was no higher than 3;000 ft. in the area Aircraft X needed to fly across in order to reach the airport. Using the information provided by Aircraft Y; Aircraft Z; and the approach plate; I felt it was the last reasonable option to guide Aircraft X north toward the airport; over terrain at 4;000 ft.Aircraft Z established visual contact with Aircraft X about 10 miles south of the airport and remained in close proximity. The pilot of Aircraft X reported the airport in sight while heading north over Gravina Island near Nichols Passage and Blank Inlet at about 4000 ft. Shortly thereafter; we received confirmation from KTN FSS that the aircraft had landed safely on Runway 29.I am not sure there is much I could recommend that would prevent future [priority handling] of this type. It is not uncommon for pilots to encounter difficulty in Southeast Alaska; particularly those unfamiliar with Alaska flying. Perhaps more robust outreach to pilots from the lower-48 concerning the multitude of factors that present greater risk in the area is warranted. Weather; procedural and service limitations; lack of suitable landing sites; and the need for greater safety margins could all be presented to summerleisure flyers who visit our airspace.The pilot of Aircraft X performed incredibly well during a challenging situation. The pilots of Aircraft Y and Aircraft Z were crucial to my situational awareness and contributed directly to the successful resolution of this incident. KTN FSS and my colleagues at ZAN provided timely and useful assistance. All are to be recognized and commended for their efforts.

column121: At GS intercept; 2000; on the ILS XX and as I was setting the missed approach altitude; 2;500; the outer ALT ring was in 1;000s increments. I called the GA to Tower; and their instructions were runway heading to 2000. Since we were almost already at the GA altitude; the Captain stopped the go-around configuration at go-around flaps. We assumed a very quick return/rejoin was about to happen so he maintained gear down; flaps 2; and 170 kt.During our vectoring back to final with Approach Control; an ECAM was triggered simultaneously with autopilot disconnect cavalry audible alert; and the Captain said; 'TOGA LOCK?' He immediately accomplished a match/mash. ECAM showed AP (Autopilot)/ATHR (Autothrust) OFF; SLATS LOCKED and WINGTIP BRAKE. He maintained PF role as it was now raw data; with zero PFD (Primary Flight Display) information beyond airspeed; altitude and VSI. There were no characteristic speeds and no min/max symbols; Vls; Vmo; etc.; apart from the blue-selected speed caret. I ran the QRC; the QRH; and LAND APP procedures; as well as comms. The Captain elected to not declare an emergency; as Approach had broadcasted we were priority. We verified the approach was the appropriate one and reloaded it; a quick cursory brief about speeds; and we were cleared for the approach. One attempt was made to cycle the FDs for some guidance; to no avail. Autothrust would not engage. The Captain had to hand-fly the approach raw data. He successfully landed; we cleared the runway; and taxied to the gate.Slow is smooth and smooth is fast. In my haste to correct a simple mistake; I made a blunder. No fault go-around policy is great! There's no way of knowing if we'd have seen the slat lock if the first approach was flown to a landing. I had approximately XX hours on type.

column121: [The] flight departed ZZZ; [runway] XXL and at 400 ft. we were given a heading of 360. As soon as the turn was initiated a loud bang was heard from below and behind the cockpit. The noise then went away. A few moments later FA (Flight Attendant) 1 called up and reported a loud banging noise from 2R. There were no ECAM or any other indications in the cockpit - all displays were normal - nor was the noise audible from the cockpit. After getting the airplane stabilized and the after-takeoff checks completed; I sent the FO (First Officer) back to investigate. It was confirmed that a loud banging was obvious in the cabin. A return to the field was planned; ATC notified; [priority handling was requested]; FA's briefed for a precautionary landing; Dispatch notified and CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) requested. Runway XY was requested as this was an overweight landing; and the QRH procedure was followed. A smooth landing followed; the aircraft was brought to a stop after clearing Runway XY and the airplane inspected by CFR crew. The comment was that; 'A door was missing.' No other damage noted; and the flight taxied to a gate uneventfully. A walk-around revealed the 2R slide door departed the aircraft; followed by the slide. The noise was from the inflation supply line which was banging against the fuselage and wing root. A write-up for the missing door and raft was entered into the log along with the overweight landing notes. [The cause can be found through] perhaps confirmation of all maintenance items accomplished during the inspection at ZZZ immediately previous to this event. [I suggest to find the] determination of why the slide/raft door failed and [to find] appropriate remedies [to be] taken to preclude future issues.
column123: I was assigned FO (First Officer) on [the] flight. I arrived at aircraft and the Captain was already at the aircraft. I performed the preflight walk-around and noted no issues. All checks for preflight were normal. We were cleared for takeoff on Runway XXL; initial climb to 5000 and heading 290. Takeoff was normal. The Captain called for AP (Autopilot) on and pulled heading at turn altitude. Climb power reduction and clean-up was normal. We were handed off to Departure and checked in. Departure gave us a climb to 7;000 and 360 heading. I confirmed 7;000 with ATC and the Captain set 7;000 and I confirmed it. As he turned the heading knob to 360; a loud bang was heard from behind the flight deck. The #1 FA (Flight Attendant) called and reported the bang and a clunking noise near 2R door. No ECAM or warnings were displayed.The Captain retained the aircraft; leveled at 16;000 as cleared; and set speed to 245. We completed all checks and asked ATC to remain at 16000 as we needed to check out something. They approved that and asked if we were [requesting priority handling]. We replied not at this time; but we will need to check some things. The Captain then asked if I was OK with going back and checking things out as the sound could not be heard on the flight deck. The FA came forward and I went to the cabin and inspected the area and heard the banging she described. I returned to the flight deck; described what I heard and what I felt was happening and suggested that we return. The Captain agreed and formulated a return plan. He completed all notifications [and] reviewed all procedures with me. We [requested priority handling] and returned to base for an overweight landing.The Captain performed the landing as per QRH procedures. He brought the aircraft to a stop on the taxiway as CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) could inspect the aircraft; and they informed us that there was a door open and everything else looked OK. We taxied to the gate; followed shutdown procedures; and then went down to inspect the aircraft. At that time; we found that the 2R slide door and slide were missing and the inflation hose was hanging down and had struck the fuselage. The Captain the entered entries in the AML for the damage and overweight landing.My concern is that when we checked the system pages to see if we had any systems issues; there were none indicated. The doors page showed all the slides green and the white 'slide' indications. I.e.; normal armed condition. Had the green box that indicated the 2R slide shown amber; we would have been alerted that the door was in fact open - in this case gone - and would have had a better idea of what we were dealing with.

column121: While passengers were boarding I was notified by Flight Attendant A that a passenger had a smart bag that they could not put on the cart because they could not remove the battery. column123: After being notified by ground service agents and flight attendants that one of the passengers has in his/her possession a smart bag; both Captain and I reviewed the FOM regarding the smart bag policy (FOM page #); and the Captain called the supervisor. column121: I was coming back to my home airport after a fuel stop; there was weather coming in and I was trying to land before the storm got to the airport. I entered pattern at a 45 degree entrance to the downwind of Runway XX and flew the rest of the pattern. On short final; I was at landing speed of 90MPH. I landed long on the runway and tapped the brakes on landing which entered my aircraft into a porpoise. Being too far down the runway; I knew I could not pull out of it and needed to keep the airplane on the ground. I pulled the power to keep it down and the prop struck the ground which then collapsed the nose gear and brought me to a stop. Analyzing the situation; the first mistake I made was trying to beat the storm. This was the root to everything that happened. Next; I was coming down too fast and landed too long. I also tapped the brakes; which commenced the porpoise. If I was put into this situation again; I would have diverted to another close airport and waited for the storm to pass. What I have learned from this is to never try to beat a storm; along with don't rush to get down and go around when you need to go around. I am very lucky to have walked away from this situation and it will forever be an experience to learn from and never repeat.

column121: Enroute to ZZZ; I tuned to ZZZ's UNICOM and it sounded like the pattern was very busy. [I] decided to change plans and go to ZZZ1. I got airport information from the sectional map and noticed *RP. As I approached the airport; I could hear transmissions from a Piper Pawnee departing Runway XX towing a glider. I announced entering a right downwind for Runway XX; then base Runway XX; and final Runway XX. About mid-final; the tow plane announced left downwind Runway XX. I saw the tow plane heading [towards the] opposite direction above me at about my 11:00 position. I looked inside for a few seconds to complete my final GUMP check. The tow plane announced left base Runway XX. I saw the tow plane about my 9:15 to 9:30 position approximately 300 ft. laterally and 30 ft. to 40 ft. above me. At that point I realized I must not be transmitting. As I started to do a go-around; UNICOM announced; 'You have traffic.' He replied; 'Thank you;' and immediately entered a climbing right turn. I did not try to troubleshoot the radios at that critical phase of flight. I did not feel it was safe to go around and enter the traffic pattern considering the other aircraft in the area and not being able to transmit.When getting airport information from the sectional I failed to notice the asterisk next to 'RP' and assumed right traffic. Right traffic is for gliders and gyrocopters. Airplanes use left traffic. At airports where both left and right traffic exist; I would suggest simply putting 'TP' for traffic pattern. That way neither can be assumed and would require further research. After entering CTAF in com1; I noticed the 'com1/com2' transmit selector was already in com1.I failed to adequately research airport information. I failed to manage my radios. I failed to ensure communication with UNICOM and traffic. It won't happen again. I enrolled in a ground school and I am getting additional instruction.

column121: Arriving in TUS we had briefed the RNAV RNP Y Rwy 11 approach.  Our clearance was for the ZONNA 1 arrival which took us from SSAND to OTUKE.  Just outside SSAND we were cleared to fly the lateral course for the RNAV Y.  We cleaned up the box and turned on to the course.  The next fix was LUYEG; our clearance was to cross at 11;000 feet cleared for the RNAV Y approach.  We slowed to 240; went flaps 1; did the LAVS procedure.  The FMA went to PATH and looked normal.  We read the Approach checklist.  I checked the FMAs again; it indicated SPD not PATH.  There was no VNAV scale to indicate high or low on the path.  I selected V/S and slowed the rate of descent.  Before I could enter the next stepdown altitude in the MCP; ATC called with a low altitude alert.  There was no EGPWS warning.  I disconnected the A/P and initiated a climb.   We were in VFR conditions.  We reengaged the A/P and selected 9;500 feet for a crossing altitude at HODPU.  We did the LAVS procedure outside of HODPU.  The FMA went to PATH and looked normal until it crossed the fix and then it went to speed.  After that we used the A/P to fly the lateral course put each crossing altitude in the MCP.  On final I disconnected the automation [and] flew a visual approach.  First Officer did an excellent job monitoring; calling out deviations; and analyzing the problem.  We delayed reading the approach checklist until the FMS was correct for the approach that we intended to fly.  I was distracted by the checklist reading and that caused a delay for me to recognize that the FMA for the vertical mode was no longer in PATH.  We had asked the ABQ Center Controller to clear us onto the approach [but] he told us to make our request to Approach Control.  It meant that we were making changes to the FMS just before turning on to the approach.First Officer and I discussed the FMS setup; the approach; our procedures in the debrief.  We were unable to determine what error caused the airplane to not fly the RNAV approach correctly.  It would have been helpful to do everything earlier; complete the changes to the FMS and read the Approach checklist well before we were cleared onto the approach path.  That would free both pilots to monitor the automation and catch deviations sooner.

column121: While setting up beverage cart; myself (4); 2; and 3 all at the same time noticed an abnormal smell. It smelled electrical and went from a level 2 to a 10 within seconds; and haze was also noticed. I pulled galley circuit breakers; turned chillers; and coffee makers off while 3 called flight deck and informed them of the situation. We diverted to ZZZ1. The entire incident was approximately 30 minutes. The three of us (2; 3; 4); experienced headaches; nausea; and dizziness.After deplaning in ZZZ1; we; as a crew; needed to debrief. We had NO place to do so. Ultimately; we all sat in the one restaurant that had seating. We politely had to request the loud music be turned down; as we didn't feel well; as well as needed to debrief. Scheduling had only called number 3; and was having her relay our account of what happened through her. Scheduling should have called EVERY crew member for our account of the incident from us DIRECTLY. Tracking was called and said 'we heard two of you want a [day off]'. None of us had any idea where that came from. In the meantime; Name 1 from safety had text or called us. He told us You all need to get out of your uniforms IMMEDIATELY; take a hot shower and wash our hair IMMEDIATELY '. He said to contact him if the company gave us any sort of push back. The company did give us a hard time. They told us in order to get a hotel; that we would be removed and coded as a sick call; using our sick time. Our Captain; was listening to this on speaker phone; and he told the company that this was a diversion due to fumes; and questioned why our crew would or could possibly be charged with a sick call and sick time taken away. Keep in mind; there were still approximately 50 passengers that were unable to be rerouted for one reason or another. It was our impression; that after FIVE hours sitting in the ZZZ1 airport; the company needed us to work the flight back to ZZZ to get said passengers back. I called tracking back; and after a very long wait on hold; told her that we took Advil and wanted to be reinstated to work the flight back. The agent had indicated to us that there were NO flight attendants laying over that could relieve us. We had also gotten back in touch with Name 1 from safety; letting him know we had no way of showering and getting out of the fume filled uniforms. I believe the only reason we were reinstated to work the trip is because the company wanted to get the passengers back to ZZZ without any regards to how we felt or the ordeal we went through. Each crew member should have individually been contacted by scheduling. We were dealing with two different people; and neither seemed to know what was going on."

column121: [We] departed HNL for a training flight. This was both a biannual flight review and a night currency flight to be shared between us. It was an uneventful flight with training completed as needed. Upon returning to HNL and accordance with the Approach Controllers; we held over Ford Island for sequencing. We were then given clearance to land on Runway 8L. The landing was uneventful.Taxi instructions were then given to us - turn right on taxiway G; left on B; right on E; and hold short of Runway 4L; the left seat pilot read back the instructions verbatim and confirmed the hold short instructions. We began to taxi; and then I took the the flight controls midway down Bravo. The intersection of taxiway B and E is listed as Hotspot 3 on the HNL Airport Diagram. Before we arrived at E; Tower made another call to confirm the hold short instructions and they were read back correctly; again from the left seat pilot. As we made the turn from B to E; we did not see the Runway 4L hold short lines and unknowingly taxied onto an active runway.This near 30 feet horizontal runway incursion put us directly in front of a departing [aircraft]. The [aircraft] was at rotation speed when they spotted us in front of them and [they] were able to lift off and bank the airplane to the right; overflying us.I had control of the aircraft from the right seat at the time; but the responsibilities between the two of us were unclear and controls were exchanged on the ground; but radio were handled from the other pilot. Also adding to the confusion was a lack of experience and recency with night operations in general; night operations at HNL; never having landed on runway 8L or taxied from 8L - I only had one other night flight at HNL X months prior. All of these factors contributed significantly to this inadvertent runway incursion and near miss.

column121: During take off; the decision was made by the PIC(self) to abort owing to a bang and the aircraft pulling left requiring extreme right rudder use. column121: With just 0.9 hrs of PIC time YTD; I arrived at my flying club's towered home field; ZZZ; rested and eager to shake off some rust. My first sign of how much rust I had came when I accepted a Ground instruction to RWY XX but taxied to the nearer RWY XY. After completing my runup; Ground advised me to taxi to RWY XX. I thanked Ground for 'that catch' and received a double-click 'you're welcome.' I paused; ensured I was focused and not letting myself feel rushed; and proceeded to RWY XX. I completed four takeoffs and landings; and after reviewing LiveATC recordings I believe that my radio communications were professional and crisp. Ground did request that I confirm one hold-short instruction; and Tower asked that I confirm a 'give way to helicopter' instruction as part of a 'hold short' read back. However; I acknowledged and complied with all instructions promptly; including hold-shorts; midfield reports; extended down winds; go-arounds; no delay etc.; using proper phraseology. A midair near-miss occurred when two Cessna's with 'XXXX' in their call signs began to turn base at the same time -- Aircraft Y from Right Downwind; and I; Aircraft Z; from Left Downwind. I mistook a 'cleared for the option' instruction for Aircraft Y as being intended for me; and radioed my acceptance for a full stop. I believed Tower had cleared me to land. The conflicting traffic had been advised of 'that Cessna on Left Downwind;' from which I further inferred my own landing priority over this newcomer to the pattern. Upon review of the recordings; it is clear to me that Tower attempted to clarify that the landing clearance was for Aircraft Y; and that the call out to my position was purely advisory for Aircraft Y -- and not a reaffirmation of a clearance for Aircraft Z to land. However; someone stepped on the frequency; and I missed the clarification. It was only after Tower instructed me; 'You need to turn right now' that I saw the conflicting traffic approximately 1/2 mile turning right base. Tower then instructed me for the first time that I was #2 for the field. I attribute this near-miss primarily to my own lack of recency; but secondarily to additional factors. I lost situational awareness of other similarly-[call] signed Cessna's entering the pattern from the opposite direction. ATC could have clarified our landing sequence earlier; or verbally emphasized the differences in our call signs. (A minute later; Tower itself briefly confused two call signs; instructing me to turn Right Base when I was already on Short Final from Left Base; Tower quickly corrected itself when I advised of my position.) It was also a very busy pattern in which to shake off rust -- for pilots and ATC alike. Simultaneous radio transmissions obscured instructions that might otherwise have been sufficiently clear. Stress was apparent: After landing; I complied immediately with Tower's instruction to exit without delay -- only to be told urgently to 'stop right now' to avoid a jet on its takeoff roll. (I appreciate Tower's urgency: I had acknowledged the hold-short instruction and was already preparing to stop; but to their eyes I was still in 'no delay' mode as I transitioned from RWY to Taxiway.) Tower similarly expressed frustration with another pilot for requesting 'a turn around a point;' a term that Tower did not recognize; they doubtless would have preferred 'a 360' or 'a circle.' When I was finished with my pattern work; I briefly expressed my appreciation to Tower and received a friendly 'no problem' in response. I think we all did what we could to be as clear as possible (urgently if the situation demanded it); and to correct our mistakes. Although it will be frustrating at times; on balance I think this is a good set of attitudes to have; especially as the entire National Airspace System shakes off varying degrees of rust coming out of the pandemic. The dangers here were addressed; but a slightly more intransigent attitude; or a slightly more congested frequency; might have tipped the balance to a midair collision.

After several minutes; we advised ZZZ Tower that we were still runway heading; at which point the controller advised us to turn right crosswind for right closed traffic to Runway XXR. While on the downwind; the controller advised us to extend downwind and he would call our base. We read back the instruction.When we were approximately .75 statute miles northwest of the airport; the controller changed our clearance to fly a close approach and we were cleared for the option. We read back the clearance and turned right base. Because we were high; we extended flaps to increase our descent rate. As I was about to turn final; the controller (a different voice this time) advised us to extend downwind; which we read back. I began an immediate climbing left turn. The controller immediately followed that clearance by clearing Aircraft Y to fly an immediate left 360. Aircraft Y was on final to either [Runway] XXL or XXR. There were multiple flight school aircraft with similar call signs in the pattern. Aircraft Y mistakenly made a right 360. I gained a visual contact on Aircraft Y; who was at my one o'clock low. I continued my left turn and climb to avoid collision with the aircraft. We extended downwind and were then given clearance to land. We landed without further incident. I believe that the hazy conditions; busy controllers; controller change or controller training; and multiple aircraft from the same flight school and similar call signs created confusion leading to this incident.

column121: I was working a Radar Sector with a Radar Associate controller. I was informed prior to the event that I would be very busy and over numbers for the sector. I was working multiple; 8 plus IFR arrivals into ZZZ using the ILS approach. The volume and complexity of arrivals/departures/and overflights in the sector was high. After an initial descent; I had cleared Aircraft X to cross ZZZ1 at or above 14;000 ft. and cleared him for the ILS approach. I inadvertently issued this clearance in a 14;600 ft. MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) area. Once my Associate Controller alerted me to the MSAW (Minimum Safe Altitude Warning) alert; the aircraft was already exiting the 14;600 ft. MIA; and as a result I did not issue a low altitude safety alert. The aircraft continued on the approach. ZZZ has shown a pattern of having very high peak demand in respect to arrivals. These spikes in demand are usually left up to the Radar Controller to take care of with little outside assistance from the Center TMU (Traffic Management Unit). This has resulted in numerous errors and other safety events as the Radar Controller is saturated. This high workload is also due in part to multiple transmitters for overflights and ZZZ arrivals and high terrain around ZZZ. I would suggest that preemptive procedures be developed for times that ZZZ is experiencing peak demand. Another possible long-term solution would be the stratification of Sectors into a high/low configuration so as to reduce the added complexity of overflight traffic. Frankly; with the volume ZZZ sees on a daily basis; especially in peak seasons; I am surprised it does not have an Approach Control.
column123: I was working the Assistant Controller position dealing with communication with Tower and point outs with adjacent sectors. Aircraft X was level at 15;000 ft. above a 14;600 ft. The aircraft descended below the MIA to 14;000 ft. before the Radar Controller realized the low altitude. No low altitude alert was issued. Spacing from adjacent sectors for ZZZ arrivals. column121: This is an informative report to highlight an issue that could be a safety and or planning concern. We were planning our takeoff data for departing ZZZ and were receiving MTOG [Maximum Take Off Gross] limitations that seemed unusually restrictive. We were a full flight from ZZZ - ZZZ1 reasonable fuel load. The advertised runways in use for departure were Runway XX; XYL. We were unable to receive takeoff data for Runway XX at our weight. The restriction on MTOG was listed as Obstacle Limitation. We tried various adjustments to get a number that would work. We were able to get takeoff data for XYL but that was limited also. We were required to do a TOGA takeoff even at a medium weight in a 319. We were concerned why the takeoff was so limited on a relatively average day with moderate weight and favorable winds. It took several calls to Dispatch to confirm that the numbers were accurate. The Dispatcher was unable to find a reason for the restrictive data. As we found out later with the help of another flight that had departed ZZZ also that morning; there was an obstacle that seemed to be the reason. Although we read the NOTAMs for the field and noted the cranes; etc; construction obstacles for the various runways; what we didn't see was that these obstacles had a significant effect on takeoff data calculations. Normally we understand that when the review is done for takeoff performance evaluations the message is that if engineering has looked at it you are good to operate as normal with the possibility of effects on takeoff data. But this was a rather significant change to the takeoff data. We were concerned that as we were quite limited to which runway we were able to use safely it could become very restrictive if conditions were less favorable. For example; heavier weight; tailwind; hotter temps. Our main concern was that there was no information to pre-plan for this restrictive data. The point of this report is to provide the information from our experience for future flights. It seemed like information from operations would have been appropriate to help us plan for and minimize threats to our takeoff planning. We wanted to encourage a further look at this threat with the intent to warn other crews of the more complicated takeoff restrictions departing ZZZ.

column123: Operating flight from ZZZ1 to SNA. Cleared to descend via the DSNEE 4 Arrival. Between CARZZ and KADYN Intersections at approximately 13;500 ft.; we received a 'Traffic; Traffic' TA with only a primary yellow circle popping up as a target with no altitude or trend information. The TA occurred about 20 seconds prior to us and the target converged. Center called 'traffic at 12 o'clock; altitude and type unknown'. The weather was VFR; but it was hazy. We scanned the immediate area above and below and did not see it.Then I looked to my left and I saw a white colored glider passing less than 500 ft. laterally and within 100 ft. vertically. I did not pick it up until it was at our 8 o'clock position and as we were descending on the arrival. We must have NEARLY HIT HIM! He was heading southeast bound.This occurrence made the hair stand up on my neck and it really shook me up. Just as I reported the near mid-air; ATC gave us a frequency change to Approach. I was so taken-aback by what had just happened; I had to ask Center to repeat the frequency. Just as I was trying to re-establish contact with Approach; I heard Approach calling us on Guard; which I thought was strange as we had only been off of Approach for less than 30 seconds. There seemed to be either a late hand-off from Center and they were looking for us; or they saw the near miss and were trying to call us. I mentioned that we had just missed a glider and we were trying to regain our composure but we had switched over in a fairly timely manner.After a busy; but uneventful approach and landing to 20R at SNA; during the taxi-in to Gate XX; SNA Ground alerted us that Approach was requesting that we call them once we parked.I called and spoke to a Supervisor. His first question was am I going to file a NASA report. I stated that I would. He took my name and number in the event that this occurrence needed further investigation. That glider was sailing on the main ridge-line just prior to entering the area. HE HAD NO MODE C transponder at an altitude that should have required him to have it. The glider was sailing on the direct arrival path of the STAR; and we are lucky that we hadn't arrived at our point of convergence 10 seconds sooner. When I saw him he was about 100 ft. higher than us at 8 o'clock as we were descending.

column121: The five of us crew members boarded Aircraft X at ZZZ just as soon as the inbound flight fully deplaned.  The inbound flight crew left the APU and APU Bleed ON.  Upon stepping aboard and entering the Flight Deck (FD); I noticed an odor that wasn't quite normal.  As I was setting up; one of the flight attendants (FAs) called me to the back to check on something.  She was standing approximately halfway between first class and the emergency exit row; and as I walked towards her the odor became readily noticeable and more intense.  I recognized it as an odor I haven't smelt in many years; that of burning oil coming through the APU driven pack.  She asked; 'do you smell that?' which confirmed my thought.  I said I certainly did and that we were not going to take this aircraft.  She said 'it's that old dirty sock smell' referring to a common term used many years ago (6-8?) pertaining to a period when there were many bad and noxious odors on the Airbus 320 fleet.  I told her I agreed and explained it was likely APU oil that was getting into the air conditioning system.  I took a few steps further aft and noticed the odor intensified the further back I went.  I believe she went to the back of the aircraft to tell another FA as I made my way to the FD to turn the APU Bleed OFF.  I briefly explained the situation to the FA in the fwd galley; and told her we were not taking this aircraft.  After turning the APU Bleed OFF; I called Maintenance and informed them of the situation.  I grabbed the AML and my iPad and headed out to the jetway to fill out the forms.  All 3 FAs were now in the jetway and my FO (First Officer) was outside doing his walk-around; preflight inspection.  I advised the cleaning crew they should also exit the aircraft; though 2 of them remained aboard as they wanted to finish as they were almost done.  The odor dissipated within a few minutes of turning the bleed OFF.  I then called my Dispatcher and advised her of the situation; explaining the noxious odor we just experienced; and that some of us already had noticeable symptoms.  Per the first items of the online Smoke/Odor/Fume Report in [the] checklist;  I asked how everyone was feeling.  The 3 FAs and myself had throat irritation; a foul taste in our mouths; and varying degrees of a headache.  Mine was slight at that time; hardly worth noting as I began filling out the S/O/F form.  My FO had been outside; therefore had minimal exposure and no ill affects.  The 4 of them then went up to wait in the terminal while I remained in the jetway to fill out the S/O/F form and AML. A few minutes later; an FA came down to inform me that another FA was feeling light headed and nauseous and that they were contacting their Inflight Coordinator to seek medical assistance.  A few minutes later; my FO came down to inform me that FA was now looking faint and had vomited.  I gave him the number to Med-Air to give to the FAs.  After completing the S/O/F report and making an AML entry; I put the AML back in the FD; shutdown the aircraft and left; intending to go with my FO to another gate (D3?) for a replacement aircraft to complete the flight to ZZZ1.  As I was walking up the jetway my symptoms intensified; particularly the headache; and upon entering the terminal it was strongly suggested I have my condition assessed.  I called the Chief Pilots [office] to confer and advise them of the situation; then I went with the FAs to [the] hospital.  The 4 of us each had POC Blood Gas; arterial tests done; and were monitored.   We were discharged shortly after midnight.  I contacted an FA to see how she and the rest of the FAs were doing.  She reported a new symptom of watery eyes; still with sore throat and headache. Another FA still had a dull headache; and the one who vomited was still not feeling well.  The first FA contacted me again later in the day for an update stating no change with her; the other one was now down to a dull headache; and the one suffering the worst now reports body aches.  My own symptoms have improved but not yet gone away; still with a mild throat irritation; a nasty taste in my mouth; and almost negligible headache. I have been on the A320 fleet for overall XX years and have experienced many of these events; particularly during that long ago time period when there was a rash of these incidents; many before the cause was determined or rectified.  I was rather surprised at how quickly and intensely the symptoms came on during this event.  This was by far the most intense experience I've had. As mentioned above; I haven't experienced this in many years.  It is my understanding that maintenance procedures had been put in place to prevent these from occurring.  I recently read a bulletin message regarding recent events occurring and a new operational procedure to remedy the situation.  I am curious as to what may have changed to cause the recent events; as it seemed to me this had been under control.  If it is a design flaw it must be fixed.  If it is a procedural matter; we must figure out what works for the health and safety of our passengers; and particularly the crew who have potential exposure many times per work day.

column123: Upon reporting to Aircraft X in ZZZ; the crew noted a smell of urine in the passenger cabin.  I figured the smell would subside once we had some airflow in the cabin as the aircraft had been sitting for a little while.  The air onboard was hot and stagnant. I started the APU soon thereafter.  In addition we requested some deodorizer to spray in the cabin. I informed the supervisor to hold boarding for a minute while we deodorized.  The crew did feel as though the smell subsided enough to board at this point.  After departure; it was apparent that the urine odor had returned and was intermittently present during the flight.  I'm surprised that I didn't hear any passenger complaints post flight. This issue was documented 2 prior times in the AFML (Airplane Log).  The corrective action block on each had stated an inspection was made and found nothing.  I initially figured that maybe a pet onboard a previous flight had caused issue and that the smell had resurfaced. Assuming the issue was resolved; we departed.  Upon arrival in ZZZ1; I notified Supervisor and Maintenance of the issue along with an entry in the AFML. I did contact the pilot on duty who in turn notified the Manager on Duty that it seemed to be more than just a cabin cleanliness issue and that at more than 1 member of the crew would be unable to continue working on the aircraft until the smell subsided as it made them feel sick.  I was told by the Chief Pilot that Maintenance would be finishing up shortly and that I would be using the aircraft on a revenue flight to a maintenance base. A maintenance inspection revealed there was a leak from the lavatory system and that it had been leaking into the insulation in the lower fuselage for some time.  At that point I was swapped to another aircraft to use.  I do understand some of the challenges in our operation and I made the initial effort to clear up the issue in a timely manner to ensure an on time departure out of ZZZ1. It is frustrating to know that this aircraft was sent back into continued service after numerous complaints; smelling of urine.

column121: During an initial flight lesson with a student; I was landing on Runway XX with a slight crosswind. Upon touching down; right at the point of adding brake pressure; a gust of wind picked up the left wing. The wind also caused us to drift aggressively to the right of the center line and pointed the nose off of the runway. I felt that I did not have enough energy to go-around; but also felt the aircraft was moving too fast for an aggressive left rudder input. I decided that the best option was to apply maximum braking in hopes of stopping before reaching the runway edge. Unfortunately; I was unable to stop the airplane before it struck a runway edge light and rolled approximately 10 ft. off of the asphalt. The aircraft nor anyone on board received any damages or injuries. Upon reflection of the event; I suspect that my failure to apply full opposite aileron for proper crosswind correction once touched down may have been a leading factor. If I had made that input; the initial uplifting left wing may not have occurred; which would have kept the aircraft pointed in the right direction. I do not regret my judgement in solving the problem after it had occurred. I believe that an attempt to go around would have caused us to strike multiple objects off the side of the runway; and an attempt to steer back towards center line could have causes the aircraft to skid/flip.

column121: After starting engines on the ramp at TEB; Aircraft X received the following instructions from the combined TEB Tower/Ground control: 'Aircraft X; Runway 24 taxi via Papa; Lima; hold short 19.' Upon receiving this ATC instruction; both crew members briefed the taxi route to include a left turn from the ramp onto Papa; a right turn on Lima; and hold short of the crossing runway. Shortly after turning left from the ramp onto taxiway Papa; Aircraft X received amended instructions from Tower/Ground: 'Aircraft X; cross Runway 19 at Lima.' Shortly afterwards; another aircraft (Aircraft Y) received a clearance to takeoff on Runway 24. Upon reaching the intersection of Papa and Lima taxiways; Aircraft X turned right onto Lima and proceeded to cross the runway. All aircraft lights were illuminated; the Pilot Flying (from the left seat) announced 'clear left;' and the Pilot Not Flying announced 'clear right' after a visual inspection of the runway environment. When Aircraft X was approximately halfway across the runway; a small-to-midsize jet passed low overhead after rotating from its takeoff roll on Runway 24 (the runway Aircraft X still believed; at the time; to be Runway 19). Among the resulting radio chatter; the departing aircraft asked what Aircraft X was doing on the runway; and tower responded 'They were not supposed to be there; sir.' Aircraft X responded with the assertion that we had been cleared to cross. Only after the tower responded did the crew of Aircraft X realize that we had been crossing Runway 24 instead of 19 as assigned. Aircraft X continued clear of Runway 24 and continued taxiing at ATC's instruction. Improper/incorrect taxi briefing between crew members. Both crew members failed to properly identify the branch of taxiway Lima that leads to Runway 19; and instead improperly concluded in the pre-taxi brief to make a right turn; rather than the correct left turn; at the Papa/Lima intersection. In reviewing the event; both crew members concluded that the taxiway diagram used to plan the taxi route had been zoomed in too far to properly identify the entire assigned taxi route. Combined Tower/Ground frequency. After receiving the clearance to cross Runway 19 at Lima; Aircraft X did not hear any corrective instructions or warnings from ATC following the improper right turn at Lima. Additionally; ATC did not specify a left or right turn at the Lima intersection. Acute angle between taxiway Lima and Runway 24 limited visibility of oncoming traffic. After turning right onto Lima; the approach end of Runway 24 was partially obscured by the sharp viewing angle behind the left-seat pilot's left shoulder. Misinterpretation of ATC instruction to 'cross Runway 19 at Lima.' This instruction was received as Aircraft X approached the Papa/Lima intersection; after which both crew members concluded that we had been instructed to turn right onto Lima and cross the runway. Failure to identify runway identification markings. Neither crew member noticed the Runway 24 identification markings while making the right turn onto Lima. After completing the turn onto Lima; all runway identification markings were behind the crew's field of view.

column121: Prior to entering the traffic pattern at UAO; I could hear over the radio that it would be very busy with all the air traffic and could sense the air traffic controller was not taking his job too serious because he had had a comedic inflection in his voice; which I've never heard any other controller use. I was told to enter left downwind for 'A' taxiway and report when abeam the tower. I entered the left downwind and reported when abeam the tower. Nothing was heard from the controller. After thirty seconds had passed I made another call to the tower and the controller instructed me to pass behind the traffic that was on right base for Runway 35. During the downwind approach I got multiple 'Traffic' advisories. This became a distraction and I reported back that I had the traffic on final in sight because I had been focused on that aircraft. This was not the correct aircraft that I was supposed to pass behind and my transmission was not corrected for by the controller so I turned for left base. As I'm turning I am getting another 'Traffic' annunciation and look out my right door. Down below I see Aircraft Y 500 feet under me. By the time the controller comes up on the radio and questions my intentions it is already too late. Luckily the Cessna saw me and began descending or else we would have been a much closer incident. I maintained my altitude and requested a descending right 360 because I had overshot 'A' taxiway. This in turn caused a fixed wing that was departing to the south from the right downwind to make a left 360 to avoid me. I proceeded down to the taxiway to park on the company ramp. I should have not got so caught up on the aircraft on final that caused me to not read back the proper clearance back to the tower. I was also distracted from the multiple 'Traffic' annunciations while I was trying to locate where these aircraft were in particular. I feel that had the controller also done his part in correcting my incorrect read back that the situation could have easily been avoided.

column121: I was flying Aircraft X. I was incoming to SQL from the north for [a] full stop landing; exiting the SFO Bravo; heading south towards the airport. SQL Tower initially asked me to enter a left downwind for Runway 30; keeping 101 freeway to my left; and they would call my left base for Runway 30. A couple of minutes later they asked me to turn left; overfly the runway and enter a right base for Runway 30. I crossed the runway at 1200 feet and began to descend to pattern altitude. SQL Tower told me to follow Aircraft Y that was on an extended right base for 30. As I was searching for Aircraft Y; I began to turn right downwind for 30 right as I noticed Aircraft Z cross in front of me....both of us executing an evasive maneuver. I told Tower that I had a near miss with Aircraft Z....and Tower responded that this aircraft was not on frequency. I was able to land safely.   Upon reviewing ADS-B data and ATC recording of the event; it appears that Aircraft Z took off from Runway 30 and was asked to follow Aircraft A; Aircraft A was told to proceed to KNBR [radio station] antenna and then proceed on course; which they did. Aircraft Z however did not follow Aircraft A and turned too early into downwind. The tower also gave Aircraft Z a very early frequency change so they were not on frequency at the time of [the] near miss. It seems to me that the failure of the Tower to verify that Aircraft Z had Aircraft A in sight was a factor in this near miss; as well as the Tower's early frequency change for Aircraft Z.

I executed a straight-in approach [planning on a touch-and-go]. I conducted my descent check in accordance with the checklist along with a 'GUMPS' check. Final approach and landing were normal. I pushed up power for the 'go' portion and the aircraft initially responded normally.  Shortly after takeoff I heard the RPMs drop and felt the airplane experience a partial power loss. I checked mixture; prop; and throttle all in the full forward position (they were) and maintained landing attitude until touchdown.  During this time I announced (incorrectly) 'engine failure' on Tower frequency. Once the aircraft was down; the engine was still running and I was able to taxi clear of the runway.  At this point; after continued power manipulation the engine stopped. I maintained radio contact with Tower until a tug arrived to taxi the aircraft back to the hangar. I documented throttle/mixture settings; fuel quantity indicators; and checked the sumps. There was no apparent damage to the aircraft or any property; and no injuries.

column121: Was flying on Los Angeles Special Flight Rules (LASFR) northbound at 4500 [feet] when my ADS-B in system gave me a traffic warning coming from the right side. The traffic was ascending into me on a current collision course. [It] looked like a Cirrus or Bonanza and were much faster than me. I tried to call them on LASFR frequency to no avail. They continued on about a 75-degree angle directly towards my route of flight. The scary part was that they were heading directly towards me but also ascending into me at the same time. They were traveling much faster than me and guessing from their speed and my speed we were on a direct collision course. I was on a special use airway in Bravo airspace and was originally nervous to descend due to possible on-coming traffic from the opposite direction as well as fear of violating Bravo airspace. Since they were ascending from underneath me I had no visual contact with them (I was in a low wing aircraft). My ADS-B system continued to give me hazard and collision warnings. I turned left to avoid them; but they seemed to turn left immediately after I did and now again were on collision course. My ADS-B system warned me that they were now within less than half a mile from me and were at the exact same altitude as me; going much faster. I still could not see them visually so at the last second I cut my power and dove about 400ft and hard left to avoid them. I now immediately saw them visually; pass overhead right above me. Since I had dived a few hundred feet they were a bit higher now and were no factor. The whole experience just overall shook me a bit but I am doing fine now. I believe one of the biggest issues of this possible collision was that nobody was warning them for traffic; as well as them not looking for me. Since I was on an uncontrolled special use frequency and was not on flight following during the Bravo transition (it is not provided there; although I was squawking 1201 which is mandated); nobody was warning me of traffic. Since I was higher than the oncoming aircraft and they were coming from my right side; if it were not for my ADS-B in system; I absolutely would not have been able to see them visually. I believe a human factor involved that did startle me more was that my ADS-B system kept beeping and flashing and trying to warn me which only incited more fear; although this was good at the moment because I took evasive action; it made me feel more startled afterward. If the oncoming plane was on flight following or an IFR flight plan; then they absolutely should have been warned about me; if they were simply flying VFR then they failed to scan for traffic and failed to see me. Overall; the incident was just more startling/scary than anything; I wouldn't usually expect anything like this to happen in such well-controlled airspace; especially since this happened within Bravo airspace (to note; they were not on the special use corridor that I was on; they were departing to the west over the ocean; so they were flying in Bravo airspace on non-special use airspace.) I wanted to just report this to get it off my chest; as well as a few friends of mine recommending I do this.

column121: Shortly after touchdown on Runway XX the plane began drifting to the left; controllability was deteriorating rapidly. The SIC was attempting to correct the drifting; I (the PIC/PM) stated we're drifting left and applied Full; Authoritative; Firm pressure to the right rudder.  The plane began to straighten out and correct right. The left tires were on the edge of the runway next to the grass and water runoff; causing hydroplaning. As the plane decelerated I was able to regain control and corrected back to the center of the runway. The SIC further assisted in maintaining control of the aircraft as we could feel the tires slipping and hydroplaning. With team work and crew coordination; we regained full control of the Aircraft again and we're able to stop and clear the runway onto a taxiway.Contributing factors include; but not limited to: Weather; rain; winds/crosswinds; darkness/night; unfamiliar airport; wet runway; uncontrolled airport; fresh grass clippings and water pooling along edge of runway; long duty day greater than 12 hours;  consecutive long duty days; multiple flights in a duty day (4th);  human factors; pilot/crew exhaustion; crew dehydration due to extreme heat and humidity throughout the day; high stress loads throughout the day; get there itis; external pressure from passengers;  crews desire to succeed and make everyone happy by completing the mission.
column123: After touchdown the aircraft began to drift to the left. Control correction was applied as the aircraft was drifting but with very little effect. As we neared the left edge of the runway the Pilot Monitoring (PM) assisted the Pilot Flying (PF) and applied full right rudder.  Due to the water collecting on the runway the aircraft did not respond very well to the rudder input until we decelerated.  At that point we had drifted slightly off the runway edge onto the grass. With crew coordination we were able to recover the aircraft back to the runway center line. We excited the runway without further incident.Contributing factors:Weather; fatigue; hot temperatures and humidity throughout the day; dehydration; lack of nutrition; end of a long duty day (arrived at ZZZ on hour 13) preceded by multiple long duty days.This event has opened my eyes a little wider to the complexity of risk assessment. In the future more emphasis will be placed on assessing external pressure; fatigue; and physiological needs.  Also more assertiveness towards these areas of risk assessment. ADM is a very complex system of checks and balances and awareness to even the slightest deviation can prevent future contributing factors to this and other events. A lot could be benefited from a personal assessment matrix to pair with a flight risk assessment matrix to help with mitigating a go/no go decision.

column121: Landing at ID24 (short grass runway) to the North which meant there is a large hump in the middle of the runway- about 15 feet high but with a short but smooth run up to it. Asked student if I could do the landing as this was the second time I had landed on a grass strip and the first time on a runway with a pronounced hill in the middle and that hill was only about 700 feet past the threshold- I knew we would be rolling over it. If you rolled over too fast it was possible for the plane to want to become temporarily airborne. There were some very tall trees on final and it was a good idea to touch down as close to the threshold as possible. The idea was to fly a very stabilized approach as low as possible over the trees and then get into the flare just as we were crossing the shore of the lake where the runway began. Set up a long straight-in over Garfield Bay; crossed the shore when I realized I did not recognize the landmarks at the lower altitude we were at; and was already descending to what I thought were the tops of the trees on final.  I think we were below the legal altitude limit a few times when considering how far from the airport we were so I climbed a little so as not to bother residents and get a better view.  Then my student who knows the area well spotted the landmarks I needed. Set up the steep approach and the rest went better than expected. Contributing factors were [the] challenging approach and landing in the type of plane we were flying had me anxious- would have been really easy in a Aircraft X. More challenging to me than landing at Telluride with a 25 gusting 35 crosswind during light snow (Aircraft Y). I did not pick out my landmarks for the approach with the idea I could not orient so well when down low. Did not do a low approach to check out the runway where I wouldn't be so worried about getting stabilized on the approach early- we just overflew the airport at pattern altitude having taken off from Timber Basin about 40 minutes earlier. Did not just do a left downwind/base/final because I was worried about being super-stabilized for the short/soft field landing.  I could have just done a longer downwind and my orientation would have been very good. The high terrain on the left downwind had something to do with my decision. How to avoid [is to] do a better job of picking out landmarks for making an approach plan to challenging airports. Fly the pattern as long as it is safe. At short unprepared strips with tall trees all around it do a low approach and check things out; ensure safety and make a good plan.

column121: Have been a 107 UAS pilot since 2016 - haven't flown in 3 years. New drone. Recently updated 107 recency; now current. Flying at dusk and tiring of practice getting manipulation skill back; decided to site see thinking I could maintain VLOS (Visual Line of Sight) further with lights.Lost situational awareness - gone further than I realized and unfamiliar with new software program map as I had only flown for getting manipulation skill back (requires tap to open and change to orientation from thumbnail map. Started getting high wind warning. Tried a different direction; and still high wind. Saw a ball field that I thought was close to house on video screen - it was the High School. Fumbled with map enough to get orientation and dropped to 200 feet to avoid high wind at 400 feet (was very little wind at ground level).Personal assessment - I was stupid to push the VLOS via lights. Training said stay closer at night; but range of drone was tempting to see. Secondly; storms coming in later so higher wind at altitude could've likely been seen if I'd looked at the weather. But weather was still and pretty on the ground. I will be back to my smaller world of VLOS without aid of aircraft lights. Truly frustrated with my normally disciplined self.

column121: Aircraft X departed [Runway] XXL and I requested that they make an early turn to the north so I could depart an IFR small transport behind them. Shortly after clearing the small transport for takeoff; I hear MAYDAY on the frequency; and it was Aircraft X with an engine out. They requested to land Runway XY. I was working the Tower all by myself; so the first thing I did was go and cancel take off clearance for the small transport; and then left them in position on the runway. I had aircraft taxiing and cleared to cross Runway XY; so I also went to them and took away their crossing clearance. I cleared Aircraft X to land Runway XY (after incorrectly saying Runway XZ first); and then I immediately went to the hand held radio to alert emergency services since I was also working CIC (Controller in Charge). Aircraft X rolled onto Runway XY safely and exited onto Runway XXR and then onto a taxiway.I canceled the alert with emergency services because the aircraft was fine; but I had to coordinate with the airport to see if they wanted to inspect Runway XY before I used it or crossed it. This entire time I had [another] small aircraft on final as well; but they were never cleared to land. I told the small aircraft to land Runway XXR instead of XXL because I had the small transport waiting there and I was still waiting to hear back from the airport. I was also actively trying to call someone to the tower to assist me with coordination and reporting since I was all alone. The small aircraft ended up not hearing my instructions; so they maneuvered on final until it was clear what I wanted them to do; and they had heard the emergency on frequency so they were aware that I was busy with that. Once that was all cleared up; Airport Ops came out to tow Aircraft X back to parking. We need more staffing. I was working too many aircraft to be able to effectively handle what was going on; especially if things were worse. I was responsible for too much airspace and ground operations simultaneously. I was unable to provide additional services during this event. The complexity of this situation was unsafe; I had to stop several aircraft from crossing the runway used for emergency landing and they were split between 2 frequencies; so read backs were not insured. We did not have enough people to run this shift; and it was very uncomfortable in this emergency situation. I was following a TMI (Traffic Management Initiative) at the time; and it was still too complex. I have said in previous reports that we need 15 people for our staffing number but I think we may need more. In order to alleviate frequency congestion; split responsibilities; have oversight; and just have one person on break to keep a minimal rotation during our high traffic volume hours we need the following:opening shift- 2 CPC7am shift- 2 CPC9am shift- 2 CPC1pm shift- 2 CPCclosing shift- 2 CPCThe above plan will allow us to have Local Controls; Ground Control and Controller in Charge all decombined and with someone on break to have a rotation that avoids anyone going over 2 hours. This plan is 10 Certified Controllers each day; and our current MOU (Memorandum of Understanding) is 7 Certified Controllers each day. Our current MOU (which we don't even meet most days because of controllers out for unforeseen circumstances). To cover 10 Certified Controllers per day and to allow for just one or two people to have bid leave each day; we need at least 17 Certified Controllers. Keep in mind if we have 17 Certified Controllers we can still lose them yo transfers so you may consider a larger number than that. IFR traffic has been steadily increasing at this airport as ever since we brought in a 2nd FBO (Fixed Base Operator); and other expansions are happening. So it wouldn't be a surprise if we may even want to regularly decombine clearance delivery eventually.

column121: We were in IMC near thunderstorms and the conditions were causing a loud static noise on our radios. Even with the radio volume turned up; it was difficult to hear. We were given another amended route clearance. The Controller spelled the first fix phonetically LEEDN and then the GOPAC 2 Arrival. Because of the poor radios; I wasn't sure of the last letter of the fix. A quick glance at the GOPAC 2 chart showed the fix LEEDR; which was just a few fixes east of our original clearance. I assumed that was the point we were cleared to. I thought I read back LEEDR to the Controller. We programmed the FMC to go to LEEDR and were given a frequency change to Chicago Center. Upon check-in; I told Chicago we were direct LEEDR. A few minutes later; Center advised us that it looked like we were left of course and asked us if we were going direct to LEEDN. That's when we noticed LEEDN was a fix on the southern branch of the arrival. We reprogrammed the FMC and then flew to LEEDN to join the arrival.

column121: Aircraft X is a MAX 8 aircraft. It was my understanding that I flew it on its first revenue flight on this flight. All operations were normal but I happened to find a 'drill tap' on the floor of the cockpit by accidentally kicking it with my foot during entry to the FO (First Officer) seat. I thought nothing of it and disposed of the errant tool and flew the flight. However I seemed to remember recently that Boeing had major issues with leaving tools and rags and [other debris] in new build aircraft. This made me think I should report it and that this and perhaps all new aircraft should be more thoroughly checked for errant tools etc. that have been left behind. A drill tap would not be something I would imagine our Maintenance Personnel would be using in the cockpit regularly; so I presume it would have been a left behind Boeing item.

column121: It was a hot day and the Flight Attendants (F/A's) were continually reminding us that the cabin was warm. We were also running about 30mins behind schedule so we felt rushed to make up time; and at the same time; cool the cabin as quickly as possible. Upon receiving our takeoff data at the gate we noticed we were going to have to do a bleeds off takeoff. It's been a while since either of us had done one so we took the time to look in the manual and review the procedure so we would properly execute the procedure. The aircraft was already warm and having MAX's long engine start sequence didn't help. After pushing back; with our departure runway practically right in front of us; being in a hot aircraft and 30 minutes late; we definitely felt the pressure to get things moving. After waving off the crew; our MAX engines finally got started. After the start during the First Officer's (F/O's) flow; he stopped at the air conditioning panel and realized we discussed the procedure for takeoff but not re-configuring after takeoff; nor had we discussed configuration taxiing to the runway. So while we waited for the MAX's engine warmup we discussed reconfiguration after takeoff as well as deciding to keep the air panel configured for takeoff; since it would be a very short taxi. After our discussion the F/O called for taxi. I released the brakes and since [the runway] was so close; I decided to do my pre-take off flow coming out of the ramp. So I chimed the F/A's and did a throttle burst all at once right out of the ramp area. And the mistake was made. We got the Takeoff Configuration Warning and horn. I stopped the aircraft; advised ATC we stopped; set the brakes and we accomplished the QRH items and with a successful throttle burst; did the Before Taxi Checklist and made an info only in the logbook. We then called for taxi and departed for an uneventful flight.Flows need to be accomplished and completed before any briefing discussions or questions take place. We both feel if we had waited to have the discussion after the FULL before taxi flow; we would have caught our mistake.
column123: After the Before Push Checklist; Captain stated it would be an Engine Bleeds Off takeoff. (First Officer was in the Yellow.) I replied it has been two years since I preformed this takeoff procedure. To mitigate this risk; I read the Engine Bleed off Takeoff procedure in the MAX AOM [Aircraft Operations Manual] to Captain to be familiarized with the procedure. We pushed back [and] started the engines. During the engine starts; the Captain stated for me to call Ground after a minute and thirty seconds passed; after engine start; because we were so close to the runway. I performed my after engine start flow when I got to the bleeds; I stopped and I asked the Captain how he would like to configure them. Once configured we agreed enough time had passed to call for taxi. As we taxied; the Captain performed the before takeoff flow. We heard the Takeoff Configuration Warning. We stopped the aircraft and performed the proper checklists to reconfigure the aircraft for takeoff. Additive conditions involved in this event: First Officer (F/O) unfamiliar with Engine Bleeds Off takeoff. Very hot cabin. Short taxi to runway. Flight Attendant (F/A) PA about the hot cabin. Once I heard the announcement. I told the Captain I had not made announcement to the passengers about the hot cabin and if he wanted me to keep the right engine bleed on before takeoff as stated in the AOM.On my next Engine Bleed Off takeoff; I will complete my normal flow so the Captain will hear 'Standby Flaps'; then go back to re-configuring the bleeds properly. [I will] become more familiar with this procedure prior to my trips in the summer months.

column121: The chart for the complex special procedure for an engine failure departing [Runway] 8L on the RATPK Departure from LAS airport shows a turn at 12.7 DME LAS to the heading of 050 degrees or continuing on the SID depending on altitude. The issue here is 12.7 DME aligns with FLAAR which is a much further point on the departure.  The turn point seems to be more closely aligned with SCAAR; which is different point on the SID for departing [Runway] 8R.  I note that point to show the location difference; not to say what the point should be.  I believe the 12.7 DME is the error on the chart and should be closer to 4.9 DME. Additionally; the BLD 325 degree radial shown is incorrect as that also aligns with FLAAR and not the turn point.As charted there is no way to identify the correct Engine Out Decision point as shown. The chart appears to be way off in terms of where FLAAR; BLD Vortac and the Engine Out turn point are located.  This procedure should be removed until corrected.  Unless we are supposed to fly to 12.7 DME; then in that case; everything beyond the turn is shown incorrectly. So that makes me suspect of all terrain shown on this chart as well.
