column121: During push with brake set; started the Right Engine. Immediately after the engine started; we received an APU Limit checklist indication. We ran the checklist which stated an exceedance had occurred and directed us to shutdown the APU; which we did. Shortly after shutting down the APU with the overhead switch; the ground mechanic stated on the intercom 'APU fire; shutdown the APU.' I then stated 'no we do NOT have an APU fire indication in the cockpit; but did get an APU limit checklist; which we ran and shut down the APU already.' He acknowledged the radio and I believe at this point went to the back of the airplane for a closer look. I assumed any smoke he had seen was from the limit exceedance and decided not to fire the APU bottle since we did not have an indication of an APU fire. After taking care of the switches in the cockpit; I went outside to investigate what had occurred and found two mechanics at the rear of the airplane with the APU compartment open; as they investigated the APU from a cherry-picker stand. From the ground; I could see no evidence of any fire either inside the APU compartment nor on the exterior of the tail section. When finished with their examination; the mechanics came into the cockpit to explain what they found. I had great difficulty understanding their English and exactly what they were saying; except that they would now MEL the APU. I understood them to say they thought it was from fluid leaking in the APU. I only found out after talking to the operations director on a phone patch on the ramp in ZZZZ; that the mechanics had used a fire extinguisher during their inspection. They did not tell me this or perhaps both my First Officer and I misunderstood them. I did not witness them using a fire extinguisher and it must have occurred prior to me leaving the cockpit to investigate. I made a write-up in the logbook. No emergency was declared because it seemed well under control. Better communication between crew and mechanics over what they did; as they should have told the Captain that a fire extinguisher was used! Now perhaps they did attempt to tell the crew and we did not comprehend what they were stating.

column121: I accepted a ferry flight for Aircraft X from ZZZ to ZZZ1.  This flight was accomplished as a single pilot operation. It was a perfectly clear day; with light winds from the south.  Aircraft X required a special ferry permit due to an inoperative stabilizer trim position indicator; coupled with an inoperative out-of-trim warning system.  Essentially; the pilot was unable to determine the position of the elevator trim from inside the flight deck; and there was nothing to alert the pilot that the trim was set outside of the takeoff range during takeoff.  I was thoroughly familiar with this discrepancy because I had recognized it and alerted Maintenance of the need for repair the night before this event.  The stabilizer trim itself had functioned normally.I felt comfortable accepting this flight; as I had been flying Aircraft X for many days prior to the aforementioned maintenance issues; and was familiar with this specific aircraft.  Before starting the engines; I re-trimmed the horizontal stabilizer by making adjustments on the flight deck and confirming the position of the trim visually from outside the aircraft.  Confident that the airplane was ready for flight; and assured that the trim was working; I started the engines and taxied to Runway XXL for takeoff.After experiencing no abnormalities prior to V1; and reaching the predetermined rotation speed; I took the plane airborne.  After attaining a climb and retracting the landing gear; I attempted to make my first adjustment of the stabilizer trim since starting the engines.  There was no response to my input.  My first reaction was to ensure that I had not switched the stabilizer trim off inadvertently; as the switch rests immediately adjacent to my right knee.  The switch was still positioned to the Captain's side.  At this point I quickly recognized the gravity of the situation; which was that I was now flying a nearly 11;000 pound airplane; and I had no mechanical assistance to maintain a level flight attitude. During the climb out; my yoke weighed approximately 70-80 pounds.In my initial radio communication with Departure; I informed the controller of my altitude and that I had no elevator trim.  I did not explicitly declare an emergency.  When asked if I needed assistance; I requested the most direct radar vector possible to join a visual approach at ZZZ1.  I knew from my preflight planning that they were landing to the south at that airport and Runways XXL and XXR were in use.  This meant that from the point at which I began my first turn to the point at which I joined final approach was a straight line just under 15nm long.  This reduced the physical burden on me significantly versus returning to ZZZ; as flying the airplane became noticeably easier in straight and level flight.I also requested a lower altitude than the 9;000 feet MSL that I was cleared to.  Departure requested that I maintain 8;000 feet MSL as there were military aircraft operating in ZZZ2 airspace at 7;200 feet MSL.  The vector I was given took me directly over the top of the military airfield.  I visually observed several military fighter aircraft engage in sharp right turns to remain clear of me laterally.  During level flight; I allowed the airplane to accelerate to approximately 215 KIAS.  Every bit of airspeed I gained translated into a lightening of my controls; and made it possible to continue flying without exhausting the strength of my arms.  It is possible that while at this speed; I descended under the Class B airspace into the Class E airspace that lies north of ZZZ1 and west of ZZZ2.  Meaning; under my authority as PIC of an aircraft under 14 CFR 91.3; I may have inadvertently violated 14 CFR 91.117 as it pertains to the maximum speed of an aircraft in Class E and Class D airspace. The conclusion of this flight was a safe landing at ZZZ1; followed by an uneventful taxi to the company maintenance hangar.  I believe that I conducted this 8 minute flight as well as could be expected of any pilot with a similar level of knowledge and experience.  My familiarity with the aircraft and the surrounding area; my current level of physical fitness; as well as the timely response and assistance from air traffic control led to the safe outcome of the flight.

Using the auto pilot for the approach I ended up descending below minimum altitude for the final approach fix and continued well below glide slope until I was approximately 1200 AGL at which point I disconnected autopilot; increased power to help arrest the descent rate; caught up to the glide slope and hand flew the rest of the approach. I relied too heavily on the autopilot and lost situational awareness. I also could have asked one of the other pilots to act as copilot.I think it would be safer to not have new hire Captains fly without an FO (First Officer) in hard IMC for multiple legs even if it is just a reposition flight. And if there is a crew member on board they should sit right seat.

column121: Aircraft X departed ZZZ1 for ZZZ behind schedule due to a deferred APU and excessive cabin temps. Prior to descent crew performed arrival brief discussing the landing on Runway 26 at ZZZ. The plan was to be fully configured; on speed at the created waypoint at 1;000 feet AGL. During vectors it was determined the flight was going to be heavy for landing; crew extended drag to help with landing within the maximum safe landing weight. At that time; crew became distracted with weight; terrain and visually flying to the final approach course when crew descended prematurely below our briefed 1;000 foot AGL waypoint. Crew was still approximately 3 miles on an extended base leg. Crew maintained visual separation with terrain. It was identified that we descended below 1;000 AGL down to 800 AGL. Crew initiated corrective action and climbed back to 1;000 AGL. Upon reaching 1;000 AGL; crew proceeded to turn final and land without further issue.In this scenario; crew became distracted with managing landing weight; flying a non standard visual approach without guidance in the vicinity of terrain. For the next time; I would've fixed the landing weight issue prior to beginning the approach. In this case the amount was so small that a simple delay vector would've solved our issue. The crew could've then focused on the visual flight path to the runway. Also for the future I would; I'd also incorporate more of the autopilot until at a safe altitude to help with workload management. For the future maintaining the altitude and autopilot until approaching a base to final turn could resolve premature descents. In the future I could also be more specific and clear about which altitudes and how soon I expect to descend to those altitudes and waypoints when transitioning below 10;000 MSL building a better shared mental model.

column121: After a 5 hour maintenance delay to change a flat tire; we departed for ZZZ1.  We executed a normal; flex; CONF1 takeoff from [Runway] XXL in VFR weather with light winds and a light aircraft.  I was PF (Pilot Flying) and was hand-flying the departure.  At approximately 1;000 AGL I heard several loud bangs from the right side of the aircraft.  My first thought was bird strike but the CA (Captain) called out 'engine failure.' I called out 'my aircraft' and we determined there was a problem with the #2 engine.  I don't recall any ECAMs but I do recall seeing the #2 EGT was high.  I was continuing to hand-fly and CA suggested we reduce thrust to idle on the #2 engine.  I agreed and we reduced the thrust and the surging and vibration ceased and the engine parameters went into the green.  CA suggested an immediate return to the departure field and [advised] ATC and coordinated a downwind turn and level-off.  I engaged the autopilot and prepared for a return to runway XXL with an ILS approach. CA set the FMGC up for the approach and I flew the downwind and base.  CA advised the FAs (Flight Attendants) to prepare for a precautionary landing and gave a short PA as well.  ATC vectored us to the ILS and cleared us for a visual approach once I had the field in sight.  I executed a normal landing on XXL and we taxied clear on taxiway 1 and had the fire department inspect the aircraft.  CA made several PAs instructing the passengers to remain seated and that the situation was under control.  I noticed the #2 EGT was increasing and approaching the upper limit and we shut the engine down as the fire department was inspecting the engine.  CA coordinated with operations a return gate and once the fire department was done and deemed the aircraft safe to taxi we returned to gate.  The passengers deplaned normally.  CA then called Dispatch to advise them of our return.We both determined the safest course of action was to get the aircraft back on the ground as soon as possible.  This was made easier with good weather; no air traffic; and being below max. landing weight.  We were only in the air ten minutes and this didn't give us time to do much troubleshooting or communication with anyone except ATC and the flight attendants.  I was 100% busy flying the aircraft the entire time; but due to excellent ATC and constant communication with the Captain/PM; I felt in the yellow most of the time and in the green for the final approach and landing.  I only felt I was 'in the red' for the few seconds between when the engine began surging until the CA said  'engine failure.'  That statement immediately told me what was happening and I snapped into our trained procedures.   We continued to discuss the plan and agreed that a quick return to the field was best throughout the short flight.  Since the engine seemed stable at idle and we had no ECAMs we decided not to complicate things by troubleshooting but rather execute a quick precautionary landing.  I feel our combined experience in the Airbus as well as constant precise communication and exchange of ideas led to the successful outcome.  We backed each other up; trapped errors; and executed our plan efficiently and effectively. I don't see this event being preventable; but I think our training and emphasis on SOP and communication made for a good outcome.

column121: My First Officer noticed while checking the hazardous cargo pallet; there was a '4.3 DANGEROUS WHEN WET' box loaded on the very bottom of the pallet; with several boxes of other DG (dangerous goods) on top. It had been raining steadily for several minutes during loading; so the pallet had about a half inch of water or more that had puddled on the floor of the metal pallet. The pallet had plastic wrapping around all the boxes and of course the plastic was also wet due to the rain. But since this box was loaded on the bottom we couldn't tell if it was totally wrapped in plastic or bare to the pallet flooring. Also if there was a rip in the plastic; it could get the box wet. So I told the ramp agent I needed to see bottom of the box. The Ramp and DG Agent did not understand due to language issues and initially they put styrofoam under the box. My First Officer used Google translate and they finally understood. When they took the box off the pallet and showed it to me; it was wet on half of the bottom of the box; the box had absorbed a good bit of water as it looked darker. We had them remove that small box from the plane. It would have been easy to over look this!! My First Officer deserves a recognition for his attention to detail!! The DG Specialist most importantly needs to understand this could have been a very serious issue! I believe the package contained Lithium Phosphorus. 'Dangerous When Wet' DG should never be on the bottom of the pallet for this very reason. The cause was a poorly built DG pallet and a misunderstanding of how this box could easily get wet in the conditions presented. Ensure DG specialist at ZZZZ understand this issue and re-train as necessary.

column121: Right after takeoff; Flight Attendant Name  and myself smelled a strong odor. Smelled like chemical/acetone to me. I went out into cabin; the odor was strong for about 5 rows from back galley. I asked the passengers if they had used anything like nail polish; or anything with chemical base. Everyone said no. I asked if they smelled it; they said yes. I looked and felt in overhead bins found nothing. My eyes were burning. I went and told Name that I couldn't find the source of odor. She called Captain to report what was happening. The Captain said she'd get back to her. We then notified the number one flight attendant. Then the Captain made a PA announcement that we were returning to the airport. And that we'd be landing in about 15 minutes. I'm still out in cabin trying to find anything that was causing the smell. After Captain's announcement; passenger in 25F hands me a open wipe packet with the used wipe in it. She said she used it right after takeoff.  It was the exact smell. It had a concentrated eucalyptus oil in it. I asked her why she didn't tell me this when I first came out into cabin. She said she didn't hear me. There is no way she didn't hear me. To prove my point; when the Captain said we were returning to airport; giving no reason why. This passenger then hands me this wipe packet. She did hear me but for whatever reason didn't admit she had used this product right after takeoff. Now that she realized the repercussions of the situation; she admits to using product. I took used packet to Name to let her smell it; we both agreed this was the odor; F/A called to tell Captain. But everything was already in motion to go back and land. The Captain makes an announcement to passengers that we are returning due to a odor in cabin. And that it needs to be accessed. At the gate firemen came on with meters to test the air. It was all good. Name showed them the eucalyptus packet. We followed procedures in every way.
column123: Climbing out of ZZZ at approximately 12;000 MSL we got a call from the aft flight attendant.  She reported a gaseous odor similar to kerosene; that was making her eyes water. column121: While I am submitting this report late; let it be known that I began drafting notes on the below report on the afternoon of Date when the events were fresh in my mind. Please accept this report even though it is late. It would have been submitted in a timely manner but I have been consumed with caring for my health and that of my fellow Flight Attendants.I have a varied work history which includes [professional medical experience]. Before I was furloughed [on] Date and after I returned from furlough; I flew high time; however; I am an inexperienced Flight Attendant; as I only have approximately 800 hours of flight time. I find myself often relying on my recollections from training when I am faced with events that are out of the ordinary. In my short time as a Flight Attendant; I had not previously experienced a fume event. While I remember them being discussed very briefly in training; I feel that I was personally ill-prepared on how to handle the situation that happened to me and my crew on Date. I was in possession of a lanyard card from the union regarding fume events that I was able to reference as a guide during the situation; however; the actions the card indicated were not sufficient in protecting my crew that day. I believe I failed in my duty as a Flight Attendant to protect the crew and passengers in the incident that happened onboard Aircraft X on Date due to my inexperience and also due to incapacitation which was caused by the inhalation of fumes.On Date I was scheduled to work Aircraft X ZZZ to ZZZ1 on Boeing 737. At approximately XA:20 during taxi out after the safety demo Flight Attendant 2 Name and Flight Attendant 4 Name 1 called the forward cabin indicating that they smelled a strange odor in the aft galley. They could not describe the odor so I (Flight Attendant 1) went back to check it. I did not detect any unusual odor as I made my way through the cabin. In the aft galley I removed my face mask but did not detect an odor. Flight Attendants 2 and 4 indicated that they could still smell a faint odor but I could not. Flight Attendant 4 indicated that she had recently (within the last 3-4 weeks; I believe she stated) experienced a fume event and that 'it smelled the same.' Flight Attendants 2 and 4 indicated the odor was/had been coming from aircraft left; specifically the aft-most aircraft left corner of the galley. I took deep breaths in the area they indicated the odor was coming from in an attempt to detect it. They said it smelled like 'a dirty bathroom mixed with gasoline.' I did not smell anything unusual but they insisted that they did. I continued to attempt to smell the odor because I could sense that they were very concerned. I called Flight Attendant 3 Name 2 and requested that she come to the aft galley. She came back and immediately said that she smelled something unusual; describing it as 'hot dust on electrical wires.' I was still unable to detect any odor but I informed Captain of it via the interphone in the aft galley. I gave him the descriptions of the odor per the other Flight Attendants (FAs) and added that I could not smell it. He indicated that we had 'passed through a lot of exhaust from other aircraft.' I informed him that none of us smelled exhaust. I again relayed what the other FAs had smelled. He said we would return to the gate. I immediately returned to my jumpseat at the forward entry door. While we were still taxiing back to the gate my nose started running which was approximately 5 minutes after I had been in the aft galley. This was somewhat alarming to me because it was very sudden and profuse; and I became worried for the FAs 2 and 4 in the back. I called to check on them but I cannot recall what they said. We arrived at the gate at approximately XA:35; disarmed the doors and did the all call. At this point the order and timing of events is slightly unclear to me as I believe I was incapacitated to the point where my decision-making abilities were negatively affected; I am aware that we were on the aircraft for quite some time until at least XE:00 but I think it was closer to XE:30 when we deplaned. My sense of time was off from around XA:25 when I called the Captain to report the odor until after we deplaned. The event felt like a blur but I have recalled everything accurately. During this period of time I felt slow; like I was hiking at a high altitude. I was not thinking clearly. I had difficulty articulating the situation to passengers and I felt like I was at a loss for words; which is abnormal for me. Throughout the incident I recall the FAs 2; 3; and 4 having to sit in the flight deck behind the Captain (CA) at times due to lightheadedness; and they all appeared ill. I regret not putting them on O2 immediately and I regret not insisting they get immediate medical attention; especially for FAs 2 and 4 who both looked particularly ill. FA 3 also at times appeared glassy-eyed and like she did not feel well. FA 2 told us that she felt nervous and lightheaded as she was doing the safety demo; she had been in the aft galley the longest. FA 4 had also been in the aft galley for a significant period of time.After we arrived back at the gate and did the all call; I believe FAs 2 and 4 immediately came to the forward galley. I recall FA 2 sitting in the flight deck. She appeared glassy-eyed and her eyes were red and watering. She indicated that she did not feel safe on the aircraft. I told the Captain that my nose was running but that I had not smelled the odor. FA 4 and FA 2 answered the CA's questions as a report was filled out. Two maintenance employees boarded the aircraft. I relayed the information regarding the odor's location and description that the other FAs had given. I told them that I did not detect an odor but that my nose was running. They proceeded to the aft galley. Approximately 20 or 30 minutes after exposure I began to feel a raw burning sensation in my throat and my voice became hoarse. I indicated this to the Captain. I had the urge to cough but tried not to so as not to alarm passengers as they were still onboard; but I coughed several times onboard (also after we deplaned and on the way to the hospital; and occasionally still have the urge to cough). While onboard I started to develop a light headache in spite of having taken ibuprofen earlier that morning and again at XB:00 for reasons unrelated to this event. In hindsight I believe I was incapacitated as my decision-making abilities were questionable by this point.Passengers began to question whether or not it was safe for them to been the aircraft since the Captain had made an announcement about an unusual odor. I advised them that it was; which I now regret. No voluntary deplaning announcement was made. At one point; a Flight Service Manager expressed concern for us FAs; indicating that we looked like we needed fresh air and that it was unfortunate that we had to remain on the aircraft due to passengers being onboard and minimum crew requirements. More passengers eventually started complaining about still being onboard the aircraft. FA 3 indicated to me that she did not feel safe on the aircraft. I asked the Captain if we were going to deplane. He said; 'it's not up to me. They've got to make the call.' It was my impression at the time that he was referring to the gate agents when he referenced 'they' but I did not ask him to clarify. I was not thinking clearly and vaguely wondered why it was not up to him as he was the Captain. I regret not pressing the matter further and I failed my duty to keep the crew and the passengers safe. At one point a passenger asked for a snack. I did not feel comfortable going to the aft galley but I did not want the other flight attendants to go back there either because their complaints of their symptoms were worse than mine (they reported shortness of breath; feeling so faint that they had to sit down while I was comfortable standing up; and tingling lips and limbs; burningtongue; etc.; and I could see their eyes were glassy and watering) and they had been in the aft galley longer than me. I tried to hold my breath as I entered the aft galley to retrieve the snack for the passenger but I was not able to hold it for more than about 10 seconds which struck me as abnormal. Those passengers in the aft-most part of the cabin questioned whether or not they were safe being on the aircraft due to the odor the Captain had mentioned on the PA. I do not recall what I told them but I think I indicated that it was safe to be on the aircraft which I now deeply regret. As I made my way forward from the aft part of the galley; more passengers started complaining about being kept on the aircraft. When I returned to the flight deck I indicated to the Captain that the passengers had been on board (since boarding) the aircraft for over two hours without food or water. I again asked the Captain if we were going to deplane and he said he stated that the aircraft was 'going to be taken out of service soon.' I regret not pressing the matter further.At one point the flight attendants and I were the only employees at the forward part of the aircraft and I believe the only employees on the aircraft. I was nervous about this because I felt like no one should be on the aircraft. I called the gate multiple times but the line was busy so I called Ops again. I believe I told them that the passengers had been held on the aircraft for over two hours with no food or water and that we should deplane but I can't remember if I said this to Ops or to the gate agent (when I finally reached them after my call to Ops); or both. Either Ops or a gate agent told me at one point on the phone: 'Tower says you guys are going back out' or something along those lines. I did at one point get ahold of the gate agent and I indicated that passengers had been on the aircraft for over two hours without food or water. I believe he said that the Captain and the chief pilot were at the gate discussing the matter. This gate agent indicated to me that he agreed that passengers should have been deplaned as soon as we returned to the gate and that we had been held on the aircraft too long; and he stated that if it had been up to him the passengers would have been deplaned immediately upon returning to the gate. I again regret at this point not insisting the passengers be deplaned for their safety and for the safety of the crew. I regret not initiating an emergency deplaning which I believe would have been advisable given the state of incapacitation of me and my fellow crew members.Throughout this entire time all three FAs told me multiple times that they did not feel comfortable on the aircraft and that they believed passengers should not be on the aircraft. Prior to deplaning my runny nose resolved but my raw/burning throat did not. At one point I noticed my hands trembling slightly for no reason but I minimized this symptom and did not mention it to anyone. I regret not speaking up when the other FAs expressed their concerns to me. Eventually we deplaned somewhere between XE:00 and XE:30. We were advised that the flight had been re-crewed and I believe he said that there would be an aircraft swap. I then heard an announcement at the gate after we deplaned that there was to be no aircraft swap. I was gravely concerned for the oncoming crew but I wrongly assumed they would ultimately not take Aircraft X. I told one crew member that 'I didn't smell any odor but I'm having symptoms' as I walked by her at the gate but I did not have time to elaborate; as we were going to immediately seek medical treatment. I assumed that the aircraft would not go since the Captain had stated earlier to me that the aircraft was 'going to be taken out of service soon'. I assumed the fume report would be or had been filed. I assumed the new crew would not be put in any danger. I regret not staying at the gate and speaking up; and I feel it was my duty to try to protect the
column123: On Date I boarded Aircraft X servicing route from ZZZ to ZZZ1 around XA:30 as the #2 Flight Attendant on a 737 aircraft. I got straight to work in the back due to the flight basically starting to board right as we arrived to have a delayed departure time of XB:07. I believe the original departure time was XA:00. I set up all my carts and did everything I needed to get done throughout the boarding process; we then armed our doors and cross checked and proceeded to go off to do the Safety Demo once we pushed back. It was at that time I started to feel very lightheaded and didn't feel too well. I ignored it and figured it would go away. Once we did our final safety checks we all sat down in our jumpseats and proceeded to inform Flight Attendant (FA) Name I was feeling light headed just so she would be informed. About two minutes later I started to smell an odd odor; the only way I could best describe it is a dirty bathroom smell mixed with gasoline. I wanted to make sure I was really smelling what I smelled so I asked FA Name if she smelled it and she did not. She came over to my jumpseat and immediately did smell it. We both wanted to be sure so we called back FA 1 Name 4; she did not smell anything and continued to keep smelling to be sure; she saw our concern and took into account that I was also lightheaded so she called FA 3 Name 3 back to see if she could smell it. Right away FA Name 3 did smell what she described as a burning electric smell. FA Name 4 made the call to the Captain and told him of the odor we were all smelling; he informed us we had just passed a lot of planes and exhaust; we informed him that was not what we smelled. So we proceeded back to the gate.Upon arrival to the gate; Captain informed the passengers that the flight attendants smelled an odor that was off so we would be returning to the gate. After we verified and disarmed doors and cross checked we proceeded up to the front. At this point I was extremely light headed and it had felt like I was moving very slow. FA Name and myself sat in the flight deck and answered all of Captain's questions that he had for the report he was filling out. At this point all four flight attendants were experiencing symptoms (shortness of breath; light headed; sore throat's; running noises and tingly lips.) we all clearly did not look well. For some reason we did not deplane and I regret not seeking medical attention when we got to the gate due to my heightened symptoms. I was pretty out of it so I wasn't really sure what exactly was going on between the gate agent and Captain. I do recall Captain saying he had no say on if we could deplane the aircraft (which was kind of a shock to me due to this being his aircraft). I did notice that passengers wanted to get off the aircraft due to them being held on it for so long without food or water. FA Name 4 was doing a great job handling the passengers during all this even though she too was having symptoms of her own. All in all I believe the passengers and the crew were held on this aircraft for two hours. I then with glossy eyes proceeded to tell the Captain that I needed to get off the plane due to feeling like I might pass out. At this point nothing was done to get us off. Name 5 from inflight came down and said he wished he could let us off because we clearly needed fresh air but due to FAA minimum crew we could not do that. I did hear that the plane might be going out of service but then I also heard from the gate agent that this plane was going to pushback soon. I informed FA Name that I did not feel safe on this plane and she said the same thing. We all got together and said that we would not be taking this plane back out due to how ill we have all become. Finally around XE:30 the gate agent came on and told everyone to deplane and that there would be a crew swap and an aircraft swap. As we got our bags to leave we headed up to the gate where we heard the gate agent say that there indeed was not going to be an aircraft swap and that did not sit well with me. FA Name 4 and myself quickly warned one of the crew members that were going to work the plane to ZZZ1 that we are all ill and going to seek medical attention; I also told her to please stand her grown with this. We did get in contact with that crew and you will be receiving reports from them that will describe what happen to them. At this point we are walking to go to the onsite clinic to get us checked out; halfway through terminal I grabbed onto the wall and almost passed out. Inflight manager Name 5 got me a wheelchair and told me to take deep breaths and we proceeded to the clinic. The nurse said to get blood work done we should go to the nearest emergency room. Name 5 tried to set up transportation from the numbers we were given but he could not reach anyone so we ended up taking an Uber. At the hospital we all were given chest X-rays; EKG and arterial blood work for carbon monoxide. FA Name; myself and Name 4 all came back clear since the incident had been so long ago but unfortunately FA Name 3 did still have carbon monoxide in her blood; she was then put on 100% oxygen for 40 min and more blood work was done until she was also cleared to be discharged. The next morning we went to catch our deadhead to go home and we all were clearly completely out of breath from just walking from TSA to our gate which is very abnormal. Date 1 after we all got home I received a message from FA Name 4 that she was back in the emergency room due to her heightened symptoms and that the nurse told her to go. The next day Date 2 we received a message from FA Name that she too was back in the ER due to stomach pains. Later that day I became very dizzy and was having trouble breathing so I called FA Name 4 and she drove me to the same ER she went to after I called the nurse and gave me the all clear to do so. I was put on a breathing tube to help open up my airways and was prescribed and inhaler; FA Name 4 who was with me also was prescribed an inhaler for her too. We are now all at home Date 3 resting and we cannot return to work until symptoms are completely gone. I have a note stating I can't go back until Date 10 and if needed to extend because not fully recovered the doctor will extend it. This 737 should have been taken out of service after seeing what it did to us four flight attendants. Instead they put four new flight attendants in clear danger. We did come in contact with two FAs that worked that flight and I will let them tell their own stories but at least three out of the four are seeking medical attention and one had to call off mid sequence for feeling so ill. It's a complete shame that this aircraft is still out there flying and will continue to fly and affect so many more people. A fume event is not to be messed with and I hope the company will do something about this and take this seriously.

column121: Busy day at the airport in the ZZZ traffic pattern. I heard a slightly garbled message about a Piper Cub entering a tear drop for the 45 to Runway XX as I was turning crosswind. I continued looking for the cub but did not see it and made my downwind turn and radio call. About halfway through downwind TCAS alerted me that there was something closer than a mile about 300 feet below me even though I was at TPA (Traffic Pattern Altitude). Worried I was over top of another aircraft I turned left and then right aggressively to check under the wings and nose for an aircraft and I did not see anything. Passed the numbers on downwind and started my descent to base. Called my base turn; heard something garbled. Then heard someone calling 'the Diamond' to which the pilot said I had gotten within 100 yards of him and that I should watch for traffic better. I did look; I had been in the pattern practicing all morning; I made clearing maneuvers to make sure there was nothing in a blind spot but at the end of the day I did not see him. While radios are not required; he obviously had one. Some of the hardest things to see while in the air are airports and other planes. It also would have been beneficial had the Piper Cub been at published TPA and even though not required; when within a very busy non towered airport; clearly announcing his position.

column121: Preflight and runup was normal. Engine operation was good. Began taxiing on the runway. Full power was applied and engine instruments were all in the green (RPM; pressure; and temperature). Airspeed was increasing slowly initially at first; but RPM increased as airspeed increased and I reached rotation speed of 60 to 65. I reached my normal Vx speed of 65 to 70 MPH. I had seen the climb-out of another aircraft and it appeared to be windy so I decided to add a little more speed to that as a buffer for safety. I had briefed this prior to takeoff and was aiming for 70 to 75 for the climb out; for obstacle avoidance and wind buffer. I also had briefed and prepared for a wind shift as I got above the trees; as this is a standard precaution that I have regularly made at this airport (because of the location of the trees) and was prepared to expect it (as is regularly briefed for an eventuality such as this). This is a part of my normal before takeoff emergency brief. As soon as I got nearing the tops of the trees I felt the lift reduce and the stall horn began. The controls were sluggish and I knew instantly that I needed to lower the nose to prevent a stall. I lowered the nose and tried to nurse it back up but very quickly realized something needed to be done as the runway was reducing and I didn't feel comfortable in the lift being generated being able to take me over the trees. I made a quick decision to reduce the power and attempt for an aborted landing. I pitched over; touched down; and hit the brakes. I realized that the runway was coming to an end and the hill was going to slope down. So I attempted to turn the aircraft using the rudders and was successful in slowing the aircraft and not going down into the sloped hill. Then; managed to stop the aircraft at the end of the runway. Once the aircraft was stopped; the engine was running; I pulled the mixture; switched the mags to off; and turned off the master. Post-incident inspection showed apparently minor prop damage (a ding in the prop) and nothing else appeared to be damaged. Postflight discussion with the pilot of the initial observed aircraft and he stated that he also felt the wind shift and was struggling to climb. The climbout seemed a little low to me; but it was not readily apparent to me that it was solely because of the winds. I surmise that a windshear event occurred from the changing wind direction because of the trees. Luckily; I had briefed for this eventuality and knew what to do. Things that went right:- Proper brief prior to takeoff which covered a change in wind due to the trees- Proper speed-wind buffer: this resulted in the lift that WAS available at that time and contributed to a safe landing without exceeding the critical Angle of Attack.  - Managed to stop the aircraft with minimal damage; and no occupant damageThings that went wrong:- Initial observation of the struggling climb of the aircraft on departure should have resulted in more hesitancy to depart to begin with

column121: I experienced a ground loop. Wind was 260 at 8kts; and tower had me land on Runway 16. My plane has conventional gear. Suddenly the plane turned right into the wind; despite my pressing left brake.We ended up in the weeds of the runway safety area; about 50 feet from the runway but facing towards it. I did not drag a wing tip or strike the prop. Neither I nor my passenger suffered any injury. Got grass between the left tire and the rim; and a shallow gouge in the tire's inner sidewall where it took off the brake bleeder valve. No other damage to the aircraft. Could start up; but could not taxi straight. Operations / Fire towed me back to my hangar. I called Tower with a report as requested; and gave a report to the Operations / Fire agent. I suspect I failed to keep the control stick into the wind on roll-out.

column121: We were on a repositioning flight to ZZZ on an IFR flight plan in VFR conditions. Upon being handed off to Approach; ATC instructed us to descend to 2000 feet and fly a westerly heading to join a right downwind for Runway 9 at ZZZ. We reported the airport in sight for the visual. ATC said that we would fly for several more miles to allow for a departure. ATC then instructed us to fly a heading of 360; cleared us for the visual approach; and to contact ZZZ tower. We complied with all instructions. As we turned a 5-mile base to final; we attempted to contact the tower three times as we continued our descent. At 900 feet; the tower finally responded and told us to immediately turn to a heading of 120 and climb and maintain 2;000 feet. As we began the turn and initiated a climb; tower announced several times in the same radio call that we needed to expedite our climb as there was traffic at 1;000 feet at our 12 o'clock; less than a mile. We aggressively climbed from 1;000 feet to 2;000 feet and was instructed to contact Approach for further vectors. ATC vectored us to a 9-mile right base and once again cleared us for the visual approach. We landed without further incident. After clearing the runway and asking ground control for a phone number to speak with the manager. The controller asked if it was about what just happened. We replied yes. She stated that it was Approach that gave the suggested heading of 120 that put us in direct conflict with the GA traffic that was at traffic pattern altitude on the right downwind for Runway 9. She said that it was Approach's fault and offered the TRACON phone number if I wanted it. I declined and informed her that I would file a NASA report and that the midair was entirely too close.

I could see the mountains in the distance and the pier about 8 miles to the southeast. Rather than continuing to orbit; I decided to fly along the coast past the pier and back. As I descended through about 800 feet; suddenly; there appeared a banner tow aircraft just barely above and slightly to the left. Even though I had visually cleared the area in front of me; I should not have flown a shallow; wings level; straight-ahead descent. column121: I am the owner of a Mooney M20E and have >300 hours in this plane. The flight in the late afternoon was a demonstration flight for a friend of mine who is considering beginning pilot training. He has done informal training many times over several years including with me; and has excellent instincts and innate skills that indicate he will be an excellent pilot. In addition; he has significant knowledge about airplanes; airplane systems and general aeronautical/ aviation information. Weather conditions were VFR and not challenging in any way. There were some mild clouds and precipitation in the area but we had no difficulty avoiding them throughout the flight.I flew left seat and handled all engine controls and critical phases of flight; takeoffs; landings; radio calls; etc. He had controls for much of the enroute time and legs of traffic patterns. We did standard maneuvers; mostly practice traffic patterns and landings at ZZZ1; which is close to ZZZ and is the most commonly used training field for many pilots out of ZZZ; including myself. We did three touch and goes and one full stop/ taxi back at ZZZ1. There was no indication of a gear problem for any of these several extensions or retractions. I have very recently done solo training flights with similar or greater numbers of gear extensions and retractions in a similar span of time with no indication of problem. After close to an hour of flying; we returned toward ZZZ for our final stop. We entered a long right base for Runway XXR; and at the appropriate time put the gear switch down. For the first time ever in this plane that I know of; there was a gear extension problem. The gear motor activated and could be felt extending the gear. It seemed mostly normal; but perhaps a little louder/ more forceful than usual. It stopped abruptly; it seemed to have taken a usual amount of time; but the gear on this plane do normally extend quickly and I could not be certain the motor had run as long as usual. The two gear down lights (one on the panel and one on the floor) did not illuminate. The gear actuator circuit breaker had popped out. I tried resetting the circuit breaker twice; but it did not stay in. The gear switch had no effect at this point; as expected with the circuit breaker tripped. The feel of the plane in flight felt as though the gear were down with the expected amount of drag.I advised ZZZ tower that we were breaking off the approach for troubleshooting of a gear problem; and headed generally north of the field in coordination with the controller. I pulled out the Owner's Manual; and my passenger assisted in reviewing the manual gear extension procedure; with which I am very familiar. I have practiced this on the ground a few times over the years at the time of annual inspection with the plane on jacks. I have also practiced it in the air at least once in this plane.With my passenger reviewing the steps out loud for me; I extended the gear manually. The hand crank did not reach a stopping point and the gear down lights did not illuminate. I checked the visual floor indicator; which is there as a backup in case of electrical failure; and the 'GEAR DOWN' sign was visible as normal when the gear extend; with the alignment bars lined up normally as per my memory of how they typically line up. Many additional cranks on the manual extension handle on several more tries had no further effect on anything that I could tell. We were concerned we might have a broader electrical problem of some type leading to failure of the indicator lights; even though the gear appeared to be fully extended. I checked another indicator light on the panel in the same cluster as the 'Gear Down' light (the 'Ram Air' light); which was working properly. I could find no other signs of electrical failure on board. There was no smell or sign of smoke.At this point; I contacted ZZZ tower and coordinated a low pass down Runway XXR to get a visual check of the gear. The tower controller was ableto see the gear well and reported all three appeared to be fully extended. The plane was performing well and maintaining control was not an issue. I was able to aviate; navigate and communicate easily and without difficulty; and to go through the appropriate manual gear extension procedure with plenty of time and focus. My passenger remained very calm; focused and helpful throughout. Neither of us became anxious or nervous; and we were able to communicate well and work together well. He was an asset to me functioning as part of the crew; even without formal pilot training. The ZZZ controller(s) likewise were extremely responsive; helpful and professional.I did not seem to have any additional options to try to get the 'Gear Down' lights to illuminate. I was fairly confident that the gear were fully extended. We were in no immediate danger; and there seemed to be no other emergency reason to land prematurely; although the possibility of some larger electrical system problem remained in my mind. As such; I decided that spending extra time in the air for additional attempts at troubleshooting was no longer wise and that we should land safely while conditions were good.The landing on Runway XXR was smooth; well controlled and uneventful. The wind was nearly straight down the runway and was light. I most often land with no flaps; and chose to do so in this case as well. I made sure to land with excellent technique; touching down gently just above stall speed; well aligned with the center line and with minimal control inputs. I made sure not to use the brakes; and I elected not to use the elevator for aerodynamic braking; as I wanted to avoid any unnecessary forces on the gear. I allowed the plane to roll out long on the runway; and all appeared to be going well. I let the tower know that I intended to roll out long due to the unknown status of the gear. Runway XXR is 7;500 feet long; I touched down not far past the numbers; and rolled out nearly to taxiway 1 for a total rollout distance of about 3;500-4;000 feet.After we had dissipated most of our forward speed without incident or sign of additional problem; I began a very gentle right turn toward the 'high speed' exit for taxiway 1. At that point; the plane began to settle toward the ground toward the left; with the front and right settling down very quickly after. The prop struck the runway and the engine quit; the plane skidded about 30 feet and came to a stop at a mild angle off center line. The impact with the runway was surprisingly soft from our standpoint. I quickly shut off the master switch; magneto switches; and fuel selector; and we exited the plane quickly and easily. There was no fuel spillage; smoke or fire. Neither of us sustained any injury of any kind.Using a heavy boom truck; we were able to gently lift the plane off the runway via the engine mount. I was able to easily manually extend the gear fully; and again was unable to get the 'Gear Down' lights to illuminate despite the gear being verified fully down; and the manual floor indicator properly aligned. While being towed away; the plane again settled to the ground toward the left when initiating a fairly gentle slow turn to the right. This time; only the left gear folded.At the time; shortly after; and for the next day or two I believed that I had properly pushed the crank forward to engage the manual gear extension mechanism and allow the handle to work properly. This is one of the basic few steps needed in the manual gear extension procedure; and I had done it many times. It is a small handle and lever located at approximately the left side of the left pilot's knee; and is easily reachable with your left hand. After reflecting on the events and going back to visit the plane; in fact I had not properly pushed that lever all the way forward. It appears that the manual gear extension mechanism will apply enough lowering force even when not properly engaged to allow the gear to fully or nearly fullyextend; but without the crank properly engaged it appears that you cannot get enough force to fully lock the gear in place.At the time of the [event]; although I and my passenger were under good control and responding well to the situation; I was approaching or beyond 14 hours since I had woken up and gone to work early that morning. I believe that pushing the end of my duty day; as well as familiarity with the procedure and not double checking myself that I had followed every step properly were contributing factors in my failure to fully lock the gear. I believe I could have prevented the gear collapse had I followed the checklist and double checked every step.We have not yet jacked the plane and examined all of the relevant components. Whether or not there is some other structural damage to the gear extension mechanism or any of the components involved; and whether or not we are able to ultimately demonstrate that the gear down lights were or were not in fact working; it does not change the fact that I did not properly complete one of the necessary steps on the checklist for manual gear extension. I also failed to catch this omission with a thorough review of the procedure and circumstances after the gear lights failed to come on. I allowed myself to give too much weight to the possibility of an indicator failure and did not continue to troubleshoot more when I have the ability to do so. I also believed that my familiarity with the procedure was sufficient that I did not consider that I might have omitted or failed to properly complete a step.As I reflect on this; it gives me a sense of humility and a reminder of my own fallibility; and reinforces that I need to double check checklists and critical steps at all times. My belief that my left hand had done what it was supposed to with respect to the one missing step was simply inaccurate. I could have and should have caught the error with a careful review of the circumstances; and there was not an emergency pressing need to get the plane on the ground immediately. I will carry this lesson for the rest of my life. Fortunately; no one was injured; and the mechanical and financial damage to the plane are the only costs. But it is still a humbling fact that I did a basic part of managing my aircraft incorrectly and caused damage as a result. In another circumstance; I or someone else could have been hurt with such an error. I will redouble my efforts to be meticulous for procedures; checklists; and review of critical items at all times. In addition; I will be more careful with respect to aircraft operations beyond 12 or 13 hours since waking up in the morning on any particular occasion.

When we arrived at the gate; our flight had begun deplaning. We were told that they had sat out on the tarmac for 2 hours before they were able to get to the gate and deplane so the aircraft could be checked out. During deplaning; Name 1 (the #4) and Name 2 (the #2) called the union and Name 3 to talk to them because we were very nervous about flying on this aircraft after it just came back to the gate and had to have us re-crew it due to a fume event. We did not know the original crew personally but as they deplaned they warned Name 2 and Name 1 that we should not get on that aircraft because something was wrong with it and that they were on the way to the hospital. They were shaken up; pale; and were visibly ill. One of the girls even had to get a wheelchair to wheel her out of the terminal. I immediately felt very unsafe about proceeding forward on this trip. Seeing the crew so visibly ill from a fume event and then being expected to take that aircraft right back out and move on like nothing happened is extremely terrifying and irresponsible of the flight deck. Our health and safety clearly was not a first priority in this instance. After original crew and passengers deplaned we were immediately sent down to the aircraft and the agent wanted us to check our equipment so we could board again and get this flight out as quickly as possible since it was so delayed. I was the first FA on the jet bridge; and I ran into the maintenance man on his way out. He told me he did an inspection of the aircraft and it was cleared to fly. He said he could smell stuff in the aft lavs but that everything was clear. He told Name 2 when he saw her that it was all good and to not get on and break anything. This was all happening so fast that it was hard to process it all and I was very uneasy and felt pressure to work this flight. After I got on the flight; the Captain was dismissive of the event. He informed me that he thought the previous crew was being overly cautious because two of the four flight attendants had just recently been through an incident on one of their trips that they had not been able to fully recover from; so that is why they turned around; but he did not think there was a serious issue to be concerned with. I interpreted this as the Captain thinking the previous crew was overreacting and that he did not take their concerns seriously. He and the First Officer said they attributed the fumes to there being a lot of aircraft congestion on the way out and that they thought it would be fine this time around. They said to let them know if we experienced anything this time; but it seemed as though the flight was going no matter what based on the flight deck's attitude. They continued to dismiss our fears before boarding started again saying it was fine to fly on this aircraft and that maintenance didn't see a problem. I was hesitant with this news because maintenance was on their way out not even 5-10 minutes after deplaning took place; and I did not think that was a substantial amount of time to do a thorough check of the aircraft. After the Captain informed me of this; my other crew members got on board and they asked me what he said. Name 2 was especially nervous because she has a health concern that if mixed with a fume event could be life threatening; so she went into the cockpit and had a long talk with the Captain. I'm not exactly sureof what he said to her because I was out of earshot but she told me he was dismissive and also mentioned what he said to me about the other 2 flight attendants from the other crew being overly cautious due to their past experiences on a trip. Name 2 told me that the Captain also made a joke when she expressed her concerns about how his mother thought he was the smartest guy in the world but there is always a chance that I'm wrong. We re-boarded passengers on the flight without there being a substantial amount of time to pass after it was deplaned the first time (like 15-20 minutes). During boarding; passengers kept asking me if it was safe to fly; and I told them that the Captain had told me he thought it was due to congestion from other aircraft that caused the smell the first time and that maintenance had cleared us to fly. The Captain never once made an announcement to the passengers to update them on the situation and reassure passengers once they re-boarded. Name 1 called Name 3 during boarding and asked Name 1 to ask the Captain if he had filled out the cabin odor fume report. Name 1 called me since he was in the back to ask. Name 2 had come to the front during boarding and she ended up being the one to ask the Captain. The Captain's response was that he had never heard of the cabin odor fume report before. There was another report that the union wanted us to ask about (the report is named with numerics) and when Name 2 asked the Captain about this he said he was going to pull it up but we never actually saw him do it. He then changed the subject with Name 2 to talk about his vacation that he was going on at the end of the trip. I had COVID back in Month and ever since I recovered; my taste and smell have not returned; so I am not a good judge on if there was an odor in this aircraft. However; Name 1 and Name 2 mentioned they smelled something gross in the back of the aircraft. Once in the air; Name 1 and I started feeling very light headed. Name 1 and the #1 Name 2 also started having a bad headache. During the middle of the service; there was moderate turbulence that continued the duration of the flight. We ended up having to suspend service because it was too dangerous to be in the aisle. I even felt like I caught some air at one point. We hurried to secure the carts and ourselves in the back. This is not what this report is about; but I think you should know that the Captain did not communicate with us the entire time about the turbulence or when it would end. We had to call him to ask if the turbulence would continue the rest of the flight and if there was a different altitude we could try because we were all feeling whiplashed in the back and queasy. He said we should suspend service and that he would make the announcement to the passengers about it. Name 1 then had to call him about 15 minutes later after the initial call to see if he was still going to make the announcement because he had yet to do it. He finally made the announcement to the passengers that we would not be completing the rest of the service due to the turbulence. However; he called the #1 Name 2 to make sure she had completed first class service because he wanted to make sure the customers were getting what they paid for. The Captain's unprofessionalism and lack of care for the flight attendants and our safety was astounding. Once we landed he and the First Officer were one of the first ones off the aircraft and they left to go straight to the van for their layover. These pilots ran off right when we landed. It was evident that the Captain was in a hurry to start his layover and had no concern for health and safety of his flight crew. He never once checked on us or asked us how we were feeling from the fume event or the turbulence. Now you have at least two flight attendant crews sick and a Captain and First Officer that could care less. Was this airplane truly airworthy? Name 1's headache continued for the next 3 days. On the second day of ourtrip; after we worked from ZZZ1-ZZZ2 Name 1 had to call out because he threw up mid flight; had a horrible headache; and had an upset stomach. He said his symptoms started that first flight from ZZZ-ZZZ1 and only continued. We had to get a standby from ZZZ2 to finish the trip with us. I have felt extremely lethargic ever since that flight. It feels like I took 10 Benadryl. I have had a very foggy brain and have slept non-stop. Writing this report is the longest I have stayed awake since I got home from that trip. I have also had shortness of breath. Name 1 and I went to the ER on Date 3 and got our hemoglobin levels tested and our chest x-rayed. Our hemoglobin levels were normal but that is to be expected since we went 48 hours after exposure. We called out on flight because we felt so sick and unable to fly. I talked to nurse when I called the number and after describing my symptoms she told me she was going to have me stop right there and recommend that I go get checked out at the ER and call her back within the next few days after I was checked out. I am still experiencing extreme brain fog; exhaustion; and shortness of breath. At the end of the day; we felt forced to get on an aircraft that had an issue and work Aircraft X to ZZZ1 because the union told one of the other flight attendants if we didn't we would get in trouble with the company and a refusal to fly. We have been given points against us when we were injured on the workplace in a fume event of some sort and now we are having our jobs jeopardized by points. The points are penalizing us for being sick and being taken to the hospital on a work injury/fume event. Why would a company that I give my time to penalize us for a work related injury? I want to recap that you have 2 crews that are sick with a Captain who was absolutely unprofessional; unsafe; and dismissive. This is a serious safety issue; and with this aircraft still flying you are risking the safety and health of passengers and crew members. Train your pilots and ground staff (the Tower and Ops) on how to handle fume events. We should have never taken this aircraft after knowing that 4 flight attendants were taken to the hospital sick and now we are all sick. At the end of the day; this flight deck crew and the company is responsible for our illnesses. I have not received any calls from our department. It is like no one cares how sick we are. This is my first fume event and I have had no guidance on how to handle this and proceed from here. Communication is key.
column123: I was on standby on Date at XA:00 sign in & was called at XE:15 to work the flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I was assigned position 4 on the trip with 3 other crew members. I made my way to the gate & as I arrived there were still passengers getting off the aircraft. I went over to the side & started talking to the crew that I was going to be working with. We saw the other crew come off & they did not look okay; the crew came over to us & said that the airplane had just had a fume event & that it wasn't safe for us to fly. We continued down the jet bridge after scanning in with the agent; upon arrival to the aircraft I saw that Maintenance was on board & talking to the Captain. As we got on we asked the Captain what had happened & if the airplane was safe to fly. He began to say that the other crew was just smelling fumes from the congestion on the taxi way & that it was nothing to be worried about. As I got to the back of the aircraft I smelt a terrible pee smell which seemed to be coming from the aft lavatory's. I informed the Captain but he said he was aware of the situation in the back. Our number 2 made sure to go up front & ask a bunch of different questions to the Captain about the aircraft & what had just happened. The Captain didn't give us much information with the plane & so I called the union. As I called the union; I was told to ask for a cabin air quality check; upon asking the Captain for this he said it was not necessary & that he wasn't needing one done. We tried our best with not feeling safe going on this aircraft; we boarded up & began pushing back. Upon push back; I was informed that 3 of the 4 flight attendants on that flight before us were headed to the hospital & one had to be wheeled out in a wheelchair. We were already taxing & there was nothing we could do at this point. We got up in the air & I started to have a terrible headache; later in the flight the number one came to the back & said that she was having a headache as well. We thought nothing of it for the most part; we then began to all feel light headed. We continued onto ZZZ1. The headaches continued onto the next day when we were working our flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2. About 30-45 away from landing I began to feel super nauseous from the flight & ended up getting sick on the flight. I proceeded to call the Captain to call tracking & have a standby waiting at the gate for me because I wanted to get off of the trip because I started feeling so sick. I got off the trip went to my hotel & slept for 12 hours before waking up. I was foggy & very out of it; very unlike me in any way. I still had my headache even after I had taken my medicine that I had been given by a doctor a while back for pain. The headache continued through the night & I was deadheading on a flight the next day; I was very very exhausted & short on my breath. I got on the plane not thinking much about it. As we were in the air I started to feel light headed; like I was going to pass out once again. Upon landing I got a message from the other crew informing me that 2 of the 4 had been in the ER still. One of the flight attendants did test positive for carbon monoxide poison. I proceeded to call the injury number and report everything to them. I was informed that I needed to go to the hospital & get checked out. Me & the number 3 flight attendant ended up going to the hospital together to get checked out; all of our tests came back normal but the doctor said that was to be expected since it was so long after exposure. He said there was a very good chance that is what it was but the test didn't show it. He gave us a note & recommended us stay rested & healthy. I don't believe that I should be punished with points for the company's inability to properly check the aircraft & deem it not safe. I should not be receiving any points for the situation as it was an injury on duty & was reported to the company in a timely manner. The points should not count against us in this event since it was a fume event. The points are given to us for being proactive about our safety & well being; Why would a company that I work for & give most of my time; want to give us points for a situation we believe is linked to an unsafe aircraft. We now have 2 crews who have been sick & however many after the fact. You have a Captain who was not in charge enough to say he wanted an air quality check of the aircraft for the safety of his crew & passengers. You still have this aircraft in service & are potentially putting other people's life & health at risk. Pilot & airplane need to be taken out of service for endangering passengers & crew members.

column121: I was flying with a private pilot student to practice landings at ZZZ1. We departed ZZZ; and arrived midfield at ZZZ1 at XA:40 local time according to my ADSB track log. Other traffic in the pattern was using Runway XX; so we made right traffic for XX. The student and I completed two laps in the traffic pattern for XX. On our third lap in the pattern; we were flying in front of another Skyhawk in the pattern; Aircraft Y. At XA:57 we turned base to final for runway 26 and made a radio call on CTAF. We heard Aircraft Y call base behind us. At XA:58; just past the numbers of Runway XX; I saw Aircraft Z low and climbing towards us. I could see his tail number. I called my controls and executed a go around and a turn to the right. I attempted to raise Aircraft Z on the radio; but had no answer. Aircraft Y responded to my calls and advised me that the aircraft appeared to be making a left crosswind turn and exiting the pattern to the north. I attempted to raise the pilot on 1XX.X; in case he maybe just had the frequency wrong; but this did not work to raise a response. My student and I exited the traffic pattern to the north to gain altitude. Then; re entered right traffic for [Runway] XX with a 45 degree entry to the downwind. We continued to make our radio calls for the traffic pattern. As we turned base for XX; I observed on my ADSB that Aircraft Z had made a 180 degree turn from his heading and was now headed directly for us; 300 feet high and descending. I took the controls and called a go around; extending the base. The aircraft was now at my altitude; close and lining up for the base to final for Runway XX. I had not heard any radio calls from the aircraft. We exited the ZZZ1 area and departed to another area until we could contact approach to get clearance back in to ZZZ for a landing. After the incident; I called the pilot of Aircraft Y to confirm what had happened. The pilot mentioned that they had landed at ZZZ1 and talked to a mechanic who witnessed the incident and talked to Aircraft Z after he had landed. According to the mechanic; the pilot of Aircraft Z said that they had a radio failure. It is unknown to me what transpired with the aircraft after that.

column121: I was involved in a rapid decompression event of an aircraft. I was acting as pilot in command of a reposition flight. We were filed under an IFR flight plan. At the time of the event we were cruising at FL410 and on frequency with ZZZ Center. While in cruise flight; roughly 1:10 into the flight we started experiencing a loss of pressurization in the cabin. I made my First Officer aware of the decompression; immediately donning the oxygen masks and requesting a descent from ATC. The frequency was cluttered with radio chatter and I was having trouble transmitting to ATC that we needed an immediate descent due to the loss of pressurization. Due to the hazardous nature of our situation I began a descent without being able to communicate with ATC. My First Officer immediately input the emergency squawk code of 7700 into our transponder to relay to ATC that we had an emergency. ATC saw our descent and queried us 'Aircraft X verify level at FL410.' I replied with 'We need a descent now.' ATC then cleared us to FL240 where we began running checklists and were able to stabilize our cabin altitude.Once we had the situation under control we informed ATC that we were no longer [in need of priority handling] and that we had our cabin altitude stabilized. My copilot and I agreed that the situation was under control and that our cabin altitude was stabilized enough to where we could safely continue our flight to our destination at FL240. We flew the remainder of the flight and landed safely without other incident.

column121: I received flight following enroute to ZZZ. After ATC approved my frequency change and squawk code change to 1200. I switched to CTAF frequency and AWOS. I made radio calls that I was approaching airport from several miles away and would be doing a 45 degree entry for [Runway] XX; full stop. I then made my radio call for a 45 degree entry on the 45 degree entrance for Runway XX right traffic. Preceding traffic did an entry via base leg and landed on Runway XX without incident. I proceeded to enter via 45 degree entry and made my turn to downwind right traffic at about 1;006ft MSL. I continued to make radio calls that I was right turn downwind XX for ZZZ. I heard nor saw no other traffic in the pattern nor making radio calls for ZZZ. No traffic appeared on my ADS-B in Stratus 2I unit either. Abeam numbers of Runway XX; I reduced power and start about a 500/min descent and was scanning for traffic and scanning for proper distance for a turn to base. As I descended a silver high wing banner towing aircraft came into view coming from the opposite direction slightly above me on downwind (maybe 35 feet above me) and was transitioning through the traffic pattern of ZZZ towing a banner. There was no time for a radio call at the closing rate of the two aircraft and I abruptly made a descending right turn to avoid a head on collision. The banner tow plane did not turn initially but made a right turn after I called on the radio letting him know he flew through the downwind leg of in the opposite of the pattern at ZZZ and nearly collided with me. He then made a right turn and proceeded to fly west toward the bay to avoid the pattern. He said he had no idea what I was talking about and was cursing on the radio. I then realized that he never saw me. I continued to make my base leg radio call and final approach radio call and landed without any other problems. This collision was avoided.

column121: Planned flight for the day was to ZZZ1 (for fuel) then to ZZZ. Preflight planning conducted with assistance from ForeFlight mobile application. Departed Runway XX. Climb to 1500 MSL; 14 min cruise to ZZZ1 with landing. Landed at ZZZ1. The flight was conducted satisfactorily. The aircraft was then fueled as necessary.Secondary preflight planning was completed. Satisfactory takeoff and climb out to 7;500 MSL. Approximately 29 minutes; started to notice engine roughness with a significant drop in tachometer RPM. The Pilot in command (PIC) took over as sole manipulator of control and emergency checklist for engine failure in flight initiated. Looked for suitable landing area. Increased in engine RPM occurred and became within glide distance of ZZZ. Engine roughness and drop in RPM began again and ZZZ Tower contacted; advising of need for precautionary landing due to engine roughness. Decision was made to not [get priority handling]. Smooth and satisfactory landing made at ZZZ. After slowing and attempting to turn off Runway; the aircraft did not have any right turning authority. Airplane would only turn left in circle when power applied. Suspected right tire or brake malfunction. Contacted the Tower and asked for permission to shut down aircraft on runway to inspect aircraft.Aircraft was satisfactorily shut down on Runway XY with airport crew arriving for assistance. On post flight walk around; it was found that the right tire became flat; no other external damage grossly observed. Also found to have fluid leak within right pilot side inside firewall. Aircraft was towed to FBO for diagnostics of engine and repair of right tire. When asked if needed to report anything to Tower or FAA; the ZZZ airport crew stated nothing was needed. Furthermore; the Tower did not mention of any need to provide any post flight report during communications. No accident or serious incident occurred.There were a few factors found on post-flight that may have caused the problems:1. Engine Roughness: The engine was new with approximately 28 hours on the engine. Engine during break in period was using Aeroshell 100W. Furthermore; this flight was conducted with cruise altitude at 7;500 MSL. Miscommunication and ill-information about any special procedures regarding aircraft break in were not discussed between aircraft owner and PIC. PIC was told to use 100W oil from previous aircraft owner (box in back of aircraft). Furthermore; the aircraft owner did not provide engine overhaul information or procedures needed for aircraft. On mechanic review; it was found that the left magneto was rotated 17 degrees causing the engine to overheat; an oil line by the firewall was damaged causing a leak; cylinders were glazed; induction air leak; and some crankcase oil leak. Overall a combination of these factors is what probably lead to engine roughness. Post flight testing; the engine performed within specifications 2250 static RPM; 600FPM climb; 2350 dynamic RPM. Engine oil consumption has increased; likely due to glazed cylinders; and is being sent to Company1 for re-honing. Furthermore; the magnetos are being sent in to [Company] Magneto to be re-checked.2. Right Flat Tire: No noted gross evident issues on pre-flight inspection for tires; struts; fairing; or braking systems. Landings was smooth and satisfactory. Theory for tire damage could be due to stuck break after landing and prior to right turn out to taxiway; in conjunction with weak spot on tire and/or a foreign object on runway and/or other. Tire was satisfactorily repaired at ZZZ. Reviewing this scenario there are a few factors to consider. There needs to be improved communication between aircraft owner and operator (PIC); especially during critical times where specific procedures are needed (such as a new engine break in). The right tire flat is a chance occurrence; and I do not think that the flight could have been handled different to prevent. The pilot did all in power to safely shut down the aircraft and immediately check out airplane to prevent any further damage.I have had a clean pilot record; commercial license and CFI. I will use the lessons from this flight for myself and all future students for the purpose of discussing complete airplane maintenance with airplane owners (especially new airplanes); what to do when engine becomes rough; and procedures to follow with a flat tire.
