column121: While on right downwind at Traffic Pattern Altitude (1000 MSL) to land runway XX at ZZZ; I reduced power abeam the arrival end of runway XX and started my descent. I was momentarily looking at the airport runway as I reduced my power. I then returned my vision to straight ahead and spotted a high wing airplane towing a banner approximately 100 feet below me; coming directly at me from my 11-12 o'clock position. He was less than 1/4 mile away when I first spotted him. At that time my altitude was approximately 950 feet. I immediately added power and pulled up as he passed no more than 100 feet below me and no more than 100 feet to my left. After he passed under me; he turned out to the west and departed the area at the same altitude. I made a radio call to the aircraft telling him he nearly hit me but he did not respond. Prior to that time; I had made 5 radio calls announcing my position and intentions beginning 8 miles north of the airport.The banner tow plane flew right through the ZZZ traffic pattern; directly opposing downwind traffic on the right downwind and between 100 and 150 ft. of traffic pattern altitude. He should not have been flying through the traffic pattern and was not communicating with aircraft in the area on the CTAF. He was initially in my forward blind spot; just under my nose. I spotted him when I lowered my nose to start my descent for landing on the downwind leg. He was a high wing aircraft (fabric body; silver colored) and likely did not see me above and slightly to his left. The approaching banner tow aircraft was not spotted until he was less than 1/4 miles ahead. Contributing factors were:1. His position in my forward blind spot below the aircraft nose. 2. A second factor is that the banner towing aircraft was approaching head on and provided a small profile for both the aircraft and the banner.3. He was flying through an active traffic pattern with aircraft actively communicating on the CTAF.4. He was not communicating his position or intentions on the CTAF while operating in the airport traffic pattern5. He was flying a non-standard traffic pattern leg; i.e.; opposed to downwind traffic.6. He was approaching from a position that was at first spotting; slightly outside the traffic pattern. Aircraft in the traffic pattern are dividing attention between the traffic pattern and the runway environment. My attention was diverted toward the runway for a few seconds just prior to the time the aircraft was first spotted.7. The banner towing pilot has a dangerous habit of flying through the traffic pattern at this airport as described in the additional incident below which occurred earlier on the same day. Additional Relevant Information:Earlier that day another pilot had a near miss with the same aircraft at the same location. He also had to take evasive action to avoid the aircraft. In his case; he was on right base for runway XX and the banner towing aircraft was just above his altitude.

column121: Aircraft X was issued a descent to 2500 feet but as soon as I said 2000; the pilot started to read back 2000. This caused the 500 (of the 2500) to be blocked and when I un-keyed; I just heard the call sign portion of the transmission. The aircraft descended to 2000 feet and asked for an altimeter setting and I noticed the aircraft below the 2500 minimum vectoring altitude (MVA) and assigned altitude. I issued low altitude alert and instructed them to climb to 2500 feet.  I missed the read back. This all stemmed from the aircraft departing ZZZ with a known mechanical issue and low on fuel. They had diverted to ZZZ earlier (unknown to me) and was trying to reposition back to ZZZ1.They departed ZZZ1 minimum fuel and would not accept an approach at ZZZ1 that was consistent with the flow of traffic. I should have [requested priority handling] for the pilot immediately and handled it as one. The pilot put the FAA in a tough situation as I was trying to do my best to help the pilots who were in a bind; but I also missed many things I should have done.I did not ensure the aircraft had the weather and NOTAMs at ZZZ1; [request priority handling] for the aircraft; advise them of their position when vectoring them on to the localizer; allowed them to intercept the localizer inside the final approach fix. I did not catch the lack of read back when I issued 2500 MVA altitude and they over keyed me with a read back of 2000. Issue a brasher to the pilot.  I need to make sure all the phraseology and regulations are followed on our side (ATC)However; Aircraft X's principle operations inspector needs to investigate if the flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 was conducted legally and safely. It was very apparent the urgency to land immediately after taking off from ZZZ. This should not have happened. This caused me to make shortcuts and put the FAA at risk of liability as well as put the pilots at risk of missing something like landing on runway XX at ZZZ1; a closed runway. The pilots were wanting to land on runway XX at one point.
column123: Upon departure from ZZZ to ZZZ1; a short 5 minute or so flight; we were given a heading and an initial altitude of 3000 feet on initial departure. Given we were taking the plane in for maintenance; the plane had enough fuel to meet the minimum FAR requirements for an IFR flight. While setting up for the approach at hand; we were told by the controlling facility to descend and maintain 2;000 feet which was read back. A couple minutes went by as we were being vectored in for the approach and ATC gave us a low altitude alert followed by a command to 'descend and maintain 2;500 feet MSL'. Having already been cleared down to 2000 feet initially after we asked for lower; we read back the instruction for 2;500 feet followed by a 'we were initially cleared down to 2;000 feet MSL'.At that point; the controlling facility told us that they weren't going to debate over it and we instigated the climb to 2;500 feet. We only meant to reiterate the initial 2;000 foot altitude instruction for clarification purposes; not for argumentative purposes; as that was the initial instruction given to us after all. After landing; we received a phone call to contact the appropriate controlling facility to clarify the situation. We pulled the tapes from the appropriate controlling facility at the time of the incident and the tapes coincide with our initial hearing of '2;000 feet MSL;' not '2;500 feet MSL'. The altitude is clearly heard as 2;000 feet being the instruction given and 2000 feet being the instruction read back; not '2;500'. In order to keep a situation like this from reoccurring; an articulate tone should be adopted in order to hear and say the correct altitude assigned. Given that a weather system was rolling through as well; that added extra workloads on both us; the pilots; along with the controlling facility.

column121: Aircraft X was on a vector descending to 5;500 feet for the GPS approach. Aircraft X read the heading and altitude assignment correctly. Aircraft X was issued a base turn heading 060. I then told the pilot to 'check their altitude immediately' and that the MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude) in the area was 5;400 feet. I received no response so I repeated the climbing instruction with an amendment to maintain 5;400 feet instead. I then asked the pilot to read back the altitude assignment. The pilot did not read back the numeric altitude. I then instructed Aircraft X to join the final approach course upon reaching 5;400 feet. I observed Aircraft X reach 5400 feet quickly and safely. Aircraft X was cleared for the RNAV/GPS Approach and landed without incident.I recommend having a quarterly conversation with the local flying community around BTV's airspace. There are a multitude of flying clubs and academies that can benefit from a conversation with BTV ATC. The format for these conversations could include in person tours; sit-downs; or e-mail correspondence. Events like this can be avoided; in my opinion; by explaining the importance of understanding altitude assignments; approach information for our lengthy; step-down; ILS and RNAV/GPS Approaches and expectations. Most of the flying community around BTV flies in and out of uncontrolled airports."

column121: During an 18-hour duty day with multiple discrepancies; write-ups; MEL's; a rejected takeoff; a turnback to the gate; and other issues; we departed Runway XXL at ZZZ for the ZZZZZ RNAV departure. We had just finished 5 hours on the ground dealing with a hydraulic 3 elevator shutoff valve and inoperative 3-2 non-reversible motor pump; and had briefed the possibility of an associated flight control problem on departure. During the initial climb; we were instructed to maintain 250 kts and acknowledged. Our speed did not require a high-speed climb. Repeatedly during this event (prior to slat retraction; and intermittently all the way to final cruise altitude); we got am amber-boxed engine 1 compressor vibration indication; averaging 4.5 units of vibration. This required retarding power on engine 1 (up to one knob-width; and up to 7-10% N1 reduction); to bring the vibration out of the amber range. When reaching 3;000 feet and just beyond ZZZZZ1 on the ZZZZZ; we began the clean-up process on schedule; and upon slat retraction; the airplane rolled left. I countered with considerable right aileron. The strong rolling moment occurred coincident with slat retraction. Shortly after; we got a master caution and two level 1 EAD messages (SEL LSAS LOB OFF; SEL LSAS RIB OFF); for which I called for the [Relief Pilot] and FO (First Officer) to address and confirm before selecting off. As that occurred; we got a caution light with a lateral fuel imbalance (LAT FUEL UNBAL); which occurred three more times (four total); along with a 2;000 kg drop in fuel quantity (repeat write-up). While focused on the control issue; I allowed airspeed to increase briefly above the 250 kts limit; estimated to be 270 kts; before decreasing speed again to maintain 250 kts to 10;000 feet ATC did not mention the overspeed; but the [Relief Pilot] did call 'airspeed.' The ZZZZZ departure includes a restriction to remain below 3;000 until ZZZZZ1; then a climb to 15;000 or above; by ZZZZZ. My priority was addressing the control issue; but adjusted pitch per the flight director to return to 250 kts. No further variations from the speed schedule occurred during the remainder of the climb; or flight. Additional distractions occurring in series (except the engine vibration indication; which occurred intermittently throughout the event); one after the other; did not cause the airspeed excursion; but certainly worked to divert attention; and increase cockpit workload.I became aware of the amber boxed vibration indication about the time we entered the 1100 ft. ceiling; departing ZZZ. I became aware of the rolling moment immediately upon slat retraction; and the airspeed excursion upon the 'airspeed' call by the [Relief Pilot]. I did note the pitch attitude below that commanded by the flight director; and noted speed increasing; but the intent was to increase airspeed through slat retract speed to 250; and I focused on the immediate concern; the rolling moment. I did not notice the speed exceed 250 until the [Relief Pilot] brought it to the crew attention with the 'airspeed' call. At that time; I observed approximately 270 on the airspeed indication; and increased pitch to the flight director pitch bar to reduce speed. The FO was occupied retracting slats; and performing the follow-up flow associated with my call; 'slats retract; after takeoff checklist.' Aside from being distracted by the rolling moment; the illumination of the amber compressor vibration indication on engine 1; subsequent LSAS failure; and fuel imbalance were contributing errors to detection; and detection was voiced by the [Relief Pilot]. I became aware of the LSAS issue; and the lateral fuel imbalance issues; with illumination of the master caution light. The LSAS issue caused loss of autopilot 2. I delayed autopilot engagement until the series of issues were addressed; given that they included flight control and subsequent autopilot engagement problems. Once those were addressed and we were outside the busier airspace; the enroute climb and remainder of the flight until descent; were largely uneventful; except for continued monitoring and adjusting of engine 1 throttle position to prevent high compressor vibration. The period of time between detection of the event and the filing of this report is accounted by the end of a long duty day; the necessity of filing another report on the previous leg rejected takeoff in ZZZ1; and then flying home.We had briefed the possibility of a flight control problem; given the return to the gate for the system 3 Hydraulic elevator shutoff valve; and associated 3-2 non-reversible motor pump. The fix on the ramp had been to add another two gallons of fluid to system three; with the explanation that 'maybe the gauge is just reading high.' I did not find that explanation satisfactory; but following an engine run in which the problem did not reoccur; maintenance was satisfied; the write-up was signed off; and we departed. About the time we entered the cloud layer; the amber-boxed engine 1 compressor vibration alert illuminated; and power was reduced on engine 1 slightly (up to one knob width) to reduce the vibration indication. This indication came and went; as we climbed; necessitating further slight reductions in power. The flight control problem which occurred after departure (strong left rolling moment; coincident with slat retraction) did not match the potential problem (possible elevator shutoff valve actuation and NRMP malfunction); but did merit attention; during which time I let the airspeed slip. I focused on leveling the wings and reduced angle of attack. I should have maintained pitch with the flight director; but divided the task of roll and pitch to prioritize directional control; while addressing the uncommanded rolling moment. Additional subsequent illumination of the master caution with the LSAS failure; and the lateral fuel imbalance level 2 warning and master caution illumination; were peripheral distractions; as was the engine vibration issue. I was hand flying at the time; and believe it was better to be hand-flying with the potential to feel a problem; than have it masked by the autopilot. Had the autopilot been flying; the speed excursion would likely not have occurred; but we may not have seen or felt the rolling moment as much; if at all. I did feel a shift in the controls when the LSAS was selected off; but couldn't say afterward exactly what I'd felt. In retrospect; the best course would have been to focus on the flight director while addressing the roll. The natural tendency when experiencing that event (rolling moment); for me; was to decrease angle of attack slightly; which I did; which resulted in the excess speed as we accelerated while cleaning up. The rolling moment was caused; I am certain; by asymmetric slat retraction; the degree of asymmetry I couldn't say; but it was significant in feel and the amount of aileron deflection needed to counter the roll. There was no buffet. It was significant enough that on arrival in the ZZZ2 area; we briefed the possibility of the same event when extending slats; and I hand flew the descent and arrival; configuring slats early. A rolling moment did occur; but not to the same degree as departing ZZZ. (We also experienced a strong rolling motion that resulted in heading change; with autopilot engaged; when deploying speed brakes; and observed speed brake asymmetry on the configuration synoptic page; and determined not to use speed brakes further on the subsequent ZZZ2 arrival). These aircraft discrepancies; while important; should not have detracted from the basic task of flying the airplane; or maintaining the assigned/required 250 kts. on departure from ZZZ. Additionally; the subsequent illumination of the master caution light several times with LSAS failure and lateral fuel imbalance issues served as peripheral distractions. The tendency for engine 1 compressor vibration to show high with amber-boxed indication; repeatedly; and to require the engine power to be retarded repeatedly; was also a distraction. Retarding power on the no. 1 engine further caused a slight yawing motion; and subsequent potential rolling moment. Flying all night and then a five hours of trouble shooting on the ramp in a hot airplane didn't help; prior to this takeoff.My reaction to the high compressor vibration indication on engine 1 was to retard the No. 1 throttle slightly; the problem was known and a recurring one which had become a repeat write-up. My reaction to the 'airspeed' call was to note the speed and increase pitch to the flight director pitch bar; after observing airspeed in excess of 250 kts. I followed the flight director command while re-acquiring and holding 250 kts; and flying the departure. My reaction to the subsequent master caution illumination was to direct the First Officer and [Relief Pilot] to work together; specifically on the LSAS issue; because with one FCC affected; I wanted confirmation on selecting the correct switches off. The lateral fuel level 2 warning was familiar; as it keeps happening and keeps being written up on this airplane. On arrival; I wrote it up again. The engine vibration was a repeat write-up that was squawked multiple times; and was subsequently written up again on arrival in ZZZ2. On arrival in ZZZ2; the [Relief Pilot] asked if I thought we should file an report; and I advised that yes; I thought it prudent. I advised the crew to file what they saw; individually. After that; I was occupied discussing multiple discrepancies and write-ups with Maintenance; and with the incoming crew as they arrived. It was a very long night and day; and a full duty day. We had a rejected takeoff; ATC directed; at ZZZ1 on the first leg; and I had to write a report for that; after arriving at the hotel. I made that report; and the next day flew home; where I slept for an extended period. This report is submitted outside the 24-hour window; when I had rested adequately to be awake to write it. I did write up the flight control issues; to be addressed by Company Maintenance Personnel.My actions were my own; and my responsibility. I was the Pilot Flying; and the Captain; and I was hand flying; and regardless of distractions; should not have allowed the airspeed excursion to occur. That said; we should not be seeing so many discrepancies and issues; especially on one flight (let alone one phase of flight simultaneously or subsequently in close succession; and especially not items which have been written up multiple times). These issues ranged from multiple flight control issues to fuel system indications and issues; engine vibration; and even a TCAS fail during the initial climb. The subsequent issues that occurred on the flight including multiple items that were repeat write ups; including a level 2 fuel lateral fuel imbalance several times during the departure. The LSAS failure is also a repeat write-up. I do not include these as excuses for failing to maintain the airspeed at 250 kts; as that was my responsibility; but these are certainly things which do not need to be happening on every flight; as a regular part of flight operations; and this can be fixed. So far as preventing this specific event from occurring again; my counsel is to point my finger at myself and what I would say to anyone else: 'fly the damn airplane.' I need look no farther than myself as the reason for failing to maintain 250 kts as cleared; and as required by the regulation; and as the captain; the buck stops with me. We can prevent it; in my cockpit; by my not allowing it to occur again. The question will arise why the autopilot was not engaged earlier in the series of events. I had briefed a hand-flown departure. The engine vibration; while a distraction; did not rise to the level of needing automated intervention; and was familiar; having occurred previously and been a repeat write-up. The rolling moment was not something I wanted masked by engaging the autopilot;

column121: I was doing student training in the vicinity of ZZZ at FL270. The clouds were building in the area and climbing up through our flight level in a relatively short amount of time. The ATCAA (ATC-assigned Airspace) was just south of our position and went hot while we in the area. Center restricted our working airspace clearance to remain north of the ZZZ airport and we accepted. The weather and high clouds were just a few miles north of ZZZ and started to severely limit our maneuvering airspace and we were getting boxed in between staying out of the weather and complying with the airspace clearance. During crew swap; I briefed the incoming pilot about the weather/high clouds and the requirements to stay north of the ATCAA. I also advised him that it was probably time to depart the area as it was becoming unworkable due to the building weather. I showed him that my student was currently on a heading that was pointing in the direction of the weather (approximately 040 heading) and he would need to turn south before the aircraft entered the cloud and possibly picked up ice. I did not specify; but I intended for the turn to be made to the right where there was still clear air. It also should have been a manual bank heading to steepen the bank angle enough to avoid flying into the ATCAA. I assumed he understood what I wanted him to do; but I did not get any communication from him that he was confused about my instructions. He said he's got it and then proceeded with the crew swap and dismissed my student from the flight controls. After the incoming pilot sat down; he commanded a left turn with the autopilot (14 degrees of bank) and turned right into the clouds. The aircraft began picking up icing and he [contacted] Center to avoid flying into more weather/icing. Upon my student exiting the ground control station; I began talk to him about his handover briefing and I did not notice the aircraft turning left until it was already in the weather. I debriefed with the incoming pilot later and he told me at the time of the crew swap; he had no idea where the clear air was and therefore was forced to exit the area immediately which resulted in him eventually [contacting] Center in order to get clear of the weather.

column121: I was assigned D-side to Sector 02/17 after a 40 minute break from position. By the time I sat down on position the R side was already too busy to give me a briefing and we already needed a tracker which we did not receive for 30 minutes. The Warning Areas were active up to FL 500 with an aircraft doing air work at FL450. There was a line of extreme precipitation from ORL to the warning areas which did not allow any northbound traffic. The northbound traffic was deviating from the adjacent sector to the west (Sector 65/68) and eventually they started handing them off to us on vectors climbing into the weather while we had opposite traffic southbound head on. Meanwhile; while this was happening ZJX KEYSTONE and ST AUG Sector (J58/J76) told us that they could not take the aircraft northbound if they were going to enter the warning areas. I started pointing the aircraft out to the military so ZJX could take them and they still refused and had us vector the aircraft out in an attempt to not violate their airspace. Meanwhile I was told by my CIC (Controller in Charge) to tell ZJX that we are unable to take any more aircraft and that they need to hold their aircraft. column121: On the RNAV Stadium Visual to runway 29 we were vectored behind an Airbus 321 on the ILS to 22R.  We joined the visual at GIMEE with the airport and the [A321] in sight.  We had been cleared to land prior to crossing GIMEE.  Tower reported winds calm; ATIS had winds 200/6.  Prior to SLIMR we were configured and slowing to approach speed.  At approximately 1;500 ft AGL I called for the landing check and called to the FO that [the A321] appeared to be crossing the numbers and spacing looked good.  Continued in LVAV/VNAV till the autopilot rolled us out on final at about 1;000 ft AGL.  At this point PAPI showed slightly high and corrected to visual glide path.  A rapid right roll was encountered just prior to touchdown causing contact of the right main. This slowed the roll but aircraft was still rolling right.  Immediate left aileron was applied along with deployment of the auto speed brakes quickly caused the left main to touch down.  Roll out was normal from this point.  Wing drop was so rapid that I thought the right gear leg had collapsed.  The event occurred so quickly that there was not even time to consider a go-around.  The application of power and lifting off again would likely only have exacerbated this situation placing us at a bank angle at low speed with an at the time unknown problem.  During debrief we determined that the event occurred just prior to the intersection with Runway 22R and was likely a wake turbulence event.  An ACARS generated report showed a max bank angle of 6.9 degrees with a predicted wing tip strike at a bank angle of 7.5 degrees.  The FO inspected the aircraft for possible damage; none was found.  The event was reported to Tower; but they did not seem concerned.  I contacted Clearance Delivery to get more information on the preceding aircraft.  CD took more interest and sounded like it would be reported.

The FA calls back and says it is coming out of the gasper vents in the galley and it was getting stronger after I turned off the recirculating fans. We were waiting for parking crew at this point and in 44c temps I was trying to keep as much cool air as possible. Eng bleeds were both turned off. APU bleed on ; left pack high ; iso closed. We could not smell anything in the front; so I figured it wasn't from the left pack or APU. At the gate; ground air was hooked up and the second the jetway was up and door opened I instructed via the pa for all passengers to grab their belongings and exit the plane. After the passengers deplaned; I went to the back and could smell the residual coming from the gasper. It was a melting plastic smell. column121: I elected to perform a high speed aborted takeoff due to pop up severe weather conditions. Prior to departure; the weather was VFR and clear. Small thunderstorms were developing around the area north of the airport; but nothing was seen while taxiing to the runway. Both crew members engaged weather radar with an upward tilt; with nothing indicating the possibility of weather impacting departure. ATC issued a takeoff clearance for runway XX and advised us of a small cell of extreme precipitation north of the airport; and said it didn't appear to be a factor. We were lined up on Runway XX; facing south; and could not see any adverse weather around us. After initiating the takeoff roll; at around 100 knots; we encountered immediate extreme precipitation and wind forces. Visibility was reduced to 0 (I could not even see the nose of the aircraft). Simultaneously; ATC advised of 40-60 knot windshear over the runways and of a micro burst. Due to being unable to see out of the windshield and feeling the wind forces coupled with the windshear and micro burst warning; I elected to abort the takeoff. I estimate that the abort was initiated at 115 knots accounting for the reactionary delay of retarding the thrust levers. The flight attendant verified no one was injured. Aborted takeoff procedures were followed; and after a follow up with maintenance; dispatch; we were able to depart normally after the cell had passed.The conditions were not present at the time of takeoff; and no one (flight crew nor ATC) had a way to predict such a rapid; immediate change. We used wet takeoff numbers as a precaution since there were storms in the forecast while at the gate. I believe all parties involved functioned proficiently.

column121: En route from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 we were directed by the physician on call to divert to ZZZ which we had just passed at FL350. The Captain gave me controls of the aircraft and radios and began the fix strategy. We were given a heading direct to ZZZ and began a descent to the airport. We began the approach on a visual right downwind as there was a cell to the north and west of the airport we wanted to avoid. Selected speed was chosen as we slowed down; however; when managed speed was selected the aircraft accelerated because I had not activated the approach. We captured the error; however; these few seconds caused us to be high and fast. Given the already high-altitude airport and compressed diversion time for the medical issue; we elected to do a visual left 360 and rejoin final. We had selected the final approach fix altitude; however; when we did our left 360 turn it took us away from the airport. The Tower Controller alerted us that he had an altitude alert and we climbed back to the 7;200 feet altitude for the fix we were now joining the ILS. We continued the approach without further issue.Cause - 1. Compressed; high pressure with the medical emergency of passenger with 60/40 blood pressure.2. Out of sequence normal approach and landing with the diversion that greatly compressed our time from top of descent to landing. 3. Choosing ZZZ - high altitude/high terrain as a divert airport.4. Loss of situational awareness as we made the turn away from the airport.Suggestions -1. Take vectors out for a longer final approach.2. If possible; choose diversion airports that have less threats. 3. If a turn for an airport is needed to descend or slow - make them towards the airport not away as altitude is less likely going to be an issue with regards to terrain avoidance.
column123: During a medical divert we were high and fast.  On approach we accomplished a left 360 to descend. We never descended below 6;300 feet before the FAF.Visual approach; high and fast resulted in loss of situational awareness.  Avoid visual approaches when in unplanned situations; get vectors for an instrument approach.

column121: During the preflight of the aircraft; my student performed the inspection. He called me in when he was having trouble removing the oil dipstick of the right engine to inspect oil level since it was secured very tight and was hot to the touch. I came out there with a napkin to use as an insulator for our fingers and managed to loosen the dipstick by using both my hands. I checked the oil level and handed the dipstick to the student for him to do the same. He placed the dipstick back in and secured it; and I doubled checked that the stick was secure by loosening and retightening it. I then proceeded to run my own quick check of the aircraft by verifying the oil in the left engine and checking the fuel quantity onboard. We found no issues with the aircraft and proceeded with the flight.About an hour into the flight; we were in the south practice area performing Vmc demo with the student at the controls. During the maneuver; I had noticed an oil slick starting to form off the right engine. For the maneuver; we were operating the right engine at full power while the left was idle. To make sure we are all on the same page; I pointed out the slick and had him start turning back to ZZZ. I instructed him to scissor the throttles; go full power on the left engine and idle the right engine. I immediately called up our dispatch and informed them of our engine trouble while they coordinated preparations at the school; airport; and rescue services as part of the company procedures. About three minutes after we idled the right engine; the oil temperature was rising to the limit. Since we were holding 3;000 feet at the time with an idling engine with good performance; and I did not want to risk having a seized engine I elected to shut the engine down and feather it. We informed dispatch; and then followed the appropriate checklist. And elected to continue to ZZZ since they still needed time to prepare the field for our arrival with emergency services; familiarity; and long runways available. On the way back; I shifted my attention to the student and briefed what happened; and what we are going to do from now. During this time; I had him at the controls flying while I ran the checklists with him. I briefed that I would have him fly to ZZZ but once we start maneuvering; I will take the controls for descent and landing. As we were nearing the field; dispatch called us requesting we circle the field if performance allows for a few minutes while they still waited for rescue to arrive. Once we were about 3 miles south at 3;000 [feet]; dispatch called again telling we do not need to circle anymore; and that the airport will not call rescue. I really did not want to stay in the air longer than we needed to; and changing the plan now would have increased risks; I opted to continue to land. I took the controls at this point; and since we needed to lose altitude; I decided to fly a normal pattern and flew down to make a normal 45 entry for runway 20. Runway 20 was the longest runway with most favorable wind conditions. The landing was successful. The airport was closed for our recovery; and we planned to shut down on the runway and get a tow; but I was nervous about another aircraft behind me on short final; so I used the remaining speed of the aircraft to turn off onto the taxiway at about 10 knots.During the post flight inspection; we could not see anything out of place other than the oil streaks. We checked the dipstick and saw that it had slightly loosen but appear to be seated. But when maintenance performed their inspection; they determined the oil dipstick was cross threaded. They determined this was the most likely source of the oil leak. Only about a quart of oil was lost in flight.I think obviously the biggest factor here was the dipstick not secured properly. I was not aware how easily the dipstick could be cross threaded. The biggest learning moment for me was paying closer attention to how the dipstick is seated. In the specific aircraft; the dipstick sits directly on the engine block; and you can only easily see the dipstick from a top view unlike other aircraft I operate such as the other [aircraft type] where the dipstick is sits on a pipe that protrudes from the engine where the dipsticks cap is visible from the side. I think what also did not help was the fact we used a napkin to hold the dipstick during the preflight; which also visibly covered it. I think from here on out I am going to make sure some gloves are accessible and emphasize to my students the potential risk of cross threading.However; I am concerned about the airports handling of this situation. It was revealed when we landed; the airport management seemed to have not deemed our situation important enough to call in fire rescue as a precaution. They also have seemed to do a poor job of closing the airport as aircraft were still taking off and landing even when they announced multiple times over the radio the airport is closed. When I landed; a aircraft was flying not too far behind us in the pattern; and I had to move the aircraft on a single engine off the runway out of concern they would land on top of us which added the risk to us. But in the end of the day; the aircraft made it back in one piece; and most importantly my student and I made back safe.

column121: After conducting an aerobatic practice flight; I entered the pattern on the 45 degree leg to downwind behind two other aircraft; a Cherokee and a C182.  The Cherokee was operated by the local flight school and was in front of the C182.  The C182 was flying a wider than normal downwind; 3 times the size recommended by the airport.  The Cherokee did the same and flew a 1.7 mile long final with no other traffic in front of him.  This caused me to perform two 360 degree turns to increase spacing.  I also performed S-turns on final but got too close to the C182 so I went around.  During the go-around the C182 announced that he was disabled on the runway.  I orbited and then started to divert to ZZZ1 but realized that I did not have enough gas to get there.  I returned to the ZZZ pattern; declared a fuel emergency on CTAF and landed without incident on taxiway A.  My low fuel state was caused by two factors: the excessively large traffic patterns flown by flight schools causing two 360 deg turns; s-turns; and a go-around; and the limitation of the Extra 300/S to prohibit aerobatic flight with fuel in the wing tanks limiting the amount of fuel on board to 12.9 gallons.The FAA must push flight schools to fly tighter traffic patterns. column121: While flying on an IFR flight plan from to ZZZ1 at 4;000 feet the Controller contacted me and asked for my altitude. When I learned I could get in without having to shoot an approach I asked to be vectored and stated that I was not declaring an emergency at the time. I was cleared direct and informed he would call ahead to advise of the situation. I was unable to acknowledge as my Garmin 650 would not transmit; nor would the Narco that's our COMM2. I squawked 7600 and hit IDENT. I was able to hear the controller trying to raise me but couldn't respond. The GPS screen went black about a minute later so I decided to descend to get below the clouds. I continued towards ZZZ with no electronics. I next connected my cell phone to the blue tooth on my headset and called my father who is also a private pilot and asked him to telephone the Tower; tell them I'm requesting priority and that I will be landing on Runway 23 in about 15 minutes and that I was experiencing an electrical failure. I noticed electrical sparks coming from under the co-pilot side of the panel when I was about 2 miles out so I killed the master power and the alternator immediately. My landing was largely uneventful and actually better than I was expecting; given the conditions.

Lightning reported on the finals to all Runways; airspeed fluctuations reported on final; audible Wind Shear Alerts continuous all runways; 15 knot wind shift approaching the SLC Airport. Light to occasional moderate chop reported in the area. Tailwinds on final.Aircraft Y vectored to a 15 mile right base; cleared for Visual Approach to Runway 17 at SLC; switched to Tower. Traffic Management Unit calls down to TRACON through speaker in the Supervisor's console that Aircraft Y had a Lightning Strike and coordinated a heading 270 at 9;000 feet. I responded Radar Contact. Tower initiated the Heading 270 on a 9 mile final at 9;000 feet; which you never do; however; Aircraft Y was coordinated at 9;000 feet.  I kept Aircraft X expediting to 6;000 feet; which would not be an issue as long as Aircraft Y leveled at 9;000 feet. This was not the case as I observed Aircraft Y continuing descent through 8900 feet and continuing.  Recognizing this immediately; Aircraft Y appeared to be an Emergency aircraft not knowing what altitude he would be stopping at; I issued traffic to Aircraft X followed by a Traffic Alert with a heading 270 immediately to avoid a mid-air collision; all the while I was still not talking to Aircraft Y performing evasive maneuvers in my airspace.As soon as Aircraft X was past Aircraft Y I would then have divergence. I turned Aircraft X to heading 340; and issued a Low Altitude Alert and climbed him immediately to 7800 feet; while doing so I see Aircraft Y turning to the same north heading 340 at 8000 feet; with Aircraft X just West of Aircraft Y on a parallel course; and not talking to Aircraft Y in my airspace; not having lateral separation; I immediately turned Aircraft X to heading 310; all the while trying my best to achieve some sort of radar separation; and avoid a collision; until I find out who is talking to Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y at 8;000 feet is not what coordinated nor approved by me in my airspace; and a Heading 270 off the finals is never performed; for this exact reason. This is an unsafe operation with traffic in the downwind. Aircraft Y at 8;000 feet leaves no options at all.After determining the adjacent sector controller; who is only certified on those positions; was working Aircraft Y; in which Tower switched him to my airspace; when I had conflicting traffic. The adjacent sector controller provided zero communications to me; even though I repeatedly asked who was working Aircraft Y and what is he doing?  After I had Aircraft X squared away; they just happened to say 'Aircraft Y had your Aircraft X in sight and was maintaining visual separation.'This would have been nice to know.When an aircraft is coordinated to be 9;000 feet then have the aircraft be at 9;000 feet; not at 8;000 feet; which leaves the final sector Controller absolutely no way out. No attempt was made to by Tower who assigned 8;000 feet; or by the adjacent sector who received the aircraft at 8;000 feet to advise the sector who owns the airspace with an aircraft in direct conflict. When a heading of 270 and 9;000 feet is coordinated with another sector; a Departure Only Sector; then make sure he enters the airspace for which that specific coordination was originally made; and not another sector that has conflicting traffic with that type of coordination.No coordination or even a point out was attempted to be made to the appropriate sector in which the vital coordination directly impacts. When Visual Separation is applied between two aircraft that are in direct conflict with each other; it is absolutely a top priority to ensure that all parties involved receive this valuable bit of information.When a Controller takes it upon themselves to accept the responsibility of an aircraft in someone else's airspace at an altitude that is in direct conflict with an aircraft that you are not in communication with and at a different altitude than what was previously coordinated; then it might be a top priority to advise Controller working the aircraft in his own airspace that he is in direct communications with that visual separation is being applied. When a controller is taking evasive actions to prevent a mid-air collision with an aircraft that you are talking to; that is not in your airspace; and you are providing control instructions to; don't sit quietly when you hear 'Who is talking to Aircraft Y'?

The aircraft was out of 8;500 feet when I took the handoff and checked on out of about 9;400 feet climbing to 16;000 feet. I climbed the aircraft to 2;6000 feet as I had no traffic in the area. The majority of my attention was focused on the south side of the sector where I had a VFR aircraft inbound to ZZZ2; an IFR aircraft inbound to ZZZ2 who was just out of 40;000 feet 45 miles from the airport as well as an additional VFR aircraft who was climbing and descending that needed lost communication procedures. Shortly after climbing Aircraft X; he reported that he needed to level off at 100 feet due to traffic above at 10;500 feet; I looked and I did see the numbers XXX on the scope but the target associated with these numbers was obscured by the target from Aircraft X.I was trying to figure out if there was actually traffic there and if there was traffic there why I had not received any kind of CA (Conflict Alert) indication (nothing was flashing at all) and since this was well within the lateral and vertical confines of Approach's airspace why they had climbed the aircraft into traffic within their airspace. I acknowledged Aircraft X and approved his request to level off; at that point he told me he was responding to an RA. I was surprised by this; but just asked him to report on course and when he resumed his climb. A few minutes later he told me that he was going to report the incident. At that time I responded trying to calm him down and let him know that I had already notified the supervisor that he had responded to an RA. A few minutes after that; Aircraft X pilot informed me that he was going to report it as a 'near midair'. Again I attempted to defuse this situation; informed the Controller in Charge and told him I would contact Approach to find out more details. We then gave him the information to contact the Center Operations Manager in Charge as well as the Approach Control Supervisor. Approach Control should have called the traffic and not shipped me the aircraft until they were clear. The Conflict alert should have been going off for several minutes; which would have alerted both myself and Approach Control to the unusual situation. At that point I would have seen the non-associated VFR target and called the traffic. We should have better staffing so that we aren't working 6 day work weeks and running 2 under on busy shifts. Everyone is burnt out; exhausted and probably not as sharp as they would be.
column123: On departure out of ZZZ;  we received a RA after encountering a near mid-air collision. The event occurred around around 30 to 40 miles south of ZZZ. The Captain was Pilot Monitoring and the First Officer was Pilot Flying. The First Officer was hand flying at the time of the event. We were climbing to 16;000 feet as instructed and talking to Departure Control. 16;000 feet was our initial altitude assigned on the ground in ZZZ. We received a handoff climbing through approximately 8;000 feet and contacted Center. After we checked in with Center; I noticed traffic straight ahead at 10;700 feet depicted on the scope and we were climbing toward them. We were not notified by ATC of any traffic and once myself (First Officer/Pilot Flying) noticed the traffic at 5 miles; I called 'traffic 5 miles 10;700; I'm going to level off' and began to level off immediately around 9;000 feet and did not climb above 10;000 feet.We got a TA; and I began a slight left turn as I noticed on TCAS that traffic was crossing left to right of our course. As the Captain was calling Center to ask about traffic in the area we got a visual on the traffic and immediately started a descending left turn to avoid traffic; simultaneously we received a descending RA and complied. The converging aircraft passed off our right wing and appeared to make a left turn also to avoid our converging course. We never saw the converging aircraft change altitude more than a few hundred feet. We notified Center of the RA event and returned to normal flight. Prior to departure; we briefed General Aviation traffic as the biggest threat in the departure briefing and I think that helped our awareness.General Aviation traffic not on a IFR flight plan or talking to ATC. Departure or Center not notifying of traffic. Timing of handoff from Departure to Center occurring at the event. Suggest attentiveness to traffic.

column121: [Personnel were brought to] PTKK to finally fix the PAPI lights that have been inoperative for months. The Runway 4 PAPI was no longer NOTAM'd out. However; upon arrival [to] PTKK; we tried multiple times to turn them on to no avail. We asked TKK Radio to try and he was unable to turn them on either. Then arriving PTSA; the PAPI was inop for Runway 5 with no NOTAM. Then arriving [to] PKWA the Runway 6 PAPI is also NOTAM inop with shortened runway construction. So now we have the three shortest runways PTKK 6;000 ft.; PTSA 5;700 ft.; and PKWA (now down to 6;000 ft. with construction) having inoperative PAPI lights for the prevailing wind runway. Add this to PGSN not having PAPI/VASI installed even though the Jeppesen Approach chart indicates there are VASI; and we have 4 airports in the Guam region with no visual guidance. Poor trend; especially for night time operations and new crews coming on board. Unsatisfactory trend. [We're] lucky we have light and empty airplanes with very few passengers allowing for short landing rolls.
column123: I write this not relating to a specific flight but relating to a safety issue at PTKK airport. For the past 2 years; the PAPI at PTKK Runway 4 has been out of service. Sometimes this is noted on the NOTAMs and sometimes it is not. The safety issue is that PTKK is the proverbial 'black hole' airport which gives very limited visual reference. This makes flying a visual approach very challenging. In fact; an article 'Black Hole Approach' concludes with the statement 'The best way to combat these often subtle and insidious factors (relating to the Black hole effect) is to avoid straight-in; visual approaches at night without glide slope guidance; especially when overflying the infamous black hole.' Engineers conducted an extensive study of the problem. The results were published in a report entitled; 'Flight Deck Work Load and Night Visual Approach Performance' They concluded that the problem is exacerbated by many factors but the factors that stood out to me are those that are present on nearly all PTKK approaches. They are:1. A runway length/width combination that is unfamiliar to a pilot. PTKK is 6;000 ft. long with absolutely no overrun on either end. It is shorter than most runways and that effect is amplified by the fact that there is no paved safety area on either end. SNA is famed for being short but it is 5;700 ft. long PLUS over 1;000 ft. of paved safety area on the approach end to Runway 2L. It actually has almost 7;000 ft. of pavement. PTKK only has 6;000.2. Substandard runway and airport lighting. PTKK has had broken PAPI for at least 2 years. The only other airport lighting is the runway edge lights and some taxi lights. There are no MALSR lights. There is no big city lights to help with visual reference. 3. Peering through a rain-soaked windshield can convince a pilot (because of refraction) that the aircraft is too high and can result in an error of as much as 200 ft. of altitude per nautical mile from the runway. It is very common to have an island induced rain shower right off the approach end of Runway 04 at PTKK. Now we are flying this approach late at night; windshield covered in rain; poor lighting; and absolutely no backup source of glide path information as I will explain later due to the way the RNAV approach is built. 4. An airport that is situated at a slightly lower elevation and on a different slope than the surrounding terrain. This is PTKK. The runway is on the northwest side of the island at sea level. The island rises quickly to the southeast to an elevation of 2;700 ft. in less than 1 mile. 5. An approach over water or unlit terrain means that the visual reference points are at a distance where altitude and sink rate are more difficult to judge. This is PTKK. Absolutely no ground reference from the IF of FIGBY until the runway nearly 10 miles away. The problem is further exacerbated by the fact that the only approach we have to Runway 4 (most commonly used because of the prevailing trade winds from the NE) is the RNAV (GPS) Runway 4 approach. Everything works fine with VNAV and LNAV until we reach the missed approach point of HAMAX. Notice that HAMAX is 2.2 miles from the end of the runway. So here you are; flying the approach as usual in VNAV and LNAV and you have the usual rain shower between FASPO and the runway. You are tired because it is now after midnight and you are over the dark ocean with no ground lights in sight and the PAPI's are not working as usual. You approach the waypoint HAMAX and the flight director bars (your only vertical guidance at this point) suddenly command a pitch up and a turn to the left. Why?? Because you have hit the missed approach point and the guidance tells you to go around. This isn't common for most approaches. It throws off even seasoned pilots. You can see the runway lights through the rain soaked windshield but again with no PAPI; you have now lost all vertical guidance. You are now at 660 ft. above the ocean and continue based on a fuzzy view outof the windshield. Are you stable for that 500 foot callout? I guess so; hard to tell if we're on the vertical path...Is this safe? I would submit that in my opinion that this is the most dangerous flight we operate. Why do we do it in the middle of the night? I am not talking about the hopper. That is daytime and is doable. We don't currently have an aircraft availability problem like we did when we were busy. Why not do this flight in the daylight? Why not get those PAPI's fixed? They've been broken for 2 years! Why not get the RNP approach finished. That would solve the whole problem if we actually had vertical guidance to the runway instead of losing it right at 660 ft. where we really need it.

column121: During Cruise we received an ACARS message from the company [Dispatch] that they had left 1768kg (initial message said 1768lbs but was later corrected) of Dry Ice off the DG manifest.  We began to send follow up messages back and forth to confirm the location and total quantity of the dry ice.  It was determined that the total quantity was 1884kg vs the DG manifest value of 166kg.  Basically; 2 cans worth of Dry Ice had not be accounted for on the DG manifest.  The crew deployed the Drager CO2 monitoring system immediately and was also directed to do this from the company.  We also ran the QRH for this event.  Upon further review; it was determined by crew and Dispatch that the dry ice quantity on board not only exceeded normal FOM limits; but was over the supplemental limits in the FOM.  I began a conference call with the Dispatcher; DO; and Flight Operations.  Based on all the information; they recommended we deploy the CO2 monitoring system and keep a close eye out for any elevated CO2 levels; but that we should be able to continue safely to our destination which was another 8 or so hours away.  We knew if the levels were elevated we could follow the QRH and use oxygen to breathe safely and divert if needed.  We also knew that we were flying right over ZZZ1 in about an hour which we could just divert to immediately to remedy the problem.  This would give us time to get ready for the divert and allow us to burn enough fuel to get below maximum landing weight.  So basically our options were 1) continue or 2) divert.  We woke up the Captain to provide him all of the data so he could make the decision.  With all the data and the opinions of the crew; he decided we should continue.  The decision was supported by the crew and Dispatch.  The rest of the flight was uneventful.  Obviously; undocumented hazardous materials is a big deal and could have serious safety concerns.  Luckily everything worked out here.  Once the issue was identified; Dispatch was a little slow to get us all the info and to provide input.  I believe this was because the Dispatchers had a shift change.  I think this led to information slowly being provided to all parties. The cause was someone [erred] in the chain of [custody] during loading; documenting; and manifesting must have made an error which led to this dry ice not being manifested.
column123: Approximately 20 minutes into flight; we received a message via ACARS from Dispatch that 1768lbs of dry ice went on the aircraft unmanifested and to please use supplemental dry ice procedures. At that time the RFO was in the jump seat and he retrieved; turned on and distributed a Drager monitor to each crew member. Once established in cruise; CA proceeded to the CRM as planned/briefed and RFO took the left seat. Subsequently we received message that the unmanifested dry ice was 1768kg; not lbs. We confirmed with  that the 1768kg was on the main deck along with the 116kg that was manifested ; for a total of 1884kg of dry ice on the main deck. The main deck limit is 1814kg. DO stated that he and dispatch agreed; that with all systems on the aircraft functioning properly and with FOM 10.37 DRY ICE SUPPLEMENTAL PROCEDURES in place; we were OK to continue to destination; however; if Captain desired to divert that would be appropriate as well given the over-limit situation. At that time; we had just passed the east coast of [State]. Diverting to a [company name] base at that time would have required dumping fuel in order to land under MAXLGW. FO and RFO discussed and determined that we would arrive overhead ZZZ1 on current flight planned route at MAXLGW and that if a divert decision was made; ZZZ1 was the most appropriate divert base. One hour prior to arriving overhead ZZZ1; FO awakened the CA in the CRM and informed him of the situation and [Dispatch's] deferral to him on a divert decision. CA agreed that continuing on  was appropriate. FO/RFO informed [Dispatch] via ACARS of decision to continue to [our destination] using dry ice supplemental procedures. Rest of flight was uneventful. A [contributing] cause was it had something to do with this being a chartered/non standard flight.

column121: While on our first attempt to land at COD we were vectored onto the RNAV to Runway 4 visual conditions prevailed and we were using the RNAV primarily for additional terrain clearance continuous moderate turbulence and windshear persisted on the arrival. ATC vectors and my attempts to maintain an airspeed that buffered against the rapid ups and downs of the green line and the rapid fluctuations of the indicated airspeed left us high and fast on our first attempt so we initiated a go-around missed approach. There was a significant tailwind down the valley that sheared to a headwind at the surface this contributed to us being high and fast.While we were climbing out we were instructed to climb and maintain 15;000 feet and were given vectors back to TOCUD. Approaching TAKBE the Captain requested a turn direct to TAKBE from ATC. Being at 15;000 [feet] we couldn't lower the flaps [so] the Captain instructed me to set 12;200 [feet] for TAKBE and start down. I complied with these instructions and as we dropped below 15;000 [feet] we began lowering the flaps and configuring.Shortly after starting our descent ATC issued a low altitude alert and stated that his minimum vectoring altitude was 15;000 [feet]. We were visual with both the mountains and airport in sight but failed to get proper approval from ATC for the visual approach before descending. As a side note we were being shook pretty good by the continuous moderate turbulence and I was really having to work the thrust levers to maintain a safe airspeed. We informed ATC that we were visual and we were cleared for the approach to Runway 4. We successfully landed on our second attempt. At no time was the safety of the fight or terrain clearance an issue and no EGPWS cautions or warnings were issued.Confusion on my part of the Captains instruction to 'sneak / start down'. It was the last leg of long hot sweaty day with multiple Captain swaps delays and MX issues; heat fatigue and dehydration were setting in and the turbulence and windshear created a very challenging flight environment.Once we goofed up and should have made sure that we were cleared for the visual prior to initiating a descent from a clearance altitude. column121: While climbing out at approximately a little over 10;000 feet we received a pitch trim caution. I was hand flying the aircraft as we were maneuvering around some build-ups in order to avoid unnecessary turbulence; the caution light came on when I used the trim to command more nose up trim to properly trim the aircraft for the climb.The First Officer ran the Pitch Trim Caution E&A checklist. This would not clear the malfunction and the checklist confirmed that our pitch trim was jammed in position and we would have no AutoPilot for the remainder of the flight. The aircraft was trimmed for a climb at approximately 200 knots at a 5 degree nose up attitude. I contacted Dispatch and advised them of the situation and spoke with Maintenance (MX) control. When discussing what my intentions were; myself and Dispatch agreed that we would continue to ZZZ for the moment but I'd evaluate the situation a little closer to ZZZ1 once we were in cruise flight.Once we reached our cruising altitude of FL240 it became apparent that the amount of nose down force that needed to be maintained on the control column was substantial. Furthermore in order to minimize the amount of nose down forces required on the yoke to hold altitude and to comply with the E&A checklist the airspeed had to be maintained at just over 200 knots IAS; greatly increasing our time enroute to ZZZ. The First Officer and I had a discussion as to the wisdom of continuing the flight all the way to ZZZ under these conditions and determined that the more prudent course of action was to divert to ZZZ1. I also believed that the pace of ATC operations into ZZZ1 were much more favorable for an abnormal landing than in the busy airspace of ZZZ. I called Dispatch and the Dispatcher agreed with my decision and we diverted to ZZZ1. We followed the E&A procedure for this landing and landed without incident in ZZZ1 and taxied to the gate. After landing in ZZZ1 and speaking with the MX personnel waiting for us I debriefed the crew with the exception of 1 FA that had already left the aircraft before I could get to the back (approx. 5 minutes or so after deplaning ended) in order to make her DH back to ZZZ1. I also spoke with [NAME] and we debriefed the flight.This was a situation that I hadn't seen pop up before as either a FO or a CA on the Dash 8-400 and I might be mistaken but I'm not sure I've seen this particular situation in the SIM either. Although the situation was certainly manageable it might be a good scenario to incorporate into future SIM sessions just so pilots can get an idea of what the aircraft feels like when the pitch trim is inoperative.

column123: We were taxiing in from landing on Runway XXL in ZZZ. During the approach there was moderate rainfall. Our taxi instructions were to taxi via Taxiway XY; Taxiway XZ; Taxiway XA; Taxiway XX; hold short of Runway XXC at Taxiway XX. [At] the first bend on Taxiway XX as it turns from a south to a southwest heading; the aircraft almost completely lost traction. The nose wheel understeered and the aircraft continued straight ahead even as the taxiway turned. The Captain applied braking and the main tires also lost traction immediately. I also applied the brakes on the First Officer's side because I thought we were going to depart the taxiway. The aircraft skidded approximately 15 feet and nearly departed the prepared surface. At the last second; the aircraft slowed enough to allow the nose wheel to regain some effectiveness. The Captain was able to steer the aircraft back toward the centerline. There was a short; but secondary loss of traction [and] as we overshot the taxiway centerline; the aircraft was still in a partial skid.I have never seen an aircraft moving that slowly lose traction on a wet taxiway. I estimate the aircraft was moving at 15 kt. when the turn began. Both the Captain and I agree that this was something neither of us expected or have ever seen in our combined experience on the 737. I do believe any prudent pilot would have taken the turn at the same speed considering the conditions. It's my feeling that there was some issue with drainage or that [that] stretch of pavement is unusually slick during rainy conditions. I notified the Ground Controller of the event and reported braking action as fair to poor. I asked them to inform other aircraft of the slippery conditions on Taxiway XX between Runway XXL and XXC.

column121: There had been a ground stop for passing storms to the east; which were now 1/3 of the way between ZZZ and ZZZ1. The Captain gave a briefing and asked the Flight Attendants to remain seated the entire flight due to the cells we'd be flying around and the potential for turbulence. He also made this part of his welcome aboard announcement.We took off and were given a 090 heading; transitioning north of the group of cells. This group of cells gave us a small option north toward ZZZ2 VOR and a small option south between cells. Neither path had a significant advantage over the other.Once we were abeam the northern track; ATC gave us a hole they depicted on their radar to our 1 o'clock position. We opted to continue straight; but ATC said straight looked worse to them. We conversed back and forth with them and the hole appeared to our right and clear skies on the back side. We maneuvered right; then left to make a perpendicular path through the hole. The bottom of the hole was higher than our altitude and we were given a climb from 17;000 to FL210. We tried to establish this climb at 250 kts. to stay slow for possible turbulence. This was made difficult by the fact we had an MEL for the speed bug. The speed bug jumped from the upper 200s into the lower 300s; back and forth throughout the flight. It was distracting and was the first time either of us had experienced this particular anomaly in nearly four years. Just prior to penetration; we could see heavy lightning coming from the cells immediately left of our path; extending toward the area we were originally going toward.As we climbed to FL210; we penetrated the lower portion of the hole and into IMC. Throughout the encounter; we had moderate turbulence and heavy to extreme rain. Our ice detection caution message activated; as well.We estimate the pass took 30 to 45 seconds to transition. I tried to transmit to ATC not to send anyone behind us; but never received a response.Once in clear air; I tried ATC again and they said they'd been trying to reach us to say the hole had closed up on their scope. We never their transmission either.In discussion after passing into clear air; neither of us felt we'd encountered hail. The sound of the rain striking the window and body of the aircraft were consistent with heavy to extreme rain.I checked on the Flight Attendants to make sure they were ok and to make sure the passengers were ok; and everyone was. We landed without incident and discovered damage during the walk around.The first area I noticed was the radome. There were extensive areas where the paint had been removed and the composite material underneath was exposed. There were three areas where horizontal slices in the composite material were visible. There was at least one area where a circular area was compromised. Most of the damaged paint and material were on the upper half of the radome. There was one hole that was previously covered during the preflight inspection that was now exposed due to speed tape coming off the aircraft. We conducted numerous; slow and methodical visual inspections of the exterior of the aircraft over the course of the next two hours. The only other damage was an unidentified antenna on the top of the aircraft. It was located aft of the VHF 1 antenna and forward of the upper beacon. POH and PRM (Pilot's Reference Manual) searches failed to produce an identity to this antenna; and might possibly be a wifi antenna installed after manufacturer documents were printed.The Captain notified [Maintenance Control]; the Chief Pilots; and Dispatch and briefed them on the incident and the status of the aircraft. Our Contract Maintenance arrived about an hour later and began making an evaluation of the damage. Our return flight was eventually cancelled and we rode the brakes for Ground Personnel while they repositioned the aircraft. We left the aircraft with Maintenance and proceeded to the hotel. After the flight; the Captain and I debriefed our flight and the incident. The flight attendants and the passengers were secured at the time due to crew briefings and the announcement that the seat belt sign would stay on and the flight attendants would remain seated throughout the flight. As previously noted; we had north and south options that were basically equal. Since our radar conflicted somewhat with ATC; we applied their observations into our decision making process in accordance with good CRM procedures. We had convection on our left and right sides and clear blue skies ahead. Our ability to climb over the IMC we entered could have been better facilitated if we began our climb sooner; however there was a small layer that obstructed our view and we were too close to the hole when the height of that IMC was determined. Again; this was further complicated by not having our heading bug to help with pitch reference and avoid a lower than desired speed or increasing over the turbulence penetration speed.

column121: On a flight intended for ZZZ to ZZZ1; I noticed a little way into the cruise portion of the flight that my hydraulic pressure was low. I confirmed that the hydraulic pump switch was in the ON position; and then cycled the switch to see if this would resolve the problem. When I did that; the radio stack lost power with the switch in the ON position and the pump did not activate. Moving the switch to the OFF position; the radio stack returned to life. I performed this action again with the same results: with the pump switch in the ON position; the radios died; but in the OFF position the radios returned to life. I imagined that the pump system had shorted out somehow and left the switch OFF and used the manual pump handle to restore pressure. At that point; I decided not to fly all the way to ZZZ1 but instead to ZZZ2; which was somewhat closer (although still an hour ahead) and where the propeller was scheduled to be inspected the next day; thinking to repair the pump at that same time.Flight continued normally after this for some time; until I noticed that the landing light switch was in the ON position; and I moved to turn that switch off. When I turned off the landing light switch; the radios again failed. Recycling the landing light; radio master; and master switches did nothing. The next day; the Mechanic discovered that the battery terminal connector was broken; not the hydraulic pump; and it was this that explained the electrical failures.The problem had actually started before the flight: the landing immediately prior to this flight had resulted in a significant nose wheel shimmy due to the castering nose wheel not being aligned with the longitudinal axis of the plane (This can happen in this plane when the nose wheel has been down in the water and it casters; during a water takeoff there is no runway to naturally realign it). The shimmy had probably caused a pre-existing crack in the terminal connector to nearly; but not completely; open the circuit. So the engine start; taxi; takeoff and climb were normal; but additional vibration and heat caused the crack to spread until finally it broke completely. So at first there were wonky partial failures and then a total failure later in the flight.

column121: I am a Private Pilot working on my commercial ticket. I need dual time in complex so my Instructor and I decided to fly from ZZZ1 to ZZZ; do a full-stop taxi-back and return to ZZZ1. I picked up VFR flight following en route and talked with ZZZ2 Approach and ZZZ3 Approach. Approximately 10 miles from ZZZ; ZZZ3 switched me to advisory so I called ZZZ Tower. Tower instructed me to enter a right base for Runway XX and report a 2 mile right base. There was one other aircraft also intending to land at ZZZ; who was also going to be reporting a base.I don't recall exactly what Tower said when I called my 2 mile right base; but was instructed to look for traffic. I assumed the traffic would be closer to the airport than me; considering that they had entered the pattern prior to my arrival in the Class Delta airspace. They had reported a 2 mile base before I reported mine. I looked 12:00 to 3:00 (straight ahead and along to the numbers) but could not see any traffic. I glanced at the ADS-B traffic on my iPad but did not see any markings there to indicate traffic (aircraft do not require ADS-B in the area at ZZZ). Finally; I saw traffic a few hundred ft. away from me; at my 11:00; at just a slightly lower altitude. This traffic was flying a significantly wider base than is standard (more than 1/2 to 1 mile from the runway threshold). I initiated an immediate 90 deg left turn; then flew a 270 right turn to enter the final approach.When Tower asks me and other traffic to report a 2 mile right base; I am assuming that I will have a 1/2 to 1 mile final; and that I am just on an extended base leg. I'm wondering if the other pilot flew to a 2 mile final; and then called that as their 2 mile base. I know ZZZ is a Class Delta; but I don't believe they get any supporting radar from ZZZ3. If they were using their eyes to sequence us; then their advisories were unhelpful at best. I don't believe that ZZZ Tower had any accurate idea of where the traffic in the air was at any moment. ZZZ was unaware of how close we came to a collision; and didn't seem to care when I told them I was turning onto a downwind; and then doing a 180 to final. I am the Pilot in Command so [I] take full responsibility for my actions; which were correct in that moment to avoid a collision; but I received no further instructions; which would have been an issue if there had been anybody on a straight-in.In the future; I will be more cognizant of scanning left and right when looking for traffic ahead on a right base. I will be less dependent on Towers with no radar backup to provide me with accurate traffic advisories; or any at all. I believe that Tower Controllers need to be more cognizant of where the traffic is in the air so they can provide better traffic advisories. If they aren't sure where an aircraft is; they should be telling the number 2 airplane to keep a wide scan; rather than acting like everybody is flying a standard pattern.

It was a confusing sequence from getting the instructions on the rollout and given two different runway crossings with two different instructions. It would have been nice to have been given time to clear the runway and then take down instructions when I wasn't still focused on the landing during a critical phase of flight. Simple taxi instructions such as one taxiway to the ramp or one runway crossing isn't too hard to remember but still hard during a critical phase of flight. However; two runway crossings while rolling and complex instructions were confusing. The controller had a high work load and asking for conformation on the runway crossing probably didn't help her but I felt like I needed to verify. Then the confusion on my end didn't help crossing XXR. Being told to taxi via XXR weren't the instructions I was thinking of getting and made me second guess crossing the runway. Coming to a stop and asking for more clarification on frequency would've been the best thing to do. XXR wasn't a runway in use at the time and I cleared the area so I felt comfortable to cross; along with being told to taxi via XXR; I believed I had been cleared onto the runway.

column121: I was practicing my aerobatic routine in Aerobatic Practice Area (APA) waivered airspace just north of HGR and had a ground observer. The airspace NOTAM was active and the area is depicted on a sectional chart and is in software for current navigational systems. However; my concern is that I'm getting traffic coming through the airspace.I feel there are a few things that could be done to enhance the safety of my current operation. I'm writing you because I'm concerned the FAA will just close it down if I suggest there is a safety issue. The current waiver requires me to monitor Potomac Approach during my operation. That possibly may help; but sometimes there is so much chatter that it would be difficult to catch a call and their main purpose is to keep IFR traffic out of my waivered airspace. In the past I would monitor HGR Tower and they were more helpful because they would look for traffic and be able to warn VFR traffic that they were communicating with also. My aircraft does not have the ability to monitor 2 frequencies simultaneously; so I'm currently only monitoring Potomac Approach as required by the waiver.   As you know; TFR's are depicted boldly on digital navigational software devices. Could 'Hot' APA's also be depicted boldly like TFR's? That would be a more obvious warning to other aircraft than just a drawing on a chart. Obviously; all pilots should be familiar with published NOTAMS in their route of flight; but we know that doesn't always happen. Also allowing HGR Tower to call out possible traffic conflicts would be helpful but please don't let the FAA close the area again for months until they have time to amend the paperwork! I did contact a representative from Potomac Approach about my concern and am waiting for a reply. Even if he is able to allow me to monitor HGR Tower instead of Potomac Approach; it would still be helpful if Hot APA's could show up as obvious as TFR's on digital navigational aids. Your consideration in this matter would be greatly appreciated. Thank you.

column121: I was flying on an instrument flight plan from SEE in San Diego to ZZZ1 outside of Denver and filed via Foreflight. The flight plan of direct was accepted but I assumed a SID. Given that SEE was MVFR I studied the departures including the Mission Bay Two (obstacle) Departure which seemed the most likely. I noted that this was a procedure which required tracking multiple radials of different VOR's; and I know from experience that modern glass panels (Garmin G600 and Garmin GTN 750) do not recognize these departures and they must be manually configured tuning the VOR's and radials.Shortly before departure; Foreflight via cellular connection gave me an expected route which was an odd route as it contained over 20 waypoints; but I programmed it into the Garmin GTN750 after engine start. There was no SID assigned. Normally when a SID is assigned its included in the expected route. So; I assumed SEE direct the MZB VOR. The weather was good VFR. So; I did not brief terrain clearance. When I called Ground Control; I was told it was a complicated route and asked if I was ready to copy it all down. I also advised that I had also received the route electronically. To make it faster I wrote the expected route on my knee board and followed along as the Controller gave it to me. I believe the route was the same; but I cannot rule out confirmation bias. I read the route back and received a 'readback correct'I took off on runway heading and noted that if I made an immediate turn to MZB I would not be able to out climb the terrain so continued on runway heading. It was VFR and I had the terrain in sight at all times. When I was handed off to Departure I was asked by the Approach Controller why I was not turning right. (presumably to follow the  obstacle departure). She further immediately called a terrain alert. I advised the terrain was in sight and was not a factor. The  Approach Controller then directed me to fly a heading and advised of a possible pilot deviation. It [is] possible that the Controller specifically called out the obstacle departure and I missed it due to confirmation bias. However; I believe the obstacle departure was not mentioned either due to it being a VFR day or common practice for the field and part of an unduly complicated clearance. The obstacle departure definitely did not populate as the Foreflight expected clearance like other SID's. I have screen shots of this. As a corrective action; I believe that obstacle clearances need to be built with waypoints and published like any other SID so they worked  with automated clearance delivery mechanisms and integrated avionics

After the application of right rudder; the aircraft veered even further left; which is when he decided to abort the takeoff by pulling the throttle to idle and applying brakes.
