We asked ZZZ TRACON (Approach Control) for direct ZZZZZ1 to avoid the thunderstorm cell. We were anticipating a visual approach to Runway XXR because the most recent ATIS (weather report) was reporting only Few and Scattered clouds at the airport with adequate visibility for a visual approach. The TRACON Controller asked if we would be able to 'get the airport?'My First Officer and I were slightly confused by his phraseology and tried to discuss what the Controller meant. At that time; we were within a few miles from ZZZZZ and just about to level off at 3;000 feet. The Autopilot Mode Control panel was in Vertical Speed (Altitude Acquire) and LNAV to ZZZZZ. I was anticipating going to ZZZZZ1 and was ready to change the altitude to 2;800 feet in MCP for the autopilot. We were then cleared on a 160 degree heading to join the final approach course of 128; and cleared for the approach. I didn't hear the Controller say 'maintain 3;000 feet until established.' I selected VOR/LOC and dialed 2;800 feet into the autopilot Mode Control Panel. Because we were in a descent and in Altitude Acquire; the autopilot continued to descend towards 2;800 feet.My First Officer said we were supposed to maintain 3;000 feet. I had missed that part of the clearance so I dialed 3;000 feet into the Mode Control Panel; but by that point the aircraft had descended below 3;000 feet and was continuing to descend and would not ever capture 3;000 feet. I was also trying to slow the aircraft and get it to capture the localizer. Seeing that we weren't going to level off; I tried to use Vertical Speed to make the aircraft climb back to 3;000 feet; but it was continuing to descend. Our descent was exacerbated by the fact that I still had the speedbrakes deployed almost to the flight [descent]. ZZZ TRACON (Approach Control) said he he had a low altitude alert and his MVA [Min Vector Altitude] was 2;800 feet. We were now at about 2;300 feet. I disconnected the autopilot and autothrottles; started a climb and we decided to go missed approach. I finally stowed the speedbrakes; climbed to our clearance altitude and we then got re-vectored by ZZZ TRACON for another approach to Runway XXR and landed safely.
column123: We were being vectored around some weather coming into ZZZ and were given a descent to 3;000 feet and direct ZZZZZ outside of ZZZZZ1 on the ILS XXX. There was some confusion as ATC asked if we would be able to get the airport. I wasn't sure if he meant visually or altitude wise. After a pause; as I pondered his meaning; I responded that we were IMC. At the time; I didn't think we were high; so I assumed he meant visually. Just a couple miles outside of ZZZZZ; Captain asked for a turn to ZZZZZ1. I paused because I was anticipating a vector shortly to intercept the final approach course. I then asked ATC for the turn inbound; and ATC responded that he was just about to give us a vector and then provided the clearance. We were given a 160 heading to join and maintain 3;000 feet until established and cleared for the ILS to [Runway] XXR. This extra communication ultimately caused a delay in getting turned in. Because it all got really busy; I didn't see that Captain dialed in 2;800 feet. So; I don't think it acquired 3;000 feet and was now descending below it. Then I think 3;000 feet was reset into the MCP and yet the aircraft was still descending. All of this was happening while I was replying to ATC and I didn't realize what happened until after we talked about it later. We triggered a low altitude alert; and ATC informed us that we were to maintain 3;000 feet until established. I responded that we were correcting. Captain was climbing back up to 3;000 feet and we were slightly south of the localizer. I figured by the time we got back to 3;000 feet; we would then be high for the approach and not being established on the localizer; I said we should go-around. Captain agreed; and we did. This whole thing took me out of the Green; made me feel rushed and got behind in my responsibilities. A go-around was the best decision.

column121: Climbing through 7;000 feet on the ZZZZZ SID; the aural warnings for airspeed; fire and pressurization came on.  The First Officer and I scanned the flight deck for unreliable airspeed; fire warnings and any possible pressurization problems. We were in agreement that none were present and could not locate the source of the warnings; I elected to disengage the autopilot and auto throttles; to verify control of the aircraft. The First Officer and I searched again for any indication of fire or airspeed issues. We found none. With the fire bell still sounding we elected to return to ZZZ and request priority.   ATC was notified and vectors given back to Runway XX. Having just departed and well over the gross landing weight; we planned the longest runway available.  I notified the A Flight Attendant; to prepare the cabin for landing and that we had about 10 minutes to touchdown.The First Officer computed the landing data and a visual approach was planned. Landing weight was XXX;000 pounds; and the Ref Speed 1XX. ATC provided vectors to a base leg and we were cleared for the visual approach. The landing and rollout were normal and I elected to let the aircraft roll to the end and turnoff; stop the aircraft and allow CFR to inspect for fire. As soon as I stopped the aircraft; I made a PA to the Flight Attendants and Passengers to remain seated. Ground was contacted and we spoke directly with fire command. No evidence of fire was found to exist. The First Officer computed the brake cooling module for and potential issues that would prevent us from parking at the gate or cooling required. None were found. Coordination with ZZZ Operations as to our situation and a gate was completed and we taxied to gate X. At the gate we were met by the Fire Crew; ZZZ Maintenance and Ground Operations.  The warnings continued to sound and were not able to be silenced by Maintenance Personnel. I made two logbook entries for the discrepancies and the overweight landing and gave a debrief of the event to the Maintenance Personnel. Dispatch was contacted and informed of the situation and we agreed to talk later as my main focus was still dealing with passengers and Ground Ops. After passenger deplaning; the aircraft was handed over to maintenance and the First Officer and I went to the Crew lounge; where we contacted Dispatch and conducted a debrief of the events with the Chief Pilot.
column123: This event occurred while departing ZZZ from Runway XX; climbing out on the ZZZZZ Departure at about 7;000 feet. I was the PM; and had just completed the final flap retraction and a radio hand off to ZZZ Departure. All of a sudden; numerous alarms/warnings sounded on the flight deck and were extremely loud. The PF stayed focused on flying the aircraft in the high density environment. I quickly started to scan all of the panels; Master Caution and Warning indications; pressurization panel; cargo fire panel; fire handles; flight instrumentation; airspeed; AOA; and standby indicators. There were NO indications of any light or malfunction anywhere on the flight deck and all aircraft flight parameters seemed normal.The Captain made the decision to advise ATC and return to ZZZ; on Runway XX. Meanwhile all aural alarms continued to sound very loudly which made communication difficult. We discussed the situation. We had just about every major aural alarm sounding at once; with the exception of wind shear. With no other indications presently indicating any kind of system malfunction; we concluded the best option would be to get the aircraft on the ground. This would be an overweight landing by about XX;000 pounds; on a long runway in day VMC conditions. The Captain coordinated with the cabin and operations. We computed landing data; briefed; and ran checklists. We were cleared a visual approach and the Captain completed an excellent uneventful landing to Runway XX. We cleared the runway at the end. I coordinated with CFR (Crash Fire Rescue equipment) and requested them to thoroughly evaluate the aircraft for any fire/smoke issues. I also ran the numbers for any brake cooling issues. The CFR Chief stated there were no indications of fire or smoke. There were no brake cooling issues. ZZZ Ops cleared us to gate X. We resumed taxi to the gate; with CFR following us to ensure absolute safety.We parked the aircraft at the gate and were met by Maintenance and the Fire Chief. THE ALARMS WERE ALL STILL SOUNDING. Maintenance came on board and tried to figure it out; to no avail; prior to us leaving. Passengers were safely deplaned and sent to another gate for continuation to ZZZ1. With the alarms still sounding at the gate; the Captain and I both commented on how fortunate we were to have on noise cancelling headsets; otherwise communication would have been nearly impossible. This was a very unusual emergency and I hope that we are provided follow-up with the cause of the malfunction.

column121: New Captain was PM; LCA (Line Check Airman) was flying from right seat on arrival into IAH. Approach kept us so high the entire time we had to get approval to miss the altitudes. Aircraft on other arrivals were holding and we were expecting the same. We were cleared to descend via the GUSHR arrival; and had to use full speed brakes the whole time but we made 10;000 at 250kts; and were able to make the bottom altitude at GUSHR at 6000 and 210 kts. Big rain shower at 15 miles out on the final of 8L. By the time we went by the rain shower it was mostly north of our course but there was rain and lightning coming out of the shower. TCAS showed traffic on 8R behind and above us. We could see him out of our window.  We were told to hold 200 knots till about 10 mile final. At this time; traffic somewhere; behind us we think; said they needed to go around because of rain and lightning. Approach gave us a frequency and switched us to tower and told us to tell them our speed.  We switched to the Tower frequency but must have put it in wrong; and when we tried to check on to what we thought was tower; another approach told us it was the wrong frequency. To go to the Tower; we looked up on the Jepp chart and the Tower frequency for 8L was 120.725. We called Tower on 120.725 and they cleared us to land. On final after that; a monitor came on and told us to change to 119.82. We switched to 119.82 and it was the same Tower Controller as 120.725 and she cleared us to land a second time. After landing we were told to contact ATC for possible pilot deviation. We had no idea why. We contacted the ATC Ops Manager who said there was a possible conflict with the traffic on 8R as that traffic was so close that had he not seen the airport and been given a visual we would have been too close and had a separation issue.1. We were cleared for an ILS. There was no PRM operations being used or advertised.2. The tower frequency they were using; 119.82 is nowhere on the IAH 70-9 page; dated 16APR21; effective 22APR21. ATC Ops Manager said Houston has been using frequency 119.82 as Tower for a few weeks because coverage was poor on the other frequency in some areas; but that frequency (119.82) is not published anywhere. 3. After talking with ATC Ops Manager; we verified in the NOTAMs there was nothing about 119.82 being used anywhere.4. Why is approach cramming the planes on approach so close that a momentary loss of communication results in loss of separation?

column121: As Captain; I was the Pilot Monitoring and the First Officer was the Pilot Flying for this flight. On the take off roll at approximately 90 to 100kts; I hear the First Officer make the comment 'There seems to be a lot of airflow through this window'. I glanced over and to see from my point of view that the window appears to be closed. I shift my eyes back to the runway centerline; airspeed and engine instruments while thinking about what he said. At approximately 110kts; it becomes loud with high airflow into the flight deck. The First Officer shouts 'My window is open'. I quickly glance over to his side to see he has his left hand on the control wheel and is holding the R 2 flight deck window closed by the window lock lever with his right hand. I immediately took the controls. At this time we are approximately 120kts just prior to V1 (129). I took a quick glance at my First Officer and back to my instruments; I saw that we were Vr + 8 to 9kts. I then rotated. I saw a positive rate of climb and shout 'gear up'. The First Officer assumed pilot monitoring and raised the landing gear. I shouted 'Can you crank the window closed at all?' He responded 'No; it won't close'. At this point; Tower had advised us to contact Departure. I selected the Center Autopilot; VNAV & Heading Select with a heading of 360 as assigned. I opened the speed window and remained at Flaps 5 to prevent the airplane from accelerating. I figured the faster we would go; the louder the flight deck would be and the more the First Officer would struggle to hold the window in position. The First Officer shouts 'I can't hear anything from ATC.' Around 3;400 ft. I contacted Departure and informed them that we need to stop climb and return to the airport because we have a flight deck window opened. We were given a left heading of 270 and to maintain 4;000. We performed the after takeoff checklist. My First Officer states 'I can't hear anything from ATC but what do you need from me?' I responded 'ATC is giving us vectors back to ILS RWY XX. If you can; get flight deck performance for Runway XX and set us up for the ILS RWY XX; I'll do a quick brief; then we will do our Descent and Approach checklist.' With one hand still on the window crank; the First Officer did just that and along with his flow. ATC gave us another vector and asked if we need more time. I told ATC that we were not ready and asked to continue heading at 270 and 4;000. Once we were set up; briefings and checklist were complete; I advised ATC we were ready for the approach. Since I was flying while doing the radios myself and the First Officer with only one free hand available; I decided it would not be prudent to be heads down and message Dispatch through ACARS. I felt the priority was to fly the plane and get us safely on the ground. I informed ATC 'We [request priority]; 2 souls on board and approximately 4 and half hours fuel on board'. ATC asked the nature of the [situation] and I replied 'We have a flight window cracked'. I meant to say cracked open; however; the noise from the airflow was a little distracting. ATC gives us an intercept heading of 100 and clears us for the approach. We were stable; fully configured; and all checklists were complete prior to the final approach fix. At 800 feet AGL we broke out of the clouds. I had the airport in sight and disengaged the autopilot. A normal landing was made at approximately 265;000 lb. We informed Tower that we did not need assistance and taxied to parking. Upon taxi in; I do not know if the First Officer closed the window or left it in its previous condition from flight; opened. Perhaps he left it alone so that Maintenance could inspect. I wrote up that the First Officer R2 flight deck window opened on takeoff/climb and I waited for them to inspect. There was no damage or defects noted.I honestly do not know if it was a Flight Deck Window malfunction or if it was ever truly locked. Both of us had opened our Flight Deck Windows on the ground during preflight because the APU was off and the temperature was in the 70's. About 30 minutes prior to block out; I started the APU and we closed our windows. In the Before Start portion of the checklist; I verified my flight window was closed and locked with strut at a 90 degree position. I heard the First Officer respond 'Closed and locked'. I could see his Window Lock Lever was in the forward and locked position; however; I could not verify if his decal showed 'CLOSED' nor if the strut was at a 90 angle simply because of the angle from where I was sitting in the Captain's seatI think that in the moment; the First Officer did a great job of prioritizing aircraft control in such a critical phase of flight. To be in the high speed regime of takeoff; so close to V1 and to keep 'aviating' while a huge startling distraction occurred was commendable. He also; kept his head in the game and jumped to the pilot monitoring duties without delay. He prompted me for the after takeoff checklist as we were about to level off at 4;000. If I could have done one thing over; I would have shouted 'My controls' in a louder voice. I didn't take into consideration that the First Officer could not hear well at that point.I'm also appreciative of our Company training video made by Boeing of a flight with the flight deck window opened. I'm glad that I was shown to me during my 767 upgrade training. I never thought I would be in that situation but thankfully I had some idea of what to expect. The plane will be extremely loud and distracting but it will safely fly.
column123: During takeoff my window opened immediately after the CA (Captain) called '80 knots; thrust set.' I was PF and saw the window rolling aft. I grabbed the window handle with my right hand while continuing to fly. I maintained runway centerline and described what happened by shouting cross cockpit to allow the CA to have the information and make an appropriate reject decision. About 10 knots before V1 the CA took the aircraft. I couldn't hear him verbally call V1 due to the cockpit noise and open window. Perhaps I didn't hear him call V1 because he had already taken the aircraft. Regardless it was loud and my audio panel wasn't set up to compensate for the noise.When the aircraft rotated I immediately assumed the role of Pilot Monitoring. He shouted to raise the landing gear and I did. The CA flew and took the radios because I had shouted cross cockpit that I couldn't hear ATC well enough to communicate. Both of us had to compensate because of the noise. The CA selected heading select and turned left to our assigned heading of 360 and elected to select VNAV and Center Autopilot Command almost simultaneously.The CA requested to stop climb around 5;100 MSL and informed me that we would return to ZZZ. Around this time I had determined that as long as I held the window with a good amount of strength it wouldn't roll open. I adjusted my interphone and ATC freq to Max volume so that I could hear. I then asked the CA if he was ready to run the After Takeoff Checklist and we did. Everything from that point forward was standard and in order except that the CA had to turn the Standby Attitude Indicator to ILS mode because I had one hand holding the window; the CA [advised ATC]; and did the radios. After we landed all roles were normal and the taxi in was standard.This situation is dynamic. I think perhaps a better verbal transfer of aircraft control on takeoff roll but we effectively handled the situation. I thought the CA was going to reject the takeoff. By the time he processed what was going on he decided it was safer to continue the takeoff. It was loud and we coordinated the best we could in this situation.

column121: While descending via the CHINS4 arrival into BFI (Seattle/King County Boeing Field); on the segment between 'HUMPP' and 'AUBRN'; passing approximately 14;500 ft. MSL at 250 kts. IAS; I encountered wake turbulence. Temporary loss of control was experienced as the aircraft rolled right; back left; and strongly back right again - with the final bank angle in the roll estimated to be beyond 30 but not more than 50 degrees wing down to the right before I could fully react. During the course of the roll and recovery; automation (including autopilot and auto throttle) was disengaged; and at no time did the EGPWS 'BANK ANGLE' warning sound. I stopped the roll and regained controlled flight with full and smooth application of left aileron; while adding power and climbing out of the perceived vortex. Once clear; automation was restored; the event briefed amongst the crew; and I instructed the PNF (Pilot not Flying) to radio Seattle Approach indicating we had 'encountered wake turbulence' and that 'we were attempting to re-establish on the arrival'. The Approach Controller acknowledged the transmission and advised we were following a Boeing 737-900 series sequenced for SEA (Seattle). From there; a normal descent and approach was conducted to the destination airport. No aircraft faults/failures/malfunctions/warnings; nor exceedances were experienced at any time before; during; or after the event. I was aware of the altitude and spacing regarding the traffic ahead on the arrival; with use of TCAS indications and relative altitude; as well situational awareness provided by our aircraft's INAV display. Spacing and distance appeared more than adequate considering the flight conditions; as the preceding aircraft was consistently indicating around 2;500 ft. below our level and well ahead on the arrival. At no time were we given advisories from ATC in regards to traffic ahead; nor caution on wake turbulence.This event was truly unexpected; however; I must credit flight training providers with modeling extremely accurate wake turbulence simulation scenarios that helped me to quickly identify; and recover properly from this real life upset. Experiencing this is a reminder that wake turbulence can be encountered during a descent profile - especially on an RNAV arrival with 'at-or-above/below' vertical crossing restrictions that could result in brief level offs at slower airspeeds which could lead to preceding aircraft generating stronger than expected vortices.

column121: Aircraft X had landed [Runway] XXR and stopped on the runway to question the exiting instructions. This delay in exiting caused the next [Runway] XXR arrival to go around. Then; an airport vehicle requested permission to inspect the runway because there's some local airport procedure to sweep the runway behind a [type aircraft]. There was a full sequence of arrivals to [Runway] XXR and [Runway] XY. Then; while the Local Controller was sorting out the Aircraft X arrival; the succeeding go-around; and the airport vehicle; Aircraft Y ([Runway] XXR) and the Aircraft Z ([Runway] XY) tied at the intersection. ASDE-X (Airport Surface Detection Equipment) alarmed; Local Controller issued a late go-around.Actual time on position may not have been a factor; rather the lack of staffing to open other positions and reduce the Local Controller's workload. There were only two of us in the tower at the time; simply because no one else was available. We had asked; and been told that we would be getting more people at XA:30z. Positions in the TRACON were also combined; and despite the fact that management had kept 3 tower-certified controllers down [in the TRACON] to 'get time'; one controller was working both the runways Arrival position; and vectoring the final to Runway [Runway] XY having to sequence in with the intersecting [Runway] XXR arrivals. The search for more controllers is on-going. What else can one do; when asking for more staffing; and being told to just wait?
column123: I was working Local Controls combined. I had Aircraft X land Runway XXR. I told the aircraft to exit the runway at taxiway. An airport vehicle asked to check the runway behind the Aircraft X as per our SOP (Standard Operating Procedure). Aircraft X then stopped at taxiway on the runway an asked if I was sure I wanted him to clear there as he is a [type aircraft]. I said affirmative. It was then too close for the next arrival to land safely so I sent him around. I then got the airport vehicle on to the runway but had to have him exit early as more arrivals were too close. It was then that the ASDE-X (Airport Surface Detection Equipment) alarmed informing me that the next [Runway] XXR arrival and [Runway] XY arrival were in conflict. I sent the [Runway] XXR arrival; Aircraft Y; around. Aircraft Y was about to touch down when he executed the go around. I had become distracted by the situation with Aircraft X and vehicle. By the time I was made aware of the tie between the [Runway] XY arrival and [Runway] XXR arrival the ASDE-X had alarmed. I would give more space behind Aircraft X to do the runway sweep and maybe have local controls split during the push.

They got all the way to about 3 minutes from the field before they stated that they had the field in sight and wanted the Visual Approach. They had been assigned present heading and to maintain 9 thousand; but then I cleared them for the Visual Approach. Shortly after the aircraft informed they were VMC and were just going to do local maneuvers while they 'come up with a plan'. They had not begun their descent; and I asked if they were cancelling IFR; and they said no. I told them 'approach clearance cancelled; maintained 9 thousand' and I neglected to give them routing. A hit (radar update) or two goes by and they make a slight left turn and I assign them a heading for terrain. A few hits later; they made a turn into the 9700 foot MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) at 9 thousand feet. The pilot was cleared for the Visual; and the last thing I expected them to do was to turn about 160 degrees away from the airfield. They're allowed to climb; descend; and turn; on a Visual Approach; but they're required to keep the field in sight; which they obviously can't do on that easterly heading; so I'm not sure why they turned that far east. Additionally; I don't think a Visual Approach clearance enables an aircraft to just hold and 'come up with a plan'. I get updates every 12 seconds; and I kept waiting; and hoping; that the pilot would fly their assigned heading. I'm not sure how long it took for him to be established on the turn; but if I had updates every second; I would have known he wasn't taking my turn; and climbed him. This airspace area needs an Approach Control. I believe that if there had been faster updates on the data block; I would have taken different action.

column121: In VFR conditions and clear of clouds on final approach to Runway XXL in ZZZ. ATC vectored us behind two other aircraft on final for the same runway and assigned us a speed of 160 kts. The aircraft was already configured with approach flaps and slowing. Tower advised that the aircraft in front of us had slowed further and advised us to slow to minimum approach speed. We fully configured the aircraft for landing and continued to slow. Tower advised we were still 60 kts faster than the preceding aircraft and requested us to do an 's' turn to the north to provide further spacing. The Pilot Flying; using the autopilot; initiated a 90 degree turn to the north (right) and continued to descend. We were clear of any traffic. The parallel runway was closed. About 80 degrees perpendicular to the approach course; using the autopilot; the Pilot Flying turned the aircraft back towards the runway. I; the Pilot Monitoring advised him to slow his descent rate; we were continuing to descend while maneuvering; using the autopilot the Pilot Flying slowed the rate of descent. At about the same instant at 2.5 mi from the end of the runway. Tower stated that he had a 'low altitude alert' on us and he advised us to 'initiate a climb'. The altimeter showed 860 ft above the water. The electronic glide path showed one dot low. The Pilot Flying immediately disengaged the autopilot pilot and applied back pressure to the controls. The aircraft immediately recovered to 1;100 ft agl. The Pilot Flying continued the turn towards the runway and descended on the glide path. At 1;000 ft agl; I; the Pilot Monitoring; reported 'stable'. I confirmed our landing clearance. At 500 ft agl; I reported 'stable'. We continued and landed. There were no TAWS warning triggered by the event. No alarms 'glide slope' or 'terrain to low' triggered.Less automation. Had the Pilot Flying turned off the autopilot for the maneuver and hand flown the aircraft; responding to the rate of descent would have happened in a more timely manner and an altitude low waning would have probably not been triggered. Hand flying would have managed the rate of descent better.

I immediately jumped up and opened the galley door and shouted to the fueler to stop because the Right engine was running. It took him approximately a minute to understand what I was saying and he stopped fueling. We took on about 1000 lbs total. I contacted the ramp and he said that they were Other Company and not under his direct control. I informed him I would write up the incident. Rest of the flight was without incident.Have a notice to the pilots and to stations directed specifically at the rampers and fuelers that aircraft cannot Hot refuel. This seems to be more of we're finally busy and COVID is over so we're rusty and rushed. I had a second incident at ZZZ on the return flight. We arrived at the gate in ZZZ without incident. I shut down the left engine while leaving the right one running since we had no APU. The ground crew had trouble hooking up power and before I shut down the second engine; I saw the AUTO XFLOW INHIBIT status message. I had the First Officer immediately head to the galley door to have ramp stop fueling which was just starting. I was mostly deplaned and power was coming up so I killed the engine. The First Officer got the fueler to stop and we took on less than 100 lbs. I discussed with ramp personal reminding them not to start fueling until the engines are shut down. column121: We were dispatched an aircraft that had previously been reported with a directional control discrepancy with the right main gear (time frame between this being reported and me getting this aircraft I assume was less than 15 min). This aircraft was not taken off the line for maintenance to check. In the aircraft book I had not seen this discrepancy listed when I opened it. I had gone out and done a preflight of the aircraft and did not see any issue with either landing gear (treads and wheel pressure were all fine and no sign of brake fluid leak). We took off with no incident. We proceeded to ZZZ where we did a few landings. I noted that the aircraft slid a bit which I thought was my new student locking up the brakes. I told him; 'I have controls' and told him to get off the brakes (also visually inspected his feet were off). I assumed it was due to improper use of brakes and we continued to do landings. On our last takeoff at our rotation speed; I noticed the aircraft's right wing dip and an 'odd' experience in the rudder pedals. I believed it was a gust of crosswind (as we experienced this multiple times during our ground reference maneuvers earlier). I took controls and had us climb. However; after thinking about the sensation I got from the rudder pedals I came to the conclusion that my wheel might have been deflated. I decided I wanted to fly back to ZZZ as the runway was longer; wider and ATC could inspect my gear. I came in and Approach addressed me as 'priority aircraft' which I responded that we were not in an emergency as I wanted my tire inspected first before I declared my situation as an emergency (At no point did I declare myself as an aircraft in an emergency). Once I was handed off to Tower I noticed an ambulance and firetruck holding short of the runway. I did a low approach for [Runway] XXR where I was told my gear looked fine. I concluded with a landing and noticed no issue on my landing or taxi. Maintenance followed me back and inspected the tire which they found no issue with.I do respect the fact that as the PIC of this flight I hold the final authority for the safety of the flight. However; this aircraft should not have made it through to be redispatch moments after it was just reported as 'having a discrepancy'. At the time I heard 'Green' aircraft in the pattern. If I was a few minutes early or late a 'Green' could have easily been given this aircraft. Sending a solo student up with an aircraft with known directional control issues very easily could have resulted in a far worse safety report. I believe an outdated software resulted in this. There were a lot of people this problem slipped through and all of us had been trained by the best flight school in the world. I believe any aircraft that has been reported not fit to fly should be marked by the computer system and shouldn't be able to be redispatch. As noted above; this problem had slipped through a number of very well trained personal. Just like the swiss cheese model when analyzing an accidents or incidents. This problem should have been picked up but its wasn't and I believe this highlights a vulnerability in our procedures. This problematic aircraft could have very easily ended up in the hands of a solo student. I would recommend software that allows the dispatcher the ability to straight away remove an aircraft from the line without having to wait for the aircraft's book to be brought in. Or simply marking an aircraft as having been reported as having a discrepancy.

Not knowing how fast the aircraft was going to approach the runway; we elected to stay put and maintain visual contact with the landing aircraft. As that aircraft landed; another aircraft (PC-12) announced their intentions to land while on a left base to final. Again; we announced we were past the hold short line but not on the runway surface. They acknowledged our location and continued to land while showing no attempts to increase spacing for us to move our aircraft. After the second aircraft landed; we departed Runway 36 without further incident.

The trainee then told Aircraft Y to descend for traffic. I keyed up and told Aircraft X to report complete with RA and that the traffic had Aircraft X in sight. column121: I was providing on the job training on Ground 1 when the following event happened. Aircraft X exited [Runway] 25R at J and was instructed to 'taxi via B; L; hold short of K1 and contact City Ramp.' Aircraft X read back the instruction correctly. The developmental made two more calls and in the meantime Aircraft X started to turn from B onto K...one taxiway earlier than instructed. I pointed out the error to the developmental and then the developmental immediately told Aircraft X to stop. (Background: K & L are now City Ramp controlled and the only entry point to the ramp without additional coordination is via L short of K1.)We explained to Aircraft X that they were prematurely turning into the ramp and not following the issued route. Aircraft X responded by saying they had received clearance to continue on K short of K2; however we had never mentioned anything about K/K2. The Controller in Charge coordinated with the City Ramp via the phone and verified that it was safe for Aircraft X to continue northbound on K. Additionally; while this entire scenario was unfolding; Aircraft Y deviated from their taxi clearance (B; K; C; Northroute) and turned onto L. I overkeyed the developmental and told Aircraft Y to 'hold short of K1 and contact the ramp.' After the training session; I reviewed the tapes for both Aircraft X and Aircraft Y's instructions/readbacks. There were no discrepancies with either--each pilot responded correctly and timely to the developmental's instructions but failed to comply.I am writing a report about the operation of this 'LAWA City Ramp' because it continues to cause unsafe proximity events. While I was previously under the impression that the majority of the errors were due to pilot expectation bias and over reliance on familiarity (the old Northroute was on K/L); I now believe that the instructions of the Ramp Tower personnel contributed to Aircraft X's deviation today. See below:When we told Aircraft X that they turned too soon; their response was 'we had further clearance to continue via K short of K2.' It is my belief that Aircraft X called the City Ramp on their second radio while taxiing westbound on B and the ramp personnel instructed them to continue via K short of K2. Aircraft X understood this as a complete change from the instructions we provided and began to turn on K early. If this is approximately what happened; then it needs to be remedied immediately. It's unsafe to have non-ATC personnel issuing instructions to aircraft that could be confused with new or amended instructions for how to taxi/proceed on the movement area. The ramp personnel need to clearly define to inbound aircraft that the previous clearance remains the same; but once on L short of K1; they may continue; hold; etc.Additionally; this is about the actions of pilots that turn early onto L/K when they correctly were issued and read back 'the Northroute.' I previously stated that 'I'd recommend additional signage; a change to the charts; or added emphasis in the text of the 'Northroute' that emboldens how N is now the Northroute; not K or L. Or all of the above;' and my sentiments still remain. I believe there was one small change to the Jeppesen map that tried to highlight the new ramp area but bolding the Northroute and re-emphasizing that N is the Northroute could also help prevent this occurrence.

Momentarily I didn't believe it but quickly went to Aircraft Y and told him to stop.  I then immediately cancelled Aircraft X takeoff clearance. column123: Aircraft Y was holding on taxiway H short of H9. Aircraft X was told to Line up and wait Runway 25R.  Aircraft Y was then told to turn left at H and Hold Short Runway 25R. I on Local Assist went to Ground Control to see if they had Aircraft Y on frequency which they did not.  I noticed Aircraft Y start moving.  Local Control reached out again with and repeated Hold Short Runway 25R. This time Aircraft Y responded and gave a good read back of Hold Short Runway 25R.Aircraft X was cleared for takeoff and started the departure roll.  I first noticed that as Aircraft Y was turning at taxiway Lima approaching the hold bars it did not look like they were stopping; and verbal said that. I do not know if the Runway Stop Lights were working properly.  I know there were issues with that system in the past with the red lights turning off early. column123: While being vectored for ILS approach to RWY XXL at ZZZZ; the Pilot Flying momentarily began an early descent through required altitude of 2;600 feet.  I; the pilot not flying; and the jumpseat pilot gave immediate verbal corrections. Aircraft descended to approximately 2;420 feet as the Pilot Flying regained situational awareness and applied corrective action to include resetting the MCP altitude; and then reverting to manual control.  The recovery was smooth and controlled.  As the aircraft was returning to 2;600 feet; ZZZZ Radar Control called to direct climb to 2;600 feet.  I responded to ATC while the Pilot Flying completed the recovery.  Approach and landing were completed uneventfully.   This was the final segment of a 2 leg international flying pairing nearing 17 hours of duty.  All crew members were not at their best state of alertness.  Original arrival setup was for a STAR coupled to an ILS approach.  Flown arrival was very non standard. The aircraft was vectored off arrival path and given clearance to disregard many published mandatory altitudes.  This complicated arrival descent planning and may have led to the Pilot Flying losing some situational awareness.  ATC Traffic on approach ahead was a potential conflict.  This diverted my attention during the approach.Delays in positive corrective action which could have lessened/prevented the altitude deviation were potentially caused by distraction due to traffic call; lessened cognitive performance due to overnight/long duty period; lack of urgency due to VMC weather with runway in view.

column121: Early descent and low speed condition resulting in go-around. I was the Pilot Flying. Very short flight. Visual approach to RWY 15 at CHS. I was expecting the ILS approach. I missed that the GS for RWY 15 was out of service. We had briefed the OSPRI7 STAR. ATC recleared us direct to the airport and eventually direct MAMAE intersection to join the localizer for [Runway] 15 at 3;000 [feet] ft. Airport was in sight and we were cleared for a visual approach. I armed the approach and when we went into altitude capture at 3;000 [feet] I incorrectly set an altitude below 3;000 [feet] to allow the descent to continue in order to join the glide slope. I then realized we were not receiving the glide slope and were below the FAF crossing altitude at 1000ft. I disconnected the autopilot and stopped the descent. Unfortunately I did not also call for the flight directors off initially. I am relatively new to the equipment. Since we were in landing configuration of course the speed dropped rapidly. We were in landing configuration with the airport and PAPI's in sight but since the approach was unstable I decided to go around. We then flew the RWY 15 RNAV (GPS)Y to a normal landing. It was the third leg of a busy day with thunderstorm avoidance on the first two flights. It is my practice to carefully review the NOTAMs but somehow I missed the GS OTS. I haven't been into CHS as yet and the flight is very short and our ATC clearance had us high from the top of descent.Direct to a new airport on a time compressed flight for a visual at night is never in my opinion a pleasant way to conclude a long day of flying. Upon honest reflection I fully acknowledge I had a strong expectation bias for the ILS to 15. The lack of the GS and the unexpected consequences placed us in a reactionary position which is unacceptable.Our training is clear on how to capture and correct erroneous situations should they occur and we did our best to stop and correct an inadvertently entered unstable position. This was a clear example of the value and necessity of our human factors training. I know these things have happened before and I consider it my professional responsibility to not allow it to happen to me. And yet it did. Recognizing; and fully appreciating how higher than expected workload situations can present themselves is an essential aspect to our work. An increased diligence regarding the review of NOTAMs is a resounding suggestion I'm making to myself for one. Also; the need for particularly increased vigilance when in situations such as this is something I'll never forget.

column121: I was the Pilot Flying on Flight XXXX; ZZZ to ZZZ1; DATE. All was normal until takeoff roll. At approximately 110 kts a loud signal began blaring in the cockpit. ECAM was clear of any messages and master caution/warning lights were extinguished so I elected to continue the takeoff. When the After Takeoff Checklist was completed we [advised] with Tower and told them we wanted to return for an immediate landing. I had two jumpseaters that flew the A321 and they were essential assets. They assisted in determining the source of the loud sound which was the EVAC Command Signal and the EMER CALL buzzers going off continuously. Neither the signal or buzzers would silence. Jump seater 1; Captain NAME1; covered the EVAV speaker with his hand trying to muzzle the sound and provided valuable input. I transferred the aircraft to the First Officer and determined that the cabin inter-phone was inoperative and was not able to communicate with the cabin. I directed the jump seater 2; First Officer NAME1; to open the cockpit door and establish communications with the flight attendants and asses the conditions in the cabin. He reported that passengers cabin lights; emergency exit lights; and lavatory smoke detector lights were intermittently blinking on and off. I told him through the cockpit door to tell the flight attendants that we were returning to land and not to evacuate and for the passengers to remain seated once the aircraft stopped. I took back control of the aircraft and we accomplished an over weight landing. After stopping and consulting with the AARF commander we determined it was safe to taxi to the gate. Signal continued to sound until maintenance showed and pulled circuit breakers at the gate. The assistance of my First Officer along with the 2 jump seaters was absolutely essential in successful conclusion to this event. During the event; my confusion of what was actually happening might have been mitigated by a deeper understanding of the CIDS (Cabin Intercommunication Data System) system.I feel that having better systems knowledge would be beneficial to any similar future events.

column121: On a flight landing in EWR; the ATIS advertised the Stadium Visual to Runway 29.  Although the environment was busy due to the airspace congestion; everything was working out smoothly and well.  Approach mentioned to us a few different aircraft along the way to use caution for due to wake turbulence and we did use caution for the several large aircraft we saw during the terminal phase of the approach.  I do not recall; however; my Pilot Monitoring later said the Tower upon clearing us to land issued another caution for wake turbulence for a 747.  I did not see any flying aircraft that would pose any wake turbulence threat.  The approach was normal and I was right on my target speeds.  I closed both throttles all the way during the flare; and both engines settled all the way to idle.  The tires were maybe an inch or two from the surface; the yoke back bumping the stop; all the flying air gone from the wings; touchdown imminent; [when] a large gust from the left shoved the aircraft aggressively to the right.  The gust raised the left wing up and also the whole aircraft up into the air several feet. When the gust reached the tail; it shoved the vertical stabilizer right moving the nose left.  The centerline of the runway went from centered on the nose gear to well outside the main gear near the left wing tip.  There were two gusts one right after the other; both the same and having the same effect on the aircraft.  I immediately shoved both throttles all the way forward and countered with the controls to maintain orientation.  I don't recall calling the go-around; but my Pilot Monitoring says I called it right away. The air was smooth after the two gusts; the plane settled some towards the ground as it gained momentum.  Once everything was straightened out and the airplane with some flying speed now climbing from the runway instead of closing toward it; I realized my right arm was still holding the throttles against the stop.  Knowing that could be very bad for the engines; I looked inside to see how badly they were over revving and simultaneously pulled them back off the stop some.  I never got the chance to see because I noticed the left engine sitting at idle while the right engine was making full power.  That's when I realized my right leg was holding about 80% right rudder travel in.  The gear was up and the flaps sitting at 15 degrees and we were making only 125 knots.  Then after several more seconds; the left engine began to slowly make its way through the 50%'s; 60s; 70s; 80s; and finally into the low 90% of N1 speed.  With everything back to normal; we cleaned up the aircraft and settled in for the next approach.  ATC again offered us the Stadium Visual to 29 but said the ILS 22R was available.  We took the ILS 22R.  ATC never asked us why we went around.  We did not make any communications to our team in the cabin until after shutdown.  The origin of the gust was immediately very clear to both of us in the cockpit.  It was jet blast from jet engines pointed at our flight path during our touchdown; departing aircraft on 22R beginning their takeoff roll were blasting the landing zone of 29 with their engines.  Perhaps the cautionary statements we received from ATC for wake turbulence were referring to jet blast from airlines beginning to roll on the ground and not from wake turbulence from aircraft in flight.  Had I been aware this was the case; I would have never accepted 29 as a landing option.  The 22R & L runways cross Runway 29; so I envisioned aircraft departing across our landing path as they took off on the 22s.  So I would see them and be aware of the timing for jet blast and wake from landing aircraft.  However; instead; airlines were making intersection departures after the 29 intersection; shortening their takeoff distance.  So instead of crossing our path; they were starting from our left and starting their takeoff roll; and moving away to our left.  I never looked left during my landing; so I don'tknow what was there blasting us; I'm guessing something big.  Of note; due to high fuel price in EWR; we were heavy; just a few hundred pounds under max landing weight.  I would first suggest not landing small jets on [Runway] 29 at EWR when 22s are departing in the way they were.  I wasn't familiar enough with EWR to know how dangerous the circumstance would be; I've landed on 22s in years past.  I would also suggest the left engine acceleration be repaired to an acceptable level.  Waiting 15 - 20 seconds for an engine to give power in fight is not acceptable.  If neither engine had given power for that amount of time; I do not believe a touchdown without major damage would've been possible.  Even still; it took everything the aircraft had in it plus everything humanly possible I could do to prevent an accident.

column121: Inadvertent switching off of IR1 mode selector which deactivated that associated ADIRU. ADR and IR data not available. This occurred during flight one of day two of an initial Captain upgrade. The trainee came off the B777. He has been with our company for many years. The three legs of day one was extraordinarily busy. It was immediately clear to me during those three legs he had studied hard during training and had mastered much of the material. On the first two legs of day one I had a LCA (Line Check Airman) in-training watching me conduct the line check as part of that LCA's upgrade training. I commented to the new LCA not all trainees will be so well prepared as this one.This flight was leg four of the IOE and the first flight of day two. Our transportation to the airport was 15 minutes late and there was a detour so we arrived at the aircraft about 30 minutes prior to departure. Normally; I introduce myself to all the FAs (Flight Attendant). However; because we were on IOE; [we] were somewhat late to the aircraft and on Release 6. I only introduced myself to the FM. I felt I did not have time go to the back to introduce myself to the FAs assigned to the rear of the aircraft.We had been in the seat for approximately 3 hours. The upgrade Captain requested I ask the FM to prepare the meals and that we would then take a restroom break when the meals were ready. I did so. The FM called us about 25 minutes later to state the meals were ready. The upgrade Captain offered me the opportunity to use the Lav first. I declined and said he should go first and I would then go. The door chime rang and then I heard a knock. That knock is not standard. However; it occurs occasionally with legacy Company 2 flight attendants. We put on our masks. I saw the upgrade Captain move to get out of his seat; stand up; and let the FA in while he then left the cockpit. I noticed nothing odd about his movement out of the seat and to the rear of the cockpit. I saw out of the corner of my eye the FA was standing near the rear of the cockpit just behind and to the right of the Captain's seat; a normal position for a relief FA.My concentration then focused on something else. I think it was because we were getting ready to enter a large area of convective activity. I might have been looking at WSI and comparing that to what I was seeing on the weather radar. Why my gaze was generally focused forward and right I am not sure; but it was. I planned to brief the relief FA about this weather and its possible effect on their service in a few minutes. It was at that point; maybe 30-45 seconds after the upgrade Captain had left the cockpit; that for lack of a better description; 'all hell broke loose.' The cockpit went from a completely benign environment to one of confusion. The startle effect was in full force. The first warning was a continuous repetitive chime and the warning lights flashing. I immediately looked at the E/WD (Engine/Warning Display) and noted about 4-5 ECAMs listed; primary secondary and independent failures in both red and amber. I silenced the CRC (Continuous Repetitive Chime) by pushing [the] master warning light. That silenced the CRC. However; there still was an aural alert going off that I could not silence; which created a fair bit of consternation on my part. I look at my PFD and saw the FMAs were wrong. I then saw the AP (Autopilot) was off and that there was nothing where I expected to see the AT (Autothrottle) condition. I noted the aircraft climbing slightly and corrected that. I knew the AP disengaged for some reason but didn't know why. I thought about engaging AP 2 but then thought that may create new problems; so I elected to hand-fly until the ECAMs were sorted out. I saw we were no longer in NAV but again; wasn't sure why. I did see that the aircraft didn't diverge much from the 'green line' so lateral stick inputs weren't necessary. At this point ATC called to ask us something about recycling the transponder. We wereon speaker at that time; I responded we had a problem and to standby.I then noted the airspeed increasing and pulled the TLs (Thrust Lever) back; I didn't want to add an over-speed to our problems. This silenced another aural sound. I do not recall seeing a Thrust Locked ECAM or FMA which I thought would have been the source of the alert I couldn't silence. I glanced at the Captain PFD (Primary Flight Display) and ND (Navigation Display) and saw they didn't look right.The aircraft was reasonably stabilized now but; in my mind; because the ECAMs were displayed; the situation wasn't. I then told the FA to recall the trainee Captain to the cockpit. He opened the door; looked and then closed it; and said he was in the bathroom. I told the FA I knew that and I wanted him back in the cockpit now. He then had the FM knock on the Lav door. The trainee Captain returned to the cockpit and the relief FA left. The trainee Captain was incredulous when he looked at the E/WD. I told him I was hand-flying; had the aircraft and radios; and that he was to handle the ECAMs. It was at this point I noted we were about 20 knot slow; well within flying speed but slow for planned speed. I had overcompensated for my worry of overspending the aircraft. I pushed the power back up. Airspeed had fallen out of my cross-check. The trainee Captain methodically and correctly went through the ECAMs. As I recall the first several ECAMs had no action items; one ECAM had us switch the air data switch to three. At some point during this; ATC stated they now had data on us and asked if we needed assistance. We told him we were completing a procedure and to standby. Once the status messages were read and the ECAM procedure completed; I reached up to engage AP two. It did so. I armed the AT and then moved the TLs to the climb detent to engage it. Our ATC clearance was to proceed direct to a fix so we reinserted that. I don't recall having to pull or push to capture our assigned altitude but I can't be sure.It was now maybe 4-5 minutes after the initial event where I could take a breath. I recalled the ECAM and saw the ADR 1 fault. I then looked over to the ADIRS panel and saw IR mode selector one was in the OFF position. It; of course; was on for the flight up until some point in [the] last few minutes. I asked the trainee Captain if he recalls hitting the switch with his head or back as he left his seat. He said no. I then thought perhaps the switch was defective. This aircraft came to us as a through flight. We did not have to turn them on so we had no knowledge of how that switch felt by turning it on. We again discussed it and he stated he didn't recall even touching the overhead panel while leaving the seat.Because I didn't introduce myself to the FAs at the rear of the aircraft prior to the flight; I wasn't sure which FA came to the cockpit during our break. I asked the FM to ask the FA who came to the cockpit to call us on the interphone. That FA did and I asked him if he recalled touching anything on the overhead panel; he stated he did not. What I found unusual was that during the event; the FA seemed very nonplussed by the cacophony of sounds in the cockpit. I would have expected a FA to at least ask what was going on; but maybe he was somewhat shocked by what he saw and heard during his short time in the cockpit.The trainee Captain and I discussed that I would write up the ECAM and then conference Dispatch and Technical Support Maintenance Control to provide further details of what we thought may have occurred. I wanted the switch looked at but also didn't want Maintenance to search for a problem which might not exist. I ACARS'd Dispatch with the request and he set up the conference call. The communications with Technical Support Maintenance Control were reasonably good and he captured exactly what I wanted him to know and he appended it to our write-up. Since the Captain's displays were significantly degraded; we switched PF/PM roles. Fromthat point we continually deviated for weather; were put in holding; and changed our alternate three times. We over-burned by almost 5500 lb on this flight; more than on any flight I have been on in [an] Airbus. It was an understatement to say this was a busy flight. I don't know how this happened. The final flight of the day was a termination. As the trainee ran that checklist and turned off the IRUs; he stated he couldn't believe how he accidentally managed to switch that style of switch - pull and turn - off by getting out of the cockpit.I am disappointed in myself for not more thoroughly reviewing the flight manual for ADR 1 fault after things had settled down. We did not have a GPWS TERR FAULT light and no ECAM direction to switch it off so it remained on. We discussed that threat in that we were now the aircraft's GPWS system and to be cognizant of the terrain. We also discussed changing the transponder to position 2 but did not do so because there was no ECAM direction to [do] so and ATC noted no anomalies in our reporting. Also; once I saw the IR mode selector switch in the off position; I should have considered reviewing the NAV IR fault non-normal even though we didn't have that ECAM. I did not do a word search in the flight manual for ADR. Had I done so; I would have seen that there may be RVSM limitations associated with its failure and should have gone to the FOM for further information. I recall many years ago; our Line Manager at the time; wrote up in his weekly update a similar event. As I recall he wrote the trainee somehow managed to hook the window shade into that same switch and turned it off. That of course didn't happen here.

column121: We were descending on the arrival into ZZZ. We were descending at a high speed programmed into the FMC. I have over 10;000 hours flying the Next Gens and am comfortable with that descent profile. This was my first MAX flight. Somewhere in the descent the FMA changed without warning to MCP SPD (Mode Control Panel Speed). It went unnoticed. I have witnessed many Next Gens revert to VNV SPD (Vnav Speed); but never MCP SPD. There is a significant difference; in that MCP SPD gives no altitude protection. I have never seen anything like this. Somewhere around ZZZZZ/11000; we received a radio call and became distracted as the aircraft descended through 11000. I did not catch the deviation until 10;000 and momentum and recovery took us to about 9;500 feet. I disconnect all automation and hand flew the recovery as I tried to figure out what had just happened. We reported the deviation to ATC and continued to ZZZ without incident.I do not know why this happened. I can only guess that somehow LVL CHG (Level Change) was inadvertently selected. Another theory is that VNV could not keep up and reverted to MCP SPD. This happens sometimes in the Next Gens; but it always reverts to VNV SPD; which is much safer.
column123: On arrival to ZZZ in VFR conditions. Arrival information was checked by both pilots for altitude and speed restrictions prior to descent. Aircraft was cleared by approach to descend via the arrival with a bottom altitude of 8;000 feet. The crossing restriction at ZZZZZ is 11;000 feet. Prior to reaching ZZZZZ the crew saw the aircraft was in Lvl Chg (Level Change) mode instead of VNAV and was descending through 10;000 feet. The Captain (Pilot Flying) took the controls; disconnected the autopilot and returned to altitude. The FO (Pilot Monitoring) notified ATC of the deviation but no conflicts existed and was handed to the next controller.  Upon checking the FMS the First Officer determined the altitude restriction was still active at ZZZZZ for 11;000 feet. The crew briefly discussed the incident and possible errors but did not determine how or when the autopilot entered Lvl Chg mode during the descent.

column121: While at cruise at 35;000 feet in Cairo control airspace; we began to receive a series of Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting messages- ATC Fault; Unable RNP and Terrain Position.  We referenced the Quick Reference Handbook for each message but were unable to clear the faults. We asked ATC if they saw any issue with our transponder and they replied that they saw no problems. Shortly after crossing from Amman control to Jeddah on airway Y415; we received the FMC message 'Verify position'. We saw that we were off the airway to the left and ATC asked if we were on the airway. The First Officer and I put our range scales to 5 miles and noted that the left side showed us approximately 3 to 5 miles left of course; First Officer side showed the same distance to the right of course.We checked the FMC position reference pages and saw that GPS position was blank and substantial errors on the other positions - FMC; IRS and Radio. We advised ATC of the GPS failure and could not determine which source was accurate. ATC said we were showing right of course. I selected GPS off then on; selected HDG (heading) select to manually steer to course. Reselected LNAV. Nothing seemed to be working. I asked for direct to a fix further down the airway. No VORs were on this airway to use for navigation. I repeated switching heading to LNAV but the aircraft symbol did not move closer to the course line as if it was frozen. We were continually advising ATC and monitoring position reference as GPS was now intermittent and RNP-ANP errors were constantly changing. Eventually GPS began to work and we were able to get back on course.  This entire time we never received any EICAS or FMA indications of any faults such as 'GPS'; 'IRS Nav Only'; 'LNAV'.  ATC passed the information to subsequent ATC and they offered vectors if needed. After position MOGON; navigation functions all appeared normal for the remainder for the flight.

column121: Preflight; taxi; takeoff and initial climb were normal. We were flying the ZZZZZ RNAV departure when at approximately 15;000 feet the aircraft displayed a Level 2 alert; CABIN INFLO LO. I was acting as Pilot Monitoring so I began to reference the QRH; but the alert extinguished after only a few seconds. As a matter of course my First Officer and I took note of the QRH procedures for this alert should it reappear. A few moments later we heard a loud squeal seemingly emanating from below the flight deck. This in itself wasn't entirely unusual in an aircraft of this vintage; but the noise was soon followed by a level 1 alert; CABIN RATE. I again referenced the QRH and we found that; indeed; cabin altitude was rising. Passing approximately FL 210 we heard a loud BOOM and the cabin altitude increased its rate of climb. We shallowed our rate of climb to around 1;000 fpm to allow us to process the problem. Given the rate of increase in cabin altitude it was clear to me that we were about to exceed 10;000 feet; and I verbalized to my First Officer to get ready to don O2 masks. This was followed by a Level 3 alert; CABIN ALTITUDE. We donned masks; established crew communications; and I instructed our jump seater to don her mask as well (and comm was established with her). I asked ZZZ Center for a level off at FL 240 (our next available FL). Roles were established with my First Officer continuing as Pilot Flying and I as Pilot Monitoring. We followed QRH procedures for the CABIN ALTITUDE alert but it was clear that the cabin altitude could not be controlled. I [advised] with ZZZ Center and requested an immediate descent and turn back to ZZZ. We were given clearance to 9;000 feet and a left turn back to the airport. My First Officer began an IDLE descent with full spoilers while I set up navigation. Once in contact with ZZZ Approach we were offered any runway landing south. Given that our weight was well below max landing weight we accepted RWY XXR. During the descent I built and briefed the ILS approach; and as cabin altitude went below 10;000 feet we doffed masks and resumed communication on boom mics. I instructed our jump seater that she could do the same. ZZZ Approach inquired as to whether I wished to continue as a [priority] aircraft; but given that cabin altitude had stabilized and we had no other issues I declined the status (CFR did not roll). At approximately 25 nm from the airport I assumed the role of Pilot Flying. My First Officer did an excellent job in depressurizing the aircraft during the remaining descent IAW limitations. Landing; rollout and taxi in were uneventful. After landing it was discovered that the Avionics Compartment Access door under the nose of the aircraft had come open in flight. Maintenance discovered that the Avionics Compartment Access door seal failed allowing the door to open in flight. I don't have a good answer for this one. These are aging aircraft and anomalies are to be expected. I am unaware of current maintenance practices in regards to inspecting these door seals; but perhaps a greater emphasis needs to be put on those inspections.

column121: During cruise flight; the Master Caution light illuminated with the #2 engine driven B hydraulic system light. We ran the QRH and turned the pump off; and also noted that the B system indicated approximately 3000 psi but zero quantity. We discussed the possibility that although technically the conditions were not yet met per the QRH; there was a strong possibility that entire B system had likely failed or was failing and notified Dispatch via ACARS that it was a possibility. We ran the weight data for landing in ZZZ with the B system inop; and came up with approximately 1;300 feet of stopping margin with max manual braking. We let Dispatch know that even with a hypothetical total loss of the B system; ZZZ was still acceptable and they concurred with our stopping margin calculation.  The B system held steady with approximately 3000 psi until we started our descent into ZZZ with approximately 120 miles to go.  As we were descending; the psi of the B system quickly dropped to near zero and the ELEC 1 B pump Low Pressure light illuminated; along with the Flight Control B Low Pressure light. We ran the QRH for Loss of System B and calculated brake cooling; which advised staying off the gate for 30 minutes.We advised Approach of the situation and asked for delay vectors for checklists and CFR (Crash Fire Rescue)  trucks to be present at the end of the runway to check brake temps and condition after landing. We landed on the runway at the end and shut down engines at the request of CFR. CFR noted that hydraulic fluid was leaking from number 2 engine and brake temps were above 500 C. They were also concerned about hydraulic fluid on the hot section of #2 engine aerosolizing and advised we wait for cooler temps for ramp safety. CFR advised that although the brakes had cooled acceptably they were still concerned about the possible aerosolizing of hydraulic fluid from #2 engine hot section and advised we wait another 10 minutes. This all led to a lengthy ground delay but we did the best we could to keep the flight attendants and Passengers informed. In our judgement it was the safest course of action to follow CFR recommendations.

column121: I knew it was going to be a struggle getting out of ZZZ with all passengers on board when I saw the take-off performance. At 40C the margin between PTOW (Planned Take-off Weight) and MTOW was 1100 lbs. My First Officer (FO) was terrific; but it was his first trip since IOE; he had 18 hours on the airplane at the start of the sequence; and had not flown prior to training for about 8 months. In addition; it was only my second time flying the ZZZZZ departure; which has three at or above altitudes on it; which is a new thing in ZZZ.  I live in ZZZ; and consequently fly out of there a great deal.  All previous RNAV departures used to have at or below altitudes on them (to keep clear of inbound aircraft); so it never used to be an issue worrying about making altitudes on the SID.  At the aircraft; I was already concerned about two things: brake temps and having to bump passengers.  I asked my FO to pull us up numbers for 41 and 42C; just in case it got hotter; as it was likely to. In addition; I believe the winds were swinging around - runway XXR had a tailwind component at one point; so I was also looking for numbers for XYL; but due to terrain; the only runway that worked at all was XXR.  I noticed that we would be unable to make the restrictions and asked the FO to ask for altitude relief on the SID as soon as he contacted ground.  In my experience; asking for altitude relief at other airports was never an issue; so I was not overly concerned. We pushed back; and naturally were over PTOW.  I asked the FO to request a new take-off performance for 41 and 42C.  We eventually landed on a Flaps 1 take-off performance requiring thrust bump which got us legal for takeoff.  All this occurred during the short taxi from the terminal to runway XXR.By the time we reached number 1 holding short of the runway; I realized we had forgotten to ask for the altitude relief on the SID. I asked the FO to do so as we were taking the runway.  The controller; upon hearing the request; told us to taxi clear and get a new clearance.  By this time there were 6-8 aircraft in a queue for takeoff; and our brake temps were over 150 degrees.  My main concern was that if we had to leave the runway; it would get too hot to accommodate the load; and by the time we taxied for another 30 minutes; the brakes would be too hot for takeoff.  So; glancing down at the FMS; which showed that we would miss the altitude restrictions by 5-700 feet; I knew that if we delayed cleanup; we could easily make those restrictions.  I told the controller that we could manage the departure; and he again cleared us for takeoff.  I told my FO that since we were at the max performance envelope of the airplane; he should rotate very gently.  As we were rolling down the runway; my attention was fixed on the EGT; as I had not done a bump takeoff before; and the engines were exactly on the edge of the red.  He did as I asked; and as a result; we were very fast on the initial climb segment.  As we climbed out; I was fixated on the altitude.  Once it became clear that the 5;000 ft altitude (I think around 4;500 feet MSL) I relaxed a bit and told him we could clean up.  He set climb power (which was a much greater reduction than normal due to the thrust bump) and I reached for the flap lever and set flaps up.  At this time we were still wings level.  I was so fixated on the altitude; and our airspeed shortly after takeoff was so much higher than usual that I didn't take a good look at the airspeed indicator.  I believe that I retracted the flaps very early. VLS (lowest selectable speed) jumped by perhaps 40 knots; and we ended up about 20 knots below VLS.  Naturally; we were now facing rapidly rising terrain; and the SID commanded a right turn.  My FO started to turn; and now instead of being below VLS; we were in alpha floor.  I instructed my FO to lower the nose; but it wasn't happening quickly enough; so I grabbed the side stick and pushed the nose over; at the same time requesting him to let go.  There was a momentary DUAL INPUT" annunciation and a momentary noticeable low speed buffet which lasted perhaps a second.  We lost perhaps 300 feet of altitude as I got the airspeed back.  We were able to make all of the altitude restrictions and I don't believe there were any deviations from the SID.  Once we recovered; the only other item remaining was how to get the auto throttles out of alpha floor.  Eventually; we turned them off (match and mash) and back on again and that got the system back to normal.I was using my knowledge of past experience flying the old SIDs.  They didn't have airspeed or at or above altitudes; and my experience in the past that asking for altitude relief on a SID was not a big deal.  In addition; I was flying with a brand new (very sharp) but inexperienced FO; who was relying entirely on my experience.  I was also pushing to accommodate the load without having to remove passengers and/or cargo; and was worried about the brake temp issues; causing me to push to get off the ground as soon as possible.I made several errors.  The first one was not notifying clearance delivery early of our inability to make the altitude and/or airspeed restrictions on the SID.  In the past; ZZZ used to have a procedure for A321 aircraft to delay climb power/flap retraction to 3;000 AGL.  I think if we had used that procedure; we probably would have been able to make the altitude and speed restrictions on the SID.  That procedure is gone.  Second; when we finally did request relief on the SID (by this time we were on the runway) and the controller told us to clear the runway and get a new clearance; I should have done so; even if it had caused us further problems with brake temp and/or takeoff weight.  Third; having taken the decision to take off because I was certain we could delay cleanup; thus making us legal for the SID; I should have taken over flying duties.  This would have alleviated my FO's task saturation; as I was far more experienced in the airplane.  This would still have been sub-optimal; but I am confident the takeoff would have been uneventful.   Fourth; once I retracted the flaps and we were below VLS; I should have put the flaps back to Config 1.  So; there were many errors on my part; but an early intervention with clearance delivery would have solved everything.  I believe there should be a warning to the A320 Fleet about the new SIDS; and that at high temperatures careful note should be taken of the danger of not being able to make altitude restrictions on any SID with at or above altitudes; especially early in the SID; and that relief should be requested at the gate with clearance delivery. Also to note: green dot speed (min maneuver) was 245 with flaps up; so the only way to maintain 230 knot speed at ZZZZZ waypoint is at config 1.  Again; the old requirement to clean up at 3000 AGL would have solved this."

column121: After takeoff; during a turn to a heading of 270 degrees; we received an ALT and IAS cross-side miss-comparison. The autopilot also would not engage when commanded and I hand flew up to 5;000 ft. After leveling off; and receiving instructions to climb; I called for the autopilot again and it connected. During the climb; we kept receiving the IAS and ALT notices and leveled off at 16;000 ft.; FL260; and FL320. We also noted a 200 ft. discrepancy between altimeters at one point. We leveled off at these altitudes because of the miss-comparison. After leveling off; for a minute the miss-compare would go away and we would continue the climb. During the climb and at one of the level-offs; we tried using our alternate static sources. This seemed to work on the Captain's side but the miss-compare came back when we started to climb again. The Captain then ran the airspeed unreliable checklist to see if it would be any help but nothing in the checklist seemed to be a fit for the problem we were encountering. The cause of the problems was not obvious and the checklist did not seem like it was of any help. Also; during the climbs; the FCP was not usable. All of the windows for airspeed; heading; and altitude only showed - - - -.With the problems we were having and not being able to identify the cause combined with the prospect of having to hand-fly and the encounter weather; we felt that continuing to ZZZ1 was not an option should the problems become worse. If we did in fact have an unreliable airspeed; we would be directed to disconnect both AFS and FD switches off which would mean having to leave RVSM; which would lead to higher fuel burns and hand-flying in heavy thunderstorms. [The problem was identified] when the amber IAS and ALT alerts were presented on our PFDs (Primary Flight Display). If I had to guess I would say that the aircraft had some sort of computer issue that was presenting the airspeed and altitude to the displays with differing data and a comparator caught the difference and alerted us. Our first reaction was to fly the plane. I started asking the Captain what his airspeed was as I figured that was more important than altitude. Once we were at a safe altitude and maintaining a safe airspeed; we began to troubleshoot and discuss the problems. There is nothing that we could have done as pilots to prevent this.
column123: On the climb out the EIS detected intermittent ALT and IAS miss-comparisons between Captain and FO's (First Officer) PFD (Primary Flight Display). Stopped climb at 16;000 ft.; the issue went away. We then decided to continue to climb but had to stop at FL260. I had the FO put his STATIC AIR to ALT. Problem went away for about 1 minute and then came back. I then selected Captain STATIC AIR to ALT. This time; the issues went away for a few minutes. We decided to continue the climb but had to stop at FL320 because the problem came back. I ran the emergency non-alert AIRSPEED UNRELIABLE checklist; but the issue was not resolved. At 27100 ft.; Captain's IAS/MACH 336/.830; FO's IAS/MACH 330/.816. At every level change attempt FCP window indicated - - - -. The altitude difference between [the] Captain and FO was over 200 ft. Since AP (Autopilot) #2 was deferred and if we disconnected AP #1 we would not be able to remain in RVSM; we contacted company and returned to ZZZ. No emergency or special handling was required. [The problem was identified by the] amber IAS and ALT on Captain's and FO's upper left-hand corner of the PFD. [The cause was] failure annunciations… cross-side miss-comparisons generated when the EIS detected significant differences between the displayed data of the Captain's and First Officer's instruments AIRSPEED and ALTITUDE. [The response was to] climb to [a] safe altitude; maintain speed; and attempt to address the issue at hand. Maintenance issues cannot be forecasted.
