There was a discontinuity between PLADE and CI28; which I closed up. Once we reached PLADE; I asked my FO (First Officer) to set 7;100 ft. in the mode control panel which is the minimum altitude at CI28 and started a VNAV descent with the intention to arm the ILS just prior to CI28. At approximately 7;600 ft. we received a warning 'too low terrain'. We could visually see the terrain and started to level off; then; very quickly received 'terrain; pull up' with amber showing on the terrain display.  I immediately complied by going into the CFIT recovery procedure. We climbed to approximately 8;000 ft. and leveled off seeing that we were well clear of all terrain (no more warning and terrain indicator showed us to be clear). We then reassessed. At that time; we were very close to CI28 and had plenty of light from the city and a very bright moon. We were also in a good position to continue to the airport; so I continued to an uneventful landing.
column123: We were landing Runway 28 in Guadalajara. Night VMC conditions with moonlight provided adequate visual references. We were set up to land Runway 28 using the ILS DME2 or localizer Runway 28 with the transition for the ILS DME 2 with the IKBAN transition. At the last minute; Control told us to descend via the LIVRI 1D arrival. After changing to this arrival in the FMS; we realized that we needed to descend quickly. To complicate matters; Control give us directions to go direct to PLADE. I estimate Control shortened our arrival by 40 to 50 miles in giving us the arrival change and direct PLADE which greatly compounded our decent plan. This caused us to have to execute an expedited decent while having to re-program the FMS and plan for this new routing. I verbalized terrain that was to our right as we were turning direct PLADE and both the CA (Captain) and I correlated this to what we were seeing on our terrain displays. Prior to reaching PLADE; Control cleared us for the ILS Zulu Runway 28. However; we heard cleared for the ILS Two. I attribute this miscommunication to language barriers. CA asked me to set 7;100 ft.; which would've been correct for ILS 2 but 7;700 ft would've been correct for ILS Z. We got the 'too low; terrain' oral warning followed by the 'terrain; pull up'. CA commanded auto pilot off; stow speed brake (Even though they weren't in use); pitched up and added full thrust. We had the terrain in sight the whole time; as well as the Runway environment. We climbed approximately 500 ft before determining that we could safely continue the approach without incident. We landed on Runway 28 without incident.

column121: Since we have taken delivery of more 737 Max aircraft; I have noticed that aircraft are coming with the aircraft headset attached to the sidewall of the aircraft.  The method this is accomplished; wires the headset wires into position near the headset jacks in such a manner that they cannot be removed.  The problem starts when pilots open the window; to talk with ground crew; ventilation; wing inspection; etc.  At this point; the wire becomes tangled; and stuck in the window mechanism.  The result is that the window is not completely closed; or that the headset cord is damaged; requiring replacement.  In addition to the costly factors above; if a crew were required to egress through the window; its possible the additional tanglements from the wire might prevent the window from opening completely.In the past month; I have personally observed two maintenance write-ups where damage occurred to the headset wire. One was on the FO (First Officer) side; one on the Captains side.  An additional write up involved a return to field; because the window wasn't properly closed despite the window handle being over center.There is no requirement to wire into position the headset (most of which are unused by pilots anyway).  Many other airlines fleet do not have the headset wired into position in this manner.

column121: We were doing a late night flight to Evansville on the visual approach for Runway 22 and the FO (First Officer) (Pilot Flying) drifted below the glide slope as he went to full visual not cross referencing a glide slope. I told him he was sinking below it and about that time we received the glide slope warning as he was correcting. Pilot Monitoring stated the Pilot Flying was too low and below the glide slope while shortly after the glide slope GPWS went off.I believe the cause of this was improper scan of the Pilot Flying while transitioning to the visual part of the approach and also it being late at night and being tired on the last leg of the day.The Pilot Flying climbed the airplane back on to glide slope and proceeded with the visual approach and a good landing.Keep a continuous scan in and out of the cockpit while on a visual approach; especially when there are no PAPIs.
column123: While hand flying the approach around 500 ft. to Runway 22 in Evansville; I allowed the aircraft to drift below glide slope. The Captain; who was PM (Pilot Monitoring) noticed and informed me I was getting low. I also received a 'glide slope' aural warning. I quickly corrected pitch and power to get back on glide slope and landed without any further issues. The Captain informed me I was getting low; and the 'glide slope' GPWS aural alert. I believe the cause was my insufficient scan of the flight instruments; as well as transitioning from the glide slope to scan the runway environment. Since it was nighttime; and since Runway 22 in Evansville has no VASI or PAPI; I believe my sight picture was incorrect; and I judged the aircraft to be higher than it was. I corrected pitch and power and returned to the glide slope for a normal landing. I believe I can do a better job of scanning the flight and navigation instruments while on approach; especially to an airport with no VASI or PAPI.

column121: After passing ETP (Equal Time Point) on RZZZ1 eastbound past ZZZZZ at flight level 380. level 1 hydraulicaulic pump 3R off during cruise with associated amber 'T' displayed above pump on hydraulicraulic synoptic page. This is the standby pump for Engine 3. It was indicating an overheated condition. Operations notified via ACARS. Satcom was not working properly. Could not connect. Referenced QRH (Quick Reference Handbook). Next; level 1 hydraulic 3 off; system pressure zero; temp 35C; quantity decreasing rapidly from 10.4 gal to 1.8 gal. Pressure zero; temp 35C; both hydraulic 3 pumps off; system in auto. Referenced QRH; stabilized situation. Over the next 2 hours; contacted Maintenance; as a crew using CRM (Crew Resource Management) reviewed QRH and other sources for next possible scenarios. Attention to level 2; hydraulic 3 fail checklist. Observed during that time period; hydraulically quantity 3 increased to approximately 8.9 gal with a temperature of 3C prior to descending to ZZZ. With more than one plan/upcoming scenario ready to go; as a crew we started the descent into ZZZ. Direct ZZZZZ1 6000 ft. ILS XXR. We started to configure for the ILS at 16 miles due to a request from ATC to slow further to 180 kts. 'Slats extend'...about 4 seconds later level 2 alert hydraulic 3 fail. Complied with QRH; requested priority handling with ZZZ Tower; manually lowered the landing gear and proceeded to land uneventfully on runway XXR. AP2; flaps 35; no auto brakes; 400K landing weight. Restrictions for PW (Pratt Whitney) engine thrust reverser inop and limitations for turning right. Once clear of the runway we worked with ZZZ airport operations to confirm there was no excessive fluid/fire coming from the airplane. As expeditiously and safely as possible we taxied clear of the north runway complex so other aircraft could land. In contact with ZZZ Ramp/ZZZ Tower we devised a safe taxi plan to exit the North complex and meet a tug. Once at the designated point ZZZ Maintenance showed up promptly and towed us back.

column121: During initial descent into ZZZ noted slide [slight] odor near last 10 rows of main cabin while accomplishing landing safety compliance check.  Thought it strange but was still not sure of its origin or validity. It was not until Flight Attendant #2 stated; 'Do you smell that...?' I acknowledge the unusual odor -- about XA:58. I left my jump seat and proceeded into main cabin walking as far as the over wing exit seats.  As I approached the mid-cabin; the odor was strongest and clearly recognizable...; Category A (musty/dirty sock) odor.  I witnessed a couple of passengers wave their hand under their nose and questioned; 'Pew; what is that smell?' I returned to my jump seat and confirmed the odor with Flight Attendant #2 who then attempted to contact the flight deck (both a routine and emergency call) ...; neither call was answered.  A few minutes later; flight attendant #1 came to the aft section and explained the Captain was too busy with the approach and would call us back after landing about the odor.  The odor diminished somewhat after landing.  As the aircraft taxied to the gate; the Captain called to explained he believed it was due to a 'cold soaked aircraft'; much to do with humidity etc.  As he continued his explanation; I witnessed a significant amount of mist/condensation being expelled through the lower side panel vents.   I noted a slight minor burning sensation in my nose which dissipated a few minutes after landing.  Due to another delayed inbound flight; our aircraft was required to wait 1hour and 12 minutes before reaching the parking area.  I collected my luggage to deplane the aircraft and noted the odor of musty/dirty socks was still significantly prevalent towards the middle section of the aircraft.  I brought this to the Captain's attention; and he too noted the odor. He further explained how it could also be from a 'mildewed filter' (shaped like a sock) which simply needs to be changed on this aircraft.'  However; he further stated that it had 'nothing to do with Turbine Oil.'   We deplaned the aircraft without further incident.  I advised the outbound crew (while walking to the terminal) about the odor event which had transpired during the inbound flight.  [A] report and notification to [union name] also submitted.
column123: We were getting ready to prepare the cabin during the descent into ZZZ and I noticed a musty odor in the aft galley. I briefly uncovered my nose to get a better sense of the smell and determined it was a very distinct stinky sock odor. The #4 [Flight Attendant] came to the aft galley about 1-2 minutes after I first noticed the odor. I asked 'do you smell that?' and told me that he did as well. He then did a walk through in main cabin. He said the odor was even stronger around the exit row area and that he noticed a couple of passengers waving their hands over their face. Because we were well into the descent; I made the decision to immediately contact the Captain to inform him of the situation. I called the flight deck once with a routine call and then an emergency call; but neither were answered. The #1 came to the back galley and told us 'The Captain knows about the situation but is too busy on the approach right now.' The #4 pulled up his manual and we both agreed it was a Category A Odor. After landing the odor dissipated somewhat; but was still noticeable. I had tingling/burning sensations in my nose and felt light headed for about 5-10 minutes. The Captain called us after we came to a stop and said 'Sometimes that odor appears when descending into a humid environment.' We waited to deplane for over an hour and the smell was still noticeable; although not as strong as when I initially noticed it on the descent. After deplaning the captain walked through the cabin and agreed that the odor was prevalent; but specifically said 'It's not from an oil leak.' He explained that's there's a filter that's literally shaped like a sock that could become dirty and can cause the cabin to smell like a dirty sock. We deplaned the aircraft and I notified one of the inbound crew members of the smell when passing by.

column121: When arriving MQY from the South East sector; our routing has us over waypoints associated with the SWFFT RNAV Arrival but without 'flying' the published arrival as it only serves BNA. Traffic landing MQY is kept at a higher altitude consistently resulting in late descents requiring a high rate of descent such as the 17;000 feet 35 miles from the airport we experienced today. This is opposite of the efforts being made for constant rate descents. This late descent is compounded by the requirement to land on Runway 32 at MQY which is a straight in approach from this arrival path. This creates an extremely rushed approach environment for not only the loss of altitude but also a reduction in speed in preparation for an approach. Additionally; this arrival path puts aircraft directly overhead MBT which is a heavy training airfield. The combination of training aircraft combined with a high performance jet aircraft with a high descent rate creates a high possibility of an inflight collision or separation issue with aircraft that are not likely talking with ATC. The other potential with being kept high is the inability to become properly stabilized for the approach into MQY which could lead an aircraft to have a runway excursion. There is no reason that a modification to the RNAV arrival to incorporate MQY and surrounding airports to better facilitate the flow of traffic vertically and provide for better stabilized arrivals and approaches couldn't be created.

To compound this issue; the route of flight today went overhead of MBT which has/had high volumes of flight training aircraft in the vicinity of the airport. The possibility for traffic conflicts; TA/RA's and unstablized approach conditions are high in this scenario.

column121: I was attempting a landing at ZZZ; Runway XX; at approximately XA:45 in a 1976 Cessna 172M with a 160 hp Lycoming engine. I was the sole occupant. It was a hot day and density altitude was about 4;950 ft. at the time. As I flared for touchdown over Runway XX; the wings lost their lift in the thin air and heat emanating from surface and the plane dropped 5+ feet causing it bounce even higher due to the spring steel landing gear. At first I tried to salvage the landing on the amount of runway I had left but after a successive bounce and drop it was clear that I was experiencing a severe oscillating (porpoising/bouncing) effect that would not end well for me or the airplane. Coming off that bounce I then applied full power for a go-around. On the subsequent landing I held the nose up as long as possible after the mains touched down. The nose wheel was indeed flat but I was able to taxi from the runway and exit the aircraft. There was no prop strike but apparently the bounce(s) left a wrinkle in the firewall. The airplane was subsequently flown; repositioned; by a pilot/mechanic to ZZZ1 and is awaiting repair at an airframe repair shop there. I was not hurt in this incident.

column121: The context is flight instruction for a CPL certificate in the North Perry Practice Area (Concentrated Flight Training area A-291B) located to the North West of Miami International Airport. The day was bright and VFR but as often in South Florida in summer; quite hazy due to extremely high humidity and thermal and proximity to the Everglades. On that particular day; the traffic in the practice area was intense; most flight schools in the surroundings taking advantage of a break from the daily storms and general difficult weather we had been having for the past month and a half. My student and I were practicing CPL maneuvers (steep turns; Chandelles; Lazy Eights); in the southeast corner of the practice area making repeated announcement of location/direction of flight/and maneuvering on the frequency. As we were practicing Lazy Eights at about 2;700 ft. I spotted and heard on the common frequency two traffics practicing and maneuvering; at about respectively 3 to 4 NM; one approaching from the north and the other from the west. We therefore moved further to the southeast; temporarily exiting the training area; in an E airspace below a section of the Miami International B airspace with a 4;000 ft floor; made another call on the frequency indicated our position; intentions; directions and maneuvers.Our airplane was not equipped with ADSB-In and we were therefore only relying on visual scanning to spot other traffics. As we were in the middle of Lazy Eights I suddenly spotted; what I guess were the same the two previously spotted traffic; this time less than a mile away; one of them heading in our direction roughly 100 feet below us. We were at that time at 2;800 ft. We had to take evasive action; doing a steep 180 to the south and climbing slightly above 3;000 ft. while making further radio calls to make sure those traffic and others in the area were aware of that situation.By the time we completed our escape maneuver we were at the very edge of that section of the MIA B airspace were the floor is 3;000 ft. Checking for the position of the other traffic; which by now had also taken actions to re-establish safe separation between us; and acknowledging that we were clear; we turned back to the north while descending below 3;000 ft and re-entering that section of the B with floor at 4;000 ft.Obviously traffic is a major concern in concentrated training areas and risks are increased by VFR days such as this one; were the visibility is affected by the summer moisture haze. Usually the western; northwestern portion of the area has a less dense traffic; but that day the global movement was such that we had to be slightly on the outside of the southeastern edge.

column121: I was conducting a local flight in the training area doing practice maneuvers for my CFI (Flight Instructor) check ride. I am a commercial rated pilot with instrument rating. I conducted some ground reference maneuvers and after completing those I started a climb for 2;500 feet. During the climb; my 30 minute timer went off and I changed the fuel tanks.  Within a couple minutes after changing the tanks; the engine suddenly suffered partial power loss and the RPM dropped to 1;000 RPM and stayed there. I began to troubleshoot (my first thought was that it was related to the fuel selector.) I ensured that the throttle and mixture were full; the then swapped the fuel selector back to the left tank. I attempted to crank the engine; but it was still running. I continued my ABC emergency checks and called Approach and alerted them to my engine trouble. The engine did not stop at any time; but the RPM stayed at 1000 RPM. I told Approach of the situation and told them I was landing in a grass field. At this point; I fully committed to landing in the grass field. The field had tall grass and lots of berms. The berms and drag from the grass caused the nose gear to collapse and the right wing to hit the ground. After landing I turned everything off and we exited the aircraft. I used a hand held radio to contact Approach and let them know we were fine and no injuries. We proceeded to contact local authorities; the company I rented from and the owner.

column121: I was approach the ZZZ from the north; preparing to perform a touch and go at the airport before flying northbound back towards ZZZ1. Before beginning my VFR descent; I obtained the current weather at the airport; and I found that the wind would be favoring Runway XX at the airport. From there I determined that in order to conduct a standard pattern entry; I should overfly the airport at 1;700 ft. MSL or 500 ft. above pattern altitude; and then perform a 225 degree turn to enter the left downwind from a 45 degree angle to Runway XX. At 10 miles; I began to announce my intentions regularly at intervals of approximately 2.5 miles.At a distance of around 5 miles from the airport; a Piper Pawnee preparing to tow a glider announced that they would be making a right downwind departure from Runway XX; towards the east. This would be the only transmission I noted from this aircraft until I would be touching down on Runway XX. I continued approaching the airfield and I had the two aircraft in sight. As the Pawnee turned downwind; I noted that my flight path would create a collision hazard; should I have continued my descent. As such; I immediately applied full power and climbed to 2;800 ft. MSL. I continued to watch as the Pawnee; with its glider in tow passed underneath me by approximately 500 ft. Climbing was likely the best evasive action in this case because I was in a high wing Cessna; while he was in a low-wing Pawnee. Had I descended; we both would have lost visual contact with each other and no additional action could have been taken should it have been necessary. The factors which appear to have contributed to this event appear to be the Pawnee pilot's lack of communication when departing; thus preventing me from restructuring my arrival plan so that I may safely avoid him. Additionally; he utilized a non-standard right downwind departure that was not charted at the airport for Runway XX. I believe that the Pawnee pilot could have extended their crosswind leg so as to remain well clear of me. On my own part; I should have taken earlier action to increase separation such as maintaining 3;000 ft. over the airport; as I was indeed aware that he would be making right traffic and climbing out of the airport. I had misjudged the climb rate of the Pawnee; and as such suspected that I could pass in front and above them before there would have been a collision hazard.

Due to low AGL; nearby towers and already having 20 degrees of flaps in; I am hesitant to enter a forward slip and descend faster (aircraft type placards state to avoid forward slips with flaps). It's possible that I'm also reaching the end of my endurance- coming back from an hour of pattern practice at ZZZ1 where conditions were gusty. My flight time at this point was around 1.6 hours; and my flights up to that point at typically max of 1.8.I have debated if I should have immediately turned right or even left. While I had the right of way (a lower craft engaged in landing); the right of way isn't going to help me if I end up in a midair. In the end I think it was correct not to turn- the pattern was extremely busy; there were higher towers to the right and planes on extended down wind to both sides. I could have caused another NMAC by turning suddenly. ATC was aware of the situation; issuing instructions to Aircraft Y and I was going to pass safely- although close- below.While I pass under (300-400 ft. estimated?) Aircraft Y either completes a right 360 or an S-turn; and ends up in an extended left downwind.Because I am below the ideal approach path to Runway XX; I put power in and arrest my descent. I actually end up too high for the runway and decide to do a go around. The go around is uneventful and I land safely. I believe Aircraft Y actually landed in between my go around and actual landing.
column123: Moderately heavy traffic relative to ZZZ; training in progress; everything under control of the Trainee until I noticed an aircraft turning base without any sequence or landing clearance yet. This aircraft was initially part of a flight of two who had just separated in the downwind; because we have to issue separate landing clearances at ZZZ; the AID (Aircraft IDentification) is Aircraft Y. Multiple inbound aircraft on either downwind and on straight in.I key up and say 'Aircraft Y and flight; both of you guys; Don't come in on base; there is traffic at the [VFR reporting point]; so don't come in on base right now; you are going to follow the guy on a 3 mile final' The [VFR reporting point] is 3 mile final; Aircraft Y is starting a 1 mile right base so this is plenty of time to catch and correct this pilot. The second aircraft from the original flight of two responds traffic in sight and immediately corrects back to the downwind. I respond to 2 other calls then scan back to ensure Aircraft Y was correcting; he wasn't; I say 'Aircraft Y it looks like you are doing exactly what I said not to do; unless the radar is deceiving me here.' Pilot responds 'Aircraft Y was already on base'; I respond 'OK; well I just said don't go on base; you missed that part; so let's go right turn back to the north downwind for both you and the other guy (his flight wing man; who was following instructions)' Pilot responds 'Affirm; right turn; north downwind; Aircraft Y'. I tell the original wing man to now turn base; he correctly responds; I then scan back and see Aircraft Y not following instructions; again the pilot does the opposite and starts a left turn towards final before correcting right and continuing for the north downwind. I then say 'Aircraft Y are you literally on final right now cutting someone off?' Pilot responds 'No; I'm trying to get out of here; we're turning; Aircraft Y'I advise the traffic on final 'Aircraft X; the guy in front of you is moving out of your way; Runway XX cleared to land' His response seemed to be partially blocked but I heard 'Aircraft X'.All aircraft eventually land; brasher warning was not issued. The pilot of Aircraft X called the tower a couple hours later and said he wanted to file a NMAC. He said he was aware of the situation developing and heard the controller (me) several times tell the other aircraft not to turn base and issue instructions which the pilot of Aircraft Y repeatedly disobeyed. I should have issued a traffic alert to both aircraft; but at the minimum to Aircraft X.

column121: Near mid-air collision at the approach end ZZZ. It was almost a perfect storm that could have put us in a nearly unavoidable accident had the timing been a few seconds different. I was number one on final (RNAV Approach; VFR conditions; approximately 1/4 mile from threshold; visual landing) ahead of Aircraft Y on a survey mission landing for gas. The other aircraft was a Airtractor crop duster operating from a semi-trailer full of chemicals parked on the ramp. The pilot reported that his radio was marginal; but they had no replacement. His ground crew reported that he was using a hand-held radio. He made no calls before getting to the runway; and may not have even had the radio on until taking the runway. He certainly wasn't listening to it. He says he made a call taking the runway; but the FBO said it was more like a call after he was on the runway and rolling; and I didn't hear it or recognize it as there were also two aircraft operating same runway alignment; same frequency. I believe he took off from the midfield intersection just short of the midpoint of the 6307 ft. runway opposite direction to the one with two aircraft on final who had been making multiple position reports on CTAF. Winds were being called as calm until I was on three-mile final when they went to about 9 kts. crosswind. He obviously didn't visually clear the final approach course as he took the runway because I had all lights on (three strobes and three landing/taxi lights) and would have been quite visible had he looked.He was likely concentrating on centerline (tailwheel aircraft with a crosswind); and I was concentrating on the aim point on short final (end of the runway) so I could turn off at midfield with Aircraft Y behind me. When I was about ¼ mile on final; he came into my field of view just above the pavement less than 1000 ft. from the end of the runway. I went around and broke right; but he didn't deviate before he passed out of my view under my wing as I banked away. We passed abeam one another just south of the approach end of Runway XX. I doubt he saw me before I was wing-up passing him on his left.

We briefed and commenced the approach; completed the QRH; ran brake cooling and reviewed the plan one last time. The PF flew a very nice approach at Vref 40 + 30 to a smooth flaps 1 landing with AB3 required and selected. On rollout I suggested he quickly disarm the AB and let the aircraft roll out at max reverse thrust to allow for more brake cooling. column121: When we arrived at the airplane the flight deck was around 34 degrees; but it soon cooled to around 28. Everything else was normal until the Captain stepped out to use the restroom. As soon as he sat down the ground crew pulled the ground power; but we had not yet switched over to the APU; so everything shut down. The Captain switched to the APU; but the right FMC did not start back up; and we got a R FMC FAIL status message. After about five minutes it did come back on without incident. We pushed back and started normally; but after about two seconds after I selected the status page on the lower EICAS we got a PACK 1 status message. The Captain reviewed the procedures; but because we had already blocked out and did not get any EICAS messages we continued. After starting up with the packs all off the flight deck warmed up quickly; but we knew as soon as we took off it should start cooling. At around 1;000 ft. the Tower gave us the Departure frequency and I checked in successfully. By the time we reached 5;000 ft. we were concerned by how little airflow there was; and the observer pilot asked for the ECS page to verify that the airplane was pressurizing. It seemed to be normal; and we monitored the air; but still figured as we climbed the flow would increase. Around FL180 Departure called us on guard and said; 'Aircraft X; if you can hear this transmission contact...' The Captain and I agreed that she hadn't called prior to that and I dialed in the frequency. I couldn't reach them; so I asked for another frequency. I didn't realize how much the heat was affecting me; but on the third frequency I asked the Captain to attempt to call. When he transmitted; I could hear that his call wasn't going out; and I finally recognized that we had lost the left comms. I didn't want to change the right radio from guard; because that seemed to be the only way they could reach us; so I used the center radio and was able to reach ZZZZ Control. Shortly after that we got an EQUIP COOLING EICAS message; and the third seat pilot began to run the checklist; and I asked for a level off altitude of FL300. ATC came back with FL290; but we were at FL288 and empty; so I said we would do our best. We ended up climbing to FL295 before we could get level; and promptly descended back to FL290. At this point we began to discuss returning when we noticed that the secondary attitude indicator was leaning to the right; but our wings were level; so we all agreed we should return. We told ATC we needed to return and explained that we were having equipment cooling issues. They assigned us the arrival and Runway XXR; but the workload was continuing to accelerate; and we were all sweating profusely; and told them we would like to get vectors to the ILS for XXR. I gave them the fuel remaining; souls on board; and tried to explain that we were safe; but needed to return soon. We completed all checklists; and uneventfully landed; taxied; and parked the airplane. I didn't realize until we were on the ground how much the heat in the flight deck was affecting me. Even with the lack of traffic in the vicinity; I am surprised how long it took me to recognize the radio failure. In the future I will be more cognizant of the heat and it's affects not only in seeming to increase workload; but also decreasing focus and clarity.
column123: I had gone to the lavatory on the ground prior to departure. Before I returned to my seat; the external power was pulled without my permission; and the power to the aircraft was interrupted; as I sat back down; I selected the APU power source and after waiting a bit; the R FMC would not come back. We called Maintenance up and the FMC returned to normal. We ensured all of the data that we had input was correct and then continued onward to push. The aircraft was extremely hot; and we know that they had just established air as we were arriving at the aircraft. The interior cabin was at 36 Celsius and we agreed that the aircraft should cool after takeoff. After starting we noticed a Pack 1 status message; but there was never an associated EICAS message. We followed our checklists and proceeded with taxi. After takeoff; the airflow never increased and the FO (First Officer) selected the EICAS page as we all were wondering if we were even pressurizing. The gaspers were blowing at about 5%; but cool air was coming out. It was still extremely hot in the aircraft; and the 3rd observer seat first officer said that he had hardly to no air coming out of his gasper. At around FL250; we began receiving radio calls on 121.5 and it was at this time with trying to transmit out; and different frequencies that we realized the radios were not working; except for the center. The Pilot Monitoring was able to get the right radio to work intermittent; and immediately we got the Equip cooling EICAS caution message. I continued to fly the aircraft while the crew ran the QRH and attempted to maintain contact with ZZZZ. At this point; we all agreed the best course of action was to return to ZZZZ. We were given a level off to FL290 after an initial climb clearance. We were given this rapidly; as were already in a climb; but I arrested the climb and descended back from FL295 to FL290. We were given vectors and further descent. At this point with descent power; there was almost no airflow. We [received priority] to get on the ground as safely and quickly as possible. My standby instruments were also showing erroneous. We landed in ZZZZ without further incident. After touchdown; the airflow suddenly increased to normal. Maintenance was briefed with the logbook; but I was not given the nature of the aircraft's issues before we headed back in to rest.

column123: SOF Event during departure with an immediate return to the departure airport (ZZZ). First Officer (FO) was the pilot flying. Ground Ops and taxi out to runway XXL were uneventful. I loaded the FMS for arrival and began a descent/vectors for the ILS runway XXL approach. At this time the Captain completed the Smoke/Avionics Smoke/Fumes QRH Quick Action procedure and informed the passengers and flight attendants of our intention to land. We were over maximum landing weight by roughly 4;000 lbs.; but elected to proceed with the descent checklist and land instead of working through the QRH procedure for Overweight Landing due to time. column121: The runway incursion occurred when a new CFI and myself were doing a night flight for the said CFI to become night proficient again in small GA aircraft after not flying GA in a long time. ZZZ Tower had closed 30 minutes prior and we were the only aircraft working in the pattern. I said that we should practice a power off 180 when the incursion occurred. As we turn from base to final and get closer to the runway; we did not see anything on the runway that would have warranted a go-around. After seeing it was a vehicle of some sort I initially believed that the sweeper had moved off into the grass; however the driver came over after we landed and said he was still on the runway. We landed 300 ft. past the vehicle to the best of my knowledge so there was no immediate concern for a collision.I believe that the situation would not have occurred had several things happened. A breakdown of communication had occurred in the chain of events between the aircraft and the Ground Operations in terms of knowing the position of where everyone was. We made a downwind call but did not make subsequent calls due to the high workload of the power off 180 maneuver. I cannot confirm if the ground vehicle did or did not make a call; but to the best of my knowledge they did not make the call saying they were on the runway.

At the time I was aware of a TBM aircraft behind and faster then me on an GPS approach for an avionics check; as well as another aircraft 500 ft. below me passing right to left. Tower told me to turn base which did make sense to me considering I was 5 miles out. I reported to Tower that there were two [similar N-numbers] on frequencies. He then told Aircraft Y to turn base followed by an instruction to me to turn to a heading of 070. I read back 070 but confirmation bias; and still rattled by the near miss; I turned to a heading of 170 thinking that he wanted me to turn an extended base to final; essentially cutting off the faster TBM closing on me. Tower asked me to read off my current heading and I reported flying 175 only then realizing the mistake. I was advised to make a right turn to intercept the final of Runway XX and report turning through 270 degrees. Already heading south this happened in less than 30 seconds. Now inbound on final for landing I was advised to copy a phone number on the ground for a possible pilot deviation. Finally on a half mile final I asked Tower twice if I was cleared to land Runway XX; and they advised me that I was 'still cleared to land XX' when I had not previously been given a landing clearance. Once on the ground I contacted Tower via phone and we discussed the situation; agreeing that parties were at fault a that a lot of events contributed to the situation.I believe that there were 3 main human factors causes that led to this incident.First the Tower was overloaded with inbound; transit; and outbound traffic and was unable to properly give traffic advisories to inbound and departing traffic.Second that Tower instructed me turn base when an aircraft with a similar call sign was the intended recipient even though it didn't make sense to me and at the time. column121: On a step climb around FL300; between ZZZ and ZZZZZ; we noticed a weather cell we wanted to deviate around. The Captain had already briefed the FAs (Flight Attendants) about the en route weather; that we would most likely have some bumps; that we were keeping the seat belt sign on; and to use caution. We were in full IMC and our radar return showed that a turn to the left would be best. We requested an initial left turn of 20 degrees but almost immediately we encountered heavy and extreme precipitation and ultimately had to turn 80 degrees. We were given the necessary deviations but then told to go direct ZZZZZ when able as well as climb to FL340. We also encountered moderate and possibly severe turbulence. We experienced both positive and negative G's. The speed tape never went into the red but the trend vector showed both rapid climbing and simultaneous descending trends that took up the entire top to bottom range of the speed tape. The plane was moving quite a bit as we were both in updrafts and then subsequent downdrafts getting bumped around. After about 5 minutes when we could actually get everything sorted out; we called back to check on the status of both the Flight Attendants and Passengers. FA1 answered and she proceeded to tell us there was an accident in the aisle and she would call us back. FA2 was about mid aircraft doing her beverage service when we encountered the worst of the turbulence. She thought she had hit her head and beverages had been thrown from the cart and some passengers tray tables into the ceiling. We consulted our FOM and made the decision we needed to contact Dispatch and make them aware to coordinate with [Maintenance Control]. We continued to keep checking on the FAs for the rest of the flight and as we got closer; FA1 called and said FA2 had requested In-Flight to meet us at the gate. Upon block in; [flight attendant representative] and member of [Company] met the aircraft. CA (Captain) called Dispatch/[Maintenance Control] to explain event and to assess if an aircraft inspection for severe turbulence was required. Based on our reading and interpretation of FOM on the definition of severe turbulence; we determined we encountered severe turbulence. However; [Maintenance Control] said because the autopilot did not disengage; that there was no 'momentary loss of aircraft control' and it was only moderate turbulence which does not require an aircraft inspection. The aircraft was not removed from service; boarding for the next flight started immediately; and [Company] took FA2 for a medical evaluation.Pilot interpretation of FOM differed from [Maintenance Control]. [Maintenance Control] did not accept our interpretation of severe turbulence. It kept them from having to inspect the aircraft and delaying the flight schedule. Any disconnection of autopilot is apparently the determining factor in deciding if aircraft control is lost. There needs to be a more clear definition of what severe versus moderate turbulence is and pilot experience should be held in account. Safety should always be the priority over schedule integrity.
column123: On final climb out from FL300 to FL340 between ZZZ and ZZZZZ intersection; we had to deviate for weather. Seat belt sign was on and FA (Flight Attendant) briefing and PA to passengers included weather/ thunderstorms in the area and to expect a bumpy ride on the climb out. We were in and out of IMC conditions as the weather radar depicted a buildup. We discussed a plan for deviations prior to the radio frequency change that we received at the same time. We continued the left turn to approximately a 270 degree heading due to the intensity of precipitation and increasing turbulence; while still trying to climb to FL340. In the turn and climb; we encountered moderate to potentially severe turbulence: VSI showed +/- 2000 fpm climb; ASI showed a white positive and negative trend vector for the entire range of speed tape; and we experienced zero G and positive G due to the turbulence.Once clear of the weather; we immediately called the FAs to get a status of the cabin. FA1 answered and she said there was an accident in the aisle. A few minutes later; she called back and reported that FA2 believes she hit her head on the ceiling and the surrounding passengers in the area agreed. Beverages had spilled on to passengers and were also dripping from the ceiling. Throughout the rest of the flight; we were in constant communication with the cabin on the status of FA2 and the passengers; as well as Dispatch/[Maintenance Control] via ACARS. FA1 requested that inflight meet us at the gate for FA2.Upon block in; a member from inflight and from [Company] met the aircraft. Based on our reading and interpretation of FOM on the definition of severe turbulence; we determined we encountered severe turbulence. However; [Maintenance Control] said because the autopilot did not disengage; that there was no 'momentary loss of aircraft control' and it was only moderate turbulence which does not require an aircraft inspection. The aircraft was not removed from service; boarding for the next flight started immediately; and inflight took FA2 for a medical assessment.Pilot interpretation of company FOM definition and procedures differed from [Maintenance Control] definition and interpretation of company FOM defined severe turbulence [Maintenance Control] decided NOT to err on the side of safety and do a precautionary severe turbulence inspection of the aircraft due to their interpretation of the FOM severe turbulence definition; solely based on the fact that the autopilot did not disconnect during the event in order to save the integrity of the flight schedule. In the interest of safety; a severe turbulence inspection should have been conducted and a better definition of severe turbulence needs to be updated in company FOM defining what 'momentary loss of aircraft control' means. Safety should always be a priority over schedule integrity.

Shortly after; he left so I then called Maintenance Control and told them the temperature control knobs left in auto were not sufficient to cool the plane at any position; and that if you moved the knobs to manual; it was blowing out warm air immediately followed by hot air within 5 minutes. Maintenance Control replied that he didn't understand as the technician said it was 'OK for service; and only 25 degrees in the cockpit.' My statement to him was 'Absolutely not. It is right now indicating 32 degrees and nothing is fixed. Did you want me to send you a picture of the temperature?' I did not receive a reply as we talked about what the issue could be. I stated to Maintenance Control; 'I have seen this before multiple times and I think either a duct connection is loose; or there is a tear or leak somewhere; did you want me to send a picture of the cockpit temperature to show you what is indicating?' I still received no reply that he wanted evidence so I then asked him for the number I can send it to. When provided and after I sent a picture; he replied 'CABIN temperature looks pretty normal for a summer day' but mentioned absolutely nothing about the cockpit. He thought the plane was 'heat soaked' but I reminded him it had already been running for an hour and a half. I was then instructed and proceeded to run ground air inside the cabin and directly point it at the cockpit. It dropped 8 degrees from 33 to 25 in 20 minutes. I then had the ground air disconnected and within 20 minutes the cockpit heated back up to 31 degrees; and 5-10 minutes later it was again at 32. After writing it up a second time and being told from Maintenance Control it's still probably just 'heat soaked'; the same technician from before came back and I told him what we did. He replied while mumbling something about 'maybe we got some parts lined up and we'll take a look.' The First Officer and I went back inside to cool off and let Maintenance work on it. After 5-6 hours of Maintenance continuously working on the plane; I called Maintenance Control to get an update. Apparently; the technicians did in fact discover a leak(s); and were proceeding to put a sleeve(s) on. An hour later it was still not done (about 6-7 hours of continuous work since the second write up). I then was removed from Aircraft X by scheduling.Cockpit indication and hot feeling in the cockpit.Hot airplane that would not cool down without external air and feeling pressured to take a hot airplane to ZZZ1 for service.Refused the aircraft twice.The main concern is current maintenance practice. I was able to get the technician to agree that it was warm inside the cockpit even though he signed offthe aircraft as 'OK for service' because they could not find anything wrong. I will give the benefit of the doubt that maybe the technician relayed bad information to Maintenance Control and read the temperature of the cabin instead of the cockpit; however; he still told them it felt fine when clearly the temperature control knobs were not functioning properly. There was a second technician that stated the same about it being OK for service. Since the first write up; Maintenance Control had me troubleshoot it for up to 4 hours with/without the technicians. After going through 2 large bottles of water; sweating profusely; and being asked to run the ground air into the back of the aircraft instead of the front this time as it was probably still 'just heat soaked;' I said no and needed a break. Also; I mentioned that based on experience it was probably a leak or tear. Sure enough; after having the technicians look at the aircraft a second time; this is what they found and worked on for several hours. The fact I refused the aircraft twice and they 'found an issue' the second time leads me to believe they knew all along. Especially considering the fact the technician admitted to me that the cockpit would not sufficiently cool but yet signed it off and told maintenance control it was fine. A chief pilot called me to get more information and while I did not feel pressure from him directly to take it; it was clear that the company for one reason or another needed to get this plane to ZZZ1. Again; I did not feel pressure from the chief pilot directly; but I could not help but think everyone in Maintenance knew this plane could not get stuck in ZZZ. I also believe that troubleshooting for Maintenance up to 4 hours is excessive when it was clear the aircraft was not heat soaked but instead was not self-sufficient to cool on its own. I am not a maintenance technician nor one with the most experience; however; I felt undermined from the technicians signing it off and Maintenance Control having me go through the motions of 4 hours of troubleshooting and not one person taking my advice that I had seen this exact issue multiple times. More believably I was ignored and every trick was pulled just to get the aircraft to ZZZ1; i.e.; being told constantly by Maintenance Control we can get the aircraft cool enough with PC air so that we can depart but then reminding them the packs are not working properly and keep heating the plane up. Regardless; the technicians constantly tried to tie the issue to me implying that I was the problem and ultimately it was my call. If this was the case; I do not see why they would have had to work on the aircraft for several hours following my second write up.

column121: The aircraft in question was operating with MEL 27-XXX open; Spoilers #2 or #4. After engine start on both legs; an ECAM message was received regarding the spoilers but this was disregarded as a result of the MEL. Upon further reflection; these messages should have triggered further investigation on my part; as the presence of such an alert was not mentioned in the MEL. However; I had noted a write-up in the MEL about spurious messages - made by a Check Airman - which was subsequently signed off by Maintenance as essentially being unimportant. The aircraft had flown 4 legs the day prior with the MEL active. Also; at the time of this incident; I had approximately 100 hours of experience in any Airbus aircraft.The first leg of the day was flown uneventfully. Immediately after takeoff on our second leg of the day with the same plane; an ECAM caution and audio alert was triggered for a F/CTL SPLR FAULT. The message subsequently cleared itself; but then a few seconds later; would trigger again. This cycle repeated itself approximately every 20-30 seconds for about 20 minutes; until the flight reached FL270; where the message stopped cycling and instead remained. Initially; after exiting the sterile period; ACARS messages were sent and a brief exchange ensued. An emergency return to ZZZ was offered as an option; but given that we were well above maximum landing weight and the ECAM did not require us to land as soon as possible; I elected to continue the climb.Upon reaching cruise altitude; I transferred the flying duties to the FO (First Officer) and verbally contacted Dispatch and eventually Maintenance Control. Maintenance had no inflight suggestions and stated that they would look at it when the plane is on the ground. At this point; the Dispatcher and I discussed our options. Since the ECAM mentioned FUEL CONSUMPTION INCREASED and FMS PRED UNRELIABLE and we still had just under 3 hours to go on a flight planned to land with just 8;000 LBS of fuel; the decision was made to divert to ZZZ1. Dispatch changed our destination and we proceeded to an uneventful landing in ZZZ1. An emergency was not declared. While on the ground in ZZZ1; one of the responding mechanics reported to me that he discovered that the MEL procedures were not properly complied with when the item was deferred and that Spoiler Pair #2 was inadvertently deactivated instead of Pair #4. Apparently; the aircraft had flown 4 legs in this condition prior to our operating it. He mentioned to me his concern that on the [day prior]; a previous crew; the previously mentioned Check Airman had also apparently experienced a similar condition; wrote it in the logbook; only to have Maintenance simply clear the entry by writing 'info noted.' He expected that the aircraft would be taken out of service to fix the underlying issue. However; the decision was made to clear the write-up that I made and allow the deferral to continue. Based on the information that was relayed to me by this Mechanic; it appears that the initial error of deactivating the wrong spoiler pair was attempting to be covered up. This is very concerning.My relative inexperience with Airbus aircraft allowed me to be lulled into a false sense of security when it came to ECAM messages that appeared to relate to the MEL item. Seeing a write-up about spurious messages being handled the way it had been also led me to believe that there was nothing out of the ordinary; when realistically; there was a major error made by a certificated Mechanic. In retrospect; what was displayed on the F/CTL page should have alerted me to a problem; with both Spoiler Pairs #2 and #4; but I assumed that this was the same display that the mechanics and all of the other pilots who operated the aircraft before me also saw. The MEL does not give us specific guidance as to what should be displayed on this page with the MEL active; but I presume that the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) procedure referenced should tell the Mechanic whatshould have been displayed.More information in the MEL document detailing what exactly should be displayed on the SD (System Display) and what messages the crew should or shouldn't expect for a given MEL. Also; if there was indeed an attempt to cover up a maintenance error; I think this case should be used as an example as to how to properly correct an error.
column123: After takeoff we got an ECAM for flight spoiler fault that was reoccurring. We had this aircraft on the previous leg and got the ECAM and cleared it but this one kept returning. We still thought it was associated with the MEL on the Aircraft Spoiler Surface 4 INOP but Spoiler Surface 2 was also INOP. The Captain had reviewed the logbook before the previous flight and seen another crew had this happen and Maintenance had signed off [that] it was normal for the MEL. The Captain got in touch [with] Maintenance through Dispatch and they wanted us to divert to ZZZ1. We diverted and landed uneventfully.I think Maintenance improperly deferred the Spoiler Surface 4 and after a crew wrote it up; did not verify it was correct. The MEL should have had us view the Flight Control page instead of the HYD SD page for amber information of #4 Spoiler ONLY amber or #2 Spoiler ONLY.

column121: All of a sudden; the Captain stopped mid-sentence and said; 'Look at that!'  He pointed to the 1:00 right position; and we passed by a large; round; unknown object to the right at our altitude.  Based on the speed of passing; it seemed to be stationary.  It was large (much larger than a Mylar balloon); dark gray and silver/shiny; stripes (stripes of its form/shape) from top to bottom.  It seemed to have a pinch point at the bottom.  I didn't see anything attached; but the Captain said he saw a rope or something dangling behind it.  Soon after our shock; ATC gave us a handoff and we reported the object.  He was unaware of its presence. I reached out to the [nearby]  pilots to see if anyone knew anything.  One pilot responded: 'We got a message from our chief pilot this morning - balloon off SWO 100 radial 12.4nm & tethered balloon by Company.' The message the pilots in SWO received correlates with the location of our event.  I've never known of a tethered balloon at 32;000 feet.  Makes one wonder if this balloon got loose; especially given the rope the Captain saw.  If so; shouldn't ATC have been notified?  A bit more right today; and I may not have been able to write this report; along with the more than 200 people we had onboard.

The airport was on a north wind operation that day; so we used the taxi lane on the south end in order to make an upwind turn to access the fuel island.Five days later we start hearing from other pilots how 'pissed off' [a] hangar owner is that we used the taxi lane in front of [their] hangar adjacent to the taxi lane. Aircraft and other vehicles are often parked dangerously close to the taxi lane in front of [the] hangar; so taxiing requires great care to avoid collision. Many times the hangar occupants shut down; leave aircraft unattended; and block the taxi lane. This causes other aircraft to use the downwind taxi lanes causing unsafe operations; especially for tailwheel aircraft. Being considerate of each other is imperative to aviation safety.

column121: An aircraft in crosswind for Runway 29. Aircraft Z is 4 NM to the South West 1;000 feet above pattern altitude; announcing intentions to enter the downwind. My aircraft (Aircraft X) is 2 miles to the south at pattern altitude; announcing intentions to enter on the 45 for midfield downwind [Runway] 29; have the crosswind and 4 mile traffic insight. I announce to the now downwind traffic that I have them insight and will sequence behind them at the midfield downwind Runway 29. Aircraft Y departs Runway 29 and announces crosswind to perform touch and goes on Runway 29 (CFI and student). Aircraft Z announces performing a 360 for spacing. I believe that Aircraft Z was facing away from the field and did not see Aircraft Y in crosswind. I hear a radio call that Aircraft Z has cut off Aircraft Y; I look at my MFD and see the two aircraft appear very close to each other. The CFI in Aircraft Y announces that they will be performing a 360 for spacing behind the 'cutting aircraft'. I am closer than I would like to the aircraft in front of me and stay 100ft higher and slightly to the right to keep the aircraft insight. Aircraft in front announces intentions to full stop land; and I announce that I will extend downwind for spacing. Aircraft in front calls base; I continue on downwind. Aircraft in front calls final; I call and turn base. I call and turn final upon seeing the Aircraft on short final and deem spacing to be appropriate for the Aircraft to vacate the Runway. Reviewing the radio calls; my call to Final was stepped on. Aircraft Z calls base; I'm expecting him to be behind me on base. Aircraft in front calls that they are on the runway and will be vacating; I verify that spacing looks good. My passenger (2nd GA flight) calls for traffic to the left; I look and see the Aircraft Y in downwind. 5-10 seconds later the broadside of Aircraft Z passes in front of the windshield at 100ft or less; same altitude. I call 'go around sidestep left' as I can see the shadow of Aircraft Z on the right of me. I announce intentions to depart crosswind to the south. Not hearing any calls from Aircraft Z I become concerned. Using my MFD; I identify the call sign of the aircraft involved and ask if they are OK? They respond they are OK and that they are in Downwind. I believe that Aircraft Z confused my radio calls for that of the Aircraft in front of me. I believe that the near miss with Aircraft Y after his 360 for spacing caused him to lose situational awareness. I believe that my call for final being blocked did not help Aircraft Z's SA. I believe that the lack of availability of pattern work at ZZZ/ZZZ1/ZZZ2 is making non towered fields like LMO busier than they should be.

column121: I'm working two radar sectors combined. Total normal for the summer. Even if it wasn't normal we don't have the staffing to split it off. I'm working about X airplanes at the time. Sure; not a lot. Two airplanes are going the same direction. I separate the two airplanes via altitude separation. One's an IFR small aircraft (Aircraft Y) west bound on the airway at 10;000 feet. The other is a VFR small aircraft (Aircraft Z) west bound restricted at 9;500 feet wanting 10;500 feet. There's an air carrier jet (Aircraft A) which was a departure off of PSP heading east bound. Then there's this IFR small aircraft (Aircraft B) at 14;000 feet without a proper scratchpad flashing at me from the Center from the east. There are thunderstorms in and around the area so I suspect it's someone deviating. So I call the flight data and get a full route. Of course; thunderstorm or not; it's a bad route. I don't take radar; I have some time to deal with that issue later. Now here are the two players. The first one is what this whole story is about: Aircraft X.I release Aircraft X on the RNAV departure. I then go over and deal with the skydiver at the Banning Airport (BNG). This is a problem. It's been somewhere between 2 to 4 years since someone [opened] a skydiving joint in the middle of a pass in between two large mountains. Many reports [have been filed] about this. Now; I will give you all this much; the skydiving is finally depicted on the VFR chart.However; the folks at SCT have dropped the ball. There's no Letter of Agreement (LOA) with us and the BNG skydiving operation. We have an LOA for every other skydiving organization within SCT. There's no definitive anything on what should or shall happen with any of the procedures. We have a little piece of paper taped to the radar sector for controllers to spout off on the recorded line to invoke their Article 65 rights. Doesn't that seem like a glaring issue? Is it because no one has died yet or there haven't been enough TCAS RAs or significant event/MORs (Mandatory Operation Report) filed yet to have to worry about it? The BNG jumper calls two minutes. I give my two minute call. I call the Hemet sector and give them the notice that the jumper is two minutes out. [I have] to coordinate with a separate sector about a jump zone that is on the border of three airspaces and there's nothing written anywhere about who's responsible for what?The initial altitude for departures off of 31L is 8;000 feet. The lowest altitude you can issue off of 31L is 5;000 feet. There was about a two year period where it was 400 feet but that changed when PSP was absorbed into SCT. I'd like to mention to everyone that's ever seen the craziness of the Minimum Vectoring Altitudes (MVA) of PSP that the Cath1 departure is runway heading until about 5ish miles before it's a right turn to the east into the valley. So the Aircraft X goes up the final (if you will) to Runway 13R. The MVAs look scary but it's a pretty clear shot...albeit not for very long at all. JEXOT which is the Final Approach Fix for Runway 13R is supposed to be crossed at or above 2900 feet which is 7.5 miles north of the airport. It was also 10 miles visibility and Sky Clear that day. Upon Aircraft X's second call he checked in either at 3;000 or leveling at 3;000. Either way; it wasn't what it was supposed to be. I was literally in disbelief. I asked him again; 'Verify assigned altitude?' To see an aircraft where he was at there at 3;000 feet wasn't shocking. It gets a little warm in the summer time at PSP. Climb rates are bad. Once it was verified; it was clear there was a problem. I solved it. I issued 'Climb and maintain 8;000.' I think I said it twice just in case.[I was told] I should have issued a low altitude alert. The FAA 7110.65 says; 'low altitude alert check your altitude immediately the MVA in your area is...' The altitudes are a little hyperbolic but it's the truth. Look at the MVAs. They're insane and there are a lot of them. I didn't assign 3;000 feet. He needed to climb. I believe the .65 literally says; 'Give first priority to separating aircraft and issuing safety alerts as required in this order.'  That's what I did. I separated the plane from the terrain. So Aircraft X is up to 8;000 feet. He's flying the departure. Everyone's separated. He's passing traffic so I assign a higher altitude. 'Aircraft X climb and maintain 15;000.' He reads back 16;000. I immediately catch it and fix it. He clears a higher MVA so I want to turn him on course. I tell him; 'Aircraft X turn left heading 360 when you are able proceed direct to YUCCA.' We do this 1;000 times a day. He reads back 260. I catch immediately. 'Negative; 360.' Honestly; I don't think I used his callsign. That's on me. But he reads it back. Should be fine right? I'm guessing CRM (Crew Resource Management) wasn't optimal that day. He definitely turns right; not left; to a 260 heading. I think it was at this moment that I noticed a VFR aircraft departing the BNG airport within two minutes of jumping. I say; 'Safety alert (almost ironically I know since I didn't say low altitude alert with the Aircraft X)' to the BNG jump aircraft and I inform him about the traffic.I know there are safety alerts even though the phrase safety alert isn't phraseology. It gets the message across. I hold the jumper and ask if he's talking to the departure. Unsurprisingly he's not because the departing traffic isn't on the UNICOM.  That's when I notice the Aircraft X is turning right instead of left. Now he's heading for terrain and two unsuspecting small aircrafts. I deem that trying to turn back to the left would be a catastrophic decision. I felt that just continuing the right turn but stopping the climb would be the absolute safest decision. So; phraseology didn't work the first time so I go to plain language. I say something to the effect of; 'Aircraft X it looks like you turned right instead of left. That's okay; just continue your right hand turn to a heading of 030 and just stop your climb for traffic.' Not sure if it matters or not at this point but I did ask the Aircraft X; about two minutes before; when he was out of 3;000 for 8;000 that I wanted to triple check to make sure that he was assigned 3;000 by clearance delivery.So because I had said that; I was a little concerned that maybe the Aircraft X would think that he was in trouble and he might not have been as responsive as I would have liked him to be. That's why I said the whole 'that's okay' bit. I just didn't want him to go into a mountain and I didn't want him to say; 'you said right not left' all the while he's not turning. It happens way too often. So I stopped his climb. Well; I asked him to...but he didn't. He was at about 8;100 feet when I said stop your climb. He wasn't exactly climbing at 4000 feet a minute either. I could have said climb and maintain 090 but he was converging with a small aircraft that was out of 9;300 feet for 9;500 feet and another small aircraft above that guy at 10;000 feet. column121: I'll start off by saying that the South Area had 6 Controllers and 1 D side trainee; but no Supervisor.  The East Area had 6 Controllers and 1 Supervisor.  The South Area was forced to operate while the Supervisor position was combined with the Operations Manager in Charge.  While working 68; Sealord was active above my stratum for everything but W136A/B.  There was a few scattered areas of precipitation around SAV; and a line west of SAV that forced the traffic between sectors 66/50 to deviate into my sector.  Sector 47/48 was combined and very busy. ZDC did what ZDC does best; as they slammed the door on sector 47/48.  Scrambling; the East Area begins rerouting every aircraft into ZTL.  ZTL did what ZTL does best; as they then slammed the door on the East Area as well.  This caused us all to put everyone into no notice holding.  Like dominoes falling south; everyone stopped taking hand offs for aircraft headed towards ZDC and put everyone into holding.From here; chaos ensued.  Information was limited; we had no Supervisor in the area to talk to Traffic Management Unit or the other areas to figure out what we needed to do.  I basically had one hole around SAV everyone was flying through; and Sealord had the rest of my airspace.  Regardless; I had to begin no notice holding.  I didn't know how long this would be; so I made a plan to hold aircraft at odd altitudes in two different locations (SAV and GIPPL).  My plan was to hold south at both points; so I could successfully hold a lot of aircraft if I needed to. I began by first issuing holding instructions to Aircraft X to hold south at a point just east of SAV at 33;000 feet.  The next aircraft I was given was Aircraft Y at 33;000 feet.  I issued holding instructions to him to hold south at the GIPPL intersection at 33;000 feet.Between every transmission of mine; I was trying to get the attention of the Supervisor in the East Area.  If you listen to the tapes; you will hear me say 'say again' very often.  This is because it was impossible to try and get help; while also keeping up with their check ins/requests.  He was the only one around that wasn't plugged in and trying to create order from the chaos.  He of course was very busy (and doing well at taking care of his own area) so it was hard to steal him away to try and figure out what was going on. At some point (I had too much going on to see the exact time) conflict alert initiated between the Aircraft X and Aircraft Y.  I expected the Aircraft Y to be south of GIPPL; thus no factor for the Aircraft X when I gave the holding instructions.  The Aircraft Y must have plugged in north instead of south; because he was head on with the Aircraft X.  I issued traffic alerts and turns; while climbing the Aircraft X to FL340. There was a loss [of separation].I don't know at this point if I issued the holding instructions incorrectly or if I had missed a bad read back.  This could have been my mistake or it could have been a pilot deviation.  Either way; there was too much chaos to catch any unexpected pilot actions.  ZDC giving no notice to stop all hand offs without any kind of heads up is ridiculous and dangerous.  It would be a completely different story if they had put us on alert and given us routes to issue if it happens.  This also would have given ZTL a heads up and then we could have all worked together on a safe and expeditious plan. There should have been a staffing trigger tonight.  Any time that is brought up; everyone freaks out and refuses to ever use the word 'staffing'.  This happens constantly.  The South and East areas having 6 Controllers a piece is not ok.  Maybe this is conversation better spent as a hotline call?  What is so wrong with slowing traffic due to low staffing?  It is no different than getting slower service at a restaurant because they are low on servers.  It's semantics; and semantics should never interfere with safety. That is our number one job after all. Tonight was dangerous and this kind of practice needs to stop.  It won't though; so I'm going to stop wasting any more time.  Staffing is terrible; we constantly get stretched too thin; we don't ever really have a proactive plan; we get very little support from Command Center; and sometimes that swiss cheese thing the FAA likes to tell us about comes true and then there's a loss.

column121: While reviewing the SID and release prior to departure (ABQ3 Runway 8); the First Officer and I noticed that the required climb gradient was very steep. We determined it may be difficult to meet the gradient and contacted Dispatch for guidance. I was unable to get in touch with Dispatch via phone. I then contacted a base chief pilot for guidance; who referred me to the Director of Operations. I was unable to get in contact with the Director of Operations until after departure. I then contacted another chief pilot for guidance and was referred to contact Dispatch again. I was able to talk to Dispatch and asked if we needed to run the climb analysis tool that we perform in ZZZ since this gradient was much steeper than ZZZ. Dispatch informed me that there was no need/requirement to run the analysis. I verified multiple times that this was the case; even with a steep climb gradient. Dispatch confirmed that no climb analysis was needed.I briefed the First Officer that we would need to fly a performance climb and ensure we were above 1;600 ft./min at a 200 Knot climb. After takeoff; we maintained the highest practical climb performance with E-climb; but were unable to maintain the needed vertical speed for our airspeed. We tried leaving the flaps at 9 and after that didn't work; flaps up with a climb below 200 Knots. I estimate we maxed out at 800 to 900 ft/min at 180 Knots. It was apparent that we would not be able to climb at the required rate with any configuration/speed and we made a right turn as assigned by ATC. We avoided terrain by executing the turn; but in IMC or without a quick turn crews would be in danger of CFIT. I was able to get in contact with the Director of Operations after landing to explain my concern with this departure. He pointed me to Training Bulletin XYZ; which referenced SID climb tables. This bulletin references ZZZ SIDs and it was not readily apparent (at least to me) that it would apply to other airports. After referencing the data cards; it appears that the required climb gradient of 470 Ft. per NM may not be achievable by the aircraft. While technically; there is a sentence in the training bulletin that states applicability to other airports; we have not received any training; memo; daily read; email; etc. on climb analysis at airports other than ZZZ. I was also a bit frustrated that it is recently getting harder to contact support resources by phone. I spent about 20 minutes trying to get help on a safety sensitive concern with no real available/wrong answer. While I take responsibility for this event; I followed the note on the training bulletin to contact dispatch when in doubt. I believe the company needs to issue a training; memo; etc. to make other pilots; Dispatch; and Management aware of the need for this analysis at other airports and include this on the 10-7 pages. I think this threat could result in CFIT if not corrected. While ATC would hopefully intervene; a crew could run into a situation where a GPWS (Ground Proximity Warning System) escape maneuver may not physically be able to clear the terrain without a non apparent turn in IMC.

column121: Preflight up through takeoff on this flight was normal ops.  I was sitting as the relief pilot with NAME being the PIC and flying pilot and NAME1 being the SIC and pilot monitoring.  During the takeoff roll and at rotation; the flying pilot rotated normally after the 'ROTATE' call and pitched up to approximately 4 to 5 degrees and then stopped rotating any further.  We were very heavy (382;094 TOW).  We had a stop margin of approximately 2;000 feet and the end of the runway was rapidly approaching.  After a moment or two; the flying pilot continued the rotation and we proceeded on normally.  After takeoff and past sterile cockpit; the flying pilot communicated to us that the airplane just didn't seem to want to fly and he held the lower pitch attitude for a moment to allow the aircraft to accelerate a bit and avoid a potential tail strike.  During cruise with my time in the seat; the flying pilot and I discussed the issue a little bit more; determined that we might be heavier than the weight and balance paperwork stated; and agreed to really check the pitch attitude on final approach at the calculated REF speed to see if that was another indication of being heavier than we thought we were.  We did find that some airspeed had to be added to the calculated REF speed to maintain the normal pitch attitude during the final approach.  Upon blocking in; we pulled out the landing REF speed chart in the QRH Inflight Performance section and found that with the additional airspeed we had to add to maintain the normal; fully configured; landing pitch attitude; it was conceivable that we may be UP to 20;000 pounds heavier than what was stated on the paperwork.  We called the Load Master up to the flight deck and he said that flight was loaded at the point of origin in ZZZZ1; he was not involved with the loading process (or maybe more accurately; he wasn't involved in the weighing of the cargo) but was just given the numbers from those that were and that we had around 20;000 LBS of cargo in the lower cargo compartments along with all of the passenger weight. The PIC placed a writeup in the logbook to alert the outbound crew (the airplane continued on to ZZZ1 with the same Passengers and cargo) and we all agreed that we needed to make someone else aware of the issue (I elected to inform the Duty Pilot) and to ensure the outbound crew knew of the situation since we wouldn't see them ourselves.  During the limo ride from ZZZ to ZZZ2; both the PIC and myself made unsuccessful attempts to reach the duty pilot through both Pilot Support and Dispatch.  During the subsequent limo ride and discussing the issue further; the PIC wondered if there was a chance that the ground crew in ZZZZ1 was using KILOS as unit of measure rather than pounds (very possible given the 20;000 LBS of cargo we reportedly had vs what the potential difference in weight we noticed with the landing REF speed).  The PIC was dropped off at the ZZZ2 airport for a commercial flight and the FO (First Officer) and I continued onto the layover hotel.  It was agreed that the PIC would continue to communicate the issue to someone in hopes of alerting the outbound crew of the situation.  I was texted later by the PIC that he did get a hold of the Fleet Captain and discuss the issue.

column121: On arrival at the departure gate; I inquired about station provision of international documents - Hawaii Reference Guide; plotting chart; and AIREP forms. Agent had no idea what I was talking about; claiming that the Hawaii flight is a domestic operation. The FOM clearly includes Hawaii operations under the flag operations description; and Hawaii is specifically addressed in the international operations sections of FOM - to include the need to use a plotting chart on random routes and the AIREP form when making non-CPDLC (Controller Pilot Datalink Communications) position reports. On this flight; the SATCOM system was placarded INOP which meant I would need to make position reports - thus; the need for an AIREP form. The Hawaii Reference Guide includes both plotting chart and AIREP forms as required paperwork to be checked prior to departure. I called Operations to ask for an AIREP form; but was told that they had no idea what I was asking for. We have been operating Hawaii and ZZZ1 flights out of ZZZ for years. If the FOM is going to require certain forms and documents; it would be very helpful to have these documents and forms available at the departure station. The same situation is now occurring in HNL as well - no international forms are being provided since they state that flights to the mainland are considered 'domestic' flying. But random routes are occasionally used and position reporting is still required. If there is no requirement for an AIREP form to be used in the CPDLC environment; the FOM and reference guides should be updated to reflect that their use is no longer required.Conflicting treatment of Hawaii operations - domestic for some purposes; international for others. Lack of clarity on what forms and documents are actually required to be used or made available for Hawaii operations. Lack of availability of international forms and documents at departure stations for international operations. If the FOM requires the use of documents and forms on international flights; it would be very helpful to have those forms actually available at the departure station. The mixed status of Hawaii operations - considered international flag operations by the FOM for some purposes but not for others - causes confusion as to which rules actually apply. This needs to be clarified.
