column121: I was pilot flying; my CA (Captain) was pilot monitoring. After receiving instructions from Approach to slow down to 170 KT until a 5-mile final; we got an IDG (Integrated Drive Generator) fault message. The CA pulled out the QRH and tried to address the issue. Shortly after; we got a multitude of issues. We notified ATC and we agreed that we would be safe to land. Slat flap fail; AT/AP (Autothrottles/Autopilot) disconnect; and more. Suddenly we lost all screens and everything went black. The RAT (Ram Air Turbine) deployed and I had to continue flying using the Captains PFD (Primary Flight Display). The CA [requested priority handling] and was cleared by Approach to land and swap to Tower.CA told the FAs (Flight Attendant) we were making a precautionary landing. Tower said they had the trucks rolling and landed as best we could normally. We dropped the flaps on schedule and noticed that the Slat Flap Disagree persisted. The CA then took over the controls with ample time before the 1;000 feet call and I swapped roles to PM. We notified ATC that we could not verify [if] the gear and flaps were down. Luckily; Tower notified us that another plane verified they were down. We landed uneventfully and taxied to the gate under our own power. No passengers were hurt; only the first row or two knew something was abnormal due to the RAT vibrations; the rest of the passengers were unaware of the incident. [The cause was an] internal electrical malfunction at a time of high workload. Potentially go-around and troubleshoot If issues happen on final.

We saw them cut us off and executed a turn to our right to avoid and then another turn once clear to follow them in the pattern. As we entered the downwind leg; I determined we were too close for a safe pattern and told the student to execute a right 360-degree turn for spacing. I announced this on CTAF and we did the turn.While this was occurring; the unknown Cherokee was proceeding down the downwind leg and failed to notice Cessna 172; Aircraft Z; on an extended downwind/base leg. Aircraft Z had announced its intentions of doing so once [it] joined its downwind leg in order to provide spacing for another aircraft already in the pattern to complete a full-stop landing. This unknown Warrior proceeded to turn a base leg too close to the runway and effectively cut off Aircraft Z on final. The unknown Cherokee then overflew final; turned its own final leg; and proceeded to fly final within 100 feet. wing tip-to-wing tip of Aircraft Z. Aircraft Z then proceeded to execute a go-around and depart the area to the south afterwards. The unknown Cherokee did not make another radio call and proceeded to go around; departing ZZZ's pattern to the north from what I could tell.After talking to the other pilot in Aircraft Z; we determined that when Aircraft Z was on its entry leg into ZZZ's pattern the unknown Cherokee was following Aircraft Z in trail very closely. To make spacing; he announced he would execute a left 360. However; in reality he turned into an opposite direction downing leg and made a 180-degree turn after to reenter downwind on the correct direction. In doing so he effectively entered right where I; in Aircraft X; was making my turn and cut us off. All of this could have been fixed by proper radio communication on the part of the unknown Cherokee. The Cherokee should have also used standard pattern procedures and not nonstandard ones. If he had completed the 360 like he said he was going to he wouldn't have cut us off and standard procedure usage wouldn't have led to Aircraft Z being cut off as well.

column121: I was vectoring Aircraft X into ZZZ for an ILS Approach. He was vectored through final and left high for VFR traffic on the localizer. He called the field in sight over the Final Approach Fix; was cleared for a Visual and switched to ZZZ Tower. He turned towards ZZZ1.  VFR aircraft above 1500 feet near the localizer are a conflict because 2400 feet is the crossing altitude for the Initial Approach Fix ZZZZZ. VFR aircraft departing ZZZ or ZZZ2 Class D southbound are in a head on conflict with any aircraft on the localizer into ZZZ. IFR aircraft often end up being too high for a localizer approach because they can't descend because of VFR traffic on the localizer and they get a Visual Approach instead. It's also not uncommon for aircraft to be vectored through the final approach course to avoid traffic or descend. Both of these courses of action can disorient pilots; but there is nowhere to break them out without creating another conflict somewhere else. A few miles east of the localizer is higher terrain. An aircraft at 3000 feet within 10 miles of the airport will not be able to climb to the Minimum Vectoring Altitude in time. If the aircraft continues on a vector north to parallel ZZZ1; they could conflict with a departure off of ZZZ1; likely a prop on a 020 heading climbing to 3000 feet.  ZZZ1; ZZZ; and ZZZ2 are so close to each other that it can be confusing which airport they see when they aren't able to fly a straight path inbound because of VFR conflicts.ZZZ localizer approach course need to be controlled airspace. VFR aircraft should not be able to fly on or through the localizer without talking to ATC. It's impossible to predict the actions of a VFR aircraft not on frequency. They climb; descend and maneuver around traffic they do see; sometimes making 360's.

column121: Departing Runway XXR at ZZZ over the shoreline at approximately 1;500 feet AGL; the Pilot Flying (PF) began a required turn to the left for heading of 210. The PF immediately verbalized a flight control abnormality stating that he is feeling resistance in the control wheel and that it couldn't be turned more than about half-scale deflection to the left; as if it was hitting the designed maximum stop.We continued the climb and the PF asked the Pilot Monitoring (PM) to take controls to see if the resistance was the same on both sides. The PM took the controls and agreed that the resistance was the same on both sides. Neither the PF nor the PM tried to force the control wheel beyond the point of resistance since the plane was still controllable in the normal range of operation up to 30 degrees angle of bank.The PM pulled out the QRH section 9.8 Jammed or Restricted Flight Controls. The PF continued to fly the SID as the PM ran the QRH and discussed the situation. The first thing we noticed about the QRH was that Step 4 required the use of Maximum Force to overpower a restricted system; however; this step did not seem to apply to us because the aircraft was controllable in the normal flight regime. This step introduced some doubt and confusion with the crew.We agreed that we didn't have a jam; but the maximum control deflection was restricted. Upon reaching Step 7; we had to decide whether the controls were normal or not normal. This step also introduced some confusion because we reasoned that since we both were able to make right and left turns under normal conditions up to 30 degrees angle of bank; the controls were for all intents and purposes normal. However; we still had the restriction; which gave us concern; and that full control wheel deflection was not normal.At this point; the crew decided to contact Maintenance and Dispatch on ARINC VHF radio and use all available resources to discuss the situation. The radios were very scratchy and there was a lot of feedback when the company keyed their microphones. All parties agreed that QRH 9.8 was the appropriate checklist for the situation; but the decision to continue or divert to the nearest suitable airport was still to be determined.As a crew; we felt that we were in a gray area between normal and not-normal flight controls but relayed to Maintenance that we felt comfortable continuing on to our destination. All parties agreed. En route; we continued to discuss the situation and it occurred to us that even though we could maneuver the plane normally; it was unknown whether an upset recovery might be diminished or not in the event of an encounter with wake turbulence; jet wash; or a rudder hard-over event. Such a condition might require Step 4 of the QRH to overpower the restriction with both Pilots. As a precaution; the crew asked ATC to keep the aircraft clear of potential wake turbulence due to restricted flight controls but that we were not declaring an emergency at this time.On final approach in full configuration; the PF experienced some ground convective turbulence and verbalized that he hit the resistance once during the approach as he was trying to counter the turbulence. This was unexpected; but the crew was able to land the aircraft safely.

column121: [There was a] nose gear tire issue followed by a loss of System A Hydraulics. We were flying Flight XXXX from ZZZ to ZZZ1 on (date). As we were rolling down the runway; we heard a loud bang from the nose gear area. It went away as quickly as it arrived; engine parameters were normal as well as directional control. After the takeoff; we talked about what it could have been. During the climb to our cruising altitude; we decided to call ZZZ Tower back and ask them to inspect Runway XR for any clues to what had happened during our takeoff roll. It took a while before we got an update from ZZZ Tower. They had found a two feet by two piece of rubber. We immediately contacted Dispatch and Maintenance; and we discussed various options. We were now in cruise and still bound for ZZZ1; when all of sudden the Number 1 Eng Hyd A LOW PRESSURE light started to come on and off a few times. We got the QRH Checklist and ran the HYDRAULIC PUMP LOW PRESSURE.I looked down on the instrument panel and noticed the System A Hydraulics quantity was down in the low 20's percent. We could watch that number was dropping fast. We now went quickly over to another chapter in the QRH; to LOSS OF SYSTEM A. We also [requested priority landing] with Center; and they immediately gave us direct to ZZZ1 airport. We determined that it was likely that a possibly piece of rubber had hit some of the Hydraulic lines. We quickly updated Dispatch about our loss of Hydraulic A quantity; and that we had [requested priority landing]. Dispatch gave us the Landing Distance information data; and we compared it to our own. We were all in agreement to continue and land in ZZZ1. We informed our Flight Attendants about our situation and what they could expect from our landing. We flew overhead ZZZ1 airport; and manually extended our landing gear per QRH. After completing all the steps in the QRH; we lined up with Runway XXL and landed. I immediately noticed the tiller was «locked» and unusable upon landing; and had to use rudder and differential braking to get back on center line. Both NORM and ALT nose wheel steering where both unavailable. We elected to stop the aircraft on the runway; and asked the Fire Trucks to visually inspect the aircraft from the outside. After getting the OK from them; we had Company Maintenance meet us on the runway with a tug; and to tow us clear of the runway. We had just cleared [Runway] XXL when the tow bar snapped; and they had to get another one. Once we got the second one; we were towed over to Gate X where our passengers were able to deplane.
column123: Departed ZZZ Runway XR. On takeoff roll; prior to rotation; a noise was heard similar to a hand slap on the front of the aircraft. Takeoff was continued with no adverse indications. As we continued to climb; the Captain and I assessed the probable cause of the noise. ZZZ Tower was advised of possible FOD on the runway. Before we were out of range of ZZZ Tower; we inquired for any findings of the FOD. Tower advised a piece of tire rubber was found on the runway. Still unsure whether the rubber was from our aircraft or a piece we hit on takeoff roll; we continued the assessment. Dispatch was brought into the loop and we all agreed to continue. As we continued to discuss the current situation; the #1 HYD LOW PRESSURE light illuminated and we ran the HYDRAULIC PUMP LOW PRESSURE QRH Checklist. SYSTEM A HYDRAULIC quantity was noted to be around 20 percent. SYSTEM A HYDRAULIC quantity continued to drop. LOSS OF SYSTEM A QRH Checklist was started. [After] reassessment of the loss of HYDRAULIC SYSTEM A and the noise heard at takeoff; [they] led us to believe that we had blown a tire which had damaged the hydraulics. A [priority landing was requested] with Center and direct ZZZ1 was issued. We continued discussions with Dispatch; as well as informed the Flight Attendants of our current conditions; plans and what to expect on arrival in ZZZ1. All went as planned with the completion of the LOSS OF SYSTEM A Checklist and landing on Runway XXL in ZZZ1. The only unexpected item on landing was no nose wheel steering on landing. Both NORM and ALT nose wheel steering was inoperative upon landing so we were unable to exit runway. CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) met the aircraft on the runway to assist. Aircraft was towed to the gate from the runway.

column121: Just prior to push out of ZZZ we received and Air Bleed Message. Maintenance interrogated the system and MEL'd the message iaw MEL XX-XX. Enroute the Purser called and stated 'we have an issue; in reviewing our manual we have a Class A fume event in the forward galley. It smells like dirty gym socks.' I've had fume events in the past and I know the ramifications to the safety of the crew and passengers. We also have received good training during [Flight Attendant Training]. In the cockpit we didn't smell anything. All three flight attendants confirmed the same smell. With a Jump seat rider in the cockpit; I made the decision to take a quick bathroom break. Upon reaching the front right galley is was prevalent; mild and persistent. Upon returning to the cockpit I had the purser remain in the cockpit. I used air cell to call Dispatch and maintenance. With pilots; purser; dispatch and maintenance all on the phone call we jointly made the decision it's best to divert to a suitable airport. Over the vicinity of ZZZ2 and ZZZ3 we evaluated diversions to outstations; continue to ZZZ4 or ZZZ5. We were 570 miles from ZZZ4 and 240 from ZZZ5. Knowing ZZZ5 was just as close as spiraling down from FL380 and the aircraft would be grounded; we took into consideration passengers re-accomodation; medical response; inflight support and aircraft replacement. ZZZ5 was the best option and the joint decision was made to proceed to ZZZ5. I asked the First Officer (F/O) to [request priority] from ATC and we proceeded direct to a fix on ILS [Runway] XXR and landed and taxied to the Gate. With the jump seater being pregnant and the review of other events where fumes become hard to smell after long exposure; I requested everyone in cockpit to wear oxygen. I ran through QRC and [other procedures] multiple times to make sure we didn't miss any steps. Managing and reassessing the issue I think we did a pretty thorough job. I even turned on APU and ran bleeds to trouble shoot and nothing was working. The smell persisted in a mild to moderate amount especially in descent according to Flight Attendants (F/As). The purser had F/As rotate to mitigate one persons exposure. With a full aircraft we couldn't move anyone. Upon landing and shutting down we de-masked and opened up flight door. The first officer immediately noticed the smell and we left shortly after securing the aircraft.  I was not aware that the F/As had on the previous leg noticed any smell. They all reported after the event that the dirty socks smell was present on the previous flight. When I took over the aircraft I was again blind sided by this. The F/A in aft galley even said she replaced her socks thinking it was her feet. So my suggestion is to continue to encourage communications from the cabin and have these experiences validated and documented even if there is the slightest question to certain smells. I don't know if the Air Bleed message would have an impact on this event but if so maybe adding instructions to confirm with crew no odors prior to MEL. Having these Name (Purser) able to locate his references on his tablet was huge in assisting me with my QRH.

column121: Instructing student on dual flight from ZZZ. Pre-flighted aircraft and fueled up and sump check good. Taxied to [Runway] XX. Run up checks were all within tolerance. Took off [Runway] XX and had normal performance for the weight and heat of the day. Getting around 300-400 FPM climb after crossing through 50 feet above the runway. Did our check of engine gauges; all green. Contacted Approach around 800 feet MSL and were told on course heading; started turn to NW and experienced partial power loss from 2;250 to 1;800 RPM. Instructor said 'what was that?' I took controls from my Student and remained Pilot Flying till we landed. Checked mixture full rich; throttle full; fuel pump on; and switched fuel tanks. Made a call to Approach and turned back to the airport. Was switched over to Tower and requested priority as we could not maintain altitude and safe airspeed. Did not lose total engine power until after we landed. Made sure Student was OK and calm. Picked a field and put in one notch of flaps; then full flaps once the field was made. Turned 180 degrees at 30 degree bank and aimed for first 3rd of runway. Touched down as smoothly as possible and used parking brake to come to a stop. Engine died as we rolled to a stop. Called emergency personnel; no injuries or visible damage to the plane; surprisingly. Plane overhead spotted us.
column123: We did the run up and pre-takeoff checklist and everything was checked out. We made a call to Tower and were cleared for takeoff on Runway XX. We took off with 10 degrees of flaps and full power and started climbing; and engine was sluggish due to high heat index; but within normal operating range. We did our initial climb check with engine gauges and Departure was contacted. Altitude was reported as 800 feet MSL and climbing; we took out the flaps; and turned toward our heading. At 1;000 MSL we had a partial power loss before we reached our heading. I noticed the partial power loss right away and exclaimed; 'What was that?' to my Instructor and instructor took controls. We switched the fuel pump on and then verified mixture and throttle were full and then switched fuel tanks. Nothing changed. We established proper pitch for best glide. My Instructor made a call to Departure; but then was switched to Tower and made a call. We were cleared to land Runway XY; but aborted landing because we were too far from the runway. Instructor put in 10 degrees of flaps and found a field. Instructor put in full flaps and did 30 degrees of bank to align with the field while descending rapidly. At 100 feet AGL; instructor pulled power to idle. Instructor then flared to land and we touched down. We immediately pulled the parking brake as the engine had total power loss and the propeller stood still. We stopped before the trees and switched off fuel pump; master; and turned off magnetos. We got out and started contacting the appropriate people. We opened the engine compartment to check things out and made sure the propeller was OK. An airplane found us and began circling and emergency personnel arrived. We left the airplane in the field and walked to meet with the personnel and they took it from there.

column121: Was instructing in owner's aircraft. He wanted to practice takeoff and landings in the pattern at ZZZ. We did three three pointers. They were acceptable. Not greasers but nothing fundamentally wrong. We then did two wheel landings. Again; acceptable but not greasers but no warning flags. It was getting hot and thermal activity was affecting the landings so we decided to do one more and then call it quits. He did an acceptable wheel landing and at first everything was OK. Straight on the runway and wheels down. He then put the tail down - prematurely in my judgement as we still had a lot of speed (not excessive). The plane immediately yawed to the right. I intervened and applied full opposite rudder (I think he did as well) but it did not stop the yaw. This aircraft has no brakes on the instructor side so unable to apply brakes. The pilot did not use brakes to control the yaw. We ended up in the grass next to the runway. The pilot was pretty shaken up so I taxied back onto the runway and to the tie down. We determined there was no damage to the aircraft. I recommended to the pilot to have the tail wheel inspected in case there was some issue with it.I was surprised that we had the yaw to the right after what appeared to be an acceptable wheel landing. There were no wind gusts or other factors that I was aware of. It was either a result of lowering the tail too quickly (gyroscopic precession) or there is an issue with the tail wheel mechanism.

column121: While taxing; a situation arose where the aircraft I was operating; Aircraft X; and a separate C172 training aircraft were instructed to taxi in opposing directions on Taxiway XX at ZZZ Airport. I was instructed 'to taxi via XX and XY to [Runway] XZL and maintain right of XX for opposite traffic' after leaving FBO.Abiding by this instruction; I maintained right of the taxiway and an opposite Grumman aircraft passed our left side of the taxiway; with us on the right. Having believed the opposing traffic no longer a factor; I returned to normal taxi while still maintaining right of taxiway; however; with less vigilance; believing traffic no longer a factor. My instructed taxi procedure at the Skydiving Facility is to taxi nose high to alleviate nose wheel pressure thus putting less wear and tear on the nose wheel Oleo Strut. This can make distant traffic difficult to see. We are also urged to taxi rather quickly to save time by skydiving management to save time. As I approached a 45 degree bend in Taxiway XX; eastbound on the Taxiway; my aircraft briefly went over to the left side of the Taxiway. I was unaware that there was another opposite bound Aircraft; having thought only the Grumman was the traffic I should have been looking out for. Our quick taxi; and brief cross to the left; startled the opposing C172 traffic--who was instructed to taxi right side of XX; from XA; to FBO. This prompted them to alert Ground Control that we were too close and a possible collision existed. I applied brakes and moved further to the right of the Taxiway to make room for the opposing traffic and passed with normal intended separation.To avoid a recurrence of a similar situation; I believe it would be helpful to alert pilots of specific traffic when special bidirectional operations are in use on Taxiways. This will aid in helping pilots to stay more alert of specific traffic to be aware of. Also; skydiving operators should be advised to use caution when bidirectional taxiway operations are in effect. Ground Control holding conflicting traffic could also improve safety; by holding traffic at originating positions to allow for non-opposite direction use of the Taxiway with only one permitted on the Taxiway at a time.

column121: Aircraft X was assigned the unadvertised XYL for arrival (advertised as a departure only runway) to accommodate for the required runway inspection by airport ops after this type of aircraft arrives or departs. It's easier to stop traffic and inspect the departure runway.  Aircraft Y checked on 10 to 15 miles out and I cleared them to land and advised that traffic would Line Up and Wait/depart prior to their arrival. I was very focused on my sequence because we were in weather reroute program and there were numerous in-trail restrictions over most (all?) departure fixes. I got too focused on the departures and did not appropriately scan for the arrivals progress. When I instructed Aircraft Y to Line Up and Wait; Aircraft X advised that they were going around. I responded with a subsequent go around and maintain 3000 feet shortly after followed by a 300 heading after coordinating with Local Control. Aircraft Y crossed the Hold Short Lines but not the edge line. I will add a memory aid to my personal technique to prevent this from occurring again. I plan to use an empty strip holder to conservatively predict where the arrival will fit in with my departures. For example; if the arrival is 10 miles away I would put the blank strip 2 departures back and not depart beyond the blank strip without reassessing the situation. This will force me to periodically check on the progress of the arrival to my departure runway.

column121: Aircraft X checked on approximately 30 [miles] north [of] CUL airport requesting to descend. Marginal VFR to IFR conditions in airspace. Attempted to request type approach and verification from pilot. Pilot advised they could not hear me and switched radios. The pilot switched but was broken and unreadable and when the pilot called back; I attempted to switch to standby transmitter but the pilot could only get me '2x5'. I told the aircraft to proceed direct the IAF for the RNAV 18 approach at CUL. The pilot responded 'proceeding direct HGOOD; cleared RNAV 18 approach.' I chose not to respond to the pilot as the pilot seemed to be having difficulty possibly with radios or navigation with the weather; so I chose not to reiterate 'cleared RNAV 18 approach'. Moments later I observed the aircraft at 2;000 feet level direct to the IAF (not on a published portion of the approach). The MVA in the area is 2;500. I then pulled the approach plate to verify the crossing altitude at the IAF (2;100 feet) and pulled up the VFR chart located above the position to verify obstructions in the area. There were no obstructions on the route of flight above 800 feet which the aircraft was more than 1;000 feet above. I chose not to climb the aircraft and accepted the altitude as variance of what I thought was an appropriate altitude considering the following: 7110.65 4-8-5 Specifying Altitude:'Specify in the approach clearance the altitude shown in the approach procedures when adherence to that altitude is required for separation. When vertical separation will be provided from other aircraft by pilot adherence to the prescribed maximum; minimum; or mandatory altitudes; the controller may omit specifying the altitude in the approach clearance.'  Additionally; I was thinking of the example given in 4-8-1 for RNAV approaches of the 7110.65:'Aircraft 1 can be cleared direct to CENTR. The intercept angle at that IAF is 90 degrees or less. The minimum altitude for IFR operations (14 CFR; section 91.177) along the flight path to the IAF is 3;000 feet.'After the event a controller who had seen the altitude asked what was going on with the Aircraft X from earlier at 2000. I told him the situation and what I thought was an appropriate response. He told me that he does not believe that applied to this circumstance. I followed up with two additional more senior radar controllers who agreed that an altitude should be given but didn't know what 4-8-5 was in reference to. The next morning I asked a supervisor about the scenario and asked what 4-8-5 refers to; he showed me an approach plate for ORD with multiple crossing altitudes on the approach. I asked him how he knew that this is what that paragraph referred to and he just noted experience.I would recommend clarification of 4-8-5 in the 7110.65 to be more easily understood to which scenario this applies. Additionally; in the example given in 4-8-1 for RNAV application; the use of minimum IFR altitude is confusing as this altitude could be lower than an MVA for the area. I would change this to MVA; or DVA if applicable; to ensure better understanding that a lower MIA than MVA is not acceptable on an unpublished route.

column121: We operated the ZZZ to ZZZ1 flight. The landing numbers were run for Runway XXL with the ATIS showing south winds at about 7 kts. and temperature about 90 degrees. Normal flaps 30 approach was flown and I used thrust reverser to about 100 kts. before getting on the brakes. Normal brake pressure was used and we took the high speed taxiway. Taxi time to the gate was about four minutes; and I released the parking brake once we were in the chocks.The Operations Agent came in and asked if we 'got on the brakes'.  I said no and he said that our Company has blown about six plugs in the last couple weeks. I received a call from the Operations and was told what happened. I also called Maintenance and answered some questions regarding the flight. Everything on this flight was normal and I believe we did not brake the aircraft down more than a normal landing.  We actually mentioned there was no reason to brake hard due to the three minute limitation on the MAX.Might consider leaving the gear down on such a short flight. Using the carbon brakes; it would be nice to have a temperature gauge for the brakes.
column123: Our first indication that there were any concerns was as the Operations Agent met us upon arrival in ZZZ. He asked if we had used heavy braking on landing because recently he had seen 6 events where the wheel fuse plugs had deflated the tires on this particular flight. The Captain immediately ensured that the parking brake had been released to allow for improved cooling. The oncoming FO (First Officer) met us after he completed his walk-around. He noted that the brakes seemed pretty warm. However; at this point the fuse plugs had not melted yet. We turned the aircraft over to the new crew and headed to the hotel. The Chief Pilot called the Captain at the hotel to inform him that the fuse plugs had melted and deflated the tires after we left. I do not believe the landing data indicated that brake cooling was required. Once at the hotel I tried to re-run the landing data to confirm that there wasn't a brake cooling message. There was not; as far as I could tell; but I could not recall the actual landing weights. I also tried to run the brake cooling module but couldn't get it to run because the release data had expired. This led me to go dig in the books for the brake cooling charts. I believe the brakes on speed was approximately 100 kts.; because I remember seeing the runway exit coming and checking the speed as I felt the increased deceleration from the Captain applying the brakes. Using this and estimated landing conditions I used the Landing Data Charts in the MAX performance manual. This indicated that no special brake cooling procedures were required. However; I noted some interesting facts in this section of the airway manual: If we had used Autobrakes 3 and VRef 145; it puts a lot of additional energy in the brakes; requiring at least 40 minutes of cooling time; and possibly into the 'Caution' for hot brakes; depending on the landing data used. The cooling time chart seems to suggest that 7.3 minutes of cooling Inflight Gear Down is equivalent to 50 minutes of cooling on the ground. The text in that section states; 'Total energy is the sum of residual energy plus energy added.' This is important to note since the previous flights of this particular aircraft had landings at high elevations on high temperature days.

column121: This report concerns the unscheduled separation of the #4 - outboard right main wheel - from the aircraft on takeoff from Runway XX in ZZZ. We began the trip receiving the aircraft from the previous crew at the gate in ZZZ1 one leg prior. There were no abnormalities on the pre-flight; no abnormalities that had not been cleared; and no major abnormalities of any kind recorded in the logbook or in the previous logbook that was in the can for the aircraft. The previous crew verbally told us that it was performing well when we received it from them. The first leg; ZZZ1 to ZZZ; operated smoothly with nothing out of the ordinary occurring. The post flight after that leg revealed no discrepancies of any kind. We pushed back from ZZZ; and our taxi route towards Runway XX included left- and right-hand turns as well as brake applications; and the aircraft continued to operate normally with no signs of any abnormality on the wheels.When we performed the takeoff; shortly after we selected the landing gear up; Tower called us and told us it looked like we lost a tire on the runway. The takeoff was so smooth that we weren't sure if we had in fact lost a tire as we had no indication in the cockpit of any system abnormalities; and the aircraft felt like it was operating normally. We knew there was construction around the runway in about the position we would have lifted off the ground at; so I thought that perhaps it was misidentified construction debris - although we hadn't seen any debris on the runway prior to takeoff. We asked them to perform a runway inspection to determine if it was our tire while we contacted Dispatch to obtain some identifying information about it; as well as to make a plan of action in case it was our tire. We contacted ZZZ Operations after some attempts; and asked them to remain at the airport to assist in identifying the tire and in case we needed to return to ZZZ.We decided not to relay to Dispatch through Operations because we initially had trouble reaching them and we believed that their Operations radio was a handheld and would not have good signal at altitude and location we would need to hold at. We decided to continue climb so that we could contact Dispatch through AIRINC. We discussed the possibility of flying by ZZZ Tower to have them identify if we were missing the tire and which one it was; but at that time we were still not sure that it was our tire and we were unsure if we would have enough fuel to do that and still proceed to ZZZ1 if that was what Dispatch wanted us to do. We made the judgement call that Dispatch would most likely have us continue to ZZZ1 due to the long runways; good emergency services; and having the finest Operations and Maintenance staff there to assist. We continued to climb along our filed route while ATC attempted to identify the tire. Shortly after that; we advised the Flight Attendant (FA) of the potential situation and that we were most likely continuing to ZZZ1; and we would wait to advise the passengers until we were sure and close to ZZZ1 to avoid panic. She said that she would take the time to review some information in her manuals. We chose to continue at a speed of long-range cruise or slower - 180 IAS being the safe speed used when structural damage is suspected - because we were unsure if there was debris on the wheel assembly that could become dislodged and damage something else; or if losing the tire had already damaged something.It took about 30 minutes to 45 minutes for us to make contact with Dispatch after that. We attempted AIRINC; Station Operations on 4 or 5 different local frequencies; relaying through company aircraft; or through another frequency. We attempted using different transmitters in case there was debris from the tire that had damaged an antenna. We were unsuccessful; so ATC attempted to call Dispatch. This took time because ATC was attempting to call using an old company number with an old area code. It was further delayed because we werebeing handed off to new controllers periodically and we had to apprise them each of the situation and have them attempt to make contact. ATC did make contact and Dispatch instructed us to continue towards ZZZ1. After that; we were advised that it was in fact our tire. We requested priority handling and continued to ZZZ1. After this determination; it took roughly 15 - 30 minutes longer for us to contact Dispatch on AIRINC.We had time with a low workload in cruise because we couldn't contact Dispatch through AIRINC yet; so we used the time to review our manuals and the QRH for the related procedures. In the QRH we decided that the Landing with Abnormal Landing Gear Procedure was the most applicable. We began to brief and discuss this procedure while trying to make contact with Dispatch through AIRINC. When we did make contact with Dispatch; [they] advised us that they thought it was the #1 wheel - the left main outboard. We told him that the procedure called to induce a fuel imbalance and to burn off as much fuel as possible before landing. We asked his opinion of going into holding on the way in to ZZZ1 to do so; and he agreed.After this determination was made; we said we would call back again and terminated the call because our radio transmitters made it very difficult to talk to ATC and Dispatch at the same time - there appeared to be interference or override between VHF 1 and 2. We began cross-feeding fuel to make the left side as light as possible and briefed the FA assuming that the #1 wheel was the one we had lost. We told the FA that there was a good chance that it would be a normal precautionary landing and that we would most likely come to a stop on the runway; or exit the runway if able; but most likely would not taxi to the gate. We decided to request for fire trucks; busses; a tug; and a GPU to be standing by. After we were done briefing the FA; we continued to discuss the procedure for approach and landing. The first step of the checklist was to notify the passengers; so we used some time to create an agreed-upon script to brief the passengers without inducing panic - which I would later administer when we were holding near ZZZ1. We noticed that this procedure appeared to be designed to cover both structural landing gear issues as well as tire and wheel problems. We were not sure if we had structural problems or not resulting from the loss of the wheel; so we briefed the procedure including several decision times - such as what we would do if the gear extended normally vs. if the gear did not extend normally vs. if we lost the hydraulic system when the gear was extended; etc. The result which did occur which we briefed was that the gear extended normally and the remaining tire; brakes; and steering operated normally for the landing.The decisions which we briefed involved in this were as follows. We left the GPWS switch in the on position because that switch's function is to silence alerts when the gear is not sensed down and locked. No fuel imbalance was established; and with our and Dispatch's agreement due to the relatively light weight of the aircraft; small practical difference the imbalance would make; and for ease of procedure application in the interest of safety. We did not pull the emergency gear extension lever due to the gear extending normally and indicating locked down by both indicating systems. Our understanding is that the emergency gear extension handle simply opens the uplock boxes; which had already been opened successfully; and that pulling the emergency gear extension handle could potentially impede us during egress if an evacuation was needed. We discussed at what time the bleeds should be selected off for approach. I had never selected the bleeds off in this aircraft in flight before; so the Captain and I had different opinions about when it should be done. We ended up selecting them off at 500 ft.; which I now agree with in hindsight. The remaining items of the checklist would be completed after we were already on the ground. We briefed that we would complete these steps if there was some kind of fire; severe damage; or loss of control evident at touchdown; but we would otherwise move slowly and discuss these steps due to the potential hazards of aircraft control involved with performing them.While we were discussing this; Dispatch called on AIRINC again and corrected that we had actually lost the #4 - outboard right main wheel - rather than the #1 as said earlier. I asked him if he was sure and made sure that Maintenance had checked the serial numbers on the wheel to be positive. After Dispatch told us this we re-briefed the Flight Attendant for the #4 wheel.After we were all thoroughly briefed; we began our delay vectors around ZZZ1 to burn down to roughly 2000 lb. as instructed by Dispatch; I gave the PA to the passengers. When we had burned enough fuel; we began the ILS to Runway XYR - the longest and most familiar runway for us in ZZZ1. The gear extended normally and we saw no abnormal flight characteristics or any system abnormalities. On touchdown; as briefed; I began using the tiller to steer the aircraft early; and we felt it pulling slightly toward the right. However; not nearly enough to warrant the emergency engine shutdown. We were able to control the aircraft throughout the rollout to maintain centerline. We chose not to try to turn off the runway as it would be a left turn-off; which would put the most weight on the right side; and we were unsure of the quality of braking that we had. We used reverse only until we were at a slow walking speed and only then used brake application to bring the aircraft to a stop on the runway centerline abeam the XX taxiway exit where the firetrucks and Operations were waiting.Tower gave us the discrete frequency to use. The firetrucks came onto the runway and asked us to shut down the #2 engine so they could inspect. We complied and they said the remaining tire seemed to be in good condition and asked us if we wanted to exit. We said no; we would like to deplane the passengers and then be tugged. While Operations was setting up to deplane the passengers; we briefed how we would manage shutting down the #1 engine in order to deplane; and requested the GPU to be connected so we could deplane with lights on without killing the batteries. When the GPU was ready; we connected; Operations pinned all 3 gears; we shut down #1; checked the after-landing and -parking checklists; called the Flight Attendant; and then began deplaning to the busses. While the passengers were deplaning; Operations connected the tug. When the passengers were clear we prepared to sit in the cockpit while Operations tugged us to Gate XX. We monitored the tug process; arrived at the gate; and began conducting the postflight inspection and filling out the logbook. I completed the logbook while the Captain called the Chief Pilot to begin debriefing.I suggest that Station Operations be provided with better radio systems; or that the ACARS system be utilized in our aircraft. It was difficult for us to establish a reliable communication with Dispatch due to a combination of poor-quality radios and not many base stations being occupied due to the time of day. A communication with Dispatch was very necessary in order for Maintenance to verify which tire was missing so that we could adjust our procedures.

We happened to have a jump seater commuting home and he provided me some data from the website Flight Aware. Flight Aware shows Aircraft Z at 475 ft. when they started to climb/Go Around; and ATC had previously cleared Aircraft Y to depart. On departure ATC said 'Sorry to Aircraft Z' and Aircraft Y acknowledged with 'Yeah we were confused.' I told/instructed Aircraft Z to 'go around;' after nobody else would say anything and the fact the two planes were on what appeared to be a collision course. It seemed as though ATC was unaware they had two planes going to the same runway.

column121: On the final phase of the Visual Approach; backed up by the ILS Runway XY to ZZZ; with the intention to capture the glide path from above; the Auto Pilot (AP) and Auto Throttles were disengaged. Prevailing conditions were Good Visibility and varying Tail Winds of up to nine (9) Knots. During the final portion of the descent to touchdown; with a visual transition to the PAPI reference already established (PAPI were showing 3 RED-1 WHITE); the Aircraft descended below the referenced visual glide path; with the tendency to fly over the Runway XY overrun area at an altitude (AGL) of less than 50 ft. The moment the Captain; having the Pilot Monitoring (PM) duties; mentioned his estimation for being low on the glide path; the aircraft was overflying a point short of the RWY by about 500 feet. He consecutively called for a Go Around; which was immediately executed by the PF (Pilot Flying). The Flight landed after a RADAR pattern on the same runway uneventfully.[The cause was] Human Factors / Pilot Flying error on visually estimating the projected Glide Slope to Runway XY; with the current Tail Wind conditions. Root cause is the initially higher angle of descent / rate of descent to capture the glide slope from above; that ended up to an over correction - reverse situation of flying finally lower than the projected/correct slope. [I suggest] earlier Aircraft configuration for the Final Approach Phase and timely request from the ATC for lower altitudes / earlier descent to the recommended altitudes that lead to a better projected sequence of flying tasks.
column123: FO was flying pilot. Performed visual approach and FO had a hard time trying to catch the glide slope from above because he was trying to slow down and put flaps down while on OPEN DESC. FO called for 'the bird'; which caught me off guard because it is the first time anyone has asked for the flight path vector while trying to intercept the ILS and while disconnecting the AP. He not only disconnected AP but also eventually the auto thrust without previously briefing it. I told him to never disconnect the auto thrust again while trying to save a visual approach. Finally he was established on the ILS. Below 500 feet he said he was going to follow the PAPI. I glanced down at the VSI to make sure we were stable and when I looked backed up we had 4 red on the PAPIs and at the same time we received a GS GPWS warning. Became unstable. I loudly and sternly called 'unstable; go-around.' Performed go-around as RA called 50 feet. FO performed a soft go-around. I overrode his decision after he brought back TL (Thrust Lever) to CLB and I pushed TL to TOGA since we were in ZZZ (high airport elevation) with high OAT. I honestly could not tell you the altitude when the FO brought back the TL to CLB. I wanted to make sure we were safe since the go-around was performed at 50 feet from an unsafe position. At 50 feet RA; aircraft was not anywhere near the approach end of the runway. Came back for an uneventful landing.FO descended below glide slope and PAPI showed 4 red.Soft Go-around procedure should be changed or at least highlight the need to take into account airport elevation and OAT when deciding to make a soft go-around from a low altitude with an obvious performance deterioration.Soft Go-around procedure should be changed or at least highlight the need to take into account airport elevation and OAT when deciding to make a soft go-around from a low altitude with an obvious performance deterioration.

column121: After takeoff at approximately 500 ft. AGL; we received an EGT (Exhaust Gas Temperature) Overtemp ECAM.  We continued to thrust reduction altitude; requested priority handling; and followed the ECAM protocol which resulted in shutting down Engine #2. We completed all necessary tasks associated with an event of this nature and returned for an uneventful overweight landing at ZZZ.Contributing factors were a slight tailwind (new T/O data was obtained); heavy weight due to fuel tankering resulting in an APU bleeds on takeoff.Difficult to say; OAT was not excessive but perhaps there was an issue of some kind with the engine resulting in it exceeding EGT limits.
column123: Before departure at the gate; my Captain and I discussed possible threats prior to briefing. While the weather was nice; the two that came to mind were that while the ATIS reported wind as calm; it is not unusual to have a takeoff clearance with a tailwind; and secondly that if we had to return to field; we would be overweight for landing. As a matter of technique; I always load a return ILS into the longest runway at the departure airport in the secondary flight plan in case of a return to field; we discussed this and agreed it was a good idea.After discussing these threats; we noted that our Performance Data showed a TOGA takeoff; APU off. We requested a Performance Data with 5 kt. tailwind applied; which showed a TOGA takeoff; APU on. We entered the data for normal takeoff; but kept the we new Performance Data if needed.Upon switching to Tower upon approaching Runway XXC; we noted that the previous takeoff clearance included a tailwind. We entered the new data; ensured that flaps and APU were set appropriately; and verified that all were correct. Shortly after; we were given clearance to takeoff.The takeoff roll; takeoff; and initial climb were all normal. Somewhere around 500-800 ft.; we heard the 'ding' from the ECAM. The Captain stated 'my aircraft'; and after noting that it was not an quick action or ECAM exception; I noted it was simply an advisory ECAM with no actions; 'ENG 2 EGT High Temp'. I noted a temperature as high as 971. After thrust reduction; the ECAM then displayed the actions 'Thrust lever 2 ... idle; ENG Master 2 ... off'. We were now aware that we would be shutting down the number 2 engine. We requested priority handling and leveled at 4;000 ft. With the autopilot on; we changed controls so that I was the Pilot Flying; my Captain running the checklists; and we shut down the engine.With a maximum landing weight of 171;519 lbs.; and we were over 188;000 lbs.; we elected to slow the aircraft and deploy flaps in order to increase our fuel burn and get as light as we could before landing. My Captain completed all appropriate checklists while I coordinated with ATC. Reprogramming the MCDU for our return to field was now as simple as hitting Secondary Flight Plan and Activate Secondary. After all QRH checklists were complete and everyone was notified; my Captain asked me 'is there anything you can think of that we have missed?'; which I answered; 'No; I cannot.' We concluded with our approach briefing; with emphases on single engine and overweight procedures; completed the descent checklist; and got vectors to final. The Captain resumed control of the aircraft for approach and landing.Approach and landing were uneventful; landing at a weight of 184;400 lbs.; approximately 157 kts.; and 100 FPM descent rate or less. We came to a stop on the runway for inspection from ARFF (Airport Rescue Fire Fighting); and we immediately turned on the brake fans and monitored brake temperatures. ARFF did not note any high temperatures or leaks. We then taxied to Gate XX with ARFF following us.The takeoff clearance with a tailwind made us change from TOGA; APU off; to TOGA; APU on takeoff. This change in takeoff thrust may have been enough for the engine to overtemp shortly after takeoff. A takeoff clearance with a headwind would have been a lower thrust takeoff. In our case; the Performance Data even indicated that [Runway] XXC would have been a reduced thrust takeoff.ZZZ airport needs to be better about airport operation being in line with wind direction in order to minimize the frequency of tailwind takeoff and landing clearances.

column123: While on dogleg to final for RWY 34L; descending to 2;400 feet MSL following preceding B737 by 3.5 NM encountered wake turbulence while on autopilot. column121: On Runway XX approach into ZZZ; I attempted to lower the gear by placing the landing gear handle down to extend the gear. During the extension process; both main gear green lights came on but neither the red or green light came on for the nose gear. I told ZZZ Tower that I needed to go around due to a system malfunction. After completing the go around; I followed the QRH procedures. The QRH procedures did not correct the unsafe nose gear condition. I then asked for priority handling and I contacted Tower for permission for a low pass to have them see if they could confirm the status of the nose gear. They said it appeared like all my gear was down; but they were not certain as it was night and it was difficult for them to have good visibility of the nose gear. After the low pass; I went back through the QRH checklists again to try to correct the condition. Once it was determined the nose gear would remain in an unsafe condition; I prepared for a potential nose gear up landing. At that time; I took the time to brief the Jump Seater and we reviewed the egress checklist. Since the Jump Seater was an experienced pilot; I handed the egress checklist to the Jump Seater and had him read through it. We discussed egress options in the event I became incapacitated. We briefed the scenario several times to ensure we had a clear understanding of what to expect and what actions we may need to take. After all appropriate checklists were ran and briefed and the approach reviewed and briefed; I elected at that point to land. I flew the ILS for Runway XX. I followed QRH guidance to land on the mains and hold the nose off the runway while gently lowering it as appropriate. In accordance with the procedures; I pulled the stop and feather pressed the stop button and turned the fuel and hydraulics off. After safely coming to a stop on the runway center line; I asked the Jump Seater if he was ok or if he was injured he said he was not injured and was safe. I assessed myself and reported to ATC that we were both safe. I completed the remaining items of the egress checklist and we exited the aircraft.Nose wheel door failure.Run the checklists; keep the Jump Seater informed and remain calm.Metro nose gear door inspections more often.

column121: TOGA APU bleed on config 2.  Cleared for takeoff; at about power stable and 1.5 EPR Engine 2 FAIL message (no fire indication) and single chime. Notified ATC of reject and needed to clear runway. Started ECAM procedures; at the same time another airline notified us over air that we had a fire on our number 2 engine. We then proceeded to extinguish fire with push button and squib. After finishing up procedure and coordination with CFR to make sure no fire was present we set up to be towed back to gate with no further incident.Apparently; Airbus is having issues with this config for takeoff. TOGA APU bleed on.Coordination with Airbus on reliable and safe max effort takeoff configurations.
column123: Day 3 of a 3-day; early departure; last leg home.  Gate XXX; short taxi to runway XXR.  Allowed the engines to warm up for three minutes while on the ramp to get the five minutes required before takeoff.  Winds were reported 280 degrees to approx 300 degrees.  From previous experiences from flying the Airbus in and out of ZZZ; the winds can switch to a tailwind component very quickly when they use runway XXL/R for departure; so I expected a potential tailwind.We were cleared to line up and wait on runway XXR.  The aircraft was lined up with the center line and the parking break was set.  Control was then given to the FO as we awaited takeoff clearance.  Once it was received and we read it back; we immediately experienced a single chime; which normally would indicate that perhaps the airplane was not configured for takeoff.  Upon looking at the ECAM; we had an ENG 2 FAIL ECAM alert.  Normally when we encounter ENG FAILs in the simulator; we are presented with a master warning and three chimes.  This was a singular chime.  I immediately told the FO we needed to clear the runway as there was a 90 degree taxiway (1) on the right side of the runway just 50 yards or so from us.  FO advised tower we needed to clear for a warning.At this point I initially thought this might be a false warning.  There was definitely a surprise factor to all of this.  As we were clearing the runway (right turn) at taxiway 1; I glanced at the EGT and it was red.  At the same time; another airplane that was getting ready to take the active runway said he saw fire coming out of out right engine.  I stopped the aircraft on taxiway 1.  I had the FO call for the CFR vehicles.  The FO wanted to run the ECAM procedure; but I had him check the Quick Reference Card first as I remembered there was either a quick action or ECAM exception procedure that needed to be run prior to executing the ECAM procedure.  The FO started to look that up... I called back to the cabin and asked the flight attendants to check to see if there was any smoke in the cabin or any sign of fire coming from the engine.  The answer was that there was no evidence of fire or smoke; from the #3 or #4 FA.  When I returned to the FO; he said the QRC procedure he found was for an ENG FIRE on the ground.  After considering a possible evacuation; my focus shifted to getting the engine shut down.  Since we had no indication of a fire from the cockpit (other than high EGT) nor any evidence from the cabin; we ran the ECAM ENG FAIL procedure and elected to discharge a fire bottle into the #2 engine.  I made a PA to the passengers telling them we exited the runway due to an alert we received in the cockpit and to expect some emergency vehicles come around the aircraft.   The fire trucks were not present at this point; so we asked the other airplane if they could see any evidence of fire.  They couldn't see from their vantage point; so I taxied the aircraft South on taxiway 2 to taxiway 3 (50 yards?) to see if they could see any evidence of continued fire.  They still could not see; so I stopped the aircraft at taxiway 3 and waited for CFR to show up.  No fire indications in the cockpit; such as aural fire warning or ENG FIRE ECAM; other than the excessive EGT with the ENG FAIL ECAM.Once CFR arrived; communications were hampered as they were not on a dedicated frequency yet.  I queried the tower and they gave us the right frequency to be on; when they arrived.  CFR scanned the aircraft and did not find any hot spots. At this point; we had finished the ECAM procedure and were looking for any follow-up procedures (which is the next step in Airbus; non-normal methodology).  The FO couldn't find them.  They used to be in the QRH and were on [specific] paper... easy to find.  Since a previous; major QRH revision; they are no longer on [specific] pages but are found within the QRH itself.  I told the FO not to worry about finding them... that much of the material was not going to be applicable.  I redirected our focus back to the STATUS page so we could discuss the current situation of the airplane.  The big thing was that we had no nose wheel steering; so we summoned ops to get us a tug and advised CFR to follow us under tow.  It took an inordinate amount of time to get a tug out to us (maybe 30 minutes or more); but seemed like hours.  Made several PA's explaining that we were still waiting on our tug.Eventually towed back to the gate.  Maintenance met the aircraft and asked about EGTs; duration; and the fire bottle status.  I told them I remembered seeing an EGT of 669 at some point... maybe for 30 to 60 seconds.  AML entry was made indicating all of this.When all of this was occurring during a short amount of time; I originally thought that maybe this was a false alert (only a single chime).  After exiting the runway and realizing the extent of the emergency; I thought that perhaps we had the presence of flames due to a compressor stall; exacerbated by a wind that may have shifted to a tailwind.After returning to the gate; I was in contact with the Fleet Captain... who asked if the APU was ON for takeoff.  I replied that it was.  In Airbus world; you can do a Max power takeoff and run the packs from the APU; freeing-up the engines; giving you a little more power for takeoff.  That was the case this morning.  The Fleet Captain indicated that the ENG FAIL ECAM was caused by having the APU bleed ON.  Apparently; this causes back pressure on the engine bleed and is a known issue.  Tech Ops is increasing ground idle to prevent thisAfter speaking to the Fleet Captain; he mentioned that the QRC procedure (requiring completion before doing the ECAM alert) entitled ENG FIRE on GROUND is a procedure used when there is no electrical power to the aircraft.  It is a procedure that is to be used in that situation.  Perhaps I misunderstood him as our conversation occurred after the adrenaline started settling down a bit; but maybe it needs to be explained to the flight crews (the correct use of that particular QRC procedure).Also; the FO had difficulty in finding the ECAM follow-up procedures; to the point where I said we need to move to the final step of assessing the STATUS (page) of the airplane.Finally; communication from the tower on how to communicate with CFR/ARFF when they arrived could; be improved upon.  In retrospect though; we never said the word 'emergency' to them.  My instructions to the FO were to get the trucks rolling now... not very clear perhaps and maybe was a factor in the initial comm problems with CFR.Advised the Duty Chief that we were done flying for the day.  The adrenal rush was subsiding and he was very helpful in accomplishing that for us.

column123: On Final Approach to XXL in ZZZ and configuring from flaps 25 to flaps 30 at about 1;500 feet the trailing edge flap needle indicators displayed a split and the flaps stopped at approximately 27 degrees. The LE FLAP TRANSIT light was also illuminated. After taking a few seconds to realize what was happening and coming through approximately 1;000 ft the Captain called for a go around. column123: On climbout passing approximately 21;000 feet; we got an ECAM indicating loss of the green system; LO G Press; and another green system ECAM but I cannot recall it now. The CA (Captain) and I split up the flying and comm duties; he advised the FA's (Flight Attendant) of our situation; and sent a message to Dispatch. I also advised ATC to let ZZZ know we would be a full-stop on the runway and would need to be towed. We were given priority handling back to ZZZ and we briefed the approach and threats of a go-around since the gear could not be retracted once it was hand-cranked down. The CA flew the approach XXL and the landing and stopping at the end of the runway was uneventful. We dropped the landing gear pins to the tug team and got towed back to the gate. We debriefed once we were off the aircraft and the passengers disembarked. The CA was cool; calm; and collected and flew a textbook approach. column121: After takeoff; passing approximately 2;000 feet MSL; the First Observer noticed a status message and a momentary Bleed 2 EICAS message. Upon review of the bleed control panel; he noted #1; #2; and #4 bleed off lights were illuminated with the bleed switches selected open. He quickly looked at the synoptic page and verified #1; #2; and #4 bleed valves were closed. I directed a climb to 10;000 feet to get above most VFR GA aircraft; and we leveled at 10;000 feet to begin assessing the situation. Radios were transferred to the Pilot Flying from the right seat and the First Observer; Second Observer; and I began to assess the situation.We observed the following Status MessagesENG 3 FIRE LP BBLEED OVPRESS 2BLEED PRV ENG 3There were no EICAS messages present.ECS (Environmental Control System) Synoptic was reviewed and we confirmed that only the #3 Bleed Valve was open.To assist ATC; we climbed to FL180 and leveled off; continuing to assess and evaluate the situation. We elected to cycle each malfunctioning bleed valve independently; but the #1; #2 and #4 valves remained closed. We did not cycle the #3 valve as it was the only source of air available to the aircraft.I initiated a conference call with Dispatch and Maintenance Control. The decision was made to return to ZZZ. Since we would be overweight I asked Dispatch if they wanted us to dump fuel; or burn it off. I was given approval for either choice.The crew agreed the best course of action was to return to ZZZ and burn down to the maximum normal landing weight by creating excessive drag. We held at low altitude for approximately 15 minutes to burn down to normal landing weight; uneventfully landing on XXC with flaps 30 and Autobrakes 3.It should be noted that during the descent; and any time engine thrust was reduced; the #1; #2; and #4 Bleed Valves opened and operated normally. The malfunction re-manifested itself anytime thrust levers were advanced.Our collective assessment was the #3 PRV had failed creating a manifold over pressure situation. However; we did not conduct any inflight trouble shooting of the #3 Bleed Valve to preclude compounding the loss of three bleed systems and the potential to lose all bleed air on the aircraft.ATC Controllers provided excellent assistance throughout the malfunction.

column121: Overloaded TakeoffPush back; engine start; fuel indications all normal. Initial taxi took additional power to move aircraft; which is unusual in a B777-200 at typical [long distance] weights. On takeoff roll; initial acceleration was sluggish even though we were TO2 max; the takeoff roll seemed longer than normal and climbout was less than usual. We were filed for initial cruise FL350; but given option of FL370 as FL350 taken; so we climbed FL370 (FMC said Max FL391). Upon level off at FL370; aircraft struggled to maintain normal cruise Mach speed .83; and I noticed amber hook was seemingly higher than normal (about 245 kts).Shortly after level off; EICAS caution 'FUEL DISAGREE'. Followed Emergency Check List and Progress Page 2 indicated totalizer about 10;000 lbs. higher than calculated. Determined no fuel leak; and followed up with QRH review of ETOPS failures; selected fuel probes synoptic display from maintenance section in FMC; and noticed many center tank fuel probes inoperative. We called Dispatch/Maintenance conference call on satcom and sent fuel maintenance display to them; all three parties agreed no fuel leak; use calculated fuel; determined it was appropriate to continue flight.We started to burn substantially above plan; and we started to suspect we were heavier than closeout. We referred to performance manual cruise pages; 1.3g maneuver data; and .84 cruise data; and our suspicions were confirmed: amber hook was indicating maneuvering speeds for approximately 50;000 lbs. heavier aircraft; also fuel flow predictions the same.We called Dispatch and Duty Pilot; asked them to contact ZZZ Station Personnel to obtain FUEL UPLIFT in gallons from fuel company. Prior procedures required us to check this information from the fuel slip. It would have caught this serious error. Initially fuel company kept sending info strictly off our aircraft gauges; but we explained to Dispatch this was not correct; due to inoperative center fuel probes; and we strongly suspected fueler had overfilled the amount required for the flight to ZZZ1.After an hour or so; Dispatch confirmed that we were approximately 50;000 lbs. (7500 gallons) heavier than planned.Our performance data/climb; cruise; descent; and landing data were invalid. The flight crew; not knowing this situation at the time of departure; could have encountered serious consequences; if an emergency such as engine failure occurred the crew may not have acted appropriately because of the unknown situation. implications for engine failure at V1 on takeoff; implications for stopping on wet runway from V1; implications for enroute engine out performance and drift down; implications for correct Vref in ZZZ1.This is an extremely serious incident in my opinion; possibly could have been caught with a simple fuel slip check.Inexperienced fuelers; lack of back up checks by the pilots; cross checking required fuel vs actual loaded fuel; possible fuel sensor failuresRecommend having someone in the crew cross check the fuel slip provided by the fueler against the master flight plan.

column121: On a VFR flight from HTL to 48D in day VMC with unrestricted visibility and high ceilings; with a right seat Private Pilot passenger. Briefed that Runway 09/27 at 48D was NOTAMed closed; and elected to land Runway 22 given westerly winds and NOTAM.  I made multiple callouts on CTAF including base and final.  During rollout; the pilot passenger noticed and informed me of a remote-controlled RC aircraft ahead; apparently above Runway 09/27 but overflying the extended centerline of Runway 22; about 600ft from the end of Runway 22. I did not myself see the RC aircraft. Upon safe landing and shut-down we became aware that there was an RC aircraft group operating at a series of RVs south of Runway 09/27 and that this was the reason for the NOTAM. While it is completely acceptable to have RC aircraft operations in an airport environment given NOTAMs; RC operators should be briefed to avoid overflight of an extended centerline for an active runway. Alternatively; if RC operations require the overflight of an extended centerline of another runway; that runway (or the airport) should be NOTAMed closed as well.If we were either performing a touch-and-go; or had to perform a go-around; the RC aircraft would have been directly in our path and would have posed a collision risk.

column121: I took off from ZZZ in my 2008 CAW SportCruiser; an aircraft that I had recently purchased. This was my first flight from ZZZ where I had based the aircraft. I flew around the local area to familiarize myself with landmarks in a 15 NM area near ZZZ. When I returned to land; an aircraft that was returning to the airport announced their intention to land on runway XX. I set up to enter the pattern for that runway about 5 NM away and went over the approach in my mind. Then; when I was about 3 NM away; I heard a pilot announce he was entering a left downwind for runway XY. I was surprised and concerned and made changes to my power setting and flaps setting from downwind settings. I changed my approach to enter a crosswind for runway XY. I was still a little shaken by the sudden change in approach for landing. The downwind and base legs were uneventful. The final approach started well; but as I neared the runway threshold; the PAPI system indicated that I was below the glide slope. I added a little power to get back on the glide slope; but I was too far into the landing. The aircraft hit hard and then the nose gear collapsed. The aircraft slid about 250 feet on top of the nose gear fairing and cowling. The prop struck the asphalt and one blade snapped off. Fortunately; I was thoroughly strapped into the four-point restraint harness and was uninjured.In retrospect; I should have abandoned the approach when it became unstable; and initiated a go-around. This will be a very expensive lesson. I am grateful that I emerged from the experience physically unscathed.

I was receiving flight following at the time from New York Approach. I was cruising at 2;000 feet VFR. At XA:44 EDT I spotted a White Drone that came into alignment and coverage with my left-wing landing light about 20-30 feet away. The drone had 4 props.  My spotting and reaction time was within 2 seconds and I performed an evasion maneuver with a quick bank to the right and turned about 10 degrees with a bank angle of about 20-30 degrees. The drone barely missed my left-wing. I immediately then radioed New York Approach and reported the near-miss of the drone. The controller asked for a description; altitude; and if I had to perform an evasive maneuver.There was nothing I would have done differently in this case; however; it does once again bring around the constant issue of drones in the NAS. I believe that drones need to be programmed to not be able to exceed a specific altitude at any time without an FAA waiver. column121: Close call event on short final to Runway 13 and unstable approach at ZZZ after finishing a long cross-country home from ZZZ1. Event occurred after being cleared for the visual approach to Runway 13 from Approach and switching to the local advisory frequency. I made a call on the advisory frequency on a 5 mile initial to the left downwind for Runway 31; intending to enter the traffic pattern. The aircraft was descending and I was very fast; 130 KIAS; with the intent to slow the aircraft in the pattern. Switching back to Approach frequency to cancel the IFR flight plan I decided on a straight in approach to Runway 13 to save time; while on Approach I missed the local traffic call of an aircraft taking Runway 31 to depart. After switching back to the local advisory frequency I made an advisory call for a 3 mile final to Runway 13 and I was switching the landing runway. The ADS-B data link immediately showed a traffic target directly ahead and climbing from Runway 31; passengers in my airplane spotted the traffic; and the other aircraft and I communicated to ensure we would avoid each other. Being distracted by the traffic close call; handling the radio swaps; and changing our approach I did not slow the aircraft down or add full flaps. Attempted to land with two notches of flaps and very fast; floated the aircraft most of the runway with braking in the final 1000 ft. Factors and Chain of Events:1. Long day of flying; and being tired from week at ZZZ1 contributed to wanting to be home. Additional time pressure of needing to pick up the family dog from the boarder affected decision making on speeds to fly and ultimately the runway selection.2. Concerns about forgetting to close the IFR flight plan; especially when tired; under time pressures; and distractions of passengers (kids); etc; contributed to cancelling in the air very close to the local airport operations. column123: I am a Flight Instructor and was practicing landings with my student. We were practicing short field landings and were inbound for the second landing at the airport. On final the student had made the remark we were coming in slightly fast and began correcting for the correct airspeeds. The approach to landing itself was not abnormal.  It was on centerline and at a proper glidepath; just slightly fast. Due to the fact that we had been practicing short field landings; the student was aiming to flare at a point that likely should have been extended. As we flared; a little bit of crosswind caused there to be a slight sideload on the left wheel and at the time it was the only wheel touching the ground. As the Instructor; I had mentioned right rudder to get us realigned with centerline and reduce the sideloading. The student used right rudder but accidentally had his foot on the brake as well as the rudder. This caused the plane to brake solely on the right side and begin skidding down the runway. Out of fear; I believe the brake was pushed slightly more as opposed to less. At this time I started calling that I had the flight controls and the student took his hands off of the controls. At this point; the aircraft was perpendicular to the runway. Momentum had the plane still rolling slowly. I was not sure at the time if there was any damage to the tires due to side load or skidding and did not want to apply brakes in an effort to reduce damage. At this point I treated the plane as if it was a soft field landing; I used minimal braking and let the plane come to a stop in the grass directly next to the runway. I have a very small feet and know for myself that if my heels are on the ground I am on the rudder. In order to touch the brake; my leg needs to be lifted. This is not the case for most other people. In the future; I have now learned that to reduce the chances of this happening again; I will verify on short final that the students have their feet only on the rudder and not touching the brakes. Instead of teaching 'heels on the ground' I will now specify that 'balls of feet should be on the rudders'

column121: [We were] operating in a military restricted area where range rules [were] to remain in VMC. Due to increasing cloud coverage; we had to knock off our planned flight early and began preparing for return to base (ZZZ). The PIC was managing the descent while I managed the checklists. We leveled at 10;000 ft. MSL to stay below cloud deck. We were flying southbound with mountainous terrain to the west. Cloud coverage was along the entire route ahead of us; and a hot restricted area was to the east (with cloud coverage). As a crew; we discussed the forward visibility which we estimated to be about 30 NM from our present location. It looked like some rain showers ahead down the valley; and cloudy conditions over the mountains (with maybe a little better clearance in the immediate direction). On board; radar was not indicating anything appreciable returns; and weather showed just a few pixels of green.As we approached the weather; the PIC said we should turn right as he thought the weather looked better towards the mountains. I stated that the weather ahead looked better in my opinion; as it looked like we would go under some of the rain showers in the valley. PIC said he thought it was IMC ahead; and started turning right towards the mountains. I reiterated that going down the valley was our best option; especially due to the mountainous terrain to our right. He mentioned he has flown in this area hundreds of times and he knew this would be better. I again reiterated that not only were we turning towards mountains; but there was a National Park over there which required us to stay 3;000 ft. above the terrain; and would limit how low we could go to avoid weather. I estimated that going down the valley could have got us as low as 5;000 ft. MSL safely (about 2;500 ft. AGL). PIC stated that going down the valley would be impossible for us to stay VMC and maintained the heading towards the mountains. I told him that I did not see what he was seeing; and he stated it would work fine.As we approached the first ridge the PIC climbed to 11;000 ft. MSL to stay safely above the terrain (although I estimate we needed to be about 13;000 ft. MSL to avoid National Park overflight). As we continued south; we could see that it was closing in and that the bases were getting lower; so the PIC started stepping down in altitude to approximately 8;500 ft.' MSL. At one point; the PIC was getting nervous; and asked me if we should turn around. As I was super focused on trying to stay ahead of the PIC; I told him whatever you do; do not turn right; as the Terrain display was showing a 10;200 ft. peak while we were descending through about9;500 ft. MSL. The visibility was becoming much reduced and we entered some light rain showers. As we were navigating mountainous terrain in visibility that were maybe 1 NM at times; the GPWS alerted us to 'TERRAIN; TERRAIN' followed immediately by 'PULL UP; PULL UP; PULL UP.' I immediately called climb-climb-climb. The PIC's only response was to pull back on the yoke (as opposed to our training which calls for disconnect AP (Auto Pilot)/AT (Auto Throttles); pitch to PLI (Pitch Limit Indicator) and max power). I put my hand on the throttles and started to push up about the same time the AT's responded to increasing power. As the climb commenced the Terrain Warning silenced; however we did encounter solid IMC. Shortly after we broke through the line of showers; [we] proceeded back to the airfield [in] VFRThere were multiple opportunities to prevent this from happening. The first and foremost that comes to mind is that as soon as we disagreed on the course of action; we should have entered a hold to discuss it. This would have given us time to regroup and may have resulted in a better decision. Additionally (in hindsight); we could have requested an IFR flight plan back to the landing airfield per the range rules. However; we were so focused on remaining VMC that we overlooked that option; probably due to task saturation. Personalities and organizational culture are also paramount to conducting safe flight operations; and these subjects will be presented to leadership as a result of this incident.
