column121: Inbound to ZZZ on ZZZZZ arrival and Level at FL330 the controller gave us descend via ZZZZZ Arrival.  FMC was Active in the Cruise page after a cruise descent earlier from FL 360 which is normal with a Top of Descent computed to start approximately 4 Miles prior to ZZZZZ to cross at or below FL320 as the VNAV is designed to do at IDLE Thrust.  We had 12;000 feet set in the MCP per normal FM 'descend via' procedures for the arrival.   Everything was set per FM procedures; light winds; Normal descent speeds.  Just prior to the Top of Descent the FMC transitioned from the Cruise page to the Descent Page and the throttles started retarding and the aircraft started descending.  Approximately 200 feet into the descent the Pitch Stagnated and shallowed and the Path indicator 'hung' and the Airspeed started bleeding off as the throttles retarded  instead of maintaining speed and descending on the path.  I saw the FMC/Autopilot was not acting correctly so I told the FO he needed to started inputting Vertical Speed down to make the restriction.   He wheeled in vertical speed and at that time the Path 'Unstuck' and dumped out showing us 400 feet high.  He wheeled in enough vertical speed to get the descent going but since the VNAV did its normal computation of TOD so close to the FIX we crossed it approximately 240 feet high as it was impossible to react fast enough to the VNAV glitch to stay on path.   The FO did everything right per the FM procedures.  So what happened here is a very common thing that I see about 20 percent of the time that should NOT be happening and started after the Planes were reconfigured to default into VNAV Speed from Path instead of honoring PATH even if it had to dive for it.  In this case a MAX.  Most of the time when it happens you are not right on top of a restriction so you have time to correct it. There is a occasional glitch in the VNAV system I believe tied to FMC software not aircraft specific that happens and I'm not sure why when the FMC transitions from Cruise Page to Descent page.  What Happens is the FMC hits top of descent and begins to retard the throttles and pitch over but for some reason the Pitch stagnates because the path incorrectly and temporarily shallows out instead of continuing to pitch over to descend and the result is the airspeed starts to bleed off.  After 5-10 seconds the FMC comes out of this Foggy zone and the path indicator then drops out to reflect where the plane should be and it Drops out of VNAV Path into VNAV Speed because when this happens the planes usually ends up 500 feet high.  When you have room to correct it you can get the plane back on PATH before hitting a restriction but in our case since it started down so close to the fix as its designed to do we did not have room to fix it.  The only thing you can do to possibly mitigate this from happening is to force the plane into the Descent page early by hitting the 'descent now' button; which is NOT Standard but not prohibited; to get it started down.  I have never seen this anomaly happen once the FMC is established in the Descent Page even when temporarily leveling off while it waits for the next TOD if an arrival has a level segment.  This is purely an issue during transition from FMC Cruise Page to Descent page and is very random as to when it happens and should be considered a known anomaly because I have seen it so many times.  Had we not been at FL330; 1000 feet above the FL320 restriction; and had we descended from a higher Altitude with more distance from the restriction we would have had time to correct the deviation in path but in this close in situation we were not.

column121: During preflight; I found an unusual wear pattern on the #3 main tire (RH inboard). I took a photograph of the wear; showed it to the CA; and we agreed that it would be prudent to call maintenance. Both the mechanic who answered the radio when I called it in as well as the mechanic who came out to inspect it both said it was a 'common problem' and 'known issue' with the MAX; specifically the #3 tire; and the mechanic who came to the airplane added that in his opinion it's really a landing gear design issue. Maintenance ultimately ended up issuing a deferral item for the tire; deferring replacement until later (but still flagging it for replacement).Guidance in the AOM on tire wear is unclear whether the plies are body plies or tread reinforcement plies. If they are body plies; maintenance managed to convince us to depart with an aircraft that; per the AOM guidance; had an unserviceable tire.Example photos or a more detailed diagram might provide more clarity. And while tires are expensive and the Max has indeed had a number of high-profile 'issues'; if a tire is unserviceable per our own guidance; it should be replaced; whether this is a 'known issue' or not.

column121: During initial takeoff roll; at takeoff thrust setting and less than 30 kts; aircraft began uncommanded hard left turn. column121: ATC had just assigned us a descent from our cruise altitude. While in a shallow descent to the newly assigned altitude we received an 'Engine Fire' CAS along with the 'Fire' voice callout. The PM (PIC) immediately identified and reset the master warning. The PM then begun the QRH actions associated with the CAS message as I PF (SIC) suggested lower. The PIC asked for a diversion to [a nearby alternate] from ATC and also asked for a lower altitude. Upon the diversion request ATC asked for the reason why. At this point both crew members agreed this was an [critical] situation and it was declared over the frequency as a possible engine fire. The Controller then asked if we wanted to stay close to the airport and if we could expedite our descent for the ILS. I as PF began an immediate descent to 2;000 feet MSL at around 3;000 feet per minute at full forward speed. In the meantime the PM was donning their oxygen mask while still following the procedures listed in the QRH. As we were about to level off and intercept the localizer our autopilot failed. At this point I was flying the aircraft and setting up the ILS at the same time. Since the autopilot failed I immediately requested the PM to drop the checklist and finish setting up the ILS as I stabilized the aircraft from its descent. It should also be noted that at the time of level off and autopilot failure the Controller issued their first approach clearance to us. Both of us were too busy to properly read it back with everything going on. Once the localizer was set and we were stable we intercepted the glideslope slightly higher than the minimum altitude for the step down fix. I; as PF; kept the speed up and configured with gear first then flaps. I remained at flaps 15 for the landing as I wanted to approach faster to get on the ground quicker. At about 1;200-1;400 feet MSL the red 'Engine Fire' CAS disappeared with the torque decreased to slow the aircraft. I elected to descend below glideslope when the runway was in sight and within glide so we could land as close to the fire trucks as possible that were sitting on the closest adjacent taxiway to the runway. We stopped using full reverse and braking. While the PF was removing their mask I communicated with Tower asking if fire command saw any visible fire. I believe they were on ground frequency while we were on Tower so the response was never heard. After a few seconds I ordered we evacuate the aircraft since we didn't know what the actual situation was. As I was exiting the aircraft the PM (PIC) followed the remainder of the checklist to secure the aircraft for a possible fire. the evacuation was without issue and the remainder of the day was cancelled with the aircraft grounded. While we couldn't confirm a fire existed the degradation of equipment in the aircraft caused enough alarm to assume something could have been seriously wrong. We elected to not shut the fuel off and stop engine as it was still producing power and the surrounding area was IMC with low ceilings. We elected [our preferred alternate] as it provided immediate fire assistance because of their 121 service along with it was directly in front of us. Continuing the flight over water or any longer was not an option as the situation warranted quick action.
column123: We were enroute when we encountered the Engine Fire event. The Red CAS ENGINE FIRE illuminated and the aural warning said 'FIRE.' We identified the CAS; cleared the message; noted that the Red CAS ENGINE FIRE stayed illuminated and told ATC we needed to divert. The closest field was [a suitable airport]; as we turned towards the field ATC asked our intentions and means for diversion; after quick discussion we agreed we needed to [ask for expedited handling] for the matter at hand. The CAS message came to us as we had descended through 8;000 feet to level off at 5;000 feet per ATC instructions. We had continued our descent and turn towards the field as ATC read us the weather and approach being used. Using our CRM I was running the QRH items and [the Captain] was inputting the ILS into the FMS as we were navigating during the descent. While going through the QRH I was able to put my oxygen mask on and when [the Captain] was going to put his on the autopilot failed and we decided to have him handfly the airplane the rest of the way to the ground and continue without his oxygen mask as we were passing through 3;000 feet and beginning to intercept the localizer for the approach.  The full QRH was completed for an ENGINE FIRE red CAS and we evaluated the engine instruments the entire time while on our descent into the field as the CAS had remained on the entire time. We were also looking at the engine cowling and we had not seen any fire or smoke; but we were planning to get the airplane on the ground first before doing any further inspection or analysis. While handling this we were in full IMC and didn't break out of the clouds until passing through 700 feet on the ILS.  Upon breaking out of the clouds we were short final for the field and saw emergency vehicles were already standing by for us. We landed safely on the runway; signaled to [ground personnel] we were shutting down the engine on the runway; and then proceeded to evacuate the aircraft. From the first indication of the CAS message to shutting the engine down on the runway was approximately 6 minutes. After shutting down and evacuating the aircraft the fire and EMS teams rushed to make sure we were OK before proceeding to inspect the aircraft. Upon inspection and walk around with the fire crew there was no indication to us on the exterior of the aircraft that we had been on fire at any time. After completing our services with local airport authority; we had the aircraft towed back to the FBO and put in the hangar while I proceeded to talk to [Company] to let them know of our [situation] and the next steps we were doing moving forward to handle the situation. Upon reflection; I wouldn't have changed anything we had done. We deviated from items on the QRH in order to enhance our safety. The last QRH item told us to feather the engine however; while we were in IMC; we would rather use a fully operable engine to get us as close to the field as necessary before shutting it down. [The Captain] and myself had excellent CRM and delegated appropriate tasks accordingly to make sure we got the airplane and ourselves on the ground safely.

column121: While in cruise flight; approximately 40NM south of ATL; we were given clearance by Atlanta Center to climb from our present assigned altitude; FL370 to FL380. Within a few seconds of initiating a climb; we received a TCAS alert for 'Traffic'. I immediately noticed an aircraft (a large amber TCAS image on the ND (Navigational Display)) at our same altitude '00'; opposite direction. I increased the rate of climb by electing CON (Max Continuous Thrust) on the N1 page of the FMC.Literally seconds later; we received an RA to 'CLIMB'. I immediately disconnected the auto-pilot and manually advanced the power to rapidly climb out of the red displayed warning area on my PFD (Primary Flight Display). At approximately FL380; the TCAS system said to 'Level Off'. At this point I was at 38100 ft. Moments later we received the aural 'Clear of conflict'. Still hand flying; I lowered the nose and descended 100 ft. back to our assigned altitude of FL380. We had just come from an area of weather over Florida and more weather was ahead beyond Atlanta.The radar was on; and I was on a 160 NM scale. In a busy area like ATL; I recalled seeing numerous aircraft on TCAS which was normal and gave no reason for concern. After the event; both of us (Us & Company) advised ATC we received an RA. The Company pilot asked ATC 'what happened back there?'. The controller replied in a broken sounding voice something like: 'I climbed them too late…'. Looking forward; I never saw the oncoming aircraft.My FO (First Officer) said the Company jet passed beneath us from the right side at a slight angle. The last TCAS altitude I recall seeing as we passed was '-02'. Perhaps; I expected that ATC would keep us safely separated at cruise altitude. At the end of the day; TCAS prevented a catastrophic event! No suggestion. I would not have responded any differently than I did.
column123: We were flying at FL370 talking to ATL Center approximately 40NM south of ATL VOR at the time of the event. ATL center gave us clearance to climb to FL380. As we got the clearance; we got a TCAS Traffic Advisory. I reached up to zoom in my ND (Navigational Display). I saw the Yellow Square and 00" next to it. During this time; the Captain had set the new altitude; and pushed the ALT intervene button. I said to the captain; 'We are going to get an RA; get ready'. As soon as I said that; we got the RA and instructions to climb. The Captain promptly disconnected the Auto Pilot and pushed the throttles up to comply with the TCAS Climb command. I saw traffic under us under the left wing. AT FL381 we got the TCAS level off command; then a few seconds later Clear of Conflict. We returned to our assigned altitude of FL380. Company later asked ATC what the reason was for getting that TCAS. The ATL controller admitted fault and said they climbed us late. The causal factor was lapse of attention regarding two aircraft nose to nose at same altitude. ATC issued a turn to avoid traffic rather than slow to happen climb instructions. ATC having more awareness in regards to aircraft in their sector that are at the same altitude."

column121: Smokey day; still decent horizontal visibility but milky white sky. We were on flight following flying east and saw another traffic (not with flight following) on traffic system flying parallel to us on our left; also eastbound. We wanted to turn north; so we decided to make a right 270 degrees to the north in order to pass well behind that traffic. But just as we finished the turn; we realized traffic had turned right and was coming towards us. Out of the haze there appeared to be a Mooney like aircraft. It's bank; color; and convergence angle blended perfectly with the white haze. Even though traffic system said they were 500 feet above; it looked closer than that so I began a rapid descent and was soon clear of conflict. ZZZ was busy and didn't give the traffic alert until just before I saw them out of the haze. Conclusion: Be very careful of traffic during wildfire smoke; especially white aircraft on converging course; expect the unexpected when it comes to movement of other traffic; don't rely on ATC advisories.

column121: Midway through the flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 we received 'HYDR #1 PUMP 3' CAS (Crew Alert System) message. The QRH states that system operating times will take longer than expected and that no other action was required. We continued the flight after notifying home base of the situation. Quantity showed 100% on the synoptic page with a pressure stabilized at 3;000 psi.On the arrival to ZZZ1 we were given a level off altitude and 'HYDR #1 PUMP 1' CAS message appeared. Soon after pressure fluctuated between 0 and 3;000 psi. causing CAS messages to appear then extinguish when pressure was high. Due to sequencing into ZZZ1 we had extended vectors for the ILS XX circle to land runway YY. During this time The PIC and I decided we would configure early so I could get a feel of the aircraft and allow extra time for gear extension; flap extension; ect. After being established on a long final for runway XX circle YY; I asked for gear down. We received 3 red down arrows but heard what I would consider normal gear down. We then overflew the airfield so tower could view if the gear was down then executed the missed approach for the ILS XX.The tower reported the gear was down but our indication was three red arrows. After being handed off to ZZZ2 we received delay vectors to trouble shoot the gear issue. At this time hydraulic quantity on system 1 was zero. Because we had a red gear indication; PNF followed the checklist that included pulling the gear T-handle. We still had three red gear indications so we followed the checklist for the gravity free fall. Because the checklist required 190 knots for gravity gear drop I commanded the aircraft to clean wing. This set off additional 'inboard slat fail' CAS message and we added the landing distance penalty required by the checklist.The PNF then followed the checklist for the gravity gear deploy checklist. He pulled the left main gear pull-handle and I applied full left rudder per the checklist; resulting with a left main gear down green indication. As I returned the aircraft to rudder neutral the nose gear indicated down and locked. The PNF then pulled the right main gear pull handle and after applying a slight right rudder the right main gear appeared down and locked. The PNF finished the checklist and we had a three green gear indication.We determined because of the hydraulic/gear issues it was in our best interest to declare an emergency and return to ZZZ and have crews standing by in the event the gear would collapse. Airport conditions were VFR and favored runway XX. We landed the airplane as a non-event and were towed to the FBO due to the loss of nose wheel steering.

column121: During preflight fuel was indicated as follows in the 4 tank system in the PA32. L Tip 15 gal; L Main 4 gal; R Main 11 gal; R Tip 17 gal. Through past experience in this aircraft; the gauges had an accuracy of +/- 1 gallon and were considered to be accurate. Fuel was visible in all tanks. I started and taxied on R main tank with the intention of burning fuel from the R main tank to match the L main level. The handbook recommends exhaustion of the main tanks before using the tip tanks. The flight that was going to be conducted was expected to be less than 45 minutes with an expected burn of 12 gallons. Indicated fuel onboard was 47 gallons. Takeoff was accomplished with the fuel selected on R Main tank. At 500 feet as I just started my climbing left-hand turn engine power was suddenly lost. I immediately [advised the tower] and requested Runway XX for an landing. Because I was at such a low altitude I was only focused on airspeed and the best place to land; not restarting the engine. Luckily I had a local flight instructor on board who troubleshot while I flew the airplane. After switching to a tank with fuel (R tip) power was restored almost immediately. I was a bit high and fast for a Runway XX landing and had I continued for runway XX I would have had a significant tailwind. With power restored I elected to land into the wind on Runway XYR because I deemed I was within glide even if power was lost again. I landed on Runway XYR uneventfully. After shutting down it was discovered that R Main tank was completely empty however the gauge was still indicating approximately 11 gallons. Many lessons were learned and I am going to employ the following actions to prevent a reoccurrence. Have fuel gauge for R main inspected and repaired. Heavily scrutinize the level of fuel observed vs the level of fuel indicated on the preflight.

column121: We were taking off from ZZZ and on initial climb out from Runway XX. There had been several prior departures before us that had used the same runway.  Approximately 2 miles from the runway we got a traffic alert on our iPads and it was descending into us. The aircraft appeared to be heading into Runway XY and was no making any radio calls.  Our eyes immediately went outside the aircraft trying to make contact with the aircraft.  We continued to climb as he was descending into us and we made a right turn to avoid head on traffic.  Eventually we were able to make visual contact with the airplane and he was approximately 200 feet above us. After we were clear of the aircraft my scan came back inside and I noticed that we were about 100 feet into the ZZZ1 Class Bravo airspace.  Immediately a descent was made out of the airspace and the flight continued.  We did not hear the other aircraft make any calls on the CTAF throughout their flight/approach.Looking back this all happened very fast; and I would have done a couple things differently. Police and fire were waiting for me.I was uncomfortable continuing the descent without being cleared and switching frequencies without being told; but felt both actions were necessary for the safe outcome of my flight. column121: I was the R-side at Sector 38 during this event. Weather had been impacting Area 6 for the majority of the night; with a solid line from the LNK area up to the FOD area in Area 5. Then Area 5 came up with a plan to route all aircraft coming from sector 38 and 43 up over MCW direct FSD and points west. For many aircraft MCW was backtracking and turning them wrong for direction. Not only was the whole situation very unsafe; it was un-efficient as well. It seemed like TMU wasn't giving us any help with sending re routes out to Chicago and Kansas; so sector 38 and 43 had to re route every single aircraft we talked to during that 1-2 hour period. A plan should have been developed for the weather in case it did close in; which ended up happening; to route all OVR and LNK west bound traffic to the north around the weather. This would have at least pinned them all down to a route instead of having every aircraft asking for deviations at the last minute. Also; I felt unsafe working this stint not only because of deviations; but because we haven't been allowed to work an even remotely busy sector for the last year plus during normal operations. column121: Upset/wake turbulence event. Approximately five minutes prior to this event First Officer and I had completed our arrival brief and I had given a PA to the passengers that the seat belt sign would be coming on in the next 10 minutes. Ahead of us was a B787 at [our altitude]; FL360. [The B787] was directed by ATC to descend and maintain FL340. Within a few minutes we were assigned the same clearance. Shortly after leveling at FL340; our aircraft entered a rapid; shuddering turbulence; followed by a rapid roll to the right. We both immediately put our hands on the controls and recited the upset recovery call outs.  We disconnected the autopilot; though the autopilot may have disconnected by itself; and autothrottle. We both fly with our FPV (Flight Path Vector) up so we could see immediately; intuitively that we weren't stalled; but our push was slight; not even half a G; which added to our effective counter roll rate. Prior to our response to the upset; the autopilot had already put in aileron control forces counter to the roll; but the aircraft was still rolling to the right. As we took control; the aircraft reached approximately 40 degrees before the aircraft responded to our control inputs; then rolled left to approximately 20 degrees. Based on the fact we were at FL340 we left the thrust where it was positioned; possibly a slight reduction; as the energy state was good and a large thrust change was not necessary. Our altitude loss was minimal and the descent was very shallow. The recovery point at which we managed our flight path divergence started at approximately FL337; only a 300 FT loss.  Rudder may have been used - Indicated by both an overshoot; subsequent bank to the left and a report from the flight attendants that we not only rolled; but yawed. We advised ATC that we had encountered wake turbulence which had caused our descent. They offered us direct HLYWD moving us from the wake of the preceding aircraft. We then checked on the Flight Attendants and passengers to ensure there were no injuries. The seat belt sign had been off and there was a passenger in the lav; but no injuries were reported. The First Officer and I debriefed the event but; because ATC started our descent onto the Arrival; I failed to make a PA to the passengers.  After landing; I waited at the flight deck door to thank the passengers. I saw that the event was more impactful than I had realized and a PA would have gone a long way to reassure the passengers and Flight Attendants.

At ZZZ; unlike all the other airports I have operated out of over the last 30 years; it is the norm to be cut off and/or almost impacted by every type of ground vehicle; except for the fire and rescue vehicles. Quite frankly; the leaders of airport safety at ZZZ seem to find the blatant disregard for ground vehicle adherence to safety procedures as acceptable. No apologies; after the hundreds of operations I've performed parking at ZZZ gates; it is apparent that there is a serious lack of safety concern on the ramp.Better initial and continuing education and testing for all ramp personnel and ground vehicle operators. Daily observation and audits of random gate parking operations by teams of knowledgeable personnel with the authority to correct the problems. Positive incentives to follow strict safety procedures as well as writing citations to drivers for gross violations. Integrated in to this enforcement it is highly recommended to also audit and enforce strict ramp preparation after aircraft depart and before aircraft arrive to park so that the safe zone is clear of all objects AND personnel. There is no reason cones; air hoses; tow bars; etc should be within the red lines. In addition; all ground personnel should be aware of how Docking Guidance System (DGS) works and know when to pick up the wands and guide us in until the aircraft is parked. Too often; the guideman spend 50% of the time looking at the DGS so when he thinks its ok; to hand us off to the DGS with less than 75 feet to go. We don't know if the DGS is lined up properly or calibrated correctly by this time. Ive had a DGS try to get me to turn off the line in to the jet bridge because it wasn't calibrated properly from the beginning. After 10 years on this aircraft as a captain calling in these problems and writing a few reports and not seeing improvement; I am hoping these last 2 incidents and filing  reports will hopefully jumpstart a plan to get ZZZ in compliance. If all the other airports we operate in and out of can comply; I believe ZZZ can do it.

column121: I departed my home base airport on a VFR flight for the purpose of gaining experience using the VNAV (Vertical Navigation) function of recently installed GPS Navigators and an autopilot in the aircraft.  As I was intending on changing altitudes throughout the flight to test out the VNAV I decided to not request flight following and instead on my Comm 2 radio I monitored [frequency] XXX.X. The conditions were VFR with about 10 miles visibility; but there was significant haze. To best test out the VNAV functions I created a flight plan with a final fix (another airport) located approximately 79 miles from the departure airport.  My initial intent was to test out the VNAV functionality throughout that path on a few different occasions and with different step downs; then turn around at the final fix; without landing; and return to my home base airport.  While descending to 3;500 feet about 45 miles from the final fix; I flew about 2 miles north of a non-towered airport and about 5 miles north of a city.  When flying in that area; I looked at my IPad which has Foreflight and I did not notice any Parachute Jump Area (PJA) rings over that airport and expecting to see those rings in the relevant areas I did not notice the parachute symbol by the airport that appears on the VFR Sectional on the IPad.  Having successfully completed one test of the VNAV about 45 miles before arriving at the final fix; and predominately due to the haze; I decided to discontinue flying towards the final fix and to begin heading back to my home base earlier than originally anticipated.  Looking again at the IPad I did not notice any PJA rings or the parachute symbol by the airport near the city and I decided to use that airport as part of my route towards my home base airport and turned toward that airport.  Within a couple of minutes I overflew that airport eastbound at 3;500 feet MSL (approximately 2;300 AGL) while using the autopilot and noticed a small aircraft landing southbound on the airport's runway.  I then looked up about 45 degrees from the horizon and saw one open canopy parachutist about 300 feet above the airplane and another at about the 2 o'clock position 500 feet laterally and 300 feet above the plane.  It was immediately clear from their rate of descent that I would be past both of them before they would reach my altitude.  I quickly scanned for other parachutist and put my thumb over the autopilot disconnect switch; but not having any idea how many parachutists were out there and not seeing others except for the two with which I recognized I was not in a collision course; I thought that maintaining heading and altitude would make me as predictable as possible and it would give any other parachutist that could see or hear me the best opportunity to avoid me.  Thus; I covered the controls to use them to override the autopilot if needed but did not disengage the autopilot or perform any evasive maneuvers.    Upon landing; I immediately checked my iPad again to see if there were any PJAs over the airport; and none were present over that airport; and I then noticed there were no PJAs depicted anywhere over any airports.  When looking at the IPad on the ground I did identify the Sectional's parachute symbol near the airport.  I then compared my IPad's Foreflight map display with that on my IPhone and saw that the IPhone displayed the PJA rings.  The next day I contacted Foreflight as I could not identify the difference in the settings that was causing the IPhone to display PJA rings and not on the IPad.  They very quickly pointed me to a setting for Airspace that I had not enabled on the IPad and as soon as I enabled it; the PJAs showed up on the IPad. I believe my over reliance on Foreflight's PJA rings caused me to not inspect the map closely enough to identify the parachute symbol by the airfield near the area that I was not originally intending to use as a turn around point.  Verifying that this setting is enabled is now a checklist item for me; and when there are changes to a plan that will cause me to fly near an airport; regardless of the altitude over the pattern; I will more closely inspect for the parachute symbols even if there is no ring depicted on Foreflight.  Also; even when engaged in local flights that require maneuvering and changes in altitude and that may place me near multiple airports; I intend to request flight following.

I watched Aircraft X turn towards the localizer; he had a good read back; and was descending out of 067. Shortly after I saw them through the localizer still on H080 and at 052. I advised them they flew through the localizer; and turned them first H030; then H020 to join but quickly realized that they would not turn before the entered an adjacent 060 MVA [Minimum Vectoring Altitude]. I issued a low altitude alert and advised they climb to 060 immediately. When they got to the MVA I vectored them back to the localizer. I asked if the pilot had received the localizer; and he responded affirmative. On the next attempt; I kept them at 060 and asked to report established. They flew through the localizer again; and said they were not receiving it and requested the RNAV RWY XX. I vectored them to final for the RNAV RWY XX; and they were able to establish on final and I cleared them for the approach.Leading up to this event; our facility had just finished working our cargo arrival rush; and traffic had slowed significantly. I was on West Radar; but then got the East Radar controller off position and worked them combined. After a period of about 30 minutes; traffic had built up to moderate levels and moderate-high complexity. This was due to wildfire smoke in the area; and nearly all aircraft being IFR. Our visual separation LOA with ZZZ2 was turned off; and I was staggering approaches between ZZZ2 and ZZZ; and also had a 3 aircraft sequence into the ZZZ1 airport; which has a temporary fire tower in operation. This caused multiple inbound calls via landline for the 3 arrivals. I had a high workload with multiple shout line coordination's from ZZZ3; ZZZ ATCT; and ZZZ2. The FLM was helping with my strips; and another controller came in and after the traffic had slowed a little we split the positions again. It was during this cool down period that the MVA violation happened. The 2 aircraft ahead of Aircraft X both flew the ILS [Runway] XX without issue. When I turned and cleared Aircraft X for the approach; he was in a good position to join final and was descending well; and I remember I was not concerned about them intercepting the localizer.I had been watching my strips print out; and realized it was going to get a little busy but wouldn't be a big deal. However; a military aircraft departed ZZZ2 into the radar pattern; and we got a divert from ZZZ4 to ZZZ1; and some of the coordination's that happened were unforeseen. I just didn't recognize how busy I would become in time to ask for help before traffic became difficult. Of course I will be more diligent in my scan and also recognizing overload situations and ask for help sooner. I think just having Hand-off staffed would have alleviated the overload; and my scan would likely have been better without such a high peak of workload followed by the lull of less traffic. I will also consider vectoring to a longer final and having aircraft join at 060 instead of 050.

column121: SWAP night at ZZZ (Severe Weather Avoidance Plan). I had just arrived at work for the mid and taken over the two local positions from the outgoing controller. I settled in and started working the traffic and Aircraft X was one of the first few aircraft I cleared to land after taking over the position. It was VFR conditions after weather that had impacted the airport earlier had moved well out of the area. Everything seemed routine except it was busier than usual due to the weather delays as traffic was landing and departing on parallel runways. Ground Control was open and working the outbound departures to runway XXL. At ZZZ; traffic must cross runway XYR in order to access runway XXL because the runways are staggered. Ground control was taxiing Aircraft Y on taxiway 1 and I learned afterward that the aircraft was instructed to hold short of runway XYR. As Aircraft X was approaching runway XYR (our arrival runway) I noticed the taxi light on Aircraft Y was still illuminated and the aircraft seemed to still be in motion. I quickly scanned the ASDE-X (Airport Surface Detection Equipment) and as I looked up; Aircraft Y's data tag started to flash. I issued a go around clearance to Aircraft X as soon as I saw that Aircraft Y was not going to hold short. The ASDE-X did issue a go-around alert; but I had already been issuing the go-around clearance. I climbed Aircraft X to 3;000 feet on runway heading. As Aircraft X was starting into a stable climb; I issued a turn to a 300 heading away from the traffic departing runway XXL that had been cleared on a 245 heading prior to the go around and was already on departure roll. Aircraft X was then switched back to approach control for resequencing and landed about 10 minutes later without incident. Aircraft Y was then issued a runway crossing clearance by Ground Control and instructed to contact the Supervisor in the TRACON once the aircraft was parked on a taxiway.No recommendations. In a telephone interview with the flight crew by the Supervisor; it was learned that the crew was confused by the lights (ZZZ has wigwags at all the hold short lines and it is unmistakable where to stop for the runway) and failed to stop at the hold short line on taxiway 1.

column123: We were doing the ILS Z Runway XX into ZZZ. Night time; good visibility; no clouds. ATC had us at 9;500 feet; turned us to intercept final outside of ZZZZZ and cleared us for the approach. Autopilot was on. We were flaps 1 about 190 knots at the time and about 22 miles on final. We intercepted the localizer and the glide slope at about the same time. At which point we were busy setting touch down zone; putting flaps down and gear. A moment later ATC gives us an altitude low warning; climb immediately to 8;600 feet. The flying pilot ( first officer) immediately disconnected auto pilot and initiated climb. We were around 8;100 feet; on the glide slope; auto pilot on when this was initiated from what we could tell. We had just passed ZZZZZ (FAF; but 17 miles out). The controller mentioned they had some glide slope problems just a week or two prior; and asked us if we were ok to proceed visually. Still being over 10 miles out; runway and PAPI in site; and glide slope still showing slightly below us; we proceeded visually with reference to PAPI and GS. The problem may have been from the auto pilot intercepting the LOC and GS at the same time and possibly overshooting the GS as it sometimes does when far out and possibly exasperated by configuration changes. This all happened about 15 to 20 miles from touchdown. Or it could have been from a faulty GS signal that they have had problems with previously.

column121: When we arrived in ZZZ to start our trip we meet with the inbound crew to discuss the inbound leg and aircraft.  There was no mention from them about any odors or problems with the aircraft.  When we boarded the aircraft we were over come by a strong smell throughout the plane. Looking back it was strange the previous crew didn't mention this. It was similar to a strong carpet cleaner smell or an odor like when you clean an oven.  There was no indication of fire or smoke much less any indications of a malfunction.  We discussed the issue with the crew and found no reasons not to continue safely.  As we boarded the aircraft several passengers started to complain especially in the rear cabin about the odor.  We discussed what the cause of the smell could be and determined that it was not a safety of flight issue since we could not isolate any problems. All systems operated normally.  We agreed to continue on the short flight to ZZZ1 hoping that at altitude the fresh air would dispute any smell.  We felt that since there was smoke all around the area from west coast wild fires that could possibly be the cause.  At cruise the smell seemed to disappear in the cockpit but as we got closer to our destination the FA'S informed us that it remained in the cabin.  There was no smoke or any indications of a malfunction. They then stated that many passengers complained that they were starting to get headaches and feel bad.  We asked if there any immediate concerns and were informed there were none.  Inbound we decided to inform maintenance control that there was an odor which seemed to be coming from the gasper vents via an MRM entry so that on arrival they could trouble shoot and see if they could remove it. After landing we started the APU and received a low oil level indication.  Not sure if this contributed to the problem or not as we accepted the aircraft in ZZZ with the APU operating and had no indications of any problems at that time.  Arriving at the gate we noticed that the smell in the cockpit remained but the cabin was stronger.   We had an hour on the ground before our next flight so felt that the problem could be resolved.  After block in we meet with maintenance and he noticed the smell as well.  His feeling is it smelled like burning oil.  We had no indications at any time of an overheat or fire on any system.  I then received a call from Name our Chief Pilot to contact Name 1 in Maintenance Control for some questions. I was asked generic questions about the entire flight to help trouble shoot the problem. As I stated everything went great expect for the strong smell.  They removed the aircraft from service and we continued our trip with another aircraft.  The entire crew handled the situation professionally and with merit.  I applaud how we worked together to assist passengers needs and answer any questions or concerns they may have had.  The flight was concluded safely and professional with our [company] principles.

I refused the aircraft on the basis of safety-of-flight because I felt the aircraft was unsafe to operate with an unknown wheel brake issue coupled with an inoperative thrust reverser.The primary causal factor for refusing the aircraft was the unknown reason for the hot brakes. column121: After pushing back on the ZZZ ramp; we went to start the engines.  During the start; the Blue Hydraulic pressure gauge came up low; just to the yellow line.  Note that the Blue Hydraulic system had been serviced in ZZZ by Maintenance while we hub turned.  In consultation with ZZZ Maintenance; we shut down in position and they went to service the Blue Hydraulic.  After some time the Blue Hydraulic was back in the Top Hat.  Cleared off Maintenance; and restarted engines.  After start; When the bleed air transferred over to the packs; we immediately started getting smoke in the cockpit.  I initially smelled it.  Then with the rising sun coming in my side window; you could clearly see the smoke (vaporized Skydrol?)  coming out of my air vent starting to fill the cockpit.  The intensity of smoke increased with time.  We opened the windows for fresh air and shut off the packs.  Approximate about 3 - 4 minutes of chemical exposure.  We wound up taxiing back to the gate and eventually shut down the engines.  I felt a little light head; a scratchy throat; and was beginning to cough.  Captain had some similar issues.   After speaking with Chief Pilot; and self-evaluating our symptoms; we were driven to the local ER to get checked out.  At the hospital; poison control was contacted; X-ray's were taken and a breathing treatment administered before being released. Exact cause for this issue is still unknown to me...but it clearly has to do with the servicing of the Blue Hydraulic system and possible failure of aircraft parts.

column121: After landing on Runway XXL at ZZZ; we cleared off the runway at Taxiway 1 and was instructed to hold short of Runway XYL. Tower subsequently cleared us to cross Runway XXL and hold short of Runway XYR.  We proceeded to taxi to satisfy the clearance.  In an attempt to try to clear Runway XYL and also hold short of Runway XYR we encroached on Runway XYR causing a go-around of an aircraft attempting to land on Runway XYR. I believe this event was caused by an impossible clearance in combination with an attempt to comply with it. In hindsight; we should have recognized earlier that the clearance was not possible to comply with and should have communicated that to Tower.
column123: Flight was uneventful through departure; enroute; ILS Runway XXL; landing and rollout on Runway XXL; ZZZ.  Weather was VMC. Told to clear right on Taxiway 1 and hold short of Runway XYL.  Executed uneventfully.   We were then quickly given clearance to 'Cross Runway XYL on Taxiway 1 and hold short of Runway XYR.'  The Captain executed that clearance to the absolute best of his ability; set the parking brake; and turned off the taxi light short of Runway XYR.  The Captain pulled up very close to Runway XYR; in order to no longer obstruct Runway XXL.  In his estimation; the nose wheel was short of the Runway XYR hold short line; and the aircraft was only on Taxiway 1; not at all on Runway XYR; but he was trying to fit a 209 foot long B777 in a very small space.In hindsight we should have said 'Unable' to the impossible clearance; but we did not see that the space available on Taxiway 1 between the runways was insufficient until we were committed to cross Runway XYL.  The aircraft was short of Runway XYR; and to the best of his estimation was clear of Runway XYL. At this point I realized we were crossed the hold short line and saw the landing aircraft on final. I spoke up and said I think we are on the active runway for the landing traffic. Seconds after I brought that up to everyone's attention; the tower then directed the small aircraft (I believe a PC-12) on extended final to Runway XYR to go around. All crew members had taxi charts open.  Solid procedures were used.  Everyone understood the clearance.  There was no confusion at all; until we crossed Runway XYL on Taxiway 1; then I noticed we had crossed Runway XYR hold short line and saw the traffic on final.  Debriefed that we should not have accepted the clearance and should have said 'Unable' to attempting to fit a B777 on Taxiway 1 between Runway XYL and Runway XYR.Attempting to do the impossible; to meet a clearance to fully cross Runway XYL and hold short of Runway XYR; to fit a B777 on Taxiway1 between Runway XYL and Runway XYR at ZZZ. Also; a misunderstanding of the controllers expectation (due to local knowledge). We should have transmitted one of two things.  Best choice would have been to transmit 'unable' to the clearance and hold our original position short of Runway XYL; even though cleared to cross.  Second; once committed to cross Runway XYL; and in observance that the task was impossible to transmit; 'We are holding short of Runway XYR; but still obstructing active Runway XYL.'  We should have done this and left more room between the nose of the aircraft and Runway XYR.  Clearly; we could have been more directive in the situation.  One suggestion would be to have Tower change the comm to transmit; 'Cleared on to Runway XYL; but hold short of Runway XYR.'  That would convey the point that they understand Runway XYL will remain obstructed.  In that case; we would have not been concerned with obstructing Runway XYL and left more room between the nose and Runway XYR.  Better still; have Tower wait until such a time as they can clear a B777 across both runways at once.

column121: When cruising at FL350 and deviating right of course for thunderstorm avoidance on a heading of 075 we began to encounter blow off and overhangs from other cells in the area reducing visibility to IMC. ATC was overwhelmed and could not give us requested higher altitude and due to high traffic in the area we did not initiate a further deviation right of course until we could ask ATC. Our radar was operating and being manipulated by the Captain showing no cells along our route of flight. We did not realize our radar had failed (no cockpit indications) and suddenly we were in a extreme thunderstorm cell. Our altitude deviated considerably 1;500 feet up and 700 feet down from FL350. We encountered light hail extreme precipitation and severe turbulence. Upon exiting the cell we immediately flew towards clear air and made the decision to divert to ZZZ. Suspecting possible negative G limits had been exceeded and concerned about possible aircraft damage. ATC was able to immediately accommodate our diversion and I landed on runway XX at ZZZ without further issue. The radar and possible turbulence damage was written up in the maintenance log and the company notified according to SOPs and Op Specs. Ensure all radars are operational and checked regularly by Maintenance. Also release this incident to the entire pilot group so that they are aware of this possible issue when operating near thunderstorms.

At this time it is unknown (from a pilot's  perspective) as to what could have prevented the malfunction of the autopilot; and cause it to self-engage.

column121: In cruise heading north on flight following with Travis Air Force Base RAPCON at 5;500 feet at 167 KTAS.  Travis called out a descending C17 on approach into Travis with a caution for wake turbulence.  Assumed I was above their trailing wake but flew into the turbulence and experience rough turbulence as we crossed the wake.  Hit my head on the ceiling and the contents of the cockpit got tossed up in the air. Lesson learned:  Don't try to gauge the altitude of wake turbulence.  It's too hard to pinpoint where the risk is.  Either climb well above it or turn around go the other way.  I could have easily turned away and climbed to avoid it completely.  I misjudged the location of the wake turbulence. Appreciate Travis RAPCON calling it out.  I just didn't adjust enough.

column121: During the approach to landing at ZZZ on runway XX; the TIS traffic warning on the GPS came on. I was at 500 ft and descending to the runway.  I believed it to be an 'echo' of my transponder; which sometimes happens; so I reset it and continued with the approach and landed (The conflicting traffic was showing +200 ft).  An observer on the ground came into the terminal office and asked to see the pilot of the flight that had just landed.  I introduced myself and he asked me if I had seen the helicopter over the airport. I explained that I could not see them as they were in the cloud layer and could not hear them; of course. I had made three position reports during my approach to the airport; but none were made by the military helicopter; which is not unusual.  It is my estimation that the crew of the helicopter turned on their transponder to let me know of their presence as they saw me on their traffic awareness system.  While it is not a common practice for the military to have their transponders on during operations; it would be invaluable for them to do so while on training missions that would get them close to civilian aircraft and airports.

column121: I was working as TRACON Data for West in position of R1.  I did not notice my Controller drop the tag for Aircraft X.  About 5 minutes later; I coordinated a point out with Lone Rock sector control on Aircraft Y at 8;000 who would just clip our NW airspace.  My Controller; being busy and trying to clean up his scope for a position transfer to me; was dropping tags on several aircraft above our airspace.  He mistakenly dropped Aircraft X.A few minutes later; I was relieved of position and busy taking the position brief for R2 control position.  The new R1 TRACON Data Controller took a call from Lone Rock and was asked if he talking to Aircraft X.  He; of course did not know who they were talking about since the aircraft was a splat with no information.  The R1 Controller asked me if I knew who that was; and I not hearing with the noise in the TRACON; said something like; 'Of course not; that was a point out; I was thinking they were talking about the point out I took on Aircraft Y. Shortly after; the R2 controller figured out the splat was one of our aircraft and took corrective action to avoid the two aircraft getting any closer.The NOTAM that was produced for departing aircraft from OSH during EAA Experimental Aircraft Association contributed to this. Expecting dozens of aircraft to pick up IFR flight over DLL VOR at the same point at the same time is inviting loss of separation.  Many aircraft filed incorrectly; leading to much frequency congestion.  One pilot in particular; during my following 30 minutes on the R2 scope wanted to argue with me that he filed correctly; when he didn't.  Several aircraft were in Lone Rock and Dubuque sectors looking to pick up their IFR; requiring further point outs and coordination. Several aircraft required 6/10 [Flight Plan]  amendments in order to gain their flight plans.  Most aircraft were at same altitudes and required valuable frequency time for separation; to ensure they were at correct altitudes and separated from other IFR aircraft.  In short; the EAA Air Adventure is a set up for controllers at my facility.  The loss of IFR separation is almost inevitable given the volume; complexity and inherent confusion at certain heavy periods.  There is probably no recommendation I can give other than tell a certain number of aircraft to pick up IFR at different points; or just have them fly VFR."

column121: Aircraft X was 12 miles Northwest of ZZZ on a base heading 220 at 3;000 feet being vectored to the ILS Runway XXR at ZZZ airport. I observed an unidentified VFR target depart ZZZ1 airport climbing out of 1;700 feet southbound. At first the the target was flying away from Aircraft X but then I observed the target start a a turn to the east. I then assigned Aircraft X heading 250 anticipating the VFR target would make a turn to the north east to avoid the immediate incursion into the ZZZ Class C airspace. This caused Aircraft X to go through the final for Runway XXR and I climbed Aircraft X to 3;100 feet because the new projected flight path would be into a higher Minimum Vectoring Altitude. I then anticipated the VFR target would turn east bound once it got north of the Class C. So I took Aircraft Y off the arrival who was 10 miles north west of the airport on the downwind. I stopped his descent at 5;000 feet when I would normally descend aircraft at this phase of flight to 3;000 feet. It then became apparent the altitude adjustment wasn't going to be enough so I turned Aircraft Y to a 220 heading. The VFR target did make a turn to the east once north of the Class C climbing opposite direction into our arrival corridor at ZZZ. The VFR target did eventually contact another controller for an IFR pickup in my airspace.This event only had a positive outcome because this happens so frequently I have become overly cautious and I guessed correctly what the non participating aircraft was going to do every step of the way. I could have easily guessed wrong and could have had a dangerous situation develop into a crash. I recommend an airspace change that would extend controlled airspace over ZZZ1.

column121: Halfway through our flight our B-Flight Attendant asked to come into the flight deck and talk with us. When she got to the flight deck she indicated that there was a very strong cleaning/bug spray smell in the aft galley. Additionally; our C-Flight Attendant was complaining of coughing and having a hard time taking a deep breath because of the strong cleaning smell. Our A-Flight Attendant didn't smell anything. No Passengers were indicating concern and we didn't smell anything. The Captain asked the Flight Attendant (F/A) if she was medically concerned; and if so; we would patch through to medic so she could communicate her concern. All the F/As indicated they were feeling OK and did not want to contact medic. They just wanted someone to look at the aircraft in ZZZ. At that point the Captain told her we would put the packs to high to help eliminate the strong cleaning odor. We also contacted Dispatch through ACARS to discuss the situation and see if there was an anti-microbial spray completed the night before. Additionally; we informed Dispatch that the F/As were not comfortable taking the aircraft on our next leg. Dispatch wanted a patch through ARINC to get F/As; operations and medic on the line for a conference call.  During their discussion; Dispatch sent us an ACARS message to divert to ZZZ1. As a result; we notified ATC of our intention to divert. The Captain notified the F/As and Passengers of our intent; as well.As a precaution we accomplished the Smoke; Fire; or Fumes QRC and referenced QRH Smoke; Fire or Fumes Checklist in case the situation escalated. Dispatch notified us the aircraft had been sprayed the night before with antimicrobial spray. We communicated with our A-Flight Attendant on what to expect on landing; taxi; and at the gate. We kept in constant communication with the A F/A to constantly reassess our situation. On our descent into ZZZ1 medic recommended the two Flight Attendants having issues breathing use the portable oxygen. With that information; we [advised] ATC to have Medical Personnel standing by. We then accomplished all appropriate checklists and landed uneventfully.The anti-microbial spray the night before was a bit much. That needs to be more regulated. I think the call to divert was a good call; but happened very fast. Our Crew day also ended up being super long with this diversion on our first leg. We were OK to continue after the diversion; but that kind of day; with what we went through; is probably not completely safe.

column121: Immediately after takeoff; the horizontal trim failed. Neither pilot could activate the electric trim. column121: Recently FDK completed its Runway 5/23 extension from 5;219 ft to 5;819 feet. The next chart cycle date reflected the runway/taxiway markings.  As of cycle 2108; all of the FDK airport diagram and approach charts now show the runway 5/23 at 5;219 ft again. The reasoning from the airport manager was the FAA approach plate 'people' said that since they have not done an approach assessment (to be performed in March of 2022); that they would not allow the runway to be shown as extended; and the group unilaterally changed all airport/approach charts to show the runway shortened; but with a 600 feet relocated threshold and a taxiway leading up to the new unmarked runway threshold in cycle 2108.  Cycle 2107; the previous cycle; properly showed the runway's extension.  Also to note; the RNAV approach that services Runway 5 has been NOTAMed NA since the completion of the runway extension. Fun to note; that the RNAV approach was allowed when the runway was shortened by about 500 feet to 4;700 feet during runway extension construction without a NOTAM showing un-coincidental glideslope/PAPI relationship. This is no longer an issue; although it was brought up by local based charter pilots as being unsafe and improper.The following instances may occur.  An aircraft landing Runway 23 at night; may rightfully assume they have 600 feet past the Runway 5 threshold markings to exit at Taxiway A1; when in fact; there is no pavement past the Runway 5 threshold.  This can cause a runway excursion by confusion of the actual markings and the chart diagram. Aircraft may proceed onto Runway 5 from Taxiway A1 to pull up to the 600 foot relocated threshold; causing a runway incursion.  May cause pilot confusion or disorientation when a pilot lands or departs runway 5/23. Changing a diagram that does not depict the actual markings without a proper NOTAM or notification by the Tower is extremely reckless behavior and should not be tolerated as standard practice.Requested Fix: NOTAM the runway length to 5;819 feet; NOTAM to disregard the relocated threshold and revert the airport diagram and all approach charts to the Cycle 2107 depiction of the airport diagram/layout. Do not allow the FAA Approach Office to unilaterally change the airport diagram's of airports without concurrence of all related parties; and if the FAA Approach office does not have the concurrence; the office should perform a good faith effort to mitigate all safety issues.

column121: I'm a new CFI with 475 hours total time and 6 hours instructing. I was approached by another CFI that teaches at a local flight school to see if I was interested in doing part time instruction. He instructs in a Piper PA-28-161. We scheduled to meet. Two days prior I sent the CFI a message asking what I could do to prepare for the flight and if there was a specific lesson I should be prepared to teach. He called me the day prior to the flight and said there was nothing to prepare for; 'we're just going flying'.  He then asked if I could instruct a student that day. I said no based on not having any experience in their aircraft; personal insurance in their aircraft; or proof of employment. On the day of the flight; I arrived as scheduled.  The CFI/Pilot in Command was already at the airplane with a 'new' student.  This was to be the students 'intro' flight. They had already preflighted the airplane. I sat in the back seat. The CFI/Pilot in Command took off with window and top of door not latched. I reminded him while we were taking the active runway but he said there was a law on this aircraft that they could takeoff with the door all the way open. Once we took off he gave his student the flight controls. The CFI/Pilot in Command asked his student if he had ever touched a cloud. The student said no; and the CFI/Pilot in Command took the controls. He immediately flew next to a cloud and had the student stick his hand out the window. We were flying in a broken layer. He then asked the student to fly directly between two clouds; which had a very narrow gap; definitely not within legal cloud clearances. At this point I asked if there was any traffic awareness and found out there was no traffic advisory or ADSB on the aircraft. After approximately 20 minutes; we full stop landed at ZZZ and the CFI/Pilot in Command asked me to move to the front seat.  I asked; 'left or right'?  He said; 'actually get used to the right seat please.'  I asked if I could sit left for the first time since this was a different model Piper than I have previously flown with somewhat different avionics. He said 'no; sit in the right. This isn't an evaluation; I'm flying.' The student sat in the back seat. The CFI/Pilot in Command performed the takeoff and then gave me the flight controls at 300 feet. During our climb to 7000 feet I noticed that the Alternator Amps read 0.  I alerted the CFI/Pilot in Command who pulled out the checklist and asked me what that meant if the alternator failed.  I said; 'that means we have roughly 30 minutes of battery life left and we should head back to the airport.'  He told me the alternator failed last night on a long cross-country trip and their maintenance technician didn't have time to come inspect it today; but not to worry because they had a second battery besides the main. He also showed me how he cycled the on/off switch and that power was restored. He went on to say that they bought and installed 'crappy overhauled alternator' which was likely the issue. We stayed within 15 miles of ZZZ and the CFI/Pilot in Command asked me to demonstrate stalls. He then took a map from the backseat and covered the entire instrument panel; restricting my view to standby instruments or even the tachometer. I said 'I'm not going to do a stall without being able to see my rudder.' He told me it was an outside maneuver and I didn't need any instruments to do it. I stated again; 'I'm not kidding; I'm not doing it without my instruments. I've never done that before and I do not want to get into a spin.' He reluctantly took the map down.  I demonstrated a stall and then he did multiple falling leaf stalls on his own to show how I didn't need my instruments. At this point he asked me to demonstrate a falling leaf and when the power was pulled I heard the engine choke slightly. At this point we were getting very far over the ocean and I said I was done with stalls and wanted to go back toward shore and ZZZ.  He took the controls at thispoint.He then asked the student (now in the back seat); 'do you think (my name) ever played the toilet paper game?' I asked what it was and he told me I was about to find out. He then flew out over the water and dropped two rolls of toilet paper out the window. He then pulled the power and in a nose-diving turn aimed right between the two falling rolls. The goal he said was to hit the toilet paper on the wing. He gave me controls at one point; but I told him my fear of the toilet paper getting in the cowling and he said it wasn't an issue. He got down to 2500 feet and I told him I didn't want to go any lower over the ocean. He said we were taking it down to 1500 feet. Then we flew back to ZZZ and he told the tower he wanted to do a go around.  He told the student that we were going to float over the runway at 6 inches.  We did this until we got to the 1;000-foot bars on the departure end of the runway when I told him to add power and start going around. He flew it all the way to the numbers and then finally pulled up. I thought we were going to crash as this was so last minute.He then asked me if I wanted the controls and I said yes. We stayed in the pattern. When he asked tower for another go-around; I called them back saying it was going to be a full stop. He questioned my decision and I told him I wanted to end the flight. After we landed; I noticed there was zero fuel indicated in our right tank and the left was reading full. This had to be incorrect as I visually checked the tank prior to flight and it was half full. As the flight progressed I felt more and more unsafe. By the end of the flight I was sure that mine and the students safety were in jeopardy and I can't help feeling that I should have done more to stop it.

column121: During the second leg of our day on a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 sudden turbulence was encountered. Approximately 3.5 hours into the flight while descending through an estimated 27;000 feet; we felt a bump which we both agreed was likely Clear Air Turbulence. The remainder of the flight was uneventful. The aircraft was not adversely or noticeably affected in its ability to fly and no buffet or shudder was noted in the flight controls. After landing and unloading the line crew notified me that the right engine cowling was missing. Upon further inspection it was noted that the right engine cowling was in fact missing and the horizontal stabilizer had likely been struck at the time the engine cowling separated from the aircraft.
column123: The flight was from ZZZ to ZZZ1. After preflight inspection; we had an uneventful takeoff out of ZZZ. At an altitude between 35;000 feet and 25;000 feet during the descent we hit momentarily clear air turbulence. We both agreed that it was turbulence. We continued our descent into ZZZ1 as briefed. After a normal approach and landing we parked the aircraft then assisted the passengers with their bags and they went on the way. On post flight walk around we discovered the right engine cowling was missing and a small dent in the leading edge of the tail of the aircraft. That is when we suspected that the clear air turbulence was caused by the right engine cowl departing the aircraft. ZZZ Tower; our company operations manager; and the FAA were then notified.

column121: I departed ZZZ shortly after XA00 from runway XX; heading west. Shortly after I put my gear up at approximately 100 knots airspeed and a couple hundred feet of altitude the engine started to run rough and appeared to be losing power. I made an immediate left turn to return to the runway. I was planning to land on runway XX however; the engine appeared to be losing power and airspeed. I lowered the nose to maintain airspeed and decided to attempt to make it to runway 6 with the runway lights visible. I felt that I was too low to make the runway and raised the nose to gain some attitude and give up some airspeed. At which time i heard a felt a loud bang and immediate vibration. After that point I pointed the aircraft towards the runway lights; dropped the landing gear. Although this all happened very quickly; I think a couple of minutes or so it felt as though the engine was intermittently losing and gaining power.After I landed about mid field; I was able to brake and maintain control. The vibration was mild and the engine continued to run. I stopped on the taxi way just off the runway and checked the engine gauges; verifying good oil pressure and temperature and fuel flow; was normal. I taxied to my hanger.Inspection revealed some dents in the left wing; engine cowling and damage to the 3 propeller blades. I called [an FBO] and explained the incident. He brought a replacement prop and installed it. Shortly after this I started the engine and did a run up which was all normal and smooth. I then flew the plane a couple of miles to [the FBO]. Further inspection revealed some vegetation in and around the wing gap seals. Although I did not see what I hit. I suspect it was a tree top somewhere off the airport property.

column121: I was traveling eastbound over the south end of ZZZ 4;800 feet under broken cumulus clouds at 6;500 feet.  I was monitoring the ZZZ1 glider CTAF flying with Mode S transponder squawking XXXX. I monitor Fore-flight to provide TFR's and NOTAMs.  No TFR's or NOTAMs were noted. A falling skydiver appeared at 11 o'clock out of the cloud deck. I attempted to turn right and another appeared at 3 o'clock. Then it appeared a half dozen or so were falling around and past me out of the clouds. I continued east to leave the area and then saw skydivers under canopy headed north toward the airport ahead of me. They had fallen in the blue sky area south of the airport. I may have passed one closer than 500 feet but can't say for sure.  Next I saw the Drop plane headed north to the airport in front of me wag his wings acknowledging he had seen me. I could not see the jump aircraft before the jumpers exited the aircraft at 12;000 feet or so; because they were above the cloud I was flying under. Many of the jumpers fell through the cloud and I did not see them until they fell clear 1;500 feet above me.ZZZ TRACON was probably monitoring the operation however failed to see my transponder or provide alerts to traffic in the area not listening to approach control. It is impossible to see and avoid jumpers falling through clouds.  It is impossible to see the jump aircraft above the clouds. Jump operations should not be allowed in uncontrolled airspace with clouds when see and avoid rules are to be followed.

column121: I was doing a training flight with my student. Our first four touch and goes went fairly smooth. The fourth touch and go we landed; cleaned up our flaps; visually checked our left flap was up; and added power. I was taught to visually check our flaps to make sure the motor works. I checked my left one and the motor was working. Previous flight instructors never stressed the importance of checking both flaps before taking off in case of a rod failure. I am not sure when our right flap rod broke. Our take off and landing appeared normal. After climbing 50 feet; we rolled to the left. I added right rudder to counter the roll and regain aircraft control. We made a much smaller pattern to get back to the runway we took off from. Our climb performance was poor. I made sure to keep airspeed up knowing if we stalled we would spin with the asymmetrical flaps. We safely landed without any damage to ourselves or airplane. Maintenance on the field replaced the rod on the same day and deemed the rod failure was metal fatigue. There were no signs of over-sped flaps. Although some POHs allow the first notch of flaps above the white arc; I stress to my students to never put in flaps if above the white arc. It is very easy to add too much flaps. Other instructors at the school do not teach it the same way as I do. Although not confirmed; I personally believe this could have caused the metal fatigue and the rod finally decided to give up during our flight.

column121: Departed ZZZ VFR. Our destination airport was ZZZ1. Standard FAA Telephone Weather Briefing was conducted by co-pilot. That information [was] High Pressure; No Significant Weather; Winds Aloft at planned Altitude - 7 knots. NOTAMS/TFRs Checked. Flight Planned distance was 440 miles. Altitude was 6;500 feet. Engine was Leaned as per Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH). Aircraft Fuel Gauges were Operational. At 15 miles from ZZZ1 the Engine began to Sputter. I positioned the Mixture Control to Full Rich; Turned On Aux pump (A) and switched fuel tanks. The Engine Came Back Alive.3 Minutes Later; the engine began to sputter again. I switched to AUX Pump 2. The engine came back alive momentarily; then quit. At this point; I was descending at L/D Max Whilst Looking for a suitable landing site. A country highway was selected; and used. The off airport landing was uneventful.  No Injuries or damage to equipment or property occurred.I telephoned the FAA right-away; and advised them of the situation. After FAA Approval; we put fuel in airplane; [officials] blocked [the] road; and I took off (solo) Flying the airplane to ZZZ1. At ZZZ1 an FAA Field Inspector met me; and I gave him a written statement of the events. The airplane has 'Engine Blow-BY'. The oil turns black in 15 hours of operation. The manual (1979 Aircraft X) 'Book Performance Values' are not accurate. The Engine was Consuming 11.1 Gallons per hour; that should not be. I should have stopped for fuel sooner! Do not believe older owner airplane manuals/POHs. If fuel guages read low to empty - believe them!!

column121: I was preparing to conduct a Part 91 IFR flight from OAK. My clearance was Runway 30; CNDEL4 Departure EBAYE AVE EHF and to climb via the SID. Upon reaching Runway 30; I was holding on Taxiway Whiskey behind an A321. After the A321 started its takeoff roll; I watched and noted the point at which it lifted off. At the same time I was instructed to 'Line up and wait'. After what I thought to be a very short time; less than a minute from lining up; I was cleared for takeoff with a caution warning for wake turbulence. Upon reaching Vr and prior to the A321's rotation point; I rotated and began my initial climb. I had 1900 ft set in my Altitude Select as I was to cross LECHE at or below 2;000 ft; on a heading of 296 degrees which I had set on my DG's bug. At approximately 600 ft I engaged the autopilot. Almost immediately after entering IMC conditions at approximately 700 ft; I entered very heavy turbulence. I disengaged the autopilot at which time the plane entered an un-commanded roll to the left. I tried to recover but the plane was shaking very violently and kept wanting to violently roll to the left between 35 to 40 degrees of bank angle. The plane was really not responding to my control inputs; at least not according to my flight director. I really had no idea what was happening at the time and was very startled. At first I thought I might have a control surface failure. Then I realized that I must have flown through and was now within the A321 wake vortices.  I had a very hard time controlling the aircraft. I was worried if I could not keep the plane out of an upset condition; I was way too low for a successful recovery. I could also hear that my passengers were very uncomfortable.  At this point; I just reverted to flying 101; aviate; navigate; communicate. I hit my Takeoff/Go-Around switch which also disengaged the yaw damper and put my command bars at a 10 degree nose up and wings level command. At that point I was just trying to concentrate on putting the airplane symbol into the command bars and just keep wings level. All the while keeping my eye on my TCAS for any aircraft near or around me. (I never got one traffic warning or alert during this whole event). At some point a controller came on and began giving me vectors. I had not yet talked to the controllers or advised them of my situation as I had not gotten to the communicate" part yet. I was also told to squawk my assigned transponder code. I had selected the code prior to taxi but failed to enter it. At approximately 1800 feet I began to try to level the airplane but was having a hard time doing so. I did not want to push down too hard and put the plane in an excessive negative G situation. I think I passed the max altitude by 150 ft but; immediately corrected to 1800 ft. When I was switched to the next frequency I was still attempting to regain my composure and just follow the controller's instructions. The turbulence completely disappeared out of about 2;500 feet. Out of 10;000 feet; I cancelled IFR and continued VFR with flight following. The rest of the flight was uneventful until I was advised by NorCal of a possible pilot deviation and was given a phone number to call upon landing.  How the problem arose: Inadvertent flight into wake turbulence. Contributing Factors: Too early release behind a heavy aircraft. IMC Conditions. Failure to ask for a possible short delay to my takeoff clearance due to wake turbulence. How it was discovered: Difficulty in controlling the aircraft due to violent and uncommanded aircraft attitudes. Corrective Actions: Maintain wings level attitude. Follow ATC Instructions. Perceptions: Fear of possible loss of control in IMC conditions and very low altitude for recovery. Judgements: Just fly the plane. Aviate; Navigate; Communicate. Decisions: Do whatever it takes to keep wings level attitude. Factors affecting the quality of human performance: The startle effect. Actions or Inactions: Have hand written; 'Enter Squawk Code';in my Pre-Taxi Checklist. Just did what I could to fly my plane out of an inadvertent but bad situation."

column121: During cruise at 7;500 feet  MSL with a properly leaned engine and (nearly) full fuel; the engine on the aircraft suddenly lost power.  The engine struggled to maintain idle speed at full power.  I [requested priority handling] when the fuel controls (mixture and throttle) were checked and the problem persisted.  When enroute to the closest landing location it was found that the engine could be coaxed to approx 2/3 power by pumping the throttle in and out.  Upon landing; a mechanic looked over the fuel system (to include sumps and fuel strainer) but found no issues.  During a subsequent run-up; the engine performed as expected without issue.  When the in-air engine issue occurred the outside air temperature was noted to be approximately 45 degrees.
