column121: I began this trip with my flying First Officer (FO) starting leg 3 of his transition operating experience from the Airbus; one International Relief Officer (IRO) relatively new to the fleet and still not yet consolidated; while the other IRO was a seasoned FO on the 777 fleet.We pushed back from gate.  After the left engine start was complete we noticed a strange and unfamiliar odor that wasn't readily identifiable.  A brief discussion took place on the flight deck about the possibilities of the odor origin and all agreed it was not an electrical smell so we continued with the right engine start procedure.  Within seconds of the right engine start completion; smoke was noticeable in the cockpit along with a very strong and identifiable electrical burning odor.  We noticed flashing switch lighting on the overhead panel; specifically the window heat switches but no EICAS warnings had appeared.  Thoughts of Swiss Air flight 111 many years ago instantly entered my mind and rather than execute a lengthy non-normal procedure; I made the decision based on being on the ground that we would be better off in the long run to remove power immediately from the aircraft.  I elected to shutdown both engines at that point and have one of my IROs open the door and check in the back with the purser and check if the cabin had smoke as we were assessing whether to initiate an evacuation or not at this point.  There was a lot of ground traffic around us in all directions; both automotive and aircraft; and I was wanting information as to just how bad things were in the cabin before committing to an evacuation. XXXXXX reacted above and beyond any expectations I had and promptly reported back with the following information:Door 1R Flight Attendant (FA) had seen smoke coming from the floor area around the jumpseat as well as the seat 1L floor area.  The customer in seat X was relocated away from the smoke area.  I was told there was some smoke in the galley and forward seats but that was it and that it appeared to cease escalating and that the floor was not hot. XXXXXX had also opened up the electronics (EE) compartment door and performed a visual inspection that revealed a scorched panel with no visible fire.  He mentioned; that while the scorched panel was warm; it was not hot and felt certain that whatever had precipitated the event had stabilized and all we had was smoke at this point with electrical odor. With that firsthand information and no further comments from the FAs; I made a PA informing the customers and inflight crew of the situation; realizing there probably were flashing lights along with some smoke in the cabin we were certain there was no further reason to suspect a fire and that we would be returning by tow back into the gate.  I would later find out from the FA and Passengers through sharing of information in the boarding lounge that it was the initial PA that was responsible for de-escalating anxiety and growing concern that would later facilitate a timely and orderly deplaning of the aircraft at the gate as well as all but 2 of our original customers re-boarding the new jet. It was  XXXXXX's 'eyes on' first hand assessment along with the purser and 1R door FA assessment that the smoke had ceased to proliferate that led to de-escalating my thoughts of evacuation onto a busy tarmac and into that of a tow back to the gate and expedited deplaning.We contacted ramp and explained our situation... 'XXX on taxiway has smoke in the cockpit with all engines shut down and requested that they facilitate a tow back to the gate right away'.  The ramp agent working the frequency appeared agitated with us and told us we would need to contact Maintenance to coordinate.  I repeated with urgency; our situation as unable to taxi and needing their help with coordination... I received no answer.  XXXXXX; my other IRO assumed the responsibilities of communicating with ramp trying to facilitate help and continued to receive a comment that 'if wecould just taxi back it sure would make things a lot easier'.  I continued to make PA to let folks know our progress and what the plan was when we got to the gate.  We had shut down all fans and other electrical items such as cabin services and entertainment.  Later we would discover that the APU had actually auto-shutdown and we were on battery only.  The smoke had gotten pretty thick in the cockpit but was now beginning to subside while we were being towed back to gate.  We requested Airport Rescue Firefighting (ARFF) be standing by should things deteriorate and instructed operations to let Ramp know that we did not want any cargo doors open for fear of possibly fueling a bad situation with large amounts of fresh air.  Once at the gate; we coordinated with airport personnel that we had no electrical power to enter a log writeup  and subsequently completed the additional paperwork for Maintenance with regard to smoke.  I was able to inspect the cabin and had noticed quite a bit of smoke during the deplaning.  I would later find out from the flight attendants; that the smoke did not actually start appearing in the aft sections of the cabin until the door was opened and passengers started deplaning.  Once off the jet; I debriefed my crew using company CRM skills; spoke with and briefed Chief Pilot as well as submitted the required incident report before making my way to the next aircraft.  I met with our inflight crew at the new aircraft and spoke with each of them to thank them for their calm and professional approach to what had potential to have been a very different outcome.  Everyone assured me that [they] were fit and ready to continue with our new jet into ZZZZ.  I did speak with one FA who waited for me outside the flight planning room.  She wanted to tell me she had experienced a headache and was removing herself from the trip. I made a PA in the boarding lounge thanking everyone for remaining calm and following their crew member instructions and proceeded to offer a very high level explanation of the event while praising the highly experienced crew I had to work with who were quick to identify and de-escalate the situation allowing us to deplane orderly and continue to ZZZZ with this new jet. We were fortunate that this happened on the ground and that we had the option of simply and quickly removing the power from the aircraft.  We all felt certain that after seeing the pictures; that had this happened in flight; we would have never had time to run a multi-page procedure hoping to isolate before something unrecoverable may have occurred within the electrical system ultimately affecting a successful outcome.A few things to note after our cockpit crew debrief:Of interest is that we elected to open the cockpit windows to vent the smoke.  I suspect that because we were on the ground; no one ever mentioned the memory item of donning the O2 mask or the thought that we might exacerbate the problem by opening the windows.  We did however consider this idea as it pertained to opening the cargo doors as we were being towed back. We train 'smoke in the cockpit/cabin' in the simulator and it can become somewhat of a spring loaded evacuation solution as we don't have any outside cues from which to assess.  In real time with real visual feedback in the moment; one gets an overwhelming reality check as to just how dangerous an evacuation of 250+ people can be on a busy tarmac if there are other options.  It may pay dividends to assess the risks and current information prior to committing to an evacuation. In retrospect; after seeing the scorched panel; it is believed that the initial odor was that of burnt dust and paint before the onset of obvious electrical smoldering.  It may also be worth a precautionary discontinuance of starting with any odor that is not readily identifiable. With both engines shut down; we were surprised to later discover the APU had also auto-shutdown contributing to some confusion as we were on battery only. Moving forward; I will now add to my before pushback ritual; the review of a telephone number for operations as we all felt strongly that we spent precious minutes trying to solicit help on the radio from ramp when we could have probably made a phone call directly to Ops to help coordinate all of the services.

column121: Crew departed late due to brake accumulator issues on previous aircraft; and a potential one on this aircraft.Ground Ops were completely normal and the FO (First Officer) had no problems deploying the flaps to 3 for takeoff.Takeoff was normal and as we were turning to an assigned heading; we reached the cleanup altitude. I called for flaps 1 and noticed that the FO had some what I felt was minor difficulty bringing the flaps up to 1. This is not unusual; a hand slips; or the lever used to move the flap handle out of the detects isn't gripped correctly for easy retraction. I thought little of it.When I called for flaps UP; the raising was again delayed; and I noticed my FO reaching around with his right hand to put both hands on the flap lever to get it up. We talked about him having trouble getting them up; and I flew the aircraft only to ensure that I did not over speed the flaps. Eventually he was able to get them up which I saw on the speed tape on the PFD and I verified on the display; and flap handle position.We discussed what had happened a bit but decided to focus on safely exiting the terminal area and getting to altitude since the aircraft was now in the safe; and proper configuration. We made a plan to contact Maintenance Control at cruise and notify them of the problem and get advice about continuing the flight.After reaching altitude; the FO told me what he had encountered and explained how difficult it was to move the lever that released the flap handle from the detent to raise the flaps.A phone patch was initiated with dispatch and Maintenance Control and we discovered that our radio 2 wasn't able to receive over long distances. We ended up substituting radio 3 for radio 2 and temporarily disabling ACARS to complete the phone patch. Maintenance Control was very helpful on the phone patch and felt like he knew what the problem was. Maintenance Control was asked if he felt the aircraft should continue to ZZZZ; and he wanted it to go to a maintenance hub. As a Captain; I agreed with that thought process and asked the Dispatcher to bring in the Ops Manager so that we could all agree on a plan of action. We could have landed the aircraft at ZZZZ if there had been a flap malfunction; but the aircraft would have been stuck there quite a while.Eventually after consideration of landing lengths; the close to overweight landing weight of the aircraft; and the potential for wet runways in ZZZ1; that the best and safest place to divert the aircraft would be ZZZ1 in case the flaps would not deploy normally. Consideration was based on the worst case; flaps up scenario.Destination was changed with ATC once the plan was agreed upon by all parties and the phone patch was terminated and ACARS restored.Maintenance Control was asked via ACARS if we should leave the flaps down after landing and they asked them to retract them as much as we could.Fortunately; the landing in ZZZ1 was uneventful. The flaps deployed normally. Upon taxi-in. The flaps were retraced to position 1; where the handle binding began to be very difficult to overcome.Upon arrival at the gate; after shutdown; I tried to move the lever that releases the flap handle from the detent and found that it was impossible to move with just one hand.
column123: We were doing a flaps 3 takeoff from [Runway] XXL. After the acceleration altitude; and above flap retraction speed; the pilot flying called for flaps to 1. I noticed; while moving the lever from 3 to 1; that the flap lever was nowhere near as smooth and free moving as it usually is; rather; it was quite difficult to move. As we accelerated through flap 1 retraction speed; it took considerable effort to get the lever out of the detent. I mentioned it to the captain who quickly made sure to raise the nose and not over speed the flaps as I used both hands to get the flap lever compressed and moved to the up position. The flaps moved as expected; with no issues; the flight control page showed normal; and the hydraulic page showed normal. We continued the climb out of ZZZ; and when reaching a safe altitude; I took the controls and radios with ATC; while the captain initiated an incredibly detailed conversation with dispatch and Maintenance Control. After exhausting every bit of information we could give; and every insight Maintenance Control had; the decision was made with dispatch and everyone in planning that they were talking to; to divert to ZZZ1 instead of potentially having a flight control issue on landing in ZZZZ; on a shorter runway; at an international station; and then leaving the plane there. We didn't [request priority] but asked approach to slow down early to get the flaps out and make sure they extended. We had planned every contingency for having to go around and then [request priority] if they didn't; and were ready to run whichever QRH abnormal procedure would have applied based on where the flaps ended up. On the approach; the flaps came down just fine and a normal landing was made. After landing; we planned; with maintenance approval; to attempt to retract the flaps but to stop if they locked again and not force anything. The lever was much less stiff from flaps full to flaps 1 than earlier; but again locked at the detent there. We left the flaps at 1 into the gate; let ramp know to tell anyone they could; and had maintenance meet us there. Sounded like they were going to replace the entire flap lever section.

After properly executing the resolution advisory; we narrowly missed the conflict aircraft and proceeded back to ZZZZZ1 and did the RNP to Runway YY for normal landing. We never saw the conflict aircraft however they did have us in sight; and I don't recall who the conflict aircraft was. There were two jets in holding. We think the controller got our call sign confused with someone else for the 090 vector. English as a second language may have been a factor in this event. Both the F/O (First Officer) and myself remember hearing our call sign in the 090 vector. In the end it was TCAS that saved the day.

column121: The flight was conducted by an experienced ATP-AMEL owner as PIC and training Captain and an experienced commercial AMEL pilot as Trainee. No passengers were on board. The purpose of the flight was a training mission from ZZZ to ZZZ1 and back to ZZZ and for aircraft familiarization and to run an errand in ZZZ3. The flight landed ZZZ1 uneventfully after about 2.0 hours and estimated 28 gallons of fuel burn. Fuel on board at departure from ZZZ was 70 gallons of 84 gallons maximum usable and flight on only the main tanks (48 gal avail; 28 required) was planned. The two pilots parked at the FBO and requested fuel to be topped then proceeded to take the crew car to town for a couple hours to take care of some business in town and get lunch.Upon return to the FBO line service had already serviced the aircraft and a receipt for 26 gallons of fuel was provided. The pilots performed the pre-flight on the aircraft. The ATP checked the fuel quantity visually on the left side and the commercial pilot checked fuel visually on the right side. By verbal agreement the fuel was observed full in all 4 tanks left and right. The receipt for fuel purchase showed approximately the expected amount of 26 gallons burned on the previous flight.Approximately halfway back to ZZZ from ZZZ1; at about 1.3 hours flight time; the right engine failed. The ATP took over controlling the aircraft and completed all of the memorized and checklist emergency procedures and diverted to ZZZ2 in visual conditions. The landing was uneventful with no damage to the aircraft; no injury to the pilots and no passengers nor ground personnel were involved.Upon inspection of the aircraft the problem was determined to be the right main fuel tank was empty. This should not have been the case because it held 27 gallons usable and the 1.3 hour flight should've only burned 8-9 gallons on the right side; flown entirely on the main tanks. The aircraft was fueled at ZZZ2 and the left main took 8.5 gallons commensurate with fuel burn estimates. The fuel selector valves and fuel strainers were tested repeatedly and found to be in working condition. There were no evidences of fuel leakage and the tanks all held fuel properly after refuel. The inescapable conclusion is that the FBO failed to fuel the right main tank. One can account for the volume of fuel added at ZZZ1 prior to departure because auxiliary tanks and main tanks were not full at original departure. This made the quantity placed on board commensurate with the quantity used yet it is inexplicable why the Fueler would have not fueled the right main tank. The right main tank would have had 10 gallons in it. This is commensurate with the one 1.3 hour flight to the point of failure. The pilot in training who checked the right main tank either saw what he expected or saw a glare but didn't properly check fuel quantity on the right main tank. Corrective actions for the future: The PIC should always supervise the personnel during fueling to alleviate any confusion about where the fuel is to be placed. Secondly; the PIC should always check fuel tanks visually himself never trust even another experienced pilot to do that for you. Also; while fuel gauges are properly never to be trusted as a reliable fuel assessment or fuel planning tool and many pilots properly rely on visual checks of fuel and fuel burn calculations; a gauge that show a grossly different from what was visually checked should indicate that a visual recheck is required. Also; stay current on emergency procedures. In this case being absolutely current on engine failure procedures and knowing where VMC alternate were made for an uneventful approach and landing.

column121: Flying at 31;000 ft. and the pressurization audible alarm sounded; and we noticed that the cabin pressure was climbing.  It was at 9;800 ft. normally; but had risen to 12;500 ft.  I donned my oxygen mask as the cabin pressure over the next 1-2 minutes rose to a maximum of 15;500 ft.  At 15;000 ft. we began an emergency descent.  As we were setting up for the descent the emergency descent mode (EDM) on the plane took over and began turning the plane 90 degrees from its present course; I deactivated the EMD and corrected the heading back to a safe heading (bad weather was all around us).  I then notified ATC that we would need to begin an emergency descent due to pressure loss in the cabin.I requested 15;000 ft. altitude; and was cleared to descend (while I was already descending).  Once we reached 15;000 ft. the pressurization system began to catch up and the cabin pressure had stabilized at 7;200 ft. MSL.  We flew the remainder of the flight at 15;000 ft. and monitored the cabin pressure.  We landed without incident.  The 3 passengers reported to me to be fine.  The passenger oxygen masks were deployed when the plane began the EDM.Once on the ground i contacted the FBO to determine maintenance and repair requirements.  The problem had occurred before in very rare identical situation.  Rain/ice conditions.  Apparently; a slight amount of moisture in the door seal forms ice; and the seal breaks allowing for pressure from the inside to leak out.  Once we reached a lower altitude the pressure reached normal; and the remainder of the flight was uneventful.After discussions with the FBO I was able to clean the seals and on the flight out; we monitored the cabin differential pressure closely up through 12;500 ft.  Our plan was to return home at 12;500 ft. if there was any indication of an issue; but the cabin differential remained at 6.0 psi the entire flight.  We have added to the preflight checklist; to wipe down door seals prior to each flight.

column121: I have not taken the COVID vaccine.  Because of this; I expect to lose my job in XX days or less.  I flew a scheduled trip; ZZZ to ZZZZ; on Date 1 and returned Date 2.  I am new to the [aircraft type] fleet and have XX total hours on type with XY hours towards my hours required for consolidation.In training; I was taught the importance of discussing threats before a trip with the other pilots.  My dilemma was deciding whether to tell the other pilots that I am distracted because of my upcoming termination or not to tell them.  I decided not to tell them because; having never met them before; I was concerned that this information might be perceived by them as anything from a minor annoyance with me to a possible outrage.  Prior to both flights; I addressed all my concerns and considered myself fit for duty.  Although I just recently completed training on the [aircraft type]; I am proficient in my skills.  I was convinced that should any non-normal situation occur I would be competent and able to properly perform my duties.  What I did not expect to encounter was the anxiety and inner conflict I experienced once airborne.After the flight; I was unable to go to dinner with the other pilots on the overnight because I do not have a vaccine card which is required in Country.  I felt uneasy about giving a vague reason for declining the invitation because I was uncertain about revealing the truth about my vaccination status.  While in ZZZZ; I thought about the inner-conflict that I am experiencing; anxiety about losing my job; and concern over possible discrimination by other pilots and/or cabin crew members should they become aware of my vaccination status. I was pilot flying on the return leg to ZZZ and I found it more difficult to concentrate on simple tasks especially since I am new to the aircraft.  I was also unable to sleep during my rest break and unable to eat very much due to the heightened anxiety I was experiencing.  My landing at ZZZ airport was not as good as I had hoped.  The inner tension was compounded by my uncertainty as to whether I should have confessed my vaccination status to the other pilots and what would happen to me if I made a mistake and they found out later that I did not tell them.The unexpected level of anxiety never reached a point that I would consider dangerous; but the possibility of increased errors was apparent to me.  The conflict that I experienced because I did not reveal my vaccination status at the onset of the trip was an unnecessary distraction imposed on me by the company.  In addition; I did not want to introduce an issue to the other pilots that could cause a hostile work environment.  At the end of the flight; at the gate in ZZZ; I told the other pilots that I was unvaccinated and would be losing my job soon.  I could sense their concern and as they are both true professionals; they seemed empathetic with my plight.I have not yet determined the best way to deal with my predicament and since there is no guidance from my union or the company; I will probably conceal my vaccination status on my next trip.  I would hope that there would not be any hostility directed towards me if I revealed my status at the beginning of my next trip; but considering the contentiousness of the situation I am unsure.  I believe that my training and prior experience make it easier for me to deal with these types of distractions than others.  I am very concerned for those who may be unable to effectively manage their personal problems caused by the vaccine mandate.I believe that the company's vaccine mandate has created a potentially dangerous work environment that could impact safe operations.  The divisiveness caused by the vaccine issue; the unknown side effects for those already vaccinated and the prospect of impending job terminations have culminated and become; in my opinion; an inherent risk to aviation safety.

As we descended I scanned the radar altimeter and noticed it fluctuating between 1;300-900 feet. We were configured at flaps 25 and I verbalized this to my FO (First Officer) as I temporarily leveled our descent and checked our distance from the runway. DME was NOTAMed out of service so I put [the] runway on fix page during brief and it showed around 4-5 miles. Bar altimeter was 2;300 with 800 ft elevation so we determined that hilly terrain was causing the spike. By this time radar altimeter normalized above 1000 ft and we had selected flaps 30 so we continued approach to landing.Approach brief covered obstacles but I did not take into account hilly terrain in the area. Also; our desire to facilitate ATC requests to keep speed up and accept visual approach.At unfamiliar airports during night operations it is advisable to let ATC vector to the initial or final approach fix.

I thought this might be important because of the restricted visibility and poor runway conditions so no one would commence a takeoff or an approach with our airplane parked on an active runway. Tower understood clearly our intentions there was no miscommunication. Our approach was normal and normal procedures were utilized in the event. The airplane performed exactly as we anticipated. The event overall was a well orchestrated event; [the] Captain showed excellent leadership; CRM and cockpit management skills. [The] Captain reacted calmly and confidently as I backed him up during the process. I posed questions and [a] hypothetical to ensure we had all of our bases covered and [the] Captain was very respective the few I had to offer. I would also like to note that ZZZZ Approach and Tower performed above expectations despite a slight language barrier we all had an understanding of what we needed and they were able to provide that with ease. Lastly ZZZZ Company Operations performed flawlessly we couldn't have asked for anything more. column121: Acceptance flight for new UAS was being conducted in the field with LAANC authorization.  Since this was a first flight; the vehicle was placed in a hover approximately 15 feet for observation.  After approximately 1 minute and with no control input from the RPIC (Remote Pilot in Command); the vehicle went into abrupt left graveyard spiral.  This is the expected flight behavior for motor failure in a quad configuration.  The failed motor was identified on postflight inspection and replaced with a spare motor.  Subsequent flight exhibited the same motor failure after approximately 3 minutes; however there was no damage due to keeping the vehicle in a low hover.  Operation Center was notified of the event. Tech support from the manufacturer revealed that the vehicle software was not properly matched to the controller software.  A field software update was applied and subsequent fixed; low hover testing was successful for approximately 10 minutes.  Build up testing was accomplished to demonstrate the vehicle to be fully mission capable.1) Future acceptance testing (first flights of a vehicle or new config) should follow the procedure used today.  Fly in a fixed; low hover for several minutes to validate vehicle stability before conducting further checks.  2) This incident highlights the importance of ensuring proper software configuration on components of the system:  flight controller; gimbal; ESCs (electronic speed controller); and controller.  Although the manufacturer had been involved with a software update the previous day; even they missed verifying this configuration with us until it was revealed on the acceptance flight.

column121: Flying from ZZZ to ZZZ1 takes approximately four hours in this aircraft. Normal fuel management requires the takeoff and the first hour on the mains; then two hours on the auxiliary tanks; finishing the final hour on the main tanks. There was a tail wind that day so the distance traveled on each set of tanks increased. Just prior to ZZZ [VOR] the final fuel switch was made from the auxiliary tanks to the mains. Approximately twenty minute later; the left engine started to surge. Scanning all engine monitoring instruments showed normal temperatures; RPM; fuel flow; and manifold pressures being matched by each engine. The engine returned to normal cruise profile for about fifteen to twenty seconds; then surged violently. Thinking it may be a fuel contamination problem; I switched the left tank back to the auxiliary tank knowing that there was approximately fifteen minutes of fuel remaining. The left engine continued to surge and RPM of the left engine would not go above fifteen hundred RPM. I contacted Approach; apprised them of the situation and requested vectors to the closest airport; which happened to be ZZZ2. They vectored me towards ZZZ2 when the engine decided that it had had enough. The aircraft was handling erratically; so I decided to cage the engine and make the approach and landing on the remaining right engine; I had seven thousand feet to descend to airport elevation with only ten miles to accomplish it; so I circled the airport to the south to keep a right hand pattern into the airport. There was a successful landing and difficult taxi to tie down where I was met with the local [officials] and rescue squad. An inspection a couple days later with a certified A&P found that there was a leak around the filler cap on the left main tank which allowed the low pressure over the wing to suction out the entire tank. The main filler caps are hid from the pilot's view by the engine nacelle. I believe that after three and a half hours of flying through IMC up to the point of the incident weighed heavily on my initial decision not to cage the engine; but to try to troubleshoot problem and on this particular aircraft; the fuel gauges are obscured by the power levers and my initial scan failed to see the amount remaining in the left main tank.

After a normal approach and touchdown; during rollout while the tail was still in the air; I could feel the rudder starting to become less effective and the wind wanting to push the tail to the left; so as quickly as I could I got the tail wheel planted firmly on the ground to help with directional control. As the plane was slowing down through an estimated 35-40 kts. the plane started to veer to the right; I immediately applied full left rudder and pumped the left brake to make sure that we were getting maximum effectiveness out of the left brake. After rolling about another 100 ft.; I realized that it was not likely that we were going to be able to get the plane straight again; so then I applied maximum right brake also and was just trying to get the plane stopped before it went off the side of the runway. When we were about 100-150 ft. from going off the runway the Copilot also applied maximum braking; but nothing we did was able to keep the plane on the runway; we went off the right side of the runway about 1;000-1;200 ft. from the end. The plane stopped quickly in the soft mud that was just off of the runway. We then did a quick assessment of the passengers and after none of them reported any injuries we evacuated the passengers and then secured the aircraft. There were no known pre-accident mechanical issues with the aircraft. Of the passengers and 2 crew members on board; there were no reported injuries. After the incident was over as I was back on the ramp; I was able to observe the windsock for a while. I noticed that the wind would be anywhere between 5 and 15-20 kts. and the direction would shift between approximately 060 and 150 degrees. At the time we landed I would estimate that the clouds were about 2;000-2;500 ft. broken-overcast and greater than 10 miles visibility. The ceilings and visibility did deteriorate throughout the day.

In conclusion; during the flight back from ZZZ1 to ZZZ we knew the head wind was more than we had factored for so we recalculated midair and that is where our mathematical error came into play. A simple addition mistake caused us to land just short of the runway that night.

column123: After push back and disconnect from the tug; the left (#1) engine was started. Upon commencement of the right (#2) engine start a very faint electrical odor was sensed. We deemed it prudent to call door 1 to inquire if the flight attendants also noticed any smell or smoke; to which they responded negative. as the right engine became stabilized after start the smell became worse and a shuddering or thumping sound was heard. No flight deck warnings occurred but there appeared to be some electrical malfunctions on the overhead panel (window heat lights flicking on and off). We decided as a crew that shutting down both engines promptly was the best move; to remediate the situation as quickly as possible. After both engines shut down; the APU failed leaving us with battery power only. At this time we noticed a small amount of smoke in the cockpit; but decided it was not dangerous enough to issue an emergency evacuation of the aircraft. The second Relief Pilot went into the cabin and stated there was smoke there as well; and he could see what appeared to be a burn mark in the amp compartment. With only one operable radio we had to switch between communication with Ramp Tower and Operations. This caused some confusion as to who we should be talking to; in order to get an expeditious return to the gate. The Ramp Tower controller did not seem to think the situation was urgent and this may have led to a delay in having a tug and ground crew called to return us to the gate. Flight attendants and passengers were briefed and there were no adverse events in the cabin. We returned to the departure gate uneventfully. The student had completed 7 previous touch and go's with no issues but on the 8th lost directional control after touchdown and ran off the runway. The student in question had 51 hours of total time and approximately 3 hours of solo time before the occurrence. The lack of ADM (Aeronautical Decision Making) and physical motor skills to keep the plane on the runway led him to have an excursion. Corrective action is to make sure that he is not challenged with directional control and talk about decision making if something just doesn't seem right.

Pitched to return to glide path and failed to pull throttle enough and airspeed increased. I didn't notice it until I crossed the threshold and was still doing 118kts. Normal approach with 10% flaps is 100. There was also a gusty crosswind and I was focused on maintaining alignment and centerline. Ended up landing almost 2;000 feet down the 5;000 feet runway. Continuing to maintain centerline; I saw the end of the runway coming up quickly and braked hard; speed then was 49 kts. Crossed the end of the runway into the grass at approximately 20 kts; continued to slow; executed a hard left turn and rejoined taxiway. Subsequent inspection showed no taxi light damage and no damage to gear. I need to maintain a closer watch on airspeed even when dealing with gusty crosswind; don't get fixated.

column121: Student and instructor were on a night cross-country. Traffic pattern was entered and to verify wind direction we did not descend on downwind but continued on an upwind leg to ensure we would be ready for the landing. We turned crosswind and downwind and did our before landing procedure. Student was slow to configure the aircraft which extended the downwind leg further than desired and upon turning base we noted we were low on the VASI. The student made a correction to get back on/above the glide path which was too little. I as the instructor was too late and too slow to inspire a more aggressive correction until the top of the tree came into view. I took control of the airplane and landed uneventfully and taxied to parking. There was no indication of flight control malfunction nor any indication of a loss of engine RPM. Subsequent inspection revealed slight damage to the right main landing gear fairing and damage to the left horizontal stabilizer fairing. I suspect that the propeller may have been impacted but there was no sudden stoppage of the prop. Of note; when the runway lights were activated by the CTAF; the lights on the north side of the runway from midfield to the departure end did not illuminate. What did come on was all of the lights on the south side of the runway and half the lights on the north side from the approach end to midfield. Also; I'm aware that the VASI glide slope angle is set higher than a three degree glide slope because of obstructions (trees) and the angle used to be published in the Chart Supplement; but that information is no longer available.

column121: The following is my best recall of the events between approximately XA:00 and XB:30 Zulu on Date which resulted in damage to the aircraft.Student: Private Pilot seeking a Multi Engine add on ratingThe day's lesson was an introduction to engine failure procedures in the aircraft. We had previously covered these procedures in our simulator; most recently on date [two days prior]. Before the flight we reviewed the lesson plan; which was to include:1. I would conduct all communication with ATC during the flight so that he could focus on procedures.2. A simulated engine failure on takeoff to be verbalized by me as 'engine failure' with the student responding by retarding both throttles to idle and declaring an aborted takeoff. He did not respond to my first call; but on the second call of 'engine failure' he followed the procedure correctly.3. Simulated engine failure on climb out by retarding one throttle to idle and with the student following the appropriate response flow; then resetting the throttle for climb to the practice area. This went according to plan.4. Upon reaching maneuvering altitude in the practice area (4;000 feet) a simulated engine failure with fuel selector set to Off and the student following the response flow and troubleshooting checklist. This was followed by securing the engine per the checklist; then restarting per the checklist. This all went according to plan.5. Demonstration and practice of the VMC maneuver with engine failure simulated by throttle setting. This went according to plan.6. Return for landing; with simulated engine failure by throttle setting. This went according to plan.After landing; I requested a taxi back to the ramp as I thought the student was maxed out for the day based on previous flights and how much we had covered. However; as we had about 40 minutes left in our lesson block he asked if we could do some pattern work. Per his request I requested taxi instructions to Runway XXR. Once reaching the hold short line for [Runway] XXR I failed to recognize that the remaining flight was no as longer planned; and failed to develop and verbalize a brief specific to it. I was still operating under the assumption that we were practicing simulated engine failures per the original flight plan. In hindsight I believe that the student was operating under the assumption that we were setting up for pattern work with no planned (simulated) failures. We received clearance to take off and the student entered the runway following all normal procedures. He advanced the throttles for takeoff; and once we were rolling; but before positive airspeed indication; I retarded the right mixture control to idle cutoff (which we had done in the simulator on the previous lesson). The student did not respond to the engine failure; keeping both throttles full for take off. We immediately started veering south toward the right side of the runway. I called for the student to retard the throttles; but he did not respond. I moved the right mixture control full forward to restart the engine in an effort to eliminate the asymmetric thrust and regain directional control; but by then we were crossing the runway edge and about to run into a taxiway location sign (Taxiway 1). At this point the student did retard both throttles to idle. The nose wheel struck the location sign and the left propeller struck either a runway edge light or a taxiway light. We stopped on Taxiway 1; but in the process made a looping turn and ended up facing east on the taxiway. The Tower controller called to ask if we were alright and I responded that we were. I requested and received taxi instructions to our maintenance hangar. After clearing Runway XXL on the east side I provided more detail to the Tower controller and informed them that I would call with additional detail once I was back at the office; which I did. Additionally; Operations and Security personnel came to the office and took a statement from me. At this point the student had already left the school.Contributing factors:1. My failure to properly brief the unplanned scenario with the student and anticipate the potential failure.2. The student's failure to follow established procedure.3. No brakes on the right side limited my options for regaining control.

column121: New operator of sUAS asked for tips from an acquaintance who is a private pilot and commercial remote operator. With a small group of onlookers the new operator demonstrated the drones capability looking intently at display and launching it within 2 ft of an onlookers face. The new operator immediately launched the drone over a ridge of trees and out of sight head down on the display. I commented that he needed to have the drone in sight at all times to which he laughed and replied 'No. That can't be; what would be the fun in that' he proceeded to inform me that because the UAS was below 0.55 lbs that it was exempt from FAA regulation. As the new operator blew past 400 feet AGL he asked what was the max altitude again? To which I responded accordingly. A round of laughter commenced as the operator received a notification on his display that he may be violating the law. The new operator reached a maximum horizontal distance of 1;600 feet which he complained was too little and was sure the software was preventing him from going farther as he had gone 6;000 feet without issue before.From takeoff to landing this operator never had visual contact with the drone.The new operator flew recklessly in a corridor popular with manned commercial scenic tours; GA aircraft sight seeing; and GA aircraft coming in to BHB.When informed of the regulations the operator laughed; indicated that it did not apply to him; and if he were to get in trouble he would blame it on a blog post he read. Blatant disregard for FAA regulations; the safety of others; and no expectation of consequences.FAA should make something similar to the commercial remote operator course for recreational operators and make it mandatory for any UAS that has the capability of exceeding 400 feet vertical or horizontal.FAA should also crack down on manufacturers who are clearly advertising their products and encouraging use in disagreement with law.

The Controller asked if Aircraft Y was descending OPD  to which I replied yes and asked if the aircraft was radar contact. She replied no because the aircraft was not separated from Aircraft X. These aircraft are procedurally separated. I was forced to turn Aircraft Y but as I issued the turn away from approach; the Controller accepted the hand off. I don't believe this alleviates the need to know basic procedures of separation before plugging in and controlling traffic. column121: Aircraft X was departing on the ZZZ1 Obstacle Departure Procedure which climbs on a heading to intercept a VORTAC radial. The aircraft was NW bound; as expected; when the pilot advised that they were not receiving the VORTAC and requested a radar vector. The aircraft was at 3;200 in a 4;000 ft. MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude). I explained that I was unable to vector and issued a low altitude alert. I advised the pilot to remain on the DP (Departure Procedure) if able.Aircraft was above EOVM (Emergency Obstruction Video Map) altitude; very near the airport; and on a general heading that mirrored the departure procedure and would clear the 4;000 foot MVA in a timely manner. The aircraft then turned towards the east and higher terrain. I re-issued a low altitude alert; instructed the aircraft to expedite the climb and upon reaching 4;000 ft.; turn to a heading of 270. The aircraft reached 4;000 ft. and turned westbound. I put the aircraft on course and notified management. Reports from other aircraft indicated the VORTAC was functioning.I was instructed by management that I should have issued a vector to the aircraft below the MVA because it was an emergency. I was talked to and warned to be more cautious and issue headings when a pilot asks for them when they are below the MVA. I did the wrong thing by issuing a low altitude alert. A vector below the MVA would have been more appropriate in this situation. I will learn from this situation. I consider myself fortunate for not being disciplined officially and am grateful I was only 'talked to' about this egregious lapse of control judgment.

column121: Received vector for initially an ILS to Runway 8R.  Intercepted LOC just outside JELLI at 5;000 feet.  Upon interception; glideslope captured aircraft autopilot began a 'substantial' descent (1;500 feet/min).  At first I didn't think anything about it. Shortly after; we were cleared a visual approach.  We were fully configured before MATON; and passing MATON I felt low on the approach; it was too shallow and looked wrong; and then I noticed our altitude was 1;200 feet MSL (1;100 feet AGL) when it should have been about 2;000 feet MSL.  Flight Director still showed us on glide path.  I immediately called out we were 800 feet low for some reason.  Suspecting an instrument issue; I disconnected the autopilot; turned off the flight director; and began hand flying.  We had been cleared a visual shortly after LOC capture and were visual; so I completed the final segment flying purely visually.  I even took the precaution of having the First Officer deselect the ILS in the nav radio tuners.  At approximately 1 mile from the runway threshold; I noticed 2 aircraft holding short on the north side of the approach end of 8R waiting clearance to cross.  A B737 was holding short on Taxiway NE; and a E-170 was holding short at NR.  It appeared those aircraft were causing interference of the glideslope signal resulting in the indications we were receiving on our instruments.  Our manual recommends backing up a visual approach with the ILS; when available.  However; good airmanship and situational awareness must always be maintained. An additional item: ATC gave us no call about our low altitude on the approach.  I couldn't find it above anywhere on this form; but I could also consider this an incident which was successfully recognized and resolved in time with no incident. I have seen aircraft waiting to cross untold number of times; but never have I seen glideslope interference such as I saw during this approach.

column121: After pushback from Gate XXX and given our taxi instructions 'XX-XY-XZ etc...' to XXL for departure; we commenced our single-engine taxi. While I was taxiing at a slow speed; taxi light on; I noticed a truck that appeared to be stopping on the roadway across Taxiway X between XZ and XY to give way to our aircraft. However; the truck did not stop and they rolled right through Taxiway X without giving way to our aircraft. I applied brake pressure to prevent the plane from hitting the truck. Due to the slow taxi speed; we did not think the braking action to prevent the collision was too firm to knock anyone down or warrant a drastic brace from anyone if they were up. We notified ATC about this taxiway incursion and they asked if there was an Operations car on frequency to go after the truck. We took off; were in cruise; and were past the CP (Critical Point) - [middle of the flight] - when we set up for the first bathroom break. I went out first and I asked [the] First Class Flight Attendant (FA); 'If everything is all right back here.' They responded; 'Yes.' I went to the bathroom; came back up to the cockpit; and was talking to the Purser who also said everything was 'fine' as well. When the First Officer (FO) came back he then informed me that [the] FA informed him that when I had to brake to not hit the truck; she hit her right side against the forward galley wall with some of the quarter turn edging. I then called back and asked if she needed medical help in ZZZ1. She replied that she was icing it and took Tylenol and she would not need medical attention in ZZZ1." I asked the other FAs if they were all right; one stated that they didn't even feel the braking action and two others stated they felt it as they were standing but everyone else was fine. To be clear; the first time I was told something was wrong was past the CP. Before departure I briefed the FAs that if there is anything wrong or abnormal; even if we are in sterile cockpit; do not hesitate to call up and let us know. Also; during the flight; no calls to see if [there were] medical personnel on board to help with an injury were made by the FA crew.Prior to the top of descent when we set up for another bathroom break; the Purser came in and I asked him how [the] FA was doing. He said; 'She seems fine; she wants to go home; she's just a little sore.' When I went out; I asked how she was doing. She stated; 'She wanted to call in enroute injured; but then wanted to deadhead home.' I told her; 'I don't know that they will be able to deadhead her home; but if she is enroute injured please let me know and I will contact Dispatch.' She then said she was 'enroute injured.' I said; 'Do you want medical treatment in ZZZ1.' She said; 'No.'I then texted Dispatch that we had an FA who was enroute injured and would call them when we landed per the reporting requirements. I also requested priority handling and asked the paramedics to meet the aircraft to evaluate her; just to be safe. We landed without incident. When the paramedics came on board; [the] FA refused additional medical care from them and stated to the FO; 'Why did you call them out; you didn't need to do that.' Appropriate reports were made per the manual to the Dispatcher [and others]."
column123: During our flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1; most of which was uneventful; we had a minor injury on taxi out of our galley Flight Attendant (FA); but we were not notified until after the CP (Critical Point); [middle of the flight]. On taxi out we had to stop taxi for a truck that did not stop as we were taxiing X XY XZ from Gate XXX. As we came to a stop at the XX XY intersection; we at the time were more concerned about the truck that did not stop; and believed that we did not stop too abruptly for the truck but just more startled that it did not stop. Hindsight; we did not hear any clunking or hitting - and although we stopped slightly faster than normal; we did not realize that [the] FA may have been knocked off balance a little bit. We did make a call to Ground to let them know that the truck did not stop but we quickly continued our taxi not thinking too much of the incident. column121: We almost slid off a taxiway.  After landing [Runway] 27R in rain; we were cleared on C1 and proceeded southbound on Z.  At the first right turn; I heard the Captain say; 'Oh [no]' and looked up to see us slowly sliding straight for the edge lights as my CA heroically held full right tiller and popped the reverse.  We also heard a loud; sustained grinding noise from the nose wheel as we slid across its tread.  The taxiway was noticeably wet with relatively new (slick) paint markings; plus we were operating a MAX that carries extra energy while taxiing.  We informed ATC of our issue as we were able to return the airplane to the centerline.  We continued to the gate after checking with our FA and PAX (all were well).  Upon parking; my CA went outside and was able to verify that no contact was made with any lights or grass; and the airplane was undamaged.  Flight concluded uneventfully.We were vigilant regarding the weather and ready for unexpected things while flying; but our attention became divided on the ground and our senses softened.  Plus; Runway 27R is not a typically assigned runway.  Normally; a slow taxi in wet conditions; as ours was; is sufficient to keep things safe.  But in this case even that was not enough.  Additionally; we are relatively low time in the MAX (CA w X legs; FO w XXhrs); so while expecting things to be different it may also be true that our reflexes were simply not mature.We later learned from a local ORD based pilot that this corner is notorious for being very slick when wet; given the nature of the pavement; paint; and its downhill gradient.  This was news to us and would make an EXCELLENT addition to the company pages!!
column123: After clearing the Runway 27R at C1 we proceeded on to taxiway Z. At the first right turn on taxiway Z; I proceeded to make the right turn to follow the taxiway centerline but the aircraft would not turn. The nose wheel began to slide. The taxiway was wet at the time. We were in a 737 MAX at idle thrust and riding the brakes. The taxi speed was between 8 and 10 knots. I managed to keep the aircraft on the taxiway with aggressive braking. The taxiway was wet and with the strong residual thrust the aircraft nose wheel could not get enough grip on the painted surface of the centerline. It also seemed like the aircraft was tail heavy and that might have reduced the weight on the nose wheel.Go even slower when taxiing the 737 MAX with wet surface conditions.

column121: I was acting as Pilot Monitoring on Aircraft X enroute from ZZZ to ZZZ1. We were climbing through FL270 just west of ZZZ2 when [the] Captain selected the cowl anti-ice switches to on position in response to a layer of clouds we were about to climb through. Within a few seconds of him selecting the cowl anti-ice; I noticed immediately that there was a loss of information on the Captain's side PFD (Primary Flight Display). The Captain had lost his white FMS course needle; a red RA flag appeared below the altitude tape; and on both PFD's; FMS1 in the FMA (which at the time was the active mode) had a red line through it. I called out this issue to the Captain; and he analyzed the situation to attempt to identify what information he had lost; which functionalities he still had; and which QRH checklist could be run to solve the issue. I do not recall what the active lateral mode in the FMA turned to after the Captain's side navigation information disappeared; but in troubleshooting; the Captain decided to transfer control of the aircraft over to me; as my navigation instruments were still working. We managed to arm and capture FMS2 on my side and continue flying the assigned route. We were still climbing in VS mode; now through FL280. I noticed that several functions of the FCP (Flight Control Panel) were now unavailable; including the SPD knob; and VS wheel; rendering it impossible to use any vertical mode of the autopilot. I informed the Captain that these issues may affect our ability to enter RVSM airspace; to which he agreed and informed ATC as such. ATC assigned us to descend now to maintain FL270. Unable to use any vertical modes of the autopilot; I had to disconnect the autopilot and hand fly down to FL270. I was still able to set an altitude in the altitude selector; so upon reaching FL270 I was able to reconnect the autopilot; which held altitude without issue.Meanwhile; the Captain continued to troubleshoot; looking through the QRH for what the issue might have been; and what checklist to run. He also notified the company of what components we had lost and called the flight attendants to tell them not to start any new service. At this point; ATC was aware of the situation; and an emergency had not been declared as; at the time; safe operation of the aircraft was not in question. As we were unable to identify what was causing the many failures; the Captain began suggesting a diversion to ZZZ2; which at this point we were only 25 miles east of. He began talking with ZZZ2 Maintenance and Dispatch over the radio to attempt to identify the problem and find the appropriate QRH checklist. After consulting Maintenance and Dispatch; together they were unable to identify the appropriate QRH checklist to run. The Captain and I discussed the possibility of a diversion. Given the descent and approach would need to be hand-flown on raw data (since the autopilot and flight director were rendered unusable beyond flying straight and level); all navigation information as well as RA on the Captain's side was unavailable; and there was inclement weather at ZZZ1 due to the approaching hurricane; we made the decision to divert to ZZZ2 (which at the time was VFR). Dispatch was made aware of the decision and notified ZZZ2 Ops; and told us they were prepared for our arrival into ZZZ2. We notified ATC of the decision to divert; and ATC began giving us radar vectors to ZZZ2. An emergency was still not declared as the Captain and I were still able to safely operate the aircraft in VMC and good weather conditions; and priority handling was not necessary; and ZZZ2 was not busy.Given that navigation information was only available on my side; I hand flew the rest of the flight while the captain made appropriate announcements; collected required information for landing; and set up the aircraft. We conducted a visual approach backed up by the ILS to Runway XXL at ZZZ2. The entire descent and landing was hand flown; as vertical modes were unavailable;including the ability to capture a glideslope. I was able to receive vertical and lateral information from the ILS; but the Captain's side was not; so he had to revert to cross-side information for the approach. His RA was also unavailable; so he had to make his call outs based on the information on my PFD. A normal; stable approach was conducted to a safe landing. We parked at Gate X. Maintenance came on board; and after a quick diagnostic; determined that the airplane would need to be hangared for further investigation. The passengers were deplaned and moved to a different aircraft. The cause of this event was maintenance-related. An unidentified failure occurred that resulted in a loss of multiple sources of navigation information and autopilot functions. Events like these can't always be prevented. I believe my training well prepared me for the outcomes of this event; and allowed me to return the aircraft to the ground safely.

column121: Myself and an Instructor flight planned to do a commercial long cross country going ZZZ1-ZZZ2-ZZZ-ZZZ3. The flight plan read that we would have used up less than half our fuel (50 useable per POH) going to ZZZ2. We departed ZZZ1 having a ground speed much higher than expected of 125-131 using up less fuel than expected. Other than deviating around clouds and cells it was an uneventful flight. I have done this flight before and last time made the smart decision of fueling up in ZZZ2 to go back to ZZZ1. When we landed this time in ZZZ2 during day light; It was shown that we had used about 21 gallons. Leaving 29 gallons remaining. Then once our preflight was done in ZZZ2 we jumped in the plane and started it up. At this point it was night time. The plan was still to go to ZZZ. So we departed and start to head in that direction.  We found ourselves deviating around storms and making sure we are of course not running into airspace. We found that we had a greater headwind than expected and our ground speed ending up being around 90. When we were en route to ZZZ the engine began sputtering south of ZZZ4. I thought we were having an engine failure because throughout the flight I had constantly been checking the fuel gauges to show we had fuel. I turn the fuel pump on and switch the tanks from left to right. Once I was complete the engine ran normally. It was after this that I said to the Instructor that I wanted to get on the ground as soon as possible. He reassured me that we had plenty of fuel based on the aircraft fuel gauges and the secondary JPI. The left fuel gauge read a quarter of a tank of fuel when we ran out. We were still going toward ZZZ and continued. We contacted ZZZ Tower and they instructed us to enter left base and report a 3 mile final for Runway XX. We enter the base to final and report a 3 mile final. Followed by the Tower's instruction that we were number two and cleared to land on Runway XX. On about a 1 mile final we had the engine sputter again. I turn the fuel pump on and switched tanks from right to left hoping there was a possibility we have a little bit more fuel in there to keep the propeller going. Unfortunately; there was no more fuel even though the gauges read there was and the JPI indicated we had 8.8 gallons remaining when the engine died. The Instructor [advised] Tower and we then landing on [the] highway.

column121: I was the Pilot Flying. The weather in ZZZ was deteriorating quickly. Thunderstorms; heavy rain and wind were moving towards the airport. On downwind we could see the airport through the spotty rain showers and were number 3 for the RNAV XX approach. The previous two aircraft reported light turbulence; heavy rain; negative windshear; and they broke out right at minimums. The weather radar depicted a large cell just to the south of the airport moving in quickly and one at the very end of the runway moving towards the airport. Lightning was also depicted on the weather radar. We broke out right at minimums with heavy rain on short final however the runway was visible and I continued with the remainder of the approach visually. At about 300 ft. I encountered a wind gust that caused the aircraft to go above the VASI glidepath slightly. I recovered by lowering the nose of the aircraft and also being cognizant of the increase descent rate that would occur. Even though there was heavy rain; the runway was still visible. With the heavy rain and wipers on max rate; it was difficult to hear anything else. My First Officer informed me that he heard an alert through the aircraft speakers that sounded like 'Don't Sink' but it could have been 'Sink Rate.' He wasn't sure. I glanced at the VSI and it was indicating about a 1;200 fpm descent rate. Speed was about 10 kts. Fast. I arrested our descent rate and got back on the VASI glidepath. I removed my headset from my ear to hear any further aural warnings. At about 100 ft. with a VSI of 850 FPM I also heard 'Don't Sink' in conjunction with the 100 ft. aural call. The descent rate had been stabilized and it was evident that a safe landing could be made within the Touchdown Zone. We were both quite certain there was no question that a safe landing could be made and also; if we initiated a go-around we would have gone directly into the thunderstorm at the end of the runway. I decided that the safest course of action at that given time was to land. I elected to land the aircraft rather than follow the Company requirement of initiating a go-around when a 'Don't Sink' Alert was received. The landing was uneventful. We touched down in the Landing Zone as briefed. Deceleration was smooth and as we were taxiing towards the gate the ensuing thunderstorms enveloped the field but the wait for our gate was not that long. We arrived at the gate a bit behind schedule. Company policy is quite clear on what is expected and required when encountering this; or any other EGPWS Alerts. I think our situation was a little precarious due to the weather; heavy rain; wipers and also a lack of direct communication as to what was heard. A prevention in this situation would be to not be in this situation. Hold; wait out the storm. Divert as necessary. Company aircraft send Aural Warnings through the speakers. There are some aircraft where the speaker volume is not that loud. Better planning and briefing would also be a factor in preventing this from happening.
column123: I was Pilot Monitoring during RNAV XX Approach to ZZZ. Last weather report from tower was 10 miles visibility and winds 150 degrees at 23 kts. gusting to 28 kts. with no reported wind shear however it was evident visually as well as on radar that a thunderstorm was rapidly approaching the field from the south.  Because of this we were vectored north of the field and cleared the approach. We discussed the published missed approach would take us toward the incoming storm and how to mitigate the risk if we had to go missed approach. At the DA; the runway was in sight (despite a quick to develop rain shower between the FAF and DA) and would remain so throughout the landing; thus we continued the approach. However; on the descent from the DA; the gusty conditions resulted in the aircraft being above glideslope and in an effort to correct glidepath; the aural 'Sink Rate' sounded on short final; followed by a sink rate call from me. The PF (Pilot Flying) made appropriate corrections; maintaining a stable airspeed despite the gusty conditions; and landed in the Touchdown Zone without incident. The post flight report noted a max sink rate of 1;215 fpm. Although the sink rate aural caution sounded; I feel the safest action was to continue the landing considering the runway remained in sight from the DA to touchdown; airspeed remained stable and a go-around would result in flying the aircraft toward the fast moving thunderstorm enveloping the airfield.

column121: While cruising at FL410 west of DEN [airport]; the Captain and I were analyzing a severe thunderstorm complex on our route of flight over NE. Our route of flight was DBL-HCT (Hayes Center)-OVR-BDF. I referenced my JeppPro app and suggested a route to the south; via HYS (Hays)-BDF. The Captain verified the routing with the dispatcher who agreed with the plan. The Captain then radioed Denver Center and requested the weather reroute by asking for 'direct Hayes Center direct Bradford'. I saw that on my JeppPro chart the VOR we wanted to fly to was 'Hayes'; but I knew I often heard 'Hayes Center' referred to on the radio so I thought to myself it was a colloquial reference to the same fix. When the Controller asked for us to repeat the request; I reminded the Captain 'Hays' but he repeated 'Hayes Center'; and I didn't speak up more forcefully again thinking it wasn't quite correct but it was colloquial reference to the same fix. I entered HYS into the FMS; verified it with the Captain and executed the turn; approximately 10 degrees right. A few minutes later we were issued a frequency change to a new Denver Center Controller who answered our check-in with; 'it looks like you're on a shortcut.' The Captain explained that we had received a new clearance due to weather from the previous Controller and said that we were 'direct hotel-yankee-sierra direct bravo-delta-foxtrot.' The Controller said something like 'I'll make sure that's updated for you' and that was the end of the discussion. At that point the Captain and I went back and reconstructed why the Controller seemed unaware of our routing and at that point I realized the Hayes vs. Hayes Center confusion - that there are two frequently-used NAVAIDs in close geographic proximity with extremely similar names.

column121: During the enroute climb at approximately FL270 on Aircraft X ZZZ1-ZZZ2 we encountered visible moisture below 10 deg c so I turned on the Cowl Anti ice. Immediately; my PFD red flagged the following; RA; FMS1; flight director and lost my bearing pointer; I took a second to evaluate the situation and quickly realized we were going into RVSM so I notified ATC that we had lost instruments and we needed to descend which we did. We transferred controls on the FCP to the FO (First Officer) side and quickly realized we had lost all pitch modes and the vertical speed wheel. We also noticed the speed knob and heading bug wasn't working. We decided to hand fly and I started communicating with ATC and Dispatch/Maintenance through the ZZZ3 operations. I started to look for possible failures in the QRH that may help explain what we lost and a solution with no success. I decided ZZZ3 was a good diversion airport but still was trying to figure out the problem so we slowed down. After some time looking through the QRH and trouble shooting the FCP I decided it wouldn't be safe to continue to ZZZ2 and into hurricane conditions with the instrument failures we had so I called for the diversion to ZZZ3. We were VMC the whole time so I didn't feel the need to declare an emergency. I notified the FAs (Flight Attendants) about our situation and assured them they were safe and this wasn't an emergency. I made a brief announcement to the passengers that we were diverting for loss of some of our instrumentation. We successfully landed in ZZZ3 called maintenance and did an aircraft swap. I made a passenger announcement both on the plane after landing and at the gate explaining what happened and what they could expect as well as made myself available at the new gate for questions in case anyone needed reassurance. After the plane swap we continued into ZZZ2 without incident.Unknown. Multiple equipment failures. Possible QRH for FCP failures.

column121: When we arrived at Aircraft X at spot XX; the APU was running and the other crew was deplaning. My crew; boarded the plane at gate and started to do our preflight inspections to get the flight ready. While I was doing my originating flow; the APU auto shutdown and only displayed a 'fail' light. I grabbed the E&A [Engine & APU] and ran the checklist; which only asked if there were any other lights illuminated. The answer was no so the checklist was complete. At this point it started to get warm on the plane; and we were just starting to board our specials. I allowed the APU to stay off for a few minutes; and then opted to turn the APU on again since there were no other indications of an issue. I started the APU again and it started fine; and the generator also came online fine. When I pressed the bleed air switch; the cabin and cockpit instantly started filling with heavy smoke. I instantly shut the APU down; and turned around to Flight Attendant A and told them to get the passengers off. By then; we only had about 5 passengers or so on the aircraft. After deplaning the passengers; I asked Ops to call the Fire Department to come and make sure there was nothing still burning on the airplane. They came and verified that there were no hot spots in the airplane. Maintenance was notified and the crew did a short debrief to insure we were still safe to fly. We continued our flight about an hour later.
column123: We had a plane swap; exiting crew said everything was fine; we got on. Captain was starting the APU then a [circuit] breaker blew and cabin lights went out... Captain did his checks... restarted APU... by this time we had our specials and people who needed extra time about 10 total on board. I was helping a women to her seat when I looked up and saw the end of cabin had smoke at that exact time Captain said to stop boarding. I immediately got on PA and instructed everyone to deplane.   Captain called Fire Department and Maintenance they found no hot spots. We got our bags off then went to another plane to continue into ZZZ1.  Captain was great and asked if we were both OK.   Very thankful this happened while on the ground.
