column121: While climbing out of ZZZ1 enroute to ZZZ I noticed that in RVSM we were close to having a 200 ft. discrepancy between mine and the FO's (First Officer) altimeter.  We didn't go beyond 200 ft. difference and never got an ALT miscompare message.At cruise (FL350) the difference was roughly 130 ft.During descent in to ZZZ; I don't know when exactly it showed up; but I noticed at roughly FL330 during the descent we had a ALT message flashing on my altimeter.  I thought maybe the BARO knob on my side or the FO side got bumped.  I checked and saw that all three altimeters were showing STD.  Then the message went away only to show up 100-200 ft. later.  I looked at the altitudes and saw that we were either 200 or greater but not more than 220 ft. off. But then the next 100-200 ft. we were 200 ft. or less on the miscompare and the ALT message went away only for in the next 100-200 ft. for the ALT message to return and the discrepancy being 200 ft. or greater.It back and forth intermittently until roughly FL290; possibly lower; I do not recall when exactly the issue stopped.I sent an ACARS message to Dispatch to inform them and so that they could inform maintenance so that the issue could start getting worked on when we got to the gate.I also informed ZZZ Operations on the in range call what was going on and that we would need maintenance.I was looking through the QRH to see if there was a checklist for it just in case even though I was pretty sure there wasn't one.This being the first time that this has occurred to me; I unfortunately did not think to reference the standby altimeter to try to help isolate where the fault may lie; as the issue went away while I was diligently looking for a checklist and the issue was intermittent.  Also because it was intermittent and went away on its own I also did not think to inform ATC since we were already in the process of exiting RVSM.No other messages on any display unit; including the EICAS; showed while this was happening nor throughout the remainder of the flight.We landed in ZZZ without incident.I should have known that there wasn't a checklist for this issue and I need to read back up on alt miscompare procedures and how it affects RVSM and what to do.  I should have informed ATC and I should have referenced the standby altimeter to help isolate the problem.  Otherwise I think we did everything else correctly.After working with Maintenance in ZZZ it turns out the number 4 probe had failed even though we didn't get any messages other than the ALT message on the altimeters.  Maintenance said that there when they initially went through their task that there wasn't any active or logged faults with the system and that they had to do another task to isolate where to problem was; in this case the faulty probe.
column123: In ZZZ; during descent we had an ALT disagree message during descent.Upon arrival into ZZZ we had everyone deplane; had maintenance come on and do some checks.They were able to isolate the issue and ascertained it was going to be a lengthy delay.We got word that our new departure time was going to be XE:00 so we got a day room.We got back to the airport at XD:15 for the re-report time.Upon arriving at the aircraft I was informed that there was still work to do but that they just needed to tape a cover back onto the plane for one of the pitot tubes.After that they still needed to do some testing and that it would be about 30 more minutes.So; we went to the crew room to wait for the work to be done.I went back out several times to get updates and each time the return to service kept getting pushed back.Finally; once it became a return to service time of XG:00 I realized that we were going to be within an hour of our FDP (Flight Duty Period) time out in ZZZ1.So; I called scheduling and got a wheels up time of XG:55 before the pilots timed out and due to contractual issues that the main cabin door needed to be closed at XG:34. I was told that Maintenance would call ZZZ Operations who would then call me in the crew room when Maintenance was done in the flight deck and that we could go to the plane; preflight; board; and wait for the maintenance log to come back so we could hopefully get out in time.The call did not come in until roughly XG:10.We went out to the aircraft; I told the flight to not rush the preflight. I told them to take their time; not to slow down so that we didn't hit our times; but so that something wouldn't be missed; prevent mistakes; keep us legal and not on the wrong side of SOPs and Regs.We were able to accomplish our preflight in a timely matter; board in a timely matter; and we were able to get the MCD closed at XG:32. The AML (Aircraft Maintenance Logbook) hadn't returned yet so I figured let's get the door closed so that we hit the Flight Attendant contract time and that hopefully the AML would arrive soon and could be handed to us through the flight deck window.I called Dispatch to make sure we were on the correct revision since we had a hard time getting our IFR clearance. I verified all the fuel and time values along with the correct revision. A few minutes after that a Ramp crew member came to the flight deck informing us that the fuel truck had arrived. There was apparently some confusion about fuel. I initially dismissed the fuel truck only to decide that I should make sure that wasn't any last second changes. So; I called Dispatch to re-verify our fuel numbers. There wasn't any changes and I moved on to the next step.Some time after this the AML arrived around XE:40-XE:45.After the cabin secured and we started our air start checklists due to the APU being INOP.At this point I knew that our timeline most likely wouldn't work but that it would close and that we needed to give our best effort.Right as we got to the part in the checklist to apply air to the aircraft for the air start; the FAs (Flight Attendants) called and informed us that a passenger had gotten up to use the lavatory. I told them to let me know when they had returned and were seated.I told the ground crew to apply air but that we were going to wait for the passenger to come out of the lavatory since the cabin was no longer secured. I do not know if this was the right call but I thought that it was the best call in regards to safety.After a minute or two we got a call from the FAs that there was a possible passenger removal situation going on. I asked what was going on and they informed me that the passenger was being non-compliant with the face mask and was being non-cooperative and nasty in the process.Knowing that we as a whole crew were feeling stressed; tired; and unhappy about all the delays I made sure to ask had we been on time; no maintenance; still XA:30; would this situation rise to the passenger beingremoved. They talked about for a few seconds and agreed that it wasn't. I then instructed them that since he was still being non-compliant; go back one more time and see if we can get him compliant and in line or that we would then look into removal and top report back.After a minute or two I was called back and the FAs informed that the passenger was apologetic and now being compliant and we were good to go.At this point; with the cabin re-secured; I turned back to do the air start. I glanced at the clock to check our time and it was XG:51. At this point I knew that there was no possible way to get the air start; taxi; second engine start; and wheels up at XG:55.I conferred with the FO (First Officer) if he was in agreement and if he was willing to do an extension. He gave valid reason for not doing an extension and agreed with me that there was no possible way that we could get wheels up by XG:55. The reason I asked him was just to get a second opinion and he reaffirmed everything that was already thinking. I had already decided once I saw it was XG:51 that we were done; that there was no point in starting the engines; wasting fuel; taxiing out and turning back. The most efficient and economical path was to admit defeat on there being no possible way to make it off by XG:55 for FDP limit reasons and throw in the towel.We had been fighting a losing battle; we did everything we could to safely get the plane going in time and we just had too many issues pop to delay us going out.I then informed the ramp that we had timed out and to pull the ramp back to the plane and that I would inform the Flight Attendants to do arrival procedures and that we were going to deplane.The FO and did after landing and parking flows and checklists.I then exited the flight deck to tell Flight Attendant A that we were done and to do arrival procedures and that I would inform the passengers.I wanted to be out in the cabin for the announcement to not only own the decision but to not leave our Flight Attendants hanging to deal with potentially irate passengers.I made the PA informing them what was going one; the regulations on duty limits; that we tried our best but unfortunately had timed out and that we need to deplane; that they would be taken care of inside the terminal and apologized profusely for the situation.The passengers got off; mostly understanding; some were understandably irritated; but left without incident.I called crew scheduling to let them know and it sounded like word had gotten around already.We waited with the plane until a hotel was assigned. We then shut down the aircraft; secured it; turned it over to the ramp crew; and left the airport.It was a comedy of setbacks. It was just one thing after another. If it wasn't for the passenger; or the maintenance; or the air start due to the APU being broken; take any one or two items out of the equation and we most likely would have made it. It was a losing battle from the get go; we just didn't know it until the time came were there was no possible way to get out in time.I believe we did everything safely; timely; accurately; with safety and service in mind. At no time did myself; the FO; or FAs intentionally slow down the operation for the goal of timing out. The times we slowdown was to make sure things were done safely and correctly; to catch our breaths; and move on the next step to be completed; all with safety in mind.I do not know what else we could have done. We were ready and on time until the passenger; air start; AML delay; fuel confusion came about. It just wasn't our day.That being said; in order to help speed up AML paperwork we should seriously look into getting electronic AMLs and maintenance. This has a huge potential to cut down the time it takes to get paperwork done. Plus; since we would have access to the AML on our iPads and that the AML lives in the cloud that anyone in the operation can access; we wouldn't have to wait for the AML to come back tothe aircraft. Just like in [program] we would get an alert that the AML is finished; review the changes; sign off on the review; and be on our way in a significantly shorter time.In addition to that; ZZZ is not only a base but also a place where maintenance takes place. There shouldn't be an excuse to not have parts and/or the tools necessary to get jobs done. We shouldn't be having to rely on parts and tools being flown in and we definitely shouldn't be relying on borrowing tools from [other airline] like our maintenance had to do today. I understand that it would be expensive to do all of that but is it more expensive than what we just paid for crew to stay in ZZZ in a more expensive hotel; giving 500-dollar voucher to the passenger in addition to getting them hotel rooms and food vouchers? More expensive than the domino effect that just occurred down the line. Vouchers and hotels were given to those passengers in ZZZ1 no doubt. It's more expensive to not give our Mechanics the resources to do their jobs in a timely fashion than it is to try to save money on parts and tools. Also; across all [aircraft type]; things are failing at; to me; an alarming rate. Be it in the cabin or on the flight deck; these planes are not that old and should not be having things break this much; this fast. We need to stop kicking the can down the road and actually fix things rather than defer and hope for the best. Also; we need to figure out why things are breaking so much so often so soon. This is getting embarrassing and the 3rd major delay; break; cancellation in the past week for me and in talking with other crews and ramp crews; I'm not the only one experiencing these issues. We clearly have systemic issue that we are either unable or unwilling to address and sooner than later it is going to bite us real hard and cause a serious incident or accident.

column121: During a morning approach; BJC was busier than usual. It took three calls to establish two-way communication with Tower; during which a right 360 was completed for spacing. On approach; ATC cleared us straight in for a left base on Runway 12L; then with about 2 miles to go; handed us off to Tower Frequency 2 and changed us to Runway 12R. After changing; we continued the southbound approach 'behind Aircraft Y'. about a half mile from the airfield; over US 36; we saw not one but two [aircraft]; same altitude and 1/4 mile apart; heading for us west-to-east up US 36. I felt that this was loss of separation and far too close for comfort; and uncommanded (By ATC) evasive action was taken including a sharp right turn and an arrested descent; to allow the aircraft to pass under and behind us. No traffic advisory was given (possibly because the other two were on Tower 1 frequency); and it felt as though Tower had no idea where we were. After nearly missing; Tower cleared us No. 1 for Touch and Go on Runway 12R; and we completed our touch and go in front of Aircraft Y on right traffic behind us for the same runway. During the climb-out; the Controller gave us a traffic alert for a 'helicopter on your left' (he was on our right). It felt to me as though the Controller was over-saturated and had no idea where the aircraft he was in control of were located. I also believe there was a lack of communication between Controller staff in the tower during the hand offs from Tower 1 to Tower 2; as the receiving Controller seemed to have no idea where we were; what we were doing; or what we were previously cleared to do. To have the FAA breathing down ZZZ's throat for recent mid-airs (both of which were pilot error and had nothing to do with ATC); and then to be directed into a near-collision on base by BJC Tower; is unacceptable; and tells me that the FAA doesn't care until something makes the news.

column121: We were cleared for takeoff by ATL Tower immediately behind a 757. As the 757 was not calling himself a heavy; I guess no wake turbulence separation was required. After takeoff; at about 1;000 feet AGL; we encountered a rolling motion to the left due to the 757 wake turbulence. I applied right aileron and the aircraft rolled wings level. I followed the magenta line on the NAV display; and we hit the 757 turbulence again. The aircraft rolled left; I applied right aileron but this time the aircraft continued to roll left. With full aileron input; the aircraft slowly came back to level flight. The 757 was climbing above us to our left. I checked the wind display on the NAV display (ND) and the winds were calm; so no help to move the wake turbulence out of the departure ground track. For safety of flight reasons; I decided to offset slightly to the right of track to get into clean air. At this point we were flying the 082 heading away from the south runway complex. It was a clear night and no aircraft were south of us. Once in clean air; I turned direct to RONII; but my ground track was slightly right of the magenta line on the NAV display. Now that we were safely flying; I was asking the First Officer (F/O) to let Departure Control know we were off track when Departure Control called us and asked if we knew we were south of course. We told him we had offset our track to avoid the wake turbulence we encountered; he replied that no deviation was allowed on the departure and gave us a phone number to call about a potential pilot deviation.If indeed the 757 was not a heavy; then no procedures were violated in having us take off immediately behind him. Had there been some wind in the climb out we probably never would have encountered the wake turbulence. As it was; I had the choice of fighting the wake turbulence and staying on the ground track or offsetting. Since I had one encounter that required full aileron input; and then was slow to recover; staying in the turbulence was not an option. The 757 was left of us. Had I attempted to offset to his left (north of track) I would have had to cross both turbulence vortices. Moving slightly to the right was the only option I could safely make.
column123: Climbing on the VARNM Departure off [Runway] 8R; we experienced moderate wake turbulence from the (other carrier) 757 ahead. Captain was Pilot Flying and decided it would be the safest course of action to deviate right of course; without notifying Departure. He deviated around two degrees right and we were immediately questioned by Departure. I responded to Departure; 'Yes; we are deviating right for wake turbulence.' He said we could not do that and to contact this phone number.

column121: Took off from TPA from Runway 19R on the ENDED Nine DP. There was a small TS cell south of the field and the Tower was calling approximately 20 kts. loss of airspeed on the climb from Runway 19L. Runway 19R looked clear to us so we didn't [think] much of it. As we were cleared to takeoff from Runway 19R; we used reduced thrust and Flaps 1. On the climb; we entered IMC and turbulent conditions as we penetrated the cell. I suddenly noticed that the vls was starting to climb up and overtake my airspeed; the vsi had a downward trend and suddenly changed to amber and the 'DON'T SINK' aural warning was triggered. I immediately pushed the thrust levers to TOGA and said 'TOGA Thrust; stow speed brakes' and executed the Windshear (WS) escape maneuver. We continued the maneuver to approximately 5;000 ft. and the Captain reported to Departure that the ENDED Nine DP is not feasible due to the presence of that TS. After 5;000 ft. MSL; we turned on course to the north en route back to ZZZ.

column121: We departed Tampa Runway 19R on ENDED9 STAR following 2 previous departures with no adverse reports. When cleared for takeoff; we observed heavy rain from a building storm about 3 to 4 miles South of field over I-275 bridge. On taxi out during the brief time when radar was pointed at weather; return displayed as a narrow band of red about 2 to 3 miles across from North to South spreading East to West well inland to East and ending over the bay to the West. We had been facing North with no view of storm for the past 10 or so minutes. Takeoff roll and climb was normal and we had penetrated the band of heavy rain by about 1000 ft MSL. Nearing S speed passing about 1;500 ft MSL; airspeed began to hesitate then decay and rate of climb turned to a descent of about 1;500 fpm down. GPWS sounded with 'DON'T SINK DON'T SINK' and First Officer (FO) reacted with TOGA and increase in pitch. The descent was arrested and climb continued. Lowest radar altitude was about 1;200 ft AGL. Total time was about 10-15 seconds and we never encountered any lateral course deviations nor any typical entry or exit parameters of windshear- just the vertical aspects. We reported the microburst encounter to Tampa Departure and advised that our flight path should be avoided by any subsequent departures.

column121: When we arrived at the plane the APU was already running.  During our preflight we were notified that we would be transporting a large quantity of dry ice and would need to use the dry ice supplementary procedures.  One of those procedures is to turn the temperature in the compartment with the dry ice to as low as it gets.  We did this.  Upon engine start we noticed that the right pack 'INOP' light was on with an associated EICAS message.  As I was going through my after start flow (flap handle; APU off; engine heats; left pack; right pack) when we got to right pack we started troubleshooting the issue.  We followed the QRH which required a 5 min wait time to see if the issue is fixed.  We proceeded to taxi while we timed the 5 min.  After the 5 min the pack reset and worked normally.  We believe that the high OAT and humidity caused the pack to freeze up and fault due to the low selected temperature.  On taxi we also had to balance some fuel due to the APU burn on the ramp.  Operations were normal to the runway.  Once we started our takeoff at 60 knots we got a right bleed off message.  Captain executed a rejected takeoff and we exited the runway.  After cleaning up the aircraft and completing the rejected takeoff QRH checklist we contacted Maintenance and trouble shot the problem.  We soon discovered that the bleed air isolation valve was open.  In troubleshooting the pack issue after start; I had not finished my flow and closed the isolation valve.  So on takeoff the air from the left engine overpowered the right and closed the right bleed valve giving us the offending message.  We re-ran our checklists and made sure our brake temp cooling was OK and departed uneventfully. Multiple non normal issues caused the flight crew to miss a flow item.

column121: L2 door was making a noise that was louder than just the whistle you usually hear. More of a medium pitched hum. Called the pilots. They said cabin pressurization looked OK on their end. I looked at seals and put my ear up to an area that looked a little looser. It was definitely louder as we explored that seal. About a minute later I started to feel lightheaded and my ability to control my breathing/focus start to feel altered. I asked the Flight Attendant 'C' in the back of she was feeling different at all. She ended up feeling weird; too. Things started to feel like it was harder to focus and spin/euphoric feelings. Harder to breathe. She said; 'We need to get out of here.' And we immediately headed to the front. I felt that I immediately needed oxygen right away and to tell the pilots that something was wrong. I felt faint-like; was grey in color; and sweat on forehead. I felt like I was having a hard time with my ability to communicate as I was speaking with the pilots. The focus/cloudy feeling in my head was unusual and anything I've ever experienced. My breathing felt shallow and also rapid at times. I was able to tell the pilots and immediately went on oxygen. It took a while for my head and body to be able to focus and for the symptoms to lessen. Used almost a full bottle of oxygen.Sat in aircraft right; inboard jumpseat for landing; with the pilot's permission; in order to stay away from L2 door.Still was feeling lightheaded; cloudy; hard to focus feeling even after we landed throughout the night. And a little lightheaded the next day; too. Was checked out by the paramedics and went to the hospital to get checked out as well. FA 'C' felt better than I did more quickly but also mentioned she had never been through that before as well... and had never felt those feelings before; either.Maybe there was an air quality issue on my side that I was more exposed to? Or slight decompression/lack of oxygen by my L2 door. I did notice it smelled like dirty socks in the back galley later when I went to the back of the plane. Sat in L2 jumpseat; aircraft right; inboard for landing to avoid sitting by the L2 door for landing. With the captain's permission.I recommend having the door and cabin area on the particular tail number monitored.

At approximately 5NM from the airfield; priority landing status announced on CTAF to other aircraft operating in the pattern and practicing instrument approaches. At approximately 3NM west of the approach end of RWY (Runway) XX; the aircraft would no longer maintain level flight. A descending left 180* turn directly to a grassy field was executed. Configuring the aircraft for landing; an additional 90* turn to the south was made in order to land length-wise into the field. After maximum braking; the aircraft came to a stop in the southwest corner of the field; approximately 30 yards from the field perimeter. Landing rollout was approximately 960 ft. No injuries to the pilot; no damage to the aircraft; and no damage to property occurred. A number of local emergency personnel and vehicles responded within 5 minutes. Local media also arrived on scene as well as some witnesses. Word was passed to the property owners regarding the occurrence. Aircraft recovery efforts are forthcoming; and the plane will be disassembled and trucked home.

column121: After we landed in INL we had a runway excursion with a GA aircraft. While on approach we heard the GA traffic make radio calls about being inbound about 3-5 miles north of the field. We notified them of our location of about a 10-mile final for Runway 32 and they said they would wait for us to land before landing themselves. They also called us; 'In sight'. After we landed we advised on the radio we were back-taxiing; and as we were turning around we saw the GA traffic landing while we were still on the runway. They stayed well clear of us and were able to exit the runway so we could back-taxi with no issues; and no evasive maneuvering was required at any point.GA traffic apparently not being aware of the risk of landing on a runway we were still on. While he had us in sight I did not have him in sight or on TCAS; and therefore did not know exactly how close behind us he was. Construction in INL requiring back-taxiing and therefore a longer landing time than usual that the GA traffic was probably used to. Try to advise GA traffic earlier if a need to back-taxi is required.
column123: We were flying into an uncontrolled airport and made two-way radio contact with another aircraft north of the field coming into land on the same runway we were. He told us that he would let us go first since we were much faster than him and that he would follow us and be #2 to land. Normal radio calls occurred after that and we landed without incident. Because of construction there are no taxiway turn offs available on the runway and a180 degree turn and back taxi is required. After coming to almost a stop and just about to turn around I made a radio call stating that we would be back taxiing on the runway. Once we just about completed our 180 degree turn we saw the other aircraft about 50 feet off the ground at the other end of the runway in his landing flare. So we pulled as far to the side of the runway as we could just in case he made it down to us. We stayed still until he landed and pulled off on the taxiway about 2;000 feet down the runway where we needed to exit. Once the other aircraft was clear we continued our back taxi to the exit point without incident.The other aircraft stated he saw us on about a one mile final and would be number 2 to land. A contributing factor could be that he never actually saw us or he just disregarded us. Being that he was in aircraft type he might have just assumed he had plenty of runway to land and turn in before us without it being an issue on his end. Poor communication on his end as well; very few radio calls almost all of them were non standard; no tail number; no position reports at all outside of being north of the field; and simply stating 'I'll follow the jet'. A pilot with little regards to aviation safety more or less.The only thing I could think of is maybe more communication. We could have tried getting back on the radio real quick and attempting to have the other aircraft go around. By the time we saw it however; he was basically on the ground

column121: ZZZ was preparing for multiple taxiways being closed and aircraft back-taxiing to [Runway] X despite NOTAM prohibiting. Runway X was in use. It was the preferred calm wind runway and all aircraft were departing and landing 04. Taxi to X from the hangars requires crossing the approach end of [Runway] YY. I stopped at the hold-short line for YY; announced my intention to cross the runway; [and] turned on my strobes and checked for landing traffic in both directions. Not seeing any; I started to cross the runway and looked to my right; there was an aircraft on a takeoff roll on [Runway] Z. He did not announce he was taking off and did not have strobes or a landing light on. There was never any real chance of collision unless he aborted the takeoff and was going to run off the end of the runway; as the approach end of YY is at the very end of the runway.Several factors contributed to this chain of events. First; I scanned for landing traffic and did not consider an airplane taking off of Z as that runway is never used for takeoff. I've been at that airport for many years and never seen an aircraft take off on Z. Second; the pilot for some reason decided to use Z when all other aircraft and there were multiple aircraft flying; between coming and going for the airshow and high density of training on the field; were using X. Third; the pilot failed to broadcast he was departing Z; which he should have done multiple times just because all other aircraft were using X.I realize that a pilot is free to use any runway he chooses at an uncontrolled airport; but in this case with high density traffic and the favored runway being X; it was a poor choice. It does not excuse my failure to look both for landing and departing traffic. Perhaps the FAA should consider a rule change whereby airport management can actually designate an active runway at the field for given weather conditions.

column123: After taking off from ZZZ I climbed to 3;500 ft. MSL; heading northwest to clear the ZZZ1 Class C airspace with a VFR flight plan to ZZZ2. I checked to see if we had any circuit breakers popped out and none of them were popped out. I then began a right turn towards ZZZ and got in contact with ZZZ1 Approach to [request priority handling] and I said that we are turning back to ZZZ. column121: Eglin Missions Coordinator had called the day before to try to approve Aircraft X and Aircraft Y; IFR at at 14;000 feet and 15;000 feet; to do holding north of R2915; just to the west of CEW; for a few hours. They were denied; correctly; by the Supervisor.  That is right in the way of all departures and arrivals into PNS Approach and VPS Approach; as well as PNS N MOA (Military Operating Area); and some departures/arrivals into PAM Approach.  You will be hard pressed to find a worse spot in the entire US airspace to have two aircraft hold for hours; during the middle of the day. They were planning on doing some sort of military targeting or work from that position south into R2915; repeatedly.After being denied on one day they launched anyway on the next day; and claimed to be VFR; at two IFR altitudes.  When I took over the sector they had already been approved as pointouts by the previous controller; who had also voiced objections to the Supervisor; but VPS Approach or missions decided to launch them anyway; in spite of being denied the previous day. I worked for probably an hour and a half with Aircraft X and Aircraft Y in the way; moving perhaps three dozen civilian and military aircraft around these two 'VFR' aircraft at IFR altitudes. There was no loss of separation; but it greatly increased overall complexity and workload; with little communication or teamwork from VPS Missions.  As far as I understand; VPS approach controllers were not exactly happy with these aircraft in the way either; nor was PNS Approach.  If there had been more weather in the way; this could truly have been a colossal headache and possibly led to multiple separation errors.Note that the controller relieving me eventually; did not want to take the sector; and invoked Article 65 on the recorded briefing; as well as informing management that he was uncomfortable with the situation. At the time; PNS N MOA was active; just north of the Aircraft X and Aircraft Y holding area; as well as Rose Hill [MOA]; along with the standard high level of inbound/outbound traffic; all directed at CEW; during this time of day.  I cannot stress enough how poor of a spot that is to have aircraft holding; especially at those altitudes.Never allow this again.  VFR or IFR; the FAA cannot allow the military to use up hundreds of square miles of airspace; and then take up even more airspace when they are unable to stay inside there already vast released airspace.  They are literally putting civilian traffic in danger.  If they must run some sort of targeting mission at R2915; come in from the south. Do not go north out of R2915. Missions coordinators at ZJX must deny these sort of insane requests by default; not approve them and then have the area supervisor try to be the voice of reason at the last second; let alone the controller at the sector. Readers unfamiliar with Crestview sector (R10) will not realize how crowded this airspace gets regularly; let alone with added aircraft holding right in the center; that are not in communication with ZJX; and have a poorly defined holding track/mission.

column121: Climbing through approximately 500 ft. AGL in a right turn to 360; the departure heading selected on the MCP by the FO (First Officer) prior to takeoff; the FO's flight director; FD2; failed; the MCP (Mode Control Panel) altitude window indicated 50;000; not the pre-takeoff selected altitude of 3;000; and the FO's command bars biased out of view. The PF continued the climbing turn using PFD (Primary Flight Display) raw data in night-time VMC conditions. Cross-checking respective PFDs revealed no flags or indications as to the specific failure.In the busy initial climb segment; confusion as to the cause of current flight instrument condition gave way to confidence in the raw data. Directing the PF to continue to climb using raw data; I attempted to select 3000 ft. on the MCP; the altitude knob spun freely without any effect on the window. I then turned off the FD1 and FD2; reselected 3000 ft. in the MCP altitude window; confirmed the heading bug was at 360; selected heading; and turned the FD switches back on; FD2 first; in an attempt to restore FD2 guidance for the PF. Immediately upon switching on FD2; the MCP altitude returned to 50;000 and no command bars appeared on the FO's PFD.Switching to Departure Control; ATC gave us direct routing to the first fix; ZZZZZ; and continue climb to 11;000. I asked ATC for a heading; mentioning our concern that our navigation might be unreliable. They provided a 010 heading which when selected; had no effect on the FO's heading bug. Changing heading on the MCP failed to change the bugs on the FO's ND (Navigation Display) and PFD compass displays. I confirmed compass heading on the wet compass corresponded with both the Captain's and FO's compasses. They asked if we needed to declare an emergency; I declined as we had good raw data and were still diagnosing the malfunction.I attempted a second reset of FD2 with the same negative result. Leveling at 11;000; the PF reported the autothrottles were not holding commanded airspeed; we disengaged the autothrottles. Turning both FDs off again and selecting FD1 on provided accurate command bars on the Captain's PFD. We agreed that continuing using raw data was possible; and that full FD capability was available from FD1. I transferred aircraft control to myself and agreed with my FO's suggestion of going to the QRH for additional troubleshooting/procedural steps. A satisfactory QRH procedure to handle this malfunction was difficult to find and both FMS1 on the Captain's ND and FMS2 on the FO's confirmed FMC operation. We asked ATC for direct down range and confirmed FMS accuracy using FD1 guidance of MCDU1 entered direct routing. I engaged the autopilot and autothrottles and we continued on course using LNAV/VNAV.We discussed the status of the aircraft and the conditions at our destination; ZZZ. We elected to continue to ZZZ where we completed the trip without incident. I submitted an electronic logbook entry and called Maintenance Control after arrival. Approximately 35 minutes into our hour-long flight; I realized we had not requested [the] planned climb above our initial cruise altitude; FL310; and that contingency fuel had been burned during a slower climb than normal. Burn; alternate; ZZZ1; and 45-minute FAA fuel was still available; though a missed approach would have compelled diversion to ZZZ1. The FD2 diagnosis and distraction lead to the initial loss of SA regarding erosion to our fuel state. Beginning descent and approach planning brought for our new fuel and prepared us for contingencies. Communication throughout was key to understanding the status of the aircraft and mitigated the initial startle and confusion at such a low altitude early flight stage.
column123: We were cleared for takeoff by ZZZ3 Tower with instructions to turn to heading 360 and maintain 3;000 ft. The pilot flying which was me; the First Officer; put 360 in the MCP and deselected LNAV. We took off and as we were climbing through about 500 ft.; the command bars disappeared and altitude went to 50;000 on both the PFD and MCP. We leveled at 3;000 on heading 360. ATC gave us climb to 11;000 and direct to a fix. The Captain told him we needed a heading we were having trouble with the flight director. ATC gave us a head of 010 and climb to 11;000 ft.The heading bug on the First Officer's PFD and MFD was stuck on heading 360 but was 010 on the MCP and on the Captain's displays. The Captain checked the PFD heading with the compass and it matched. We had no flags on the PFD or MFD. The Captain turned off both flight directors and then turned them both back on with the First Officer's being the master. When he turned it back on; the altitude went back to 50;000 and we could not change it. The command bars never came back. We saw that the Captain had a flight director and that his heading bug would turn with the MCP. The Captain then turned the FDs off and put his FD as the master. When he did that; the altitude went back to normal. On the FO's (First Officer) displays there was still no FD and the heading bug was stuck on 360 but now the altitude was correct. We continued the flight to ZZZ with the Captain flying.

column121: After landing on Runway 22R; we contacted Ground who advised us to taxi via Bravo; November. Since Bravo was directly off the nose of the aircraft; the Captain assumed; and I didn't disagree; that November was somewhere down Bravo closer to our arrival gate. Unfortunately; November was also directly across the nose and nobody noticed it until the Captain has commenced the same turn which resulted in a Boeing 787 taking out some taxi lights the week prior. As we were taxiing northbound on Bravo; Ground gave us a phone number to call which led to an intra-cockpit discussion of what we might have done wrong. Not finding any fault on our own; the Ground Controller advised us of the incorrect turn as we continued to taxi to the gate. This discussion never ceased until we were already into the gate area. No attempt was made to contact the ramp prior to entering the ramp area because ATIS stated (paraphrased) Company extended ramp procedures not in effect". When we read that during the approach briefing; we incorrectly thought it meant "Company ramp procedures effect". If the latter statement had been correct; we would have been correct to taxi to the gate with Ground...who had been talking to us the whole time. The expectation bias of believing that the ramp was closed; combined with the continuous chatter from EWR Ground led to us believing we were OK to taxi to the gate. When Ground finally let us go; I switched to Operations vs. Ramp for gate and we were told to contact Ramp...who was more than a little upset. Apparently the Captain hadn't followed the correct wide-body line but had followed the taxi line which met the one we were already on. The wide-body gate is not well marked as such at the intersection of all these lines to make it readily apparent to us; although a post-incident discussion and analysis showed us that the textual description of WB taxi lines is clearly something we could and should have seen. Despite having sufficient clearance; which was visually confirmed; Ramp was understandably angry with us for not contacting them and for following the eastern; rather than center taxi line."
column123: Landing 22R we exited highspeed B4. During arrival briefing we discussed that the normal ground flow was for arrival traffic to utilize A; as B is used for traffic taxiing out. Exiting B4 ATC said to join N and contact Ground. That intersection is a junction of B4; N; A & B. Obviously a dynamic situation as we are clearing the runway and changing controllers. We joined N and as we switched to Ground Control made the hard right turn onto A consistent with our arrival briefing and consistent with the need to clear the runway rather than stopping leaving the rear of the aircraft still on the runway. After switching to Ground; the controller inquired as to our turn onto A. The controller queried us wondering if the signage was not clear. He referenced a recent incident where taxiway lights had been damaged by a wide body making a similar (or same) turn recently. He suggested that we were not the first ones to make this turn. In a follow up phone call we suggested that the instructions be more specific; such as 'join N and a right turn on B' so that there is no guesswork on anybody's part. EWR ATIS indicated 'Company expanded ramp procedures not in effect'. We were still with Ground discussing our runway exit as we approached the alleyway. Ground control did not switch us to Ramp Control. On our 'late' switch to Ramp Control we discovered we were on the wrong frequency. Upon coming up on the correct Ramp Control; we were admonished for entering the alleyway before contacting them and for being on the wrong line". Contributing factors were 1) missing the note regarding using the center of 3 lines for wide-bodies; 2) the fact that the only graphic depiction of the lines is not on the ramp diagram; not on any of the 10-7's; not on the gate page. It only appears on the secondary JeppPro AMM display of 10-9; and 3) The lead in line from RK ties into the left alleyway taxi line rather than the center as in every other similar situation I have ever seen. 4) There is considerable anxiety and distraction caused by ongoing company responses to Covid. While Covid has knocked the wind out of the travel and airline industry; the company's actions to pile on additional unnecessary restrictions and requirements add a huge level of stress; anxiety and uncertainty; adding completely unnecessary and avoidable threats and distractions to the conduct of our duties across the board! I am making more mistakes and I am witnessing my crew members and others like ground staff; ramp agents and maintenance personnel doing the same."

I further insisted that we call Maintenance and Dispatch to report both of these items and was met with a tirade of sarcasm; trying to put me down. CRM at this time was at an all-time low. He finally agreed to do the 3-way call only as a further attempt to try and put me down. It turned out the items he didn't want to write up; Maintenance still wanted to him to write up in Miami. I think that further irritated him.Takeoff was normal; but as we reached 5000 ft. AGL the Captain turn round to me and expressed his further annoyance at me; saying we're going to have to talk about this. column121: I was conducting a routine cross-country flight to ZZZ1; then back to my departure location ZZZ. The flight to ZZZ1 went as planned. We landed on Runway XX and were asked to back-taxi on the runway by ATC in order for us to depart back to ZZZ. We departed from Runway XX and headed back southwest. We climbed to 4500 MSL enroute back to ZZZ. Approximately 20 miles out I began my initial descent. As I began this descent; I also tuned into the CTAF frequency as Tower was closed at this time. Approximately 10 miles out I made my first position report. I made a secondary one at 6 miles. Upon reporting at 6 miles; I was under the impression that I was the only one in the airspace as there was no other plane making reports. Upon this; I began to set up for a 6-mile final straight into Runway XX at ZZZ. I made another position report at 4 miles and then another 2 miles. Once I reached 1 mile out; I made the announcement that I was on short final. I continued my descent until I had reached the numbers and started my round out. Upon doing this; my ADS-B announced that there was traffic on short final at 6 o'clock. This traffic had not made any position reports and gave nobody in the airspace an indication for what he was doing. Upon hearing this; I made the decision to land in order to avoid a possible midair collision with this traffic.Continuing my flare; I was dealing with a 15 kt. headwind which I had flown with through my entire approach. Upon flaring; I decreased power and the wind shifted from a headwind to a crosswind that became in excess of 17 kt. As a result of this; I side-loaded my right main landing gear. As an attempt to keep the nose gear off for as long as possible; I increased power to aid in my attempt. After doing this the crosswind sheared to a tailwind; which as result forced my nose straight into the ground. With the increase in power and the direct nose impact; this resulted in the aircraft bouncing. As a result of the bounce; I initiated go-around procedures. As a I began to gain altitude; the aircraft who was not talking to anyone came to a stop on Runway XY. As a precautionary measure I flew 10 miles out and climbed up to 2500 ft. I soon turned towards the airfield and began making position reports every mile as an attempt to make contact with this aircraft. Unable to make any sort of communication with this aircraft; I overflew the field to try and see his exact position. I observed that he was off the active runway and on a taxiway. Upon noticing this; I made the decision to go in and land. This decision was based upon the fact that I was unaware of any possible damage to the aircraft and I had no exact way of telling what this other aircraft's intentions were. Upon making my base to final turn for Runway XX; this aircraft turned off the taxiway and departed Runway XY. I made a landing on XX and was able to taxi back to the hangar.As I taxied up to my hangar; this aircraft was finally able to make contact with me as he reported radio difficulties. Upon performing a normal shutdown; I got out and examined the aircraft and the only direct observation that could be made was that the tube of the front nose gear tire had gone flat. It was only once the cowling was removed that the damage to the firewall was observed. A learning experience that I will take away from this is to be more aware of potential traffic surrounding me and in my airspace. The most important one I believe is to be more aware of the possibility of windshear on final. This better preparation and awareness I believe; would help me to respond better if a situation like this were to occur again and I was called upon to take action. Having this type of experience will benefit me as before; I did not have the chance to be forced to react in a situation like this. Having gone through this will help me to learn from my mistakes and allow me to correct them and perform an appropriate response to these less-than-ideal landing conditions in the future. I also believe that I need to learn to be more hesitant about adding power in a situation like this and learn to make more accurate or precise adjustments that might be necessary.

column121: We were given a late hand off by the previous controller to Salt Lake Approach control controlling the LEEHY arrival. On check in Approach Control contacted us first and it was apparent that he was task saturated and that the sector was extremely busy. He told us he needed to give us a 'box pattern for spacing' and gave us a heading westbound over Utah Lake. We complied with this heading and the instruction to descend to 14;000 ft. and reduce speed to 190 KIAS. We were then given another heading turning us to our left and back towards the approach course. It was at this time that we got a traffic advisory of an aircraft that was in the direction we were now turning towards with the latest vector from ATC. The aircraft was climbing towards us as we were descending and turning as per the ATC instructions. Almost simultaneously ATC realized the situation and gave us a traffic alert at the same time the aircraft gave us an RA to descend. The Captain immediately disconnected the autopilot and began to comply with the instruction to descend. At this time I was looking outside doing what I could to see and avoid the traffic. At this point we were in a layer of smoke and visibility was low. I was able to spot the traffic as the aircraft was passing above us. It was very close; only a few hundred feet. It is hard to judge distance without anything to base the measurement on. Just prior to me seeing the traffic the TCAS system made the annunciation to monitor vertical speed and as the aircraft was passing off our right we got clear of conflict. It took us a minute to get back with the controller and he gave us a new altitude and heading to join the final approach course into Salt Lake. We made an uneventful landing on Runway 35 in Salt Lake and once safely parked contacted Company to figure out next steps. I believe the cause of this event mostly had to do with improper instructions from ATC. I obviously did not have the big picture of the traffic environment in that sector like the controller did. However I could tell he was task saturated and had more aircraft to control than he could safely handle. We were not aware of any potential conflict until beginning the turn to the heading the controller gave us which put us in conflict with the other aircraft. In the future I will attempt to be even more vigilant at situational awareness. I believe this event has only renewed my sense of importance on this matter. Furthermore I would suggest that the controller of this sector not be controlling more than one sector as it seemed he was. I believe that the controllers task saturation was potentially the largest contributing factor in the event. I am glad that we responded so promptly to the resolution advisory and were able to resolve the conflict. The training we had at Company prepared us well for this situation and I am glad that I have practiced it many times in training.

column123: On descent; realized right engine was stuck at full power. Pulled thrust back with no response. Advised ATC unable to comply with descend via; and we were working a problem. Advised ATC; and requested delay vectors. Discussed with FO (First Officer) no alternative but to shut down via severe engine damage IAC/QRH. We both noted probably a disconnect of sorts from thrust lever to engine. FO and I agreed with course of action.  I kept FO Pilot Flying; felt PM (Pilot Monitoring) tasks were more complex. Checklists completed and prepped for landing single engine Runway XXR. Requested 35-40 mile final after delay vectors. Began to send Dispatch a message via ACARS but ATC made for a very busy cockpit; with many requests and turns. I did notify FA (Flight Attendant) of issue; that we were shutting down engine due to over speed; and expect a normal landing with Aircraft Fire/Rescue vehicles to meet plane. Explained announcement to make to passengers; and she complied. Advised FO at anytime he could transfer controls to me if he felt the need. Landed without incident; Aircraft Fire Rescue vehicles did inspection; and we taxi'd to gate.I'd suggest an IAC/QRH option taking into account a failed thrust lever; not just uncommanded acceleration. It's not a problem to 'be a pilot' and make the right decision; but this scenario should be addressed at the procedural level should it reoccur.

I was flying the aircraft when we experienced a sudden loss of engine power; followed by complete engine loss. I gave controls to the other instructor and began troubleshooting / running checklists - Checked fuel selector / gauges; mixture/throttle; carb heat; and were unable to get it restarted. We turned south for a cornfield and began preparing for an off field landing while I contacted ZZZ Tower to let them know of our situation. No injuries or damage to the aircraft / property. I called Clearance Delivery and asked them to let ZZZ Tower know that we were okay. I spoke with various agencies over the next 30 minutes. I let them know we were okay and the plane was undamaged. We shared our location with flight school management; who then drove out and brought extra fuel. We began straining fuel; which all came back clean. Then added approx 5 gallons to each fuel tanks and did a thorough run up on the engine - All gauges were green and no issues seen. After discussing we came to the conclusion of carburetor icing affecting engine performance. We were at a relatively low cruise setting with high humidity due to showers/storms in the area. When troubleshooting in the air earlier; pulling the carb heat had no affect on engine RPM. We commenced a soft/short field takeoff from the cornfield and landed safely back at ZZZ.

column121: I was on Center [sector] ZZZ. Aircraft X was handed off to me from ZLA [sector] ZZZ1 on the ARLIN3 arrival; assigned a 070 heading left of course for weather. When the aircraft checked on; I called the weather [and] told them I would need to vector them north of the weather but south of the GLADDEN MOA/ATCAA (Air Traffic Control Assigned Airspace) that was active. I turned them to a 085; trying to aim them towards the 2-mile gap between the north side of the weather and the 3 miles I needed to keep from GLADDEN. The last vector; I think a 100; I needed to clear GLADDEN by 3 miles; the aircraft refused and I ended up 2 miles from GLADDEN. On their refusal; they said they were in weather and the chop was pretty bad. The pilot was pretty willing to work with me on vectors as I was trying to front-load them with information on the military airspace and the need for expedited compliance on the vectors. I think I even mentioned the two-mile gap I had to play with.Prior to all of this and taking over Center [sector] ZZZ; I took over the area as CIC. As I took the area; the FLM told me that he needed to go to breakout briefly; but was going to stop by the northwest area to have them recall GLADDEN because the weather was building north of the R2306/8 restricted areas  which were hot FL800 and below and GLADDEN and YARNELL; and we were running out of room for the arrivals. Soon after; the Area X FLM at ZLA called me to ask about the weather and said they had one SDL and one PHX arrival heading our way. We still had room at the time to wedge them north of the weather and get into the terminal area without risk of hitting the 3-mile buffer of GLADDEN; but I was worried about weather building as the R-side on the sector at the time had told me that the weather had doubled in size in about ten minutes. Aircraft up as high as FL410 were also deviating. I told the Area X Supervisor that we still had room and that we could vector nort;  plus it was too late for them to move them as they were out of room.Soon after; the STMC (Supervisor Traffic Management Coordinator) called me to ask me about the weather and I mentioned that the FLM had tried to get the northwest area to recall GLADDEN; a recently changed local procedure about recall of airspace. The STMC said that they needed GLADDEN - I think that was what he mentioned - and that they would be shutting off the IZZZO/KEENS departure because of the weather and that they would also be turning off the HYDRR arrival. He asked about the FYRBD departure because of weather over MOHAK and the J2 corridor - a single corridor that goes between two restricted areas - and said that aircraft were getting through so long as they were above FL280.After that I took over Center [sector] ZZZ; and I alerted the FLMs. The swing Supervisor had just arrived; and the previous FLM had just shown up from breakout to a IWA on the IZZZO departure. ZZZ3 sector; south departure; called the D-side Trainee on the sector to ask about them since they said the IZZZO was shut off; and had asked about a 270 heading. Swing Supervisor said put them over IZZZO since; at the time; we still had some room to go north of the weather. I had a subsequent SDL aircraft in addition to an aircraft at 110; Aircraft Y I think was the callsign; that I had to vector in the same basic spot. Bottom line; someone; or multiple someones; missed at least three aircraft at higher altitude on these routes - seemed to be the satellite airports. Additionally; there were three aircraft; one Aircraft Z; on routes below 140 that were also missed. As I was leaving the sector; there was Aircraft A on the BLH arrival going to PHX; that was attempted to be handed off to me with a DL (Departure List) in the 4th line. I tried to call ZLA ZZZ2 about them twice; they didn't answer; and then I saw the aircraft turning north; so I believe they finally turned them north go to north of all the ATCAAs. When I left the sector; the entire gap between GLADDEN and R2306/8 was fully blocked with weather and was completely impassable.First; R2306/8 was hot FL800 and below for a solar powered UAV at FLXXX; operating in various altitudes. I'm not really sure why the restricted areas needed to be blocked off at such a large altitude for one aircraft. We could have deviated to the right into the restricted areas if ZLA was more dynamic in scheduling the restricted areas; something like FLZZZBDDD.Second; TMU at both Center and ZLA have been behind the power curve this year in being dynamic and proactive in trying the move aircraft for weather. Arguably; our monsoon weather this year has been particularly brutal; and our traffic is up at our highest levels; 10% above our norms according to our ATM. However; moving aircraft in a dynamic manner due to how fast our monsoon weather develops is vital; and it has been absolutely abysmal this year.Third; recall of military airspace and the ability to change military airspace in an unorthodox manner has been something of a disappointment this year. Our Safety Representative has been trying to effect change through a process that would better coalesce procedures for recall of airspace into one unified procedure and one point of contact per area.Fourth; moving aircraft is good for weather; but TMU missed all of the satellite airports - at least that is how it appeared - and all of the Category C aircraft. When ZLA [sector] ZZZ1 called about Aircraft X; the D-side OJTI told them that the arrival was shut off; and ZLA [sector] ZZZ1 said they hadn't even been told.

He said he didn't know that was not acceptable and the first Supervisor advised that Radio-Pharma shipments could not be split in the forward bin. column121: When Aircraft X from ZZZ arrived into ZZZ1; the aft cargo compartment was offloaded by my belly person Name. After the offload was complete Name informed me that there was damage to the cargo compartment. There was a metal strip that became loosened and a gap between the 2 belly panels existed along with the screw hanging. I notified control first of the aircraft damage that I needed maintenance. Manager Name1 said the rubber strip will be repaired at the end of the days flight. I told him its not the rubber strip in the floor. It was a metal strip between the belly panels. Manager Name 1 told Manager Name 2 to come to the gate to see what it was. Manager Name 2 came out a few minutes later and we showed him the video of the damage. Manager Name 2 notified the tower of the damage. Manager Name 2 told me that maintenance will come out and look at it. A short time later a collaboration between me and Manager Name 2 was that I was going to load as far as I can to the damage. The outbound load was only showing about 39 bags and it was Flight XXXX to ZZZ2. My crew and I specifically belly person Name 3 completed the load to that point and we still waited for maintenance. Name 3 was in the belly saw the damage while we waited for maintenance. At about XA:06 Manager Name 2 came to tell me that the Tower said its good to go. I told Manager Name 2 how is Tower going to tell me 'Its good to go' and to push it when no one looked at the damage. I felt that this was unsafe from what I was trained in the past. Any damage to the belly was supposed to be repaired in order to help contain a fire if one should happen to break out. I proceeded to inform the pilot in command of what the damage was. This flight was piloted by Captain A. As per the conversation he was unaware of the damage. He wanted to call maintenance to get clarification. After my conversation with the Captain; I was contacted via the radio by the Manager On Duty (MOD) Name 4. MOD Name 4 asked if I had a push crew and I said yes we are all present. Within about 5 minutes MOD Name 4 came out to Gate XX and wanted to know why we didn't push and why am I pushing 'this issue' with the flight crew. I told him that from what I was trained in the past any damage to the belly had to be repaired. Any belly damage and missing/broken/damaged nets were considered 'NO GO' items that needed to be addressed. He asked me if I was a mechanic and are you qualified to make this decision. I told him no. Then I asked him the same question in return. MOD Name 4 said no and he was told by someone (not sure who he didn't tell me) that it is good to go and will be addressed down line. He seemed to become upset with me and my decision to contact the Pilot In Command on my concerns of safety. He also wanted to see me in 'The office' later. Short time later my push driver told me the Captain wanted to talk to me again. The Captain wanted to know what's going on. I told him that MOD Name 4 is upset that we didn't follow his instruction to push. The Captain said that I did the right thing on reporting the damage and that it is his license on the line as well if something should happen. The Captain wanted to talk to MOD Name 4 on the headset. MOD Name 4 declined. I was directed by MOD Name 4 to take my lunch and talk to him later. I went inside and contacted [a] union representative. The union representative came to the ready room and I had told him what happened from my point of view. The union representative spoke to the Captain for a long period of time. After the conversation Captain and union representative both came back into the ready room and in front of my entire crew and myself; he told me I did the right thing by bringing it to his attention and he will take care of this incident on his end. I was given the Captain's information if I needed follow up. The flight eventually pushed out about 54 minutes past departure time.

column121: During an IFR flight Date from ZZZ1 to ZZZ I encountered clouds and thunderstorms that were not forecast during the planned flight. The area of the thunderstorm was also not showing any data on my MFD XM weather display. I requested to climb from 15;000 ft. to 16;000 ft. expecting to be clear of the clouds; was cleared to 16;000 ft. The cloud tops were rising so requested and was cleared to 17;000 ft. The clouds were rising fast so I then requested lower and to deviate to the north to stay clear of the clouds. Was cleared to deviate as required; at or above 8;000 ft. What had been a broken layer of clouds was rapidly joining together and evident I could not fly below them either. I requested a report from ATC of what was ahead; the controller said all she had was light rain at my 11:00 but clear between our current location and ZZZ. I told ATC that it looked like a 'wall of water ahead of me; and could I get vectors to stay clear'. ATC said I could go direct to ZZZ and be clear of the rain. I turned direct ZZZ and almost immediately upon entering the cloud I encountered severe turbulence; reduced power to slow to 120; turned autopilot off; was attempting to hold attitude; airspeed; then altitude. We were clearly in an unexpected thunderstorm with severe downdrafts and updrafts that caused very erratic airspeed and altitude. There was severe static on the radio making communication difficult. Frequent lightning strikes was causing the static. I received some garbled and static filled transmissions from ATC to climb; which I acknowledged and attempted to comply with but was extremely busy trying to maintain control of the attitude and airspeed. Prior to getting clear of the thunderstorm the Center Controller handed me off to the Approach Controller; during this time communications were very hard to hear with the static; so I am not sure I received all instructions. Once I switched to the Approach Controller and was clear of the cloud; I got the weather at ZZZ and requested vectors for the RNAV Runway XX approach. ATC gave vectors to final with minimum altitude that was 3;000 feet high; ATC had me change to ZZZ Tower. I told tower I was too high so they approved making a 360 degree turn to loose altitude and cleared to land. Balance of the flight was uneventful.I understand the Center radar has a delay so it would be good to be reminded of that before accepting a vector for weather or trust there is not a thunderstorm.

After the traffic my student pointed out passed in front of us we angled toward the base leg. then I realized that traffic is not a light transport. Then I inspected the final for Runway XXR and saw a light transport about 250 ft. below; and about 500 ft. north east of us. I took over the airplane and maneuvered to avoid flying in front of the light transport. [The] maneuver was successful and we flew behind them. A good radio transmission  would be 'we do have a traffic over X location please confirm that is our traffic.'

I was the Pilot flying I asked the PM (Pilot Monitoring) to tell ATC we need to stop climb. We stopped at 12;000 feet. We pulled out the checklist. I noted a Cabin Altitude of 11;000 feet. We ran the appropriate Checklist. We descended to below 10;000 feet. The CAB Light went out. I did [request priority handling] since its part of the checklist procedure. While we were not that high. I was not sure what was going on? As I had never had an issue in an XLS with pressurization. The controller was in Normal so? The passengers never noticed anything. We were closer to ZZZ1 than turning back to ZZZ so we pressed on with the issue under control. Plus the ZZZ1 ATC [Center] Folks while they can be aggressive; are some of the best in the world if I had an issue I wanted their help into some great Airports with assistance. We performed a normal landing. After landing once we had some light I noticed that the Auto/Man switch had been moved to manual so I knew then what the issue was we were in manual mode. I pointed that out to the FO (First Officer). He is very new to the plane. It was night and dark and a long day. He moved a wrong switch and when doing the after Take off check did not notice the issue. Its a learning process. For me too have to watch new guys which is my responsibility as a Captain and its my ship. The good thing we caught it before it was a real issue.

column121: Working combined feeder sectors; typical arrival traffic; not busy but not slow. Aircraft X was arriving ZZZ1 via the ZZZZZ arrival and had been issued a descent to 8;000 feet as is normal for an aircraft in their position.  Suddenly; Aircraft X announced that they had to level off because they had almost hit what they were describing as a Aircraft Y that was skimming along the tops of the cloud layer at approximately 10;000 feet.  I had not previously observed traffic in the vicinity of Aircraft X; but upon their comment I did observe a primary only target emerging just east and behind ASA's radar target.  I informed the supervisor of the event and subsequently issued the information to Center; because the primary target appeared to be continuing into their airspace and there were other aircraft inbound from that direction.Had I observed the primary target converging with Aircraft X; I would like to think that I would have issued the traffic regardless of the fact that it was only a primary return.  Issuing traffic would likely have not prevented the incident; because even with traffic issued I would not have altered the descent instructions.  However; traffic being issued would undoubtedly have prepared the crew more appropriately. It is also worth mentioning that we observe false targets in our airspace on a relatively regular basis.  I would be naïve to assert that it is possible to issue traffic on every primary target to every aircraft 100% of the time.  Particularly given that I was working both the feeder sectors combined; which essentially means my scan is the entirety of our airspace.  Had the feeder sectors been split; there is an additional possibility that my scan would have caught the primary target and I would have issued traffic.Additionally; while I believe the primary target was technically just outside of the Mode-C/ADS-B Out veil around ZZZ1 at the location that the incident occurred  my guess is that the aircraft departed from a satellite airport underneath that veil (even if just barely).  To my knowledge no aircraft contacted the facility today to inform us of their intentions to operate in the vicinity of this incident without Mode-C/ADS-B Out capabilities.  So; the aircraft's compliance with applicable regulations pertaining to their equipment may have averted this incident as well.

column121: Flew a 737 Max from ZZZ-ZZZ1.  During single engine taxi to [runway]; called for the delayed engine start with what I thought was enough time to reach runway at a normal pace and fully prepare for takeoff.  I even briefed the need to take into consideration the slow engine start cycle as part of the workload management process.  The engine start process took so much time that we were finishing checklists (at a normal pace) when we were cleared to line up and wait.  The checklists were complete and the FO (First Officer) and I both agreed that we were ready for takeoff prior to takeoff clearance.  As we took the runway; an LCA (Line Check Airman) on the jumpseat pointed out that the 3 minute warm up time was not complete.  We asked the Tower for 30 seconds on the runway and then took off.  The rest of the flight was normal. While the buck stops with the Captain; there were a few factors that led to this inadvertent deviation.  This leg was my 3rd in the Max.  This was a threat that was briefed in preflight.  While I knew we needed more time for the engine to start; it was much longer than I planned for.  Additionally; the FO did not start a timer after the engine start for some reason.  Because the FO did not call out that the warm up time was not finished; it was forgotten.  What I took away from this event was that the start sequence on the Max takes at least 6 minutes - approximately 3 for the start; and 3 to warm up.  Another take away is that even though FO's normally track this time and report it as necessary; I need to monitor this much more closely.

column121: After combining the STAR waypoint onto the RNAV waypoint in the FMS; we re-entered the altitude due to the FMS EPIC load 27.3 known issues of 'melding' altitudes. We just re-entered the altitude in the FMS on the fix which acted as a 'vertical direct to' and deleted all of the crossing restrictions between our current altitude and the set altitude. This removal of all the crossing restrictions went unnoticed.We noticed the terrain below us. We could still see it and thought it seemed a 'little close.' We both had our terrain pages up and I noticed the highest terrain was 11;700 ft. and we were still at 14;800 ft. This error continued unnoticed as our attention turned towards a diverting aircraft from a nearby airport to our destination due to weather. Our approach would take us close to that airport; so I instructed the FO (First Officer) to keep terrain up on his side and I would take a look at the radar on mine. After a few minutes of looking at the weather; we determined that it was not a threat. About that time; we received a 'low altitude' call from the very busy ZZZ Approach Controller. We immediately leveled off; even though we still had the terrain in sight. We discovered the error; re-entered the remaining crossing restrictions; and continued. The remainder of the flight continued without incident. We never received any GPWS alerts.I mis-applied the 'Action Required' from our Flight Operations Bulletin. We should have deleted the 'melded' altitude and then re-entered the correct one. Instead; I just re-entered the crossing altitude and did not re-verify the crossing restrictions. Since we both had verified all the altitudes prior to the descent checklist; it gave us the confidence that they would still be there.While I take full responsibility; the FMS 'issues' are just waiting there for a slightly distracted crew; with weather. We would have had no issue; if I complied with the actions in the Flight Operations Bulletin; but there are a lot of them to keep track of that are not observed on a daily basis.
column123: On a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1; on ZZZZZ Arrival into ZZZ1 with planned RNAV RNP Y XXL. Cleared direct ZZZZZ1 and descend via ZZZZZ. Approximately at ZZZZZ2 the Approach Controller issued clearance for the RNAV Y XXL. The Captain; PM; connected ZZZ1 from the approach to ZZZ1 on the arrival. Because of the Flight Operations Bulletin about altitude melding; the Captain selected 9000 ft. and re-entered it. The FO (First Officer); PF; confirmed it. The aircraft entered a shallow; steady descent to 9000 ft. at ZZZ1. The conditions were VMC and both pilots saw the terrain. There was a large thunderstorm near ZZZ2 VOR. The Captain was adjusting the radar when ATC issued a low altitude alert between ZZZZZ3 and ZZZZZ4. The Captain had the FO level off the aircraft at 12;000 feet. The Captain re-entered the correct altitude at ZZZZZ4. The rest of the approach went without further incident. We never received a GPWS warning.I checked all the altitudes on the arrival and trusted they were correct in the FMS. I was mostly concerned about the aircraft making the crossing restriction at ZZZ1 at 9;000 feet. where we melded fixes. When the Captain and I confirmed / activated the 9000 ft. in the MCDU; I didn't realize that we accidentally just created a 'vertical direct to' and deleted all altitudes between ZZZZZ2 and ZZZ1. So when we flew over ZZZZZ5 and ZZZZZ4; there were no altitudes next to the fixes on the flight plan page. [I suggest that] on a STAR after crossing every fix; have the PF read off the chart 'next fix; ZZZZZ5; 16;000 feet.'

column121: During maneuvers in practice area; we were practicing stalls going from south to north. The practice area frequency was monitored and all our radio calls were made for location; direction of flight; altitude; and maneuver type. No conflict was identified from other aircraft. Upon completion of the stall; we got a traffic alert for an aircraft traveling northwest to southeast at our 11 o'clock 500 feet above us. They didn't make any radio calls before; during; or after the event. I took the flight controls and performed a 180-degree descending turn to south; 1000 feet below our altitude. This solved the traffic conflict.The traffic crossed through the practice area and wasn't on our frequency as far as we could tell. I should have maintained more vigilant attention to traffic de-conflicting; both visually and with the ADS-B. Going forward I will double-check for traffic with a visual scan and verify with the ADS-B. Even if traffic is clear to begin a maneuver; it may be a conflict by its completion. If a similar situation arises in the future; I will adjust heading and altitude prior to starting the maneuver.

column121: My team was supporting wildfire efforts in the Western US. I was the RPIC (Remote Pilot in Command) for the operations. We flew our UAS (unmanned aircraft system) under the authority of the appropriate state dispatch agency we were contracted to; within TFRs associated with the firefighting efforts. Operations consisted of flying within the TFR; at approximately 3;000-5;000ft AGL to provide infrared mapping; real-time video; and hot-spot location for ground firefighting personnel. Our aircraft are equipped with Mode A/C/S ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast) out transponders; which were operated for all flights. We maintained radio communications with both the TFR controlling entities as well as with other aircraft within the TFR on assigned air-to-air frequencies. All operations were conducted normally and safely. According to our interpretation of normal contract-type UAS procedures set up by the BLM (Bureau of Land Management) PMS-515 (Publication Management System-515) entail having a 'carded' [qualified] UAS Manager (UASM); employed by the contracting agency assigned on-site to the contractor. The UASM coordinates SGI (special government interest) Waivers for contracted Type 1 and 2 UAS platforms. The state contracted UAS for firefighting; the state was not aware of most of the federal procedures for contract UAS; and was not able to provide a qualified UASM for our operation. I reviewed our operational documents as well as NWCG (National Wildfire Coordinating Group) PMS 515 after the mission was complete. As a result of the review; I realized an ECOA (Emergency Certificate of Authorization)/ SGI Waiver for BVLOS (beyond visual line of sight) flight had not been attained for our operations. We planned operations going forward. I immediately contacted the FAA SOSC (System Operations Support Center) to obtain the necessary SGI-COA for all subsequent planned operations. A plan and alternate plans were readied for future operations in support of that wildfire. For the remainder of our mission calendar; we were not able to find a suitable Takeoff/Landing area (LRZ) within the boundaries of the TFR. Further support flights were not able to be flown. All further flights of this nature will have the proper SGI/ ECOA Waivers for BVLOS flight in place prior to launching the aircraft. This step has been added into our preparation checklist to ensure it is not missed in the future; regardless of the management/ interface assets available or assigned.
