column121: Fume event.  We loaded the passengers and had a maintenance issue with my oxygen mask that they had to run to the hanger so we were going to be delayed slightly.  The Captain started the APU.  The Gate Agent came down and asked if Maintenance was there for the smell.  We didn't realize that it smelled on the plane as we were already acclimated to it.  It took a few minutes of discussion and trips to the jetway and outside to clear our noses and realize there was a smell.  I went down to the tug to see if the smell was from outside but it wasn't.  I asked the flight attendants about it and they all thought it was from outside also until they walked to the back of the plane and it was getting worse.  They called us and we both decided to turn off the APU bleed and get the people off.  I talked to the agent and she said just send them up and I made an announcement that we had a maintenance issue and everyone needed to deplane.  The total time was about 25 minutes; 15 minutes to realize the extent of the problem which got progressively worse; and 10 minutes to deplane all but one wheelchair that took another 10 minutes to find a wheelchair.  Afterwards; Chief Pilot met us at the gate and we called air medical service. It was a waste; the person couldn't understand us; and told the Captain he was fine.  Name told her that's not what he said as he was sitting next to him.  We debated going to the hospital but went to the company medical center and home. We feel the APU was the factor that caused [the event]. Not having the fumes would be the best; but the agent being aware and speaking up reduced the severity of the event.  It allowed us to act faster than we probably would have not realizing the severity.

column121: A lot going on that culminated into a low altitude caution on approach to Runway XXR. The RNP approach was loaded into the FMS in the normal preflight planning. I did not catch this error and thought it was the RNAV XXR that we were flying during the initial descent and approach; which is the approach we were cleared for. On the base leg prior to the ZZZZZ fix; we noticed the error and the box was not sequencing correctly. I instructed the FO to 'handfly' to make the 90 degree turn to final while I went heads down to get the correct approach in the box. The FO started a turn but also a descent and we received a caution obstacle aural warning from the aircraft. I instructed the FO to immediately correct and to climb to the correct altitude. At that time we also received a query from the control tower for a low altitude alert and we were 800-1000 feet below the minimum vectoring altitude at that point on the arrival. We corrected the altitude error and climbed to be at ZZZZZ1 (FAP) at the correct altitude.   I neglected or misread what approach was actually loaded into the FMS. The turn to  final should have been a turn only and not a descending turn. I was removed from monitoring while heads down reloading the approach so I did not monitor the hand flying properly. It was the end of a long day; and the last 45 minutes of the flight was dodging weather in and around ZZZ. This all happened very quick and was a bit of a wake up call to me how quickly it went from normal to a situation that had the aircraft in a low altitude situation. In hindsight; I should have just asked ATC for a vector to buy time and get reestablished on the approach instead of trying to save the approach and fix it while asking the FO to hand fly. The safest course of action would have been to get a vector.
column123: On the late downwind leg of the approach; of the second leg for the day; after multiple deviations due to weather; the CA & I realized the approach loaded in the box differed to that which was briefed. That is; RNAV GPS instead of RNAV RNP . Although this was recognized; changed & executed just after the IAF; the aircraft did not respond accordingly; and as PF I initiated hand flying to correct the base to final turn; of which we momentarily overshot. Whilst hand flying & commencing a 30 degree turn in the descent at the IF; insufficient back pressure was held & the aircraft lost approximately 700-800 ft before establishing on final. This was immediately recognized and corrective action was taken to reestablish the correct altitude; whilst an aural 'Obstacle' warning was heard & moments later; an ATC advisory was received. The approach was stabilized before 1000 ft; we broke out around 900 ft & landed safely. This event was initially due to a combination of complacency & distraction... where we were dodging multiple cells en route; and failed to amend the previously entered approach in the box (*as loaded prior to departure). We held off amending the box; until we were in range to receive the latest ATIS; and at that time; became busy avoiding weather; and then once closer to the field; there was multiple traffic & very busy ATC communications. To ensure this is not repeated; I will also be thoroughly going over the box during the approach brief; and verify my intentions regarding when I shall be arming the approach & what I then expect to see on the FMS.

column121: A large portion of what happened was because of weather around the sector and through out the state of Florida.  It caused for 'not normal' procedures to be used; re-routes; and added traffic coming from additional sectors.  We also had the airspace and procedures in our airspace recently change with Metroplex; and their is still a learning curve.For this specific incident; Aircraft Y was on the VIICE arrival descending out of FL340 for FL240.  Then FLL was being rerouted and Aircraft X was on a south heading to get spacing.  Both aircraft were handed off to our sector Y).  Then coordination went on between the 2 R-sides; and the sector X R-side offered a point out on the Aircraft X turning on course.  I think experience of X R-side vs sector Y R-side was a factor in sector Y R-side accepting the point out on an aircraft he probably should of called radar on and worked.  Aircraft Y was also on a weather reroute; and I think his heading vs his route; gave both controllers the feeling they had more time to resolve the conflict.  I brought the potential conflict to the attention of my R-side.  Aircraft Y had never checked on; so sector Y R-side  leaned over to sector X R-side and told him to be careful of the situation.  That's when sector X R-side told sector Y R-side that sector Y R-side should already be in communications with Aircraft Y.  At that point sector Y R-side reached out to Aircraft Y and told him to fly a heading of 180 and maintain FL280.  Sector X R-side then told the Aircraft  X to turn to a heading of 270.  Although the turn was issued late; the reaction time of the Aircraft Y pilot and the response/performance of the plane was also not anticipated.  The turn was a lot wider and longer than what was expected.  Now the sector Y R-side also told the Aircraft Y pilot to stop his descent and maintain FL280 when the data block reflected FL281.  Meaning the aircraft had already descended through; had to level off; and then climb back up.  I honestly don't know [what to do about the situation].I think experience was a factor with the sector Y R-side as  a newly checked out CPC.  I think they learned a lot today; and looking back would of done things differently.  As for a procedural change or how to keep it from happening in the future I don't have an answer.
column123: Weather in the South Florida Area. Miami Approach was temporarily holding Miami Arrivals then opened. Next Fort Lauderdale arrivals were being held. Initially I was not aware the location or spelling of PEAKY or the BHHIA1 arrival. I placed my first FLL aircraft on a heading 270 and advised to expect revised clearance. I placed the second aircraft Aircraft X on a heading of 180 to gain the necessary 15 miles in trail spacing that was being requested. Both my FLL aircraft were PVD up onto sector Y which is the adjacent sector to X on the south side. There was difficulty attempting to locate the new arrival and input into the system. It was not an item in the drop down routes. Aircraft X currently heading 180 for the initial requested in-trail spacing was then given the revised re-route PEAKY BHHIA BHHIA1 FLL. At the same time now flashing with Aircraft Y; another aircraft; EGLL ZFP PTOON VIICE1 MIA. I had worked Aircraft Y; descended to FL240 and handed off to Sector Y. I could hear next to me the sector Y R-side controller attempting to turn Aircraft Y to a heading of 180 and I turned Aircraft X to a 270 heading; then 290 heading and then a 360 heading attempting to maintain positive separation. Separation was lost. We are currently in the initial weeks of the revised Metroplex. Sector X; Y; and Z have been recently altered; adjusted both in design; altitude stratum and procedures; new fixes; airways and descend/climb VIA clearances. Initially Aircraft Y was direct PTOON descending to FL240; handed off to Sector Y. At this time I thought all was well and was involved in Issuing clearance to the FLL arrivals. column121: While on an approximate 3-mile final to Runway XX at ZZZ in a Cessna Skyhawk 172S with a pre-solo student pilot; ZZZ Tower cleared a regional jet for takeoff. Departing aircraft was either a Regional Jet CRJ700 or an Embraer 175 E-175. The Tower Controller gave myself and my student the option to either 'extend upwind and expect landing clearance in 3 minutes;' or 'make a full stop taxi-back landing.' I made a transmission stating; 'Full stop taxi-back; Aircraft X.' Then we were cleared for a full stop taxi-back Runway XX. I advised my student we will come in on final approach slightly high and land long; desired touchdown point being the 1;000 ft. white blocks rather than the numbers 'XX.' After our higher-than normal approach to avoid wake turbulence from [the] departing jet and longer-than-normal touchdown point; I had to brake aggressively to make the right turn onto Taxiway XX. My student and I got off the runway; completed the items on the 'after landing' checklist; and then contacted Ground on [frequency]. I felt an abnormal shimmy coming from the nose wheel after letting the airplane slow to a stop on Taxiway XX; holding short of Taxiway XY. We then received our clearance to taxi via Taxiway XY to Runway XX. While holding short Runway XX on Taxiway XY; my student completed the 'pre-takeoff' checklist items and made his radio transmission for 'right closed traffic.' Tower told us to line-up-and-wait Runway XX and he also advised us of traffic coming in on final. I cannot remember if they were 5 miles out or 3 miles. During our takeoff roll I felt a slight shimmy coming from the nose wheel again; same sensation as when we first slowed to a stop while exiting on Taxiway XX. I also noticed our pitch attitude during the takeoff roll was slightly lower than normal. We continued with the takeoff because traffic was close behind us for Runway XX. I did not want to abort the takeoff and make the traffic behind me have to go around; so I decided to have my student continue with the takeoff. After reaching our right downwind leg; we advised Tower we would be making a full stop landing. I advised my student we would be making a soft-field landing; to keep as much weight off the nose wheel for as long as possible; because I suspected an issue with the nosewheel. The soft-field landing was successful; and the nose wheel did not make contact with the ground till rounding the turn to exit Runway XX on Taxiway XZ. Once back pressure was released and the nose wheel made contact with the ground; the issue became apparent. The nose-wheel tire was completely deflated. Tower then asked if I could make it to the other side of the hold-short lines and I replied that I could and that I would bring the aircraft to a stop on the 'Compass Rose.' Tower then temporarily suspended operations on Runway XX so personnel could make a FOD inspection. Then two firetrucks and two county airport vehicles crossed Runway XX on Taxiway XZ to assist my student and I on the Compass Rose. We then pushed the aircraft to its parking space. A county airport worker called for clearance to cross Taxiway XA before we continued back to our parking space.My personal assessment of the factors leading to the deflated nose wheel tire and the temporary closure of Runway XX. An issue with the ATIS recording at the beginning of the flight was the first abnormality in a series of abnormalities on this flight. During this flight leading up to the events described previously; my student and I were advised to extend upwind and fly runway heading; make right traffic; make a 360; extend our upwind; and finally come in to land. A desire to come in and land after being delayed for so long caused me to make the decision to make the full-stop taxi-back under time-sensitive circumstances; rather than taking Tower's other option presented to me; which was to extend upwind and expect a landing clearance in another 3 minutes.After the full-stop taxi-back and after we were told toline-up-and-wait and that traffic was on final for Runway XX behind us; I decided to commit to the takeoff rather than to abort to prevent the traffic behind me from having to go around; despite my feeling that something was wrong with the nose wheel.Pressure from Tower and the busy environment of the ZZZ airport that day; along with the added pressures and obligations of instructing a pre-solo private pilot student led me to make two errors. Failing to ask to taxi back to our parking space during the initial shimmy experienced on Taxiway XX. Failing to abort the takeoff out of fear of causing an inconvenience to another pilot.Although my student was doing most of the manipulations of the flight controls and making most of the radio calls; I was responsible for the hard-braking to make Taxiway XX; and I was on the controls during the soft-field landing and during the left turn to exit Runway XX on Taxiway XZ. I was also the pilot-in-command; therefore the responsibilities of this flight were mine; and I should have aborted the takeoff when I suspected an issue with the nose wheel.Traffic pattern was busy; my student and I were only able to make 2 landings with a Hobbs recording of 0.9 hours for the pattern-flight. No one was injured during this flight. Winds were variable during this mishap and weather was not a factor. I am not sick; I am not on any medications; I am not stressed; I have complied with Federal Aviation Regulation (FAR) 91.17; I got well-rested sleep the night before and was not fatigued during the flight; I am emotionally healthy and stable. The aircraft was thoroughly preflighted. All preflight checklists were adhered to and completed; FAR 91.9(a) adhered to.

column121: I departed the ZZZ in the afternoon on a training flight with a student who I had been working with in Aircraft X. I had been flying this aircraft most of the day and had observed that we had seven quarts of oil and 25 gallons of fuel; plenty for the local training flight; before we departed. Leaving the airport; we proceeded southbound to practice stalls and steep turns at altitude. At this point in the flight; the aircraft's engine was running smoothly; and the engine instruments were indicating normally. Having spent several hundred hours teaching in this particular aircraft; nothing seemed amiss. After completing these maneuvers; I tactfully asked my student to realign the directional gyro and smoothly pulled the throttle to idle as soon as his right hand left it; simulating an engine failure. As my student completed his required tasks and circled above his selected field; I periodically 'cleared' the engine - smoothly increasing the power to 1500 RPM to ensure that it was running normally during the exercise.When [we] reached an altitude of roughly 800 ft. AGL; I instructed my student to go around. He applied full power and the engine performed normally as we began to climb out. After gaining several hundred ft.; the engine began to shake violently with almost no warning; and a significant loss in power was noted. I reduced the power as the engine felt as if it were going to shake itself off of its mounts. I took control; pitched for best glide; and ran the memory items from the engine failure inflight checklist without success. Gliding towards a field; I began to adjust the power setting and after increasing power from idle several times; the shaking began to dampen. Nearing the field; the engine began to run smoothly again and I elected to climb away from my landing point and proceed to ZZZ1; a X;XXX ft.-long grass strip 3 or 4 miles away. I figured that the much safer landing at ZZZ1 was worth the risk of another 'engine failure' on the two-minute trip over.On the way; my student tuned in ATC and [explained our situation]. After an uneventful landing under power at ZZZ1; I was met by a breathtaking amount of firefighters; EMTs; and [other public officials]. After hearing that I had landed at ZZZ1; the aircraft's owner; who happens to be an A&P Mechanic; drove out to the field. After inspecting the airplane and performing a run-up; the owner determined that there was nothing visibly wrong with the aircraft or the engine and elected to fly it back to its home base of ZZZ. The next morning; it was flown to a repair station in ZZZ2 where we are currently waiting for a diagnosis of the problem.In my opinion; engine roughness and power loss of the duration that I experienced 30 seconds to a minute could either be carburetor icing or fuel contamination. The air temperature was nearly 80°F with a very high temperature/dewpoint spread; making carb icing unlikely. Furthermore; carburetor heat had no effect on the engine shaking and power loss. Fuel contamination could be another possibility. However; I did observe my previous student sump the tanks when the aircraft was last refueled and we were an hour into the flight when the power loss occurred; which makes contamination seem unlikely. Regardless; I was happy with my decision to land on a nearby grass strip instead of attempting to get a suspect airplane back to the airport and feel that I set the right example for my student.

column121: We were approaching the airport from the west on an IFR flight plan. We called the airport in sight roughly 13nm from the field and Approach Control handed us off to Tower. Our company aircraft was ahead of us and already talking to Tower. They were told to enter a left base for Runway 2. We then checked in and gave our position and informed Tower we were on a visual approach for Runway 2. We were told to enter a left base for [Runway] 2. We then saw that our company was just ahead of us by maybe 2 miles and I turned right (to the south) and pulled the power; lowered the landing gear and configured to slow to our final approach speed to ensure separation between us and our company aircraft. Shortly after we were cleared to land on Runway 2. On about a 3-4 mile final and fully configured; we heard tower tell a small aircraft to enter left base; Runway 2. To our surprise; there was a small aircraft just ahead of us and to our left on the base leg. I told the PNF (Pilot not Flying) with me that the small aircraft was very close and was going to hit us. I had to push the nose down and turn to the right while the PNF simultaneously told the Tower Controller about that other airplane. At the same time; the small aircraft began turning final; right into our path. Within a matter of seconds the Tower controller told the small aircraft to go around and he started climbing above us. Since we were faster and below him; I turned back onto the extended centerline and stabilized the approach. This happened on about a 2 mile final. The PNF and I were both in shock that this had happened; especially since the tower was supposedly going to alleviate close calls in the pattern. Upon landing; I called the Tower to speak with a supervisor to discuss what had happened. The supervisor had gone home for the day but the person who answered the phone was the controller who was working tower position at the time of the incident. I told him that we were upset that another plane had come so close to us. I told him that in my XX years of flying; I had never come so close to another airplane in the air and that it shook me up. He said that the small aircraft had reported both us and the company small transport in sight; but I don't remember hearing the small aircraft call us in sight until he pointed us out and told us to go around.I think a major factor in this incident was the fact that the new tower had just begun operations that morning. I also think the controller; not being familiar with the local terrain and area contributed as well. Lastly and what I think is a major factor and was a total surprise to me; was the fact that the tower does not have a radar feed from BNA. In other words; it's a matter of the controllers asking for position reports and trusting that airplanes are where they say they are. From a safety standpoint; this should be added very soon.

column121: This occurrence happened after maneuvers. We were practicing normal takeoffs and landings at ZZZ which had a crosswind component of 10 kt. After a first attempt and go-around; we decided to try again. On the second approach in; we proceeded to come in slow; 50 kt.; and I prompted my student to add in power. However; he was frozen and too fixated to notice the low airspeed. I should have promptly issued a go-around and should have taken the controls. However; I was not forceful enough and was not able to take the controls from my student to go around; resulting in a rough landing and a tail strike. We ended up going around and did not feel there was any difference in controls and continued back to ZZZ1.Later after pushing the plane back; we noticed the damaged tail piece and the bent tail strike protection. This could have all been avoided with just a simple go-around. At the slightest feeling of something not going right - for example; not being lined up or being too slow on final - a go-around will ultimately save a bad landing from happening. The student and the instructor should always be communicating and be aware of the situation that is happening. A positive exchange of controls should be practiced frequently so that the exchange can be flawless and can prevent situations where a student may be fixated or task saturated. The reaction to go around was not quick enough and resulted in the tail strike. Task saturation is a real thing; especially if a student pilot is being introduced to a new airport and also uncontrolled airport operations as well. To wrap things up; going around is your best option and positive exchange of controls should be practiced not only when braking; but also while in the air; even in critical phases of flight.

I just was unable to clear him because of the arrival sequence.The ZZZZZ STAR is a lightning rod for deviations and errors. In this particular situation; it is too close to a 6;300 foot MVA; which means any slight deviation almost guarantees a low altitude event. The MVA's should be reassessed to see if a more reasonable buffer can be created adjacent (east) of the STAR.One other thing I could have done is to keep the arriving aircraft at 7;000 feet; but I wanted to get them as low as possible to get below weather and to see the field; especially in a situation that was already high workload/high complexity. I was counting on the pilots to fly the procedure accurately; which isn't unreasonable since arrivals preceding Aircraft X did not encounter any issues making the turn at ZZZZZ1. But because of the small margin for error; Aircraft X definitely won't be the last.

column121: I was the First Officer and pilot monitoring on our flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. This was the last leg of a three-day trip. We taxied out on time and parked to wait out a ground stop. ZZZ was just starting to get the worst of a tropical storm. Convective SIGMETs for embedded thunderstorms covered much of the mid-Atlantic states. The ground stop lifted and we were able to depart 2 hours and 2 minutes after pushback.The first part of the flight went fine; and we were clear of weather until contacting Approach Control. The controller gave us good vectors; but we still had to penetrate some moderate rain showers. Our aircraft was an older 321 with CRT screens and the old radar display; and it was night by this point. This made it difficult to know the intensity until we were very close to the depicted weather. We were able to keep clear of magenta turbulence indications on the display; yet we still encountered moderate to severe turbulence with speed indications +/- 20 kt. below 8;000 ft. Upon turning base; we were in a clear area and could see one more cell crossing the final approach course. Traffic ahead that had just flown through the same cell reported moderate rain and smooth ride. Our ride was worse than that; and after configuring we got an aural predictive windshear warning; 'GO AROUND; WINDSHEAR AHEAD.' We initiated a go-around. The ride was moderate and there were big airspeed fluctuations; but we didn't get a reactive windshear alert. Approach vectored us back for another ILS. The downwind took us around more moderate intensity rain and turbulence. Approach informed us that traffic behind us had landed; and that we were the only one to go around so far. I believe two aircraft landed between our first approach and our second attempt.Our second approach also resulted in a go-around. When we encountered the heaviest part of the rain; airspeed loss was unacceptable and we initiated the go-around. We did not get a predictive windshear alert. I don't recall if we had a reactive windshear warning; but almost instantly we had multiple ECAM warnings and cautions. The autopilot disconnected and Captain assumed manual control - he was pilot-flying throughout the event. The ride felt very similar to how the simulator presents a windshear event. Recovery felt like it took forever. With no autopilot and multiple F/CTRL ECAM messages; we were fully caught up in recovering to a normal state. We climbed up to 3000; which was [the] missed approach altitude. Flight director guidance was fluctuating a lot; and we turned off FD 1 and 2.Re-configuring the aircraft after the approach was delayed; the airspeed trend arrow indicated a very imminent flap over-speed condition. I asked the Captain if he wanted flaps up; and then raised them when he indicated in the affirmative. My perception here was that we were in level flight and accelerating rapidly. In retrospect; I misjudged our energy state and failed to follow the prescribed schedule for flap retraction; retracting them too quickly. As the flaps were retracting; we were somewhere around 3;100 ft. correcting for 3;000; in moderate turbulence. These factors all compounded; resulting in a low-energy state and stall warning indication. I'm not sure what the auto thrust was commanding at this point; or if it had reduced thrust for us to descend back to 3000. I believe I yelled; 'Nose down!' and Captain responded that he was full forward stick. I momentarily pushed my flight stick forward and was corrected by the aural 'dual input' alert. Captain recovered the aircraft. I gave ATC a quick description of our flight control computer problems and they climbed us to 5000 on vectors. We began the process of going through the ECAM malfunctions; with me working the ECAM. The autopilot was inoperative for the rest of the flight. F/CTRL ALTN LAW was next. There is no follow-up for this. I believe the next was F/CTRL ELAC 1 PITCH FAULT and F/CTRL ELAC 2 PITCH FAULT. I know that's the checklist I went to; but after the fact I can't say whether it was the ELAC PITCH FAULT or a generic ELAC FAULT. The pitch fault follow-up prohibits resetting an ELAC in flight; and so we did not attempt a computer reset. The ELAC FAULT reset procedure does allow a reset in flight if you do it one at a time and there are no uncommanded maneuvers happening.After follow-ups; I called Dispatch to see if we could go to ZZZ2 or ZZZ3 or ZZZ4. We had around 12;000 lb. of fuel. ZZZ4 appeared to have storm cells at the field but ZZZ2 and ZZZ3 were clear. I expressed that we were hand-flying with degraded flight controls and needed a clear airport. Dispatch gave us a minimum fuel of 8.0 to go to ZZZ4 if we could not get into ZZZ. Ultimately; ZZZ updated us that winds were shifting straight out of the north; and they could turn the airport around for us. The non-normal section of the [manual] confirmed we had enough runway landing distance. The final for XXR was clear of storms; and we were able to shoot the ILS and land.So many factors were at play here. At the time we entered ZZZ airspace we had been on duty for 10 hours. We were navigating around severe weather in a tropical storm with the old-style radar. It was working well; but overall; it just doesn't provide the clarity that the new radar presents. We were in continuous turbulence of varying intensities; occasionally severe; before our first approach. Our picture of what the weather was doing was not as clear as the situational awareness that can be achieved in cruise flight. We were relying on ATC vectors through areas that other aircraft had just previously flown. Reports from other aircraft indicated acceptable conditions; or conditions that we could plan for by following severe weather avoidance guidance. The predictive windshear system did its job the first time and we had a clean go-around. Other aircraft landed after our missed approach and conditions were ok. Startle factor played a huge role on the second attempt. Windshear plus multiple ECAMs and autopilot failure created a complex and dynamic situation. We were getting bounced all over the place. We were struggling to get the airplane under control. The monitoring challenge was huge because of the turbulence and the degraded flight controls. I was making FCU inputs in between running checklist items. I had sent an ACARS to Dispatch asking where we should go and listing our system failures; and got no response. The crew phone app worked well enough; but I was frustrated that the feedback we got was that it would be preferred that we hold for ZZZ or go to our listed alternate. I'm sure the Dispatcher could hear my frustration. I am glad that we were able to safely continue to ZZZ; but I wanted to get the plane on the ground without dealing with any more threats to the flight. Holding between thunderstorms with no autopilot in alternate law is an unnecessary risk. I'm not sure why the ground stop for ZZZ was lifted. After the flight; we learned that there had been 7 confirmed tornadoes in the area right around ZZZ. These storms were moving very quickly. It looked like it was possible that ZZZ would clear up before we got there; but there was a good chance it would not. Our decision to go was based on having a lot of fuel; and two alternates. Our second alternate was ZZZ3; which remained clear. This meant that if at any point the path ahead looked bad; we could turn around and have an escape plan. The weather moving in from the south across the final ended up being the worst that we would encounter. If we had delayed this flight by another hour; I think we would have been better off.
column123: On first approach; got a windshear warning and went around. On second approach with moderate to almost severe turbulence; we hit a heavy rain shower. From what I remember we were configured for landing when we hit turbulence. Right then from what I can remember; the autopilot kicked off with the nose pitching up and the speed tape coming up. I pushed the power to climb and tried pushing the nose down. At first; nothing was happening. We did get a low-energy warning too. The plane did recover and started to respond to control inputs. On the ECAM we had F/CTRL ALTN LAW [and] ELAC 1&2 PITCH FAULT. I was flying; the FO (First Officer) did the ECAM and follow-ups and communication. No resets in the air so we looked at going somewhere I could shoot a visual approach. ZZZ Approach had us flying a box pattern until we figured out what we wanted to do. ZZZ Approach then gave us the option to land on XXR and visibility was adequate for a visual. We made an uneventful landing in normal law and gusty crosswinds. I'm guessing we hit the rain at the wrong time.ATC did a good job vectoring us between. The aircraft in front of us just had heavy rain and a smooth ride. Cells were building very fast. I'm thinking that one of the probes froze up momentarily; giving us the speed tape fluctuations. One thing that bothered me was that we couldn't get a hold of Dispatch right away; even after [communicating our situation] over ACARS. The FO did a great job with all the ECAM and checklist procedures.

The only thing I/we were unable to accomplish was getting the manual gear release handle back in the stowed position. At one point [the] FO actually got out of his seat to try and stow it; with no luck.After running the checklist and getting the gear down and locked; I notified Dispatch and Maintenance via ACARS of our situation. I also called our FA (Flight Attendant) and notified her of the situation and informed her we would be returning to ZZZ. After I notified our FA; I made a PA to the passengers and informed them of our situation and that we would be returning to ZZZ. ATC provided priority handling for us. After all appropriate checklists were accomplished; everyone was notified; and everything was coordinated; we headed back for landing.ATC was keeping us north of the field the whole time we were running checklist. Initially; we planned to land on XXL because of our position. After I informed ATC there was the possibility of losing our steering and needing a tug off the runway; I asked if we could take XYL. We accepted XYL as our landing runway and got vectored onto the ILS for a visual approach and landing. Landing was normal. The FO touched down very smoothly with a very slow rate of descent. We taxied off the runway and to our gate. During our taxi into the gate; we got a HYD 3 HI TEMP [and the] hydraulic temperature of System 3 was 93 degrees. FO ran the QRH for that as I taxied in.Once we parked safely at the gate; a Gate Agent came onto the airplane and talked to myself and the FA. She said the customer service representative at the gate wanted to keep the passengers on the airplane until we got the situation figured out. I relayed that message to the passengers; also letting them know that the door was open and if anyone didn't want to remain on the airplane and they felt like they needed to get off the airplane they could. Maintenance arrived at the airplane and I told him what had happened. The nose gear didn't come up when I selected the gear up and we had to do an air return. I have no suggestions. Would like to see this scenario in the sim.

column123: This was the last leg of a six day pattern. Fatigue was not the primary cause; but certainly a contributing factor. This was an OE flight with the FO (First Officer) being the PF (Pilot Flying) and trainee. The PM (Pilot Monitoring) was a Captain LCA (Line Check Airman) and two other FO's were onboard. The flight was being vectored around weather for a visual approach to Runway XX. The autopilot was engaged; we were above the glideslope; and approximately 5 miles from ZZZZZ our altitude was above 8;000 feet. I mentioned that we seemed high; and soon after the gear and speedbrakes were extended. I also spoke of the pitfalls of getting ALT before G/S capture and that using vertical speed instead of FLCH was the correct way to solve that problem. We did get ALT and the FO disconnected the autopilot which significantly increased the work load. I switched to Tower; and shortly after we went from above glideslope to approximately 1 dot below. Speedbrakes were extended; flaps were going to 25 and then 30. Tower issued a low altitude alert; and the FO responded back to glidepath. We never heard a GPWS glideslope warning. After securing the airplane at the gate; all four of us thoroughly debriefed the event. We emphasized automation management and specifically the result of turning off the autopilot which significantly increased everyone's workload. Another emphasis was situational awareness and how the 787 does not slow and descend as quickly as the 777 the FO had previously flown. We also talked about monitor crosscheck and the need to speak up earlier to address an approach that is becoming high and fast. Finally; I talked about leadership effectiveness and my lack of being more assertive instead of allowing the student to continue into that situation. Additionally; during the debrief for my own knowledge and clarity; I asked the other pilots if the speedbrakes had been retracted by 1;000 feet; the autothrottles had remained engaged; the glideslope was captured and if we had met the stabilized approach criteria. The others agreed that was the case. Finally; perhaps the training center could include a training scenario where the glideslope needs to be captured after the FAF with ALT engaged.

Approach calls us and says they have a low altitude alert on use as we were now below the minimum vector altitude for that area.  She asks if we missed the turn and I said 'No'; that the aircraft has a turn radius as we are turning to the north. She said minimum vector altitude was 10;900 feet and we were at 10;300 feet. We stopped our descent and the aircraft dropped out of the approach mode. Approach asked if we had the terrain insight; luckily for us it was clear with 10 mile visibility and we could see cultural lighting on the hills and knew terrain was not an immediate factor. None of the Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System annunciated and we were always in either the black or hashed green on the ND. Back on the inbound course; we selected a lower altitude and armed the approach. Nothing further.Center gave us a speed and we didn't get relief until we asked Approach. This higher speed resulted in a larger turn radius than had we been at the mandatory 210 knots restriction at ZZZZZ2. They also gave us direct to a Fly-Over fix with a 90 degree intercept; which set us up to fly through our final approach course; and asked us to cross ZZZZZ2 at 11;000 feet instead of the mandatory +13;000 feet restriction.   This was all done to keep the other aircraft from getting a vector or slowing down. Don't give direct to a fly-over fix with 90 degrees of turn required at the fix; especially at night; at lower than published altitude; and in mountainous terrain.

column121: First Officer's Qualification Line Check which concluded First Officer's IOE (Initial Operating Experience). First Officer was Pilot Flying. Check Airman was Pilot Monitoring. Normal arrival via SILCN5.KLIDE for ILS 30L at SJC. Shortly after KLIDE; both pilots became aware of flashes of intense blue laser light illuminating the windscreens for 1 to 2 seconds. Pilot Flying continued the approach referencing the instruments rather than scanning outside. Pilot Monitoring reported the threat to NORCAL Approach. After the handoff to SJC Tower; another burst of the same blue laser light appeared; this time from the right side of the aircraft. The flight leveled off at 3;300 feet and the Pilot Monitoring reported the latest burst to the Tower Controller.The distraction of both the laser events themselves and the reporting of the events to NCT (NorCal TRACON) and SJC Tower caused the Pilot Flying to lose track of the briefed stabilized approach plan. The delay in configuration caused the aircraft to be well above the glide path past the final approach fix. There was no way to continue the approach and remain within stabilized approach criteria; so the crew executed a missed approach. column123: Flight was final leg of First Officer's (Initial Operating Experience) with the Captain as Line Captain. Line Captain was Pilot Monitoring while First Officer was Pilot Flying. The Pilot Monitoring continued to scan for additional evidence of directed laser illumination and landmarks for reference; but did not mention the initial burst to the Pilot Flying. Several seconds later; a subsequent burst of flashes of light appeared to illuminate the windscreens; at which time the Pilot Flying also saw the light.Pilot Flying reported the incident to the NCT Approach Controller; and passed along generalized street locations of the position of the light. Within a minute; at the time of handover to SJC Tower; the flight was subjected to a third illumination burst viewed peripherally by the Pilot Flying; with the Pilot Monitoring noting the dazzle effect of the light on the flight deck windows. At this point; the flight leveled off at approximately 3;300 feet and the Pilot Monitoring contacted the Tower Controller; reporting the continued laser illumination from the same vicinity.At this time; the Pilot Flying noted that the flight was well above the vertical path and was not yet configured according to the briefed Stabilized Approach Plan. The crew immediately began speed reductions and configuration for approach; but soon determined that the flight was 'well above' the glide path and well past the final approach fix. The crew discontinued the approach at approximately 2;700 feet and climbed to maintain 3;000 feet per Tower instruction; and soon switched back to NORCAL for vectors back to final.Subsequent vectors to final and final approach and landing via the ILS to 30L were uneventful. The Pilot Flying drew the flight deck sun shades as a precaution from possible further laser illumination. There were no further illuminations observed during this second approach.It appeared that the source was from a club establishment that was using a laser light source with some reflective device that was reflecting the light upwards. The illumination appeared to be random and unintentional. The atmospheric conditions were clear with very little particulate in the air; which did not refract the laser light when it was directed away from our aircraft; neither crew noted any laser light being directed anywhere other than at our aircraft.

column121: While on approach to Runway 30 and flying the ILS 30 approach the aircraft automation intercepted the glide slope from below after a momentary fluctuation from the glide slope signal. For a split second the glide slope indicator fluctuated from full up to full down about 15 miles away from the airport. At that moment the aircraft automation captured the glide slope from below and the aircraft started an abrupt pitch up attitude. To fly the glide path and at that moment I disconnected the autopilot and continued the approach manually (there was no deviation from ATC instructions). The glide slope indicator did that a second time right before landing again along with the flight director. It took us a bit to understand why that happened; but here is my theory.When landing west in Miami; the airport uses Runway 30 for landing and 27 for takeoff (intersecting runways). Every time an aircraft was cleared to take off Runway 27 the moment that aircraft passed adjacent to the glide slope antenna there was a fluctuation with the glide slope indicator in the aircraft; and with the flight director since they were coupled. We flew this approach many times and on different aircraft since then and every time the same thing happens. When an aircraft is cleared for takeoff from Runway 27 and passes the glide slope antenna we received a fluctuation (full pitch up and down from the flight director and glide slope signal). My recommendation would be for the FAA to investigate and see if this is true. Also for the time being I would recommend the airport uses the RNAV approach to Runway 30; or publish an amendment to the approach to not allow an autopilot coupled approach. Thankfully we caught this situation early when we got the abrupt pitch up attitude of the autopilot following the flight director and glide slope signal; but it can easily turn into an unusual attitude situation if caught off guard.

column121: Prior to departure we briefed the multiple MEL/CDL (Configuration Deviation List)/NEFs (Non-Essential for Flight) on file for this aircraft including MEL XX-XX-XX AUXILIARY POWER UNIT. While the Form sticker said BLEED APU LEAK; the APU as a whole was deferred; so we briefed and followed the procedures for MEL XX-XX-XX as opposed to MEL YY-YY-YY (which was not listed). While in cruise at approximately XA50Z the EICAS displayed caution message BLEED APU LEAK while the APU was inoperative; off and the APU BLEED button was pushed OUT. MEL XX-XX-XX makes no mention of BLEED APU LEAK being an expected EICAS message but the QRH procedure did not make sense to me in this situation. My FO (First Officer) and I decided together it would be best to contact Maintenance for further insight; so I transferred the radios and flight controls to the FO and proceeded to contact dispatch via ARINC (Commercial Radio) at around XA53Z. After a normal exchange with ZZZ1 Radio and patching into our Dispatcher I requested to talk to Maintenance and the Dispatcher responded that 'Maintenance would not talk to me in flight and to follow the QRH' even after insisting several times. We proceeded to follow the remainder of the QRH and had to descend to FL300 and continue the flight with single bleed. Upon arrival into ZZZ2 I made the appropriate entry into the AML (Aircraft Maintenance Logbook) for a BLEED APU LEAK EICAS caution message. In my opinion this was a complete breakdown in CRM between the flight crew and Dispatch/Maintenance. I accept responsibility if this MEL was incorrect and should have been YY-YY-YY; but if that is the case; it has been incorrect for 10 days worth of flights. When I saw the APU deferred as a whole I considered that an acceptable solution to an APU Bleed leak; however there is no mention in XX-XX-XX of any special procedure for BLEED APU LEAK EICAS message. Furthermore; I do not have the full information in flight as to why the APU was deferred as opposed to the APU BLEED over a week prior to this event. I believe our decision to contact Maintenance for further guidance via ARINC was sound; and if they had simply answered our call for help we could have avoided descending to FL300 with a single bleed/PACK. There are numerous examples of NTSB accident reports where a safer outcome was achieved thanks to the pilots communicating with Maintenance while in flight; and throughout my training with Company I have always been trained to use all resources available. While I do not know whether Dispatch refused to talk to Maintenance or Maintenance refused to talk to me; I strongly recommend this practice of not allowing pilots to contact Maintenance during irregular situations in flight cease immediately.

As I approached minimum altitude; I was slightly below glide-slope and right of course. I was able to recognize the airport environment; but did not have forward visibility and could not identify the runway environment. I began to initiate the missed approach at about the same time the tower instructed me to go around.  Since it appeared ZZZ1 was below minimums I elected to divert to ZZZ2. I landed at ZZZ2 without incident.I was not aware that I may have created an unsafe situation until I was contacted via phone by the FAA ASI on Date. I was informed at that time that ATC had forwarded the incident for investigation. It appears that at the termination of my approach; before initiating the missed approach procedure my aircraft overflew the adjacent taxiway where two airliners were holding.

column121: This is the second time I have landed at ZZZZ1 (the first was a normal IFR landing at dusk 2 years earlier). ZZZZ1 is a high use uncontrolled training airport located under ZZZZ's Class B airspace. It proved to be a very busy afternoon with 4 to 6 aircraft simultaneously in the pattern. Some pilots had very limited English proficiency. The ATIS listed in ForeFlight for ZZZZ1 is actually for ZZZZ so the Runway information is misleading. The lack of clear communications and the traffic density resulted in my experiencing Task Saturation for the first time since I completed my training 20 years earlier.Issue 1 - Unexpected runway change. Based on my communications with ATC I was expecting to land on Runway XX from my IFR approach and did not have warning that Runway XY was the active runway until after being instructed by ZZZZ to change to the ZZZZ1 Unicom. After listening to the ZZZZ1 Unicom I broke off my approach to Runway XX because I found the conflicting runway was in use and sought to understand what the traffic was doingIssue 2 - Confusion TCAS/sight/radio reports. As I approached the airport; the aircraft I saw in the air; corresponded with the aircraft I saw on the TCAS screen. The self-announcement pattern positions from the aircraft appeared to correspond with what I saw in the air and on TCAS. What I did not realize was the aircraft I saw were not the ones reporting the positions I heard. There were likely others in the same relative position at the opposite end of the field at the same time. I consequently unintentionally set myself up for Runway XZ thinking it was Runway XY. I did a 45-degree entry into what I thought was the left downwind leg for Runway XY and a heard conflicting mid field downwind traffic report which I could not locate and decided to exit the pattern and reenter. Another pilot informed me I was actually on the upwind side for Runway XY and I subsequently set myself up in sequence for entry into the pattern for Runway XY.  As I was in the downwind someone used 20 seconds on the Unicom asking for a weather radar for an area 20 miles report north of the airport. On downwind I slowed down for the aircraft in front. The only part of their call sign I could understand was Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y called base. I called base. Aircraft Y called final. I extended my downwind a bit and later called final. I lost sight of Aircraft Y and as I was trying to reestablish their location; I lowered the nose to see. Aircraft Y eventually came into my view as I was abeam him; but I could not reduce speed further to get behind him. He was low and to the right of the final approach course. In hindsight my best guess is he was doing 65 kts. or less (my minimum normal approach speed is 80 kts.) When I had become aware we were converging I advised him and he said 'sir that's illegal ??? theres off the words two cows on the left on final' [Verbatim]. I was trying to make sense of what he had just said and was preparing to go around but then I heard him say 'Going around for Runway XY' at which point I thought the safest thing to do at that point was continue with my landing on Runway XY. There was no injuries or damage to either aircraft.As I was focusing on situational awareness another pilot consumed 20 seconds on the Unicom asking someone on the Base radio to check the weather radar well north of the Airport. Having the pattern frequency used for other purpose reduced everyone's opportunity for situational awareness. ZZZZ ATC was very insistent I understood they were holding the airspace open for me and twice read me an 800 number to call on the ground. I felt pressured to cancel IFR while in the air. After landing I later saw a sign in the Pilot Dispatch area saying 'keep the Unicom Free' and advising the use of XXX.XXX for Weather and Airport information. However; the frequency is not published in [our database] and when a local CFI and I tried it a few days later we found it was inoperative.The pilot in Aircraft Y I conflicted with was often impossible to understand; even though he had made several radio calls; I could never establish what his call sign was. Variations in US/Country X procedures. I entered the pattern per US VFR entry rules; I was not aware the [country] rules do not allow for two of the common US VFR entry methods. Given its location relative to the ZZZZ Class B airspace the remaining VFR entry options are very limitedI found having coverage terminated by ATC with limited prior airport information severely impacted my situational awareness; resulting in the beginnings of task saturation. Use of the Unicom for non-essential communications reduced opportunities for everyone to provide position reports. I lost a sense of where Aircraft Y was; and when Aircraft Y came into my view I was already abeam him. Normally I would have immediately gone around but I was trying to understand what he was saying.I have since reviewed the [country] VFR pattern entry rules with a local CFI and done several VFR pattern entries with him at ZZZZ1. I have booked time with my regular CFI to reevaluate and refresh my VFR skills and go over the incident with him. In future I will assume my runway can be reassigned to anything at anytime after arrival and will study every runway before arrival and map out the situational awareness should I be required to change. I will put the Common traffic frequency in Radio two and monitor ten miles out (well before instructed by ATC) to determine what runaway is being used rather than wait until the controller says to switch.A dedicated ZZZZ1 ATIS (rather than using ZZZZ's) that included announcing the active runway in use would have reduced confusion and would do a lot to help be prepared for the current traffic pattern. A dedicated ZZZZ1 ATIS with weather remarks appended (rather than using the common Unicom frequency) would have reduced the need for other pilots to ask someone to check the weather and increased the available time for all pilots to provide position reports. Audit students' ability to clearly communicate in English when in the pattern and especially under stress.

column121: Airport Operations witnessed this event from the ground. A C172 took off to remain in the right closed traffic pattern from Runway XX. Next to take off was a Mooney M20. As the C172 was partway through their crosswind; the M20 turned a very early right crosswind with the intention to depart to the east. In doing so; the M20 cut inside the pattern. The C172 turned right downwind and was now on a perpendicular collision course with the Mooney. The M20 passed in front of and slightly below the C172.Immediately after this near miss; Tower queried the M20 if they were aware of the local departure procedures. The M20 replied 'not really' - they were a transient aircraft. Tower clarified that the ZZZ departure that they were shooting was to be flown via runway heading until past the diamond-shaped waterway; then turning east. This M20 turned before the waterway; producing a very early crosswind turn.Here's a friendly reminder to GA pilots to familiarize themselves with local approach and departure procedures when flying out of unfamiliar airports.

column121: On a typical week-end trip with friends; we wanted a drone shot in a scenic location; so I searched recommended spots and found that Red Rock was a popular spot; confirmed on the map that it was far enough from the airport and that it was far enough from the wilderness area; so we went there. Into the hike we came across a sign indicating that the wilderness area started there; a bit closer than the map seemed to indicate; so we canceled the plan; and I hiked back to the car to put the drone back in the trunk; and we went for the hike again. After the hike; we had such great views that I figured we could still do a panorama shot safely while staying outside the wilderness area. A friend was the designated watcher; and I quickly prepared the drone for a quick shot while our friends waited. I took off and went to a safe altitude of 400 ft.; and started heading towards Red Rock mountain to frame the shot properly. Then the phone screen dimmed suddenly and became harder to read; but I could still clearly see that I was still far from the mountain and the wilderness area; so I headed towards it. What I didn't realize is that the phone had been heat-soaked in the car in the Arizona summer sun all afternoon; and had stopped updating the screen altogether. So while it displayed a picture of the drone safely at a distance; the drone was actually advancing; so I was surprised and confused when the designated watcher called that the drone was out of sight. We talked; and as I went to show him the video feed; the screen went dark. When I turned the phone back on; the connection with the drone was lost.Given last position and direction; it probably crashed near the summit of the Red Rock mountain; hopefully too high to endanger anyone. But it's a touristic wilderness area; so I checked with a ranger who said it was not a problem; that it happens all the time. I'm still worried that the drone likely crashed in a wilderness area; and really hoping it didn't endanger anyone. It's very frustrating as I was trying to do things safely and legally. I should have realized faster that I had lost video feedback and was flying blind. Instead I allowed myself to be distracted by the dimming of the screen. Next time I will pay attention to the heat of course; and should something confusing happen; I will come back and land to sort it out.

column121: I was asked to train a CPC-IT with over a decade of radar experience and with over half of the allocated hours allowed for the position at hand. Traffic was light and I kept getting distracted by the Data position near the radar scope. I had to stand further away than I usually would because of the constant traffic in and out of the data position; noise from the load speaker; and trying to have some social distancing for COVID.  I have made many complaints about the data position being a complete distraction and today it most certainly was a contributing factor to a NMAC.Aircraft X departed ZZZ and the tower put the aircraft on a 250 heading. The aircraft never checked in and I scrambled to call the tower so they could climb and switch the aircraft before it crossed directly over the obstruction depicted on the video map and below the MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude). While this was going on; there were 2 other aircraft on frequency that were becoming a conflict. Once I realized that the trainee was not doing any of the instructions me or the supervisor was giving; I took over the frequency to prevent a loss of separation. Unfortunately; in my scramble to coordinate with all the appropriate sectors and facilities that Aircraft X was seconds from violating; I missed a readback from Aircraft X and they took another aircraft's instruction. I did not notice Aircraft X turning northeast bound immediately because of the coordination at hand and Aircraft X turned right at Aircraft Y that was VFR on frequency. I instructed Aircraft X to turn left and climb; but Aircraft X was already too far in the turn and I continued the right turn back to the east. I however did expect Aircraft X to climb in a timely manner in which they did not. This in turn created a dangerous situation that forced Aircraft Y to turn to the north to avoid the traffic. Although traffic was issued to Aircraft X; I did not see how close the aircraft actually got from the distance I was forced to be from the scope and my coordination efforts that needed to be done.I believe this event happened from combination of multiple events and some expectation bias.  The Data position being a major distraction; COVID social distancing; ZZZ tower procedures allowing an aircraft to depart on a heading at an obstruction and maintaining an altitude below the MVA; Aircraft X not checking in; training on the position; expecting the CPC-IT to not freeze up; Aircraft X not climbing in the timely manner that I assumed they would have; and most importantly; I take responsibility and will definitely lose sleep over the fact that in my scramble; I missed the read back that ended up putting 2 planes in a dangerous situation.My recommendations to hopefully minimize any such event from occurring again would be to:MOVE THE DATA POSITION!Change the departure pie for ZZZ departures off Runway XX.

column121: I was flying pilot. Approach was fully briefed. AMOS 1E STAR; transitioning to an RNP approach from HADAS. Descending in VNAV Path. Cleared direct MORIA and cleared the approach. Normal stable descent; normal procedures and speed reduction. MORIA waypoint in the FMC must have had 3;000A instead of 3;600A; because we crossed MORIA between 3;600 and 3;000; when the altitude we should cross MORIA at is 3;600 or above. It is on the chart as 3;600A. We became aware when the controller questioned our altitude at MORIA and if we has visual terrain clearance and the runway in sight; which we did. We landed without incident in a stable configuration throughout the approach. Upon reflection; I do not know how that altitude at MORIA in the FMC was 3;000 instead of 3;600. Fatigue a factor after a long overnight flight. 1st time flying the trip with a 4th pilot; which disrupted expected rest pattern. We had multiple GPS outages on the descent and it was distracting as we were discussing the backup plan of an ILS should the GPS not return. Although this is a known issue of the GPS outages in that area; this particular outage lasted much longer throughout the descent than my previous experience. As a result; I had both approach plates queued and it took away from my normal progressive crosscheck of chart against glass routine on RNAV approaches. Regardless of distractions; as the flying pilot I need to do a better job of progressively checking the progress of the VNAV points on the approach. It is not enough to check the altitudes during the approach briefing and then rely on the data to all be correct. Fatigue after a long flight should have heightened my awareness of potential omissions or errors in the data. I have learned from this event and will increase my awareness and cross-check moving forward.
column123: While descending into TLV we were flying the AMMOS 1E STAR to HADAS and then the HADAS transition to  an RNP Approach.  We were cleared for the approach.  We were proceeding when the controller asked us about our altitude.  I said we were going to cross MORIA at 3;000 feet.  He said it should be 3;600 feet. He then asked if we had the terrain in sight. We said we had the terrain and the airport in sight. We then realized that somehow the FMC altitude for MORIA had switched from 3;600A to 3;000.  We continued to the field and landed without any further problems.  First time into TLV.  Very concerned about the special procedures for the clearance to enter airspace by 180 miles and the loss of GPS signal during the descent.   Delaying vectors and multiple speed changes added to distractions from monitoring FMC altitudes and possible changes to those altitudes.  Language barrier also present with controllers. They had to repeat themselves a few times and we had to as well. Very difficult to understand how or why the wrong altitude was in the FMC.  I may have let my guard down once all the earlier problems had been overcome. Especially after a 9 hour flight.  I should have continued to monitor better and not trust the automation and VNAV.

column121: On climbout of ZZZ Flight ABC we experienced a 1000 pound differential between main tanks on initial departure/climb-out.  The Captain pointed to the wing fuel quantity indicators and the left was amber indicating an imbalance between wing tanks.  We were on center tank feed so no fuel should be used in this condition.  I continued flying to a level off at FL260 and the CA ran the QRH for a fuel imbalance followed by the me backing him up by going through the QRH to confirm our situation. The CA plotted our fuel to the next waypoint which was ZZZZZ and were 1000 lbs below planned. Within a few minutes our fuel was 1500 lbs below planned fuel to the next waypoint ZZZZZ. The decision was made to request priority handling; shutdown engine #1 per the QRH; and return to ZZZ.   I ran the non normal checklists; cleanup items; and reviewed the evacuation checklist. The CA flew the approach and landing which were uneventful; stopped the aircraft on the runway; and had ARFF check for a visible leak. After confirmation that there were no fuel leaks we taxied the aircraft to parking and shutdown the aircraft normally.There are no causal factors by me that played a role in the event.I believe an aircraft history should be pulled to check for any history of fuel quantity malfunctions or any fuel system maintenance has been   completed for this this tail number.
column123: Fuel imbalance developed during climb of 1000 lbs - left wing low within minutes of departure. Leaving 10;000 feet. Cabin crew was asked to perform a cabin walk through with attention paid to possible fuel emissions visible aft of wing from No.1 engine. No visible fuel leak was evident as communicated by cabin crew. We stopped climb at FL260. Position; time and fuel comparison with Flight Plan Review showed us 1000 lbs low at first fix after level off as we ran QRH IMBAL checklist. Subsequent FMC PROG fix (fix name: ZZZZZ) initially showed us estimating 1000 lbs low crossing the fix; then 1500 lbs low; then 1700 lbs low as we approached ZZZZZ. FMC PROG fuel estimate deterioration occurred rapidly over the course of just a few minutes. QRH IMBAL checklist led to Fuel Leak Engine Checklist - parameters indicated probable fuel leak No.1 engine - which led to Engine No. 1 shutdown. All checklists to include precautionary landing checklist were performed. ATC and Dispatch notified. Flight attendants and Passengers advised of return to ZZZ for a precautionary landing.  Single engine landing was performed - Captain flying. After landing we stopped on the runway; ARFF inspected aircraft; found no leaks or damage; and we taxied to the gate. The following AML entries were made: 1) possible fuel leak leading to engine No. 1 shutdown; 2) info to maintenance item: No 1 engine windmilling time 15 minutes; 3) info to maintenance item: landing was accomplished below maximum landing weight. Report made to Dispatch of engine failure and emergency declaration. FO did a great job - especially so given his approx 100 hours in seat and on type. Comment: cabin crew kept cool and were professional. Comment: I made every effort to be both clear and deliberate during each step of the event; to solicit FO's input; and - as we returned to ZZZ - I slowed the aircraft approximately 20 miles from the field and kept the cockpit CRM 'in the green' to the maximum extent possible.

column121: On short final we encountered wake turbulence from a heavy that had landed on the parallel 28R and I executed a go around. The controller told us to fly runway heading and maintain 3;000 ft. As we were climbing we received an RA for traffic that was in the departure corridor at 2;000 ft (a Cirrus). The First Officer had the Cirrus in sight. Wake turbulence dictated a go around and a Cirrus in the departure corridor were the cause of this event. I always anticipate a missed/go around; however I don't believe ATC anticipated us going around and allowed the conflicting traffic to fly through the airspace. I am in no way blaming ATC because that may be standard practice for them.

column121: We were proceeding direct to HEVVN when ATC instructed us to cross LEGGT at FL270.  The RNAV arrival had already been loaded in the FMS and briefed with the altitude crossing restrictions confirmed in the flight plan.  FL270 was set and confirmed in the Altitude Preselect and the VNAV was armed.  The airplane intercepted the VPATH and we were given a frequency change.  When the Pilot Monitoring (PM) checked in with the controller advising we were FL28.5 descending to cross LEGGT at FL270; the controller responded that we were past LEGGT and to confirm our crossing restriction.  The PM advised ATC we had an issue/conflict with our FMS and ATC cleared us to expedite a descent to FL190.  The rest of the flight was completed without further event.Reflecting back on the event; I think there are several factors that contributed.  First; the MAATY1 RNAV Arrival is one of the new arrivals as part of the greater Florida Metroplex airspace revamp.  However; the first two fixes in our flight plan on the arrival; HEVVN and LEGGT; are the same first two fixes on the FOOXX5 arrival.  Up until the last month; we had routinely flown the FOOXX5 arrival into TPA numerous times each month for the last several years.  From my perspective; one of the key important differences between the FOOXX5 and MAATY1 arrivals is that all the altitudes listed in the FOOXX5 are 'expect'; while in the MAATY1 they are published as mandatory (without 'expect').  Another key difference is that in the FOOXX5; the procedure calls for a crossing restriction 'AT' LEGGT at FL270...The new MAATY1 procedure calls for a crossing restriction 'AT OR ABOVE' LEGGT at FL270.  When previously loading the FOOXX5 arrival into our FMS; we had to manually enter the crossing altitudes into the flight plan since all of the altitudes in the procedure were 'expect'.  When loading the MAATY1 arrival into our FMS; all of the altitude restrictions are automatically loaded into the flight plan.  So; today when we loaded the MAATY1 into the FMS; both the PM and myself saw the 'at or above FL270' at LEGGT that was automatically loaded in the flight plan when the procedure was selected.  We both mistook that as crossing 'AT FL270'.  Hence; when our VNAV VPATH was intercepted; it had us crossing LEGGT 'at or above FL270' as properly depicted in the published procedure - despite our ATC clearance to cross LEGGT 'AT' FL270.In short summary the factors contributing to this event were:1) New MAATY1 RNAV ARRIVAL in use with common fixes from FOOXX5.2) Same altitude with difference constraints between MAATY1/FOOXX5 ('Expect' FL270 'AT' LEGGT in FOOXX5 vs. published 'AT OR ABOVE' FL270 at LEGGT in MAATY1).3) FMS programming error in FMS VNAV/lack of close cross-checking altitude constraints vs. ATC clearance by crew.4) ATC issuing a crossing restriction at a fix (LEGGT 'AT' FL270) on the assigned RNAV arrival that differed from the STAR published restriction (LEGGT 'AT or ABOVE' FL270) without emphasizing the change.To prevent this recurrence; we as a crew will be much more diligent in cross-checking altitudes in the FMS flight plan whenever crossing restrictions are issued by ATC; specifically when differentiating between crossing 'AT' vs 'AT or ABOVE'.  We will also query ATC if there are any questions when the clearance issued by ATC contradicts published altitudes or crossing restrictions in a procedure. I also think it would be beneficial for all involved if there was a way for ATC to emphasize crossing altitude instructions whenever they differ from published altitudes or crossing restrictions in the SID/STAR.  I think something along the lines of 'descend via MAATY1 except cross LEGGT AT FL270' may have helped in this scenario; though it is possible that may be too redundant or possibly be cause for additional confusion for other crews/controllers.  It comes down finding a way to differentiate between the assigned clearance of crossing a fix 'AT' compared to the published restriction'AT or ABOVE'.
column123: While flying the MAATY1 arrival yesterday into TPA; we were given an altitude restrictions to 'cross LEGGT at FL270.'  27;000 was entered into the altitude preselector and FL270 was already pre-programmed into the FMS; as this is the altitude shown on the arrival. VNAV on the auto-pilot was armed; and we intercepted the VPATH to FL270. We were given a frequency change and when I checked in I said that we were '28;500 descending to 27;000 at LEGGT'.  The controller said that we had already crossed LEGGT and asked what our previously assigned altitude restriction was. I saw that we were on the Glide Path to 27;000 and wasn't sure immediately why we hadn't arrived at 27;000 at LEGGT.  I said that 'we were assigned 27;000 at LEGGT and that we were having an FMS issue.'  The detail that the crew failed to notice was that the FL270 is an AT OR ABOVE altitude as depicted on the arrival plate and as pre-programmed in the FMS.  We used the VNAV mode on the autopilot and the display on the G5000 appeared to be bringing us to 27;000 at LEGGT. We were then cleared to FL190 and told to expedite; which we did.  Later we were given MAATY at 13;000 and 250kts and the FMS functioned as expected.  After taking some time to diagnose the issue; we learned that the FMS was pre-programmed to cross LEGGT AT OR ABOVE FL270.  Not to cross AT FL270 as instructed. After thoroughly debriefing the flight; there are multiple factors as to why I believe this event occurred.1) The implementation of the new arrivals from the Florida Metroplex and the similarities (and subtle differences) between the MAATY1 and the FOOXX5 arrivals.2) Even though the altitudes in the FMS were briefed; the crew failed to notice the altitude constraint difference between the pre-loaded altitudes in the FMS and the clearance received from ATC.3) ATC used an altitude restriction from the FOOXX5 as an altitude restriction on the MAATY1.4) ATC did not emphasize the difference between the clearance and the published arrival.1) The pilots have been flying the FOOXX5 arrival regularly for many years.  The FOOXX5 says to EXPECT LEGGT at FL270; and it was very common for the controllers to issue this restriction. We would always enter FL270 AT LEGGT manually into the FMS. By entering the altitude manually; we always create an 'AT' altitude. Since the new procedure shows the same altitude at the same point I think that it is easy for the crew to assume that the FMS will cross LEGGT at FL270; just as it always has. However; 'AT OR ABOVE' FL270 is now pre-programmed in the FMS and the auto-pilot will not cross LEGGT at FL270 like it did previously.  It now requires re-entering the altitude into the FMS as an 'AT' altitude if the controller issues the 'cross LEGGT 'AT' FL270' like they have done for many years.  2) To prevent this from happening in the future; the crew must be sure to cross-check the constraints ('AT OR ABOVE' vs 'AT' altitudes) for the arrival.  The crew must also be aware that ATC altitude restrictions MAY NOT coincide with the published arrival procedures and must be sure to cross-check each clearance.3) There are similarities between the FOOXX5 and the MAATY1 in that they use some of the same fixes (HEVVN and LEGGT).  The published altitudes at LEGGT are subtly different.  FOOXX5 publishes expect LEGGT 'AT' FL270 and MAATY1 publishes cross LEGGT 'AT OR ABOVE' FL270.  The controller used the altitude constraint from the FOOXX5 as opposed to the altitude constraint on the MAATY1. The controller that issued 'cross LEGGT at FL270' may have issued that clearance hundreds of times in his career from the FOOXX5 and may not think anything of it; even though this clearance differs from the published altitude in the MAATY1. With MAATY1 programmed; the FMS in our aircraft schedules the crossing of LEGGT somewhere between FL280 and FL290 since it is projecting a 3 degree glidepath to GOJOE between FL260 and FL210 and MAATY AT 13;000. To make our FMS cross LEGGT 'AT' FL270; it requires reprogramming the altitude restriction in the FMS.  This is easily missed since the altitude displayed next to LEGGT is FL270 within the FMS.  4) If a clearance differs from the published arrival procedure; it would be helpful if ATC would emphasize that difference. For example 'Descend via the MAATY1 EXCEPT cross LEGGT at FL270.' Going forward the crew will also be sure to question ATC when a clearance does not match a published procedure.

column121: Pre-flight document review: Flight Plan indicated extra fuel; cruise at FL320 due to APU use. MEL 24.01a also listed on flight plan.Arriving Captain (CA) briefed me on aircraft status; MEL 24-XX-X for #1 IDG: Requires running APU; Max Altitude 33;000 feet. Otherwise there were no other problems with the aircraft (as reported by CA).Once in cockpit; CA & First Officer (FO) review of MEL 24-XX-X indicated a requirement to (M) c) 'Operator ensures the APU oil quantity if adequate for the intended flight.'* Both CA & FO interpreted this to mean APU Oil quantity check prior to each flight.* CA called Maintenance to ensure and APU oil quantity check was accomplished.* Maintenance came; read the log book & MEL; concluded that an oil quantity check was not required.Pre & post-engine start procedures of MEL were successfully accomplishedDuring departure (approx. 8;000 feet) got 'VENT SKIN VALVE FAULT'; accomplished ECAM procedures (Blower & Extract to OVRD). QRH and Supplemental procedures were reviewed; flight continued.At cruise altitude (FL32;000 feet) we started selecting potential divert fields with adequate runway length; putting fixes and 100 nm rings around. We updated them along the path; and pre-briefed our plan in case of generator failure.Approx 80 NM SW of ZZZ; got 'ELEC GEN 2 FAULT'; with IDG temp high.  Accomplished ECAM procedures; including disconnecting IDG.  Now single generator ops.At this point PM (CA) requested immediate assistance'; nature of problem; and told ATC we were turning toward ZZZ; required vectors for immediate approach & landing. At this point; CA tasked PF (FO) to take ATC comm; descend & set up for ZZZ arrival. FO passed SOB and fuel state.CA briefed Flight Attendants; Passengers; then took back ATC radio duties. Crew set up & briefed ILS XX approach to ZZZ; reviewed non-normal procedures; contacted ZZZ OPS for gate assignment. FO flew arrival and landing to ZZZ Runway XX in VFR conditions.After landing taxied to gate XX; wrote up Generator #2; debriefed to Maintenance personnel.Cause -1. Aircraft was dispatched away from a major maintenance base with an inoperative IDG/Generator.2. MEL does not clearly describe APU oil quantity check (one time; or prior to each flight).3. MEL does not require the opposite side IDG oil level to be checked.4. MEL category B allows too much time. Believe this MEL should only be for a single flight (ferry) to a maintenance base.Suggestions -1. Review MEL 24-XX; rewrite to clearly define oil quantity check requirements. Ensure both APU & other IDG are serviced/checked prior to EACH flight.2. Review Airbus failure data for IDG's; consider re-setting MEL 24 from cat B to single flight only.3. Review maintenance records for this aircraft; specifically the IDG servicing. Determine why/how BOTH IDGs on the same plane can fail within 3 flight legs/2 days. Possibly the units were both serviced at the same time but improperly; or contaminated; or serviced with improper fluid.
