column121: I was completing my run-up at the arrival end of Runway XY of ZZZ when I witnessed a runway incursion event that could have resulted in two accidents involving three aircraft. Across the runway from me; Aircraft Y taxied up and was holding for landing traffic on Runway XY as well. I radioed the Aircraft Y pilot on CTAF to say that I would hold for her to depart first; since it was a skydiving ops plane and I was in no hurry. The landing traffic Aircraft Z touched down (it was a small single engine of some kind) and Aircraft Y taxied onto the runway as soon as Aircraft Z passed us. The Aircraft Y pilot did not wait for Aircraft Z to exit the runway and instead throttled up and began accelerating down Runway XY towards Aircraft Z which was still rolling out; about midfield. If this wasn't bad enough; another pilot [Aircraft A] on short final decided not to go around but instead to land on Runway XY with two aircraft ahead of him. I do not remember what type of aircraft this third plane was; a small single-engine of some kind. The Aircraft Y pilot had to abort her takeoff and slam on the brakes to avoid hitting Aircraft Z; which rolled all the way to the departure end of the field before finally exiting. Aircraft Y exited the runway just in time for Aircraft A to roll out behind it without a collision. What caused the problem: 1. While Aircraft Y might have been OK to 'line up and wait' on Runway XY; she should not have begun her takeoff roll until the runway was clear. Pilot displayed impatience and was counting on Aircraft Z to exit promptly; which it did not. With traffic in the pattern; even the decision to line up and wait was not a very prudent one.2. The third; landing plane should have executed a go-around. The runway was occupied with two aircraft ahead of it. 3. Smoke/haze in the area may have been a factor; although the visibility was at least 3-5 SM and I don't believe that the runway was obscured from view at any time.

Aircraft Y then announced downwind for Runway XY. I then told the applicant that in the event of go-around; both engines were available. The applicant continued while I searched for traffic in haze and seven mile visibility. The applicant reported a three (3) mile final. I continued to scan for Aircraft Y. I told the applicant that I had not spotted the traffic and then radioed that we were on a one and one-half (1 and ½) mile final. In response; Aircraft Y stated they had us in sight. I asked them to go-around. Instead; they called they were turning final for Runway XY. When the applicant called one hundred feet (100') above minimums; I spotted Aircraft Y. At that time; I told the applicant the runway was in sight and the applicant removed his foggles. I pointed the traffic to the applicant at one to two o'clock and less than a quarter (1/4) mile and again asked Aircraft Y to execute a go-around; which he then did as he flew over the top of us at the intersection of Runway XX and Runway XY. As the applicant flared to land; the tail struck the pavement. Only then did I realize that the applicant failed to complete the before landing checklist; by extending the gear; which I; in turn; failed to observe.
column123: On Date I was taking a multi-engine commercial check ride with Designated Pilot Examiner [DPE] Name. I was the pilot in command for the flight. After flying the maneuvers we set up for the ILS XX into ZZZ. We had a simulated engine failure during the approach. ZZZ approach approved frequency change and gave no traffic advisories. I made a 5 mile final call on the CTAF followed by a 3 mile final call. During a 2 mile final Aircraft Y made a final call for Runway XY. I still had the foggles on and the [DPE] was searching for the traffic. I announced we reached the DA; and at that time name told me to remove the foggles. He was still searching for the traffic and talking to the other aircraft. Aircraft Y announced they would go around and I continued my approach inbound for Runway XX. With all the confusion and concerns of a mid-air collision i failed to complete the before landing check. It wasn't realized that the gear was retracted until the tail struck.Distraction and pressure were two major human factors that contributed to this incident. The other aircraft distracted me from completing the before landing check. In addition; the pressure of flying the approach and completing the maneuver within standards played a role.

column121: Vectoring student onto RNAV XX into ZZZ at 3;000 feet; 11nm South of the field; we switch to CTAF to start monitoring incoming traffic. On an estimated 030 heading giving the final vector to intercept for the RNAVXX; we hear our first transmission from the King Air stating '15nm South descending out of 5;000 feet inbound runway XX; ZZZ'. I tried to find the traffic visually and on TCAS but we could not visually see them as they were almost fully behind us and TCAS did not show any traffic in the area they reported; so I immediately made a radio call on CTAF declaring; 'ZZZ traffic; Aircraft X; 11nm South; intercepting the RNAV XX; 3;000 feet descending to 2;600 feet; King Air traffic you can overtake us before we come in.' The King Air advises the traffic call and states; 'We have someone on TCAS; that should be you.' With two-way communication established we continued with our approach descending to 2;600 feet expecting the King Air to sidestep and overtake us.  After a few seconds of no communication; the King Air appears on our TCAS showing plus 2;000 feet about 13nm South of the field on an extended final for runway XX. As the traffic was behind us and high there was no way for me to visually identify the oncoming aircraft. As I couldn't maintain visual separation myself; I stated on CTAF 'We would appreciate 1;000ft of clearance while you overtake.' We received no response from the King Air.  The TCAS altitude separation continued to reduce from 2;000 feet to 1;000 feet. As the traffic came within 1nm; altitude separation was under 1;000 feet and continued to rapidly reduce; I had my student began a descent to try and avoid a potential collision as it appeared the King Air was going to continue descending directly into our reported altitude. As the traffic passed overhead about 7nm from the end of the runway; the last TCAS message noted in the cockpit was +500ft and the traffic alerting system sounding from the G1000. During the descent to gain separation; we had to maneuver down to 1;900ft just to maintain a +500ft separation as the King Air continued to descend directly on top of us with no indication of leveling before crossing overhead. When I first gained a visual of the aircraft; it appeared the separation was much lower than the +500 feet last seen on the TCAS and estimated between +300/+400 feet. After the traffic was no longer within NMAC distance; I stated on CTAF; 'You could have given us some more clearance'. The King Air responds with; 'We gave you 500ft; learn to fly your airplane.' If he had 500ft of separation it was because we descended 700ft to avoid him. Multiple other CTAF transmissions were made between us after; fighting between who was at fault and who wasn't following the regulations. After landing; another crew that was on an approximate 1nm final for runway 36 stated that the separation on their TCAS as the King Air overtook us was +300 feet. The whole incident from first radio contact to final radio transmission between the two crews was an estimated 3-4 minutes. No injuries during the incident. There are several witnesses besides the two aircraft that were involved that are willing to corroborate the situation; their information will be available upon request.

column121: This type of event happens way too often in the Ocean area of ZMA.  I have been at work before working sector 62 or 63 and the same thing has happened to me so I feel compelled to write this report. On Date there was a massive equipment failure. GDT (Radar and comm site) failed along with the GDT frequencies. The ZNY ATOP system failed also; along with the Santo Domingo ADE (Flight Plan Processing) system.Because we are only one source of RADAR coverage and only one site of frequencies at sectors 62/63; when these fail it makes it impossible to provide safe air traffic services to the flying public. The Ocean area is in desperate need of some redundancy as we are constantly in danger of losing our only source of surveillance and usable frequencies. Whether it's because of maintenance or every year during hurricane season. If these type of events happen once it's one too many. Controllers were put in harms way and took drastic measures to maintain some type of order and safety to the flying public. It could've been horrible for everyone involved. Thankfully; there was no need to be on the evening news because of a catastrophic event. We need overlapping sources of surveillance and we need more coverage and back ups for the frequencies. We feel there is a lack of attention in the Ocean area and the flying public isn't aware of the potential danger. If the airspace was over CONUS (Continental United States) we would not be asked to deal with this. We are constantly having to use landlines to speak to foreign facilities because of the failures on the MEVA's [Multi National Network System; Mejoras al Enlace de VOZ del ATS].  Please look into these issues and finally do something.
column123: I was working R62 combined with sector 43 and 63. The GTK radar failed around XA:30Z together with all frequencies at the GTK site. I was unable to communicate with any airplanes under my control initially. I started broadcasting on 121.50 off the ZIN site; and tried to advise all airplanes on frequency 126.45 and 135.20 that we had lost the radar and the frequencies; followed by an advisory to use extreme caution. There was also a lot of weather in the sector with a majority of airplanes in sector 62 and 63 deviating.  I also kept broadcasting on 121.50 informing the airplanes to use extreme caution due to the outages; and to try to reach me on frequency 123.77 (ZIN site). I also tried reaching out to airplanes from the ZIN 126.45 site; but that frequency is very unreliable and I was unable to communicate there initially. After having re-established communications with numerous aircraft; now on frequency 123.77; I was able to take appropriate actions to separate airplanes that needed vertical separation; and re-routed some northbound airplanes to the west towards frequency and radar coverage. I established vertical separation with these airplanes. With the help of surrounding sectors; surrounding facilities and great teamwork in the area; we were able to avoid any disastrous consequences.We need a new backup frequency site that can cover the entirety of sector 62 and 63; and more importantly an additional radar/ADS-B feed that will prevent us from going non-radar. We cannot rely purely on non-radar procedures if we lose the frequency. There needs to be a push to fix these problems! Additionally; we need to make sure the backup frequencies actually work properly. 126.45 at ZIN was working horribly and could not be considered as a reliable backup frequency; especially during times it was most needed.

column121: During climb out; FA (Flight Attendant) called on intercom to report a very loud banging noise behind the wing area; aircraft right side; row 31. FA said it sounded like someone pounding on the fuselage with a sledgehammer repeatedly. We leveled off at FL280 immediately and reduced speed from 280 KIAS to 250 KIAS. I asked the FO to look for a nearby field with good weather.  FA recorded the noise via video on her cell phone and brought it to the cockpit. After reviewing the video; we decided to divert to ZZZ. We notified dispatch and coordinated with the FA's and informed the passengers. During the descent and configuration of the aircraft for landing at ZZZ; with the flaps at 5deg; I called for Flaps 10 while the aircraft speed was at 209 KIAS. I immediately said 'delay that stay at flaps five.' I believe the FO moved the flap handle out of the 5 detent and returned it immediately. The flaps remained at 5 degrees and I continued to slow the aircraft. I called for gear down an Flaps 15; flaps 25; flaps 30 landing checklist. I noticed the stick shaker indicator on the airspeed tape was in an unusual position and cross checked the configuration to find the flaps were at 5. We were at approximately 1200 feet when I announced 'going around'; but did not hit TOGA as I did not want GA thrust. At this point; the FO and I were convinced that the two problems were related; that there was some structural damage to the flaps.We climbed to 5;000 feet and referenced the Checklist for FLAPS - TRAILING EDGE FLAPS DISAGREE. We returned the flap lever to 5; then selected 2. The flaps retracted to 2. The checklist directed us to 'Proceed normally.' We had a discussion about what that meant and were not comfortable with extending the flaps again; with suspected mechanical damage to the flaps already existing. We got a phone patch with Maintenance Control and dispatch on HF and discussed the two issues and our checklist. They had no additional advice. We discussed the plan to land in the current flap configuration (flap 2); using the flap up speeds with Maintenance Control and dispatch. The FO had already assessed the landing distance and we referenced the FLAPS- TRAILING EDGE FLAPS UP LANDING checklist. We landed on RWY XXL at ZZZ; at VREF 40 + 40 + 5. I used auto brakes 3; and rolled to the end of the runway. We had the fire/rescue look us over for damage prior to proceeding to the gate. They reported a large cable hanging from the satellite antenna. The PSEU (Proximity Switch Electronics Unit) light came on after landing. The FO and I debriefed the events in detail post flight and during the next two flights. It was not until the following morning; that I realized that in all likelihood; I caused the flap malfunction by calling for flaps 10 at 209 KIAS. The SATCOM antenna seal failure noise was significantly concerning; and I assumed the flap issue was directly related.

column121: While making our descent at approximately 8;000 feet on the ZZZZZ1 arrival we noticed the Emer/Parking brake 'on' light and a 'PRKG BRK NOT RELEASED' caution on the EICAS Illuminated with a Master Caution. We responded by requesting a heading with ATC and let them know we were working an issue. As the PM; I accessed the QRH and looked up the EICAS message and competed the procedure. We attempted twice to cycle the parking brake per the QRH procedure with no effect. After reading the note in the QRH that states 'Expected potential tire burst during landing' we opted to request priority handling; requested CFR to be available due to a potential parking brake issue. Upon touchdown there was no indication of loss of steering control. We taxed off the runway and then asked CFR to make a visual inspection of the tires and brakes. During the inspection the engine had reached their cool down period and the APU was on and 100%. I instructed the FO to terminate #2. About a minute later and after the CFR's inspection came up negative for any abnormalities we began taxiing via ATC instruction. As I began straightening out onto the taxi line by making a soft left turn the aircraft responded normally and then after several seconds the aircraft started to make an un-commanded right hand turn. I immediately added more left on the power steering tiller and the aircraft initially responded but then went back to the right. I stopped the aircraft; turned on the HYD pump 1&2 from auto to on. The FO open the HYD status page and saw no abnormal indications but there was a cyan advisory message that read EMER BRK FAULT. The aircraft did taxi normal and we were able to taxi to the gate without issue. Once we deplaned the passengers the FO and I were asked to stay behind to accomplish a taxi check. Later; we terminated the attempt to complete a taxi check due to no ground crew personnel available. Crew scheduling was called and they asked us to be at the airport in the morning for sign in. I left the airport via hotel shuttle to the hotel. The Crew was given an early van time the next morning. When we arrived at the aircraft the next morning I was asked to complete the taxi check.  After completing the taxi check maintenance issued MEL XY-Z and released the aircraft for revenue flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I explained to maintenance that there were issues with the MEL and it does not state that I would have to turn on the hydraulic pumps on and that only by turning the pumps on would I get power steering and asked if they still agreed it was good for revenue flight. With the pump issues maintenance decided that they were not going to release the aircraft for revenue flight. Shortly there after I was asked to do a ferry flight with the loss of directional control being the open write-up and source for the ferry flight permit (I'm not sure if that statement is exactly correct but that is my understanding after maintenance explained the process). Once we received the permit we prepared the aircraft with a manual weight an balance and pushed off the gate. During the takeoff brief both the FO and I spoke about how we would have to turn the #2 electric hydraulic pump from auto to on for taxi; and opted to do so for taxi and landing as well. In addition to that we talked about how we would get a 'no takeoff brakes' aural message while executing the taxi checklist and checking the T/O Config. We were also prepared to get warnings and cautions during the takeoff roll due to the 'no takeoff brakes' status the aircraft thought it was in (some of us may have seen something like this in the sims). Lastly we were prepared for the caution 'PRKG BRK NOT RELEASED' once airborne and that we would disregard all of those as long as they were associated with the parking brake being on. When we executed to takeoff from runway XY R at ZZZ; Literally everything we discussed happened. We received continuous master warning light with chimes and 'not takeoff brakes' aural messages until reaching 80 knots and then shortly after rotation we received the master caution for the 'PRKG BRK NOT RELEASED'. After climbing through 2;000 to 3;000 feet the master caution for the parking brake disappeared and was never seen again for the remainder of the flight. When we landed there was no abnormal emergency brake light on or emergency brake fault advisory on the EICAS. The landing and braking was normal as the night before and we taxi it to the company hanger. We were then taken via van from the maintenance hangar to Gate X where we used the jet bridge to get back into terminal on date; [2 days later]. All but the #1 FA was scheduled to take off on the next company flight due to depart [later that evening.] After about an hour sitting at the airport both the FO and I concluded that for safety reasons it would be best that we remove ourselves from the flight due to fatigue. I called crew scheduling on behalf of the FO and myself and we were both removed from the last turn of our sequenceMidway during a sequence dominated by evening flying with late starts and late ends we had to respond to an Emergency landing with the possible loss of aircraft control. Then during the taxi to the gate after a normal landing onto the emergency runway we lost aircraft directional control. The FO and I stayed were asked to stay late to help maintenance and then given minimum crew rest to come back and again to help maintenance early in the morning which was a disruption of our sleep cycle by several hours. After the uncertainty of continuing with our normal sequence we had to ferry a broken aircraft including dealing with a plethora of false warning; cautions; and advisories that would have normally cause rejected takeoffs and emergency declarations. Upon arrival to the airport we would have concluded the completely abnormal and stressful day with a 3 hour sit follower buy a 3 hour evening flight.

column121: Trip started with FA (Flight Attendant) Brief re: Weather enroute and at ZZZ at Arrival; Passengers got same brief. Twice enroute I had FA's take their seats due to Company Alert; and Weather deviation around Utah; no issues...90nm from ZZZ; I briefed the Passengers of the weather and Arrival info; expecting a bumpy ride on the descent; and that we would be landing; and then parking at Gate XX; at XX:35 ZZZ Time; 30 minutes to landing. 20 minutes to landing; I made a PA for the FA's to take their seats; as a precaution. We were cleared direct ZZZZZ and to keep our speed up. We were then cleared to descend via the ZZZZZ and transition to 310 kts.; as we were #1. We were then given a heading for vectors to the ILSXX Approach; and descend to 12;000 ft.At 12;000 ft.; I cycled the seat belt switch and stated 'Flight Attendants prepare for landing' over the PA; early on purpose. We were then given Descend to 8;000 ft.; followed by a turn to downwind and descend to 4;000 ft. We were IMC; it was 9 degrees Celsius; 29.49; and strong winds and moderate rain. Descending from 5;000 ft. to 4;000 ft.; we encountered severe turbulence; the AP kicked off and the airplane pitched up and down erratically.I hand flew the airplane to regain control of our Flight Path; and we settled down at 4;000 ft. and re-engaged the AP. We were then given a descent to 3;000 ft.; followed by a heading to Intercept the ILSXX Approach Course; and cleared for the approach. We broke out at about 2;000 ft.; configured for a full flap landing; encountered 30 kts. headwind on Final; followed by a 10 kt. tailwind on landing; and made a normal landing.As we were rolling out; we got a call from the back (FA's); and the FO (First Officer) answered as I taxied clear of the runway. She informed me that the #2 FA hit the floor hard on her left side; and could we ask for Medics to meet us at the Gate.We were met at the Gate by 2 ZZZ Airport [Officials]; and they checked out our #2 FA. They recommended that she go to the hospital; as did I; so she could get a proper check out. It was also recommended that at least 1 other FA go with her. The FA's then left the aircraft; as did the FO.I stayed with the aircraft; so I could note in the logbook that an aircraft inspection would be needed do to our encounter with severe turbulence. FA did not go to hospital; and returned to work the next day.The 2 AFT FA's did not take their seats when instructed; by my PA: 'Flight Attendants take your seats'. FA's need to follow instructions; i.e. when told to Be Seated; then Take Your Seat.

An emergency was not declared but the nature of the issue was given. Dispatch was contacted initially via ACARS; given the failure and fuel onboard; then subsequently via ZZZ Radio.After discussions with the dispatcher and calculating the fuel onboard all parties were in concurrence to continue to ZZZ. Requested for the Dispatcher to call ahead and have ZZZ ensure the longest runway was made available for the landing and to provide any assistance to facilitate 'short cuts' and weather avoidance to ensure arrival with sufficient fuel. Final cruise altitude was 14;000 feet and speed was 220 KTS to comply with the flap speed restriction and a 10 kt buffer for turbulence associated with weather. ATC was advised and provided assistance in find the shortest way around weather and direct to points on the arrival into ZZZ.Passengers were than advised via PA due to a performance issue that presented itself on the climb out of ZZZ1 the aircraft will be limited to 14;000 feet and a slower speed than flight planned causing our arrival time to be approximately 15 minutes after scheduled arrival. Additionally Airline was aware of the issues and would be watching and looking at any possible misconnects and proactively make any re-bookings if required in ZZZ. Flight Attendants reported no issues with the passengers and everyone seemed to be in good spirits.Thirty (30) Minutes prior to arrival flight attendants reported a strong 'mechanical/electrical' smell beginning aft of the wing root and extending back towards zone 6 in the cabin. Dispatch and Maintenance was advised; flight attendants asked to monitor and advise of any changes and systems were monitored via the various system pages for any indication of further subsystems degradation to which none was found.Flight was vectored to join final for Runway XYL ZZZ. Items in QRH (prior to landing) were accomplished aircraft landed with no issues; exiting Taxiway X and parking at gate XX in ZZZ.
column123: Climbing out of ZZZ1; immediately after take off; received the 'flaps fail' caution message. Completed QRH and made the decision; with Dispatch and Maintenance input to continue to ZZZ. Flight was limited to 15;000 feet and 230 knots due to the flaps being stuck at 8. A much less fuel efficient route; so we required shortcuts when the weather would allow just to make sure we had plenty of fuel. With approximately 30-45 minutes left in the flight the flight attendants reported a mechanical or electrical smell.  No smoke was observed.  We discussed diverting to another airport but our options were limited since we had to increase our landing distance and roll.  Discussed the fact that the smell was probably associated with the failure and no other indications to suggest a fire so we continued to ZZZ.  Landed on the longest runway in ZZZ without any issues. The training received in the sim helped me be well prepared for a situation like this.

I was at 1;500 ft. when I made the call. As I was leaving the hills behind me and crossing the bay I was getting progressively worried about visibility due to haze. I slowly descended to pattern altitude (800 ft.) and about 2 miles from the airport (keeping about 80-85 kts.); starting to panic as I could not see the runway and most things around it. I had been given instructions for right traffic on Runway XX. I descended to about 450 ft. when the Controller asked me to make a right 360 and get back to pattern altitude. I had completely passed the runway - I told ATC I cannot see the runway. ATC gave me headings and eventually was able to clearly see the runway; joined the pattern and proceeded to land. column121: I was practicing landings at ZZZ. It was a night flight where I was planning to do five total stop and goes. ZZZ does what they call either a 'racetrack' pattern or a 'figure 8' pattern for their runways. That night; with the winds considered; led for Runways XX and XY to be in use. After accepting their pattern; I executed my stop and goes alternating between both Runway XY and XX. All was going well until I was on right downwind (right traffic) for Runway XX. (This would have been around my 3rd landing). I had traffic behind me essentially following me (doing the same thing) and I had a CRJ off to the northeast inbound for Runway XY. I was cleared to land for Runway XX by the time I was on right base. As I was entering final; ATC had told the CRJ to slow down obviously because I was cleared to land for XX. (XY and XX are intersecting runways). As I was on final; ATC called up and instructed me to make 'little delay' on Runway XX of which I was cleared for. They had then called up again and instructed me to do a low approach instead a little bit after. I was confused what they meant by this call so I questioned them that they wanted me do something in relation to XY and XX; however; their call up again was still confusing. They had instructed the traffic that was behind me who was on right downwind at the time to also do a low approach where they gave them more instructions in terms of altitude etc.This confused me more. As I was on short final; I had interpreted a low approach to mean 'to steepen your approach' 'land...ASAP' ~ low approach. There was much happening in the background: ATC talking to everyone; me trying to configure my aircraft to land and trying to interpret what they meant. On short final though; they had told me to do a low approach again (reassuring that I was going to) and I repeated that I would. I failed to query them by asking them what they meant by a low approach exactly. I continued the steep approach to a landing because that is what I had thought they wanted me to do. I landed trying to make little delay (from what I remember) before the landing markers for Runway XX and did my full stop. I saw the CRJ then land on Runway XY a few 2;000 ft. from where I was and then was instructed to hold position. Afterwards; ATC had cleared me to takeoff Runway XX once again with no further problems noted. ATC never told me to contact a number nor mention anything of a pilot deviation. They were very accommodating and actually came back up to mention myself and the other traffic in the pattern that they thank us for our corporation because everything happened quickly and the CRJ came in a bit faster than we all had anticipated on. I kept questioning myself what they meant by 'low approach' the rest of the flight.When I got home that night; I looked up what a 'low approach' meant; and I was shocked; scared; and embarrassed. I was not sure why I was unable to distinctively understand what they meant by low approach during that moment. I contacted our Flight Operations and spoke to him roughly around an hour about the occurrence. We began talking about the FAR/AIM in terms of definitions of 'low approach' and he gave me recommendations on what to read in the FAR/AIM. We also went over what the NASA form was and why I should report one. I now understand the meaning of the amended clearance and will begin furthering my search on other possible ATC phraseology as well for basic knowledge we all should be very familiar with.

We were doing the GPS XX approach at the ZZZ airport while self-announcing our position and did not hear anyone else on the CTAF frequency. As we are about .2 miles from the threshold of the XX Runway at ZZZ; tracking the GPS radial for landing on short final; my instructor immediately puts in full throttle. column123: Me and My student were shooting a VFR GPS practice approach to Runway XX. We did a full procedure starting at ZZZZZ. We made traffic calls using distance instead of fixes so VFR traffic would know our position. (Example: ZZZ TRAFFIC Aircraft X IS 11 MILES NORTH OF THE FIELD SHOOTING THE GPS XX PRACTICE APPROACH TOUCH AND GO ZZZ). We made call outs at 11 miles (IAF); 5 miles (FAF); and short final (2-3 miles). When we were final approach fix inbound I noticed on my MFD of our G1000 an ADSB hit that was +23 above our altitude at FAF and east slightly north of the field heading northwest. I assumed the traffic was passing by as I had not heard call outs other than us for ZZZ and began to focus more on my student who was on his second ever approaches lesson and thus required a higher amount of monitoring and supervision than a student who was more experienced with approaches. On short final; maybe 10-20 seconds from touch down I glanced from the student to the MFD and noticed a MFD hit in yellow that was nearly on top of us and slightly behind at +100 ft. I looked back and to my left out a rearward window to see the engine slight belly of a T6 coming down on top of us. I immediately took control from the student and evasive action applying full power; flaps up and offset further down and to the left of the runway crossing the threshold about that time. The next time I saw the T6 was about 3-5 seconds later in a climbing right turn mid gear retraction. I called up and asked 'T6 IN ZZZ ARE YOU ON FREQUENCY?'. They replied that they had not heard us. We let them know we had not heard them either and would be filing a safety report with NASA. I think contributing factors to this was the T6 being a low wing and us being a high wind making visibility poor between both aircraft in close proximity. Further more me being task saturated with the student and assuming the aircraft was passing by ZZZ at FAF. Based on the tone of the T6 Instructors voice I got the impression that they were just as surprised to see us; leading me to believe they were also just ask task saturated teaching their student.

column121: The following is a narrative of the flight to the best of the Instructor's recollection. Incident occurred on DATE. The exact time is unknown; but it was sometime after XX00; likely closer to XX00. The flight was a pre-solo cross-country progress check for a private pilot applicant in the flight school's 141 program. Student was given a cross-country flight route to ZZZ but was instructed the entire flight would not be completed and he would be requested to fly a diversion to an unplanned airport during the evaluation. He presented a weather brief for the route of flight during the ground portion. Following a satisfactory ground examination; local weather was reviewed; and it was determined the flight could commence.Student's pre-flight was observed and mirrored by Instructor prior to commencing flight. Student properly used checklists. Start-up; taxi; and run-up were completed within standards using checklists. Systems appeared nominal and nothing out of the ordinary was observed or experienced. Takeoff was conducted within standards; systems appeared nominal and nothing out of the ordinary was observed or experienced. Climb out was conducted within standards with checklist usage at appropriate phases of flight (after takeoff and cruise); student's leaning of the fuel system was observed to be done appropriately; systems appeared nominal and nothing out of the ordinary was observed or experienced. The flight departed the ZZZ1 Delta airspace to the North-East and the evaluation proceeded through the cross-country navigation/lost comms/lost procedure portions with a satisfactory performance by student. Systems continued to appear nominal and nothing out of the ordinary was experienced.Student was then given a scenario (told he was experiencing high oil pressure) requiring him to make a decision on a diversion location. No systems were changed; it was a simple verbal scenario. Based on the information available he elected to divert to ZZZ2 and was instructed to divert and plan to make a touch-and-go. He appropriately set up the aircraft's navigation systems; radios; etc. and procedure in-bound to ZZZ2; making appropriate radio calls along the way. His actions inbound and during the descent were observed. He properly adjusted the mixture during the descent. Systems appeared to remain nominal and nothing out of the ordinary was observed.Student completed the touch-and-go and was instructed to navigate back towards ZZZ1. Appropriate checklist usage and actions were observed during the climb back to 7;500; including leaning procedures. Systems remained nominal and nothing out of the ordinary was observed. Somewhere near the south edge of the town student was given a progressive simulated emergency. He was first told we were experiencing high oil pressure and then high oil-temp. He immediately made the decision to turn back toward ZZZ2. Thereafter he was told he was experiencing partial power-loss and RPM was reduced to approximately 2;000. Student immediately pitched for 68 kts. Thereafter student was told the scenario progressed to an engine fire. He reduced throttle to idle; called out his memory items; banked and began to dive. He was told the fire was out and he pitched for 68 kts. while turning for a simulated off-field landing location somewhere near the town. It was noted the stall horn kept coming on anytime the aircraft got even slightly slower than 68 kts. The propeller continued to turn; systems appeared nominal; nothing out of the ordinary was experienced.At approximately 1;000 ft.; when it was determined student would be able to safely reach his selected simulated off-field landing location; he was instructed to commence a go-around and return to ZZZ. Student advanced the throttle and the engine did not respond. Student was observed bringing the throttle out and advancing a second time. At that moment he informed Instructor the engine was not responding. Instructor immediately took control of the plane; ensured it was at best glide speed (68 kts.) and; given the low altitude (estimated below 1;000 ft. at this time); advanced throttle and mixture to see if engine would respond. The propeller continued to turn; but the engine did not respond. Instructor directed student to tune 121.5; then Instructor requested priority; and began to go through off-field landing/engine secure memory items while conducting what was in essence a power-off 180 maneuver to the field Instructor had selected at the outset of the original emergency scenario. Instructor did not continue to students selected field because of power lines in the area and its proximity to structures. From the air; the location selected by Instructor was a cornfield with what appeared to be a flat access road immediately in front of it; and a flat dirt-field preceding the road. It appeared readily accessible to emergency responders and several work trucks were observed near the train tracks running parallel to the field. In addition; no power lines were observed in the vicinity of the selected field. Once turning 'final'; Instructor recalls ordering unlatching of the cabin doors; but specifically instructed not to open until the aircraft came to a stop. Instructor made conscious decision to not turn off master so that flaps could be used to the slow the aircraft down as it approached the ground. The flaps were deployed prior to landing. Instructor recalls maintaining approximately 68 kts. for the longest possible period of time and that the stall horn kept activating around 65 kts.Touchdown was normal in that the main gear touched first; Instructor believes somewhere on the dirt field. Instructor continued to maintain back pressure for as long as possible; but within moments the aircraft struck either the slightly raised dirt road or the ditch; which caused the aircraft to flip onto its roof. Aircraft came to a stop. Instructor ordered unlatching of harnesses and egress from the aircraft. No serious injuries were observed on scene.Though at this point Instructor is uncertain of what caused the engine to fail; I do believe it would be wise to include a requirement in the ACS that during any simulated emergency where the engine is brought to idle; the applicant should continuously clear the engine (like what is allowed in steep spiral descent during the commercial check-ride). If that standard were included; it may have been possible to detect the issue earlier.

column121: As my private students and I returned from a local practice area; we were told to enter midfield right downwind for Runway XX. We were approximately 8 miles west of ZZZ at this point. Continuing inbound; we heard several other people coming back into ZZZ from practice areas and some other transient traffic. Just before we turned onto downwind at 1900 MSL; I looked up and to the right to saw an Aircraft Y also flying on downwind above me. When I turned downwind; I could no longer see him; as he was 6 o'clock high. At 2;400' MSL; Aircraft Y reported having us in sight and tower clear them to land as they are flying over top of us.  I noticed on the MFD that their ADS-B target had resulted in a traffic alert that was getting closer and descending. I pushed the nose forward and checked in with Tower abeam the numbers. The traffic passed over us very close. Seeing +02 on the MFD for the traffic; I initiated a left turn just as tower was instructing a left 360. I noted 1600 MSL on the altimeter; so I had descended 300' from traffic pattern altitude to evade the Aircraft Y. On final; I heard the Aircraft Y tell tower; 'we were extremely close to that downwind traffic on base.' Tower responded with; 'well he said he had you in sight; and Roanoke vectored you in that way; so I don't know what else to say about that.' We performed our touch and go and final lap before making a full stop. Bottom line; the Aircraft Y was overtaking me from the rear; told Tower he had me in sight; and was then cleared to land. I took evasive action; and even so; the traffic got within a few hundred feet of our aircraft. If we had not had ADS-B in; they might have hit us as they descended through Traffic Pattern Altitude.

column121: I split legs with this other 74-year-old Captain and I'm in the right seat. He slowly brings the power in and then we get the configuration callouts; red lights; yellow lights and white lights (pitch trim setting) and then he proceeds to ignore my 4 abort takeoff calls. Configuration red lights (trims and we were trimmed majorly nose down... After ignoring the aural; visual and vocal call outs; he rotated around 165kts - plus; muscled it into the air then couldn't keep altitude. Started 200/300ft descent at around 800/900ft. Told me he couldn't keep the nose up and ask me to help; so I took the airplane from him with a nose down attitude at over 250KTS; trim was inoperative; [I] used pitch trim bias to arrest the descent and elevator disconnect after that; never got back above 1;000 AGL. Brought it back around and landed. We completed the all necessary checklists. And when I called for 'trims' before takeoff... he said 'check'.  Rotated around max tire speed of 165. Then once airborne; while nosing down we're doing somewhere over 250; well past the red tape for flaps 8 degrees. That's when I took the airplane. I took the airplane and then delegated tasks to him while I flew us out of that situation. I got him to adjust power and adjust the pitch trim bias up; and engage elevator disconnect. While I kept us airborne.  I was speaking with ATC the entire time.  Wheels up to wheels down was 6 minutes.

column121: At approximately XX:15 am the GTK radar site was out of service and no targets appeared on the screen. First safety issue: Greater than 90% of ocean area only has secondary radar. We don't have primary radar. The point may be moot in this scenario but should be noted and addressed. At approximately XX:18 am we had lost the entire GTK frequency site which includes 126.45; 125.1; and 135.2. Second safety issue: At this point 2 entire sectors (62 and 63) do not have any radar services; primary or secondary; or any direct radar sites to communicate with aircraft. In short; there are approximately 35 planes and 7;000 people that cannot be seen or communicated with; and 102;480 square miles of airspace that is completely unworkable and as dangerous as the National Airspace System could possibly be for more than 10 HOURS!Controller relayed through aircraft on the nearest frequency site (ZIN) to relay on guard to separate aircraft in conflict within the 102;000 square mile zone of equipment failure. Third safety issue. The ZIN site used for sector 43 to relay to the 102;000 square mile dead zone had only 1 of the 2 working frequencies! 126.45 on ZIN transmitter was working but not the receiver.Coordination was accomplished with all surrounding facilities to include; Santo Domingo; San Juan; adjacent ZMA sectors; and Miami Approach to ground stop aircraft. ZWY Center was called to reroute planes through different ZMA sectors and SJU (San Juan) Center. At approximately; XX:45 am the ADE with ZWY (New York Oceanic Airspace) failed and 0 flight plan information was being transmitted to ZMA from ZWY. At this point; I shut off all ZWY flights to ZMA and requested every single plane being rerouted out of ZMA entry points to Jacksonville Center. Fourth safety issue: Complete ADE failure with New York Center and 0 flight plan information transmitting between Centers.It is only by the grace of a higher power that there weren't any TCAS alerts; RA's; or even worse an aircraft accident. If the recommendations and solutions presented in this report isn't taken seriously or implemented in any capacity there will be loss of life...'. This should be prioritized as immediately. Some sort of backup frequency site should be established for sectors 62; and 63. There have been plans for a second frequency site at MBPV. A second site in a different location would have meant the world to this area that day. Although; we would not have radar; the Controllers in this area have been trained and know the procedures to successfully and effectively work under non radar conditions; providing a working frequency is available.In comparison; CONUS (Continental United States) airspace has BUECS (Backup Emergency Frequency) sites to help with theses types of failure; along with other multiple back up options. These two sectors and all others in the OCEAN area literally have zero backup options. We desperately need backup options and more over lapping frequency coverage. Although; I understand that this may be expensive and that foreign territory is involved; the monetary price to pay now will pale in comparison to the eventual punitive damages forced to be paid to the families of the affected. The GTK radar site fails and is listed out of service at a staggering rate. This site is completely unreliable; and is the reason that the OCEAN Controllers are so well trained in non-radar procedures. The solution would be allowing radar feeds from SDO; or any other feasible facility with ZMA. Also; prioritize space based ADS-B that didn't meet the efficiency criteria due to an approximately 98% accuracy rate; or the ground based ADS-B as long as it is not collocated with the faulty GTK radar site. It must be separate to allow for one failure to not affect both systems.In conclusion there is so much more that can be done in ZMA OCEAN area; there is not weather radar; primary radar; backup frequencies; a working EBUS (Enhanced Backup System) or dark system (backup radardisplay); accurate altimeter stations; etc... These 2 solutions to problems encountered on Date; are about as important a safety issue as there can be. If the agency truly believes safety is the number one priority; these issues will be resolved as if life depends on it because it actually does.

column123: During cruise; about halfway into the flight; the Flight Attendants called from the aft galley to say that one of the ovens was smoking heavily. They kept watch over the oven and it was cooling off rapidly. There was no further incident. When I went on my break; about thirty minutes later; I went to the back to check the status of the oven. The oven was cool and the Flight Attendants continued their watch over the oven until we landed. Upon landing; a Mechanic came to inspect the oven and he suspected a grease fire on the aft fan of of the oven. He gave me an engineering smoke/fumes questionnaire to fill out; which I did.The Flight Attendants did a great job taking care of the situation and I was very impressed with how they handled the situation.

column121: We were briefed by inbound crew that they had spoiler float.  When we got to aircraft; we found out that the number 10 spoiler had been deactivated.    Everything was normal below 10;000 feet.  As our speed increased above 250 knots; we had a very slight yaw/roll to the right and auto pilot put in left rudder.  As we climbed our speed increased further and so did left rudder.  Finally; we got over 320 knots; rudder went left with foot pedals to 3.5 degrees left.  Simultaneously; we received the Yaw/Roll Asymmetry EICAS Warning.  The checklist had no procedure.  It just said to land at the nearest suitable airport. Knowing that we had a deactivated spoiler at takeoff; I sent the First Officer back to look at it.  He was unable to see it even with his flashlight.  We asked to hold at present position because we were about to go over mountains.  We reread the deferral to see if this is one of the expected messages we could get as a result of the spoiler being deactivated.  It was not.  We then called Dispatch and got a phone patch to Maintenance Control.  I told him our situation and that I thought the spoiler was floating.  I asked if the Roll/Yaw Asymmetry EICAS was a possible message for our deferral to which he replied no.At this point; unable to determine the cause of the EICAS; we stopped our climb at 30;000 feet; [notified ATC]; found a new place to hold; got permission to dump fuel; and proceeded back to ZZZZ.  Dump altitude was 30;000 feet down to 18;000 feet.  As our speed decreased; the rudder slowly centered.  By the time we reduced to 250 knots; it was zeroed.  Landing was uneventful at max certified weight except we had hot brakes. After we got back to the hotel; I found the inbound crew.  They said they only had 2.5 units of left trim.  This makes sense because at altitude; the IAS is only around 270 KTS and do to speed restrictions at ZZZZ they never went over 300 knots on descent.  After talking to the inbound crew; I then called Maintenance Control and gave them a full in-depth review of what happened.  I asked him to call me when they found out something so we could prepare our rest cycle.Five hours later; Maintenance Control called me and said the rod on the PCU Actuator was incorrect.  Apparently; our maintenance manual has two ways to lock out a spoiler.  One is to use a Rear End Cap and the second is to use lock out plates.  Our Maintenance manuals don't specify which one to use and apparently; they used the wrong method.  After maintenance talked to Boeing; Company is going revise their manuals to reflect the preferred lockout method for each specific situation.  They suspect we had a sheared shaft but won't know until we bring the aircraft home with the spoiler locked out using the Lock Out Plate Method.  Note: We used all 4 pilots in this event.  We had one flying the entire time and that was his only job.  We had one in the back of the aircraft checking out the spoilers and helping with checklists including the diversion guide.  We had another rereading the Maintenance Required Document and looking up the possible EICAS messages we might receive with a spoiler deactivated and assisting with checklists like fuel dumping and giving the flight attendants the brief.  I was overall in command talking to Dispatch and Maintenance Control and coordinating a plan.
column123: We were briefed by the incoming captain that they had a flight control problem coming into ZZZZ. We ran the checklist and it said land at the nearest suitable airport. Everyone then worked together after talking with maintenance to return to ZZZZ. We ended up dumping about 110;000 pounds of gas and came in for [a] max gross weight landing.

column121: Fume event. Entire crew on jetway. Jetway broken. Aircraft with ground crew member in flight deck. APU on packs on all doors shut. Once door opened I entered aircraft went into flight deck and smelled the dirty mold sock smell and got off jet. Fumes started to enter jetway most of us left jetway. Fumes caused eye irritation and sore throat at time of this writing.  Maintenance tried to get the Captain and First Officer to do engine run ups after this incident.Ground crew who was in flight deck during tow most likely did not have training in the dangers of this type of fumes. I spoke directly to the station manager about how dangerous fumes are and how long [operator] was exposed. [Manager] said [operators] could not [be forced to] get blood tested. The ground crew members were exposed for over 10 minutes that I am aware. I am sure it was more like 10 to 20 minutes.I reviewed the QRH checklist for smoke/fumes. It needs [to be] improved. I suggest [company] look at what [other carrier] have done with their checklist and procedures. I have heard their mechanics are required to wear protection for engine runs etc.; after this type of event. [Company] maintenance should not be requesting pilots to trouble shoot with no protection after fume event. They asked us to return to jet and do engine run ups.
column123: Plane was brought from the hardstand to gate. All crew was on jetbridge waiting to get on plane. The plane door was open and the FO (First Officer) and I entered the plane. He went into cockpit and I was in 1st class galley. I went to put my luggage away and told FO that the plane smelled awful. He agreed and we both got off. I got FA's [Flight Attendants] and we went halfway up the jetbridge and then the smell started coming up the jetbridge. We then went into the terminal. I called OPS and Crew Tracking. Paramedics checked us out and we deadheaded to ZZZ1 and we called [doctor] and were sent to [clinic] in ZZZ1 to be looked at.If you are involved in a fume event; the 1st thing once you call and report it; they should advise you to immediately step outside for fresh air. The doctor told us we need to do that. Second; it should be mandatory to immediately have blood drawn and tested for CO poisoning. We were under the impression that they would do that in ZZZ1. By the time we got there; it was too late to be tested.

column121: It was the FO (First Officer)'s leg into ZZZ. He had briefed the ILS approach which was the landing runway on the ATIS. A flap 40 degree landing was planned. The weather was VFR at the field with a cloud base at roughly 4;000 ft. MSL. ATC had us on a left downwind and turned us on a 90 degree base to final for Runway XXR. The FO had a 2.0 mile ring around the FAF ZZZZZ in the box to be fully configured for landing by then. And to the best of my recollection we were fully configured by the FAF. Runway XXR was in sight and ATC cleared us for the visual approach which was backed up by the ILS XXR. As we turned on to final for the Runway XXR at ZZZ; an accelerated red airspeed zipper came up on the bottom of the speed tape. There was an 'airspeed low' aural warning. The FO pushed the power in immediately; a stick shaker was felt; and the red airspeed zipper came down for the top of the airspeed tape. The FO disengaged the autopilot. There was very narrow gap on the upper and lower red zippers on the airspeed tape and the FO flew between the narrow gap. The FO stated; 'I'm not sure what is going on'. The chain of events happened at a very accelerated pace. Then the aircraft accelerated and the red zippers opened up and I called out ' watch your speed'. I remember seeing the aircraft accelerate near 159-160 kts. and I saw the red zipper on the top of the airspeed tape at 162 kts. In recovery; the aircraft climbed approximately 200-300 ft. We had Runway XXR in sight and the FO was in good position to land. I asked the FO if he was good with landing or if he wanted to do a go-around. The FO elected to continue the approach. Considering what we had just experienced; I felt that was a good choice. The FO continued the visual approach flying on the ILS XXR glide slope and localizer. At 1;000 ft. the FO made the 'stable' call out. At 500 ft. I made the 'stable' call out. We experienced no more airspeed red zipper indications or aural warnings for the remainder of the approach. The FO had a good landing. Upon landing I saw that the speed brakes did not automatically deploy so I manually deployed them. I noted after clearing the runway that due to the distractions; I failed to finish the 'below the line' checklist which I later mentioned to the FO. After the flight the FO and I decided to call Maintenance Control to discuss what had happened to us. Maintenance Control notified me that our Aircraft X had a 'history' of unreliable airspeed and that the FO's pitot tube was changed out. The Maintenance Representative voiced concern that it may be that our aircraft had a much 'bigger' maintenance issue and he wanted to pressure test the pitot system before releasing the aircraft. I put the 'write-up' in the maintenance book. I notified the outbound crew of what had happened and that my understanding was that Maintenance was on the way. ZZZ Operations was notified as well.I agreed with the Maintenance Representative that Aircraft X possibly had a bigger Maintenance issue at hand. When I called out 'watch your speed' as the airspeed was approaching 160 kts.; the First Officer had the same indication and matched mine. I have never seen anything like this event ever. So it seems possible that the airspeed was correct but the red zippers were not correct. Due to the distractions on final approach; I did not complete the Before Landing 'below the line' checklist and this did not register until touchdown when I had to manually deploy the speed brakes.I did not complete the Before Landing 'below the line' checklist. A go-around could have possibly helped in this situation but I do feel now as I did then; that the safest thing to do was land the aircraft straight ahead.

column121: When the fuel stick calculator was first approved for MD11; I had an aircraft that was not on a level ramp (roll attitude) with a number 3 fuel quantity on deferral. I used the online fuel stick calculator to try and verify the fuel quantity in the #3 tank. The numbers were off significantly. I used the maintenance manual procedure to correctly measure the quantity and it matched the known quantity. Afterwards I did more research and found that the web based fuel stick calculator to be inaccurate with the RH wing tanks of all fleets if the ramp isn't level. The problem stems from the fact that there is only one selection for wing tanks and that selection includes both left and right tanks. The calculator gives the same quantity for left and right tanks regardless of the roll selected. I had sent emails to the website contact and the Director of Maintenance office. Periodically throughout the last 6 years I have been sending emails to the office and discussed with my managers trying to get this corrected. About 6 months ago there was a read and sign about the importance of doing accurately sticking the tanks. This prompted me notifying the Maintenance office about the problems with the calculator again. I checked today and it still hasn't been corrected. I haven't heard back and I'm out of ideas to get this resolved. I believe the FAA would be very concerned if they were aware. Correct the calculator by making each tank a separate entry with its own table of quantities instead of combining left and right wings.

column121: In the event that occurred on Date a crossing restriction was assigned to my aircraft to cross ZZZZZ 10nm SW at 10;000 [feet]. I set that in my preselect on my altimeter and on the Garmin. Initially I missed the altitude at first and he repeated 10;000. I read back ZZZZZ 10nm SW 10;000. I reconfirmed with the passenger who decided to sit in the front with me and he confirmed that is what he heard (I also have his contact information). I began to get the plane into its descent to meet the restriction. I set the plane to meet its descent altitude right at 10000; 10 nm SW of ZZZZZ. At this point it had already been VFR conditions and turbulent through FL180. As I passed 15;000 I began noticing we were not going to make it over the mountain according to the chart and the visual out of the cockpit window. I leveled at around 13;500 to 13;800 (with Visual Separation). Again I had visual separation during the entire situation. Then I began to try and question ATC; I called 4-5 times several on Center and I believe twice on 121.5 (guard). I finally got the controllers attention when he ask probably perplexed at how low we had become. I read him back the crossing instructions he assigned over the radio; after confirming it; he apologized and stated if I could keep my own obstruction clearance; I confirmed I could; then assigned an immediate climb to 15;000 which I gladly executed. He had also in-between that claimed he assigned 16;000 (sounding unsure to me). I continued in bound and today the situation was avoided. Landed safely at ZZZ1 with no alert systems being activated.In this situation I should have caught the issue in the initial stages of the decent. I had ZZZ1 weather playing as the plane was descending and got it. In the descent as stated this is when I noticed the mountains becoming very close and compelled me to level off. I again tried to reach Center; I might have been too low for his receiver to hear me. I also tried Guard with no luck. Fortunately I finally got a hold of him. In this instance I could have leveled off soon instead of setting the auto pilot so meticulously maybe getting fixated on aviating. However; I do know the rules 'Aviate; Navigate; Communicate'. I aviated and then caught this situation happening in the Navigating Phase.As for ATC their Job is just as important as mine. I reconfirmed the altitude and crossing restriction. However; the error in altitude (if it was 16;000) was not caught. It also sounded like on Center that he became a little over saturated himself. I was not focused on it but he seemed [inundated] with multiple frequencies and more aircraft than a controller could handle by themselves. It sounded like some delay occurred somewhere. He apologized which initially made me wonder where the error occurred. I know his job is stressful and busy. I hope he submits a report on his end to see his perspective if anything were to come of this.As for correcting the situation I believe confirming altitudes and crossing restrictions is important. But in the mountains more than ever. From now on I will be double confirming my crossing restrictions and verifying plates before any descent is made to verify the crossing altitude.As for ATC I am not a controller and I know their worst fear would be to lose a plane. I know he was busy and probably [inundated]. But both sides keeping their ears peeled is ever more important.The Important thing is the situation was corrected and nobody was harmed. I used my skills to the best of my ability and I know the controller was giving his best too.

column121: I requested VFR flight following to ZZZ1 (a westerly departure) on the ground with ZZZ ground.  I was issued a squawk code and frequency.  I was subsequently cleared for takeoff by ZZZ Tower.  I was on initial climb out and began a turn to the west. I heard an aircraft report; 'we have a Cherokee right in front of us'!  At that moment my traffic information system called; 'traffic same altitude nine o'clock'.  I looked again to my left and saw a high wing aircraft within 100 feet of me at the same altitude!  He was so close I thought we were going to collide!  I had little time to react and the aircraft passed within a few feet behind me.  I pressed the PTT switch and said; 'that was close!'; to which the (presumably) pilot of the other aircraft responded; 'was that on purpose'?  I responded; 'of course not'!  I don't understand this comment.  It was as if Aircraft Y saw the impending convergence and decided to remain on course even though I was on his right side.  A few seconds later ZZZ Tower initiates my hand off to contact Approach.  I responded with; 'ZZZ Tower; go ahead with your telephone number' as I was incredibly shaken up from the extreme near miss and wanted to debrief post landing.Why did the controller not prevent this?  many minutes after my near miss the ZZZ Tower controller comes on frequency and advises all traffic the radar is out of service or intermittent.  I understand that equipment can fail however; he should have had a mental picture of proceedings and not cleared Aircraft Y for an extended right downwind to Runway XX when I was departing for a westerly destination.After landing I called the ZZZ Tower at XX35 and spoke to Name; the ZZZ Tower supervisor.  I discovered the following. I think the near miss aircraft was Aircraft Y.  A flight school aircraft based at ZZZ. There is an apparent familiarity between the controller and the (presumably) CFI onboard Aircraft Y.

column121: I filed a VFR flight plan as a private Part 91 pilot in my Lake Amphibian aircraft between ZZZ and ZZZ1. I was given a cross border squawk code and was using it flying north towards my destination. My aircraft has a current IFR pitot static system certification and my instrument ticket is current. On a VFR flight in suddenly deteriorating ceiling and visibility; I was flying low over the water in a place noted on the chart as Name enroute to ZZZ1 in what is clearly class G airspace. I was under some pressure to arrive at XA45 in ZZZ1 due to customs wanting a landing within 15 minutes before or after the filed time of arrival. I have quite a bit of experience flying low over the water in class G airspace; able to land in low visibility ceiling conditions. At approximately XC15; flying low over the water I suddenly and completely unexpectedly hit the water. I had already configurated the plane to a flaps down; mixture full rich; prop pitch flat attitude; for a water landing were it necessary to do so. But; I did not anticipate the plane hitting the water and when it did so the let down on the water was extremely violent. The plane pitched up in the air and back down slamming onto the water extremely hard. The plane came to a stop and myself and my single passenger were in dense fog. I [climbed] out of the cockpit with the plane on the water and stood on top of the cabin and looked at as much of the airframe as I could see to ascertain if there was any damage in the place as detectable in that portion of it visible floating above the surface of the water and saw none.There being no visibility and ceiling sufficient to fly in we displacement taxied for some 20 minutes. Being on the surface of the water and too low to contact anyone by radio my passenger called [number] and informed them that we would report back airborne if we were able to find a ceilings and visibility adequate to fly in. After 20 minutes of displacement taxiing on the water we got airborne and arrived a short time later in ZZZ1. I [received priority] going into the pattern because we did not get an up and locked light on the gear and wondered if we would get a down and locked light before landing the plane on the runway back to ZZZ and do a grass landing adjacent to the runway gear up rather than do that on the water or suffer a gear collapse landing on the runway. Tower was helpful. When I cycled the gear down I got a down and locked signal on the panel and proceeded to land the plane on the runway without incident.I flew home later that day and have not been able at this point to find damage to the airframe. It may be the case at the time of annual when I pull up the floorboards I will discover some bent frames but that is to be determined when I perform the inspection. The take away lesson in all of this is that despite not liking to set the plane down in saltwater because of a several hour clean up to prevent corrosion it is obvious to me that I need to be willing to do so if encountering lowering ceilings and visibility as I did when the event occurred.

column121: We left for ZZZ to do takeoff and landings. On takeoff; we were on the left tank; and left the left fuel gauge changed to empty. I pointed this out to the owner; he tapped on the gauge and it showed almost full. We entered the pattern and got no gear down in the annunciator panel I pointed this out to the owner and he said the gear is down and didn't seem surprised. We verify this with a small window on the floor between the front seats. We did several takeoff and landings and never got an annunciator panel gear down indication. The last landing was to be a short field landing. I reminded him not to get below 75 knots until in a low flare and ready to land. Previously his airspeed varied a lot on final. On a half mile final he was exactly at 75 knots. He seemed to be working hard on maintaining 75 knots. I was really focusing on his airspeed to be sure he didn't get below 75. Just seconds before touchdown we heard a 'go-around' on the radio we didn't know who it was for; why; or where it was coming from. No mention of plane type or reason. A few seconds before touchdown we both scanned the runway to be sure there was nothing on the runway. No gear down indication on the annunciator had been routine each time. I was guilty of confirmation bias that the gear was down. Fixating on the airspeed contributed to the incident. At no time during the landing did we get a gear warning or stall warning. In the future if the annunciator light becomes inoperative; I will use the small window on the floor each time in place of the annunciator light.

column123: Aircraft X contacted Tower in a wide right downwind; cleared for visual approach RWY XXL at ZZZ. I was working local control and cleared Aircraft X to land RWY XXL. After turning about a 12 mile right base; Aircraft X reported Aircraft Y a couple hundred feet above him a mile back. column121: GPS ECAM messages started occurring and going away as we got close to ZZZ. Captain notified ATC and GPS jamming was confirmed. This was a distraction for the rest of the flight. Approaching the terminal area and we had to put the jamming issue to the side to concentrate on the approach segment. Vectors were given off the ZZZZZ arrival for Runway XX; 6500 ft. prior to FAP; then cleared for the approach. I was high and was at a high rate of decent and needed to bleed off speed. I noticed the glide slope below and turned the AP (Auto Pilot) off and hand flew to get down and aligned with Runway XX. Configured to late even though we briefed the possibility of unstable approaches and the need to set up early. At 1;000 ft. call out; was unstable. Performed soft go around. While performing this; vectors and altitudes were given by Tower. Left turn and climbing instructions were given. Captain was task saturated with ATC instructions and the heading knob giving him issues; I tried to assist and accidentally turned the speed knob down instead of the heading bug. It stood at 100 and during the climb I noticed the speed decaying towards vls. I remember saying out loud; why is the speed dropping. I leveled off to keep the speed from hitting vls. Then noticed I turned the wrong knob. I asked the Captain to increase my speed. More vectors were given. Speed was increasing. AP turned on by me because I realized that could help the situation. I shouldn't have touched anything since AP was off. Captain was trying to set up the MCDU (Multipurpose Control Display Unit) for the ILS again. Captain asked for the aircraft so I can try it. Vectors to the LOC were given. We joined it; cleared for ILS. We configured early and landed safely.  Initially; the GPS jamming played a big role in distracting us. ECAM messages kept popping up; then disappearing. Captain kept trying to troubleshoot the issue. I noticed this as we got closer to the airport and simply said to him to let's focus on this arrival brief so we don't get behind. I briefed the issue of the go arounds due to aircraft being unstable on this approach. So we tried to be ready early but was too high and descending fast to fix the issue as well as off course with the vectors given. Additionally; I failed to not let the Captain handle the FCU (Fuel Control Unit) while I was flying. A lot was happening in a short time with vectors and completing the soft go around. I noticed the issue the Captain was having with the knobs on the FCU and tried to help. I should have turned on the AP; then work the FCU while the Captain handled the radios. Hand flying while doing a go around added to the stress during this event [I suggest] Configuring early. AP on while doing the go around. Situational awareness when turning knobs on the FCU. column121: Cleared via the RUGGD 2 RNAV SID. Maintain 230 KTS. Cleared to takeoff almost immediately behind a B757. Calm winds. We were heavy enough that 230 KTS was barely above green dot speed (min safe speed for an Airbus). Encountered up to moderate wake turbulence. No way to climb above it based the slow climb speed and being a heavy A321. Continued off and on until almost BUBBY waypoint. Eventually asked for a slight left upwind heading but it helped only a little.ATC clearing us to takeoff too close behind a B757. 230 KT demanded climb speed. We didn't demand a takeoff delay behind the B757 even though both aircraft are 'large'. We also didn't demand a higher climb speed.A B757 is still a hazardous aircraft to take off behind. Even our ADS-B system labels them as a 'high vortex' wake as opposed to simply 'large'. The FAA needs to re institute heavy wake separation behind B757s instead of cramming in more departures by deciding a large behind a 757 doesn't need any wake separation. I will be asking for at least 30 sec after liftoff or at least 1 minute after brake release when taking off behind a B757 from here on. The FAA should also be aware that an A321 is not the best performing aircraft.

column121: During takeoff roll; the jet's nose began to rise when the First Officer (FO) reduced forward side stick pressure to neutral. I visually noticed the jet's nose rising and holding a nose up pitch. The mains didn't feel as if they had extended struts and lifted off. I checked the side stick indications on the PFD (Primary Flight Display) and it had been removed so the jet definitely thought we were in the air. The FO applied forward command of the side stick but not enough to force the nose wheel back to the ground. He didn't want the jet to go into the landing mode with max auto brakes already selected as we do normally for takeoff. By this time I checked the airspeed and it indicated 120 KIAS (approx 40 below V1). We continued to accelerate to V1 and Vr. I told the First Officer to use caution on rotation. He neutralized the side stick and the jet had enough elevator command in neutral position to gain altitude. As we moved into the 2nd segment of the climb; the jet flew normally due to the auto trim adjustment after takeoff. When we reached TOC (Top of Climb); we reviewed our actions including trim settings and performance numbers for takeoff and everything checked out as normal. I even remember checking the performance trim setting against the CG trim setting in the Fuel Pred page of the FMGC after engine start (my normal 'gross error' check on every flight). We could only determine that the jet may have been loaded in error or the load numbers were reported with an error to Maintenance so we sent an ACARS message to the Dispatcher asking for a baggage loading audit on arrival. Dispatch responded telling us the Sector Manager would command the audit at our arrival. Request result of load audit for any ASAP recommendations.

column121: Maintenance did a tail rotor inspection that morning; and needed me to do the run up to check the balance afterwards. Why I didn't look at the directional of the rotors when I looked at them; I don't know aside from complacency and reliance on the RII. column121: Aircraft X departing ZZZ the left main gear would not retract. The number one priority at the moment for us was to get back and land as soon as possible as we were not sure about the possible external or internal damages that those bangs might have caused. I contacted tower and made sure to have fire trucks waiting for us down the runway. Shortly after landing; we stopped at the runway and asked fire trucks to inspect the engines. There were no signs of damage so we continued to the gate.As of now we are not aware of the exact cause; but we're expecting it to be a mechanical malfunction.

column121: My day started at XA:30am to assist with the AAIP (Approved Aircraft Inspection Program) inspection on the back up aircraft. Removed tail rotor blade individually for AAIP Zone 12 section A0312.10.2 inspection. I loosened both attaching bolts; removed one nut/washer; removed bolt; pivoted tail rotor blade away from the mount and reinstalled the bolt and washer/nut; removed other mounting hardware in the same manner to preserve hardware installation location. I took the blade down to a bench to clean and inspect. Reinstalled the inspected blade in the reverse of removal. Repeated the process for the second blade. I was aware the blades are easy to install backwards; but somehow that happened with one of the blades. I had the Lead mechanic look over the work; for installation and cotter pins.The Pilot also looked at the work. All three of us missed that one blade was installed backwards. During the initial run up for track and balance; the Pilot commented how rough the tail rotor pedals felt; I observed the tail area shaking more than normal and told the pilot to shut it down. Only one engine was started and at ground idle. I was thinking at the time that maybe I had dropped a washer during the removal/installation. After shut down; The Lead Mechanic came out asking what was wrong; I told him we had a bad vibration and he noticed the tail rotor blade installed backwardsStarting later in the day today would have allowed for more rest prior to working for me. Due to my assisting with the heavy maintenance on the base aircraft as well as taking care of my base aircraft in [another city]; the past 2 weeks have been full of fairly long days. Having a more thorough RII / CYA; standing back and looking at the big picture and not focusing just on cotter pins being installed. I could have marked the blade before I took it off to help ensure I got it installed correctly as well.
column123: We were going to start an A/F zone 12 inspection by completing the tail rotor sections; essentially visually inspect the system; remove the tail rotor blades from hub (hub is still on aircraft) inspect attachment and dynamically balance tail rotor. I left the hangar to run over to the [other company location] to look for some equipment and the base mechanic stayed to remove the tail rotor blades. When I returned he told me he had the blades off and back on and was just finishing the cotter pins. when he was finished I looked at the back side of the blades and verified that cotter pins were installed; the pilot was informed of what was done and she looked it over as well; we  pushed the aircraft out to start the balance runs. I went back into the office to work on the paperwork and heard the aircraft start 1 engine and immediately shut down. After shut down it was determined that one tail rotor blade was installed backwards. At that point I looked up the measures to take for high vibrations and contacted my [supervisor].This aircraft is a backup aircraft covering heavy maintenance on our base aircraft. Slow down; since the base has been under stress given the maintenance on primary aircraft and the mechanic had to drive up we should have started the maintenance later in the morning to allow for more rest. Most importantly I should have stood back and looked at the big picture of the blade removal and not focused on the attachment of the blades.
