column121: We were departing ZZZ Runway XY. I was the PM and the FO was the PF. After getting clearance to line up and wait; I taxied the aircraft onto the runway; stopped; and handed control to the FO. I said 'your brakes; my radios'. The FO assumed control by stating 'my aircraft' but subsequently realized that the rudder pedals were not locking in position when she applied pressure with her feet. She tried to make an adjustment and it again did not lock. I assumed that she was having problems securing the pedals; and knowing that my rudder pedals were secure; I stated 'my aircraft' and stated something to the effect that I would do the takeoff. I planned to takeoff and hand controls in cruise; but then decided that since I did the takeoff that I would do the landing and she would fly the next leg of the sequence. The takeoff was uneventful. During cruise she tried to secure the rudder pedals and had no issues. After landing while taxiing to the gate; she asked me if she could check the pedals. The pedals again were not staying in position when she tried to lock them. I wrote a maintenance entry in the logbook describing the fact that the FO rudder pedals could not be secured. The FO during cruise had expressed concerns about the rudder pedals on the older Airbus 319 as this had been her 2nd or 3rd flight where the pedals could not be secured.The FO's before takeoff flow does not include a rudder check as the CA does. The only time that the FO notices that the rudder pedals cannot be secured (if not checked at the gate prior to pushback) is when control is handed over prior to the takeoff roll. A suggestion would be to include a rudder position/adjustment check during preflight as it would be difficult to do an FO rudder check during taxi the way the check is done by depressing the button on the tiller.
column123: Date 1This morning we were departing from ZZZ to ZZZ1.  I was the pilot flying departing on Runway XY. I began the takeoff and had my feet on the rudder pedals.The rudders moved and I tried to quickly adjust them. They slipped again and I told the Captain. He quickly took the controls and continued the takeoff roll with normal rudder control on his side.At this point the thought was I had not properly locked the rudder pedals in place when I set them.Once in cruise I started to think about some previous experiences I have had with the rudder pedals over the last year.In-flight I repeatedly pressed on the rudders and confirmed they were in fact locked in place. Although it appeared there was no issue with my pedals at this point the captain continued to be the pilot flying. During taxi in ZZZ1 I asked if I could check my rudders to see if in fact the issue was resolved but once again they would not lock in place I could push them forward and aft freely. A similar scenario happened to me on two other occasions with a different aircraft.Date 2From ZZZ2-ZZZSame scenario however it occurred at V1/R so I rotated and gave the Captain the controls. After passing through 10;000 feet it appeared that my pedals were again working correctly so I became the pilot flying again and continued for landing at ZZZ. On touchdown the position of the pedals went from 1-2 all the way to 12. The Captain took control of the aircraft. We wrote up the malfunction in the logbook and asked maintenance to come out so we could explain what had happened.Date 3I arrive at work to fly another turn to ZZZ3 from ZZZ and immediately checked the logbook.I found that the rudder pedal position was on MEL for positions 0 to 3.Since I set my rudder pedals within that position; I asked the Captain to refuse the aircraft citing safety concerns.I have pictures of the write ups and logbook entries.Date 4ZZZ4-ZZZSame aircraft as Date 2 and similar situation. Just prior to starting the Departure roll the rudders slipped in position and I quickly corrected them for takeoff. The remainder of that takeoff was normal. However; I was certain that I had properly set my rudder pedals back at the gate and checked them.I went back to my records and realized this was the same aircraft I had a problem with approximately six months prior. I briefed Captain on my previous experience. In cruise the pedals remain locked in place as normal. I was the pilot flying and on touchdown on Runway XY in ZZZ as I applied brake pressure the rudder pedals again went all the way to 12.Once again; we entered all the information in the logbook and requested maintenance come to the gate so we could explain the situation. The Captain requested follow up through a report but to my knowledge he had never received any.This morning almost 11 months from the original time this happened and in a different aircraft. I did not expect it to be the same problem. Initial I thought I had made a mistake and not locked the pedals. Unfortunately; it appears it is the same problem as on the other aircraft and I am quite concerned. This is potentially serious malfunction that has happened on two different aircraft. I am happy to provide any further information that could assist in making sure this safety concern does not happen again.Some additional notes- I understand from my systems knowledge there is no difference in the positioning of the rudder pedals whether in the air or on the ground. However; all three times the pedals seem to stay locked in place in the air.- At the gate when I reset my rudder position; I always push on them to confirm they are locked in place. A suggestion my Captain had was to possibly add a rudder check for the first officer during taxi. This added check may be another barrier for the crew.[Suggest] Inspections of malfunctioning item that has caused this in two of our aircraft that I am aware of.

column123: Arrived at gate saw unusual EICAS Slat drive message. Entered as MRM code and called TLV Operations to have maintenance come to aircraft. Maintenance worked the issue and cleared the item. We communicated to Nicosia we had a flight control issue; declared emergency and told of our intentions were to return to TLV. We requested hold and informed Nicosia we would have to jettison fuel as well. Nicosia authorized the fuel Jettison. We entered hold about 118 miles North of TLV and worked the Slat drive EICAS and the un-annunciated fuel jettison checklist. Both checklists completed successfully. It had been the FOs leg but after checklists had been completed I opted to fly the airplane back to TLV.We were within 180 miles of TLV which required us to talk to BGN control to request re-entry into their airspace and to also declare the emergency. They asked if we were a priority aircraft and we affirmed. During the hold we tried to Satcom dispatch after we had already notified them of the nature of the issues via ACARS and included our intentions. Satcom was weak so we sent ACARS to dispatch to work out our landing distance needed with our slat drive malfunction. We came up with approximately 7;000 feet runway needed and dispatch came up with 7;200.  After checklists completed and fuel jettisoned down to MLW we requested clearance to TLV. TLV offered us straight in RW 12 which we accepted. column121: Before take-off; I performed my normal pre-takeoff checks; and everything was perfect; including a brake check; flight controls free and correct; auto pilot off; and trim set for takeoff. I also had a passenger who is an experienced RV pilot that I frequently fly with him; either in his airplane or mine.  I was cleared for takeoff on Runway XX by the Control Tower. My normal takeoff procedure is to do a soft field takeoff; where I have the control stick full aft as I start to feed in power. As the airplane starts to roll and increases speed; the nose wheel comes off the ground; and I relax aft pressure on the stick and hold the nose wheel off the ground until the airplane flies itself off the ground. On the day this occurred; I was in takeoff attitude; with the nose wheel off the ground; and was accelerating down the runway. I started to feel forward pressure on the stick; which became heavier and heavier. I glanced down at the trim indicator and it showed a full nose down trim indication. I immediately pulled power to idle to abort the takeoff and was now focused on keeping the airplane under directional control and getting it stopped. As I applied braking to stop the airplane; I realized that I was getting close to the south end of Runway XX. I applied heavy braking being careful not to skid the tires and risk a blow-out. When I reached near the end of Runway XX; I felt that I was still moving too fast to safely make the 90 degree left turn onto Taxiway Alpha. I elected to taxi straight ahead and get the airplane stopped or go off the runway pavement and into the grass. I was not able to get the airplane stopped; so I went off the runway pavement and approximately 20 ft. into the grass. I made an immediate 180 degree turn back onto the runway pavement; made a right turn toward Taxiway Alpha and exited the runway onto Taxiway Alpha. After clearing the runway; I called the Control Tower and advised them that I had aborted my takeoff and that I had a malfunction with my trim and that I was going to troubleshoot the malfunction while I was in the run-up area for Runway XY; and I would call them back with my intentions. My airplane is equipped with electric pitch and roll trim; which is activated by a hat switch located on each control stick grip.  After troubleshooting the system; we determined that I had experienced a runaway trim condition. I called the Control Tower and informed them that I wanted to taxi back to my hangar. They gave me the taxi clearance and I taxied to my hangar. The airplane is grounded until I can get a satisfactory understanding and repair to the electric trim system. There was no personal injury to me or my passenger and there was no damage to airport property. The main gear fairings were scraped on the bottom presumably when the aircraft transitioned from concrete to the grass.

column121: I am submitting this report because This is the second time I've experienced this situation. After sending an email to [the] Manager the first time and not getting a response; I am submitting this report. It has been a relatively new procedure to leave hydraulic switches off during preflight inspection. It used to be that hydraulics switches were always left on. Because the hydraulic pumps were off during our preflight inspection; we did not observe the hydraulic leak that was present. During the 'Pushback' checklist when the hydraulic switches were finally turned on; we received an 'RF' message on the EICAS within about 4-5 seconds. I then contacted Maintenance Control. Upon Maintenance Technician arriving; he advised we had a serious hydraulic leak spraying fluid all over the wheel well. Long story short; we ended up being almost 2 hours delayed getting the leak repaired. If we had NOT received the 'RF' message; we would've most likely had taken off with this leak and would've gotten a B hydraulic low quantity or even worse loss of hydraulic B pressure inflight!I've asked many people in several chief pilot offices; and sent emails to training and no one has offered a reason; other than standardize with other fleet type. I believe this is a safety issue. Leaving the hydraulic pumps off during preflight makes observing possible leaks impossible.

column121: Leveling at FL240 during descent into ZZZ; ATC asked us to report our altitude because she was not receiving anything from us. When we looked down; the Captain noticed that IFF 2 had a fault and switched it to his side. At about that time we both noticed a power surge which made my clock blank momentarily and the Captain noticed lights on his panel flash. Next we had a series of lights come on spaced apart by a few minutes at first and then began to come on more quickly as time passed. First we had a cooling fan supply light. Then when cleared to descend via the arrival; I pushed recall and noticed the left pack light remained illuminated. Suspecting something wrong with the power distribution system; I cycled through electrical panel wafer switch positions and found no amps coming from TR 2 or 3 and negative 3 amps on the battery. I hacked my clock. About 5 minutes had already passed. I took the radios while the Captain ran the checklist for the pack light next and shortly after; we lost the left aft fuel boost pump. I told the Captain I thought we had a power distribution problem and we were draining our battery. I thought we might be slowly shedding components due to their power sources being associated with the battery. As we passed 10;000 ft. I told the Captain and he put away the book and ran the landing checklist. While on the descent; I recommended [requesting priority handling] so we could land ASAP. I configured early in prep for a slam dunk and the Captain and I agreed to starting the APU just in case. By this time we were on base and more lights had come on. We lost the B Electrical Hydraulic Pump; had a right side window over heat light; battery discharge light; TR fail light; and a few pitot lights had come on. Then while turning to final; I noticed the short vectors would overshoot me so I clicked off autopilot and turned. That's when I noticed I had no electric trim. The Captain manually ran the trim for me as we slowed and configured and we had an uneventful landing. After the fire trucks greeted us and found no hot spots around the E & E bay; we discussed whether we had enough power on the battery and I noted the time had been 17 minutes from when I noticed the negative amps on the battery and started the clock. We continued to taxi to the gate and after the fire crew came up I went with them down to the E & E bays to do my own inspection. I didn't see or smell anything. Aircraft X is an old airplane. The older planes get the more they will have gremlins like this. Maintenance discovered a faulty number 2 generator or regulator with some certainty that an Aircraft phase was not getting to the busses. How many more lights would have come on eventually? Just thank goodness we were so close to landing when it failed.

column121: While giving instruction; we were performing pattern work at ZZZ. After successfully executing several take off and landings; we were holding short of XXL. The previous three patterns were right traffic patterns. To the best of my knowledge; all other local traffic was also right traffic patterns. We were given clearance to take off; and this time asked to fly left traffic. I initiated a normal takeoff and began to climb out. As we were climbing out; we experienced electrical problems; and the alternator dropped off line. I completed a right turn on crosswind and another right turn onto downwind and leveled at pattern altitude. After we were stabilized on downwind; we performed an alternator reset; and the alternator came back on line. At this time the Tower Controller informed me that I was supposed to make left traffic. I immediately recalled my takeoff instructions at that point; and knew I had made inadvertent right turns during the confusion of the electrical issue. I apologized on the Tower frequency and no further mention was made. We landed uneventfully and as we taxied back to the holding point at XXL; I apologized again. We then executed two more turns in the pattern making right traffic. On the second; and final pattern; we experienced the electrical issue again. And the alternator dropped off line. At this time I informed ZZZ Tower that we were experiencing electrical problems and we needed to land. We declined to [request priority handling]; but the Tower Controllers were outstanding; giving us priority to land. We landed uneventfully. ZZZ Ground asked if we needed any assistance; and I said I believed we did not and taxied to the Hangar. The airplane is currently down for maintenance; to trouble shoot the electrical problem. I believe the confusion of the electrical issue lead to fixation on my part and I defaulted to what we had done the previous three times. We should have ended the flight after the initial electrical occurrence; but we believed it was a one off occurrence. Since we were planning to stay local; I was not writing down the takeoff instructions. In the future; I plan to write down takeoff instructions for all flights.

column121: This report was composed by an Instructor at FBO (at ZZZ). I am not the Students primary Instructor. A Student had to initiate a go-around after getting close to 'traffic to follow' while on short final to Runway XX. The private pilot Student completed FAR 91.103 requirements before proceeding with his local pattern flight. Weather was not a factor during today's mishap. ATIS information (XA56Z) reported winds calm; 10 miles visibility; sky condition clear; temperature 29; dew point 2 degrees Celsius; altimeter 29.97; visual approach to Runway XX. Fuel onboard was 20 gallons. Student was also familiar with Runway lengths as well as takeoff and landing distances. Student had on his person government issued photo ID; medical; proper logbook endorsements; and Student pilot certificate. Onboard aircraft (required documentation complied with).Student's last flight was 9 days ago. An aircraft had dropped FOD on the active XX Runway while the Student was on a solo flight in the pattern. Runway XX was closed temporarily while airport vehicles were dispatched to find the FOD. Meanwhile the Student was told to hold South of Runway XX. After the Student asked for clarification the controller told him to make 360s south of the airport. Student made 3 360s south of the Runway; meanwhile the FOD was found and Runway XX operations were resumed. Student then re-established himself on the left downwind for XX when he was then told to extend his downwind. Student was told number 3 to land Runway XX. Student waited till number 2 traffic was 45 degrees off his left shoulder before turning base. Student quickly overtook traffic on final and initiated a go-around while the traffic to follow was still on short final. Prior to this go-around Student had been told to initiate a go-around by Tower. A compilation of unfamiliar radio calls in the traffic pattern; 360s; downwind extension; a temporary runway closure; and two go-arounds narrowed the margin of safety and nearly exceeded the Student pilot's piloting capabilities; leading to a close spacing on final which lead to a go-around. The Student pilot feels remorse for what happened and the event has been debriefed in detail. The Student pilot has learned from his mistakes. The primary cause was pilot error; a high workload led to decreased situational awareness in the pattern.

column121: Aircraft X experienced an upset aircraft state as a result of severe turbulence encountered on approach to ZZZ Runway XXR. The aircraft pitched to approximately 20 degrees nose up and 10 to 15 degrees left bank; disengaging the autopilot and causing the autothrust to increase power toward max. The airspeed decayed from 250 KIAS to 220 KIAS as the aircraft climbed from 10;000 ft. to 10;900 ft. before upset recovery procedures returned it to stable flight at 10;000 ft. and 250 KIAS. There were no injuries as passengers and flight attendants were seated early in anticipation of turbulence. There was no aircraft damage. Aircraft X made an uneventful landing on Runway XXR. The severe turbulence encounter was reported to Air Traffic Control and the Company. A full debrief was conducted with Flight Operations.Prior to descending into ZZZ; the First Officer (FO) and I discussed concerns about thunderstorms and convective activity in the terminal area. We had plenty of gas and I noted that ZZZ1 weather was excellent. I briefed the flight attendants to be seated approximately 20 minutes before touchdown. I then confirmed that they were seated. I made a PA to the passengers that I expected very bumpy conditions and I emphasized the need for them to obey the Fasten Seat Belt sign. The FO and I briefed windshear precautions; indications; and procedures while inbound to ZZZ2 for the ZZZZZ [arrival]. We did not re-brief the Upset Recovery procedures as they had been briefed prior to departure. (In retrospect; I think this could be good to review when windshear concerns are expressed as the windshear could result in an upset.) We were initially cleared on the ZZZZZ arrival. We loaded the Runway XXL ILS approach. Shortly into the descent; we had an AUTOFLT RUD TRIM 1 FAULT ECAM. I wrote it up as we were descending. Shortly after that; ATC vectored us off the arrival. ATC did not tell us what we should expect; but I heard several aircraft ahead of us receiving clearances to ZZZZZ1 for what I assumed would be the remainder of the ZZZZZ arrival. Radio communication congestion was significant. I sensed ATC was struggling to manage the number of arrivals from the north. I did not hear anyone receiving holding clearances. Holding might have alleviated the density of traffic and eased the friction for ATC. Eventually; we were told to do a 360 degree turn. Out of the turn; we were cleared to descend to 10;000 ft and given a heading of 190deg. I had heard another aircraft given a vector toward the ZZZZZ2 intersection; so I put it on the fix page for situational awareness. At that time; I was watching the radar which showed a cell next to the ZZZZZ2 intersection and another cell to the southwest. The two aircraft ahead of us were vectored through that gap. A 777 was behind us. At that time; we still did not know what arrival or approach clearance to expect. As we passed through the gap between the two cells; ATC said to advise when we could take a turn direct to ZZZZZ3. We did not have ZZZZZ3 loaded into the FMC. The FO did not know what ZZZZZ3 was. I asked him to load it and I spelled it out. (We still had Runway XXL loaded.) As we tried to get ZZZZZ3 loaded; along with the remainder of the ILS XXR approach; while still in the gap between the two cells; we experienced the severe turbulence and upset. After recovering the aircraft; I gave direction to the FO to load DIRECT ZZZZZ3 and I spelled it again. He did so; and we turned direct to the fix. He then connected the rest of the approach and it was flown uneventfully.As far as the execution of the Upset Recovery procedure; I did not comply with all the procedures. I also did not verbalize the steps and I did not silence the autopilot aural which resulted from the disconnect for quite some time. I had trouble focusing on the instruments and the 'Startle Effect' was significant.
column123: Descending into ZZZ on the ZZZZZ arrival; we were taken off the arrival. I am assuming it was because of the convective weather in the area. We had flown in from the north and were being vectored west away from ZZZ. It seemed ATC was overwhelmed with all of the aircraft and bad weather in the area. Because we knew there was adverse weather around the airport the Captain sat the passengers and flight attendants well in advance. At one point while being vectored west we were told to fly multiple different headings which eventually made us complete a giant 360 degree turn. At the end of the turn I noticed that ATC was vectoring aircraft towards ZZZZZ2 intersection which seemed like ATC had found a gap they were funneling aircraft through. I pulled up ZZZZZ2 intersection on the fix page so we could see we where it was in relation to our position on the nav display. ATC gave us a heading of 190 that was towards ZZZZZ2 intersection. At this point ATC did not tell us which runway or routing to expect. While flying on a heading of 190 and 250 kts. at 10;000 ft. we flew into a cloud and at that point we experienced an upset event of severe turbulence. The aircraft gained about 900 ft.; dropped 30 kts.; banked 10-15 degrees and disengaged the autopilot. The Captain was flying and immediately returned us to straight and level flight. The Captain reported the incident to ATC and I checked in with the Flight Attendants and no injuries occurred in the cabin. After the event ATC told us to go to ZZZZZ3 intersection and to expect Runway XXR. We landed the airplane and contacted the company about the event.

column121: During climb passing approximately FL280 the flight attendant called and informed me that a passenger believed we were trailing fuel out of our #2 engine.  All engine indications appeared normal including engine fuel flow.  Checking our fuel we determined we were showing an imbalance of approximately 1500 pounds with the right wing being low. We continued to monitor to determine if the fuel imbalance remained stable or if the imbalance was increasing. We received a second call from the flight attendant informing us we had a company A320 instructor pass riding. He and I spoke and he told me it appeared to be fuel trailing the #2 engine. I sent the First Officer back to the cabin for a visual inspection and told him to look forward and aft of the wing and specifically any damage he might see on the forward edge of the wing.  While he performed a visual inspection; the flight attendant in the cockpit showed me cell phone video of the leak. I leveled off at FL380 and verified the fuel imbalance was increasing to about 1700lbs with the right wing on the low side.  I referenced the QRH for fuel leak and sent dispatch a message that we had a fuel leak; needed to divert and would be shutting down the #2 engine. The First Officer returned and informed me of the same information and we began running the fuel leak QRH.  Dispatch recommended ZZZZ and looking at our distance and time required for descent I determined it to be a proper divert location. I [requested priority] with ZZZZ Center and requested an immediate turn to ZZZZ and descent to FL 200. The First Officer and I ran the fuel leak QRH which directed an engine shutdown for a fuel leak out of the engine or pylon followed by the engine shutdown checklist.  We shut the engine down in an idle power descent and I started the APU. I then transferred flying duties to the First Officer.  ZZZZ Center handed us off to ZZZZ Approach. ZZZZ is an non radar airfield. They told us to report 30 miles from the airfield and asked if we could maintain VMC.   Weather was scattered to broken with some vertical development but was sufficient to maintain VMC and the field was reporting 6;000 scattered.  Approach gave us a descent to 7;000 and offered the [non-precision] Approach to Runway XX. I asked for the ILS for XX. Approach asked if we could fly a visual to Runway 26 and conditions were sufficient for that and we were cleared for the visual approach. We never received guidance information on our ILS though it was programmed correctly. After an uneventful landing by the First Officer we taxied to a hard stand. Foreign Country aviation authorities inspected our certificates/medical/airworthiness certificate/insurance certificate which the company instructor was very helpful working that while I worked with operations. Operations moved the passengers indoors to a gate seating area. I worked with the Chief Pilot and Maintenance Control. They informed me that the passengers would be taken on a flight from ZZZZ-ZZZZ1-ZZZ. I made several announcements and trips to the gate holding area and informed all passengers of our plan.  Most of the passengers had left carry-on bags on the aircraft; but Foreign Country security wouldn't let them return to retrieve it. I coordinated with Station Operations to have aft air stairs brought up so we could get the passenger to come back and file front to back through the airplane to retrieve their items before their inbound flight arrived and coordinated with Foreign Country security.  Foreign Country security eventually agreed but only allowing 4 passengers at a time.
column123: On climbout from ZZZZ1 we were passing FL280 when the Flight Attendant (FA) called us.  He said a passenger (who is a pilot) said that it looked like fuel was coming out of our #2 engine.  We monitored the fuel page.  The engine fuel used totals were identical; as were the wingtip tanks.  The inboard wing tanks showed an imbalance of 1000 pounds.  Over the remaining 5 minutes of our climbout we watched the imbalance increase to 1400 pounds.  During this time we got another call from the FA.  He put us on with an Airbus Instructor that was non-revving in the back.  He told us it appeared that fuel was coming from the engine exhaust.The Captain took over the aircraft and I went back to look for myself.  There was nothing visible on the front of the wing or the front of the engine.  I went back to row XX and could clearly see a fluid coming out of the exhaust of #2.  I returned to the flight deck and told the Captain.  We ran the Fuel Leak checklist and it directed us to shut down the engine.  After starting a descent to FL200; we did so.  We secured the engine and talked to dispatch.  He directed us to either ZZZZ1 or ZZZZ.  ZZZZ1 was further and the weather was reported as suboptimal.  We chose ZZZZ.The Captain and I turned the aircraft back to ZZZZ and finished the descent to FL200.  We briefed up the approach and I took control of the aircraft.  Approach control informed us there was no radar service.  We used the local MSA to ensure terrain clearance until we were clear of the clouds and could see the airfield.  I maneuvered the aircraft to a 6-7 mile final and we configured the aircraft for landing.  There was no glideslope which we knew; but the localizer wasn't working either.  We confirmed with Tower that they could see us and that we were lined up on the correct airport.  During the confusion we forgot the Before Landing Checklist; but the Spoilers Not Armed message reminded us.  We accomplished the checklist and were fully stable and complete by 500 ft. AGL.Landing was normal; the Captain took the aircraft around 80 knots on the rollout.  We taxied clear to a hard stand near the terminal.  Most of the passengers deplaned into the terminal.  We coordinated with the Foreign Country equivalent of the FAA; as well as dispatch and maintenance.  After the passengers got on the rescue airplane; we closed up the plane and went to the hotel.

column121: I was the Pilot Monitoring while on an Initial Operating Instruction flight training with a new First Officer (FO).  During climb out of ZZZ on the ZZZZZ7 Departure Procedure; a smoldering singe smell  resembling an electrical or wire insulation became apparent to me at approximately 8;000 feet.  As we climbed through 10;000 feet; the smell became very strong; and my FO and I mentioned the smell simultaneously.  I called my flight attendant and inquired if she also smelled the fumes; to which she said; 'yes it is pretty strong.'  I asked her to check areas of potential fire including the forward closet; galley; lavatory and cargo areas. I requested to stop my climb at 12;000 feet; notified ATC about the fumes resembling a potential fire.  We also requested to return to the airport in ZZZ; and [requested priority handling] and descended to 8;000 feet under ATC clearance.                                                                                                      We notified the flight attendant we would be returning to the field in about 10 minutes and to expect a briefing shortly. I elected for the FO to continue flying the aircraft.  Given his experience level I continued communication with ATC; ran checks; and coordinated with the flight attendant. The FO and I donned our O2 Masks and ran the smoke evacuation QRC/QRH checklist.  After that initial check was complete I coordinated a report with the flight attendant; ACARS dispatched about the return to field; and made a brief passenger announcement.  By this time; we had an ATIS; approach and landing data for an approach to ZZZ; and were on a about 12 mile base to turn for ILS XXR into ZZZ.  I briefly looked at the smoke fumes checklist as well.  Given the time to landing; it became apparent there would be no time to diagnose the source of the fumes and we already 'vented' the cabin.  All circuit breakers were in and systems performed normally.  I elected to stop that check; take the controls from the FO; and make an overweight landing in ZZZ.  Priority personnel had been notified and were waiting to inspect the aircraft.  Upon [arrival] no reasonable indications of external fire or smoke; I taxied the aircraft to the gate with Crash Fire Rescue following.  After shutdown; passengers were deplaned normally with no known injury to passengers or aircraft damage.
column123: We departed runway XXR on the ZZZZZ7 departure after making the initial turn direct to ZZZZZ and climbing I began to smell what was a burning wire or a rubber insulation smell. When we approach closer to 12;000 feet the smell was extremely strong and that is when I questioned the Captain if he too was smelling the burning smell. After confirming this; the Captain called the flight attendant who also confirmed this smell coming from the forward part of the aircraft. After confirming our suspicions; the flight attendant began searching in the forward part of the aircraft and the rear to observe the baggage compartment. The Captain told me to keep flight controls and he began to observe systems pages and the circuit breakers. We saw nothing; which we began running checklists in the QRH. I programmed the approach back into ZZZ; the Captain requested priority handling and from there we donned our oxygen masks. After confirming crew communications; I got the ATIS and built the approach; and the Captain handled communications and checklists. ATC brought us around very quickly to the final approach course and with suspicion of fire the Captain and myself did not want to waste any time. We continued on the approach and with a heavier than normal aircraft; once everything was set up the Captain landed the plane. We had the support vehicles waiting and followed us into the gate. We had them look for visible flames and tried to get thermal scan on the aircraft. We had advised Dispatch of what happened and maintenance as well. [The] Captain performed extremely well through the process and as a cockpit I believe we did very well as a crew considering the circumstances.

column121: Myself; a Commercial pilot; CFI-I and a Private Pilot who owned the aircraft were flying back into ZZZ and had requested the overhead break approach. The approach controller cleared us for the approach and informed us to report a 2 mile initial for the approach. At the same time a C172 was on the ILS XX at ZZZ above us. When we reported the 2 mile initial for the overhead break we had just passed underneath the C172 and subsequently lost visual contact on the aircraft as they were above and behind us. The tower cleared us for a right break over the departure end of Runway XX and to wait for the tower to call the base turn. I am not sure why but both myself and the other pilot on board misinterpreted the exact location to start the approach. We both believed that we should start the turn over the approach end of Runway XX; even after correctly repeating back the instructions for starting the turn on the departure end. Again; I am not entirely sure why two experienced pilots both misinterpreted a relatively simple instruction; but a misunderstanding between pilot and controller was evident. The pilot who was on the radio asked the control tower for clarification on when  to start the break and we were met with no answer. I began the right turn over the approach end of the runway. The control tower immediately requested to know what our intentions were. Again; we asked for clarification on when to start the turn on the break and the tower instructed us to continue the downwind and wait for clearance to turn base. This was where the major mistake was made; as I continued the right turn into the final approach corridor. I am not sure why I made this mistake; most likely due to stress and loss of situational awareness; however I believe continuing the right turn was probably the worst reaction to those stressors as I knew there was an aircraft somewhere near my altitude and on a converging path. The appropriate reaction would have been to turn away from the final approach corridor. We came close to colliding with the C172; although I never had visual contact on the aircraft so I am not sure how close. A few key points that I believe helped in creating the misunderstanding were the clearance for the overhead break. The intentions of the tower and the intentions of the pilots were very different in this case. The tower needed us to extend our upwind and then extend our downwind. We were anticipating an overhead break approach where we kept a tight break into a descending approach onto final. I believe both myself and the tower could have made our mutual intentions clearer to each other to help avoid this near miss from happening. I believe there was also an error with the sequencing of the aircraft. We were brought in underneath an aircraft on the ILS and that led to loss of SA; knowing that we were going to be turning back into the direction of that plane.
column123: Doing an overhead break approach to Runway XX at ZZZ I was given instruction to break over the departure end of the runway and land #2 behind traffic on final.  I have done the overhead break approach over 100 times and have always gotten break over the numbers or midfield.  I know now that the controller wanted me to break over the far end of the runway (over number XY); not over the number XX.  I didn't understand the sequencing and asked for clarification 3 times.  The controller repeated the instructions twice (which I still didn't understand) and the 3rd time didn't answer me.  I broke over the numbers XX and announced my break to the controller and asked if we were cleared to land.  I was still at 1500 ft. AGL and turning right base; and the controller told me to establish on the down wind.  At this point I was not clear which way to go and was eventually told to maintain heading and climb (in a series of radio calls).  We came around and repeated the maneuver and was cleared to break over the numbers without any issues.My mistakes were not understanding that I was expected to break at the far end of the runway (which was the first time I had ever gotten this direction); not understanding what the controller wanted me to do when he realized we broke early; not asking for a go around early in the process because of the lack of understanding on my part.

column121: While conducting a student training flight under Part 91; I had asked my student to track the 270 radial to the ZZZ VOR/DME. Approach had told me they had indeed not; and was not seeing any traffic in my area. I continued to keep the traffic in visual contact as they proceeded north; evidently unaware they had almost been in a mid-air collision. I then resumed my instructional responsibilities as normal and proceeded back to ZZZ1 for touch-and-goes.It is possible I became distracted as a result of trying to relay information to my student; but also that the incident aircraft was not equipped with a properly reporting transponder. Whatever the reasoning; I do believe this could be resolved in the future by equipping the facility with the ability to read ADS-B sources; as the other aircraft in the near collision was reporting ADS-B data according to my cellular device; allowing me to view their registration number. It also could be prevented by equipping the aircraft I was using with an ADS-B in receiver; to view said data.

column121: On a flight in Aircraft X; I was the PIC (Pilot in Command) with my son. I have provided my son two ground sessions of about 1 hour each before allowing him to sit in the front seat of the aircraft. I always fly from the backseat and felt comfortable flying there. During a planned touch and go; I aborted the touch and go and ended up off the runway 60 ft. into the EMAS (Engineered Material Arresting System). There were no injuries and very little damage to the aircraft from entering the EMASBackground: We took off and flew for 30 minutes and on return to ZZZ; the DEEC (Digital Electronic Engine Control) light illuminated indicating the DEEC reverted to a manual mode. This had happened on a previous flight earlier in the day and I reset the DEEC as I had done on the previous flight and the DEEC returned to normal operation. I had it in my mind to do one touch and go when we returned to the pattern at ZZZ and failed to change my plan as the smart thing would have been to full stop and investigate the problem since it was the second occurrence of the day. I flew a normal overhead pattern; completed the before landing checks and was cleared for a touch and go on Runway XX. I flew a stable final approach and landed the aircraft on speed; with full flaps; in the touchdown zone of Runway XX. I landed in the touchdown zone of Runway XX on speed with full flaps. I selected flaps 25 and smoothly brought the throttle up to take off power. The aircraft accelerated but at a slower rate than normal. I looked inside and saw 64% N1 and decided to abort the touch and go. I estimate I was just past mid field at this time. I brought the throttle to idle and applied the brakes with the brake lever on the stick. The airplane didn't decelerate. I tried a second time and got the same response so I grabbed the emergency brake lever and began a slow gradual application so as not to skid the tires. I should have made sure the nose was fully lowered and the nose wheel weight on wheels switch was fully depressed but in the moment I could see the end of the runway coming up and didn't make the correct decision. I had been able to use the normal brakes correctly I would have stopped the aircraft before entering the EMAS at the end of the runway. If the nose wheel weight on wheels switch is not fully depressed; the normal braking system is deactivated. During the stopping process; I thought about shutting down the engine to help eliminate residual thrust; but had my hand on the emergency brake lever. I also thought about going to 0 flaps; a technique emphasized on my checkride; but again had my left hand on the emergency brakes.I should have never flown the aircraft after it had an uncommanded switch to manual DEEC mode until Maintenance had inspected the aircraft. Secondly; I should not have attempted a touch and go after an uncommanded reversion to manual DEEC mode. During the abort; I should have pushed forward on the stick and selected 0 flaps before reaching for the emergency brake lever as it would have afforded me anti-skid braking and would have prevented me going off the runway. If there was a malfunction with the nose wheel weight on wheels switch we will never know as that was part of the very minor damage done to the aircraft when it went into the EMAS. I have debriefed thoroughly with two other Aircraft X qualified pilots who helped identify the errors and instructional fixes. I have reread the manual and reviewed a similar accident investigation finding on an Aircraft X who also aborted a takeoff and had similar mistakes as the mistakes I made.After the main wheels touched the runway; I smoothly brought the throttle to take-off power position; and selected flaps to the take off position for the touch and go. I felt the aircraft accelerating but less than normal acceleration. I decided to execute an aborted take off procedure. I brought the throttle to idle; moved the stick forward to lower the nose to the runway and applied brakes.

column121: Climbing out of ZZZ I was on an IFR flight plan in VMC conditions in a climb just about to transition altimeter setting to 29.92 transitioning into the flight levels.  Engines were set at climb power (37.5' Mp 2400 RPM full rich) and the autopilot was engaged on Nav mode Direct ZZZ1 in Vertical Speed mode at about 800 FPM climbing at approximately 155-160 KIAS.The nose yawed hard right and I heard a tone change in the right engine.  At this time I disconnected the autopilot to hand fly the aircraft.  The mixtures were already full rich so I advanced the props forward to 2500 RPM.  I normally would have pushed both throttles full forward but knowing I had more than sufficient obstacle clearance below me and not wanting to put additional stresses on the left (good) engine I left the Mp on that engine at 37.5' and pitched for airspeed of 155.  Normally you would pitch for VySE however to maintain cooling and a higher margin of directional control I intentionally kept speed at 155KIAS and accepted any change in vertical speed which may have resulted.  I [notified ATC] and on multiple occasions told the controller to stand by and I did some trouble shooting and made a decision on what to do.  Leaving the left engine at about 37.5' and now at 2500 RPM I noted the right engine was producing only about 15' of manifold pressure; flowing 38 GPH of fuel with good pressures and oil temps with CHT's decreasing quickly.  As I moved the right throttle forward thrust rapidly decreased on the right engine causing more yaw.  When I decreased throttle to verify the thrust came back somewhat.  I made the decision to shut down; feather and secure the right engine which I did.I trimmed the aircraft and considered what was going on thinking this was likely an issue with the right turbo based on my engine inputs.  Although the engine was secured and I knew I could make an emergency landing single engine I decided to attempt one restart on the right engine under the thought process that one good turbocharged engine and one engine essentially operating as normally aspirated was better than one turbocharged engine and a feathered engine.  My aircraft has a digital engine monitor so if the right engine ran out of oil pressure or produced pressures or temperatures out of range I would get a visual alarm on the annunciator light in front of me.I told the controller that I wanted to divert to ZZZ2 and I turned towards the airport.  The controller cleared me to ZZZ2 and told me to let him know when I had the ATIS information.  Hand flying the aircraft with a very frightened wife beside me I tuned in ATIS on my Comm 2 wishing the controller had given me the altimeter; wind; runway in use field elevation and a vector and a frequency for tower.  I descended to pattern altitude and made an entry onto a right downwind and switched to tower.  Tower told me they briefly saw me trailing smoke.  I asked whether the smoke was black or white and they said it was white.  They stated white so I now knew I was losing oil somewhere.  I made a partial flap landing (20 degree) at 110 KIAS and made a slightly long landing.  After clearing the runway I shut down the right engine and performed an after landing checklist.  With the assistance of Ground I taxi the aircraft to the FBO and began making arrangements to get my wife home on a commercial flight and I called ZZZ Center; my Mechanic and an experienced CFI to get the link on how to file a report. Contributing factors were my relatively low time in type and time flying high performance turbocharged aircraft. I believe that my actions were for the most part good however I am still on the fence as to whether restarting an engine after shutdown was a good idea or whether I should have kept it feathered and headed straight for ZZZ2 with it feathered.  Factors affecting human performance were primarily fear and adrenaline.  I was very shaky during this event.  I believe that my biggest mistake was not being more firm withATC.  I should have requested in no uncertain terms that ZZZ Center give me the local altimeter setting runway in use winds and tower frequency when I wanted them.  I should not have taken my attention away from flying the aircraft single engine to turn in ATIS on my Com 2 and try to get basic information while listening to him direct other aircraft.  In the future I will remember that ATC is there to assist me and I will be more direct with requests during an [urgent situation].All in all I think everything turned out fine.  The failure appears to be catastrophic failure of the outboard turbo on the right engine.  A post mortem on the turbo and further inspection and oil analysis of the oil; screens and engine components and an analysis of the data from the engine monitor will tell shed further light on what happened.

column121: Upon landing at ZZZ for fuel; a normal wheel landing was conducted on Runway XX; which was in use per ATC. Landing was smooth and as airspeed bleed below 40 kts.; tail settled to ground smoothly after slightly floating. Once tail was on the ground; it felt like something bit into my right main and aircraft canted hard right. Full left rudder and left brake were applied but I was unable to maintain directional control of the aircraft as it skidded towards the runway edge at approximately 35 degrees. As the aircraft slowed and braking became more effective; the aircraft canted back towards the left and stuck the wingtip on the ground and came to a stop on the runway. I noticed that I had trouble moving the aircraft on the ground due to an issue with my right main gear but was still able to taxi off the runway. Being current on the aircraft after spending some time away from flying the Pitts was extremely helpful and this situation would have undoubtedly ended different if I had not attended that course.

column121: The Jeppesen approach plate for Denver RNP to Runway 26 seems to have an inappropriate speed restriction for the initiation of the RF legs from both sides of the airfield. Both speed restrictions require an 'AT 210 knots;' all other RNP approaches similar in design have 'Below 210 knots.' The use of a hard 'AT 210 knots' for our aircraft means you must be in a manual speed control mode which is not desired for the approach being flown. Clean maneuvering speed (212-215 knots) of the aircraft is typically above the speed requiring the use of flaps and a manual speed window be open; which is a non-standard configuration for this type of approach.  Recommend the approach plate be updated to show 'Below 210' knots max speed at the initial fix.

I was about 1 hour into the flight. Winds at 8 kts. gusting to 17 were being reported at ZZZ; so I made a plan to use Runway XX; a turf strip with favorable winds. As I neared ZZZ at about 10 miles out I noticed traffic was using Runway XY at ZZZ. I listened again to weather and the winds had calmed and no gusts were being reported. I decided to change my plan and set up to land on Runway XX.My approach was normal and everything was smooth until the last instant; just after touchdown; my plane lurched to my left. I pushed in throttle to get airborne. I had 40 degrees of flaps in at this time. The plane lifted free of the ground and stayed there; climbing only a slow rate and now at a 30 degree angle corresponding to direction the plane was facing as it left the runway.I now found myself heading toward the airport hangers and climbing slowly with little airspeed. I knew I was now straight into the wind and at this slow an airspeed a turn seemed not a good choice. I cleared the hangars and slowly let out some flap angle to gain some speed. I climbed slowly; reducing flaps a bit and keeping the nose and climb angle slight.After the plane was cleaned and climbing I flew straight at 2;000 ft. to calm down. This had all happened very fast and I took a few minutes to go through a cruise checklist. I now resolved to indeed land on Runway XX and set up a pattern for that strip. This landing went very smoothly and I taxied in and tied down the plane.As I thought about this it is my thought that I may very well have hit the left brake upon touchdown.

column121: During a training flight with a student we experienced an electrical failure/fault with our ammeter indicating a discharge. My student and I flew to another airport 50 NM away from our home airport for a night flight to satisfy PPL (Private Pilot) training requirements. We preflighted the aircraft and all systems were operational. Our runup was uneventful with normal indications and the ammeter showed an appropriate charge indication. We completed two full stop taxi-back landings at the other airport and departed back towards our home airport. About 25 minutes from our destination we heard an odd feedback in the headset and noticed the ammeter was ticking and indicating a discharge. We attempted to cycle the master switch/alternator switch but that did not remedy the situation. We heard the radio start to sound garbled as well. I elected to discontinue the training flight and head back to our home airport where the airplane could be serviced. However; due to the discharging battery; I turned off all electrical equipment in the aircraft including navigation lights and ADS-B out to conserve power so that we could put the landing light and navigation lights on during our approach and landing. This resulted in us not having ADS-B out or navigation lights on in airspace in which they are normally required. I felt it necessary to deviate from the regulations in order to safely get the aircraft back into our home airport where repairs could be made. I also avoided known busy airspace so as to deconflict from any other traffic in the area. We landed uneventfully and the plane was squawked so that it can be inspected.

column121: I took off from ZZZ on a reposition flight to ZZZ1. At 900 ft. I turned the autopilot on with the master switch. At no point during the event did I ever engage the autopilot by selecting a mode. The 'ready' annunciation turned on and then it turned off. At the time I was flying runway heading. Approach then gave me a right hand turn at which time I noticed the turn coordinator had frozen and was not turning with me. It had previously worked fine on the ground. I decided to return to ZZZ. Approach gave me another right hand turn and that is when the aircraft controls became very stiff. It was difficult to turn the aircraft and even more difficult to hold altitude. After I leveled out in that turn; approach attempted to make a radio call that was very broken up and I asked her standby. She then informed me I was almost completely unreadable but when I asked her standby a second time she heard me a little better. I recycled the autopilot master switch and it once again showed ready and then the ready disappeared. I turned the autopilot master switch back off and pressed the red autopilot disconnected button but nothing changed. I then leaned over to try to pull the circuit breaker. After a few moments of not being able to pull the circuit breaker; I still couldn't get it. At this time I requested priority handling. I said if [I] could get out of IFR I would like to [have] the Approach Controller turned me again to more of a downwind leg for Runway XX. Another aircraft called and said they had the field in sight at 2000 ft. and 5 miles from the runway. I told Approach to send me there. She gave me a small turn and descended me to 2;000 ft. When I made it to 2;000 ft.; I checked the trim to see if moving forward and back would alleviate the problem. I moved it backwards (towards nose up) and everything with the trim seemed to be working properly but have no affect on the controls stiffness. I pushed the trim wheel forward and then back to level flight. At this time; the aircraft had started a small descent which the VSI also showed but the attitude indicator showed a 10 degree nose pitch up. After returning the aircraft to level; I noted the attitude indicator was becoming sluggish and not matching the movements of the aircraft as quickly as it normally does. The stiffness of the controls wanted the aircraft to pitch nose down and made it difficult to turn; however when I got to just outside the final approach fix flying in the opposite direction; I was still unable to see the runway so I had to shoot the ILS Runway XX into ZZZ. The only reduction in stiffness came when I pulled the power for in range and it lessened the pull I was having to put on the yoke to maintain altitude and heading. All engine gauges including the suction gauge were normal throughout the event. I was met at the hangar after landing by the Airport Support Personnel and [other] airport personnel. I wrote up the aircraft afterwards and discussed everything that happened per [each] instrument with the Mechanic so he could have a better picture of the situation.

We checked the overhead pressurization panel and saw that the cabin climb indicator was indicating a rapidly climbing cabin. The cabin altitude indicator was also increasing. We donned our oxygen masks and I elected to follow the Rapid Depressurization Checklist in the QRH. We [requested priority handling] and were cleared to descend. We descended to 10;000 ft. then completed the remaining normal procedures checklist before diverting to ZZZ. One major factor in the event was crew communication in the cockpit. With the speakers on and the breathing noises carrying over the interphone we had to repeat ourselves numerous times increased the workload of the event. Reading the checklist and verifying the actions combined with ATC instructions; the Flight Attendant briefing and announcements to the passengers proved to be challenging. Another factor was the decision to go with the checklist that I felt was the safest for the passengers and crew. I felt that taking any extra time to look at the other checklists that may apply would be time consuming and compromise our margin of safety. [I suggest] reviewing and using oxygen masks in the simulator more.

column121: After preflight at the airplane's home base of ZZZ; I departed alone for ZZZ1. All systems are normal at this time. In ZZZ1; I take four (4) friends for short; individual flights totaling 0.9 hours. I get 5 gallons of 100LL from the ZZZ1 self service fuel pump; a pump I am familiar with; before beginning my return flight to ZZZ. I am accompanied by Name; as a non-pilot passenger to help with the ground handling and hangaring of the airplane at ZZZ. I preflight the airplane; inspecting control surfaces; landing gear; engine compartment; oil level; and fuel sump. I have 10 gallons of fuel at takeoff; equivalent to at least 1.5 hours of flying with reserves. Engine start up is normal; as is run up. No indicators of any malfunction were present. My passenger and I take off from Runway XX around XA:30pm and head south-south-east to fly over [named] Lake while climbing to 6;500 feet at a consistent vertical rate of 200-300 ft/min. At approximately XB:10 I begin my descent from 6;500 ft. At 5;500 ft. I notice RPMs are hovering around 1;400. I open the throttle to return power and the tachometer does not change. Our rate of descent is -500 ft/min and airspeed at 90 mph. I pitch to best glide speed of 60 mph and begin to try to restore power through carb heat application and cycling the magnetos. No change in tachometer as we cross 4;000 feet. I declare to my passenger our engine is out and we will be making an off field landing. Searching for southward facing open fields; I locate my landing spot and begin to circle over the field. At 500 ft. I cross Farm Road X and prepare for final landing in the field I have selected. I fly over the hay field; clear the fence; and touch down in the cow pasture. As the wheels touch down; the prop stops wind milling and I apply brakes to prevent a collision with the next fence. Once the plane is stopped I instruct my passenger to get out of the plane and meet me at our rendezvous point behind the tail; power off radios; magnetos; and shut off the fuel. It is XB:18. Taking a few moments to collect myself; I attempt to restart the airplane. The engine starts and runs for 1 minute; but shortly dies thereafter. With the sun starting to move lower in the sky; my passenger and I begin walking to find the property owner. The owners arrive; the [local authorities are sent] to assess the situation; and the FAA is contacted. No damage to any persons; property; or the airplane are sustained.

After one of my touch-and-go's I climbed to 700 ft (Traffic pattern altitude - 300 ft) and started my crosswind turn. The C152 saw me cutting in front of them at nearly the same altitude as we were both about to turn left downwind; and took evasive action to create vertical separation by descending to 600 ft. At this time the instructor contacted me on the radio and asked if I could see him visually. I asked where he was. He responded that he was in a left downwind for XX. At this point; I saw the C152 below and in front of me. I slowed down; but continued to fly downwind (Problem 2). I intended to extend my downwind until after the C152 turned left base for XX. I did not see it turn base; and instead of contacting it to see what their intentions were; I turned base and started a descent thinking that they were leaving the pattern (Problem 3). At this time; the instructor in the C152 once again asked if I still held him visually; at this point the C152 came into view below and right of me flying in the same direction (left base for XX). I then maintained my altitude at 800 ft; turned and over flew the runway at that altitude. The C152 made a full stop landing. I completed another pattern and made a full stop landing to discuss the incident with the instructor in the C152. He help provide the details for this incident. The third plane in the traffic pattern was not a factor during this incident. What should have happenedProblem 1. I should have maintained a near exact position of the other aircraft in the pattern; especially the one right in front of me. On takeoff; I was dwelling on my last landing instead of putting my full attention on flying and collision avoidance. I should have waited to turn left crosswind until after I had seen the C152 turn left crosswind and ensured proper separation.Problem 2. At this point; I should have made a right turn out of the pattern and climbed to create both vertical and horizontal separation and to give the lower critical aircraft room to maneuver at a safe altitude.Problem 3. I should have communicated with the C152 instead of making assumptions. I should NOT have turned base and should NOT have descended without knowing exactly where the C152 was and ensuring there was not collision factor.

column121: During cruise at FL400 the oil filter bypass light for engine #2 EICAS message began blinking and then remained on steady. I told the First Officer to continue flying and to advise ATC of the problem. I said I would reference the QRH 'ENGINE OIL FILTER BYPASS'. Reading the checklist we realized the procedure might have us shut down the engine. We asked for a descent from FL400. There was traffic below us at FL390 so ATC said it would be a minute before we could descend. We started to look for a suitable diversion airport at that time. I sent a message to Dispatch to 'call me'. We waited to retard/reduce the power to idle (as stated by the checklist) until the descent was initiated due to drift down airspeed restrictions at FL400 and traffic right below us. The oil filter bypass QRH required us to shut down the engine because the light did not extinguish when the throttle was brought to idle. We continued the checklist and shutdown #2 engine with the (MAX) 'ENGINE FAILURE OR SHUTDOWN' checklist. We [requested priority handling] with ATC. Dispatch responded within a few minutes but the frequency was garbled and somewhat busy. Communicating with Dispatch we received weather and NOTAMs for ZZZ2 and ZZZ3 and we collectively decided to divert to ZZZ3. Dispatch said they would send landing data for Runway XXR at ZZZ3. I also looked up the non-normal landing distance performance table. So many performance non-normals it was hard to find the One Engine inoperative section. Later I realized the aircraft/config performance non-normals table was alphabetized! It was an idle descent all the way down as the airport was only 80 miles away from where we shutdown the engine so we did not have to consider the drift down QRH. Dispatch stayed on the frequency if we needed any more assistance. I advised the purser [and] communicated with the passengers to advise them of the problem and our need to land in ZZZ3. We asked for extended vectoring with ATC to complete checklists and approach briefings. The First Officer continued to fly as we had discussed this during the descent and he was comfortable landing. Based on the situation and conditions I felt he was more than competent to execute a safe landing. Checklists were completed and an uneventful single engine approach and landing were completed. Airport Fire Department met the aircraft after landing and we taxied to a hard stand where passengers were able to deplane via air stairs. The First Officer and I had a meaningful debrief. I then contacted Dispatch and the Chief Pilot to debrief. A logbook entry was made and I had a discussion with Maintenance regarding the engine shutdown.
column123: We were operating Aircraft X from ZZZ to ZZZ1 on a B737 MAX-9. We had completed a delayed flight from ZZZ4 and had to do a quick turn in ZZZ. I started preparing the flight deck while the Captain did the walk-around and dealt with jumpseaters and a new-hire pilot doing an 'observation ride' with us in the flight deck jumpseat. With the preflight done; we pushed on time and started both engines on push-back due to the long start times on the LEAP engines. Both engines; specifically #2; appeared to start normally. Taxi out; takeoff; and initial cruise was normal. Approximately; 50NM East of ZZZ2; we had a #2 Engine 'Oil Filter Bypass' flashing amber annunciation. I took the radios from the Captain and continued to fly while he looked up the MAX QRH for an oil filter bypass. The first step in the checklist is to disengage the auto-throttles. So we did that. The next step is to retard the affected thrust lever until the bypass light extinguishes or the throttle is closed. The Captain said we needed to descend to close the throttle since we cannot maintain FL400 on a single engine. I looked up the engine out info page on the FMC to see what our target altitude should be. It said FL244. The Captain quickly sent a 'Call Me' ACARS message to Dispatch. While he did that I requested a descent to FL300 with ATC; because we felt there was a chance the bypass light would extinguish as we retarded the throttle on our way down to FL300. This piqued the interest of ATC which appropriately asked if we needed any assistance. At that time; I told them to standby due to us running a checklist. On our descent; we closed the throttle completely and the bypass light did not extinguish. Per the checklist; step 3 says if the light does not extinguish we are to proceed to the Engine Failure or Shutdown Checklist. We were a little surprised there were not any more steps involved with the checklist; such as checking other engine indications for corroboration. So before proceeding to engine shutdown we re-examined the fault; we made sure we were in the correct checklist; and that we had not erred or missed anything that would prevent an engine shutdown.  Our conclusion was that we had not and an engine shutdown was necessary. After securing the engine; [I requested assistance] with ATC and requested FL240; I also began slowing the aircraft down to a more drift-down speed so we would not get too far away from ZZZ2; which appeared to be VMC; as well as prevent us from having large amounts of asymmetrical thrust at level-flight at a low altitude. While this was occurring; the Captain was briefing the Flight Attendants. He was also coordinating with Dispatch. Dispatch informed us that the weather in ZZZ2 was not VMC and he recommend ZZZ3 instead due to weather. Hearing Dispatch on frequency was a challenge due to the lag in relays; static on the frequency; and other parties transmitting on the same frequency. That is one area specifically that I feel could use improvement. Communicating to Dispatch should be as easy as communicating to ATC in a high stress; time limited situation. After agreeing of diverting to ZZZ3; I notified ATC of our new destination and we received vectors direct to the airport. The Captain made a PA to the passengers to explain the situation and plan. Next; the Captain began running the single engine landing checklist to prepare for landing in ZZZ3. I simultaneously began loading the ILS XXR approach in the FMC and prepared the aircraft for an approach into ZZZ3. We requested a delay vector for an extend final so we had ample time to complete all the checklists. Once we were set up; we completed the deferred items and began configuring the aircraft for landing. We had emergency equipment standing by upon our arrival as a precaution. The XXR runway was plenty long for our brakes 3; flaps 15; increased Ref speed approach; and we made an uneventful single engine landing. We were able to taxi under our own power to the ramp for passenger deplaning via air-stairs and busing to the terminal. We ensured everyone safely exited the aircraft and submitted a maintenance write-up for an engine oil filter bypass annunciation with a corresponding inflight engine shutdown. I feel everyone worked well together with excellent CRM including the Company new-hire observation First Officer; Name. I also feel safety was not in jeopardy at any time.

column121: After starting engines and completing the before takeoff checklist on the ZZZZ Ramp; ZZZZ Tower Control cleared us to back taxi & lineup/wait runway XX; and the I correctly read those instructions back to the controller.  Before taxiing onto the runway from taxiway C--which is approximately 3;500 ft. from the approach end of Runway XX--we verified that both the runway and final approach areas were clear; especially since it was still dark out; wet runway;  and the weather was reported scattered at 2;000 ft AGL.With about 2;000 ft. of taxi distance remaining; both the Captain & I observed an approaching aircraft's landing lights breaking out of the weather.  (Call sign of that aircraft is unknown.)  Captain observed on TCAS that the approaching aircraft was only about 500 ft above our position at field elevation.  At no time did we hear communication between the approaching aircraft and tower prior to observing the landing lights.  This also highlights that the actual weather on approach to Runway XX was significantly lower than the reported 2;000 ft. scattered.I immediately communicated via tower freq 'The approaching aircraft needs to go around; we are still on the runway' at which point we observed a climb from the approaching aircraft while the tower controller and approaching aircraft pilot were communicating in non-English.  With the approaching aircraft go-around underway; we completed our back-taxi; and were cleared for an uneventful takeoff & departure shortly thereafter.We operated strictly IAW flight manual and ICAO procedures; to include maintaining SA of the aerodrome environment which allowed us to see the traffic and direct the go-around; preventing a more dramatic outcome.  The cause is very simply sub-standard Country ATC operations that allowed this situation to arise.  (Regrettably--and even though this was the first experience for me in the dozen or so times I have operated in Country--events like this are purportedly not uncommon in Country based on fellow pilots' accounts.  Country operators do not adhere to the highest standards of ICAO procedures.)  In this case; it is safe to assume that there was a likely ATC coordination breakdown between approach and tower controllers since we were cleared onto an active runway while an approaching aircraft was on final approach.  And for whatever reason; the approaching aircraft was not on tower freq until well inside the final approach fix; otherwise we would have heard the check in.  Also; had it been VMC; we would have likely seen the aircraft on approach and declined to take the runway.NEVER get complacent operating in Country.
column123: We were given clearance to back taxi and to line up and wait on Runway XX in ZZZZ. column121: Wake turbulence encounter following a Boeing 747 on final approach. On radar downwind in VFR conditions we were cleared a visual approach following a 747 that was already established on final.  On the dog leg to final I was descending to arrive at the FAF at what would be a normal intercept for glideslope to runway 07R. Autopilot and autothrottles were connected at this time.  I noted on TCAS that we were 6 miles behind the heavy as we were about be aligned on final. Suddenly we encountered the wake turbulence from the preceding aircraft and the aircraft rolled quickly to the left. I took over controls manually and disconnected the autopilot and autothrottles while simultaneously recovering the airplane from the sharp bank to the left. The event happen very quickly; so I am unsure as to what bank angle we reached but estimating more than 30 and less than 45deg. We received a roll authority alert as the auto pilot had been unable to maintain level flight with the quick onset from the wake turbulence.  The aircraft recovered and we re-established ourselves on final. I mentioned to the First Officer that I was going to climb and maintain above the preceding aircraft flight path and also stay above glide slope for the remainder of the approach; planning to touchdown at 2;000 feet. The rest of the flight was uneventful and we landed normally in Anchorage.Looking back on this event I could have easily avoided encountering the wake turbulence.  When cleared for the visual approach behind the 747 I should've maintained my altitude instead of starting a gradual descent. I had plenty of time to descend later and descending at that time only increased the chances of encountering the wake. At the time; I was considering the fact that our distance was adequate and that we wouldn't have any issues following the 747 using normal visual cues /angle approaching the runway. I was wrong.  Even 6 miles behind the heavy the turbulence was strong and the rolling tendency abrupt. Not worth the risk; not to mention the discomfort to the passengers and crew. In the future I will certainly keep this in mind for a visual behind a preceding heavy aircraft to avoid this type of encounter.

column121: This report is for the dangerous situation of inadvertently approaching an airport in mountainous terrain. at night at too low of a height above the airport.This issue happened because I did not crosscheck information provided by the Garmin GTN 625 Navigator for VNAV profile with airport information.  The button sequencing on the GTN 'zeroed out' the 1;000ft AGL offset I programed into the VNAV feature.  This appears to occur with all GTN 6xx/7xx navigators.I was flying a personal flight to SAF.  I knew that I would be arriving at night; and planned to approach from the Albuquerque area to avoid terrain.  In order to have a safe approach to the airport; I setup VNAV in my GPS Navigator; a Garmin GTN 625.  I used the VNAV feature to give a 3 degree glide path to a point 1 mile from the airport at 1;000ft AGL.In setting up the VNAV; for altitude I entered a value of 1;000ft; then hit the MSL/AGL soft key to enable AGL.When I reviewed the added point VNAV waypoint in the flight plan on the GTN; it autofilled a crossing altitude of 6;349ft MSL.  I had understood this to be the MSL altitude of 1;000 AGL.  When approaching the airport; I descended through 7;000ft and noted that the terrain illuminated by city lights appeared closer than the approximately 1;600ft I was expecting.  I arrested my descent; and climbed visually to an appropriate height visually with the airport in sight.  I finished my traffic pattern and landed.  I noted that the elevation of the field was 6;349 MSL.Later I tested my keystrokes in the GTN625.  I tried to enter a VNAV waypoint with the following keystrokes:Enter 1;000ftHit the MSL/AGL buttonUpon doing this; I noted that when you hit the MSL/AGL button; the altitude/height reverts to 0.  I learned that you must enter the AGL value AFTER hitting the MSL/AGL value.  I also learned to always check your VNAV crossing altitudes with the chart.

The C-172 asked if I saw him; and I acknowledged I did; under the belief he was taking evasive action to keep us separated. I continued on to turn base and then final for a full stop on XX.Though separation existed; it was closer than needed be.  I thought by performing a loop; I provided adequate time and distance for all in the pattern; but in hindsight; given the pattern was busy I should have left the pattern entirely and rejoined when spacing was favorable.
